div.head: Irregular, Doubtful, and Emended Accidentals
div.p: The following is a list of emendations made in the Variorum text where in Q1(u) and in about 110 additional lines from F1(u) an obvious typographic irregularity of no substantive importance has been rectified by an obvious emendation. Where the irregularity might have resulted from a cause other than typographical error, or where its correction is uncertain, the text has been left unaltered. In the following notes the lemma is the reading of the the Variorum text as emended, and the first siglum is that of the edition (if any) from which the emendation is drawn; mere typographical rearrangements are not traced to a source in an early edition. The rest of the note either records a rejected Q1 or F1 reading or indicates that Greg (1940, pp. 81–105), having inspected all twelve extant copies of Q1, found the reading doubtful. In the latter cases Greg’s distinction between uncertain marks of punctuation (i.e., those clearly intentional but too obscurely printed to be identified) and doubtful marks (i.e. those perhaps not intended as punctuation at all) is here preserved.

div.head: Unadopted Conjectures
div.p: The following is a list of conjectural readings that are not recorded in either the textual or the commentary notes. Most of these readings are taken from printed editions or commentaries; a few are from manuscript sources. I have attempted to note the earliest occurrence of each reading and all later occurrences that seem to have been arrived at independently; mere secondings of someone else’s conjecture have been ignored.

div.head: The Texts
div.p: Defining the nature and interrelationships of the texts in the first three printed editions of King Lear—the First Quarto (1608), the Second Quarto (1619), and the First Folio (1623)—has proved as difficult for Shakespearean editors as defining the nature and interrelationships of the three Synoptic Gospels has been for Biblical scholars. The problem has been called the Mount Everest of bibliographical studies; Everest has so far proved more conquerable. The following discussion will first survey what has been learned and thought about the production of each of the three original texts of Lr., and then will survey the wide range of opinion about their relationships to each other and to Sh.’s intentions.

div.head: The First Quarto (1608)
div.p:
The printing history of Sh.’s King Lear begins on 26 Nov. 1607, when a book bearing that title was officially approved for publication and the following entry was made in the Stationers’ Register (Book C, fol. 161v, as transcribed in Greg, BEPD, 1:24):
Na. ButterIo. BusbyEntred for their copie vnder thand[es] of Sr Geo. Buck knight & Thwardens A booke called. Mr Willm Shakespeare his historye of Kynge Lear as yt was played before the king[es] maiestie at Whitehall vppon St Stephans [deleted k]night at x&ptilde;ist&mtilde;s Last by his maites servant[es] playinge vsually at the globe on the Banksydevjd
This entry records the facts that the prospective publishers of the First Quarto (1608), the London stationers Nathaniel Butter and John Busby, senior, had secured from the king’s official censor, Sir George Buc, Master of the Revels, allowance to publish the manuscript of Lr. in their possession; that the wardens of the Stationers’ Company had granted them (for sixpence) a license to publish this title in London; and that Butter and Busby had further guaranteed their ownership of publication rights by paying (the usual four pence) to have this entry made in the Register. However these two men may have acquired the manuscript of Sh.’s play, their conduct in securing approval for its publication was completely normal and regular. Since 1604 Butter had already published several plays, including the apocryphal The London Prodigal (1605), whose title page announces William Shakespeare as its author; none of his other plays came from the King’s Men. Between 1599 and 1609 John Busby is listed in the S.R. as owner (usually joint-owner, twice with Butter in 1608) of seven play MSS, two of which, printed as bad quartos H5 (1600) and Wiv. (1602), were versions of Chamberlain’s Men plays. The title pages of only two of these plays list Busby as publisher; he was apparently more interested in acquiring plays (and transferring ownership) than in selling them (see Johnson, 1985, p. 2).

When Q1 appeared early in 1608 it bore the following title page:
M. William Shak-speare: | HIS | True Chronicle Historie of the life and | death of King Lear and his three | Daughters. | With the vnfortunate life of Edgar, sonne | and heire to the Earle of Gloster, and his | sullen and assumed humor of | Tom of Bedlam: | As it was played before the Kings Maiestie at Whitehall vpon | S. Stephans night in Christmas Hollidayes. | By his Maiesties seruants playing vsually at the Gloabe | on the Bancke-side. | [device <McKerrow> 316] | LONDON, | Printed for Nathaniel Butter, and are to be sold at his shop in Pauls | Church-yard at the signe of the Pide Bull neere | St. Austins Gate. 1608.

This first edition is often called the Pied-Bull Quarto after the designation of Butter’s sign in the imprint, differentiating it from Q2, whose title page lacks that detail. Pollard (1909, p. 76): John Busby was obviously the provider of the copy, as his name disappears from the imprint. Greg (1940, p. 381): He may have sold it outright to Butter on registration. From the printer’s device Furness (ed. 1880, p. 357) conjectured what Daniel (facs. 1885, p. iv) and Pollard (1909, p. 53) confirmed, that the printer was Nicholas Okes. Okes had only recently begun his career as London printer, first as partner in a printing shop on 29 Jan. 1607 and then as its owner on 13 April, and he had never printed a play. Butter apparently chose him to print Lr. simply because of an ongoing business relationship: between February 1607 and June 1608 Okes printed nine of his books. Blayney (1982) has studied in detail Q1’s place in Okes’s output. Bartlett & Pollard (1939, pp. 46–7) identify and locate the twelve extant copies of Q1. Modern facsimiles include that of C. Praetorius, ed. P. A. Daniel, 1885; the Sh. Q. Facs., ed. W. W. Greg, 1939; that in Shakespeare’s Plays in Quarto, ed. Michael J. B. Allen & Kenneth Muir, 1981; and that in The Complete King Lear, 1608–1623, ed. Michael Warren, 1989. Manuscript corrections in 17th-c. hands appear in seven of the extant copies of Q1; these are listed in Greg (1940, App. IV, pp. 115–28).

Though several quartos of plays by Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, and others had advertised their author’s name on their title pages, Collier (ed. 1843, 7:351–2) finds it worth remarking that the appearance of Sh.’s name prominently at the head of both Q1’s title page and the first page of text is a peculiarity found in no other Shn. quarto if indeed in any other book of the period. He assumes that the purpose was to ensure that purchasers would be able to buy Sh.’s play rather than King Leir (1605). Brooks (2000, p. 71) suspects that the italic capitals of HIS also emphasize Sh.’s authorship. Blayney (1982, p. 82): The name of William Shakespeare in large print on the title page would not have helped sales by virtue of adding several hundred buyers to an already large potential market—it would merely have removed some of the risk that the book might not sell at all.…Most of Shakespeare’s plays had a relatively undistinguished publishing history before 1623. Moreover (pp. 97 and 148, fig. 6), the same large type from the head of the title page was simply reimposed at the head of the first page of text as a common economy. The only other quarto naming Sh. in large type is the 1609 Sonnets. Brooks (pp. 59–60): The material reality of Lear’s initial publication is somewhat inglorious. The edition probably ran to no more than seven hundred copies, and it seems unlikely that it sold very quickly, because no further edition of the play appeared until Thomas Pavier’s [1619]. Nonetheless he emphasizes (2001, p. 153) the singularity of the Q1 title page, designed to market the book on the merits of its author’s name.

The contents and wording of the title page are probably the invention of Butter, not Sh.: see n. 0.3. Greg (1940, p. 381): The prominence given to the author’s name on the title-page, and also probably the explicit mention of Edgar’s story, are due to a desire to distinguish the piece as clearly as possible from its predecessor of three years before, the old King Leir. The latter was, no doubt, still on sale, and Butter must naturally have been anxious lest it should be passed off on the unwary as his own more recent publication. The advertisement of court performance before James was certainly designed to attract purchasers; it has also led some editors to believe that the Q1’s text was based upon the prompt-book used for that performance, a doubtful idea (see ). Someone has carefully adjusted the SR’s phrase at Christmas Last to in Christmas Hollidayes; the original phrase, at the date of entry, had referred to 1606, but on a title page dated 1608 it would have erroneously referred to 1607. Blayney (p. 83) believes that the vague substitute is intentionally misleading, suggesting that Lr. was last month’s play rather than last year’s.

div.head: The Quality of Printing in Q1
div.p: Craig (ed. 1901): The Pide Bull edition is perhaps the very worst specimen of the printer’s craft that ever issued from the Press. Bowers (1947, p. 40): The elaborate stop-press corrections…seem to me to indicate that Okes was doing his conscientious best to produce the best text he could from his miserable manuscript, a copy so difficult to decipher that even the proof-reader at his comparative leisure could not always determine the manuscript reading. Lear is perhaps not by ordinary standards a carefully printed book, but I submit that the evidence shows it was not a wilfully careless one. Blayney (1982, pp. 29, 184–5), considerately: There were printers whose worst was worse than Okes’s—but not very many, and not much worse.…[Q1] can fairly claim a place among Okes’s half-dozen worst-printed books of 1607–1609. Nonetheless (p. 30), In some superficial respects Lear does not appear to be particularly bad: the paper (not supplied by Okes) is of moderately good quality, most of the type was only a few months old, and literal misprints of certain kinds are comparatively infrequent. Register was satisfactorily made, the page-depth is almost entirely consistent, and most of the catchwords are right. But…some of the effects of cheap-minded expediency become all too evident. It will be shown that Okes failed to anticipate a serious problem [type shortages] which arose from the combined facts that Lear was his first play-quarto and that he chose to print it in a certain way.…The printing-house problems could have been largely avoided had either he or Butter spent a few shillings on a transcript. Okes’s certain way here was seriatim setting instead of the setting by formes usual in Okes’s other books and in play quartos generally, and it suggests special problems. The unusual seriatim setting of Q1 Ado, for instance, probably reflects the fact that three-quarters of the play is in prose, much harder to cast off in manuscript than blank verse lines. Only one-quarter of Lr. is prose. Blayney (p. 184) proposes a different cause: It is perfectly evident that the manuscript itself was a difficult one. Lear was set seriatim quite probably because the manuscript was difficult to cast off for the more customary setting by formes.

The mislining of verse and prose, the sparse and often illogical punctuation, and numerous nonsensical readings tempt Daniel (facs. 1885, p. iv) to imagine that the printer was a foreigner, imperfectly acquainted with English. Adee (ed. 1890, pp. xvi–xviii) expands this hint into a fantasia, imagining a foreign-born type-setter, perhaps a German from Wechel’s shop in Frankfort, or a Fleming who knew French, composing by ear from the voice of an assistant (an illiterate fellow…from the rural districts) who read the manuscript, a custom, then quite common. (The custom, which would require two men to do the work of one, was unknown in England; see A. W. Pollard, ed., Richard II, 1916, p. 35, R. B. McKerrow, Introduction to Bibliography, 1927, pp. 241–6, who can find no basis for the practice and admits it only as a remote possibility, and van Dam, 1935, p. 5, who quotes McKerrow [Transactions of the Bibliographical Society 12, 1931, p. 253] and a 17th-c. printer who refers to it as an early usage, presumably a continental practice abandoned long ago.) Adee even imagines that Q1 may have been printed by Wechel in Germany, but is disposed to dismiss this theory without more evidence—fortunately, since the type came from Okes’s shop. To even the most casual glance Q1 is manifestly full of errors; but from the beginning, students of its text have wrestled to distinguish between those probably arising from the manuscript used by the printer and those owing to the compositors’ ineptness. Two examples:

Chambers (1930, 1:465): Many of its misreadings might well be due either to actors’ blunders or to mishearings.…Mislineation is a constant feature in Q. The verse is often put wrong by an initial error, and runs from central pause to central pause, until another error or the end of a speech recovers it. Occasionally it is altogether unmetrical. Prose is printed as verse. Still more often is verse printed as prose, throughout long passages, in a way which cannot be explained either by errors of composition or by marginal insertions in copy. Moreover, Q has practically no punctuation except commas, even in places where both logic and enunciation require heavier stops.

Doran (1931, pp. 21–5, 51): There are upward of one hundred and twenty-five errors in Q1 which seem to have been caused by failure on the part of the printer to decipher his manuscript correctly; such errors are most abundantly represented in Q1.…[22] In Q1 there are about thirteen errors which have the appearance of being due to mishearing.…[24] Its punctuation is light, but systematic, even if simply so. Commas are the mainstay, being used to mark clauses, sometimes phrases, and sentences in speeches which contain more than one. Periods are rarely used except at the end of a speech. Colons and semicolons are sparingly used. Question marks and [25] inverted semicolons (both marks used to signify exclamations as well as interrogations) appear more frequently. It is clear that the term faulty punctuation can be applied only to the negligent omission of any mark at all between sentences, to the misplacement of a mark…, and to punctuation which distorts the sense and shows that the printer did not understand the meaning of the passage in question or that he inserted a mark when he thought he had come to an appropriate place.…[51] The first quarto of King Lear does not always give the contracted form when it is required. When it appears, it is frequently without the apostrophe, e.g., Q1. opposd : F. oppos’d.

Greg (1940, pp. 63–80) records misprints, mostly minor typographical ones. Of many turned letters he notices esp. (p. 64) turned s, whose remarkable frequency near the end—more than two dozen instances in sheet L—leads him to suggest an influx of s types cast the wrong way up. Likewise nullas are used for o. Wrong-font letters are usually roman for italic capitals. Wrong-font punctuation marks are very frequent; there are five kinds of question marks, plus the mark like an inverted semicolon (Greg thinks it is really a form of question-mark). He records abnormal but not unusual kinds of spacing variants, and (p. 66) notes speeches ending without a stop or comma, the latter sometimes used to mean that the speaker breaks off.

The seriatim setting of the text was established by Blayney (1982, pp. 184–5, 112 ff.). (P. 184): Lear was set seriatim (quite probably because the manuscript was difficult to cast off for the more customary setting by formes), and this fact caused unprecedented problems of type-supply.…[185] [Lear] is exceptional not only as a quarto, a play-quarto, and a Shakespeare Quarto, but as an Okes quarto. (P. 112): Despite all the compositorial misreadings in Lr., the compositors made few typographical errors such as turned letters, inking spaces, and roman/italic wrong-font settings; there are few wrong-font errors except in sheets I–L. Many of their stylistic errors may be attributed to shortages of type. (Pp. 129–31): Lear placed a heavy strain on italic E because of all the Exits and Enters, Edgars and Edmunds; substitutions of roman, swash, and defaced letters begin in upper H4v (B) and I3r and I3v (B), I4r (C), and I4v. Similarly VV begins to be substituted for W. (P. 142): I suspect that the change to Duke. (which is how Albany is described on his entrance at K4v14) was nothing more than a simple expedient adopted because the A box was empty. (P. 144): What Lear used in the quantities most unprecedented in the pica books of 1605–7 was space-metal.…Distributing the marginal space-metal from Lear sheet L would have been a necessity.…[147] Okes may have increased his stock of Ws during work on Lear.…[150] The demands of seriatim work require rather more type (and not only headlines) than is needed for setting by formes. It seems evident that the fount was not really adequate to the task.…The shortage of type is another factor which affected the work—and consequently the text—from time to time. He estimates (pp. 145–7) the numbers of types that Okes owned.

One consequence of Okes’s limited stock in space types was his decision to use a narrower measure in parts of the text where a preponderance of verse would have required heavy leading between the end of the verse line and the right margin. Wilson (facs. 1931, p. [iv]): The most extraordinary feature of all [is] that while one third of the play is printed in lines 3 1/4 inches broad, with words tucked in, above, or below the end of the line whenever they would otherwise cause it to exceed this breadth; the rest of the play runs between 3 3/4 inch limits and pays no attention to the narrower restrictions. In other words, the printer of the Q. must originally have assumed that the whole copy was in verse (which would naturally fall into a 3 1/4 inch setting), and only later have discovered his mistake. What this betokens I have no notion. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xvi, n. 1): Two different lengths of stick are used, the shorter (about 3 3/16 inches).…The longer stick measures 3 11/16 inches. Like Adee, Greg (1936, pp. 178–9) and Williams (1949–50, p. 180) both assume that the compositor used two different composing sticks of different lengths (of 80 and 93 mm., according to Williams). McKenzie (1973, pp. 125 ff.) gives the lengths of the two measures as 93–94 and 80–81 mm., which he equates (p. 126) with 23-ems and 20-ems. He deduces that Okes was short of pica quads and used the long measure throughout, (p. 127) but indenting it wherever possible by adding large quads at one end, thereby avoiding wasting spacing material. The difference between the two line lengths in King Lear is regularly 3-ems and it results, not from a change of measure, but from the compositor’s indenting his stick by using a quad which, running up the head of the stick, served to indent two, three, or four lines at a time. He attributes (p. 128) several irregularities in the text to such indenting to a narrower column: the spelling daugter (1290), the omitted article in a womans seruices (2296), the accidental omission of and appointed guard (2990+1), and the omission from Q(u) of A letter (2715), later added within the narrow measure in place of a 3-em pica quad. At 1775 the Exit. is similarly set within the narrower measure, while above (1770) it has been set to the right margin [by some irregular adjustment of the spacing quads, since it sits between typographic lines].

Although the evidence for the narrower measure—such things as turned lines, the use of ampersands and numerals for words, truncated spellings and speech prefixes, irregular left margins, crowded lines lacking spacing and punctuation, etc.—is often clearly present, it is often difficult to determine exactly where the indentation of the measure begins and ends. There is clear evidence that the short measure was used on the following pages—B1v–B4v, E2v, E3, E4, E4v, F1, F1v, F2v–F4, G1, G1v, G3, H1v, H2v–H4, I2, I2v, I3v, K1, K2, K4, L1v, L2, and L3—and it is possible that it was also used on the adjacent or intervening pages E3v, F2, F4v, I3, K2v, K4v, L1, and L2v, and perhaps a few others. Overly long lines are moved into the left margin at 1228, 1231, 1289–90, 1477, 1952–3, 1960–1, 2405–6, 2471–2, 2499, 2525–7, 2708, 2781, and 3174, an entrance direction is moved into the right margin at 1595, names are abbreviated within the line at 82 and 1613, speech prefixes are shortened at 1554, 1601, 1960–1, 2426, and 2943–4, and one is omitted altogether at 1448. Catchwords are set within the shorter margin on F2v, F3, L1v, and L2v, showing that they were set within the stick; usually the catchwords are set full out, showing that they were added in the galley.

The methods and quality of printing in Okes’s shop, and their effects upon Q1, have been exhaustively studied by Greg (1940) and Blayney (1982). The first compares minutely, letter and point, all extant copies of Q1, and defines the extent of stop-press correction of errors during its printing; the second reconstructs from the data of recurring types and other bibliographical evidence the chronology of production and the division of labor and the working characteristics of its compositors. These are treated in the next two sections.

div.head: Press-Variants and Proof-Correction in Q1
div.p: The recognition of press-variants in Q1 was complicated for nearly a century by the variant readings in another issue of the play, very similar to Q1, that only gradually came to be recognized as a later, separate edition, Q2. Vickers 6(1981):81: On King Lear…in the 1778 edition Steevens disputed a reading given by Jennens [ed. 1770] (attaskt) since it was in neither of the Quartos he knew (it comes from the corrected state of Q1). He subsequently stated that there were two Quartos which differ from each other, though printed in the same year, and for the same printer (IX, pp. 403, 452), only to retract this opinion later (p. 564). But by 1793, in response to Malone’s statement that both Quartos read We, and that of which the first signature is B [i.e., of Q1], reads:—We that too late repent’s, Steevens can reply that My copy of the quarto, of which the first signature is A [i.e., of Q2], reads:—We that too late repent’s us, (XIV, p. 69). In the 1790 edition Malone had reported that the First Folio must have been proof-corrected during printing, since he had discovered copies in varying states (I, part 2, p. 157), and now Steevens applies the discovery to King Lear: some of the quartos (like the folio 1623) must have been partially corrected while at press ([ed. 1793] XIV, p. 76). Having recorded more variants, he postulates the existence of a third Quarto (pp. 87f.). Boswell (ed. 1821, 2:652), following a note by Malone in a copy of Q1, also describes three editions. Clark & Wright (ed. 1863–6, 8:xiii–xv) finally demonstrate that there were only two, one existing in copies having differing corrected sheets. Unfortunately they identified Q2 as the earlier edition, only later (Ellis, 1869, 1:217 n.) retracting their error. Nonetheless, by collating six copies of Q1 they discovered more than a hundred variants among copies of Q1. Koppel (1877, pp. 67–70; summarized in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 364) supports their argument that many of the corrected readings derived from the original manuscript from which Q was set.

Halliwell (ed. 1865, 14:362–3) had preceded Clark & Wright in distinguishing Q1 as the first edition and Q2 as the second, and in pointing out that no two copies of Q1 that he had seen contained precisely the same text. Halliwell also said in a supplementary volume (1871) to the Ashbee facsimiles of the Shn. quartos that twelve copies of Q1 were known to exist and needed to be inspected. It was now becoming apparent (see Adee, ed. 1890, p. x) that no copy of Q1 was like any other because each contained a different mixture of corrected and uncorrected formes. Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 356–7) mistakenly thought that such a mixture was due to piecemeal printing and carelessness on the part of the binder. Pollard (1909, p. 53) gives the correct explanation: While the edition was being printed the proofs of several sheets seem to have been read with the manuscript, and numerous corrections introduced. The copies of these sheets which had been printed without correction were not, however, destroyed, but mixed promiscuously with corrected copies, so that there are different combinations of corrected and uncorrected sheets in the different extant copies of this edition.… McKerrow (1927, pp. 207–13) describes the process of stop-press correction of formes after printing has begun.

Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xi) also raised the question of how authoritative Okes’s corrections were: The corrections were made on a re-examination of the MS. from which the Qo was printed. In many cases the corrector succeeded in decyphering the words which had in the first instance baffled the printer; in others he himself appears to have failed and to have had recourse to conjecture and again, some of the corrections he made were once more blundered by the printer. Instances of successful correction are patent on every sheet. Ridley (ed. 1935, p. ix): That the alterations in the corrected sheets do often in fact give the correct reading of the MS. there can be little doubt; but there seems to me very little evidence that they were at all universally arrived at by a consultation of the MS. And, if they were not, we are more likely to be near to what Shakespeare wrote when we are looking at the efforts of a stupidly honest compositor struggling with a writing which he could not read [i.e., setting the uncorrected state] than if we rely upon an ingenious emender [producing the corrected state]. Having examined six copies of Q1, Daniel (pp. vi–xi) laid the groundwork for the systematic study of Q1’s variants, finding and tabulating corrections existing in all sheets but B, I, and L. (There is no sheet A, only an unsigned half-sheet bearing the title page). Refining his results, Doran (1931, pp. 11–12, 20) finds that sheets C, F, and H have the inner forme corrected (C twice), D, E, G, and K the outer forme, and that sheets B, I, and L are uncorrected. (P. 12): That Shakespeare had anything to do with the corrections in the first quarto of King Lear is, from the conjectural nature of some of them, at least doubtful. Greg (1933, p. 251) shows in addition that both inner and outer formes of K were corrected, to make the catchword on K4 recto agree with the changed first word on K4 verso. He further (1940, p. 4) singles out Doran’s very suggestive discovery that in every variant sheet the variants are confined to one forme or side of the sheet, the other forme appearing in one state only, and adds that still more suggestive was the fact that it was not quite true, citing the anomaly of sheet K.

Greg’s (1940) monograph, based on a collation of all twelve extant copies of Q1, describes exhaustively and definitively the differences between them, showing in tabular form (p. 11) which formes are corrected in which extant copy. In collating twice as many copies as Daniel he finds about a third more variants. (Pp. 15–16): The total number of alterations here listed is 167, of which 148 are substantive and 19 consequential.…[16] Omitting these [i.e., two instances of type-shifts], Daniel’s total is 124…The number of substantive variants that I have been able to add is therefore 24, besides the 19 consequential.

Blayney (1982, pp. 220–1) adds five incidences of shifting type as being press-variants: 1065 Father, 1378 sp eake,commands, 1931 c.w. Lear., 2053 turnover (master,, 2864+2 and 2866 him nd mee. | Our. He also shows three words in E4v where three damaged types were replaced. (P. 221): If unnecessary sophistications of spelling and punctuation are…described, nearly a third of the variants in Lear can be considered as miscorrections. He believes (p. 222) that the corrector was probably Okes himself. He provides a consolidated list (pp. 593–7) of all the known press-variants, including a few not noted by Greg and a few of his own conjecturing:

row.cell: the wast and spoyle of his
old, he met the might mare
coster or my bat- | tero be

div.p: Note (p. 597): Five formes of Lear show quite clear evidence of the use of copy—outer D, outer E, outer G, inner H, and outer K. [See nn. 819, 820, 867, 1039, 1220+3, 1790, 1792, 1794, 1888–9, 2132, 2289, 2297, 2673, 2674, 2677, 2990+1.] No other Okes quarto of 1607 or 1608 shows the influence of copy in so many formes, and few formes show as many copy corrections as are found in any one of those five. While Lear can hardly be described as an outstanding exception to Okes’s normal standards of correction it is neverthless somewhat unusual.
A similar though not identical list of press-correction variants is given in Michael Warren, ed., The Complete King Lear, 1989, Introduction to Part 2: The First Quarto, pp. VIII–XIII.

Greg (1940, pp. 10 ff.): If we disregard C altogether as anomalous (with only two real corrections and three states), and K(i) as merely consequential [upon a change made in K(o) at 2971; see the table above], we find that there exist [in the 12 copies] altogether 72 variant formes, of which 32 are in the original and 40 in the corrected state.…[13] For the other five formes the figures [for corrections] are: D 16, E 33, G 25, H 33, K(o) 27. But even in the more heavily corrected formes the distribution is very uneven.…They tend to occur in groups…[of] fifty passages containing from one to thirteen changes each. He suggests (p. 41) that because of preliminary correction before presswork began, possibly on proofs taken from galleys (p. 56; McKerrow’s suggestion) or standing formes, further systematic proofing of Lr. was not planned; but that the incidental discovery of errors in C, requiring two interruptions of presswork, showed the need for regular proofing, which began in earnest in D, continued through K, and (pp. 191–2) tapered off near the end, where I and L are invariant and may not have been corrected. (P. 54): The corrector and proofreader could not (always) have been the same person (Okes), because in at least one case (1220+3 contaned/temnest) the corrector misunderstood the reader’s marks. Greg also (p. 37) lists and discusses six non-substantive variants between uncorrected and corrected pages, due to type shifts, some but not all due to unlocking the formes for correction. He rejects (p. 49) as improbable and unnecessary the possibility suggested by Bowers (1938) that two presses were used on Lr.

Blayney (1982, pp. 217–18) revises Greg’s figures: Eight of the twenty-one formes are known to have been corrected at press. The variants in five of them suggest that reference was made to the copy. There is also evidence (provided by anomalous types) that at least four formes received some kind of correction before the presswork began.…[218] It seems likely that thirteen formes of Lear (including the titlepage) were proofed against copy before presswork. The proofing was certainly…unskilled, bungling, and inadequate, but there are no valid grounds for denying that it happened, and several formes contain typographical evidence for the fact that some kind of correction took place. Three of those thirteen formes (the inner formes of sheets C, F, and K) were revised at press, and the copy was not consulted because it had already been used in the earlier correction. Eight formes seem to have escaped proper correction, but were probably read without the copy (either in the type or from foul proofs) so that the worst typographical blemishes could be removed. Five of them (the outer formes of sheets D, E, G, and K, and the inner forme of sheet H) were corrected at press, and the copy was very carelessly consulted for some of the errors that were actually noticed. Three formes (outer F and both formes of sheet I) may well have been printed without being read against copy at all—but even they had been corrected in some fashion, as typographical evidence in two of them demonstrates.

div.head: Order of Printing and Compositor Identification
div.p: Besides helping to explain many erroneous readings in Q1, Greg’s evidence of press-correction seemed to offer a basis for reconstructing the press-work on the edition; the fact that on some sheets only the inner forme revealed press-correction, on others only the outer forme, as Doran had shown, seemed to be possible evidence for determining the order of the printing of the formes. Greg’s initial explanation (op. cit., pp. 50–55) was challenged by Bowers (1947, 1948), who offered an alternative hypothesis; Blayney (1982, pp. 89–90) conveniently summarizes and questions both:

p.quote: Greg put forward a theory concerning the order in which the formes of each sheet had been printed. After the eight type-pages [i.e., both formes] of a sheet had been set and imposed, he suggested, a proof was pulled of each forme. The presswork began with whichever forme was still on the press, while the other forme was corrected as necessary. That corrected forme, which is invariant in surviving copies, was then given to the pressmen while the other was taken for correction. The pressmen first perfected those sheets which had already been printed on one side with the uncorrected forme, and then printed the rest of the heap. Finally, the formes were exchanged again, and sheets printed only with the invariant forme were perfected by the corrected state of the variant forme. Uncorrected copies of any variant forme were therefore always printed before the invariant forme, and corrected copies were always printed after it.

Bowers found this theory unlikely, and offered a more detailed reconstruction confirmed partly by the evidence of the running-titles. The printing began, he suggested, with whichever forme was first made ready for the press. An early pull was read and marked for correction, and the forme was then removed so that the type itself could be corrected. While it was off the press a proof of the other forme was pulled, but the first forme was given back to the pressmen as soon as it had been corrected. Not until all copies of that forme had been printed were the sheets perfected by the second forme.

It should be noted that the basis of both theories was the assumption that there was a constant relationship between the proofing and the order of printing. Bowers also took account of the evidence of recurring headlines, but treated that evidence as merely corroborative. When the headlines of sheets F and H appeared to contradict his proofing theory, therefore, their failure to recur properly was attributed to delays in the presswork. But the order in which the formes of a sheet were printed can be directly determined by the use of a raking light, and such an examination invalidates both reconstructions. [A raking light beamed across the surface of a printed page may reveal raised impressions made by the types perfecting the verso side of the sheet, after the first side had been machined.] The order of Lear formes is not dependent upon the state of any variant forme, and sheets F and H were in fact printed in the order suggested by the headlines.

The reason why Bowers could not find a more regular pattern in the reappearance of headlines is that the skeletons were not kept intact from forme to forme; instead, headlines were separated from the skeleton’s furniture and reused separately as new pages were composed. (Pp. 124–5): What happens in Lear is that head-[126]lines recur individually, their pattern dictated by distribution and composition rather than by presswork. And when inner G was stripped, not one of the pages on which the headlines reappear had been even partly set. (Pp. 137–8): Many pages were not supplied with headlines until just before imposition; the pages may have been left in a galley until a forme was stripped, and on one occasion the compositor tied a page before it had a headline.

div.p:
The following chart shows the recurrences of each headline (identified by Bowers’s [1947, p. 21] numbers), and the lack of a regular pattern of recurrence:

II B2v (then pied?)
III B3 C4 D3v F2v G3 H3v K3v
IV B4v C3v D4v E4 G1v I3 L2
V C1v D3 E3v G1 H4 K3
VI B2 D1 F1 G3v I3v L1v
VII B1v D2 F1v H1 I4
VIII B4 D1v E3 F4 H2 K2v
IV B3v D2v E4v F4v G4 I2v K1v L3v
X C1 E2 G2 I2 K4
XI C2v E2v F3 G4v H4v I1 K2 L4
XII C3 E1 F3v H1v K1 L2v
XIII C4v E1v G2v H3 I4v L1

Blayney (1982, pp. 78–85): Lr. was printed between two other quartos, after John Pelling’s A Sermon on the Prouidence of God, finished on about 9 December, and before The Cobler of Canterburie, begun during the second week of January. (P. 144): From type evidence it is clear that something no longer extant may possibly have been set between Lr. and Cobler, which precedes Henry Hoddesdon’s The Forme of Friendship (late January to early February 1608).

(Pp. 89–90): While the order of formes in each sheet is a useful datum, it does not reveal very much about the order in which the pages were set—and it is of some textual [90] importance to know whether or not the copy for Lear was cast off for setting by formes (i.e., marked to assign particular lines to particular pages to be set out of sequence, a practice that sometimes resulted in changes to the text in order to fit it onto a preassigned page). Blayney therefore uses other means to deduce the order of setting and printing, in particular the method, most fully developed by Hinman (1963), of analyzing various kinds of typographical evidence, particularly the recurrence, from one sheet to another, of distinctive types. His most important discoveries are that the text was set seriatim rather than by formes, and that this method sufficiently strained the resources of Okes’s limited stock of type that the text was sometimes affected. He is able to reconstruct with great exactness the chronology of printing and the place of Q1 in Okes’s output of 1607–8:

(Pp. 99–100): The watermarks reveal that the paper was nearly absent from Okes’s other books and was therefore provided by Butter: Okes used (p. 100) ten edition-size units of the paper identified by marks 1 and 2, and a half unit of mixed paper…[which] formed half the heap for the first complete sheet printed—after a half-unit of the main stock had been used for the title half-sheet.…With a few exceptions, all copies of sheets B, C, and E–L were printed first on the felt side of the paper.…[101] Sheet D differs in that the precedent (outer) forme was printed on the mould side in all but two copies.

(Pp. 148–50): Work on Lear probably began during the second week of December 1607, by which time Nathaniel Butter had delivered the copy, received an estimate, and delivered the paper [enough for 500–750 copies, Blayney guesses].… [149] [Perhaps] sheets B–G, and perhaps also outer H, were printed at half-press by a single pressman.…Half-sheet A and sheets B–F would have taken a little less than two weeks to print at half-press. This would bring the printing of sheet G fairly close to 24 December, on which date the printing house would have closed for about a week. Blayney guesses the interruption occurred at some point between the distributions of inner F (H1v29) and outer G (H3r26).…When the setting reached the middle of H3r a second case was brought into use. A second compositor (C) seems to have set part of H4v and the first page and a half of sheet I while B worked on the remainder of sheet H. After the next distribution B took over where C had finished, while C set another passage from about I3v16 to I4v25. B probably finished the end of I4v before C’s passage was complete, and set K1r before the next period of simultaneous work. Sheet I was the only sheet after C of which the inner forme was printed first. The rate of presswork appears to have increased after the first forme of sheet H had been printed, and suggests that a second pressman began working at that time.…Work probably finished during the second week of January 1608.…At no point in the work (after C3v, that is) is there reason to suspect that any part of the copy was cast off in the usual sense.…But in another sense the whole text must have been cast off, in that the number of sheets it was to fill had been predetermined.…From the somewhat crammed appearance of the last three pages it would appear that the final (but not necessarily the only) adjustments were left rather late.
The following is a sheet-by-sheet summary of the sequence of printing, as determined by Blayney, mainly from the evidence of recurring recognizable types.

The first, unsigned half-sheet (p. 148): The first part of the book to be set was the titlepage, which was then distributed before line B1v12 had been set. (P. 96): The titlepage is printed on the second recto of an otherwise blank half-sheet. The collation therefore suggests that the titlepage was printed last, after it was found that there was to be no final half-sheet with which the title could be printed. Had Okes started with the titlepage the text could be expected to begin on A3r, and Bowers quite reasonably assumed that work began with sheet B. The first unusual feature of Lear as a printed book, therefore, is that the titlepage was in fact printed first. The first two lines of the title page and much of the third were reused above the beginning of the text proper on B1r. Type from the upper part of the title page was reimposed to form part of the head-title. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xiii): Q1 [i.e., the text] may have begun on signature B in the printer’s uncertainty that a preface or prologue was to follow the title and so left a vacant signature to the last. Blayney (p. 96), rather: Okes seems generally to have attempted to end the text either on the final recto of a gathering or on the verso before the final leaf—thus allowing a blank to protect the print when folded or stitched copies were stored without wrappers. For the same reason he preferred to leave a blank leaf before the titlepage where possible.

Sheet B (p. 148): The pages of sheet B were set in unknown order, and the outer forme of the sheet was printed first. (P. 101): They were possibly set seriatim. McKenzie (1973, p. 130 n.): In King Lear outer B was printed first and the type was deeply impressed. When the inner forme was printed and the sheet perfected, a quad [inked] in B3v of the inner forme touched the raised impression of the word Foure printed on B3r. (See the right margin opposite 229.) Blayney (p. 102): The most recently distributed types should (in theory) reappear first. The headlines, on the other hand, are taken [intact] from the first pages distributed—though not invariably. (P. 103): Headline b from B2v does not reappear and may have been pied.

Sheet C (p. 148): The last two pages of sheet C were set seriatim, and the same is therefore likely to be true of the whole sheet. The inner forme was ready for imposition before C outer and was printed first. During printing the press was stopped twice for trivial corrections.

Sheet D (pp. 103–5): D was set seriatim. The headlines from B inner were used on the first four pages of the sheet, probably added as each page was finished; then the headlines from C inner were given to the last four pages of D, probably as each was completed. D inner was finished and probably imposed first, (p. 104) but outer D was the first to be printed. (P. 105): The printing of outer D was stopped and numerous corrections were made.

Sheet E (pp. 108–10): E inner was set and imposed first, but E outer was printed first. (P. 109): Bowers [1947, pp. 22–3, 26] assumed that the headlines from each wrought-off forme were transferred to pages which had already been set.…[As a result he] indicated the distributions somewhat later than they actually occurred.…Outer D was partly distributed nearly four pages earlier than Bowers believed, and no very substantial interruption need be assumed. Some small delay did happen between the machining of inner D and outer E, possibly no more than was required by ordinary additional maintenance presswork. (P. 110): Outer E underwent numerous press-corrections, some requiring reference to copy, and three replacements of damaged type (not discussed by Greg).

Sheet F (pp. 115–17): In sheets C, D, and E, variants are found only in the first forme to be printed. The fact that the only variants in sheet F are found in the inner forme therefore suggested to Bowers that presswork began with that forme. In fact the outer forme was printed first. There are only a few trivial variants, none of which suggests that copy was consulted.…[117] Bowers found that the prior use of F(o) headlines suggested another major break in presswork between sheets F and G. But since the pages of outer F were in fact the first available, no such interruption is in evidence.
Sheet G (p. 117): While outer G was being printed the press was stopped, and the forme was corrected fairly extensively…[with] reference to copy.

Sheet H (p. 118): Because of the correction of H1r to agree with a change in outer G (see n. 2064–6), It is a reasonable assumption that outer H was proofed before presswork began. (P. 126): The reason for the disappearance of distributed types from G from H4v18 to I1v25 is that these passages were set by a second compositor working at a second case, very likely given a physically separable sheet or leaf of the copy. H4v18–I1v25 was therefore probably set simultaneously with H3r26–4v17. (P. 128): Outer H was printed first; inner H has variants, several of which required reference to copy.

Sheet I (pp. 128–9): On the division of labor in sheet I between the former and new compositors, see the next section below. (P. 137): The most reasonable explanation of the apparent increase in the rate of presswork [after the new compositor began to share the setting]…is that the majority of Lear was printed at half-press [i.e., with only one pressman] and that shortly after the advent of a second compositor, a second pressman joined the crew. (P. 131): For the first time since sheet C the inner forme (of I) was printed first. No variants have been found in either forme in the surviving copies, although there is reason to suspect that Q2 may possibly have been printed from a copy with at least one page of the outer forme in a later state. If so, then the variants were in the second-printed forme.

Sheet K (p. 134): The outer forme of K was printed first. Both formes are variant, but only the outer forme suggests reference to copy. The K4r catchword was altered in consequence of a change to the first word of K4v. The only other change in inner K is a completely unnecessary spelling-change [vew] in K3v.

Sheet L was set all from one case. (P. 142): Outer L was printed before inner; there are no variants in either forme. Meyer (1994, p. 142): Usually the inner forme is printed first in seriatim printing while the last page is being set; in Q Lr. the last page was blank, so the outer forme could be printed while the seventh page [in the inner forme] was being set. (P. 143): The compositor found his last two pages drastic[ally] crowded; commas were unspaced, and Edgar’s two split lines are merged with other lines (i.e., printed on the same typographic line with another speech). [In fact two short lines of Lear’s and three of Edgar’s are so printed.]

div.head: Compositors
div.p: Adee (ed. 1890, p. xvi) first detects two compositors, on mistaken grounds: that the one using the longer composing stick set up his text much worse than the other using the shorter stick (both compositors used both lengths). In an influential study Williams (1948–9, pp. 61 ff.) claims that I can show conclusively [from spelling preferences and running titles] that only one compositor [whom he calls B] was engaged in the production of Lear. This view was generally accepted by Greg, Bowers, Duthie, and others, and was repeated as recently as Halio (ed. 1973, p. 8, n. 3). Honigmann (1965, pp. 310 ff.), however, detected a second compositor, whom he named Compositor C. From tests such as the irregular apostrophe, preferred spellings, the use of number abbreviations, ampersands, and tildes he distinguishes a compositor B, willing to follow copy, from a modernizing compositor C. He thinks B set Lr. down to the end of Act III (two-thirds of the way down H2), and C thereafter (from H2r28 to the end). He nonetheless leaves open the possibility that one compositor set Lear, changing his habits as he went along. (P. 314): Acts I–III and IV–V resemble each other so closely in typographical and other features.…The exclamation mark, comparatively rare in the Quarto, occurs in roughly the same proportions in both sections; the same is true of the dash (consisting of three hyphens); there are two pairs of brackets and two speeches ending with a colon in Acts I–III, one pair of brackets and one speech ending with a colon in Acts IV–V; both sections have one erroneous catchword (F3v; K4, press-corrected), and both have one long catchword hyphened (C2 predomina-; I1v More-). That the break occurs between acts suggests that Q may have been divided into acts. An Oxford dissertation by Feather (1972) also undertakes to distinguish the compositors, with only partial success.

Using not only spelling evidence and headlines but patterns of recurrence of recognizable types throughout Q1, Blayney (1982, pp. 151–87) further differentiates Honigmann’s two compositors, accepting their names B and C and identifying them with two different cases of type in Okes’s shop, called case x and case y respectively. Like Honigmann he finds (pp. 157 ff.) that sheets B–G and the first part of sheet H were set by one compositor working alone, from case x, but thereafter by two compositors working simultaneously at two cases, C working more slowly than B. Presumably B, who alone set the first two-thirds of the book, also set the title page; at least he transferred several of its lines to the first page of text (Blayney, pp. 96–9). (P. 160): C’s total contribution to the book amounts to approximately 455 lines—the equivalent of nearly twelve pages.

The tabular summary of compositor stints given below identifies their pages and the TLN numbers of the portions of text on those pages:
Compositor B (case x) Compositor C (case y)
B–G (0.1–2064)
H1–H4v17 (2065–2347) H4v18–I1v25 (2347+1–2381)
I1v26–I3v15 (2383–2542) I3v16–I4v28 (2543–2659)
I4v29–K1v2 (2660–2723) K1v3–K2v1 (2724–2809)
K2v2–L1v18 (2810–3072) L1v19–L4r36 (3073–3303) (case x)
For doubts about Blayney’s evidence and reasoning in identifying Compositor C, see Werstine (1985, pp. 123–4).

As is usual in compositor studies, the division of work indicated by types, headlines, setting habits, and the like is reinforced by the evidence that in his stints each compositor preferred certain alternative spellings of frequently used words. Blayney’s identification of these supersedes similar work by Williams and Honigmann, and his results (pp. 163 ff.) are summarized here:
Compositor B preferred doe, goe, here, King (with capital); -or and -our indifferently, sometimes -er; -s (without apostrophe), -’t (with apostrophe); -’th, -t’h, -th’, oth’e (with apostrophe); O; -’d (with apostrophe); -ee (in be, he, me, she, we) frequently, though -e preferred; beene.
Compositor C preferred do, go, -or, -s (without apostrophe); -th, othe (without apostrophe); O; -d (without apostrophe); -ee (in be, he, me, she, we) seldom, since -e preferred; bene?
Other spellings sometimes used as discriminants proved inconclusive or inconsistent. (P. 166): Honigmann (p. 311, no. 7) thought i’st was a determinant, but C uses it only once, and it is not uncommon, because a compositor who used the st ligature had to put the apostrophe before it. (P. 169): -t’h is more likely a printer’s than a penman’s irregularity, since in some secretary hands th is practically a digraph, whereas for a printer t and h come from separate boxes. Though Honigmann thinks it is rare and therefore likely to be from the MS, it is found in other Okes books, so it may be compositorial. (P. 168): The use of ô for preferred O, begun by C (2375), then set twice by B (2703, 3043), possibly reflects (unclearly) type shortage. (P. 169): After f, ch, sh, k, p, x, and unvoiced s, the elided participle always takes -t.…After c the practice varies. When i is used in the participle, the forms are either -ied or -ide. When y is used, there is variation. (P. 171): In the use of terminal -ie and -y there is no clear distinction between B and C. No word in Lr. has -ie after a vowel. B, C, and almost every other Jacobean compositor usually set -ie after lower case f and s in order to use a ligature (fi or si). (P. 176): C preferred -ie, while B’s practice was extremely inconsistent. B preferred -ie in justified lines and may possibly have had a preference for -y in unjustified text. But he was so prone to the influence of several factors, especially that of type-supply, that one could hardly use this group of spellings as a reliable discriminant. (P. 177): Both B and C preferred the long form -esse to -es.

The spacing of text on the page and in the line may also distinguish compositors. (Pp. 178–81): C took little trouble to center stage directions even approximately. B set all SDs to the full measure even in pages set entirely to the short measure. Their spacing of punctuation is not distinctive, however. Neither B nor C sets a space before the comma at the end of a verse line (as Folio Compositor C does), though there are a half-dozen probably accidental ones. Spacing of medial commas is difficult to determine because commas from at least four founts were used, and their centering on the type may have differed from fount to fount. In addition, (p. 180) Okes seems (from irregular margins) to have owned a few off-center capitals, and some ys that sometimes have extra space after them within words. The majority of terminal commas before which a thin space might be suspected follow either y or short s—the latter sort used initially or medially only 44 out of 2,567 times in Lear.…[181] C set approximately 20% of his unjustified commas without a space. B’s overall average was considerably higher, but he is inconsistent, and sometimes may have had a space shortage.

As for Q1’s inadequate pointing, (p. 182): When C became confused by the pointing (or absence thereof) in copy, he reacted by resorting to what might be called do-it-yourself punctuation. A line which quite evidently required a medial pause [somewhere in it]…would be given a comma, thoughtfully placed in a prominent position at the end of the line where a reader [or proof-reader] could find it and insert it where necessary, sometimes several times on one of C’s pages. (He gives exx. from H4v33–I1r2, I1r23–5, K1v5–6, K2r12–13, K2r16–19, L3r1–2.)

(Pp. 185–6): It seems likely that only three men worked on Lear before the Christmas holiday. Compositor B set the type, one pressman printed the sheets at half-press, and a third party (quite probably Okes himself) proofed at least some of the formes. In addition to Okes, the resident staff of the house included (or consisted of) two apprentices: Thomas Corneforth (bound to George Snowdon [Okes’s predecessor] on 9 September 1605…) and John Reynolds (bound to Okes on 26 March 1607…). One would also expect Okes to have had at least one journeyman under contract as long as there was work to be done…and to have hired others as the needs of the work in hand dictated. [186]…Compositor B could possibly have been one of the apprentices, or, if he was temporarily absent for the holidays, a journeyman. After Christmas, C seems to have worked more slowly, and perhaps less competently, than B. This tends to suggest that he was a less experienced compositor, and in C’s case I think it quite likely that he was an apprentice.…I suspect, however, that the later formes of Lear were the work of a normal staff of four men. It is likely that Okes generally hired one journeyman of each trade, and that each supervised one apprentice. Both apprentices may have been able to set type…but not necessarily so. Under those conditions, if C was an apprentice compositor then B was probably not. And in that event the most likely reconstruction is as follows. Journeyman B began setting type for one of the apprentices to print. After Christmas the apprentice C (who may have been the pressman in December) began to set type alongside B.…[187] By the time that inner H was printed, the house was back to normal strength.…There is a reasonable chance that C was either Thomas Corneforth or John Reynolds. Or Okes himself might have done some of the setting when short-staffed, and since he had been a master printer for only ten months, the inexperience evident in Lear may sometimes be his.

div.head: Features of the Q1 Text
div.p: Q1 is remarkable for its large number of textual errors, and has sometimes been classed with the so-called bad quartos which show signs of serious memorial or theatrical or other corruption. Its many suspect readings are recorded and discussed throughout the textual notes, commentary notes, and textual appendices of this edition. While a considerable number of its readings are nonsensical or patently wrong, the general quality of the text has long suffered from invidious comparison with that in the First Folio, whose superior printing and authorized publication by Sh.’s fellow actors have long led to the easy conclusion that the F text of Lr. was in all ways superior and that its readings should generally be preferred to those in Q1 unless there was strong reason to do otherwise. In the case of the some 850 verbal variants between the Q1 and F texts, there has long been a strong presumption that the F readings were generally superior and the Q readings likely to be inferior or corrupt. At the same time Q1 contains some 300 lines, apparently authentically Shn., that are missing from F1, and often its individual readings have seemed preferable to those in F; such considerations have led a few editors, notably Jennens, Ridley, and Halio, to rely heavily upon Q in their modern editions. Since the 1930s a remarkable reevaluation of Q1 has been under way, until in the past quarter-century it has come widely to be thought of as equally authoritative with F1, despite its numerous errors and poor printing. The chief foci of discussion have been verbal differences between Q and F, particularly a kind of aural variant interpreted to imply oral transmission and mishearing of textual details; variant and erroneous lineation of verse and prose; faulty punctuation; and variations in the accessories, particularly speaker identifications and stage directions. Apparent verbal omissions that are supplied in F1 are discussed separately in the section Passages Not in Q1 (see ).

Adee (ed. 1890, p. xvii), who imagines a foreign-born typesetter composing from dictation, lists seven readings revealing his phonetic blundering. Adee’s choice exhibits the difficulties of all such later identifications: in 328 lets hit/let vs sit, Q is more likely to be right and F wrong; in 755 great pallace/grac’d Pallace, both Q and F make sense; in 1211 Stobing (corr. Stopping) his messenger/Stocking his Messenger Q makes poor sense, but the error could as well be graphic (misreading) as aural; the same is true of 1902 O light/a-light; in 2602–3 dogge, so bade/Dogg’s obey’d, an instance included in any list of hearing errors in Q1, mishearing is a real possibility, but the cause may instead have been graphic confusion: see n. 2602–3. In 1685 haue a corne/of a Corne and 3278 rat of life/Rat haue life, the similarity in sound between of and have may have led to error in the first case (though it makes adequate sense) and certainly did in the second; but rather than being an actual mishearing, this common confusion of these two words of similar sound could have occurred in the mind of a scribe or compositor, holding a phrase phonetically in his memory while rendering the text in script or type. McKerrow (1927, p. 254), Doran (1931, p. 125), and van Dam (1935, p. 99) all quote William Blades, Common Typographical Errors with Especial Reference to the Text of Shakespeare (Athenaeum, No. 2309, 27 Jan. 1872, p. 114): Every compositor when at work reads over a few words of his copy, and retains them in his mind until his fingers have picked up the various types belonging to them. While the memory is thus repeating to itself a phrase, it is by no means unnatural, nor in practice is it uncommon, for some word or words to become unwittingly supplanted in the mind by others which are similar in sound. From the time of Gutenberg until now this similarity of sound has been a fruitful source of error among printers.

Adee represents as well the tendencies in later critics to find aural errors if they believe that Q1’s text was taken down from dictation or during a performance, but to be skeptical of them if they think the text was reproduced from script or type. Doran (1931, pp. 124–5), who disbelieves in a text created by dictation or stenography, accordingly admits the presence of only a few possible aural errors: 682 doe weare/to weare, 870 ought/oft (though ought is a recorded spelling variant for oft), 1564 not the deed/not the need, 2248+4 Mobing, & Mohing/(not in F); 2379 in sight/incite, and 3278 rat of life/Rat haue life. Several other potential examples could easily be misreadings or misprints, or no errors at all: 248 may know/make knowne, 411–12 I apprehend/Ile apprehend (if I = aye, there is no error in Q), 741 weaknes/weakens (transposed letters, possibly merely a typographical error), 742 lethergie/Lethargied (possibly a compositor omitted a letter), 2551 argue-proofe/Agu-proofe (since in context argue-proofe makes no sense, it is more likely an accidental typesetting error than a deliberately written term; see n. 2551). She lists 45 Confirming/Conferring and 88 confirm’d/conferr’d as good variant readings similar in sound, thereby casting doubt that the Q readings are erroneous at all; if they are, they could be graphic errors. As for 867 attaskt [Q(c)]/at task, Q(u)’s alapt is less likely an aural error than a misreading of MS ataxt; see n. At 947 aske/act, Q may be right and F may be a misreading or sophistication; see n. At 1211 Stopping [Q(c)]/Stocking, Q(u)’s Stobing was quite possibly a misreading from MS, since there are other b/k and p/k errors; see n. At 1671 taske/taxe, the words were apparently interchangeable; see n. In variants at 1685, 1728, 1914, and 2401, Q may have been correct; at 172 That sorrowes makes as good sense and syntax as That’s sorry, and troope sets forth as good as troopes set forth. She rejects five other presumed Q errors as being merely ignorant spellings on the part of the printer; 1657 caterickes and Hircanios are spellings not otherwise known, but vaunt-currers, cushings, and Fauchon are all established spelling variants. The Q variants 328 lets hit, 1096 clamarous, 1029 is crackt, 1995 dearer, and 2380 right are all correct and their F counterparts erroneous.

Advocating stenographic origin of Q1, Adams (1933, p. 157) suggests further examples: 117 mistresse/misteries, 117 might/night, 817 the worst/thee worth, 1505 hot bloud in/hot-bloodied, 1576 lamely/tamely, 2182 experience/esperance, 2626 shoot/shoo, 2627 fell/Felt 2783 exposd/oppos’d, 2783 warring/iarring. The strong graphic resemblance between the words in each pair suggests an alternative explanation for the Q readings, not all of which are clearly wrong.

Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 79–82), believing that Q1 was dictated to a scribe, lists the most noteworthy of Q’s aural errors. Those not previously suggested are 882 where/were, 1804 thy one/thine owne, 2175 dungell/Dunghill, and 2525 Bare free/Beare free. None needs to be an error of hearing: where, one, and dungell are all recorded spelling variants, and Bare occurs in a crowded line set to a narrow measure, and so could be either a compositorial error or an adjustment. Six other words Duthie thinks might be mishearings but might as well be reproductions of popular pronunciations: 1135 ruffen, 1930 venter’d, and 2014+15 cushings are all recorded spelling variants; 2551 argue (ague) Duthie (p. 413) explains as a misreading of too many minims in copy; and 424–5 aurigular and 1657 caterickes are both unknown spellings of unusual words having many other variants suggesting a wide variety of pronunciations.

Ingham (1967, pp. 81–4) surveys all the examples previously offered, finding those unmistakably aural fewer than generally supposed. Nine that she cannot explain by a mishearing of contemporary pronunciation may not be aural errors of any kind, but only…mistakes (several may not even be mistakes). The rest (all but 3241 Fauchon, a common spelling, are listed above) represent contemporary pronunciation, usually vulgar or advanced; these could be errors of a listening scribe, or a compositor’s homonymic substitutions, or evidence for (authorial) foul papers.

Stone (1980, pp. 190–200), believing that Q was reported from performance, assembles a list of some seventy Q readings that are either phonetic errors or somehow involve phonetic confusion, including, in some dozen cases, possible confusion on the part of a compositor. The term error is freely applied to words that Stone is usually the first to wish to emend, including more than a score of Q readings that are the same as those in F, and another half-dozen in which Q is at least as defensible as F. Another two dozen readings are easily explained as compositorial misreadings of graphically similar words or (in a half-dozen cases) as literal typographical errors (1219 speake/speakes, 1261 else/elfe, 1627 Arte/note, 1902 O light/a-light, 2014+8 tral (tral or tryal), 2525 Bare/Beare), another six or seven are simply unusual spellings of obviously correct words, and another half-dozen are homonymic substitutions (1542 chanc’st/chanc’d, 1794 their/there, 2654 here’s/heares, etc.) that could be attributed to a compositor’s memory. Two or three are textual cruxes involving unique or puzzling words (1148 to intrench/t’intrince, 1271 Tuelygod/Turlygod, 1889 caese/Sesey), and a few other Q terms can hardly have been misheard for their F counterparts (1247 and/their, 1409 fruite/Tombe, 3245 or/and).

On the whole, the case for the presence in Q of aural errors pointing to an oral stage in the transmission of its text is less than compelling. Maguire (1996, pp. 197–8) gives examples of aural errors from contemporary dramatic texts and modern newspapers to exemplify their weakness as diagnostic evidence for reporting of Renaissance texts. They can arise in almost any mode of transmission. We cannot exclude the possibility of mishearing by a scribe of a dictator, or by a compositor of himself (compositors provide a complicating mnemonic link in that the text is carried from a ms to a composing stick via their memory).…[198] Thus, aural errors cannot function as proof of memorial reconstruction, and the infrequent appearance of such errors in our suspect texts shows that they are not even a strong feature.

div.head: Punctuation
div.p: Whatever Sh.’s own standards and habits of punctuation may have been, the pointing of Q1 Lr. is inadequate by the measure not only of modern practice but even of the house style of the Folio text of Lr. published fifteen years later. The punctuation in Q1 is light, erratic, and incomplete. The comma is the mark mainly used throughout, consistently where one would today expect points denoting heavier pauses; periods are often replaced by commas or are missing where one would expect them; and other marks are seldom used. Chambers (1930, 1:465): Q has practically no punctuation except commas, even in places where both logic and enunciation require heavier stops.

Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 106) gives the following tabulation of marks within (but not at the ends of) speeches in the first two acts; the line numbers refer to lines of print in Q:

I.i 295 302 5 5 7 1 –
ii 147 175 5 4 3 1 –
iii 25 28 1 – – – –
iv 259 320 4 1 9 5 4
v 42 33 1 – – 1 –
II.i 113 154 3 1 2 1 1
ii 160 173 1 – 5 – 1
iii 21 31 – – – – –
iv 294 318 – 2 7 1 4
Total 1356 1534 20 13 33 10 11
A full-width horizontal brace, pointing down
87
There are only two pairs of round brackets ( ) in these two acts. Speeches usually close with the proper punctuation marks; on three occasions an interrupted speech ends with a dash, made of three hyphens. Question marks follow exclamations some fifteen times. Halio (ed. 1994, p. 7): Commas were sometimes used to indicate hyphens, citing 2189 poorlie,leed (u)/parti,eyd (c).

Greg (1933, p. 253; 1942, p. 95) surmised that the printer had before him copy that was…altogether without punctuation, (1942) a not unusual situation: Some autograph manuscripts…are notoriously deficient in this respect (1933), and We know that manuscripts were often inadequately punctuated (1942), citing Sir Thomas Moore. Bolton (1960, p. 435): The most cursory examination of facsimiles and reprints of Elizabethan dramatic manuscripts will make evident how very few punctuation marks the dramatists of the time normally used. He points out that in the three pages of Sir Thomas Moore, in the 147 lines sometimes attributed to Sh. there are in all 33 speeches only one punctuation mark (a period) ending a speech, and within the speeches only 35 commas, 5 periods, 4 semicolons, and one apostrophe. Although it is not necessary to believe that the lines in Moore are Sh.’s, there is reason to think that his own punctuation was also light. Alexander (1945) distinguishes two styles of punctuation in Sh.’s plays, a heavier, regular house style imposed in F1 by Jaggard’s compositors, and Sh.’s own lighter, more fluent style, observable in plays supposedly set from his MSS, as in Q2 Rom., Q2 Ham., and F Cor. [the latter possibly scribal]. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxx, n. 1): In an unpublished paper P. Alexander argues that the punctuation of Q resembles that of good quartos. Graham-White (1995, p. 73): Peter Alexander long ago [1945] called attention to how in the Second Quarto of Hamlet (1604/5) [printed by James Roberts] certain phrases stand punctuated in the midst of an unpunctuated complex and noted that punctuation is supplied within the lines but not at their ends. Peter Blayney [1978, p. 17] points to similar instances in the First Quarto of King Lear (1608). This is an old tradition: John Skelton’s Magnyfycence and Bale’s King Johan regularly mark the caesure with a virgule or comma, respectively, but not the line end. In many ways the principle seems to be the one that Helen V. Baron noted [Wyatt’s What Rage, 5 Library 31 (1976), 199] in Thomas Wyatt’s poetic practice, taking for granted a slight break at the ends of lines and only punctuating them where there was a complete break. The pointing in Q1 may have been made even lighter by the printer; according to Blayney (1978, p. 21, n. 9), Okes was short of full stops and colons.

Hammond (1994) shows that the punctuation in surviving authorial and scribal dramatic MSS before 1610 is generally very light and incomplete. As in Q1 Lr., speeches commonly lack terminal punctuation, commas generally appear in medial position, and there is no attempt to punctuate what seems self-evident. Neither authors nor scribes were as concerned with pointing as compositors were when producing printed books. (Pp. 221–2): Generally speaking, prompt-books had actually little cause to concern themselves with punctuation; the inflexion and delivery of the lines was the actors’ business.…[222] There is little if any evidence that the punctuation of authorial and scribal dramatic manuscripts was purposefully selected before 1610 or so; rather,…its very casualness until the influence of the compositors began to make itself felt suggests that it is a noisy [i.e., insignificant], or accidental, element in the text. Maguire (1996, p. 222): The New Bibliographers frequently exclaimed over the paucity of punctuation in Q King Lear. They did not consider that this might indicate an author’s lightly punctuated manuscript, even though they were well aware of the under-punctuation in hand D of Sir Thomas More; and they never explained why they viewed this feature as suspicious (of whatever they suspected) in Q1 King Lear. For the record, punctuation has little value in the study of memorial reconstruction, for, as Moxon tells us, it is the responsibility of the compositor.

div.head: Prosody and Lineation
div.p: There has been considerable comment on two, sometimes related, features of the verse in Q1 Lr.: the presence in many lines of verse of apparently superfluous syllables, and the confused and often erroneous division of the verse lines into irregular meter or prose, or of prose into false verse. The distinctions among these media are sometimes difficult to make because at this time in his career Sh. was writing verse often of great metrical freedom and even roughness, sometimes matching the agitated or distracted moods of the speakers.

A few lines in Q are hypermetric because of the presence of one or two words, usually vocatives, expletives, or interjections, that add syllables in excess of a regular pentameter line. Greg (1933, pp. 253–4) calls such expansions of the text redundancies, including also loose phrasing (74 selfe same/selfe, 1516 that lies within/that’s in, etc.) and repetitions (785 and 805 goe go, my people; 765 and 824, yet…daughter), neither of which need derive from actors. Stone (1980, pp. 18–19), like Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxv) and others, calls such expansions actors’ gag(s)—words or phrases improvised by actors to accompany a movement or gesture, to emphasise an effect, or simply to cover a lapse of memory. In fact he can find fewer than a score of these in Q1, all brief and otherwise explainable. Most of them are vocatives such as Sir, King, Madam, or My Lord indicating and showing deference to the recipient of the speech; F1 removes some as being redundant but keeps others, as it does also a few interjections such as Alack and O and Euen so, and a couple of qualifiers, then and heere. As for the vocatives, some may have been intended to occupy a separate line at the beginning of a speech, and as extrametrical monosyllables and dissyllables they are common enough throughout Sh.’s canon: see nn. 60 and 731. The same is true of interjections such as Why, How, and How now (see n. 361). There is no reason to think that these features in Q1 are anything but authorial. Doran (1931, pp. 126–7): Expletives [(p. 127) such as sir, come, how now], when they add a foot to the normal line, are sometimes taken to be interpolations by actors. But in the first quarto of King Lear, they do not occur in the lines of certain actors more than in the lines of others. They appear most frequently in the first part of the play and are distributed among all the characters. I take it that Shakespeare, himself an actor and with his ear trained in the theater, wrote the lines pretty much as they stand in the first quarto. Moreover, he probably wrote his verse by ear and not by the counting of syllables.

Conversely, there is a scattering of short lines throughout the text (e.g., 42, 45, 58, 1036, 2347+22, 3069, 3253), and here again there is no reason to attribute them (as van Dam, 1935, p. 14, is inclined to do) to any agent but the author. Chambers (1930, 1:229–30): Shakespeare made constant use of short lines for exclamations and interjections, for formulas of [230] welcome and dismissal, and for changes of address. To a growing extent he tended to end his speeches in mid-line. The beginning of the next speech does not always complete the line. Short lines occur also in mid-speech, and often with fine rhythmical effect. There is a pause for meditation or gesture, or for reversion to the business in hand. The cadence of a broken line seems to have pleased Shakespeare’s ear.

On the other hand, the mislining of verse in Q1 is egregious and extensive, occurring in about a third of the lines of the play. Doran (1931, p. 128): It is true that a great deal of the verse is printed as prose; but it is also true that much of it, even most of it, is printed as verse. Much of this, in turn, is incorrectly aligned, but, for all that, large portions of the text are correctly printed.…More than half of each of the following scenes is correctly printed: [1.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.1, 3.4, 4.1, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3]. Hubler (1935, pp. 425 ff.) estimates that Q1 prints 61 lines of prose as verse, but that (p. 426) the rest of the prose, about one-quarter of the play, is set correctly; that 500 lines of verse are set as false prose; that (p. 427) 1580 verses are lined correctly; and that 650 verses are lined incorrectly (see further ). Much of the Quarto lining, two-thirds of it, is good, and in agreement with the Folio except for about 100 lines of verse for which Q and F give different but equally good lining. His estimates are accepted by Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 90; in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 133 ff.), Muir (ed. 1952, p. xx, n. 1), and others. Andrews (1971, pp. 47–92) methodically lists all the lines of verse and prose mislined in Q1.

As for prose-verse mislineation, Doran (1933, pp. 36 ff.) thinks it must derive from a much-revised MS, perhaps resembling that of Sir Thomas Moore: Additional or revisional matter occurs written in that manuscript in three ways: on the margin beside the place where it is to be included, on slips pasted over cancelled matter, and on separate leaves inserted between the leaves of the original manuscript. Hubler (1935, pp. 426 ff.) attributes it instead to the printer: One can understand how a compositor who had been setting up long passages of blank verse carried the rhythmic pattern of it in his head, and broke up short passages of prose into lines of approximately blank verse length.…[Sh.’s later] verse tends to be loose, and the prose is often rhythmic, with the movement of blank verse. This is particularly true of transitional passages [between prose and verse]. (P. 428): As in other texts, the typesetter occasionally set long or short lines: It is reasonable to suppose that the compositor…read his text not by lines but by clauses, and that he sometimes ended a [429] line with a clause when he should have added a word or two from the next clause to fill out the line.…The number of short lines in the Lear Quarto is practically negligible.…The mislining consists in the lengthening and crowding of lines for the purpose, I think, of conserving space, giving many exx.; Greg (1936, pp. 175–9) disputes this idea with many examples. (Hubler does not consider the effect on some of his instances of the narrower margin used on many pages, and does not know that Q1 was set seriatim, eliminating the most common reason for most compression to save space.) As for long lines, Hubler describes (pp. 434–8) the manner of their occurrence: I find forty-two lines of six feet or more [e.g. 129–30] which are long because the compositor has set up the half-line with which the speech begins and the following line as one line.
