There are ninety-seven lines [e.g. 2422–3] which are long because the compositor has set up the half line with which the speech ended and the preceding line as one line. And there are one hundred and one lines which are long because the compositor has set up three lines of verse in the space of two [e.g. 1153–5], or four in the space of three [e.g. 2323–6].…[438] Of the mislined verses of the [Lr.] Quarto, five times as many are set up as prose as are mislined in any other way.

Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. 136) rejects Greg’s suggestion (1936, p. 176; 1942, p. 95; withdrawn 1955, p. 387) that the lining was done by two compositors, one more able at it; indeed, I cannot think that the task of verse line-division would be added to the burdens of Jacobean compositors. (Blayney has shown that one compositor set most of the play.) Likewise Stone (1980, p. 26, n. 25) thinks that unlined copy is an unlikely assumption a priori, and that compression of verse into prose and vice versa cannot be due to setting by formes (as in F1), because such mislined passages are as likely to be found at the beginning of a page as at the end. (Blayney has shown that the setting was not by formes.) Stone’s own explanation (pp. 26–35) is that the compositor was working from a piecemeal theatrical report in which verse lineation was often unclear; but the features that he imagines in such a report—uncapitalized lines of about the same length, confusing enjambements, caesuras, and midline sentence capitals, verse passages beginning with a short line, and so on—could as well appear in an author’s rough draft, and confuse Okes’s compositors, who were wholly inexperienced in setting dramatic verse. Uncapitalized verse lines of roughly the same length as prose lines are not necessarily signs of either authorial or reported manuscripts, since they may be found in the dramatic transcripts of the professional scribe, Ralph Crane, who prepared printer’s copy for five plays in the First Folio. Like a number of contemporary playwrights, possibly including Sh., he apparently expected compositors to transform his less formal practices of writing out verse into the somewhat different and more regular style of print presentation. Orgel (1994, pp. 278–84), demonstrating how often uncapitalized verse in Middleton’s holograph and scribal manuscripts is indistinguishable from prose: Capitalization was a common printing convention, not a manuscript one.…[284] The question of verse versus prose was a less pressing one to Jacobean playwrights, and to those concerned with the transmission of their texts, than it has been to the subsequent editorial tradition. It was, for purely practical reasons, of most immediate concern to the typographer.

Urkowitz (1980, p. 163 n. 11) quotes from a letter from Blayney (16 January 1979): Okes’s type-supply led to a surprising amount of the Q mislineation. Lear was the first play-quarto ever printed by Okes or by his predecessor in the same business (founded 1598), and from it Okes learned that one can’t print a play seriatim with 120 lbs. of type bought for printing prose pamphlets by formes. Blayney (1982, pp. 7–8): Two-thirds of the Quarto verse is divided in what editorial tradition has accepted from F as the correct form. Elsewhere there is [8] textual evidence…which suggests that Q’s copy was mislined at certain points in particular ways.… And there is abundant bibliographical [not textual] evidence throughout the Quarto which shows that the lineation and punctuation of the printed book were continually affected by a printing-house problem which had nothing whatever to do with the lineation, punctuation, legibility, or authority of the copy. Though Blayney has not to date explained how a printing-house problem caused mislining, presumably a shortage of space types led to the use of a narrow measure in pages full of verse, and possibly to the frequent setting of verse as prose or of prose as verse within that measure. Greg (1936, p. 179) makes such a suggestion about 1656–68: Here the quarto compositor began by simply filling his (narrower) measure and in effect treating his copy as prose, though he prefixed perfunctory capitals to the lines. He then decided for verse and cut up his copy into irregular lengths, though with no apparent regard for metre. The second speech is in fact prose, but having made up his mind for verse, the compositor proceeded to cut this also into lengths. Perhaps the line-lengths were not dictated simply by compositorial choice (Greg) but at least in part by exigencies of type-supply. For evidence that the mislineation was largely due to the compositors’ inexperience rather than deficiencies in the manuscript, see below ().

div.head: Accessories
div.p: Like the other Shn. quartos, and unlike F1, Q1 Lr. is not divided into acts or scenes.

Doran (1931, p. 81): The designation of the major characters as well as of the minor ones is more exact and consistent in the folio than in the quarto. In the latter text, Albany and Cornwall are both, at times, referred to in the directions and speech labels as Duke. Regan once enters as Dutchesse ([1117]), Regan and Goneril as the two Ladies ([2982]), and Lear as King ([1273]).…The phrase the two Ladies is of no help to a prompter when three ladies have roles.

Greg (1955, pp. 377–8): [In] the descriptions of characters…there is a good deal of inconsistency and some ambiguity. The worst is over the two dukes. Cornwall is [378] often Duke both in directions and speech-headings, and so is Albany, both before and after Cornwall’s death. Otherwise inconsistency is no more than sporadic and does not lead to uncertainty. Regan is once Duchess [1117] in a direction, but always speaks under her own name. Lear is occasionally King in directions [1273, 2645] but never as a speaker. Edgar in disguise is once Tom in a direction [1997], but still speaks as Edgar. Edmund is always Bastard except in the directions of the fifth act and once [1117] in the second. Oswald is Steward in directions, except on his first appearance (in i. iii) when he is a Gentleman (Gent.)…; he speaks twice as Oswald in i. iv just before he has been called by name.

Maguire (1996, pp. 269–70): Edmund in the sd at i2r [2430] is [270] a mistake for Edgar (a mistake which occurs in reverse in the dialogue at h3v, 12) [2283]. Lear’s name is spelled Leir, as in the sources, at 256, 265, 269, and 788; the aberrant spelling suggests an author early in the composition of his play being unconsciously influenced by the spelling of his chief source, the old Leir play. Gloster is called Leister in a SD at 1586; and Cor. at 176 has been improbably referred to Cornwall (see n.).

Doran (1931, pp. 82–3): The directions for entrance of characters are more specific in the folio. Sometimes in the quarto only the first character who speaks is provided for in the direction for entrance.…[83] The entrances of characters during the progress of a scene generally appear in the right-hand margin one line ahead of or on the same line with the first speech of the entering characters.

Greg (1955, p. 378): The record of entrances and exits is very defective: some sixteen entrances and twice that number of exits are unmarked. The most noticeable are at [291], Exit Lear and Burgundie, where at least Cornwall, Albany, and Gloucester also leave the stage, though not in company with the King; at [874], Enter Lear, though Kent, the Fool, and a Servant are with him; and at [1227], where there is no exit for Cornwall, Regan, and Edmund. In every respect the quarto text is unsuited to representation. Further entrances are missing: 579 Knight, 809 Lear, 1273 Foole and Gentleman, 1403 Gloucester, 2299 Albany, 2739 Edgar?, 2743 or 2771 Lear, 2927 Edgar, 3050 Herald, 3216 Edgar?, and Servants or Attendants at 203, 538, 919, 1117, 1403, 2059, and 3216. Further exits of named characters are missing: 40 Gloster (and Edmund?), 201 Kent, 446 Gloster, 576 Steward, 578 Knight, 621 Steward, 803 Lear (and Kent, Fool?), 829 Lear, 841 Fool, 864 Steward, 942 Curan, 965 Edgar, 1236 Gloster, 1332 Lear, 1396 Gloster, 1411 Kent, 1733 Lear, Kent, 1807 Fool, 1968 Lear, Kent, Gloster, Edgar, and Fool, 2000 Gloster, 2056+18 Edgar, 2080 Oswald, 2171 Gloster, 2239 Old Man, 2265 Edgar, Gloster, 2293 Bastard, 2731 Edgar?, 2919 Cordelia, Lear, and Army, 2936 Edgar, Gloster, 2968 Lear, Cordelia, 2981 Captain, 3056 Regan, and 3210 Edgar? The exits of various Attendants, Servants, Gentlemen, Soldiers, Officers, etc. are unmarked at 135, 578, 605, 606, 763, 770, 785? 803, 875 or 881, 922, 979, 1227, 2062, 2083, 2171, 2358, 2645, 2843+9, 2968, 3056, 3120, 3186, and 3210. Exit needs expanding to Exeunt at 528, 1995, –2056, 2176, 2176+9, 2347, 2347+56, 2381, 2428, and 2742.

Doran’s expectation and Greg’s firm belief that missing entrances, exits, and other stage directions would have been carefully provided in an official playbook have been shown (e.g., by Long, 1985, 1999; Werstine, 1990, 1999) not to be borne out in the handful of manuscript playbooks that have survived. The absence or irregularity of such accessories may very well be authorial in origin, but since extant theatrical manuscripts reveal that such features would usually not have been changed by the bookkeeper, they can not be taken to distinguish between an early draft and a playbook, as Greg thought they could. In all probability the manuscript behind Q1 Lr. could have been used as a playbook if such imperfections were its only fault. Q’s variants of character names are relatively few and seldom confusing. Only eight entrances for named characters are entirely missing, and these might have been considered unnecessary by author or company. Two or three (at 809, 2927, and possibly 2739) are omissions of directions for a character to re-enter soon after an exit; such omissions are so common in extant manuscripts—Werstine (privately) supplies examples from Second Maiden’s Tragedy 224, 335–84, 1998–2023, The Captives 2464–2512, Woodstock 748, Charlemagne 1136–1219, and Two Noble Ladies 403–83—that the re-entrance and ensuing speech may simply have been considered part of a continuous action, needing no separate direction. At 2771 (in Q) Lear may not enter but be revealed sleeping in an alcove. At 579 and 919 an attendant is addressed mid-speech as he enters; presumably the direct address took the place of a direction (although entrances for major characters in similar situations are added in the margin at 462, 948, and 1595). At 2299 Albany’s approach is noted in the previous line, and in 3051–8 the Herald is summoned or addressed by name three times as he approaches. In these four latter cases entrance directions may have seemed unnecessary, even redundant. Twice (874, 1273) major characters are unnamed when they enter in conversation with the King, and a Captain (Gentleman in F) returning with him is overlooked at 3216; in effect they are his attendants, and the actors would know to enter when Lear entered. Perhaps the same assumption explains the absence of Gloucester’s name from 1403 (Q), since he is only a mute onlooker throughout the scene until his exit at 1586. On four occasions (203, 538, 1117, 2059) anonymous attendant servants are similarly unspecified, naturally accompanying their masters in order to play a part in the ensuing scene. Such defective entrances would be mended in a modern promptbook or reading edition, as most of them are in F, but they probably would not have troubled a Jacobean book-keeper or discouraged a company from basing a performance on Q. As for missing exits, their presence is seldom essential because actors know when their part in a scene is done.

Doran (1931, p. 83): The directions of the quarto are descriptive…as though Shakespeare, in composing the directions, had visualized the action that was required. F1’s terse and definite directions, by contrast, leave the actors to care for their own business, and focus on the practicalities of timely entrances, properties, and off-stage atmosphere, such as music and storm.
Greg (1955, pp. 375–7): The stage-directions in Q are fairly full and clearly visualized.…[377] The directions in Q have all the appearance of normal author’s directions.

Maguire (1996, pp. 269–70): sds are attentive to details of staging, e.g. processional order (b1v) [37–8], action (Shee takes a sword and runs at him behind: h2r [2155]; Exit King running: i4v [2645]; sleepes: e3r [1250]).…There is one permissive sd (two or three: h1r [2089]). Two scenes give an advance indication of Edgar’s entrance in the lh margin (c2v [462], d3v [948]; the marginal indication A Letter prefaces the reading aloud of the letter on c1v [381].…[270] One sd is imperative: draw and fight (h1v) [2152].

div.head: The Copy for Q1
div.p: Serious attempts to identify the nature of the copy from which Q1 Lr. was set begin in the middle of the nineteenth century, and though they invoke a variety of evidence, they rely mainly on the many deficiencies in the Q1 text, particularly its many verbal errors, faulty punctuation and verse lineation, apparent mishearings, and presumed omissions of passages supplied later in the First Folio. The prevailing conviction for more than a century was that a manuscript so flawed, resulting in an edition so riddled with errors, must have been obtained by some kind of underhand means or piracy and consequently, despite its regular entry in the Stationers’ Register, was published surreptitiously without supervision from Sh. or his company. Such a provenance would explain the play-text’s low quality and its failure to be corrected authoritatively while in press. In 1931 that prevailing opinion was challenged powerfully by Doran, who concluded that the MS behind Q1 was probably Sh.’s own autograph. Her argument was repeatedly dismissed by Greg, largely on impressionistic grounds, and for several decades many other textuists, swayed by his immense authority, proposed alternatives to it; but it has in recent years become generally accepted. The following discussion will consider in turn the several theories of provenance, and the arguments that have been made for and against each one.

div.head: Theatrical Manuscript
div.p: Several theorists take Butter’s claim on the title page—that his edition presents Lr. As it was plaid before the King’s Majestie—to mean that Q1 was printed from a playbook representing that particular performance.

Knight (ed. 1840, pp. 391–2; ed. 1842, pp. 4–5): Whether Lear was piratical, or whether a limited publication was allowed, it is clear, we think, that by some interference the continued publication was stopped. [Knight was unaware of Q1619.]…From the somewhat ostentatious precision with which Butter mentions this circumstance [of court performance], may it not be conjectured that he obtained a copy, used upon that occasion, from some one of the players—perfect to a certain extent, but still not the author’s copy? (The players are not known to have had regular access to the playbook, which was kept by the bookholder, but ordinarily to parts containing their own lines.) Idem (ed. 1842, 1:xv f.): Lr. and Tro. were probably acted for the first time before the court of James I., and it is not impossible that the copies so used were out of the control of the players who represented these dramas; and that some one, authorised or not, printed each play from the copy employed at these private representations by the King’s Majesty’s servants. The utter dis-[xvi]regard of metre in the Lear proves that the edition was not printed from the author’s copy. Delius (1875, p. 128): Q was set from a complete copy of the theatre MS. as it then existed. Fleay (1879, p. 119; cf. 1886, p. 238; 1891, 2:191): In the Quarto we have the version of the play then [26 Dec. 1606] performed…somewhat altered…for Court performance, but very carelessly copied and erroneously printed. The alteration that made this copy none too legible was censorship of passages possibly offensive to James (but which survived in F1): see nn. 439–40, 440–1, 842–55, 1631–8, 1734–49. Ingleby (1881, 2:120): Q is a surreptitious copy of a revision of the original, played at Court, December, 1606.

Adee (ed. 1890, p. xx), on the assumption that Sh.’s company was travelling in the provinces during much of 1606–8: The coast was clear for Nathaniel Butter, who probably had no difficulty in bribing some hanger-on of the Globe, on whom the eye of the master no longer rested, to loan him the prompt-copy of the play, thus brought down with its interpolations and acting-cuts to the state in which the Master of the Revels approved it for acting before the King [Dec. 1606]. The original manuscript may not unreasonably be supposed to have been taken by Shakespeare to the provinces, whither the King’s company returned after the Whitehall function, although no record survives of Lear’s having been played during the tour.…Thumbed and worn, interlined, crossed-out and marginally noted, this prompt-copy must have been a puzzle to the compositors. (If the King’s Men had been playing Lr. in the provinces, they would have brought with them the playbook, bearing the Master of the Revels’ license to perform the play.) Adee adds further circumstances (pp. xxiv f.): The prompt-copy used from early 1605 until the last special revival at Whitehall in Dec. 26 1606 (after which it was not performed again) was purloined or surreptitiously borrowed to use in printing Butter’s Quartos [i.e., Q1 and Q2]. It contained errors made by the scribe who prepared the prompt-copy from Sh.’s MS (omissions of words, some eyeskip); theatrical alterations (pruning of speeches, lines added by the author to explain the situation or make the action more continuous, and actors’ interpolated gags); and probably a few censorial touches by Sir George Buck, the Master of the Revels.

Having alleged (1909, p. 53) that Q1 was printed from an unusually illegible playhouse copy, Pollard (1920, p. 50) locates it among several other piracies and offers a pipe dream that Busby coerced the King’s Men into allowing him to publish it duly printed from a playhouse copy. Busby supposedly bought rights to Leir and threatened to publish it unless allowed access to Lr., a possibility also entertained by Rhodes (1922, pp. 4–5). (In all probability Leir was published before Lr. was written; see .) Others who follow Pollard’s lead are Lee (1916, p. 396), who like Fleay hypothecates a badly transcribed playhouse copy; Rhodes (1923, p. 21), who abandons his earlier (1922, p. 66) opinion that copy for Q1 was assembled from players’ parts and settles instead on the playbook itself; and Adams (1923, p. 521), who opts for the original prompt copy, later (1933, pp. 135–63) preferring a shorthand report.

Granville-Barker (1927, p. 224) speculates that Q and F may derive from separate promptbooks containing alternate acting versions (though not that those books served as printer’s copy), and Wilson (facs. 1931, p. [iii]) imagines their use in different theaters. Greg (1942, pp. xxxvi, 93) toys with the idea before (1955, p. 375) agreeing with Walker (1953, pp. 51–2), who scouts it. Her grounds are that changes to the play after it went into performance, whether made by author or bookkeeper, ran the risk of confusing the actors, and that the omissions from Q1 seem too pointless to represent a coherent attempt to shorten the play.

Van Dam (1935, p. 9): The announcement of royal performance on the title page means—if true, and why should it not be true?—that the play was reported or that it had a prompt-book origin. The length of Q forbids the assumption of a reported play but it does not gainsay prompt-book origin. The prompt-book may contain much more than was played, for we know that lines on the left margin [in extant playbooks] indicated suppressed passages. His attempt to edit the first scene of Lr. on this assumption is less than successful, however, involving him in extensive and often improbable emendation; see .

Greg (1955, p. 378), quoted above, voices what is now the general opinion: that because of its defective exits and entrances, particularly those that omit the names of characters, the quarto text is unsuited to representation. Duthie (ed. 1949), Stone (1980, p. 20), and others point out that the Q1 SDs ignore details of great practical importance to the book-keeper—sound effects (the storm passes unremarked except in dialogue), essential props (stocks), exact numbers (two or three [2088], and others [2349–50]). Clare (1990, p. 132) speculates (unnecessarily and improbably) that Butter may have entered a playbook bearing Buc’s licence for performance, though the text in Q1 bear[s] no relation to a carefully prepared theatrical prompt book and…had a different provenance.

Nonetheless Bolton (1960, pp. 427 ff.; cf. 1956, pp. 180–1) imagines that Q’s copy was a promptbook used in early performances, and that the absence of words, SDs, lines, and passages from Q (though present in F1) was owing to playhouse wear and tear to that promptbook, whose losses had been only imperfectly restored by the book-keeper, perhaps with the help of actors’ memories. Assuming that theatrical MSS had 40 or 50 or 60 lines per page, he cites (p. 427) nine pages on which such omission-causing illegibilities occurred, at 45, 439, 1281, 1372, 1598, 1734, 2184, 3035, and 3170–3 (B1v, B3v, E1r, E4r, F3r, F4v, H2v, L1r, and L3r [or L2v]) and claims that in each case, another omission [unidentified] appears some 40 or 50 lines later, presumably at the foot of the verso of the leaf. This ragged MS, he believes, became Butter’s copy. (P. 438): After receiving Shakespeare’s manuscript and while writing out the actors’ parts and making the fair copy [presumably for the playbook], the playhouse scribe probably did a little editing of his own [i.e., adding SDs and brief textual variants].…I assume that the author’s manuscript was used for a promptbook [presumably a second promptbook in addition to that made from the fair copy].…But when the lower portions of nine of its thirty-odd sheets had worn away, the manuscript was discarded as useless. Someone retrieved it, however, from the trash basket, and sold it, late in 1607, to Nathaniel Butter and John Busby.…The [Q] compositor…worked from the tattered leaves themselves.

Bolton’s theory is questionable on several grounds, and no one has ever accepted it. If, as Bowers and Blayney agree (see ), the MS behind Q was so miserable—disorderly and frequently illegible—that it baffled both printer and proofreader, it would also have been difficult for the acting company to use and the censor to review. Evidently, as Doran first argued (see ), a transcript was made from it before it passed to Busby and Butter in 1607, and it is entirely probable that this transcript, bearing the Master of the Revels’s license, became the company’s official playbook and the basis for actors’ parts. It is not known that Sh.’s company kept and used multiple promptbooks, and a manuscript as troublesome as the original draft apparently was would not have served such a purpose easily or well. Greg (1955, p. 382, n. 19) objects that a MS used between the play’s composition (1606) and registry for publication (1607) would not likely be badly worn. Honigmann (1965, p. 127 n.) casts doubt because several Q omissions (at 269, 774, 833, 857, 1014–15, 1036, 2816, 2890) remain unexplained by Bolton, while at 1373–5 and 1379, and again at 3035 and 3037, there are two apparently connected variants; if they were both worn out of Q it is unclear how the lines between them (1376–8 and 3036) survived. Jackson (1983, p. 343 n.) concedes the bases of Bolton’s argument—that some of Q’s most significant divergences from F occur at approximately 50-line intervals, and that dramatists did pen about 50 lines per MS page; but he argues that over half of the F-only passages do not fall in the expected position, and attempts to show by experiment that many F-only passages might fall into these positions by chance (as, in Q1, 18 stage directions fall within 40 to 50 lines of another stage direction). Other objections might be made: that there is apparently no wear on intervening leaves; that the wear affects passages of widely different lengths; and that most if not all of Q’s supposed omissions are now thought to be Folio additions.

div.head: Reported Text
div.p: In recent years the sheer length of Q1 Lr. has led an increasing number of scholars to doubt that either it or the somewhat shorter F1 version could ever have been performed in its entirety within the normal contemporary playing limits, in which case Q1 can not represent a performing text of the play. For arguments that the printed texts of Sh.’s longer plays can not represent playing versions, see, especially, Hart (1934, pp. 77–153; 1942, p. 136), Chambers (1944, pp. 40–1), Smidt (1964, p. 162; 1988, pp. 25 ff.), Carroll (1988, p. 229), Melchiori (1992, pp. 200 ff.), Orgel (1994, pp. 251–2), Dutton (1996, pp. 82 ff.), Gurr (1999, pp. 68 ff.; 2004, pp. 123–4), and Erne (2003, pp. 131–73). For some actual and projected playing times of Lr., see . Nonetheless, the idea that Q1 was reported from an actual performance has had a long life, and many elaborate arguments have been erected for and against it. It has seemed to offer an easy explanation of many of the kinds of deficiencies found in Q1, especially its scanty and erroneous punctuation, mislining of verse (see, e.g., n. 287–90), and apparent errors of hearing. On the other hand, it offers difficulties of its own, and virtually all of the errors that may be attributed to reporting are equally susceptible of other interpretations.

In perhaps the earliest application of this explanation to Sh.’s texts, John Roberts, in An Answer to Mr. Pope’s Preface to Shakespear. By a Stroling Player (1729, sig. D2), supposes that Heminges and Condell’s stolne and surreptitious copies must have been taken by the Ear or (D2v) by other fraudulent Means. Similarly Theobald (ed. 1733, 1:xxxvii f.), talking generally, not about Lr. in particular: Many Pieces were taken down in Short-hand, and imperfectly copied [xxxviii] by Ear, from a Representation: Others were printed from piece-meal Parts surreptitiously obtain’d from the Theatres, uncorrect, and without the Poet’s Knowledge. Steevens (1766, 1:9) imagines a more legitimate kind of reporting: Were I to indulge my own private conjecture, I should suppose that his blotted manuscripts were read over by one to another among those who were appointed to transcribe them; and hence it might easily happen, that words of similar sounds, though of senses directly opposite, might be confounded with each other. Similarly Theobald (1888, p. 412) doubts that Q1 could be taken by shorthand from the stage, and suggests that the poet dictated his poetry to an amanuensis. Knight (ed. 1838–43, 1:392): From the defective verse in Shn. quartos we may judge…that in the stage copies the pauses of the blank verse were either disregarded as a guide for the actors, or that the printed copies were produced from a report made in some way or other by persons at the representation, or by the repetitions of the players themselves, who would not mark those pauses.

As for Lr. in particular, Knight (ed. 1840, n. 525–8): The quartos…not only confound the differences between prose and verse, but give us the verse in the most inexact and capricious manner, presenting every appearance of a reported text—a copy taken down as the dialogue was spoken,—in which case it would be very difficult for a reporter to detect the beginnings and ends of lines, and to mark what was intended to be metrical and what not. Such features, along with mistakes of the ear, added expletives, and omissions, persuaded Schmidt (1879, pp. 2–5; rpt. 1880, pp. 3–7) that all the Shn. quartos were likely to have been reported texts. Greg (1942, pp. 90–5) accepts Schmidt’s and Chambers’s (1930, 1:159–62, 465–7) belief that Lr. is a reported text somehow based on an actual performance: Besides frequent and indifferent variants, we find in the quarto all the usual stigmas of a reported text: redundancy, whether through the actors’ introduction of vocatives, expletives, or connective phrases, or through their lapsing into looser and more commonplace phraseology, merging into paraphrase; anticipation [of later lines], recollection [of earlier ones], and assimilation; vulgarization [of ideas or phrasing], and mere breakdown through failure of memory. He adds (p. 94) mistakes of the ear, misassigned speeches, and (p. 95) disregard of metre and its inadequate and often erroneous punctuation. We could well imagine that the printer had before him copy that was altogether without punctuation or metrical division. Greg (1955, p. 380–1) gives a similar list of stigmas, including breakdowns and improvisations. He continues, however, to be uncertain about the manner of reporting. Believing that the text in F1 presents the shortened and possibly censored version of Lr. prepared for the original production, Greg (p. 381) finds any performance of an earlier uncut version such as is found in Q1 wellnigh incredible: Had there been a report of a stage performance it would almost certainly have given us a garbled version of F rather than anything resembling Q.

div.head: Stenography
div.p: Of all the theories explaining the means by which the text of Q1 Lr. might have been produced by reporting, the most widely accepted has been shorthand copying from performance (presumably by graphite pencil, not by pen). Some form of shorthand had existed since the mid-1580s: Timothy Bright published his Characterie in 1588, Peter Bales The Writing Schoolmaster in 1590 (rpt. as Brachygraphy, 1597), and John Willis The Arte of Stenographie in 1602. As evidence of the growing popularity of short writing Davidson (1996, p. 422) lists eight later titles published 1618–28, all, of course, too late to have had any effect on Q1 Lr. There is some evidence that sermons, the greatest moneymakers for the publishing trade, were occasionally taken down by shorthand and published; see Matthews (1932, pp. 248–9; Davidson (1996, p. 419; 1998, pp. 302–6). Sermons, spoken in quiet places in a slow and measured delivery, on largely familiar themes in a familiar vocabulary, could be susceptible of shorthand copying; whether a stenographer in a bustling playhouse could capture the rapid interchange of dialogue, with its wide vocabulary and unpredictable tones, while noting accurately the identity of each speaker and recording all entrances, exits, and stage business, is not so self-evident. Although Sir George Buc wrote (1612) in The Third Universitie of England (as first published in Stow’s Annals, 1615, p. 984) that they which know [brachygraphy] can readily take a Sermon, Oration, Play, or any long speech, as they are spokẽ, dictated, acted, & uttered in the instant, he did not name any play so taken, and doubt remains that any exists.

In fact, only two statements by the same contemporary playwright suggest the practice. First, Thomas Heywood complained in the preface to The Rape of Lucrece (rpt. 1638) that some of my Playes have…accidentally come into the Printers hands, and therefore so corrupt and mangled (copied onely by the eare) that I have beene… unable to know them. Second, in a Prologue probably written about 1632 (Greg, 1936, p. 176) and published in 1637 in anticipation of a corrected edition of Part I of If You Know Not Me, You Know Nobody (N. Butter, 1605), Heywood made a similar complaint of that play’s original unauthorized publication: some by Stenography drew | The plot: put it in print: (scarce one word trew:). As for the first claim, there is no certainty that copied by the ear refers to shorthand; though Greg (1936, p. 174) thinks it is natural to suppose that this was what he meant, Matthews (1932, p. 244) denies that the phrase necessarly implies that shorthand was used. As for the second claim, it is difficult to know what is meant by drew the plot, since the term plot, though only then coming into critical use, had some of today’s ambiguity, and could mean simply an outline or synopsis of the action. Since Heywood says he was unable to know his reported plays, and that stenography reported scarce one word true, he may have meant by plot not a full verbatim report but a sketch that someone amplified. In any case If You Know Not Me (1605) is not known to be a reported text, nor is it certain that in 1637 Heywood knew that it was (Hubler, 1935, p. 423; Greg, 1936, p. 173; Kirschbaum, 1945, p. 702; Dace, 1971, p. 29). Greg (loc. cit.): Indeed, I would go so far as to say that if Heywood’s piece, as printed in 1605, represents approximately the best that could be achieved by Willis’s system of Stenography, or any other method current at the time, then we must rule out shorthand altogether as the method by which the quarto text of Lear was obtained.

Though such English editors as Malone, Dyce, and Collier had suspected that stenographic notes lay behind some of Sh.’s worst quartos, such as H5 and Wiv., the first attempt to derive Lr. in particular from a stenographic report taken down in the theater was that of Schmidt (1879; rpt. 1880), which initiated a series of German studies on a number of plays; see Dewischeit (1898, pp. 176–8), Matthews (1932, p. 243), Förster (1937, p. 1). For Schmidt, who thought that all of Sh.’s quartos represented pirated texts, the theory of stenographic notes explained Q’s differences from F: the verbal omissions and variant readings were attributable to failure of the actors’ memories, as were the insertion of expletives such as come, how, sir; and the verbal errors and faulty lining of verse were due to the stenographer’s mishearing. He does not discuss which system of stenography might have been used. Though Fleay (1876, p. 62) quickly endorses the theory, Adee (ed. 1890, p. xx) rejects it because Q1’s business is carefully attended to, the entrances and exits are tolerably accurate, and the continuity of the action is such as to preclude the idea of a short-hand or imperfectly memorized theft. Doran (1931, p. 122) offers further disagreements: Schmidt’s theory requires a version performed in the theater before it was abridged as in F; Q’s verbal errors seem not aural but misreadings from manuscript or misprints, connected with the form of the correct written word; and Lr. is unlike other bad quartos, which show clear evidence of oral transmission, are shorter, contain lines repeated in different parts of the play, anticipate later lines, transpose scenes, and contain much corrupt verse and many errors of mishearing and nonsense. The first quarto of King Lear, on the other hand, despite its misprints, misreadings, omissions, and faulty printing of verse, is substantially the same play, line for line, as the folio.…The amount of irregularity…varies with different scenes but not with the parts of different characters.…[124] I doubt even if a stenographer could have produced so good a text. Idem (1933, pp. 35 ff.) develops what she admits is an unprovable hypothesis that the disturbances in Q1 are due not to stenography but to Shakespeare’s own revisions either as he wrote or later; Stone (1980, pp. 24–6) rejects it.

Despite its many general problems, several eminent authorities endorse the idea of stenography. Chambers (1930, 1:161–2, 182): [Shorthand] may very possibly…be a factor in King Lear (1608) and Pericles (1609). Both have long continuous passages of verse printed as prose, and in King Lear these, although [162] fairly adequate textually, are almost entirely punctuated by commas. They look to me like the result of shorthand notes well taken, but not properly worked upon at the stage of transcription. Punctuation and metre are of course always the weak points of a report.…[182] I conjecture that [the lines of false prose] are the notes of a shorthand reporter, which he has taken down with approximate fidelity, but has not felt able, or has not troubled, to arrange as verse. There is some confirmation of this in the fact that they are almost entirely punctuated with commas. (But authorial MSS such as Sir Thomas Moore and Believe As You List use mainly commas.) Greg (1933, pp. 253–6; cf. 1942, p. 95; 1955, p. 387, Note B): The general impression left by the Quarto is that the printer had before him copy that was entirely undivided metrically and altogether without punctuation.…Such redundancy is characteristic of actors and is a marked feature of reported texts. He further argues that exclamations, expletives, and vocatives in Q must derive from actors, not the author, as do also loose phrasing and (p. 254) actors’ exaggeration and bombast (of which he gives no examples). The mistakes of hearing are the reporter’s; (p. 255) repetitions in the text are due to the actors, as are syncopations (omissions) and (p. 256) confusions of sense. The better, Folio readings are the more original, not revised improvements; the Quarto readings are generally degraded.

Not all find the evidence of mislineation and mispunctuation persuasive. Hubler (1935, pp. 440–1): The errors of the Quarto differ from the errors of other books [which were not reported] more in quantity than in kind, and if a thing can happen once without a reporter, it can happen several [441] times. The irregularities of the Quarto are more numerous because the book is a singularly bad piece of printing. Though Heywood protested stenographic piracy, he also complained in Apology for Actors how his printer, mistaking of sillables, misplacing halfe lines, coining of strange and never heard of words, refused to correct them in an errata sheet. The mislining of verse and prose in Q1 is more likely to be the work of a compositor than of a stenographer. (Pp. 426–40): Q1 actually sets up little prose as verse, mainly in transitions between verse and rhythmic prose, where the compositor might have been confused. One-quarter of Lr. is prose, correctly set in Q1 (except for 61 lines). (P. 426): One can understand how a compositor who had been setting up long passages of blank verse carried the rhythmic pattern of it in his head, and broke up short passages of prose into lines of approximately blank verse length.…[Sh.’s later] verse tends to be loose, and the prose is often rhythmic, with the movement of blank verse. This is particularly true of transitional passages [between prose and verse]. (P. 427): Q1 lines 1580 verses correctly and 650 incorrectly. It lines long passages correctly (e.g. the last 145 lines of 2.4), which a stenographer would be unlikely to do. (P. 428): Many of the mislined verses in Q1 are long and short lines (e.g. 287–91, 510–11), but printers create these in Q2 and (p. 429) other books; they are not necessarily the work of a stenographer. (P. 428): It is reasonable to suppose that the compositor…read his text not by lines but by clauses, and that he sometimes ended a [429] line with a clause when he should have added a word or two from the next clause to fill out the line. We do not need to imagine a stenographer.…The number of short lines in Q1 is practically negligible; most of the mislining consists in the lengthening and crowding of lines for the purpose…of conserving space. (P. 430): In 287–91 Q mislining destroys rhymed couplets, which a stenographer would not be likely to do. (P. 434): In the First Quarto I find forty-two lines of six feet or more which are long because the compositor has set up the half-line with which the speech begins and the following line as one line [e.g., 129–30]. There are ninety-seven lines which are long because the compositor has set up the half line with which the speech ended and the preceding line as one line [e.g. 2422–3]. And there are one hundred and one lines which are long because the compositor has set up three lines of verse in the space of two [1153–5], or four in the space of three [e.g. 2323–6]. (P. 438): Of the mislined verses of the [Lr.] Quarto, five times as many are set up as prose as are mislined in any other way. Four short passages [669+1–+4, 688–91, 1729–33, 1900–3] are rhymed, (p. 439): and so are more likely mislined by the compositor than by a stenographer; the compositor was trying to save space. The same is true at 2023–30. (P. 440): Other examples show conscious compression and a few carelessness.

Greg (1936, pp. 175–83) replies: A stenographer does not produce mislining directly. His shorthand report will contain no indication of line-division at all. And it is a longhand transcript of such a report, undivided metrically and practically unpointed, that I postulated as copy. The actual misdivision would, of course, be the work of the compositor, as Mr. Hubler contends. And the compositor may very likely have been trying to save space.… [176] But if compression was really the object [of the Q printer, as Hubler imagines],…why did the compositor waste space by setting up sixty lines of prose as verse…? Moreover, at least two-thirds of the verse is correctly lined…with no attempt at compression. (See nn. 287–90, 293–6, 1656–64, 2745–9 for Greg’s arguments that the compositor was not trying to save space.) Space-wasting false verse may have been occasioned by the compositor’s use of the shorter measure. (P. 182): If a compositor setting verse in the narrow measure comes upon a short prose speech, he will be tempted to split it up into verse lengths rather than transfer what he has already set to the galley and start afresh with a longer composing-stick; besides, frequent changes of measure would make the adjustment of the furniture more difficult. He says he has observed no instances in Q where an unscrupulous compositor carried over the last few words of a long verse line to the beginning of a shorter line below (as Hubler suspects happened at 287). He believes on these grounds alone that it is unlikely the Q compositor (p. 183) persistently upset the correct line-division for the sake of a problematic saving of space. More probably the compositor was struggling with an undivided transcript from stenographic notes.

From almost the beginning, those espousing stenography attempted to derive particular errors in Q1 from one or another of the kinds of stenography available at the time—those invented by Bright, Bales, and Willis. Dewischeit’s (1898, pp. 170–220) early choice of Bright’s Characterie (1588) made it the preferred system for several German scholars who followed him, particularly Stössel (1932, 1937) and Förster (1937). Dewischeit argued that because in Bright’s system the same sign could represent several synonyms, it could explain such Q/F disagreements as stoops/falls, offence/fault, respects/regards, heare/harke, bring/fetch, and smite/strike, in which, as Schmidt believed, a correct (F) reading had been supplanted, through stenography, by an incorrect synonym in the pirated (Q) text.

Matthews (1932, pp. 243 ff.) analyzes Bright’s system and does trial transcriptions to show its inadequacy. His students’ reconstruction from the only known transcription by an actual student of Bright resulted in synonym errors averaging 51%. His main argument (pp. 249–51) is that Bright’s symbols (characters) are too few and their significations too inexact to represent the vocabularies found in Sh.’s plays, especially within the time constraints of the playhouse. Bright’s system had an alphabet of 18 signs to which could be attached 12 end-signs—a hook, stroke, circle, etc., which could be written horizontally, vertically, or inclined to the right or left, for a total of 48 variant end-signs, not all of which were used for every letter in Bright’s original alphabet; the total of variants was 537, each representing a common word. For additional words, synonyms or antonyms could be represented by one of these standard words with the first letter of the synonym or antonym written small before it. A dot to the right made a noun plural, or in various positions showed the tense of a verb. (P. 251): Great speed was needed to search the mind for synonyms or antonyms (from a large vocabulary), and (p. 253) great pains for the transcriber later to make any sense of the symbols, as Matthews shows with several examples. Moreover (pp. 256–7), a collation of Elizabethan editions of Spenser’s Poems shows that Elizabethan printers could commit printing errors extraordinarily similar to those that could be yielded by Bright’s shorthand—substitution of synonyms for the original word, (p. 257) erroneous pronouns, number of nouns, spellings, etc.

Dewischeit based his theory mainly on wrong synonyms, as did some of his followers, but (p. 260) the errors are not what one would expect in Rom., H5, RIII, Wiv., since the bad-Q reporter would have had to omit the distinguishing initial letter, the one thing that gave him the right clue to the synonym. Conclusion: (p. 262) Bright’s Characterie…was an impracticable system in which to report plays.

Rejecting Doran’s hypothesis that Q’s verbal variations from F could represent Sh.’s own revisions, since most of them are so insignificant and indifferent that he would not have troubled with them, Adams (1933, pp. 135 ff.) invokes Bright’s Characterie as the only explanation for the errors in Q1. (P. 145): Since its symbols were written in narrow columns from the top to bottom of the page, as in Chinese, it was not suited to record blank verse; accordingly…we find the verse-lining [in Q] almost a complete wreck. (In fact, hundreds of verses are the same in Q and F.) Similarly Bright’s system indicated punctuation by a period under the character where there was a pause, but inferior periods also indicated other things, such as plurals and tenses; hence the nightmare of punctuation in Q. He explains the difficulties of inferring from the symbols for Bright’s 558 charactericall words, representing all the fundamental ideas in the language, the precise synonym or antonym for that word, its relationships to other words, its inflections, and so on; such inexactness might explain Q’s verbal variants from F’s correct words.

In addition, Adams assembles (pp. 157–63) further evidence that the stenography was taken from theatrical performance. Like many others who argue for a theatrical report, he adduces examples of faulty hearing of what the actors said: (p. 157) 1505 hot bloud in (for F’s hot-blooded), 755 great (for grac’d), 2379 in sight (for incite), and so on. (A comprehensive list of supposed aural errors is given at ; all of them have been given alternative explanations as compositorial mistakes, misreadings, spelling variants, etc., and in many cases the Q reading has been thought superior or correct.) In several pairs of words F’s word could have been easily represented by one of Bright’s characterical words; since Q’s word required a more difficult, roundabout symbolization, it must represent an actor’s substitution heard by the stenographer. Similarly, where Bright has a character for both variant words, the actor made the change—more than a hundred of them—from the correct F alternative. Sometimes the actor altered more than a single word, and sometimes added expletives, vocatives, and qualifiers, or changed word order or reworded in order to make the lines clearer. Adams attributes to the actors 123 changed words, 30 transpositions, and 65 additions of colorless exclamations or phrases, while admitting that there are other kinds of errors due to poor Q copy, evidence of reworking by Sh., and corrections from the proofreader.

This case for the use of Bright was utterly demolished by Doran (1935, pp. 139–57), arguing that the kinds of errors that Adams attributes to shorthand can all be attributed more probably to other causes, and that Q is too good a text to represent a stenographic report, particularly when it agrees with difficult readings in F that Bright’s system could not have duplicated in Q. If, as Adams believes, Q represents a reported text, then a source of corruption—memorial corruption by the actors—was active before Bright’s Characterie: Only the presence of variants which could be exclusively traced to Charactery, or of a large proportion which could be most conveniently explained by it, would admit of such a conclusion; but it is doubtful if these conditions can be met. Even without the agency of actors, a number of similar variant readings may be introduced by…the memories of…scribes and compositors. Moreover, there are even fortuitous instances of pairs where the Quarto reading, although capable of explanation by Bright, looks somewhat as if the manuscript had been misread. It is evident that we have to do with a plurality of causes, which makes impossible a strict demonstration of the use of Bright’s shorthand.…Even supposing Q1 to be a reported and therefore secondary version of the play, the original from which it was taken is clearly not F, but a primary text which underlies both and which underwent more or less alteration to become the version represented in the Folio.

She proceeds (pp. 142–8) to evaluate Adams’s evidence, distinguishing which kinds of Q variants from F may have been produced by Charactery, and which cannot be shown to have done so, giving numerous examples from Lr. of the latter. Given these limits on such evidence, only 26% of Q’s variants in verb form can be explained by Bright, and only 17% of its pronoun variants. When the Q reading is more unusual than that in F and is not one of Bright’s primitive forms (including those with the allowed terminations -ed, -ing, -er)—e.g., reuengiue/reuenging (Bright revenge), reposure/reposall (Bright repose by rest) stople/stop (Bright stop)—corruption by Bright is hard to show, because Q’s reading may be right or result from some other cause. Variants like circled/circle, immediate/immediacy, and intelligence/intelligent may represent d/e or c/t misreadings of a manuscript. Derivative variants (i.e., forms inflected from Bright’s primitive words found in F) could easily be errors made by an actor, copyist, or compositor, and are easily found in good texts such as R2 and Ado. As for the main evidence used by Dewischeit and Adams, pairs of Q/F synonyms supposedly related (as in Bright’s 200 pages of tables of some 4500 synonyms) to a common stenographic symbol, Doran finds that only 3 of Adams’s 24 pairs of synonyms prove to be related to a common word in Bright, while in 11 of the 24, each member of the pair is related in Bright to a different word, and so would not have been associated in the stenographer’s mind by Bright’s system. Of the about 130 Q/F synonyms or near-synonyms in the whole play, only 14 are related to a common word in Bright or have the Q reading which would best represent, in Charactery, the Folio reading. In 12 other cases the opposite is true: F rather than Q has the Charactery word. Since comparable results can be found in plays where no influence of stenography is suspected (e.g., R2 and Ado), synonyms are not an adequate test of its use.

Her second line of argument (pp. 149–57) is that Bright’s system could not have produced so good a text—or one so close to F’s—as Q’s. For example, in Edgar’s famous description of Dover Cliff (2445–63), a stenographer must have obtained an almost perfect transcript, since Q and F agree almost completely. Doran shows what a stenographer’s notes for this passage would have looked like in Bright’s system, and then how impossible it would be to reproduce Edgar’s F speech perfectly from them, since many of its words have no symbols or are not in Bright’s tables of synonyms (e.g., sir, chough, yon, bark, her); the same is true of prefixes and inflectional endings. Bright cannot show the use of one part of speech for another (Knee as a verb, looped and windowed raggedness), and even simple compound words (e.g. into, within, upon, therefore) would require the time-consuming finding and combining of two symbols plus two marks. There is no guarantee he would reconstruct from his symbols such words in Lr. as fraught, pight, remotion, covert, stelled (not starred), squiny, etc., or Kent’s invective against Oswald in 2.2, or the names of Harsnett’s devils, or Edgar’s dialect. Lear’s vocabulary contains scores of words not in Bright’s lists. In addition the stenographer had to note every change of speaker, while listening for almost three hours to a rate of speaking as high as 175 words per minute. Modern stenographers cannot work that fast for so long. Reconstruction from notes (sometimes erroneous), which were mainly an aid to memory, can not guarantee reconstruction of the form and character (including verse) in which the words were spoken. Bright’s system was neither bad enough nor good enough to produce the text in Q1.

Like Doran, Matthews (1935, pp. 481 ff.) declines to attribute most of Q’s incorrect synonyms to Bright’s system, arguing that they do not begin with the initial letters which should have been prefixed or suffixed to the symbols for the correct (F) word. Since the same character might refer to several equally valid synonymns from Bright’s lists, Charactery lent itself to paraphrase rather than verbatim reproduction. He concludes that most of the Q divergences from F cannot be attributed to Bright’s Charactery, and that all can be otherwise explained.

Förster (1937, pp. 1 ff.) offers the last defense of Bright against Doran and Matthews, attempting no answer to Doran’s demonstration that Q1 Lr. contains much that Bright’s system can not account for, and providing no new information and no new arguments beyond some unsubstantiated claims—that a stenographer would work quickly and nimbly because he had memorized all of Bright’s 4500 synonyms, that Elizabethans spoke more slowly than we, that a Jacobean performance of Lr. might have lasted for four hours, etc.

Duthie (1949, pp. 2–9), who taught himself and practiced Bright’s system, makes essentially the same criticisms of it that Doran and Matthew did, concluding (p. 8): Shakespeare, whose vocabulary is so very rich, would present the charactery-writer with great numbers of words which he would have himself, on the instant, to relate to suitable characterical words. Time and again the stenographer in the theatre, attending a performance of King Lear, would have to stop and think; meanwhile the actor would be away ahead. A text of Lear taken by Characterie during performance could not possibly be anything like so full and accurate as that of the quarto. The system could produce only a mere skeleton of the play.

The second stenographic system, Peter Bales’s Brachygraphy, takes its name from the third section of his The Writing Schoolmaster (1590), reprinted in 1597 and with the new title A New Year’s Gift to England in 1600. Everyone agrees that it is no improvement on Bright’s system, which it closely resembles. Matthews (1933, pp. 81–2) describes it as a brazen plagiarism: The basic signs are the ordinary Latin letters, each susceptible to 4 diacritical marks in 12 positions, giving 48 variants of each sign. Each variant is assigned one of about 530 commonly used words, almost all the same as Bright’s characterical words. Bale also uses Bright’s system of antonyms and synonyms—a downstroke on the left for an antonym and on the right for a synonym, and an optional first letter of the compared word. Comparisons, number, and tense are left to the memory, only the present tense and singular number being used. Phrases are compressed. The table of synonyms is stolen from Bright. Duthie (1949, p. 12): As in Bright’s system, feats of memory were continually required to find synonyms instantly; besides, the twelve positions of the periods, commas, tittles, etc, around each alphabetic letter required such care that error was inevitable.

The third shorthand system conceivably used for Q1 Lr. was John Willis’s The Arte of Stenographie (1602), the first alphabetic shorthand and before long the dominant system, going through 14 editions and, according to Matthews (1932, p. 246), the basis for over a hundred systems published in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Initial vowels and all consonants were represented by the appropriate letters of the alphabet, but medial vowels were indicated by where the second consonant was placed in relation to the first: a second consonant above indicates medial a, a superscript consonant to the right indicates medial e, directly beside indicates i, subscript to the right indicates o, underneath indicates u. Matthews (p. 247): A transcription…would, therefore, be liable to show words which, because of errors of position, had the right consonants but the wrong vowels [citing examples from Matthias Levy, Shakespeare and Shorthand, 1884].…But always there is a far simpler explanation; wrong vowels don’t prove the use of Willis’s shorthand. Nonetheless, because it was the best of the contemporary systems, it seemed to Greg (1933, p. 256), Matthews (1933, p. 83), Price (1936, p. 226), and others the most likely to have been used, if any was.

Duthie (1949, pp. 12 ff.), having learned Willis’s system well enough to transcribe passages from Q1 Lr., provides the most thorough and detailed critique of it, finding both that it is unequal to verbatim recording and that it is unnecessary for explaining Q1 errors, all of which could arise from other causes. Since Willis’s symbols represented letters or sounds rather than words, it was unlikely to lead to the erroneous substitution of one word for another, as Bright’s and Bales’s systems might. On the other hand (pp. 29–34), many difficulties with Willis’s alphabet led to slow and misleading transcription: many symbols could not be joined cursively but required distinct movements and lifting of the pen, taking as long as longhand to write; and joined or juxtaposed characters required great care in their positioning and size and shape to avoid ambiguity or error. Willis recommended ways to represent words other than literatim in order to speed note-taking: by recording only the first few letters, first and last syllables, or first letter only; by using conventional characters from outside his alphabet; by omitting verb and other inflections; by leaving omitted rhymes to be supplied from context; by abbreviating clauses, sentences, and common sayings; by getting only the gist of a speaker’s argument, catching only the Verbes & Substantiues, and other Wordes essentiall to the speech deliuered. All of these shortcuts might lead to a strain on the memory and misinterpretation when the speech was reconstituted from the notes. Moreover (p. 25), If the Q text had been transmitted in this way we should certainly expect to find a consistent variation of standard between passages full of passion, presumably delivered impetuously, and passages of calmer mood, presumably delivered more slowly. And yet there is in Q no such consistent variation. Duthie examines several such passionate speeches, finding them nearly word-perfect. Similarly (pp. 73–5), there is no difference in standards of reporting between earlier and later parts of the play, and the Q text is not characterized by persistent imperfection at the beginnings of speeches (the stenographer having had to pause to identify and note down the name of the character speaking), nor after stage directions.

To prove that all or most of the variants in Q1 Lr. can be attributed to the actor or the compositor, he examines hundreds of them. (Pp. 50–1): Some 75 variants beginning with the same letter could all be due to a compositor’s misreading of longhand, and some of Q’s non-existent words—disuetur’d, snulbug, festuant, conspicuate—could not have derived from Willis’s abbreviations of words. (Pp. 61–9): Errors attributable to the compositor include omission of the final letter, omission of a single medial letter, misunderstanding of longhand abbreviations, corruptions through influence of neighboring words, and a compositor’s making out only part of a word. He gives two lists of memorial corruptions, the first possibly showing an actor remembering or anticipating a word elsewhere in the text, the second possibly showing a compositor making a substitution while carrying groups of words in his head between reading them in copy and setting them in type. Many of the supposed errors of hearing, taken to indicate a reported text of some kind, may be of these kinds. And while in Willis’s stenography a misplaced dot could result in an a appearing for an e, e for i, o for u, and vice versa, (p. 73) these vowel errors are just as likely to be produced by the misreading of longhand.

Finally, he expresses the doubt, often expressed, that a stenographer could take notes undetected in a public theater, especially if he had to return more than once to complete and perfect his notes. Greg (1942, pp. 95–6) had offered a possible way around this objection: The evidence does not force us to believe that all performances were restricted to anything like two hours: we know that some given at court lasted much longer. Moreover at such a special performance a reporter, if he got in, would be more difficult to detect and also more difficult to remove—and we know that Lear was acted at court. The idea is absurd on the face of it: who in a court audience knew shorthand and was likely to break decorum by surreptitious recording of a royal entertainment for a few pennies, or to risk exposure for doing so? Kirschbaum (1945, p. 6, n. 17): This is letting speculation run away with itself. Similarly Duthie (1949, p. 75): To me the idea that Lear was pirated by stenography at a court performance is quite incredible. Shakespeare’s company of actors was under the direct patronage of the King: surely no stenographer would dare to try to purloin the entire text of one of their plays within the court surrounded by powerful friends of the company, even in the presence of the King himself. Alternatively, Greg (p. 96, n. 1) hypothecates a private performance for which the play was originally written; no such performance is recorded.

Despite the occasional cavil (e.g., Walton, 1971, p. 270 n.), Duthie’s study put the theory of stenography to rest for almost a half-century. It led even a long-time (if uneasy) defender such as Greg to abandon the notion (1933, p. 256): If it is indeed a reported text it must have been taken down by shorthand; (1936, pp. 175, 180): I rather doubt the capacity of any seventeenth-century system of shorthand to produce a text so generally accurate as this [Q1 Lr.] appears to be.…[180] [But] I see no escape from the conclusion that it was based on a shorthand report. If I could imagine how otherwise such a text could have been obtained, I would gladly dispense with the stenographic theory, for, as I said before, it introduces quite considerable difficulties; (1940, p. 431, n. 1): Q contains a (presumably shorthand) report obtained from performance; (1942, p. 96): I cannot but conclude that some kind of shorthand was employed, however little I like the conclusion; (1951, 2nd ed., p. [e]): [Duthie’s] dismissal of shorthand I cheerfully accept. So also McManaway (1952; 1969, p. 333): The difficulties of a stenographic reporter in the playhouse can be readily imagined: swift speech, rapid action, entrances and exits, and much that is calculated to transport the imagination beyond the endeavor of the hands. In a word, there was no adequate method of reporting plays by shorthand in Shakespeare’s day—certainly the text of the First Quarto of Lear was not so reported.

Only Davidson (1992, 1996, 1998) is reluctant to abandon Willis’s system as an explanation of the errors in Q1. She agrees (1992, p. 80) with Duthie that stenography was too slow to record the fast-paced delivery of Jacobean dramatic performance. She proposes instead that Willis’s stenography may have been used to copy a manuscript directly (whether from authorial, theatrical, or some other source), or (1996, p. 419) to cop[y] a playscript or recor[d] a memorial reconstruction; in the upshot (1998, p. 307), Q1 Lear could have been copied in shorthand from a manuscript. Since she never proposes any specific details about the circumstances under which such a manuscript might have been obtained or copied or to what end licit or illicit, or how it would have found its way to Nathaniel Butter, her theory is hard to evaluate and less than convincing. The theatrical manuscript or playscript would presumably be the official playbook which, because it bore the Master of the Revels’ license for performance, would have been kept securely in the company archives, not easily accessible without the company’s permission. One may doubt that the King’s Men gave permission to copy their book in the understanding that a novice printer would publish without supervision an unexamined, uncorrected, error-filled transcript, during the two decades when only three other of Sh.’s plays were first published. Davidson suggests that the purpose may have been illicit, emphasizing that all the shorthand manuals advertise their enabling of short, swift, and <above all> secret writing (1992, p. 81). One can only imagine that such secret writing would have had to occur in the Globe playhouse; a longhand copy made openly elsewhere would have taken far less time and have been more accurate than one made by copying the play first in stenographic symbols and then later reconstructing it fully from those symbols. No one with free access to the play for even a few hours would double his work in this way. The notion of a stenographer visiting a theater by stealth to acquire a manuscript must seem today an anachronistic throwback to the heyday of theories of piracy popular a century ago but now generally abandoned as unjustified and unnecessary; see Maguire (1996), and Blayney (1997), who shows that publication of playbooks was not very profitable.

As for Davidson’s evidence, its weakness is that all of it is susceptible of interpretations other than derivation from shorthand. She criticizes Duthie for under-emphasizing the phonetic basis of Willis’s system, whose rules directed the stenographer to abbreviate and truncate words, omitting vowels, final consonants, repeated letters, aspirated letters (h, w, y—none of which today is called aspirated), verb inflections, or anything else without weight or matter that may be supplied from memory or context during longhand transcription. She concludes (1992, p. 85) that the rules for short-writing show an extraordinarily high correlation with the pattern of unusual textual features found in…Q Lear. At least half of her evidence is of no weight whatever; most of the spellings that she attributes to the influence of stenography are recorded as common variants throughout the 16th and 17th centuries: alow, assalted, bereved, bloes, bruse, choghes (choughs), cocknay, codpis, comand, crum, currers (couriers), deboyst, dungell(y), flea (flay), frend, gard, gasted, gessingly (gesse+ing+ly), giltless, go(o)ddeven, gotish, grones, Hagh (dial. Haw), hathorn, hedier (hedy+er), hollow (holla), holp, imbossed, injoy, intire, jelous, lam, lothed, mise, myrackles, nether (neither), obrayde, oke, old (wold), one (own), oth, paromor (paramor), pother/pudder, quesie, reskue, roges, roring, ruffen (ruffian), slue (slew), soiorne, sumter (sumpter), sutes, thourt (thwart; cf. athourt), tosted, tuch, vew, welk’d (whelked, welk’t), wher(e) (were), wosted. She attributes truncated words and names in the text to stenographic abbreviation, citing 82 Cord., 1613 Reg, 1290 daugter, and 2673 bornet and beniz; in fact these and many other truncated words and speech prefixes occur in crowded lines set to the narrower measure used in Q1; and at 2673 the full forms must have existed in the MS, since the proof-reader (apparently no stenographer) restored bounty and benizon from copy. Omissions of letters—in devo(r)se, gosmore (gosimor), ruslngs—are common even in better-printed texts such as F1, and maidenlest reappears in Q2 and F1, not stenographic texts; the apparently or possibly dropped final -y in euer(y), honest(y), men(y), speed(y), sorrowes (sorry) might seem explicable by one of Willis’s rules, except that the omissions of initial and medial y in our/your, bod (boyd)/buoy’d, list/lyest, and tr(y)al could as well suggest a compositor’s difficulty with the script. No inferences can be drawn about words so rare as to have no fixed spellings: arint, Fretereto, Obidicut, Stiberdigebit, snulbug, Tuelygod; and surely a stenographer utterly unfamiliar with these words would have copied them out in longhand. Attraction of nearby letters, as in the eliding or repeating of similar consonants—hee’s so/he so, leape the/leapt the, I much/I am much, descryes Standst/descry Stands, Postes shall/post shall, troope set/troopes set, shoot a troupe/shoe a troope—are easily explained by a scribe’s or compositor’s inexactly reproducing words temporarily held in his mind. Likewise many graphically or phonically similar pairs of Q/F variants can be attributed to exactly such compositorial or scribal errors of memory or to simple misreading of a difficult script: after/hasten, a nellthu night more/he (a) met(t) the night mare, as/is, blesse/blisse, can/con, come on bee true/come, vnbutton, dogge, so bade/Dogg’s obey’d, dowre/Dowrie, enridged/enraged, fate/father, Father/fault, great/grac’d, a rat of life/a rat haue life, shall of/shall haue, heard/howl’d, houres/yeares, immediate/immediacie, in sight/incite, lancht (lācht)/latch’d, may know/make knowne, mistresse/mysteries, Mobing/mopping, Mohing (?)/mowing, nor/nere, now/no, no, oreturnd/ore-whelme, peruse/pierce, say/saw, sees/saies, shady/shadowie, spirituall/Sphericall, spurres/spirits, Stobing/stopping, strange newes/strangenesse, strong/strange, the/thy, them o’/T(h)om o’, thrald/thrild, vent/vext, vntender/vntented, We/Woe, well/will, wits do/wits to, your liking/your oe’r-looking. Where ordinary explanations of Q1’s features exist, there is no compulsion to accept a less likely explanation such as swift and secret copying, in the playhouse, of a protected document.

Stone (1980, pp. 13–40), like several predecessors, thinks that such Q1 features as mislining, inadequate punctuation, apparent aural errors, nonsense and garbling of names, etc. are best explained by a verbatim theatrical report from performance, made for sale to a piratical publisher, but he proposes a longhand rather than shorthand report. Though more time would be needed to make a copy, he estimates that four performances would be adequate for the job. On his first visit to the theater the reporter would get down as many of lines as he could, leaving hiatuses that he would fill in, and errors that he would correct, at subsequent visits. Such a piecemeal process, including the supplying of missing lines in the spaces left for them, would account for much of the mislineation in Q1. (Pp. 36–7): Such a process would also account for inattention to sense or grammar, multiple small errors as to verbal endings, particles, conjunctions or pronouns, minor omissions, and phonetic errors. Since these persist in Q1, the printer’s copy must have been the original longhand report, not a transcription, which would have cleaned up mislineations and other glaring errors. He assumes hasty writing, because words are occasionally run together or more often divided (my rackles, A’jax, so phisticated, ma hu, a nellthu might more, per du, many fould, where so ere, or’e heard); the writer lifted his pen or more likely graphite pencil and then left too big a space when he put it down again. To Duthie’s belief that a reporter attending to the spoken lines could not also supply accurately the speech attributions and stage directions, Stone replies (p. 25), He might have an assistant to note entrances, exits, the distribution of speeches and so forth.

In addition to the usual objections about the difficulties of taking notes accurately and undetected in a busy public theater, Stone’s theory invites new ones. The reporter’s visits to several performances would need to be spread out over many weeks, since a typical stage run was eight to twelve performances over four to six months, or an average of two performances a month (Knutson, 1991, p. 33); even if the stenographer managed to attend each time an opportunity presented itself, his memories from previous afternoons would dim. After deducting the time and expense of four visits for himself and of at least one for an assistant—especially if longhand writing required seats, costing two or three times the basic price of admission—his modest sale price of (at most) 30s., after such extended efforts, would be further reduced. Besides, as Halio (ed. 1994, p. 5) asks, Would any publisher spend good money on such an inevitably messy manuscript? To date, no one has embraced this theory.

div.head: Dictation and Memorial Reconstruction
div.p: When Pollard (1909) distinguished good Shn. quartos from the bad quartos Rom. (1597), H5, Wiv., Ham. (1603), and Per., he called attention (among other things) to textual features suggesting that oral transmission and memorial error had corrupted better, more Shn. versions of these five plays. For several decades thereafter textual scholars explored various ways in which actors’ or others’ memories might have shaped these and other texts. Kirschbaum (1945, pp. 702–6) surveys many of these studies, finding such diverse narratives as reconstruction of a play by either a single actor or a group of actors; from either memory of performance, or with the aid of actors’ parts and plot, or from memorization of the playbook manuscript; by dictation or copying; for the purpose of performance in the provinces, or for sale to a stationer or another company. Although Pollard and most scholars consider Lr. to be more a good than a bad quarto, many of its features—multiple errors, bad pointing, mislined verse, apparent mishearings—sufficiently resembled those in the bad quartos to encourage scholars to look for signs of memorial reconstruction and dictation in this text as well.

The notion that texts of certain Shn. plays might have been assembled from actors’ parts with the help of the plot excited a certain interest in the 1920s, but was soon discredited (see Chambers, 1930, 1:153–5; Greg, 1955, pp. 156–8). Rhodes (1922, p. 66) suggested that Q1 Lr. was an assembled text but within a year he abandoned the idea (1923, p. 21). No one has seconded Small’s (1946, p. 178) unsupported speculations that Shakspere dictated much of his writing to an amanuensis skilled in shorthand, probably scenes or at least changes in his manuscript; or, if Sh. did not, that the prompter and the actors certainly did. Nor has anyone claimed, as has been suggested for other plays, that an audience member rewrote the play from memory after attending several performances; in any case, as has been argued by Hart (1934; 1942), Chambers (1944), Smidt (1964; 1988), Gurr (1999; 2004), Erne (2003), and others (see above), Q1 Lr. is probably a longer version than was ever performed.

Pollard & Wilson (1919) argued that the bad quartos had been reconstructed from memory by pirate actors, not recorded by shorthand reporters, and that those actors had to recall not only their own parts but (presumably less accurately) all of the other roles in the play. Greg (ed. Wiv., 1910, p. xxviii) and Alexander (1929), among others, believed that from their accuracy one could name the actors responsible for the reconstructions. Doran (1931, pp. 123–4): Since the amount of irregularity in the first quarto of King Lear varies with different scenes but not with the parts of different actors, the [124] pirate actor cannot be considered as an agent in its production.…[126] Act I, Scene iv, for instance, is particularly corrupt. Some of the worst passages occur in Lear’s lines, but the errors are unmistakably due to illegible manuscript; Goneril’s last speech (ll. 359–67) is just as bad.

Moreover (p. 124), Almost all the errors in Q1…are misreadings from manuscript or misprints.…Emphasis is to be laid on the relatively few errors of mishearing. As for anticipated and recollected lines, supposedly characteristic of memorial texts, (p. 127) there are only three phrases which could possibly be construed as such, i.e. at 175/181, 731/746/833, and 785/803, repetitions mostly missing from F; of Doran’s surmise that Sh. may have repeated words occasionally and in revising tried to get rid of some of the repetitions (from the F text), Smidt (1964, p. 161) says, This seems to me an eminently sensible explanation.

Kirschbaum (1944, p. 197) theorizes that the bad quartos result from a reporter memorizing from a theatrical MS, a theory that (Hypothesis, 1945, pp. 697–715) he applies to 20 bad quartos, including Lr. He believes (pp. 711–15) that it explains the quality of the SDs, especially imperatives for offstage noise, which seem not to derive from performance. He gives only two from Lr., neither clearly theatrical or imperative. He also thinks that Lr. is too long to be recreated from hearing at a rehearsal or performance, and argues that playhouse MSS must not have been completely inaccessible. His further argument (True, 1945) that inferior details in Q are due to the actors’ misrepresenting of Sh.’s superior original, represented by F, does not persuade Maguire (1996, p. 86), who shows how the same facts could support an opposite argument, that Q represents a first intention, F a later revision. Neither Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 75, 116), Muir (ed. 1952, p. xviii), nor anyone else embraces the idea of a single reporter. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 130–1) I find this quite incredible; the text, with all its imperfections, is too full and good for [133] that. Doran (1946, p. 229): If anyone were able to filch and keep the book long enough to memorize it and then painfully to set it down as he recalled it, he might save himself considerable trouble by copying it out in the first place. One might also object specifically to the argument as applied to Lear that Professor Kirschbaum finds an amazing number of mishearings in a text that the reporter is supposed to be recalling primarily from a script, not from a witnessed performance. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xvii): A man who perused the prompt-book for any length of time would have aroused suspicions unless he were the book-keeper himself who is ruled out by other considerations.…Such a surreptitious borrowing would presume great carelessness on the part of the book-keeper. In any case, Q does not read much like a playbook, as, for example, Duthie (ed. 1949), Greg (1955), Stone (1980), and Clare (1990) imagine a playbook to be.

Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 75–8), having rejected a stenographic report, decided that Q1 Lr. represented a memorial report made to a scribe by the entire company, probably while it was on a provincial tour and temporarily deprived of its promptbook (hence of licence to play), probably in 1605–6 (too early a date). Such a group report had been proposed by Greg for Orlando Furioso (Two Elizabethan Stage Abridgements, 1922, p. 354) and by D. L. Patrick for R3 (The Textual History of Richard III, Stanford, 1936). The report must have been made by the entire company because no role is more accurate than any other (p. 75): There is no consistent variation in the standard of the reporting of the speeches of different characters.…[78] All the actors met together and dictated their parts in turn to a scribe (perhaps the book-keeper) who wrote down what they said as fast as he could. The actors thus virtually gave a performance of the play, and upon this performance the Q text entirely depends.
