The actors made such mistakes as they doubtless habitually made in performances in the theater—anticipation and recollection, inversion, the introduction of gratuitous exclamations, vocatives, connectives, etc., synonym-substitution, vulgarization, metrical breakdown, omission, patching. The report was probably in prose (pp. 98–105) with a minimum of punctuation, and a transcript of it had to be prepared for use as a promptbook, after which the original report, cursorily edited, served as printer’s copy.

Duthie concedes (p. 116) that his theory is highly conjectural, pure speculation, and that he is confident only that the Q1 text is reported, but not by shorthand or a few actors. Since Lr. may have been written in 1606, the date of the tour may be too early an occasion for a reported text, and a text reconstructed in the provinces would lack the Master of the Revels’s license for performance. Other doubts have been expresssed. McManaway (1950; 1969, p. 319): Curiously enough, however, the editor [Duthie] has nothing to say about how the scribe’s first draft was released to the publisher, or to whom; and there is little speculation about why this rough manuscript (the equivalent of an author’s foul papers) was sold, rather than the prompt-copy conjectured to have been derived from it. Nathaniel Butter’s entry of his copy in the Stationers’ Register suggests that there was nothing surreptitious in his acquisition of his copy, yet an experienced printer [Okes was not experienced in dramatic MSS] should have recognized the difference between such a manuscript as has been described and a normal book of the play or even a set of author’s foul sheets. It remains to be discovered who was the agent that sold the manuscript of Lear to its publisher. Greg (1942; 2nd ed., 1951, p. e): Duthie’s proposed alternative [to shorthand] seems to be the only one critical ingenuity has to offer; still I do not feel altogether happy about it. Idem (1955, p. 380): This explanation has been rather reluctantly accepted for want of a better, and is now probably that most widely current. It was cautiously accepted also by Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xviii f.) in his popular and influential edition.

Kirschbaum (1951, pp. 169 ff.) has many doubts: A supposed tour by the King’s men in which they did not possess their prompt-book for King Lear sets up a second hypothesis to bulwark the first hypothesis, that of plural memorial transmission. And, of course, this second hypothesis demands a third, not supplied by Professor Duthie, to account for the missing prompt-book. And a fourth, not supplied by Professor Duthie, to explain why actors on a provincial tour should not make an abridged version but one considerably longer than the prompt-book used around 1620 in the city.…Time after time, for particular Q corruptions Professor Duthie has to give involved explanations in which actor, scribe, and compositor play an unbelievably complex game of simultaneous error. And even then everything is often not accounted for. (P. 170): Kirschbaum asks how one actor habitually allowed himself to be robbed of a line [95] by another actor’s telescoping two speeches [jumping from 93 to 96], or how one actor [in 84] anticipates another actor’s line [252]. Similarly, on the reassignment and omissions in 3170–7, (p. 171) It also looks as though a memory which omitted the Albany speech remembered that Albany had a speech here and hence gave Edgar’s combined two speeches [3171, 3173] to Albany [in Q]. Were three memories [Gent., Alb., Edg.] plus a compositor’s erring eye at work here, according to Professor Duthie—or was one memory? Similarly, Q’s misplacement of 3181 between two of Albany’s speeches—which makes two speeches of Albany’s one [in F]—would require faulty memories of three actors. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xix) concedes the force of Kirschbaum’s objections. Eventually Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 131–2) also agrees: This theory is not impossible, but it is cumbersome. And if the company’s [132] purpose was to produce a substitute prompt-book, why is the Q1 text so much longer than that of F1?…Q1, then, does not look like an actors’ reconstruction, and my 1949 theory had better be abandoned. Jackson (1983, pp. 314, 341 n. 10) considers Kirschbaum’s refutation decisive, adding (p. 331), Variants produced by authorial revision…may closely resemble variants produced by corruption,…inevitably creat[ing] apparent evidence in the original text of anticipation, recollection, transposition, synonym substitution (vulgarization), omission, interpolation, and even metrical breakdown—all the traditional stigmata of a memorial report. (There may be other causes than authorial revision.)

Next, Walker (1952, pp. 376–8) develops a theory involving dictation, actors, memorial contamination, and even Sh.’s foul papers. The better parts of Q1 seem to me remarkably free from memorial contamination and they are, I think, good text which can only be reconciled with the undoubtedly bad text of much of Acts i–ii and v.iii in one way: by supposing that the manuscript from which Q1 was printed was dictated to a scribe from an authoritative manuscript, that the reader was an actor familiar with parts of the play, and that (either from haste, laziness or over-confidence) he used his memory rather than his eyes for those parts of the play with which he was well acquainted but perforce paid more attention to his manuscript when his memory did not serve.…Given dictation, with memorial contamination, to a scribe who was a phonetic speller, had a bad handwriting (or wrote in haste), who had no feeling for metre and was apt to misapprehend what he heard, what emerged in Q1, printed from his manuscript, is understandable in the light of the Folio.…The manuscript behind the quarto was, I judge, dictated from foul papers. It clearly represented an earlier recension than that behind the Folio. The stage directions…are the kind of stage direction we find in quartos printed from foul papers. The speech prefixes are similarly of the type we are accustomed to regard as Shakespearian: casual…, variable…and indifferent. The Q1 omissions are, therefore, presumably not cuts to shorten the play for representation but omissions due to carelessness or haste.…[378] I would suggest a boy actor (perhaps Goneril) or a walker-on as Attendant, Knight and so forth. The principal actors were, we must assume, men of choice and unlikely to have been involved in this kind of dishonest enterprise. Whoever made the report did not steal the foul papers, to avoid discovery. The passages peculiar to the quarto seem free of contamination, and must have been omitted from the acting version in the Folio. None of the passages peculiar to the quarto suggests vulgarization or interpolation, and there is certainly nothing in them that seems as spurious as the close of iii.ii, peculiar to the Folio. A year later (1953, pp. 42–9) she refines and expands this theory. The transcript was made by a non-professional scribe because the spelling and bad handwriting are persistent throughout and are not Shn. (She does not give any evidence or argument that the hand could not be Shakespeare’s.) The SDs are full and leisurely or abruptly inadequate; These features suggest that the manuscript was based on foul papers rather than on fair copy or prompt-copy.…We must suppose that the copy of the foul papers was not made for use in the theatre but that the foul papers were copied surreptitiously with a view to publication. The mislineation, mistakes due to misapprehension, phonetic spelling and bad word-division suggest aural copying. The concentration of memorial errors in 1.1 and 5.3 points to the boy actors who played Goneril and Regan. Memorial contamination is always heaviest when they are both on stage and more evident in scenes where only Goneril appeared.

Greg (1955, pp. 382–3) finds Walker’s argument fresh and ingenious but tricky and unconvincing. He doubts that one can distinguish between memorial contamination and other kinds, or that a couple of boys could have gotten hold of the foul papers and found opportunity to transcribe them in the playhouse (and if they were able to convey them to some more private and convenient place, there would be less need for haste and therefore less temptation to rely on memory); and he thinks that there is still much corruption that cannot be accounted for if F is approximately correct. Walker’s argument also contradicts the impressions of Doran, Duthie, and others that in Q1 no role is associated with more textual errors than another. Walton (1955, pp. 136–7; 1971, pp. 273–80) finds instead a different distribution of Q/F variants, equally inimical to the idea of two boy reporters. Using lists, prepared by Duthie in his 1949 edition, of apparently corrupt or inferior Q readings, Walton calculates that Q errors lessen throughout the first four acts and then increase in the last. The average rate of error in number of lines per variant (i.e., between variants) for each act is (in 1955) 7.2, 8.9, 10.5, 19.9, and 9.7, and (as revised in 1971) 6.6, 8.5, 8.4, 16.4, and 9.6. He dismisses the possibility that the actors’ memories (as they reconstructed Q) would have gradually increased in quality (i.e., agreed more with the acting script supposedly better represented in F) in 1–3, soared in 4, and deteriorated in 5 (leading to a rise in variants in the last act]. Nor was the copy damaged and then repaired partially and unevenly by memorial reconstruction (Greg’s suggestion to Walker, 1953, p. 50), for we would have to imagine that it had been damaged (and therefore correctly repaired) most in the middle, least in the beginning and end. Idem (1971, p. 272): As well…there is the fact that a large number of memorial errors are to be found in places where neither Goneril nor Regan is on stage, citing 3.1 to 3.6, where Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 7–8) cites twenty-one probable memorial errors. Having abandoned his own notion of group reporting, Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 130–1) modifies Walker’s theory: There is no significant variation of standard [of textual accuracy] between characters which would suggest memorial reconstruction by one or a small number of actors; some form of dictation from possibly damaged foul papers seems preferable. Walker’s surmise that the boy’s memory of his role contaminated the text as he read it does not, however, account for apparent memorial errors in scenes where Goneril and Regan are not present. He therefore modifies her theory with his own suggestion of memorial anticipation, which explains memorial corruption…of a kind not easily attributable to Miss Walker’s explanation. The anticipations are often unconvincing (see nn. 44, 45), and Smidt (1964, p. 134) shows that similar anticipations can as well be found in F, citing 39–41. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 315) still gives qualified assent to Walker’s theory to account for Q’s film of corruption. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 138–9) thinks it improbable that anyone would substitute his memory for the text, and substitute text so different from copy as to be extempore playwriting, frequently in perfectly rhythmic lines (see the three most contaminated scenes 1.1, 2.4, and 5.3) and containing readings often preferred by editors to those in F.

Jackson (1983, pp. 326–7) disproves Walker’s claim that supposedly memorial variants really are most frequent when Goneril and Regan are on stage. In those 14 scenes in which Goneril and Regan are entirely absent, Duthie’s memorial variants exist at the rate of 1:23.8 lines; in the other scenes they occur at the rate of 1:20.0 lines, an insignificant difference, which shrinks to nothing when opening and closing scenes are disregarded: (p. 327) the rate for Goneril-Regan scenes then falls to 1:22.5 lines, virtually identical with 1:23.8. Walker showed an increase in Q/F variants in 1.1 after Lear’s entrance with his daughters, but in 2.4 (which she thought was more memorially contaminated than any other scene except 1.1 and 5.3) the incidence of variants bears no relation to the presence of Goneril and Regan on stage.…The section in which neither is present is…almost exactly the same length as the section in which both are present; yet the former contains seven of Duthie’s memorial variants, the latter six.

Werstine (1990, p. 79) shows that Walker undermined her own case by logical contradictions: While Greg [ed. 1910] had identified the actor behind the memorial reconstruction of Quarto Wives by that actor’s presence in scenes in which the text was most accurately reported, Walker identified her actor-reporters by their presence in what are allegedly the most corrupt scenes—the ones for which they would, it is said, have relied on memory. Before Walker had finished, however, she had contradicted her own criterion for identification by arguing that the text of Goneril’s and Regan’s speeches and of speeches addressed to them is superior to the text of the rest of the speeches within the scenes for which these boy-actors were present. Now the accuracy of the report again, as in Greg’s study, becomes the identifying mark of the reporters. According to Walker, then, these boy actors paid attention to dialogue only when it was addressed to them or to be uttered by them—hence their many errors in other speeches in scenes in which they were present; nevertheless, when they came to transcribe the speeches to which they had been so inattentive, they relied on recollections—recollections that, according to Walker’s narrative, were never theirs. Since memorial reconstruction by actors can scarcely be maintained as a theory if there is doubt whether actors paid attention to the dialogue in plays in which they performed, Walker, in her attempt to apply Greg’s theory of memorial reconstruction to Lear, wound up calling the basis of the theory itself into question.

Maguire (1996, pp. 269–70, 324), having comprehensively studied the cases to be made for all supposed memorially reconstructed texts, Shn. and otherwise, on the basis of such features as external echoes, internal repetitions, formulaic phrases, inserted phrases or episodes, omissions, inconsistencies, stage directions, and speech prefixes, concludes that Q1 Lr. is not memorial reconstruction. The complexity of Walker’s theory and the shakiness of much of the evidence have dissuaded most scholars from endorsing Walker’s explanation; in time, a simpler one came to seem more likely.

div.head: Shakespeare’s Rough Draft
div.p: Although Capell (ed. 1768, 1:3 ff.) concedes that several of the quartos published in Sh.’s lifetime fit Heminge’s and Condell’s description of diuerse stolne, and surreptitious copies, maimed, and deformed by the frauds and stealthes of iniurious imposters, he names fourteen plays whose quartos deserve to be vindicated against the self-serving slurs of the editors of that lame edition F1: Let it then be granted, that these quarto’s are the Poet’s own copies, however they were come by; hastily written at first, and issuing from presses most of them as corrupt and licentious as can any where be produc’d, and not overseen by himself, nor by [11] any of his friends.…It may be true that they were stoln; but stoln from the Author’s copies, by transcribers who found means to get at them: and maim’d they must be, in respect of their many alterations after the first performance.…[12] The very errors and faults of these quarto’s…are, with the editor [Capell], proofs of their genuineness; For from what hand, but that of the Author himself, could come those seemingly-strange repetitions [of passages in LLL and Tro.],…those imperfect e[ntries]…? (It is not clear whether by transcribers Capell meant only scribes or possibly printers, and he does believe that these author’s copies were fairly come by.) He includes Q Lr. among the fourteen vindicated quartos.

Similarly Malone (in Boswell, ed. 1821, 1:203) in general preferred the early quartos to counterpart texts in F1, except for Wiv., H5, and Q1 Rom. (Q1 Ham. was unknown before 1823): With respect to the other thirteen copies…, they in general are preferable to the exhibition of the same plays in the folio; for this plain reason, because, instead of printing these plays from a manuscript, the editors of the folio…printed the greater part of them from the very copies which they represented as maimed and imperfect, and frequently from a late, instead of the earliest, edition; in some instances with additons and alterations of their own. Although most Sh. editions of the first half of the 18th century were reprints of the Folio (mainly F4), most editors made extensive use of the quartos (particularly Jennens, ed. 1770), and many modern editors now believe as Capell and Malone did that several early quartos were set from Sh.’s own papers. The onset of Foliolatry, however, was at hand, and its beginnings may be seen in the editions of Peabody, Knight, Verplanck, Hudson, and others from the 1830s, 1840s, and 1850s; many of the quartos became devalued thereafter, and from the end of the 19th century until almost the end of the 20th Q1 Lr. was considered an inferior text—if not actually a bad quarto, at least exhibiting a badly corrupted text whose connection to Sh.’s MS had been broken by some kind of scribal, stenographic, or memorial intervention.

Such denigration of Q1 should have ended with the scrupulous and thorough study by Doran (1931) of the texts of Lr., and her conclusion (p. 39), I believe that the first quarto was printed from Shakespeare’s original manuscript. (P. 122): We have seen how unevenly the first quarto is printed, with much of the verse wrongly aligned or printed as prose. I know of no satisfactory way to account for this state of the printed text unless it be that it was printed from a manuscript which contained a good deal of revised and rewritten matter. For several decades the implacable opposition of Greg to this idea (though he admitted the force of much of Doran’s case) dissuaded others from accepting it and even led Doran to renounce it in part. In the past three decades, however, thanks to the bibliographical work of Blayney (1980) and to recent critical claims that Q and F Lr. represent Sh.’s original and revised versions, Doran’s conclusions have come to be generally accepted.

In a later essay Doran (1933, p. 35, n. 3) refers to a seminal essay that appeared in the same year as her book, on the provenance of dramatic texts. McKerrow (1931, pp. 263 ff.): Surely the companies themselves must have had good manuscripts of the plays which they owned, seeing that in every case a legible copy must have been produced for the perusal of the censor. [264]…In the case of plays the printer very often did not get anything like so clean a copy to work from as he did in the case of other books; he did not in fact get a fair-copy at all, but as a general rule, the author’s original from which the fair copy had been prepared.…If…the author’s copy contained revisions or corrections, or was not clearly written, we may suppose that a transcript would be made from it by a scrivener.…This professional fair-copy would, of course, be the one to be submitted for licence, and would in due course become the prompt-copy.…[265]…They would surely have been reluctant to hand over the actual prompt-copy to the printer, for this—bearing, as it usually would, the licenser’s signature—was their authority for acting the play.…[266] And as a rule there would, I think, have been another copy—namely, the author’s original manuscript.…Although an experienced theatrical scrivener might find it easy enough to make a fair-copy from, it might well puzzle a compositor used only to working from clean manuscript. Parts of McKerrow’s argument have been challenged—Blayney (1982, p. 184, n. 2) warns that play-quartos cannot be singled out as a special category in respect of incompetent printing, and Werstine (1990, p. 70) rejects the idea that the playwright’s manuscript would be revised in consonance with a producer’s suggestions—but neither objection affects Doran’s argument (which in general McKerrow’s essay supports): that (p. 122) Sh.’s rough draft was copied to make a fair copy which became the company’s official playbook (or promptbook), and then that this same rough draft found its way to Nathaniel Butter to be the copy for Q1. To prove her theory she had to challenge two reigning orthodoxies: that Q1 represented some kind of reported text, and that F1 had been set from a marked-up copy of Q1. Her method was to compare Q and F variants and errors to show that they clearly derived from the same original, and that this original was evidently a manuscript, not a printed quarto.

Her strongest evidence (pp. 91 ff.) is a group Q/F variants in which Q is right, F is evidently wrong, and F seems to derive from a misreading of written script, rather than from the compositor’s supposed copy, an exemplar of Q1 into which correct readings and additions from a playbook had been written marginally or interlinearly. For example, at 1151, Q’s Reneag (renege) is clearly right, while F’s nonsensical Reuenge seems the result of a common n/u misreading. (P. 91): If a [Folio] compositor had a correctly printed [i.e., Q1] word before him [in his copy], why should he set an incorrect word whose form in Elizabethan handwriting resembles the written form of the correct word? He might of course misread words in the additional or corrected portions written by hand [by a copy-editor, collator, or corrector] on the printed text [Q1], but since the corrector would not have written reneag, for example, above the correctly printed word reneag, the compositor could get the misreading reuenge only from a manuscript. Similar most significant cases are (pp. 92 ff.) 988 lancht/latch’d [from lācht in the MS], 1013 spurres/spirits, 1026 strange newes/strangenesse, 1150 Bring/Being (an r/e misreading, common from MS but not print), and 1152 gale/gall (an l/e misreading, found e.g. in Ham. and Tro.), (p. 93) 1148 to intrench/t’intrince (both reduce too to to, which may have been in the MS), 1307 panting/painting (the MS had three minims), 1833–4 foord/Sword (a common s/f misreading), 2353 femiter/Fenitar (the F compositor missed a minim), (p. 94) 2452 walke/walk’d (a common d/e misreading), 2530 coyning/crying (coỹing in the MS), 2866 heare/heard (d/e misreading), and 2898 Hard/Heere (e/d). Among a score more possible examples are 1839 blesse/Blisse, 1861 iustly/Iustice, 2027 tike/tight (read as tite) and trũdletaile/Troudle taile, 2319 thereat inraged/threat-enrag’d (the hyphen proves the erroneous change intentional, not resulting from the accidental loss of e from there-), 2369 distresse (written distres)/desires, 2384 set/fet (misreading of script long s), and 3087 Despight (written Despite)/Despise. She lists further a dozen more examples (p. 95) of variant good readings in which Q is (in the opinion of most editors) preferable and F’s readings may be misreadings of the original MS forms (though some could be printer’s substitutions), and some fifteen more (pp. 48–9) instances in which either F or Q might be defended and either might be a misreading of the other. The sum of these necessitate the conclusion that the folio was printed directly from a manuscript, especially since the errors in the folio which appear to have such an origin are distributed throughout the play.

A second class of variants implies that the same MS that led to error in F also led to the same or a related error in Q1. Since in the majority of cases of Q/F disagreement throughout the play F gives correct readings for Q’s erroneous ones, (p. 96) Most of the words which gave difficulty to the printer of Q1 must have been either read correctly by the [original, pre-Q] transcriber [of the fair copy which became the playbook] or amended by Shakespeare [or someone] in the transcript, because they appear in correct form in the folio [which derives from the playbook]. It is not unlikely, however, that certain words would be misread by both the printer of Q1 and the transcriber of the playhouse copy; nor is it unlikely that some of these misreadings would escape Shakespeare’s eye when he revised the transcript. Examples are 1329 Historica (a common misreading of [presumed] histerica), (p. 97) 2799 where did you dye (a common misreading of when), 2114 you haue sent (a possible error for haue you sent), and (p. 98) 460 maidenlest. Conversely, Illegible words in Shakespeare’s manuscript must have produced…divergent errors, where both Q and F are wrong, but differently: 117 mistresse/miseries (for an illegible mysteries or misteries in the MS), 2499 sommons/Somnet (for illegible sommet or sommit), 1505 hot bloud in/[99]hot-bloodied (for hot-blouded), 1183 flitkering/flicking (for flickering, a common t/c misreading, found also in 3005 imediate/immediacie, 2280 curre/terror, 2070 intelligence/intelligent), possibly 355 tooth’/to’th’ (for top the), and 1844 What, his/Ha’s his (for What have his). The only explanation, therefore, that can be made of the striking similarities between the texts in either certain or possible errors is that a common manuscript source, in which some mistakes were made and in which some words were illegibly written, is at the basis of both the first quarto and the folio. This manuscript must have been the one from which the first quarto was printed and from which the playhouse transcript [the playbook] was copied. As we have seen…the playhouse transcript is represented in the folio. Cf. n. 2354 on hor-docks/Hardokes.

One further class of variants leads to the same conclusion (p. 100): those in which F is closer to uncorrected Q readings (Qu) than to corrected ones (Qc), suggesting a common source ignored or misread by the Q1 press-corrector. Examples are 1378 come and tends/commands her (Qc)/commands, tends, (see n. 1378); Come and tends seruise cannot be a misreading of commands her seruice, but it may easily be a misreading of commands tends seruice.…It is [101]…just as probable that the reading of F is based directly on the manuscript as that it is derived from Q1); 2054 (both Take vp to keepe [Qu] and F’s Take vp, take vp may [it is not impossible] be misreadings of Take vp the King [Qc], but Qu and F are so close to each other in the form of letters as to suggest that F’s reading was in the manuscript); 1786 crulentious/tempestious/contentious; 1204 ausrent/miscreant/ancient; 2990+1 To saue…/To send…and appointed guard/To send…(The phrase and appointed guard may have been an afterthought by Shakespeare written in the margin, where it was missed by both the playhouse scribe and the printer of F; see CN); (p. 102) 2297 My foote vsurps my body/A foole vsurps my bed/My Foole vsurpes my body (all three states are acceptable, but Qc seems furthest from the reading of the MS); 2300 whistle/whistling/whistle (the corrected reading may be just a modernization); 2309 seemes/shewes/seemes; 2324 Iustices/Iustisers/Iustices (the Q correction may be due to justification of the line; see CN); (p. 103) 1063 prise/poyse/prize; and 2189 poorlie,leed, [MS ledd?]/parti,eyd/poorely led. On occasions when F does agree with the proper correction in Qu, as in 2280 curre/terrer/terror, 2289 coward/command/command, and deseruing/discerning/discerning, F’s good readings could not have been arrived at independently, and so must have come from correct readings in the manuscript (playbook), whose scribe, like the Q press-corrector, properly read the rough draft. (P. 104): The fact that the folio was printed directly from a manuscript and not from a copy of Q1 altered in accordance with it is incontrovertibly proved by the occurrence of new errors in it [F] which can only be misreadings of manuscript. These may sometimes be misreadings of the transcript [i.e., playbook] by the folio printer rather than misreadings of the original manuscript by the transcriber. (Stone, 1980, p. 89, also finding many F readings to derive from a MS, improbably believes that, fifteen years later, it was the same manuscript as that used in the setting up of Q.)

As for other kinds of evidence, Doran (pp. 104–6) considers the punctuation and spelling, finding a few cases of common mispunctuation between Q1 and F, faulty punctuation added in F where Q has none (which might result as easily if the printer were setting from a lightly punctuated manuscript as if he were following Q1 itself), and at least two passages (1786–7, 2676–8) which reveal a misunderstanding of the sense on the part of the folio printer that could not have arisen if he had been printing from Q1.

Similarly the faulty lining of verse and prose in Q and F suggest to Doran (pp. 106–9) that both texts derive from a manuscript in which lineation was imperfect and unclear. Certain passages of verse and prose are faultily printed in both Q and F, sometimes similarly and sometimes differently. Passages of verse and rhythmic prose mixed together are usually printed as prose in Q and sporadically as verse in F. Where Q and F both line verse wrongly but in different ways, there may be a variety of causes, including decisions by author, scribe, or printer. (P. 109): Cases of misalignment in F, in which Q1 is printed correctly, are corroborative evidence that F was printed directly from a manuscript rather than from Q1. In matters of alignment the F MS frequently differs from Q because of revision, particularly the excision or addition of passages in F, requiring adjustment of lineation. Identical errors of lining in both texts, however, would seem to derive from the same original manuscript. She points to 4.6, where in both Q and F verse lines 2563–73 and 2601–15 are wrongly printed as prose, as others seem to be at 525–8, 918–20, and 1921–4. Such passages lead her to speculate (questionably) that Sh. sometimes wrote out passages of verse as prose. Other instances of similar Q/F mislinings might be cited. At 2603–8 and 2612–15 both texts erroneously make prose of good verse; apparently the lineation in the MS was very unclear. At 310–12 both texts incorrectly set prose as three lines of identical bad verse. At 2359–60 both Q and F misdivide a line to produce the same erroneous heptameter. At 2967–8 both texts fail to make Come a separate line, as virtually all modern editors do. At 710–11 both texts imperfectly line a verse quotation, burying two of its rhymes within the lines, while at 1966–8 they set identical triads even though F’s first line no longer rhymes; though not exactly errors, these irregular lineations seem to reflect a common original. Similarly at 726–8 the Fool’s jingle, set as two rhyming lines by editors since Pope, is run continuously into the prose sentence in both Q and F, as are phrases set by modern editors as verse quotations at 1878–90. In a number of other cases (e.g., 1249–50, 2377, 2563–73) modern editors alter identical Q/F lining, presumably believing that both texts make the same error; if so, both texts may reproduce an obscurity or misleading detail in the original manuscript.

Doran finds in Q1 most of the traits of orthography that Wilson (1923, pp. 122–4) finds in the other Shn. quartos. (P. 132) Shakespeare’s spelling was characterized by earlier forms, together with a good many unstable forms, and in these respects King Lear agrees with the other quartos. Of the errors due to misreading in other quartos that Wilson thinks reveal characteristics of Sh.’s handwriting, four are common to books of the period, but one in particular seems to him Shn.: a mistaken for o. If so, Doran believes, we have evidence of his hand in the manuscript of the quarto, namely, in the misreadings 890 con for can, 2607 tottered for tattered, 2131 lou’d for bare, 1901 night more for nightmare, 1902 O light for alight, 2176+5 bedlom for bedlam, and 1415 deptoued for depraued, adding (p. 133) I do not press this evidence.

Doran’s use of spelling evidence has been evaluated and refined by Halio (ed. 1994, pp. 6, 10–12), who discriminates Shn. spellings from those that might be either authorial or compositorial. The list of Shakespearean spellings that Doran derives from John Dover Wilson’s study [1923] is superseded by compositor studies with regard to spellings of do and go; but oo as in foord and strooke, and ou as in ould, could (cold), unfould, and hould, suggest authorial spellings, especially as they appear in other quartos. The same may be true for crewell, reuennew, hower, and a number of other unusual spellings. More revealing, perhaps, are the minim and other misreadings characteristic of Shakespeare’s manuscript as found in the printing of other quartos, such as q2 Hamlet.…[10] Words could be and often were spelt phonetically, according to the way the writer—or compositor—mentally heard them. As a consequence, words in Q1 that end in -s (rather than modern -ss or 17th-c. -sse), that against modern usage have single medial consonants or double final consonants after a short vowel, or -ck- for -k- after -n- may not point to an author. (P. 11): On the other hand, a marked tendency to use -ea- for -ei-, -ie-, or -e- appears, as in ceaze [277], perceau’d [1315], pearce [869], fleash [1120], tearmes [1187], shepheard [2014+19], leachers [2728]; and, conversely, spellings such as deere (for dear [81]), neerely [311], apeer’s [589], cleerest [2518], do point towards manuscript provenance.…[Cf.] the frequent use of initial -in- for -en-, as in intire [263], inioy [388], intirely [427+2], intreat [1189], indeuour [967], inraged [2319], inough [2580], indure [2861], indur’d [3168+7], imployment [2975]. Shakespeare clearly preferred a for he in some constructions…as well as I for ay.…Some curiously separated syllables, probably the result of penmanship, may be Shakespearean:…many fould [983], so phisticated [1886], how ere [2311+5], a hight [2500], a squint [3015], Sweet hart [2021]; cf. n. 2602–3 on so bade.

Halio also (p. 12) lists Q1’s contractions with or without an apostrophe, finding only a few likely to be distinctively Shn.: y’ar, th’are, at’h, ath, a’you, ant, alate. Honigmann (1996, p. 160) also notes a Shn. tendency to substitute y for modern i, to double consonants, and use -full for -ful. Greg (1955, pp. 385–6) notes that the aberrant spelling Leir (256, 265, 269, 788), probably a holdover from the sources, is more likely due to Sh. than to a compositor (Dace, 1971, pp. 91–2 makes the same point about the source spellings Rag. 325 and Ragan 331), and that Q’s spelling Gonorill is that of the sources, while F’s Gonerill is probably someone’s change in the playbook.

Following up on her suggestion (pp. 109, 128–30) that mislining in Q1 was sometimes caused by revision in Sh.’s original manuscript—indeed (p. 131) that [Q1] must therefore have been printed from a manuscript which had once contained an older form of the play, but which had been added to, patched, and revised in the margins, on pasted slips, on interleaves—Doran (1933, pp. 34–58) develops a highly speculative theory that such revision is largely concerned with certain sets of themes and purposes, primarily dramaturgic amplification to make the plot more plausible and interesting, and interpretive changes (p. 40) which reveal profounder reflection on Shakespeare’s part, either concerning the potentialities of his characters or the significance of human actions in general. The parts of the play generally close to the sources Leir and Sidney’s Arcadia are bibliographically regular, and so probably represent Sh.’s earlier, unrevised writing. Consistent printing irregularities in the part of the plot dealing with Edmund’s intrigues suggest that Sh. came to see possibilities in his character that he later developed by revision, thereby expanding the ethical dimension of the play (and making the manuscript harder to read). (Pp. 44–5): Also, since textual disturbance occurs in all but the last of the allusions to the French invasion, Sh. may have revised them in order to give earlier and fuller preparation for it. Furthermore (pp. 47–9), irregularity in reflective passages on nature as a controlling force, social obligations, and eternal justice suggest that they are later additions or revisions reflecting Sh.’s deepening apprehension of the meaning of the play’s actions. Similarly (pp. 55–6) irregularities in a few passages owing to Montaigne and in others preparing more carefully for Lear’s madness suggest later revision, the play growing in meaning as Sh. wrote and thought about it. The weakness of Doran’s argument is that it all depends on an unprovable hypothesis: that textual roughness signals later revision. But Sh.’s struggle with deep reflective passages could have occurred concurrently with his original reworking of his sources. If the roughness has other causes—Sh.’s writing in a white heat of creation, not pausing to clarify his punctuation and lineation of verse—it may signify the very opposite of revision. Some passages might signify one, some the other. At the most her argument may give possible corroboration for the inference that Q1 was difficult printer’s copy because it was a much-revised authorial manuscript.

The notion that Q presents a much-revised text in which traces of an older version of the play may be detected has been repeated by Craig (1961, 1962; see below) and more recently by others. Smidt (1990, pp. 129 ff.) argues that certain unconformities—loose ends in the plot, changing conceptions of character, odd repetitions, misalignment of verse—show that Shakespeare’s revising hand was evidently at work before the copy underlying the earliest text of the play was completed. Like Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 148–9), Smidt suspects that inconsequential rumors of impending civil war between Albany and Cornwall are remnants of an earlier stage in the plot (see nn. 938, 1638+1); he thinks the degradation of the roles of Kent, the Fool, and Edmund in the course of the play show that Sh. (p. 136) abandoned or changed early conceptions en route and left major as well as minor loose ends and inconsistencies (see, e.g., n. 2347+52); and that other untidiness and irregularity in 1.4 and 3.7 results in surprises and odd repetitions and contradictions that suggest redrafting and rearrangement in several scenes (see nn. 785, 830–3, 853, 2060–71). Inconsistencies in Lr. have long engaged critical attention, and have been explained in other ways than as traces of revision—see, e.g., Bradley (1904, pp. 256–60, 445–66), Booth (1983, passim), and Knowles (1999, pp. 33 ff.). Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 401–2) also detects traces of an earlier stage including an invasion by French forces with the King of France at their head, a notion resisted by Knowles (1999, pp. 279–81). Even if there is any likelihood in these theories, they lend little weight to the idea that Q derives from a rough draft, since the evidence on which they are based might have survived in Q through other provenance.

The part of Doran’s argument that drew most scorn from Greg (1933, pp. 254–61) was her proposal that while writing, Sh. sometimes failed to distinguish between verse and prose, writing out whole passages as rhythmic prose; the transcriber preparing the playbook attempted to align most of these properly, and Sh. corrected more of these and other stylistic faults in the playbook itself. Defending his theory of a shorthand report from performance, Greg intuits that certain changes are more likely to derive from actors than from the author (p. 253): I find it quite impossible to believe, with Miss Doran, that any writer, however familiar with the stage he might be, would in composition either deliberately or unconsciously introduce these features [redundant interpolations, mislineation, poor punctuation] which unnerve his language and destroy his verse, and then prune them away in revising the acting version. For the most part, however, Greg’s refutation is impressionistic and rhetorical. About 89–91, now generally thought to be revised in F1, he scoffs (p. 256), If anybody can see revision in this passage his conception of poetical composition must be radically different from my own. Similarly (p. 260), Miss Doran adduces…a large number of [graphic] errors…many of which I venture to think cannot possibly be of this type, offering a fanciful alternative explanation of only one of them. He restates her arguments in caricature, and then derides the caricature (p. 256): She pictures Shakespeare fumbling after his expression, and even after his meaning, with the clumsiness of a novice. That he evolved the seemingly inevitable expression of passage after passage from a welter of confused, inept, and commonplace phrases, is hard to believe. And when we are further told that the revision was carried out on the already prepared book of the play, we can only wonder what must have been the feelings—and the language—of the prompter who had to use it. He repeats (1942, p. 89; 1955, p. 378) the same kinds of objections, though conceding that in many respects Q1 look like foul papers. Doran (1941, p. 474) came to find her theory dubious, and in letters of 1971 and 1976 questioned her notion that Sh. had written out verse almost indistinguishable from prose (Dace, 1971, p. 110; Urkowitz, 1980, p. 164, n. 14). Very recently Thomas (1995, pp. 579 ff.) has continued to reject authorial MS for Q, whose errors of mishearing, mislineation, and mispunctuation can only be due, he thinks, to (p. 583) some form of oral transmission, and Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 121, 157) remains suspicious that extrametrical words in some lines might have originated with actors.

Despite Greg’s withering hostility, however, other editors were occasionally receptive to Doran’s ideas. Alexander (1939, p. 167): The Folio text of the contemporary Timon shows how irregular an early Shakespearean draft might be. We need not be surprised that Shakespeare did not write Lear in perfectly regular blank verse, but in powerfully rhythmic phrases that could later be given a smoother outline. (Much of the jumbling of blank verse, rhyme, and prose in Tim. is now attributed to Middleton’s co-authorship; see Vickers, 2002, p. 261.) Brooke (ed. 1947, pp. 153–5): The Quarto is much too good to be a reported text.…It presents a very full and essentially faithful version of the play, such as would be produced by a printer struggling honestly (however ineffectually at times) with a difficult handwriting and yet more difficult style. The two most glaring faults, which have done much to injure its reputation, are its frequent inability to distinguish verse from prose and its scandalously light punctuation.…For these things Shakespeare was largely to blame. His remarkably flexible and sinuous blank verse in Lear, his habit of beginning and ending speeches in the middle of lines, and of mingling prose and poetry without warning [154] in the same scene makes the division of a passage into its constituent verse units, once the visual distinction has been obscured, a work for none but a trained prosodist.…The very badness of the Quarto in these respects is, in the circumstances, rather a testimony of authenticity, for it is not likely that any one but the poet himself would have produced a manuscript as disorderly as the one from which the first Quarto was evidently printed. It must have been a manuscript in which margins and capitalization were so disregarded that verse and prose looked alike, and in which punctuation and legibility were at a minimum. Within two years after the writing of the play no such manuscript is likely to have been in existence except the author’s foul papers or personal draft. He cites several speeches (1564–86, 1809–17, 2948–59) in which Q1 came almost as near perfection as the text of Lear can come.…It is not likely that Burbage himself could have recited Lear from memory with as little error as appears in the better pages of the Quarto text. That such lines [156] could have been so well set down from the recollection of a hireling actor or by any kind of stenography then known exceeds credibility.

Craig (1961, p. 13) endorses Doran’s belief that Q1 reflects the disorder and illegibility of Shakespeare’s revision.…Typographical and formal irregularities are more than three times as frequent in the parts derived from Sidney as in the parts derived from the Lear tradition. This seems to render unnecessary, indeed impossible, the theory that the first quarto version was either taken down by shorthand from a performance of the folio version or put together by the process of memorial reconstruction, since neither a stenographer nor a reporter would thus discriminate against the minor plot, or could have done so had he so desired. He soon thereafter (1962) defends Q as an indispensable document which allows us to see Sh. at work. (P. 60): No pirate actor, no reporter, no memorial reconstructor whosoever could have produced such a text.…The quarto was printed from Shakespeare’s original manuscript with all its imperfections and all its phenomenal greatness on its head. How else could it show us the bare and patent ribs of a masterly construction? Like Doran he bases his argument on the distribution of good and bad verse. (Pp. 59–60): The parts of the original Lear story are in 1234 lines of good blank verse; the Gloucester story in 270 lines of prose, except that elements of feeling and imagination (Edmund’s soliloquy, other parts of 1.2, and the imaginary cliff in 4.6) are in 120 lines of verse; and Tom’s Bedlam-beggar patter (c. 150 lines), the Fool’s speeches and songs (c. 254 lines), and Lear’s mad talk are abnormal. If we…add together 1234 lines of good blank verse devoted to the Lear story as Geoffrey tells it, about 700 lines in prose and blank verse devoted primarily to the Gloucester story and the 566 lines in aberration by the Fool, the Bedlam and the crazed king, the total is roughly 2500 lines. There are 3528 lines in the [Q+F] play, and if we subtract 2500 from that, we get a remainder of 1028. To the highly original end of the play we may concede the 28 lines and say that there remain 1000 to be accounted for.…They are devoted to what might be called the nexus of the two plots—their interrelations and their matchless unification. They present the base intrigue between the Bastard and the elder daughters of Lear. They make the blinding of Gloucester a result of his loyal support of Lear.…[60] Those one thousand lines contain more than seventy percent of all the well advertised irregularities that appear in the quarto of 1608. In these lines we see Shakepeare at work…the powers at play. Similarly Smidt (1964, p. 161): In my own judgment the Quarto Lear is almost as often superior to the Folio as the other way about.…There is little indubitable mishearing, but a good deal of misreading in the Quarto, and it is to be suspected that the copy was in a rough handwriting and was perhaps lacking in punctuation and in verse division, at least for long stretches.

Ridley’s use of Q1 for his edition (ed. 1935) had been considered eccentric, but his judgment was seconded by Halio (ed. 1973, pp. 12–14), who accepted Doran’s conclusion that it derived from an authorial MS, and based his edition on Q, with importations from F (as authoritative corrections from a playhouse manuscript). (P. 13): Even if Q was not repaired autograph (Greg’s suggestion, and a possibility that cannot entirely be excluded), in accidentals—e.g. spelling, capitalisation—as well as in stage directions and other matters Q seems closer to Shakespeare’s manuscript than the version printed in Jaggard’s printing shop fifteen years later, when spelling and punctuation had considerably altered, and when the two compositors who set up the text—from the corrected Q—were hardly the most reliable ones for the task. (Folio compositors B and E are now thought to be more reliable than once supposed. On B in particular, see Werstine, 1983 and ).

Largely on bibliographical grounds, Blayney (1982) asserts the idea of an untidy authorial manuscript. He believes (p. 184) that the difficult quality of the MS probably accounts for Okes’s departure from the more customary, type-saving method of setting by formes, through casting off. Both Urkowitz (1980, p. 154, n. 15) and Wells (1983, p. 13) quote, from Cambridge University Press’s Prospectus for his book, Blayney’s opinion that its copy was a much-altered autograph manuscript containing the unpolished but probably near-final text of a play differing in some important respects from the play as we know it. Although Blayney emphatically disbelieves that F Lr. represents Sh.’s revision, his opinion about Q’s provenance has been consistently cited by scholars who, beginning with Warren (1978), have argued that Q1 and F1 Lr. represent two equally authorial versions of the play. Thus Urkowitz (pp. 130 ff.) refutes Greg’s and Walker’s arguments against author’s foul papers, particularly their arguments that corrupt passages, misassigned speeches, spellings that suggest mishearing, light punctuation, mislined verse, and memorial contamination indicate another provenance. He concludes (p. 140) that the agent most likely to have produced all the Shn. features supposed to be erroneous in Q is most likely to have been Sh. himself, in his rough draft. Taylor (1983, p. 388): Those who deny that Quarto Lear was set directly from Shakespeare’s foul papers must, among much else, explain why its vocabulary differs so radically from that of other memorially contaminated quartos, and, as Hart (1942, pp. 21–66) showed, is different from the vocabulary of the rest of the Shn. canon.

Blayney’s demonstration that neither Nicholas Okes nor his predecessors in the same shop (founded 1598) had ever printed a play quarto, and hence had never had to deal with conventions of setting and punctuating dramatic verse from a less-than-perfect dramatic manuscript, has been a confirming if not clinching argument for rough-draft copy for Q1. A more experienced printer might have demanded cleaner copy; a scribal transcript might to some degree have regularized spelling, punctuation, and lineation, and would have avoided the need for seriatim printing to which Blayney (see above, ) traces lineation and other printing problems. The kind of unclear lining and lack of capitalization and punctuation found in other extant authorial dramatic manuscripts, such as Massinger’s holograph playbook of Believe as You List and the collaborative Booke of Sir Thomas Moore, seem to confirm the likelihood that a rough draft by Shakespeare would have led Okes’s inexperienced compositors to produce the kinds of mistakes found in Q1. If Q1 was set from a rough draft, then a reasonable inference is that in that MS at least Sh. wrote verse in lightly punctuated, uncapitalized lines hard to distinguish from prose written out in lines of comparable length. Exactly such features are found in the three pages of Addition II in Sir Thomas Moore, which many scholars have suspected and others have ardently maintained (or denied) to be Sh.’s lines written in his autograph. Commentators on Lr. frequently make the comparison, without necessarily affirming that the lines in Addition II are Sh.’s: see, e.g., Doran (1933, pp. 30 ff.), Greg (1942, p. liii), Flatter (1952, pp. 35–8), Bolton (1960, p. 435), Dace (1971, pp. 88–94), Urkowitz (1980, pp. 132–3), Maguire (1996, p. 222), Wells (ed. 2000, p. 86), and others. For recent examples of the extensive literature on whether the Hand D additions are Sh.’s, see Vickers (2002, pp. 39–43, 67–70, 87–90) for a vigorous assertion that they probably are, and P. Werstine, Shakespeare, More or Less (Florilegium 16, 1999, pp. 125–45) for a scathingly skeptical argument that there is no good reason to think so. Whether they are or not, the Moore MS is one of several contemporary authorial manuscripts evidencing writing habits that, had Sh. shared them, would help explain features of Q1.

The distribution of the lining errors in Q1 also supports the idea that they are largely due to the inexperience of the compositors (rather than to an extraordinarily disorderly manuscript). Since the Q compositors were able to set two-thirds of the verse correctly, a majority of the verse lines in the manuscript were evidently distinguishable from prose and were conscientiously reproduced by the compositors. On a number of occasions each man, having set several overlong or incorrectly divided lines, was able to recover and to proceed with the correct lineation, which must therefore have been clear enough in the manuscript: see, e.g., 218–19, 305–8, 1037–41, 1062–8, 2056+8–+18, 2307+4–+6, 2713–14, 2906–16, 2946–7, and 3153–62. As was the general custom in dramatic verse, speeches throughout the play sometimes began with a part-line that was meant to link metrically with a preceding part-line to form a full pentameter; these initial part-lines were customarily lined separately in dramatic manuscripts. In 1.1 Compositor B set three of these (102, 148, 245) correctly, perhaps setting them off as introductory phrases of direct address rather than as metrical links; but for the next thousand lines he failed to set a single one of them in a separate line. Instead, he was prone to run the part-line and following line together, beginning mislineation that might sometimes go on for several lines (see, e.g. 82, 225, 234, 265, 302, 1170, 1191)—a kind of error that reappears almost four dozen times throughout the play in the work of both compositors. From 1303 and 1426 onwards, however, first Compositor B and then his partner began to set some of these initial part-lines correctly, giving about three dozen of them typographic lines of their own. Less frequently, though continually, both compositors made the inverse error, running a concluding part-line, intended to link metrically with the next speech, up into the final full line of the speech, producing a hypermetric line: see, e.g., 81, 291, 1605, 2148, 2303+17, 2347+41, 2472, 2706, 2809, and 3140.

The reason for such erratic lining of linking part-lines is more likely to be found in the compositors than in their manuscript. It is far less likely that an experienced dramatist such as Sh. would almost wholly neglect to indicate separate linking lines in the first two-fifths of his play and indicate them only sporadically thereafter, than that the two compositors, being inexperienced in setting dramatic verse, had little or no inkling of one of its common conventions until they were somehow enlightened partway through the play. Since neither man seems to have had a very good ear for blank verse, despite reproducing a majority of the lines faithfully, it would not be surprising if both of them continued in their former manner to set some of these linking lines incorrectly until the very end of their work. Compositor B in particular seems not to have had a good ear, since he (and he only) set some sixty lines of awkward false verse, and since he even failed repeatedly to recognize rhyme (see, e.g., 287–91, 1916, 2030, 2056+6–+7). Compositor B was also responsible for most of the five hundred lines of verse incorrectly set as prose. Much of this false prose, appearing in short passages intermittently with verse, probably reflects (whatever other causes may have been operative) his limited ability to hear and recognize blank verse rhythms, or perhaps his failure to devote close and continual attention to them; but the concentration of about half of B’s false prose within six pages of one early quire (D; 712–1034) may suggest another cause. Those six pages amount to about one day’s work; it may be that for a day or so, for some unknown reason, this compositor simply took fewer pains to distinguish verse from prose in his manuscript, though he subsequently gave better attention to such matters for the rest of his stint. In any case there is no other similar concentration of false prose until the notoriously difficult mixture of verse and prose (2554–649) set by Compositor C in the latter half of 4.6; the early concentration in quire D may therefore indicate a temporary lapse on the part of Compositor B. In short, there is some reason to suspect that the manuscript’s lineation may not have been so inadequate as the printers were unskilled. Blayney (1982, p. 187), identifying the likely compositors: [Thomas] Corneforth and [John] Reynolds were probably about 21 and 17 respectively. Corneforth had been an apprentice for two and a quarter years, and Reynolds for eight months, while Okes himself [just turned 28] had been a master printer for only ten months. It is not very surprising to find occasional signs of inexperience in Okes’s early books.

On more than one occasion Werstine (see esp. 1990, p. 69) has cautioned that since we have no extant Shn. autograph of a play, our notions of what it would look like are entirely inferential, or purely ideal. Such a caveat is a necessary and salutary antidote to the overconfident assertions of Greg, McKerrow, Wilson, and other new bibliographers about the particular characteristics of Shn. foul papers—their lineation, punctuation, nature and placement of stage directions, regularity of speech prefixes, and the like. Nonetheless, to say that a category of manuscript is purely ideal is not to say that such manuscripts had no real existence or are now entirely unknowable. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. We may safely assume that if a fair copy were made of any work, the original rough draft must have contained enough obscurities to justify such expense and effort. There seems little doubt that a fair copy was made from the manuscript behind Q, and that its copyist was confused by many of its illegible readings, deciphering them in ways reflected in comparable misreadings in Q1. That the difficulties in the manuscript were many and considerable is indicated by the large number of erroneous readings and even press-corrections in Q1 that baffled both compositors and proofreader. That Q1 was set seriatim rather than, as would have been usual, by formes, strongly suggests a manuscript too disorderly for ordinary casting-off. Such a manuscript would probably have presented real difficulties, even if not insuperable, to both a censor and an acting company. Despite the claims of the editors of F1 that Sh. made scarse…a blot in his papers, ample evidence survives in the early printed editions that he occasionally reworked passages, and any author in the heat of creation is likely to form letters poorly, change his mind about word-choice or meter, and make changes and deletions accordingly, within or above or beside the line. A number of critics, such as Doran and Smidt, believe they can detect evidence of imperfect revision more easily in Q than in F, and editors such as Taylor and Halio believe that the vocabulary and orthography of Q are characteristically Shn., suggesting an autograph more than a scribal transcript or reworked playbook. While it is true that none of these features of Q1 prove irresistibly that Sh.’s rough draft was its copy, such an inference seems to explain these features better than any other that has been offered. For such reasons, among recent editors of the play—e.g. Halio (ed. 1973, 1994), Wells & Taylor (ed. 1986), Bevington (1988), Weis (ed. 1993), Foakes (ed. 1997), Orgel (ed. 1999), Wells (ed. 2000), and others—there is general consensus that an authorial rough draft, not yet annotated for theatrical use nor vetted by the censor, lies behind Q1 Lr.

As a consequence of this new consensus, which has grown throughout the past half-century, Q1 Lr. has undergone a remarkable rehabilitation. In 1942 Greg (pp. 100–1) could declare that the quarto is a reported text, badly printed and arbitrarily corrected, of small textual value, and express the hope that his discrediting of it would result in 300 of the 400 Q readings in the standard (Globe) text being replaced by F readings. Kirschbaum (1945) could confidently argue that in virtually every case of Q/F disagreement, the Folio reading was preferable to the Q variant. Today the opposite opinion is widely held—that the Q1 text, deriving from Sh.’s rough draft, represents Sh.’s play in a state close to what he originally presented to his company for them to enact, while the later F text, apparently altered by a number of indeterminate agencies, may in many respects be further removed from his authorial intentions, and in that respect may be a less authoritative text, whatever its other values.

How Sh.’s own autograph found its way to a printer lacking the experience to deal with its difficulties, and was published evidently without supervision by either its author or the company that owned the play, can only be speculated upon. A draft in such a rough state as seems to lie behind Q1 would almost certainly have needed to be transcribed into a fair copy for licensing and use in the theater, and Doran (1931) provides textual evidence that such a transcript was made and lies somewhere behind F1. Either Shakespeare made the transcript himself, possibly making some of the changes that appear in F1 (a possibility urged by Honigmann, 1996, pp. 20–1, and others), or he or his company hired a scribe to do it. An autograph transcript seems unlikely on two counts: as Doran (p. 133; see above, ) and others have pointed out, the persistence of many manuscript errors in the fair copy behind F suggests a scribe other than Sh.—perhaps the prompter— since Sh. would have been too familiar with his own script and with the text that he had recently composed to be misled by his original manuscript. He may have read over the transcript, making a number of verbal or formal changes, which he could have done without the aid of his original draft and with no aim at perfection; Doran notes (pp. 134–5) that in the extant promptbook of The Second Maiden’s Tragedy the author (Middleton) failed to correct all the scribal errors (and left the verse lines uncapitalized, as they must have been in the draft behind Q1 Lr.). In any case it is hard to imagine Sh., after making a fair copy for the company, giving his original draft to presumably unfamiliar publishers such as Busby and Butter for unsupervised publication by a new and unknown printer, Nicholas Okes.

Alternatively, either the company or Sh. himself engaged a scribe to make a clean transcript. Bowers (1986, p. 21) inclined generally to the former practice: It may seem probable…that a commissioned playwright like Shakespeare, a shareholder in the company, need not have been bound by the conventions applied to outsiders. Instead, I suggest, Shakespeare ordinarily submitted his working papers, and that the company thereupon had these transcribed. Since the company, however, was probably gone from London during much if not most of 1605–6, because of plague and touring, Sh. might have had to hire his own scribe. In any case, if after receiving a clean transcript made by a professional scribe or its own book-holder the company retrieved and held the rough draft for safe-keeping—and there are serious doubts that they regularly did so—then either Busby and Butter acquired it by the kinds of surreptitious or piratical means commonly imagined a century ago but not much credited today, or the company itself sold it to Busby and Butter. Halio (ed. 1973, p. 12 n. 21) can imagine the latter: A simpler explanation is that the players sold the foul papers when the play was no longer new. After 1603, however, the company seems to have had little interest in selling its plays to publishers. The Chamberlain’s Men had evidently sold a number of Sh.’s plays in the past, but after the 1603 quarto of Ham. (entered to James Roberts in 1602) had appeared, the King’s Men (which the company became on 19 May 1603) seem to have significantly changed their attitude towards selling plays. Erne (2003, pp. 101–14, esp. 109): The four-year period from 1605 to 1608 saw the publication of no fewer than fifty-two plays written for the commercial stage.…While Shakespeare’s plays account for more than 18 percent of all the (commercial) plays printed in the ten years prior to 1603, that figure is down to less than 4 percent for the ten years after 1603. Besides Lr., only Tro. (1609) and Per. (1609) found their way into print, until eventually Oth. (1622) appeared just a year before F1. It is by no means certain that these four plays were published at the wish of the King’s Men, and two are now thought possibly to have been set from transcripts, not foul papers.

Moreover, it is doubtful that the company could have sold foul papers even if they had wished to do so. Greg’s (1942, p. 31; 1955, p. 106) insistence that playwrights were required to submit their foul papers to the company along with their fair copy, the former to be kept in the playhouse for safe-keeping, is based on no evidence and has been increasingly challenged (see, e.g., Bowers, 1955, p. 15, 1966, p. 17; Werstine, 2000, pp. 32–6). If the playing companies as a rule preferred to receive and keep relatively fair copy, then the apparently very rough (miserable or difficult) draft that editors now think lies behind Q1 Lr. was probably not the manuscript that the King’s Men accepted as the basis of their 1606 playbook; nor is there reason to think that they acquired that draft and held onto it until later, presumably some time in 1607, they sold it to Busby. It is not clear why they would have made an exception to their new policy of minimal or no publication of plays in order to sell Sh.’s draft of Lr. themselves or to encourage a scribe to sell it; nor is it clear why, if they had a choice, they would have dealt with Busby, previously known to them (if at all) only as the publisher behind the bad quartos of H5 and Wiv. Nor is it easy to imagine that if Sh. (rather than his company) had hired the scribe to make a fair copy, he would have encouraged him subsequently to transfer the rough draft to Busby, or that Sh. himself would have effected such a transfer; as Erne (p. 107) says, What appears to have been the state of the manuscript from which King Lear was set up does pose a problem…if we wanted to assume that Shakespeare cared about its publication.

One other, and possibly more likely, scenario may be imagined: that after a professional scribe, hired either by Sh. or his company, had delivered his fair transcript to the King’s Men, for some reason he did not immediately return his rough draft to Sh., and eventually, knowing that the company possessed and was using a clean transcript, made his own arrangements to sell the original rough draft to Busby, who had considerable experience in acquiring play manuscripts from various persons connected with the London theaters. The publishers’ regular entry of their book in the Stationers’ Register suggests that they had no doubts about their rights of ownership to the MS; they may have bought it fair and square from the author’s or company’s own scribe. It may be that such a transfer from scribe to publishers was the easier because of the plague: if Barroll’s (1991, p. 173) estimates are correct, the playhouses may have been open for only three months in 1605–6 and for only one in 1606–7, and continually closed between the time when Sh. was probably finishing his play (in the second half of 1606) and the time when Butter published it early in 1608. Gurr (1996, pp. 304–5) records that in 1606–7 Sh.’s company spent much of their time touring outside the city, and Sh. may have spent much of his time on tour with them or in Stratford working on Mac. and Ant. He may not have gotten around to, or even thought about, retrieving his MS of Lr. from its transcriber. For his part the scribe, holding an unclaimed and superseded MS of a play that in 1607 had already been produced, might well have been induced to sell it to Busby, who in 1606–8 was acquiring MSS of plays from several companies. There is no need to assume the kind of piracy of a manuscript that Pollard (1917, 1920) and others believed in a century ago; to Busby, the speculative purchase of an available manuscript of his third Shn. play may well have seemed simply an ordinary and straightforward business investment such as he often made. Johnson (1985, p. 15): According to the business practices of the time, these manuscripts [of Shn. and other works], not having been entered by other stationers, were seen as fair game.

At best these unprovable speculations describe a possible (if not likely) route by which Sh.’s rough draft might have reached Okes’s printing house. Whether it did so in fact is a separate question; today there is widespread (though not universal) agreement among textual scholars that it did.

div.head: The Second Quarto (1619)
div.p: There is no entry for Q2 in the Stationers’ Register, probably because it was published surreptitiously with a misleading title page. Erne (2003, pp. 255–8) has recently argued that the group of plays among which it appeared in 1619, rather than the so-called bad quartos of the 1590s and early 1600s, were the stolne, and surreptitious copies referred to by Heminge and Condell in their prefatory remarks to the First Folio (1623). If so, it is remarkable (or at least ironic) that they seem to have used some of this group of quartos in preparing copy for F1: see Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 145–7).

The title page, as transcribed in Greg (BEPD, 1939, 1:399), reads as follows:
M. VVilliam Shake-speare, | HIS | True Chronicle History of the life | and death of King Lear, and his | three Daughters. | With the vnfortunate life of Edgar, | sonne and heire to the Earle of Glocester, and | his sullen and assumed humour of TOM | of Bedlam. | As it was plaid before the Kings Maiesty at White-Hall, vp-|pon S. Stephens night, in Christmas Hollidaies. | By his Maiesties Seruants, playing vsually at the | Globe on the Banck-side. | [<McKerrow> device 283] | Printed for Nathaniel Butter. | 1608.

Bartlett & Pollard (1939, pp. 48–50; cf. p. 130) identify and locate thirty-two extant copies of Q2; Dace (1971, pp. 183–4) lists these (failing to identify the University of Virginia copy as Bartlett 534) and adds three more (copies owned by Mrs. Donald F. Hyde, Texas Christian University, and the University of Illinois). Modern facsimiles include that of C. Praetorius, ed. P. A. Daniel, 1885, and that in The Complete King Lear, 1608–1623, ed. Michael Warren, 1989.

div.head: The Printing of Q2
div.p: Except that it bears a different printer’s ornament, and lacks the reference in its imprint to Butter’s sign of the Pied Bull, Q2’s title page virtually duplicates the wording and layout of Q1. It therefore advertises two falsehoods—the name of the publisher, and the date of publication—that led to centuries of confusion. In fact, as was not discovered for almost three hundred years, Q2 was not issued by Butter in 1608, but printed by William Jaggard for Thomas Pavier’s Shakespearean collection of 1619 (see below). The printer’s ornament on the title page, McKerrow 283, was used by William Jaggard before and after 1619; the first two lines of the title page, minus a comma, are reused in the head-title under the Roberts-Jaggard headpiece of royal arms (Pollard, 1909, p. 53). There is no tailpiece. As Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xi) first demonstrated by readings common to both editions, Q2 was printed from a copy of Q1 that had sheets D[o], G[o], and H[i] in the uncorrected state. Subsequently Doran (1931, pp. 19–20) showed that that copy also had sheets E(o) and K(o) in the corrected state. Though she admits the further possibility that corrections of a few Q1 errors—371 Ba. om., 620 lubbers, length, 1520 callit, 1686 hut she—may derive from corrected sheets of C(i) and F(i), she concedes that the corrections are obvious ones that the Q2 printer might have arrived at independently. Andrews (1971, p. 48): It also appears that the Q1 copy contained the corrected sheets of C inner and K inner, and [contrary to Doran] the uncorrected sheet of F inner. Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xiv) imagines that Q2’s added 1640+2 Gent. Good Sir may be from an otherwise unknown corrected state of sheet I(o) in an unknown copy of Q1; for other explanations see n. –2640. Stone (1980, pp. 152–5) finds some misreadings in Q2 so odd and unnecessary—473+2 amities/armies, 1644 feare/doubt, 1703 Powther/Thundring, 1910 furie/fruite, 2452 beach/beake, 2454 a boui/aboue, 2546 euery thing/all, 2561 lacke/want, 3109 answere/offer, 3295 goard/good—that he hypothesizes, but does not assert, a lost intermediate Qx behind Q2, containing these variants. Greg (1942, p. l [= 50]): It is possible, though I think not likely, that one or two readings in the second quarto of King Lear may be of this nature— i.e., may be derived from an unrecorded corrected state of the sheet.

The Pavier quarto of 1619 is a copy but not a page-for-page reprint of Q1. Knowles (1982, p. 192): The collation of Q1 is A2 B–L4; the text begins on B1 and ends on L4, and it is printed 38 lines to a page. The collation of Q2 is A–L4; its text begins on A2 and ends on L4, and it is printed 37 lines to a page. Thus 79 pages of text in Q1 are stretched into 85 pages in Q2.…A line of white space is added before most entrance directions; stage directions in the margin and stage directions or speeches doubled up in the same line with another speech or part-line in Q1 are usually lined separately in Q2; a few turnovers and turnunders are carried down and indented to make a separate part-line; and there is some deliberate relining. Like Q1, Q2 is not divided into acts or scenes.

As Daniel (facs. 1885, pp. xi–xiv) was first to note, Q2 is on the whole better printed than Q1, introducing both new corrections (especially of lineation and punctuation) but also new errors (especially omissions). Adee (ed. 1890, pp. xix) notes fewer contractions, tildes, wrong-font characters, uneven spacings, and makeshift marks of punctuation to supply type shortages than are found in Q1. Stone (1980, pp. 129–30): Q2 is much neater typographically than its predecessor. It shows a more generous use of space, hence a clearer lay-out.…Capitals and italics are somewhat more liberally and more rationally employed than in Q1. Punctuation is very much improved: errors are corrected and a greater diversity of stops replaces Q1’s ubiquitous commas. Many misprints are emended, as are most spelling mistakes, and a rather more up-to-date system of spelling is adopted generally. [Fn.: The following spellings, for example, and all those analogous to them, are consistently altered: maister to master; graund to grand; cary to carry; drawen to drawne; hould to hold; nise to nice; cursse to curse.]…Attempts have been made here and there to correct the line-arrangement, speech-prefixes or stage-directions which in Q1 are obviously faulty. Readings are emended, if not always happily; on occasions a word is added or deleted to perfect the sense. Details are freely altered, though not as frequently as in F: we find an occasional substitution of he for a, or if for and, but for the most part these indifferent changes consist in the contraction of certain locutions (e.g. where’s for where is) and the expansion of contractions.…[130] We find, as is only to be expected, a series of fresh errors, chiefly misprints and omissions. Honigmann (1996, p. 53) notices the occasional expansion of colloquial contractions (ith, at’h, ’t, thar’t, you’l, You’r, tha’re, etc.) and adding or dropping of a final -s. (P. 139): The main thrust of the substitutions in King Lear (1619) is away from the old-fashioned or colloquial towards the more modern or formal.

Knowles (1982, pp. 192–3): The result of…clean copy and a regular house style was very accurate casting-off for Q2. Despite occasional inconsistencies, all three compositors were able to adhere fairly closely to style and needed to make few adjustments in spacing and lining. Only one page is a little short, and a small handful of [193] others show a little crowding, none of it very serious. Except in cases of deliberate relining, the length of the prose line in Q2 follows that in Q1 very closely.…Perhaps it was to approximate the Q1 line more accurately that the two compositors who set sheets A and B both seem to have reset their measure from 94 to 95 mm. starting with sheet C.…[201] In order that Q2 should pass for Q1 under casual inspection, Pavier or Jaggard may have intended to keep L4v blank. As Doran (1931, pp. 29–30) notices, the last two and a half pages, beginning with line 3192, are compressed so that the text ends at the bottom of L4r; most of the verse more than two lines long is printed as prose, and new half-line speeches are put on the same line as a previous short speech, until by the time he has reached line [3284] in the middle of the last page, he has gained a little on Q1, so that he can set up the rest of the page in good order, with the verse properly aligned and half-lines on separate lines. The short half-line 3214, which would not fit at the bottom of L3, may have been dropped altogether to avoid a widow at the top of the crowded next page. Lines 938–40, 3100, 3102, and the half-line 3168 seem to have been omitted by oversight.

All significant differences between Q1 and Q2 in verbal variants (including speech prefixes and stage directions), punctuation, and lineation are recorded in the textual notes of this edition. The detailed discussions of these differences in Doran (1931, pp. 20–38), Van Dam (1935, pp. 31–8), Dace, 1971, pp. 204–10), Andrews (1971, passim), Stone (1980, pp. 257–75 et passim), and many editions are represented in the commentary notes. Doran notes that Q2 corrects a number of obvious errors in Q1 but not less obvious ones, and even repeats some readily apparent ones. She finds (p. 21) no evidence of an independent manuscript source; often corrections are partial, introduce new errors, and differ from the obviously right F reading, while unintelligible passages remain. A number of indifferent variants (p. 32) consist in the addition of a word—such as an exclamation, a connective, an adverb, or a pronoun—sometimes filling out an elliptical sentence, sometimes altering the syntax, frequently disturbing the meter. (Pp. 33–4): The Q2 printer often substitutes synonyms: hath/has, does/doth, touches/toucheth, shew’d/shewne, those/these, which/that, on’s/of his, true to tell/truth to tell, euery thing/all, and the striking feare/doubt (1644), Powther/Thundring (1703), and lacke/want (2562). Such substitutons as he for a…and if for and…, occurring almost every time these forms appear, were probably made deliberately with a view to rendering the text more formal. (Pp. 26–8): Q2 supplies six of the missing exits [829, 942, 1227, 1239, 2936, 2968] and one entrance for a single character [2927]. Twice it adds, to directions [874, 1273] noting only the entrance of Lear, the names of other characters who enter with him, but not all the characters; (p. 28) it omits an exit (2843+11) and substitutes an exit for an exeunt (1073). It makes minor improvements or corrections in the wording and location of stage directions, and supplies or regularizes a few speech prefixes. (P. 35): The addition of a part-line speech Gent. Good sir at 2640+2 improves the meter and bridges two contiguous speeches by Lear. Van Dam (pp. 29–38) lists numerous examples of Q2’s corrections of Q1’s erroneous spellings, misprints, omitted words, wrong words, redundancies [e.g., a phrase in 801], and transpositions, and its three omissions of unintelligible phrases—your most deere (2632), for you her owne for Venter (2723+1), and yet are I mou’t (3075).
