He finds the substituted synonyms generally to be modernizations. Andrews (pp. 43–4) thinks that the survival of many obvious errors suggests that on the whole the copy was unrevised, and that therefore both substantive and accidental changes in Q2 Lr. are probably compositorial. This judgment is reinforced by his discovery (p. 175) that in quires A–H there are on average 22 substantive changes per quire, whereas in quires I–K, set by a different compositor, there are twice as many. Nonetheless Stone (p. 129) finds Q2’s calculated alterations of readings, lining, and stage-directions to be unmistakable signs of editing in Q2. It is of course possible if not likely that Pavier or Jaggard made some editorial corrections in the Q1 copy and that the compositors added further changes, in both cases emending by light of nature or in accordance with printing-house style, not from an independent manuscript.

Some sporadic and partial correction of Q1’s verse and prose lineation occurs in Q2. Doran (1931, pp. 25–6): The greater part of lines too long or too short have been left as they were, but a few have been altered. Most of the changes have been made in lines which will not scan in Q1 because the alignment of the verse is incorrect; if the passages were properly aligned [in Q1], the changes introduced into Q2 would impair the meter. This consideration may be taken as proof that the printer of Q2 did not in these places derive [26] his alterations from an independent source.…[28] In the matter of printing verse as prose and prose as verse, and of incorrect alignment of verse, the second quarto conforms closely to the first quarto until…[2705; I4v], where a deliberate attempt at amendment begins.…[29] The frequency with which attempts are made to set right the alignment, beginning at [2705]…is striking after the comparative faithfulness of reproduction in the earlier portion of the play. Even here we are hardly justified in explaining the changes as having come from reference to an independent source, for the alterations…do not always completely remove the difficulty. The new compositor who began work in quire I oddly mislined Gonorill’s letter (2716–21) as verse, perhaps to stretch copy. He was especially enterprising in relining verse and prose in the next quire, K, but in the last quire, L, was largely forced to ignore correct lineation in order to compress the text so as to end at the bottom of L4r. Andrews (1971, p. 91): Quire K was set by a compositor about eight times as likely to attempt to alter wrongly aligned verse and nearly three times as likely to succeed in rendering proper alignment as the compositor[s] who set the earlier pages of the quarto. Throughout Q2, however, the majority of Q1’s mislining remains uncorrected.

Doran (pp. 24–5, 114) also describes Q2’s fuller and more correct punctuation: Q2 appear[s] to have been punctuated according to the rules of the printing-house, somewhat modified by the individual preferences of the compositors.…[25] A number of passages faultily punctuated in Q1…are repaired in Q2, not always, however, without removing them still farther, in meaning, from the sense intended by Shakespeare.…[114] The punctuation of Q2 is heavier than that of Q1, with more semicolons and periods at the ends of sentences within speeches; …from the middle of Act IV, Scene v [at about 2402, I2r] (where it is probable that a different compositor began to work), Q2 is as heavily pointed as the folio. Andrews (1971, pp. 239–40) finds 482 punctuation changes in A–H—an average of 60 per quire—and 413 changes in I–L—an average of 138 changes per quire. The tendency towards heavier (rather than equal or lighter) punctuation is more marked in the last three quires: there are 340 instances in A–H (42.5 per quire), 339 in I–L (113 per quire). Obviously one compositor was more assiduous than another in regularizing punctuation according to his own or a printing-house style. Stone (1980, p. 135): Q2 retains few punctuation errors from Q1. Punctuation on Q2 A–H is fairly light, and close to Q1. Commas are redistributed, several are added and some dropped, question marks are supplied when necessary; and a few semi-colons introduced to separate sentences and to mark the heavier pauses, though by no means according to any consistent principle. Sheets I and K [he should add L], on the other hand, present a different picture. Not only is a much larger number of stops added to those in Q1.…Colons and full-stops appear in quantity for the first time, outnumbering semicolons. In appendices (pp. 257–67, 274–5) he totals Q2’s changes of each kind of punctuation mark, listing them not by pages in Q2 but by corresponding columns in F1 (thereby excluding Q-only lines); from F qq5 (corresponding to Q2 I1) onwards, Q2’s punctuation becomes markedly heavier, reflecting compositor preferences. (P. 274): All dashes and brackets (parentheses) in Q1 are retained in Q2, and more are added. Q2 also adds a number of question marks, and an occasional exclamation mark, and puts colons after nine speech prefixes on the last page.

Doran (1931, pp. 115–17): The spelling in both Q2 and F is more accurate and more systematic than in Q1. The second quarto shows a fairly consistent change from Q1 in the following respects: -ie/-y, -ay-/-ai-, -oy-/-oi-, often also -y-/-i-; -ea-/e + e following a consonant, or to ei, ie, ee; often ie/ee; -ea- more consistently for long open e; oa/long o; close o towards the sound oo; double consonants after a short vowel; -e after a long vowel and consonant, and in -nes/-nesse; in-/en-; and to more modern forms, as maister/master, madame/madam, prethe or prithee/prethee. (P. 117): Not a great many more capitals occur in Q2 than in Q1; when there are more they generally appear in spots. Q1 capitalizes titles, sometimes terms of address, sometimes nouns of family relationship, usually natural objects and names of animals, sometimes political terms; in addition, Q2 nearly always capitalizes Letter (because letters are significant to the plot), often Army, and usually Noble (even as an adj.). Andrews (1971, pp. 265–317) shows how there are different patterns of spelling and italicization in the first eight (A–H) and the last three (I–L) quires of Q2.

div.head: Press-Variants and Proof-Correction in Q2
div.p: Dace (1971, pp. 184–6): Collation of…thirty-three…copies reveals very few variants which are clearly the result of press-correction. There are, of course, occasional instances of type inking too lightly or heavily or perhaps the frisket slipping slightly. In only one of these cases does it seem likely that the press may have been stopped. Even in this instance, G3, the evidence seems more against than for press-correction having occurred. There are two erroneous variants—the [185] failure to print the final n, and part of the preceding o in prouision (last word, line 1) in roughly half the copies collated and the absence of a period after Exit (last word, line 7) in nearly half.…On L3, line one,…there are eight different combinations of spacings between the letters within [one] word.…It is unclear whether the eighteen sheets examined in which all the letters are correctly contiguous are the result of press-correction or simply represent a state preceding those in which slippage has occurred. Dace, like Furness (ed. 1880, p. 288), does not find the omission of 2659 thats all noted in jen and cam1, and suspects simply editorial eyeskip to 2662, which lacks the words. Their omission from pope and han1 is probably a metrical emendation. (P. 186): Sheet A provides the only obviously press-variant page.…On A3 we find…bgot for begot at line 26 and matry for marry at line 33 in some five or six copies; these are also the only variants discovered by Knowles (1982, p. 193 n.).

div.head: The Date and Auspices of Q2
div.p: When 18th-c. scholars finally began to distinguish between what are now known as Q1(uncorr.), Q1(corr.), and Q2, still mistaking them for three separate editions published in the same year (see ), their more difficult task was to establish the relationships between them, first of all chronological precedence. Capell (1783, 3:C1v) reverses Q1 and Q2; Halliwell (ed. 1865) correctly gives precedence to Q1; after preparing their text, the Cambridge editors Clark & Wright (ed. 1866, pp. xv–xvi) realize (having found Q1 corrected readings repeated in Q2) that they might have reversed Q1 and Q2; and in Ellis (1869, 1:217 n.) they admit and correct their error. Their solution to the puzzle led Furness (ed. 1880, p. 359) to utter his unfortunate declaration, It is comforting to reflect that to decide upon the precedence, in point of time, of these editions, or, in other words, which is Q1 and which is Q2, belongs wholly to the province of Bibliography; it has no bearing whatever on the elucidation of the text of this tragedy. Because in recent years evidence has indicated that Q2 in some way influenced the text of F1, its relationship to Q1 and its relative textual authority have taken on considerable importance.

Delius (1875, pp. 125 ff.) still considers Q1 and Q2 of equal authority, but Daniel (facs. 1885, pp. xi–xiv) establishes that Q2 is a mere copy of Q1, having no independent manuscript authority but reflecting both corrected and uncorrected sheets of Q1. Moreover, the Pide Bull edition commences the play with Signature B., leaving Signature A. to the last for Title and supposed preliminary matter;…a reprint…would naturally begin, as in Q2, with Signature A.…It marks a few additional exits and entrances. It is, however, marred by many omissions and by following a copy of its predecessor which contained at least three uncorrected sheets. It has just four variations from Q1, which might perhaps he considered to rise to the dignity of independent readings: [1399 vp ’ith paste, 1644 doubt not, 1703 Thundring, 2546 all I saide]. It also preserves [or supplies] one speech [2640+2 Gent. Good Sir.].…Compared then with Q1, Q2 will be found to be of distinctly inferior authority.…Q2 being a mere copy, its concurrence with either [state of Q1] can hardly be worth consideration.

Not until the early 20th century was Q2 Lr. accurately dated, only after it was identified as part of a group of plays printed in the same year (1619) though bearing title pages dated from 1600 to 1619. That curious and rather shabby collection (Greg, 1955, p. 12) of plays known or sometimes thought to be by Shakespeare—Parts 1 and 2 of The Whole Contention betweene…Lancaster and York (2 and 3H6), Per., A Yorkshire Tragedy, MV, Wiv., MND, Lr., H5, and 1 Sir John Oldcastle—had been reprinted in 1619 from earlier quartos or octavos originally issued by a variety of printers and publishers; this new collection, now known as the Pavier Quartos, was printed by William Jaggard (whose shop would soon print F1) for the publisher Thomas Pavier, who was apparently planning to bring out a collection of Shakespeare’s plays. Several bound collections of these ten plays have in fact survived. The brilliant literary sleuthing that revealed the truth behind their several falsified title pages has been recounted by Richard Altick in The Scholar Adventurers (1950, pp. 189–95).

Greg (1908, pp. 113–31, 381–409) first proposed that the ten quartos bound together in a 17th-c. binding were not remainders—three were dated 1600, two 1608, three 1619—but were all actually printed in 1619 despite the differing dates on their title pages. Eight had a printer’s device and numerals not used until 1610 and a type font not used until 1617, and all were printed on the same papers, bearing the same group of watermarks, which would not have been available over a span of nineteen years. (On rare Pavier watermarks bearing dates of either 1617 or 1619, see Stevenson (1951–2). In each quarto the printer imitated an original edition. Greg inferred that initially three of these editions were printed in and dated 1619, but that when Pavier for some reason got nervous about his undertaking he issued others under their original dates, possibly seeming to sell off the remainders of editions printed years before by other publishers in order to avoid challenges to copyright. Pollard (1909, pp. 81–104) reports that he and Greg became suspicious of the quartos because they did not specify the printer, publisher, and publisher’s address, but rather the initials T. P. (for Thomas Pavier) on five of the title pages; because around 1619 William Jaggard was using two of the printer’s devices appearing repeatedly in this group of quartos; because a font of Roman type used in the suspect quartos was a new kind also used in F1 in 1623; and because the spelling in each suspect quarto was generally more modern than in its (older) counterpart, evidently reflecting the habits of Jaggard’s compositors. The clinching proof was provided by Neidig (1910, pp. 145 ff.), who showed by photographic overlays that seven of the nine title pages were printed in part from the same setting of type, parts of which were transferred from one title page to another; these therefore were (p. 154) not printed nineteen years apart, but within a few days of each other. The order of printing that he established for these title pages—WC, YT, Per., MV, Wiv., Lr., H5, and SJO—has been generally accepted as the order of printing of the plays themselves, with the exception that Per. follows WC, with which it shares continuous signatures. On the evidence of watermarks Blayney (1972, pp. 196–7) provisionally places MND before Lr., and Knowles (1982, p. 195) has found the supporting evidence that a number of distinctive types in the last three sheets of MND appear in the first three sheets of Lr. Wiv. is printed in a larger and different font than that used in Lr.

Chambers (1930, 1:134–7): The Contention and Pericles have continuous signatures and were clearly designed for issue together.… William Jaggard succeeded to the printing business of James Roberts about 1608, and by 1617 had associated in it his son Isaac Jaggard.…The reprinting of 1619 was no doubt done in concert with Pavier who owned the copyright of five of the plays.…Presumably licence was obtained from Johnson for the use of Merry Wives of Windsor, and from Butter for that of King Lear. Of the other three, Midsummer-Night’s Dream was probably derelict, and Merchant of Venice may have been believed to be so. Blount’s registration of Pericles had already been overlooked, and there is nothing to show that Gosson had any copyright. The shortened imprints suggest that the title pages were originally meant for half-titles in a comprehensive volume, which would naturally begin with a general and more explicit title-page.…It was nothing to Pavier and Jaggard that they were reprinting bad texts and ascribing to Shakespeare plays that were not his. Perhaps Shakespeare’s fellows viewed [136] such proceedings with less equanimity. On May 1619 a letter was addressed by the Lord Chamberlain to the Stationers’ Company directing that none of the King’s men’s plays should be printed without some of their consents. Its exact terms are not preserved. But they appear to be recited in a letter of similar import written on 10 June 1637 by Philip Earl of Pembroke, then Lord Chamberlain, and brother of William Earl of Pembroke, who was Lord Chamberlain in 1619, asking the Stationers to stay publication of any King’s men plays without their consents. Pavier and Jaggard [137] may have issued all the ten plays. It is perhaps more likely that they had already abandoned the continuous signatures and perhaps the idea of a comprehensive volume, had separately issued those dated 1619, and had the rest ready in print.…Whatever the events of 1619, they can have left no enduring malice between the King’s men and the Jaggards, since it was again from their press that the collection…the First Folio came. From the facts of Pavier’s life—that he was at the time publishing religious books rather than plays and was just entering the governing councils of the Stationers’ Company—Johnson (1992, pp. 35–40) concludes that Jaggard, not Pavier, was the instigator of a straightforward scheme to put into print a collection of as many plays as were available, not a complete collection, and that Pavier collaborated by lending the copyrights on the plays he owned (WC, YT, SJO, H5, apparently Per.), by negotiating permissions for Lr. and Wiv., and by assuming or appropriating rights to the more-or-less derelict MV and MND. The faked imprints, Johnson suspects, were intended not to deceive the copyright holders but to avoid protest by the acting company or their agents, who ultimately may have concluded that plays being offered as old goods offered no competition to their planned new and improved Folio. Whether Pavier and Jaggard had conceived of their enterprise as a straightforward business venture, exactly why and when and how the players and other publishers may have objected to the project, what effect Pembroke’s letter may have had, and how William Jaggard and his son Isaac were persuaded to transfer their attentions to the larger project of the First Folio of 1623 have been much speculated upon and discussed; see Pollard (1909, pp. 100–4), Greg (1924, pp. 139–44), Greg (1955, pp. 9–17), Kirschbaum (1955, pp. 227–43), Greg (BEPD, 1957, 3:1107–8). Blayney (privately): Since Jaggard’s name did not appear on any of the 1619 quartos, there’s no reason to suppose that any of the players ever guessed that the culprit was the printer they knew best (because of his playbill monopoly). So that even if it had been the players who chose Jaggard to print the Folio (as it almost certainly wasn’t), we can’t assume that they’d forgiven him for a known transgression.…We shouldn’t credit them with knowing all that we know.

div.head: Order of Printing and Compositor Identification
div.p: Furness (ed. 1880, p. 357) thinks that Q2 was set up piecemeal by two compositors probably from two different shops, whose division of labor was marked by the short line 1910 on F4v, and by the growing carelessness of the first compositor evidenced by the grossest misprints near the end of that page. There was no change of compositors at this place, however.

Doran (1931, pp. 36–8), more rigorously, detects changes of style of setting, beginning with spelling changes in 4.6 (from 2430, I1r), more correct lining in 4.6 (from 2705, I4v), heavier punctuation in 4.5 (from 2402, I1r), and, in 4.7 (from K1r), both greater liberties in emending copy and the careless omission of several necessary words and a line (3102), all of which indicate a different compositor beginning work on sheet I(o). Up to that point the punctuation of Q2 is slightly heavier than that in Q1, more frequently ending a sentence in the middle of a speech with a period, a semicolon, or occasionally a colon. But in the latter portion of the play, The change from medium to heavy punctuation is marked especially by the increased use of colons and periods. [38] Colons instead of semicolons for breaking up long speeches begin to appear in the latter half of Act IV, Scene v. Moreover, on I1r, in 4.6 (at 2430) the name Glocester changes to Gloster and the speech prefix from (generally) Glost. to Glo. for the rest of the play except for one instance of Glocester to fill out a prose line to the margin (3061). Van Dam (1935, p. 39 n.), arguing that the same compositor may have had a change in mood, is the first of many unwisely to dismiss or ignore Doran’s demonstration of two Q2 compositors.

Although Williams (1953, p. 458) proposes on the basis of spelling tests that Jaggard’s Folio Compositor B set Q2 by himself before going on to set F1 Lr. by himself four years later, he finds troubling discrepancies in the quality of work which he can only explain as reflecting F1 copy. The basis of his comparison was wrong, however, since, as would eventually be discovered, Compositor B was only one of two compositors of F1 Lr., and probably had nothing to do with Q2 Lr. Kable (1967, pp. 235 ff.; 1968, pp. 131 ff.)’s extends Williams’s faulty premises beyond Q2 Lr., asserting that all of the Pavier quartos were set by Compositor B. As a result, Kable’s study of compositorial preferences in the spelling of more than 500 words throughout the Pavier quartos—his overwhelming evidence of B’s work—confuses the spellings of more than one man, none of whom was necessarily Compositor B. The misidentification has led to misguided characterizations of both the Pavier and the Folio compositor, e.g. Prosser (1981, p. 161).

Three studies dispensed with the notion that Lr. and the other Pavier editions were all set by (later) Folio Compositor B. Andrews (1971), by studying exhaustively the differences in prose and verse lineation, number of substantive variants, punctuation, and spelling between the first eight and the last three quires of Q2 Lr., confirmed Doran’s hypothesis that a second compositor had set the latter part of the play. Eventually (27 Dec. 1973, p. 5) he came to concede that his Compositor B might not be Folio Compositor B. Blayney (1972, pp. 182 ff.), after reviewing the names of compositors (the five known Folio compositors A–E and possible others) in Jaggard’s shop, cautions that it is impossible to assume that any one of them worked on both the Pavier quartos and the Folio. From discrepancies in spelling preferences between Q2 and F Lr. he further concludes (p. 193), It would appear to be a valid inference that compositor B did not set the Pavier Quartos—at least not in entirety. From a definite pattern of alternating skeletons in the first nine plays Blayney makes the further inference that the Pavier quartos were composed throughout by (p. 202) simultaneous setting of alternate sheets by different compositors, if by compositor may be meant a series of stints by more than one man. Stone (1980, p. 137) adds confirming evidence: Pages [of F Lr.] set by compositor B…all show a punctuation approximating much less closely to that of Q2 than pages set by Compositor E. Howard-Hill (1982, p. 16) notes that in sheets I–L of Q2 the compositor changed Q1 copy Glost. to Glo. 29 times, but in the same places in F [2430–2732] Compositor B set his characteristic Glou.

The probable order of printing was normal and is that found throughout the Pavier quartos: the quires were printed in alphabetical order, and the outer forme was printed first. Evidently A(o) was printed first, because parts of its title page (A1) were reused on A2; and in quires B, G, H, and K certain type breakages in the running titles first appear in the inner forme but not in the (previously printed) outer forme.

Andrews (1971) records in detail the compositorial preferences in the first eight and the last three quires of Q2 Lr. Compositor 3 (Andrews’s B), who set the latter pages, aggressively corrects erroneously lined verse and prose, and his attempts are more often than not successful. He is responsible for at least twice as many changes of punctuation and substantive alterations as his predecessors were, and his spelling preferences are quite different. The habits and preferences of Compositors 1 and 2, on the other hand, are quite similar. When Andrews’s data for his composite Compositor F (who is assumed to have set all of A–H) are divided between the actual Compositors 1 and 2, only slight differences are discernible: Compositor 1 is more ready to reline faulty verse: 11 passages of 26 lines to Compositor 2’s 4 passages of 7 lines. Similarly Compositor 1 is somewhat freer to make substantive alterations: changes toward greater formality (5 to his fellow’s 3), added words (9 to 5), added phrases (2 to 0), added stage directions and a speech prefix (4 to 2), and deliberate omissions (4 to 1). In each category Compositor 1’s changes outnumber Compositor 2’s, for overall totals of 24 to 11 changes respectively, each in about one-third of the play. There are also noticeable differences in the way they spell a few words: Compositor 1 spells eye by its variant spelling eie 13 times, Compositor 2, three times. Compositor 1 changes ile to Ile once, Compositor 2 five times. Compositor 1 uses young 6 times and yong once; Compositor 2 uses only yong, 3 times. On the whole, however, the two men seem to be very similar in their habits and preferences—not surprisingly if they worked in the same shop under the eye of the same master.

div.head: The Third Quarto (1655)
div.p: The third and last 17th-c. quarto of Sh.’s Lr. did not appear until a quarter-century later, during Cromwell’s interregnum, when the public theaters had been closed and dismantled. Its entrance in the Stationers’ Register for 4 Apr. 1655 is transcribed by Greg (BEPD, 1:63; cf. 1:338) as follows:

quote.p: Mr. Wm. GilbertsonEntred for his Copie by Vertue of an Assignmt und[er] the hand & seale of Edward wright the [3] bookes or Copies following.vizt.
1 The Tragicall history of King Leire, & his 3. Daughters.…to wch. assignmt, the hand of Mr. Norton warden is Subscribed.js. vjd. [E 339].

div.p: Q3 appeared in the same year with the following title page (cf. Greg, BEPD, 1:400):

quote.p: M. William Shake-speare, | HIs | True Chronicle History of the life | and death of King Lear, and his | three Daughters. | With the Vnfortunat life of Edgar, | sonne and heire to the Earle of Glocester, and | his sullen and assumed humour of TOM | of Bedlam. | As it was plaid before the Kings Maiesty at Whit-Hall, vp-|on S. Stephens night, in Christmas Hollldaies. | By his Maiesties Servants, playing vsually at the | Globe on the Bank-side. | [ornament] | LONDON.| Printed by Jane Bell, and are to be sold at the East-end | of Christ-Church. 1655.

div.p: Jane Bell, who had inherited her husband’s business, printed this work under the misapprehension that she held copyright to Sh.’s Lr. Kirschbaum (1938, pp. 308–11; cf. 1959, pp. 247–9) explains the confusion: though Butter must have sold to the publishers of F1 and F2 the right to print Sh.’s play (perhaps first as Q2), Jane Bell also published it in 1655. This was probably an unwitting infringement of copyright, due to her confusing the old King Leir (1605) and Lear. The widow of Edward White assigned Leir to Edward Allde on 29 June 1624. It passed posthumously to his son-in-law Richard Oulton on 22 April 1640, and its title was misspelled in the Stationers’ Register as Lear. Jane Bell came into possession of this copyright, and mistakenly supposed she had the right to print Sh.’s play, not the old Leir. As Greg (1:338) notes, The copy is not included in the transfer from John Wright sen. to his brother Edward on 27 June 1646. Leir had not been reprinted since 1605. See also . Berger & Lander (1999, p. 402) wonder how readers in 1655 would have responded to the title page, which reproduces that of 1608: There was no king’s majesty; Whitehall would not have been used for theatrical events; and the Globe…had been pulled down in 1644.
Bartlett & Pollard (1939, pp. 50–1; cf. p. 130) identify 16 extant copies of the Bell quarto. There is no modern facsimile or edition.

Q3 is a copy of Q2. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xiii) notes its many senseless changes due to careless printing, giving a single example: the Q1/Q2 SD at 32, Sound a Sennet, becomes in Q3 Sunday [Sundry?] a Cornet. Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 358–9) is more severe: American gallantry suggests commendation of this edition, but candour hushes every syl-[359]lable of praise. It is a reprint, page for page, of Q2, and has almost reached the limit of incorrect typography. Walton (1971, pp. 103 ff.) lists some two dozen variants from Q1 and Q2, but not the following: 23 yeare/years, 97 heaue/haue, 378 too/to, 1638+3 feet Q1/fee Q2/see Q3 (which shows that Q3 was printed from Q2), 1893 all/and all, 2303+1 it/its, and 2865 be-met/be met. Four of Walton’s variants (at 73, 1804, 2426, 2945) also appear in F, but are so ordinary and insignificant that they hardly show F1’s or F2’s influence on Q3. Because the text of Q3 has no independent authority, its readings are recorded only occasionally, as curiosities, in the textual notes.

div.head: The First Folio (1623)
div.p:
On 8 Nov. 1623 the first comprehensive collection of Sh.’s plays, the First Folio, was entered in the Stationers’ Register (Book D, p. 69), as here transcribed in Greg (BEPD, 1:33; cf. 3:1109–12):
Mr. BlounteIsaak Iaggard.Entred for their Copie vnder the hands of Mr. Dor. Worrall and Mr. Cole warden Mr. William Shakspeers Comedyes Histories, & Tragedyes soe manie of the said Copies as are not formerly entred to other men. vizt. [Here follows a list of half the plays].

Edward Blount was co-publisher with Isaac Jaggard, who had recently taken over the printing business of his late father William. The Dr. Worrall who granted official license to publish was Thomas Worrall, chaplain to the Bishop of London, and George Cole was then Upper Warden for the Stationers. King Lear is not named in the entry because it had been formerly entred to other men, Nathaniel Butter and John Busby, in 1607. In F1 Lr. occupies sigs. qq2–ss3, pp. 283–309 of the section given to the tragedies. In all copies p. 308 (sig. ss2v) is misnumbered 38. Lee’s (1902) census of extant copies has been superseded by West (2003). All previous facsimiles, such as those of Lee (1902), Methuen (1910), and Kökeritz-Prouty (New Haven, 1954), have been superseded by Hinman’s (1968; 1996) synthetic facsimile assembled from the best pages of copies in the Folger Library. Wilson’s (1931) facsimile of Lr. alone, along with Vietor’s (Marburg, 1886; rev. 1892) parallel-text edition, has been superseded by Warren’s (1989) facsimiles of the single text of F1 and the parallel texts of Q1 and F.

div.head: Order of Printing and Compositor Identification
div.p: On the basis of spelling variants of a few common words, such as do/doe and go/goe, Satchell (1920, p. 352) discriminates two compositors at work in F1 as a whole; Willoughby (1932, pp. 55–6), using the same kind of evidence, thinks it probable that there were at least two more. Cauthen (1952–3, pp. 73 ff.), on similar evidence, asserts that all of Lr. was set by one man, now known as Compositor B, an idea that Walker (1953, p. 62) accepts; both are mistaken. Using a wider range of evidence—the centering of entrances and varying spellings of Gloster/Gloucester/Glouster, Williams (1953, pp. 451–6) distinguishes two compositors in Lr. Hinman (1957, pp. 3 ff.), using typographical evidence of distinctive types, rules, and headlines, as well as spelling preferences, identifies three more F1 compositors: C and D in the Comedies, and (pp. 4–5) a Compositor E who was responsible for not only the Folio texts of Tit. and most of Rom. (except for 2 pages by Compositor B, cc1 and the last half-page of Rom.), but also for significant parts of Tro., Ham., Lr., and Oth. In his great study of the printing of the whole of F1 (1963, 2:157, 270–93) Hinman makes his final, all but definitive assignments of pages of F1 Lr. to Compositors B and E. After Cairncross (1972, pp. 369 ff.) attempted to overextend E’s work throughout F1, Howard-Hill (1976) more carefully sifted his evidence and concluded (1977, pp. 14–19; 1980, pp. 158–9, 176) that it could support his re-attribution of 22 1/2 pages to Compositor E, as well as 3 additional pages, including ss1 and ss3 of Lr. These attributions were confirmed by Howard-Hill’s own typographical test of the internal spacing of commas within short lines, and are now generally accepted—see, e.g., Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 151 [not the erroneous summary on p. 154]).

Hinman established that Lr., like all other F1 plays, was set by formes from cast-off copy—i.e., copy marked with estimates of just what text would fit on each page of print, so that the pages could be set out of order. He distinguished two compositors, Compositor B, working at type-case y, and Compositor E, normally working at type-case x but ultimately moving to case y or a composite case. The order of the printing of quires and the distribution of work that Hinman outlines are as follows, except that pages marked with an asterisk are those reassigned to E by Howard-Hill. The double bar signifies an interruption of the work, during which Compositor B set the end of Rom. and twenty-one pages of Tim.; parentheses signify forme-mate pages from other plays than Lr., namely Ham. (qq1r-v) and Oth. (ss4v-6v); Oth. ss3v-4, set by E, would precede ss5 if it were included below.

The lines of Lr. set by each compositor are as follows:
Compositor B: 1–94 (qq2), 353–484 (qq3v), 735–863 (qq5), 1426–91 (rr1vb), 1618–1744 (rr2v), 1862–2738 (rr3v-rr6v). Total: 1425 typographic lines.
Compositor E: 95–352 (qq2v-qq3), 485–734 (qq4–qq4v), 864–1409 (qq5v-rr1v), 1492–1617 (rr2), 1745–1861 (rr3), 2739–3302 (ss1–ss3). Total: 1861 typographic lines.
Either B or E: 1410–25 (rr1v)

The casting-off of copy may have led to the occasional compression or stretching of the text to fit it within its pre-assigned pages, with consequent textual alterations. Page qq3v is a densely filled page lacking any of the customary white space before and after the two entrances and Edmund’s forged letter; its crowding has been suspected to be the cause for the shortening of a word and a phrase and the omission of three lines: see nn. 438, 446, and 427+1–+3. In the second column of qq5v, the generous use of white space, including the line of space wasted on Edgar’s exit, suggests the reverse, the stretching of copy to fill out the column; that may account for the setting of Curan’s prose in short lines of false verse, and the setting of one verse line as two: see nn. 929–32, 938–42, 961–2. In another crowded column on rr1, six lines of rhymed verse are compressed into three, but then as if in partial compensation a line of verse that could be turned over is set as two: see nn. 1322–7, 1333–4. At the end of page rr1v, filling out a very full column, the penultimate line of verse is set as two: see n. 1489–90. A very full rr2 may not be responsible for the omission of the names Lear, [Glo]ster, Kent, and Foole from the Exeunt at 1586 and for the lack of names after the Exeunt at 1613, since both instances reflect F’s normal style in this play. Near the end of page rr2v two Q words are omitted from a crowded line, spoiling meter: see n. 1733. At the beginning of a quite full page rr3 the compositor has set two short rhymed verses as one line: see n. 1746. The most egregious stretching of the text occurs on ss1, the last page of Lr. to be set; nine lines of verse are divided and set as eighteen, and one or two phrases may have been added to the text: see nn. 2745–9, 2816, 2826.

Compositor B was an experienced workman who set more lines of F1 than any other compositor, in 35 of the 36 plays. Hinman (1963, 2:513) found it pleasant to wonder if he was a John Shakespeare, son of a Warwick butcher, bound to William Jaggard in 1610 and freed in 1617. Because of anomalously inaccurate work on 1H4 analyzed early on by Walker (1954), he long had a reputation for habitual carelessness and high-handed freedom in altering his copy—an odd reputation for a man trusted with so much work. Werstine (1978) begins his rehabilitation, showing in Ado, LLL, MND, MV, Tit., Rom., and (later) Tro., all F1 plays set from lightly annotated quarto copy, a higher rate of substitutions than in 1H4 but a much lower rate of errors of omission or interpolation, and of semisubstantive changes and alterations in stage directions. He concludes (p. 253), Compositor B must lose his notoriety as a compositor unusually prone to take liberties with his copy, a judgment soon endorsed by Reid (1982, p. 337) and further supported by Werstine (1983).

As Hinman (1963, 1:392–5) shows, Lr. exhibits Compositor B’s essential identifying traits: an almost absolute preference for B’s spellings do, go, heere, and for the ou spellings of Glouster and Glou. Some of B’s other spelling and setting habits are detailed in Howard-Hill (1980, pp. 162–77), Werstine (1983, pp. 261–87), and Reid (1985). Many of these are significant only to distinguish him from other compositors, but some of the following traits might affect the nature of the text itself. According to Howard-Hill (1980, pp. 162–77), B has a clear preference for -ee- (hee’l, sheel, wee’l) and -l (in the foregoing, and they’l, you’l). B often uses contractions in short lines: abbreviated forms such as &, M., Rich., yu, ye, and yt appear in 40 lines on B’s pages throughout F. B strongly prefers to turn a long verse line around to the beginning of the next, with indentation, rather than turn it over or under into white space at the end of the line; he never does either of the latter in Lr. B hyphenates initial weak a (a-while), and liberally uses abbreviations or tittles for justification. B preferred x’th elisions in the Comedies, but in the Histories and Tragedies moved towards x’th’. B profusely uses monosyllabic endings in -ee (bee, hee, shee, wee, yee). In the tragedies B preferred (with only 4 exceptions) -oo- in too’t, doo’t, intoo’t, vndoo’t, etc. Taylor (1985, p. 21): B’s traits include sophistication of a to he, and expansions of…in’t to into’th. Werstine (1983, pp. 283–4): We might predict, on the basis of B’s rate of omission in other Folio plays that he would have omitted no more than four or so words from his stint on Lear.…[284] Compositor B probably did not omit even a single line from his copy for the Folio version (but see n. 427+1–+3).

Compositor E appears fairly late in the printing of F1; he did not work on the Comedies or Histories. He set most of Tit. and Rom., two initial pages of Tro., a half-page of JC, and at least one and possibly three additional pages of Ham. before commencing work on Lr., setting from quarto copy for the first three plays and probably from some kind of manuscript in the following three. From the facts that he begins by setting from quartos (not from more difficult manuscript copy), that he worked slowly, that his early work is full of errors, that practically everything he set was proofread more than once (since it contains stop-press corrections), and that he did not set complicated title pages and was often employed merely in distributing type, Hinman (1957, pp. 10–20; 1963, 1:200–26, 2:157, 272–81) concludes that he was a recent apprentice, and tentatively identifies him as John Leason, who was bound to Jaggard on 4 Nov. 1622. He would in the normal order of work, after setting qq2v, have set qq2 and then qq1v, respectively the title page of Lr. and the final page of Ham., both bearing printer’s ornaments and oversize type; from the fact that Compositor B set these pages instead of E, Hinman deduces that E was still too inexperienced to handle complicated typography. During an interruption of his stint on Lr. he set a number of pages of Oth., and after Lr. a few more pages on Oth., Ant., and Cym., in all cases probably setting from manuscript copy.

Compositor E’s preference for do, go, and heere was similar to that of his eventual partner and (probably) mentor, Compositor B, but as Hinman (1963, 1:392–5) and Bowers (1964, pp. 183–4) show, he was more likely to reproduce here from his copy. Hinman observes that E is absolutely constant in spelling Gloster and Glo. without a u. Howard-Hill (1980, p. 164) shows additionally that whereas Compositor B puts a space after a comma in a short line three times as often as not, Compositor E omits the space eight times as often as he includes it. Of his many other characteristics noted by Howard-Hill (pp. 162–77), the following might affect the nature of the text: E shares B’s clear preference for -ee- (hee’l, sheel, wee’l) and for -l- (in the foregoing, and in they’l and you’l), but uses -le 47 times to B’s 10. He seldom uses contractions or abbreviations in short lines. He strongly favors turning under long lines of verse, and does not turn them around to the next line, indented, as B does. E never hyphenates the initial weak a (as in a-while), and virtually never uses abbreviations or tittles for justification. In general E follows copy spellings of words for which he has no established spelling preference. He prefers the elided form x’th’ but unlike B occasionally sets xth’. He uses monosyllabic endings in -e almost exclusively (e.g., be, he, she, we, ye), and except for too’t prefers the short spellings do’t, into’t, vndo’t.

Comparing Compositor B’s and Compositor E’s alterations from known quarto copy for several F1 plays, Werstine (1983, pp. 263–71) assesses their relative kinds and rates of error. E is most given to literal errors, then substitutions, then omissions and interpolations, then transpositions. Neither E nor B makes many omissions, interpolations, or transpositions, but both make numerous substitutions, literal or otherwise. Two-thirds of E’s substitutions (118 of 174) are of a single letter (by deletion, addition, change, or transposition), suggesting he had difficulty reading his copy. Particularly striking among Compositor E’s literal substitutions are his frequent deletions and additions of final -s, accounting for one-third of his literal substitutions and one-fourth of his total substitutions. Compositor B makes this kind of change only 10 times; instead, he more usually substitutes words which are orthographically dissimilar…but similar in meaning. At least two-fifths (70) of E’s substitutions result in obvious nonsense, only about one-fifth of B’s do (so that his substitutions are harder to recognize without known copy). B sometimes adds a more difficult word, E always is dedicated to simplicity. Generally both compositors change only a single word. More than half (26 of 45) of B’s changes affect pronouns or pronominal adjectives, and copulas or auxiliary verbs, rather than (more important) nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs. One of six is a recollection of a word just set or an anticipation of a word about to be set.

Their least frequent kind of alteration is transposition; E transposed words once per 629 lines, B once per 409. Four of E’s nine transpositions make nonsense, none of B’s six does. Interpolations are comparatively rare; B’s are sophisticated, E’s naive, often nonsense, and more than half the time erroneous or unmetrical. B is more sensitive to verse, and three of his changes disguise errors in copy. Both changed only single words—pronouns, articles, linking or auxiliary verbs. Compositor B never added half-lines, adjectives, verbs, or expansions. (P. 270): Much in evidence in the Folio [1H4] are the effects of an apparent impulse to impose formal, balanced syntax upon colloquial and elliptical prose speeches—an impulse that cannot be detected elsewhere in Compositor B’s work, and so probably derives from the copy. Omissions are twice as frequent and far more serious in E’s work than in B’s. On six occasions B omits the first or last word(s) of a speech, to justify a line; E omits medial words carelessly for no apparent reason. Only two of B’s nine omissions disturb verse; twenty-four of E’s do so. E’s forty-six omissions include adjectives and adverbs and some verbs, as well as some inessential pronouns and prepositions; these are likely to be memorial errors, resulting from holding phrases in the mind while setting. B has few omissions. E omits several lines, three from eyeskip, B omits only one, excluding probable censorship.

From such figures one would expect that only a small portion of the hundreds of variants between Q1 and F1 Lr. are attributable to the F1 compositors, both of whom seem to have been generally competent and careful. Estimates of their accuracy in Lr. are especially difficult to make because virtually all attempts to attribute individual variants to them have until now been based on the doubtful premise that their copy was a marked-up exemplar of either Q1 or Q2—a known text against which their variants could be measured. If, as is now coming generally to be thought, their copy was instead a scribal manuscript containing differences from Q1 and Q2, many if not most of the F1 changes could easily derive from the scribe or his own unknown original, not from the compositors; in fact, many of the F1 variants seem more probably to derive from such a manuscript source than from marked-up printed copy (see ). Since the qualities of such a hypothetical manuscript can be known only inferentially and imperfectly, it is of little help in assessing the roles of Compositors B and E in shaping the text of Lr. At most one can record those instances where editors have suspected that F1 readings were the result of compositorial intervention, along with their reasons for thinking so; the line numbers in the two following paragraphs refer to the commentary notes where suggestions of such intervention are recorded.

In the case of Compositor B, he has been suspected of omitting words or phrases, often in order to justify a line, more often than Werstine’s figures would lead us to expect: he has been held responsible for the omission of a half-line (769), a phrase (2640+1), a pair of words (2288), individual words (60, 73, 459, 463, 1914, 2426, and 2572), and of letters either in order to shorten words (60, 404) or from oversight (9, 1995, 2035, 2319). Obversely, he is credited with adding words (463, 1980, 2194, 2544) or letters (1664, 2070, 2079). Of the considerable number of verbal substitutions attributed to him, only a few have involved substantial differences of meaning and are usually attributed to various kinds of misreading or errors of aural memory (421, 744, 755, 769, 823, 1428, 1914, 2285, 2369, 2380, 2516, 2530); he may, however, have mistakenly substituted one long passage instead of merely adding it (1631–1638+12), though that error is more likely to have been scribal. A number of his verbal substitutions are so indifferent or insignificant as to suggest either unconscious sophistication or scribal changes in the copy (738–40, 1660, 1710, 1935, 2228, 2453, 2563, 2596, 2647). Changes of punctuation (e.g., 2025, 2693, 2718), capitals (1951, 2248+3–+4), and italics (1880) are of course impossible to attribute to a compositor rather than a scribe, as are many of the more substantive changes.

Compositor E has been suspected of omitting four lines (527+1–+2, 1226+1, 2874+1) and possibly other lines and phrases (110+1, 1016, 1294+1–1296, 2838+1–+2, 2859+1, 2864+1–+2, 2981+1–+2, 2990+1), of failing to omit two lines (667–9), and of adding a line at 2936. He may have omitted words at 235, 527, 1008, 1266, 1634–8, 1828–9, and 2775, and letters at 194 and 3045. He may have substituted one word for another at 235, 247, 531, 628, 642, 867, 1007, 1016, 1183, 1603, 1790, 1844, 2743, 2783, 3028, 3084, 3159, 3210, and 3242, though some or most of these substitutions may have been scribal. Some of the above and several others may have been the result of words being carried in his memory as he set, such as 159, 328, 552, 1057, 1336. Eyeskip may have been involved in the reassigning of lines at 204, 628, and 1227, and simple misreading at 1026, 1151, 2871, and doubtless other places. Three kinds of changes do seem to be characteristic of his habits: the addition of -s or -es at 182–4, 530, 675, 727, 1263, 1270, 1828, 2966, 3029, 3033, 3084, and 3107; the omission of -s at 301, 329, 691, 1222–3, 1228, and 1409; and the substitution of your for you at 867, 929, 1407, 3217, and 3256. Without considering apparent errors of lining and punctuation, which might be scribal, it is possible to see at a glance that this relatively inexperienced compositor appears to be more prone to error than his partner Compositor B.

div.head: Press-Variants and Proof-Correction in F1
div.p: Tangible evidence of proof-correction in F1 exists in surviving proof-sheets bearing the corrector’s marks; some of these are noted by Greg (BEPD, 3:1112), and several are reproduced by Hinman (facs. 1968, pp. 910–23) from originals in the Folger Library. One such proof-page for Lr., sig. qq6v, p. 292 (Compositor E; conjugate with Ham. qq1r, p. 218, Compositor B) in Folger copy 48, is not reproduced in the Hinman facsimile but is in Blayney (1982, 1:240–1). Hinman (1950–1, pp. 145–53; cf. 1963, 1:233–5) also reproduces it (Pl. I) and discusses it in some detail: The changes called for are not numerous—only five in all [see below]. These changes were all made, and must have been made, indeed, before any large number of uncorrected [147] states had been printed off: 76 of the 82 copies examined (or about 92.7%) show the corrected state of this page. Hinman finds in the corrections no necessary reference to copy, since the errors are patently compositorial and the errors and their corrections are obvious. [151] The almost complete absence of correction from the Ham. page suggests that the proof-reader returned a sheet after correcting only one of its pages. Perhaps he gave a separate corrected sheet to each compositor, or was worried about inexperienced E. Hinman (1953, pp. 284–5): Most of the variants in the Folio do not imply reference to copy. There can be no doubt that the proof-reading for many of the Tragedies was primarily intended to eliminate obvious error rather than to guarantee the most faithful possible reproduction of Shakespeare’s text. The changes called for by the proof-reader are often extremely inconsequential, [285] and seldom indeed do they reflect reference to copy. He exemplifies this claim with press variants in Lr. sig. rr3r, p. 297, where among 9 variants the corrected skinso: ’tis is more corrupt than the uncorrected reading. Blayney (Hinman facs. 1968; 2nd ed., 1996, p. xxxi) agrees that in general throughout F1 corrections were made without reference to copy, but disputes Hinman’s estimate of their number: The claim that approximately 750…pages (including about half even of the pages set by E) were never proofed at all is entirely without foundation. If inking variants are excluded, 789 pages are not known to have been corrected at press—but as D. F. McKenzie pointed out in 1969 [pp. 42–9], Hinman overlooked the fact that it has always been customary to proofread all pages before beginning to print them. The only corrections that can usually be detected are changes made after uncorrected copies have already been printed…but the presence of press-variants can hardly be taken seriously as evidence that there had been no prior correction.

Hinman (1963, 1:227): At least two Folio formes [of Lr.] were corrected three different times in the course of their printing; several formes were twice corrected; and formes that were corrected once are very numerous. Werstine (1980, p. 133) believes that the Church copy at the Huntington Library shows a forme, qq1v:6, that was corrected not three but four times; but Blayney (Hinman facs., 1968; 2nd ed., 1996, p. xxxi) claims a misunderstanding owing to an error by Hinman: The first state of an inking variant at qq6b52 (TLN 1089) was wrongly described by Hinman as if a real variant ([1963,] vol. 1, p. 307), and neither of the copies in which he claimed to have found the reading was accessible to Werstine in 1980.

Doran (1931, p. 94) correctly records an apparent press variant in rr3—1860 foule/foole—in the Halliwell-Phillipps 1876 facs. Blayney (privately) identifies this variant as one of many resulting from retouching of pages photographed from the Staunton facs. of 1866. In the Hinman facs. (1968) and Warren facs. (1989), the second o is apparently simply a u bent almost closed at the top, looking like an o. McManaway (1977–8, pp. 19 ff.) reports that John Crow found another sheet with further corrections on p. 297 (sig. rr3) of the Church copy of F1 at the Huntington Library. Some of these corrections are not recorded by Hinman 1:310–11. Hinman’s 1778 good/good is not here, nor 1839 T aitor/Traitor; new here is 1782 Keut/Kent and 1834 Q ag-/Quag-. 1843 ag ai ne remains unchanged in all sheets, apparently. Blayney (1982, pp. 239 ff.) finds in the Huntington Church copy most of Hinman’s variants, but comments on several: in 1777 Foole, the F and second o are faint; in 1778 good there are only improperly inked letters, not a variant; in 1782 Kent, what McManaway thought was an inverted u was only a clogged n which was cleaned or replaced; in 1834 Quag-, contrary to McManaway, a faint u was only leveled, not replaced; in 1843 ag ai ne, the word was marked for correction but was unchanged; and in 1851 Traitor there is only a faint r. For a correction possibly gone wrong, see n. 1380. Werstine (1993, pp. 235–7) points to an apparent variant in rr4v, 2165 he/be; but there and in the Hinman facs. (1968) there seems to be only a bent or clogged letter.
