3279 thouno thou no
3282 this, looke this? Looke
The e in the second word of the stage direction He dies. in [3283] was evidently pulled.…Hence we find He di s.…He dis.…[312] H edis.…Hedis.…and so on. Clearly…these are only accidental variants.
(P. 325): Summary: thirteen pages proof-corrected; 51 variants in all, [50] of them in material set by E.

Howard-Hill (1980, pp. 177–8): Unusual attention was given at least to the superficial correctness of E’s formes. His 50 variant pages [in F1] contain 300 press-variants whereas B’s 17 variant pages provide only 39 variants, many of which are textually insignificant.…[178] Although compositor E came to be entrusted with manuscript copy, it remained the practice in Jaggard’s printing-house to read E’s pages more frequently and more thoroughly than those set by other compositors.

div.head: Features of the F1 Text
div.p: All descriptions of the F1 text of Lr. inevitably become comparisons with the Q1 text. To begin with, Q1 and F1 are of different lengths, though their differing lineations of verse and prose, and their different widths of the prose margins, make an accurate numerical comparison difficult. In the Warren facsimile (1989) the through-line-numbering of the Q1 text ends at 2986 and of the F1 text at 3302, though in fact Q1 is the longer text. These are counts of the numbers of typographical lines in the original editions; most line-counts are based on modern edited texts, particularly those of the Globe edition of 1864 and the Riverside edition of 1974, since these were the bases of the Bartlett and Spevack concordances respectively; in these texts the original erroneous prose and verse lineation has been corrected. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 3), who edits both Q and F texts separately, counts 3063 lines in Q and 2890 lines in F. The main differences between the two texts are the absence of almost a tenth of the Q1 lines from F1 and the presence of more than a hundred lines in the Folio that are missing from Q1. Using the text of the first Cambridge edition (1866), Koppel (1877, p. 70) estimates that Q contains 287 more lines than are in F1, and that F1 contains 110 lines absent from Q1. Furness (ed. 1880, p. 359) gives the remarkably different estimates of 175 and 50 lines respectively. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxiv): My count gives to the Folio, over the Quarto, 84 words scattered singly or in pairs, 35 half-lines of three to six syllables each, and 88 full lines.…This substantially agrees with Koppel’s computation. The Quartos exceed the Folio by some 50 scattered words, 25 half-lines, and 242 metrical lines. Warren (1978, p. 95) counts 283 Q-only lines, and Blayney (1982, p. 1) counts 285 and 115 lines unique to each text. Weis (loc. cit.) computes percentages of difference: out of a grand total of 5,953 lines some 400 lines, or approximately one-fifteenth or 7 per cent of the two texts together (10 per cent of Q and 3.5 per cent of F, a comparatively small percentage of the textual material). All agree that the overall difference of length between Q1 and F1 is, in an edited text, about 175 lines. In this edition the Q-only material is enclosed by half-brackets within the text, and F-only material (except for minor particles) is enclosed within asterisks. Possible explanations for the presence of lines in one text but not the other are given in separate sections below.

The second notable difference between Q1 and F1 is a large number of verbal variants between them, many of them indifferent, some of them quite significant. Walker (1953, p. 60) counts rather more than eight hundred and fifty verbal variants between the quarto and Folio texts, excluding those which are manifestly nonsense; Walton (1971, p. 275 n.) estimates about 930 variants. Wells (1983, p. 6): More than 850. In fact, a computer-assisted count of all substantive verbal changes between Q1 and F1, including minor variants of number, verb agreement, word order, alternative grammatical forms, alternative names for characters in the accessories, location of stage directions in a different line, etc., yields a total of 1284, in addition to another 104 differences between Q2 and F1. Doran (1931, pp. 39 ff.) characterizes these and other differences: Although in [F1] there are a number of single words which are evidently wrong but whose correct meaning cannot be ascertained without reference to the reading in the first quarto, there are no passages which as wholes are unintelligible. In the first quarto, on the other hand, besides many more errors in single words, there are also a number of passages of several lines in length which would defy elucidation if the corrected sheets or the folio did not furnish a clue to their meaning. Some unintelligible passages are to be found even in the corrected formes. There is a good deal of faulty punctuation in the first quarto, but very little in the folio.…Metrical irregularity is much more frequent in the first quarto than in the folio. The printing of verse, with a few exceptions[, is] correct in the folio.…In both texts there are a few lines of prose (not the same ones) set up as verse. The first quarto presents a continuous text, not divided into acts and scenes; the folio text is so divided. The stage directions are more complete and more precise in the folio. In short, the folio is by far the more regular and satisfactory text of the two.

div.head: The Absence of Q1 Passages
div.p: The following are the most significant omissions from F of Q-only passages, usually of a half-line or more, all of them discussed in detail in the commentary notes: 110+1, 427+1–+3, 473+1–+6, 522+1–+4, 527+1–+2, 669+1–+11, 744+1–+4, 857+1 (see n. 857–9), 1220+1–+4, 1226+1, 1294+1 (see n. 1294+1–1296), 1622–1622+8, 1638+1–+12 (see also n. 1631–1638+12), 2014+1–+30, 2056+1–+4, 2056+5–+18, 2176+1–+9, 2248+1–+5, 2303–2303+17, 2307+1–+6, 2311+1–+8, 2347+1–+56, 2640+1, 2723+1, 2775+1–+2, 2783+1–+4, 2838+1–+2, 2843+1–+11, 2859+1–+3, 2864+1–+2, 2868–2868+5, 2874+1, 2981+1–+2, 2990+1, 2997+1–+5, 3051+1, 3058+1, 3168+1–+18. These passages are collected (in edited form, without TLN) in Halio (ed. 1992, pp. 293–309). It will be seen that only about 32 of these (typographic) lines are missing from Act 1 (2–925), about 6 from Act II (927–1613), about 77 from Act III (1615–2176+9), about 114 from Act IV (2178–2843+11), and about 39 from Act V (2845–3002). This total of about 268 typographic lines amounts to some 285 lines in an edited text in which verse lining has been corrected. While it is conceivable that a few of these almost 300 lines unique to Q1 were omitted from F1 by accident or oversight on the part of the printer, the possibility that all or most of them were omitted for that reason has always seemed (except to van Dam, 1935, pp. 75 ff.), improbable in the extreme. For that reason the two most usual explanations for their absence from F are that they are lines from an early version, identical or similar to that found in Q, which were subsequently cut from the F text, or that they represent later additions, in Q, to an early draft similar to the text found in F.

The latter possibility was advanced when it was more widely believed that Q represented the playtext performed at court in 1606. Thus Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxviii f.) believes that what appear to be F’s omissions of passages are, instead, useful and functional later additions to the promptbook which was copy for Q1. These Q-only passages without exception, round out the scene, give the players good acting speeches, or serve to explain the situation and fill rude gaps in the narrative which their non-existence would occasion. Most of them are in Shakespeare’s style.…There are twenty-six passages and bits of quick dialogue which seem to be padding supplied to meet the clamors of the actors who craved fuller parts with more stage opportunities. (P. xxix): Edgar gets three generous pads, and Albany gets three interpolations [in 4.2]…rounding Albany’s character and emphasizing the nobleness of his nature.…The Bastard’s speeches are expanded in four places…but not importantly. Lear, Gloucester, Goneril, Kent, the Doctor, and the Captain have [in Q] among them eleven short additions to their parts, nearly all of which help the stage business, while none of them suggests any special cause for omission [from F] in a revision for the sake of abridging the action.…The Gentleman’s account of Lear in the storm [1622+1–+8] is so in keeping with the whole context that it is hard to conceive of it as an afterthought [which Adee thinks it is]. Kent’s allusion to the secret emissaries of France [3.1; 1638+1–+12],…Goneril’s speech [4.2; 2307+1–+6], the [xl] entire scene [4.3; 2347+1–+56]…between Kent and the Gentleman,…and the subsequent short dialogue between the same characters [4.7; 2843+1–+11], are explanatory and read like our modern carpenter’s scenes. If, as seems probable, these passages were not in the first sketch of the drama, it is not easy to see how the audience could well have understood the threatening movement to place Cordelia and her alien husband, the French king, on the British throne. I believe them to be accretions upon the original draft, added after the first [public] performances [in 1605] for the same reasons that Albany’s part was swelled, to emphasize the danger of the French invasion, and to point the patriotic justice of its defeat by British arms, even though the catastrophe entailed the death of Cordelia and Lear.…[The revisions] professed due reverence to patriotism and sturdy Anglican teachings by bestowing the crown in the natural order of things on Albany, a native prince, whose moral worth and kinglike qualities had been steadily kept in sight and in constant increase [through Q additions].…[If] the exquisite description [in 4.3] of Cordelia’s sweetly mingled love for her father and grief [xli] for his woes…be, as I think, an aftermath, Heaven be praised, for it is one of the ripest and richest on English pages.…

p.quote: It may be objected that this theory involves the lengthening of the play during its stage life, whereas the normal course is toward curtailment.…The drama is not, in fact, much expanded by the added passages. It is not an excessively long tragedy, as things ran in those days.…Eight of [Sh.’s] plays…are longer.…[xlii] I conclude, therefore, that the Folio is in substantial accord with the first manuscript sketch, and that the two hundred lines or so by which the Quarto exceeds it are in the main legitimate acting additions.

div.p: Similarly Perrett (1904, p. 219): By far the greater number of lines in Q1 after IV, i, which are not given by F1, are of later date than the F1 text. Q1 appears to represent a revision of the play by Shakespeare himself, at least in IV, ii; IV, iii; IV, iv (Gent. changed to Doct.); IV, vii and V, i. Further than this I am not prepared to go at present, but I hope to return at some future time to a question no less difficult than interesting.

The argument now seems wrong on many counts. Adee names one of its main weaknesses: that normally, during initial preparations for staging and after experience in performance, one would shorten a long play, not add hundreds of lines to it. Nor would it have been usual to add these lines mainly in the latter half of the play, the usual place for cutting to speed the action to its close. Lr. may not be an excessively long tragedy for Sh., but it is much longer in both its Q and F versions than the vast majority of contemporary plays, and in the opinion of a growing number of scholars was too long for performance within the two to three hours normal in the public theaters. Moreover, by general agreement (see ) the text printed in Q could not easily have served as a performance text; its stage directions are both inadequate and sometimes untheatrical, and the manuscript was apparently often illegible. F on the other hand does show considerable preparation for performance; if its more careful stage directions, verse lineation, and punctuation were added to the first manuscript sketch after the Q version had been performed at court, thus producing a second, later acting version, one would expect to find the 300 lines already added to improve Q also present in F, but they are absent.

Finally, many passages in F show alteration of the lining and sense such as would result from the excision of the Q-only lines, whereas there is not evidence in Q of awkward patching to accommodate the Q-only lines as additions to its original text. In F, 474 follows 473 abruptly and stands alone as a short line; it is less likely to have been written that way originally than to result from the excision of the six lines (473+1–+6) which appear seamlessly in Q (Halio, ed. 1992, p. 266). At 829–30 the absence of two Q-only phrases produces in F a pentameter line consistent with its context, Q prose relined as F verse; one would have had to omit the Q phrases to produce the verse lineation in F, whereas there would have been no obvious need to add them to the prose in Q. Lines 1220–4, like much of the verse in Q, are mislined as printed, but in fact if properly lined they form regular pentameters. The absence from F of Q’s 1220+1–+4, however, requires the addition of three unnecessary expletives to restore the pentameter, fairly clear evidence of a cut and subsequent adjustment of meter in F (Duthie, ed. 1949, pp. 174–5). Q’s lines 2783+1–+4 appear in a passage of regular meter; their absence from F is followed by three lines which rearrange unmetrically the next two and a half verses found in Q. The most likely explanation is that after the original Q lines were cut from the F text, the next few remaining Q lines were redistributed in order to fill or disguise the gap left by a cut ending in mid-line (Stone, 1980, p. 118 n.); it is unlikely that the reverse happened—that several irregular lines now stand in F as originally written, and that they were regularized in Q by the addition, not of a needed word or two, but of several new lines. Other examples might be given.

Similarly, the absence of Q lines from F is sometimes accompanied by a gap in the sense. Chambers (1930, 1:467): F omissions…leave lacunae at [669+1–+8, 744+1–+4, 2303–2303+17, 3168+1–+18]. In the first of these, a question about sweet and bitter fools is left without a reply, followed instead by an unrelated riddle about eggs and crowns; in the second a transition is missing between Lear’s question about who he is and his next about what is Goneril’s name; in the third, the vituperations of Goneril and Albany seem disconnected and lacking sufficient context to occasion them; and in the fourth, the absence of Edgar’s account of banished Kent’s disguise and services to Lear leaves without preparation Albany’s instant acceptance of his sudden appearance a few moments later. Among other non sequiturs is that bracketing the absent mock-trial (2014+1–+30) in 3.6; Lear’s wish in 2013–14 to attack an unnamed them with burning spits seems not mad or extreme enough to occasion Edgar’s and Kent’s aghast remarks at 2115–19, and only Regan remains of the them, Goneril being named only in the missing lines. In 3.1, the absence of Kent’s instructions to the Gentleman to meet and report to Cordelia at Dover (1638+1–+12) results in his being sent, at the end of the scene, to find her at no specified place for no stated reason except to show her Kent’s ring. In all these cases the apparently fragmented F sequences are less likely to represent an original version (later smoothed out in Q) than a subsequent version resulting from inexpert cutting.

Moreover, the majority of the large passages missing from F have seemed to most commentators to be inherently undramatic: more expository, narrative, descriptive, sententious, poetic, or ornamental than actively developing characters or plot. As such they have seemed the kind of material more likely to have been cut from a long play (F) than added to it (in Q). Knight (ed. 1840, p. 393): The poet sternly resolved to let the effect of this wonderful drama entirely depend upon its action. Doran (1931, p. 70): The bulk of the omissions from the folio can be shown to have been carried out according to a definite purpose of abridgement. A number of passages, including one whole scene, which are expository, non-dramatic, and nonessential to the working out of the plot have been omitted. Bibliographical proof of the omission of [4.3] from the folio text after the [playbook] transcript was made is the survival of Septima in the scene heading; see n. 2743. Chambers (1930, 1:467): In the main we probably have to do with ordinary theatrical cutting. It is not unintelligent, affecting chiefly narratives of episodes in France and elsewhere away from the main action ([1638+1–+12]; [2307+1–+6]; [2347+1–+6]; [2868–2868+4]; [3168+1–+18]) and some dialogue between servants ([2176+1–+9]; [2843+1–+11]), a bit of poetic description ([1622–1622+8]), Edgar’s sententious rhymes ([2056+5–+18]), some interchanges of amenities between Albany and Goneril ([2303–2303+17, 2307+1–+6]). The chief loss is in iv.3, where the introduction, if only in narrative, of Cordelia is important to bridge the interval between her earlier and later appearances. Wilson’s (facs. 1931, p. [iii]) suspicion that the difference in length…suggests as least the possibility that the Folio was connected with one theatre and the Quarto with the other has won no support.

The notes on the omitted passages listed above propose many kinds of reasons for their omission, but simple shortening of a long play is a recurrent one, especially if the omitted material may be considered redundant or otherwise unnecessary. At 1622–1622+8 the Gentleman’s description of Lear defying the storm repeats what is enacted a few moments later. Lear’s mock-trial of his daughters (2014+1–+30) may have been cut to reduce what is one of several scenes of his madness. Kent’s and Edgar’s meditations (2056+1–+4, 2056+5–+18) at the close of 3.6 comment on the action without advancing it much. The same might be said of the discussion of the servants at the end of 3.7 (2176+1–+9) after Gloucester’s blinding. Edgar’s catalogue of the fiends tormenting him (2248+1–+5) is not necessary, and it is hard to imagine Sh. or someone else returning to Harsnett to supply it in Q. The omissions from Albany’s interchanges of amenities with Goneril in 4.2 (2303–2303+17) are largely philosophic generalities which do not affect the outcome of the argument, and Goneril’s further abuse of Albany in the same scene (2307+1–+6) is mainly reassertion of her earlier contempt. The poetic descriptions in 4.3 (2347+1–+56) mainly help to reintroduce Cordelia, who will speak and act for herself in the next scene, and the reportage of ongoing activity is not needed to follow the ensuing events. Kent’s conversation with the Gentleman at the end of 4.7 (2843+1–+11) is all expository gossip, none of it essential and part of it false. In 5.1 Albany’s brief explanation of his motives for fighting is missing, but as ruler of half of Britain he will have to fight the French invasion in any case. In 5.3 Edmund’s account of his actions (2997+1–+5) is not needed to justify them. Finally, Edgar’s long account of his meeting with Kent may seem too much like the static exposition of the classical nuntius, impeding the denouement unnecessarily, especially since the audience is already familiar with most of Kent’s aid to Lear. Moriarty (1913, p. 457): In an effort to improve the dramatic sequence a master in stagecraft would cut out even passages that had undoubted excellence. Taylor (1980, pp. 29–30): What is cut is eminently [30] dispensable, particularly backward-looking reflection on what has happened.

One may still insist that the omission of any or all of these passages for theatrical abridgement is an artistic mistake, as many commentators have done—e.g., the Clarkes (ed. 1864, 1:xxxvi; ed. 1868, 3:459), Herford (ed. 1899, 9:5), Muir (1983, pp. 101–4: savage, they damage [the play] fatally; rpt. 1985, p. 66: deplorable), Brown (1988, pp. 163–5; cf. ed. 1996, esp. nn. 3146–62, 3168+1–+18, 3184, 3192–3215), Clare (1995, pp. 46–7). For that reason some of these critics and others—e.g., Theobald (ed. 1733), Malone (ed. 1790), and Verity (ed. 1897) in numerous notes, Delius (1876, pp. 125, 138–40), Fleay (1879, p. 120), and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 21)—assert that the cuts were probably made not by Sh. but by members of his company. The question whether F1 represents a thoroughgoing revision by Sh. himself is discussed in a separate section below.

Of the remaining possible reasons for the F1 omissions, including adjustments in characterization, thematic emphasis, or stage effect, all are noted in the relevant commentary notes. A common suggestion is either official censorship by the Master of the Revels or self-censorship by Sh. or his company. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:370; summarized in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 360) believes that the censorship occurred late, at about the time of the death of James (in 1625). Most propose censorship much closer to the date of composition, concerning (in 473+1–+6) strained relationships between James and his son Henry, or between James and his queen Anne, or between Lady Howard and Essex; or the midlands food shortages of 1608; or (in 669+1–+11) monopolies and misbehaving courtiers; or (in 1638+1–+12) the neglect of port defences, and here as well as in 2307+1–+6 and 2868–2868+4 the notion of war with France; or (in 2010–12) James’s liberal granting of knighthoods; or (in 2014+3) his attraction to boys; or (in 2014+1–+30) false justicers and the question of equity jurisdiction. Censorship has seemed possible to Chambers (1930, 1:467), Doran (1931, pp. 135–6), Greg (1955, p. 387), and others, but is doubted by Stone (1980, p. 125 n.), who thinks that F represents a revised version dating from ca. 1616–20. Taylor (1983, pp. 75 ff.), wishing to attribute F changes whenever possible to authorial revision, attempts to show that at most the omission from F of one speech (669+1–+11) and one additional word (at 459) can reasonably be attributed to Sir George Buc. This argument has been controverted by Patterson (1984, pp. 58–73) who, arguing that Lear is ambiguously both type and anti-type of James (especially on the question of Union), finds in the play’s ambivalence a sign that the writer is working under constraint, and that Sh. felt required to remove allusions to kingly folly, disorders in the state, knightings, monopolies, banquets, and invasion from France. Clare (1990, pp. 132 ff.) is inclined generally to agree, though emphasizing official pressure more than self-censorship, and assuming (improbably) that the F1 revisions predate the 1606 performance before the king. Worden (1987, pp. 45–62) is skeptical about the impact of censorship, which often ignored blatant topical allusions, a point also made by Halio (ed. 1992, p. 78 n.). Foakes (1993, pp. 98–9) apparently considers censorship at best a remote possibility: James I himself and his officials would surely have seen a general analogy with himself in an elderly monarch [James was forty years old, Lear eighty] whose hobby was hunting, whose retinue was [99] distinctive in its foregrounding of a Fool, who during the central acts is evidently insane, and whose authoritarian views ultimately destroyed himself and his entire family. James did not go insane, or destroy himself and his family, and we have no evidence that he was disturbed by seeing the [censored?] play; but it does not seem likely that a censor would overlook the larger analogy and merely tinker by removing a few passages and references to France. The supposed excision of references to France was not thorough and may have been incidental rather than systematic (see nn. 1638+1–+12, 2347+1–+56); or it may have represented self-censorship (Halio, ibid.). Such mild and general satire and local allusion as occurs in Lr., if offensive at all, is not the kind of outright heresy, impudence, or sedition that Buc was usually watchful for. Indeed Gurr (2004, pp. 182–4) argues that Lr., chosen by the Master of the Revels (the censor himself) for Christmas performance in 1606, was the most explicitly loyal of all the plays Shakespeare wrote for the company’s royal patron, that it flaunted the company’s allegiance and caused no uproar. He does not suggest that any of the F1 omissions were the result of censorship for that performance, but points rather to an absence of censorship. Murphy (1987, pp. 56 ff.) agrees that Q Lr., with its reminders from Harsnett of the sufferings of persecuted English Catholics, would have been wholly congenial in 1606 to James’s intentions of regalian toleration of loyal Catholics, but that by 1614 (after Sh.’s retirement) the King’s Men might have decided to self-censor parts of scenes 3.6 through 4.3 which (p. 57) had become dangerously topical between 1610 and 1614 after Lr. (p. 63) had become entangled with seditious players [in Yorkshire, 1609–10; see , ], persons with close ties to the Gunpowder Plot [Sir John Yorke and Sir William Ingleby], and a Star-Chamber case [1614] of sensational import.

The many other possible reasons for the omission of Q lines from F are given in the commentary notes. The absence of most of the shorter passages, of a line or two, has been attributed by one critic or another to compositorial or scribal error; but as Werstine has shown (above), it is unlikely that either Compositor B or Compositor E was responsible for so many omissions. Doran (1931, p. 69): No omissions from F are provably accidental; conceivable candidates are 770, 1226+1, 2775+1–+2, 2838+1–+2, 2859+1–+3, 2864+1–+2, 2874+1. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:370; summarized in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 360) suggests omissions due to the obscurity which speedily falls on local allusions, or allusions to passing events, of which no play of Shakespeare contains more; both outdated topicality (see nn. 473+1–+6, 2248+1–+5) and general obscurity of language (see nn. 2640+1, 2723+1, 2783+1–+4, 2997+1–+5) have repeatedly been proposed. Tieck also proposes reduction due to the lack of an adequate actor; for suggestions that altered casting led to changes in the text, see nn. 2176+1–+9, 2303–2303+17, 2775+1–+2, 3051+1. Knight (ed. 1840, p. 393) imagines cutting to give an actor relief from the physical exertions of playing the role of Lear, and Muir (1983, p. 112) speculates upon cutting to reduce a cast on tour. Stroup (1961, p. 128): F’s cutting of over 300 lines may well indicate a falling off of popularity of certain roles, especially those of Edgar, the Fool and Cordelia. Of these some forty-two lines are taken from Edgar, including some of his best rhymes; some twenty-eight from the Fool; and some ninety from Kent and a Gentleman, many of which deal with Cordelia. Tieck (op. cit., p. 371) further suggests a desire to simplify the plot, and to avoid complications; on possible intentions to remove improbabilities or contradictions by cutting, see nn. 2176+1–+9, 2347+1–+56, 3058+1, among others. Finally, some passages may have been cut because they were found not to work: the mock trial was too close to comic, 4.3 was too sentimental, etc.

div.head: Passages Not in Q1
div.p: The following are all of the F-only lines and words significant enough to have been discussed by commentators; only particles of no real importance and SDs have been omitted from the list. Their typography, including the spacing on the page and their enclosing asterisks, reflects that of the text of this edition. They are assembled here to enable an easy overview of their nature and extent; critical discussions of their provenance, significance, language, etc. are represented in the commentary notes, and are summarized below.

lg.l: while we
Vnburthen’d crawle toward death. Our son of Cornwal,
And you our no lesse louing Sonne of Albany,
We haue this houre a constant will to publish
Our daughters seuerall Dowers, that future strife
May be preuented now.
(Since now we will diuest vs both of Rule,
Interest of Territory, Cares of State)
and with Champains rich’d
With plenteous Riuers,
The Vines of France, and Milke of Burgundie,
Striue to be interest.

div.p: The fact that a great many of these passages are only a word or two long has encouraged the suspicion that they were accidentally omitted from Q by reporters or printers and were restored to F from either the original or another manuscript. Such an explanation is less common today than it was in the late nineteenth and first half of the twentieth century, when the text of Q1 was widely believed to be corrupted by shorthand or memorial reconstruction (see. e.g., Chambers, 1930, 1:467; Walker, 1953, p. 51; Greg, 1955, pp. 375, 381). In any case, in a few instances the loss of a word or phrase or even of a line or more may still be thought to have occurred in Okes’s printing house. Occasionally the crowding of a line or page in Q1 has been thought to result in the omission of words: see nn. 2632, 2890, 3247, 3277–83, 3280, and 3282–3. Ordinary eyeskip has been suspected at 69–70, 1296 (see n. 1294+1–1296), 1798–9, 2627, and less probably at 439–44, 487–93, 842–55, and 1419–24, where the sheer length of the absent passages lessens the possibility of their having been overlooked. Compositorial carelessness or accidental oversight has been suspected at 382, 589, 787, 1281, 1350, 1373–4, 1379, 1397, 2243, 2597, and 3100–1, and more dubiously at 54–5, 94–5, 176, 1599–1600, 1819, 1982, 2007–12, 2543, and 2936. In most of these cases a gap in the sense has suggested an omission from Q, but in many cases mere improvement in F1 has seemed an equally likely alternative. In a few cases Q material is missing from F because it has apparently been replaced by erroneous substitutions in F: see 823, 1016, n. 1294+1–1296, possibly 2538–9, and the long and crucially important 1631–8, any of which may involve scribal rather than compositorial error. The notion that Q lines on touchy subjects were removed by a censor and later restored in F has seldom been entertained: see nn. 439–44 (political and social criticism), 1631–8 (bribery), 2007–12 (James’s knights), and 2608–12 (corrupt judges). The idea of censorship in Q1 is improbable on two counts: Q is not now generally thought to print an acting text which would have been submitted to the censor, and the same George Buc who objected to passages in 1606 would not likely be pleased to approve them for restoration and publication in 1623, or for public performance during the interim.

Somewhat clearer evidence that words absent from an earlier Q text were supplied in a later F text are the several occasions on which imperfect verse in Q has in its place metrically better verse in F. In most of these cases words are present in F which are not needed to complete the sense of the lines but which do perfect the meter. There would be no clear reason why regular lines in F should have been disrupted in Q by the omission of one or more unessential but otherwise unobjectionable words, but good reason why someone preparing the generally more carefully polished F text should have added an unessential word to yield metrical regularity to an imperfect Q line, of which there are many. There seems no necessity, except to complete or improve a line, for words to have been added in F at 92, 125, 344–5, 789, 1036, 1350, 1397, 1416, 1651, 2040, 2627, 2639, 2641, 2890, 2936, 2948, 3113, 3135, 3269, and 3280; see also . Adjustment of verse accompanied changes of sense in 787, 1798–9, 2243, 3175, and the part-line 3037 may have been added to restore the metrical pattern disrupted by the addition of the part-line 3035. At 1798–9 the Folio apparently restores material omitted from Q by eyeskip, thereby also restoring metrical regularity. At 1599–1600 the Folio improves one hypermetric line by interpolating two new part lines; there would have been no reason to do the reverse, and the additions may be non-authorial because one of them includes a detail (the king’s departure on horseback) quite inconsistent with the ensuing action. The several verbal adjustments in 3170–8 evidently result from the need to reline after F’s omission of a long passage from Q; and several F-only words in 3277–83 accompany the relining of Q prose as verse and the inclusion of an F-only line and a half.

Conversely, F contains a number of words or individual lines which serve a clear purpose absent from Q—giving new information, expressing new thoughts, adding emphasis by repetition, summoning a servant, giving a directive, etc.—but whose presence involves disruption of meter. It is much more likely that these represent purposeful additions in F, imperfectly assimilated to the verse patterns, than that they were removed from Q either in order to smooth the meter or that they produced that consistent result incidentally to other purposes. Such may be the case at 50 (see n. 45–50), 269 (see n. 268–9), 352, 833, 961–2, 2816, 2826, and 3247. At 50 and 833 apparent F additions result in hypermetric lines; at 487–93 an apparent addition requires the relocation of a Q phrase; at 1322–7 the F lines may be inferior in both sense and meter to the apparently original Q text; at 2007–12 the F lines interrupt a coherent train of ideas in Q; at 3035 and 3037 F lines appear to have been inserted into perfect Q meter.

A number of lines present only in F have the appearance of additions to pad out actors’ parts or to emphasize their dramatic presence in a scene. As if to compensate for his disappearance halfway through the play, the Fool is given additional (non-Q) satiric comments and a song at 1322–7, an inconsequential gibe at mad yeomen and their gentlemen sons at 2010–12, a pointed farewell (going to bed at noon) at 2043, and, most remarkably, the long and extraneous Merlin’s prophecy at 1734–49, a solo turn that most commentators believe to be a spurious interpolation added to pad the Fool’s role. Possibly Kent’s swearing by Juno at 1296 was intended as an added touch of humor; Edmund’s Fa, Sol, La, Me (466), Edgar’s O do, de, do, de, do de, and Lear’s Sa, sa, sa, sa may be actors’s gag adopted in rehearsal. Edgar’s cry from within the hovel at 1819, better occasioning the Fool’s terrified response, gives Poor Tom a more dramatic entrance in F. Albany and Cornwall are given lines that emphasize their presence at 176 and 774, and so possibly is Kent at 1281, and Goneril’s brilliant sarcasm An enterlude (3035) is a gift to any actor.

Several passages serve to give useful information that is more likely to have been added for clarification in F than omitted (detrimentally) from Q. Such may be the introduction by name of Albany and Cornwall in 45–50, the identification of Cordelia’s suitors by name in 90–1, facts about Edgar’s whereabouts in 487–93, and details about the impending conflict (spies, the behavior of the dukes) in 1631–8. Other words and lines seem to have been added to emphasize ideas or feelings by repetition, as in 94–5, 352, 774, 1379, 2826, 3280; one would expect emphasis to be added to a later version, not deleted from an earlier one.

In any case, the majority of the F-only passages, especially the longer ones, are now thought to be additions to the Q text. Moriarty (1913, p. 470): Many of them bear so directly on [plot] sequence that it is straining probability to suppose that if they had been in the original draft they would have been cut out [of Q] either by players or managers. See also, e.g., Doran (1931, pp. 56–68), Stone (1980, pp. 238–48), Urkowitz (1980, p. 14), Taylor (1983, pp. 376 ff.), Halio (ed. 1992, pp. 277–88). They seem designed to complete, or expand, or clarify, or provide transitions within existing Q passages—again, the kind of material more likely to be added to a later version than cut from an earlier one. In most cases these additions do not add anything startlingly new, but seem mainly to be functionally useful expansions of existing material. Most of them are brief, perhaps reflecting their subsidiary role; except for the repetition in 3282–3 of doubts in Lear’s mind about Cordelia’s state, none of them originates a new direction in the action or a new interpretation of character or theme. They are on the whole supplementary rather than transformative. Several serve the expository role of clarifying motive by making it more explicit: see nn. 45–50, 54–5, 842–55, 1807–8. Several clarify meaning by supplying apparently missing words, without which a line or phrase is less clear or even nonsensical: see nn. 382, 1798–9, 1982, 2632, 3100–1. Others provide a phrase of transition (see nn. 2543, 2597, 2627) or of conclusion (see nn. 2890, 3282–3). Quite a number seem designed to amplify a speech or an episode. A few of these fill out a discussion with further argument (see nn. 1373–4, 1419–24); others provide personal reflections which affirm or further develop motive and character (see nn. 2184–7, 2243, 2295). Several amplify the meaning of a passage, either by making it more explicit (see n. 439–44) or by further pursuing an idea (see nn. 2608–12, 3019). Virtually all of them have the appearance of limited local improvements. Who, and how many people, might have made such additions, and whether they are part of larger patterns of revision, are questions discussed in a separate section below.

div.head: Accessories
div.p: The F text, unlike the Q text, is thoroughly divided into acts and scenes, and its divisions in general agree with those in virtually all modern editions except those based on Q or F alone. The two exceptions are that F makes modern scenes 2.2–2.4 one continuous scene, and that it omits the whole scene 4.3, putting the numbers of the successive scenes in Act 4 off by one from those in modern editions and concordances based upon them. For arguments whether 2.3 ought to or may be considered a separate scene, see n. 1251–72; for explanations of F’s inconsistent naming of its own 4.6 as Scæna Septima, see n. 2743. Greg (1940, p. 303; 1946, p. 229) is undecided whether the act-scene division is authorial, theatrical, or editorial, eventually (1955, p. 388) settling on the last. Unless the act divisions were gratuitously introduced into F copy by a scribe familiar with texts of academic or classical plays, they probably derive from a theatrical manuscript that somehow lies behind F. If so, they do not reflect performance in the Globe, where act intervals were not observed or marked in playtexts (Jewkes, 1958, pp. 97–8), but may reflect indoor performance in the Blackfriars Theatre, where intervals allowing for the trimming of candle wicks and for entr’act entertainments seem to have been a regular practice (Gurr, 1970, p. 116; 1980, pp. 160–1; Stone, 1980, p. 107). Taylor & Jowett (1993, pp. 30–43) argue that act-pauses derive from the Blackfriars but (pp. 240–2) that scene-divisions would have been scribal additions.

The deficiencies of character-designations and stage directions in Q have been detailed above (). In general F corrects these deficiencies, and in a few cases makes alterations that apparently reflect changed conceptions of the staging. F supplies all the entrances of named characters which are lacking from Q except possibly for the Fool at 809 and possibly for Edgar at 2739, and provides the entrances of all attendant characters except for a Knight at 579 and a Gentleman at 919 and 3216. Likewise the missing exits for named characters are supplied except for Regan 3056, possibly Kent 1411, and the Steward at 621 and 864 (and two Q exits are erroneously omitted at 2298 and 2334). Q’s missing exits of attendant characters remain unsupplied in F; they are generally clear enough from the dialogue, and evidently both major and minor actors were trusted to leave the stage once their presence was no longer required. Exits are expanded to Exeunts at 291, 528, 925, 1995, –2056, 2176, 2347, 2381, and 2742 but not at 1227, 1733, and 2081, and are added at 1968, 2265, 2219, 2936, and 3302. At 2879 Q’s Exeunt is replaced by F’s more specific Exeunt both the Armies; on the other hand, proper names in Q are omitted from F’s exits at 1586 and 2081, in accordance with F’s usual style. The locating of an exit two lines earlier at 3117 is accompanied by the reassignment of a speech at 3119 and may indicate either revision or accident; see n. 3119.

On the analogy of changes in the playbook manuscript of Massinger’s Believe as Ye List (1631), Doran (1931, p. 83) surmises that directions for entrance have frequently been moved forward several lines in F1 Lr. to serve the practical theatrical need of preparing for timely appearance on stage, and so may be evidence of the prompter’s hand; she cites those at 1358, 1468, 1890, 2039, 2072, 2088, 2188, 2267, 2526, 3182, 3184, and 3264. The inference is doubtful: of the thirty-seven mid-scene entrances common to Q and F, twenty-five appear in precisely the same place and five more (including those at 1468, 2072, 2088, and 3182) are in practically the same place (in F, a mere three to eight words away from their location in Q). At 2188 and 2526 F’s entrances are not a word early; rather, Q’s are placed two and three lines too late, perhaps because the Q compositor, inexperienced with dramatic texts, did not see the need to insert a stage direction from the margin into the middle of a speech. All of Doran’s other instances may reflect special adjustments in staging rather than a general inclination of the bookholder to mark certain entrances early. At 2039 Gloucester may enter five lines before he needs to speak so as to avoid covering the Fool’s exit from the play at 2043. F’s entrance direction at 3184 may reflect experience gained in performance that more time was needed to carry on two bodies before attention is called to them in 3194. A group entrance at 1997 is split so that two entering characters precede one or two others by a few lines, and the reverse happens at 2267. The first change might make some difference in stage effect, but the second would not; the bookholder did not mark Oswald’s entrance two lines earlier (at 2267) in F in order to prepare for his timely appearance before speaking, since he enters simultaneously with two other characters and one of them (Goneril) speaks two lines before he does. Of the remaining two entrances cited by Doran, only that at 1358, which comes (anomalously) two lines earlier than the character’s first speech, is not explicable by some adjustment in staging; that at 1890 is marked four lines before the entering character is noted by the others on stage, perhaps because in both texts Gloucester’s approach in the dark by torchlight is meant to seem slow and halting. At 948, F’s entrance is actually 3 lines later than Q’s marginal direction.

A number of sound cues are added, particularly Storme [and Tempest] (1584, 1655, 1780, 1843, 1880, 1942), Flourish (202, 291, 1073, 2982), Hornes within (538), Tucket within (1466), Trumpet (3058, 3061, 3062, 3063, 3064), Alarums (3107), and (probably) with a dead March (3302). These seem more probably to have been added to the theatrical playtext to govern performance than to the F1 edition to aid readers. Added processional details are with Drum and Colours (2349, 2845, 2864, 2918, 2938), in a chaire carried by Seruants (2771), in conquest (2938), and with a dead March (3302), but F omits one bearing a Coronet,…then…then…next (37–8) and at the third sound, a trumpet before him (3067), both changes probably reflecting altered staging. The descriptive, indefinite, and apparently authorial Enter Gloster, brought in by two or three is replaced in F by the terse Enter Gloucester, and Seruants, and the descriptive meeting (927) by the functional seuerally, a term also found at 1075, and at 1615, where it replaces Q’s descriptive at seuerall doores. Q’s descriptive A drum a farre off (2737) and with Cordelia in his armes (3216) reappear in F, however. F adds only a few laconic directives for stage action: Glou. reads (382; replacing A Letter), Kent here set at liberty (1405), Reads the letter (2715), Herald reads (3059), Fights (3107), He dies (3283). At 3184 both the placement of the direction (eight lines early) and its language (bodies brought out, not in) suggests theatrical rather than literary (authorial) provenance. Q’s descriptive direction Shee takes a sword and runnes at him behind is replaced with the terser and more indefinite Killes him, and a number of directions indicating bodily actions are removed altogether: with his rapier drawne (1117) sleepes (1250), draw and fight (2152), led by (2191), He kneeles (2473), He fals (2480), mad (2526), running (2645), they fight (2696), He dies (2703), with her father in her hand (2919), with a bloudie knife (3169). These changes may indicate that the actors were entrusted to furnish their own appropriate business, without prescription. F does add He dies at 3283. The brevity and reduced number of the F directions generally may suggest that they derive not from the original authorial directions usually found centered or in the right margin but from the repetitions of such directions placed by the book-keeper in the left margin so that they would not be missed (Long, 1985, pp. 129–30). The functional identities or roles of several attendant characters are specified more exactly in F: Gentleman/Steward (506, 509, 518, 524), Gentleman/Messenger (2312), others/Gentlemen, and Souldiers (2349), their powers/Gentlemen, and Souldiers (2846), the powers of France/Soldiers (2918), others/soldiers (2982), one/a Gentleman (3169). On F’s replacement of Q’s three Gentlemen with a Gentleman while leaving needed attendants unnamed, see n. 2630.

There are only three mentions of properties (with Torches, 970; with a Torch, 1890; a chaire, 2771) and one of costume (armed, 3067); Q’s Coronet (147) and a bloudie knife (3169) are named in the dialogue but disappear from directions. Indications of properties that one might expect to find in a modern promptbook or acting edition are not added to F. No chair, bench, or stool is called for at 39 to serve as Lear’s seat or throne, if he has one, nor is a chair specifically called for at 2098 and 2139 for the binding and blinding of Gloucester. A bench for mock justices is unnecessary in F’s truncated 3.6, and if Lear falls asleep on a bench at 2040, it is not mentioned in dialogue or direction. A number of portable properties must have been assumed to be the responsibilities of the actors who presented them—a map (42), a key (491), ropes (2091), a crown of weeds? (2526), a looking glass (3221), a feather (3227), two written challenges (2582?, 3058), and many letters or notes (353, 875, 1242, 1980, 2061, 2328, 2400, 2416, 2709, 2884, 2970, 3113). Similarly, other properties are unnamed because they are items of the characters’ personal dress, ornament, or arms—a purse or a gratuity from one (622, 1642, 2249, 2465, 2533, 2611), swords (962, 1103, 2154, 2679, 3080, 3094, 3105, 3208), the Fool’s cockscomb (625), Poor Tom’s blanket and horn (1261, 1846, 2032), Goneril’s chain? (2289), Lear’s crown of weeds and gauntlet (2526, 2537), Albany’s and Edmund’s gauntlets (3040, 3045), Edgar’s batton (2694). Lear’s piece of toasted cheese (2536), gauntlet, and challenge may be only imaginary, as may be his block (2625) and Poor Tom’s head (2022), whatever they may be.

F corrects obvious Q errors in the names or assignments of speakers at 172–3, 1448, 1586, 2283, 2430, 2724, and possibly at 580; it introduces a new error at 628 and possibly others at 204 and 658. In Q, Edmund is always referred to as Bast. in speech prefixes and as Bastard in directions until 4.5; the single previous exception is in the anomalous Edmund in the direction at 1117, which, also anomalously, names Cornwall and Regan only as the Duke and Dutchesse. Q’s four other Edmunds include one apparent false expansion of Ed. (for Edgar) at 2430 (after Edmund was named twice in the dialogue of the previous scene) and 2846, 2896, and 2939; since all of these were set by Q’s chief compositor, B, who had generally set Bastard previously, his change of style may reflect a change in the MS. F’s Compositor E duplicates Q’s Edmund in all directions except at 1117, where he may be following a completely rewritten SD; at 1752 he also sets Edmund in the direction though keeping Bast. in two speech prefixes. F Compositor B also sets Edmund at 1970, having used that name at 2 (his only previous opportunity to set the name in a SD), along with the speech prefix Edm. (29, 32, 34); he also, however, keeps the prefix Bast. on the same page (at 1972, 1979, 1985, and 1990). Compositor E also sets the prefix Edm. at 487, 493, and 498, perhaps (as Walton, 1955, p. 157 suggests) following his copy, where added lines at 487–93 required the addition of a new speech prefix and perhaps resulted in the alteration, by reviser, scribe, or compositor, of the two adjacent ones. Doran (1931, pp. 81–2): Bastard cannot [82] apply to anyone else; it is therefore not imperative to make his designation uniform. Since the character is virtually always called Edmund in the dialogue, occasional changes to that name in the accessories can hardly be surprising. Whatever they may suggest about the nature of the F copy, none of these variant names makes the least substantive difference in the text or in performance. The same may be said of the change from Q’s prefix Duke to F’s Alb. throughout 1.4 (768–872) and in the latter half of 5.3 (3192–298), and from Q’s Duke to F’s Albany in the directions at 768 and 2982. Likewise there is no significance in variations on Cornwall’s name; whereas Q uses the prefix Duke. from 1025 to 1612 and Corn. from 1971 to 2173 (all set by the same compositor and therefore probably reflecting copy), F uses Cor. or Corn. throughout; and whereas Q uses several variations on and combinations of Duke and Cornewell or Cornwall in directions (37, 1024, 1117, 1403, 1970, 2058), F always uses simply Corn(e)wall. Q’s Dutchesse (1117), two Ladies (2982), and King (1273) are in F all replaced by proper names. F consistently regularizes references to Oswald, who is named in the text only at 833, 848, and (in F only) 857; in Q he is Gent. or Gentleman at 506, 509, 518, and 524, Oswald and Osw. at 857+1 and 859, and otherwise Stew. or Steward; in F he is always Ste., Stew., or Steward. The aberrant spelling Edmond, found a dozen times in F, may be the preference of Compositor B; see DP 9–10. F’s spelling Gonerill, found neither in the quartos nor in any of the sources, is probably scribal; see DP 15, and below, , . F’s changes from Q1’s Rag. (325) and Ragan. (331; Q2 Regan) to Reg. also indicates likely scribal regularization in playbook or F copy.

In a number of cases, alterations in speech prefixes may reflect changes in the staging, such as keeping rapid dialogue moving among more characters (Doran, 1931, p. 81), and are frequently taken as evidence of conscious revision; nonetheless, in most cases the changes may either reflect an error in F or the correction of an error in Q, as the respective commentary notes make clear. The transposition of Goneril and Regan at 301 has generally been thought an indifferent variant. The reassignment of Goneril’s two Q lines to Lear at 1477 has been widely thought to be simply a correction. Q’s assignment of 3119 to Goneril as her exit line has been so generally preferred to F’s assignment of it to Edmund as to suggest error in the latter text. If the transfer of Lear’s dying words to Kent at 3285 is also an error, as it may be, it has yet seemed to many critics so fraught with meaning as to seem an intentional revision. The transfer of single lines or part-lines may slightly enhance the roles of the Fool (at 744), of Cornwall (at 1134, 1227, 1597, and 1601), of Goneril (at 1594), and of Albany (3012), though F error has been suspected in all cases. The reassignment of 3064–5, along with the omission of 3051+1, somewhat reduces Edmund’s role. The division of one full line of Albany’s at 3171–3 into two half-lines assigned to Edgar and the later transfer of Albany’s part-line 3210 may be designed to enhance Edgar’s part very slightly, though the reasons for doing so, and possible differences in stage action, remain obscure and debatable. The transfer (at 3298) of the play’s last speech from Albany to Edgar, which has been invested by some recent critics with a great weight of meaning, may nonetheless be merely an error; the change of one verb-form in the speech (from haue to hath, 3300) may be merely a compositorial or scribal sophistication, not a confirmation of intentional transfer. Though the change of the last word in line 3026 suggests that the line’s reassignment from Bast. to Reg. is intentional, both Q and F versions have been defended. There seems to be no doubt, on the other hand, that the reassignment of lines from Doctor to Gentleman in 4.4 and 4.7 is the consequence of merging two roles into one; see n. 2349–50.

Many commentators have contrasted the incomplete, descriptive, often vague and inconsistent directions and character designations in Q with the more complete, specific, consistent, terse and businesslike treatment of such matters in F, concluding that the former represent authorial provenance and the latter derivation from a document regularized for use in the theater. For examples, see . Greg’s (1955, pp. 384–5) assessment is typical: A glance at the stage-directions…will show that most of the graphic touches that give them life in Q have disappeared. This is consonant with the comparative austerity of a prompt-book, in which directions are pruned to what is needed on the stage.…On the other hand [385] the book-keeper is solicitous about stage noises…and properties…, occasionally about action…and ceremonial…, and generally about such supers as he can afford.…As a rule the directions in F owe nothing to their form in Q.…The entrances and exits in F are almost complete.…Character indications too have for the most part been made consistent and explicit. Similarly Stone (1980, pp. 107–12), after a lengthy review of all the changes in the F text’s accessories, concludes that F derives from some kind of theatrical manuscript. Since recent studies of extant manuscript playbooks (e.g. Long, 1985, 1999) reveal that regularization of entrances, exits, and character descriptions seldom occurred in them, such changes in F1 may represent editing for a reading edition rather than theatrical provenance. A few commentators have detected signs that the playbook was at some point altered for presentation on a stage other than the Globe—see Rhodes (1923, pp. 108–9) and nn. 1251–72, 2771.

div.head: Playbook Copy
div.p: Many features of the F text have been generally taken as evidence that it has been influenced in some way by a manuscript adapted for theatrical use. Its most striking feature, its omission of almost 300 Q lines which are not absolutely necessary to furthering the plot, has seemed most probably explicable as theatrical cutting to reduce an overlong play to something closer to a normal playing time. Collier (ed. 1843, 7:353): It would seem that the folio of 1623 was composed from a manuscript, which had been much, and not very judiciously, abridged for the purposes of the theatre. Whether judicious or not, and whether performed by actors, author, or some other agent, theatrical abridgement is accepted by virtually all commentators since Theobald (ed. 1733) (see ). Whether or not censorship of the playbook was responsible for any of F’s omissions has been argued inconclusively; see .

This impression of F’s theatrical origin is reinforced by many other signs that an authorial rough draft, such as the one that Q1 seems to be based upon, was cleaned up and improved for theatrical purposes. Doran (1931, pp. 79, 85): The designations given in the quarto to the minor characters suggest that Shakespeare applied them indiscriminately, not having in mind the particular way in which the parts would have been assigned. When the play was performed, it was necessary to cast these parts. In order that there should be no confusion, the designations were changed whenever necessary, so that two different actors were never called by the same general term, such as Gentleman or Captain. The appellations were made to have individual significance. This fact…seems to me sufficient proof that the folio manuscript served as the prompt-copy in the theater.…[85] [The Folio] supplies correct readings for many errors in the quarto which could not have been corrected by the printer unaided; it contains more than a hundred lines not in the quarto at all; and it has many variant readings and alterations which cannot be attributed to a transcriber or printer. This manuscript is a copy of an earlier form of the play. As seen above (see ), F regularizes and modifies the accessories in ways that suggest but do not always prove preparation for practical use in the theater: missing entrances are supplied, as are sound cues and some stage business, and directions are made more terse, precise, and practical. The merging of two roles (Doctor, Gentleman) into one in 4.4 and 4.7, and hints that the staging of Lear’s appearance in 4.7 and of the trumpeter’s presence in 5.3 may have been altered for changed stage conditions, also indicate a theatrical document. The act-division in F (though perhaps not the scene division) may also reflect stage practice after 1609; see . Wells (1983, p. 9) To a considerable degree, the Folio represents actual theatrical practice.

Whether F copy was actually the allowed book or playbook or prompt-book used as the basis for actual performances is another matter. Doran (1931, p. 122; cf. pp. 85, 89), finding ample evidence that F copy was manuscript rather than a printed quarto, and that it contained evidently authorial revisions and theatrical annotations, identifies prompt-book copy: From the manuscript which was later given to Nathaniel Butter to print [as Q1], a fair copy was made; this transcript, somewhat revised, abridged for acting, supplied with the necessary annotations by the prompter, altered in the direction of explicitness with regard to the assignment of the minor parts, and marked and licensed by the censor, was used as the theater prompt-book and finally turned over to Jaggard and Blount in 1623 as part of the copy for the First Folio. Van Dam (1935, p. 72) and Craig (1961, pp. 14–15; 1962, pp. 60–1) agree, though inclining to an autograph prompt-book rather than a scribe’s transcript. As is evident from the inattention to correction and regularization in extent playbook manuscripts, the notion that the playbook served as a promptbook (a modern term), used continually backstage during performance to prompt actors in their entrances, lines, and business, is anachronistic; the actors probably had to rely mainly on their own memories and stage-sense and perhaps as well on the plot of the scenes posted backstage, on cues and reminders in their own written parts, and on occasional rescue by book-keeper or fellow-actors. The fact that someone supplied very full entrances and exits in the F text probably indicates that Lr. was not set directly from a playbook, in which such additions were generally made only sparingly if at all, but from a regularized manuscript designed to aid readers.

There are in F Lr. no clear stigmata, such as actors’ names in the text, to indicate that it was set from a playbook, and several other considerations weigh heavily against the possibility. The first, pointed out immediately by Greg (1933, p. 260) and Parrott (1934, p. 206), is that the allowed book, bearing the Master of the Revels’ official licence for the performance of the play, was too valuable to be sent to a printing house, where it might suffer damage or loss. The casting-off of copy so that two compositors could simultaneously set F Lr. by formes would entail extensive marking-up and perhaps cutting-apart of that copy, and would risk the danger of staining by ink or lye or other printshop liquids. Bowers (1986, pp. 15, 25): The printing of a quarto may be taken as implying the destruction of its manuscript.…It should be taken as an axiom, I believe, that the Folio editor would not release the promptbook itself (or any other sole manuscript) for printing: the annotation of printed copy for Richard III and Troilus and Cressida instead of the use of the manuscript itself seems to be sufficient evidence for that.…[25] In my private opinion no Shakespeare play was set directly from the prompt-book, the last copy that would be permitted to leave the theater for ruination in the printer’s shop, unless we may except one or two early works so long out of the repertory that the prompt-book had no value—but I do not know what plays these were. So also Howard-Hill (1985, p. 173). Taylor & Jowett (1993, p. 242) concur, finding no clear instance in F of prompt-book copy.

Furthermore, an increasing number of recent commentators have argued that the text of Lr. is much too long to have been performed within normal playing limits, and that therefore it cannot represent the playbook on which actual performances were based. Hart (1942, p. 132): The folio text is not an acting version, because this abridged version would be five hundred lines longer than the maximum length of a two-hour play. Smidt (1964, pp. 161–2): In fact neither the Quarto nor the Folio text is likely to have been a stage [162] version, though both may derive from a book marked with theatrical omissions, some of which were observed in the printing and some not. Carroll (1988, p. 229): Given the time limitations of actual performance, and the length of both Q and F, is it not reasonable to suppose that neither Q nor F were ever actually performed in their entirety? If the text of F Lr., like that of other Folio plays, is apparently too long for performance yet shows signs of preparation for theatrical presentation, the question of what kind of theatrical manuscript other than a working playbook it can derive from needs to be faced, and will be discussed below (). For the moment it suffices that a working playbook representing one or another actual performance of Lr. may be thought unlikely to have served as Folio copy.

div.head: Q1 Copy
div.p: For a hundred years, discussions of possible printer’s copy for F1 were dominated and corrupted by one erroneous (though plausible) idea: that the Folio text somehow derived from a copy of Q1. For many decades the idea that F had been set directly from a marked-up copy of Q1 held sway. As more and more difficulties with that idea were discovered, variations on it were proposed—e.g., that a copy of Q1 had been used in conjunction with some other form of copy, or that a scribal transcript of Q1 had either formed the basis of the company’s playbook behind F copy or was indeed itself the F copy. Not until Howard-Hill (1986) demonstrated that not a single piece of evidence conclusively showed F1 dependence upon Q1 (see n. 2990+1) was the notion eventually abandoned.

The idea originates with Daniel (facs. 1885, pp. xvi–xxi) who, finding that a few Q1 errors were reproduced in F1, concludes that therefore a copy of Q1 (with uncorrected sheets E, H, and K), altered by comparison with a manuscript copy of the [shortened] play preserved in the library of the theatre, was printer’s copy for F1. Since the careless scribe did not correct, with the aid of that more perfect theatrical manuscript, all of the errors found in Q1, they were reproduced in F from that Q1 copy. As commentators would in time point out, the F errors were either no errors at all, or were significantly different from the Q readings, or could have come from an alternate source. Daniel himself cites six instances where F1 is closer to Q2 than to Q1—534 raiz’d, 1063 prize, 1136 gray- (incorrect hyphen), 1155 smoile, 1255 vnusall, and 3074 tooth:—but he minimizes their significance and concludes despite them that to Q1 must be attributed the part parentage of F1. Craig (ed. 1901, p. xiv) and Goggin (ed. 1910) are early adherents to Daniel’s theory.

Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxiii) first offers an often-repeated objection: that such printer’s copy would be difficult to produce: Letting alone the difficulties of interlining the passages not found in the Pide Bull, there remains the incredible labor of making blank verse out of the Quarto’s mangled and halting prose-setting. He offers an alternative explanation of the Q/F similarities, likewise often-repeated: It is easier to fancy that the later compositor may have had in his pocket a copy of the Pide Bull…, and with its aid eked out sense when the copy was hard to follow. Pollard (1909) inconsistently (as Rhodes, 1923, pp. 108–9 points out) both accepts and rejects Daniel’s theory, accurately asserting it (pp. 53, 76) but thereafter (pp. 110, 121) stating that Lr. was printed from manuscript without use of an earlier printed quarto, an assertion repeated by Wilson (1924, pp. 66–7).

Daniel’s chief champion was to be Greg (1928, pp. 14–15, 38–40), who accepts Daniel’s theory as fact but is troubled that the text of King Lear is considerably better than on our textual theory it has any right to be. Soon thereafter (1933, pp. 257–9) he focuses his defense on two readings in F, 867 at task and 2990+1 and appointed guard, which he insists must have been derived from a corrected copy of Q; both examples seemed at first persuasive but ultimately proved inconclusive (see nn. 867, 2990+1). He subsequently (1940, pp. 139–42, 154; 1942, pp. xviii, xxxiii, xlix, 98–9; cf. 1955, p. 384) adduces the same examples, urging his opinions that a marked-up quarto would not have been illegible and would have been less trouble to prepare than a fresh transcript, giving no evidence for either view.

Greg’s case (1928) is confuted by Doran (1931). She gives (pp. 40–2) more than a dozen examples (see, e.g., nn. 2128 through 2138) of Q errors which in F could not have been corrected without recourse to an independent manuscript, though she concedes that these corrections might have been transferred to a quarto. She subsequently (pp. 86–9) shows that the score of F readings that Greg derives from Q1 could as well have come from a manuscript common to Q and F. Finally (pp. 91–6), after detailing the difficulties of marking and using Q1 copy, she lists numerous new F errors which must have been compositorial misreadings of manuscript forms, not of words printed in Q1: An editor who undertook to correct a copy of Q1 from the playhouse manuscript [i.e., playbook] would have had to write in all the variant readings, both corrections of [Q] errors and good [playbook] variants; he would have had to delete [from the printed text of Q] all the excrescent words which impaired the meter and which were not in his text; he would have had to supply lost parts [i.e., passages], ranging from a single word to eighteen lines; he would have had to mark out all the lines which had been omitted from his text; and he would have had to indicate line divisions of the great amount of verse that is either wrongly aligned or printed as prose. These alterations would have required a great deal of patching and inter-[90]lining, and for the latter there is little room in the printed quarto. It is a question whether such copy would not have been very difficult for the [F1] printer to follow, and whether, if he had been using it, he would not have made more errors than he did.…It would appear to be simpler and more satisfactory both for the editors and for the printer to have used the [playbook] manuscript itself as copy.…Moreover, in the transcript [i.e., playbook] there must have been fewer errors than in the printed quarto, and the verse, if one may judge from its state in the folio, must have been correctly aligned. She further doubts that the numerous slight changes in speech prefixes and stage directions, and the shifts in positions of the latter, none of them of any significance to a prospective reader of F, would have been marked in a copy of Q1.

She concludes, Proof positive [that Q1 was not copy] lies in the fact that among the fresh errors in the folio text…are a number of manuscript misreadings.…If a compositor had a correctly printed word before him, why should he set [in F] an incorrect word whose form in Elizabethan handwriting resembles the written form of the correct [Q] word?…[Instead of] the correctly printed word reneag [1151], the compositor could get the misreading reuenge only from a manuscript; she adds (pp. 90–5) some fifty more examples of such wrong or inferior F readings deriving from manuscript forms of words. (P. 96): This manuscript must have been the one from which the first quarto was printed and from which the playhouse transcript [i.e., playbook, represented in the folio] was copied.…The compositor of the folio may indeed have referred to the printed quarto at times, but, from the misreadings which he has allowed to come into his text, it is evident that he did not refer to it when he most needed to do so. The only explanation, therefore, that can be made of the striking similarities between the texts in either certain or possible errors is that a common manuscript source, in which some mistakes were made and in which some words were illegibly written, is at the basis of both the first quarto and the folio. Her evidence of manuscript misreadings in F has been accepted and supplemented by Stone (1980, p. 55) and Howard-Hill (1982, pp. 14 ff.); the latter notes that Compositor E’s portion of Lr. contains twenty spellings that do not occur anywhere else in F, including other pages that he set, and so are more likely to reflect copy than his own preferences. On thirteen occasions the Q1 form was not transmitted to F, evidence that Q1 did not directly supply E’s copy.

Gradually other textual scholars have accepted Doran’s arguments for rejecting Q1 copy. Brooke (ed. 1947, p. 156) adds others, disbelieving that the Folio editors…went out of their way to put one of the stolen and surreptitious copies they were deploring at the base of their purer text. It would be easier to write out clean any average page of King Lear than to do the relining, re-punctuating, capitalizing, transposing, and substituting of words necessary to make a Quarto page conform to the Folio readings—and the difference to the Folio printer would have been unspeakable. Considering that Heminge and Condell had in their service experts whose business was the making of fair copies, but whose skill in textual collation may well be doubted, it would have been asinine to adopt so cumbrous and dangerous a means of reproducing their theater manuscript. Williams (1953, pp. 456 ff.): A heavily annotated quarto would make poor printer’s copy; moreover, it would be more difficult to collate and annotate some pages of the Lear quarto than it would be to transcribe directly from the [playhouse] manuscript that [457] was being used for reference.…In Q, the name is invariably spelled Gonorill, and if more than the first three letters are used in the speech-heading, the fourth letter is invariably an o. In F, the name is invariably Gonerill, and in speech-headings, if more than the first three letters are used, the fourth letter is invariably an e.…[458] It is impossible to believe that a corrector of Q1 should have marked this change throughout the play, even in the speech-headings. It therefore seems safe to conclude that in the copy from which F was set, the name was consistently spelled Gonerill. Craig (1962, p. 61): More than two thousand changes, some of them long, would have been necessary, and they simply would not have been legible if made on the soft paper of an Elizabethan quarto. Smidt (1964, pp. 156 ff.) attacks Greg’s evidence that F’s at task (867) and and appointed guard (2990+1) derive from corrected pages of Q1, pointing out that numerous other details on those pages are absent from F. (P. 158): And it does seem hard to suppose that a copy of the Quarto should have been prepared with a number of relatively insignificant annotations (like…had and on) and that the editor would then proceed to strike out whole lines in it because they were not contained in the manuscript he was consulting.…A common manuscript source seems a simpler and more reasonable solution.…[160] And if the Quarto was consulted occasionally where the manuscript presented some problem of interpretation or deciphering, there would have been nothing surprising in that. What would have been surprising is the use of a Quarto heavily annotated with all kinds of insignificant variants, yet retaining a number of quite remarkable misreadings, mislineations etc. to be perpetuated in the Folio.

Similarly Stone (1980, pp. 8–9): Hundreds upon hundreds of changes are involved, a large number of them affecting matters of small detail. Plurals are substituted for singulars and singulars for plurals where, from the [9] viewpoint of sense, either would do equally well; that is often carefully altered to which; betwixt, you, oh become between, ye, ah; elsewhere between, ye, ah become twixt, you, oh.…Minor alterations of another, less indifferent kind—the substitution, addition or omission of pronouns, conjunctions and the like, changes of tense, or word order and so on, which do not leave the meaning unaffected…must be, and always are, presumed to derive from the authoritative manuscript copy. If they do, they bear witness to a fairly high degree of care and accuracy in the collation. It is all the more extraordinary, then, to find the collator committing so many oversights and blunders. The number of errors in F, in fact, errors which cannot be ascribed to compositorial mishaps, puts the collation theory to considerable strain. He also notes (pp. 82–9) that some pairs of readings in F seem to derive one from an uncorrected and the other from the corrected state of the same forme, a possibility that is naturally excluded if he were working from a single printed copy, and it is unlikely that he collated two or more copies of Q1, which exactly complemented each other.

Nonetheless the theory died hard. Williams (1953, p. 460), accepting Greg’s evidence that F Lr. was in some way dependent on Q1, hypothesizes that the prompt-book…was a conflation of good pages from Q1 supplemented by inserted manuscript leaves to replace corrupt passages of Q1. Reluctant to let the official prompt-book leave their possession, the company permitted a scribe to make a transcript of this conflated text to serve as the copy for the First Folio. (Presumably the scribal copy had F’s spelling Gonerill throughout rather than Q’s Gonorill.) Walton (1955, pp. 156 ff.), relying heavily on Greg’s unproved opinions about the convenience and legibility of marked quarto copy, assails Williams’s theory of a transcript of conflated prompt-copy, and Williams’s claims that F’s speech-prefixes could not have derived from Q. Like Williams’s arguments, his are vitiated by incorrect compositor identifications (see Howard-Hill, 1982, p. 14 n.), and his collator’s or compositor’s readings in F are equally explainable as (occasionally imperfect) regularization in scribal F copy. Walton (1971, pp. 57 ff.) reasserts F1’s dependence on Q1, but his argument (pp. 152–97) that various substantive errors in F derive from Q ignores Doran’s case that they could as well have derived from a common manuscript behind Q and the playbook ultimately behind F. Walker (1953, pp. 5 ff.) gives several examples of faulty F punctuation and readings supposedly derived from Q1; unfortunately, none is clearly an error, and as Jackson (1983, p. 341 n. 8) points out, Werstine’s (1983) demonstration that Walker exaggerated F Compositor B’s inaccuracy undermines Walker’s account of the copy for Q just as seriously as it does her account of F. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 122 ff.) follows Greg in finding the evidence of and appointed guard and at task conclusive, and inclines to Williams’s theory of a scribal transcript based on Q1 and inserted manuscript replacement pages. Though, like Walton (1955, p. 64), he is even willing (p. 128) to entertain the idea that such a transcript might have been made by two scribes of different habits, he continues to doubt (pp. 129–30) that there are any pages in F that can be said not to depend on the edited quarto itself.

Since Stone (1980, pp. 41 ff.) cannot believe that F’s frequent failure to correct Q errors and its frequent introduction of new ones is consistent with Q1 copy, and since he rejects Doran’s argument that a common authorial manuscript lies behind Q1 and F (preferring to believe Q1 a reported text), he proposes an alternative theory: that, to replace the lost playbook (lost perhaps in the Globe fire of 1613), Sh.’s company, after his death, hired another playwright to reconstruct a new playbook from both Q1 and the original (and still extant) reported manuscript behind Q1, adding his own revisions; that a scribe copied this marked-up Q1 to make a new prompt-book, which endured further revisions; and that then both this new promptbook and a marked-up copy of Q2 derived from it were used by the two compositors setting F1. This highly speculative and extraordinarily complex narrative, freely multiplying entities and events known and unknown, has never found a champion, and has been criticized by Reid (1982, pp. 329–31) for its logical inconsistencies and such gratuitous hypotheses as a lost quarto between Q1 and Q2. The belief of Fleay (1879, p. 119) and Lee (1916, pp. 446, 558) that many or all of Sh.’s MSS had perished in the Globe fire has been shown to be without factual basis or probability by Pollard (1909, p. 119), Baldwin (1927, pp. 138–9), Greg (1942, p. 135), and others, and a number of F texts are thought to derive from the company’s extant playbooks or transcripts of them (Wells & Taylor, 1987, pp. 145–7). Clearly one of Stone’s purposes is to provide an explanation different from Greg’s of what look like traces of Q1 in F. Since he rejects Q1 copy for F1, he is ready to question and revise (pp. 249–51) Greg’s (1940, pp. 144 ff.) identification of some of the uncorrected and corrected states of Q sheets in that supposed copy. Taylor (1983, pp. 355–67) still follows Greg in accepting and appointed guard as evidence of Q1’s (indirect, he believes; cf. 1985, p. 23) influence on F1, but takes a hint from Stone to account for that influence, by hypothecating a revision made in a copy of Q1 and later transcribed into a promptbook which was subsequently used to mark up Q2 copy for F—a stemma almost as complex as Stone’s.

Any basis for continuing to claim Q1’s influence on F was finally removed in two essays by Howard-Hill, who first (1982, pp. 1–24) demonstrated, from the two F compositors’ uncharacteristic failure to reproduce spellings of unfamiliar words found in their supposed Q1 copy, and from their misreadings derived (as Doran had argued) from manuscript rather than printed copy, that they must have been setting from a manuscript, not directly from Q1. His subsequent (1986) examination of all the evidence for Q1 copy gives the coup de grace to the theory, though his argument is unnecessarily complicated by the assumption that at least one Q1(c) reading must have been also in the playbook, and that an annotated Q2 was the first stage in preparing F1 copy.
