(Pp. 421 ff.): The object here is…simply to discover what evidence requires Q1’s direct involvement in the copy for F.…[422] When F shows a reading that corresponds to a variant of a corrected forme of Q1, one cannot be certain whether the reading provides evidence of the influence of the quarto upon the Folio text or whether it just shows that the [F] collator had introduced [into his Q copy] the correction from the promptbook, as he was charged. Similarly, when a variant from an uncorrected forme appears in F, one cannot assume the correctness of that variant, because the ordinary human fallibility of the collator may have led him to overlook an error that he may easily have corrected from the [playhouse] manuscript had he noticed the variation. The intervention of the collator between the quarto and Folio texts prejudices almost without exception consideration of the variants which appear to link the two printed texts.…[423] The further intervention of Q2 complicates the matter even further. Out of six possible classes of agreement between Q1(u), Q1(c), Q2, and F, the two offering the strongest basis for direct Q1 influence on F are represented in Greg’s argument by only one example each. The strongest, where Q1(u) agrees with F but not with Q1(c) or Q2, occurs at 2990+1, where Q(u) and F lack and appointed guard; Howard-Hill provides (pp. 427–30) an alternative explanation of the absence of this phrase from F, and still others have been offered (see n. 2990+1). The next strongest case, where F reproduces a Q1(c) correction that is really a blunder, is at 867, where the texts have the variants alapt [misreading of ataxt]/attaskt/a-lapt/at task; but (p. 425) the readings are probably simple spelling variations (see n. 867). For two other unlikely F retentions of miscorrections, of after to hasten and of retinue to returne, see n. 864. Possible further evidence that F did not follow Q1 occurs where F introduces errors in departing from Q1 readings (see nn. 1787, 2676) and linings (see nn. 929–32, 938–42, 1753–70).

In order to engage on their own terms the arguments of Greg and others for Q1 copy, Howard-Hill provisionally grants the possibility that a quarto (either Q1 or Q2, the latter edition a copy of Q1) was collated with the company’s playbook to produce copy for F1. The possibility that F readings agreeing with either quarto may have been supplied by a collator or scribe not from those quartos but from the 1623 playbook manuscript makes it impossible to show, on the basis of substantive readings, an influence of either quarto on F. Indeed, if he is right that, even granting such a collation, there is no provable bibliographical connection between Q1 and F1, then no such collation of quarto with playbook need be posited at all, and Doran’s (1931) alternative explanation may be entirely correct. If in 1606 an experienced scribe made a clean copy of Sh.’s rough draft, and that clean copy became the basis for the company’s playbook, and if in time either Sh. or others in the company corrected some of its occasional verbal errors, the result would be a text of relatively superior accuracy such as we find in the edition derived from that playbook, F1. And if Okes’s inexperienced compositors subsequently set Q1 from that same difficult rough draft, their resulting edition would naturally differ from F1 in a considerable number of variant or erroneous readings. Often the Q1 proof-corrector would have solved obscurities in the text in ways similar to the solutions of the playbook scribe (or of the company), in which case it might appear that F1 had derived its readings from Q1; in a few cases, as Doran shows, the obscurities in that manuscript would have misled both Q1 compositor and playbook scribe in related ways. Nonetheless, despite such apparent similarities, the Q and F texts could have been arrived at quite independently, at least in the matter of their substantive readings. Since Howard-Hill’s examination of the evidence, no one has claimed a close relationship of F1 with Q1.

div.head: Q2 Copy
div.p: Daniel (facs. 1885, pp. x f.) declares that there are many points of resemblance between the Fo and Q2, which might cast a doubt on Q1’s parentage of the Fo text, but after listing six examples he is content to leave this question to the judgment of the reader. The examples are 534 raz’d/raizd/raiz’d, 1063 prise (Q1[u])/prize/prize, 1140 gray beard/gray-beard/gray-beard (erroneous hyphen; but cf. 1036), 1155 smoyle/Smoile/Smoile (and 1156 and/if/if), 1255 vnusuall/vnusall/vnusall, 3074 tooth./tooth:/tooth: (erroneous colon, replacing Q1’s erroneous period). For almost a half-century, only Herford (ed. 1899, 9:6) seems to have taken Daniel’s invitation, suggesting that F was well printed…from a copy of Q2 rather carelessly corrected by the more severely abridged and amended stage MS. Since he offers no explanation, he may be confusing Q1 and Q2, as the Cambridge editors had done; their influential edition was reprinted in 1892 without correction of this error (see 8:vii, n. 2).

Doran (1931, pp. 109–21) investigates the question with characteristic thoroughness and scrupulousness, and rejects the notion of Q2 copy for F. The F printer would have adopted Q2’s corrections commands her (1378) and and appointed guard (2990+1), but does not; and the fact (p. 110) that none of the conjectural emendations in Q2 have come into the folio text weighs against the supposition that the printer of F used a copy of Q2 corrected in accordance with the [playbook] manuscript. She supposes instead that the printer of F occasionally referred to a copy of Q2. She doubts the significance of any of Daniel’s similar common spellings except vnusall, where F does seem to copy a misprint from Q2. At 3073, the only apparent case of common mispunctuation she finds throughout Q2 and F, even if F picked up Q2’s unexpected colon (tooth:), the printer did not adopt the incorrect verse lineation of the quartos, apparently following his MS instead; and in the next line he replaced Q1’s yet are I mou’t Where is with a phrase not in Q2, Yet am I Noble as. At 3206 she finds it striking that in Q2 and F the lines begin with Send and the Captaine (3208 is omitted); but the differences in verbs (3206 hath/ha’s), speech prefixes (3210 Alb./Edg.), and lineation (3209 Giue it the Captaine) indicate that the printer was using a manuscript and perhaps only referring to Q2 as backup.

Nonetheless she attempts (pp. 112–14) to account for more than two dozen verbal resemblances between Q2 and F against Q1. In virtually all cases she finds them to be regularizations according to the known house style of the printer who set both Q2 and F or as unconscious and natural adjustments by Jaggard’s compositors. Significantly, she finds unusual numbers of these resemblances in passages in 1.4 (553–676) and 2.2 (1138–1227); later analysts would find it significant that both passages were set by Folio Compositor E. Similarly, she attempts to explain (pp. 114–15) why in the matter of punctuation, F is closer to Q2 than to Q1.…The punctuation of Q2 is heavier than that of Q1, with more semicolons and periods at the ends of sentences within speeches, and heavy punctuation, with colons and periods plentifully used, characterizes the latter text [F] throughout. The places of closest agreement between Q2 and F, therefore, are where Q2 has the heaviest punctuation. F does not also agree with Q2 when the latter is more lightly punctuated. Moreover, even the passages which are similarly pointed do not agree exactly.…F will have a colon, perhaps, where Q2 has a semicolon. Such resemblances are probably to be explained by Jaggard’s house style, so that (p. 115) probably only those passages in which the punctuation in the two texts exactly coincides for several lines—and perhaps those only when they also agree very closely in spelling, capitalization, or readings—need to be considered as significant—as evidence that the F compositor was consulting Q2. Likewise (pp. 115–17) the more accurate and systematic spelling in both Q2 and F probably reflects printing house rules rather than influence of Q2 upon F; in a few cases F even reverts to unexpected older spellings found in Q1 (578 wher’s, 810 fiftie, 991 noyse, 2403 busines; cf. 1267 wodden). Doran does not suggest, though she might, that these may be survivals in the playbook of spellings in Sh.’s original rough draft, which lies behind Q1; in any case they do not derive from Q2. She examines in detail (pp. 118–20) all the passages in which there is closest correspondence between Q2 and F, finding in all of them differences from Q2 in wording, spelling, and even punctuation which suggest a manuscript source. Greg (1933, p. 260, n. 1; 1940, pp. 188–9) remains skeptical of any Q2 influence on F; van Dam (1935, pp. 73 ff) finds it plausible that a compositor using Q2 as an aid to reading his manuscript occasionally adopted readings from it unconsciously, and possibly even intentionally.

Cairncross (1955, pp. 252–8) seeks to find further Q2-F links, in support of his theory that F Lr. was set from composite or multiple copy—i.e., from both marked Q1 and marked Q2, the editor correcting in advance on one quarto, and handing it to the compositor while he proceeded to correct the other (p. 258). His case is weakened in many ways, particularly by his erroneous belief that Folio Compositor B alone set up both Q2 and F Lr., a supposed link between the texts upon which he bases several arguments. Moreover, unaware of Doran’s earlier criticism of Daniel, he accepts Daniel’s six exemplary readings as Q2F errors rather than as ordinary spelling variants. Without doing a thorough collation or providing a complete tabulation, he asserts on the basis of a random collection of minor changes in spelling and punctuation in Q2 and F—all of them improvements that any compositor or scribe might make independently—that Q2 copy (altered in accordance with the promptbook) was used as copy for F in at least the following [Q1] signatures: B4, C1v, D4, E1v-E3v, E4v, F1r-F2v, G1r, I3r, K1r, K2, K4r. Had Cairncross known of Compositor E, he might have pointed out that text from 12 of these 17 pages were set by him, and the other 5 by Compositor B. In a footnote (p. 258) he lists Q2F agreements provided privately by Alice Walker: parentheses at 1026, 1544, 2746, 2824, 2831, and 3147–9; dashes at 576, 871, and 1580; a period for aposiopesis at 832; the placement of a SD one line early at 497; and verbal omissions at 1227 and 2723. Again, Cairncross might have pointed out that all but two of these (832, 2723) were in lines set by Compositor E, had he known of him.

Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. 126) questions Cairncross’s theory of a playhouse editor working from the promptbook in Jaggard’s shop, imagining instead that such a precious possession would be kept in the theater, where one or two scribes could have annotated sections of Q1 and Q2 and delivered them alternately to the compositors. This would have been a more time-consuming and inconvenient method of producing copy than hiring a scribe to make a fresh transcript of the playbook, and such divided copy, presumably produced seriatim, would have been difficult to cast off and to coordinate with Folio production by formes set out of page order. Walton (1971, pp. 101 ff.) lists twelve indifferent variants—those similar in meaning—introduced in Q2 which reappear in F1, but thinks that except for the spelling vnusall, the F variants are all routine, practically automatic improvements upon Q1, needing no source in Q2. In an appendix (pp. 282–6) he considers all the evidence used by Daniel and Cairncross, concluding that all of their examples are (p. 286) either simple corrections of obvious errors, purely indifferent variants, or trivialities of spelling or punctuation. The reading vnusall is merely an error due to haplography, the second u being forgotten on account of the first; and its appearance in both Q2 and F may be simple coincidence, especially since, as Doran (1931, p. 120) says, its apparent derivation from Q2 in F is not supported by close agreement throughout the speech in readings, punctuation, or capitals.

Horsman (ed. 1973, pp. 231–2), entertaining Cairncross’s hypothesis of composite copy, and accepting some of his evidence that Q2 influenced some F pages more than others, suggests that Compositor B set from a marked Q1 and Compositor E from a marked Q2. This hypothesis is developed in detail by Stone (1980, pp. 129–40): general similarities of spelling and punctuation in Q2 and F, he thinks, are due to Jaggard’s house style being applied in both texts, and so are not especially significant. Since both are edited texts, in which obvious misprints are emended, small functional words are supplied or deleted as required by sense or meter, and common colloquial locutions expanded or contracted according to taste, it is unsurprising that on several occasions their revisions coincide; indeed, with its far greater number of small alterations, F more often than not disagrees with the changes in Q2. There remains, however, a small residue of identical readings, agreements between F and Q2 against Q1, which it would be much more difficult to explain away as in the nature of things predictable. They consist of [132] (a) common anomalies of spelling, (b) common omissions apparently unprompted by the context, (3) common interpolations apparently unnecessary to sense or metre and (d) common substitutions where the original requires no emendation. He states that there are only ten certainly significant examples—(a) 534 raz’d/raiz(’)d, 1255 vnusuall/vnusall; (b) 1227 my good Lord away?/my Lord, away., 3208 the Captaine/[om.]; (c) 562 canst doe/canst thou doe?, 667 Doo’st/Do’st thou, 2813 mocke,/mocke me:; (d) 629 on’s/ones, 2684 durst/darst (Dar’st), 3113 stople/stop—and six more doubtful ones—(a) 177 Physicion/Physition, 292 farewell/farwell, 1779 tyrannie/tiranny, 3117 arraine/araigne; (d) 464 sith/sigh(e), 3261 So thinke I to/So I thinke too/I so I thinke—a much smaller list than Doran’s, because he ignores other common spelling variants (prize, pezant, rellish) and obvious corrections. (P. 134): Despite these similarities, F cannot have been set solely from Q2, since F frequently agrees with Q1 against Q2, as in retaining mislineation at 2990–2990+1.

Punctuation, Stone believes, is decisive in showing that F derived only partly from Q2. (Pp. 136 ff.): The punctuation of F is heavier than that of Q2, and more correct, but it does not differ significantly in the positioning, at least, of the stops. The Q2 additions to or alterations from F show an alternating pattern. (P. 137): The parts of the text which most faithfully reproduce the pointing of Q2 coincide exactly with the pages of F set by compositor E.…Compositor E must have been using a specimen of Q2 as his copy [or to supplement his copy?].…[Stone’s attributions precede Howard-Hill’s demonstration that Compositor E set all of quire ss.]…We find, too, that certain errors and anomalies in the Q2 punctuation are transformed to F—again, on these pages only. Finally, of the fourteen readings shared between F and Q2 which we have isolated [see p. 276] as most likely to be significant, all occur on these same pages [with one exception].…B’s pages… show no connection at all with Q2—no shared readings, no common anomalies or errors of punctuation.…The signs are, rather, of derivation from…manuscript derived from Q1:…erroneous punctuation…[and] frequent manuscript misreadings.…[Stone concludes that] the specimen of Q2 was altered by reference to the [prompt-book] manuscript employed by B, and that this preparation of the [Q2] copy was effected in the printing house. (P. 148): Since there were two compositors, and the prompt-book was not unbound, a second copy was prepared from Q2, whose punctuation was largely reproduced in F.

Stone lists (pp. 257–67) for each page of F the number of sentence punctuation marks originating in Q2 that reappear on those F pages. What his tabulation reveals is that E’s pages, correctly assigned, show much more than seventy percent acceptance of Q2-only punctuation, and that B’s show much less acceptance, as low as thirty-six percent, usually in the forty or fifty percent range. That is, consistently E shows more influence from Q2. Stone also (pp. 268–73) discusses a few anomalous cases where Q2 copy seems excluded because F agrees with an inferior Q1-only reading; the evidence is equivocal at most. Among his examples are eight instances in which F actually differs from both quartos (at 1415, 2023, 2029, 2239, 2359, 2510, 2511, 2601), in only one of them (2029) being clearly wrong. In fifteen additional cases the Q2 reading is slightly preferable by modern usage but is at best an improvement, not a correction of the Q1-F readings, which are all acceptable by contemporary usage, and are neither erroneous nor misleading. While in all these cases it is true that F does not agree with Q2, as one would expect it to do if Q2 were F copy, a compositor merely consulting a copy of Q2 might not have been impelled to adopt the Q2 punctuation in these cases. Thirteen of the passages were set by Compositor B, ten by Compositor E, numbers from which probably no conclusions may be drawn. Stone gives five more examples, of an agreement of Q2 and F against a superior reading in Q1, supposedly showing the opposite, the use of Q2 copy; these examples all were set by Compositor E. But here the evidence is even more inconclusive: at 969 Q2 and F are actually more correct, at 3073 all of the texts are incorrect, and at 3138 all equally acceptable. Stone specifically records (pp. 274–5) the use in F of dashes and brackets (i.e., parentheses), which are rare in the quartos and Folio. Dashes are treated equally by the Folio Compositors: two new Q2 dashes are repeated in F (576 [E], 1580 [B]), two are not (172 [E], 2141 [B]). Parentheses provide clearer evidence of Q2 influence: Brackets introduced for the first time in Q2 are, in turn, repeated in F, always by Compositor E (at 102, 1544, 2786, 2824, 2831, 3147–9). The occasion for adding parentheses in these cases, however, would have been easily recognizable independently of copy, some already having in Q1 a comma at one end of the phrase.

Stone’s figures do seem to indicate some kind of influence of Q2 upon the text of F1, especially if not exclusively through the agency of Compositor E; but whether it supports his conclusion that E’s copy was a marked-up copy of Q2 is far less certain. For many of the changes of punctuation and lining between Q1 and F, no Q2 influence is necessary—see, e.g., nn. 994–5, 995, 1255, 1580, 1792, 2813, 3074, 3113, 3206–8—but the fact that they occur in passages set by Compositor E is notable. If Q2’s punctuation had entered F as Halio (ed. 1992, p. 66) suggests, by way of a scribe making a transcript from a worn playbook and consulting a copy of Q2 to remedy its obscurities, one would expect the Q2 influence to appear more or less uniformly throughout F, not more frequently in Compositor E’s pages than in Compositor B’s. On the other hand, conceivably Compositor B applied the Jaggard house style for punctuation differently than did the novice Compositor E; after studying B’s use of exclamations, colons, brackets and semicolons, Taylor (1985, p. 65) concludes: Unlike Compositor E, Compositor B heavily interfered with the punctuation of his copy, to an extent which makes it much more difficult to use punctuation as evidence of Folio copy.

Pursuing the idea of divided copy, Taylor (1983, pp. 44 ff.) argues that Compositor B set from a promptbook, Compositor E from a marked copy of Q2. From pages of Tit., Tro., and Rom. that E set from known quarto copy, it is evident that he tended to preserve his copy’s punctuation three to six times as often as changing it; in Lr. his ratio in following supposed Q2 copy is about 3:1. Compositor B follows copy punctuation much less closely. Taylor concludes (p. 59), The Folio’s agreement with a change in the nature of Q2’s punctuation [due to a change in compositor]…is one of the strongest possible indications of a direct link between Q2 and F1. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 175), however, rejects the argument as illogical: E’s similar (though quite variable) ratios (3:1 to 6:1) in other quartos and in Lr. may be (p. 176) merely a measure of his general fidelity to all kinds of copy and so does not prove that Lr. was set from quarto copy; he might achieve the same ratios using manuscript copy. Taylor also attempts to show that E set more of the indifferent verbal variants apparently derived from Q2 than did Compositor B, but Doran (1931, pp. 112–14) had discussed almost all of these and shown they could have been arrived at independently in F and so were not demonstrably derived from Q2; see also below, and nn. 2879 and 3206–8. One therefore cannot claim that E adopted more Q2 verbal variants than did B, nor conclude therefrom that E is more evidently using Q2 as copy than is B; see also n. 2842–3. In fact Taylor admits (p. 53) that he has not attempted to see if Compositor B set from Q1, Q2, or manuscript (i.e. promptbook); he merely suggests that given E’s inexperience, he might well have been given printed copy when B was not. He does give spelling evidence that B was influenced by some other source than Q2, since for several F words B uses spellings that depart from both the Q2 reading and his own usual preferences. To explain the presence in E’s pages of two or three apparent press-variants present only in Q1, Taylor hypothesizes (pp. 55–6) that the promptbook whose readings were supposedly transferred to Q2 copy for E’s use was itself a transcript from a revision of the play made in a copy of Q1.

In a subsequent essay published in the same year, Taylor, 1983, pp. 115–16) argues that Compositor B also set sometimes from Q2 copy: My own guess is that both B and E worked from marked-up printed copy [Q2] till near the end of rr3, and that B then took over (at TLN 1853…), setting the next 6½ Folio pages (900 lines) directly from [promptbook] manuscript; Q2’s influence clearly resumes in column b of rr6v, and on the next page E resumed work, setting the remainder of the play from annotated Q2 copy. Certainly, the various highly irregular exchanges of copy between B and E described by Charlton Hinman [1963, 2:272–3]…—exchanges that are almost without parallel elsewhere in the Folio—make it extremely unlikely that, for quire qq at least, two separate blocs of copy were prepared in advance for the two compositors. Moreover, the effect of these exchanges of copy is that Compositor E did not set three pages of King Lear—qq3v, qq5, and qq2—that would else have fallen to him. These three pages contain virtually all the major Folio additions in quire qq: eleven lines on qq2, six on qq3v, thirteen on qq5. Such additions, by interleaving or annotation, would have [116] produced much messier copy, and Compositor B might well have been given the affected passages for that reason. Hinman’s own alternative explanation of E’s not setting qq2 is that he was not experienced enough to set title pages (see ); B would naturally have set qq5 if E were already at work on its forme-mate qq2v; and there is no way to know that E would necessarily have been given qq3v for his first page of Lr. These assignments of work need have nothing to do with the quality of the copy.

Howard-Hill (1985, pp. 174–5), having doubted that the players would have allowed B to set from prompt-book, adds further objections to this theory of double copy: When the play was cast-off apparently the equivalent of qq4–6v; rr1–3v was initially assigned to compositor E. There is also some reason to believe that the beginning of Lear (qq2–3v) was also included in his stint, for of those four pages B shared with E only the first forme of the new play (qq3v:4), and qq2:5v in which B set the title-page, as he usually did in F. Compositor E set the first portion in text order, the second in reverse order with occasional intervention by B. After B finished setting Timon, E, who had started to set Othello in intercalary formes ss3v:4, ss2v:5, completed Lear ss1–3 unaided; accordingly, his original stint was to consist of [485–1986] and [2739–3302] at least. The original assignments, interpreted in the light of the pages eventually set by the two compositors, indicate that compositor E was charged with the main responsibility for Lear. B’s assignment seems to have been limited to rr4–6v, although his greater efficiency (and possibly because E was doing most of the distributing) enabled him to set parts of E’s stint from time to time. If this interpretation of the printing order for Lear is correct even broadly, further doubt must fall on the distribution of copy [175] suggested [by Taylor]. The proposed stemma entails that the more difficult copy—an exemplar of Q2 with profuse handwritten corrections and additions from the manuscript—was assigned to the less experienced compositor, the one Jaggard expected to set most of the play—while the relatively easy manuscript was given to Jaggard’s most experienced man. (N. 14: Taylor [p. 365] argues that the copy of Q1 revised by Shakespeare would not itself be acceptable as a prompt-book and must have been transcribed for that purpose. On the other hand…if the prompt-book of the revised play consisted of the first prompt-book with corrections, deletions, and additions added from Shakespeare’s manuscript of the revision, with some pages of the prompt-book newly written out,…a manuscript of this kind might not have been acceptable as printer’s copy even if the players had been willing to deliver up the authorized book to the printer. In such an event, a transcript of the prompt-book would be necessary.)

Jackson (1983, pp. 314 ff.) finds irresistible (p. 328) Taylor’s theory that Compositor E used a copy of Q2 edited in accordance with a promptbook based upon Q1, but he argues (pp. 346–9) that the verbal variants, punctuation, and spellings in F strongly suggest that Compositor B was not setting from marked-up Q2 copy. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 178, nn. 16, 17) remains skeptical: Jackson supports the hypothesis of B’s manuscript and E’s Q2 copy with two arguments which an intermediate transcript would seriously confuse, and another (that the indifferent variants connecting F and Q2 are far more impressive in compositor E’s pages than in B’s) which more likely points to the well-known differences between the compositors’ capabilities and respect for copy than to distinctions in the copy itself.…Jackson…points to Q2 links in B’s stint in F. Therefore, the copy of both compositors had links to both Q1 and Q2, an observation not accommodated by Taylor’s stemma but consistent…with a postulated intermediate transcript influenced by Q2.

Taylor (1985, pp. 17 ff.) attempts again to prove not only that Compositor B used Q2 copy but that he used it throughout—that is, both B and E used annotated Q2 as their copy. In the process he discovers (pp. 30 ff., pp. 48 ff.) a longer list (than that in his 1983 essay) of words of which Compositor B’s spellings in Lr. depart from both Q2 and his own preferences, strongly suggesting the influence of a different source than Q2. In addition, a number of other features suggest that B was working from something other than Q2 (p. 65): an inexplicably low number of brackets are used and (p. 68) virtually no semicolons are reproduced from (Q2) copy; nonetheless (p. 69), B’s use of colons and semicolons in Lear by no means establishes his use of manuscript (though it would certainly be compatible with that hypothesis). Furthermore (p. 70), The Folio also contains, as Stone observed, a number of lines where acceptable Q2 punctuation has been altered for the worse, errors which Taylor insists remain dubious as evidence of manuscript copy, possibly being traceable to the compositor, or to (p. 71) a Q2 annotator who may have occasionally altered his Q2 in accordance with his MS. In the upshot, though still rejecting as implausible (p. 56) the possibility that someone prepared a special transcript which copied the accidentals of Q2 while incorporating many substantive readings from some other manuscript, he finally concludes that (p. 71) Both Compositor B and his partner appear to have worked from the same kind of copy. That copy was either (most probably) Q2, or some sort of transcript which had been influenced by Q2 to an extraordinary extent. Two years later Taylor, in Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 530), still holding out for Q2 copy, is yet more amenable to the idea of a transcript: Logically, no amount of correspondence between the substantives and incidentals of Q2 and those of F can prove that F was set from Q2, rather than from a remarkably faithful transcription of Q2. Halio (ed. 1992, pp. 64–5) doubts Q2 copy, showing that some of Taylor’s evidence is subject to alternative interpretation; see nn. 2745–9, 2718. Weis (ed. 1993, pp. 4–5) inclines to marked Q2 copy in association with some intermediate MS reflecting features of Q1. Mowat & Werstine (ed. 1993, p. lvii) acknowledge that editors sometimes suspect annotated Q2 copy.

Although Blayney (1982–) has never published his conclusions about F copy, some of them have been partially reported on by others—see, e.g., Howard-Hill (1986, p. 435, n. 24), and the following from Halio (ed. 1992, pp. 67–8): Blayney…weighs the evidence for and against annotated q2 as copy for f.…While the preponderance of q2/f agreements in quasi-substantives, punctuation, and spellings clearly demonstrates f’s indebtedness to q2 as against q[1],…it does not prove q2 was itself the copy for f. As Doran and Howard-Hill argue, it need only have been consulted during the setting of f. Blayney’s extensive examination of punctuation demonstrates that f could not have been punctuated without constant reference to a copy of q2 (his emphasis) by Compositor E, who set most of the work, and probably frequent reference to it (or another copy) by Compositor B.…The copy for f probably derived from a transcription of annotated q [serving as the revised playbook].…[68] In general, then, substantive readings and alterations derive from the manuscript; accidentals and orthography from q2. Like Blayney, Howard-Hill (1982, p. 23) prefers to think that Q2 was used only as a means to interpret the promptbook, though where Blayney apparently thinks Q2 was so used by the compositor(s) during the setting of F from a transcript, Howard-Hill believes it was consulted by the scribe as he made that transcript. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 123–6), while admitting a significant relation between Q2 and F, is not specific as to how they were combined for composition. He doubts that a marked Q2 alone would have been sufficient copy: It is…difficult to imagine how large changes or expansions, for example, the addition of seven and a half lines, together with seventeen other changes in the text and several more in stage directions in [29–71], could have been written on to [Q2] A2v, which is pretty solidly packed with printed text. He speculates therefore that the compositors sometimes worked directly from a manuscript derived from prompt copy and otherwise, for the ease of setting, where possible from Q2. The mechanics of such a system are unclear, as is any reason for marking up Q2 at all if the compositors already had a manuscript.

While there is ample and persuasive evidence that Q2 somehow influenced the punctuation of F, the evidence that it influenced verbal readings in F is much more sparse and subject to varying interpretations—see, e.g., nn. 562, 676, 829, 969, 990, 1227, 2813, 3113, 3208. An independent, computer-aided count and sort of readings in F which agree with or differ from those in either or both of the quartos yields results which on merely quantitative grounds cast doubt on the idea that the F compositors were working from Q2 copy. In the case of substantive variants, including all changes of word, case, number, verb tense or mood, word order, added or omitted words, phrases, or lines, denomination of characters, and location of stage directions, the F compositors set 90 readings that agree with Q2 readings and some 1300 that differ from Q2. If the compositors were following their copy as closely as they usually did, then these 1300 non-Q2 readings would have to have been entered previously by hand, interlinearly or marginally, into the 85 pages of the Q2 copy, at an average of more than 15 per page. Most of the objections against marked-up Q1 copy—the labor involved in preparing it, the indifferent nature of the majority of the variants, and the difficult printer’s copy that would result—would apply to such marked-up Q2 copy.

As for the 90 substantive readings that appear in both Q2 and F, virtually all of them could have been arrived at in the copy behind F without any influence from Q2. They are divided roughly proportionally between the two F compositors, if 7 regularizations of the Q1 anomaly Duke. to Alb. in Compositor E’s stint are discounted: 29 of the readings, or 34% of them, were set by Compositor B, who set 43% of the lines in the play; 54 readings, or 65% of them, were set by Compositor E, who set 57% of the lines. Of B’s readings, 8 may be discounted because Q2 simply agrees with readings in one of the states of Q1, which might have been copied from the MS behind Q1 into the playbook behind F1. Another 10 are obviously correct readings replacing (in both Q2 and F) obvious errors found in Q1. Three modernizations of the pronoun a to he may reflect either Jaggard’s house style in Q2 and F or the regularization of a scribe preparing copy for F, since they occur in the stints of both compositors. Two other readings are unnecessary but natural improvements: the provision of the pronoun object you, which fills out the meter in 2146, and the correction of the spelling heares in 2654; both could have been made automatically in both texts by a regularizing compositor or scribe. B’s two readings most suggestive of Q2 influence are the dialectal chill (for 2695 ile) in the context of several dialectal speeches, and the omission of the obscure or apparently nonsensical and for you her owne for Venter at 2723; but the first of these is only one of several instances of F’s adjustments of the dialect in this passage (see n. 2688–97 and textual notes), and the second may represent omission from the playbook behind F to avoid difficulty (see n. 2723+1).

The evidence is almost as sparse in Compositor E’s stints. In twenty-one cases Q2 simply agrees with one state of Q1, and in twenty cases both Q2 and F make obvious corrections of obvious errors. There are two possible Jaggard or scribal modernizations from a to he and one from and to if. There are five unnecessary but natural improvements that might be made automatically by a compositor or regularizing scribe: the provision of a pronoun subject thou (562, 667) and a pronoun object me (2813), the expansion of a’th to the clearer on thy (676), and the change in number from rights to the possibly more likely right (990). Three coinciding readings are suggestive of Q2 influence, but in each case they might have been made independently in the two texts: the change from the unfamiliar stople to stop (3113), the omission of the apparently redundant the Captaine (3208), and the omission of good from my good Lord (1227). Various explanations of these three readings have been offered (see the respective commentary notes), and if there was Q2 influence in these few cases, it might have been through momentary consultation of that text rather than through its continual use as F printer’s copy.

Another kind of evidence against Q2 copy is the number of times in which F ignores Q2 variants and restores Q1 (or playbook) readings. Compositor B fails to reproduce thirty-nine such Q2 readings; of these he does not reproduce ten that are Q2’s erroneous attempts at correcting Q1 (e.g., 775 lessen, 1910 Fruite, 2297 head, 2452 beake, 2454 aboue), nor the one improvement—the addition of 2640+2 Gent. Good Sir—sometimes adopted by modern editors. Q2’s erroneous omissions of small words (1491 Sir, 2590 no, 2654 that) are rectified, its unnecessary small improvements (415 shal, 749 you, 2358 do, 2393 a, 2472 tis, 2635 a, 2722 &) are not reproduced, and neither are its indifferent synonyms (750 one, 1648 doubt, 1950 has, 2254 doth, 2562 want, 2644 and) nor its pointless or erroneous changes (2036 garment, 2263 shall I, 2330 to, 2456 peebles, 2485 thought had, 2546 all, 2583 on’t, 2628 sonnes in law). Similarly out of 65 possibilities Compositor E ignores 24 Q2 errors (e.g., 864 after) and erroneous omissions; of the latter, F restores (doubtless from the playbook) two lines omitted at 938–40, the single lines 3100 and 3102, and half-lines at 3168 and 3214, but also, more surprisingly, hypermetric words (2760 good, 2768 that, 3223 Why) omitted from Q2. F also ignores five out of ten apparently deliberately changed words, including some occasionally adopted by later editors (186 make, 1585 om. hundred, 2799 where, 3118 Monster), fourteen pointless or erroneous Q2 alterations, and a number of unnecessary Q2 sophistications of conjunctions (694, 1337 If), verb forms (197 hath, 1165 doth, 2983 shewne), pronouns (2881 one, 3077 What’s, 3228 that), and transposed words (2895, 3133, 3223). If Q2 had been printer’s copy, it is hard to imagine why these mostly insignificant Q1 (or playbook) readings would have been restored; they would have had to be written into the Q2 copy by an extremely assiduous and punctilious editor. It is easier to believe that they derive from a different kind of copy where they would naturally occur without needing to be restored. So Howard-Hill (1985, pp. 177–8): The proposed stemma can accommodate [Compositor E’s] 36 Q1 forms [among his 200 departures from Q2] only if it is assumed that the Q2 collator altered, for instance, fastened to fastned, butterd to buttered, he is to he’s; it is, however, implausible that sporadic alterations of this kind would have engaged his attention.…The mixture of apparent Q1 and Q2 variants, then, witness to the compositor’s inconsistency (lack of fidelity to copy or his own spelling preferences) or his faithful reproduction of the forms of a different kind of copy.…[178] The printed copy must have been marked with a multitude of insignificant variants of a kind that editors of play texts at the time rarely concerned themselves with, or…the editor…produced just about the most unlikely kind of copy for an inexperienced compositor one could devise.

On the other hand, both F compositors fail to include phrases found in both quartos: for possible reasons for Compositor B’s omission of five Q2 words at 2640+1 and for Compositor E’s failure to adopt Q2’s three words and corrected lineation at 2990+1, see the respective commentary notes; one would normally expect the adoption of both phrases if Q2 had been copy. One would also expect F to reproduce the verse lineation of 2716–21, where Q2 set this prose letter as verse to stretch cast-off copy on the last page of the sheet. Finally, F abounds in new readings that could not easily derive from Q2 copy. At 988 F’s latch’d is not a likely misreading of Q2’s launcht, though it could be of Q1’s lancht or the playbook’s hypothetical lãch’d or lãcht. At 1794 F’s beates there, differs completely from Q2’s beares their⁁ in words and punctuation. At 2253 Compositor B did not conjecture F’s slaues from Q2’s stands. At 3128 Compositor E sets the anomalous Edmond, contrary to his usual and Q2’s spelling Edmund, most probably following a copy other than Q2. Howard-Hill (1982, p. 14): The very unusual spelling pry’thy makes it unlikely that E set directly from a copy of the [second] quarto.

div.head: Scribal Transcript
div.p: Rhodes (1923, p. 108) offered the faint suggestion that a manuscript, rather than Q1, lay behind F1, and that the same bad writing may have produced the same printer’s errors in both prints. Doran (1931, pp. 91–6; see ) found more than fifty verbal errors in F1 which she thought could only be explained as misreadings of manuscript forms, as well as punctuation errors (pp. 104–5) that could not have originated in printed copy such as Q1. From several such errors Stone (1980, pp. 100–4), thinking that the playbook was burned in the Globe fire of 1613, deduces behind F a transcript from the original Q1 copy (which he improbably believes was a reported text). Doran, however, finds (pp. 40–2) that F1 corrects most of Q1’s verbal errors because the scribe making the transcript of Sh.’s original rough draft (which would become the playbook behind F) correctly read the manuscript forms in it that the Q1 printer did not—a simpler and likelier explanation than Stone’s. Similarly Kermode (1994, pp. 99–102) points to several F corrections of Q verbal errors (at 43, 45–50, 74, 88, 94–5, 117, 1147–8) which he believes could only derive from an authorial manuscript behind both Q1 and the original transcript of Sh.’s rough draft. Doran assumes that that original transcript, which became (with revisions) the official playbook, was the manuscript used by Jaggard’s compositors; today, however, there is general doubt that the players would have given their precious playbook to the printers. Kermode, instead (p. 99): The prompt-book [with its corrections of Q errors] may itself have been copied by a scribe who provided a text for reading rather than playing, and this went to the [F1] printer. McManaway (1955, p. 155) proposed a transcript from Q1, a theory entertained by Blayney (apud Howard-Hill, 1986, p. 435, n. 24) and recently by Halio, ed. 1992, pp. 67–8. Howard-Hill (1982) demonstrated that spellings in F1 could not have been derived from any known printed copy and so proposed (only provisionally and temporarily) a transcript of Q2. Though initially resistant to this suggestion, Taylor has since (in Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 531) admitted its possibility, and in Taylor & Jowett (1993, p. 241) its likelihood: If—as the quartos give us good reason to believe—Shakespeare himself did not mark or number scene-divisions in his manuscripts, and if theatrical functionaries were not interested in adding such divisions, then the presence of scene-divisions in a Folio text is excellent evidence of a scribal transcript. In addition (1987, pp. 530–1), characters enter seuerally three times (927, 1075, 1615), a formula that occurs in only three other texts (Shr. 4.1.178 [1811], Jn. 5.6.1 [2550], TNK 2.1.16 [633]), of which Jn. is scribal and the other two may be; and the use of here in the SD at 1405 is also extremely rare in texts thought to be autograph, and may be a scribe’s alteration for the convenience of readers, not for use in the theater. Stone (1980, p. 60) is attracted by the efficiency of a transcript of the playbook—Is it not very strange that the prompt-book…was not itself transcribed? No purpose can possibly have been served by a preliminary transference of corrections from the manuscript to Q—but because he remains convinced that there are traces of Q1 in the F text, he rejects the idea. Like Williams (1953, p. 460), who doubts that the company risked giving the playbook to the printer and so permitted a scribe to make a transcript of this…text to serve as copy for the First Folio, Halio (loc. cit.) is prepared to accept that the manuscript behind F1 is such a transcript of the playbook itself, as are Kermode and Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 126). Such a theory receives support from much recent work on other Shn. plays; it is evident that for quite a number of plays either the King’s Men or Jaggard were willing to invest the 2–3 shillings (less than $50 in modern currency) that a transcript would cost in order to supply good printer’s copy and keep the playbook out of danger. Besides the several transcripts prepared by Ralph Crane (of Tmp., TGV, Wiv., MM, WT, probably Cym., and possibly 2H4 and Oth.), transcripts by other scribes have been detected behind (among others) AYL, TN, H8, and especially several plays in the Tragedies section of F1—JC, Ham., Oth., Mac., Ant., and Cor. The originals of these transcripts have seemed in most cases to be theatrical documents, most likely the playbooks.

Among the evidence for a scribal transcript behind Lr. is the presence throughout F of numerous trivial changes from both quartos which seem not to derive from a playbook. Because these changes have no theatrical significance it is difficult to imagine anyone in the theater making them in the official book. Moreover, they are not particularly representative of, and sometimes they are the opposite of, the vocabulary, spelling preferences, and grammatical forms found elsewhere in the Shn. canon. Nor are they the kinds of changes that Folio Compositors B and E are known regularly to make in their other texts. They seem most likely to reflect the habitual stylistic changes (regularizings, formalizings, improvements) that a professional scribe might contribute to a text as he was copying it.

Doran (1931, pp. 44–52) distinguishes several such kinds of variants in F, attributing them either to the scribe (not Shakespeare) who prepared the fair copy that became the playbook, or to the F printers who used that (revised) playbook as copy. (She knew nothing, of course, of the stints and habits of Compositors B and E.) She notes some fifty occasions when a noun (and usually the verb it governs) is unnecessarily changed from singular to plural or the reverse; see, e.g., note 163. Similarly several particles are changed. Q1, supposedly deriving from Sh.’s rough draft and therefore likely to preserve his spellings, regularly prints towards, sometime, and (as adverb) beside; F changes these consistently to toward (206, 494, 938, Compositor E; 2050, 2078, Compositor B), sometimes (697, 1270, both E), and besides (1616; cf. 1019). She does not note that farther (1639, 2241, 2467, 2931) is consistently changed by both compositors to further, the preferred form elsewhere in Q1, Q2, and F. Werstine (1983, p. 276): Both B and E changed towards to toward, and, in one instance (TLN 938), E apparently followed manuscript copy in setting toward, since this line is missing from the second quarto. Thus the toward variants must derive from copy, not from the compositors. The Folio is likely to modernize the older forms hath and hast to has or haue (404, 1918, 2649, B; 632, 3206, E), though they remain unchanged by each compositor at 197 and 1950 and are reversed by E at 1143, 1835, and 3300. Likewise the second-person subjunctive in Q1 sometimes becomes the indicative in -st in F (552, be/be’st, 1080 loue/lou’st, 1097 denie/deny’st; cf. wilt/wouldest, all E). In Q1 (and Q2) thy is frequently used before a vowel; in F it is changed by both compositors to thine in almost half the cases (167, 181, 676, 1804, 2346, 2580, 2595, 2597). Since the modernizations of a to he by both compositors (585, 897, 1473, 1947, 2215, 2515) are all anticipated in Q2, they may reflect only Jaggard’s house style. E’s two alterations of and to if (1119, 1156) probably reflect copy, since he did not make this change independently when setting from printed copy elsewhere (Werstine, p. 277), while three other such alterations in Q2 (694, 1337, 2644) are ignored by both compositors, indicating that they were not setting from Q2 copy. That in Q1 (and Q2) is changed to which by both compositors (259, 724, 733, 761, 781, 816, 1316, 1350, 2654, 3188), that is altered to who or whom (235, 1146, 2911, 2985, all E), B corrects whom to Who (825) and Who to Which (2232) while E alters What’s to Who’s (1616), and both men ignore Q2 changes of which (3077, 3228). Werstine (p. 279): Lear is almost unique among the Folio tragedies in preferring who[m], where, and which to quarto copy that. Virtually none of these changes serves any purpose in the theater, many are trivial, and some verge on the pedantic. While it is impossible to rule out authorial correction, they are both inconsistent with Sh.’s known style in Q1 and more rigidly regular in matters of grammatical usage than he customarily was. They seem more likely to reflect the habits of a scribe whose profession it was to turn rough drafts into smooth copy.

Still other such minor changes throughout F are more obviously non-Shn. In Q1 ye appears twice (2142, 2693); F Compositor B changes the first to you once (2142), but then both compositors add ye six more times (490, 821, 1120, 1157, 1542, 2469). In the stints of both compositors, the quartos’ vm or them is changed to ’em (908, 1399 twice, 1845, 2014, 2549 twice, 2968; cf. F-only 2611); as Waller (1966, pp. 4–5) shows, this abbreviation is virtually absent from the good quartos and from F1 plays then thought to be set from author’s papers, and appears in F almost exclusively in plays now thought to be set from transcripts. Waller similarly shows that the elision o’th (and its variants) is rare in the quartos (though there are four in Q1 Lr.) and is plentiful in Folio texts set from transcripts; in F1 Lr., both compositors alter of the (701, 746, 1105, 1464, 1502, 1662, 2511; cf. 2550), at the (1133), and ath or at’h (1400, 1613, 1860, 2399, 2794) to the evidently un-Shn. o’th, and convert a to o’ thrice (700, 1666, 2399; cf. 704, 1105). The elision i’th’ occurs never in Q1 but 25 times in F1 Lr. The elision th’hast occurs only four times in all of F1, three of them in Lr. 5.3 (2979, 3129, 3135); Q has thou hast in all three places. Both F1 compositors abbreviate Q1’s (and Q2’s) hath or haue to ha’s (632, 901, 1710, 1844, 2691, 2692, 3206; cf. 1338 ha’dst and F-only 2010); since the good quartos almost always print has without apostrophes (74:3, excluding Oth.), their presence here hints at a transcript (Wells & Taylor, 1987, pp. 531, 618). Ibid (p. 531): The overwhelming predominance of do’s [15:1 over Sh.’s characteristic does] in Folio Lr.…suggests scribal interference, since both B and E usually follow copy in this variant. In Q1 I would is variously abbreviated I’d, id’e, and ide, in Q2 the abbreviation is uniformly ide; none of these abbreviations appears in F1. Instead, Compositor E (who never elsewhere in F1 abbreviates I would) sets Il’d three times (913, 1392, 3218) and I’ld four times (637, 1009, 1157, 1372); and Compositor B sets only I’ld (twice, at 2151 and 2205), a form he uses only a dozen times elsewhere in F1, preferring I’de almost twice as often. These consistent departures from Q1 and Q2 in favor of readings in F not usually favored by either compositor strongly suggest a transcript regularly using an l and an apostrophe; indeed, most other occurrences of I’ld in B’s work appear (except for Tro. 4.5.204 [2776] and 4.5.253 [2825] and Tim. 4.3.260 [1909]) in texts now thought to be set from transcripts. Doran (1931, p. 50): Nearly always when a full form [of of, the, is, terminal -ed or -est, etc.] appears in Q1, which requires, for metrical reasons, to be elided in pronunciation, the contracted form is given in F.…[51] These contracted forms may have been introduced into the folio text by [a scribe], or they may be due to the folio printer. One discovers a good deal of contraction of this sort throughout the pages of the First Folio…. (P. 52): But in F Lr. there appears to be nothing systematic about the changes, since in about as third as many cases Q contracted forms are expanded. A computer count and sort of variants in the pages of Rom., Tit., and Tro. set by Compositors B and E from quarto copy reveals that they introduce such contractions about once or twice per page on average; in Lr., full forms on which both quartos agree are contracted in F at the rate of almost seven per page, suggesting that the majority originated in the copy.

Taylor & Jowett (1993, pp. 248–52) note that the good quartos and Folio texts that they think are set from Shakespeare’s rough drafts overwhelmingly prefer the spelling O, which they deduce was Sh.’s preferred spelling after his first eight plays; the preponderance of the spelling Oh in several late plays (Ham., Oth., Cor., Ant., and Cym.) seems due to the influence of an unknown scribe’s spelling preference. In both quarto texts the preponderant form is O, but in F this has been changed by both compositors to Oh at 606, 1328, 1397, 1415, 2301, 2311, 2313, 2589, 2631, 2703, 2725, and 2878, while ah has become Oh at 2202 and a new Oh has been added at 2295. Taylor earlier (1985, pp. 45–7) notes that in the Comedies and in 1H4 Compositor B follows his printed copy’s O and Oh without exception, and in Tit., Rom., and Tro. virtually so, returning to O only twice in those three plays. Only in R2 and R3, whose printer’s copy is still problematic and doubtful, does he alter to Oh a total of seven times. Compositor E is elsewhere completely faithful to his copy, never altering to Oh except in plays probably set from transcripts. Taylor’s argument that the much higher ratio of change to Oh in Ham. and Oth. does not support scribal copy for Lr. lacks force, since the transcripts for these plays could have been prepared by different scribes; Honigmann (1996, pp. 74–5) surmises that two or more men [i.e., scribes or editors] worked on the[se] three tragedies [placed consecutively in the Folio], perhaps simultaneously. He even speculates, on the basis of the uncorrected 1147 holly, 1225 (and 1760) worsse, and 1143 (and 1835) hath (changed from has), all spellings characteristic of Ralph Crane and very unusual in Sh., that part of the Folio page’s copy, or part of Act 2 scene 2 of King Lear, appears to have been written or corrected by Crane. Of other tests which Honigmann (pp. 138–40) applies in order to detect scribal copy, one elision occurs frequently in Lr.: where both quartos agree in the, Compositor B elides to th’ twelve times and E tenty-five times; in randomly selected pages set from quarto copy in Rom., Tit., and Tro., Compositor B introduces this elision only twice in a dozen pages and Compositor E never at all in ten pages. In F Lr., therefore, they were following neither quarto copy, nor their own preferences, nor (according to Waller, pp. 4–5) Sh.’s prevailing usage outside of plays set from transcripts.

To Doran (1931, pp. 117–18), the use of Edmond (2) and Edmund (1970) in place of the quartos’ Bastard, and of Edm. (2, 29, 32, 34) instead of the quartos’ Bast., indicates a manuscript source; Goldring (1983, p. 150) makes a similar argument about the anomalous Edm. at 487, 493, and 498, which may have been introduced incidentally through a Folio addition: see . Williams (1953, p. 460), noting that the quartos consistently spell Gonorill and both F compositors consistently spell Gonerill, reasonably concludes the copy must have been a manuscript having that spelling. Except for Walton (1955, p. 159), Horsman (ed. 1973, p. 232), and Stone (1980, p. 151), no one believes that either compositor volunteered such a change of spelling or that it was changed throughout his quarto copy. Taylor (1983, p. 393) claims that Sh. derived F’s spelling from one of his sources, Higgins, but there it is always spelled Gonerell. Idem (1985, p. 54) does argue that if in 1H4 someone changed Q5’s Falstalffe consistently to F’s Falstaffe, the same could have been done for Gonerill; but the two cases are not analogous. By 1623 the name had long been Falstaff in the quartos of 2H4, Wiv., and H5, and must have been so in the theater. There was therefore good reason so to regularize it in F1; there was no evident reason whatsoever to change the spelling Gono-, standard in all the sources, to F’s unique Gone-. This inexplicable and thoroughgoing alteration suggests a scribe who mistakenly or carelessly started spelling the name one way in his transcript and kept doing so throughout.

If, as now seems likely, a scribe prepared fresh copy for F1 Lr., he may have had a significant effect on that text. Doran (1931, pp. 43 ff.) lists examples of the kinds of substitutions of colorless words, verbal transpositions, and (p. 133) metrical improvements through contractions, omissions of expletives, and forms of the relative, all of which she thinks would be within the power of a scribe to make. Dane (1995, p. 324): Many indifferent Q/F variants of transposition are consistent with the notion of material dependence (i.e., not an author revising a text, but an object being copied professionally). The small changes suggesting a scribe also seem to point to usages later or more modern than the original style in Q1. Greg (1955, p. 357), on Oth.: The frequent spellings ’em and ha (for haue in place of the earlier a) point to a late Jacobean original. Blake (1991; 1996, p. 171): As a general rule it may be said that F [Lr.] contains spellings, grammatical forms, and lexical items which suggest a more advanced state of the language. It is possible that many of these changes could have been introduced by the compositors at the printing of F. If Q is a memorial construction, as is often supposed, it would have had to be set up in type by someone who was either deliberately archaizing the language or who was trained in a somewhat old-fashioned school. This seems improbable. Similarly Honigmann (1996, pp. 138–42), on Oth., judges that many of the kinds of changes listed above look like modernisations, away from the old-fashioned or colloquial towards the more modern or formal, produced by scribes (or compositors) who tidied the text, updated it, converting a messy play-house script into a reading text fit for an expensive Folio. He shows (p. 53) that Jaggard’s compositors often expanded colloquial contractions when setting Q2 Lr. from Q1 four years earlier.

div.head: Revisions and Other Changes
div.p: For the first three centuries after publication, the attempts to explain the differences between Q and F Lr. are based on general impressions, not bibliographical evidence. The majority of commentators believe that Q represents an earlier version and that F incorporates theatrical changes made by author, actors, or censor; a few trace features of both texts to the interventions or failures of their respective printers.

Pope (ed. 1725, 1:xvi–xxi) blames the actors for lopping Q passages to shorten some scenes (1:xvii), for adding a few trifling and bombast passages (1:xvi), and for reassigning speeches to themselves (1:xix). Moreover, those members of Sh.’s company who edited the text for F1 introduced many faults: arbitrary Additions, Expunctions, Transpositions of scenes and lines, confusion of Characters and Persons, wrong application of Speeches, corruptions of innumerable Passages by the Ignorance, and wrong corrections of ’em again by the Impertinence of those editors (1:xxi). Unfortunately he specifies only a few of these in his notes, and none of the Alterations or Additions which Shakespear himself made. Theobald (ed. 1733), who begins the editorial conflation of Q and F texts of Lr., restores from Q an occasional passage retrench’d by the Players, for Brevity’s sake (see, e.g., nn. 2307+1–+6, 2843+1–+11, 2997+1–+5, etc.) or a speech misassigned by them (see n. 3298) but does not attribute changes to authorial revision. Johnson (ed. 1765) thinks that F represents Sh.’s riper but hasty revision to shorten the play for stage representation (see, e.g., nn. 1638+1–+12, 2347+1–+56, 2843+1–+11). For Capell (ed. 1768) some variants represent authorial revision (see nn. 473+1–+6, 744+1–+4, possibly 1736–48) but most are compositorial errors or editorial cuts or sophistications (see nn. 1622–1622+8, 1631–8, 1631–1638+12). Malone (ed. 1790, 1:xii f.) generally accuses the F editors of additions and alterations of their own in plays reprinted from quartos, and frequently prefers Q readings to those he thinks are due to the F editors’ ignorance, blunders, and lack of understanding (see nn. 111, 188, 1800, 1828–9); he also thinks that the F text was cut by the actors (see n. 2843+1–+11). Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:370; summarized in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 360) suspects censorship. Knight (ed. 1840, p. 393) believes that Sh., and not the F editors, cut the purely descriptive passages, sternly resolved to let the effect of this wonderful drama depend entirely upon its action. Staunton (ed. 1859, 3:55) has doubts whether the curtailment is the work of the author, being not always judicious, and finds that some of the substitutions are inferior to the language they displace, but he is certain that the additions…bear the undoubted mark of Shakespeare’s mint. Hudson (ed. 1881, p. 4), however, detects several passages in F (923–4, 1734–49, 2376–81, 2945–6) and one in Q (2056+5–+18) that are certainly not written by Shakespeare. Delius (1875, pp. 125–47) thinks that omissions from Q were in part due to printers’ blunders and in part to clumsy editing, and that the abridgement of F, often so carelessly performed that Sh. could not have had a hand in it, was carried out by actors after Sh. left the theater company and retired to Stratford; this reverses his earlier position (ed. 1854, 1:I–II) that Shakespeare made the revisions in F. Fleay (1879, p. 119) dates the actors’ abridgement 1616–22, Ingleby (1881, 2:120) query after 1613. Boas (1896, p. 438 n.) also credits the actors: There is no need to suppose that Shakspere himself had a hand in the abridgement, or that the folio is his revised version of an earlier text. Reed (1902, p. 89) proposes that the revision was made by Francis Bacon.

The essays of Tieck and Koppel (1877, pp. 63–102; summarized in Furness, ed. 1880, pp. 364–7) reach opposite conclusions and employ arguments still being used a hundred years later. Tieck considers more than a hundred pairs of Q/F verbal variants, finding that in most cases the Q readings are ductus literarum errors of scribe or printer, or at least their substitutions of inferior synonyms; or that Q omissions of words spoil, while F additions improve, the meter; that Q omissions are not passages later added by Sh. to F, but are real gaps which Shakspere could not possibly have left himself in his original work; and that F cuts could not have been made by Sh. He offers a general rationale against Shn. revision: Is it probable that Shakspere—supposing that he revised the text—would have given himself the trouble of making all these innumerable minute alterations without any apparent reason, instead of making any deeper and more essential improvement? Or, is it not more probable that some copyist,—who attached but little importance to Shakspere’s words as such,—in the haste of his work, substituted, either wilfully or carelessly, an expression which occurred to him, a particle, a mood, or a numeral, for the one used in the original?… [139] Had Shakspere, in the leisure of his Stratford life, re-examined his drama with a view to altering it, his revision would have left deeper traces on it than is the case. The theatrical abridgement was done by the company, not the author: Shakspere allowed the company for which he wrote to do as they pleased with his plays.…This drama was, like all Shakspere’s other dramas, their property, which they could treat as they pleased. Moreover (p. 140), It is very doubtful whether the actors would have thanked the poet for a complete revision of the text,…[seeing] what awful confusion the restudying of the text, altered in a thousand particulars, would introduce among the actors.…The actors did not want a revised text of King Lear, but only one somewhat abridged.

Koppel, on the contrary, argues that whatever Sh. may have felt about his future literary fame, as actor, manager, dramatist, and theater-poet he had an immediate and practical interest in supervising what his company did with his play. Koppel therefore reviews most of the Folio additions and cuts, arguing that on the whole they might be Sh.’s work. (P. 70; Furness, p. 365): The original form was, essentially, that of the Quarto, then followed a longer form, with the additions in the Folio,…then the shortest form, as it is preserved for us in the Folio.…[82] It would have to be assumed that these additions…, made, perhaps, not all at the same time, gradually so increased that at last a reduction proved to be necessary. In the cutting (p. 87; Furness, p. 366) we may…see the artist’s hand, though in some cases doubtfully: Often Shakespeare was careless in regard to secondary incidents. Indeed (p. 96), It is also possible that different passages were stricken out at different times, and in part also by different hands. In the same year Schmidt (1879) accounts for Q’s inferiority by the theory that it is a shorthand report of performance of an earlier and original version of the play; like Delius he denies (p. 6) that there is any reason to think that Sh. made the revision found in F, with all its trifling changes of words and phrases that change nothing and that would have been a nuisance for the actors to rememorize.

Such impressionistic assessments continued well into the twentieth century. Herford (ed. 1899, p. 5): Of the authenticity of all the passages peculiar to either text there cannot be a doubt, and there is a strong prima facie probability that all are derived from the same original version, so long a play being inevitably curtailed in performance.…[6] A subsequent Shakespearean revision cannot be absolutely dismissed.…But a study of the variants rather suggests that they can be wholly explained from the twofold operation of blundering printers [in Qq] and semi-intelligent actors [in F1]. Cunnington (1910, pp. 445–53): F1 admittedly shows signs of stage corruption and shortening because it was edited by the actors, but also shows signs of authorial revision. (P. 446): Usually the new matter [in F] is not necessary to the sense and would show no gap if omitted.…[Also, it] sometimes shows traces of afterthought, as if it had been added when the original was not absolutely fresh in memory.…The folio corrects a great many obvious blunders; but, apart from that, is by no means always the better text.…[453] The revision [is] practically confined to making omissions and additions. …The added passages… are explanatory, to intensify the dramatic effect, and sometimes to strike a far deeper note.…There is everywhere improvement. Moriarty (1913, pp. 451 ff.), a strong advocate of authorial revision, anticipates later theories of streamlining: after the publication of Q1, and possibly after his retirement to Stratford, Sh. attempted to [453] improve a play by revising it without in any sense rewriting it, and by making comparatively few changes.…[454] He inserts here a line and there a longer passage that would make the [plot] sequence more natural or more convincing, and [his skill] is no less evident in his adroit removal of whatever delayed the movement or too manifestly obtruded itself into the current of the plot.

From the end of the century onwards into the next, notes of doubt or agnosticism are common. Dowden (1877, p. 136): The opinion that the later text—that of the folio—exhibits a revision of his own work by Shakspere is not supported by sufficient evidence. Craig (ed. 1901, p. xiv): We cannot with any certainty determine whether the author was in any way responsible for their [Q/F] differences. My study of the two texts leads me to believe that he was not. Bradley (1904, p. 448), considering some textual difficulties: I think it more probable that the defects referred to arose from carelessness or other causes than from Shn. revision. Neilson & Hill (ed. 1909, p. 3): The Folio apparently represents a later revision of the play, cut down in some instances for stage presentation, but in other cases competently revised, perhaps by Shakespeare himself. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 224 ff.): A producer must ask himself whether these two versions do not come from different prompt-books, and whether the Folio does not, both in cuts and additions, sometimes represent Shakespeare’s own second thoughts.…[227] I recommend a producer to found himself on the Folio. For that it does show some at least of Shakespeare’s own reshapings I feel sure. The notion of two promptbooks was considered and rejected by Wilson, Greg, and Walker; see . No one now believes that Q1 is based on a promptbook, and in fact Granville-Barker often prefers Q readings, and notes (p. 141), We may do best, as students, to approach King Lear, not even through the Folio,…but through the yet greater simplicity, the very crudity of the Quartos, which record neither acts nor scenes and often leave us guessing whether characters are on the stage or off. Chambers (1930, 1:467) suspects a mixture of theatrical cutting, possible censorship, and at least one non-authorial interpolation. He elsewhere (1:298, on R3) rejects any conception of Shn. revision limited to the smoothing out of metre and the substitution of equivalent words, without any incorporation of any new structure or any new ideas, requiring that the actors relearn their parts with an infinity of trivial modification. Harrison (ed. 1937; rev. 1949): There is nothing to show whether Shakespeare or one of his company made this revision. Kittredge (ed. 1940, p. viii): The [Q/F] differences…by no means warrant the theory that Shakespeare ever re-wrote his King Lear or subjected it to a substantial revision. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 124–5): There is no basis for any theory of a Shakespearian revision separating Q1 and F (apart from whatever share Shakespeare may have had in the work of abridgment).

After the Cambridge editors’ (ed. 1863–6, 8:xiii–xv) disentanglement of Q1(u), Q1(c), and Q2, Koppel’s (1877, pp. 67–80) and Daniel’s (facs. 1885, pp. v–xii) analysis of Q1 press variants, and Greg’s (1908) and Pollard’s (1909) accurate dating of Q2, theories of the derivation of F become increasingly affected by considerations of how that text might have been altered during the printing process, by scribes, compositors, and proof-readers. In addition, the methodical study of extant quartos and folios and of surviving dramatic documents led to increasingly informed considerations of the possible influence of censorship, theatrical revision by authors and others, stenographic reporting, scribal transcripts, theatrical adaptation to different playing spaces, and the like. Doran (1931, pp. 39–56), while making a case for authorial revision in F, scrupulously attempts to segregate all of the F readings which may be attributed to the intervention of compositors, scribes, and perhaps a censor. Printers or scribes might be responsible for the small alterations of pronouns, prepositions, articles, and the like, and (as the printers of Q2 demonstrate) for the substitution of commonplace synonyms. Less predictable substitutions in F (e.g. 1194 coniunct/compact, 3009 aduancement/addition, 84 richer/ponderous, 3084 my tongue/mine Honours) or alterations which leave the meter intact (680 lesse wit to lesse grace, addition of 1296 By Iuno, I sweare I, 158 reuerse thy doome to reserue thy state, and many more) indicate that (p. 56) the two texts have different manuscripts as their basis, and that they exhibit certain variations which could not have been produced through the agency of printers and transcribers. Moreover, F contains some hundred lines not in Q. She assumes that such deliberate revisions as are evident in F are the work of Shakespeare, though she never reinforces that supposition.

Whereas van Dam (1935, p. 71) believes that F qualitatively is too inferior a text to represent Sh.’s revision, Greg (1942, pp. 89 ff.) opposes Doran’s (and others’) idea of authorial revision largely on the basis of textual and bibliographical evidence. This persuades him that Q and F differ because Q1 is an inauthentic text reported from performance, F derives from the prompt-book (probably revised somewhat for revivals), and F copy (which Greg believes is a marked-up Q1) was further altered by a sophisticating editor. His rejection of authorial revision is, however, mainly based on intuitions of Sh.’s manner of working. (P. 89): We have no evidence whatever that such persistent and wholesale revision was anything but exceptional in Elizabethan dramaturgy, and…it appears particularly unlikely in the work of so fluent a writer as Shakespeare.…Nor can I believe that the folio represents a conceivable revision.…That [Sh.] should rewrite a play in order to make a lot of verbal alterations is surely not in character, and (n. 2) There is no suggestion of any structural necessity for revision in…Lear. The arguments of Doran and Greg are presented above in detail; see .

In the 1960s a different question was increasingly debated: if F included Sh.’s second thoughts, did that fact give the F text an especially preferred status? Ridley (ed. 1935) could not accept that F, despite its typographical superiority, was an independent and superior text, and so he based his edition on Q, adding F-only passages in brackets. In his Arden edition of Oth. (ed. 1958, pp. xliii–xliv) he argued by analogy with Keats’s revised Eve of St. Agnes and Wordsworth’s 1850 Prelude that second thoughts are not always improvements, hence that Sh’s own revisions need not be preferred in a modern edition. Smidt (1964, pp. 101–2) concluded that the Quarto Lear is almost as often superior to the Folio as the other way about, and that perhaps Lr. was a play which exist[s] in equally authentic variant editions, perhaps resulting from scribes interpreting his manuscripts differently. This essay persuaded Duthie (1965, pp. 32–3; Ger.) that, despite his long-standing belief that F was a Shakespearean version, the question of independent versions needed to be taken up again and debated seriously. His tentative conclusion was that, even if Sh. himself made or sanctioned changes in the promptbook for theatrical reasons, one need not adopt these changes in a modern edition. Sh. gave the manuscript to the players in the form which his artistic intelligence (künstlerische Sinn) wished it to have; any changes that he approved for technical considerations in the theater were outside (p. 33) his purely artistic purpose, and surely he would want posterity to concentrate on his purely artistic conception. If, however, Shakespeare himself made later changes for purely artistic or literary purposes, then we may have in Q and F two Shn. versions of Lr. Honigmann (1965, pp. 121–8), in answer to Ridley, finds evidence of Sh.’s artistic revision in incidental metrical irregularities introduced into F (at 269, 774, 833, 857, 1014–15, 1036, 2816, 2890, and 3247), and rejects Ridley’s comparison with The Eve of St. Agnes and The Prelude, both revised when the quality of their authors’ work was falling off: a Shakespearian fair copy, on the other hand, would be very much a contemporary of the foul papers. (As Doran has shown, however, it is unlikely that Sh. made his own fair copy from foul papers, though he might have revised one made by a scribe.)

If, as these critics had intimated, Q and F were independent and equally authoritative Shn. versions, what could be the justification for conflating the two texts into one, as had been the practice since Theobald? Granville-Barker (1927, p. 224): If F excisions and additions represent Sh.’s second thoughts, where Quarto and Folio offer alternatives, to adopt both versions may make for redundancy or confusion. The if is crucial, of course, as are the presumed motives for revision. Furness (ed. 1880, p. 359): By whom were these excisions made…? By the master himself, or by the actors? Are they made in accordance with a plan, or hap-hazard? Was the object to shorten the play, or to emphasize dramatic effects? In taking up these questions, Warren (1978, pp. 96 ff.) begins with provisional suggestions—There may be no single ideal play of King Lear.…F may indeed be a revised version of the play,…its additions and omissions may constitute Shakespeare’s con-[97]sidered modifications of the earlier text, and…we certainly cannot know that they are not—but ends eight pages later with far more coercive language: Q and F (p. 105) must be treated as separate versions of King Lear,…eclecticism cannot be a valid principle.…What we as scholars, editors, interpreters, and servants of the theatrical craft have to accept and learn to live by is the knowledge that we have two plays of King Lear sufficiently different to require that all further work on the play be based on either Q or F, but not the conflation of both. The long-debated question of whether the changes in F were Sh.’s or someone else’s is not directly addressed, let alone decided, though Warren concedes (p. 106) that that is my suspicion, citing several other critics who share that opinion, and he asserts his belief that the F changes have authority and that at least one of them represents (p. 98) probably what Shakespeare wrote. In arguing that Q and F embody two different artistic visions, both possibly Sh.’s, Warren uses the kind of argument employed earlier by Moriarty (1913, pp. 456–7)—that the changes in Q are related to changes in F, and changes in F interrelated with each other. (P. 98): New material is included in F that appears to make up for the omission. The interrelated Q/F changes reflect in particular changed conceptions of the characters of Albany and Edgar. (P. 99): In brief, the part of Albany is more developed in Q than in F, and in Q he closes the play a mature and victorious duke assuming responsibility for the kingdom; in F he is a weaker character, avoiding responsibility. The part of Edgar is shorter in F than in Q; however, whereas in Q he ends the play a young man overwhelmed by his experience, in F he is a young man who has learned a great deal, and who is emerging as the new leader of the ravaged society. For the interpretations of passages upon which these conclusions rest, and for rejoinders, see nn. 1294+1–1296, 2056+5–+18, 2184–7, 2303–2303+17, 3168+1–+18, 3210. (Coghill, 1964, pp. 179 ff. had similarly argued that changes in F Oth. were serially connected.)

Warren’s premises are immediately challenged by Stone (1980, pp. 114 ff.), who finds in the F version too many remaining errors and obscurities, obtuse mistakes and misconceptions, unnecessary corrections, fussy regularizations of grammar, syntax, idiom, logic, and meter to justify thinking F to be a Shn. revision. In the F additions as in the smaller revisions throughout he finds features of the style of Philip Massinger—involuted syntax, a fondness for periodic sentences and parenthetic construction, stiltedness and tortuosity, a logical and methodical turn, a vein of pedantry, and fastidiousness with regard to verbal usage and grammatical and syntactical orthodoxy—as described by T. A. Dunn, Philip Massinger (1957, pp. 214 ff.). From topical evidence he dates this non-Shn. revision 1616–20. Taylor (1983, pp. 401–4) plausibly rejects some of Stone’s topical allusions and ideas concerning F copy, but his argument (1983, p. 443, n. 97) that Lr. contains none of Massinger’s favorite words is without weight, since there is little opportunity in the F additions for such words as apostasy, embryon, scarabs, imp feathers, etc. Conversely, the presence in Lr. of forms not usual in Massinger (has, i’th’, ye) does not rule him out as reviser, since these forms may have been added to Lr. by a scribe. Taylor also attempts (pp. 395 ff.) to rule out all other likely hired revisers, failing to find their stylistic markers in Lr., and attempts to prove some of the revisions Sh.’s by means of dubious image clusters (see nn. 1322–7, 1828).
