As for Stone’s date of 1616–20, Taylor remarks (p. 351), Even to speak of the date and the authorship of the redaction presumes something we have no right to presume: that all the changes between the Quarto and Folio versions were made at the same time and by the same man; two pages later, however, he argues that Sh. made all the revisions ca. 1609–10.

Like Warren, Urkowitz (1980, p. 3) declares that in many specific details—of dialogue, stage movement, spectacle, characterization, and plot—either of the two early texts is superior to the modern version; that the Folio text represents a careful and dramatically sensitive revision of the Quarto; and that the revision could have been made by no other than Shakespeare himself. He argues (pp. 16–17) that alterations in F change characterizations, adjust the rhythms and sense of the dialogue, reshape individual scenes, and revise entrances and exits. For his examples (pp. 21 ff.) of interrupted actions which thwart audience expectations, and for responses of other critics to his interpretations, see nn. 176, 970, 2014+1–+30, 2311+1–+8, 2630, and 2632. For his examples of changed effects of players’ entrances and exits (due to reassignment, cutting, or amplification of speeches, to changes in stage business, or to relocation of exits or entrances), and for critical rejoinders, see nn. 202, 204, 854–5, 1227, 1477; 1594, 1597, 1601; 2056+1–+4, +5–+18; 2176+1–+9, 2347+1–+56, 2744, 2843+1–+11, 2936, and 2981+1–+2. For his examples of interrupted exits which create surprise by frustrating expectation (of an exit), and for other interpretations, see nn. 1631–1638+12, 1631–8, 1634–8, 1639–40, 2349, and 2731. For his examples of F changes that result in a different conception of Albany’s character (morally ambiguous) and role (reduced), see nn. 2864+1–+2, 2868–2868+4, 2868+5, 2869, 2898, 2997+1–+5, 3026; 3035, 3037; 3051+1, 3119, 3194, 3210, and 3295. Overall, the changes in F produce better, especially more complex, drama, and so may therefore be taken to be Sh.’s own revisions. (Pp. 147–8): The dramatic boldness, sensitivity, and power demonstrated by the variants in the Folio declare that only a masterful playwright is at work.…[148] Careful comparison of the Quarto and the Folio texts of King Lear offers abundant lessons in Shakespeare’s own style of enriching the performance of his plays: surprises, quickenings of rhythms, and the repeated endowment of movement with meaning. He attempts (pp. 144–6) to eliminate non-authorial cutting, especially the company’s shortening the playing time (by a mere twenty minutes) or reducing the number of actors. On F changes in Albany’s role see also Gurr (1988).

Warren’s and Urkowitz’s claims that F intentionally presents an author’s (probably Sh.’s) different characterizations have met with skepticism. Concerning Edgar, Vickers (1981, p. 406): Warren’s method reflects a contemporary distrust of Shakespearean characters who are presented as paragons or as morally admirable. Clare (1995, pp. 59): Rather than being authorial revisions, some of the F omissions may have been made (perhaps at another time, and quite possibly under protest, whether by the author or by somebody else) in order to enhance…a star performance in the role of Edgar. Concerning Albany, Edwards (1982, p. 697) would expect more extensive revision from an author: In the first place, the recharacterization is pointless; and in the second, if Shakespeare had wished to refashion Albany’s part it is certain that he would have rewritten at least one speech. He would not have worked entirely by excision. The new quality of Albany seems to me the fortuitous result of playhouse cutting. Bevington (1987, p. 510): Many cuts in F look like cuts of necessity for performance. Albany’s part…is markedly reduced, but not his philosophical position.…Folio still permits him to say [2323–4]. Muir (1983, p. 101; 1985, p. 65), contra Warren: The modification of the characters of Albany, Kent, and Edgar were the results of the cuts, not the motive for them. Thomas (1984, p. 510): Leaving aside…the puzzling question of why Shakespeare should have wanted to transform a morally clear character [Albany] into an ambiguous one, I question the ambiguity itself. Certainly, the Folio in IV.ii and elsewhere has cut some of Albany’s expressions of moral judgments. But these cuts bring into even clearer relief the two Folio speeches [2323–6, 2344–7] which, as Urkowitz himself says [p. 91], declare Albany’s moral system, fiercely and unequivocally.…No other speech in the entire play more unequivocally states a belief in a benevolent universal power than the first.…It seems to me a violation of common sense to assume that Shakespeare undertook a revision of his play directed mainly to a transformation in the role of a relatively minor character, and that he accomplished this transformation almost entirely by cutting, without adding a single meaningful new line to clarify his supposedly changed vision of Albany for his audience. Honigmann (1990, p. 58), questioning whether Sh. or anyone ever revised by reassigning speeches, as between Albany and Edgar in 5.3: Shakespeare excelled in making his dramatis personae speak in character—he, surely, would be the last writer to switch around speakers’ names quite so freely. Clare (1995, p. 45): Even retrospective analysis cannot render Albany peripheral to the final stages of the action, and nowhere do the revisionists satisfactorily explain why Shakespeare should have felt his diminution to be an improvement. Terms such as moral ambiguity and complexity are simply subjective judgments expressed in weighted vocabulary with a positive spin as compensation for a lack of substance in argument. A lack of definition becomes an ambiguity, which then becomes a subtlety, which is in its turn accounted part of a strategy of revision.

Nonetheless, similar claims are advanced for other characters, on the same grounds that F changes were interrelated in an intentional revision. As McLeod (1983, p. 167) puts it, thematic consistency to the co-ordinate variation suggests purposeful differentiation. The contexting of many changes (some erroneous) of single words results in differential reading. (Pp. 170 ff.): In the first scene Gonerill [F] need not be such a bitch after all, though Gonorill [Q] may be.…[171] F offers a vision of somewhat greater moral ambiguity. In 1.3 (while she is urging insults and insubordination towards Lear and planning a future showdown with him) Gonerill’s actions in F are relatively cool and reasoned, in Q Gonorill has lost her grip on herself, taking on monstrous dimensions. (P. 178): In 1.4, F’s Gonerill is coming to the boil slowly, whereas Gonorill’s reactions are manic depressive alternation. In 2.4 Gonorill enters (p. 181) on the offensive, in F silent and on the defensive. For other representative arguments, see nn. 1033–43, 1419–24, 2014+1–+30, 2864+1–+2, 3119. Conversely, F weakens the good daughter, according to Ioppolo (1991, pp. 167, 177): The omission in the Folio of the lines found in the Quarto recasts her as a submissive, nonpolitical, and nonmonarchical daughter who embodies strength only when present on stage.…[177] Because the Folio text lacks [4.3] and [the contrasting desc. of Goneril in 2311+1–+6], it weakens the establishment of moral strength in Cordelia by reducing her at this point in the play to a supporting character rather than a fundamental one. Honigmann (1993, p. 941): If so, it is not clear to me that Shakespeare improved the play in revising it. Only Foakes (1993, pp. 106, 109–10) seems much persuaded of the changed effects.

Warren (1983, pp. 60, 63, 70) argues that although Kent’s character is not different in Q and F, his role is diminished so that Cordelia’s and Edgar’s (primarily) may be enhanced. (P. 63): During and after 3.6 in the Quarto all Kent’s major plot functions are taken from him; a previously dynamic figure, Kent-as-Caius becomes static.…[He] atrophies, ceasing to have a clear dramatic purpose. (In F, 17 of his speeches are omitted, amounting to 336 words. Except for 3.6, which cuts 2 speeches of 51 words, only Act 4 is significantly involved, and the vast majority there—11 of the 17 speeches, 204 words out of 336—disappear with the cutting of 4.3, whose omission was certainly not occasioned by a wish to reduce Kent.) To Warren the motive is inconsequential. (Pp. 60–3): Whether as a central aim of the revision or as an incidental consequence of revisions with other major objectives, the part of Kent undergoes such substantial change…that in the Folio he becomes a marginal figure until his entrance just prior to Lear’s final scene.…[63] All Kent’s major plot functions are taken from him.…Instead he becomes mainly an emblematic figure…a spokesman for humane values.…The more concentrated dramaturgy of the Folio, however, has no room for Kent’s choric utterances. Smidt (1990, pp. 131) independently thinks that F’s cuts in Kent’s part continues a degradation already begun in Q from a young, staunch defender and challenger to an older, more passive, suddenly decrepit man anticipating death. Clare (1995, p. 42), contra Warren: Kent retains an essential plot function: first, in getting the king to Dover, and then (albeit by default) enabling him to wander off alone. Neither is he necessarily static when it comes to the battle. His intention personally to fight for Lear is implicit in the short exchange with the Gentleman which F omits from 4.7.

Even the part of the Fool, who disappears after 3.6, is thought to be revised. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 219, 230): As a result of revisions which affect 54 lines out of 225 in the Fool’s part, in Q he is a natural, in F cool and rational, a wise and worldly jester, more urbane and more oblique than his precursor [in Q].…[230] The F Fool is dramatically superior to his Q equivalent; the only writer capable of surpassing Shakespeare at the height of his powers was Shakespeare; therefore the Fool’s part was revised, not adapted. For examples of his arguments see nn. 628, 658, 744, 744+1–+4, 1322–7, 1734–49, 2007–12, 2014+1–+30, 2014+9–+10, 2043. Calvo (1992, pp. 48–9): Kerrigan is mistaken in attributing superior literary merit to F and in identifying these changes as evidence of authorial revision.…Sometimes…the Folio impairs rather than improves the Quarto, discussing 625–39; cf. nn. 669+1–+11, 669+6–+7. Foakes (1985, pp. 37 ff.): I do not believe the contrast between the texts is as clear-cut as Kerrigan claims.…[39] I see no warrant here for asserting that the Fool senses his irrelevance or is leaving Lear, or that he is changed from a blathering natural to a canny rationalist, or that (p. 40) the Folio Fool [is] superior dramatically to the Quarto Fool. However (p. 43), The Folio version makes the part more consistent by emphasising the displacement of the Fool from Lear’s immediate concern [and sympathy] in the latter scenes, and expanding his function as sardonic social commentator. Idem (1993, pp. 99–105) further develops these and other arguments, emphasizing Sh.’s complex and many-sided conception of the Fool in both texts. (Pp. 104–5): The changes made in F thus continue to suggest varying perspectives on the character.…[105] Shakespeare took pains by small additions in F to keep alive the King’s tenderness for his knave even as the Fool is displaced by Edgar to become a more marginal figure. He does not say why Sh. must be the reviser; some of the Fool’s F additions, including occasional quips and jingles and particularly Merlin’s prophecy in 3.2, are often thought to be spurious (see, e.g., nn. 1322–7, 1734–49, 2010–12, 2043), and the cut of the mock trial from 3.6 may not be authorial (see n. 2014+1–+30).

Notable in a supposed authorial revision of Q Lr. into a different play is the relative lack of change in F to the central character, the King, whose part includes 22% of the words in the traditional text. Taylor (1983, p. 416) judges that Lear’s role is no less strenuous and commanding in F than in Q, and Clayton (1983, p. 121) finds no radical abbreviation of dialogue or simplification of philosophical issues. Werstine (1988, pp. 2 n. 4, 11), doubting distinct authorial versions of Lr., points out that unlike these minimal changes in the role of Lear, the revisions in Ham. affect mainly the protagonist. What local changes Clayton detects, and how he thinks that they affect dramatic purpose, theatrical effect, and thematic significance and systematically prepare for a different ending to the play, may be seen in nn. 43, 45–50, 1888–9, 3168+1–+18, 3282–3, and 3285. Foakes (1993, p. 109): F adds a few lines for Lear which explain his motives in dividing the kingdom…[and] might be seen as softening a little the impression of absolute domination and arbitrary use of power conveyed more strongly by the text in Q. (In both Q and F versions of the scene, however, he still disowns and punishes Cordelia, threatens and exiles Kent, and treats the King of France with contempt.) F’s added lines 3282–3 allow for the possibility that he dies in joyful delusion that Cordelia remains alive; so the F text makes his death more richly nuanced than in Q, though in both Q and F death comes as a release from suffering, a kind of bitter benefit. (Lear has similar delusions earlier in the scene in Q.) Clayton does not explain why the changes are Sh.’s. Taylor (1983, p. 427): F makes Lear’s death strikingly similar to Gloucester’s…[with] some sense of hope, transcendence, spiritual consolation. Whether Lear’s death is significantly changed by F’s two added lines has been much disputed: see n. 3282–3. If Sh. revised the play while writing the late romances, one might expect more. Bradley (1904, p. 252): I believe Shakespeare would have ended his play thus [as Tate did] had he taken the subject in hand a few years later, in the days of Cymbeline and the Winter’s Tale. Foakes (1993, pp. 107–8) points out that Q repeatedly tries to generate pity and compassion for the suffering of Lear and others in passages that the less emotionally coercive F excises.

Others find structural and thematic reasons for F’s changes that suggest authorial revision. Taylor (1980, pp. 28 ff.) makes the final battle between Cordelia’s and her sisters’ armies crucial evidence of Q/F revision. For the battle itself the Quarto and Folio present identical texts. But of the war as a whole the two texts present significantly different versions. The cutting of several references to France, first attributed by Doran (1931, pp. 73–6) to the censor, Taylor finds to be key to a larger design. (P. 31): F systematically removes verbal and visual reminders that Cordelia’s army is French, so that Cordelia seems to lead not an invasion but a rebellion, like Bolingbroke’s or Richmond’s. …[F thereby] deliberately excis[es] an extraneous political complication. For altered details in earlier scenes that supposedly prepare for this difference, see nn. 1631–1638+12, 1631–8, 2307+1–+6, 2349–50, 2917, 2918, 2938–9, 2968, 3051+1, 3054. (P. 34): It is hard to believe that such a succession of inter-related changes happened by accident, and it would be churlish (let alone unnecessary) to attribute them to anyone but Shakespeare. Idem (1983, p. 426) rehearses the claims that in F the war is turned from foreign invasion into something indistinguishable from civil war, and that the revision accelerates the pace, raises our hopes for Cordelia’s resistance, removes any explanation for her eventual unexpected defeat, removes extraneous political complication, and translates a somewhat irrelevant foreign invasion into the incarnation of a civil chaos set in motion by Lear’s abdication.

Among several others, Honigmann (1980, p. 151; 1985, pp. 4–5) is persuaded by this argument that it was indeed Shakespeare who revised the play. Thomas (1984, p. 509) disagrees: The changes made in the Folio text with reference to the war are not beyond the power of any competent man of the theatre and in no way disturb the structure of the play. Foakes (1993, p. 107): Although some notable references to France are omitted from F…, enough remain still to make it clear in F as well as in Q that Cordelia arrives at Dover at the head of a French army.…In the entry at v.2…the Colours shown by them would presumably be those of France.…Thus the loss of some references to France in F does not bring about a radical change; indeed the omission of some verbal allusions is perhaps more than compensated for in the use of colours to provide a visual emphasis as the various armies march over the stage in the last act. Knowles (1999, pp. 270 ff.) answers all of Taylor’s individual claims, concluding generally that apparent differences between the stage directions of an author’s draft (in Q) and those of a theatrical playbook have been exaggerated by over-literal interpretation. (P. 273): There is no reason to think that the Q and F scenes [4.4, 5.3] are different in any essential way, and (p. 274) Cordelia’s forces are of mixed nationality in both texts.

Among those arguing for authorial revision, several repeatedly make the argument that the abridgement in F is not merely theatrical cutting but artful authorial reshaping in order to streamline the action and heighten emphasis on certain parts of it. Taylor (1980, pp. 28 ff.): The cuts in 3.6, 3.7, 4.2, 4.3, and 4.7 strengthen the narrative line, largely by accelerating and clarifying the movement toward war. The effect of cutting one scene is to streamline the plot (p. 29), another cut strongly establishes the narrative momentum, and helps sustain the play through the long, leisurely scenes at Dover. By increasing the narrative momentum and giving relatively more emphasis to the war theme the Folio strengthens an audience’s expectations of armageddon, and thereby makes the anticlimax [i.e., the brief battle] when it comes not only sharper but more unmistakably meaningful. The cuts in Acts 3 and 4 clearly and strongly establish the narrative expectation of war, and they reduce the amount of time Lear himself is offstage and bring forward the build-up toward war, the Goneril-Regan-Edmund intrigue, the return of Cordelia, the reunion of Lear and Gloucester, and the reunion of Lear and Cordelia. What is cut is eminently [30] dispensable, particularly backward-looking reflection on what has happened and (1983, p. 424) explicit moral commentary. For similar arguments see nn. 2014+1–+30; 2056+1–+4, +5–+18; 2176+1–+9, 2347+1–+56, 2843, 3168+1–+18. Leggatt (1992, p. 181): The Quarto, being more discursive and moralizing than the Folio, is closer to the play’s roots in popular dramaturgy; the revision makes the play more elliptical and sophisticated.

This critical line has evoked many objections. Muir (1983, pp. 105, 112): One has only to look at the second act of Hamlet to know that stream-lining was not always one of Shakespeare’s priorities—perhaps it never was. Stream-lining is the tragic flaw of certain directors who imagine that a play is more dramatic if it is stripped of its poetry.…[112] I do not believe that the Folio alterations were made by Shakespeare himself in order to improve the play.…Shakespeare may have been reluctantly responsible for cutting it down to size, but the cuts may have been made when he was no longer there to protest.…The cuts do not improve the play: they damage it fatally. Idem (1985, p. 65): [Taylor] supposes that our objections to the cut at the end of Act 3 are those of literary critics, incapable of seeing the dramatic advantage of omitting explicit moral commentary. This leaves me speechless. Explicit moral commentary has been a feature of all great drama from Aeschylus to the present day. See further Muir’s comments in nn. 2303–2303+17, 2347+1–+56, 2843+1–+11, 2981+1–+2. Carroll (1988, pp. 231, 244): The language of speed seems to govern all arguments about the F revisions in 3.6.…To say that a deletion leads to a faster playing time of the surviving material is merely a tautology. How could it not? Every omission necessarily results in streamlining and acceleration; what is not effectively shown is why this acceleration and streamlining are really virtues. Indeed, the very metaphors used by these scholars—positives like streamline and accelerate rather than, for example, abort or truncate—beg the question of the argument. This kind of non-argument, in which a valorized terminology is substituted for logic and evidence, may be used to justify any deletion.…All these assertions…have in common…an implicit poetics of drama which exalts simplicity of structure and speed of performance over complexity and difficulty. He shows that the arguments of cutting for speed elsewhere are not invoked in defenses of the adding of the Fool’s prophecy at the end of 3.2; see n. 1735. (P. 244): Their arguments are fundamentally circular. Had Q not contained the mock trial but F had added it, they would no doubt have been able to demonstrate the superior theatricality of F and the theatrical genius of the reviser; they would have been right. Cantor (1996, pp. 449–50): Such aesthetic judgments are unhistorical, modeled on the modern cinematic fast cut. Modern Shakespeare productions are often characterized by attempts to create the effect of fast cutting on stage, usually through the use of blackouts and sudden illuminations. But there is no evidence what-[450]soever that Elizabethan productions sought to achieve similar stage effects.…Elizabethan drama seems to revel in exploring the motivations of its characters in long, reflective speeches (remember To be or not to be). Clare (1995, pp. 46–7) counters the argument of improved theatricality by showing that in all the major productions of Lr. at the RSC and National Theatre, 1962–1993, virtually all of the Q passages (except two in 5.3) were usually restored. He also gives his own justifications, on dramaturgic grounds, for restoring several passages: see nn. 2014+1–+30, 2303–2303+17, 2347+1–+56, 2843+1–+11.

A different doubt about the claim that Sh. revised Lr. in order to make it a different play is the one voiced by Delius (1875, p. 139), Chambers (1930, 1:298), Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, pp. 124–5), Edwards (1982, p. 697), Thomas (1984, p. 510), and many others: that too little is changed in F. Expanding on Taylor’s (1983, p. 376) remark that the F additions do not include new narrative material, structurally important incidents, or scenes, Knowles (1995, pp. 32, 45–6; cf. 1997, pp. 63–4): If the text of King Lear printed in the Folio represents a second authorial version of the play,…it is remarkable for its limited means of revision. Except for cutting, which could be theatrical rather than authorial, the major substantive changes in F are usually additions of a line or more to existing Q speeches, generally designed to expand or clarify motive or meaning, and hundreds of small verbal changes; most of these changes are explainable as editorial, scribal, or compositorial error, correction, or sophistication, and the vast majority of them make no practical difference. There are in Folio Lear no new scenes, characters, or episodes; no rearrangements of plot or scenes or speeches; no omissions or renamings of named characters; no new speeches to introduce new themes or different motives. The few reassignments of speeches have seemed to editors to be in most cases either errors or the corrections of errors.… Except for cuts and local additions of lines and an occasionally significant verbal substitution, the speeches and actions of the characters remain on the whole unchanged. Most remarkably, virtually no speech of any length seems to have been either wholly reworked or replaced by a different one. The only apparent exception is Kent’s long speech to the Gentleman in 3.1; this is the only place where a revised speech seems to have been substituted in F for a different one in Q. [For an alternative explanation—erroneous insertion, not substitution—see nn. 1631–4, 1634–8].…[45] [Apparently] the additions intended for Kent’s instructions in 3.1 are of exactly the same kind as the Folio reviser or revisers made elsewhere—not the recasting of a whole speech or substitution of one for another but merely two additions of a few lines clarifying meaning or motive, such as are found in Lear’s speech at [45–50] and [54–5] and at numerous other points in the play. They are local improvements, not significant revisions. Throughout F, speeches are not rewritten but merely cut or augmented. Rasmussen (1997, pp. 445–6): In Ham., phrases and lines are cut by artful, surgical excision from within speeches; in Lr., they are trimmed off the ends of speeches and scenes, suggesting different hands and purposes. Stern (2000, p. 106) surmises from this difference that, unlike Ham., Lr. is a full-play revision, requiring the wholesale rewriting of prompt-book and actors’ parts. There is no reason to think so: so few lines have been added to any actor’s role that most of them could have been added marginally in playbook and parts, where, moreover, cuts and new cues could have been indicated without any recopying at all. Folio additions of one pentameter or more affect only eleven of Lear’s speeches, three of Goneril’s and the Fool’s, two of Edgar’s and Regan’s, and one each of Gloucester’s, Edmund’s, and Kent’s. Except for the Fool, Goneril, and Regan, no character is given a new speech of more than one line, and no speech of any length is rewritten.

Recent assessments of the changes in F Lr. have in fact tended to conclude that at best they represent partial adjustments of the same play rather than a complete rewriting into a different play. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 164): The trivial or indifferent character of many of the variations which are brought forward to illustrate revision can allow readers reasonably to suspect that…the distinctive literary consequences of the variation are more a measure of the critical sensitivity of the scholars who interpret them than an indication of a purposed, consistent revision of an existing play into another distinct form. Foakes (1993), receptive to many of the arguments for authorial revision (streamlining, nuancing of characters and themes, etc.), reviews most of them sympathetically, but denies that a wholly different play results. (P. 110): At the same time, the reworking of King Lear is not so thorough as to mean that we have to think of two plays; (pp. 135–6): Though the changes between Q and F modify the presentation of some characters and events, their impact on the shaping of the play can be seen as one of emphasis or balance.…The details may vary considerably, as in variants in a large narrative painting or a long novel, so that it is nuanced differently, but not essentially changed.…[136] The changes in the Folio King Lear sometimes clarify, as in the opening scene, sometimes seem designed to make the balance of sympathies more even, as in the exchanges between Goneril, Regan, and Lear, but more often remove passages that coerce the audience’s emotions, so again leaving more to their imagination; (p. 212): The revised King Lear of F is thus significantly different from Q, though not as radically different as [some] authors…would have us think. Mueller (1994, pp. 614–15): The differences betwen the texts of Lear are not that great, as is shown above all by the easy conflatability of the versions of Lear into a composite text. The quarto and folio versions of King Lear share a rump text of about 2900 lines, while about 300 lines occur only in [615] the quarto and some 100 lines only in the folio. Editors of a composite text…face no serious problems of redundance or contradiction in extended passages. If the versions of King Lear were as different as they are now claimed to be, the business of constructing a composite version should require much more thorough-going editing than it does. Ryan (2002, p. 3), more bleakly: Objections to the two-Lears hypothesis have dealt it a series of body blows from which it looks unlikely to recover.…The problem is that that most of the cuts and revisions are not convincing on artistic or theatrical grounds anyway.

Wells (1983, p. 10) We should be justified in an initial assumption that the Folio alterations were Shakespeare’s own. Most of the recent supporters of Shn. revision, as Elton (1988, p. 343–4) complains, simply assert as fact that Sh. was the reviser, without argument, let alone proof. It is a reasonable assumption that as a sharer and chief playwright of his company Sh. could have been involved in shaping the play for its original production or a later revival, but it is impossible to know that he was; and he would have had no part in any revisions made in the decade between his retirement and the publication of F1. In an examination of fourteen manuscript plays bearing the customary marks of official abridgment, Hart (1942, pp. 132 ff.) demonstrates the conservatism, theatrical tact, and structural and stylistic skill with which a practised abridger generally did his work. Nonetheless, a general impression is often urged, that the revision of Lr. is so brilliant that only Sh. was capable of it. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 146 ff.): It is unreasonable to declare that theatrical cuts, changes, or additions were made without the active involvement of Shakespeare himself.…[147] The dramatic boldness, sensitivity, and power demonstrated by the variants in the Folio declare that only a masterful playwright is at work.…[149] No compositor is held responsible for the brilliant strokes of stagecraft, no copyist is needed to have a rich supply of Shakespearean synonyms at the tip of his tongue, no bookkeeper is required to have acted suddenly in an innovative manner.…All that is needed is Shakespeare, capable of preternatural brilliance, well within his observed capacity to strike us dumb with amazement. Similarly Honigmann (1982, pp. 154–5; cf. 1985, p. 5), persuaded that the supposed interrelation of F changes implies a single reviser: It makes sense to assume that we are dealing with one revision of the play, rather than two or more; that one person decided that Edgar and Act iv could be improved (and how many of the King’s Men would perceive that, before it was done?), and that the same person, working through the play, interpolated such masterly lines as [2608–10].…The variety of styles in these additions is also significant.…Do we really have to multiply revisers?…We should…ask whether one person could have composed in the strange variety of styles found in F’s additions, viz. (1) the [155] rough style of Who…not [1631 ff.], (2) the dense imagery of Plate…gold [2608 ff.], (3) the Fool’s doggerel [1736 ff.]. We know of one person particularly given to such variety, who employed all three styles elsewhere. Must we look farther?…A major revision by someone other than Shakespeare seems unlikely, when one considers the converging evidence: strategies of revision that imply an awareness of the minutiae of characterization, and a quite exceptional sensitivity to background plotting; the cleverness with which F’s additions have been stitched into existing material; the variety of the reviser’s styles, all of them Shakespearian styles. Who, other than the author, when a monumental master-piece has been completed, would still think about improving it and would re-touch it at so many points, and so delicately? Who, other than Shakespeare, was capable of dramatic thinking at this level?

Like many others, however, Muir (1983, pp. 99–113) argues that the dramaturgic effects of the cuts and additions are, as often as not, anything but the work of a supreme dramatist; rather (p. 112), The cuts do not improve the play: they damage it fatally. Whoever was responsible was the first of the vandals, to be followed by Tate and a long line of actor-managers and directors. See nn. 487–93; 2056+1–+4, +5–+18; 2176+1–+9, 2303–2303+17, 2347+1–+56, 2843+1–+11, 2981+1–+2. Murphy (1987, p. 58): Not only do I see no compelling reasons to think that Shakespeare made these revisions in order to improve King Lear poetically or dramatically, I maintain that properly understood, the First Quarto Lear gives us the full sweep of Shakespeare’s powerful tragedy. Viswanathan (1990), finding losses as well as gains in F’s changes, doubts authorial revision. Clare (1995, p. 38) answers Honigmann’s rhetorical questions: The passage…masks essential subjectivity by deploying a weighted vocabulary—one that invokes here a general sense of authoritative intervention and of theatrical craftsmanship, without actually telling us anything very specific. Strategies of revision, an awareness of the minutiae of characterization, a quite exceptional sensitivity to background plotting, re-touch so delicately and dramatic thinking at this level are all impressive phrases, but what exactly do they mean? While apparently referring with authority to theatricality, Honigmann actually betrays a rather limited sense of what constitutes theatrical process…[which continues] [39] not only from production to production but also (within the run of a given production) from one performance to the next.…In such a company [as Sh.’s], the answer to Honigmann’s question who other than the author would think about improving a particular play, would be likely to be (again, quite properly) everybody else involved. It is not dramatic thinking at an inordinately high level for an actor to examine whether or not his lines can be made to work. Rather, it is his job. Clare challenges several of the revisionists’ arguments about Q/F variants, framed in such terms of theatricality,…often extrapolating very dubious projections of the consequences of those variants in performance: see nn. 2014+1–+30, 2303–2303+17, 2347+1–+56, 2843+1–+11. Meyer (1994, pp. 130 ff.) argues that several of F’s crucial alterations are the work of compositors: see nn. 3277–83, 3283, 3285. Recently Honigmann (1990, pp. 58–9; 1996, pp. 144–5) has himself changed his mind and urged further consideration of possible kinds of non-authorial corruption that probably exist in F Lr.

Carroll (1988, pp. 227–9): The new orthodoxy with which I would take issue here is the interpretive privileging of the Folio text over the Quarto text.…In seeking to establish that the revisions in the Folio were made by one person, and that that person was Shakespeare, some of the authors …resort to questionable critical assumptions and dubious interpretive practices…[reflecting] their own form of bardolatry. The Folio version is better and its readings preferred, in effect, because it is later; they assume that Shakespearean genius always improves upon itself. The Folio version, more specifically, is said to be better on the stage—the revisions are theatrically justified [Wells, 1983, p. 19].…Shakespeare…revised it in light of his experience of the earlier performance of the play.…The result is inevitably an evolutionary, even teleological argument.…[229] The possibility that Shakespeare’s own theatrical revisions might not be an improvement is never taken seriously. Trousdale (1986, pp. 216 ff.), without denying the existence of two Lears, similarly questions the validity of inferring authorial intention from formal features: The arguments that have been used to wall in the two kingdoms are arguments that can be used as well to dismantle them and posit a conflated text.…[220] Is it not possible that the Quarto Albany might be perceived not as a different version so much as a flawed version; and is there, in fact, any way that is not simply arbitrary in its reading of the text of determining what the character of Albany was meant to be?…[221] If it is possible…to determine hierarachies of artistic patterning within a text and if such patternings are objective and ipso-facto author-determined, then does it not follow that the superior formal patternings that a succession of editors discerned in the conflated text must also be thought to have authorial sanction.…[223] Dramatic texts in particular…cannot be reduced to a single author or a single form because they are in origin the collective endeavors described on their title pages.

Indeed some deconstructionist and materialist critics, emphasizing the text as a fluid social construct subject to theatrical, printing-house, and societal forces beyond the control of the author, deny that F Lr. represents Sh.’s final intention. (The congeniality of arguments both for and against revision to modern schools of critical theory is summarized by Knowles, 1999, pp. 266–9.) Goldberg (1986, pp. 213 ff.): Shakespeare was a reviser of scripts subject to numerous contingencies; there never was a King Lear.…[214] We have no originals, only copies. The historicity of the text means that there is no text itself; it means that a text cannot be fixed in terms of original or final intentions. At best, Shakespearean practice authorizes the dispersal of authorial intention. He criticizes the critical conservatism of revisionist critics: The kingdom has been divided, but Shakespeare reigns supreme, author now of two sovereign texts.…[215] Moreover, the two texts seem to offer these critics further opportunities to practice a character criticism that goes back to Bradley, or to argue for formalistic structures in the plays that are equally suspect. Likewise Holderness (ed. 1995, pp. 49 ff.) questions the revisionists’ preference for F. (P. 50): The implicit critical judgment is underpinned by an instinctive preference for a more naturalistic mode of dramatic writing.…In the Folio text Warren finds some of the structural integrity, stylistic consistency and psychological verisimilitude of the naturalistic well-made play.…What he finds unsatisfactory, chaotic and potentially confusing is that inventive deployment of exactly those theatrical techniques we think of as proper to the early modern public playhouse: ensemble company acting; metadramatic self-reflexivity; fantastic improvisation of meagre theatrical resources; and the subversive carnival energies of vigorous and sceptical popular culture.…[51] [But] If…the hypothesis of revision were accepted, all that is necessarily implied is that there were obvious conflicts of artistic direction within the contingent theatrical culture. Perhaps the distance between Folio and Quarto does represent, in miniature, the movement from a more experimental to a more naturalistic mode of theatrical construction that certainly took place across the period. But these are symptoms of historical process, and do not readily facilitate judgments on a common scale of quality between the texts that are fundamentally incommensurable, precisely because culturally diverse. He speaks deprecatingly (p. 53) of the great metacategory of the author and the outdated critical concept of authorial intention, and (p. 55) of the conservative critical agenda of (p. 54) Bradleian character-criticism. Ryan (in Hunter, ed. 1996, 2005, p. 151): The rigidity (and indeed old-fashionedness) of the conceptions used (two artefacts, each having the status of a literary classic, each to be protected from addition or subtraction) bears little relation to the status of unprinted theatrical texts, present in the playhouse as open resources from which different performances could be drawn for different occasions (such as performances at court, or in the country).

Nonetheless, a few serious attempts have been made to identify the author of the F revisions. No one has been persuaded by Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxvi), who suspected in F1 Lr. the editorial hand of Ben Jonson. Stone (1980, pp. 127–8) finds Philip Massinger’s style in some of the F additions—involuted syntax, periodic sentences, parentheses, grammatical and syntactical orthodoxy—an identification denied by Taylor (1983, p. 443, n. 97) but so far not rigorously tested by anyone. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 195 ff.) argues that the kinds of revision found in F Lr. are more typical of an author than of another reviser: the latter cut, inserted and substituted sizeable pieces of text without altering the details of his precursor’s dialogue. Revising authors, by contrast, though they sometimes worked just with large textual fractions, tended to tinker, introducing small additions, small cuts and single-word substitutions. Because of its many small changes, therefore, F Lr. falls firmly into the category of authorial revision. Unfortunately for his argument, Lr. also evidences some large cuts and additions, and Kerrigan admits that (p. 204) authors sometimes worked… like adapters. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 163): Even setting aside the concessions that revising authors sometimes worked with large textual fractions and that they only tended to tinker with the text, it does not seem to me that this material is sufficient to support a generalization that adapters add or chop, and authors tinker. Rather, unremarkably, the evidence seems only to indicate that the purpose of the revision (a term which may [164] include reworking, adaptation, cutting, enlarging, and tinkering) determines the kinds of textual variation, and not the origin of the textual alterations. Similarly Rasmussen (1997, pp. 452–3) denies that Kerrigan’s generalizations are hard and fast rules: Rowley and Marston, e.g., made sizable revisions to their own plays, and non-authorial revisers, e.g. Birde and Rowley, introduced numerous single-word substitutions. Differences in form cannot be used to distinguish authorial from non-authorial revisions. Many other agents besides a reviser, of course—actors, bookholder, a theatrical editor preparing F1 copy, scribes, compositors—singly or cumulatively might introduce many indifferent verbal variants.

Taylor (1983, pp. 386 ff., 462 ff.) attempts to show, from the occurrence of rarer words (those used two to ten times in the canon) in those parts of Lr. that exist only in Q, only in F, or in both texts, and from their occurrence in other plays, that the F additions were made later than Q and that their vocabulary is typically Shn. (P. 386): The vocabulary unique to the Folio [i.e., the whole F text, not just its 100 lines of F-only additions] would appear to have been written later than Q, [389] or by another writer. It does not have any significant links (as Q does) with the plays from As You Like It to Othello; its strongest links are with the four plays The Winter’s Tale, Cymbeline, The Tempest and Henry VIII.…Neither the rare vocabulary of Q, nor that unique to F [throughout], has any remarkable number of links with Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, Pericles, or Coriolanus. He discovers, however, that Q as a whole has stronger vocabulary links with plays of 1609–13 than with plays of 1606–9, and that Q-only passages omitted from F have fewer links with later plays. He concludes that this would be a natural consequence of Shakespeare’s having extensively revised the play at some point after Coriolanus and before Cymbeline, during which process these rare words in Q which were recopied would have been positively re-endorsed and re-enter[ed] Shakespeare’s active vocabulary. Moreover (p. 390), unusual words occurring originally in Q and later added elsewhere in F occur in F in the immediate vicinity of their appearance in Q; to Taylor this suggests a mind being fitfully influenced by the (earlier) vocabulary of the text it has just been reading, revising, and copying. Moreover (p. 400), Shakespeare’s genuine works all include an unusually high proportion of new or rare vocabulary [p. 444, n. 105: the rate of words occurring only once or twice elsewhere is about one in 12 lines]. In lines unique to F Lr., the proportion (one rare word to every eleven, twelve, or thirteen added lines) is decidedly high—and typically Shakespearian.

The reappearance in F of unusual Q words—(p. 465) In 11 of 17 cases…the occurrence in F follows that in Q—could mean only that one or more revisers, not necessarily Sh., or editors or scribes, could have repeated them in an F passage after being struck by them in a previous Q-only passage. Similarly, the reappearance of such words in other plays at about the time of Cymbeline could mean only that shortly before writing those later plays Sh. had been reading with interest the new Q edition of Lr. (very likely published without his or his company’s approval), not necessarily that he had been revising it. To argue that the numerical proportion of new rare words is Shakespearian does not establish him as their author, since there is no way to show that Sh. would have added exactly those rare words, and that no one else would have; they might simply represent another adapter’s different vocabulary.

Looking at the roughly 110 lines added to F, rather than at the vocabulary of F as a whole, Knowles (1997, p. 61; 1999, p. 286) extracts from them ten words found nowhere else in Sh.: buzz (n.), enguard, unfitness, speculations [concretely, = spies; in two other uses it means power of sight], furnishings, able [v.], hurtless, snuffs [= huffs, pl. and without in], packings [= plottings], and machinations, the latter in two F additions (at 442 and 2890). The first nine are clustered in just three of the added passages (842–55, 1631–8, 2608–12) totalling about twenty-six full lines; this average of one unique word to every three lines is many times Shakespeare’s usual rate and suggests a writer with a different vocabulary. One of these passages in particular, 1631–8, has frequently been thought, on the basis of its clotted sentence structure, to be non-Shakespearean (see n.). One could add unburthen’d (46) and disquietly (443), though Sh. often uses burthen’d and disquiet; and interest (91) is not necessarily a unique use of the word interess’d. It is notable that the F additions contain several interjections not found elsewhere—O do, de, do, de, do de (1839), suum, mun (1879), se se (2031), Sa, sa, sa, sa (2645), and the unique oath My breath and blood. It is also interesting that in one short added passage (439–44) containing two unique words (machinations and disquietly) are two other words used in senses not found elsewhere in Sh.: hollowness (= falseness) and ruinous (= pernicious; elsewhere = decayed).

These rare words seem not to derive from Sh.’s sources; Harsnett uses machinations once (A3v), but two other words in quite different senses: speculation (singular, = fanciful idea) and packing (singular, = fraudulent dealing, trickery). Nor do they seem part of the idiolect of any contemporary dramatist, though many of them were common in theatrical use, especially in years nearer to F (1623) than to Q (1608). The OED and the two electronic databases Early English Books Online (EEBO) and English Verse Drama (EVD) reveal that buzz as a noun appears in several plays, the earliest being Chapman’s Widow’s Tears 2.1 (1603–9), Dekker’s Match Me in London 5 (1611–13), and Massinger’s New Way to Pay Old Debts 5.5 (1621–5). Though unfitness had appeared in Sidney’s Arcadia 3.24, it does not appear on stage until Middleton’s Old Law 2.1 (1615–18) and Brome’s Queen’s Exchange (1629–32). The use of able as a verb taking the object it or him (but not ’em) occurs in Chapman’s Widow’s Tears (1603–9), Middleton & Rowley’s Changeling (1622), and Middleton’s Game of Chess (1624). The adjective hurtless (= harmless) appears in the anonymous Caesar and Pompey (1605), Volpone 2.2 (1606), Fletcher’s Woman’s Prize 3.3 (1611), and elsewhere at about this time. The verbal noun packing meaning fraudulent dealing appears in the singular once in Sh., but nowhere else in the plural or in the sense complottings; it appears only rarely in other plays, as once in Leir 1635 (1605) and Massinger’s Great Duke of Florence 3.1 (1627). The term machination(s) is used in Barnabe Barnes’s The Devil’s Charter 1.4 (1607), John Stephens’s Cynthia’s Revenge 3.2 (1613), Massinger’s Believe As You List 2.2 (1631), and Ralph Freeman’s Imperiale 2.2 (pub. 1639). The adjective ruinous (= pernicious, not decayed) occurs in Chapman’s Revenge of Bussy 5.1 (1601–12) and Byron’s Conspiracy 2.1, 4.1 (1608), Middleton’s The Witch 1.2 (1609–16), and Webster’s Devil’s Law Case 4.1 (1610–19). Though furnishing occasionally appears in the phrase furnishing of a masque (Middleton, Revenger’s Tragedy 4.1, 1606–7; Anon., Masque at Gray’s Inn, 1618), it nowhere appears in the sense trappings, pretexts. Likewise speculation, usually meaning thinking or power of vision, is never used concretely to mean a person (or instrument) that gathers intelligence. Sh. uses the phrase in snuff after the verbs be or take, meaning be offended, but neither he nor any other dramatist uses the noun by itself in the singular or plural meaning a fit of indignation; a huff (OED sb.1 5), though the word is used off the stage often enough. The verb enguard appears nowhere else. These words suggest a reviser with an idiosyncratic vocabulary, perhaps in some cases reflecting a familiarity with the contemporary theater, but probably not Sh.’s lexicon. It is true that in at least one Q-only passage there is a concentration of somewhat unfamiliar words that cannot be attributed to a reviser: see n. 473+1–+6. In those lines, however, the diction seems intentionally mannered for comic effect; there is no such obvious intention in these F-only passages.

One other verbal feature that may suggest a hand other than Sh.’s is the repeated adding, cutting, eliding, or transposing of single words in order to make smoother verse. Doran (1931, pp. 49–50) attributes the removal from F of extrametrical terms of address such as sir or madam, the general regularity of the verse in F, and the correct alignment of the verse and prose to a careful revision, perhaps by Shakespeare. Smidt (1964, p. 154): One of the editorial tasks of Heminge and Condell may have been to regularise the verse and…they may have done away with a good many redundancies on no other authority than their own, and even added words if occasion demanded. Honigmann (1965, pp. 121 ff.) cites some dozen passages in F (269–70, 771–6, 831–4, 853–60, 2814–18, 2888–95, 3245–50, 1014–17, 1372–9, 3033–8, 1033–7) where derangement of superior Q verse indicates revision. Knowles (1997, pp. 74–5; 1999, p. 282) notes some 130 lines which in F seem to have been altered to make smoother meter, a trait uncharacteristic of the later Shakespeare. The reason for the changes in some of these lines may not be solely or even primarily metrical improvement, but that motive is clearly there in most of them. See the commentary notes for the following lines:
a.Omission of individual words or phrases: 74, 96, 115, 168, 177, 194, 221, 256, 258, 348, 520, 524, 527, 731, 741, 746, 770, 829, 834, 836, 918, 953, 964, 1184, 1196, 1203, 1231, 1512, 1527, 1530, 1532, 1673, 1800, 2124, 2127, 2156, 2198, 2221, 2224, 2457, 2584, 2756, 2772, 2877, 3022, 3073, 3076, 3108, 3115, 3181, 3209, 3217, 3279.
b.Addition of individual words or phrases: 42, 77, 210, 344, 748, 754, 789, 817, 834, 864, 947, 950, 957, 979, 1021, 1029, 1036, 1147, 1206, 1277, 1331, 1350, 1363, 1392, 1397, 1416, 1434, 1599–1600, 1803, 1940, 2040, 2084, 2146, 2164, 2243, 2400, 2486, 2508, 2557, 2614, 2639, 2641, 2645, 2688, 2798, 2890, 2936, 2948, 2966, 3037, 3113, 3118, 3135, 3269, 3277, 3280.
c.Substitution of words or forms that improve meter: 100, 261, 344, 710, 1148, 1163, 1174, 1247, 1301, 1311, 1440, 1516, 1711, 2356, 2359, 2493, 2523, 2605, 2657, 2774, 2799, 3178, 3279.

Such changes do not always result in improvement, however. Added words result in hypermetric lines at 60, 715, 961, 1059, 1380, 1453, 1952, 2479, 2826, 2842–3, and 2990, as do substitutions at 806, 1585, 1756, and 2606–7. Omitted words produce short lines at 73, 527, 769, 1451, 1733, 2228, 2640, 2812, 2863, and 3208. Relining of Q verse or false prose, and revision of the Q text, occasionally result in imperfect verse in F—e.g., at 50, 58, 84, 144, 349, 774, 806, 833, 930, 1016, 1377, 1380, 2461–3, 2638, 2816, 2828, 2873, 2967–8, 3083–5, and 3207–8.

In short, such changes result in metrical improvement three times as often as in disruption; if changes due to relining or consequent upon other revision are excluded, metrical improvement results five times as often as not. Clearly there has been a consistent attempt throughout the whole text to polish the verse. Knowles (1999, p. 282): Since in his later years, when he is imagined to have revised Lear, Shakespeare was given to increasingly free and irregular verse, such a form of revision as is found in these 125 lines would seem to be uncharacteristic of his writing at that time. Idem (1997, pp. 74–5): It looks suspicious that in a supposed rewriting of Q Lear, whose jagged rhythms often suit the moods of the speakers or stresses of the occasions, he would add, cut, or alter hundreds of words apparently to write smooth, regular verse.…[75] It is easier for me to imagine a company member or hireling attempting to supply such correct regularity to Lear while reworking or recopying it, than to imagine Shakespeare working so contrarily to his own recent habits. Since Folio Compositors B and E do not make such changes in other plays, these verbal additions, deletions, and substitutions must have been in the Folio copy. Unless they had previously been introduced into the playbook, their most likely source in F copy is a scribe who persistently made small improvements in his transcript of that theater manuscript, or a reviser (probably other than Sh.) who vetted that manuscript before transcription.

The question of authorial intention has also vexed incidental speculations about the precise nature of Sh.’s possible involvement in any revision, theatrical or otherwise. Many of the foregoing quotations of critics have touched on repeated arguments—that the Sh. who reportedly seldom blotted a line was not given to the habit of revision, that revision after the prompt-book had been prepared and the actors had rehearsed their lines would have been discouraged as a great inconvenience to the company, that significant additions to the playbook would require its resubmission to the Master of the Revels for licensing, that as both author and shareholder Sh. would have had an investment in participating in any revision, that once he turned over his script to the company it became their property not his, that he expected his long plays to be cut and revised as a matter of course, that his consent to have changes made amounts to a kind of generalized intention, and so on. The speculative nature of all these arguments has rendered them inconclusive, and no further quotations expressing them are offered here. One way of avoiding the issue is to assert that the true publication of a play was on stage, not in print, so that the final stage version, insofar as it may be known, most probably represents Sh.’s intention. Since F Lr. is evidently a later version than Q and is apparently derived from the company’s playbook, it should be accepted as the preferred, more authoritative version. This has been a principle of the Oxford edition Wells (ed. 1986, pp. xxxiv–v): The very fact that those texts of his plays that contain cuts also give evidence of more literary revision suggests that he was deeply involved in the process by which his plays [xxxv] came to be modified in performance. For these reasons, this edition chooses, when possible, to print the more theatrical version of each play. (In fact the edition prints both Q and F texts of Lr., as early and later versions of the play, and Wells in his single-volume edition of 2000 bases his text on Q.)

This influential argument—that the F version represents Sh.’s intended theatrical publication—has recently lost some of its force in the face of growing doubt that the F version of Lr. does in fact represent a version ever played upon Sh.’s stage. It is almost certainly too long to have been played in its entirety, and may (in its full length) have been intended for reading, not playing. Hart (1942, p. 136): [I] think it most improbable that either the quarto text or the folio text…was itself an acting version.…The total amount of curtailment is far too small.…[F Lr.] is nearly a thousand lines longer than…plays written in 1623.…I can offer no explanation… except that Heminge and Condell tried to offer [Sh.’s overlong plays] to the readers cur’d, and perfect of their limbes. Chambers (1944, p. 40), having considered all the documentary and statistical evidence and the experience of several modern readings and productions: I think…that the full texts of Shakespeare’s longest plays, as we have them, including at least eleven plays of over 3,000 lines, were no more likely than Ben Jonson’s to have been actually presented at the Globe or Blackfriars. Bowers (1966, p. 206, n. 39): The literary form given a play for publication could well differ from the theatrical form intended by an author after rehearsals in the matter of cuts and other adjustments. Smidt (1964, pp. 161–2): In fact neither the Quarto nor the Folio text is likely to have been a stage [162] version, though both may derive from a book marked with theatrical omissions, some of which were observed in the printing and some not. Idem (1988, p. 25) attributes the printing of theatrical omissions to editorial greed on the part of Heminge and Condell, who piously preserved Sh.’s plays absolute in their numbers, as he conceiued thẽ,…retaining lines and passages meant, or even marked, for deletion. Orgel (1994, pp. 251–2): The plays Shakespeare’s company performed were shorter than the plays Shakespeare wrote for them.…[252] But most editors and critics go to extraordinary lengths to avoid dealing with the notion.…It is often claimed, for example, that two hours is an approximate figure, which in the 16th century could mean anything up to four hours; that if you read very fast you can get through the text of most Shakespeare plays in around two hours; even that the Elizabethans spoke twice as fast as we do. Gurr (1999, pp. 69 ff.), contra the Oxford editors: It is a fairly desperate hope to retrieve much of the original performance conditions from the written records, let alone any settled performance text, since (p. 70) there was an inherent difference between the original company’s own written playbook and the text the players performed. The ideal or maximal long text approved for performance by the Master of the Revels contained the poem of Lr. and was kept as an archival copy. It was from the basis of that ideal text that the more minimal reality [the play] was drawn out for performance. The minimal versions changed according to the local and immediate conditions of performance. That is, actual performances would have contained fewer lines than in the maximal allowed manuscript, and the actual lines spoken would have differed from one production, and possibly from one performance, to the next. F1 Lr., evidently derived from the maximal playbook, is longer than any text ever seen in contemporary performances.

For proof of the pudding, a number of performances of Lr. have been timed. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 146 n.) reports that Nugent Monck, in his Maddermarket Theatre, performed a Lr. cut down to 2590 lines, with a ten-minutes interval, in two hours and a half. At that rate a Q version of 3063 lines would take a full three hours. Monck was not performing in a large amphitheater, requiring louder and slower speech, and his rate would not allow for the customary jig or time for filling and clearing a large hall. Chambers (1944, p. 40) reports that Lewis Casson expected his 3071-line acting text to take two and a half hours in performance at the Old Vic; in fact it took three hours and eleven minutes. Chambers also cites Levin Schücking’s report that a Ham. of 3,762 lines performed at the Old Vic without act-intervals took four hours and twenty-two minutes; at that rate a Q Lr. without intervals would take more than three hours and a half.

A related argument is that Sh. imagined his plays not simply as theatrical vehicles, to be variously adapted to changing stage conditions, but also as unified poems to be recreated in the theater of the mind, presumably by the great Variety of Readers. Chambers (1944, pp. 40–1): Are we to infer that Shakespeare, like Jonson, wrote for publication, and let the players, in the meantime, do their worst?…[41] For whom…did he write? For himself? It follows, if this is so, that we must to some extent qualify Dr. Granville-Barker’s view of the plays as raw material for acting. And perhaps, after all, we may have to resort to our firesides when we wish to capture the full significance of their tragic or comic intentions. Both Melchiori (1992, pp. 200 ff.) and Dutton (1996, pp. 82 ff.) argue that Sh.’s long plays survive in two forms, a longer one intended for readers and one or more shorter adaptations for stage performance. Everett (1998, p. 230): Defining a play by Shakespeare as a dramatic script only, and laying it down that differing Quarto and Folio texts illuminate the writer’s struggle to adjust his words to the stages of his time, revisionists reduce the poet’s astonishing imagination to the two or three printed versions they have in front of them. King Lear must have existed in Shakespeare’s head not as two or three versions but a thousand: ideas, gestures, names, rhymes, songs, buttons, curses and courtesies, thunder and lightning, weeds, blank verse, gods and toasted cheese, bodies, boys, a girdle, kneeling and dying and speaking. To get this turned into the agonizing and brutal and beautiful world of King Lear as we have it—or almost have it—must have required from him acts of formative balance that stun imagination. On related but different grounds, Erne (2003, pp. 131 ff.): Sh. intentionally wrote his long plays with a future print readership in mind, and presented to his company something like the overlong texts preserved for readers in F, from which he expected his company to cherry-pick shorter acting versions from time to time. (Pp. 135 ff.): The problem of the length of many of Shakespeare’s plays becomes soluble…once we accept that the text as it has come down to us may be more than a reflection of what would have been spoken on stage. Conversely, crucial evidence for Shakespeare’s interest in a readership can be derived…from the sheer length of about a third of Shakespeare’s plays.…[140] If we held that Shakespeare produced plays solely for the theatre without any considerations for their appearance in print, the length of his plays would clearly pose a problem.…[143] The tragedies and histories are of a length far exceeding what is necessary for a stage play because Shakespeare simultaneously conceived of them as literary drama with which he hoped to increase his reputation. Instead of presenting Sh.’s plays as they were acted in the London playhouse, the Oxford editors and their followers (p. 136) produce conflated texts, approximations of what was acted…along with much material that was never, nor was ever intended to be, performed. If these commentators are right, then F Lr. is therefore not Sh.’s final revision but represents as much of his original conception (though not necessarily all of it) as was preserved in the company’s official playbook, almost certainly with an admixture of theatrical alterations.

div.head: The Evolution of the Texts
div.p: It may be useful to summarize what we seem to have learned about the texts of Lr. in the century and a quarter since Furness devoted twenty pages to that subject. The basic difference between our understanding and his is one of assumptions about what can be known: Furness and others of his age believed that from the quartos and folios, despite their many variants and imperfections, one could conceivably reconstruct an edition of the play that would represent Sh.’s final intentions for its presentation to the world and posterity; today we are more aware of how the play of Lr. has always been in constant flux, in the theater and in print, evolving from one state or version to another. Recent study of the three basic texts has been largely devoted to forming hypotheses about the temporal and causal relations between them, in an attempt to construct a narrative that accounts for their particular qualities and differences from one another. Since, in the absence of any of the manuscripts from which the texts were printed, such a reconstruction must be based entirely on inferences from the printed texts and from general knowledge (such as it is) of theatrical and publishing practices of the time, the best one can hope for is a theory that is coherent within itself and consistent with the facts presently known and with opinions generally accepted. There is no certainty that such a theoretical narrative coincides with what actually happened.

In the beginning there was a draft, or possibly many drafts, or many revised pages within one draft, until Sh. was sufficiently satisfied with his new play to release it to his company. The apparently very rough (miserable) draft of it that most editors now think lies behind Q1 was almost certainly not the manuscript that the company accepted as the basis of their 1606 playbook; instead they apparently received a clean transcript, probably made by a scribe rather than by Sh. himself. Greg’s belief that the company insisted on acquiring and keeping rough drafts in addition to their fair copies has been rejected by Bowers, Werstine, and others for lack of any evidence. If they are right, then there is no reason to think that it was from the players that Busby and Butter acquired the rough draft lying behind Q1, since the players would have had no known reason to possess it at all. On several grounds it seems equally improbable that Busby or Butter acquired it from Sh. himself, who apparently had had no previous dealings with either them or their printer Okes. One other possibility, suggested above, is that those publishers acquired the draft from the scribe who had prepared fair copy. Since between 1603 and 1623 Sh.’s company seems to have refrained from publishing most of its new plays, they probably did not encourage one of their scribes to convey the rough draft of Lr. to Busby (previously known to the company, if at all, only as a publisher of the bad quartos of H5 and Wiv.). Nor, if he cared at all about the publication of his play, is it likely that Sh. would have recommended such a transaction. Both plague and touring records indicate the likelihood that both Sh. and his company were away from London most of the summer and fall of 1606 and most of 1607; in their absence a scribe might have agreed to sell the now superseded MS in his possession, some time before its entry in the Stationers’ Register on 26 Nov. 1607.

If, as is now widely accepted, Nicholas Okes did work from Sh.’s rough draft, then the first quarto edition of Lr. brings us as close to a Shn. manuscript as we are likely to get. There is no reason to multiply entities by imagining that still another scribal transcript lies between Sh.’s final draft and Q1, since a scribal transcript so difficult to read and print as the copy for Q1 evidently was is scarcely to be imagined, and no one has proposed such a manuscript. From the evidence of the text printed in Q1 we may infer that the final authorial draft contained a play which, at nearly 3100 lines, was longer than all but six of his other plays and far longer than the usual range of 2000 to 2800 lines (averaging nearly 2400 lines) for plays of the period (see Erne, 2003, pp. 141, 147). In the opinion of a growing number of scholars (see ), such a play would have been too long for performance, and hence too long to have been reported or reconstructed, either by audience members from actual performances or by actors from performing scripts held in their hands or minds. It would follow as well that the Q1 version of the play, despite its execrable printing by Nicholas Okes, represents the play more or less as Sh. imagined it when he completed its compositon in 1606. The Q1 text is not, that is to say, a gross corruption at the hands of actors or reporters, but the play essentially as Sh. originally intended his company to receive it. Indeed, one of the most remarkable results of the last few decades of textual study of Lr. has been the rehabilitation of Q1 from a text sometimes despised and rejected as a bad quarto to a text now widely thought to represent Sh.’s original intention with less interference from printers, actors, scribes, and other agents than the texts found in later editions of the play. Until recently only Ridley (ed. 1935) and Halio (ed. 1973) based their editions mainly on Q1; now we suddenly have editions of Q by Wells & Taylor (ed. 1986), Weis (ed. 1993), Holderness (ed. 1995), Wells (ed. 2000), and the editors of this New Variorum volume.

The scrupulous bibliographical study of Q1, especially by Greg and Blayney, has also enabled more informed inferences about the quality of the manuscript lying behind its text. Nicholas Okes’s complete inexperience in printing dramatic texts, his reliance on seriatim setting (suggesting a messy, untranscribed manuscript) rather than on customary casting-off and setting by formes, and the resultant type shortages, all suggest qualities of the manuscript that would help to explain features of the printed text as we have it. Both the high rate of printers’ errors and nonsense in the text and the extensive and often unsuccessful proof-corrections documented by Greg are evidence that the manuscript was often illegible to both printer and proof-reader, perhaps in part because it was much overwritten, as rough drafts commonly are, with marginal or interlinear corrections, deletions, insertions, transpositions, and the like. A transcript of the manuscript would not have been necessary unless it contained a considerable number of at least some of such kinds of blemishes. Doran believed that she could discern, from stylistic evidence, points in the text where large-scale revisions had taken place. From Okes’s compositors’ failure to supply adequate punctuation or correctly to line much of the verse it seems evident not only that they had little experience with dramatic manuscripts but also that the manuscript itself was deficient in indicating pointing and lineation. There would be nothing surprising in the latter fact: even if Sh. had given little attention to punctuation and verse lineation in the expectation that a scribe would later improve and regularize such matters at least minimally, the extant playbooks represented in Greg’s Dramatic Documents (1931) reveal that in even fairly finished transcripts the punctuation is often sparse and inadequate and the verse lines uncapitalized and therefore hard to distinguish from prose. The several additions to the play of Sir Thomas Moore, easily sampled in the transcribed and facsimile pages included in the Riverside Shakespeare (ed. 1974, pp. 1686–1700; rev. 1997, pp. 1780–94), reveal that authorial inattention to the formalities of punctuation, line capitals, and even verse-line length was quite usual in an Elizabethan dramatic manuscript. Features of Q1 which long seemed to be strong evidence for aural reporting of the text of Q1 now seem attributable to the inexperience of Okes’s printers and to quite normal features of an authorial draft. In addition to its apparent illegibility and its inadequate pointing and lining, the manuscript’s freedom from other signs (e.g., actors’ names, fuller sound cues, etc.) that might suggest theatrical use, further support the inference that this draft was probably never the basis of any actual production, at court in 1606 or elsewhere (though one cannot rule out that possibility).

Before the draft-version of Lr. could be used by the company, it probably needed first to be transcribed into a fair copy that could be read by the Master of the Revels and that subsequently would become, or become the basis of, the official playbook and ultimately of the actors’ parts. There seems to have been no intermediate transcript between the rough draft and the final playbook; as Doran has shown, a number of erroneous and doubtful readings in F1, which was based, if not directly, on some state of the playbook, are clearly derived from the same unclear handwriting that caused similar or related readings in Q1. These common errors in Q1 and the playbook also show that Sh. was in all probability not the person who wrote out the fair copy, since he would not have been repeatedly misled by his own handwriting in copying it. The scribe would have been either a scribe hired by Sh. himself (or by an agent) or else a member of the company, probably the book-holder; the former may be the more likely, since at a time when Sh.’s company was showing little or no interest in publishing his plays, there is no obvious reason why (after transcription) the book-holder would have conveyed the original manuscript of Sh.’s newest tragedy to unfamiliar publishers such as Busby and Butter. In any case a scribe experienced in preparing playbooks might have been expected to tidy up some details of punctuation and lining and perhaps intentionally or unconsciously to make verbal changes and substitutions; any or all of these scribal changes might later have survived in the F1 text. In reviewing the scribe’s work, Sh. might also have made changes in the text before passing it on to the company. If, however, he finished the play in Stratford during the plague months of the summer and fall of 1606, and his draft was subsequently sent or brought to London and there transcribed by a copyist familiar to Sh. or his company, then Sh. may not have had an opportunity to review, let alone carefully proofread and improve, the transcript. That possibility might explain why many verbal and other errors survived in the playbook and onwards into F1.

Once the company had received the fair copy and had secured the Master of the Revels’ allowance of performance, they would have adapted the play at least in time for performance at court on 26 Dec. 1606 if not for public performance before then. Their first task would have been to reduce it to playable length, by marking passages that could be omitted from performance. They would not have had to get permission from the Master of the Revels for such cutting; he had approved the lines that could be played, not decreed that all of them had to be played; and it is not certain that he himself censored any lines. Extant playbooks reveal that omissions were regularly marked in three ways: by the crossing out (or underlining) of individual words and lines, by a vertical line in the margin bracketing speeches to be cut, or by x-ing or cross-hatching through passages or scenes. The passages marked for omission may have been different from one week or month or revival to the next, as experience during production and performances suggested; they may have been made by different hands at different times for a variety of reasons. As Orgel (ed. 1999, p. xlv) says, The folio version represents…not necessarily the only version the company had performed in the years between 1605 and 1623; indeed, as he implies elsewhere (1994, p. 251), it may not have been a performance version at all, given its great length.

Some of the cuts seem ultimately to have become permanent, surviving into the text of F1, such as the excision of the mock trial in the middle of 3.6, of episodes at the ends of 3.7 and 4.7, and the whole of 4.3. Cuts of other passages may have been considered provisional, experimental, occasional, or temporary; since the text that survives in F1 is still too long to have been performed, these additional passages, perhaps marked lightly by a vertical line in the margin rather than obliterated, may have been restored when printer’s copy for F1 was prepared. If recent scholars are correct that F1 Lr. is too long for the usual playing time of two to three hours, then it is certain that more cuts were once marked in the playbook than are observed in the F1 text. There can be no doubt that Sh. expected his overlong play to be cut for performance, but whether he was present for or personally approved or took part in the cutting cannot be known; anyone can cut a text, at any time. He may have hoped, and the F1 editors may have concurred, as Smidt and Erne and others have suggested, that printed versions of his plays would survive in something like their full original length, absolute in their numbers, as he conceiued thẽ. Light marginal marking of cuts in the playbook would have made easy their restoration in the printed edition.

Besides shortening the original version, the company, with or without Sh.’s participation, would in all probability have made minor adjustments that suggested themselves during production or in subsequent performances. The book-holder may have taken care of a few such mechanical matters as supplying needed entrances and sound cues, providing names missing from directions, relocating or recasting action directions, and the like, though the notion that he would do so exhaustively or even extensively has been shown to be unsupported by the evidence of extant playbooks (see Long, 1985, 1999). Some such changes may have survived in F1, and there may have been other and different ones that have not survived, but in general F’s almost complete set of entrances and exits indicates a concern not generally found in theatrical manuscripts and suggests that many if not most of such changes in F may have been made later, in 1623, to aid prospective readers of F1, not the ongoing company. Obvious verbal errors and misleadingly lined verse would very likely be corrected to ensure accurate actors’ parts, and perhaps some rhetorical punctuation would be added for the same reason, though again existing playbooks do not suggest that the actors would have required thorough editing of this kind or that book-keepers troubled to provide it, and few exemplars of actors’ parts survive. The several additions of one to five lines in 1.1 (45–50, 54–5, 69–70, 90–1, 94–5), apparently designed to make motivations and relationships as clear as possible in the opening scene, could well have been added at this early stage, though of course they and others like them could have been added later.

A basic assumption of those who have urged that F1 represents Sh.’s own revision of the play is that all (or virtually all) of the changes were made at one time by the same person. That article of faith is incapable of proof, and seems improbable for many reasons. For one thing, the playbook on which F1 is based could have been modified at any time between 1606 and 1623; during the last ten of those years Sh. would not have been in the company, nor would he have been alive during the last seven. If Lr. remained in repertory during those years, or was revived at least once, any number of theatrical exigencies, rather than authorial second thoughts, could have occasioned adjustments to the text. Speeches might have been tailored to the different audiences of court, the Blackfriars Theatre, great houses, and provincial towns, or to audiences in different years. In 2.2 the stocks may be revealed in a discovery space in Q1, in F1 they are specifically brought out; in 4.7 Lear is apparently discovered asleep to the sound of music in Q1, but carried in without mention of music in F1. To several commentators (see nn. 1251–72, 2771, 2775+1–+2) these changes have suggested a change of venue from the Globe, well equipped with a discovery space and musicians, to a stage without those amenities.
