That new stage is less likely to have been the one at court in 1606 or that in the Blackfriars Th. after 1609, both spaces easily supplied with music and a discovery curtain, than one of the less commodious, probably improvised playing spaces (including the halls of great houses) encountered on tour from 1607 onwards. Possibly, as has been suggested, topical references became in time outdated and were cut (see, e.g., nn. 473+1–+6, 2248+1–+5). Roles might have been cut down because of changes in personnel, or episodes reduced because actors proved weak (see, e.g., nn. 1622–1622+8, 2014+1–+30, 2303–2303+17). Roles might have been augmented to clarify motive or simply to provide particular actors a little more prominence (see, e.g., nn. 842–55, 1419–24, 2184–7). The several additions to the Fool’s part (744, 1322–7, 1734–50, 2010–11, 2043) might have been included as a favor to the actor, Armin or (after 1610) a later one, to compensate for a foreshortened role, or they may reflect a clown’s improvisations as he grew into the role. In the minds of many critics, some of the cuts in F1 seem too clumsy to be authorial, and a number of F additions have seemed suspiciously un-Shn. in manner (see esp. n. 1734–49) or in vocabulary (1631–8, possibly 439–44, 842–55, 2608–12). The majority of the F additions are of a phrase or a line or two, and seem quite possibly local and piecemeal improvements rather than parts of a wholesale revision of the play. They are so limited and change so little of the essence of the play that they may never have been reviewed by the Master of the Revels, especially if they were added piecemeal over time.

As long as textual scholars were convinced that certain readings in F could only have derived from Q1, there was some reason to hypothesize, as several have done, a revision (by Sh. or someone else) made in a copy of Q1. Now that Howard-Hill has argued persuasively that direct Q1 influence on F1 cannot be shown, however, there is no reason to suppose that the alterations evident in F1 need have been made anywhere but in the playbook itself. Most of the F1 additions are brief enough to have been interlined or added in the margin, and the two or three clearly too long for such marginal insertion could have been tipped in on added slips; such a method has in fact been suggested for at least one passage (see n. 1634–8) to explain a resulting textual crux. Marginal corrections are exemplified in the pages of Middleton’s Believe As You List and Glapthorne’s The Lady Mother in Greg’s Dramatic Documents (1931, specimen pages 8 and 9), as are slips with additional lines pasted in, or flown on the page, in The Second Maiden’s Tragedy (specimen page 4). Moreover, such alterations could have been made piecemeal over many years by many people, possibly but not necessarily including the author; Werstine (1988, p. 25) notes that in the dramatic manuscript Thomas of Woodstock, for example, there are annotations, including added passages, in no fewer than nine hands. One repeated objection to the theory that Sh. undertook to revise Lr. all at once, after an interval of several years, possibly in Stratford, and in quite limited ways, is the lack of any clear motive for taking on the task. There is no such problem if the changes were made gradually and pragmatically by the company as a result of their experience in production and performance over several months or seasons.

After the playbook had been marked with adaptations for its first season of performances, it could conceivably have been vetted one or more times by Sh. or (especially after 1613) by another person or persons, possibly the book-holder, possibly a hired dresser of plaies. The practice of revision was universal…in the London theatres from 1590 to 1642 (Bentley, 1971, p. 263; cf. Chambers, 1930, pp. 211–15). A review and overhaul might be occasioned by a revival, especially of an older play or in a new theater; or an editorial redaction might (less frequently) be undertaken in anticipation of printed publication. As Bentley (ibid.) says, Almost any play first printed more than ten years after composition and known to have been kept in active repertory…is most likely to contain later revisions by the author or, in many cases, by another playwright working for the same company. Knutson (1988, pp. 257–8), seconded by Thomas (1995, pp. 573–4), argues that revision for a revival was not common or necessary before 1603; McMillin (1987, p. 76), however, insists that changes of personnel after a gap of some years might well require revision, since Elizabethan repertory companies…depended on intricate patterns of doubling. If a reviewer/reviser of Lr. were hired in anticipation of a revival, he would likely be responsible for some of the F additions which reveal a non-Shakespearean lexicon—some words of which seem to have been more current ca. the 1620s than a decade or two earlier. If he were hired to redact the text in anticipation of publication, he could have made many of the verbal substitutions and grammatical changes that seemed to him preferable even though not absolutely necessary for theatrical purposes; and he is the most likely candidate to have added, cut, changed, or transposed individual words to smooth the verse in a style untypical of Sh. near the end of his career.

Taylor (1983, p. 376) concedes that the F additions are quite limited, consisting only of alterations here and there, and Thomas (1984, p. 508) thinks that such limits argue against authorial revision: Inconsistencies and ambiguities in Lear—e.g., misleading indications of growing conflict between the two dukes, or the false report (see n. 2319–20) that Cornwall killed the servant in 3.7—have been left untouched. Many commentators have noted that the changes in F regularly result in passages more remote from Q1’s original sources, topical reference, and vocabulary: see esp. Kerrigan (1983, p. 219), Jackson (1983, p. 338), Taylor (1983, pp. 353, 367–76), and Marcus (1988, pp. 148 ff.; 1991, pp. 171–2). If so, some of the revisions may have been made considerably later than the King’s Men’s move into the Blackfriars Th. in 1609, often suggested as the occasion for revision.

Before the publication of F1 (it now seems probable) a clean transcript of the playbook was prepared, both to avoid exposing the playbook to the ravages and dangers of printing-house use and to provide the compositors with legible copy (see ). Near the conclusion of F1’s printing, several plays apparently had been or were being transcribed—JC, Mac., Ham., Lr., Oth., and Ant., and a few others—beside a few thought to have been transcribed by Ralph Crane. Except for Crane, not so much is known about theatrical scribes as about F1 compositors. One might expect a single scribe to copy the whole play, and since Crane’s identifying traits are not evident throughout F1 Lr. as a whole, the transcript seems mainly to be the work of another, different, and unknown man hired by Jaggard. Honigmann’s (1996, pp. 74–5) discovery, however, of at least one passage [1147–1225] including spellings characteristic of Crane (but not of Sh.) raises the possibility that at this time, in order to complete the transcripts expeditiously for F1 printers, more than one copyist might have shared the work on a given play. In any case the scribe(s) might have affected the text in several ways. If the act and scene divisions in F1 Lr. were not already found in the playbook, in consequence of one or more revivals at the Blackfriars, a scribe probably supplied them. He seems also to have misunderstood what to do with a slip pasted in at the beginning of 3.1, and so produced a famous crux: see nn. 1631–1638+12 and 1634–8; and he may have erroneously substituted other F for Q material at 823, 1016, 1294+1–1296, and 2538–9. Like Crane, the scribe may have habitually formalized and regularized the text to a considerable degree according to his own habits and preferences, and he is probably the source of the majority of small verbal changes of number and case agreement, interchanges of synonymous prepositions or relative pronouns, modernizations of forms of verbs, etc. which a scribe might intentionally or unconsciously introduce into a text meant for readers but which are changes pointless for a theatrical reviser to make. The transcript was evidently good enough to allow for accurate casting-off and dependable printing. It was also faithful enough to the substance of the playbook so that word forms and erroneous (if usually plausible) readings in the playbook that were caused by the letter-forms in Sh.’s rough draft were transmitted unchanged to the printed text of F1.

With the appearance of Compositor E, the second quarto, Q2, re-enters the scene, since E seems to have been influenced by its spelling and punctuation. Q2’s limited effect on the substantive readings in F1 rules out its use as printer’s copy; the suggestion made by Doran, Howard-Hill, and others that it was merely consulted during the typesetting may explain sufficiently the nature and extent of its influence on F1 (though the question needs further consideration). A computer-aided tabulation of changes of apostrophes, capitals, hyphens, italics, spellings, sentence punctuation, and elisions reveals that in each category both compositors depart from Q2 at least as often as they agree with it, and in most categories the rate of difference is several times higher than the rate of agreement. One would not expect so much difference if Q2 were printer’s copy. (Only in spelling does E agree with Q2 about as often as not, while B differs almost twice as often; even in punctuation, E differs somewhat more often than not, while B differs several times more often.) In all categories Compositor E remains closer to Q2 than does Compositor B, indicating Q2’s greater influence on his work. There is a simple explanation why Q2 accidentals should appear more often in the work of Compositor E: he was a relatively inexperienced and inexpert workman, and before Lr. he had been setting mainly from easy printed copy. Except for a half-page of JC and one and possibly three more pages in Ham., Lr. was his first extended attempt to set from manuscript copy, and relatively legible though the transcript must have been, he would naturally have resolved any problems that it presented by consulting a printed edition. Q2, produced in the same printing house four years earlier and not yet sold out by its London booksellers, would have been more easily acquired than a copy of Q1, printed a decade and a half earlier. Compositor E’s many literal errors suggest he had trouble reading the copy. He may even have checked Q2 continually, for security. Doubtless both compositors introduced substantive changes, including errors; more of the latter were expected from Compositor E, evidently, in view of the extensive proof-correction of his work. Both men occasionally compressed or stretched the text because of casting-off.

This hypothetical account of the evolution of the texts of Lr. is consistent with known theatrical and printing practices and with present editorial consensus (insofar as there is one) about the probable origins of the Q and F texts. It allows for the possibility that some of the revisions in F might be authorial but recognizes also that numerous other hands could have intervened and in all probability did. It provides a stemma simpler than most of those recently proposed, particularly in not requiring a report from performance(s), revisions in a copy of Q1, the transcription of a second playbook, and a marked-up copy of Q2 (for various stemmatic diagrams see Taylor, 1983, pp. 360, 366). The imagined lines of transmission in the present account are more simple and direct: Shakespeare’s original manuscript was the basis for Q1, which was copied in Q2 and Q3; a transcript of that manuscript was the basis of the original playbook, which remained in the playhouse, subject to occasional limited alterations, until it was again transcribed to make printer’s copy for F1. Both F compositors worked from that later transcript, though the less experienced one also regularly consulted Q2 for further guidance.

The F1 text was reprinted three times during the 17th century, as F2 (1632), F3 (1663–4, from F2), and F4 (1685, from F3). (Lr. was not included in the partial reprint of F4 now known as F5; see Rasmussen, 1994.) None of these reprints has independent authority; the quality of the emendations found in them, especially the intelligence and imagination of those introduced by the editor of F2, is discussed by Black & Shaaber (1937). The dramatist Nicholas Rowe, engaged to revise F4, produced two editions of 1709 and one of 1714 which incorporated many emendations and improvements to the text, notably additional act-scene divisions, indications of locality, and stage directions. Pope, in his edition of 1725, began the modern fashion of conflated editions by restoring some 105 of the Quarto lines omitted from the folios; Theobald, in his edition of 1733, restored another 123, drawing these from Q2, a copy of which he owned (see Seary, 1990, p. 233). Capell (ed. 1768) and Jennens (ed. 1770) restored another score of Q lines, and Ridley (ed. 1935) a final pair. Until very recently virtually all editions of Lr. have been synthetic combinations of Q and F lines.

The general rationale for such a synthesis has been prudential: not to lose lines that Sh. may have intended to be part of his play. Undoubtedly Shn. lines had been cut from Q, perhaps by actors or censors or printers; some if not all of the lines added to F have seemed (to many editors) acceptably Shn.; both, it has been argued, should be preserved from loss, at least in a modern reading edition. From time to time editors have debated whether one version of the text, Q or F, were not more authentically Shn. than the other, and a few—Jennens, Malone, Ridley, Halio—have expressed some partiality to Q. In the past quarter-century the idea that Q and F represent equally coherent and valid but significantly different authorial versions of Lr. has led to a number of separate, unconflated editions of each play. Most recently, the idea that neither Q nor F represents the play that Sh. or his company intended to be performed has cast doubt on the most important rationale for these separate editions. Q and F are the basic documentary texts, and editions may still justifiably be made of either of them; but exactly what is being edited in each case is now less certain that what once was thought. An edition of Q will apparently offer essentially the text that Sh. originally wanted to present to his company, but probably more of it than he expected to be acted; an edition of F will include less than he originally wrote, but probably also more, and in any case will represent an artifact produced not simply by Sh. but in all probability by members of his company, scribes, possibly a censor, possibly a hired reviser or redacter, and printers.

The versions of Lr. that Sh.’s company actually performed and Jacobean audiences saw, however, may be no longer recoverable. These were probably considerably shorter than those in either the Q or F text, comprising a selection of scenes and passages that might be different from one production or even performance to the next. Our best guide to what parts of the play have seemed essential to the playable core of Lr. may be the history of the text as it has been altered on the stage in four hundred years of playing. This edition provides such a history (see ), drawn from printed theatrical editions and extant promptbooks. One viable choice for future editions may be once again a conflated text, not pretending to recover one or two lost ideal authorial versions, but providing an archive of possibilities, arranged as coherently as possible, from which actors and producers will, as they always have, make a selection. So thinks Dieter Mehl (personal letter, 28 Jan. 1996): I…would probably opt for a conflated text again if I had to edit it. This…has the advantage of serving the theatre better, because directors can have no use for two texts and will return to a conflated text anyway, possibly executed with less competence than the conventional editions. Similarly Melchiori (2003, p. 25) makes a plea in favour of conflated texts. Men of the theatre should be provided with as full texts, including variants, as are available in the original printings. It is their task to choose, select, and cut in order to suit the circumstances in which the plays are to be staged. Such editions may also, as Smidt, Erne, and others have recently suggested, realize Sh.’s intention that future readers have fuller access to the whole range of his tragic vision in Lr. than can be available in any particular performance. In their overall outlines the texts in such editions will, of course, be closer to Q than to F, as conflated editions have always been, restoring or retaining 300 Q lines and adding or retaining another 110 from F.

div.head: The Date of Composition
div.p: As is true for most of Sh.’s plays, Lr. may be dated within a span of a few years but eludes more precise dating. If, as is now generally thought, the Q1 (1608) text derives from a much-revised rough draft, it probably substantially represents the version of Lr. that Sh. first presented to his company, before any theatrical adjustments were made. That version was almost certainly completed between 1603 and late 1606, and most scholars are inclined to place it near the end of that period, in 1605–6; but when it was begun or mainly composed cannot be known with certainty.

div.head: External Evidence
div.p: William Warburton first brought Samuel Harsnett’s Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures (1603) to the attention of Lewis Theobald (see ), who noted (ed. 1733) similarities of language and of detail between it and some of Edgar’s speeches (see nn. 1827, 2248+1–+5). Malone therefore, in his chronologies of Sh.’s plays (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 1:322; ed. 1790, 1:353), dates Lr. later than Harsnett, as do most editors. Only a few commentators reject Harsnett’s date of publication as a terminus a quo for Lr. Merriman (1908, p. 648) suggests that Sh. may have learnt the names of the devils which he used in Lear directly from Southampton, and long before 1603, since the Earl of Southampton’s nearest kinsman was George Peckham, on whose ancestral lands in Denham, Bucks., Harsnett’s exorcisms took place. Such communication with Sh. would probably have had to occur long before Harsnett’s book, since between 1598 and 1603 Southampton was much preoccupied with a new marriage, disgrace at court, involvement in the Irish wars and the Essex rebellion, and trial and imprisonment; and there is no evidence of any contact with Shakespeare during these years. Usher (1908, p. 206) thinks that Sh. could have known the names of the devils long before Harsnett’s book appeared, citing Bishop Latimer’s use of flyppergybes in a sermon of 1549 (see n. 1895); but there the word probably means a mere prattler, not a devil. Trotman (1919, p. 312) similarly argues that Sh.’s devil names may have been common knowledge, from folklore or the Morris Dance, from which Sara Williams, one of Harsnett’s demoniacs, may have got them. He also thinks that the name Frateretto may have been common beggar’s cant; see n. 2004. Usher further argues that power struggles among the Jesuits, beginning with the Wisbeach [or Wisbech] stirs of 1594–5 and coming to a head in 1600–3 when Bishops Bancroft and Harsnett were interviewing witnesses, would have been a continuing source of alehouse gossip that Sh. could have heard. Trotman thinks also that Sh. may have read Harsnett in manuscript. Such speculations are of course impossible to prove or disprove. Bowen (1965), pp. 2–7) argues that since at every point where Lr. echoes Harsnett, Harsnett is quoting the manuscript Book of Miracles (1585–6), it could be the source for Lr., which Bowen thinks was written by the Earl of Oxford before Harsnett wrote his book. Similarly Cairncross (apud Marder, 1974, p. 25): Harsnett got his material from an earlier book, which he mentions, and which describes the events referred to that happened in 1586–7. Probably Robert Cecil provided a copy of the Miracle Book to Bishop Bancroft and the Ecclesiastical Court of High Commission in about 1598 (Brownlow, 1993, p. 22); it is unclear how Sh. would have had access to this or another copy of it. Since the Book of Miracles no longer exists, and is only cross-referenced from time to time in Harsnett’s margins, it is impossible to say what use he (let alone Sh.) may have made of it. Against all such fancies, particularly Usher’s, Law (1908, p. 358) offers the sane reminder that (as Theobald had pointed out) Lr. echoes from Harsnett not only a few devils’ names but factual details such as the hysterica passio and terms such as mopping and mowing. Because of the thorough study of such links by Muir (1951; 1952; ed. 1952), Bullough (1973), Brownlow (1993), and many others, no one now seriously doubts that Lr. is profoundly owing to Harsnett’s book for names, vocabulary, themes, images, and moods (see ) and therefore postdates its publication.

Weak corroboration of a terminus a quo of 1603 is provided by Sh.’s evident familiarity with several of the Essais of Michel Eyquem, Seigneur de Montaigne (see ), whose English translation by John Florio was entered in the Stationers’ Register 20 Oct. 1595 and 4 June 1600 and was published in 1603. Scholarly disagreements whether Sh. was influenced by Montaigne before 1603, perhaps from reading Florio’s translation in manuscript, are the more inconclusive because all three books of the Essais had been available in French since the fifth edition of 1588, and Sh. apparently knew enough French to sprinkle it (unidiomatically) throughout H5 and perhaps to read Belleforest. No doubt, however, he read at least Florio’s English version of Montaigne, since he absorbed a good deal of its vocabulary.

A terminus ad quem date of Dec. 1606 is provided by the entry in the Stationers’ Register on 26 Nov. [1607] for Mr Willm Shakespeare his historye of Kynge Lear as yt was played before the king[es] maiestie at Whitehall vppon St Stephans [deleted k]night at x&ptilde;ist&mtilde;s Last (Greg, BEPD, 1:24). The Christmas last before the date of this entry would have been in 1606, and the King’s Men received payment for playing before James on St. Stephen’s Night (26 Dec.) of that year (Chambers, 1923, 4:173). This entry doubtless reflects the claim on the title page of Q1, As it was played before the Kings Maiestie at Whitehall vpon | S. Stephans night in Christmas Hollidayes. Though this title page was in all probability devised in 1607 by Nathaniel Butter for the manuscript of Lr. that he had somehow acquired (see n. 0.3), there is no reason to doubt its claim of court performance on 26 Dec. 1606, a claim which would have been risky to make if untrue, and easily falsifiable. Barroll (1991, pp. 154–5): Though there is no royal court record of the title of any play performed by Shakespeare’s company before the king between 1606 and 1611,…the reference is obviously to December 26, 1606, a matter not under any dispute.

How long Lr. had been in existence before Christmas 1606 is the real mystery. Craig (ed. 1901, p. xxiv): It should be placed well within the year 1606.…My reason is that the fact that it was performed before James the First at the end of 1606 points to this year; the plays selected on such occasions being seldom or never old plays. Similarly Ridley (ed. 1935, p. xiv): There is a certain probability that a play to be performed before the King’s majesty was more likely to be a new play than one which had been before the public for a year and a half. Halliwell-Phillipps (1882, pp. 144–5; 1889, 2:339): If the tragedy had been produced any length of time previously to the Christmas of 1606, it would be difficult to account for the evidences of its popularity [i.e., entry in Stationers’ Register and publication] accruing only in the following year. Plausible though these arguments sound, they are complicated by two other external facts. The first is that Shakespeare’s company had played before king and court only four months earlier. Fripp (1938, pp. 653–4): Three times [Sh.] played before King Christian of Denmark during his visit to his sister, Queen Anne—twice at Greenwich, where His Majesty stayed on 18–24 and 28 [29?]–31 July and 8–9 August, once at Hampton Court, on [654] 7 August. The other complication is theater closings due to the plague. The possible interrelation of these two facts, summer performance and plague, have been most fully explored by Barroll (1965; 1991), as follows.

Barroll (1965, p. 129 n.): In terms of repertory, there might have been a problem here, for ten plays had been presented before James in the previous Christmas season [1605–6]. If material presented both to Christian and James had to be new, at least to James, then plays performed this summer might well have been written in the previous spring.

Idem (1991, pp. 154–5, 176–7): Plague had closed the playhouses throughout the late spring of 1606, the entire summer, and even the autumn. Indeed, the king had not come to London for the usual All Saints’ Day celebration on November 1 and November 2 when, during the first ten years of James’s reign, plays were performed in all but the most difficult circumstances (all having to do with plague). Indeed, no holiday plays by any city company were presented before the king in autumn and winter 1606 until that St. Stephen’s Day—much later in December than holiday court playing usually began. Thus, with the public playhouses being closed by plague, the first play to have been produced by any city company either in the public playhouses or at court since the August enter-[155]tainment of the king of Denmark was, in fact, King Lear; this situation has not generally been recognized.

p.quote: Was King Lear then new on St. Stephen’s Day, 1606? Most probably new to the court. The tragedy could not have been performed at court during the king of Denmark’s visit, for Shakespeare and his fellows (or the master of the revels, responsible for court entertainment) would hardly have inaugurated the long delayed Christmas season with a play King James had seen as recently as four months earlier. By the same token, King Lear would not have been shown during the previous (1605–6) Christmas season, for one can assume that a performance of the same play before the king would not be featured in two successive Christmas seasons.

If these assumptions seem valid, then there are difficult alternatives in trying to estimate the date of the first production of King Lear. It either saw its debut at court on December 26, 1606, or, if it was first presented at the public playhouse, it was at a time too late for performance at court in Christmas 1605–6; if the play had been new and already in existence by Christmas 1605, it would have been presented then at court and thus not presented again in December 1606.

In these circumstances, the first time after the Christmas holidays of 1605–6 when public plays were possible was the spring of 1606, at such a time when the absence of Lent or of plague allowed playing. Easter was April 20, 1606.

But, it might be objected, with King Lear already in production in this spring, would not the tragedy have been an ideal choice for the king of Denmark’s visit in August? It would indeed seem so. On the other hand, given that King Lear would almost certainly not be presented at court twice within a four-month period (August-December), one must assume that Shakespeare and his fellows chose not to perform it during the visit of the king of Denmark even if the tragedy was ready. The king of Denmark saw only three of the King’s Servants’ plays. Thus, one must argue that King Lear had its debut either at court on Christmas 1606 or in public between April and June 1606 before plague returned to London. [Fn. 3: The playing dates for the King’s Servants during the holiday season 1605–6 are not known; payment was in a lump sum on March 25, 1606 (in the middle of Lent). The Prince’s Servants came to court on Shrove Monday and Shrove Tuesday (MSC, 6:43), so Shakespeare’s company did not.].

div.p: Chambers (1930, 1:468): The difficulty about 1606 is that the earlier part of 1606 seems also to fit best for Macbeth, and that the time-table left available by plagues…makes it unlikely that two Shakespearean plays appeared almost concurrently at this date and none at all in 1605, which was clearer from sickness. On the whole, perhaps Lear is the easier play to put back to 1605.

Barroll’s argument that if Lr. had existed by Christmas 1605 it would have been performed at court then rather than in 1606 is a hard one to overcome. As for why it may not have been performed for the Danes during the summer of 1606, possibly James’s queen, Anne of Denmark, knew the tastes of her sports-loving brother Christian IV and recommended lighter fare than Lr. for his visit; in fact, at times the Danish visit seems to have been celebrated with scandalous drunkenness and debauchery (as reported by Sir John Harington; see Fripp, 1938, p. 654). If, as Paul (1950, pp. 317 ff.) has argued, Mac. was the last of the three plays performed at Hampton Court on 7 Aug., being suitably complimentary to James to serve as a decorous conclusion to Christian’s visit, that one tragedy might have been thought enough to display the company’s tragic skills. Lr. might have seemed even more de trop if, as Paul surmises, a second tragedy, the Danish play Hamlet, had already been performed. In fact, however, no one knows what plays the King’s Men performed; the only known title, the lost playe called Abuses: containing both a Comedie and a Tragedie—apparently some kind of tragicomedy—was performed by Paul’s Boys on 30 July (Chambers, 1923, 4:121).

One important fact external to the play remains to be considered: the publication in 1605 of the anonymous True Chronicle History of King Leir, a major source for Lr. That event has been taken to show either that Sh.’s play had already been written or that it was yet to be. Malone (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 1:322; ed. 1790, 1:352–3) gives Lr. priority: It seems extremely probable that its first appearance was in [ed. 1790 specifies: March or April] 1605; in which year the old play of K[ing]. Leir, that had been entered at Stationers’ hall in 1594, was printed by [353] Simon Stafford, for John Wright, who, we may presume, finding Shakspeare’s play successful, hoped to palm the spurious one on the publick for his. In his 1790 edition Malone goes on: The old King Leir was entered on the Stationers’ books, May 8, 1605, as it was lately acted, a statement that he evidently thinks can apply only to Lear. As for Sh’s evident borrowing of one of the passages of Leir if it had not been acted recently, (ed. 1778) the old play had been in possession of the stage for many years before 1605 [ed. 1790 goes on:] and without doubt he had often seen it exhibited; nor could he have found any difficulty in procuring a manuscript copy of it.…I suspect, however, the old play had been published in 1594. So also for Staunton (ed. 1859), the printing of Leir in 1605 was mainly in consequence it would seem of the great popularity of the present drama [i.e., Lr.] then running at the Globe Theatre. Malone’s theory has found many adherents and defenders; if it is true, Lr. may have been written some two years or more before the Dec. 1606 performance at court, as Furness (ed. 1880, p. 377) points out: After imputing to Simon Stafford an intention to deceive the public, Malone is obliged to put the date of the performance as far back as March or April, 1605. It was on the eighth of May in that year that Stafford entered his book at Stationers’ Hall, and if Shakespeare’s Lear was then on the stage, or had been lately, it must have been written some months before. If, as Malone supposes, it was performed in March, it must have been written in January or February, in order to keep it within the year 1605. Law (1936, p. 49): The title-page on the 1608 Quarto of Shakspere’s play seems to stress the genuineness of its text as opposed to the spurious article of 1605 vintage. For this and other reasons I would date the Lear in 1605, a little before the reprinting [sic] of the anonymous Leir.

An odd and inconclusive line of defense for Malone’s position is offered by Fleay (1879, p. 119): The old Chronicle History could not have been described as Tragical in 1605 [S.R.] had not a tragedy on the subject been lately acted, nor could the tragedy have been any other than Shakespeare’s.…[J.] Wright, however, had not the impudence to put Stafford’s Tragical History on his title-page though he kept the lately acted, which was probably, as far as the older play [Leir] is concerned, not true. Accordingly, when the real tragedy [Lr.] was issued in 1608, But[t]er marks his edition as the genuine Dirty Dick, by putting Chronicle History on its forehead; only in the Folio does the real name of Tragedy appear. The date, then, is early in 1605. According to this logic, a false Stationers’ entry for Leir, calling it a tragedy, occasions in return a false title page for Q Lear, calling it a history. As Perrett (1904, p. 97) drily remarks on this fantasy, Leir is undeniably called a Chronicle History on its title page: Only in the S. R. is it called a Tragical History. To confine the deceptive title (if there is any guile in the word Tragecall) to the private papers of the Company of Stationers was a remarkably ineffectual attempt at a fraud upon the public. Many have in fact defended the characterization of Leir in the Stationers’ Register as tragical. Thus Furness (ed. 1880, p. 378): If the spectacle of a respectable elderly king, reduced to such an extremity of hunger as to induce his faithful attendant to offer him his bare and living arm as an article of diet, be not tragic, it is difficult to say what tragedy is. Moreover, Dryden in his Preface to The Spanish Friar speaks of a Tragedy ending happily. The half-title of Tate’s version of this very play reads, The tragedy of King Lear, and we all know that the declared purpose of that version was to turn it into a comedy; and when we find even Campbell, the poet, in his Remarks on this play, speaking of this same King Leir as a tragedy, I think we ought not to be too severe on an Elizabethan printer for applying to it the same title. Verity (ed. 1897), Craig (ed. 1901, p. xix), and others agree. Perrett (1904, p. 99) points out that in Leir Cordella calls her own story tragick (645), and that Collier (1843) titles the play The Tragedy of King Leir. Greg (1940, p. 383) finds the argument foolish: No stationer at the time would have regarded it as anything but a chronicle play. Bullough (1973, p. 270): But do S.R. entries usually describe accurately the genre of plays?

Law (1906, p. 474) provides an explanation of how the word might have been applied accidentally: as may be seen in a facsimile of the two Leir entries provided by Halliwell (ed. 1865, p. 362), the actual entry was first Tragedie but then corrected in the same hand to Tragecall historie: It seems probable that this error alone is responsible for the use of the word in the entry [rather, in both entries of that date]; perhaps neither Stafford nor Wright thought of employing the adjective till after the mistake was made. Greg (1940, p. 383 n.): If, as we may suppose [because of the 1594 entry and the 1605 title page], the manuscript had The True Chronicle History it would account for the partial correction. Perhaps the clerk carelessly or hastily misread true chronicle as tragecall and, having inattentively written Tragedie, turned it into the required adjective and correctly added historie. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxii), who wants to date Lr. early, in 1604–5, thinks that the mistake in the Register was not due to the publisher, who titled his book The True Chronicle History, but to someone else—presumably the clerk in the Stationers’ office—who shared the general knowledge that the story of the play was already known as a tragedy.

Nonetheless, Law and many others continue to think that Stafford’s decision to publish Leir was occasioned by a play about Lear lately acted, and that this was more likely to have been Sh.’s new tragedy than the old drama (which has also been called a comedy and romance) revived from the early 1590s. Thus Schelling (1902, p. 191): The registry in 1605 of the old play on Leir as a tragedy, although it ends happily…is a sufficient proof of the recent performance and popularity of a new play—and that a tragedy—on the story of Lear and his daughters.…Such a republication of an old play upon the revived popularity of an old theme is among the commonest proceedings of the time; he gives no examples. Pollard (1917, pp. 52–3; 1920, pp. 50–1) even erects a wild theory that one of Q1’s future publishers, John Busby, having been stymied by the King’s Men from pirating any of their plays after H5 and Wiv., may have been in a position to annoy them by printing the old play of King Leir (with an i)…when Lear (with an a) was first being acted in 1605. There is no evidence whatever of any connection of Busby with Leir. Greg (1940, p. 382): I find it very difficult to believe that this respectable but old-fashioned play, dating back in all probability to about 1590, had been divers and sundry times lately acted in 1605, especially if the playhouse manuscript had been for years in the hands of stationers. But no one now believes, as Greg did, that playbooks regularly were conveyed to printers, and the manuscript behind the 1605 imprint does not appear to come from the theater (see below).

Others think a revival in 1605 of the old Leir altogether possible. Furness (ed. 1880, p. 378): Simon Stafford, in all likelihood, tells the truth when he says his King Leir was latelie acted. I dare say it was a popular play; it is quite a good specimen of the third-rate class of comedies, and its success was sufficiently marked to suggest to Shakespeare a tragedy on the same subject. Verity (ed. 1897): Indeed it has been plausibly argued [Lee, DNB 51 (1897); 1973, 17:1315] that, instead of the publication of the old play being due to the success of King Lear, it may have been the revival on the stage of the old play and its publication that suggested the subject to Shakespeare. On the whole, then, I do not think that we can do better than to accept late autumn of 1605 or early spring of 1606 as the true date of King Lear. Chambers, having first said (1923, 4:25), It seems a little improbable that Leire should have been revived as late as 1605, later reverses himself (1930, 1:470): On the whole I think it is likely that Leir had been lately acted shortly before Lear was written, and gave suggestions for it. Greg (1940, pp. 382–3), though doubtful: If this was so, it is of itself sufficient to explain why a publisher into whose hands the manuscript had come should have thought it worth the printing…; there is no need to seek inducement in the chance of passing it off as Shakespeare’s, and Malone’s main argument falls to the ground.…[But] before accepting it one would like to know what company was supposed to have given the performance.…[383] And if it was not true (or if its only excuse was that the piece survived in the provinces) the publication of the play calls for an explanation. There were not many ten year old plays printed between 1600 and 1608. Bullough (1969, p. 43): Probably Leir’s revival in 1605 was the result of the Annesley scandal (see ). Idem (1973, p. 270): Revivals of old-fashioned pieces were not unknown. Mucedorus, a much looser piece of romantic writing, was revived in 1611, with some additions, by Shakespeare’s company, before the King. Taylor (1982, p. 407 n.): And if someone was attempting to pass the play off as Shakespeare’s, why not simply put W. S. as the author, as was done on other occasions? Finally, there is little evidence that Shakespeare’s play was (as Greg’s dating assumes) strikingly successful; very few contemporary allusions to it have been found. Patterson (1984, pp. 70–1): It is highly probable that its appearance [in print] at that time was motivated by the publication of John Thornborough’s [pro-Union] Joiefull and Blessed Reuniting (1605?), which described England and Scotland as siblings competing who could love their king most.

As with Harsnett’s book, a number of commentators speculate that Sh. might have been familiar with Leir before its publication in 1605. Malone (above) offers three possibilities: that Sh. had often seen it exhibited, that he had procured a manuscript of it, or that the play had been published earlier, in 1594. Unfortunately no evidence exists to support any of these conjectures (see below). A number of parallels have been detected between Leir and other early plays by Sh. (1 & 2 H6, R3, Jn., R2, Shr., MV, Ado, AYL, Ham.): see Law (1912, 1960), Greg (9 Mar. 1940, p. 124), McNeal (1958), Pearson (1981), Skura (1993), and Mueller (1994). Though in virtually all cases the points of resemblance are dramatic and linguistic commonplaces that could have originated in many other sources than Leir (see Knowles, 2002, pp. 18–27), Wells (ed. 2000, pp. 11–12) is inclined to accept them as evidence of Shakespeare’s familiarity with the old play long before it was published; he is careful to add, nonetheless, that Long familiarity with King Leir does not, however, preclude the possibility that Shakespeare wrote his play after Leir had appeared in print, and that he consulted the text afresh at this point, so his indebtedness to it does not certainly help with the dating.

Others speculate that Sh. had acted in the play or that his company had inherited the playbook. Only two performances of Leir are known. Henslowe’s Diary (ed. Greg, 1904, 1:17; ed. Foakes & Rickert, 1961, p. 21) records fairly large receipts on 6 and 8 April 1594 for performances of kinge leare, presumably at the Rose Th., by the Quenes men & my lord Susexe to geather. Henslowe’s 1594 Leare is generally supposed to have been owned by the Queen’s Men at that time (Greg, 1940, p. 378); it is not listed in Henslowe’s catalogue of Sussex’s plays in 1593–4 (Diary, ed. Greg, 1904, 1:16; ed. Foakes & Rickert, 1961, pp. 20–1), and it was entered to Edward White on the same day as another Queen’s play, Friar Bacon. Gurr (1996, p. 175) thinks that the Queen’s Men and Sussex’s probably played on alternate afternoons, and that Leir belonged to the Queen’s Men, an opinion reinforced by McMillin & MacLean (1998, p. 88). A month later, on 14 May 1594, entry was made in the Stationers’ Register of a book apparently not subsequently published entitled the moste famous chronicle historye of Leire Kinge of England and his Three Daughters (Greg, BEPD, 1:11, 337–8). These two records, in Henslowe and the Stationers’ Register, probably refer to the same play.

Since Malone, most scholars have been inclined to assume that it is also the same play (or at least an earlier version of it) published a decade later in 1605. Law (1906, pp. 465–70) and Greg (BEPD, 1:11, 34, 53, 55, 337–8) give the circumstantial evidence. The 1605 Leir was the first publication of John Wright, who obtained the copy by transfer from the printer Simon Stafford, on the condition that Stafford print the book. Wright had been an apprentice to Edward White, who had first entered Leire for publication in 1594. Law (p. 169) suspects Wright of piracy, but it is unlikely that Wright would have begun his career by illegally appropriating the copyright of his recent master, or that White would have allowed this act of theft and ingratitude. Greg (1940, pp. 379–80) rejects the idea: If this had been stolen from another stationer it is unlikely that the publisher [Wright] would have risked entering it in the Register or would have put his name and address on the [380] edition he issued. Moreover, it is clear from the entries themselves that the copy had been obtained not by Wright at all, but by Stafford. White apparently retained his 1594 copyright until his death in 1613, whence it passed to his son and heir Edward the younger, who operated his father’s shop until his own death in 1624. On 29 June 1624 the younger White’s widow transferred ownership of a Leire (and other plays) to Edward Aldee (Allde), who died in 1627. On the death of Allde’s widow the copyright for Leir was assigned to her stepson Richard Oulton on 22 Apr. 1640. White’s heirs evidently assumed continuous ownership of the play.

Nonetheless John Wright, the printer of the 1605 Leir, must also have considered himself its owner until he died in 1646; though Leir is not named in the transfer from John Wright senior to his brother Edward on 27 June 1646, on 4 Apr. 1655 it was transferred from Edward Wright to the bookseller William Gilbertson. Thus, either there were two Leirs (or two quite different versions of it), or else one version about which there were differing claims of ownership, one extending from Edward White in 1594 to Richard Oulton in 1640, the other from John Wright in 1605 to William Gilbertson in 1655. The existence of two Leirs before Sh.’s Lr., one from the 1590s and another perhaps more recent one, remains a possibility, but the play published in 1605 has structural, thematic, and stylistic traits that seem to place it in the early 1590s. It is a distinctly old-fashioned play, and McMillin & MacLean (1998, pp. 33, 92, 100–8, 133–4, 146–7) show that its qualities are all typical of Queen’s Men plays of the early 1590s. The probability that two old plays on Leir had existed simultaneously in the 1590s—one ultimately printed in 1605 and another now lost—seems remote. Much more probably there is some kind of continuity between the play entered by White in 1594 and the book published by his former apprentice Wright in 1605. A possible account of such continuity is offered later in this essay.

If the Leare played at the Rose in 1594 and the Leir published in 1605 are the same play, the question still remains how and when Sh. became acquainted with it. Conceivably he had acted in the play at the beginning of his career, as Wentersdorf (1950, p. 128), Craig (1951, p. 32), Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxii), Pinciss (1974, p. 133), McMillin & MacLean (1998, pp. 160–2), and others suggest. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxii): There is a possibility that Shakespeare acted in King Leir; and as Perillus is on the stage when all save one of [Muir’s selection of eight] parallel passages are spoken, that may have been Shakespeare’s role. Unfortunately for this theory, several dozen other parallels occur when Perillus is not on stage. Muir does not suggest a company, theater, or date for Sh.’s performance. Though Sh. may have acted with the Queen’s Men before their leaving London in May 1594, as Pollard (1929, pp. 13–21), Pinciss (1974, pp. 129–33), McMillin & MacLean (1998, pp. 160–6), and others are inclined to believe, most scholars would not assert that possibility to be a certainty. The staging of his plays by one company after another in the early 1590s may suggest rather that he was with Lord Strange’s Men until 1592 (1H6, Tit.), then with Pembroke’s company until it broke up in 1593 (2 & 3 H6, Shr., Tit.), then perhaps briefly with Sussex’s Men until they broke up in spring, 1594 (Tit.), and thereafter with the Lord Chamberlain’s Men (Chambers, 1923, 2:338; Gurr, 1996, pp. 175–6, 262–3, 269–72). One cannot therefore claim with any assurance that he acted Leir (or any other play) with the Queen’s company. If he were with Sussex’s Men at the Rose in 1594, however, he could have seen the Queen’s Men perform Leir at that time, and later remembered some of its details.

Some editors, such as Wells (ed. 2000, p. 11), argue that Sh.’s memory was exceptional, and that he would have retained sufficently sharp memories from either seeing or acting in the play a decade or more earlier. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxii) compares the way echoes of Coleridge’s reading appeared years later in The Ancient Mariner. The apparent indebtedness of Sh.’s Lr. to Leir for nearly a hundred details of action, character, ideas, phrasing, and vocabulary (see ), however, seems to imply, to a growing number of commentators, a close and recent acquaintance with the old play rather than merely memories of a distant performance. If that is the case, and if Sh. wrote Lr. before Wright’s edition of 1605 appeared, he must have had access to either an earlier printed version or a manuscript of Leir. Virtually no one accepts Malone’s assumption that an edition of 1594 was printed; no copy survives, and Greg (1910, p. 516; cf. 1940, p. 379) thinks that it is improbable that White ever produced that edition, since the new edition of 1605 was preceded by a fresh entry. Had an earlier edition existed, John Wright would not have made a second entry, but would have registered a transfer from White. The entry of 1605 practically proves that that of 1594 had been inoperative. If so, Sh.’s only alternative to the 1605 printed edition was a manuscript.

Exactly how Sh. might have acquired such a manuscript has never been fully accounted for. Greg (1940, p. 385) imagines that when the moribund Queen’s company broke in 1594 they sold to Edward White a manuscript of Leir too debased for him ever to publish, but that they disposed more prudentiallly of the play’s promptbook, which first remained as a pledge in Henslowe’s hands, then passed to Alleyn, who was leading the joint Strange’s-Admiral’s company, thence somehow to the Chamberlain’s, where eventually Shakespeare used it, and then was careless enough to let it get into the nimble hands of Simon Stafford, who printed it. Of this tissue of speculation Greg has the assurance to say, This, of course, is guesswork but not altogether improbable, not too fantastic, conceding I have no great liking for this hypothesis. Both Knutson (1991, p. 9) and Gurr (1996, pp. 279–80) also speculate that some Queen’s Men playbooks migrated to the newly-formed Chamberlain’s Men in 1594, but neither can identify any such books, or even any former Queen’s Men who entered the new company and might have brought playbooks with them. If the Chamberlain’s-King’s Men had ever acquired their own manuscript of Leir, most probably the old Queen’s Men playbook, bearing the Master of the Revels’ license to perform, then one might expect a performance of Leir, which had had very good receipts at the Rose in 1594, soon afterward; but it is not among the list of seven plays performed jointly or alternately by the Admiral’s and Chamberlain’s companies at Newington Butts two months later, between 3 and 13 June (Henslowe’s Diary, ed. Greg 1904, p. 17; ed. Foakes & Rickert, 1961, pp. 21–2). Moreover, Sh. did not attempt to rewrite Leir for another eleven years, until about the same time when a publicly available printed edition appeared in 1605. There is simply no reason to think that Sh.’s company owned a manuscript of the play.

Probably only a very limited number of manuscripts of the play ever existed, and it is unclear how Sh. would have acquired any of them. There is no reason why either the manuscript acquired by Edward White in May 1594 or the manuscript acquired by Simon Stafford in 1605 would have been accessible to Sh. before he wrote his play; both were entered for copyright as publishable investments, and in both cases the copyright passed to heirs; neither stationer would be likely to let his property out of his hands before he had made some use of it. Nor would another manuscript held by a company performing the play in or shortly before 1605, as Wright’s title page probably implies, have been made available to the chief playwright of the pre-eminent rival company, the King’s Men, to aid him in writing a competing play on the Lear story. Simon Stafford, of course, had been able to acquire a manuscript of Leir at about the time Sh. was starting to write Lear. How that manuscript made its way from its original owners the Queen’s Men to Stafford, and what kind of manuscript it was, have never been explored; but these questions are key to understanding the appearance and the nature of the 1605 edition of Leir.

Since Greg’s time until very recently our thinking about the Queen’s Men has been clouded by some serious misconceptions. Whatever Henslowe meant when he reported in May 1594 that the Queen’s Men recently brocke & went into the contrey to playe (Diary, ed. Greg, p. 4; ed. Foakes & Rickert, p. 7), they did not cease to exist as a company; rather, they ceased to be a company centered in London, instead touring widely and successfully in provincial towns (as they had done for most of their existence) for almost another decade. The list of their known activities assembled in McMillin & MacLean (1998, pp. 175–88) records more than a hundred provincial performances through late 1602, possibly into early 1603, after which, upon the Queen’s death, they disbanded. When they left London in 1594 they apparently did not sell off their stock of playbooks, but rather a variety of less valuable duplicate copies of their plays. It seems to have escaped notice that of the known or most likely Queen’s plays sold to publishers in 1594 and 1595—Friar Bacon, The Famous Victories of Henry V, The True Tragedy of Richard III, Selimus, The Old Wives Tale, and possibly James IV and Locrine—not one of them, in the opinion of their recent editors, derives from the company’s playbook. Clearly the playbooks, with their licenses from the Master of the Revels, were being preserved for use in the provinces, as they may well have been until the company ultimately ceased to exist upon the Queen’s death in 1603.

It is therefore entirely possible that the title page of Stafford and Wright’s edition of 1605 tells the truth. The Queen’s Men could lately (until 1603) have performed this respectable and formerly successful play divers and sundry times (in various provincial towns). Upon the dissolution of the company in 1603 the sharers would have sold off the remaining assets, including such properties as the playbook of Leir. Stafford might have invested in the manuscript either because the subject of a divided kingdom seemed timely or (equally probably) because the play had recently shown itself to be viable on the stage. The failure of the title page to name either company or theater, which has aroused some suspicion (see Greg, 1940, pp. 380, 382–3; Wells, ed. 2000, p. 11), is easily accounted for: the Queen’s Company had not had a home theater for a decade, and there would be no advertising value to Stafford’s naming a provincial playing company that had been defunct for the past two years. The play had never been published, and Stafford registered his ownership on 8 May 1605, intending to publish it then. Immediately, however, doubtless owing to the care or good memory of one of the wardens of the Stationers’ Company, he was made aware that Edward White still held copyright from 1594. Having paid good money for his manuscript, he might naturally have approached White to find a way to salvage the situation. Lee (1909, p. xi) and Michie (1979; 1991, p. 4) have suggested that Wright was allowed to publish Leir as a result of a friendly negotiation between the master, White, his former apprentice, Wright, and the third party, Simon Stafford. White may have found a way to do two good deeds at once: allowing Stafford to print the play, and helping his recently freed apprentice Wright to start his career by publishing it. This would explain the coincidence (Greg, 1940, p. 380) that young John Wright ever got involved in Stafford’s transactions at all. With the supervision and approval of one of the wardens, Mr. [William] Leake, White arranged to transfer publication rights to his former apprentice Wright—not necessarily the recognized ownership of the property in question…but only whatever right or claim [as purchaser of a manuscript] Stafford might have to it (Greg, 1956, p. 80). Because Stafford was stipulated in the Stationers’ Register entry as the printer, he could after all make some profit on his original investment. Since the manuscript behind Leir (1605) shows no signs of theatrical provenance, but seems rather to be an authorial or scribal fair copy (Jewkes, 1958, p. 201; Michie, 1991, pp. 16, 21), quite possibly White, to help make Wright’s first publishing venture as successful as possible, allowed the printer Stafford to use his original clean, non-theatrical copy—the kind of copy typically released by the Queen’s Men in 1594, and the actual copy for which White still held copyright—instead of the marked-up and worn theatrical copy that Stafford would most likely have acquired from the actors. Later John Wright (or his heirs) may justifiably have assumed that, since he had entered and published the book, the rights to it were now his. The question of ownership, if anyone was even aware of it, seems never to have become an issue. (For further development of this theory of provenance, see Knowles, 2002, pp. 27–35.)

In the upshot, we know that a printed text of Leir existed in 1605, and that Sh.’s Lr. was influenced by many details of the version of the play appearing in that text. Sh.’s borrowings from the old play now seem to many scholars to be too numerous and specific to be explained as memories of his seeing or acting the play twelve or more years earlier; rather, he seems recently to have used a written or printed version of it. His access to a manuscript, while a possibility, is not demonstrable or easily accountable. Though many possibilities may be imagined, the most likely inferences are that Sh. used the 1605 edition, and that his completed play therefore postdates it.

div.head: King and Court
div.p: Many commentators have suspected topical allusions to King James, his policies, court, family, and beliefs: see nn. 7, 39, 141, 439–44, 473+1–+6, 514, 552–3, 561, 669+1–+11, 669+4, 669+6–+7, 669+10, 669+11, 682, 751, 842–55, 1089–90, 1328, 1536–8, 1638+1–+12, 1734–49, 1739, 1741, 1865–78, 1968, 2007–12, 2037, 2248+1–+5, 2303–2303+17, 2497, 2546–7, 2608–12, 2703, 2948–59, 3295, 3298, and DP nn. 2, 5, 6, 9–10, and 16. Even if all of these allusions are actual, they are of little help in dating, since virtually no one doubts that Lr. is a Jacobean play.

Much criticism, following Chalmers (1799), has concerned itself with the relevance of the division of the kingdom in Lr. to King James’s hope to unify England and Scotland (see nn. 7 and 1968, and , ). Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxiv): Between 1604 and 1607 King James was trying to get Parliament to approve of the union of England and Scotland and referring in speech after speech to the misfortunes that division brought to early Britain. Draper (1937, p. 182): Sh. intended his play to illustrate the evils of disunion. Wickham (1973, pp. 36–7): Unlike Leir, Sh.’s play identifies the husbands of Goneril and Regan as the Dukes of Albany and Cornwall; up to 1605 these were titles of James’s two sons. Evidently Sh. chose to dramatize the story of Lear the divider as antitype to James the uniter and peacemaker. That Shakespeare, both as a Groom of the King’s Household and as principal play-maker to the King’s personal company of actors, should have elected to co-operate in the active propagation of these ideas [James as pacific uniter of Britain and of Christendom], as far as his artistic conscience as poet and dramatist would permit, strikes me as neither surprising nor unnatural. Kernan (1995, pp. 96): King Lear glances at current politics in the opening act, where the old king of Britain makes the mistake of dividing his kingdom, thereby replicating the House of Commons’ continuing refusal to end the separation of the kingdoms of England and Scotland. Patterson (1984, p. 69): If we assume a date of late 1605 to late 1606 for the composition of King Lear, we can also assume that it followed all of the other contributions to the Union controversy. Not one of them alludes to the Lear story, even when, as in Munday’s pageant [Triumphes; see below], or Herbert’s Prophecie, or Thornborough’s Joiefulll and Blessed Reuniting, substantial attention is paid to the chronicle history of Britain. It is hard to believe that Thornborough, in particular, could have developed the metaphor of sibling rivalry and the competition to see who should love their king…most without some references to King Lear if the play were already current in the London theater. Thornborough’s undated pamphlet is assigned conjecturally in STC to 1605; Patterson thinks it also predates the publication in 1605 of Sh.’s source Leir (see above).

Malone (ed. 1790, 1:353) thinks in fact that the attempt at Union provides a very precise limit for dating Lr.: This play is ascertained to have been written after the month of October, 1604, by a minute change which Shakspeare made in a traditional line, put into the mouth of Edgar:…I smell the blood of a British man [1968], where British man is substituted for the traditional English man in recognition of James’s efforts: Though a complete union of England and Scotland, which was projected in the first parliament that met after James’s accession to the English throne, was not carried into effect till a century afterwards, the two kingdoms were united in name, and he was proclaimed king of Great Britain, October 24, 1604. Chalmers (1799, pp. 416 ff.) similarly argues for an even earlier limit: The fact is, that there was issued from Greenwich a royal proclamation, on the 13th of May, 1603; declaring that, till a compleat union, the King held, and esteemed, the two realms, as presently united, and as one kingdom: and, the poets, Daniel, and Drayton, who wrote gratulatory verses, on his accession, spoke of the two kingdoms, as united thereby, into one realm, by the name of Britain; and of the inhabitants of England and Scotland, as one people, by the demonina-[418]tion of British. This argument is repeated by Drake (1817, 2:457–8), Craig (ed. 1901, p. xv), and Goggin (ed. 1910).

Skeptics, however, doubt that the use of British in 1968 has any significance. For one thing, the word was in common use. Halliwell-Phillipps (2nd ed., 1882, p. 285; 8th ed., 1889, 2:339): British occurs more frequently than English in Sh.’s source-play Leir. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905, p. 143): Spenser, in his 1590 account of Leyr (FQ 2.10), uses Briton, and it is, in fact, common throughout The Faerie Queene. Moreover, as Knight (ed. 1840, p. 394) noticed, In the folio edition of 1623 the latter passage [2703] is given, Upon the English party, where the 1608 quarto reads Brit(t)ish, thus reversing the kind of politic substitution that Malone thought he discerned at 1968. Wright (ed. 1875, p. xv): It is well not to lay too much stress upon [the variants].… It might be inferred that the line [2703] as it stands in the folios was written before Oct. 1604, and that it was corrected before the play was printed [in Q] in 1608. But it is at least as likely that Shakespeare, writing not long after 1604, while the change was still fresh, and before the word British had become familiar in men’s mouths, may inadvertently have written English and subsequently changed it to British (at 1968, but not, presumably, at 2703). Though this line of argument is repeated by Craig (ed. 1901, p. xxi) and Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. xxxiv), it is probably false; no one now believes that Q is a later, more carefully corrected state of the text than F.

Wright (ed. 1875, pp. xvi–xvii), without insisting too much upon this, suggests that in 442–4 (Machinations…Graues) there may be a reference to the Gunpowder Plot of Nov. 5, 1605; many have agreed. See nn. 437–43, 473+2–+3. Chambers (1930, 1:468) speaks for the skeptics: The reference to machinations, hollowness, treachery and all ruinous disorders ([442–3]) is hardly specific enough to bear pressing as a reminiscence of the Gunpowder Plot. Wickham (1973, pp. 36 ff.) seems to think such an allusion would be premature: The drift away from revenge tragedy and towards regenerative tragi-comedy in the first decade of James’s reign…has its true origins in the political consciousness of the British peoples saved from foreign invasion and civil war by the peaceful accession of James I in 1603, by the timely discovery of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, and the final ratification of the Union of the two Crowns by Act of Parliament in 1608…. (P. 39): James’s triumphant entry to London in 1604 was celebrated in pageantry by Jonson, Dekker, Middleton, and Webster, upon the triple theme of Peace, Plenty, and Regenerative Power. In 1605 Anthony Munday did the same in the first Lord Mayor’s Show of the new reign, The Triumphes of Re-united Britania, featuring Brutus, Albanact, Camber, and Locrine, and celebrating James as a second Brutus. (P. 40): The Gunpowder Plot was one month later, and the miraculous escape of the royal family only reinforced the myth of a second Brutus bringing Troynovant. (P. 41): Thos. Heywood was just then writing Troia Britanica (1609), and it served as theme for several later masques and shows. (P. 42): Shakespeare can hardly have chosen to revert, via Holinshed and The Faerie Queene, [from the tragi-comedic Leir] to Geoffrey of Monmouth’s original account with its tragic catastrophe for both Lear and Cordelia unless it was planned and scripted very early in James’s reign—i.e., before the Gunpowder Plot.

In fact, the supposedly allusive lines are not present in Q (1608) but appear as one of the later (and undatable) additions in the Folio (1623); they are therefore of no help in dating the original composition of the play. If the much-revised rough draft lying behind Q1 had been written after Nov. 1605, an allusion to the Gunpowder Plot, if Sh. had intended one, would have been more timely and therefore more likely to appear in that draft than as a later addition to F. The absence of the lines from Q may indicate either that Sh. intended no such allusion there or that the Q text as a whole predates 5 Nov. 1605. The lines must have been added at some point to the theatrical manuscript lying behind F, but when and why they were added is uncertain (see n. 439–44); the longer after the play’s first known performance at the end of 1606, the less likely that the added lines were intended be recognized as specifically topical. One may speculate that they were added to the theatrical manuscript before the 1606 court performance, but they could as well have been added at any time before 1623, for various reasons. If an allusion to the Gunpowder Plot exists in F, it is of no help in dating the original composition of the play.

Other supposed allusions to James’s personal behavior and the nature of his court seem equally unhelpful in fixing a date for the play. The reference to monopolies at 669+10 (see n.) has been thought to allude to James’s granting of too many monopolies, but that royal practice had been abused throughout the reigns of all the Tudor monarchs and was especially an issue some fifteen years after the first performance of Lr. Goneril’s several complaints against Lear’s excessive retinue of knights have been thought to allude satirically to James’s wholesale creation of many Scottish knights in 1603–4 (see nn. 669+1–+11, 751, 842–55); but Lear has not recently enlarged his court, and Goneril’s complaints that his retinue is too expensive for a hostess to maintain and a possible military danger besides are not the reasons why many English subjects resented the Scottish influx into James’s court. Goneril’s unproven claims of the misbehavior of Lear’s knights have been taken as a topical reference to the drunkenness, gluttony, and promiscuity that occurred during the visit of the King of Denmark and his followers during the summer of 1606 (see nn. 669+11, 751). Pearson (1949, pp. 140–1): The visit of the Danish monarch had been celebrated with such a riot of drunkenness and fornication [described in Fripp, 1938, p. 654] that even Sir John Harrington was shocked. But those carouses involved both English court and Danish guests on holiday, disorderly ladies and men both, not an entourage of British knights providing attendance and protection to their former sovereign. Kernan (1995, p. 96): Lear’s fool would immediately have caught the attention of an audience at a court where there had been no official fool since the time of Henry VIII until James, with his pawky sense of humor, brought with him from Scotland Archie Armstrong, who was no doubt fooling it in the audience that Christmas [1606]. In addition, Shakespeare…felt by this time that he could sail fairly close to the political wind in allowing the antagonisms in the House of Stuart between father and children to play about his story, citing Patterson (1984, pp. 59–60; cf. 1989, p. 115–16). Finally, if an allusion exists to James’s preoccupation with hunting (see n. 514), it can hardly refer to any single year of his reign.

div.head: Other Contemporaries
div.p: Similarities have been found between Lear’s and Gloucester’s parental problems and the plight of several English contemporaries (see ). Most attention has been given to the legal actions between October 1603 and December 1604 concerning the mistreatment of the aged Brian Annesley by two of his daughters and his protection from them by a third. If this legal case was a source for Lr., it would provide a slightly later limit for date of composition than such other sources as Harsnett and Montaigne. An earlier analogue discovered by Sisson (1951), occurring in 1589, can have no relevance to dating Lr. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 92): A more prominent case [than Annesley] heard in Star Chamber between June 1604 and June 1605 was that of Sir Robert Dudley, bastard son of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Queen Elizabeth’s favourite, having analogies with the relationship of Gloucester and Edmund; see . If Sh. was influenced by this case, a somewhat later date of composition is implied. Pearson (1949, p. 139) fancifully finds an analogy in Sh.’s own life: Conceivably the birth of this natural son [William Davenant] prompted Shakespeare to create the bastard Edmund in King Lear (1606). Though Davenant, born early in 1606, liked to claim poetical kinship with Sh., John Aubrey’s mischievous report that he was his actual son is one of the unproved Shn. myths; and why Davenant’s begetting would lead Sh. immediately to portray Gloucester’s bastard son as a ruthless villain is anything but obvious.

div.head: Meteorology
div.p: Supposed allusions to two kinds of meteorological events, eclipses and spring storms and floods, have also been detected and applied to dating the play. Eclipses are referred to in both Q and F, in 433: these late eclipses in the Sunne and Moone, and in 470, these Eclipses. Hudson (1872, 2:350): A great eclipse of the Sun took place in October, 1605, and had been looked forward to with dread as portending evil; the more so, because an eclipse of the Moon occurred within the space of a month previous. And John Harvey had, in 1588, published a book wherein, with the wisdom of nature, he had reasoned against the common belief, that such natural events were ominous of disaster, or had some moral significance in them. Therewithal, in November, 1605, the dreadful secret of the Gunpowder Plot came to light; so that one at all superstitiously inclined might well say that nature finds…effects, and that machinations…graves. Taking all these particulars together, we have ample ground for inferring the play to have been written near the close of 1605, or somewhat later. The conclusion of course rests on the assumption that mention of an eclipse in a play refers to an actual event outside the play. Moreover, as Greg (1940, p. 384) remarks, We might argue that the allusions…are a later insertion. There is nothing whatever to indicate that they are; but on the other hand they are in no wise essential, and it would have been easy enough to work them in.

Hudson’s argument is immediately picked up by Moberly (ed. 1876), Fleay (1886, p. 237), Boas (1896, p. 438), and others, but most influentially by Wright (ed. 1875, pp. xv–xvi): The solar and lunar eclipses of 1590, 1598, 1601, and 1605, he notes, had been forecast by the said John Harvey in his anti-astrological work A Discoursive Probleme concerning Prophesies (1588, p. 119). Harvey predicted that the solar eclipse of 2 Oct. (O.S.; 12 Oct. N. S.) 1605 would be especially dramatic, and darknes appeere euen at midday, the Moone at the very next full immediately preceding hauing likewise beene Eclipsed. Wright says, It can scarcely be doubted that Shakespeare had in his mind the great eclipse, and that Lear was written while the recollection of it was still fresh, and while the ephemeral literature of the day abounded with pamphlets foreboding the consequences that were to follow, when he refers to eclipses and their consequences in 433 and 470. Harvey says, however, that two Eclipses in the space of one month, are no great strange nouities, and he apparently gets his predictions from other astronomers, since he gives the dates matter-of-factly, not as revelations. He also names the years 1606, 1607, and 1608 as other years notable for eclipses. The allusion has more recently been accepted by Chambers (1930, 1:468), Greg (1940, p. 377), Kittredge (ed. 1940, p. viii), Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 128), and some others.
Those doubting this way of dating use two lines of argument: that no actual eclipses need be referred to at all, but that if one or more is, there are several other candidates besides those in 1605.

Halliwell-Phillipps (1889, 2:339): Allusions to such matter as storms and eclipses are exceedingly treacherous criteria. Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xxii f.): [Sh.] may not have been thinking of any particular eclipse.…Several remarkable eclipses had been of recent [xxiii] occurrence. In the year 1598 there was on the 7th of March [N. S.] a large partial eclipse of the sun visible in England, preceded on the 21st February [N. S.] by a large partial eclipse of the moon, and followed on the 16th August by a total eclipse of the moon; while in the year 1601 an annular eclipse of the sun occurred on the 24th December, which was preceded by two lunar eclipses in that year—one, a small partial eclipse, on the evening of the 15th June; the other, a large partial eclipse, nearly total, on the evening of the 9th December—all predicted by Harvey (though not always for the right day) in 1588, and confirmed for Craig in 1901 by W. H. Wesley of the Royal Astronomical Society. Doubts about the particular allusion are repeated by Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905, p. 143), Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. xxxii f.), Ridley (ed. 1935, pp. xiii f.), and others, because of other eclipses of 1590, 1598, 1601, 1607, and 1608. Parr (1953, pp. 73–4): It is not unreasonable to suppose, of course, that Shakespeare [74] might have referred in King Lear to the eclipse of the sun in 1601 and any one of the many eclipses of the moon from 1598 onward. It is especially notable that Shakespeare mentions eclipses in no play written prior to 1601, but that he alludes to them somewhat frequently thereafter…[in Ham., Oth., Lr., Mac., Ant.]. Since the large majority of notable eclipses visible in England during Shakespeare’s lifetime occurred from 1598 onward, it would seem that all of Shakespeare’s allusions to eclipses might have been suggested by actual eclipses of the time—i.e., not only those of 1605. Citing (p. 73, n. 6) Theodor Ritter von Oppolzer, Canon der Finsternisse (Wien, 1887; [tr. Donald H. Menzel & Owen Gingerich, New York, 1962]), and J. Fr. Schroeter, Sonnenfinsternisse von 600 biz 1800 N. Chr., mit 300 Karten (Kristiana, 1923) on the occurrence, visibility, and duration of the eclipses, Parr goes on: There were lunar eclipses clearly visible in London in 1596 and 1598, as Oppolzer (pp. 367–368) will show. The solar eclipses visible in London throughout Shakespeare’s lifetime were not very numerous, occurring (according to Schroeter, pp. 10, 149–151, cxix-cxxii) as follows (Gregorian Calendar):
March 7, 1598 10:20 a.m. Total
December 24, 1601 1:01 p.m. Partial
October 12, 1605 1:08 p.m. Total

There were solar eclipses in Europe also in 1590, 1594, 1596, 1600, and 1610, but Schroeter’s charts of the paths of these eclipses show clearly that only the three listed above were visible in England. If Shakespeare always remained in England, he never saw an eclipse of the sun until 1598—one lasting for more than two hours, and unusually conspicuous because it was total. Levy (2002, p. 76): While solar and lunar eclipses do take place within two weeks of each other, it is rare that they are prominently visible from the same spot. In early 17th-century London, however, this happened twice. The annular eclipse of 1601 was preceded just two weeks earlier by the nearly total lunar eclipse on December 9th, which was visible in the early-evening sky. And the 1605 total solar eclipse was preceded by a pre-dawn partial lunar eclipse on September 27th.…But in 1605 the autumn eclipses came on the heels of a lunar eclipse that had taken place that spring—on the evening of April 3rd Londoners were treated to a nearly total lunar eclipse.…Shakespeare might well have had the three eclipses of 1605 in mind.

Because Elizabethan discussions of eclipses date them according to the old-style (O. S.) Julian calendar used in England until 1752, and modern dating uses the new-style (N. S.) Gregorian calendar, there has been much error and confusion in literary discussions of this issue. Moreover, the visibility in London of the 1598 and 1605 eclipses is disputed by Ward (1933, pp. 878, 909) and Collins (1933, p. 896). The times and visibility (weather permitting) of all these eclipses are confirmed by Buckley (1963, pp. 253, 255–6) on the authority of the directors of the Nautical Almanac Offices of the Naval Observatory of Washington and the Royal Greenwich Observatory, and they have recently been confirmed by Dr. James Lattis of the University of Wisconsin Space Astronomy Laboratory, using both von Oppolzer’s Canon and Fred Espenak’s online Five Millenium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses, -1999 to +3000 (http://sunearth.gsfc.nasa.gov/eclipse, 2001). Levy (2002, p. 76) cites the Annales Célestes du Dix-Septième Siecle by the 18th-c. French astronomer Alexander Guy Pingré, including a clear notation that from London, at least the ending of the great solar eclipse of October 1605 was recorded. The sky was also clear enough for observations to be conducted from France.…It was also the eclipse that led King James I to write to his friend Robert Cecil, earl of Salisbury, scoffing at judicial astrology.

Those urging that topical allusions to recent eclipses would have been recognized by the audience of Lr. give evidence of contemporary interest in such events. Collins (ed. 1931, pp. xiv f.): The eclipse of [10 July, N. S.] 1600 [which was total over Spain] was supplemented by a partial eclipse of the sun on [xv] Christmas eve, 1601, which provided fearful portents the same day in thunder and lightning over London, and an earthquake [citing the letter from Dudley Carleton to John Chamberlain, S.P.Dom., cclxxxii, 48]. On the 8th [18th, N. S.] November, 1603, the moon was eclipsed, and on the same day there was a conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter.
