Men’s minds reverted to the similar, though astrologically not so alarming, conjunction of the same planets in 1583, when the years immediately following ha[d] been a time of disaster.…The general uneasiness concerning the approaching conjunction, and the double eclipse of the sun and moon in 1605, is apparent very much earlier in the frequent references to them both, as in verses 32–3 of John Norden’s Vicissitudo Rerum (1601). Apparently inferring Sh.’s own interest in such matters, Harrison (1933, p. 856; ed. 1937, pp. 15–16) finds verbal similarities between Gloucester’s lines 433–44 and Edward Gresham’s Strange feareful & true newes (dated 11 Feb. 1605 [O.S.; 1606 N. S.]), which claims that planetary alignments (especially of Saturn and Jupiter), The Earth and Moone’s late and horrible obscurations, and wandring planets have terrestrial effects: new Leagues, Traytrous Designements, Catching at Kingdomes, translation of Empyre, downefall of men in Authoritye, æmulations, Ambition, Innouations, Factious Sects, Schisms, and much disturbance and trobles in religion and matters of the Church. There is not much overlap in the particulars of this and Gloucester’s catalogues of disasters, which may be merely formulaic: see n. 433–44. Harrison nonetheless concludes, If Shakespeare had this pamphlet in mind, it follows that Lear was written after February and before Christmas, 1606, when it was performed at Court. His subsequent clarification somewhat weakens his case (1933, p. 896): Nowhere did I suggest that Shakespeare was referring to any particular eclipse.…The prodigies described in the pamphlet were not eclipses, and occurred in June, 1605. Taylor (1982, p. 412) finds another mention of eclipses in the contemporary play, George Wilkins’s Miseries of Enforced Marriage (which he dates June 1605–May 1606): When dus [sic] the Sunne and Moone borne in one frame | Contend, but they breed Earthquakes in mens harts (2350–1). It seems likely both playwrights are referring to the same events.

Doubters remain. Parr (1945, pp. 47–8): The argument that these late eclipses shows [48] Lear to have been written after the eclipses of September and October, 1605, is somewhat weakened when we consider what prognostications concerning them were on the London bookstalls in 1604 and earlier. Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxi f.): If we accepted Harrison’s theory we should have to suppose that King Lear was written in the last ten months of 1606. But astrological jargon inevitably varies little; and there are closer parallels with Gloucester’s remarks in Florio’s Montaigne. There were several earlier eclipses that would still be remembered by the audience. [He cites the three in 1601]…[xxii] But Shakespeare may not have been referring to any particular pair of eclipses; and even supposing a reference was intended to the eclipses of 1605, he might have cunningly inserted the reference because he knew these eclipses were expected later in the year. It is therefore possible that the play was begun before September 1605; or, indeed, that the reference to the eclipses was a later addition. Stone (1953, p. 471): In any one year there must be at least two and not more than seven eclipses [solar + lunar, not equally or everywhere visible]. Four eclipses in a year usually achieved mention in the chronicles. Neither [John] Harvey nor anyone else saw anything important in the eclipses predicted for 1588. Eclipses were so common that all pronouncements on the basis of them were…made with the utmost caution. Barroll (1991, p. 133): Searching for actual eclipses as a way of dating the composition of King Lear…begs the question.…Dating King Lear via an eclipse is to assume that the eclipse talk in the play refers to a real event. But this may no more be the case than that the eye-gouging of the earl of Gloucester refers to the actual eye-gouging of some earl in the court of James I—or that the eclipses occurred just before Q2 Hamlet when Horatio speaks of how the moist star…Was sick almost to doomsday with eclipse and that the like precurse have heaven and earth together demonstrated [Un]to our […] countrymen.

Even less persuasive than his dating by eclipses is Wright’s (ed. 1875, p. xvii) dating by weather. Though despairing of fixing the season in which the storm in Act 3 takes place, he suggests the season in which the play was written: Perhaps Shakespeare began the play in the winter of 1605 and finished it in the summer of 1606, while the fields were still covered with the unharvested corn, and the great storm of March was still fresh in his recollection. One of the few who agrees, half-heartedly, is Harrison (1935, p. 896; ed. 1937, rev. 1949): March 29 [1606], a tempest of great violence broke, which wrought great damage all over Europe. There is no trace of a storm in other versions of the Lear story.…It is perhaps not too far-fetched to suggest that the storm scenes in King Lear came to Shakespeare at this time. The idea is asserted by Paul (1950, pp. 251–3). Most are not convinced. Fleay (1879, p. 120): The storm in Lear has no connection with the floods and continuous rains of [June] 1606. Furness (ed. 1880, p. 381): To suppose that when Shakespeare alludes to winter there must actually be icicles hanging by the wall, or that when he mentions flowers the meadows must be painted with delight before his very eyes, is to put a narrow limitation to his imagination. Chambers (1930, 1:468): This theory seems to limit the poet’s imagination rather unduly by climatic conditions.

div.head: Literary and Theatrical Milieu
div.p: Of the contemporary plays and other works that may have influenced or been influenced by Sh.’s Lr., the most important for purposes of dating, the old play Leir, has been discussed above at some length.

Though many have supposed it possible that Sh. drew upon the story of Ina, King of the West Saxons, in Camden’s Remaines (1605), particularly for Cordelia’s answer to Lear (see nn. 105, 106–110+1), his indebtedness is in considerable doubt: see . Muir, who (ed. 1952, p. xxiv) argues for a date of composition in the winter of 1604–5, declines (1957, p. 143) for lack of conclusive evidence to accept Camden’s work as a source, and (1977, p. 197) adds that it was probably published too late to influence the play. Musgrove (1956, p. 298): If we insist that Shakespeare can only have known Camden’s book in its published form, then the date of composition must be 1605 at the earliest. But those who hold to a date of 1604 can justifiably argue that Shakespeare’s friendship for Jonson, and Jonson’s for Camden, would make it quite possible for him to have seen the book before publication.

Sampson (1902, pp. 71–2): At the close of Act 1 of Edward Sharpham’s The Fleire [1607, sig. C3] Fleire is questioned by a group of gallants and ladies—Spark, Ruffell, Piso, the Knight, Nan, and Susan—and (p. 72) replies to their questions in a waggish, blunt way and professes to want service. It seems not unlikely that Sharpham, who, by the way, is a frequent borrower from Shakespeare, expanded the latter’s briefer and more effective scene, Kent’s application for service in Lr. 1.4. The play was entered in the Stationers’ Register on 13 May 1606 and permission to print was given 21 Nov. 1606. It is probably to be dated 1605–6, because of jests in it on Englishmen turned Britons, and its presentation at Blackfriars by the Children of the Revels (not called Queen’s or Her Majesty’s) after the Eastward Ho trouble. Its main character is modelled from Marston’s Fawn (1604–6), doubtless soon after The Fawn had been transferred from the Queen’s Revels at Blackfriars to the Paul’s boys. Chambers (1930, 1:468): There is a fairly palpable imitation of [Lr. 539–72] in Edward Sharpham’s The Fleir, i, ad fin. This was probably produced after 30 January 1606, registered on May 13, and printed in 1607. Chambers (1923, 3:490) explains the early limit: A date after the executions for treason on 30 Jan. 1606 is suggested, as in the case of Marston’s Fawn, by ii. 364, I have heard say, they will rise sooner, and goe with more deuotion to see an extraordinarie execution, then to heare a Sermon, and with this indication allusions to the Union (ii. 258) and [Dekker & Webster’s] Northward Ho! [1605] (ii. 397) and resemblances to the Fawn [1604–6; 1st ed. 1606; S. R. 12 Mar. 1606] are consistent. Kittredge (ed. 1936) is inclined to agree, as is Greg (1940, p. 377 n.): The resemblance is not very close, but I agree that it is fairly palpable. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974, p. 1249): This pushes King Lear back into 1605. Taylor (1982, p. 408): That parallel is not decisive, the direction of indebtedness being probably indeterminable, an opinion repeated by Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 128) and Wells (ed. 2000, p. 14 n.).

Brooke (1912, p. 62; cf. ed. 1947): If Sh. took the incident of the servant in 3.7, which is not in Sidney’s Arcadia, from the scene in a play his company had acted, A Yorkshire Tragedy (v.36 ff.; ed. T. Brooke, Shakespeare Apocrypha, p. 258), where a servant attempts to stop his master from stabbing his wife, then a terminus a quo for Lr. is summer 1605. The crimes upon which the play is based occurred April 23, 1605, and Calverley, the criminal, was executed on the fifth of the following August. During this interval at least two prose accounts of the atrocities were licensed in London. The uncertainty in which the play leaves us concerning Calverley’s precise fate…gives reason for the assumption that A Yorkshire Tragedy was written before the details of Calverley’s trial and execution had yet reached London. Sh.’s company is named on the title page of the 1608 quarto, but the play’s date of composition is inferential only; since it seems not indebted to the later of the two prose accounts, it is sometimes dated late summer of 1605 (Knutson, 1991, p. 209). In any case the analogy between the two episodes is not exact.

Chambers (1930, 1:469): Bradley…thought he saw signs of the influence of Lear on Marston’s Dutch Courtesan (1605). I cannot find any very plausible parallel except a bit (iii. 2. 44) about taking butter’d shrimps from horses, which recalls Lear, [1401–2]. It may be doubted that the jest is original in either play. Moreover, the Dutch Courtesan, although registered on 26 June 1605, probably goes back to 1603–4, the date now generally accepted. Following Muir (1957, p. 147), Fraser (ed. 1963, p. 192): John Marston, in The Malcontent (1604), dramatizes a feigned suicide (4.3) that seems to parallel Gloucester’s, at the Cliffs of Dover ([2480]). Other possible sources have been suggested, however: see nn. 2429, 2480.

Ashe (1950, pp. 508–11) suggests on the basis of a very few verbal similarities that a sonnet by William Strachey On Sejanus (published with Jonson’s play after that play’s second S. R. entry on 6 Aug. 1605) influenced Lr. and Tim. Though Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxiii f.) discusses the supposed similarities, which are tenuous, he rejects not only Ashe’s claims that Strachey’s sonnet influenced Lr. but also his further speculations that Strachey, a poet but no dramatist, collaborated with Jonson on Sejanus and with Shakespeare on Lr. and Tim. Instead Muir advances his own theory (p. xxiv): It would appear that Strachey, not Shakespeare, was the debtor; and this means that the storm-scenes of King Lear, and possibly the opening lines of Act IV, must have been written by 2 November 1604, when Sejanus was first registered, unless we assume that the sonnet could have been added to the copy for the play after it had been licensed.…Taken in conjunction with other evidence, the connection of the play with Strachey’s sonnet establishes the winter of 1604–5 as the most probable date. Muir gives not the slightest reason for his conclusion that Strachey was indebted to Lr. in 1604, and indeed the similarities are so commonplace as to make any influence in either direction unlikely. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974) allows that they may be accidental, and Wells (ed. 2000, p. 14 n.) thinks that even the most likely of them may be merely coincidental.

Fraser (ed. 1963, p. 192): The London Prodigal (1605), a play once attributed to Shakespeare and performed by his company, anticipates the rustic dialect affected by Edgar in his combat with Oswald (IV. vi). The King’s men are named on the title page of the 1605 quarto, and the play could have been written as early as 1603. But such rustic dialect occurs in many other plays and poems; see n. 2688–97.

Taylor (1982, pp. 396–413): Jonson, Chapman, and Marston’s Eastward Ho, a possible source for Lr., could not have been available until after April 1605, perhaps at a first performance in late July or August or when first in print no earlier than mid-September (p. 407). It is a (p. 397) very light and topical city comedy, but Taylor detects parallels of structure, subject matter, and verbal detail. See . While admitting that individually, these characters and dramatic relationships might be described as common, he asserts that their accumulation, their interaction at the level of plot and structure, and the recurring similarities of detail…are remarkable. They seem not remarkable to Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 108): The evidence is not convincing, though no doubt Shakespeare did read or see this play.

Taylor also argues, on the basis of a few fairly remote similarities, that George Wilkins’s The Miseries of Enforced Marriage is echoed in Lr. He dates the composition of that play after the entry of its source in the Stationers’ Register (12 June 1605) and, because of its obscenities, before the Act to Restrain Abuses of Players of 27 May 1606. That act governed playing, not composition, of course, and profanation of the Holy Name of God rather than obscenity, and quite possibly Wilkins, known for his sordid and criminal life, was not restrained by it. An additional difficulty is that the play may have been mounted by Sh.’s company after Lr. There were only a few weeks in 1606 (between 21 Apr. and ca. mid-June) when the plague would have allowed its performance (see above), and the title page of its 1607 quarto (S. R. 31 July 1607) says As it is now playd. Knutson (1991, p. 196) assigns it to the 1606–7 season; given the apparent absence of playing in fall 1606, the court performance of Lr. on 26 Dec. 1606 may have inaugurated that season.

The verbal and thematic echoes of Lr. discovered in Tourneur’s The Atheist’s Tragedy (1607–11) and his (or Middleton’s?) The Revenger’s Tragedy (1606–7) by Schücking (1916–17), Chambers (1923, 3:499), Ornstein (1960, p. 121), Ribner (ed. Atheist’s Tragedy, 1964, p. lxiv), and others are of no help in dating Lr., since those plays postdate the court performance of 26 Dec. 1606. The parallels with John Day’s Isle of Gulls (1606) suggested by Murphy (1984, pp. 135–52) seem not close enough to establish any clear relationship with Lr.

The importance of Dover in the play, and especially the description of Dover Cliff in 2446–59, has been attributed to the recent touring of Sh.’s company. Perhaps on a hint in Murray (1910, 2:264 n.), Harrison (ed. 1937) declares that the vivid description seems to be based on observation, perhaps during a visit of the King’s players to Dover in September 1606, and Pearson (1949, pp. 138, 141) similarly says that in the autumn of 1606 Sh. had been sufficiently impressed with what he saw [of Dover Cliff] to describe it in the play [4.6]. There has been some confusion about the date of that 1606 trip. Fripp (1938, pp. 654–5) dates the visit on 4 October 1606, citing Murray (1:183–4), but Murray dates payment Sept. 16–24, and Chambers (1923, 2:212) says the company was at Dover between 6 and 24 September. Authoritatively, Gibson (2002, p. 495) and Gurr (1996, p. 305), using REED documents, identify the day as 30 Aug. 1606. Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxiv) dates a visit on 4 Oct. 1605, citing no authority but perhaps misquoting Fripp; no visit on that day is listed by Murray or Chambers (1923, 2:212; 1930, 2:333), but Gibson (p. 602) and Gurr (p. 304), though not recording Dover, list a visit to neighboring Fordwich on 6 Oct. 1605, and Gibson (pp. 566, 723) records visits to Faversham and Maidstone in 1605–6. As Fripp and Muir note, however, Sh. could have formed his impressions of Dover in an earlier visit of Aug. 1597 with the Chamberlain’s Men. Murray 1:109 dates payment 3–20 Sept. 1597; like Gibson (p. 484), Davison (2000, pp. 58, 67) dates the Dover visit ca. 3 September 1597 (when payment was made), and says that Murray and Chambers conflate 1596 and 1597 visits to Faversham. Murray (1:109) lists only 1596. After July 23); Gurr (p. 303) lists Faversham ca. 1 Aug 1596, and Dover and Faversham 1596–7. Gibson (p. 562) lists payments at Faversham on 21 Feb. and about Lam[m]as (1 Aug.) of 1595–6. Despite confusions and incomplete records, it seems that Sh. could possibly have observed Dover cliff in 1596 and 1597, so that even if he traveled there in 1605 or 1606 (and we cannot know that he was traveling with the company on those occasions), those later visits might not have inspired his writing of Lr. 4.6; at best they might have refreshed old memories, and so can not help fix the date of the play.

The Act to Restrain Abuses of Players (27 May 1606), mentioned above, has also figured directly in attempts to date Lr. Fripp (1938, 2:656–7): Doubtless he would have preserved the [657] Christian background [of Leir]… were it not for the Act, forbidding the use of God, Jesus Christ, and Holy Ghost.… in Lear he is reduced to the feeble substitutes: Gods, Powers, Wills, Heaven and Heavens, Apollo, Jupiter, Goddess, Fortune, Juno, Justicers, Summoners, Stars, Fairies, anything he can lay hold of. The idea is entertained by a few followers—Pearson (1949, p. 140), Empson (1951, p. 155), Munro (ed. 1957, 6:891)—but most commentators seem content to attribute the pagan or neutral references to deity to the pre-Christian setting of the action; see nn. DP 3–4, 116–18.

div.head: Stylistic Evidence
div.p: Since the last half of the nineteenth century many scholars have studied the entirely internal evidence of the language of Sh.’s plays themselves—their vocabulary, linguistic features such as morphology and rhetoric, and their prosody—in an attempt to find chronological developments in the style of the plays that would help to establish their order of composition. At best such attempts may indicate a sequence of the plays, not particular dates for any one of them; at worst they may suggest, and have suggested, contradictory and even absurd chronologies. General surveys and assessments of stylometric dating may be found in Ekwall (1911), Chambers (1930, 1:253–69, 2:397–408), Reinhold (1942), Barroll (1965, pp. 116–19), and Wells & Taylor (1987). Those of Chambers and Barroll are critical, skeptical, and cautionary about the limits of such approaches; that by Wells & Taylor is the most optimistic about present progress and future possibilities. Besides the practical problems of defining and tabulating stylistic features are many further complications, often hard to recognize or assess, that may skew the data: Sh.’s apparent collaboration in some plays with authors having very different styles, the evident fact that a play’s genre and sources may affect the style, possible later revision of plays by the author or someone else, possible irregularities in the actual order of composition, and so on. The notion that the plays were written as a sequence of discrete entities is itself an unprovable assumption: authors may put aside a half-completed work and return to it months or years later, so that styles of different periods may overlap in the same work, or they may work concurrently on two or more plays, whose differences of style may therefore be very hard to distinguish and order in a sequence even though the plays were in fact ultimately completed at different times. Because of the uncertainty and inconclusiveness of many stylistic chronologies, especially the earlier pioneering studies, there is need here for only the briefest account of their results concerning Lr. Attempts since 1930 are treated a little more fully.

div.head: Vocabulary Links between Plays
div.p: Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 100) describe the theoretical basis: Vocabulary may indicate chronology, if a writer’s usage of certain words follows a predictable pattern. One might hypothesize, for instance, that proximity of composition generates similarity of vocabulary, so that works composed at about the same time will have more words in common than works composed at widely separated times. This hypothesis was tested, and confirmed, in the late nineteenth century…[and] has recently been tested, much more systematically. As with other stylometric tests, however, unforeseen complications may arise. For instance, if Sh. revisited an earlier work by re-reading it, or by vetting it for a revival, or in order to revise parts of it, his renewed acquaintance with earlier vocabulary might then cause some of it to reappear in later plays then being composed, thus complicating the evidence for clear chronological development.

Sarrazin (1898, pp. 119 ff.) studies the recurrence of words used twice in Sh. (dislegomena) and thrice (trislegomena) to see how they cluster in several plays, which are therefore assumed to be chronologically close to each other. Lear has most words in both groups in common with a middle group of plays, Ham.-Mac. Though Oth. belongs to this period, it gravitates towards the earlier one, while Mac. and Lr. incline to the last period, and Cor. and Ant. even more so. Sarrazin (pp. 138–9) finds only two words unique to Tim. and Lr. and only four common to them and one other play. Tim. is impossible to date exactly because of its multiple authorship, but (p. 168) The sequence—Lear—Macbeth—Coriolanus—Antony and Cleopatra—permits hardly a doubt (Ger.). The figures yield a somewhat inexact comparison because of the differing genres and lengths of the plays compared, and because some of the unusual words are editorial choices; for Lr. these include choices between Q and F readings (e.g., hot-blooded, oeillades, retinue, fetch, pother, tart, dearn, simular, mow, nonny, spherical, stell, sessa, plate, consummation, dialect, justicer, footed, century, prize, tamely). The counts may also be incomplete: Bradley (below) finds some fifteen additional words shared between Lr. and Oth.

Bradley (1904, pp. 441–3) lists twenty words and brief phrases in common with Oth. and no other plays. (P. 442): The fact that more than half of the above occur in the first two acts of King Lear may possibly be significant: for the farther removed Shakespeare was from the time of the com-[443]position of Othello, the less likely would be the recurrence of ideas or words in that play.

Conrad (1909, pp. 244–5) reports that of some two hundred parallels of thought and expression that he finds between Tim. and other plays, most are with Lr. and MM. Lr. has the most echoes in Mac., which has fewer from Tim. and MM. Tim., he concludes, was therefore apparently written before Lr. and in the same year as MM, and presumably Mac. came after Lr. He gives no particulars as evidence.

Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxv): There are fewer verbal echoes of Measure for Measure [than of Oth.] in King Lear, but we may notice the phrase furred gown which appears in both plays [2608, MM 3.2.7 (1497); nowhere else in Sh.], unaccommodated [1886–7; nowhere else in Sh.] which is linked with accommodations [MM 3.1.14 (1217) and only Oth. 1.3.238 (586)], warped used only in these plays [Q 2014+27, MM 3.1.141 (1363)] and in All’s Well that Ends Well [5.3.49 (2755)] [also TNK and several exx. of warp in AYL, MM, WT], and evasion used only in these plays and in Troilus and Cressida [455, MM 1.1.50 (58), Tro. 2.1.69 (923), 2.2.67 (1052), 2.3.114 (1319)]. The figures would seem to indicate that Lr. was written closer to Oth. than to MM.

Slater (1978, p. 148), tabulating recurrences of rare words throughout the canon, finds that Tim. has significantly higher-than-chance links through such words with Ham., Tro., AWW, Lr., and Cor., and that Lr. has them with TN, Ham., Tim., Ant., and Cym. (p. 149): Though there are statistically significant degrees of linking [of Tim.] with Hamlet, Troilus, All’s Well and Coriolanus, they are far from reaching the magnitude of the Lear association.…Timon has a significant degree of linkage with three earlier plays, Hamlet, Troilus and All’s Well, and with one later play, Coriolanus. Lear on the other hand has significant linkages with two earlier plays, Twelfth Night and Hamlet, and with two later plays, Macbeth and Cymbeline. This suggests that Timon is more probably the earlier rather than the later play. In any case, if Timon came after Lear, it would be surprising to find that it did not have a significant excess of links with Macbeth, when Lear did.…We conclude that Timon was written at about the same time as Lear.

Brainerd (1980, p. 228), comparing the relative frequency in the plays of twenty lemmas (representing root words and their several forms) that vary numerically in relation to what is known of the plays’ chronology, and using the most sophisticated statistical method so far applied to such data, arrives at a dating of Lr. in 1606, a year later than its assumed date of 1605. Since the text used is the F-based Riverside text of 1974, the figures may reflect later F changes from the original vocabulary found in Q.

Salingar (1983, p. 165) notes the unusually close associations of themes, images, and vocabulary between Lr. 1.4 and Timon’s curses in Tim. 4.3, esp. the sequence in 176–92, of nature, man’s unkindness, womb, teems, arrogant man, eyeless venom’d worm, abhorred births, one poor root, fertile, ingrateful man, dragons wolves and bears, new monsters, and marbled mansion of heaven. [See also self-same mettle, found only in Tim. 1799 and Lr. 74 Q; it is selfe-mettle in F.]

Taylor (1983, pp. 388–90; cf. Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 128), using the data amassed by Eliot Slater (U. of London diss., 1981) to show that Sh.’s rarer vocabulary has a statistically significant correlation with the accepted chronology of the plays, concludes: The vocabulary of the entire Quarto text tends to confirm a date of original composition between Othello and Macbeth, either just before or just after Timon of Athens. On the other hand, the vocabulary unique to the Folio would appear to have been written later than Q, [389] or by another writer. On F’s vocabulary see .

div.head: Linguistic Features
div.p: Waller (1966, pp. 4–7) shows Sh. moving gradually towards more informal, colloquial usages—towards does rather than doth, has for hath, and the contractions i’th’, o’th’, th’, ’t, ’s [from is, us, and his], and ’ll. Waller does not date or order the plays. The figures for each of the features that he enumerates indicate different sequences for the plays from Ham. to Cor.; when these are averaged out—excluding the sequence for ’ll, where no regular progression is evident from the figures, and excluding all data from MM, which is based on a transcript by Ralph Crane and reflects many of his linguistic habits—the resulting sequence places Lr. after Oth. and AWW and before Tim. and Mac.

Ranson (1977, p. 14): E. B. Everitt’s tabulation of the increasing relative frequency of fourteen spelling contractions (has [for hath], ha’s, i’th, o’th, to’th, by’th, th’, -’t, ’s, a’/o’, ’a, ha’, have, ’em) places Lr. after Oth., TN, and Ham. and before AWW and Ant.

Taylor (1989, p. 121): The increasing use in verse of some twenty contractions and colloquial or poetic forms after 1600 places Lr. (Q) after AWW and Oth., before Mac. and Ant., and at about the same time as the Shn. portion of Tim. (Folio Lr. is not considered.) A note on p. 129 says of the essay Canon and Chronology in Wells & Taylor (1987), Though published earlier, that article contains a revised version of the evidence presented here. There (1987, p. 105) a tabulation of twenty-six such colloquialisms places Lr. (Q) after MM and Tim., close after AWW, and before Oth. and Mac., a placement which is (p. 106) one of some obvious anomalies…for which we have as yet no explanation. A chart on p. 99 places Lr. (QF, meaning apparently a conventional critical text based on F, with Q additions) anomalously earlier, just after Ham. and MM and before Oth., AWW, and Tim. The differences may reflect (in part) a scribe’s or a non-Shn. reviser’s intervention in the F text.

div.head: Verse Tests
div.p: Malone (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 1:[280–1]): Though the gradual disappearance of rhyme among blank verse from early to late Shn. plays might be evidence useful in determining the dates of plays, it is but a fallible criterion.

Bathurst (1857, pp. 2–3): There is a progressive increase over Sh.’s career of interrupted verse (enjambement), due to his making the verse end upon a perfectly weak monosyllable—such as if or and. This is capable of happening, where the first verse is in itself unbroken (end-stopped). Bathurst does not use this feature to establish a chronology.

Fleay’s (1874, p. 10) dating of Lr. in 1605 seems not clearly to be based on his tables of numbers of lines of rhymed and blank verse; he locates Oth. and Lr. after Mac., Cym., and Ham. and before (parts of) Per., Tim., and Cor. Using Fleay’s figures to compute the ratios for rhymed and blank verse in each play, Furnivall (1874, p. 33) and Matthew (1874, p. 312) locate Lr. after MV, MM, and Cym. and before Ham. and Oth. Fleay’s revised tables (1874, p. 38; 1874, p. 345), which discount rhyme in the context of a prose scene, make Lr. contemporaneous with Ham. and Oth. In 1876 (p. 130), 1881 (p. 120), and 1886 (pp. 237–8) he dates Lr. in 1605.

Ingram (1874, pp. 442–64) studies the progressively increasing use of enjambement made possible by lines with light endings (words on which the voice can to a certain small extent dwell, such as am, are, be, can, does, has, I, they, etc.) and weak endings (words which force the reader to run them, in pronunciation no less than in sense, into the closest connection with the opening words of the succeeding line (p. 447) such as and, for, from, if, in, or. Both are used so sparingly before Ant. that they are of no help in dating Lr. or any of the previous three-fourths of his works.
Hertzberg (1878, p. 252): The gradual decrease of alexandrines in the plays places Lr. after Oth. and Ant. and before Cor. and Tmp.
Pulling (1879, p. 458), counting speeches ending within the line in twenty plays, places Lr. after Oth., Ham., and MM and before AWW, Mac., and Cor., admitting that Oth. must be out of place.

G. König’s (1888, pp. 131–8) metrical tables give varied results: the percentage of rhyme groups Lr. with R3 and 3H6; the percentage of unaccented line endings groups it with Cor. and AWW; the percentage of overflows (enjambements) puts it after Tro. and AWW and before Tim. and Mac.; and the percentage of speeches ending within the line puts it after MM and Ham., before Tim. and H8.
Heuser (1894, p. 245), on the basis of the percentage of rhymed couplets in Lr., puts it after Wiv. and Oth. and before 1H4 and H5.

Bradley (1904, pp. 473–80) reviews the extant verse tests, making independent counts of his own. He is suspicious of those for Timon because he does not believe that Sh. wrote all of the play. He verifies the results of König’s speech-ending test (though with different percentages); finds that his overflows put Tim. just after Mac.; and decides that Ingram’s weak endings show nothing, but that his light endings yield the order Oth., Lr., Ham., Tim., Mac.

Chambers (1930, 1:273–4, 468): The time-relation of King Lear and Macbeth is not very clear. The verse-tests, as shown by Dr. Bradley, confirm the priority I have given to King Lear, but I cannot put much confidence in their application to a play like Macbeth, which can hardly be in its original form. Nor am I at all clear about the dating of Timon of Athens. This Dr. Bradley would place between King Lear and Macbeth, partly because of the resemblance of its temper to that of King Lear, and partly again on metrical grounds. But an unfinished play is even less likely than an abridged [274] play to answer to the metrical tests, and it would be hard to find room for Timon of Athens in the already rather full year 1605–6. I agree as to the temper.…[468] Bradley has argued strongly for [Lr.’s] priority to Macbeth on the basis of metrical tests,…although I doubt whether much reliance can be placed upon them in determining the sequence of contiguous plays.

Gray (1931, p. 148), averaging together the percentages of double endings, run-on lines, and speeches ending within the line, to get a truer sequence of plays than any single test would yield, places Lr. after Oth., Ham., MM, and Per. and before Tim., AWW, and Mac.

Langworthy (1931, p. 748), in a variation on the line-ending method that studies the gradually diminishing parallelism between the verse line and certain syntactic units—independent clauses, non-restrictive dependent clauses, and line-length phrases—places Lr. after Ham., MM, and Tim., and before Per. (Sh.’s portion), AWW, and Mac. A weakness of this study is that the stylistic analysis is based on a modernized (Oxford, 1925–7) text.

Reinhold (1942, pp. 88–9), according to the percentage of verse lines split between two or more speakers, places Lr. (with Tim.) after Oth., Ham., and MM and before AWW, Mac., and Ant. He notes that AWW appears remarkably late in the sequence, and he distrusts the percentage that would make Tim. contemporary with Lr. because of the suspicion of multiple authorship.

Yardi (1946, pp. 266, 268), submitting to more rigorous statistical analysis than previously the admittedly rough and inaccurate counts of variations in stress and pause made by Chambers and Fleay, places Lr. after AWW, MM, and Oth. and before Ant., Mac., and Cor. As for Tim., it belongs in 1605–6 and may have preceded Lr.

Wentersdorf (1951, pp. 161–93), averaging together (pp. 183–7) percentages for extra syllables, overflows (lines in which the sense is run on without a syntactical pause into the next; sometimes called run-on lines, and adding the figures for light and weak endings), lines split between two or more speakers, and sense-pauses within unsplit lines, and then further segregating the history plays because he thinks their deliberate, slower composition from chronicle sources resulted in more formal verse, groups Lr. (p. 165) after Oth., AWW, and Tim., whose almost identical figures seem to group them in 1604–5, and just before Mac. in 1605–6 and before Ant. in 1606–7.

Oras (1960, pp. 68, 75, 80) tabulates the gradual chronological decrease in the plays of three types of midline pauses in verse: those marked by light or no punctuation (Type A), by heavy punctuation (B), and by a shift to a new speaker (C, split lines). The figures for all three types place Lr. after Oth., roughly contemporary with Tim., and before Mac. and Ant. (the anomalously low figures for AWW in all three categories would place it after Lr. and even Mac.).

Fitch (1981, pp. 298–9) points out a weakness in Oras’s and Chambers’s sense-pause tests: This procedure makes the quite erroneous assumption that the overall frequency of sense pauses (whether within the line or at line-end) remains constant from play to play. In fact the frequency varies considerably.…Clearly, where the frequency of sense-pauses is greater, there is more opportunity for mid-line pauses to occur. A further objection to Chambers’ method is that it makes no distinction between lines containing one sense pause and those containing two or more. The only satisfactory method, therefore, is to express the number of sense-pauses occurring within the line as a percentage of the total sense-pauses for the play. Fitch makes adjustments for several plays, but not for Lr.

div.head: Shakespeare’s Development
div.p: Hurdis (1792, pp. 45–6), assuming Sh.’s steady improvement in correctness of versification and style, weight of sentiment, and discrimination of character, locates Lr. as one of the last three plays, coming just after Mac. (1606) and before JC and Ham. Except for this wildly wrong impressionistic guess, Lr. is almost always grouped with the other Jacobean tragedies and problem plays. There are two other exceptions. Discovering traces of older Blank Verse in Act 1 and juvenile use of horror in the blinding of Gloucester, Mathew (1922, pp. 250–1) theorizes that Lr. is a combination and rewriting of an early Lear and an imagined Tragedy of Gloucester, and that this revision may have been Henslowe’s Leare of 1594. Somewhat differently, Cairncross (1936, pp. 157 ff.), on the basis of a few verbal parallels between Leir and Lr. (and other works), speculates that Lr. was written early in Sh.’s career, ca. 1591 (p. 182), and that Leir, a later play, drew on it. Though the supposed parallels do not indicate which play was prior, and could derive from the other sources of the Lear story, Cairncross repeats the theory forty years later (see Marder, 1974, pp. 24–5), now dating Lr. in 1590. It is picked up and developed still further by Everitt (1954, pp. 60 ff.), who expresses (p. 173) the belief, purely conjectural and unfortified by specific allusion, that an earlier, pre-1594 version of Leir existed, that it was Sh.’s work, and (p. 174) that it came before Ironside, Troublesome Reign, and 1 and 2 Tamburlaine, in (p. 172) 1587. The notion that Leir is early Sh. is entertained also by Alexander (1964, pp. 170–1, 230–1) and Schamps (Nov. 1974, p. 33).

Dowden (1877, pp. 48, 54): Four periods [of Sh.’s artistic life] may be designated with reference to the class of works written in each, or with reference to the subjects of those works, or with reference to the kind of versification which was characteristic of each period, or with reference to Shakspere’s supposed condition and state of mind in each.…I will call the first period, In the workshop; the second, In the world; the third, Out of the depths; the fourth, On the heights.…[54] Now [in the third period] passion and crime form the subjects of tragedy, instead of error or the cruelty of fate. The bonds of life are broken: in Othello, the bonds which unite husband and wife; in Lear, the bonds which unite parent and child; in Macbeth, the bonds of kinship and of the loyalty of the subject; Antony, through voluptuous self-indulgence, dissolves the bonds which bind him to his country, and ceases to be a Roman; Coriolanus, through passionate haughtiness, also turns away from Rome, and even tries to crush the loyalties and affections which make him man—tries to lift himself into proud isolation; lastly, Timon actually severs himself, not from his country merely, but from humanity itself.…This group of plays we name…Later Tragedy.

Bradley (1904, pp. 244–6): [Lr.] is allied with two tragedies, Othello and Timon of Athens.…These are the most painful and the most pathetic of the four tragedies, those in which evil appears in its coldest [245] and most inhuman forms, and those which exclude the supernatural from the action. But there is also in King Lear a good deal which sounds like an echo of Othello.…Edmund, though of course essentially distinguished from Iago, often reminds us of him, and the soliloquy, This is the excellent foppery of the world, is in the very tone of Iago’s discourse on the sovereignty of the will. The gulling of Gloster, again, recalls the gulling of Othello. Even Edmund’s idea (not carried out) of making his father witness, without over-hearing, his conversation with Edgar, reproduces the idea of the passage where Othello watches Iago and Cassio talking about Bianca; and the conclusion of the temptation, where Gloster says to Edmund: and of my land…capable [1021–3], reminds of us Othello’s last words in the scene of temptation, Now art thou my lieutenant.…Both plays [Lr. and Tim.] deal with the tragic effects of ingratitude. In both the victim is exceptionally unsuspicious, soft-hearted, and vehement. In both he is completely overwhelmed, passing through fury to madness in one case, to suicide in the other. Famous passages in both plays are curses.…In both plays occur repeated comparisons between man and the beasts;…and the idea that this bestial degradation will end in a furious struggle of all with all, in which the race will perish. The pessimistic strain in Timon suggests to many readers…the notion that Shakespeare was giving vent to some personal feeling, whether present or past.…It is…likely to have been composed immediately after King Lear and before Macbeth. Bradley points out (passim) particular similarities (pp. 310–11 n.): There is a fool in Tim. whose talk sometimes reminds one of Lear’s fool; and Kent’s remark, This is not altogether fool, my lord [669+8] is repeated in Tim. 2.2.122 (782) Thou are not altogether a fool; (p. 327) Lr. 2201 our means secure us is like Tim. 4.3.77–8 (1685–6) (though not closely similar); (pp. 443–4) both plays contain invective about sexual vice (It almost looks as if Shakespeare were expressing feelings which oppressed him at this period of his life—i.e., in 1602–5, in Ham., MM, Tro., AWW, Oth.), as well as references to lower animals; and there are likenesses in word and phrase (e.g., Lr. 1457, cõfort & not burne, and Tim. 2361, Sunne that comforts burne) and in versification.

Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxv–vi): Themes dealt with in Measure for Measure recur in King Lear: the truancy of the Duke may be compared with Lear’s abdication from responsibility; the debate on justice and authority which runs all through Measure for Measure reappears in the mad scenes of King Lear; the idea of the oddest frame of sense [MM 5.1.61 (2418)] in madness is repeated in the reason in madness [2617] of the King; the Duke’s advice to Claudio in prison and his later comfort to Isabella—[quoting MM 5.1.397–8 (2783–4)]—look forward to several of Edgar’s speeches [apparently 2181 ff., 2207–8]; and his words [quoting 3147–9] recall Claudio’s fight for life. The sentence Keep me in patience occurs in both plays [not in Lr.; cf. giue me that patience, 1571; MM 5.1.116 (2485)]; and the next words in Measure for Measure—[quotes 5.1.116–18 (2485–7)]—[xxvi] seem to be echoed in two passages in King Lear—[quoting 306, 2728] and Isabella’s lines about Angelo—[quoting MM 3.1.92–3 (1307–8)]—have been used by Dr. Edith Sitwell as a commentary on Edgar’s words: Nero…darkness [2004].

Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxvi): There are many resemblances between King Lear and Timon of Athens. The theme of ingratitude is prominent in both; both have many references to the lower animals; both stress the natural goodness of the poor in contrast to the viciousness of the rich; and their versification is similar.…[He cites also Bradley’s similarities.] These links with other plays suggest that King Lear may well have been written soon after Measure for Measure and Othello, and not long before Timon of Athens.

Dowden’s name for the period of tragedies and problem comedies, Out of the depths, is derived from the opening line of Psa. 130, a supplication for hope and redemption. Whether the depths were Sh.’s own, or those of his period, or entirely imaginary, has received much comment.

Furnivall (1874, pp. xxxix f.), who had read Dowden’s 1875 book (Shakspere:…Mind and Art) in MS: Undoubtedly at this time a shadow of darkness fell upon Shakspere. What causes brought it, we cannot certainly tell. Private reasons the Sonnets show. He was deserted by his mistress—wrongly but madly lovd by him, in spite of the struggles of his better nature—for his dearest friend; and this for a time severd their friendship, never to be restord again as it first was. Public reasons there were: his great patron and friend Southampton was declard traitor and imprisond in 1601; was threatend with death, and in almost [xl] daily danger of it till Elizabeth’s own death in 1603 set him free through King James: the rebellion and execution of Essex, Southampton’s friend and the cause of his ruin, to whom Shakspere had two years before alluded with pride in his Prologue to Henry V., Act v. l. 30. At any rate, the times were out of joint. Shakspere was stirrd to his inmost depths, and gave forth the grandest series of Tragedies that the world has ever seen: [Ham., the tragicomedy MM, JC, Oth., Mac., Lr., Tro., Ant., Cor., Tim.]; showing what subjects were then kind to his frame of mind; how he felt, and struggld with, the stern realities of life; how he dwelt on the weakness and baseness of men, their treachery as friends and subjects, their lawless lust and ungovernd jealousy as lovers, their serpent-like ingratitude as children, their fickleness and disgustfulness as the many-headed mob, fit only to be spit upon and curst: over all he held the terrors of conscience and the avenging sword of fate.…[xliii] Now all that I have written on the succession of Shakspere’s works in relation to the man Shakspere is liable to the objector’s Pooh! all stuff! Shakspere wrote comedies and tragedies for his company just as the Burbages told him to. His comedies were produc’d for some leading comic actor, and his tragedies for his friend and partner Richard Burbage, the great tragedian. Neither reflected his own feelings, except professionally, any more than Macbeth’s or Othello’s did Burbage’s when he acted them. Take it so, if you will; but still, I say, do follow the course of Shakspere’s mind…and then ask yourself whether the choice of Shakspere’s series of subjects was fixt by others’ orders, or chance, or by his own frame of mind, his own mood.

Chambers (1930, 1:85–6): The temper of Hamlet and Troilus and Cressida leads up, naturally enough, to the long unrolling of the Jacobean tragedies. These are not without evidence of mental strain [86] and sometimes exhaustion. Shakespeare’s spirit must have been nearly submerged in Lear, and although the wave passed, and he rose to his height of poetic expression in Antony and Cleopatra, I think that he went under in the unfinished Timon of Athens. The chronology of the plays becomes difficult at this point, and it is therefore frankly a conjecture that an attempt at Timon of Athens early in 1608 was followed by a serious illness, which may have been a nervous breakdown, and on the other hand may have been merely the plague. Later (1:274) Chambers concedes that this imagined mental disturbance and breakdown of Sh. may very likely only be a whimsy of my own. Wentersdorf (1951, p. 181), however: K L was clearly written in a state of abnormal stress.

Parrott (1934, p. 54): The gloom that seems to have settled over Shakespeare’s mind in the last days of Elizabeth’s reign…deepens as he goes on to write Othello, Lear, and Macbeth. The change of tone and temper in his work has been explained by the changing dramatic fashion of the time, shifting from romantic comedy and the chronicle play to realistic satiric comedy and tragedy; but this is hardly a sufficient cause. His change of theme may have been due in part to his unceasing desire to explore new realms of art; a deeper cause, no doubt, was his growing realization of the powers of evil that lay beneath the brilliant surface of Renaissance culture and that were to show themselves in abhorrent forms during the reign of the first Stuart king. Similarly Harrison (1935, p. 896) imagines a general gloom in England caused by the death of Queen Elizabeth, anxiety over the succession, plague in 1603, dissatisfaction with the new king, debauchery and corruption at court, the Gunpowder Plot, the eclipses, etc. On the contrary, Neilson & Thorndike (1913, pp. 85–6): From all we know of his personal life, the years of King Lear and Othello were years of abounding prosperity. The lachrimae rerum that touch the mind in these stupendous tragedies are the outcome of profound meditation and vivid imagination, not the accompaniment of a cry of instant pain.…[86] The change in type of play perceptible from period to period is more safely to be explained by changes of theatrical fashion and public taste than by conjectures as to the inner life of the dramatist. Recent studies such as those of Knutson (1991) and Kernan (1995) have emphasized Sh.’s conscious choice of genre and themes to suit the desires of his company and audience and the particular interests of king and court.

Chambers (1930, 1:269), on the basis of a statement in Dr. John Ward’s Diary (1661–3)—I have heard yt Mr. Shakespeare…supplied ye stage with 2 plays every year (quoted by Chambers, 2:249)—notes that the plays in his chronology are partly arranged to provide a fairly even flow of production when plague and other inhibitions did not interrupt it. Though he goes on, [I] do not treat literally Ward’s statement that he supplied his company with two plays a year, Chambers does assign two plays to twelve of twenty-three seasons. The problem of doing so is complicated for 1605–6 by both a large number of Shn. plays and by frequent closings of the theater; the latter resulted in provincial tours, which would not be convenient occasions to prepare and mount new plays. The theaters had been closed for most of 1603, and did not open again until 9 Apr. 1604. They closed again on 5 Oct. 1605, until 15 Dec., and again from late June or July 1606 until the end of that year. The company was sporadically on tour during the spring and fall of 1603, the first half of 1604, the fall of 1605, and the second half of 1606, being supported otherwise by numerous appearances before the court at Whitehall, Hampton Court, Greenwich, and elsewhere. Barroll (1991, p. 176): The [plague] scene directs the observer to imagine clusters of Shake-[177]speare plays emerging in brief periods of intense productivity: a two-year hiatus, then Othello and Measure for Measure [and AWW?] in 1604, sixteen to twenty-two months of further hiatus, then Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, and King Lear [and Tim.?] by the end of 1606.

Paul (1950, pp. 139, 398): The sharing of rare words (aroint, germins), allusions to the Gunpowder Plot of Nov. 1605 and the hurricanes of March 1606, and the catalogues of dogs in both plays, lead to the conclusion that Lear…was written at the same time as Macbeth, but not finished and performed until more than four months after Macbeth had been given before the king [in Aug. 1606].
Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxiii): There is not much doubt that Macbeth was written by the summer of 1606; and if King Lear has to be dated early in 1606, Shakespeare must have been working overtime.

Taylor (1982, pp. 412–13): One must also take into account the probable date of Macbeth, which most scholars would regard as having been completed by the summer of [413] 1606. [Fn.: Barroll [1965]…gives convincing evidence for dating the first performance of Antony no later than 27 Feb. 1607, and probably by Dec. 1606. This would mean that, unless Antony preceded Lear, Lear itself must have been finished by the first half of 1606 (and the later in 1606 one presumes, the more implausible it becomes that Macbeth was completed before 1607).] I therefore incline to believe that the original composition of Lear was finished by some time in December 1605 or January 1606, too late to be offered at Court for Christmas of 1605. Certainly, the number of links [which Taylor urges; see above] between Eastward Ho, The Miseries of Enforced Marriage, and Lear now makes [i.e., would make] any date before autumn of 1605 most implausible, while the conjunction of influences dating from May to October 1605 suggests that composition began before Christmas of that year. Idem (1983, p. 354): I will assume that Shakespeare completed his first version of Lear sometime between October 1605 and February 1606.

Sh. may have spent part if not all of each summer at Stratford, and was there for a major business transaction on 24 July 1605 when he purchased the lease of some Stratford tithes (Chambers, 1930, 1:85, 2:118–27). If he was not touring with other members of his company when the theaters were closed in the first half of 1604, the fall of 1605, and the second half of 1606, and was at Stratford during part or all of the summers of 1605 and 1606, he may have had more time than usual to write without the other distractions of co-directing a theatrical company. He could still have been revising his final draft of Lr. (and finishing Mac. and starting Ant.) well into 1606.

head.title: The History of the Kings of Britain

div.p: The ultimate written source of all versions of the story of King Lear, as well as of the stories of King Arthur and Merlin, is the Historia regum Britanniae, written ca. 1135–8 by Geoffrey of Monmouth, Bishop of St. Asaph (1100?–1155), and extant in more than two hundred manuscripts. Geoffrey, from Monmouth in southeastern Wales and probably of Welsh or Breton ancestry, lived much of his life at Oxford, where he wrote in Latin prose his British History (as it is sometimes called), presumably in order to win recognition from the Anglo-Norman nobility and to gain advancement in the church. His claim that he was simply translating an old Welsh or Breton book, britannici sermonis, brought from Wales or Brittany and lent to him by his friend Walter, archdeacon of Oxford, is generally dismissed as a fiction; he seems instead to have drawn on Latin chronicles and literature, Welsh and Breton legends and folklore, and his own imagination. In 1155 the Norman cleric Wace translated the History into French verse as the Roman de Brut, which in turn was translated into Middle English verse as Roman de Brut (ca. 1190) by the English priest Layamon. Geoffrey’s History was widely disseminated in England and on the continent; 215 surviving MSS in Latin and Welsh are described in A Summary Catalogue by Julia C. Crick (1989). Latin editions were published in Paris in 1508 and 1517 and in Heidelberg in 1587. Perrett (1904) traces Geoffrey’s influence in some 55 versions of the Lear story up to Sh.’s. The standard scholarly edition of Geoffrey has long been that of Griscom & Jones (1929); versions from various Latin and Welsh MSS have also been edited by J. A. Giles (1844), San Marte [Albert Schulz] (1854), Jacob Hammer (1951), and Neil Wright (1985). The first translation into English is that of Aaron Thompson of Queen’s College, published posthumously in 1718; it was revised by J. A. Giles (Bohn, 1842) and reissued by J. C. Vaughan (Arlington, Tex., 1975). Other English translations are by Sebastian Evans (Temple, 1904; Everyman, 1911; rev. Charles W. Dunn, 1963), Robert Ellis Jones (in Griscom, 1929), and Lewis Thorpe (Penguin, 1966). Excerpts (in English translation) have been reprinted in Eccles (ed. 1792, pp. 469–70), Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xxxvi–xli), Satin (1966, pp. 448–55), and Bullough (1973, pp. 311–16). Because Sh.’s direct knowledge of Geoffrey is questionable (see below), most editors of Lr. do not provide excerpts as possible sources.

Lee, ed. Leir (1909, pp. xxiv f.): According to Geoffrey, whose work is a massive monument of stubborn credulity, Britain owed its name and the birth of its civilisation to one Brute, an imaginary grandson of Aeneas of Troy, who settled with a band of followers in the island more than 2000 years before the Christian era. Brute is credited with founding London under the name of Troia Nova or Troynovant, and with begetting a long line of English Kings. His son Locrine was followed in the eighth generation by Lear (son of Bladud), on whose career Geoffrey grafted the folk-tale of the three daughters [a variant of Cinderella or Love like Salt]. Lear’s royal progeny is carried by Geoffrey through six or seven further generations until its extinction amid the fatal strife of King Gorboduc’s sons, Ferrex and Porrex. With the deaths of these fierce warriors, a new dynasty of the same Trojan strain was inaugurated by Malmutius Donwallow, son of Cloten, Duke of Cornwall, a lawgiver after the pattern of Numa Pompilius of Rome. Malmutius’s descendants supplied the throne of Britain with brave occupants for ten or more centuries. His line, which included King Lud, the renovator of London, survived the Roman occupation and became feudatory to the Roman Empire. Cymbeline, who was reckoned to be coeval with the opening of the Christian era, was Donwallow’s distant [xxv] heir. Only with the invasion of the Jutes under Hengist and Horsa, and the ending of the British dynasty on the passing away of King Arthur, did the dominion initiated by Brute and his Trojan companions pass altogether to another race. To Geoffrey’s story of the ancient and long-lived dynasty, Shakespeare owed more or less directly two of his heroes—Cymbeline as well as Lear.…[xxvi, n.] During Henry VIII’s reign Polydore Vergil denied the existence of Brute and his family, and denounced as credulous invention the whole pedigree of British Kings. George Buchanan was among his disciples, and later Camden and Speed, though Richard Harvey strenuously defended the authenticity of the story of Lear and his ancestry in Philadelphus, or a Defence of Brutes, and the Brutans History (1593). Drayton, and afterwards Milton, doubted the historicity but defended poetic use of the stories. Ribner (1956, pp. 48–9): Despite a few doubters like Polydore Vergil and Edmund Bolton, We cannot doubt that the great majority of Elizabethans [49] accepted implicity the authenticity of Geoffrey’s tales. Historians defended and incorporated them, and the Tudors found it very convenient to claim direct descent from King Arthur.

Excerpts from Geoffrey’s History concerning the life of Leir, the tenth British king, are here reprinted from the English translation closest in time to Sh., that of Aaron Thompson, made in the late 17th c. and published posthumously in 1718. The typography of that edition is reproduced save that long s is printed s, and the prose is relined. Bracketed page numbers in italics are inserted at the beginning of each page, and passages referred to in the commentary notes are preceded by bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes, inserted into the text.

body.head: [From The British History, tr. Aaron Thompson, 1718.]

div.head: [50] Book II. Chap. XI. Leir, the Son of Bladud, having no Son, divides his Kingdom among his Daughters.
div.p: After this unhappy Fate of Bladud, [DP 2] Leir his Son was advanced to the Throne, and nobly governed his Country sixty Years. He built upon the River Sore a City called in the British Tongue Kaerleir, in the Saxon Leircestre. He was without Male Issue, but had three Daughters whose Names were [DP 15, 16, 17] Gonorilla, Regau, and Cordeilla, of whom he was doatingly fond, but [tln 131] especially of his youngest Cordeilla. When he began to grow old, he had Thoughts of dividing his Kingdom among them, and of bestowing them on such Husbands, as were fit to be advanced to the Government with them. But [tln 53–8] to make Tryal who was the worthiest of the best Part of his Kingdom, he went to each of them to ask, which of [51] them loved him most. The Question being proposed, Gonorilla the Eldest made Answer, That she called Heaven to Witness, she loved him more than her own Soul. The Father reply’d, Since you have preferred my declining Age before your own Life, I will marry you, my dearest Daughter, to whomsoever you shall make Choice of, and give with you the third Part of my Kingdom. Then Regau, the second Daughter, willing after the Example of her Sister, to prevail upon her Fathers good Nature, answered with an Oath, That she could not otherwise express her Thoughts, but that she loved him [tln 80–1] above all Creatures. The [tln 499] credulous Father upon this made her the same Promise that he did to her elder Sister, that is, the Choice of a Husband, with the third Part of his Kingdom. But Cordeilla the youngest, understanding how easily he was satisfied with the flattering Expressions of her Sisters, was desirous to make Tryal of his Affection after a different Manner. My Father, said she, Is there any Daughter that can love her Father more than Duty requires? In my Opinion, whoever pretends to it, must disguise her real Sentiments under the Veil of Flattery. I have always loved you as a Father, nor do I yet depart from my purposed Duty; and if you insist to have something more extorted from me, [52] hear now the Greatness of my Affection, which I always bear you, and take this for a short Answer to all your Questions; Look how much you have, so much is your Value, and so much I love you. The Father supposing that she spoke this out of the Abundance of her Heart, was highly provoked, and immediately reply’d; Since you have so far despised my Old-age, as not to think me worthy the Love that your Sisters express for me, you shall have from me the like Regard, and shall be excluded from any Share with your Sisters in my Kingdom. Notwithstanding I do not say but that since you are my Daughter, I will marry you to some Foreigner, if Fortune offers you any such Husband; but will never, I do assure you, make it my Business to procure so honourable a Match for you as for your Sisters; because though I have hitherto loved you more than them, you have in Requital thought me less worthy your Affection than they. And without farther Delay, after [tln 6] Consultation with his Nobility, he bestowed his two other Daughters upon the [DP 5] Dukes of Cornwal and Albania, with half the Island at present, but after his Death, the Inheritance of the whole Monarchy of Britain.

It happened after this, that [DP 3–4] Aganippus King of the Franks, having heard of the [53] Fame of Cordeilla’s Beauty, forthwith sent his Ambassadors to the King to desire Cordeilla in Marriage. The Father retaining yet his Anger to her, made Answer; That he was very willing to bestow his Daughter, but without either Money or Territories; because he had already given away his Kingdom with all his Treasure, to his elder Daughters, Gonorilla and Regau. When this was told Aganippus, he being very much in Love with the Lady, sent again to King Leir, to tell him, That he had Money and Territories enough, as he possessed the third Part of Gaul, and desired no more than his Daughter only, that he might have Heirs by her. At last the Match was concluded, and Cordeilla was sent to Gaul, and married to Aganippus.

div.head: CHAP. XII. Leir finding the Ingratitude of his two eldest Daughters, betakes himself to his youngest Cordeilla in Gaul.
div.p: A Long Time after this, when Leir came to be infirm through Old-age, [tln 45–50] the two Dukes, upon whom he had bestowed Britain with his two Daughters, made an [54] Insurrection against him, and deprived him of his Kingdom, and of all Regal Authority which he had hitherto exercised with great Power and Glory. But at last they came to an Agreement, and [DP 6] Maglaunus Duke of Albania, one of his Sons-in-Law, was to allow him and sixty Soldiers, who were to be kept for State, a Subsistence at his own House. After two Years Stay with his Son-in-Law, his Daughter Gonorilla grudged at the Number of his Men, who began to upbraid the Ministers of the Court with their scanty Allowance; and having spoke to her Husband about it, gave Orders that [tln 810] the Number of her Fathers Attendants be reduced to thirty, and the rest discharged. The Father resenting this Treatment, left Maglaunus, and went to [DP 5] Henuinus, Duke of Cornwal, to whom he had married his Daughter Regau. Here he met with an honourable Reception, but before the Year was at an End, a Quarrel happened between the two Families, which raised Regau’s Indignation; so that she commanded her Father to discharge all his Attendants but five, and to be contented with their Service. This second Affliction was unsupportable to him, and made him return again to his former Daughter, with Hopes that the Misery of his Condition might move in her some Sentiments of Filial Piety, and that he with his Family might find a Subsistence from her. But she [55] not forgetting her Resentments, swore by the Gods, He should not stay with her, unless he would dismiss his Retinue, and be contented with the [tln 580] Attendance of one Man; and with bitter Reproaches, told him how ill his Desire of vain-glorious Pomp suited with his Old-age and Poverty. When he found that she was by no Means to be prevailed upon, he was at last forced to comply, and dismissing the Rest, to take up with one Man. But by this Time he began to reflect more sensibly with himself upon the Grandeur from which he had fallen, and the miserable State he was now reduced to, and to enter upon Thoughts of going beyond Sea to his youngest Daughter. Yet he doubted whether he should be able to move her Commiseration, whom (as was related above) he had treated so unworthily. However disdaining to bear any longer such base Usage, he took Shipping to Gaul. In his Passage, he observed he had only the third Place given him among the Princes that were with him in the Ship, at which with deep Sighs and Tears, he burst forth into the following Complaint.

p.quote: O irreversible Decrees of the Fates, that never swerve from your stated Course! Why did you ever advance me to an unstable Felicity, since the Punishment of lost Happiness is greater than the Sense [56] of present Misery? The Remembrance of the Time when vast Numbers of Men obsequiously attended me at the taking of Cities and wasting the Enemies Countries, more deeply pierces my Heart, than the View of my present Calamity, which has exposed me to the Derision of those who formerly laid at my Feet. O Rage of Fortune! Shall I ever again see the Day, when I may be able to reward those according to their Deserts who have forsaken me in my Distress? How true was thy Answer, Cordeilla, when I asked thee concerning thy Love to me, As much as you have, so much is your Value, and so much I love you? While I had any Thing to give they valued me, being Friends not to me, but to my Gifts: They loved me then indeed, but my Gifts much more: When my Gifts ceased, my Friends vanished. But with what Face shall I presume to see you my dearest Daughter, since in my Anger I married you upon worse Terms than your Sisters, who, after all the mighty Favours they have received from me, suffer me to be in Banishment and Poverty?

div.p: As he was lamenting his Condition in these and the like Expressions, he arrived at Karitia, where his Daughter was, and waited before the City while he sent a Messenger to inform her of the Misery he was fallen [57] into, and to desire her Relief to a Father that suffered both Hunger and Nakedness. [tln 2348] Cordeilla was startled at the News, and wept bitterly, and with Tears asked him how many Men her Father had with him. The Messenger answered, he had none but [DP 8] one Man, who had been his Armour-bearer, and was staying with him without the Town. Then she took what Money she thought might be sufficient, and gave it the Messenger, with Orders to him to carry her Father to another City, and there give out that he was Sick, and to provide for him Bathing, Clothes, and all other Nourishment. She likewise gave Orders that he should take into his Service forty Men well cloathed and accoutred, and when all Things were thus prepared that he should then notify his Arrival to King Aganippus and his Daughter. The Messenger quickly returning carried Leir to another City, and there kept him concealed, till he had performed every Thing that Cordeilla had commanded.

div.head: CHAP. XIII. He is very honourably received by Cordeilla, and the King of Gaul.
div.p: As soon as he was provided with his Royal Apparel, Ornaments and Retinue, he sent Word to Aganippus and his [58] Daughter, that he was driven out of his Kingdom of Britain by his Sons-in-Law, and was come to them to procure their Assistance for the Recovering of his Dominions. Upon which they being attended with their chief Ministers of State and the Nobility of the Kingdom, went out to meet him, and received him honourably, and submitted to his Management the whole Power of Gaul, till such Time as he should be restored to his former Dignity.

div.head: CHAP. XIV. Leir by the Help of his Son-in-Law and Cord[ei]lla, being restored to the Kingdom dies.
div.p: In the mean Time Aganippus sent Officers over all Gaul to raise an Army, in Order to restore his Father-in-Law to his Kingdom of Britain. Which done, Leir returned to Britain with his Son and Daughter and their Forces they had raised, where he fought with his Sons-in-Law, and routed them. Thus having reduced the whole Kingdom under his Power, he died in the third Year after. Aganippus also died; so that Cordeilla now obtaining the Government of the Kingdom, [DP 2] buried her Father in a cer-[59]tain Vault, which she ordered to be made for him under the River Sore in Leicester. The Subterraneous Place where he was buried, had been built to the Honour of the God Janus. And here all the Workmen of the City, upon the anniversary Solemnity of that Festival, used to begin their yearly Labours.

div.head: CHAP. XV. Cordeilla being imprisoned kills herself. Margan aspiring to the whole Kingdom is killed by Cunedagius.
div.p: After a peaceable Possession of the Government for five Years, Cordeilla began to meet with Disturbances from the two Sons of her Sisters, being both young Men of great Spirit, whereof one, named Margan, was born to Maglaunus, and the other, named Cunedagius, to Henuinus. These after the Death of their Fathers succeeding them in their Dukedoms, were incensed to see Britain subject to the Power of a Woman, and raised Forces in Order to make an Insurrection against the Queen; nor desisted from their Hostilities, till after a general Waste of her Countries, and several Battles fought, they at last took her and put her in Prison; [60] [tln 3214] where for Grief at the Loss of her Kingdom she killed herself. After this they divided the Island between them, of which the Part that reaches from the North Side of Humber to Cathness, fell to Margan; the other Part from the same River Westward was Cunedagius’s Share. At the End of two Years, some restless Spirits that took Pleasure in the Troubles of the Nation had Access to Margan, and inspired him with vain Conceits by representing to him, how mean and disgraceful it was for him not to govern the whole Island, which was his due by Right of Birth. Stirred up with these and the like Suggestions, he marched with an Army through Cunedagius’s Country, and began to burn all before him. A War thus breaking out, he was met by Cunedagius and all his Forces, and upon an Attack made he killed no small Number of his Men, put Margan to Flight, and pursued him from one Province to another, till at last he killed him in a Town of Kambria, which since his Death has been by the Country People called Margan to this Day. After the Victory, Cunedagius gained the Monarchy of the whole Island, which he governed gloriously for three and thirty Years. At this Time flourished the Prophets Isaiah and Hoshea, and Rome was built upon the eleventh of the Calends of May by the two Brothers, Romulus and Remus.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Geoffrey
div.p: Since no English edition or translation of Geoffrey existed during Sh.’s lifetime, there is much doubt that the History exerted any direct influence on him. Simrock (1831; 1850, p. 121) and Dyce (ed. 1865, 7:247) suggest that Sh. might have read Geoffrey, but on the whole early commentators on Sh.’s sources such as Skottowe (1824), von Friesen (1877), and Eidam (1880) ignore or dismiss the possibility, assuming that Sh. was influenced by him only through Holinshed or some other intermediate source. Perrett (1904, pp. 279–85), however, thinks the case is strong. Sh. could have known the French or German editions of the Latin, or possibly one of the numerous MSS. Geoffrey was known to Sh.’s English contemporaries—Holinshed, John Higgins in Mirour for Magistrates, and Michael Drayton in Polyolbion (1613). Sh. would have been drawn to the original Latin by the marginal note Gal. Mon. in Holinshed (1587 ed., bk. 2, p. 12), opposite the lines to vnderstand the affections of his daughters towards him, and preferre hir whom he best loued, to the succession ouer the kingdome, which would suggest that Geoffrey might provide an adequate motive for the Love-Test. Lear’s violent and impetuous character is more like the Leir in Geoffrey and his immediate followers than the bland, bourgeois king of the old play Leir and Sh.’s other contemporary sources. Geoffrey makes Albany a better man than Cornwall, and like Geoffrey but unlike the other recent sources, Sh. pairs Goneril with Albany and Regan with Cornwall. Similarly, as in Geoffrey Lear gives away two-thirds of his kingdom immediately after the answers of Goneril and Regan; the daughters justify reducing the train because the knights are quarrelsome; the last remnant of Leir’s train, the solitary knight in Geoffrey, becomes the Gentleman in F1 (not Q’s Doctor), and his squire becomes the disguised Kent; Lear has only two companions in his misery, and is nursed back to health and newly arrayed before his reunion with Cordelia. In Geoffrey Lear is credulus pater, in Lr. Gloucester is A credulous father; the French King’s My love should kindle to inflamed respect [280] may come from Geoffrey’s Latin, Amore virginis inflammatus. Bullough (1973, p. 273) and Muir (1977, p. 197) are persuaded by this evidence that Sh. could possibly have known Geoffrey. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 94): It is possible, but I think not necessary, to believe that the dramatist consulted [Geoffrey’s history]…, which he would have had to read in manuscript and in Latin. Passages from Geoffrey’s History are cited in these notes: DP 2, 3–4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17; TLN 6, 45–50, 53–8, 80–1, 131, 141, 280, 499, 580, 810, 2348, 3214. The work is also cited generally in the following notes: TLN 7, 1749, 3037–42, 3249.

Because of the doubt that Sh. used the History, there is not much comparison of it with Lr. Eccles (ed. 1792, pp. 469–70) quotes (freely) from Lennox (1754, 3:286–91) on how Sh. made the story more absurd. Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xli f.): Sh. and Spenser rejected Geoffrey’s reason for Lear’s questioning his daughters; in Geoffrey, Leir’s knights number sixty; Geoffrey is guilty of an inconsistency in making Leir reserve for himself half his kingdom after just parting with two-thirds of it. Perrett (1904, pp. 244–5): It is the pitiable fate of the historical Cordeilla [i.e., her later death] that determines the tragedy.…What moved Geoffrey to drop the pall of darkness upon the moral tale…is the old Celtic note of the undeserved suffering of women, echoing in the sad fate of this child of Ler [sic], that [245] has given the world, through Shakespeare’s genius, its greatest tragedy. Chambers (1940, p. 12): It is, indeed, a depressing story.…Therefore it is small wonder that those who retold the story between Geoffrey in the Twelfth Century and Shakespeare in the Seventeenth have in certain cases sought to humanize and soften it.

Bullough (1973, pp. 272 f.): The Lear story does not appear in Welsh national literature, but it came into England with Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Historia regum Britanniae (c. 1135), in which Lear is the tenth British king after Brut. The name Leir, however, was that of a Celtic seagod, and the name Leicester may have had nothing to do with the king until Geoffrey made him founder of the city.

p.quote: Geoffrey adapted the tale [of the Goosegirl-Princess who told her father that she loved him like salt] but altered it, omitting the salt and making more of the natural relationship between children and parent. When Cordeilla says, I have ever loved thee as a father, nor ever from that love will I be turned aside.…So much as thou hast, so much art thou worth, and so much do I love thee, she is being jestingly ironical about her sisters’ exaggerations. She speaks plainly enough at first, but then riddles in a way that suggests to Lear that she loves him only for his possessions. What she means of course is that he has all that a father should have—affection for his children and the rights to love of a good parent; so her love for him is great. The narrative which follows is more full of feeling and more detailed than most of Geoffrey’s other stories. Cordeilla’s sad fate is not a punishment for her cryptic answer; it is a different story, arising from the divided land motif which recurs often in the chronicle; for almost invariably the partition of the kingdom leads to war. [Bullough cites Brut’s sons Albanact, Camber, and Locrine; Mempricius and Malin; Balinus and Brennius.]…The death of Cordeilla in prison after being dispossessed by the two sons of her sisters is an instance of evil reviving in a family. After this Margan and Cunedag quarrel and Margan is slain. Discord after Gorboduc’s division of Britain recurs between Ferrex and Porrex and results in the destruction of the line of Brut.

div.p: Curran (1999, pp. 1 ff.): Unlike other Renaissance history plays derived from Geoffrey’s history, Lr. does not attempt to rationalize the characters’ actions as believable history. In making no reference to a previous era, in having Regan and Goneril die without issue, and in turning the king’s triumph into failure—(p. 10) measures comparable to having Henry V lose at Agincourt—he precludes a correspondence between the play and any historical reality and de-emphasises any political message that might be extracted from it.

div.head: The Chronicles (1587)
div.p: Raphael Holinshed’s Chronicles of England, Scotlande, and Irelande (1577, 2 vols.; rev. 1587, 3 vols.), incorporating many earlier works of history, absorbed from them Geoffrey of Monmouth’s legendary histories of British kings, including that of Lear. Sh. made extensive use of Holinshed as a primary source for many plays, and Lr. has long been assumed to be one of them; that assumption, however, has recently been questioned by a number of commentators. If Sh. consulted Holinshed while writing Lr., he may also have been influenced by William Harrison’s Description of Britaine, prefixed to Holinshed’s first volume in each edition.

The Chronicles, originally intended by Reyne Wolfe, printer to Elizabeth, as a world history, was reduced in scope after his death in 1573 to a trio of chronicles of the British Isles, compiled by Raphael Holinshed, assisted by Richard Stanyhurst and Edmund Campion. The Chronicles, first published in 1577, was prefaced by topographical descriptions of ancient Britain and modern England by William Harrison. The much expanded second edition (1587), appearing some seven years afer Holinshed’s death, was chiefly the work of Abraham Fleming, aided by John Hooker, Francis Thynne, and John Stow; this is the edition used by Sh. Both editions were heavily censored by acts of the Privy Council. The full text of Holinshed was edited by Henry Ellis in 6 vols., 1807–8; the text is a reprint of the 1587 edition with censored passages restored. Selections of those parts of Holinshed which provide sources for Sh. have been edited by W. G. Boswell-Stone (1896, 1907), Allardyce and Josephine Nicoll (Everyman, 1927), and Richard Hosley (1968). Selections concerning Lear are included in Lennox (1754, 3:273–7), Hazlitt (1875, 2:314–17), Furness (1880, pp. 384–6), whose inaccurate transcript of the 1587 ed. is misdated 1574, Fischer (1914, pp. 12–16), Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 234–7), Satin (1966, pp. 453–5), and Bullough (1973, pp. 316–19).

The black letter of the original 1587 edition is here printed in roman type, and the roman and italic of the original in italic type. Long s is printed s, and the text is relined.
