The beginning of each page in the 1587 edition is indicated by bracketed page numbers inserted into the text; passages referred to in the commentary notes are preceded by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes, inserted into the text.

body.head: [From The second Booke of the historie of England, 1587]

div.head: [Book II, Chap. v.]
div.p:
[12][DP 2, tln 1968] Leir
the 10.
ruler.Leir the sonne of Baldud was admitted ruler ouer the Britaines, [DP 3–4] in the yeare of the world 3105, at what time Ioas reigned in Iuda. Mat. West.This Leir was a prince of right noble demeanor, gouerning his land and subiects in great wealth. Leicester is
builded.He made the towne of Caerleir now called Leicester, which standeth vpon the riuer of Sore. It is written that he had by his wife three daughters without other issue, whose names were [DP 15] Gonorilla, [DP 16] Regan, and [DP 17] Cordeilla, which daughters he greatly loued, but [tln 53–8, 131] specially Cordeilla the yoongest farre aboue the two elder. When this Leir therefore was come to great yeres, & began to waxe vnweldie through age, [tln 53–8] Gal. Mon.he thought to vnderstand the affections of his daughters towards him, and [tln 49] preferre hir whome he best loued, to the succession ouer the kingdome. A triall of
loue.Whervpon he first [13] asked Gonorilla the eldest, how well she loued him: who calling hir gods to record, protested that [tln 63] she loued him more than hir owne life, which by right and reason should be most deere vnto hir. With which answer the father being well pleased, turned to the second, and demanded of hir how well she loued him: who answered (confirming hir saiengs with great othes) that [tln 60–6] she loued him more than toong could expresse, and [tln 80–1] farre aboue all other creatures of the world.

Then called he his yoongest daughter Cordeilla before him, and asked of hir what account she made of him, vnto whome she made this answer as followeth: The answer
of the yoon­
gest daugh­
ter.Knowing the great loue and fatherlie zeale that you haue alwaies borne towards me (for the which I maie not answere you otherwise than I thinke, and as my conscience leadeth me) I protest vnto you, that [tln 98–9] I haue loued you euer, and will continuallie (while I liue) loue you as my naturall father. And if you would more vnderstand of the loue that I beare you, assertaine your selfe, that so much as you haue, so much you are worth, and so much I loue you, and no more. The father being nothing content with this answer, The two
eldest daugh­
ters are ma­
ried.married his two eldest daughters, the one vnto [DP 5] Henninus the duke of Cornewall, and the other vnto [DP 6] Maglanus the duke of Albania, betwixt whome he willed and The realme
is promised
to his two
daughters.ordeined that his land should be diuided [tln 7, 138] after his death, and the one halfe thereof immediatlie should be assigned to them in hand: but for the third daughter Cordeilla he reserued nothing.

Neuertheles it fortuned that one of the princes of Gallia (which now is called France) whose name was Aganippus, hearing of the beautie, womanhood, and good conditions of the said Cordeilla, desired to haue hir in mariage, and sent ouer to hir father, requiring that he might haue hir to wife: to whome answer was made, that he might haue his daughter, but as for anie dower he could haue none, for all was promised and assured to hir other sisters alreadie. [tln 275–84] Aganippus notwithstanding this answer of deniall to receiue anie thing by way of dower with Cordeilla, tooke hir to wife, onlie moued thereto (I saie) for respect of hir person and amiable vertues. He gouerned
the third part
of Gallia as
Gal. Mon.
saith.This [DP 3–4] Aganippus was one of the twelue kings that ruled Gallia in those daies, as in the British historie it is recorded. But to proceed.

After that Leir was fallen into age, the two dukes that had married his two eldest daughters, thinking it long yer the gouernment of the land did come to their hands, [tln 45–50] arose against him in armour, and reft from him the gouernance of the land, vpon conditions to be continued for terme of life: by the which he was put to his portion, that is, to liue after a rate assigned to him for the maintenance of his estate, which in processe of time was diminished as well by Maglanus as by Henninus. But the greatest griefe that Leir tooke, was to see the vnkindnesse of his daughters, which seemed to thinke that all was too much which their father had, the same being neuer so little: in so much that going from the one to the other, he was brought to that miserie, that [DP 8] scarslie they would allow him one seruant to wait vpon him.

In the end, such was the vnkindnesse, or (as I maie saie) the vnnaturalnesse which he found in his two daughters, notwithstanding their faire and pleasant words vttered in time past, that being constreined of necessitie, [tln 2743] he fled the land, & sailed into Gallia, there to seeke some comfort of his yongest daughter Cordeilla, whom before time he hated. The ladie Cordeilla hearing that he was arriued in poore estate, [tln 2773] she first sent to him priuilie a certeine summe of monie to apparell himselfe withall, [tln 141] and to reteine a certeine number of seruants that might attend vpon him in honorable wise, as apperteined to the estate which he had borne: and then so accompanied, she appointed him to come to the court, which he did, and was so ioifullie, honorablie, and louinglie receiued, both by his sonne in law Aganippus, and also by his daughter Cordeilla, that his hart was greatlie comforted: for he was no lesse honored, than if he had beene king of the whole countrie himselfe.

Now when he had informed his sonne in law and his daughter in what sort he had been vsed by his other daughters, Aganippus caused a mightie armie to be put in a readinesse, and likewise a great nauie of ships to be rigged, to passe ouer into Britaine with Leir his father in law, [tln 2376–81] to see him againe restored to his kingdome. It was accorded, that Cordeilla should also go with him to take possession of the land, the which he promised to leaue vnto hir, as the rightfull inheritour after his decesse, notwithstanding any former grant made to hir sisters or to their husbands in anie maner of wise.

Herevpon, when this armie and nauie of ships were readie, [tln 2347+2–+7] Leir and his daughter Cordeilla with hir husband tooke the sea, and arriuing in Britaine, fought with their enimies, and discomfited them in battell, in the which Maglanus and Henninus were slaine: and then was Leir restored to his kingdome, which he ruled after this by the space of two yeeres, and then died, fortie yeeres after he first began to reigne. Matth.West.His bodie was buried at Leicester in a vaut vnder the chanell of the riuer of Sore beneath the towne.

div.head:
The gunarchie of queene Cordeilla,
how she was vanquished, of hir impri­
sonment and selfe-murther: the con­
tention betweene Cunedag and
Margan nephewes for go­
uernement, and the euill
end thereof.
The sixt Chapter.
div.p:
Queene
Cordeil­
la.Cordeilla the yoongest daughter of Leir was admitted Q. and supreme gouernesse of Britaine, in the yeere of the world 3155, before the bylding of Rome 54, Uzia then reigning in Iuda, and Ieroboam ouer Israell. This Cordeilla after hir fathers deceasse ruled the land of Britaine right worthilie during the space of fiue yeeres, in which meane time hir husband died, and then about the end of those fiue yeeres, hir two nephewes Margan and Cunedag, sonnes to hir aforesaid sisters, disdaining to be vnder the gouernment of a woman, leuied warre against hir, and destroied a great part of the land, and finallie tooke hir prisoner, and laid hir fast in ward, wherewith she tooke such griefe, being a woman of a manlie courage, and despairing to recouer libertie, there [tln 3214] she slue hirselfe, when she had reigned (as before is mentioned) the tearme of fiue yeeres.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Holinshed
div.p: In 1715 Theobald (No. 10) named the Annals as the source for Lr., and two centuries later Boas (1896, p. 438) could declare, The source of the main plot is Holinshed’s Chronicle. In the interim many critics attributed to Holinshed features of Lr. that could have derived from other sources, particularly from the old play Leir, whose influence on Sh. was often discounted. Conversely, critics made distinctions between Lr. and Holinshed that are equally applicable to other sources. Eventually, in the 20th c., a more skeptical and discriminating attitude towards Holinshed’s influence began to develop.

Collins (1904, p. 274): In Lear Shakespeare’s indebtedness to Holinshed, though obvious, is very slight, and is almost confined to the first scene of the first Act, that is to Lear’s purposed partition of his kingdom—and even here there are important variations; to the replies given by his daughters, when asked to testify their affection; and to the rupture with Cordelia, and her portionless marriage with the King of France. Beyond this he borrows nothing further from the story, except the subsequent quarrel with Goneril and Regan in consequence of their ungrateful determination to scant Lear’s sizes, and deprive him of his retinue, and the subsequent reconciliation with Cordelia. For nothing else in Lear is there even a hint in Holinshed, and the catastrophe is entirely different from the catastrophe in Holinshed, and in the old play which follows Holinshed.

Perrett (1904, p. 273): The account in Holinshed…has by no means the paramount importance usually ascribed to it. Sh. had a much fuller knowledge of the story than could be obtained from this source, and differs from Hol. over a number of fundamental particulars. Specific influence of Hol. is apparent, however, at [2376 ff.], where Cordelia disavows any selfish purpose in her attempt to restore her father…; the strange statement that Cordelia was to succeed Leir as ruler over Britain may have had some effect.

Law (1934, pp. 41–3): I cannot find any convincing evidence that Shakespeare ever read a single line of Holinshed’s account of King Leir.…The Mirror for Magistrates contains the full account given by Holinshed.…I cannot find in the entire drama of Shakespeare a single phrase echoed apparently from Holinshed.

Greg (1940, pp. 397–8): Both the husbands are kings in the old play, dukes in Holinshed and Shakespeare. There seems also to be a few verbal reminiscences. In Holinshed Regan protests that she loved her father more than tongue could express [a parallel pointed out by Malone; see n. 60–6].…Cordeilla, on the other hand, announces that so much I love you, and no more; cf. [98–9].…Leir warns Gallia that he might have his daughter, but as for any dower he could have none: cf. [287 ff., 281].…Gallia takes Cordeilla to wife only moved thereto…for respect of her person and amiable vertues; cf. [264, 273].…Leir was brought to that misery that scarcely they would allow him one servant to wait upon him; cf. [1563].…After the death of Leir, Cordeilla ruled Britain till deposed by her nephews, who finally took her prisoner, and laid her fast in ward, wherewith…despairing to recover her liberty, there she slew herself; Cordelia is murdered, the command being [3212–14].

Law (1950, pp. 47–9): On certain other matters Holinshed seems to have brushed aside all previous authorities to develop individual differences. These are the date for Leir’s reign (beginning at 3105), the motive for the love test (to bestow his whole realm, not to divide it), Cordeilla’s form of address to Leir (you, not thou), and the fact that Aganippus prepared not only a strong army but a strong navy. But all of these distinctive details in Holinshed are absent from Sh.’s Lr., while incidents omitted by Holinshed are found there: Lear, not Cordelia, dominates the story; the kingdom is to be divided; the daughters are married to different dukes, as in Geoffrey; Lear makes a proviso that he and his knights will be maintained; France accepts Cordelia personally, not through messengers; etc. (P. 49): Thus Shakespeare owes nothing to Holinshed, though I believe he owes much to the old play, something to Geoffrey and other versions of the story.

Bullough (1973, p. 274): Shakespeare seems to have taken…little specifically from Holinshed.…Shakespeare seems to have wished to refute Holinshed’s implication (after Caxton) that Cordelia in invading Britain wanted to take possession of the land, for in King Lear she declares [2376–80].

Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): The spelling Regan may have come from Holinshed; it is he who marries her to Cornwall, in Leir the husband of Gonorill. Holinshed also makes the marriage of Cordeilla dowerless, and credits her with a successful invasion. Professor Muir [1955; see n. 2429] has shown that Edgar’s description of the imaginary fiend at Dover cliffs is based on a passage in Holinshed two pages earlier than his account of Lear.
Comparisons between Holinshed’s account and Sh.’s play generally emphasize the differences.

Theobald (1715, no. 10): In some Particulars of the Catastrophe the Poet has given himself a Liberty to be Master of the Story. For Lear and Cordelia are taken Prisoners and, both lying under Sentence of Death, the latter is hang’d in the Prison, and the former breaks his Heart with the Affliction of it. In this respect Sh. differs from all versions of the Lear story, of course.

Lennox (1754, 3:286 ff.): This Fable, although drawn from the foregoing History of King Lear, is so altered by Shakespear, in several Circumstances, as to render it much more improbable than the Original.…He shews us a King resigning his Kingdom, his Crown and Dignity to his two Daughters; reserving nothing to himself, not even a decent Maintenance.…

[287] Lear does not run mad till the third Act; yet his Behaviour towards Cordelia in this first Scene has all the Appearance of a Judgment totally depraved.…Lear banishes her his Sight, consigns her over to Want, and loads her with the deepest Imprecations. What less than Phrenzy can inspire a Rage so groundless, and a Conduct so absurd!…[288] The Lover who is made to Marry the disinherited Cordelia on account of her Virtue, is very injudiciously contrived to be Absent when she gave so glorious a Testimony of it, and is touch’d by a cold Justification of her Fame, and that from herself, when he might have been charm’d with a shining Instance of her Greatness of Soul, and inviolable Regard to Truth.

p.quote: So unartfully has the Poet managed this Incident, that Cordelia’s noble Disinterestedness is apparent to all but him who was to be the most influenced by it. In the Eyes of her Lover she is debased, not exalted; reduced to the abject Necessity of defending her own Character, and seeking rather to free herself from the Suspicion of Guilt, than modestly enjoying the conscious Sense of superior Virtue.…

div.p: [290] Shakespear has deviated widely from the History in the Catastrophe of his Play.…In Shakespear the Forces of the two wicked Sisters are victorious, Lear and the pious Cordelia are taken Prisoners, she is hanged in Prison, and the old King dies with Grief. Had Shakespear followed the His-[291]torian, he would not have violated the Rules of poetical Justice; he represents Vice punished, and Virtue rewarded; in the Play one Fate overwhelms alike the Innocent and the Guilty, and the Facts in the History are wholly changed to produce Events, neither probable, necessary, nor just.
Skottowe (1824, 2:97): The old dramatist, the ballad, and Shakspeare agree in deviating from Holinshed by making Lear resign the whole of his kingdom and power.

Chambers (1940, pp. 21–2): Shakespeare telescopes, as it were, two battles into one. The battle begins as the battle fought by Cordelia to restore her father to the throne: it ends as the battle in which Cordelia is captured by her foes. By thus combining the two battles, Shakespeare is able to give Cordelia one who will comfort her distress and mourn her death.…Cordelia is slain. But not by herself; there Shakespeare does depart from historic fact, as he had received it. For it is extremely unlikely that Shakespeare could have known any of the Fifteenth Century versions in which Cordelia is saved from suicide by being murdered.…[22] Suicide would be unbearable in the case of Shakespeare’s Cordelia.…The feeling of Christendom, and often of the pagan world also, has been that men and women may not kill themselves to avoid the torture or the tedium of imprisonment or sickness.

Satin (1966, p. 446): Holinshed deals more briefly [than Geoffrey] with the conflict between Gonorilla and Leir’s household knights, and with the meeting between Leir and Cordeilla.…Both of these incidents loom large in The True Chronicle and in King Lear.

Ribner (ed. 1967, p. xiv): Shakespeare made a single tragic story out of the two episodes [the actions of Lear’s daughters, the later story of Cordelia] by eliminating the interval of seven years and by identifying the rebellion against Cordelia by her nephews with the war waged by Cordelia and the King of France against her sisters and their husbands on behalf of her father. Other versions differed from Holinshed in the same way.

div.head: The Tragœdye of Cordila (1574)
div.p: Of the many poets who added to the growing bulk of The Mirror for Magistrates between its inception in 1555 and its final maturity in 1587, only one has relevance to Lr. In 1574 John Higgins published sixteen tragic poems in his First Parte of the Mirour, so-called because his tales are about earlier periods than those in the previous collections. In one of these, Queen Cordila, beginning with an account of my father Leire, describes her life and death by suicide. These sixteen poems and some two dozen more by Higgins were added to those of his predecessors in the culminating Mirour for Magistrates of 1587, where the poem about Cordila is somewhat revised. In her standard edition (1938) of the Mirror Lily B. Campbell gives the text of 1559 and the additions of 1563, 1578, and 1587; her Parts Added to the Mirror for Magistrates (1946) gives the additions of Higgins (1574, 1575, 1587) and Thomas Blennerhasset (1578). Cordila’s tragedy has been excerpted in Collier (1843, 2.3:27–40), Hazlitt (1875, 2:324–36), Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 389–91), Fischer (1914, pp. 20–6), Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 238–43), and Bullough (1973, pp. 323–32). Perrett (1904, p. 239): It is unlikely that Sh. read the revised legend of Cordila, MfM 87, in addition to the older version [of 1574], whereas (pp. 273–4) evidently he derived the detail of Lear’s squires from the earlier version, since it is lacking from 1587 (see n. 750). Though Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxvi) detects two verbal echoes of the 1587 version, they are in language that Sh. himself had previously used: see nn. 436–41, 2004–5.

The black letter of the original 1574 edition is here printed in roman type, and the roman of the original in italic type; long s is printed s. The beginning of each page in the 1574 edition is indicated by bracketed folio numbers inserted into the outer right margin opposite the first line on that page; passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by bracketed TLN numbers in the right margin, opposite the line containing the first word of the passage discussed.

body.head: [From The Mirour for Magistrates, 1574]

Cordila shewes how by despaire
when she was in prison she slue herselfe.
the yeare before Christe. 800.

lg.l: Yf any wofull wight haue cause, to waile her woe:
Or griefes are past do pricke vs Princes tel our fal:
My selfe likewise must needes constrained eke do so,
And shew my like misfortunes and mishaps withal.
Should I keepe close my heauy haps and thral?
Then did I wronge: I wrongde my selfe and thee,
Which of my facts, a witnes true maist bee.
A woman yet must blushe when bashfull is the case,
Though truth bid tell the tale and story as it fell:
But sith that I mislike not audience time nor place
Therefore, I cannot still keepe in my counsaile well:
No greater ease of hart then griefes to tell,
It daunteth all the dolours of our minde,
Our carefull harts thereby great comfort finde.
For why to tell that may recounted be againe,
And tell it as oure cares may compasse ease:
That is the salue and medcine of our paine,
Which cureth corsyes all and sores of our disease:
It doth our pinching panges, and paines apease:
It pleades the parte of an assured frende,
And telles the trade, like vices to amende.
Therefore if I more willing be to tell my fall,
And shew mishaps to ease my burdened brest and minde:
That others haply may auoide and shunne like thrall,
And thereby in distresse more ayde and comfort finde.
They maye keepe measure where as I declinde,
And willing be to flye like bruite and blame:
As I to tell, or thou to write the same.
For sith I see the prest to heare that wilt recorde,
What I Cordila tell to ease my inward smart:[DP 17]
I will resite my storye tragicall ech worde,
To the that giust an eare to heare and ready art,
And lest I set the horse behinde the cart,
I minde to tell ech thinge in order so,
As thou maiste see and shewe whence sprang my wo.
My grandsyre Bladud hight that found the Bathes by skill,
A fethered king that practisde for to flye and soare:
Whereby he felt the fall God wot against his will,
And neuer went, roode, raignde nor spake, nor flew no more.
Who dead his sonne my father Leire therefore,[DP 2]
Was chosen kinge, by right apparent heyre,
Which after built the towne of Leircestere.
He had three daughters, first and eldest hight Gonerell:[DP 15]
Next after hir, my sister Ragan was begote:[DP 16]
The thirde and last was, I the yongest namde Cordell[DP 17]
And of vs all, our father Leire in age did dote.
So minding hir that loude him best to note,
Because he had no sonne t’enioye his lande:
He thought to giue, where fauoure most he fande.[tln 53–8]
What though I yongest were, yet men me iudgde more wise
Then either Gonorell, or Ragan had more age,
And fayrer farre: wherefore my sisters did despise
My grace, and giftes, and sought my praise t’swage:
But yet though vice gainst vertue die with rage,
It cannot keepe her vnderneth to drowne,
But still she flittes aboue, and reapes renowne.
Yet nathelesse, my father did me not mislike:
But age so simple is, and easye to subdue:
As childhode weake, thats voide of wit and reason quite:
They thincke thers nought, you flater fainde, but all is true:
Once olde and twice a childe, tis said with you,
Which I affirme by proofe, that was definde:
In age my father had a childishe minde.
He thought to wed vs vnto nobles three, or Peres:
And vnto them and theirs, deuide and part the lande:
For both my sisters first he sent as first their yeares
Requirde their mindes, and loue, and fauour t’understand.
(Quoth he) all doubtes of duty to abande,[tln 53–8]
I must assaye and eke your frendships proue:
Now tell me eche how much you do me loue.
Which when they aunswered, they loude him wel and more[tln 63, 80–1]
Then they themselues did loue, or any worldly wight:
He praised them and said he would againe therefore,
The louing kindnes they deserude in fine requite:
So found my sisters fauour in his sight,
By flatery fayre they won their fathers hart:
Which after turned, him and mee to smart.
But not content with this he minded me to proue,
For why he wonted was to loue me wonders well:
How much dost thou (q[uoth] he) Cordile thy father loue?[DP 17]
I will (said I) at once my loue declare and tell:
I loude you euer as my father well,[tln 98–9]
No other wise, if more to know you craue:
We loue you chiefly for the goodes you haue.[tln 106–110+1]
Thus much I said, the more their flattery to detect,
But he me answerd therunto again with Ire,
Because thou dost thy fathers aged yeares neglect,
That loude ye more of late then thy desertes require,
Thou neuer shalt, to any part aspire
Of this my realme, emong thy sisters twayne,
But euer shalt vndotid ay remayne.
Then to the king of Albany for wife he gaue[DP 6]
My sister Gonerell, the eldest of vs all:
And eke my sister Ragan for Hinnine to haue,[DP 5]
Which then was Prince of Camber and Cornwall:
These after him should haue his kingdome all[tln 7]
Betwene them both, he gaue it franke and free:
But nought at all, he gaue of dowry mee.[tln 136]
At last it chaunst ye king of Fraunce to here my fame,[DP 3–4]
My beutie braue, was blazed all abrode eche where:
And eke my vertues praisde me to my fathers blame
Did for my sisters flattery me lesse fauoure beare.
Which when this worthy king my wrõgs did heare,
He sent ambassage likte me more then life,
T’intreate he might me haue to be his wife.
My father was content with all his harte, and sayde,
He gladly should obtaine his whole request at will
Concerning me, if nothing I herin denayde:
But yet he kept by their intisment hatred still,
([Quoth] he) your prince his pleasure to fulfill,
I graunt and giue my daughter as you craue:
But nought of me for dowry can she haue.
King Aganippus well agreed to take me so,
He deemde that vertue was of dowries all the best:[tln 264]
And I contentid was to Fraunce my father fro
For to depart, & hoapte t’enioye some greater rest.
I maried was, and then my ioyes encreaste,
I gate more fauoure in this prince his sight,
Then euer princesse of a princely wight.
But while yt I these ioyes enioyd, at home in Fraũce
My father Leire in Britayne waxed aged olde,
My sisters yet them selues the more aloft t’aduaũce,
Thought well they might, be by his leaue, or sans so bolde:
To take the realme & rule it as they wold.
They rose as rebels voyde of reason quite,[tln 45–50]
And they depriude him of his crowne and right.
Then they agreed, it should be into partes equall
Deuided: and my father threscore knightes & squires[tln 141, 750]
Should alwayes haue, attending on him still at cal.
But in six monthes so much encreasid hateful Ires,
That Gonerell denyde all his desires,
So halfe his garde she and her husband refte:[tln 810]
And scarce alowde the other halfe they lefte.
Eke as in Scotlande thus he lay lamenting fates,
When as his daughter so, sought all his vtter spoyle:
The meaner vpstarte gentiles, thought thẽ selues his mates
And betters eke, see here an aged prince his foyle.
Then was he faine for succoure his, to toyle.
With all his knightes, to Cornewall there to lye:
In greatest nede, his Raganes loue to trye.
And when he came to Cornwall, Ragan then with ioye,
Receiued him and eke hir husbande did the lyke:
There he abode a yeare and liude without a noy,
But then they tooke, all his retinue from him quite[tln 1560–3]
Saue only ten, and shewde him dayly spite,
Which he bewailde complayning durst not striue,
Though in disdayne they laste alowde but fiue.
On this he deemde[,] him selfe was far that tyme vnwyse,
When from his doughter Gonerell to Ragan hee:
Departed erste yet eache did him poore king despise,
Wherfore to Scotlande once againe with hir to bee[tln 1556–8]
And bide he went: but beastly cruell shee,
Bereaude him of his seruauntes all saue one,[tln 1560–3]
Bad him content him self with that or none.
Eke at what time he askte of eache to haue his garde,
To garde his grace where so he walkte or wente:
They calde him doting foole and all his hestes debarde,[tln 522+2–+3]
Demaunded if with life he could not be contente.
Then he to late his rigour did repente,[tln 769]
Gainst me and sayde, Cordila now adieu:
I finde the wordes thou toldste mee to to true.
And to be short, to Fraunce he came alone to mee,
And tolde me how my sisters him our father vsde:
Then I besought my king with teares vpõ my knee,[tln 2378]
That he would aide my father thus by them misusde
Who nought at all my humble heste refusde:
But sent to euery coste of Fraunce for ayde,
Wherwith my father home might be conueide.
The soldiers gathered from eche quarter of ye land,
Came at ye length to know the king his mind & will:
Who did commit them to my fathers aged hand,[tln 2347+2–+7]
And I likewise of loue and reuerent mere goodwill
Desirde my king, he would not take it ill,
If I departed for a space withall:
To take a parte, or ease my fathers thrall.
This had: I partid with my father from my fere,
We came to Britayne with our royall cãpe to fight:
And manly fought so lõg our enmies vãquisht were
By martiall feates, and force by subiectes sword and might.[tln 2868+3–+4]
The Britishe kinges were fayne to yelde our right,
And so my father well this realme did guide,
Three yeares in peace and after that he dide.
Then I at Leircester in Ianus temple made,
His tombe and buried there his kingly regall corse,
As sondry tymes in life before he often bade:
For of our fathers will we then did greatly force,
We had of conscience eke so much remorce,
That we supposde those childrens liues to ill:
Which brake their fathers testament, and will.
And I was queene the kingdome after still to holde,
Till fiue yeares paste I did this Iland guyde:
I had the Britaynes at what becke & bay I wolde,
Till that my louing king myne Aganippus dyde.
But then my seate it faltered on eache side,
Two churlishe Impes began with me to Iarre,
And for my crowne wadgde with me mortal warre.
The one hight Morgan th’elder sonne of Gonerell
My sister, and that other Conidagus hight
My sister Ragans sonne, that loude me neuer well:
Both nephewes mine, yet wolde against me Cordel fight,
Because I loude always that semed right:
Therfore they hated me, and did pursue,
Their aunte and queene as she had bene a Iewe.
This Morgane was that time ye prince of Albany,
And Conidagus king of Cornewale and of VVales:
Both which, at once prouided their artillery,
To worke me wofull wo, & mine adherentes bales:
What nede I fill thyne eares with longer tales?
They did preuaile by might and powre so faste
That I was taken prisoner at laste.
In spitefull sorte, they vsed then my captiue corse,
No fauoure shewde to me, extincte was mine estate.
Of kinred, princesse bloud, or pere was no remorce,
But as an abiecte vile and worse they did me hate,
To lie in darksome dongeon was my fate:
As twere a thiefe mine aunswers to abyde,
Gainst right and iustice, vnder Iaylours guyde.
For libertie at lengthe I suid, to subiectes were:
But they kepte me in pryson close deuoyde of truste,
If I might once escape, they were in dreade and feare,
Their fawning frendes with me would proue vntrue and iust.
They tolde me take it paciently I muste,
And be contented that I had my life:
Sithe with their mothers I began the strife.
Whereby I sawe might nothing me preuayle to pray,
Or pleade, or proue, defende, excuse or pardon craue.
They herde me not, despisde my plaintes, sought my decay,
I might no lawe, nor loue, nor right, nor iustice haue:
No frendes, no faith, nor pitie could me saue:
But I was from all hope of licence barde,
Condemde my cause like neuer to be herde.
Was euer lady in such wofull wreckfull wo:
Depriude of princely powre, berefte of libertie,
Depriud in all these worldly pompes, hir pleasures fro,
And brought from welthe, to nede, distresse, and misery?
From palace proude, in prison poore to lye:
From kingdomes twayne, to dungion one no more:
From Ladies wayting, vnto vermine store.
From light to darke, from holsom ayre to lothsom smell:
From odewr swete, to sweate: from ease, to grieuous payne:
From sight of princely wights, to place where theues do dwel:
From deinty beddes of downe, to be of strawe full fayne:[tln 1715, 2786–8]
From bowres of heauenly hewe, to dennes of dayne:
From greatest haps, that worldly wightes atchieue:
To more distresse then any wretche aliue.
When firste I lefte the crowne of Fraunce, did me exalte,
And eke my noble king, myne Aganippus true:
And came to Englande for their heynous factes, and faulte:
Which from his right and kingdom quite our father threw,
To take this realme, to raigne and treason knew:
I thinke of all misfortunes was the worste,
Or else I deeme, was some of vs accurste.
For marke my haplese fall that drawes at length to ende,
As in this pryson vile, on lyue I lingering laye:
When I had mourned long, but founde no faithfull frende
That could me helpe, or ayde, or comforte any way,
Was serude at meate, as those their kinges betraye,
With fare God wot was simple, bare and thinne,
Could not sustayne the corps it entred in.
And when the sighes, & teares, & plaintes nigh burst my hart,
And place, and stenche and fare nighe poysond euery pore:
For lacke of frendes to tell my seas of giltlesse smarte,
And that mine eyes had sworne to take swete slepe no more,
I was content sithe cares oppreste me sore,
To leaue my foode, take mourning plaintes and crie,
And lay me downe, let griefe and nature trie.
Thus as I pyning lay my carkas on couch of strawe,
And felte that payne erste neuer creature earthly knewe:
Me thought by night a gryzely ghost in darkes I sawe,
Eke nerer still to me with stealing steps she drewe.
She was of coloure pale, a deadly hewe:
Hir clothes resembled thousand kindes of thrall,
And pictures playne, of hastened deathes withall.
I musing lay in paynes and wondred what she was,
Mine eyne stode still, mine haire rose vp for feare an ende.
My fleshe it shoke and trembled: yet I cryde alasse,
What wight art thou, a foe or else what fawning frende?
If death thou arte, I praye thee make an ende?
But th’arte not death: arte thou some fury sente?
My wofull corps with paynes to more tormente?
With that she spake I am ([quoth] she) thy frend Despaire[tln 3213]
Which in distresse eache worldly wight with spede do ayde:
I rid them from their foes, if I to them repayre,
To long from thee by other caytiues was I stayde.
Now if thou arte to die no whit affrayde,
Here shalt thou choose of instrumentes, beholde?
Shall ridde thy restlesse life, of this be bolde.
And therwithall she spred her garmentes lap asyde,
Under the which a thousand thinges I sawe with eyes:
Both knyues, sharpe swordes, poynadoes all bedyde[tln 1835]
With bloud, and poysons prest which she could well deuise.
There is no hope ([quoth] she) for thee to ryse,
And get thy crowne or libertie agayne:
But for to liue, long lasting pining payne.
Loe here ([quoth] she) the blade that Did’ of Carthage highte,
Whereby she was from thousande panges of payne let passe:
With this she slewe hir selfe, after Aeneas flighte:
When he to sea from Tyrian shores departed was,
Do chouse of these thou seest from woes to passe,
Or bid the ende prolonge thy paynefull dayes,
And I am pleasde from thee to get my wayes.
With that was I (poore wretche) content to take the knife,
But doubtfull yet to dye, and fearefull faine would bide:
So still I lay in study with my selfe at bate and strife,
What thing were best of both these deepe extreames vntride.
My hope all reasons of dispayre denide,
And she againe replide to proue it best
To dye, for still in life my woes increast.
She calde to minde, the ioyes in Fraunce I whilom had:
She tolde me what a troupe of Ladies was my traine,
And howe ye Lords of Fraunce and Britaynes both were glad,
Of late to waite on mee and subiects all were faine,
She tould I had bin Queene of kingdomes twaine,
And how my nephewes had my seate and crowne:
I could not rise, for euer fallen downe.
A thousand thinges, beside resited then dispaire:
She tould the woes in warres, that I had heapt of late:
Rehearst the prison vile, in steede of Pallas faire:
My lodging lowe and mouldy meates my mouth did hate,
She shewde mee all the dongeon where I sate,
The dankeish walles, the darkes and bad me smell:
And bide the sauour if I likt it well
Whereby I wretch deuoide of comfort quite and hope,
And pleasures past comparde with present paines I had:
For fatall knife slipt forth my fearefull hand did grope,
Dispaire in this to ayde my sencelesse limmes was glad,
And gaue the blade to ende my woes she bad.
I will (quoth I) but first with all my hart:
Ile pray the Gods, reuenge my wofull smart.
If any wronge deserue the wrecke I pray you skyes,
And starres of light, if you my wofull plight do rue:
O Phoebus cleare I thee beseech and pray likewise,
Beare witnes of my plaints well knowne to Gods are true.
You see from whence these iniuries they grue,
Then let like vengeaunce hap and light on those:
Which vndeserued were my deadly foes.
God graunt a mortall strife betwene them both may fall,
That one the other may without remorse distroye:
That Conidagus may, his cosin Morgan thrall,
Because he first decreast my wealth, bereft my ioye.
I pray you Gods he neuer be a Roy.
But caitife may be payde with such a frende:
As shortly may him bring, to sodaine ende.
Farewell my Realme of Fraunce, farewell Adieu:
Adieu mes nobles tous, and England now farewell:
Farewell Madames my Ladyes, car ie suis pardu:

l.hi: Il me fault aler, desespoir m’a donne conseil

lg.l: De me tuer, no more your Queene farewell.
My nephewes mee oppresse with maine and might,
A captiue poore, gainst iustice all and right.
And therewithall the sight did faile my dazeling eyne,
I nothing sawe saue sole Dispayre bad mee dispatch,
Whom I behelde, she caught the knife from mee I weene,
And by hir elbowe carian death for mee did watch.
Come on (quoth I) thou hast a goodly catch,
And therewithal Dispayre the stroke did strike:[tln 2980, 3214]
Whereby I dyde, a damned creature like.[tln 1835]
Which I alasse lament, bid those aliue beware,
Let not the losse of goodes or honour them constraine:
To play the fooles, and take such carefull carke and care,
Or to dispaire for any prison pine or paine.
If they be giltlesse let them so remaine,
Farre greater follye is it for to kill,
Themselues dispayring, then is any ill.
Sith first thereby their enmyes haue, that they desyre:
By which they proue to deadly foes vnwares a frende:
And next they cannot liue, to former blisse t’aspyre
If God do bring their foes in time to sodaine ende:
They lastly as the damned wretches sende,
Their soules to hell, when as they vndertake
To kill a corps: which God did liuely make.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Higgins
div.p: Steevens (ed. 1773): Sh. derived from this work (1587) the behaviour of the Steward, and the reply of Cordelia to her father concerning her future marriage. Simrock (1850, p. 123), disagreeing: Sh. could have invented the behavior of Oswald by himself.

Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xlii): In Geoffrey, Leir’s knights number sixty; this number is gradually cut down by each succeeding writer, and omitted by all accounts of Sh.’s day, except Mirror for Magistrates, which has sixty, and has the daughters cut down that number and leave Lear on scanty allowance. Bullough (1973, p. 275): In his Preface Higgins asserted that he had seen a manuscript of Geoffrey of Monmouth (which I lost by misfortune).

Perrett (1904, pp. 84, 246–7, 273–4): The fact is, that Higgins was hopelessly out of his depth. The plan of the Mirror demanded a story tragical. His excessive respect for the chronicles he so carefully studied forbade him to tamper with the historical facts. He tries, and fails, to present as Tragedy what is in reality Comedy, the story of Leir, by having it related by the victim of undeserved suffering, the heroine of the inorganic tragic sequel. Clio and Melpomene between them lead him a sorry dance.—But however poor as art, his version is of very considerable importance.…Leir’s knights, for instance, are mentioned nowhere else, except in the printed Perceforest, between C[axton] and Shakespeare.…[And] the mere fact of an attempt at a tragic setting is important.…[246] In Edmund, the intriguer for the kingdom and the immediate cause of Cordelia’s death, who too late repents and confesses his guilt…, there is some resemblance to that Morgan, son of Gonerell, the subject of the next legend in the MfM, who lost his life in the attempt to make himself king of [247] all Britain.…[273] The description at [750] of Lear’s train of a hundred knights as a hundred knights and squires…is…a clear sign that Sh. had at some time seen either Caxton or MfM 75.…But while no other trace of C[axton] is visible, several points speak for MfM: —the numbers in the reductions of the train, half,…, 10, 5, 1, 0…; the title of the King of [274] France…; Cordelia’s importun’d tears, [2378]…; the despair that was to have caused her suicide, [3213]…; the resemblance between Edmund and Morgan.

Greg (1940, pp. 399–400): Cordell tells Leire: Yet shortly I may chance, if Fortune will, | To find in heart to bear another more goodwill. Cordelia tells Lear ([107–9]).…In this version alone do we find specific mention of the knights. His knights are stripped to ten, then to one; Of all this the only hint in King Leir is that Gonorill restrains her father of half his portion or pension (763, 807).…[400] It is in the Mirror for Magistrates alone that we find the couples [Gonerell=Albany, Ragan=Cornwall] as in Shakespeare, and also the exact form of the name Albany.

Muir (1957, p. 143): From The Mirror for Magistrates Shakespeare took about ten minor details, including the forms Albany and King of France, and there is one significant verbal parallel [From sight…strawe ful fayne, 2786–8 And wast…musty straw?]. Cf. also n. 3214.
Olson (1961, p. 205): Here, Lear’s sons-in-law revolt and seize power (the profession of love here has nothing to do with the division of the kingdom, but only with Cordelia’s banishment).

Bullough (1973, pp. 275–6): [Higgins] did not include King Lear but Cordila, who is there not so much for her early sufferings as because she committed suicide in prison, tells his story. In the next piece her nephew, Morgan of Albany, attributes his destruction by his brother Cunedag to his ill-treatment of her.…According to his Cordila, the love-test was made because Leire thought to give, where favoure most he fande. He did not me mislike, but she was not his favourite. Cordila admits that In age my father had a childishe minde. Leire’s division of the kingdom was meant to take place after his death, but the sisters (not the sons-in-law) rebelled and seized his crown and right. Higgins gave more details than usual of the gradual diminution of the old man’s retinue, his leaving Gonerell for Ragan after six months, Ragan’s welcome turning after a year to dayly spite; so back to Gonerell, who Bereavde him of his servantes all save one. Leire’s journey to France takes only one line. Cordila left her husband behind in France, perhaps because Higgins did not want a foreigner to conquer Britain. [Cf. n. 2347+2–+7.] In the second part of the poem, describing Cordila’s sufferings in prison, she is visited by Despair, who tempts her to suicide and offers her the knife used by Dido. By killing herself Cordila falls into deadly sin. From The Mirror Shakespeare probably took the squires of Lear’s train ([750]), its reduction by a half ([810]), [276] the suggestion that he should content himself with one or none, and Cordelia’s begging her husband to help her father ([2377–8]). Maybe Higgins’s emphasis on Cordila’s wretched end affected the dramatist. The captain at [3212–14] has been instructed To…herself. But there is no allegory here. Edmund’s excuse for imprisoning Lear and Cordelia, lest they gain popular support, may have been suggested by Margan’s motive: Fearing lest she should recover ayde.

div.head: Albions England (1586)
div.p: William Warner’s historicall map of England in the form of verse narratives was published in four books in 1586 and was successively enlarged by two to four books in each of the editions of 1589, 1592, 1596, and 1602 until it grew to sixteen books in 1606. The first instalment covered the national history from the beginning down to the death of Henry VII; the last brought it down to James I. The story of Leir appears in Book 3 (1586, pp. 58–9); any influence on Sh.’s play may have come only indirectly through the earlier play Leir, for which Warner may be the main source. There is no modern scholarly edition; an incomplete reprint may be found in vol. 4 of Alexander Chalmers, English Poets (1810). The Leir narrative is excerpted in Lee (ed. Leir, 1909, pp. 129–31) and Bullough (1973, pp. 335–6).

The black letter of the original 1586 edition is here printed in roman type, and the roman of the original in italic type; long s is printed s. The page numbers in the 1586 edition are indicated by bracketed italics in the outer right margin opposite the first line on each page; passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes, in the right margin opposite the line containing the first word of the passage discussed.

lg.l: About a thirtie yeres and fiue did Leir rule this Land,[DP 2]
When, doting on his Daughters three, with them he fell in hand[tln 53–8]
To tell how much they loued him: the Eldest did esteeme
Her life inferior to her loue, so did the Second deeme:[tln 80–1]
The Yongest sayd her loue was such as did a childe behoue,
And that how much himself was worth, so much she him did loue.
The formost two did please him well, the yongest did not so:
Upon the Prince of Albanie the First he did bestoe,[DP 6]
The Middle on the Cornish Prince: their Dowrie was his Throne,[DP 5, 16; tln 45–50]
At his decease: Cordellas parte was very small, or none.[tln 7, DP 17]
Yet for her forme, and vertuous life, a noble Gallian King[DP 3–4]
Did her, vn-dowed, for his Queene into his Countrie bring.
Her Sisters sicke of Fathers health, their Husbands by consent
Did ioyne in Armes: from Leir so by force the Scepter went:[tln 45–50]
Yet, for they promise pentions large, he rather was content.
In Albanie the quondam King at eldest Daughters Court
Was setled scarce, when she repynes, and lessens still his Porte.
His second Daughter then, he thought, would shewe her selfe more kinde,
To whom, he going, for a while did franke allowance finde.
Ere long, abridging almost all, she keepeth him so loe,
That of two badds, for betters choyce he backe againe did goe.
But Gonorill at his returne, not onely did attempt[DP 15]
Her fathers death, but openly did hold him in contempt.
His aged eyes powre out their teares, when holding vp his hands,
He sayd: O God, who so thou art, that my good happ withstands,
Prolong not life, deferre not death, my selfe I ouer-liue,
When those, that owe to me their liues, to me my death would giue.
Thou Towne, whose walles roose of my wealth, stand euermore to tell
Thy Founders Fall, and warne that none doe fall as Leir fell.
Bid none affie in Friends, for say, his Children wrought his wracke:
Yea those, that were to him most deare, did loath and let him lacke.
Cordella, well Cordella sayd, she loued as a Childe:
But sweeter words we seeke than sooth, and so are men begilde.
She onely rests vntryed yet: but what may I expect
From her? to whom I nothing gaue, when these doe me reiect.
Then dye, nay trye, the rule may fayle, and Nature may assend:
Nor are they euer surest friends, on whom we most doe spend.
He shippes himself to Gallia then: but maketh knowne before
Unto Cordella his estate, who rueth him so poore,
And kept his there ariuall close, till she prouided had
To furnish him in euery want. Of him her King was glad,
And nobly intertayned him: the Queene, with teares among,
(Her duetie done) conferreth with her father of his wrong.
Such duetie, bountie, kindnes, and increasing loue, he found
In that his Daughter and her Lord, that sorrowes more abound
For his vnkindly vsing her, then for the others cryme:
And King-like thus in Agamps Court did Leir dwell, till tyme
The noble King his Sonne-in-law transports an Armie greate,
Of forcie Gawles, possessing him of dispossessed Seate,
To whom Cordeilla did succeede, not raigning long in queate.
Not how her Nephewes warre with her and one of them slew th’other
Shall followe: but I will disclose a most tyrannous mother.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Warner
div.p: Passages from Warner’s account of Leir are referred to in these notes: DP 2, 3–4, 5, 6, 15, 16, 17; TLN 7, 45–50, 53–8, 80–1. The following notes refer to other passages in Warner: DP 9–10, 11; TLN 5, 676.
Steevens (ed. 1778, 9:349 n.): Warner is a source for the play.

Perrett (1904, pp. 89–90) makes no suggestion that this popular long episodic poem influenced Sh., but (p. 90) in first telling of an attempt on Leir’s life it influenced the old play Leir. Lee (ed. Leir, 1909, p. xxvii n.): Warner’s Albion’s England (1586) is the chief source of the old play Leir.

Bullough (1973, p. 276): In William Warner’s Albions England…Leir’s life follows that of Locrine, and occupies 48 lines (Bk. III, Ch. xiv), bewailing his miseries and asserting that Goneril did attempt | Her fathers death. His restoration is described; Cordella’s fate is not mentioned. Nothing suggests that Shakespeare was influenced by this piece.

div.head: The Faerie Queene (1590)
div.p: Books I–III of Spenser’s epic appeared in 1590; these were augmented by Books IV–VI in 1596, and by the Mutability Cantos in 1609. The story of Leyr appears in Bk. II, canto x, where, in Alma’s House of Temperance, Prince Arthur reads A chronicle of Briton kings, from Brute to Vthers rayne. Of the many modern editions, the Spenser Variorum (ed. Edwin Greenlaw et al., 1932–49) may claim prime scholarly importance. Spenser’s verses on Lear have been excerpted in Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 391–2), Fischer (1914, pp. 30–2), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905, pp. 134–5), Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 237–8), Satin (1966, pp. 456–7), Bullough (1973, pp. 332–4)

The roman and italic of the original 1590 edition are here reproduced; long s is printed s. Stanza numbers have been supplied in brackets. The page numbers in the 1590 edition are indicated by bracketed italics in the outer right margin opposite the first line on each page; passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes, in the right margin opposite the line containing the first word of the passage discussed.

lg.l: Next him king Leyr in happie peace long raynd,[DP 2]
But had no issue male him to succeed,
But three faire daughters, which were well vptraind,
In all that seemed fitt for kingly seed:
Mongst whom his realme he equally decreed[tln 53–8]
To haue diuided. Tho when feeble age
Nigh to his vtmost date he saw proceed,
He cald his daughters; and with speeches sage
Inquyrd, which of them most did loue her parentage.[tln 53–8]
The eldest Gonorill gan to protest,[DP 15]
That she much more then her owne life him lou’d:[tln 63]
And Regan greater loue to him profest,[DP 16, tln 80–1]
Then all the world, when euer it were proou’d;
But Cordeill said she lou’d him, as behoou’d:[DP 17, tln 98–9]
Whose simple answere, wanting colours fayre
To paint it forth, him to displeasaunce moou’d,
That in his crown he counted her no hayre,
But twixt the other twain his kingdom whole did shayre.
So wedded th’one to Maglan king of Scottes,[DP 6]
And thother to the king of Cambria,[DP 5]
And twixt them shayrd his realme by equall lottes:
But without dowre the wise Cordelia,[DP 17]
Was sent to Aggannip of Celtica.[DP 3–4]
Their aged Syre, thus eased of his crowne,
A priuate life ledd in Albania,
With Gonorill, long had in great renowne,
That nought him grieu’d to beene from rule deposed downe.
But true it is that when the oyle is spent,[tln 728–9]
The light goes out, and weeke is throwne away;
So when he had resignd his regiment,[tln 45–50]
His daughter gan despise his drouping day,
And wearie wax of his continuall stay.
Tho to his daughter Regan he repayrd,
Who him at first well vsed euery way;
But when of his departure she despayrd,
Her bountie she abated, and his cheare empayrd.[tln 1441]
The wretched man gan then auise to late,
That loue is not, where most it is profest,
Too truely tryde in his extremest state;
At last resolu’d likewise to proue the rest,
He to Cordelia him selfe addrest,[DP 17]
Who with entyre affection him receau’d,
As for her Syre and king her seemed best;
And after all an army strong she leau’d,[tln 2347+2–+7]
To war on those, which him had of his realme bereau’d.
So to his crowne she him restord againe,
In which he dyde, made ripe for death by eld,
And after wild, it should to her remaine:
Who peaceably the same long time did weld:
And all mens harts in dew obedience held:
Till that her sisters children, woxen strong,
Through proud ambition against her rebeld,
And ouercommen kept in prison long,
Till weary of that wretched life, her selfe she hong.[tln 2980, 3212–14, 3214]
Then gan the bloody brethren both to raine:
But fierce Cundah gan shortly to enuy
His brother Morgan, prickt with proud disdaine,
To haue a pere in part of souerainty,
And kindling coles of cruell enmity,
Raisd warre, and him in batteill ouerthrew:
Whence as he to those woody hilles did fly,
Which hight of him Glamorgan, there him slew:
Then did he raigne alone, when he none equall knew.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Spenser
div.p: References to Spenser’s account of Leir are found in the following notes: DP 2, 3–4, 5, 6, 15, 16, 17; TLN 45–50, 53–8, 63, 80–1, 98–9, 728–9, 1441, 2347+2–+7, 2478, 2980, 3212–14, 3214, 3238. References to other possible sources in Spenser are found in notes 1564–71, 1749, 1835, 1873–4, 2429, 2480, 2490–6, 2949, 3217.

Lennox (1754, 3:302): Spencer seems to have furnished Shakespear with the Hint of Cordelia’s Manner of Death.…Cordelia…hanged herself. In Shakespear, Cordelia does not hang herself, but is hanged by a Soldier; a very improper Catastrophe for a Person of such exemplary Virtue.

Murphy (1754; 1756, pp. 223–5) reprints the lines from Spenser, not to hint that they are a source but only for the sake of comparison, proving the rightness, historically and emotionally, of Tate’s happy ending.

Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xxix f.): Sh. seems to have followed Spenser in having already divided his realm into equal shares before asking his daughters to gratify his ears with loving speeches. (P. xxx): It is also practically certain…that the beautiful name Cordelia comes from the Faerie Queene; in the older versions she is Cordoylle or Gordoylle, Cordeilla, Cordeill, Cordella, Cordell (Spenser once has Cordeill). Only Spenser and Leir make Regan wed the King of Cambria, though one account makes her wed the Duke of Wales and Cornwall. Greg (1940, p. 399): FQ also shares the form Regan with Holinshed and Shakespeare.

Perrett (1904, pp. 92, 242, 273) Rhyme in Spenser’s difficult stanza is responsible for the form Cordelia…and for the hanging of the heroine (herself she hong to rhyme with strong and long.…[242] It was by no means the tradition…until 1590, that Cordelia hanged herself in prison. Wherever, outside FQ, the manner of suicide is specified, it is by the steel. [273] Knight, Craig, and others find a similarity of thought between [728]…and the comparison of Leir in FQ with a wick,…but the simile of the lamp or candle was quite a commonplace, and [could as well]…have suggested [2478]. See nn. 728–9, 2478.

Lee (1909, p. 112): In Holinshed…Leir reserves half his property for himself, and only divides the remaining half between his two daughters. Spenser was the first writer to make Leir deliberately give his whole kingdom away in two halves. Bullough (1973, p. 273): Leyr proposes to divide his realm equally until Cordelia disappoints him by her simple answere.

Watkins (1950, pp. 98–9), without claiming direct influence: The type of characterization in King Lear resulting from this combination of psychological realism and symbolical stylization…is of the same order as Spenser’s when, at his best in the Faerie Queene, he fuses abstract and concrete.…Goneril, the most astonishing characterization in King Lear, represents this fusion perfectly.…Though psychology is present…[99] she is superhuman, a symbol in the allegory toward which the play tends.

Potts (1958, pp. 180–8): Lr. owes details to Bk. I of FQ: Surely Duessa has bequeathed to Goneril her characteristic hypocrisy. When she deserted the Redcrosse Knight for Sansjoi and, at the end of the Book of Holiness, sent a desperate letter by Archimago to thwart the alliance of the Redcrosse and Una, she possibly suggested to Shakespeare an end for King Lear. Witness the letter Goneril sends by Oswald to urge upon Edmund the murder of Albany.…[181] Both intrigues fail.…The battle between Redcrosse Knight and Sansjoi in the lists of Lucifera at the House of Pride…may have helped furnish the last scene of King Lear with its pledge and exchange and its triply sounded trumpet. Potts further argues that there is an allegorical design behind the ordeal of Lear and Gloucester similar to the allegory of the House of Pride, Cave of Despaire, and House of Holiness (cantos iv–v, ix, and x). Duessa and Lucifera are haughty; so are Goneril and Regan. Lucifera looks in a mirror; so do Oswald and Goneril. (P. 182): Sloth rides on an ass and is riotous; the knights may be riotous and the Fool refers to an ass. Lechery rides on a goat, Edmund associates lechery with a goatish disposition. Envy is associated with wolves and snakes; so is Goneril. (P. 183): Lear illustrates Wrath, because he shakes with ague and wears rags. The Redcrosse Knight and his Dwarf…prefigure Lear and the Fool, emerging from the clutches of Goneril and Regan. Gloucester’s story is indebted…hypothetically to Spenser’s Cave of Despair. Gloucester’s hovel is in bleak country, like Spenser’s Cave, and (p. 185) Despaire offers a rope and knife to Sir Trevisan. Edgar comes out of the hovel, Sir Trevisan out of the Cave. (P. 186): Cordelia serves Lear as Una and Mercie serve Redcrosse, and Cordelia’s doctor is not unlike Patience, whose name refers to a subject Lear talks about, and Lear and Cordelia are reunited as Una and Redcrosse. (P. 187): Lear’s white flakes are like Contemplation’s snowy lockes. Redcrosse sees a New Jerusalem, (p. 188) Lear and Cordelia will laugh at gilded butterflies. (This argument rests wholly on commonplace similarities of vocabulary, details of action, plot devices, character, setting, and ideas.)

Weiner (1991, pp. 261 ff.): Only in Shakespeare does Cordelia’s army lose; only in Shakespeare is the captive Cordelia murdered.…[263] Shakespeare’s ending appears to reflect the play’s rejection of suicide [cf. Gloucester’s attempt].…[264] The play tries to teach us that Cordelia’s death is preferable to the one history had in store for her.…[265] Spenser can allow Cordelia to commit suicide because he is going to provide alternate [providential] views of history that will render suicide an inadequate [266] and unnecessary response to the world; Shakespeare, to the extent that he has internalized that Spenserian perspective, needs to preserve Cordelia from [mortally sinful] self-slaughter such as Goneril’s. By correcting Spenser’s history, Shakespeare affirms the truth that both he and Spenser believed lies at the heart of life’s mystery…the ultimate meaning of history. (Higgins’s Cordila moralizes her suicide as folly and mortal sin.)

Maxwell (in Wilson, ed. 1960; see n. 2429) suspects influence of the Malbecco episode in FQ 2.9–10 on Gloucester’s attempted suicide. Tobin (1979, p. 266) detects the same episode, with its vocabulary describing exclusion from a castle, a storm, lack of courtesy, blindness, Cupid, entreaties, kennelled dogs, and a dotard’s rage, finding its way into Lear in several thematically parallel scenes, e.g., II. iv, III. i, III. iv, and IV. vi, in addition to the fall from Dover cliff. Anderson (1987) finds a few possible verbal echoes of Bks. 2, 5, and 6: see nn. 728–9, 1564–71, 2949, 3217.

div.head: The True Chronicle History of King Leir and His Three Daughters (1605)
div.p: The chief source of Sh.’s Lr. is an older, anonymous play on the Lear story, evidently acted by the Queen’s Men in the early 1590s and published in 1605 at about the time Sh. was beginning to compose his play. In his Diary Philip Henslowe recorded performances of a kinge leare, presumably at the Rose Theatre, on 6 and 8 April 1594. The entries appear in a column of plays performed by the Quenes men & my lord of Susexe to gether, the companies probably playing in the same theater on alternate days. Chambers (1923, 4:25): As the play is not named in the Sussex’s repertory of 1593–4 [Henslowe’s Diary, ed. Greg, 1:16], there is a presumption that it belonged to the Queen’s. A month later, in May, Henslowe reported that the Queen’s Men brocke & went into the contrey to playe, and for the rest of their life, until 1603, the company toured in the provinces. Before leaving London for good they divested themselves of unneeded, probably duplicate, copies of a number of their plays, selling them to stationers for future publication. The printer Edward White acquired the manuscript of The moste famous Chronicle historye of Leire kinge of England and his Three Daughters, and though he registered it at Stationers’ Hall on 14 May 1594 he apparently never published it. On 8 May 1605 another stationer, Simon Stafford, registered ownership of A booke called the Tragecall [altered from Tragedie] historie [interlined] of Kinge Leir and his Three Daughters &c[es]. As it was latelie Acted. On the same day he transferred ownership to another stationer, John Wright, who until recently had been apprentice to Edward White. Later in 1605 Stafford printed and Wright published The True Chronicle History of King Leir, and his three daughters, Gonorill, Ragan, and Cordella. As it hath bene diuers and sundry times lately acted. There is no reason to doubt that these are all substantially the same play; McMillin & MacLean (1998) demonstrate that the subject, structure, style, dramaturgy, and casting of the play represented in the 1605 edition are typical of Queen’s Men’s plays from the early 1590s. The clerk at Stationers’ Hall apparently botched his 1605 entry, first writing Tragedie and then partially correcting to Tragecall historie; the printed title, however, is practically the same as the title entered in 1594, both calling the play a chronicle history. Halliwell-Phillipps (1882, p. 284; 1890, 2:338) thinks there were two plays, that of 1605 and the other of 1594 more like Sh.’s, on the unlikely grounds that Kentes woden leage in Henslowe’s inventory of props (March 1598–9) refers to the stocks, rather than to the wooden leg in Marlowe’s Faust, possibly worn by William Kemp. (Chambers, 1923, 2:168; 1930, 1:470 conjectures other plays having such a property.) The hypothesis of two plays is revived by Cairncross (1936, p. 168), Alexander (1964, pp. 230–4), and Everitt (1965, p. 11); lacking tangible evidence, it has not been generally accepted. For doubtful theories that Sh. had known Leir since the beginning of his career, either from having seen it, or having acted in it, or having had access to a manuscript of it, see Knowles (2002, pp. 17–35) and . In all likelihood Sh. used the printed ed. of 1605.

There is no satisfactory attribution of authorship; among authors proposed are Kyd, Greene, Peele, Lodge, Munday, William Rankins, and the young Shakespeare. Most recently Brian Vickers has found what he considers conclusive evidence, of vocabulary and phrasing, for Kyd’s authorship; Kyd is not known to have written for the Queen’s Men, and Leir is a typically Queen’s-Men play. Apparent echoes of Lodge’s Rosalynde (1590) and Spenser’s Faerie Queene (1590) may set the earlier limit for the date of composition, and its 1594 performance sets the later limit. Perrett (1904) and Michie (1979) agree that the anonymous dramatist selected materials from the recent metrical versions by Warner, Higgins, and Spenser, and probably did not use Geoffrey or Holinshed, as earlier commentators had claimed. After its appearance in 1605 the play was never reissued. It has been included in collections by George Steevens (1766), George Steevens & John Nichols (1779), Hazlitt (1875, 6:305–87), Fischer (1914, pp. 36–170), E. B. Everitt & R. L. Armstrong (1965), Satin (1966, pp. 458–526), and Bullough (1973, pp. 337–402), in excerpts in Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 393–401) and Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 221–34), and in separate editions by Arthur F. Hopkinson (1895), Walter W. Greg (1907), Sidney Lee (1909), John S. Farmer (1910), Michie (1979; rpt. 1991), and Cordelia Sherman (diss., 1982).

The roman and italic of the 1605 edition are here reproduced; long s is printed s. Although the lines have been given through-line numbers in the right margin, boldface scene numbers have also been supplied for ease of cross-reference. The signatures in the 1605 edition are indicated in brackets in the outer right margin opposite the first line on each page; passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes, in the right margin opposite the line containing the first word of the passage discussed.

body.head:
The true Chronicle Historie of King
Leir and his three daughters.[DP 2]
ACTVS I.

sp.speaker: [Leir.]
sp.p:
Thus to our griefe the obsequies performd
Of our (too late) deceast and dearest Queen,
Whose soule I hope, possest of heauẽly ioyes,
Doth ride in triumph ’mõgst the Cherubins;
Let vs request your graue aduice, my Lords,
For the disposing of our princely daughters,
For whom our care is specially imployd,
As nature bindeth to aduaunce their states,
In royall marriage with some princely mates:
For wanting now their mothers good aduice,
Vnder whose gouernment they haue receyued
A perfit patterne of a vertuous life:
Left as it were a ship without a sterne,
Or silly sheepe without a Pastors care;
Although our selues doe dearely tender them,
Yet are we ignorant of their affayres:
For fathers best do know to gouerne sonnes;
But daughters steps the mothers counsell turnes.
A sonne we want for to succeed our Crowne,
And course of time hath cancelled the date
Of further issue from our withered loynes:
One foote already hangeth in the graue,
And age hath made deepe furrowes in my face:
The world of me, I of the world am weary,[tln 43–6]
And I would fayne resigne these earthly cares,
And thinke vpon the welfare of my soule:
Which by no better meanes may be effected,
Then by resigning vp the Crowne from me,
In equall dowry to my daughters three.

sp.speaker: Skalliger.
sp.p:
A worthy care, my Liege, which well declares,[tln 669+1]
The zeale you bare vnto our quondam Queene:
And since your Grace hath licens’d me to speake, [A2v]
I censure thus; Your Maiesty knowing well,
What seuerall Suters your princely daughters haue,
To make them eche a Ioynter more or lesse,[tln 53–8]
As is their worth, to them that loue professe.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
No more, nor lesse, but euen all alike,
My zeale is fixt, all fashiond in one mould:
Wherefore vnpartiall shall my censure be,
Both old and young shall haue alike for me.

sp.speaker: Nobl.
sp.p:
My gracious Lord, I hartily do wish,
That God had lent you an heyre indubitate,
Which might haue set vpon your royall throne,
When fates should loose the prison of your life,
By whose succession all this doubt might cease;[tln 45–50]
And as by you, by him we might haue peace.
But after-wishes euer come too late,
And nothing can reuoke the course of fate:
Wherefore, my Liege, my censure deemes it best,
To match them with some of your neighbour Kings,
Bordring within the bounds of Albion,
By whose vnited friendship, this our state
May be protected ’gainst all forrayne hate.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Herein, my Lords, your wishes sort with mine,
And mine (I hope) do sort with heauenly powers:
For at this instant two neere neyghbouring Kings[tln 7; 42–3]
Of Cornwall and of Cambria, motion loue[DP 5]
To my two daughters, Gonorill and Ragan.[DP 15; 16]
My youngest daughter, fayre Cordella, vowes[DP 17]
No liking to a Monarch, vnlesse loue allowes.
She is sollicited by diuers Peeres;[tln 50]
But none of them her partiall fancy heares.
Yet, if my policy may her beguyle,
Ile match her to some King within this Ile,
And so establish such a perfit peace,
As fortunes force shall ne’re preuayle to cease.

sp.speaker: Perillus.
sp.p:
Of vs & ours, your gracious care, my Lord,[DP 8]
Deserues an euerlasting memory,
To be inrol’d in Chronicles of fame,
By neuer-dying perpetuity: [A3r]
Yet to become so prouident a Prince,
Lose not the title of a louing father:
Do not force loue, where fancy cannot dwell,
Lest streames being stopt, aboue the banks do swell.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
I am resolu’d, and euen now my mind[tln 53–8]
Doth meditate a sudden stratagem,
To try which of my daughters loues me best:
Which till I know, I cannot be in rest.
This graunted, when they ioyntly shall contend,
Eche to exceed the other in their loue:
Then at the vantage will I take Cordella,
Euen as she doth protest she loues me best,
Ile say, Then, daughter, graunt me one request,
To shew thou louest me as thy sisters doe,
Accept a husband, whom my selfe will woo.
This sayd, she cannot well deny my sute,
Although (poore soule) her sences will be mute:
Then will I tryumph in my policy,
And match her with a King of Brittany.

sp.speaker: Skal.
sp.p: Ile to them before, and bewray your secrecy.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Thus fathers think their children to beguile,
And oftentimes themselues do first repent,
When heauenly powers do frustrate their intent.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
I maruell, Ragan, how you can indure[tln 60–6, 74–81]
To see that proud pert Peat, our youngest sister,
So slightly to account of vs, her elders,
As if we were no better then her selfe!
We cannot haue a quaynt deuice so soone,
Or new made fashion, of our choyce inuention;[tln 1109]
But if she like it, she will haue the same,
Or study newer to exceed vs both.
Besides, she is so nice and so demure;
So sober, courteous, modest, and precise,
That all the Court hath worke ynough to do,
To talke how she exceedeth me and you.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
What should I do? would it were in my power,
To find a cure for this contagious ill: [A3v]
Some desperate medicine must be soone applyed,
To dimme the glory of her mounting fame;
Els ere’t be long, sheele haue both prick and praise,
And we must be set by for working dayes.
Doe you not see what seuerall choyce of Suters[tln 39]
She daily hath, and of the best degree?
Say, amongst all, she hap to fancy one,
And haue a husband when as we haue none:
Why then, by right, to her we must giue place,
Though it be ne’re so much to our disgrace.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
By my virginity, rather then she shall haue
A husband before me,
Ile marry one or other in his shirt:
And yet I haue made halfe a graunt already
Of my good will vnto the King of Cornwall.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
Sweare not so deeply (sister) here cõmeth my L. Skalliger:
Something his hasty comming doth import.

sp.speaker: Skal.
sp.p:
Sweet Princesses, I am glad I met you heere so luckily,
Hauing good newes which doth concerne you both,
And craueth speedy expedition.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
For Gods sake tell vs what it is, my Lord,
I am with child vntill you vtter it.

sp.speaker: Skal.
sp.p:
Madam, to saue your longing, this it is:
Your father in great secrecy to day,
Told me, he meanes to marry you out of hand,
Vnto the noble Prince of Cambria;
You, Madam, to the King of Cornwalls Grace:
Your yonger sister he would fayne bestow
Vpon the rich King of Hibernia:[tln 53–8]
But that he doubts, she hardly will consent;
For hitherto she ne’re could fancy him.
If she do yeeld, why then, betweene you three,
He will deuide his kingdome for your dowries.
But yet there is a further mystery,[tln 41]
Which, so you will conceale, I will disclose.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
What e’re thou speakst to vs, kind Skalliger,
Thinke that thou speakst it only to thy selfe.

sp.speaker: Skal.
sp.p:
He earnestly desireth for to know, [A4r]
Which of you three do beare most loue to him,
And on your loues he so extremely dotes,
As neuer any did, I thinke, before.
He presently doth meane to send for you,
To be resolu’d of this tormenting doubt:
And looke, whose answere pleaseth him the best,
They shall haue most vnto their marriages.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
O that I had some pleasing Mermayds voyce,
For to inchaunt his sencelesse sences with!

sp.speaker: Skal.
sp.p:
For he supposeth that Cordella will
(Striuing to go beyond you in her loue)
Promise to do what euer he desires:
Then will he straight enioyne her for his sake,
The Hibernian King in marriage for to take.
This is the summe of all I haue to say;
Which being done, I humbly take my leaue,
Not doubting but your wisdomes will foresee,
What course will best vnto your good agree.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Thanks, gentle Skalliger, thy kindnes vndeserued,
Shall not be vnrequited, if we liue.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
Now haue we fit occasion offred vs,
To be reueng’d vpon her vnperceyu’d.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Nay, our reuenge we will inflict on her,
Shall be accounted piety in vs:
I will so flatter with my doting father,
As he was ne’re so flattred in his life.
Nay, I will say, that if it be his pleasure,
To match me to a begger, I will yeeld:
For why, I know what euer I do say,
He meanes to match me with the Cornwall King.

sp.speaker: Ra.
sp.p:
Ile say the like: for I am well assured,
What e’re I say to please the old mans mind,
Who dotes, as if he were a child agayne,[tln 522+2–+3]
I shall inioy the noble Cambrian Prince:
Only, to feed his humour, will suffice,
To say, I am content with any one
Whom heele appoynt me; this will please him more,
Then e’re Apolloes musike pleased Ioue.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
I smile to think, in what a wofull plight
Cordella will be, when we answere thus:
For she will rather dye, then giue consent
To ioyne in marriage with the Irish King:
So will our father think, she loueth him not,
Because she will not graunt to his desire,
Which we will aggrauate in such bitter termes,
That he will soone conuert his loue to hate:
For he, you know, is alwayes in extremes.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Not all the world could lay a better plot,
I long till it be put in practice.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Perillus, go seeke my daughters,
Will them immediately come and speak with me.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p: I will, my gracious Lord.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Oh, what a combat feeles my panting heart,
’Twixt childrens loue, and care of Common weale!
How deare my daughters are vnto my soule,
None knowes, but he, that knowes my thoghts & secret deeds.
Ah, little do they know the deare regard,
Wherein I hold their future state to come:
When they securely sleepe on beds of downe,
These aged eyes do watch for their behalfe:
While they like wantons sport in youthfull toyes,
This throbbing heart is pearst with dire annoyes.
As doth the Sun excceed the smallest Starre,
So much the fathers loue exceeds the childs.
Yet my complaynts are causlesse: for the world
Affords not children more conformable:
And yet, me thinks, my mind presageth still
I know not what; and yet I feare some ill.
Enter Perillus, with the three daughters.
Well, here my daughters come: I haue found out
A present meanes to rid me of this doubt.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Our royall Lord and father, in all duty,
We come to know the tenour of your will,
Why you so hastily haue sent for vs?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Deare Gonorill, kind Ragan, sweet Cordella,[tln 2303+3] [B1r]
Ye florishing branches of a Kingly stocke,
Sprung from a tree that once did flourish greene,
Whose blossomes now are nipt with Winters frost,
And pale grym death doth wayt vpon my steps,[tln 45–50]
And summons me vnto his next Assizes.
Therefore, deare daughters, as ye tender the safety
Of him that was the cause of your first being,
Resolue a doubt which much molests my mind,
Which of you three to me would proue most kind;
Which loues me most, and which at my request
Will soonest yeeld vnto their fathers hest.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
I hope, my gracious father makes no doubt
Of any of his daughters loue to him:
Yet for my part, to shew my zeale to you,
Which cannot be in windy words rehearst,[tln 60]
I prize my loue to you at such a rate,[tln 75]
I thinke my life inferiour to my loue.[tln 63]
Should you inioyne me for to tye a milstone
About my neck, and leape into the Sea,
At your commaund I willingly would doe it:
Yea, for to doe you good, I would ascend
The highest Turret in all Brittany,
And from the top leape headlong to the ground:
Nay, more, should you appoynt me for to marry
The meanest vassayle in the spacious world,
Without reply I would accomplish it:
In briefe, commaund what euer you desire,
And if I fayle, no fauour I require.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: O, how thy words reuiue my dying soule!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: O, how I doe abhorre this flattery!

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: But what sayth Ragan to her fathers will?

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
O, that my simple vtterance could suffice,[tln 60–6]
To tell the true intention of my heart,
Which burnes in zeale of duty to your grace,
And neuer can be quench’d, but by desire
To shew the same in outward forwardnesse.
Oh, that there were some other mayd that durst
But make a challenge of her loue with me; [B1v]
Ide make her soone confesse she neuer loued
Her father halfe so well as I doe you.
I then, my deeds should proue in playner case,
How much my zeale aboundeth to your grace:
But for them all, let this one meane suffice,
To ratify my loue before your eyes:[tln 80–1]
I haue right noble Suters to my loue,[tln 106–110+1]
No worse then Kings, and happely I loue one:
Yet, would you haue me make my choyce anew,
Ide bridle fancy, and be rulde by you.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: Did neuer Philomel sing so sweet a note.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p: Did neuer flatterer tell so false a tale.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Speak now, Cordella, make my ioyes at full,
And drop downe Nectar from thy hony lips.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
I cannot paynt my duty forth in words,[tln 97–8]
I hope my deeds shall make report for me:[tln 247–8]
But looke what loue the child doth owe the father,[tln 98–9]
The same to you I beare, my gracious Lord.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Here is an answere answerlesse indeed:
Were you my daughter, I should scarcely brooke it.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Dost thou not blush, proud Peacock as thou art,
To make our father such a slight reply?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Why how now, Minion, are you growne so proud?[tln 100]
Doth our deare loue make you thus peremptory?[tln 89]
What, is your loue become so small to vs,
As that you scorne to tell vs what it is?
Do you loue vs, as euery child doth loue
Their father? True indeed, as some,
Who by disobedience short their fathers dayes,
And so would you; some are so father-sick,
That they make meanes to rid them from the world;
And so would you: some are indifferent,
Whether their aged parents liue or dye;
And so are you. But, didst thou know, proud gyrle,
What care I had to foster thee to this,
Ah, then thou wouldst say as thy sisters do:
Our life is lesse, then loue we owe to you.

sp.speaker: Cord.
Gon.
sp.p:
You were not best say I flatter: if you do,
My deeds shall shew, I flatter not with you.
I loue my father better then thou canst.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
The prayse were great, spoke from anothers mouth:
But it should seeme your neighbours dwell far off.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Nay, here is one, that will confirme as much
As she hath sayd, both for my selfe and her.
I say, thou dost not wish my fathers good.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p: Deare father.—

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Peace, bastard Impe, no issue of King Leir,[tln 764]
I will not heare thee speake one tittle more.
Call not me father, if thou loue thy life,[tln 120]
Nor these thy sisters once presume to name:
Looke for no helpe henceforth from me nor mine;
Shift as thou wilt, and trust vnto thy selfe:
My Kingdome will I equally deuide[tln 7]
’Twixt thy two sisters to their royall dowre,
And will bestow them worthy their deserts:
This done, because thou shalt not haue the hope,
To haue a childs part in the time to come,
