sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.p:
But I will proue her title to be nought
But shame, and the reward of Parricide,
And make her an example to the world,
For after-ages to admire her penance.
This will I do, as I am Cambriaes King,
Or lose my life, to prosecute reuenge.
Come, first let’s learne what newes is of our father,
And then proceed, as best occasion fits.

div.stage:
Enter Leir, Perillus, and two Marriners, in sea­[tln 2347+43–+47]
gownes and sea-caps.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
My honest friends, we are asham’d to shew
The great extremity of our present state,
In that at this time we are brought so low,
That we want money for to pay our passage.
The truth is so, we met with some good fellowes,
A little before we came aboord your ship,
Which stript vs quite of all the coyne we had,
And left vs not a penny in our purses:
Yet wanting mony, we will vse the meane,
To see you satisfied to the vttermost.

sp.speaker: 1. Mar.
sp.p:
Heres a good gown, ’twould become me passing wel,
I should be fine in it.

sp.speaker: 2. Mar.
sp.p: Heres a good cloke, I maruel how I should look in it.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Fayth, had we others to supply their roome,
Though ne’re so meane, you willingly should haue them.

sp.speaker: 1. Mar.
sp.p:
Do you heare, sir? you looke like an honest man; [G4v]
Ile not stand to do you a pleasure: here’s a good strõg motly ga­
berdine, cost me xiiij. good shillings at Billinsgate, giue me your
gowne for it, & your cap for mine, & ile forgiue your passage.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: With al my heart, and xx. thanks.

sp.speaker: 2. Mar.
sp.p:
Do you heare, sir? you shal haue a better match thẽ he,
because you are my friend: here is a good sheeps russet sea­
gowne, wil bide more stresse, I warrant you, then two of his, yet
for you seem to be an honest gentleman, I am content to chãge
it for your cloke, and aske you nothing for your passage more.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
My owne I willingly would change with thee,
And think my selfe indebted to thy kindnesse:
But would my friend might keepe his garment still.
My friend, ile giue thee this new dublet, if thou wilt
Restore his gowne vnto him back agayne.

sp.speaker: 1. Mar.
sp.p:
Nay, if I do, would I might ne’re eate powderd beefe
and mustard more, nor drink Can of good liquor whilst I liue.
My friend, you haue small reason to seeke to hinder me of my
bargaine: but the best is, a bargayne’s a bargayne.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Kind friend, it is much better as it is;Leir to Perillus.
For by this meanes we may escape vnknowne,
Till time and opportunity do fit.

sp.speaker: 2. Mar.
sp.p:
Hark, hark, they are laying their heads together,
Theile repent them of their bargayne anon,
’Twere best for vs to go while we are well.

sp.speaker: 1. Mar.
sp.p:
God be with you, sir, for your passage back agayne,
Ile vse you as vnreasonable as another.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
I know thou wilt; but we hope to bring ready money
With vs, when we come back agayne.Exeunt Mariners.
Were euer men in this extremity,[tln 1614]
In a strange country, and deuoyd of friends,
And not a penny for to helpe our selues?
Kind friend, what thinkst thou will become of vs?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Be of good cheere, my Lord, I haue a dublet,
Will yeeld vs mony ynough to serue our turnes,
Vntill we come vnto your daughters Court:
And then, I hope, we shall find friends ynough.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, kind Perillus, that is it I feare, [H1r]
And makes me faynt, or euer I come there.
Can kindnesse spring out of ingratitude?
Or loue be reapt, where hatred hath bin sowne?
Can Henbane ioyne in league with Methridate?[tln 2353–5]
Or Sugar grow in Wormwoods bitter stalke?
It cannot be, they are too opposite:
And so am I to any kindnesse here.
I haue throwne Wormwood on the sugred youth,
And like to Henbane poysoned the Fount,
Whence flowed the Methridate of a childs goodwil:
I, like an enuious thorne, haue prickt the heart,
And turnd sweet Grapes, to sowre vnrelisht Sloes:
The causelesse ire of my respectlesse brest,
Hath sowrd the sweet milk of dame Natures paps:
My bitter words haue gauld her hony thoughts,
And weeds of rancour chokt the flower of grace.
Then what remainder is of any hope,
But all our fortunes will go quite aslope?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Feare not, my Lord, the perfit good indeed,
Can neuer be corrupted by the bad:
A new fresh vessell still retaynes the taste
Of that which first is powr’d into the same:
And therfore, though you name yourselfe the thorn,
The weed, the gall, the henbane & the wormewood;
Yet sheele continue in her former state,
The hony, milke, Grape, Sugar, Methridate.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Thou pleasing Orator vnto me in wo,[tln 3213]
Cease to beguile me with thy hopefull speaches:
O ioyne with me, and thinke of nought but crosses,
And then weele one lament anothers losses.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Why, say the worst, the worst can be but death,[tln 2179–80, 2210–11]
And death is better then for to despaire:[tln 2932]
Then hazzard death, which may conuert to life;
Banish despaire, which brings a thousand deathes.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Orecome with thy strong arguments, I yeeld,
To be directed by thee, as thou wilt:
As thou yeeldst comfort to my crazed thoughts,
Would I could yeeld the like vnto thy body,
Which is full weake, I know, and ill apayd, [H1v]
For want of fresh meat and due sustenance.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Alack, my Lord, my heart doth bleed, to think
That you should be in such extremity.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Come, let vs go, and see what God will send;
When all meanes faile, he is the surest friend.

div.stage:
Enter the Gallian King and Queene, and Mumford, with a
basket, disguised like Countrey folke.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
This tedious iourney all on foot, sweet Loue,
Cannot be pleasing to your tender ioynts,
Which ne’re were vsed to these toylesome walks.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
I neuer in my life tooke more delight
In any iourney, then I do in this:
It did me good, when as we hapt to light
Amongst the merry crue of country folke,
To see what industry and paynes they tooke,
To win them commendations ’mongst their friends.
Lord, how they labour to bestir themselues,
And in their quirks to go beyond the Moone,
And so take on them with such antike fits,
That one would think they were beside their wits!
Come away, Roger, with your basket.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
Soft, Dame, here comes a couple of old youthes,
I must needs make my selfe fat with iesting at them.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Nay, prithy do not, they do seeme to beEnter Leir
Men much o’regone with griefe and misery.& Perillus
Let’s stand aside, and harken what they say.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, my Perillus, now I see we both
Shall end our dayes in this vnfruitfull soyle.
Oh, I do faint for want of sustenance:
And thou, I know, in little better case.
No gentle tree affords one taste of fruit,
To comfort vs, vntill we meet with men:
No lucky path conducts our lucklesse steps
Vnto a place where any comfort dwels.
Sweet rest betyde vnto our happy soules;
For here I see our bodies must haue end.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Ah, my deare Lord, how doth my heart lament,
To see you brought to this extremity!
O, if you loue me, as you do professe, [H2r]
Or euer thought well of me in my life,He strips vp his arme.
Feed on this flesh, whose veynes are not so dry,
But there is vertue left to comfort you.
O, feed on this, if this will do you good,
Ile smile for ioy, to see you suck my bloud.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
I am no Caniball, that I should delight
To slake my hungry iawes with humane flesh:
I am no deuill, or ten times worse then so,
To suck the bloud of such a peerelesse friend.
O, do not think that I respect my life
So dearely, as I do thy loyall loue.
Ah, Brittayne, I shall neuer see thee more,
That hast vnkindly banished thy King:
And yet not thou dost make me to complayne,
But they which were more neere to me then thou.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
What do I heare? this lamentable voyce,[tln 2188, 2552, 2743]
Me thinks, ere now I oftentimes haue heard.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, Gonorill, was halfe my Kingdomes gift
The cause that thou didst seeke to haue my life?
Ah, cruell Ragan, did I giue thee all,[tln 1547]
And all could not suffice without my bloud?
Ah, poore Cordella, did I giue thee nought,
Nor neuer shall be able for to giue?
O, let me warne all ages that insueth,
How they trust flattery, and reiect the trueth.
Well, vnkind Girles, I here forgiue you both,
Yet the iust heauens will hardly do the like;
And only craue forgiuenesse at the end
Of good Cordella, and of thee, my friend;
Of God, whose Maiesty I haue offended,
By my transgression many thousand wayes:
Of her, deare heart, whom I for no occasion
Turn’d out of all, through flatterers perswasion:
Of thee, kind friend, who but for me, I know,
Hadst neuer come vnto this place of wo.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Alack, that euer I should liue to see
My noble father in this misery.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Sweet Loue, reueale not what thou art as yet,
Vntill we know the ground of all this ill.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
O, but some meat, some meat: do you not see,
How neere they are to death for want of food?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Lord, which didst help thy seruants at their need,
Or now or neuer send vs helpe with speed.
Oh comfort, comfort! yonder is a banquet,
And men and women, my Lord: be of good cheare;
For I see comfort comming very neere.
O my Lord, a banquet, and men and women!

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
O, let kind pity mollify their hearts,
That they may helpe vs in our great extreames.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
God saue you, friends; & if this blessed banquet
Affordeth any food or sustenance,
Euen for his sake that saued vs all from death,
Vouchsafe to saue vs from the gripe of famine.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Here father, sit and eat, here, sit & drink:him to the table.
And would it were far better for your sakes.

div.stage: Perillus takes Leir by the hand to the table.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Ile giue you thanks anon: my friend doth faynt,
And needeth present comfort.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
I warrant, he ne’re stayes to say grace:
O, theres no sauce to a good stomake.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p: The blessed God of heauen hath thought vpon vs.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
The thanks be his, and these kind courteous folke,
By whose humanity we are preserued.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
And may that draught be vnto him, as wasdrinkes.
That which old Eson dranke, which did renue
His withered age, and made him young againe.
And may that meat be vnto him, as was
That which Elias ate, in strength whereof
He walked fourty dayes, and neuer faynted.
Shall I conceale me longer from my father?
Or shall I manifest my selfe to him?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Forbeare a while, vntill his strength returne,[tln 2838+1]
Lest being ouer ioyed with seeing thee,
His poore weake sences should forsake their office,
And so our cause of ioy be turnd to sorrow.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p: What chere, my Lord? how do you feele your selfe?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Me thinks, I neuer ate such sauory meat:
It is as pleasant as the blessed Manna, [H3r]
That raynd from heauen amongst the Israelites:
It hath recall’d my spirits home agayne,
And made me fresh, as earst I was before.
But how shall we congratulate their kindnesse?

sp.speaker: Per.
Leir.
sp.p: Nay, stay, Perillus, for they shall haue mine.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p: Pardon, my Lord, I sweare they shall haue mine.

div.stage: Perillus proffers his dublet: they will not take it.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, who would think such kindnes should remayne
Among such strange and vnacquainted men:
And that such hate should harbour in the brest
Of those, which haue occasion to be best?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Ah, good old father, tell to me thy griefe,[tln 2517]
Ile sorrow with thee, if not adde reliefe.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, good young daughter, I may call thee so;
For thou art like a daughter I did owe.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Do you not owe her still? what, is she dead?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
No, God forbid: but all my interest’s gone,
By shewing my selfe too much vnnaturall:
So haue I lost the title of a father,
And may be call’d a stranger to her rather.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Your title’s good still; for tis alwayes knowne,
A man may do as him list with his owne.
But haue you but one daughter then in all?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: Yes, I haue more by two, then would I had.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
O, say not so, but rather see the end:
They that are bad, may haue the grace to mend:
But how haue they offended you so much?

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
If from the first I should relate the cause,
’Twould make a heart of Adamant to weepe;
And thou, poore soule, kind-hearted as thou art,
Dost weepe already, ere I do begin.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
For Gods loue tell it, and when you haue done,
Ile tell the reason why I weepe so soone.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Then know this first, I am a Brittayne borne,
And had three daughters by one louing wife: [H3v]
And though I say it, of beauty they were sped;
Especially the youngest of the three,
For her perfections hardly matcht could be:
On these I doted with a ielous loue,
And thought to try which of them lou’d me best,
By asking them, which would do most for me?
The first and second flattred me with words,
And vowd they lou’d me better then their liues:
The youngest sayd, she loued me as a child
Might do: her answere I esteem’d most vild,
And presently in an outragious mood,
I turnd her from me to go sinke or swym:
And all I had, euen to the very clothes,
I gaue in dowry with the other two:
And she that best deseru’d the greatest share,
I gaue her nothing, but disgrace and care.
Now mark the sequell: When I had done thus,
I soiournd in my eldest daughters house,
Where for a time I was intreated well,
And liu’d in state sufficing my content:
But euery day her kindnesse did grow cold,[tln 597]
Which I with patience put vp well ynough,[tln 598–9]
And seemed not to see the things I saw:
But at the last she grew so far incenst
With moody fury, and with causlesse hate,
That in most vild and contumelious termes,
She bade me pack, and harbour somewhere else.
Then was I fayne for refuge to repayre
Vnto my other daughter for reliefe,
Who gaue me pleasing and most courteous words;
But in her actions shewed her selfe so sore,
As neuer any daughter did before:
She prayd me in a morning out betime,
To go to a thicket two miles from the Court,
Poynting that there she would come talke with me:
There she had set a shaghayrd murdring wretch,
To massacre my honest friend and me.
Then iudge your selfe, although my tale be briefe,
If euer man had greater cause of griefe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Nor neuer like impiety was done,
Since the creation of the world begun.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
And now I am constraind to seeke reliefe
Of her, to whom I haue bin so vnkind;
Whose censure, if it do award me death,
I must confesse she payes me but my due:
But if she shew a louing daughters part,
It comes of God and her, not my desert.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: No doubt she will, I dare be sworne she will.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: How know you that, not knowing what she is?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
My selfe a father haue a great way hence,
Vsde me as ill as euer you did her;
Yet, that his reuerend age I once might see,
Ide creepe along, to meet him on my knee.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: O, no mens children are vnkind but mine.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Condemne not all, because of others crime:
But looke, deare father, looke, behold and see
Thy louing daughter speaketh vnto thee.She kneeles.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
O, stand thou vp, it is my part to kneele,
And aske forgiuenesse for my former faults.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
O, if you wish I should inioy my breath,
Deare father rise, or I receiue my death.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Then I will rise, to satisfy your mind,
But kneele againe, til pardon be resignd.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
I pardon you: the word beseemes not me:
But I do say so, for to ease your knee.
You gaue me life, you were the cause that I
Am what I am, who else had neuer bin.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
But you gaue life to me and to my friend,
Whose dayes had else, had an vntimely end.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
You brought me vp, when as I was but young,
And far vnable for to helpe my selfe.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
I cast thee forth, when as thou wast but young,
And far vnable for to helpe thy selfe.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
God, world and nature say I do you wrong,
That can indure to see you kneele so long.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Let me breake off this louing controuersy,
Which doth reioyce my very soule to see.
Good father, rise, she is your louing daughter,He riseth. [H4v]
And honours you with as respectiue duty,
As if you were the Monarch of the world.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
But I will neuer rise from off my knee,She kneeles.
Vntill I haue your blessing, and your pardon[tln 2811]
Of all my faults committed any way,
From my first birth vnto this present day.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
The blessing, which the God of Abraham gaue
Vnto the trybe of Iuda, light on thee,
And multiply thy dayes, that thou mayst see
Thy childrens children prosper after thee.
Thy faults, which are iust none that I do know,
God pardon on high, and I forgiue below.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Now is my heart at quiet, and doth leape
Within my brest, for ioy of this good hap:
And now (deare father) welcome to our Court,
And welcome (kind Perillus) vnto me,
Myrrour of vertue and true honesty.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
O, he hath bin the kindest friend to me,
That euer man had in aduersity.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
My toung doth faile, to say what heart doth think,
I am so rauisht with exceeding ioy.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
All you haue spoke: now let me speak my mind,
And in few words much matter here conclude:he kneeles.
If ere my heart do harbour any ioy,
Or true content repose within my brest,
Till I haue rooted out this viperous sect,[tln 802]
And repossest my father of his Crowne,
Let me be counted for the periurdst man,
That euer spake word since the world began.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
Let me pray to, that neuer pray’d before;Mumford
If ere I resalute the Brittish earth,kneeles.
(As (ere’t be long) I do presume I shall)
And do returne from thence without my wench,
Let me be gelded for my recompence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Come, let’s to armes for to redresse this wrong:
Till I am there, me thinks, the time seemes long.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
I feele a hell of conscience in my brest,
Tormenting me with horrour for my fact, [I1r]
And makes me in an agony of doubt,
For feare the world should find my dealing out.
The slaue whom I appoynted for the act,[tln 2851]
I ne’re set eye vpon the peasant since:
O, could I get him for to make him sure,
My doubts would cease, and I should rest secure.
But if the old men, with perswasiue words,
Haue sau’d their liues, and made him to relent;
Then are they fled vnto the Court of Fraunce,
And like a Trumpet manifest my shame.
A shame on these white-liuerd slaues, say I,
That with fayre words so soone are ouercome.
O God, that I had bin but made a man;
Or that my strength were equall with my will!
These foolish men are nothing but meere pity,
And melt as butter doth against the Sun.
Why should they haue preeminence ouer vs,
Since we are creatures of more braue resolue?
I sweare, I am quite out of charity
With all the heartlesse men in Christendome.
A poxe vpon them, when they are affrayd
To giue a stab, or slit a paltry Wind-pipe,
Which are so easy matters to be done.
Well, had I thought the slaue would serue me so,
My selfe would haue bin executioner:
Tis now vndone, and if that it be knowne,
Ile make as good shift as I can for one.
He that repines at me, how ere it stands,
’Twere best for him to keepe him from my hands.

div.stage:
Sound Drums & Trumpets: Enter the Gallian King,
Leir, Mumford and the army.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thus haue we brought our army to the sea,
Whereas our ships are ready to receyue vs:
The wind stands fayre, and we in foure houres sayle,[tln 1638+6]
May easily arriue on Brittish shore,
Where vnexpected we may them surprise,
And gayne a glorious victory with ease.
Wherefore, my louing Countreymen, resolue,
Since truth and iustice fighteth on our sides, [I1v]
That we shall march with conquest where we go.
My selfe will be as forward as the first,[tln 2347+2–+7]
And step by step march with the hardiest wight:
And not the meanest souldier in our Campe
Shall be in danger, but ile second him.
To you, my Lord, we giue the whole commaund[tln 2347+9]
Of all the army, next vnto our selfe,
Not doubting of you, but you will extend
Your wonted valour in this needfull case,
Encouraging the rest to do the like,
By your approued magnanimity.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
My Liege, tis needlesse to spur a willing horse,
Thats apt enough to run himselfe to death:
For here I sweare by that sweet Saints bright eye,
Which are the starres, which guide me to good hap,
Eyther to see my old Lord crown’d anew,
Or in his cause to bid the world adieu.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Thanks, good Lord Mumford, tis more of your good will,
Then any merit or desert in me.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
And now to you, my worthy Countrymen,
Ye valiant race of Genouestan Gawles,
Surnamed Red-shanks, for your chyualry,
Because you fight vp to the shanks in bloud;
Shew your selues now to be right Gawles indeed,
And be so bitter on your enemies,
That they may say, you are as bitter as Gall.
Gall them, braue Shot, with your Artillery:
Gall them, braue Halberts, with your sharp point Billes,
Each in their poynted place, not one, but all,
Fight for the credit of your selues and Gawle.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Then what should more perswasion need to those,
That rather wish to deale, then heare of blowes?
Let’s to our ships, and if that God permit,
In foure houres sayle, I hope we shall be there.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
And in fiue houres more, I make no doubt,
But we shall bring our wish’d desires about.

div.stage: Enter a Captayne of the watch, and two watchmen.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p:
My honest friends, it is your turne to night,[tln 1638+2]
To watch in this place, neere about the Beacon, [I2r]
And vigilantly haue regard,
If any fleet of ships passe hitherward:
Which if you do, your office is to fire
The Beacon presently, and raise the towne.

sp.speaker: 1. Wat.
sp.p:
I, I, I, feare nothing; we know our charge, I warrant:
I haue bin a watchman about this Beacon this xxx. yere, and
yet I ne’re see it stir, but stood as quietly as might be.

sp.speaker: 2. Wat.
sp.p:
Fayth neighbour, and you’l follow my vice, instead of
watching the Beacon, wee’l go to goodman Gennings, & watch
a pot of Ale and a rasher of Bacon: and if we do not drink our
selues drunke, then so; I warrant, the Beacon will see vs when
we come out agayne.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p: I, but how if some body excuse vs to the Captayne?

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p:
Tis no matter, ile proue by good reason that we watch
the Beacon: asse for example.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p: I hope you do not call me asse by craft, neighbour.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p:
No, no, but for example: Say here stands the pot of ale,
thats the Beacon.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p: I, I, tis a very good Beacon.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p: Well, say here stands your nose, thats the fire.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p: Indeed I must confesse, tis somewhat red.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p:
I see come marching in a dish, halfe a score pieces of salt
Bacon.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p:
I vnderstand your meaning, thats as much to say,
half a score ships.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p:
True, you conster right; presently, like
a faithfull watchman, I fire the Beacon, and call vp the towne.

sp.speaker: 1. W.
sp.p:
I, thats as much as to say, you set your nose to the pot, and
drink vp the drink.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.p:
You are in the right; come, let’s go
fire the Beacon.

div.stage: Enter the King of Gallia with a stil march, Mumford & soldiers.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Now march our ensignes on the Brittish earth,[tln 2349]
And we are neere approching to the towne:
Then looke about you, valiant Countrymen,
And we shall finish this exployt with ease.
Th’inhabitants of this mistrustfull place,
Are dead asleep, as men that are secure:
Here shall we skirmish but with naked men,
Deuoyd of sence, new waked from a dreame,
That know not what our comming doth pretend,
Till they do feele our meaning on their skinnes:
Therefore assaile: God and our right for vs.

div.stage:
Alarum, with men and women halfe naked: Enter two
Captaynes without dublets, with swords.

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.p:
Where are these villaines that were set to watch,
And fire the Beacon, if occasion seru’d,
That thus haue suffred vs to be surprisde,
And neuer giuen notice to the towne?
We are betrayd, and quite deuoyd of hope,
By any meanes to fortify our selues.

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.p:
Tis ten to one the peasants are o’recome with drinke
and sleep, and so neglect their charge.

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.p:
A whirl-wind carry them quick to a whirl-poole,[tln 1840]
That there the slaues may drinke their bellies full.

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.p: This tis, to haue the Beacon so neere the Ale-house.

div.stage: Enter the watchmen drunke, with each a pot.

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.p: Out on ye, villaynes, whither run you now?

sp.speaker: 1. Wat.
sp.p: To fire the towne, and call vp the Beacon.

sp.speaker: 2. Wat.
sp.p: No, no, sir, to fire the Beacon.

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.p: What, with a pot of ale, you drunken Rogues?

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.p:
You’l fire the Beacon, when the towne is lost:
Ile teach you how to tend your office better.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p: Yeeld, yeeld, yeeld.

sp.speaker: 1. Wat.
sp.p:
Reele? no, we do not reele:
You may lacke a pot of Ale ere you dye.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
But in meanespace, I answer, you want none.
Wel, theres no dealing with you, y’are tall men, & wel weapõd,
I would there were no worse then you in the towne.

sp.speaker: 2. Wat.
sp.p:
A speaks like an honest man, my cholers past already.
Come, neighbour, let’s go.

sp.speaker: 1. Wat.
sp.p: Nay, first let’s see and we can stand.

div.stage: Alarum, excursions, Mumford after them, and some halfe naked.

Enter the Gallian King, Leir, Mumford, Cordella, Perillus, and soul­
diers, with the chiefe of the towne bound.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Feare not, my friends, you shall receyue no hurt,
If you’l subscribe vnto your lawfull King,
And quite reuoke your fealty from Cambria,
And from aspiring Cornwall too, whose wiues
Haue practisde treason ’gainst their fathers life.
Wee come in iustice of your wronged King, [I3r]
And do intend no harme at all to you,
So you submit vnto your lawfull King.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Kind Countrymen, it grieues me, that perforce,
I am constraind to vse extremities.

sp.speaker: Noble.
sp.p:
Long haue you here bin lookt for, good my Lord,
And wish’d for by a generall consent:
And had we known your Highnesse had arriued,
We had not made resistance to your Grace:
And now, my gracious Lord, you need not doubt,
But all the Country will yeeld presently,[tln 2868+3–+4]
Which since your absence haue bin greatly tax’d,[tln 2867]
For to maintayne their ouerswelling pride.
Weele presently send word to all our friends;
When they haue notice, they will come apace.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Thanks, louing subiects; and thanks, worthy son,
Thanks, my kind daughter, thanks to you, my Lord,
Who willingly aduentured haue your blood,
(Without desert) to do me so much good.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
O, say not so:
I haue bin much beholding to your Grace:
I must confesse, I haue bin in some skirmishes,
But I was neuer in the like to this:
For where I was wont to meet with armed men,
I was now incountred with naked women.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
We that are feeble, and want vse of Armes,[tln 2922]
Will pray to God, to sheeld you from all harmes.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
The while your hands do manage ceaselesse toyle,
Our hearts shall pray, the foes may haue the foyle.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Weele fast and pray, whilst you for vs do fight,
That victory may prosecute the right.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Me thinks, your words do amplify (my friends)
And adde fresh vigor to my willing limmes:Drum.
But harke, I heare the aduerse Drum approch.
God and our right, Saint Denis, and Saint George.

div.stage: Enter Cornwall, Cambria, Gonorill, Ragan, and the army.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
Presumptuous King of Gawles, how darest thou
Presume to enter on our Brittish shore?
And more then that, to take our townes perforce,
And draw our subiects hearts from their true King? [I3v]
Be su[r]e to buy it at as deare a price,
As ere you bought presumption in your liues.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Ore-daring Cornwall, know, we came in right,
And iust reuengement of the wronged King,
Whose daughters there, fell vipers as they are,[tln 802]
Haue sought to murder and depriue of life:
But God protected him from all their spight,
And we are come in iustice of his right.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.p:
Nor he nor thou haue any interest here,
But what you win and purchase with the sword.
Thy slaunders to our noble vertuous Queenes,
Wee’l in the battell thrust them down thy throte,
Except for feare of our reuenging hands,
Thou flye to sea, as not secure on lands.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
Welshman, ile so ferrit you ere night for that word,
That you shall haue no mind to crake so wel this tweluemonth.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: They lye, that say, we sought our fathers death.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Tis meerely forged for a colours sake,
To set a glosse on your inuasion.
Me thinks, an old man ready for to dye,
Should be asham’d to broache so foule a lye.

sp.speaker: Cord.
sp.p:
Fy, shamelesse sister, so deuoyd of grace,
To call our father lyer to his face.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p:
Peace (Puritan) dissembling hypocrite,
Which art so good, that thou wilt proue stark naught:
Anon, when as I haue you in my fingers,
Ile make you wish your selfe in Purgatory.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Nay, peace thou monster, shame vnto thy sexe:[tln 2309–10, 2347+28, 3118]
Thou fiend in likenesse of a humane creature.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p: I neuer heard a fouler spoken man.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Out on thee, viper, scum, filthy parricide,[tln 802]
More odious to my sight then is a Toade.
Knowest thou these letters?She snatches them & teares them.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Think you to outface me with your paltry scrowles?
You come to driue my husband from his right,
Vnder the colour of a forged letter.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p: Who euer heard the like impiety?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
You are our debtour of more patience:
We were more patient when we stayd for you, [I4r]
Within the thicket two long houres and more.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p: What houres? what thicket?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
There, where you sent your seruant with your letters,
Seald with your hand, to send vs both to heauen,
Where, as I thinke, you neuer meane to come.

sp.speaker: Rag.
sp.p:
Alas, you are growne a child agayne with age,
Or else your sences dote for want of sleepe.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p:
Indeed you made vs rise betimes, you know,
Yet had a care we should sleepe where you bade vs stay,
But neuer wake more till the latter day.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Peace, peace, old fellow, thou art sleepy still.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
Fayth, and if you reason till to morrow,
You get no other answere at their hands.
Tis pitty two such good faces
Should haue so little grace betweene them.
Well, let vs see if their husbands with their hands,
Can do as much, as they do with their toungs.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.p:
I, with their swords they’l make your toungs vnsay
What they haue sayd, or else they’l cut them out.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Too’t, gallants, too’t, let’s not stand brawling thus.

div.stage:
Sound alarum: excursions. Mumford must chase Cambria[tln 2844]
away: then cease. Enter Cornwall.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
The day is lost, our friends do all reuolt,[tln 2868+3–+4]
And ioyne against vs with the aduerse part:
There is no meanes of safety but by flight,
And therefore ile to Cornwall with my Queene.Exit.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.p:
I thinke, there is a deuill in the Campe hath haunted
me today: he hath so tyred me, that in a maner I can fight no
more.Enter Mumford.
Zounds, here he comes, Ile take me to my horse.

div.stage: Mumford followes him to the dore, and returnes.

sp.speaker: Mum.
sp.p:
Farewell (Welshman) giue thee but thy due,
Thou hast a light and nimble payre of legs:
Thou art more in debt to them then to thy hands:
But if I meet thee once agayne to day,
Ile cut them off, and set them to a better heart.

div.stage:
Alarums and excursions, then sound victory. Enter Leir, Peril­
lus, King, Cordella, and Mumford.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thanks be to God, your foes are ouercome,
And you againe possessed of your right.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
First to the heauens, next, thanks to you, my sonne,
By whose good meanes I repossesse the same:
Which if it please you to accept your selfe,
With all my heart I will resigne to you:[tln 3270–2]
For it is yours by right, and none of mine.
First, haue you raisd, at your owne charge, a power
Of valiant Souldiers; (this comes all from you)
Next haue you ventured your owne persons scathe.
And lastly, (worthy Gallia neuer staynd)
My kingly title I by thee haue gaynd.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thank heauens, not me, my zeale to you is such,
Commaund my vtmost, I will neuer grutch.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
He that with all kind loue intreats his Queene,
Will not be to her father vnkind seene.

sp.speaker: Leir.
sp.p:
Ah, my Cordella, now I call to mind,
The modest answere, which I tooke vnkind:
But now I see, I am no whit beguild,
Thou louedst me dearely, and as ought a child.
And thou (Perillus) partner once in woe,
Thee to requite, the best I can, Ile doe:
Yet all I can, I, were it ne’re so much,
Were not sufficient, thy true loue is such.
Thanks (worthy Mumford) to thee last of all,[tln 89]
Not greeted last, ’cause thy desert was small;
No, thou hast Lion-like layd on to day,
Chasing the Cornwall King and Cambria;
Who with my daughters, daughters did I say?
To saue their liues, the fugitiues did play.
Come, sonne and daughter, who did me aduaunce,
Repose with me awhile, and then for Fraunce.

div.note: I.e., Cenouesean, for Senonesean, Gauls from Senon, mod. Sens, on the Yonne r., SE of Paris. See Law (1955, pp. 6–9).

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of The True Chronicle History of King Leir
div.p: Theobald (ed. 1733, 5:217–18) thinks Sh. may have made the ending tragic to vary from another, but most execrable, Dramatic Performance upon this Story: which I certainly believe to have preceded our Author’s Piece, and which none of the Stage-Historians appear to have had any Knowledge of. He quotes from Leir some lines of such Poetry as one might hammer out, Stans pede in uno [Horace, Sat. 1.4.10, = efffortlessly], so that Shakespeare…may stand acquitted from the least Suspicion of Plagiarism.

Steevens (ed. 1766, 1:16): It is not improbable he might have seen [Leir], as the father kneeling to the daughter, when she kneels to ask his blessing, is found in it; a circumstance two poets were not very likely to have hit on separately; and which seems borrowed by the latter with his usual judgment, it being the most natural passage in the old play; and it is introduced in such a manner as to make it fairly his own.

Capell (ed. 1768, 1:55–9): Lear’s distressful story has been often told in poems, ballads, and chronicles: But to none of these are we indebted for Shakespeare’s Lear: but to a silly old play which made its first appearance in 1605. He cites particularly the reunion of Leir with Cordella, which includes (p. 57) a circumstance of some beauty, which Shakespeare has borrow’d;—…their kneeling to each other, and mutually contending which should ask forgiveness. In the watch scenes there is some low humour that is passable enough.… [58] Who the author of it should be, I cannot surmise; for neither in manner nor style has it the least resemblance to any of the other tragedies of that time: most of them rise now and then, and are poetical; but this creeps in one dull tenour, from beginning to end.…It should seem he was a latinist. Capell lists Sh.’s apparent borrowings: the kneeling incident; Albany’s No tearing, lady (3115), from Leir 2586; (p. 59) the patterne of all patience (1689), from Leir 755 the myrrour of mild patience; and Kent and Oswald from Perillus and the murderous Messenger.

Skottowe (1824, pp. 95, 105–10): More numerous than to all other sources combined were the obligations of Shakspeare to a drama entitled, The True Chronicle History of King Leir…, a work which must, in fact, be considered as the foundation stone of the bard’s performance.…[105] For the outlines of Leir’s character Shakespeare was indebted to [Leir].…He ascribes to Lear the tenderest love of his children.… [107] Shakspeare makes the whole of Lear’s rage and inflexibility emanate from his own mind; whereas, in the old play, much of his violence is attributable to the instigation of his fiend-like daughters.…[109] But all the subsequent passages of affection and agony,—the sublime of astonishment when Lear’s faculties are palsied into doubts of his own personal identity—all the frightful maledictions when he unites himself with the spirit of nature—all these passages own no inspiration but that of Shakspeare.

p.quote: The specific difference between the Lears of the two dramatists is, that the king of the old play yields to despondency, and resigns himself to his fate, as justly merited by his cruelty to the only child who loved him. Shakspeare’s king is full of energy and rage; and…[110] resignation and tame submission form no part of his mind.

div.p: Collier (1831, 3:76–7): The hint of the part of Kent is undoubtedly taken from the Perillus of the Chronicle History; but the latter is a poor, spiritless lamenter over the injuries of Cordella, in the earlier scenes, and in the progress of the play, instead of contrasting with Lear, he not only partakes the sufferings, but shares the imbecilities of the old abdicated monarch.…In the Chronicle History, the two wicked daughters have been bribed by the offer of the division of the kingdom, and the union of Cor-[77]della with the King of France is most absurdly conducted.…They fall in love with each other on the spot, he not knowing that she is a Princess, nor she that he is a King.…Nothing can be more tame and mechanical than the whole of the dialogue of the Chronicle History.

Kemshead (ed. 1875, pp. 13–14): Leir provides the king’s inflexibility, Goneril’s ingratitude, and the images of pelican and eagle; but All that is sublime and terrible in Shakespeare’s Lear is original [paraphrasing Skottowe];…the awful impressiveness of despair;—his dignified demeanor even in the ravings of insanity;—all this is peculiarly Shakespearean.

Furness (ed. 1880, p. 384): In reading this old drama, every now and then there comes across us an incident, or a line, or a phrase, that reminds us of Shakespeare’s Lear, and…this cannot be said of Holinshed’s story. For instance, in Leir we find a faithful courtier who defends Cordella to her father, and the old king replies, Urge this no more, and if thou love thy life [cf. Lr. 165]. And this same courtier afterwards accompanies the old king in his exile as his faithful companion and servant. Again, in the trial-scene Cordella murmurs aside her abhorrence at the hypocrisy of her sisters’ asseverations of affection. Again, Leir alludes to Gonorill’s young bones.

Verity (ed. 1897, pp. xvi f.): In the old play, as in Shakespeare’s tragedy, the king’s abdication is complete, whereas in Holinshed’s account he retains a portion of his realm and is afterwards ejected from it by his rebellious sons-in-law, Gonorill complains (as in I.3) of Leir’s constant fault-finding. In the scene of reconciliation Leir kneels to Cordella, who bids him rise. There are a few verbal resemblances [fn.: Cf. Lear’s shadow [744]; her young bones [1445]; the pattern of all patience [1688]; those pelican daughters [1856].] which sound like casual and unconscious echoes of the old piece. Individually the points of similarity are essentially trivial, but, taken together, they produce the impression that the earlier play was known to Shakespeare.

Herford (ed. 1899, p. 11): Leir made important advances in the plot, some of which Shakespeare did not disdain to adopt. Lear, like his prototype, resigns his kingdom, and does not merely determine who shall inherit it after his death. Kent is a blunter Perillus, Oswald a less masculine Messenger. Leir’s reunion with Cordeilla faintly foreshadows the ineffable pathos of the close of Shakespeare’s Fourth Act. But beyond this, the old play interests us chiefly as setting forth paths from which Shakespeare deliberately departed.

Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xxx–xxxiv) lists similarities or echoes:
1.Not only does Lear divide his kingdom, he resigns all power and authority.
2.The division of his kingdom is into equal parts.
3.Leir wants to marry Cor. to a king of Brittany, and this is the reason for the questioning of all his daughters about their love. This is not explicitly Sh.’s reason, but it influenced his mind.
4.Only in the old play does France come to Britain and take Cordella home; in all earlier versions, Aganippus deals by envoy, and Cor. is sent dowerless to France.
5.Perillus is the pale original of Kent; in other sources Lear goes to France accompanied by only one knight or soldier (and both, in one scene). Perillus grieves at Cordella’s mistreatment and wins Leir’s displeasure by pleading for her. He also laments Leir’s mistreatment by his daughters, and follows him in disguise to the end.
6.Messenger is doubtless the origin of Oswald.

But Sh.’s play is more deeply and truly pathetic: He has here fairly unlocked the gates of pity and terror; and that out of apparently such unpromising materials he should have created such a matchlessly wondrous and perfect result, must indeed be regarded as one of the greatest miracles in all art.

Schelling (1902, pp. 174–5): The older play contains only the story of Leir and his daughters: the parallel underplot of Gloucester and his sons was added from another source by Shakespeare, as was the daring picture of madness real and feigned, the pathos of the contrasted folly of Lear and the sad-eyed fool. and the wonderful climax of storm in which the warring elements of nature unite in subtle sympathy with the wild tumult of human suffering and passion.…[175] In the older play, as befits a comedy, the Gallian king’s wooing of Cordella is made much of, a feature completely subordinated in the sterner tragedy.

Tolstoy (1906; 1937, pp. 341–5): In the older play [342] there is an explanation, lacking in Shakespeare, of Leir’s anger at the younger daughter’s reply. Leir is vexed at the non-success of his cunning device, and the venemous words of his elder daughters add to his irritation.…[343] In the older play there are no tempests or tearing out of grey hairs.…Instead of the unnatural expulsion of Leir during a tempest and his roaming about the heath, in the old play Leir and Perillus during their journey to France very naturally come to the last degree of want.…Instead of the unnatural conjoint ravings of the fool, Lear, and Edgar…we have in the older play a natural scene of the meeting between the daughter and father.…[345] The whole of this older play is in all respects beyond compare better than Shakespeare’s adaptation. It is so, first, because in it those superfluous characters—the villain Edmund and the unnatural Gloucester and Edgar, who only distract one’s attention—do not appear. Secondly, it is free from the perfectly false effects of Lear’s roaming about on the heath, his talks with his fool, and all those impossible disguises, non-recognitions, and wholesale deaths—above all because in this play there is the simple, natural, and deeply touching character of Leir, and the yet more touching and clearly defined character of Cordelia, which are lacking in Shakespeare. And also because in the older drama, instead of Shakespeare’s daubed scene of Lear’s meeting with Cordelia and her unnecessary murder, there is the exquisite scene of Leir’s meeting with Cordelia, which is unequalled by anything in Shakespeare’s drama.

Perrett (1904, pp. 175, 220–6, 248, 274–9): In Leir Gon. and Reg. [are] already married, previously to the Love-test, as in no other version.…[220] Sh.’s angry, peremptory, pugnacious king is [222] very different from the weary, pious, patient, tearful, abject king of the old play.…[225] It appears as if the possibility of Leir’s going mad [in the earlier versions of the story] were never very remote, citing Leir 2083, 2196–2200. But Leir is never nearer being actually mad than is Gloucester when he says [1946, 1950]. All these [226] quotations merely show that it was a common belief that…Extremity of griefs would make men mad [Tit. 4.1.19 (1562)]. [248] The author makes Leir a pious Catholic [or Protestant; see below], anxious to tell his beads (Sc. 6) and lets Cordella reproach herself with remissness in attendance at church (Sc. 13)…. (P. 274): Perrett dismisses as meaningless a number of verbal resemblances: the pelican (Leir 512, Lr. 1856), withered branch (Leir 1242–3, Lr. 2303+4), young bones (Leir 834, Lr. 1445), etc. (P. 277): While no other version gives any adequate mo-[278]tive for the Question [of the Love-test], [Leir] makes it a stratagem on the father’s part to entrap Cordella into a diplomatic marriage. Likewise in K. L. the trial is a trick, though its aim is entirely changed. Cordelia the favourite daughter is to have the opportunity of showing herself worthy above her sisters of that greatest and best portion already mapped out for her, by openly declaring her love for her father.…The motive for the sisters’ flattery is in both plays the same. It is a counterplot, its object being to bring about the downfall of their sister.…Cordelia’s coronet is handed over to the two dukes to symbolise her complete disinheritance, the action corresponding to the drawing of lots in [Leir].…Several minor characters owe something to parts in [Leir].…Much of the activity of Goneril’s steward is anticipated in Gonerill’s parasite Skalliger, and his substitute in the latter part of [Leir], the Messenger or Murderer.…The Old Man in IV, i, owes his existence…to the pathetic spectacle of the aged and infirm Perillus endeavouring to stay and comfort his old, unhappy master.…Gloucester has something more in common with Leir in the scenes where the father, led by his aged guide, comes upon and gradually recognises the outcast child.…From the same source comes their [i.e., Goneril’s and Regan’s] plot of death upon their father.…Kent’s warning [1638+1–+3]…[279] would recall the secret landing of Gallia in Sc. 28, due to the negligent guard of the drunken watchmen. Other action in Leir accepted in Lr. are Cordelia’s asides [67, 82; cf. Leir 254, 274], Kent’s interposition for Cordelia and Lear’s threats [165 ff., cf. Leir 569], the business of the incriminating letter and the guilty one’s snatching and tearing of it [3115; cf. Leir 2586], and the alternate kneeling of Lear and Cordelia.

Lee (1909, p. xli): Something of the stage business which is associated in Shakespeare’s tragedy with the exchange of letters, e.g. between Regan and Goneril ([2328]), Kent and Cordelia ([2347+10]), and Goneril and Edmund ([2391]), seems traceable to the interception by Goneril in the old play of letters addressed to Leir ([990]) and to the passage of letters between Ragan and Goneril ([1168]).

Brooke (1911, pp. 398–9): In Shakespeare’s treatment, King Lear and his daughters lose the vague royal dignity which the earlier anonymous play on the same subject allows them, and become practically bourgeois types; while the kingdom of Britain could [399] be replaced without dramatic loss by a farm.
Adams (1923, p. 374): The old play seriously handicapped him, for its story was disjointed, its action rambling, and its theme, essentially epic in nature, ill-suited to dramatic treatment.

Tolstoy criticized omissions 2–3; (p. 148) but exposition being the most important part of any play, Sh.’s changes must have been deliberate, to heighten the characters of Lear and Cordelia. It is as if he had consciously neglected to provide the slightest motive for the actions of the King and his daughter in order that their characters might thereby stand out in greater relief.…In the old Leir the King is to a large extent justified in his wrath. He does not know his daughters, as he expressly tells us, and he does not know of Skalliger’s treachery. Considered impartially, his wrath has in it nothing that is not without cause. In the Lear of Shakespeare, on the [149] other hand, the dramatist has endeavoured in every way to make the king’s senile dotage apparent.…His pageantry court scene is but an old man’s folly, a pretence of egoistic pride.…[151] [Similarly, Cordelia] has Lear’s own nature. No ordinary person would have been so offended at Regan’s and Goneril’s speeches as Cordelia is. It is her false pride, this egoistic, overweening pride, that causes her undoing.…She is too proud to descend into the arena of wordy oratory. (P. 152): Lear and Cordelia both also share a materialistic attitude and lack adaptability to circumstances.

As for the omission of the wooing of France, (p. 155) To have presented, as in the older play, the romantic wooing of Cordelia by the King in his palmer’s disguise would have been to throw a spot-light on Cordelia and a conseqent shadow on Lear.

Law (1934, pp. 42–4): [In] the lay-out of scenes…the two plays run parallel for a considerable distance. In his first [43] scene Shakespeare places Lear’s decision to divide the kingdom, his love-test, resulting in the disinheritance of Cordelia, the determined protest of Kent and his banishment, the wooing of Cordelia by France, and the plotting of the two elder daughters against their father. Now every one of these incidents…is related in the first seven scenes of the old play in almost the exact order followed by Shakespeare.…Scene iii, where Goneril plots with Oswald against her father, corresponds closely with a scene between Gonorill and Skalliger in the old play. Similarly paralleled are the successive episodes of Kent’s care for Lear, the Fool’s reminding Lear of his folly, the quarrel between Goneril and Lear, Albany’s mild protest, Lear’s departure for Regan’s home, and the letter sent by Goneril through Oswald. Almost none of these details are in other versions of the Leir story.

p.quote: [In] Act II…the attitude of Regan to her father on his coming, the disgraceful treatment of Kent, and Regan’s shutting the doors on her father, all seem to be echoes of successive situations in the old play.…Shakespeare, after the love-test of the first scene is following neither Holinshed nor any other undramatic version of the story. Second, he is heavily in debt to the old drama for suggestions of phrase, of character, of situation, and of entire scenes. Third, throughout Act I and part of Act II [44] he follows closely the order of action employed in the old play.…So far as we can judge, Shakespeare apparently preferred the architecture of a crude play to that of faithful history unadorned.

div.p: Hart (1934, p. 141): The poet has made such great changes in and additions to the subject-matter of King Lear that what he has left of the old King Leir is scarcely recognisable. The vocabulary of the latter is much inferior to that of the Troublesome Raigne, and only twelve of its scarce words find a place in King Lear, which has a richer vocabulary than any other play except Hamlet. Idem (1942, pp. 21–66) gives detailed statistics on the recurrence of the vocabulary of Leir in Lr. and other plays. (P. 26): In writing Lr. Sh. rejected over forty percent of the words in Leir. (P. 29): Of a total of 340 rare words in Leir, Lr. uses only 18 and rejects 322. (P. 31): The small totals of rare words common to both plays offer a most striking contrast to the very large totals of the rare words peculiar to each play [340 for Leir, 742 for Lr.]. (P. 152): He treated some plays with sound texts, such as…King Leir…as raw material, varied the plot and characters, decreased or increased the length of some scenes, rejected others, added new episodes or even sub-plots, retained barely two dozen lines of the three plays [Troublesome Raigne, A Shrew, Leir], cut out nearly all the compound words, classical allusions, similes, figurative expressions, etc., and inserted his own.

Kittredge (ed. 1936, pp. 1195–6): Shakespeare owes little to the old play except the impulse to write a new one. Now and then a phrase reminds us of something in King Lear, but these resemblances are trifling. Kent may be foreshadowed by Perillus, but the likeness is shadowy indeed. Perillus is an old man, his protests are very mild, and he is not banished; therefore he does not, like Kent, disguise himself to enter the service of his master. The Messenger whom Regan employs to murder her father may have given a hint for Oswald. The business of the letter (iv, 5) is rather like a scene between Goneril and the Messenger in the [1196] old play. In various matters Shakespeare abandons the novel devices of his predecessor: as in i, 1, where the old play complicates the plot by bringing in a scheme of Cordelia’s sisters to ensure her giving an unacceptable answer.

Greg (1940, pp. 384–97): It may very well be that Shakespeare saw King Leir acted in the early nineties: it is most unlikely that he saw it often or had seen it lately when he wrote his own play. A general resemblance of situation and character might be accounted for by a retentive memory: actual verbal reminiscences would imply direct study of the text. Most recent critics, while making light of Shakespeare’s debt, are agreed in finding some measure of verbal similarity, and they therefore conclude that Shakespeare must have read the earlier play.…I do not think there is any escape from the general opinion. Shakespeare undoubtedly knew King Leir, and though he made no conscious use whatever of its language, there is clear evidence that he read it carefully not long before he wrote.…

[386] The general likeness is obvious enough despite the widely different ways in which the story is handled, and goes far beyond what we should necessarily expect in any two dramatic versions of a common theme. The structure of the love-test episode is essentially the same: particularly noticeable are the single-line asides in which Cordella comments on the protestations of her hypocritical sisters. Perillus is manifestly the propotype of Kent. The storm that reverberates through Lear is heard in the thunder that appals the would-be murderer in Leir (sc. xix). In Leir the aged king asks forgiveness of his wronged child in [2295–2304].…[387] The essence of this affecting but theatrically clumsy scene Shakespeare transmuted in two magic touches in his own play; the first when Lear awakens to recovered sanity ([2810]):…the other when he and Cordelia are brought in as prisoners and Lear says ([2950–1]).…The mildness of Goneril’s husband is strikingly anticipated in [829–50].…Ragan in the old play hires a messenger to murder Leir and Perillus: Regan bribes (I’ll love thee much) a messenger (Oswald) to murder Gloucester (both fail); while of course Edmund bribes (One step…thee) the Captain to murder Lear and Cordelia. It has also been ingeniously argued that we may find another reminiscence of the old play in the Fool’s doggerel ([669+1 ff.]).…Some such advice is in fact given by the rascally courtier Skalliger (32–8), a character whose time-serving propensities, according to Sidney Lee, helped to generate the wicked servility of Goneril’s servant, Oswald.

Greg then traces some forty subtler links of language or of thought (see commentary notes), concluding, (p. 397) In writing Lear Shakespeare did not do what he is credited with having done on previous occasions—leave standing whatever he thought good enough to pass muster on the stage: the whole thing has been fused and transmuted in the alembic of his genius. Yet it would seem that as he wrote, ideas, phrases, cadences from the old play still floated in his memory below the level of conscious thought, and that now and again one or another helped to fashion the words that flowed from his pen.

Fripp (1938, pp. 656–7): In the play of 1594 the scene is transferred to Christian times. The author introduces Scripture and moralizes. He hints at the death of their mother as a cause of the unfilial behaviour of Goneril and Regan. Lear laments her decease. Though in a moment of doting frenzy, egged on by her sisters, he disinherits Cordelia, he is a gentle, pious old man, who wants to exchange his throne for the cloister; and Cordelia is a Puritan maiden.…Doubtless [Sh.] would have preserved the [657] Christian background…were it not for the Act [of Abuses]. (The 1606 Act, however, does not forbid the representation of Christian background, only the profaning of the name of God and of sacred practices and beliefs.)

Perkinson (1943, pp. 317 ff.): Shakespeare prepares for his tragic treatment by compressing the striking initial episode of his play, which occupies four scenes of King Leir, into a prologial opening scene, heightening thereby its improbability.…[318] The purpose of the condensation and of the excision of the reason for the King’s behavior is to secure a thoroughly tragic character who can say as early as the end of Act I…I did her wrong. (P. 319): The test as a trick to justify his more opulent third he derived obliquely from Leir, though there the division was equal and (p. 320) final and the test is skillfully motivated as an independent stratagem.…

By comparison with her counterpart in King Leir, Cordelia is obviously meant to appear more innocent.…The author of King Leir attributes [Cordelia’s behavior in 1.1] to her character, to stubbornness and pride.…[321] No other version [than Lr.] concludes with the French King’s dignified dissent and a noble’s violent protest.…One effect of the condensation…is the deliberate sacrifice of the probability of Holinshed and of the old play.… (P. 322): Whereas in Leir the king begins his reconciliation with Cordelia only late in the play—after Gonorill and Ragan have both mistreated him and even plotted against his life— in Lear he begins the process at the end of 1.5. (P. 323): Since the suffering Lear thereafter endures is no longer designed to produce a change in his attitude toward Cordelia, it requires a different quality of pathos, and the King the new character of a strikingly tragic hero.

p.quote: Lear’s change…is now the result of his own inner nature prompted finally…by the Fool. The rebuffs of Goneril and Regan now bring about not the first desperate softening in the old man and the journey to France, but tragic madness; after Act I Shakespeare’s hero is helplessly acted against.…[324] By condensing the major element of the story into a temporary aberration, Shakespeare swiftly projects his hero into a period of physical ignom[in]y and, by contrast, of increasing spiritual nobility, both beyond anything in the sources.

div.p: (P. 324): Sh. accordingly changed Goneril and Regan. Their ingratitude becomes a kind of heartless reasonableness.…The source of their disintegration Shakespeare places in the Gloucester sub-plot, in their rival passions for the unscrupulous Edmund. Lear’s meeting with Cordelia begins the cure of his madness rather than (p. 325) the vengeful defeat of Goneril and Regan. Shakespeare deals in terms of personalities rather than of historical events. Sh. excises Lear’s travel to France and the victory of the French army. Cordelia’s invasion serves to reintroduce Cordelia and (p. 326) bring about the tragedy of Lear. Having bypassed so many episodes in Leir, Sh. fills out his five acts with the Gloucester subplot.

Charlton (1948, pp. 190 ff.): In its mechanical crafts for securing theatrical plausibility, [Leir] is superficially much superior to Shakespeare’s play in one or two major features. For one thing, it provides its incidental circumstances with an everyday Elizabethan colour, and often with its colloquial domestic idiom.…[191] But in an even more important respect, the old dramatist shows insight and technical skill in handling…the plot’s strain on credulity in its initial scene.…[Leir] is left with three unmarried daughters and no male heir.…[192] A courtier suggests that he should choose the most suitable from the suitors to his children, and give to the three daughters on marriage a jointure more or less, as is their worth, to them that professe. In such casual and natural way, the idea of a trial enters.…Another counsellor commends the marriage suggestions on sound political grounds: let Leir prepare for the soon-impending future by marrying his three daughters to three neighbour kings, and so secure the confederate integrity of his realm.…It is a real test, not for verbal professions, but for practical proof of the extent of his daughters’ love for him.…In Leir, the device is primarily a means to ensure a reasonable political scheme, the intelligible desire of a sonless king to find sons-in-law from whom he might wisely choose an heir to inherit him politically when his time should come. But there is no talk of immediate abdication.…[194] It is only when Leir is stung [195] to sudden fury by Cordella’s answer that he resolves on immediate division and an abdication forthwith.…In Shakespeare’s form of the story, Lear has already provided his two elder daughters with husbands before any thought of dividing the kingdom has entered his head. It is only now when the third daughter is wooed by two suitors that the provision of a proper dowry for her suggests a division.…The division will not await testamentary disposal, but will be by immediate deed of gift. Lear will abdicate. This…is all that the scene offers as ground for the stupendous unreason of Lear’s anger when he is incensed at Cordelia’s obtuse answer to his easy and formal question. For his question, unlike [196] Leir’s, had neither political nor rational purpose behind it; it was merely sentimental.…[198] [Yet] Lear becomes every inch a king; and the old play’s Leir remains nothing more than a pathetic, and sometimes testy, old man whose senceless senses are easily played on by his scheming daughters, and who takes their ill-treatment of him meekly, with many tears, and with all Christian resignation.…

[216] The outstanding feature of the older Leir’s world is its pervading and even obtruding Christianism. Its opening lines strike a distinctive note of Christian belief.…It adopts the whole institution of Christian practice, its offices, its sacraments, its liturgy and its creed.…[217] The will of God is justice: the heavens are just, and God will always succour his obedient flock.…[218] King Lear’s is a church-less and a priest-less world.…[227] A spiritual civilisation is dimly emerging and man is making or discovering a morality.

Muir (1957, pp. 143–5): Cordelia’s death takes place so long after the main events of the story that to dramatize it meant a sacrifice of dramatic unity and the introduction of new characters,…[144] [Sh.] had to avoid the seven years that elapsed in the chronicle between the restoration of Lear and the death of Cordelia. He had to make the death of Cordelia a logical result of Lear’s original error and of her refusal to flatter. He had to make Lear pay for his sin by death.…Cordelia could not be allowed to commit suicide, and therefore she must be murdered.

p.quote: Shakespeare solved the problem by bringing forward the death of Cordelia, so that she dies before her father; and the man who orders her murder does so because he hopes for the throne. This situation can arise only if she is defeated in battle.…The wicked sisters…must be killed by the working out of their own evil passions.

div.p: Sh. condensed its first eight scenes into the second part of his own first scene.…[145] Shakespeare by his ruthless telescoping leaves Lear’s motives in some obscurity.…He may have felt that Lear’s irrationality would be more credible on the stage than Leir’s stupid cunning.…The banishment of Kent and his subsequent serving of Lear in disguise are more dramatic than the continuation of Perillus in Leir’s service.…Shakespeare borrowed comparatively little from the remainder of King Leir.

Munro (ed. 1957, 6:894): Sh. telescoped into one the two battles of Leir, the battle on the invasion from France and the battle with the nephews, transferring the nephews’ battle to their mothers, Goneril and Regan. This final and single battle Shakespeare deliberately made into a token affair. See n. 2917.

Houghton (ed. 1957, pp. 17–18): It is prosaic and didactic, the verse mostly end-stopped and the imagery conventional. In some ways the probability is greater than in Shakespeare. Lear does not divide his kingdom until after Cordelia has failed him. We do not have the mixture of medieval France with pure paganism, for the atmosphere is full of references to Christianity, particularly on the lips of Lear and Cordelia. There is a fair amount of comedy intermingled, mostly from Mumford, who speaks somewhat after the fashion of the Bastard in King John.…The King is tame, compared to the awful figure we know, and is soon penitent for his treatment of Cordelia. The recognition scene where Lear and Perillus (who corresponds to Kent) meet France and Cordelia on the shore without at first recognizing them has some merit (Tolstoy found it more moving than Shakespeare!), but the comedy of the drunken [18] watchmen who let in the French army shows for what trivialities this tragi-comedy found room. In fact the play becomes less and less like Shakespeare as it proceeds.

Law (1958, pp. 121–4): Very little debt to…[Leir] is to be found in Act III.…Yet the final scene in this act, in which Gloucester’s eyes are torn out, may owe some suggestion to the attempted murder of Leir. For Gloucester, like Leir, declares that the offspring he has so favored may help him in his need, only to learn that the betrayer of his secret was his ungrateful illegitimate son.

p.quote: With Act IV the structure begins to correspond roughly to the analogous series of scenes in the old play. No longer is the dominant theme filial ingratitude, causing intense suffering, but the tender affection for their aged parents shown by the wronged children in both plots.…Shakespeare adds an entirely new set of incidents, revealing the adulterous love of both Goneril and Regan for Gloucester’s handsome bastard son.…
In his final act, Shakespeare seems to disregard almost completely the feeble lines of the anonymous play.…

div.p: [122] [Leir] is a typical Eizabethan romantic comedy of the early 1590’s, in which all the good are rewarded and all the wicked punished without the shedding of blood.…Its three longest and most important scenes of new material are full of romantic motifs: love at first sight, proxy wooing, rejection of a proposed royal lover in favor of his agent, acceptance of death as a penalty for sin, confidence misplaced in villains, sudden conversion of the wicked on threat of hell-fire, friends [123] coming just in time to prevent starvation.

p.quote: Characters follow conventional patterns [affectionate but misguided father, pious heroine, soldier-king, villainess, parasite, faithful follower, clever courtier, villainous messenger].…Power of vital characterization is certainly beyond the playwright’s skill, but each one of those listed offered some hint to Shakespeare.…A few touches of realism, such as the Messenger’s playing with his victims before proceeding to their murder, and the behavior of the drunken coast guard, reveal genuine humor, and there are several wholly indecent jestings. But the diction, especially of the verse, is pedestrian, naïve to a marked degree. The contrast with King Lear in this respect has been most unfortunate for the earlier piece.…[124] While Shakespeare owes to the play, I believe, a larger debt than is usually recognized, nowhere did he exhibit greater artistic power than in turning this crude romantic comedy into heartrending tragedy.

div.p: Watson (1960, pp. 362–6): The old play is as deeply saturated in Christian themes as Shakespeare’s is lacking in precise religious doctrines.…[365] The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir is saturated in Christian doctrine and has an all-pervasive religious atmosphere. Not only are the protagonists turning to God in their hour of trial, but also the tone and sentiment throughout the play are colored by true Christian feeling. All fundamental ethical dilemmas are resolved by reference to the Christian notions of good and evil. As Leo Tolstoy observed, this is not true of [366] Shakespeare’s tragic world.

Sternfeld (1963, pp. 160 ff.): The Chronicle…contains prose only occasionally, as in the scenes of the messenger; the king speaks exclusively in verse. Moreover, as befitting the genre of tragedy, there are no songs whatever.

p.quote: [In Lr.] the course of Lear’s development from king to madman and his recovery to true regal stature is mirrored in the prosody. His momentous decision in the opening scene…is expressed in traditional verse. In the fourth scene…[his] perturbation is expressed in prose.…As the prose scene proceeds it is interspersed by seven lyrics.…[161] There are many transitions from verse to prose as Lear is taught humility and compassion by painful degrees.…[162] This mixture of prose and lyric [in 3.2] with its indecorous frankness is characteristic of a clown’s role. [163] In the fourth scene of Act III the insanity of Lear reaches its culmination.…[Both the Fool and Edgar] sing their lowly snatches of song at him.…[164] Lear’s prose following upon Edgar’s ditty is both startling and pathetic.…In scene vi the exiled king is still attended by the fool and mad Tom and hears song by both. The fantastic criss-cross of ideas which emerges from this mingled web of prose and verse has its poetic attractions, but the comprehensive dramatic purpose is to reduce the haughty Lear to the humanity of the fool and Tom.…In the course of the mock trial which follows, Lear and Kent speak in stately blank verse but the fool and Tom have prose, except when they sing or quote a lyric.…[166] The dramatic function of the songs and the unconventional prose scenes which add grotesque and bizarre elements to the tragedy proper have been fulfilled when arrogant Lear has become wise enough to play the fool.

div.p: Elton (1966, pp. 63–71) The God of the source is not a Deus absconditus but a realizable and clearly just anthropomorphic deity; the change in Shakespeare’s work is crucial to the sense of his tragedy.…The old Leir looks back, in a sense, to the medieval, while the new Lear is relatively modern. Elton proceeds through the old play, pointing out Christian themes of God’s justice and vengefulness against sinners, the blessings of immortality, contemptus mundi, prayer, pilgrimage, faith, charity, miracle, providence, submission to God’s will, grace, and righteous victory. (P. 70): The old drama furnished a groundwork upon which Shakespeare constructed his variations: piety re-[71]mained, to an extent, in the good characters, especially Cordelia and the interpolated Edgar; but the king himself and the added Gloucester are vastly different and more complex; further, they change and develop as the characters in the old Leir do not. The thunder is taken up and expanded into an all-encompassing storm, and Lear’s attitudes toward it are a measure of his confused alterations; and, more significant, the thunder itself, perhaps for one of the first times in Christian literature, becomes ambiguous—not clearly on the side of God or the good.…From the old Leir the departures are, indeed, numerous; and those critics who still insist on viewing Shakespeare’s play as a traditional drama of redemption might, comparing the two, measure the distance which Shakespeare has traveled into complexity, ambiguity, and dubiety in his new creation.
Satin (1966, p. 447): While the bitter fool is Shakespeare’s own, The True Chronicle does provide witty comic contrast through Mumford.

Jones (1970, pp. 126–30): The play’s orientation is distinctly Puritan, and its interpretation of the legend is distinguished from that of other versions not…by being Christian but by being didactically so with a pervasive religious vocabulary, sentiments of humility, penitence, thanksgiving, and the inefficacy of human merit, and a new emphasis on moral lessons, grace, special providences, and Scripture.…The play tends to explain adversity as punishment for sin.…The good characters accept their suffering as just punishment for their sins. And they trust Providence to protect them. Leir has a predominantly Old Testament and Lear an emphatically New Testament emphasis.…[130] [Sh.] changes from a focus on Providence’s response to man’s temporal events and natural needs to a New Testament focus on the spirit prompting man’s acts and the response of Providence to man’s spiritual needs. Wittreich (1984, p. 44): In King Lear,…the emphasis is…more precisely, apocalyptic. The Book of Revelation…provides the biblical counterpart, the apt analogy, for Shakespeare’s play.

Nagarajan (1972, pp. 31–9): Sh. changes Lear from a tired old man retiring from the world to think of the welfare of his soul (p. 32) to an imperious and vigorous monarch; (p. 34) Sh. changes Cordelia from a very meek, God-fearing and humble person, resigned cheerfully to…tribulations to a woman motivated wholly by selfless filial love; (p. 38) Sh. changes the thunder from a plot device to terrify the assassin to a symbol of cosmic upheaval, and an agent (p. 39) to punish the sinful and teach reality.

Rosenberg (1972, p. 102): Lear was made to accept mistreatment with Christian patience; Shakespeare made a different, much more difficult design of man, quick to feel shame, and furious at his shaming.

Bullough (1973, pp. 277 ff.): The old play of King Leir…belongs to that numerous group of pieces concerned with early British history which extends from Gorboduc to Middleton’s Hengist, King of Kent, and beyond.…[It belongs to the subclass of] plays using chronicle material together with romantic or comic ingredients, e.g. A Knack to Know a Knave, Cymbeline.…In Henslowe’s 1594 list it comes with other pieces on early history: William the Conqueror (4 Jan.), King Lud (18 Jan.), Leire (6 and 8 April), Cutlack (16 May).…

p.quote: Leir has been called a sentimental fairy [tale] with no historical pretensions [Ribner, 1957, pp. 247–8]. The author, however, kept the main outlines of the Lear-story, embroidering it freely with pathos and romantic invention.…

div.p: [281] The tragi-comedy…is more than a sentimental fairy-story. It is a tale in which parental unkindness and filial ingratitude, sins against natural and divine law, are contrasted with loyalty, truth, and piety. Leir’s folly is set alongside Perillus’s wisdom, the selfish cruelty of the bad sisters, those fell vipers, and Cordella’s simple devotion.

p.quote: That the play has strong religious implications has already been suggested.…[283] So the anonymous dramatist of this very successful play has convincingly interpreted the story as more than a political and domestic affair, seeing it as concerned with the inmost laws of human nature and of the Divine Will.…[Sh.] struck out several scenes: Skalliger’s conversation with the bad daughters before the love-test, the coming of the suitors, the ballad-like wooing of the French King, the abortive attempt on Lear’s life, etc. But, having recently composed a highly intense and closely-knit tragedy in Othello, he was led by the epic nature of the Lear-material to revert to the manner of Hamlet, to follow his dramatic source in tracing events from beginning to end, and to enrich the social background and make it not so neutral as in Othello but pervaded with a moral and poetic atmosphere suited to the tragic perplexities of the chief characters.

With accurate details of place and time Shakespeare was not greatly concerned as his imagination immersed itself in the emotional and ethical implications of the story and initially with obvious themes embodied there, e.g. ingratitude, discord in the family, parent against child, child against parent, greed, the pathos of old age maltreated, the war of good against evil.

div.p: (P. 287): Focussing on the comprehensive folly of Lear, Sh. begins his play in a court scene corresponding to the third scene of Leir. By omitting the preparatory matter of the old play, Shakespeare makes [Cordelia’s] bald understatement a hammer-blow to the audience as well as to Lear himself.…

[289] In Leir the Gallian King does not arrive in Britain until Cordella has been driven out, and he meets and woos her in his disguise as a pilgrim. Shakespeare avoids the mild humour and naive sentiment of this scene by having the French King take her publicly in full court.…

p.quote: Shakespeare’s dramatic judgment is shown in approaching Goneril’s ill-treatment of Lear, for he omits the soliloquy in Leir (Sc. 8) in which Perillus bewails the King’s plight now that she wishes to get rid of him.…Instead, Shakespeare goes directly to the conversation between Goneril and Oswald.…[290] Shakespeare’s Lear needed no counsellor [viz., Skalliger] to make himself a bitter fool, and his Goneril does not ask advice about cutting down her father’s allowance (Cf. Leir, Sc. 9).…[292] Shakespeare jettisons the device by which Gonorill rouses Ragan against Leir (Sc. 12, 15). Ragan needs no false libels to make her hostile.…

Instead of using Ragan’s plot against Lear’s life (Sc. 15, 17) and the Messenger’s attempt on the two old men (Sc. 19) from which he is deterred by thunder and their appeals to religion, Shakespeare evokes from the thunder (sign in Leir of divine displeasure) the great storm in which Lear vies with the elements in rage and rhetoric until he goes truly mad (III.2).…The hapless wandering of Lear and his Fool were suggested by Leir (Sc. 14), where the two old men are creeping towards Ragan’s home, and by the later extremity in France (Sc. 24).…

div.p: [294] To intensify the action Shakespeare now [i.e., in Act IV] makes his most considerable omissions from the old play: Cordella’s envoy sent to invite her father to France (Sc. 16); her journey with her husband in disguise, Leir’s crossing and exchange of clothes with the seamen (Sc. 23); and, later, the embarcation of the Gallian forces, the beacon-watchers (Sc. 27, 29), the landing and the capture of Dover. Shakespeare wished to have Lear meet his daughter on British soil, to avoid emphasizing the French invasion and to bring all his characters together for the catastrophe.…[295] As in Leir (Sc. 23), the old King feels a sovereign shame which keeps him from going to [Cordelia], but is reunited in a scene springing, however distantly, from the Recognition scene in Leir, Sc. 24.…

[296] Shakespeare omits the conventional altercation between army-leaders in Leir, Sc. 30; but as in Leir, Sc. 31, the battle is merely sketched in V.2. In the old play it was the means by which Leir was restored to his throne—by foreign aid, however. Here it is the means by which he is captured by Edmund; the military aspect is entirely subordinate to the spiritual, but is no defeat of British by French forces.…
