Captaines, or Cõmaunders aboue the rest: Captaine Pippin, Marwoods deuill, Captaine Philpot, [tln 2021] Trayfords deuil, [tln 1921–2] Captaine Maho, Saras deuil, Captaine Modu, Maynies deuill, and Captaine Soforce, Anne Smiths deuil. These were [47] not all of equall authoritie, & place, but some had more, some fewer vnder theyr commaund. Pippin, Marwoods deuill was a Captaine, (marry, either cassierd for some part of bad seruice hee had done, or else a male-content standing vpon his worth), like some of our high Puntilios, scorned to sort himselfe with any of his ranke, and therefore like a melancholick Priuado, he affects Marwood to lie in the fields, and to gape at the Moone, and so of a [tln 2004–5] Cæsars humor, he raignes in Marwood alone.

Captaine Philpot, Trayfords deuill, was a Centurion, (as himselfe tels you) and had an hundred vnder his charge. Mary he was (as seemes) but a white-liuered deuill, for he was so hastie to be gone out of Trayford, for feare of the Exorcist, that hee would scarce giue him leaue, beeing a bed, to put on his breeches. The names of ther punie spirits cast out of Trayford were these, Hilco, [tln 1919] Smolkin, Hillio, Hiaclito, and Lustie huffe-cap: this last seemes some swaggering punie deuill, dropt out of a Tinkers budget. But Hiaclito may not be slipped ouer without your obseruation: for he scorning a great while (as the Author saith) to tell his name, at last he aunswered most proudly, my name is Hiaclito, a Prince, & Monarch of the world. And beeing asked by the Exorcist, what fellowes he had with him: hee said that hee had no fellowes, but two men, and an vrchin boy. It was little beseeming his state (I wis) beeing so mighty a Monarch, to come into our coasts so skuruily attended, except hee came to see fashions in England, and so made himselfe priuate till the Exorcist reueald him: or els that he was of [tln 1776, 2953] the new Court cut, affecting no other traine thẽ two crasie fellowes, and an vrchin butter-flie boy.…

[48][tln 1921–2] Modu, Ma: Maynies deuill, was a graund Commaunder, Muster-maister ouer the Captaines of the seauen deadly sinnes: Cliton, Bernon, Hilo, Motubizanto, & the rest, himselfe a Generall of a kind and curteous disposition: so saith Sara Williams; touching this deuils acquaintance with Mistres Plater, and her sister Fid.

Sara Williams had in her at a bare word, all the deuils in hell. The Exorcist askes Maho, Saras deuil, what cõpany he had with him, and the deuil makes no bones, but tels him in flat termes, [tln 2248+1–+5] all the deuils in hell.…

And if I misse not my markes, this Dictator Modu [error for Maho] saith, hee had beene in Sara by the space of two yeeres, then so long hell was cleere, and [tln 2022] had not a deuill to cast at a mad dogge.…
Heere, if you please, you may take a suruay of the [49] whole regiment of hell: at least the chiefe Leaders, and officers, as we finde them enrolled by theyr names.
First [tln 1857] Killico, Hob, and a third anonymos, are booked downe for three graund Commaunders, euery one hauing vnder him 300. attendants.…

[tln 2004] Frateretto, [tln 1895] Fliberdigibbet, [tln 2014+12] Hoberdidance, Tocobatto were foure deuils of the round, or Morrice, whom Sara in her fits, tuned together, in measure and sweet cadence. And least you should conceiue, that the deuils had no musicke in hell, especially that they would goe a maying without theyr musicke, [tln 2004–5] the Fidler comes in with his Taber, & Pipe, and a whole Morice after him, with motly visards for theyr better grace. These foure had forty assistants vnder them, as themselues doe confesse.…

Delicat, an other Captaine, or vicenarie in Sara, ha-[50]uing vnder him twenty assistants, seemes by his English name to be yeoman of the Sprucery, to see the deuils motly visards, after they were soiled with Brimstone, and sweat, to be brusht vp, and kept sweet, neate, & cleane. These were the Officers, or Commaunders names, that had taken vp theyr lodging in Sara Williams, now the [tln 1311] many, rascality, or black-guard of hell, were God knows how many in her: for all were there [tln 2023–7] tag, and ragge, cut and long-tayle, yet diuers of them it pleaseth the holie Exorcist to commaund theyr names to doe them some grace, others he lets goe out, leauing no names, but an ill sauour behind thẽ. The names of such as the Exorcist thought good to fauour, were these, Puffe, and [tln 2014+21] Purre, the two fat deuils, that had beene coniurd vp for mony, anno 84, and would not home to hell againe, till good company came for them. Lustie Dickie, Cornerd-cappe, Nurre, Molkin, Wilkin, Helcmodion, Kellicocam. These were like the Sporades in via lactea, hauing neither office, order, nor ranke; all these were Saras deuils.

Maho was [tln 1921–2] generall Dictator of hell: & yet for good manners sake, hee was contented of his good nature to make shew, that himselfe was vnder the check of Modu, the graund deuil in Ma: Maynie. [tln 2248+1] These were all in poore Sara at a chop, with these the poore soule trauailed vp and downe full two yeeres together; so as during those two yeeres, it had beene all one to say, one is gone to hell, or hee is gone to Sara Williams: for shee poore wench had all hell in her belly. And had had it still to this day for any thing we know, if it had not pleased Fa: Weston, and his twelue holy disciples, to haue deliuered her of that deuil-childe.…

[73] Heere strange tragicall exclamations filled all our eares. Deuils why come yee not? and thou Pippin (which was the name of the tormenting deuill) doost thou not reuenge my quarrell? is there no ayde, no succour left in hel? Take mee miserable caytife, and hurle mee into the infernall flames: but if eyther you will not, or cannot right this disgrace, then you launces, swords, and kniues dash thorough me: fire, dogs, plague, mischiefe consume me, house fall vpon me, earth swallow mee, [tln 1258–67] lightning from heauen deuoure mee: who can beare my burden? who can endure my heate? who can be thus torne in peeces, beeing [tln 1258–67] rent with a thousand nayles? Who would not think that hee heard Hercules furens, or Aiax flagellifer newly come from hell? Was euer [tln 1412–13] Prometheus with his Vulture, Sisyphus with his stone, [tln 2795–6] Ixion with his wheele in such a case? Did euer the [tln 991] God-gastring Giants, whom Iupiter ouerwhelmed with Pelion and Ossa, so complaine of theyr loade? Or Phaeton so bellow when he was burned with Iupiters flames, as poore Marwood heere bellowes; and roares vnder Edmunds fierie flames, and all with the onely touch of his head with his Ignatian hand?…

[94]…But when this good natured man shal heare of the more various, and more direful not whips, but scorpions, stings, and fiery serpents of the holy Church: the [tln 2567–71] blacke gloomie armour, embellished with the thicke smoake, & vapour of hell; [tln 2013] the swords, darts, and speares of fire, pointed with grisly death, that the Church doth arme her infernall souldiers (the Exorcists) withall, against the princedome and power of hell, hee will cry out with Marwoods tormented deuil, terra dehisce, ne sentiam illas plagas, earth swallow mee vp, before I come neere the scorch of those flames.…

The Poets, to strike vs with a terror of the torments of Styx, doe present before our eyes, the three Eumenides sisters, [tln 2013] the Furies, and tormentors of hell, with black vgly visages, grisly with smoake, with whips of blood, and fire in theyr hands, theyr armes gored with blood: and a huge bunch of a thousand snakes crawling down theyr haire. Let me present you an Exorcist, armed by the Church at all poynts, to encounter hell, and the deuil, you wil laugh the Eumenides from of the stage.…

[97] If the Sceptick wil pry higher, & demaund, whence the Pope, & his consistory doe borrow that diuine power, to consecrate water, candle, brimstone, Frankincense, potions, Exorcismes, nick-names, and asses eares, and to sublimate theyr nature, & put into them such a fiery scorching flame, as shal turne thẽ into serpents, and scorpions, to bite and sting the deuil, and [tln 2965] to fire him out of his hold, as men smoke out a Foxe out of his burrow: these beeing of theyr owne nature, and in shew, silly poore stuffe to hold such diuine facultie in them?…

Simon Magus the Sorcerer, sent vnto Peter the Apostle certaine [tln 2023–7] deuils in the likenes of dogges, to deuoure [98] the blessed Apostle. S. Peter being taken on a suddaine, not looking for such currish guests (as beeing belike at dinner) consecrates on a suddaine certaine morsels of bread, and throwes them to the dogge-deuils, and by the power of that bread they were all put to flight. And is not this a faire tale of Simon and his hel-dogges that would haue snapt up S. Peter, but onely for a soppe of bread?

[106]…O fidem Catholicam! that hast such a check, and soueraignty ouer all the power of hell, as that thy priests leade about deuils after them, as [tln 1282–5, 2303+11] men leade Beares by the nose, or Iack an Apes in a string, and enduest thy young Infants, with such heroical magnanimitie, as they dare play with the deuils nose.…[107]…But little did those three good Kings of Cullen know, what a powerful rich present they had brought vnto our Sauiour, whẽ they presented him with Frankincense, as little deeming of fuming any deuil in theyr way, or profugating a deuil from the body of our blessed Sauiour.…[T]he Egyptian priests…halowed them [i.e., their idols], and theyr Altars with frankinsence, and candle: you haue very wisely, deuoutly, and heathenishly, smoaked your Altars, your images, your Churches, your vestments, your reliques, your beades, your bookes, your breeches with this perfume, for feare of [tln 1840] deuil-blasting; and therefore you needed not vppon our deuil Theater to grace it with any new wonder.
[122] [Sara Williams] tels her owne tale.

At one time (saith she) [tln 2567–71] when it began to be with me, after the manner of women, the Priests did pretend, that the deuill did rest in the most secret part of my body: wherevppon they deuised to apply the reliques vnto that place?

div.head: CHAP. 21.

argument.p: Of the strange formes, shapes, and apparitions of the deuills.

div.p: It is a question moued by Scaliger: Why [tln 464] men of a melancholick constitution be more subiect to feares, fancies, and imagination of deuils, and witches, then other tempers be? His aunswer is, quia ab atra bile, atri & fuliginosi ge-[132]nerantur spiritus, qui cerebrum pingunt turbulentis phantasmatibus, because from their blacke & sooty blood, gloomie fuliginous spirits do fume into their braine, which bring blacke, gloomy, and frightful images, representations, and similitudes in them, wherwith the vnderstanding is troubled, and opprest.…

This man, though during the prime of his wit he was of a most, pregnant, ripe, and subtile discourse, yet his wit beeing deepe woaded with that melancholick blacke dye, had his braine veram sedem dæmonum, the theater, and sporting house for deuils to daunce in: for he hath in his braine, such strange speculations, fantasmes, and theoremes for deuils, as a man may see a great deale of madnes mixed with his great wit. For he holds [133] that deuils may transforme themselues into any shape of beasts, or similitude of men, and may eate, drinke, and conuerse familiarly with them, and may haue the act of generation with women, as they please. And not that onely, but that a Witch by oyntments, & charmes, may transforme herselfe into the shape of any beast, bird, or fish: that she may flie in the ayre, that she may depriue men of their generatiue power, that she may transferre corne out of one field into another, and may cause [tln 1258–67] haile, thunder, and winde at her pleasure.…[134] But out of this, and such like Heathenish dreames, what a world of hel-worke, deuil-worke, and Elue-worke, had we walking amongst vs heere in England, what time that popish mist had befogged the eyes of our poore people? How were our children, old women, and maides afraid to crosse a Churchyeard, or a three-way leet, or to goe for spoones into the Kitchin without a candle? and no marueile. First, because [tln 2514–17] the deuil comes from a smoakie blacke house, he, or a lewd frier was still at hand, with ougly hornes on his head, fire in his mouth, a cowes tayle in his breech, eyes like a bason, fangs like a dogge, clawes like a Beare, a skinne like a Neger, and a voyce roaring like a Lyon; then boh, or oh, in the dark was enough to make their haire stand vpright.…But if a Peeter-penny, or an houzle-egge were behind, or a patch of [135] tyth vnpaid to the Church (Iesu Maria), thẽ ware where you walke for feare of bull-beggers, spirits, witches, vrchins, Elues, hags, fairies, Satyrs, Pans, Faunes, Syluans, Kit with the candlesticke, Tritons, Centaurs, Dwarffs, Giants, impes, Calcars, coniurers, Nymphs, changlings, scritchowles, Incubus[,] the spurne, the mare, the man in the oake, helwayne, the fire-drake, the puckle, Tom thumbe, hobgoblin, Tom-tumbler, Boneles, and the rest: and what girle, boy, or old wisard would be so hardy to step ouer the threshold in the night for an half-penny worth of mustard amongst this frightfull crue, without a dosen auemaries, two dosen of crosses surely signed, and halfe a dosen Pater nosters, and the commending himselfe to the tuition of S. Vncumber, or els our blessed Lady?

These be the Popes, and his holy Legats, and those of his holy mission, and commission from hell their frightful crue, theyr black-guard, with which they work wonders, amongst a faithlesse, sencelesse generation: these shoute about them, attend them, and are of theyr guard, and trayne, wheresoeuer they goe, or walke, as Styx, Phlegeton, and the Eumenides doe guard Æacus in hell: with these they worke their wonders, making Images to speake, vautes to sound, trunks to carry tales, Churchyeards to swarme, houses to rush, rumble, and clatter with chaynes, high-waies, old graues, pittes, and woods ends to be haunted with lights, owles, and poakers; with these they adrad, and [tln 991] gaster sencelesse old women, witlesse children, and melancholike dottrels, out of their wits.

These Monster-swarmes his Hol: & his helly crue haue scraped, and raked together out of old doating heathen Historiographers, wisardizing Augurs, imposturizing South-sayers, dreaming Poets, Chimerial conceiters, & coyners of fables, such as puffe vp our young gallants with bigge lookes, and bombast phrases, as the booke of Lancelot du Lake, Guy of Warwicke, The Mirrour of [136] Knighthoode, Amadis de Gaule, and such like their Legends; out of these they conceit their monstrous shapes, vgly bug-beares, hydeous apparitions of ghosts: out of these they conforme, their charmes, enchauntments, periapts, amulets, characters, wast coates, and smockes of proofe, against [tln 1258–67] hayle, thunder, lightning, biting of mad dogges, gnawing of Rats, against botches, biles, cros-biting, [tln 1840] sparrow-blasting, Owle-hunting, and the like.…Why then ho, beware, looke about you my neighbours; if any of you haue a sheepe sicke of the giddies, or an hogge of the mumps, or an horse of the staggers, or a knauish boy of the schoole, or an idle girle of the wheele, or a young drab of the sullens, and hath not fat enough for her porredge, nor her father, and mother, butter enough for their bread; and she haue a little helpe of the Mother, Epilepsie, or Cramp, to teach her role her eyes, wrie her mouth, gnash her teeth, startle with her body, hold her armes and hands stiffe, make anticke faces, girne, [tln 2248+4] mow, and mop like an Ape, tumble like a Hedgehogge, and can mutter out two or three words of gibridg, as obus, bobus: and then with-all old mother Nobs hath called her by chaunce, idle young huswife, or bid the deuil scratch her, then no doubt but mother Nobs is the Witch: the young girle [137] is [tln 1840] Owle-blasted, and possessed: and it goes hard, but ye shal haue some idle, adle, giddie, lymphaticall, illuminate dotrel, who being out of credite, learning, sobriety, honesty, and wit, wil take this holy aduantage, to raise the ruines of his desperate decayed name, and for his better glory wil be-pray the iugling drab, and cast out Mopp the deuil.…

The frightful fancies, and fond [tln 991] gastful opinions, of all the other dotrels arise out of one of these two rootes; weakenes of wit, or vnstayednes in religion. [tln 1921–2] Horace the Heathen spied long agoe, that a Witch, a Wizard, and a Coniurer were but bul-beggers to scare fooles: writing thus to one that had so much wit, as to discerne a poled sheepe, from a parlous beast.

lg.l: Somnia, terrores Magicos, miracula, sagas,
Nocturnos Lemures, portentaq; Thessala rides.
That is,
Dreames, and Magicall affrights,
Wonders, Witches, walking sprights,
What Thessalian Hags can doe,
All this seemes a iest to you.

div.p:
And Geoffry Chaucer, who had his two eyes, wit, and learning in his head, spying that all these brainlesse imaginations, of witchings, possessings, house-hanting, and the rest, were the forgeries, cosenages, Imposturs, and legerdemaine of craftie priests, and leacherous Friers, either to maske their venerie, or to enritch their pur-[138]ses, by selling their Pope-trumpery (as Medals, agnus dei, Blessed beades, holy water, halowed Crosses, periapts, amulets, smocks of proofe, and such) at a good rate; as who would not giue soundly for a Medal defensiue against the deuil? writes in good plaine termes of the holy Couent of Friers thus:
For there as wont to walken was an Elfe,
There walketh now the Limitor himselfe:
In euery bush, and vnder euery tree,
There nis none other Incubus but hee.

Now see our holy Comedians, if they haue not dressed their Denham deuils, after the old Romaine fashion, fit to amaze Will Sommers with-all. Heare the graue Miraclist, how aunciently hee attires the deuil for Sara. Shee had beene diuers times affrighted with vglie visions. You shal neuer heare a prologue to a Popish possession, but it begins with that style. As she sate by the fire somewhat late with an other mayde of the same house, being both in a readines to goe to bed, they fell into a slumber, and drousing thus by the fire, there approached neere vnto them [tln 2014+21] three Cats, making a terrible noyse, and sprawling about this young mayde, one of them leapt ouer her head, and an other crept betwixt her legges: (by M[a]lleus, and Mengus his rules, this might be a priest in the likenes of a Cat: their hunt was all that way) whereat shee sodainly looking behind her: (as hauing beene vsed to such creeping Cats,) she beheld a strange huge Cat, of the bignes of a Mastiffe-dogge, staring in her face, with eyes very great, and bright, to the bignes of a sawcer. Heere is a right priests Hobgoblin, or Tom Spanner in the darke. And wil you heare Sara her selfe vncase you this bugge: Looke in her deposition. Shee was looking for egges in a bush by her Maisters house, and sodainly a Cat leapt out, whereat she gaue a startle: and this Cat, by this priestly power (O Catholicam fidem) is sodainlie Hobgoblinizd, and hath gotten a shape, as bigge as [139] a Mastiffe, and eyes as bigge as a sawcer: O monstrous Catholique faith, that canst turne ordinarie Cats in a moment into Mastiffes. You shal haue them rancked together, as they came from the Popes tyring-house, that ye may see, which deuil you like best, to set the Asses eares vpon. At supper the Cat afore-said, was turned into [tln 2023–7] a dogge, of two colours, blacke, and greene, and there-with-all, a Spaniel bayed, (and therefore Maho was certainly come.) At another time the deuill came downe the chimney in a Winde, and blew the ashes about the chamber: Sometime he appeared in the likenes of a Man: sometime of a Bright thing, that sate vpon our Ladies image: sometime in the likenes of an Irish boy, with a blacke curled head: sometime of a great Black dogge: sometime he came flying like a Sparrowe, with a Woodcocks bill: sometime like a Toade, with a nose like a Moale: sometime like a Mouse: sometime like a Minister: sometime like an Ey, without a head: sometimes like a Ruffian, with curled haire: somtimes like an Old man, with a long beard: and aboue all, he came in with a drumme, and seauen motly vizards, dauncing about the chamber.…

div.head: CHAP. 22.

argument.p:
Of the admirable finall act of expelling the deuils, and of
their formes in theyr departing.

div.p: …The first deuill that was disseised was [tln 1919] Smolkin, [tln 2021] Trayfords spirit, whom Sara espied (saith the Miraclist) to goe out at Trayfords right eare in the forme of a Mouse, and it made the poore wench at the sight of the Mouse almost out of her wits. The next deuil dispossessed was Hilcho at Vxbridge, who appeared (saith our Authour) to the possessed parties at his going out, like a flame of fire, and lay glowing in the fire in Trayfords sight, till he had a new charge. The third was [tln 2014+12] Haberdidance, Saras dauncing deuil: who appeared to the patient, like [tln 1840, 2248+2] a whirlwind, turning round like a flame of fire, and his voyce was heard by a Cooke, as hee flew ouer the Larder. Captaine Filpot went his way in the likenes of a smoke, turning round, and so tooke his way vp into the chim-[141]ney. Lusty Dicke (as seemes) did slippe a button in one of his turnes aboue ground: for he went out in a foule vnsauory stench. Delicate, and Lusty Iolly Ienkin went out, one whirling like a snake, the other in a vapor not verie sweet. Lusty Huffcappe went out in the likenes of a Cat. [tln 1857] Killico, Hob, and the third Anonymos, all Captaines, went out in a wind. Purre went out in a little whirlewind. [tln 2004] Frateretto in a smoke.

Maister Maynie had in him (as you haue heard) the Maister-deuils of the seauen deadly sinnes, and therefore his deuils went out in the forme of those creatures, that haue neerest resemblance vnto those sinnes: as for example; [tln 1873–4] the spirit of Pride went out in the forme of a Peacocke (forsooth) the spirit of Sloth in the likenesse of an Asse: the spirit of Enuy in the similitude of a Dog: the spirit of Gluttony in the forme of a Woolfe. But it is to be wondered at, that Generall Maho, at the last, and most dreadfull exorcisme of all, when hee was expelled with 22000. yeeres torment layd vppon his backe, hee slunke out without any similitude at all. And more, an ordinary Reader will wonder, that Maho, beeing [tln 1921–2] Dictator of hell, is said in the Legend of Miracles, and so noted by Sara, to haue chosen [tln 2567–71] such a strange part in Sara for his passage out, as I dare not name: and yet deuils, comedians, and their reporters may haue licence in all Courts to call all things by their name. And indeede heere lyes the wonder of all, considering that that namelesse part, the deuils port-gate in Sara, was the priests quest and haunt, which they had hunted sore, had crossed, recrossed, and surcrossed with their holy hands, had sacred, or seared vvith application of their reuerend strong reliques, and other their potent holy parts, (as you haue heard poore Sara herselfe confesse:) the deuill should once dare to come neere that part, that had been harowed, (I would say halowed) and enriched with so many precious Iewels from Rome: but you shall finde [142] the Authour noted that part, and assigned it for Maho the deuils passage vppon very sage and prudent consideration.

[194] Also she [Sara Williams] saith, that [tln 2014+13] if at any times she did belch, as oftentimes she did by reason that shee was troubled with a wind in her stomacke, the priests would say at such times, that then the spirit began to rise in her. Whereas [195] diuers times since she hath beene likewise troubled with such wind in her stomacke and rifting, and thereby perceiueth that they said vntruly, when they said that that wind was the deuil. But as shee saith, if they heard any croaking in her belly, (a thing whereunto many women are subiect, especially when they are fasting) then they would make a wonderful matter of that. One time shee remembreth, that shee hauing the said croaking in her belly, or making of herselfe some such noyse in her bed, they said it was the deuill that was about the bedde, that spake with the voyce of a Toade, and there-with they seemed, as though they were greatly afraid. But this examinate, though shee knew, there was no such cause of theyr feare, if they were indeed at all afraid, as they did pretend, yet did shee let them alone, and said nothing vnto them.

[219] This exam: [Friswood Williams] further saith, that one Alexander an Apothecarie, hauing brought with him from London to Denham on a time [tln 1835] a new halter, and two blades of kniues, did leaue the same, vpon the gallerie floare in her Maisters house. The next morning he tooke occasion to goe with this exam: into the said gallerie, where she espying the said halter, and blades, asked Ma: Alexander what they did there: Hee making the matter strange, aunswered, that he saw them not, though hee looked fully vpon them; she her selfe pointing to them with her finger, where they lay within a yard of them, where they stoode both together. No (quoth this exam:) doe you not see them? and so taking them vp, said, looke you heere: Ah (quoth he) now I see them indeed, but before I could not see them: And therefore saith he, I perceaue that the deuil hath layd them heere, to worke some mischiefe vpon you, that are possessed.

Heereuppon maister Alexander told the priests what a strange thing had happened, and a great search vvas made in the house, to know how the said halter & knife blades came thether: but it could not in any wise be found out, as it was pretended, till Ma: Mainy in his next fit said, as it was reported, that the deuil layd them in the Gallery, that some of those that were possessed, might either hang thẽselues with the halter, or kil themselues with the blades.

Now this exam: further saith, that shee herselfe did espy the end of the halter, in maister Alexanders pocket, the night before shee saw it, and the blades in the Gallery, at such time as he drew out of his pocket a certaine boxe of Wafer-cakes for Masses. Whereby shee is fully perswaded, as she saith, that he the said Alexander, [220] was himselfe the deuil, that layde the halter, and knife-blades in the said Gallerie, and as she saith, she told maister Dibdale as much, when the search was, how they should come thether.

[263] The disease I [Richard Mainy] spake of, was a spice of [tln 1328] the Mother, where-with I had beene troubled (as is before mentioned) before my going into Fraunce: whether I doe rightly terme it the Mother or no, I know not: but it is wel knowne to the Physicians in London, that be aliue, and were then of any name, that my eldest brother Thomas Mainy had the same disease, and that he died of it: and Ma: Edmond Peckham (as I haue beene credibly enformed) was likewise troubled with it. When I was sick of this disease in Fraunce, a Scottish Doctor of Physick then in Paris, called it, as I remember, Vertiginem capitis. It riseth (as he said, and I haue often felt) of a wind in the bottome of the belly, and proceeding with a great swelling, causeth a very painfull collicke in the stomack, and an extraordinary giddines in the head. With this disease I am still once in foure or fiue yeeres troubled, and I doe greatly suspect that it wil end me, as it did my brother.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Harsnett’s Declaration
div.p: Commentary on Sh.’s use of Harsnett is generally of two kinds: speculation about why he would have been drawn to an anti-Catholic satire of exorcisms that had occurred twenty years before he wrote Lr., and discussion of the influences of Harsnett’s book on the play.

As for the first, possible reasons given are the general notoriety of the events described, which had occasioned a number of books and pamphlets besides Harsnett’s and had been the subject of an inquiry conducted in 1598 and 1601–2 by the court of the Ecclesiastical High Commission; Sh.’s wish to appeal to the interests of his patron King James; his personal acquaintance with people from Stratford involved in the exorcisms; his connections with Harsnett; and his presumed sympathy with the plight of English recusants.

Theobald (ed. 1733, 5:163–4) was the first to name (in print) Harsnett’s account of the exorcisms as a source for Edgar’s Tom o’ Bedlam scenes: The whole Matter being blown up, the Criminals brought to the Stake, and the Trick of Devil-hunting brought into Ridicule; Dr. Harsenet…[164] wrote a smart Narrative of this whole Proceeding.…This Transaction was so rife in every Body’s Mouth, upon the Accession of King James the 1st to the Crown; that our Poet thought proper to make his Court, by helping forward the Ridicule of it. Theobald first learned of Harsnett’s book from Warburton in April 1729 (see Nichols, 1817, 2:209, 230, 490), and there has been some discussion whether he or Warburton deserves more credit for showing its importance to Lr. Theobald included in his edition of 1733 two notes on Harsnett’s influence on Lr. (see nn. 1827, 2248+1–+5); the long one at 1827 is written in the first person and unsigned, as is a shorter, reorganized version in Warburton’s 1747 edition at 2248+1–+5; in substance and phrasing they have much in common. David Nichol Smith, Eighteenth Century Essays on Shakespeare (Glasgow, 1903; rev. Oxford, 1963, pp. xlvii f.) notes that Warburton marked in his copy of Theobald’s 1733 ed. a number of passages in the Preface and notes for which he claimed authorship; Smith apparently relied on Aldis Wright for inspection of this edition (now in the Capell collection of Trinity College, Cambridge); Wright identified thirteen such passages in the Preface but none in the notes. Although Vickers (1974, 2:18, 507–8, 535) does not (p. 535) identify Theobald’s two notes on Harsnett among those that Warburton claimed, and does not print as being Warburton’s the shorter version of 1827 that appears in Warburton’s 1747 ed. at 2248+1–+5, he nonetheless (p. 507) credits Warburton for Theobald’s long note at 1827. Theobald at least made one contribution in correctly identifying Harsnett as the author of A Declaration, a fact apparently still unknown to Warburton in Feb. 1730 (see Nichols, 2:490). At least the two men shared some knowledge on the subject, and some of it was first published by Theobald.

Hunter (1845, 1:380–90) found links between Sh.’s TN and Harsnett’s Discovery of the fraudulent practices of John Darrel (1599), an exposure of exorcisms performed in 1586 and 1596–7 by Puritans rather than Catholics. These supposed allusions would point to Sh.’s earlier and recurrent interest in Harsnett’s writings; but the links with TN are dubious—see Furness, ed. 1901, p. 322—though they have been reasserted by Brownlow (1993, p. 107).

Stevenson (1952, pp. 898 ff.): There is nothing in Sh. comparable to this full and exact recall of a piece of polemical theology; perhaps he knew some of the Jesuits arraigned in the case. (P. 899): The wide scattering of page locations at which [Sh.] found names and phrases later copied into Tom’s part [citing pp. 47, 49, 136, 194–5, 225, 268, 278, all discussed in Malone, ed. 1790, vol. 8] indicates he read the whole of it. Harsnet [sic] set out to destroy the claims of Robert Debdale to be a miracle worker and martyr for the Catholic faith. (P. 900): Catholics in England so hated the book that they bought most of the copies for burning, to get it out of circulation. Shakespeare in his selective use of names and phrases from it gave, however, not the slightest inkling of the true contents of the book.…[901] It was the only book of polemical divinity he can be shown to have read in entirety and with care; such information as he did extract from it was tangential to Harsnet’s manifest purpose in writing the book; had Shakespeare been really interested in gathering demonological tit-bits when he read it, any number of other books better adapted to his purpose were immediately at hand.

However, Robert Debdale…had been a neighbor of the Hathaways at Shottery. A coetanean of Shakespeare, Debdale (according to Fripp [1938, p. 180]) may well have been a fellow schoolmate in the Stratford school. [In fact, since Dibdale, b. 1556, was seven or eight years older than Sh., and left Stratford for the Continent in 1575, when Sh. was eleven, he was not Sh.’s schoolmate.] Thomas Cottam, whose relics…Debdale carried about with him at Fulmer, was the brother of John Cottam, schoolmaster at Stratford during 1579–82. Debdale wrote a letter in 1580 to John Pace, who was intimate with Richard Hathaway, Anne’s father, having on 1 September 1581 witnessed Richard Hathaway’s will.…[902] The book must have interested Shakespeare not so much as a religious exposé as a revelation of happenings in Debdale’s last days. The Declaration was for Shakespeare a story of a Shottery personage important in the private world of the Hathaways and of his own family.
Munro (ed. 1957, 6:895): This [above] provides a reasonable explanation of Shakespeare’s unexpected interest in the book.

Elton (1966, pp. 89 ff.): First, as chaplain and secretary to Richard Bancroft, Bishop of London, Harsnet had been licenser of books for the press, and such a function could have brought his opinions to Shakespeare’s attentions.…

[90] Moreover, Harsnet had in a cause célèbre in 1599 licensed for the press his old friend John Hayward’s The First Part of the Life…of King Henrie IIII, eulogistically dedicated to the Earl of Essex, Southampton’s friend. Presumed Shakespearean associations with the Essex group, as well as Harsnet’s threatened share in Hayward’s punishment, might also have linked the dramatist and Harsnet. Further, the latter, like Hayward, soon found favor under James, who became Shakespeare’s royal patron.…

p.quote: Significantly for Shakespeare, Harsnet’s exposure of demonic possession suited James…. The monarch’s interest in demoniacs appears, for instance, in his Daemonologie (Edinburgh, 1597).…James had, in April 1605, proudly exposed the supernatural claims of Richard Haydock…[and] of a woman pretended to be bewitched.…James diagnosed her swelling as having been occasioned by the disease called the mother. [91]…The woman’s insensitivity to pain when she was stuck with pins…has obvious affinities with Edgar’s Tom o’ Bedlam role.…Jonson, like Shakespeare in both Lear and Macbeth (1606), drew upon Harsnet to expose pretended possession. Besides Volpone, other plays about the time of Lear and Macbeth catered to James’s interest in demonology. [He names several]…

div.p: [93] Through Edgar’s role, in turn, demonic possession and miracles are thus plainly shown to be frauds: the first, publicly assumed as part of a disguise during banishment; the second, a benevolent and admitted trifling ([2471]) played, in the audience’s full view, upon a suicidal and blind old man. For Harsnet in his Declaration had not only assailed pretended possession; he had also, like James, attacked as heathenish superstition the fraudulent belief in miracles.

Lascelles (1973, pp. 72–3): This [Sh.’s acquaintance with Dibdale] would indeed account for his reading Harsnet’s recital of [the case] with close attention; but not, surely, for his making this very use of what he found there. A personal relationship, of whatever kind or degree, would hardly prompt a man to exhibit particulars of the charges in the framework of Edgar’s grotesque impersonation.…This disgusting case is investigated without repugnance by a man who was to rise high under James I—regrettably, in the Church. Harsnet’s cart-horse irony, his ostentatious learning, and that knowledge of the theatre which enabled him to present the affair in terms of play-acting, must have gained him enough readers to account for two further editions (1604 and 1605)—including Sh.
Milward (1973, p. 54): It is even possible that the lot of such priests as Weston and Dibdale provided Shakespeare with a suggestion for his portrayal of Edgar in hiding.

Kaula (1975, pp. 18–29) finds similarities with Christopher Bagshaw’s pamphlet A True Relation (1601) describing Weston’s (Father Edmund’s) activities in 1595, and thinks that these suggest Sh.’s continuing interest in English Recusants. These similarities, however, are too general—e.g., Machiavellian practices, divisions in the community, etc.—to show any particular influence on Lr.

Bradbrook (1978, p. 194): What has not been observed is that the brutal jeers and savage obscenities of this most unchristian work combine insults to Papists with insults to players.…It was calculated to hit Shakespeare particularly hard at a particularly sensitive moment. I think the origins of King Lear are to be found in a collision between the smug pieties and exaggerated poetic justice of the old play (King Leir) and the vindictive game which Samuel Harsnett plays in his mocking pamphlet.…Among the assistants [to Edmunds/Weston, Superior of the Jesuits] was a seminary priest, Robert Dibdale, who had been Shakespeare’s schoolfellow at Stratford Grammar School [not quite; see above s.v. Stevenson].…[197] Players’ morals are insulted to castigate the wandering priests: It is the fashion of vagabond players, that coast from town to town with a truss and a cast of fiddles, to carry in their consort broken queans and Ganimedes as well for their night’s pleasance as their day’s pastime ([1603,] p. 149).…By [Harsnett’s] mocking these devilish rites as mere acting, acting itself became tainted with devilry. [Murphy, 1984, pp. 184–5, defends Harsnett’s unchristian language as the habitual language of the historic Church against heretics. He does not invent this language; it fills the libraries of Europe.]

Brownlow (1993, pp. 108–10) rehearses the personal reasons why Sh. would have been interested in The Declaration. Since there is considerable evidence that Sh.’s family was Catholic, Sh. may have had a continuing general interest in the fortunes of English recusants, and particularly those with ties to Stratford. Robert Dibdale, one of the exorcists, had been born in Stratford in about 1556, was contemporary of Sh.’s wife Anne Hathaway, and left Stratford in 1575 to go overseas (hence was not schoolfellow and not provably a friend of Sh.); he was executed in Oct. 1586. Dibdale’s sister, Agnes, married a John Pace in 1578, who in 1581 witnessed the will of Richard Hathaway (d. Sept. 1581), father of Sh.’s future wife Anne (m. Nov. 1582). Thomas Cottam, born in Stratford in 1549, who was overseas with his friend Dibdale in 1575 and became a Jesuit martyr in 1582, is briefly named a half-dozen times by Harsnett; he was the younger brother of John Cottam, Stratford schoolmaster from 1579 to 1581 or 1582, years when Sh. may have matriculated. [Honigmann (1985, pp. 40–9) speculates that John Cottam may thereafter have helped secure Sh. a position as teacher and actor in a recusant household in Lancashire.] Harsnett once makes passing mention (as Arden only, p. 85) to Edward Arden, probably a fourth cousin of Sh., who was executed as a Catholic traitor in 1584. [Sh. may have been aware of the executions of Dibdale, Cottam, and Arden before reading Harsnett, but only Dibdale, whose connection with Sh. is remote and tangential at best, plays a large enough part in Harnett’s narrative to have possibly drawn Sh.’s attention to the book.]

[129] As I have suggested elsewhere,…some of the thought and imagery of this counter-statement to Harsnett’s cruelty [i.e., Lr.] was suggested by the work of the Jesuit poet and martyr St. Robert Southwell.…[130] Robert Southwell, born in 1561, was Harsnett’s and Shakespeare’s contemporary; Shakespeare would certainly have known people [131] Southwell knew, and indeed, if Christopher Devlin’s genealogy is correct, the two men were remotely related to each other.
Commentary on Sh.’s use of Harsnett has pointed to Edgar’s impersonation of Tom o’ Bedlam, devil names and other vocabulary, a keen tragic awareness of human suffering, and possibly political themes.

Theobald (ed. 1733, 5:164): Edgar thro’ all his Frenzy supposes himself possess’d by Fiends; and…the greatest Part of his dissembled Lunacy, the Names of his Devils, and the descriptive Circumstances he alludes to in his own Case, are all drawn from this Pamphlet, and the Confessions of the poor deluded Wretches recorded by Harsnett.

Skottowe (1824, pp. 129–30): Shakspeare…borrowed, for the use of Edgar, many casual phrases, which, being inexpressive of valuable ideas, are devoid of sufficient interest to justify their individual quotation.

Paul (1950, p. 127): Edgar plays the sham demoniac thrusting pins into his bare arms and pretending to be infested with devils. To learn the tricks of this kind of fraud, [Sh.] is reading Harsnet’s book.

Muir (1951, pp. 13–21; 1952, pp. 555–6) shows parallels with Lr., mainly in Act 3, and points out a few words in Harsnett that first appear in Sh. in Lr.; these instances are recorded in the notes (see above). He further (ed. 1952, pp. 253–6) reprints the more than eighty passages in Harsnett that have a parallel in Lr., and adds (1957, pp. 152–3): It may even be suggested that the thunderstorm itself was partly derived from Harsnett, citing pp. 52, 73, 108 (see nn. 1584, 1604).

Lascelles (1973, pp. 72–3): Shakespeare, wanting devils and devil names, for a reason still to be determined, found his memory furnished with them. He had read his Declaration through.…[73] I do call in question any inference which supposes Shakespeare to have exploited this satire, and to that end foisted Harsnet’s devils into his play.…[Rather,] we have to be precipitated into fear; and—unlike the apprehension and despondency of Leir and Perillus in the old play—this pervasive fear exceeds altogether the sum of its circumstantial causes.…

[76] And so the ambiguous figure of the Bedlam beggar, sufferer or sinner or both, victim or imposter, with his presented nakedness and his infestation by fiends, has much in common with…beings in Doomsday paintings. United thus, the two images wake a deep and powerful fear, and lead to Lear’s (p. 77) preoccupation with Judgement.…Although these judgement fantasies of Lear’s madness are interspersed with references to hell and devils, they imply no appeal to, nor shrinking from, any concept of divine Justice. (P. 79): Kent’s reference to the promist end [3224], and Albany’s ensuing prayer for a termination, can refer only to Doomsday.

Bullough (1973, p. 300): Edgar is a pretended demoniac and as such his speeches from III.4 to IV.6 are full of material from Harsnett whose derisive account of the multifarious devils named in the case-histories affects his wild rhetoric and grotesque humour. Lear too shows the influence, e.g. as [1328–30], which recalls Harsnett’s Mainy, who had a spice of the Hysterica passio, as seems, from his youth, hee himselfe termes it the Moother.…As Poor Tom Edgar is, he tells Lear ([1865]) a servingman like some of the possessed witnesses, and in his ravings he declares that he has been occupied by five devils, naming some of those named by Sara Williams. Bullough suggests several other parallels: see notes 1835, 2014+21, 2514–17. (P. 301): Harsnett’s tract is a most important source, for it contributed greatly to the play’s atmosphere of trickery, deceit, and the sense of a wickedness inexplicable by reason. It helped Shakespeare to introduce a recognition that poverty, misery, and sickness of mind and body were widespread in the world.…The book gave him touches of extravagant comedy and satire; it increased his knowledge of psychological eccentricity, of human nature in distress. Above all, it added a new dimension to the Lear story by making him show the arrogant old king reduced to the lowest level of human existence, mad among madmen, yet recognizing his own lifelong indifference to other people’s sufferings.

Bradbrook (1978, p. 198): His [Harsnett’s] allegations of bawdyness mixed with sacramental rites, and the use of actors and priests to blacken one another, all in the name of religion, provided raw material for the central scenes of King Lear, more especially when juxtaposed with the docile pieties of the old play on King Leir.…It was the coming together of these incompatible works…which gave Shakespeare the extremes of the whole evil time in King Lear, its union of opposites. It is these two polarized emotional starting-points rather than the conventional ones usually mentioned that I would think illuminative of the play. They do not give us the story but they give the power drive, which injected the madness of possession into a history that was a model of reassuring providential acts.

Salingar (1983, p. 160): Shakespeare’s reaction is very unusual for him, in that he cuts out the comic—sadistically comic—vigour from his source. But at another level, it seems that Harsnett set Shakespeare thinking about episodes of sadism and moral perversion, taken from recent experience but not to be met with in any versions of the Lear story; they are documented instances of evil assuming the form of the grotesque.…Images of malevolence, torment and degradation, apparently suggested by Harsnett, stretch across Shakespeare’s play, still mainly connected with Edgar’s story, but hence also with Lear’s madness.

Murphy (1984, pp. 173, 175–6, 189): Harsnett…creates the scene in which we find not only Bo-peepe [see n. 690], and the Eeles [see n. 1398–1402], but the only source for the Fool himself that occurs in any of the known literary sources for Shakespeare’s King Lear.…[175] We call attention to Harsnett’s placing of the fool, Will Sommers [Henry VIII’s court fool and the best known fool in Tudor England], in the good play between the exorcist and the devil [1603, pp. 60–1]; he belabours them both handsomely with his fool’s sceptre, his bauble, for their dramatic performance.…I suggest that the world in which [176] Lear goes among the fools and plays bo-peep is the world of the religious enthusiasts, the gulls, who know not how to wear their wits and fall into aping and mimicking the bodily signs and words of the demons of hell. These are the wise men of Lear’s Fool.…[183] Harsnett presents us with the materials of gaiety and nightmare. This is for me exactly the note of the great scenes in King Lear, the world of the Fool, Kent, and above all, Edgar…. (P. 186): As for the antitheatrical slant in the Declaration: Muir, Brownlow, and Bradbrook have with justice underlined the pervasive lexicon of the theater in Harsnett’s satiric account of the exorcisms. In fact, the preparation for the public exorcisings is for Harsnett but a school of acting.…

[187] Professors Bradbrook and Brownlow are right to call attention to Harsnett’s contempt for the common players of his age, but he knows and loves dramatic writing, both in Greek and Roman letters and in the humanist drama of the Renaissance. He shows a genial knowledge of the old church plays, the clerkly morals. He shows not the slightest hesitation [as chaplain to the Bishop of London] in licensing for publication Thomas Nashe’s Sommers Last Will and Testament and Ben Jonson’s Every Man Out of His Humour.… (P. 189): For Harsnett the interpretations set forth in the manuals of exorcism are either a comedy of deluded enthusiasm or a devil-tragedy of treason, murder, and plot. Of course any combination of these is possible and one has a perfect formula for intertwining brilliant satiric comedy with the full power of a tragedy built upon deceit and intrigue.

(P. 197): The technique controlling Edgar’s speeches may be modelled on devices in Harsnett’s Declaration, i.e., (p. 198) the startling contrast in the voices of the persons normally and when possessed. (See nn. 1839, 1857, 1878–9, 1919, 1921–2.) (P. 200): One clear meaning of this world of darkness, devils, imprecations, revenge, and murder [in Act 3 of Lr.] is that it is a world of some English Roman Catholics (i.e. reflected in Harsnett).

Greenblatt (1985, pp. 177, 182–3), developing ideas from (1982, pp. 241–2): King Lear’s relation to Harsnett’s book, then, is essentially one of reiteration, a reiteration that signals a deeper and unexpressed institutional exchange. The official church dismantles and cedes to the players the powerful mechanisms of an unwanted and dangerous charisma; in return, the players confirm the charge that those mechanisms are theatrical and hence illusory.…[King Lear] offers then a double corroboration of Harsnett’s arguments: within the play, Edgar’s possession is clearly designated as a fiction, while the play itself is bounded by the institutional signs of fictionality: the wooden walls of the play space, payment for admission, known actors playing the parts, applause, the dances that followed the performance.…[182] But if false religion is theater, and if the difference between true and false religion is the presence of theater, what happens when this difference is enacted in the theater?

What happens…is that the official position is emptied out, even as it is loyally confirmed. This emptying out bears a certain resemblance to Brecht’s alienation effect, and still more to Althusser and Macherey’s internal distantiation.… For Harsnett the wicked are corrupt individuals in the service of a corrupt [183] church; in King Lear there are neither individuals nor institutions adequate to contain the released and enacted wickedness; the force of evil in the play is larger than any local habitation or name. In this sense, Shakespeare’s tragedy reconstitutes as theater the demonic principle demystified by Harsnett. Edgar’s fraudulent, histrionic performance is a response to this principle: evacuated rituals, drained of their original meaning, are preferable to no rituals at all. [Harsnett, of course, did not believe that the difference between true and false religion is the presence of theater. The Jesuit priests were promoting beliefs in exorcism and miracles that Harsnett and other Anglican bishops considered heretical. The difference was heresy; theater was one means of propagating it.]

Vickers (1993, pp. 240–1): [Greenblatt’s] argument develops as a (fallacious) syllogism: exorcism was denounced as counterfeit; but drama was also counterfeit; ergo, drama is a form of exorcism, or exorcism a form of drama. But the fact that opponents of exorcism used derogatory metaphors from the theatre does not mean that these are convertible propositions. Then to say that Edgar’s claim to have seen a fiend which parted from Gloucester before his attempted suicide…constitutes the play’s brooding upon spurious exorcism (p. [175]), or shows that the play effects a convergence of [241] exorcism and theater, to make such judgments is to build not upon sand but on air. The references to devils in King Lear have nothing to do with exorcism, and Shakespeare shows no interest either in the Jesuits or in what Greenblatt misleadingly describes (without ever defining) as charismatic exorcism (p. [177]).…Greenblatt reports Harsnett as saying that the hidden reality behind the imposture is…the theatre (p. [182]; my italics): but all that Harsnett says is that it is, like the theatre, a performance. Greenblatt arrives at the conclusion that if false religion is theater (p. [182]), then—the suggestion is—theatre is false religion, as proved by Edgar’s fraudulent, histrionic performance (p. [183]). Somehow all this is said to show that the official position is emptied out, even as it is loyally confirmed by Shakespeare, dutifully writing a play to show the identity of theatre and imposture (ibid.).…The further argument, that mad Lear’s discovery of the thing itself is actually a man playing a theatrical role (p. [182]), is fallacious: what Lear has discovered is a near-naked man, a poor forked animal. To start calling in question the theatricality of the theatre in these [242] terms is to step into a spiral that descends rather quickly, into itself. The link that Greenblatt attempts to forge between exorcism and King Lear is self-deluding, illusory.

Brownlow (1993, pp. 113 ff.): Shakespeare…did not merely read Harsnett to gather arcane details for Edgar’s part or to make a topical allusion, as older critics thought. The book entered deeply into his imagination, its contents to be transmuted into the iterative imagery of human suffering.…[122] [Greenblatt’s] interpretation attributes to Shakespeare and his audience a capacity for radical skepticism that seems to me anachronistic, and is based on an oddly positivistic understanding of religious faith and phenomena. Greenblatt says, for instance, that medieval resurrection plays offered the spectators ocular proof that Christ had risen and that Lear’s craving for just such proof…would seem to evoke precisely this theatrical and religious tradition, but only to reveal itself, in C. L. Barber’s acute phrase, as post-Christian(p. [181]). Mystery plays, however, prove nothing ocularly. They enact beliefs. The ending of Lear resembles a crucifixion play rather than a resurrection play. Like a crucifixion play, it leaves its spectators with a sign that no more interprets itself than did the corpse of a priest newly executed on that other kind of Elizabethan scaffold, the place of execution.…[126] Shakespeare as dramatist responds to Harsnett as presenter-critic by admitting his audience to a sight of the phenomena. Edgar performing as Poor Tom imitates some of the signs of possession.…The effect is surely not a satire on fake possession, but…an initiation of the audience into some realities that the signs of possession might portend. Similarly, when Edgar takes his father through the strange ritual of a false suicide, the effect should not be to turn the audience against miracles but to make them wonder what the definition of a miracle might be.…[127] King Lear, like Richard II, is about the consequences of the claim to absolute authority.…Harsnett’s book gave Shakespeare a microcosm of the claim to authority and its results.…

[128] King Lear is Shakespeare’s reply to Harsnett, an immense prophetic miracle play on religious and political subject matter, composed as a romantic tragedy of outrageous indecorum, appropriating or engulfing Harsnett’s own book, and situating its contents in a landscape of violence and alienation that, whether we read it as pre- or post-Christian, offers a devastating commentary on the spiritual condition of contemporary England.
Contra Theobald’s theory that Sh. wished to satirize Catholicism: [120] King Lear was acted by recusant actors in Yorkshire, 1609–10. This…does seem to prove that it was not an anti-Catholic [play].

Taylor (1994, pp. 294–5): The inclusion of King Lear in the repertory of a recusant company may surprise us.…[But] Harsnet’s Protestant book quotes extensively from a Catholic manuscript account of the same events, The Book of Miracles. Virtually everything which Shakespeare allegedly took from Harsnet could have been taken instead from the lost manuscript; at the very least, Shakespeare’s interest in Harsnet’s pamphlet might have been stimulated by the fact that it made widely available for the first time, in print, excerpts from a proscribed Catholic manuscript. What Shakespeare’s treatment utterly ignores is Harsnet’s own contribution: his ceaseless mockery of the whole idea of demonic possession. Edgar’s performance as Poor Tom, unlike Harsnet’s account, does not seem designed to provoke cynical laughter. What Shakespeare adds to Harsnet is the vindication and eventual triumph of the character most strongly associated with these popish impostures.…There can be no denying that King Lear draws [295] upon a series of incidents [rather, upon the language and details in an account of those incidents] in recent English recusant history—or that it was read by some of its first readers as a pro-Catholic play. (Only one manuscript copy of the Book of Miracles is known for certain to have existed, and since it passed from the hands of Bishop Bancroft, who possessed it in 1598, and Harsnett, who consulted it, to the archives of the Ecclesiastical Court (Brownlow, p. 22), Sh. probably never had access to it. Though Sh. borrowed details and vocabulary from Harsnet, no one has ever shown that he borrowed anything from the Book of Miracles. There is nothing definitively popish about Edgar’s act, and he performs it to save himself, not to refute or discredit Protestantism, or to vindicate Catholicism. There is no evidence that the Yorkshire players thought Lr. (or Three English Brothers or Pericles) a pro-Catholic play, and even if they did, that fact would not prove that it was.)

Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 102–4): The importance of Harsnett in relation to King Lear has been inflated by Stephen Greenblatt, who claims that in the play The Declaration’s arguments are loyally reiterated, but in a curiously divided form, since Cornwall, Goneril and Edmund are the sceptics, while The fraudulent possession and exorcism are given to the legitimate Edgar (Greenblatt [1985, p. 178]). Shakespeare’s use of Harsnett does not, it seems to me, have this kind of structural significance (see also Brownlow, 122 and n.). Edgar’s masquerade as the possessed Poor Tom is pretty much confined to one scene, and has little or no effect on the mad Lear, who sees him as a learned Theban; only the Fool is momentarily terrified by him. His possession is not fraudulent, since it serves as a [103] protective disguise, not as a means to deceive others. As Poor Tom, Edgar introduces names of devils, and the prince of darkness himself ([1921]), as fictions to support that disguise, and the action distances itself from the process of religious exorcism here (which may be fraudulent, as Harsnett argued), just as it is distanced from any specific religious belief elsewhere in the play, in spite of the many allusions to biblical texts scattered through it. It is just possible that some might have seen a connection between Poor Tom and the recusant missionary priests who wandered in disguise in Jacobean England, though they did not travel as beggars (Brownlow, 119–20).

p.quote: Shakespeare seems to have been attracted by Harsnett’s vocabulary and turn of phrase, and recalled a number of unusual words that do not occur in any of his earlier plays.…Usually they enliven a dramatic moment that has no connection with the event being described by Harsnett.…Shakespeare also picked up some ideas for particular moments in the action of his play from Harsnett. The binding of Gloucester to a chair in [3.7] echoes the way the women subjected to exorcism in Harsnett were bound in a chair (Brownlow, 234, 237, 369, 385, 386 [1603, pp. 38–9, 42–3, 220–1, 243–4]).…The idea of Lear as suffering a fit of the mother was suggested by Harsnett’s account of Richard Maynie [see n. 1328].…Harsnett’s description of the adjurations of exorcists in terms of fierce and noisy storms contributed to the rage of the storm scenes in King Lear (Brownlow, [104] 113–15). Lear’s misogynistic outburst against women, associating their sex with hell, darkness, the devil [2563–71]…was no doubt prompted by Harsnett’s descriptions of the exorcists’ treatment of women, fumigating them ([1603, p. 109])…and their assigning the inferiour parts [of women] for a peculiar lodge for the devil ([1603, p. 63]). By attacking the exorcisms as merely theatrical, Harsnett was also aligning his tract with Puritan attacks on the stage, so that his book is not likely to have appealed to many of the patrons of the Globe. If the play is Shakespeare’s reply to Harsnett, as Brownlow claims (128), it is so, I think, not as a response to the latter’s offensive authoritarianism (127), but as a recuperation of the power of theatre to embody profound truths in its shows and rituals, and make audiences feel what kings and wretches feel.

div.p: Wolf (1998, pp. 252 ff.): Shakespeare uses the symbols, language, and details of Harsnett’s Declaration to undermine the message of that pamphlet by contrasting possession with true madness, offering a sympathetic portrayal of demoniacs, and drawing a tragic portrayal of human cruelty and evil that Harsnett’s cynical politics do not admit.…[261] The sympathy that Harsnett lacks in his characterization of the demoniacs blooms even in the midst of tragic suffering in King Lear.…[263] The only redemption possible in this bleak world of human cruelty comes from human sympathy [on the part of Lear, Gloucester, Cordelia, and Edgar].…Shakespeare does not borrow from Harsnett so much as thoroughly critique him.

div.head: The Essayes, Tr. John Florio (1603)
div.p: Echoes of some of the Essais (1580–8) of Michel Eyquem, later Seigneur de Montaigne, have been detected in several of Sh.’s plays from the end of the 16th c. onward, and echoes of John Florio’s translation, The Essayes…of Lo: Michaell de Montaigne (1603), have increasingly been found in Lr. and a few later plays. It is now generally believed that if Sh. knew Montaigne, it was in Florio’s translation, which was readily available after 1603. Ellrodt (1975, pp. 38–9), however, admits other possibilities: Shakespeare…might have read the Essays in the original from the outset of his career. He may not have lived with the Mountjoys before 1602, but his friendship with the Quineys in Stratford and his early connection with Richard Field, together with scraps of French dialogue in his plays, gave William Carew Hazlitt [Shakespeare, 1902] and the Countess of Chambrun [Giovanni Florio, Paris, 1921; Shakespeare: Acteur-Poète, Paris, 1926) among others fairly sound arguments for an emphasis on his French background.…[But] The parallels so far pointed-out make an acquaintance with the original unnecessary [39] since William Cornwallis, in his own essays written before 1600, praised a translation of Montaigne circulating in manuscript. Florio’s translation, according to Frances Yates [John Florio, 1934, p. 213], was begun at least by 1598 [and, Ellrodt notes, another translation had been entered to E. Aggas on 20 October 1595.]. In the Southampton circle Shakespeare might have had easy access to the manuscript, early enough to account for the [to Ellrodt, unconvincing] parallels in Henry V, Julius Caesar and As You Like It.

The roman and italic of the 1603 edition are here reproduced; long s is printed s, and the prose is relined. The page numbers of the 1603 edition are indicated in italics within brackets, and passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes; such insertions are made within the prose line at the beginning of the page or passage.

body.head: [From Michel Eyquem, Seigneur de Montaigne, Essays, 5th ed., 3 Books, 1588, translated by John Florio as The Essayes Or Morall, Politike and Millitarie Discourses of Lo: Michaell de Montaigne.…First written by him in French. And now done into English, 1603.]

div.head: From 1.19, That to Philosophie, is to learne how to die.
div.p: [36][tln 2191–2] Consider wee by the ordinary mutations, and dayly declinations, which we suffer, how Nature deprives vs of the sight of our losse and empairing: what hath an aged man left him of his youthes [v]igor, and of his forepast life?…Were man all at once to fall into it, I doe not thinke we should be able to beare such a change, but being faire and gently led on by her hand, in a slowe, and as it were vnperceived descent, by little and little, and step by step, she roules vs into that miserable state, and day by day seekes to acquaint vs with it. So that when youth failes in vs, we feele, nay we perceive no shaking or transchange at all in our selves: which in essence and veritie is a harder death, then that of a languishing and irkesome life, or that of age. Forsomuch as the leape from an ill being, vnto a not beeing, is not so dangerous or steepie; as it is from a delightfull and flowrishing beeing, vnto a painefull and sorrowfull condition.…[37][tln 2935] [S]ince wee are threatned by so many kinds of death, there is no more inconvenience to feare them all, then to endure one: what matter is it when it commeth since it is vnavoidable?…[tln 2620–2] Death is the beginning of another life. So wept we, and so much did it cost vs to enter into this life; and so did we spoile us of our ancient vaile in entring into it.…[tln 2932–4] But nature compels us to it. Depart saith she, out of this world, even as you came into it. The same way you came from death, to death returne without passion or amazement, from life to death: your death is but a peece of the worlds order, and but a parcell of the worldes life.…[38][tln 2935] Moreover, no man dies before his houre. The time you leave behinde was no more yours, than that which was before your birth, and concerneth you no more.…

Wheresoever your life endeth, there is it all. The profit of life consists not in the space, but rather in the vse. Some man hath liued long, that hath had a short life. Follow it whilst you have time. It consists not in number of yeares, but in your will, that you have lived long enough. Did you thinke you should never come to the place, where you were still going? There is no way but hath an end.

div.head: From 2.8, Of the affection of fathers to their children.
div.p: [224][tln 382] It is meere injustice to see an old, crazed, sinnowe-shronken, and nigh-dead father sitting alone in a chimnie-corner, to enjoy so many goods as would suffice for the preferment and entertainment of many children, and in the meane while, for want of meanes, to suffer them to loose their best daies and yeares, without thrusting them into publike service and knowledge of men; whereby they are often cast into dispaire, to seeke, by some way how vnlawful soever to provide for their necessaries.…That father may truely be said miserable, that holdeth the affection of his children tied vnto him by no other meanes, then by the neede they have of his helpe, or want of his assistance, if that may be termed affection: A man should yeeld him-[225]selfe respectable by vertue and sufficiencie, and amiable by his goodnesse, and gentlenesse of manners.…[226] But a father over-burthened with yeares, and crazed through sickenesse, and by reason of weakenesse and want of health, barred from the common societie of men, doth both wrong himselfe, injure his, idely and to no vse to hoorde vp, and keepe close a great heape of riches, and deal of pelfe.…[H]ee ought willingly to destribute and bestow them amongst those, to whome by naturall decree they ought to belong. It is reason he shoulde have the vse, and bequeathe the fruition of them, since nature doth also deprive him of them, otherwise without doubt there is both envy and malice stirring. [tln 7] The worthiest action, that ever the Emperour Charles the fifth performed was this, in imitation of some ancients of his qualitie, that hee had the discretion to know, that reason commaunded vs, to strippe or shift our selves when our cloathes trouble and are too heavie for vs, and that it is high time to goe to bed, when our legges faile vs. He resigned his meanes, his greatnesse and Kingdome to his Sonne, at what time he found his former vndanted resolution to decaie, and force to conduct his affaires, to droope in himselfe, together with the glorie hee had thereby acquired.…[227][tln 522+1–+4, 1426–30] It is also follie and injustice to deprive children, especially being of competent age, of their fathers familiaritie, and ever to shew them a surly, austere, grim, and disdainefull countenance, hoping thereby to keepe them in awefull feare and duteous obedience. For, it is a very vnprofitable proceeding, and which maketh fathers yrkesome vnto children; and which is worse, ridiculous. They have youth and strength in their hands, and consequently, the breath and favour of the worlde; and doe with mockerie and contempt receive these churlish-fierce, and tyrannicall countenances, from a man that hath no lusty bloud left in him, neither in his heart, not in his veines.…There are so many sortes of defects in age, and so much impuissance: It is so subject to contempt, that the best purchase it can make, is the good will, love and affection of hers. Commandement and feare are no longer her weapons.

div.head: From 2.12, An Apologie of Raymond Sebond.
div.p: [257][tln 1882–8] The meanes I vse to suppresse this frenzie [i.e., atheism], and which seemeth the fittest for my purpose, is to bruze, to crush, and trample this pride and fiercenesse of man vnder foot; and violently to pull out of their hands, the silly weapons of their reason, to make them stoope, and bite and snarle at the ground, vnder the aucthoritie and reverence of Gods Majestie.…[258] Let vs now but consider man alone, without other help, armed but with his owne weapons, & vnprovided of the grace & knowledge of God, which is all his honour, all his strength, and all the ground of his being. Let vs see what hold-fast, or free-hold he hath in this gorgeous, and goodly equipage. Let him with the vtmost power of his discourse make me vnderstand, vppon what foundation, hee hath built those great advantages and ods, he supposeth to have over other creatures.…[259][tln 433–44] To consider the power and domination, these [heavenly] bodies have, not onely vppon our lives, and condition of our fortune:…But also over our dispositions and inclinations, our discourses and wills, which they rule, provoke, and moove at the pleasure of their influences, as our reason findes and teacheth vs.…
Seeing that not a man alone, nor a King only, But Monarchies and Empires, yea, and all this world below is mooved at the shaking of one of the least heavenly motions.…

If our vertue, vices, sufficiency and knowledge, and the same discourse wee make of the power of the Planets, and the comparison betweene them and vs, commeth as our reason judgeth by their meane and through their favour.…

lg.l: One with love madded, his love to enjoy,
Can crosse the seas, and over-turne all Troy;
Anothers lot is to set lawes severe.
Loe sonnes kill fathers, fathers sonnes destroy,
Brothers for mutuall woundes their armes doe beare,
Such warre is not our owne, forc’t are we to-it,
Drawne to our owne paines, our owne limbes to teare;
Fates so t’observe t’is fatal, we must doe-it.

div.p: [260][tln 2602] We vnderstand them [i.e., animals] no more then they vs. By the same reason, may they as well esteeme vs beasts, as we them.…And if it be (as Cosmographers reporte) that there are nations, who receive and admit a Dogge to be their King, it must necessarily follow, that they give a certaine interpretation to his voice and moving. We must note the paritie that is betweene vs.…[262][tln 1882–8] For, the daily plaintes, which I often heare men make…exclaiming, that man is the onely forsaken, and out-cast creature, naked on the bare earth, fast-bound and swathed, having nothing to cover and arme himselfe withall but the spoile of others; whereas Nature hath clad and mantled all other creatures, some with shelles, some with huskes, with rindes, with haire, with wooll, with stings, with bristels, with hides, with mosse, with fethers, with skales, with fleeces, and with silke, according as their qualitie might neede, or their condition require:…where as man onely (Oh silly-wretched man) can neither goe, nor speake, nor shift, nor feede himselfe, vnlesse it be to whine and weepe onely, except he be taught.…

lg.l: [263] An infant, like a shipwracke ship-boy cast from Sease,
Lies naked on the ground, and speechlesse, wanting all
The helpes of vitall spirit, when nature with small ease
Of throw’s, to see first light, from hir wombe lets him fall,
Then, as is meete, [tln 2620–2] with morn’full cries he filles the place,
For whom so many ills remaine in his lives race.
But divers heards of tame and wilde beasts foreward spring,
Nor neede they rattles, nor of nurces cockring-kinde
The flattering-broken speech their lullaby neede sing.
Nor seeke they divers coats, as divers seasons binde.
Lastly no armor neede-they, nor high-rear’d wall
Whereby to guarde their owne, since all things vnto all
Worke-maister nature doth produce,
And the earth largely to their vse.

div.p: Such complaints are false:…Witnes divers nations, which yet never knew the vse of clothes.…Our whining, our puling and our weeping is common to most creatures, and divers of them are often seene to waile and grone a long time after their birth, forsomuch as it is a countenance fitting the weaknes wherein they feele themselves.…The earth without labour or tilling doth sufficiently produce and offer him [i.e., a child] as much as he shall neede. [tln 1340] And if not at all times, no more doth she vnto beasts; witnes the provision, we see the Antes and other silly creatures, to make against the cold and barren seasons of the yeare.…[272][tln 2252] Lustfull desires are either naturall, and necessary, as eating and drinking; or else naturall and not necessary, as the acquaintance of males and females: or else neither necessary nor naturall: Of this last kinde are almost all mens: For, they are all superfluous and artificiall. It is wonderfull to see with how little, nature will be satisfied, and how little she hath left for-us to be desired.…
These strange lustfull longings, which the ignorance of good, and a false opinion have possest vs with, are in number so infinite, that in a manner they expell all those which are naturall.…

[274][tln 1882–8] This many-headed, divers-armed, and furiously-raging monster, is man; wretched weake and miserable man: whom if you consider well, what is he, but a crawling, and ever-moving Antes-neast?…[280] Truely, when I consider man all naked (yea, be-it in that sex, which seemeth to have and chalenge the greatest share of eye-pleasing beautie) and view his defects, his naturall subjection, and manifold imperfections; I finde we have had much more reason to hide and cover our nakednes, than any creature else. We may be excused for borrowing those which nature had therein favored more then vs, with their beauties to adorne vs, and vnder their spoiles of wooll, of haire, of fethers, and of silke to shroude vs.…[283] So long as man shall be perswaded to have meanes or power of himselfe, so long will he deny, and never acknowledge what he oweth vnto his Maister: he shall alwayes (as the common saying is), make shift with his owne: Hee must be stripped into his shirt.…[284] [tln 2200] Whence proceeds the subtilest follie, but from the subtilest wisdome? As from the extremest friendships proceede the extreamest enmities, and from the soundest healths, the mortallest diseases; so from the rarest and quickest agitations of our mindes ensue the most distempered and outragious frenzies. There wants but halfe a pegs turne to passe from the one to the other. In mad mens actions, we see how fitly folly suteth and meets with the strongest operations, of ovr minde. Who knowes not how vnperceivable the neighbourhood betweene folly with the liveliest elevations of a free minde is; and the effects of a supreame and extraordinary vertue?…Will you have a man healthy, will you have him regular, and in constant and safe condition? overwhelme him in the darke [288] pit of idlenesse, and dulnesse. We must be besotted ere we can become wise, and dazled before we can be led.…[289] It is not by our discourse or vnderstanding, that wee have received our religion, it is by a forraine aucthoritie and commaundement. The weaknesse of our judgement, helpes vs more than our strength to compasse the same, and our blindnesse more then our cleare-sighted eyes. It is more by the meanes of our ignorance, then of our skil, that we are wise in heavenly knowledge. It is no marvaile if our naturall and terrestriall means cannot conceive the supernaturall, or apprehend the celestial knowledge: Let vs adde nothing of our owne vnto it, but obedience & subjection.…Hath not God made the wisdome of this world foolishnesse?…[337] [tln 124] One nation vieweth a subject with one visage, and thereon it stayes; an other with an other. Nothing can be imagined so horrible, as for one to eate and devoure his owne father. Those people, which antiently kept this custome, holde it nevertheless for a testimonie of pietie and good affection: seeking by that meane to give their fathers the worthiest and most honorable sepulcre, harboring their fathers bodies and reliques in themselves and in their marrow; in some sorte reviving and regenerating them by the transmutation made in their [338] quicke flesh, by digestion and nourishment. It is easie to be considered what abhomination and crueltie it had beene, in men accustomed and trained in this inhumane superstition, to cast the carcasses of their parents into the corruption of the earth, as foode for beasts and wormes.…[tln 2037] Dionysius the tyrant offered Plato a robe made after the Persian fashion, long, damasked and perfumed: But he refused the same, saying, that being borne a man, he would not willingly put-on a womans garment.…[346] [tln 2446–59, 2949] Let a Philosopher be put in a Cage made of small and thin-set yron-wyre, and hanged on the top of our Ladies Church steeple in Paris; he shall, by evident reason, perceive that it is impossible hee should fall downe out of it; yet can he not chuse (except he have beene brought vp in the trade of Tilers or Thatchers) but the sight of that exceeding height must needes dazle his sight, and amaze or turne his senses. For, we have much adoe to warrant our selves in the walkes or battlements of an high tower or steeple, if they be battlemented and wrought with pillers, and somewhat wide one from another, although of stone, and never so strong.…I have sometimes made triall of it vpon our mountaines on this side of Italie, yet am I one of those that wil not easily be afrighted with such things, and I could not without horror to my minde, and trembling of legges and thighes endure to looke on those infinit precipices and steepie downe-falles, though I were not neere the brim, nor any daunger within my length, and more.…Where I also noted, that how deepe soever the bottom were, if but a tree, a shrub, or any out-butting cragge of a Rocke presented it selfe vnto our eyes, vpon those steepie and high Alpes, somewhat to vphold the sight, and divide the same, it doth somewhat ease and assure vs from feare, as if it were a thing, which in our fall might either helpe or vpholde vs.…So as they can not looke downe without giddines both of eyes and mindes: Which is an evident deception of the sight. [tln 2200] Therfore was it, that a worthy Philosopher pulled out his eies, that so he might discharge his soule of the debauching & diverting he received by them, and the better & more freely apply himselfe vnto philosophie.…[347][tln 1791–4] To a pensive and hart-grieved man, a cleare day seems gloomie and duskie. Our senses are not only altered, but many times dulled, by the passions of the mind. How many things see we, which we perceive not, if our minde be either busied or distracted else where?…[349][tln 1381–5] Moreover, since the accidents of sickenesse, of madnesse, or of sleepe, make things appeare other vnto vs, then they seeme vnto the healthie, vnto the wise, and to the waking. Is it not likely, that our right seate and naturall humours, have also wherewith to give a being vnto things, having reference vnto their condition, and to appropriate them to it selfe, as doe inordinate humours; and our health, as capable to give them his visage, as sickenesse?
