Why hath not the temperate man some forme of the objects relative vnto himselfe, as the intemperate: and shall not he likewise imprint his Character in them? The distasted impute wallowishness vnto Wine: the healthie, good taste; and the thirsty brisknesse, rellish and delicacie. Now our condition appropriating things vnto it selfe, and transforming them to it’s owne humour: we know no more how things are in sooth and truth; For: nothing comes vnto vs but falsified and altered by our senses.

div.head: From 3.9, Of Vanitie.
div.p: [574][tln 2221–2] The Gods play at hand-ball with vs, and tosse vs vp and down on all handes, Enim uero Dii nos homines quasi pilas habent [Plaut. Capt. Prol.]. The Gods perdy doe reckon and racket vs men as their tennis-balles.…[575][tln 448] Astrologers may sport themselues, with warning vs, as they doe of imminent alterations and succeeding revolutions: their divinations are present and palpable, we need not prie into the heavens to finde them out.…Who knowes, whether God hath determined it shall happen of them, as of bodies that are purged, & by long-grieuous sicknesses brought to a better & sounder state; which throughly-purged diseases doe afterward yeeld them a more entire and purely-perfect health, then that they tooke from them? That which grieveth me most, is, that coumpting the symphtomes or affects of our euill, I see as many meerly proceeding of nature, and such as the heauens send vs, and which may properly be termed theirs, as of those that our owne surfet, or excesse, or misdyet, or humane indiscretion confer vpon vs. The very Planets seeme orderly to declare vnto vs, that we haue continued long enough, yea and beyond our ordinary limits.…[592][tln 2557–71] Of the same paper, whereon a Iudge writ but even now the condemnation against an adulterer, hee will teare a scantlin, thereon to write some love-lines to his fellow-iudges wife. The same woman from whom you came lately and with whom you have committed that vnlawfull-pleasing sport, will soone after, even in your presence, raile and scolde more bitterly against the same fault in her neighbour, than ever Portia or Lucrece could. And some condemne men to die for crimes, that themselves esteeme no faults.

div.head: Comments on Shakespeare’s Use of Florio’s Montaigne
On Shakespeare’s Use of Montaigne in General
div.p: There has been continuing skepticism about Sh.’s acquaintance with and use of the Essays. The Montaigne scholar Villey (1916), having surveyed all previous studies, finds (p. 418) only coincidences of thought, no borrowings, and at best two or three reminiscences (if that) in all the parallels that have been suggested. Cent zéros additionés ensemble ne font toujours que zéro. Were it not for the parallel between Cannibals and Gonzalo’s description of the ideal commonwealth in Tmp. 2.1, pointed out by Capell (1783, 2.2:63), Villey would have no grounds to affirm that Sh. had even read Montaigne. The similarities between the authors, he says, derive from commonplace ideas on common subjects. In a later (1917) and fuller article he admits that besides the Tmp. parallel are somewhat persuasive though not decisive ones in MM and Ham. Only slightly less skeptical, Ellrodt (1975, pp. 37–9), surveying all important studies since 1940, also concludes that (p. 37) the parallel in Tmp. 2.1 is the only indisputable echo of Montaigne in Sh., though If [38] one is satisfied with probability, accumulation has some weight. But the contrast between Shakespeare’s unsettled debt and Marston’s or Webster’s obvious borrowings is illuminating. Taylor’s (1925) accumulation of some 750 words from Florio which do not appear in Sh. before Ham. is more impressive to Ellrodt than commonplace ideas that the two writers share, since similar analogues are too easily found in other writers, the classics, and collections of commonplaces. Taylor is careful to say (pp. 4–5) that though Sh. was without a doubt owing to Montaigne for vocabulary, phrases, and long and short passages, he was influenced only after a fashion in thought: he does not contend that Shakespare was in thought a follower or disciple of Montaigne. Harmon (1942) shows how many of the parallels of idea were commonplaces; Taylor (1943) reasserts that some are useful. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 251), after cautioning against exaggerating Florio’s influence: Yet as there is no doubt that [Sh.] did read Florio’s translation, it is reasonable to assume that he enlarged his vocabulary by a study of it, especially as some of these words seem to be Florio’s coinages.

Ellrodt (op. cit., pp. 46 ff.): Sh.’s main kinship with Montaigne, perhaps under the latter’s influence, was a focus on self-consciousness. (P. 47): The habit of self-analysis in soliloquy increases around the time of JC; in Ham. it causes doubts, interferes with self-knowledge. (P. 49): It seems to be generally agreed that Hamlet, Troilus and Cressida, and Measure for Measure are more consonant with the spirit of Montaigne than any other play. Out of the three plays two are tragi-comedies and Hamlet in its intellectuality has affinities with the so-called problem plays. The full tragic response calls for a heightened consciousness of identity—evident in Lear, Othello or Macbeth—not for the kind of self-consciousness that may dissolve identity. Shakespeare the tragedian had to part company with Montaigne. (P. 50): Whether Sh. would have endowed Hamlet or Angelo with so vivid a self-consciousnesss had he not read Montaigne is not answerable. This heightening of self-awareness was a process in which many minds were engaged by the end of the sixteenth century.

div.head: On Shakespeare’s Use of Montaigne in King Lear
div.p: Robertson (1897; 1909, pp. 107–10) finds for Lr. four parallel passages in Montaigne: see nn. 447, 2221–2, 2956. Hooker (1902, p. 364) points out three parallels, at least two of them noted previously by Robertson: see nn. 1882–8 (her original one), 2932–4, 2935, and 2956.

Taylor (1925) finds in the Essays ideas similar to those in passages in Lr., and points out in Florio’s tr. of Montaigne (1603) words and phrases which do not occur in Sh. before 1603 and might therefore have been suggested to him by his reading of Florio. Only a few of the passages seem closely similar (see nn. 382, 1504, 1564–71, 1791–4, 1882–8, 2557–71), and comparable ideas often occur in other sources than Montaigne. Of the 116 words supposedly echoed in Lr. (reprinted in Muir, ed. 1952, p. 250), from a total of about 750 purportedly echoed in Sh. as a whole, the great majority had already appeared in plays written from one to five years earlier than Lr. and so do not necessarily show Sh.’s recent consultation of Florio; and almost three dozen have close cognates in Sh.’s vocabulary (unquiet if not unquietly, justice if not justicer, numb if not numbed, menace (verb) if not menace (noun), etc. Only some 25 words in Lr. seem quite new to Sh.’s vocabulary; of these the majority were in common use, and in any case every play of Sh.’s contains a number of words, often of his own invention, which do not appear elsewhere in his works.

Doran (1933, pp. 51 ff.): Many of the philosophic passages in King Lear, particularly those which reflect on the relation between parents and children, on the selfish and sensual nature of man, on the difficulties besetting the exercise of justice, and on the relative nature of human values, are reminiscent of or directly traceable to Florio’s translation of the essays of Montaigne.…They have an intensity, and sometimes a bitterness, quite foreign to the tolerant, amiable skepticism of Montaigne.

Henderson (1939–40): In Lr. Sh. derived from Montaigne his skeptical attitude towards the Renaissance notion of the God-King, along with many other ideas about the brutishness of man, folly, the inadequacy of legal justice, filial ingratitude, nature, astrology, etc. Many of Henderson’s ideas are rather fanciful (Muir, ed. 1952, p. 253), depending on slight resemblances of word and ideas from very different contexts.

Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 249–53), reviewing earlier studies: (p. 251) The vocabulary evidence in Taylor shows there is no doubt that he did read Florio’s translation, and several parallels of idea, though over-urged by Henderson, are convincing that (p. 253) it would be unreasonable to deny that Montaigne had a substantial influence on the thought of King Lear. Idem (1957, pp. 161–2): It [162] seems probable that he had been reading the translation not long before he wrote King Lear.…[Like Montaigne] he exposes the weakness of unaccommodated man, he considers the influence of the stars on human destiny, he discusses the effect of dizzy heights, and he may have provided some of the material for Lear’s attacks on authority—the fact that a dog is obeyed in office, the way big sinners pass judgement on lesser sinners, and the lust of women. Idem (1977, p. 206): He may have provided some of the material for the clothing imagery pervasive in the play.

Anderson (1971): Lr., like Montaigne, continually (p. 275) reminds us that we, too, share the savage mind. (P. 276): The fragile world of Lear shares many concerns with the Essais; it is a critique of justice, reason, nature, social structure—perhaps Shakespeare’s deepest glance into the abyss. He cites esp. parallel passages from That to Philosophie and Apology.

Salingar (1983, pp. 125–53): In Lr. Sh. was owing to Montaigne for many of his ideas on the relations of fathers and children, poverty and the distribution of surplus goods, man’s ignorance of his own nature, nature’s corruption by civilization, old age, the body’s influence on the mind, passion’s dulling of the senses, human generation, civilized society, the opposition of custom and nature, the comparison of men with beasts, hypocrisy, and authority. Few if any of these ideas (or vocabulary words) need have come only from Montaigne, but Salingar finds it suggestive that clusters of both seem to derive from the same few essays, esp. Sebond, Of Vanitie, Verses of Virgil, Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children, Of Custome, Of the Caniballes, and Of Phisiognomie.

Parker (1999, pp. 3, 9–12): The Montaignean vision of radical naturalness, of unaccommodated man, both fascinates certain of Shakespeare’s characters, and generates a kind of recoil.…[10] The equation of man with the animals is, very clearly, not conducted in Lear’s spirit. It is, for one thing, consciously extravagant; Montaigne’s animals are never bestial.…[12] Montaigne remarks the ingrained contradictoriness of humanity quite as sharply as Lear, but he exhibits none of Lear’s…compulsion to resolve the contradictions.…Montaigne, whose vision is never tragic, sustains a double perspective which tolerates contradiction: licentiousness is written deeply into the nature of human life, but no less necessarily part of our foolish, self-tormenting condition is the impulse to suppress or to regulate such energies.

div.head: Other Versions and Analogues of the Lear Story

div.p: Douce (1807, 2:171–5), on the evidence of MS Harleian 7333, names Gesta Romanorum, a collection of moralized tales from Roman writers, as containing the story of Lear with different names, and he prints the story of Theodosius. Unknown to Douce, two other versions of the story exist under the title Gesta Romanorum, one also the story of the Theodosius, the other of Leyre, some tyme kyng of bretayne. Douce was followed by Knight (ed. 1840, p. 394), and White (ed. 1862, 11:201). Adee (ed. 1890, pp. xliii f.) and Craig (ed. 1901, p. xlix) cite both versions, and Hazlitt (1875, 2:315–22) prints the Leyre version. Perrett (1904, pp. 64 ff.), however, demonstrates that all three versions of the story extant in various MSS and editions of the Gesta are translations from a French prose version of Brut from the end of the 13th or beginning of the 14th c., which in turn derives from Geoffrey. (P. 69): There was an English book of the GR, it is true, first printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1510–1515.…It was a popular work under Elizabeth and ran through many editions [STC lists nine, 1502–1605]…but none of them contain more than 43 or 44 stories, neither of which…is that of Theodosius or of Leyre. [70] The Gesta Romanorum did not directly or indirectly furnish Sh. with the groundwork of his play.

div.head: Layamon, Brut
div.p: Layamon’s early 13th-c. English translation of Wace’s Roman de Brut contains a version of the Lear story deriving ultimately from Geoffrey. Although it shares a few peculiar details with Lr., it is not now thought to have been known to Sh. or to have influenced his play. The similarities are these:

Perrett (1904, pp. 43–5): Layamon presents the story in dramatic scenes, [44] the husbands of Gornoille and Regau are differentiated (one principled but weak, the other greedy), Lear goes hunting (see n. 514) and swears by Apollo, wrathfully expels Cordoille on threat of death but continues to berate her; [45] Gornoille rationalizes that Leir does not need followers when she has servants to attend to him.

Seef (1977, p. 30) adds the conception of a raging, tempestuous king and the conception of the outcast daughter as a foster-nurse of nature healing her father who lay in the field | and rested him on the earth for grief (v.3602–3).

Friedlander (1978, pp. 43–5): In addition, Layamon also anticipates Lr. in his emphasis on Lear’s folly and enlightenment. He is foolish in misreading his daughters’ declarations of love, and in his surrendering his realm voluntarily. Later Lear enumerates his own mistakes. But (p. 42) except for possible borrowings by one or two English chroniclers, there is no evidence that anyone in the Middle Ages or the Renaissance ever read Layamon.
Greg (1940, p. 400): A possible verbal echo found by Craig [ed. 1901, p. xlvi] is in fact only of Madden’s translation.

Alamichel (1992, p. 175), after listing analogies between Layamon’s Brut and Lr., urges that the former be more highly valued as an indirect source. She shows no direct influence. Speed (1996) draws further comparisons.

div.head: Robert Fabyan, Gerard Legh
div.p: Perrett (1904, p. 76): The account of Leyr in Robert Fabyan’s New Cronycles (1516; rpt. 1533, 1542, 1559) is derived mainly from Geoffrey and Caxton’s Chronicles of England (1480), and is important as the basis of Holinshed’s. Bullough (1973, pp. 273–4): His account and a brief one in Hardyng were [274] used by John Stow in his Summarie of Englyshe Chronicles (1563) and his Annales (1592). No one suggests direct influence on Sh.

Atkinson (1936, pp. 63–6): Sh. was possibly influenced by Gerard Legh’s account in Accedens of Armorie (1562, fol. 165; rpt. 1568, 1576, 1591, 1597), where Cordeilla’s answer (somuche arte thou worthie, and so will I loue the; 1568, fol. 96v, and 1576 and 1591 read instead somuch (quod she) as thou haste, so much art thou worth, and so well do I loue thee) drives Lear into a rage and causes him to order her to shun ye rage. Chambers (1930 1:336) thinks Sh. may have used Legh’s desc. of the arms of Alexander as the basis of the jest about Ajax and the lion in LLL. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxvi n.) is dubious: In none of the versions certainly used by Shakespeare does Lear tell Cordelia to avoid his presence; but such a detail requires no source; (1957, p. 141): He may have known the version in Gerard Legh’s Accedens of Armory; (1977, p. 197): The evidence that Shakespeare knew Legh’s book is inconclusive. Munro (ed. 1957) and Ribner (ed. 1967, p. xiii) list Legh as a source, without any further support or explanation.

div.head: William Camden, Remaines (1605)
div.p: Bishop Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 9:349 n.) points to the similarity of the story of Ina, King of the West Saxons, told as an anonymous anecdote by William Camden in his Remaines of a Greater Worke (1605, pp. 182–3), which if the thing ever happened, probably was the real origin of the fable. Malone (ed. 1790, 8:486), reprinting the anecdote, thinks it more probable that Shakspeare had this passage in his thoughts, when he wrote Cordelia’s reply [at 106–10]…than The Mirrour for Magistrates, as Camden’s book was published recently before he appears to have composed this play and it furnished him with a hint in Coriolanus. Camden’s book was entered in the Stationers’ Register on 10 Nov. 1604; its tale of Adrian the Fourth may be the source of a few details in Menenius’s fable of the Belly: see Bullough, Sources 5(1964):552. Stokes (1878, p. 119), Perrett (1904, pp. 121–4), Bullough (1973, p. 274), and a few others are inclined to agree with Malone that Camden may have slightly influenced Lr.; Simrock (1850, p. 123), Anders (1904, p. 141), Muir (1952, p. xxxvi n.; 1957, p. 143; 1977, p. 197), and others are dubious, thinking that the similarities may be accidental or owing to the echoes of Biblical language in each version (see n. 105). Perrett identifies the anonymous source of Camden’s anecdote as Polydore Vergil’s Anglicae Historiae (1534), the source also for Cordelia’s answer in Higgins’s Mirour, st. 12 (1587 only; Sh. used only the 1574 version).

The text of Camden’s anecdote is reprinted here in the roman and italic of the original 1605 edition; long s is printed s. The page numbers of the 1605 edition are indicated in italics within brackets, and passages referred to in the commentary notes are indicated by the bracketed TLN numbers of the appropriate notes; such insertions are made within the prose line at the beginning of the page or passage. Other references to Camden appear in notes DP 9–10 and 14, and TLN 5, 711, 1968, and 3249.

body.head: [From Grave Speeches and wittie Apothegmes of worthy Personages of this Realme in former times]
body.p: [182] [tln 105] Ina King of West-Saxons, had three daughters, of whom vpon a time he demanded whether they did love him, and so would do during their lives above all others; the two elder sware deepely they would, the yongest, but the wisest told her father flatly without flattery, [tln 106–110+1] That albeit she did love, honour, and reverence him, and so would whilst she lived, as much as nature and daughterly dutie at the vttermost could expect: Yet she did thinke that one day it would come to passe, that she should affect another more fervently, meaning her husband, when she were married: Who being made one flesh with her, as God by commaundement had told, and nature had taught her she was to cleave fast to, forsaking father and mother, [183] kiffe and kinne. <Anonymus.> One referreth this to the daughters of king Leir.

div.head: Ballad, King Leir, and his three daughters
div.p: Lennox (1754, 3:302) first called attention to an ancient broadside ballad, A Lamentable song of the Death of King Leir, and his three daughters, thereby beginning extensive argument whether it was a source or offshoot of Sh.’s play. The first extant version of it is in Richard Johnson’s The Golden Garland of Princely pleasures and delicate Delights (1620, sigs. A2r-5v), whose title page announces this edition as the third time Imprinted; no earlier imprints have survived. Johnson’s collection had gone through its 13th edition by 1690, and broadsheet issues of the ballad have survived from 1700, 1710?, ca. 1750, 1760, 1764?, 1770, 1775?, 1794, 1795?, and 1808. It was reprinted in the anonymous A Collection of Old Ballads, 3 vols. (1723–5), from whence it was reprinted by Lennox (pp. 303–8) and by Child (Ballads, 1864, 7:276–83). Bishop Thomas Percy cites Johnson (1620) in his Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765, 1:211–19), but in fact reprints the 1723 text with occasional readings from Johnson. Percy’s text is reprinted by Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:160–3, a truncated version), Steevens (ed. 1773, 9:491–5, and later eds.), Malone (ed. 1790, 8:697–702), Eccles (ed. 1792, pp. 494–500), Boswell (ed. 1821, 10:297–301), Hazlitt (1875, 2:348–53), and Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 403–7). The ballad has been reprinted in The New Story Teller, or the Historical Medley (Newcastle, 1782), in Perrett (1904, pp. 129–34), and in A. F. Hopkinson, ed., Six Old Ballads (1906), and it was edited by B. Mühry (Leipzig, 1893).

Lennox (1754, 3:302): If the ballad is prior, then From thence (for ’tis mentioned no where else) he took the Hint of Lear’s Madness, and the extravagant and wanton Cruelty his Daughters exercised on him; the Death of King Lear is also exactly copied.

Johnson (ed. 1765): My reason for believing that the play was posteriour to the ballad…is, that the ballad has no thing of Shakespeare’s nocturnal tempest, which is too striking to have been omitted, and that it follows the chronicle [i.e., Holinshed]; it has the rudiments of the play, but none of its amplifications: it first hinted Lear’s madness, but did not array it in circumstances. The writer of the ballad added something to the history, which is a proof that he could have added more, if more had occurred to his mind, and more must have occurred if he had seen Shakespeare.

Ritson (in Steevens, ed. 1793): This ballad, which by no means deserves a place in any edition of Shakspeare, is evidently a most servile pursuit…of Holinshed’s Chronicle, where, as in Geoffrey of Monmouth, the king of France is called Aganippus. I suppose, however, that the performance and celebrity of the play might have set the ballad-maker at work, and furnished him with the circumstances of Lear’s madness, of which there is no hint either in the historian or the old play.

Skottowe (1824, 2:96): The ballad is without date, but I have no doubt of its priority to Shakspeare’s Lear. Would the copyist of Shakspeare have sent Lear from Regan…to Goneril; from Goneril back to Regan; and from Regan back to Goneril?…Would the follower of Shakspeare have sent Lear o’er to France and ended with the death of Cordelia in battle and reinstatement of Lear?

Simrock (1850, p. 122): We decide [that the ballad derived from Sh.]…partly on account of the modern tone of this spiritless fabrication, partly because the poet…could find all the ideas determining the treatment of the subject in his own mind, which was not the case with the ballad-writer. That nothing is said in the ballad of the Night-Storm cannot prove Johnson’s opinion that it is older than the play, for it is clear that the author of the ballad did not mean to give an extract from the play. He meant, as the name Aganippus shows, to guide himself by the Chronicle, but could not keep himself free from the influence of the play. Others inclined to think that the play is prior to the ballad are Delius (ed. 1854, 1:vii), Halliwell (ed. 1865, 14:362), von Friesen (1876, 3:81), and Furness (ed. 1880, p. 403).

Eidam (1880, pp. 10–11): It is an exaggeration to interpret the ballad’s grew franticke mad as equivalent to Lear’s madness; the phrase waxt franticke mad in the ballad of Gernutus the Jew does not refer to actual insanity.
Halliwell-Phillipps (2nd ed., 1882, p. 284; 8th ed., 1889, 2:338): It is all but impossible that it could have been published before the appearance of Shakespeare’s tragedy.

Perrett (1904, pp. 136–40): The balladist could have derived the hint for the storm (the woods sigh and groane), (p. 137) Lear’s madness (franticke mad), Lear’s leaving his life on the bosom of Cordelia, and the deaths of Lear’s three daughters from no other version than Lr. Skottowe thinks that if the ballad came after Sh., Cordelia would not have been slain in battle and her sisters condemned to death by lords and nobles; but to relate the deaths of Goneril and Regan as they occur in the play would mean bringing in the story of Edmund and the whole secondary plot of Gloucester, and to tell both stories is clearly beyond the capacities of a simple ballad. Finally no chronicle has Lear giving away his whole kingdom on conditions (only Sh. and Leir) and no chronicle gives Lear’s train and its reductions (only Mirour and Sh.). (P. 139): In the chronicles we hear of the marriages of the elder daughters, whereas only in Sh. are they already married; thus the balladist could leave out the two dukes altogether. The ballad is unique in making Ragan the eldest, at whose court the reductions take place; Lloyd (in Singer, ed. 1856, 9:522) thinks the ballad maker remembered 2.4. I conjecture that we have here the work of a professional ballad-maker, who had some slight previous knowledge of the story, saw the play soon after its production, was particularly impressed by the final scene, and set to work on a woeful ballad; that in order to keep clear of the Gloucester story, and to eke out his impressions of the play, he looked up the historical account, (p. 140) most likely Holinshed.

Hamel (1913, pp. 310–18): The ballad’s sigh and groane refers not to a storm but to (p. 311) the compassion Nature showed. Since some chroniclers (in the Munich Brut, (p. 312) Manning of Brunne’s Story of England, Layamon’s Brut etc.) developed Lear’s grief into madness, the idea may have occurred independently to the balladeer and dramatist. (P. 313): The ballad’s unhappy ending is unlike the play’s and in a way is like the chronicles’, since Lear wins the battle, then dies of grief at Cordelia’s untimely death. In the ballad the elder sisters die, in the chronicles they do not. (P. 314): The Gloucester subplot would have seemed to a simple ballad-maker an indispensably interwoven element of the saga. The ballad-maker would also have included the French King, Kent, and the Fool, and much more, and would not have spent two-fifths of his poem disposing of the marriage and division that Sh. disposes of quickly in 1.1. The ballad is neither derivative from Sh.’s play (p. 315) nor a source of it. (P. 316): The likeness of lamentable ballad and tragedy derives from the common aim of the two writers to move their audiences to compassion. (P. 317): The ballad writer magnified and elaborated the cruelty of Lear’s treatment, and this led to the details of madness and pathetic death; and like Sh. he tried to satisfy the audience by the deaths of the wicked daughters. The play and ballad possess only a (p. 318) psychological affinity.

The fact that Bullough (1973) does not reprint or even mention the ballad probably reflects the general consensus now that, whatever else it may be, it is not one of the sources of Lr. The tune for the ballad, Flying Fame, may also be sung by the Fool in 1.4; see . Duffin (2004, p. 244): A Lamentable Song…is not to be confused with the much later broadside Tragical History of King Leare and His Three Daughters, which was printed without tune direction and does not fit this melody.

Furness (ed. 1880, pp. 403–7) reprints fairly accurately the ballad as it appears in Thomas Percy’s Reliques (1765, 1:211–19). A much longer ballad dated ca. 1670 is reprinted in The Roxburghe Ballads, ed. J. Woodfall Ebsworth, 6 (1889):717–20. The text of the ballad is here reprinted from its earliest extant source, Richard Johnson’s The Golden Garland of Princely pleasures and delicate Delights (1620, sigs. A2r–5v). Since the title page announces this as the third time Imprinted, possibly Percy took his version from one of the earlier imprints, now no longer extant. Percy uses the spellings Leir and Leare, Furness only Leir; both use the spelling Cordelia; Johnson (1620) uses only Leare and Cordela. The black letter of the 1620 text is here printed in roman type, and the roman and italic of the original in italic type; long s is printed s. The beginning of each page is indicated by bracketed signatures in the right margin.

body.head:
A Lamentable Song of the death
of King Leare and his three
Daughters.
To the tune of, When flying Fame.

lg.l: King Leare once ruled in this Land,
with princely power and peace
And had all things with hearts content,
that might his ioyes encrease.
Amongst those guifts that nature gaue,
three daughters faire had he,
So princely seeming beautifull,
as fayrer could not be.
So on a time it pleasd the King,
a question thus to mooue,
Which of his daughters to his grace,
could shew the dearest loue:
For to my age you bring content,
(quoth he) then let me heare,
Which of you three in plighted troth,
the kindest will appeare.
To whom the eldest thus began,
deare father mine (quoth she)
Before your face to doe you good,
my blood shall tendred be.
And for your sake my bleeding heart,
shall heere be cut in twaine,
Ere that I see your reuerent age,
the smallest griefe sustaine.
And so will I the second said,
deare father, for your sake,
The worst of all extremities,
ile gently vndertake.
And serue your highnesse night and day,
with diligence and loue:
That sweet content and quietnesse,
discomforts may remoue.
In doing so you glad my soule,
the aged King replyed.
But what sayst thou my yongest Girle,
How is thy loue allyed.
My loue quoth yong Cordela then,
which to your grace I owe,
Shall be the duty of a childe,
and that is all ile shew.
And wilt thou shew no more (quoth he)
then doth thy duty binde:
I well perceiue thy loue is small,
when as no more I finde.
Hence forth I banish thee my Court,
thou art no child of mine,
Nor any part of this my Realme,
by fauour shall be thine.
Thy elder sisters loues are more,
then well I can demand:
To whome I equally bestow,
my kingdome and my land.
My pompall state and all my goods,
that louingly I may
With these thy sisters be maintaind,
vntill my dying day.
Thus flattering speeches won renowne,
by these two sisters here:
The third had causelesse banishment,
yet was her loue more deare:
For poore Cordela patiently
went wandring vp and downe,
Unhelpt, vnpittied, gentle maid,
through many an English towne.
Untill at last in famous France,
she gentler fortunes found,
Though poore and bare, yet was she deemd,
the fairest on the ground:
Where when the King her vertues heard,
and his faire Lady seene,
With full consent of all his Court,
he made his wife and Queene.
Her father, old King Leare, this while,
with his two daughters stayed:
Forgetfull of their promisd loues,
full soone the same denaide.
And liuing in Queene Ragans Court,
the elder of the twaine,
She tooke from him his chiefest meanes,
and most of all his traine.
For whereas twenty men were wont,
to waite with bended knee:
She gaue allowance but to ten,
and after scarce to three.
Nay, one she thought too much for him,
so tooke she all away:
In hope that in her Court, good King,
he would no longer stay.
Am I rewarded thus, quoth he,
in giuing all I haue
Unto my children, and to beg,
for what I lately gaue.
Ile goe vnto my Gonorell,
my second child I know,
Will be more kinde and pittifull,
and will relieue my woe.
Full fast he hies then to her Court,
where when she heard his moane,
Returnd him answer, that she grieude,
that all his meanes were gone.
But no way could relieue his wants,
yet if that he would stay
Within her kitchin, he should haue,
what Scullions gaue away.
When he had heard with bitter teares,
he made his answer then,
In what I did let me be made
example to all men.
I will returne againe, quoth he,
vnto my Ragans Court,
She will not vse me thus I hope,
but in a kinder sort.
Where when he came, shee gaue command,
to driue him thence away:
When he was well within her Court,
(she said) he could not stay.
Then backe againe to Gonorell,
the wofull King did hie:
That in her kitching he might haue
what Scullion boyes set by.
But there of that he was denied,
which she had promis’d late:
For on[c]e refusing he should not,
come after to her gate.
Thus twixt his daughters for reliefe,
he wandred vp and downe,
Being glad to feed on beggers food,
that lately wore a Crowne.
And calling to remembrance then,
his yongest daughters words,
That said, the duty of a childe,
had all that loue affords.
But doubting to repaire to her,
whom he had banisht so:
Grew franticke mad, for in his minde,
he bore the wounds of woe.
Which made him rend his milk white locks
and tresses from his head:
And all with blood bestaine his cheekes,
with age and honour spred:
To hils, and woods, and watry founts,
he made his hourely moane:
Till hils and woods, and sencelesse things,
did seeme to sigh and groane.
Euen thus possest with discontents,
he passed ore to France,
In hope from faire Cordela there,
to find some gentler chance.
Most vertuous dame, where whẽ she heard,
of this her fathers griefe:
As duty bound, she quickly sent
him comfort and reliefe.
And by a traine of noble Peeres,
in braue and gallant sort,
She gaue in charge he should be brought
to Aganippus Court.
Her royal King, whose noble minde,
so freely gaue consent,
To muster vp his knights at armes
to fame and courage bent.
And so to England came with speed,
to repossesse King Leare:
And driue his daughters from their thrones
by his Cordela deare.
Where she true hearted noble Queene,
was in the battell slaine:
Yet he good King in his old dayes
possest his crowne againe.
But when he heard Cordela dead,
who dyed indeed for loue
Of her deare father, in whose cause
she did this battell mooue:
He swounding fell vpon her brest,
from whence he neuer parted,
But on her bosome left his life,
that was so truely hearted.
The Lords and Nobles when they saw,
the end of these euents:
The other Sisters vnto death,
they doomed by consents:
And being dead, their crownes were left,
vnto the next of kin,
Thus haue you heard the fall of pride,
and disobedient sinne.

div.head: Folk Tales
div.p: A certain fairy-tale lack of realism in the first scene of Lr. and the fabulous nature of much of Geoffrey’s history has encouraged critics to believe that Geoffrey (and through him Sh.) borrowed from Welsh, Irish, or Breton folktales which themselves embodied narrative archetypes found widely throughout world literature. Olson (1961, pp. 198–9): The Lear story is a simple little yarn, with the moral sticking out a mile. Originally, perhaps, it was some sort of moral apolog which became a folk tale, was dignified into history by the chroniclers, and was humanized somewhat by the poets.…It is merely an illustration of the old saw that actions speak louder than words. Of special weight, and a cause of much confusion, is the fact that the name Leir has been linked specifically with Llyr, the name of a Welsh sea or water god as well as of one or more legendary Celtic kings (see DP nn. 2, 17). von Friesen (1877, pp. 172–3) speculates that some of Sh.’s differences from his known sources may derive from his own (assumed but unproved) knowledge of British folklore about the Lear story. Others think the folklore influence may be more general than the story of one king. Folklorists have discovered elements similar to those in Lear’s story throughout the folk-literatures of the world, and more recently psychological critics have associated such motifs with presumed psychological archetypes, especially Jungian.

The story of King Lear is unknown in Welsh literature before Geoffrey, and the associations between Leir and Llyr, formerly celebrated as highly significant, now seem to be fortuitous or factitious. Perrett (1904, pp. 19, 24): There is no trace of the Lear-story in Welsh national literature. Llyr and Kreiddylad both appear there in a totally different set of circumstances. (P. 24): The filial piety of Cordeilla towards an aged, helpless parent (Perrett continues) was probably not part of the ethics of ancient Britons, but was an importation by Geoffrey from Church teachings in support of the 5th Commandment against pagan ancestor worship (as in Gesta Romanorum). The identification of Lear and Llyr persists, however, as late as Graves (1948, pp. 165, 341): [Janus] is probably also to be identified with the British god Llyr or Lludd or Nudd, a god of the sea—i.e. a god of a sea-faring Bronze Age people—who was the father of Creiddylad (Cordelia) an aspect of the White Goddess; for according to Geoffrey of Monmouth the grave of Llyr at Leicester was in a vault built in honour of Janus; (p. 341) Creiddylad (alias Cordelia), daughter of Lludd (alias Llyr, alias Lear, alias Nudd, alias Nuada, alias Nodens. Bromwich (1961, p. 429), authoritatively: The story which Geoffrey tells of King Lear is unlikely to have any basis in antecedent Welsh sources: it is a popular medieval international tale, of which a version is found in the Gesta Romanorum.

Hartland (1886, pp. 308–49) distinguishes five types of worldwide folktales about The Outcast Child, a child rejected by its parents for a slight offense. The first three are known as the Youngest-best stories and are:
1.The King Lear type, in which the conduct of the elder children is strongly contrasted with that of the the youngest. [309]
2.The Value of Salt type, in which the story of the contrasting elder children is dropped, though the rejected child is still a sister.
3.The Joseph type, in which the father’s wrath, against sons or daughter, has some other cause, often a dream.

As for the first type, (p. 311) Geoffrey’s story of Lear has not been discovered in Welsh or Cornish or Breton folk tales. The one fact with which we have now to concern ourselves is that the story of king Lear and his three daughters has never been met with in any folklore research. (P. 312): The analogous story of Theodosius in Gesta Romanorum probably derives, though indirectly, from Geoffrey.

An example of the Value of Salt (p. 313) type is a story from southwestern France (Agenais) of Peau d’Âne, in which the daughter’s answer that she loves the widowed king as she loves salt enrages him; he exiles her to death and divides his kingdom between the other two elder daughters, on condition that he stays with each for alternating periods of six months. They turn him out. The youngest, now working as a turkey keeper, goes three nights to a ball, and on the third loses a red slipper, by which the prince identifies her; but she will not marry him without her father’s consent and until he is reinstated in his rights. Clearly this is a hybrid, though the evil of the elder sisters is still insisted upon. (P. 314): There is also a Corsican variant of this story. (P. 315): The story of the Value of Salt exists in Roman, Swabian, (p. 316) Venetian, Spanish, Flemish, and Hungarian, (p. 317) Tuscan, Sicilian, Austrian (Jacob & Wilhelm Grimm, Hausmärchen 179, where it forms only part of the tale of The Goosegirl by the Spring), (p. 318) Hindoo, Basque, (p. 319) Tirolese, (p. 320) Portuguese, and Asturian versions.
(Pp. 321 ff.): The Joseph type exists in Siberian, Italian, Sicilian, Brazilian, Persian, Indian, South Slavonic, and other versions.
The other two types, the Ravens and the Language of the Beasts, have no close connection with the Lear story.
(P. 349): The framework of the [value of salt] tale has nothing to do with the marvellous and so might have developed from Märchen into saga and have been an early form of King Lear.

White (1880, p. 119) always associated Cordelia and her sisters with Cinderella and her sisters, and Cox (1893, pp. xv, 80–6), describing a variant of the Cinderella story, names the initial elements of the Suffolk tale Cap o’ Rushes the King Lear judgment—Loving like salt—Outcast heroine. (It should be pointed out that there is no complete tale about love like salt; it is a motif that appears in countless stories mainly about other kinds of events.)

Perrett (1904, pp. 9 ff.) discusses traditional tales about a love-test, starting (pp. 9–10) with a Grimm brothers tale [Märchen 179, Goose-girl by the Spring] of a daughter cast out because she tells her father she loves him like salt, and with many earlier versions of it found throughout Europe by folklorists, including Cox. (P. 11): Some versions have details close to the Lear story: the father wishes to be king no longer but wishes to divide his kingdom (Cox no. 211), wants to give his kingdom to the daughter who loves him best (Cox no. 223; cf. Holinshed), is made suspicious of his favorite by the other daughters (Cox no. 212), etc. (P. 12): The sisters may be jealous and excite the father’s anger further (Cox nos. 211, 212; cf. Higgins, Leir), and later maltreat him (Cox nos. 211, 220, 222, 312) until the outcast daughter rescues him. There is scarcely a new turn or incident given to the [13] story in the literary version from Geoffrey to Shakespeare for which a parallel cannot be found in one or more of these Cinderella variants, except Cordeilla’s warning her father against her sisters’ flattery. (P. 287): Geoffrey…was the first to apply them to Leir.

Beza (1931) cites three remotely analogous stories of love-tests from Romanian folktales, one involving the love-like-salt motif. Cocchiara (1932) collects versions of the Lear folktale from many different countries, though he hardly mentions Lr. Smith (1946, p. 172) compares the Irish tale of St. Dympna, killed by a loving but tyrannical father enraged by her disobedience to his marriage plans. Hoeniger (1974, pp. 89–102): There are no extant English folk tales on Lear: Sh. instead exploits the power of primitive myth in developing his basic themes of generational conflict and sibling rivalry. Hoeniger discusses three analogues from Corsica, Cosenza, and Calabria originally recorded by Cocchiara. Among Cinderella-like stories Tobin (1978, pp. 39–40), as Freud before him, cites the Cupid and Psyche story in Apuleius’s Golden Ass, with its impatient father and his laconic daughter whose two elder sisters show to her martial hostility.

Young (1975, pp. 309–19), surveying the many international instances of the love-like-salt and Cinderella types of narrative: (p. 310) It is now generally believed that Geoffrey’s own source was some early folktale or legend, possible of oriental origin. He looks at two groups of Eurasian folktales, some versions dating from the 9th c., classified by Aarne & Thompson (1961, pp. 175–8, 322) as Types 510A & 510B (Cinderella and Cap o’ Rushes) and Type 923 (Love like Salt). I would argue here that these two groups of tales represent an oral tradition related to the original source of Geoffrey of Monmouth’s tale of King Leir.…At the same time, I would suggest that the oral source, in the form of the 510 and 923 Types of folktale, almost certainly existed side by side with the legend of King Leir. (P. 313): It can be seen that all the versions of the 510 and 923 Types of folktale I have described possess certain features of a common pattern. All begin with a father’s question to his children which in every case demands that the children put a value on their love for their father. Invariably the youngest child refuses to flatter the father like the other children. The answer given by this child is usually the cryptic Love like salt, though in some Scandinavian and Russian version it is Love like wind in the hot sun, and in Indian versions, as we have seen, the youngest child (usually a male) insists that destiny is in his own hands, not those of the father. In all cases the father misinterpets the child’s reply ([called by many folklorists] The King Lear Judgment) and expels the child from his house. The child marries, often with a seemingly unpromising man, though sometimes with a prince. Prosperity and good fortune then attend the child and eventually there is a meeting with the father in which their former positions are reversed. When the child’s identity is revealed, the father recognizes the falsity of his original judgment when the cryptic truth of the child’s misunderstood answer to the love-test is made clear. (P. 315): In the [510 and 923 Types], as in all the written versions preceding Shakespeare’s, the father-figure is not sacrificed. Instead he comes to [316] self-knowledge… which prepares for his reconciliation and return to the status of the just parent. The conclusion…is thus comic. (P. 317): What Shakespeare does in the final act of his play, when he telescopes the Cordelia episode into the Leir story, is to cause a deliberate break in the expectations that have been evoked in the minds of his audience by their familiarity with both literary and oral sources.…Not only is Shakespeare distorting the basic pattern of his source story, but he is also distorting its inherent pattern of justice.

Dundes (1976, pp. 356 ff.) attempts to prove that much of the inherent dramatic power of the play is owing to an essential psychological dimension of the underlying folk-tale, i.e. incest. Cap o’ Rushes has the King Lear judgment and Outcast daughter; another related tale, Catskin, does not but has the functional equivalents of Unnatural [i.e., incestuous] father and Heroine flight. Aarne-Thompson tale type 510B is Dress of Gold…[(Cap o’ Rushes)], whose dress is the gift of the father who wants to marry his own daughter. (P. 358): The love like salt plot appears [to Dundes] to be a weakened form of the folktale plot in which a mad father tries to marry his own daughter. Dundes argues as if the lecherous father and the essential psychological dimension of incest were present in all variants of the Cinderella or Cap o’ Rushes tales, or at least in Love like Salt. This premise is not supported, however, by Aarne-Thompson’s analysis (510.1) of the Cinderella variants, which makes clear that the persecution of the heroine may be either a) abuse by her stepmothers and stepsisters, b) a father who wants to marry her, c) being cast out for her love-like-salt remark, or d) threat of death by a servant. Moreover, Love Like Salt is treated separately as type 923, in which there is no hint of incest. Dundes tries to get around this crucial difficulty by saying (p. 357, n. 11), Love Like Salt…can be considered as an abridged form of the basic tale type 510. Presumably one thing that has been abridged is the lecherous father, the very thing that Dundes needs in the tale as the basis of his whole reading of Lr. The love like salt folktale, he believes, is a derivative (abridgment) of an earlier one about (p. 359) daughter-father incest rather than father-daughter incest. This dimension carries over by (p. 360) projection (i.e., reversal) from the folktale to Sh.’s play. Lr. is about daughter-father incest, and revolves around Cordelia; it is a transformation of a folktale fantasy [363] concerned with a daughter’s disguised incestuous love of her father. In both play and folktale a girl, (p. 362) in sibling rivalry with her sisters for her father’s affection, is unable to express sexual love for the parent (speech is sexual), though (p. 363) Cordelia finally realizes her Electra fantasy briefly, having Lear all to herself before being led to prison and death, the latter her (p. 361) punishment for her breaking of taboo.

Thus Dundes takes a folktale that Sh. may not have known, gives it a fatherly incest motive which it apparently did not have (though other cognate tales do), and finds evidence in Lr. for the presence of Cordelia’s daughterly incest. For that evidence, see nn. 238, 1644, 1708, 2640–1, and 2949. Cf. Welch (1996), who generally agrees.

Gorfain (1977, pp. 246 ff.): In the Love Like Salt tales the father learns through experience the mistake he makes in repudiating his youngest child. In these stories the father, like Lear, prefers his youngest daughter but rejects her answer because he cannot understand her plainness.…[247] The folktale device places the female protagonist outside the home on her own so that while disguised in a lowly position, she can meet a partner. Both for the suitor and her father…the final recognition reinstates the proper social order, and emphasizes the theme of false appearances.…[248] In the same way that salt refreshes that which is flat, understanding its value renews relationships and redeems the family. Lr. uses various folkloristic forms—love contest, riddles, prophecy—but thwarts our conventional expectations about them and thereby the very notions of justice and order.

Markey (1982, p. 57): Geoffrey’s tale of Lear is comprised of three basic components: a succession myth [which Markey reconstructs from the supposed etymologies of Lear, Goneril, Regan, and Cordelia]; a folktale comprised of the topoi of the love-test, loving like salt, angry father, and reconciliation, a folktale related to the Cinderella motif [fn.: Where Geoffrey heard them and where they originated from are open questions which may never receive definite answers.…Relationship to the Cinderella type, specifically in the motif of the love-sick prince, is discernible in the wooing of Cordelia by Aganippus, King of Franks, but this episode is highly reminiscent of the marriage of Clovis with Clotilda as related by Gregory of Tours in his Historia Francorum, lib. II, cap. 28.]; and the suicide of the despondent Cordelia. First, we note that Cordelia’s suicide is apparently but another of Geoffrey’s inventions [citing Perrett, pp. 25–7]. Second, the folktale elements are virtually universal and may or may not have been part of early Welsh popular tradition. At any rate, they are not exclusively Welsh, or Celtic, or even exclusively Indo-European for that matter. Moreover, as woven around these elements, the Lear story as such has no history in Welsh tradition, but is only an artful fabrication passed off as history by Geoffrey. Note, too, that the Welsh versions of the Lear story are rather slavish translations of the Historia [citing D. Simon Evans, A Grammar of Middle Welsh, Dublin, 1970, pp. xxxiv–xxxv.].

It may be noted finally that since no one has discovered anywhere in Sh. an explicit reference or clear allusion to the particular tales of Cinderella, the goose-girl, Cap o’ Rushes, or love-like-salt, he may not have known them at all; if so, such folk-tales and motifs would have influenced him only indirectly and at several removes, if at all. One may argue, of course, that they are manifestations of mental archetypes, Jungian or not, found in many very different world cultures, including Sh.’s.

div.head: More General Archetypes
div.p: In Lr. Freud (1913; 1925, 4:246, 255–6) recognized archetypes resident in myths of the Greek goddess of love and of the German goddess of death: Is not this once more a scene of choosing between three women, of whom the youngest is the best, the supreme one [as is Cinderella, Psyche, and Aphrodite]?…[255] Lear is not only an old man; he is a dying man. The extraordinary project of dividing the inheritance thus loses its strangeness. [256] The doomed man is nevertheless not willing to renounce the love of women; he insists on hearing how much he is loved.…[But] Cordelia is Death.…The three inevitable relations man has with woman are here represented: that with the mother who bears him, with the companion of his bed and board, and with the destroyer. Or it is the three forms taken on by the figure of the mother as life proceeds: the mother herself, the beloved who is chosen after her pattern, and finally the Mother Earth who receives him again. In initially rejecting Cordelia, Lear is resisting Death and longing for the love of woman; but he carries her in at the end, accepting Death. Holland (1966, p. 65) reports that Freud in 1883 sometimes called his sweetheart Martha by the name Cordelia (when she had a sore throat and could not talk), and commenting to Ferenczi in 1913 on this essay said that its subjective condition was his particular closeness to his daughter Anna. After reading Bransom (1934) Freud wrote to that author seconding the secret meaning of the tragedy, the repressed incestuous claims on his daughter’s love; the letter is rpt. in E. Jones, Life and Work, 3 vols., 1957, 3:457–8. Garber (1987, pp. 74–86) discusses at length the relevance of this essay to Freud’s life, family relationships, and psyche.

The Jungian derivation of artistic forms from racial archetypes subsisting in the human psyche appears in Bodkin (1934, pp. 16–17, 85–6): King Lear is at once a poor, infirm, weak, and despised old man…and also in his sufferings a superhuman figure.…[17] The word king is…loaded with a significance for the sources of which we must go far back in the story of the race and of the individual.…In the life-history of the individual imagination the figures of father and king tend to coalesce. Legends and fairy stories that reflect the feelings of more primitive people towards their king are interpreted by the child in the light of his own earlier feeling towards his father.…The figures of both father and king tend to retain within those deeper levels of the mind to which poetry may penetrate, something of the mana that invested the first representative of a power akin to, but vastly beyond, that of the individual emerging into self-consciousness.…[85] Within the meaning communicated to-day to a sensitive reader or spectator of…King Lear,…something is present corresponding to the emotional meaning that belonged to ancient rituals undertaken for the renewal of the life of the tribe.…[86] Lear dies, but those who have shared with awe and pity the anguish of his last convulsion gather themselves together to sustain the gored state. For interpretive criticism that assumes or invokes primitive psychological archetypes, such as that of Stewart (1949, pp. 20–7), Holloway (1961, pp. 75–98), and Frye (1967, pp. 95–121), see , , , , , , .

Others have found archetypes closer to home in the folk play and other village rituals. Spens (1916, p. 51): Sh., having begun to write a comedy or romance, followed his usual method, humanizing his literary source by steeping it in a parallel folk-play—in this case the Elizabethan equivalent of something like the Revesby sword-play. As he studied he realized what was probably more evident in the Elizabethan form of the sword-plays, that the story of the Summer King, or Fool who is slain, is the story of pitiful human decay and death, of the passing of the generations. And so in King Lear he portrays the agony and rebellion of the individual when he realizes that the kingdom is passing from him, that in the nature of things he can no longer be the centre of the little group around him. Hewitt (1949, pp. 18–19): Possibly Geoffrey or his source adopted the annual folk-ceremony of driving out of the forces of sterility, evil, and death, in the person of a scapegoat, often representing the old year, who was treated at first with regal honours, then mocked and derided, and finally expelled from the village.… (P. 19): [Sh.’s audience probably] transferred from the ceremony to the play a feeling of the inevitability of the old king’s expulsion. Gorfain (1977, pp. 151–3): Lr. incorporates the traditional folk form of the riddle. The Fool’s riddles help express and unite…thematic paradoxes; (p. 152) they reverse the riddle’s usual rite of passage ritual (because while Lear’s understanding advances, his status is not restored); and they overturn normal relationships in a topsy-turvy realm that uses the same folk logic as does carnival, citing Bakhtin. Weimann (1978, pp. 40–1, 224–36): Details of the barking dog (2599–2602) and the little tiny wit of the Fool (1729) may derive from features of the Mummers’ folk play. But the topsy-turvydom in the Mummers’ Play, the nonsensical heritage of ritual action is replaced by a new convention of reason in madness. Zak (1984, p. 166): Wearing his crown of idle weeds, Lear in 4.6 may be presenting himself with self-conscious irony as a carnival king, the mock king of a festival of fools, whose edicts…lack any real power. Following Bradbrook (1978, p. 192), Billington (1991, p. 207): The mad king of summer, at whose court Gloucester can find forgiveness [for adultery], is also a fool king in the winter of his fortunes; but see n. 144. Hodge (1990, pp. 63–4) accepts Graves’s improbable association (see above) of Lear with Llyr, and of the Janus-like Llyr with midsummer festivals of the year’s death and renewal celebrated in Leir’s city of Leicester, and argues that Sh.’s Lr. does incorporate motifs from the festival ritual text which are not in his sources: Lear’s madness; the storm scene, where Lear’s curse is an anti-king’s inversion of a prayer for festivity; the triple-fool (i.e., the Fool, Edgar, and Kent, who Hodges mistakenly claims disguises himself as a madman/fool). But Sh. in turn departed from this ritual text in the final double death and the critique of the patriarachal protagonist and his schizoid society, and thus deliberately removed the essential quality of the festival-text as a provider of consolation, as training in how to cope with death. For other critics who discern patterns of seasonal festivals and rituals in Lr., such as Long (1976) and Liebler (1995), see .

Still others point to archetypes embodied in the medieval religious drama. Harbage (ed. 1958, pp. 22–3): Here is no soft-brained Senex, but the archetypal King. As such Lear symbolizes Mankind.…The king-figure surrogate is an understandable product of the human mind in its early attempts at abstraction, since the most imposing of single men best lends his image to the difficult concept of Man.…Early Renaissance drama was steeped in the tradition of this symbolic figure, sometimes still called King as well as Mankind, Everyman, Genus Humanum, and the like. He is always identifiable by his centrality to the action, and the mixed company he keeps—vices or flatterers on the one hand, virtues or truth-speakers on the other. And there stands [23] Lear—Goneril and Regan to the left, Kent and Cordelia to the right. Mack (1965, pp. 49–80) argues that it is difficult to account for what Shakespeare made of Leir apart from the influence of some governing archetypal themes. One is that embodied in folk and medieval renderings of the Abasement of the Proud King (as described by Lilian Hornstein, PMLA, 1964, 13–21), with their details of (p. 50) humbling pride…, nakedness and beggary and madness, loss of identity, suffering in the cold, as well as in the Biblical story of Nebuchadnezzar, who for his pride was driven mad and made to live on grass as a beast among beasts. Moreover (pp. 57–63), Lear, Edgar, and Edmund share several archetypal patterns of the Morality play, including the psychomachia externalized in good and evil counselors, the Summons of Death, the Vice posing as virtue, life as a spiritual progress, symbolic change of garments, abandonment by friends, temptation to suicide, the theme of the moral cost of Appetite, recollections of the Seven Deadly Sins, etc. (See further below on the influence of the Morality.)

For others the archetypes are recurrent patterns of human history. Wittreich (1984, pp. 37–8): Shakespeare’s sources, medieval and [38] Renaissance, delineate…an archetypal pattern: of families sparring, of kingdoms dividing, of factions warring, of history dissolving; what Shakespeare injects into the process, through his revision of those sources…, is the possibility—and only the possibility—of the world’s reconstituting itself and becoming whole again.

div.head: Medieval Drama
div.p: Jones (1977, pp. 57–9) alone finds a source in the crafts cycles. Sh. seems to have seen and in Lr. remembered medieval Passion plays: in their humiliation and casting out of Lear, Goneril, Regan, and Cornwall have a marked family resemblance…to the typical Caiaphases and Annases of the Passion plays, especially in their ferocity and capacity for physical violence. (P. 58): In the York Judgment of Jesus, Caiaphas’ words show sadism lurking under a cover of judicious restraint, the tone of which is oddly like Regan’s words spoken near the end of ii. iv…[59] with a demure quietness that is very disturbing.

A multitude of critics, on the other hand, find traces of the late medieval morality play and early Renaissance moral interludes. Few address the question of the means and extent of Sh.’s knowledge of the moralities, but take it for granted that he knew the morality manner—the general patterns of pilgrimage of life, psychomachia, allegorical personages, the Vice, coming of death, etc.; and even fewer suggest the influence of particular moralities or interludes.

Farnham (1936, pp. 437, 451–2): The grossness of the Fool…is a paradoxically delicate metamorphosis of the Vice’s shrewd irreverence and of the Vice’s lack of rational soul or moral responsibility.…[451] If one thinks…in terms of [452] the moral play, it is as though Lear loses the world only to save his soul by confession and penitence.

Kernodle (1945, pp. 186–7): The double plot and the double opening (two sets of characters in two scenes), and the balance of a dominant Cornwall in the first half and a dominant Albany in the second, reflect artistic habits inherited from the Middle Ages, figural parallels of characters and events that underline common patterns or themes. Nearer models, however, are Mirror for Magistrates, Lyly’s Gallathea and Midas, Marlowe’s Jew of Malta, and Sh.’s own R2 and AYL.

Campbell (1948, pp. 94, 102, 108–9): King Lear is, in my opinion, a sublime morality play, the action of which is set against a backdrop of eternity. Lear’s problem and his career resemble those of the central figure in the typical morality play.…The action of Shakespeare’s play is his greatly modified version of man’s endless search for true and everlasting spiritual values.…[Lear] is not so much an erring Christian as a completely unstoical man and he is converted to a state of mind which is a mixture of Stoic insight and Christian humility. (P. 102): His counselors are Kent, the Stoic plain man, and the Fool, the wise innocent. (P. 109): Lr. reflects the resurgence of medieval concepts in Jacobean drama and is a grandiose development of a mediaeval model. The morality pattern in Lr. of Mankind’s pilgrimage marked [Sh.’s] participation in a well-defined Jacobean movement in tragedy. With this influential essay Rosier (1954) agrees—Lear follows the Morality pattern in structure and the medieval homiletic structure and exemplum tradition—as does Ribner (1957, p. 252; cf. 1960, pp. 117, 136): Lear’s experience is that of every man in a sinful world in which salvation is yet attainable.

Danby (1949, pp. 40, 42): The characters…are not Morality-figures. They stand one stage nearer to actuality than the personages of allegory. The clear Morality outline is however included in the play.…[42] Edmund and the sisters can be regarded as figures in a Morality debate concerning the nature of Man. They stand for the view given expression later by Hobbes. They are opposed to the view maintained in Hooker and Bacon, and which is exemplified by Albany, Cordelia, and Edgar.

Craik (1958, pp. 93–6), more particularly, discusses the temporary fettering…of a virtue by the vices, citing Hickscorner, in which Imagination and Freewill bind Pity; (p. 94) Youth, in which Riot threatens Charity with the stocks and fetters his ankles and wrists; Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis, in which wicked clergy stock Veritie, joined later by Chastitie; (p. 95) Impatient Poverty, where Prosperitie theatens Peace with stocks; New Custom, where Ignorance theatens New Custom with stocks; and King Darius, in which the Vice offers Equity a fetter. When Kent is placed in the stocks by Regan and Cornwall in King Lear, the incident derives some of its force from this tradition.…The devices of the moral interludes are suggested more than once in King Lear; there are, for example, Edgar’s descriptions of the grotesque devil whom he feigns to have seen tempting Gloucester to despair, and [96] his speeches about the similar temptations which he claims to have suffered as Poor Tom.

Spivack (1958, pp. 413–14) sees in the earlier part of Edmund’s role a formula, the evolved product of the Christian homiletic drama: his gay alacrity in deception and dissimulation, the breach his stratagem achieves between father and son, and, beyond anything else, his absolute awareness of the moral [414] position as he merrily and cynically pits his own villainy against the susceptible credulity and nobility of his dupes, are the conventional activity of the stage Vice.

Whitaker (1965, pp. 216–17, 236, 240): In this redemptive action [the regeneration of Gloucester and Lear], the morality structure of this play…becomes especially apparent. The forces for good and evil are clearly aligned—Cordelia, Kent, and Edgar on one side; Goneril, Regan, and Edmund on the other. Edgar and even Cordelia come closer than any other characters in Shakespeare to personifying moral forces: Edgar is analogous to Knowledge in Everyman, Cordelia is [217] Love. Even the sisters approximate Lust, and Edmund is still Ambition, though with them the morality-play analogy breaks down because they are too much involved in the subordinate counteraction to act directly upon Lear and Gloucester.…[236] This simplicity and universality of exemplum is developed also by the use of thematic doubling [both Lear and Gloucester misjudge their children].…[240] On the other hand, much as King Lear may resemble a morality play in its structure, it differs profoundly in never neglecting the tragic suffering of those who find regeneration or the tragic waste of those who sink from sin to sin.

Mack (1965, pp. 60–1): Edmund’s name could be Appetite—sprung from his father’s appetite and seeking to devour all that lies in his way: brother, father, mistress, the kingdom itself.…The solid shape under the idiosyncratic accent remains that of the Vice figure of the Morality play, who confides his scorn of virtue to the spectators in a similarly insinuating tone and always [61] identifies himself for them by attacking the moral bases of the life they lead.

Jones (1971, pp. 158–9): What Shakespeare means to present, it seems, is not only the personal story of one man’s decline and death [as in the moralities]; he also gives us the closing stages of the history of a whole society, even a whole world’s destruction.…[159] Lear is himself a British king as well as a representative of Humanum Genus.

A few particular morality models have been proposed. Greenfield (1954, pp. 280–6): The symbolism of clothing and nakedness is familiar in medieval and Renaissance pictorial art and in miracle and morality plays (p. 282) and is the center of Medwall’s morality Nature. Sh. draws upon many of the traditional overtones—clothing = power, rank, human worth; falsity, error, concealment, vanity. Jones (1971, p. 188): Cordelia’s reunion with Lear in 4.7 possibly derives its essential form from a dialogue between Mankind and Mercy in Mankind, lines 804–8. Creeth (1976, pp. 111–74): Lr.’s structure originates in the fragmentary morality play Pride of Life. Its wrathful protagonist Rex Vivus, king of Britain, scorns truth told by a woman dear to him, suffers desertion by his false friends, and is restored to grace by kindness. The boy Solas and the bishop correspond to Lear’s Fool and Kent, the false friends to Goneril and Regan, and the Virgin Mary to Cordelia. Levitsky (1978), finding general analogies: Both Tim. and Lr. may be indebted to Skelton’s morality Magnyfycence for its theme of true magnificence.
Recent criticism has emphasized the ways in which Sh. adapted the morality model to radically different purposes from Christian allegory:

Potter (1975, pp. 152 ff.): King Lear is Shakespeare’s supreme, metaphysical, idiosyncratic morality play—a work of Gothic dramatic architecture that takes premises, structure and characterizations from medieval precedent, and makes of them something utterly unprecedented. It is an exploration of pain, separation, cruelty, incomprehension, madness, and futility, conducted in the guise of a spiritual pilgrimage, and it ends in tragedy. It is an extension into new philosophical and dramatic regions of the political morality tradition. Like the earliest extant morality, the 14th-c. Pride of Life, it utilizes the figure of a King to represent humanity; and (p. 153) it resembles Mundus et Infans (1508), where the mankind figure is a boisterous and proud ruler, riding for a fall.…In his pride the hero of Mundus et Infans is misled by Folly, and falls into sickness, old age and near-despair, from which he is rescued by agents of repentance.…[154] From the political morality tradition Shakespeare borrows not merely the central king figure, but also the subordinate character groups. There is, first of all, a loyal and truthful group of advisers (Kent, Cordelia) who are soon to be ignored or discharged. In opposition to this group, and in the ascendant, are a parallel company of flattering advisers wearing the disguise of virtue (Goneril and Regan and their husbands). (P. 155): The question of identity, which is posed by the tidy circumstances of a morality play like Everyman or Mankind, and answered in orthodox theological terms, is rephrased by Shakespeare to fit the unruly and expanded ideological world of King Lear, with its strange intimations of pagan determinism, medieval hope, and seventeenth-century skepticism. Gloucester and Lear, perceiving themselves to be the injured fathers of ungrateful children (Edgar and Cordelia), are in fact the duped fathers of untrustworthy children (Edmund, Goneril, and Regan). These misconceptions of identity are fundamental, and can only be corrected by bitter experience, though (p. 162) without a positive morality-play redemption; there is no transcendent deathbed repentance, no formalized good ending.…[163] As the central figure in a play from the political morality tradition, Lear is also suffering a storm in the little world of the state.…Yet Shakespeare relegates these matters to the background, in order to project and consider the greater inner conflict. (P. 165): Facing the naked Tom, Lear’s instruction by ministers of grace, in a grotesque tragic parody of the morality play sequence, leads him to a perception of truth which is insupportable, and to madness. Nonetheless, (p. 167) the religious language in 4.3 makes it abundantly clear…that Cordelia can be regarded as a minister of Christian grace.…[168] [In 4.7] Lear is…reclothed in the garments of a king. This action, the traditional morality play ceremony of reclothing the penitent hero, is Cordelia’s way of reconstructing Lear’s identity in its original rank, but in a chastened form.…It restores, seemingly, a lost soul from perdition.

Felperin (1977, pp. 87–106): The Gloucester subplot, with its deliberately archaic and artificial morality pattern of good versus evil agents, fortunate fall, and redemptive suffering, is intended to throw the deeper and fuller experience of Lear into relief. (P. 94): The air of contrivance that hangs about the Gloucester action is pervasive, and it smells of morality.…[98] The movement of the Lear action away from a morality vision thus opposes and crosses that of the Gloucester action toward a morality vision.…The change that Lear undergoes in the course of his play is not a change from one moral state to another, such as from pride to charity, but a change away from self-definition in terms of moral categories altogether and toward a new sense of existential indeterminacy, the very opposite of Gloucester’s change.

Kernan (1979, pp. 120 ff.): Of all Shakespeare’s plays, King Lear is most obviously structured in the morality-play manner.…The plot of the play conflates several standard morality patterns, the education of the prince in the nature of true government, Everyman’s discovery of who will go with him into death, and the even more basic temptation pattern of sin, repentance, and salvation.…[126] Where Gloucester’s survival was staged for him in the form of a crude play with the illusion of a miraculously harmless fall from the cliff, Lear’s regeneration is arranged by Cordelia with a more subtle emblematic play involving sleep, a change of garments, music, and the forgiveness of a lost daughter, the principal symbols of renewal in Shakespeare’s late romances.…But for all its grace and subtlety, Cordelia’s miracle play still has the configurations of an old-style play.…Act 4…is built around these two parallel scenes of regeneration.…[128] in Lear Shakespeare makes his peace at long last with the morality play.…Attractive and true as they [Edgar’s and Cordelia’s plays] may be, they are not finally in King Lear adequate realizations of experience.

Schell (1983, pp. 25, 150–95): Lear mounts so radical a challenge to the morality form, and through it a challenge to the notion that life can be understood as a pilgrimage, that one can never be entirely comfortable with either again. During Lear’s journey into the land of unlikeness—of unwise, unfatherly, unkingly behavior and ultimate madness—(p. 174) a psychomachia between appetite and order…goes on within Lear himself.…Out in the storm the psychomachia is carried on through the opposed pairs of revenge and justice.…[181] In the course of his pilgrimage Lear must discover the nature and function of social offices and the fact that his identity is bound up with them. And, most of all, he must come to understand himself, as king, as father, and as a man. But (p. 184) There is nothing systematic and very little that is cumulative about Lear’s pilgrimage. He learns the art of our necessities, (p. 185) the bonds of common humanity with the Fool, the falseness of flatterers, and (p. 186) his own fragility. (P. 187): Cordelia…confers on Lear his lost identity as father and king, even dressing him in royal robes while he sleeps. He awakens from the grave and from false notions of his own self-sufficiency. (P. 190): Only in Shakespeare’s [version of the Lear story] is his suffering treated as part of a spiritual pilgrimage in which, by pursuing all his follies to the disillusioning ends they imply, he discovers what his nature truly requires. At the end, however, (p. 194) There is no hint of transcendence or affirmation in Cordelia’s death, no clue as to what we are to make now of those teasing [earlier] allusions to grace.…King Lear…turns a familiar dramatic form against itself and the assumptions it embodies.…[195] Lear’s entrance with Cordelia’s body virtually marks the end of a long-lived way of understanding experience and of the dramatic form created to express it.

Considering Sh.’s departures from morality features, some critics have denied significant influence. Watkins (1950, p. 106): King Lear is not a Morality play like Faustus, but it has the same effect because of the unusual measure of symbolical stylization. Schoff (1962, pp. 157–72) confutes an array of critics who define Lear’s mistakes as those of a sinner—in breaking Nature’s or God’s law, in being derelict in duty or lacking in political wisdom, or in being a wrathful man. She concludes (p. 172) that Lear is not a moral exemplum, nor is Lr. a morality play. It is a play about the fearful power of evil…and its protagonist is a tragic hero whose experience…enables us to gain strength and understanding. Reibetanz (1977, pp. 59–60): The main difference between Edmund and the Vice is as noteworthy as these similarities.…Like Lear, he discovers the limitations and passions that being human bestows on him.…Except for Shakespeare’s grand variations on the type, the Vice largely disappeared from the stage after the advent of established professional theatre in London during the 1570s and 1580s. Edmund, he argues, is more likely modeled on (p. 60) the wily intriguer…who was a stock character during the first decade of private-theatre dramaturgy. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 197): Structurally King Lear is not patterned on the old morality play.…There is no pattern of spiritual development in the play. The pattern derives from its de casibus theme and is closely similar to that of Timon of Athens, a threefold pattern in which the hero begins in prosperity, then suffers rejection through the ingratitude of men (in Lear’s case, women) and finally collapses into despair and death in a hostile world where supernatural aid is not forthcoming. McAlindon (1996, p. 148) denies Edmund’s Morality roots: The character of the jocular, histrionic villain derives from the devil and not…from the Vice.…The Vice was himself an obvious derivative of the archetypal figure of evil in the Christian mythos. Furthermore, the comic and ludic conception of demonic behaviour does not originate in the medieval drama, nor…in medieval sermon literature. It was far more abundantly exhibited in the lives of the saints, in other-worldly legends such as St. Patrick’s Purgatory, and in ascetical treatises dealing with the ways in which Satan seeks to ensnare the devout—as, in the eyes of puritans, by plays and games. Edmund uses play to confuse, disguise, and destroy; Edgar uses dissembling and disguise in the service of truth and concord.

Occasional comparisons with features of the morality may be found in the commentary notes: see, e.g., those by Mack (1965) in n. 60–6, 74–81, by Bratton (ed. 1987) and Findlay (1994) in n. 335–56, and by Wilson (1957, pp. 19–20) and Salter (1954, p. 110) in n. 2303+17.

div.head: Renaissance Plays
div.p: Of the many plays about early English history that had been common on the stage before Lr., among them Gorboduc (1562), The Misfortunes of Arthur (1588), Leir (1590–4), Locrine (1591–5), possibly The Birth of Merlin (1597–1621), and many others that have been lost (see Creizenach, 1916, pp. 169–88), almost none (except Leir) have been thought to be influential on Lr. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 167): Indeed Lear remains somewhat isolated as a revival of the genre of legendary history at the height of the fashion for city comedy.

Smith (1946, pp. 169–71) speculates that the names of Gloucester, Edgar, and Edmund came from Geoffrey of Monmouth by way of a lost Admiral’s play of 1597, Uther Pendragon, thought to be the possible source of William Rowley’s The Birth of Merlin, which includes the parts The Earl of Gloster and Edwyn (his son). (P. 179): Edwyn could no doubt have suggested Edgar and Edmund, Anglo-Saxon names which do not appear in Geoffrey of Monmouth, but which Shakespeare could have found in Holinshed or Camden or almost any chronicle. Edwinus, king of Northumbria, appears in Geoffrey (ed. Acton Griscom. London, New York, Toronto, 1929, pp. 512 ff.), as does Oswaldus (pp. 525 ff.…). Gloster and Edoll duke of Chester (in Merlin and presumably the earlier play) seem to derive from Geoffrey’s Eldol dux Claudiocestrie, a militant figure immediately before and after the story of Merlin’s birth (ed. Griscom, pp. 378, 403).

Otherwise Sackville and Norton’s Gorboduc, whose protagonist was a close descendant of Lear, is the only history play (besides Leir) thought possibly to have influenced Lr. Although comparisons with Gorboduc are frequent (see nn. 6, 7, 42–3, 43–6, 436–41, 938, 1448–51, and DP 8), the first scholar to suggest its influence on Lr. is apparently Adolf Mager, in Abhandlungen zur 20. Jahresberichte der K. K. Staats-Oberrealschule in Marburg, 1890, 3:36–39 (Tannenbaum (1940, no. 1429). The evidence for influence is slight.

Perrett (1904, p. 175): A single parallel indicates that Gorboduc directly influenced Leir (and so indirectly Lr.): In Leir 1.1 the king takes counsel over the intended division, in a scene modeled on Gorboduc 1.2, where the counsellors’ advice only hardens the king in his own previous opinion; cf. Lear’s fast intent and constant will.

Levin (1959, pp. 95–6): The first play performed before Queen Elizabeth, Gorboduc, one of whose collaborators was co-author of the Mirror for Magistrates, warned the queenly magistrate against the division of her realm and even foreshadowed King [96] Lear in introducing a dissension between the rival Dukes of Cornwall and Albany.
