Mendonça (1960, pp. 42 ff.) makes the most detailed case, on the basis of fairly general similarities: In both plays there is an old king who wants to rest and thinks it is time for his children to bear the burden of responsibility.…In both, the division of [Britain] has already been planned when the play opens and, before the court scenes, it is discussed, in Gorboduc by Videna and Ferrex, in King Lear by Kent and Gloucester.…In both, the initial actions drive the monarchs to extreme suffering and death, bringing evil to their nations; human feelings grow abnormal, there is a pervasive unnatural atmosphere, good and evil are bared and placed in mortal combat. (P. 43): Both plays refer to classical gods and share a number of political and (p. 44) moral terms (govern, treason, unnatural, monster, etc.). (P. 46): In both plays evil children are tried by their fathers. (P. 47): Though in Lr. the focus of the tragic ending is on the man, in Gorboduc on the state, yet the consequences of the division, amply analyzed in the concluding scene of Gorboduc, are echoed in Albany’s lines near the end of the last scene. At the end each nation is restored to hierarchic rule.

Comparing Marlowe’s Tamburlaine, Hopkins (1996) finds broad patterns of similarity of plot (three same-sex children, mad scenes in prose, a map), themes (nationality, computation, thematization, historiography, kingship), and occasional vocabulary, all of them too general to show direct influence. Similarly Hutchings (2000): Lr. echoes the ending of Marlowe’s II Tamburlaine, where a tired old ruler, having disinherited one son, calls for a map while bequeathing his empire to two other sons.

Steevens (ed. 1778) notes a similarity between the blinding of Gloucester and that of a character in Robert Greene’s Selimus (1586–93) (see n. 2140), which, asserts Capell (1783, 1.2:172), Sh. copy’d. Ekeblad (1957, pp. 193–4): Greene’s Selimus was acted by the Queen’s Men in the early 1590s; it may have influenced R3; and it has a character named Regan (not Ragan as in Leir). An Aga, a venerable counsellor, is blinded on the stage by Prince Acomat for his loyalty to the king, and then has his hands cut off. Ronan (1986) points out further that the mutilations in both plays occur in two stages amidst sinister quibbling repartee, that each monarch has two evil and one good offspring, and that in Selimus (1193) the unjust gods are called squint-ey’d, possibly leading Sh. to use the word squint three times in this play alone. Both Ekeblad and Ronan suspect that Sh. once acted in the play with the Queen’s Men; but there is no evidence that he was ever a member of that company, and the play had been in print since 1594. Hutchings (2000, pp. 84–5): Selimus, like Lr., shows the danger of political division.

Goldsmith (Timon, 1958, pp. 32–7) finds parallels between Lear and an undated MS play, the academic comedy of Timon: Timon and Lear both complain of undeserved misfortunes and curse mankind for its ingratitude, Timon recommends a suicide like Gloucester’s attempt to throw himself into the sea, both Laches and Kent bravely speak the truth, are exiled, and put on a homely disguise in order to continue loyally to serve their unthankful masters, both scorn and beat proud foppish servants. Goldsmith, however, names several other examples of that familiar figure of the Tudor stage—the blunt-spoken, loyal-hearted Englishman, including the Plowman in Of Gentylnes and Nobylyty (ca. 1522), Plain Thomas in Woodstock (ca. 1592–5), Sateros in The Cobler’s Prophecy (1594), and Stump in A Larum for London (ca. 1600). Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 168–70) compares Timon’s curse on all mankind at the end of Act 5 with Lear’s curses in 3.2, 5.3, and 1.4, admitting that It is not that there are any very precise verbal echoes but rather a similar dynamic as Timon appeals to Jove to let the heavens fall and to return Earth to former Chaos. (P. 170): In the old comedy Timon also goes temporarily mad on occasion. (P. 171): It is unclear how Sh. could have acquired and made use of an unpublished student play. Bulman (1976, p. 103), however, supposes that the Timon comedy was performed ca. 1602 at the Inns of Court, where Sh. could have seen it.

Analogies have been found with a number of late Elizabethan and early Jacobean plays, usually not close enough to show influence on Lr.: Capell (1783, 1.2:150): The rhyming of Lear’s Fool may have been suggested by that of Will Summers in When You See Me, You Know Me (1603–5) by Samuel Rowley, who wrote and acted for the Admiral’s (later Prince Henry’s, later Palsgrave’s) Men from 1597 to 1624. Though there are no close parallels, Summers speaks rhymed jingles, proverbs, and answering speeches, and impudently exposes both King Henry VIII’s infidelities and Cardinal Wolsey’s venality. The rhymes at 3054–5 are from George Puttenham’s The Arte of English Poesie (1589, bk. 3, ch. 23), possibly the source of the Fool’s Prophecy in Lr. (see n. 1735). In his edition of the play (MSR, 1952), F. P. Wilson notes that Rowley probably acted in two plays by Henry Chettle on Wolsey in 1601; one of them included Will Summers, as did a play of 1598 (Henslowe Papers, 10 Mar. 1598, ed. Greg, 1907, p. 114; ed. Foakes & Rickert, 1961, p. 318). Neither Wilson nor Karl Elze (ed. 1874) points out any parallels with Lr.

Lamb (1808; 1813, p. 73): The situation of Andrugio and Lucio [in Marston’s Antonio and Mellida, Part 1, 1599] resembles that of Lear and Kent, in that King’s distresses. Andrugio, like Lear, manifests a kind of royal impatience; a turbulent greatness, an affected resignation. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xlii; 1957, p. 147) and Fraser (ed. 1963, p. 192) note a feigned suicide in Marston’s Malcontent (1600–4); but there are many possible sources for Gloucester’s attempt (see nn. 2256, 2480). Reibetanz (1974, p. 43) compares Lear’s entrance with Cordelia to the endings of Marston’s Sophonisba (1605–6) and Chapman’s Bussy D’Ambois (see n. 3216). Similarities of phrase and idea have been found with Marston’s Dutch Courtesan (1603–4), Malcontent, and Fawn (1604–6): see nn. 337, 459, 548, 644, 666, 967–8, 1140, 2181–2, 2572.

Craig (ed. 1901), Muir (ed. 1952), and others compare Edgar’s rustic dialect in 4.6 with similar speech in the apocryphal The London Prodigal (1603–5), performed by the King’s Men, but Kittredge (ed. 1940) lists dozens of other precedents and analogues (see n. 2688–97). Muir (ed. 1952, rev. 1957, p. 257) also proposes some influence from Jonson’s Sejanus (1603), in which Sh. acted, but it is doubtful; see nn. 563 and 1146–53, and .

Sampley (1961, p. 469) finds in Dekker’s Old Fortunatus and the Anonymous The Wisdom of Doctor Dodipoll, both printed 1600, incidents of a rejected girl taken in marriage (and thereby saved from disgrace) by a more faithful suitor. The curious coincidence of these two analogues shows a contemporary vogue for this effective turn of plot, not necessarily influence on Sh.

Taylor (1982, pp. 396 ff.) detects similarities with Chapman, Jonson, and Marston’s satirical comedy Eastward Ho (1605) and George Wilkins’s domestic drama The Miseries of Enforced Marriage (1605–7). The similarities with the latter play are few and slight, and it may have been performed later than Lr.; see . The similarities with the former are generally unremarkable or remote: a storm is described, a father kneels to his daughter (as in Leir), malefactors are (comically) tried, a servant is insolent and is tripped up, a daughter is threatened with denial of dowry, some commonplace words and thoughts occur in both plays. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 108): The evidence is not convincing.…No doubt Shakespeare did read or see this play, which could have reminded him of the parable of the prodigal son, a parable that relates to the progress of the prodigal fathers, Lear and Gloucester, in King Lear…; but the prodigal brought to penitence and reconciliation was a common theme of citizen comedy of the period, as in The London Prodigal, published in 1605 with a title-page claiming it was acted by the King’s Men and written by William Shakespeare.
Murphy (1984, pp. 135–52) finds parallels with John Day’s Isle of Gulls (1606) and Blind Beggar (ca. 1600), but they seem not close enough to establish any clear relationship.

Reibetanz (1974, pp. 39–57): Though written for the public theater, Lr. shows the general influence of contemporary private-theater drama, such as that of Marston (The Dutch Courtesan, 1603–4; Sophonisba, 1605–6), Middleton (A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, 1611–13), Chapman (Bussy D’Ambois, 1600–4; Byron’s Tragedy, 1608), Beaumont and Fletcher (Philaster, 1608–10; Cupid’s Revenge, 1607–12; Maid’s Tragedy, 1608–11), Jonson (Epicoene, 1609), Field (Amends for Ladies, 1610–11), and Lording Barry (Ram Alley, 1607–8), in its use of emblematic groupings, entrances, costumes, gestures, juxtapositions of actions and of characters, the plot-subplot configuration, reiterative actions and combinations of characters, and asides. Only two of these exemplary plays precede Lr., however. Similarly, though more fully, Reibetanz (1977): Many of the oddities, improbabilities, discontinuities, mixing of genres, the violence, absurdity, and moral simplicity in Lr. are characteristic of other Jacobean plays, by Fletcher, Chapman, Middleton, Marston. Structural features that Lr. shares with other Jacobean plays are the subordination of realism to dramatic effect; the creation of an extreme, self-enclosed play world; the anticipation of theatrical action by abstract statement; an anti-narrative sequence of strong, self-sufficient, disjunctive scenes designed to create momentary effects or dramatic emblems; a wily intriguer who acts as stage-manager to set up scenes; a subplot; an arrangement of characters into moral polarities; a clown.

Fripp (1938, p. 655), however: Never was a great work of art less in touch with its immediate context, or more completely an expression of the artist, than King Lear. We look around in vain for anything that bears the least resemblance to it in contemporary drama, or for any one outside the circle of his fellows and grave, judicious friends, who would entirely understand it. King James and the majority of his courtiers could only regard with astonishment its annihilation of commonplace morality and theology.…This incomparable tragedy [is] the noblest spiritual utterance since La Divina Commedia.

div.head: Shakespeare’s Earlier Plays
div.p: A number of critics find precedents, sometimes called sources, in Sh.’s own earlier plays, for details in Lr., which are therefore said to recall, reproduce, imitate, borrow from, be modeled on, develop, etc. their antecedents, rather than being, e.g., homologues issuing independently from the same mind.

Bradley (1904, p. 245): The soliloquy, This…world [447 ff.], is the very tone of Iago’s discourse on sovereignty of the will [1.3.319 ff. (672 ff.)]. The gulling of Gloster, again, recalls the gulling of Othello. Even Edmund’s idea (not carried out) of making his father witness, without over-hearing, his conversation with Edgar, reproduces the idea of the passage [4.1.74 ff. (2456 ff.)] where Othello watches Iago and Cassio talking about Bianca; and the conclusion of the temptation, where Gloster says to Edmund: [and…capable (1021–3)] reminds us of Othello’s last words in the scene of temptation, Now art thou my lieutenant [3.3.479 (2134)]. Cf. Black (1962) in n. 361–412 Danby (1949, pp. 57–101) traces Edmund’s ancestry far back beyond Iago to earlier Machiavellians: Richard III, the Bastard Falconbridge in Jn., and Hal, Hotspur, and Falstaff in the second Henry trilogy.

Watkins (1942, pp. 3 ff.): Like R2, Lr. is about a king falling from power, ceasing to dominate the action but dominating the play. The emphasis is on character, not action; (p. 4) both kings are self-willed and impetuous, both decline to take friendly advice and make autocratic decisions that lead to calamity, and in downfall both become passive. (P. 6): The slightly sketched and loosely related Aumerle episode in R2 becomes in Lr. a fully developed and integrated subplot to support the action during Lear’s downfall. (P. 7): Whereas York describes Richard’s degradation, Sh. shows Lear degraded in the hovel scene. (P. 9): As in R2, Sh. uses the king’s self-dramatization to characterize him and to give drama to his passivity, especially in the mock-trial. In Lr. as in R2, Sh. uses both psychological realism and symbolical stylization in the opening scene, in Edmund’s soliloquy and scene with his father in 1.2, in Goneril’s and Lear’s quarrel over the hundred knights (1.4), in Lear’s dialogues with his fool in 1.5, in Gloucester’s leap on Dover cliff (4.6), in the characters of the Fool and Goneril, etc.

Muir (ed. 1952, p. xlii): Some details of the mad scenes in Titus Andronicus are repeated in King Lear [citing 2227 and 2558 (the gilded fly), 2534 (archery), 2582 (imaginary petition), and 2619 (I know thee well enough)].…The Aaron-Tamora-Saturninus triangle resembles the later triangle of Edmund-Goneril-Albany; and Aaron has something in common with Edmund. Bate (ed. Tit., 1995, pp. 50, 87): Aaron is a member of an oppressed minority wreaking his revenge on the established powers. (P. 87): Both Aaron and Edmund are witty Marlovian villains, delighting in their villainy. Like Lear, Titus invites his daughter to share old sad stories (see n. 2952).

Mack (1965, pp. 51–5): Sh.’s own previous work is a shaping influence. From the history plays he continues the analysis of authority, the theme of shadow versus substance, the humanity shared by king and peasant, and Riot or Appetite let loose upon the realm by a monarch’s transgressive act (and a subplot to emphasize this theme). From the comedies he repeats Launcelot Gobbo’s fiend at his elbow and meeting with his blind father (like Edgar), Bassanio’s choosing the leaden casket (as France chooses the disowned daughter), Orlando’s victory over Charles (like Edgar’s over Oswald’s), MM’s probing of the relations of justice to power, Ado’s emphasis on self-deception, TN’s theme of wisdom in folly and the wise Fool, AWW’s encounter of the contemptuous courtier (Lafeu) with the foppish courtier (Parolles), like Kent and Oswald, and the resultant triumph of corrupt pliancy over virtue’s steely bones. Markels (1964) finds Lr. and TN strikingly similar in their prominent use of a domestic fool to develop a common theme, the need for domestic order.

Jones (1971, pp. 163 ff.): If we now ask how Shakespeare devised the ground-plan, so to speak, for the work which was to become King Lear,…we must look among some of his earlier plays, since, consciously or not, this is what Shakespeare must have done himself.…Shakespeare’s mind went back to the Henry VI plays which are also concerned, not peripherally this time but centrally, with the division of the kingdom.…[164] [He took] the first movement of Henry VI, Part Two (Acts One to Three [the fall of Duke Humphrey]) as a very general model for the first movement of King Lear and the second movement of Part Three (Acts Three to Five [rival claimants, decisive battle, killing of a beloved child]) as a very general model for his second movement. (P. 165): In particular 3H6 4.6 anticipates Lr. 5.3: Henry compares himself to a happily caged bird (lines 12–15 [2393–5]; cf. Lr. 2949) and offers his government to Warwick and Clarence as Protectors while he remains king in name (lines 24–52 [2405–34]; cf. Lr. 3294–5). (P. 166): Shakespeare’s conception of Lear as a tragic figure is to some extent a combination or re-configuration of two or three tragic figures in his early plays. When Duke Humphrey is baited by his enemies in 2H6 1.3 he (p. 167) leaves the stage in a passion, then returns, as Lr. does in 1.4; in 3.1 Humphrey’s enemies mass themselves against him, as Lear’s do in 2.4.

More importantly, the increasing helplessness of Constance in Jn. and final frenzy of grief for loss of her son anticipate Lear’s career, and (p. 168) in 3.1 and 3.4 her appeal to the concept of need, invocations to the heavens, and lament for her son anticipate Lear’s rhetoric. (P. 169): Moreover, the Bastard Falconbridge is important for King Lear, since his qualities are refracted into two of its characters: his bastardy and perhaps his engaging manner [and his rising progress] are given to Edmund, his loyalty and honest bluntness to Kent. Tit. also provided Shakespeare with a few points for Lear’s own character. Both Titus and Lear are aging fathers, at first passionate in wrath, later passionate in grief; both commit initial acts of folly, and suffer agonizing grief for it; and both go mad. (Jones cites also the verbal and thematic resemblances noted by Harrison, 1964.)

(P. 171): In AYL we have two sets of good and bad brothers, just as in King Lear we have two sets of fathers with good and bad offspring.…Duke Frederick foreshadows Cornwall, Oliver Edmund, and Orlando Edgar. Indeed Orlando’s journey with the aged Adam (ii. vi) comes remarkably close in feeling to Edgar’s more extended journey with the blinded Gloucester. Jones compares Adam with Gloucester, Lear, and Cornwall’s servant. (P. 173): AYL 2.7, in which Orlando meets Duke Senior, marks the point where the two plots [i.e., their respective exiles] converge, and in this function it seems to have formed the model of the great scene on Dover Cliff (iv. vi) in which Lear confronts Gloucester, and speaks of the great stage of fools in a way recalling Jacques’s All the world’s a stage.…The peculiarly comprehensive range of King Lear can be indicated by the fact that Shakespeare drew on romantic comedy as well as tragedy and the history play. Not only As You Like It but Twelfth Night and All’s Well that Ends Well contribute to the fabric of the play.…[174] They each contain a professional Fool and, in their different ways, are much concerned with the topic[s] of folly…and Law and Right.

Jones finds numerous similarities between scenes in early plays and in Lr. (P. 176): The villain Aaron the Moor in Tit. and Edmund have early soliloquies; AWW 2.3 opens with prose dialogue between courtiers, as does Lr. 1.1; both Bertram and Cordelia rebel against their fathers’ arbitrary demands; (p. 177) Helena is her own dower as is Cordelia (see n. 264); (p. 179) in TN Feste proves Olivia a fool (1.5) as the Fool proves Kent and Lear to be fools (1.4), Malvolio and Goneril are opposed to festivities, (p. 180) Malvolio and Lear impotently protest wrongs and threaten revenge; (p. 182) Kent quarrels with Oswald in 2.2 as Lafeu does with Parolles in 2.3, and Kent’s trial and punishment by Cornwall and Regan resembles the sadism of Duke Humphrey’s and Margaret’s punishment of Simpcox in 2H6 2.1. (P. 186): In 3.6 Gloucester urges Kent to carry off the sleeping Lear, as in Jn. 4.3 Falconbridge urges Hubert to carry off the body of Prince Arthur. (P. 189): Goneril gives Edmund a favor in 4.2 as Rosalind gives Orlando a chain in AYL 1.2; a supposed peasant (Edgar) kills the courtier Owald in 4.6 as Walter Whiter the pirate kills Suffolk in 2H6 4.1. (P. 193): Like King John (Jn. 5.7), Lear dies after the defeat of a French invasion, attended by faithful followers.

Lindheim (1974, pp. 169 f.): Lr. translates the central pastoral theme of AYL—the need for pity in an ideal society—from the romantic to the tragic mode. Young (1972, pp. 81–2): Lr. has a curious kinship with As You Like It.…The two plays can be paired by their concern with the nature of Nature. Thus the similarities of detail—the Fool, the banished ruler, the familial divisions, the disguises, the natural setting as mirror to individual dilemmas, the generalizations about the world—are scarcely concidental.…A strong undercurrent in As You Like It…rises to the surface in King Lear…a steady, if secondary, concern with winter wind and bitter sky, with violated vows and benefits forgot, with man’s ingratitude and unregarded age in corners thrown, with the foul body of the infected world, with the strange eventful history that ends in second childishness and mere oblivion.…[82] If As You Like It showed the pastoral doubling back upon itself, Lear shows it turned inside out. Colie (1974, p. 315): Lr. exemplifies hard pastoral, in which a harsh nature is morally educative. McCombie (1980, pp. 68 ff.): Perhaps in a spirit of discovery…Shakespeare set out to write another version of As You Like It.…Both plays are concerned with a casting out into the wilderness of a prince who goes through a process of learning. The [Gloucester] subplot concerns a faithful follower [cf. Sir Rowland] and his sons [cf. Orlando, Oliver, Jaques].…[69] The casting out of Oliver and the seizing of his estates is echoed in the turning of the villains against Gloucester; and Oliver’s recantation [which is not shown in AYL] is a comedy version of Edmund’s puzzled relenting in the face of death. Orlando sees himself as possibly becoming an outcast in quite precisely Poor Tom terms (though he never makes this comparison). The princesses, like Kent, go to liberty not to banishment. Old Adam reappears as the Old Man who leads Gloucester away after he is blinded. (P. 70): Touchstone was the source for the Fool (or perhaps the actor Robert Armin was). There are words in common, and occasional themes (wise folly, ingratitude, time, stoicism, redemption). Responding to Mack’s (1965, p. 65) claim that Lr. alludes to the structure of pastoral romance only to overturn it, producing the greatest anti-pastoral ever penned, Zak (1984, pp. 58 ff.) argues that pastoral conventions and imagery cluster around Cordelia, the Fool, and sometimes Kent, an ideal community better than Lear’s court, who work to restore nature to prelapsarian grace.

Jenkins (1987, pp. 78–9): Kent’s banishment is a more forceful version of that of the loyal servant Alcibiades in Tim. 3.5, which it echoes in many details. See n. 189. Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 168 ff.): It seems to me…likely that Shakespeare abandoned the completion of Timon at the last moment with the realization that he could achieve a much more satisfactory working of its main theme [ingratitude] in a new play, than that having achieved his greatest play he would want to go over similar ground again, only to find he’d made a mess of it. (P. 174): The satiric role is assigned to the Fool. Timon’s anger at the world (and Apemantus) in 4.3 is transformed into Lear’s anger on the verge of madness in 3.4. (P. 187): Lr. gives its protagonist a greatness lacking in Tim., basing it on King James’s ideas of kingly greatness, including (p. 195) the propriety of anger. (P. 197): The fall of Timon in one sketchy third act is developed in almost two acts (1.2–2.4) in Lr., making the tormentors next of kin. (P. 203): Timon’s misfortunes convert him into the stereotype of the raging satirist as he sees the perversity of mankind in terms of other people. Lear’s response is to look inward, to attempt to adjust to the vision of disorder his experience of suffering has presented.…The attempt…at first proves too much for him. His mind loses its hold on reality and his mad fantasies take just those forms of blind condemnation of mankind that Timon asks us to accept as a vision of reality.…[204] When Lear is fully restored to his sanity it is to meet yet again with defeat.…[205] As an exercise, like Timon, in the anatomy of anger as a response to a wicked world, it [the play] absorbs the role of the satirist into the tragic vision of man’s helpless vulnerability.…[206] His greatest achievement, King Lear,…was built on the ruins of the scourging satire of Timon, which, even with Middleton’s help, was beyond the range of Shakespeare’s humane vision.

Teague (1992, pp. 88 ff.): Lr. 1.2 echoes JC 1.3: Characters read false letters truly and true portents falsely. Edmund seduces his father into acting against Edgar, and Cassius seduces Brutus into acting against Caesar; both plays use fraudulent letters; both plays refer to ominous prodigies of nature; and in both plays the seducer is skeptical about the meaning of natural portents.…Brutus fails to recognize his friend’s hand, Gloucester does not read his son’s character, Cassius and Edgar refuse to read the portents that fill their worlds.…[92] Omitted in the sources, the false letters, the window of the closet, the betrayal of one man by another close to him are all elements of the stage motif found in Julius Caesar. Unlike Hamlet’s false commission that destroys Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, or (p. 93) the letter that gulls Malvolio, only Lr. and JC include portents of nature and a skeptic who sneers at them. (P. 96): Lr.’s eclipses are missing from the Arcadia’s story of the Paphlagonian king. (P. 99): Edgar is a Christian stoic in a pagan world; his stoicism may derive from Shakespeare’s Brutus.

Mueller (1994, pp. 200–1): AYL: As Duke Senior arrives through man’s ingratitude at court at insight (complacent and sentimental reflections on court and country), Lear rages at ingrateful man; AYL is a restoration fantasy and hence is an anti-Lear since Lear’s daughter cannot restore him. In AYL the chidren (Rosalind, Orlando) of two friends (Sir Rowland, Senior) marry; in Lr. the counselor’s son (Edmund) meddles disastrously with the king’s daughters.

An actor (and playwright) in Sh.’s company has also been named a source for qualities of Lear’s Fool and of the play generally. Robert Armin (ca. 1568–1615) seems to have joined the Chamberlain’s Men in 1600 (see Knowles, ed. AYL, 1977, pp. 374–7), replacing William Kempe as their chief comic actor. The idea that Sh. shaped parts, especially of his fools and jesters, in order to capitalize on Armin’s special talents and knowledge has been widely embraced. Besides acting in clown parts for almost a decade before coming to the Chamberlain’s company, Armin was to show his knowledge of fools and fooling in his play Two Maids of More-Clacke (1607–8); his Quips upon Questions (1601), a collection of satirical answers in impromptu rhyme to questions from an audience; and his Foole upon Foole (1600; enl. 1609 as A Nest of Ninnies), containing brief biographies and jests about famous British fools. The changed nature of Sh.’s clowns from Touchstone onwards has been attributed both to Armin’s expertise and his intellectual style of clowning.

Baldwin (1924, pp. 454–5): Join together in one man the qualities displayed in Foole Vpon Foole and Quips, filter out the realistic impurities through the imagination of Shakespeare, and you have the wise fool Touchstone. Let the resultant mixture mellow for a few years while [455] Shakespeare on closer acquaintance learns the true wisdom that underlies this man’s outer folly and you have the foolishly wise Jester of King Lear. Idem (1927, pp. 241–5): Kemp’s successor, Armin, is almost immediately reflected in the plays by the jesters Touchstone and Feste, to whom may be added the Fools of Timon and Lear.…[244] The clown changes into the sly, roguish, jesting fool of the court…from the pompous, countrified, blundering clown of Kemp.…This change in fools is not surprising when we [245] remember that Armin had evidently made a special study of these naturals.

Gray (1927, pp. 681 ff.): Here, then, was a man of rare character—the eternal clown who hid his wisdom and his charity behind a veil of mirth.…Here, too, was an actor, with a special line of acting—the natural and the crack-brained jester—the fruit of study and observation in real [682] life. No wonder that Shakspeare, who also studied and observed real life, grew interested in Armine and allowed him the fullest self-expression in his plays.…[684] In King Lear we run into a pretty problem of Armine’s influence on Shakespeare, for here is Armine’s own humour of madness run riot, and for no good reason, so far as the authority of the old play of King Leir is concerned. For Armine he constructs the character of the faithful fool.…[685] As Armine went across Moor Fields to the Curtain he must often have passed the famous Bethlehem Hospital. With his interest in the madmen of this world, he must often have noticed in the villages around London, the Bedlam Beggars.…Shakespeare was quite capable of studying such characters for himself, but…Armine, for whom they held an even greater interest, may have drawn the poet’s attention to them and may have helped him in filling in the picture.

Henderson (1939, p. 224): Like enough, Armin sometime put a definite question to Shakspere as to why he, the virtual creator of Feste and Touchstone, was being neglected in the new plays, Hamlet, Othello, and Macbeth (unless this last follows Lear, as some think).

Parrott (1949, p. 301): After the somewhat shabby way in which he had treated Armin in the allocation of parts in Othello, Shakespeare certainly owed his fellow-actor something and he paid the debt with interest by creating for him the part of the Fool in Lear.

Goldsmith (1955, pp. 60 ff.): Shakespeare went not to history but to the popular and literary tradition (or to Armin, which was the same thing) for the stuff of which he created Feste and Lear’s Fool.…[67] Lear’s Fool, however, transcends his fellows in the quality of his wisdom. He is the supremely wise fool who expresses in his heartfelt devotion to Cordelia and to his king the Christian virtues of patience, humility, and love.

Coghill (1959, pp. 6, 14): It was Armin who made this [new kind of fool] possible. Not his book, but himself, as an actor; for him, through him, Shakespeare created the witty Fool, the singing Fool, the fey, the tragic Fool.…[14] The Fool’s crazy versicles, riddles and proverbs sting Lear inwardly, and therefore give an I could have told you so satisfaction to an audience.…The second great thing he does for us is to make visible the charity of Lear.

Felver (1961, pp. 31, 59, 61): Robert Armin…originated a new style of witty, songful, intellectual, and socially mobile clowning.…[59] [In Lr.] Shakespeare develops the apothegmatic wisdom of the fool and his paradoxical reflection on the general dilemma of mankind to its highest dramatic achievement.…The Fool brings out tellingly…the saving grace of laughter.…[61] The daring of Shakespeare and Armin in creating the first and only high tragedy fool has been amply rewarded by…250 years of critical praise.

Bradbrook (1969, pp. 53 ff.): Armin enriched and changed the clowning tradition with rapid and nimble shifts of posture, acceptance of contradiction, flirts and fidgets of wit.…[69] A shrewd ironic professional, but also a little cracked, the fool bears an instinctive knowlege of Lear’s misery and remorse.…[70] In Armin’s own play, Touch is turned out of service for fidelity to his young mistress and is threatened with hanging as well as whipping.

Kinney (1976, p. 693): Now in his darker Jacobean days Shakespeare may have in mind his troupe’s new and more serious clown Robert Armin and he may be thinking too of Archy Armstrong, the fool to King James who could in his stinging barbs bring that royal personage to tears.

Somerset (1984, pp. 69 ff.) demurs: Many recent treatments of Armin are overstated and tend to focus our attention upon the actor rather than upon the mature experimenting dramatist.…[73] If Touchstone, Feste and company display Armin’s special and successful line which won audiences’ favour, why, we may ask, is this company of wise fools so small in Shakespeare’s plays?…Why are there only two other singing fools [besides Feste]?…[74] From the company’s whole repertory one gains an impression of the range and adaptability of Armin’s talents rather than a limited line.…Armin’s fools [in Foole upon Foole] are not the source for Shakespeare’s fool characters, except as Armin records a common tradition which the two authors share [quoting that work’s ed., H. F. Lippincott, Salzburg, 1973, p. 24].…[80] The reasons Shakespeare created a great stage of fools between 1599 and 1607, culminating in his unique inclusion of the fool in tragedy, are to be found in the parts themselves.…[81] Shakespeare’s fools differ widely in their attitudes to comic or tragic inadequacy, comic or tragic suffering.…The actor called upon to play these five parts…should be celebrated for his astonishing range and variety, not for his comic line. Skura (1993, p. 74) agrees: Armin seems rather to have been limited to creating ordinary clowns (and to have been fascinated by unwise, natural fools) until he collaborated with Shakespeare. Accepting Wiles’s (1987, pp. 139, 147) imaginary description of Armin’s physique, she goes on, Instead, it may have been Armin’s Richard [III]-like physique—squat, ugly, doglike—and his gift for projecting multiple identities that inspired Shakespeare to create the series of creatures occupying the same theatrical space that he had first staked out for Richard. For accounts of the roles of fools in medieval and renaissance society, and the relation of Lear’s Fool to them, see Welsford (1935, pp. 253 ff., 270), Lothian (1949, p. 7), and Wiles (op. cit.).

div.head: Classical Greek and Latin
div.p: Kranz (1938, pp. 36–8): The element of classical antiquity is partly present in Lr. because of its many allusions: Theban (i.e., Oedipus), Athenian, Ajax, Ixion, Centaurs, and such classical ideas as the opposition of custom and nature, life as a pawn or as something usurped, man as a microcosm, nothing as coming from nothing (Lucretius). More importantly, here we have as if a Senecan or Aeschylean tragedy, in which the world of the gods extends into that of men. (P. 37): The gods in Lr. are plural. Jupiter, Juno, and Apollo are named, so are Nature, the sun, Hecate, the stars, and Fortune, and are often invoked in classical forms, as in Seneca’s Oed. 248 ff. (cf. the curse on Cordelia, invoking several gods), or the imprecations for fulfilled wishes in Horace, Carm. 3.18. (P. 38): The eternal mystery of the way of the world and its justice or injustice is touched on often in Lr. in allusions to the gods’ being almighty, indiscernible, just punishers of sin, players with men’s fates, etc. Horace is referred to in nn. 1921–2, 1936, 2037, 2536.

Smith (ed. 1902, p. xxv, n. 2): The Oedipus Coloneus of Sophocles offers a remarkable comparison with King Lear. Oedipus, too, is a man more sinned against than sinning (see note, [1712–13]), but he has learned patience and self-control and has a strength of character wanting in the aged Lear. His curse on Polynices is even more terrible than Lear’s on Goneril, because it is deliberate, and does not spring from a passionate desire for revenge, and Antigone is his Cordelia. Wolff (1912, pp. 312–13, 366): Heliodorus’s story of Calasiris and his sons affected Sh. via Sidney; Sh. deliberately chose this descendant of the story of Oedipus as a foil to the story of that other Oedipus, King Lear. Many critics compare Lr. with Sophocles’s plays about Oedipus without actually suggesting that Sh. knew Sophocles, who is referred to in nn. 306, 1712–13, 1936, 2181–2, 2204–5, 2473–9.

Butler (1986, pp. 515): Cynic influence [of Diogenes and his follower Crates] is pervasive throughout the play. He shows no direct influence, however, and his evidence is mainly commonplaces, especially apophthegms of Erasmus. See nn. 1564–71, 1882–8, 1932, 1936, 2530, 2597–8.

Simrock (1850, pp. 124–5): The behaviour of the two elder daughters, and their liaison with Edmund, remind us of the two daughters of Servius Tullius; of whom the good one was married to the wicked Tarquinius, and the wicked one [125] to the good brother, until the good husband and wife were removed, and the bad came together. This resemblance is most striking in the relation of Goneril to Albany. He is the good Tarquin who has married the wicked Tullia; but she wishes to remove him out of the way, not for the sake of the wicked husband of her sister, but for the more wicked Edmund. The relation of Livy may not have been unknown to the poet.

Beginning with Brandl (1894, p. 177; 1922, p. 372), many find influences of Seneca’s Hercules Furens and others of his plays, known to Shakespeare either in the Latin or in the translations of Jasper Heywood and others (1559–66; 1581). References to Seneca occur in nn. 116–18, 117, 152, 773, 850, 912, 1242–3, 1448–51, 1564–71, 1578–86, 1580–2, 1656–64, 1659, 1936, 2056+7, 2133, 2181–2, 2480, 2620–2, 2735–9, 2795–6, 2801, 2946, 3154, 3298–9. Though Pratt (1983, p. iv) thinks it unprofitable to seek Senecan sources for Lr., he notes that in Seneca (as in Sh.) moral order in nature is threatened by the chaos of man’s nature led by passion. Miola (1992, pp. 143–74): Lear thunders in Senecan style and echoes Hercules Furens. King Lear is a tragedy of furor (or in Thomas Nash’s [sic] phrase, a Tragedy of Wrath) in [144] which Hercules Furens serves as a model.…Like all tragedies of wrath, King Lear contains elements of both revenge and tyrant tragedies.…The madness of the revenger appears in the old king’s inspired insanity as well as in Edgar’s.…The emphasis falls…on the tyrannical character—a huge and dominating creation driven by great passions, tormented by the infernal kingdom within. As in Seneca, tyrannical rhetoric, grand, expansive, and hyperbolic, expresses a personal rather than a political will to power.…[149] The transformation of nuntius into moral agent…comes to fulfilment in the person of Edgar [who is a major named character, not a nuntius].…[151] Ira is the archetypal Senecan passion.…[152] And yet, unlike Seneca’s plays…, King Lear does not feature a wrath that aims towards scelus, a crime.…Instead, Lear rages titanically and aimlessly at his daughters and his world…in thunderous rhetoric.…[160] Shakespeare reverts to the model of Hercules Furens to express a climactic moment of tragic passion and experience.…Both Hercules and Lear cry out for justice and revenge, employing an expansive rhetoric that relates human action to cosmic events and divine forces. Calling upon thunder and lightning, each locates the suffering self in the center of the universe, and dares the supernatural to destroy it. Onlookers, Amphitryon and the Fool, try to curb the surging emotion and counsel prudent self-preservation.…[161] In contrast [to Hercules’ wish for punishment and suicide], Lear’s outcry begins by expressing a desire for self-destruction but modulates to a wish for universal annihilation.…[163] Lear becomes a reluctant Senecan hero, a figure whose furor, despite his will, creates for him a new and powerful identity.…[165] Both Hercules and Lear fall into a deep restorative slumber in the presence of several sympathetic attendants.…Upon waking, Hercules asks confused questions about his location.…[167] Both Hercules and Lear understand that they have committed crimes against their own children…[and each] offers to commit suicide.…[168] Lear’s awakening reactions and his acceptance of guilt contrast sharply with the grand furor of Seneca’s Hercules.…He speaks a language of humility and contrition.…To Senecan tragedy, which so often centres on Kindermord, Shakespeare pointedly opposes an antitypal scene which features a romance reunion instead of tragic separation, before (p. 169) a final anguished furor different from Hercules’ stoic calm. (P. 173): In King Lear Shakespeare confronts and solves the dramatic problem of creating a sympathetic Senecan protagonist.

There are a few critical references to Plautus and Terence; see nn. 463, 960, 2020–1, 2221–2, 2545–7. Miola (1994, pp. 172–3, 188 ff.): Shakespeare’s most complex adaptations of New Comedy, though largely unremarked, appear in Hamlet and King Lear. In these plays New Comedy consists of inherited traditions and conventions, not specific source texts. Shakespeare’s long experience with Plautus and Terence colours and modifies his appropriation of the other sources. New Comedy shapes the secondary characters and subordinate plot lines—Polonius, Ophelia, Laertes, Gloucester, Edmund, and Edgar. Moreover, both Ophelia and Cordelia appear as Italianate versions of the New Comedic virgo, problematized. And even the main characters themselves, reprising a dazzling vari[173]ety of generic and theatrical possibilities, at times wear New Comedic masks and enact New Comedic roles: Hamlet plays eiron, Lear, the misanthropus. (P. 188): Lr. reveals analogues with New Comedy, the plays of Plautus and Terence as understood and analysed by humanistic commentary. The opening scene presents scraps and traces of New Comedic motifs—the past indiscretion of the father, the present casual, even nostalgic, acknowledgement, the illegitimate child now returned. The subsequent scheming of a son against a father for money (or in this case land) is archetypal, though here Edmund will play both adulescens and callidus servus. Like Plautine intriguers, and unlike the alleged [189] source figures, Sidney’s Plexirtus and the Iberian stepmother, Edmund speaks in soliloquy and aside, relies on wit, on his ability to fashion fit ([504]), congratulates himself on the easy riding of his practices ([502]), improvises to take advantage of occasions like Cornwall’s arrival (ii. i.). The use of a forged letter for deception…is a well-attested Plautine device.…The duel with Edgar…bears interesting similarities to…[that which] Davos stages in Andria, a standard grammar school text. In order to deceive the eavesdropping senex, the clever servant invents a quarrel with Mysis, who co-operates in the deceit but does not understand it.…[190] [Gloucester’s] recognition [in 2.1] parodies the New Comedic discovery of offspring, as this senex entirely confuses his legitimate and illegitimate sons.…Edmund early on achieves the comedic goals of land and legitimized [334] identity, but he does not rest with these achievements. Instead, he enacts literally the stock jokes of sons against fathers, attempting to realize in fact the comedic wish for paternal death.…Edgar protects himself from the dangers threatening him by use of three comedic devices that are absent from the source tale in Sidney’s Arcadia—disguise, feigned madness, the gulling of his father. The first is a ubiquitous feature of classical plays and their descendants.…[191] Feigned madness…has a specific precedent in Plautus’ Menaechmi (830 ff.).…Deceiving his father at Dover Cliff, Edgar replays inventively the familiar gulling of the senex by fast talk and disguise.…[192] Lear plays in a more specific New Comedy configuration—the familiar senex iratus blocking a marriage—though those ancient fathers generally interfere with the amours of their sons, not daughters.…The variation closest to Lear occurs in Aulularia: here the miser Euclio refuses to offer any dowry for his daughter; the suitor, Megadorus, responds…(238–9), Don’t. As long as the girl has good manners, she has dowry enough. [Fn.: Plautine commentators identified the response as gnomic, citing parallels from Plautus, Horace, Menander, and Antipater, Opera (1577), 161.]…[193] Shakespeare departs from the chronicles and Leir to recast the action into a familiar comedic configuration—the lock-out [in 2.4; cf. Menaechmi 698].…[195] Angry withdrawal and fulminating misanthropy characterize the comedic idiotes—self-important, isolated, inflexible, anti-festive, and ridiculous.…The traditional idiotes has a curious but consistent relationship with a clown, in this case, a fool.…[196] Throughout the play Cordelia exhibits the luminous spirituality of that comedic and redemptive figure [the woman as wonder from the commedia erudita].…The surging joy of their [i.e., Lear and Cordelia’s] reunion…[197] reifies in a startling way the conventional rhetoric of New Comedic reunions [cf. Poenulus 1262–70, Rudens 1172–4].…The death of Cordelia represents Shakespeare’s final, most profound, and most moving inversion of New Comedy.…[200] In one appalling moment comedic chance becomes tragic tyche.…[201] Shakespeare’s bold inversion of New Comedic practices and expectations greatly augments Lear’s power to shock and disturb. (For critics who have seen generic comedic structures, characters, and themes in Lr. see .)
Burnett (1997, p. 83) traces Kent to the clever and faithful servants of Roman comedy.

Following especially Hardison (1975) and Bate (1993), Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 107): It is not implausible that Shakespeare was affected by his knowledge of Ovid in writing King Lear, in the idea of metamorphosis or shape-shifting, in the imagery of people behaving like monsters, and in his allusions to centaurs and the myth of Ixion. See particular references to Ovid in nn. 116–18, 124, 436–41, 773, 823, 1202, 1350–7, 1580–2, 1933, 2181–2, 2516, 2518, 2567, 2775+2, 2795–6, 3217, 3224–5, 3287.

div.head: The Bible
div.p: Possible allusions to passages in the Bible, which Sh. probably knew in the Geneva translation of 1560, are indicated throughout the notes. Personages and incidents in a few books have seemed analogous to Lear and his experience, and critics often assume that one or another of these biblical analogues was in Sh.’s mind as he wrote this play, influencing its composition and its meaning.

div.head: Job
div.p: Though Lear is not notably patient, many compare his endurance of manifold sufferings to a biblical antecedent. Knight (1930, p. 191): The old Hebrew problem is restated: Lear is analogous to The Book of Job. Holloway (1961, pp. 85–9) finds general parallels with Job’s patience, affliction by storms, forsaking by family and servants, and the tragic ending: (p. 88) The materials exist for a more conventional and less protracted tragedy which could have ended well before the beginning of Act V. If we ask what extends the play further, the Book of Job reveals the answer. Similarly McCann (ed. 1964, p. xii): Job has his Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar; and Lear has his Fool and Edgar [Kent?]. Like Job, Lear is driven to question the very justice of God. As Job is humbled by God’s speaking out of the tempest, so Lear is humbled by exposure to the pelting of the pitiless storm. Job was a brother to dragons and a companion to owls; Lear chooses to become a comrade of the wolf and the owl. Job cries, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither, Lear observes, [1882–8]. In the end, Job is restored to reason, having probed the mysteries of suffering. But for Lear…there is no comfort and acceptance. Kott (1961; 1964, pp. 147, 153): From the middle of Act II to the end of Act IV, Shakespeare takes up a Biblical theme. But this new Book of Job…[has] neither Christian Heaven, nor the heaven predicted and believed in by humanists. King Lear makes a tragic mockery of all eschatologies.…[153] It is Job’s stage that constitutes the main scene. On it the ironic, clownish morality play on human fate will be performed. Nevo (1972, p. 261): The play is a Shakespearean version of the Book of Job.…Like Job, Lear takes his initial prosperity as a sign of heavenly favor; like Job in affliction, he calls the heavens themselves to heavenly account. Like Job, though he die for it, he will affirm his own conviction of what injustice is. Like Job, his natural egotism reaches beyond itself to embrace a universe of suffering creatures.…Like Job, he refuses to compromise with pain and with evil; refuses to surrender to the plot of optimistic quietism. Bloom (1987, p. 2): Shakespeare intended his audience to see Job as the model for Lear’s situation in the middle of the play, though he is unlike Job in its earlier and later parts. Fisch (1999, pp. 125–6): The hero testifies in his moral history to the force of the Job archetype but he dies in fulfilment of the laws of tragedy.…[126] What we have at the end of Lear is something different—a Promethean defiance, an assertion of Lear’s undiminished royalty.…Lear does not end in Christian fashion; he ends with a gesture of pride and defiance, which is the ironic achievement of ancient tragedy. In the subplot, Gloucester and Edgar are more consistently Joban, not Titan; the double plot (p. 132) exhibits…the opposition between the Hebraic pattern of the pilgrimage and the pattern of inevitable doom which belongs to the Hellenic mode of tragedy. Further possible parallels with the Job story are discussed by Milward (1969–70), and apparent echoes of particular passages in the Book of Job are listed by Colie (1974, pp. 128–31) and Milward (1987, pp. 158 ff.). For these and others see nn. 256–7, 306, 749, 773, 842, 1233, 1503–4, 1517, 1584, 1622+5, 1669–79, 1689, 1702–12, 1882–8, 2043, 2200, 2217, 2302, 3216, 3279.

div.head: Nebuchadnezzar
div.p: Mack (1965, p. 50), pursuing the archetype of the fallen king, finds an analogue in Nebuchadnezzar (see ). So does Battenhouse (1969, p. 297): Typologically, Lear may be said to resemble the Nebuchadnezzar of Daniel 4, who was driven from among men to eat grass like an ox until his reason returned and he learned to bless. Bryant (1977, pp. 27–8): The archetype [for Lear] is the mad Nebuchadnezzar, well known in popular art and literature, as well as much glossed in the mediaeval commentaries.…Nebuchadnezzar was noted for the sins of furor madness and superbia pride.…For his pride Nebuchadnezzar is driven from his kingdom to dwell among the beasts of the field until he has learn’d who he is in the sight of God.…Nebuchadnezzar ate grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven… (Dan. 4:33). Living with animals is, to Richard of St Victor, a clear symbol of Nebuchadnezzar’s forsaking the ways of reason. Daniel tells how Nebuchadnezzar’s reason returns to him, when he lifts his eyes to heaven (Dan. 4:34). The pattern here [in Lr.] is Nebuchadnezzar’s fall, penance, and restoration. Hoeniger (1992, p. 330): Like Lear, Nebuchadnezzar was punished with madness after casting Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into the fiery furnace.

div.head: Other Old Testament Figures and Events
div.p: Traver (1934, pp. 181–5) finds remote parallels of phrase and idea to Isaiah. Danby (1952, pp. 108–27) reads Lr. as a play about Christian patience, citing the biblical examples of Job, Tobias (whom God deprived of his sight, that he might try his patience), and David (pursued by his son Absolom). Enlarging on essays of 1957 and 1965, Battenhouse (1969, pp. 271–2) finds typological links with Genesis: the general curse refers to Adam and Eve (as Danby, p. 125) suggested; Edmund’s envy is Cain’s; the storm is the Flood; Lear’s mad talk is the Tower of Babel. Fisch (1987, pp. 49–50; 1999, pp. 137–42): The relations among Gloucester and his sons are like those of Isaac, Jacob, and Esau in Gen. 27–8. Blind Isaac touches and blesses his disguised and unrecognized good son Jacob, against whom Esau has murderous designs. Jacob becomes a penniless wanderer before final reconciliation with Esau.

div.head: The Prodigal
div.p: Battenhouse (1957, pp. 85–6), describing the facts of the play metaphorically: The play’s hero is analogous to the prodigal son [Luke 15:11–31]. He wastes his portion on harlots (which Goneril and Regan literally are in the play) and riotous living, until he is driven to eating husks with swine (as Lear does in feeding on empty memories in his hovel on the heath)…. The father who comes out to meet and embrace him is, paradoxically, a daughter, Cordelia, who alludes to the Prodigal in 4.7. [Neither daughter is literally a harlot, certainly not towards Lear; towards a different character, Edmund, who swears love to both (2902), Regan is a lusty widow seeking marriage, Goneril a wife whose adultery and husband-murder remain only wishes upon the way (2282). Lear does not ever engage in riotous living, nor spend a moment in a hovel, nor feed himself on memories (though old injustices rankle), and Cordelia does not receive him as a sinful child but as a parent and wronged old man.] Snyder (1966): Cordelia’s description of Lear in 2787, hoveling with swine, recalls the parable. (P. 362): Shakespeare found in his sources [for Lr.] a story resembling in its broad outlines that of the Prodigal Son: the protagonist starts by rejecting the one who loves him most, embarks on a reckless course which brings him eventually to suffering and want—and, paradoxically, to the self-knowledge he lacked before—and finally [363] is received and forgiven by the rejected one.…In both cases the reconciliation is presented explicitly in terms of rebirth: Lear is, in his own description, taken from the grave ([2794]); while the Prodigal’s father rejoices that this my sonne was dead, and is alive againe (v.24). Other points of contact are the references to rags and nakedness throughout the play, the reported riotousness of the knights (projections of Lear), and the presentation of Lear as a child. This biblical model also is echoed in the subplot: Gloucester also must find self-knowledge in adversity, must die symbolically before he emerges into a new state of love and acceptance; the fabricated impatience of Edgar for his patrimony is like the Prodigal’s, and in the role of Poor Tom, Edgar confesses a debauched past like the Prodigal’s. (P. 368): The importance of human love, the inadequacy of human justice, the vision of Lear as a child humbled and instructed by a tragic world—all these, like most of the incidental parallels of the Prodigal Son parable, are Shakespeare’s [369] own contributions to the Lear legend. The idea that Lear is the Prodigal, who goes wandering, not so much from his home as from his right wits, and that Cordelia takes the place of the father who receives him back from his riotous course, is offered also by Milward (1970, pp. 177–8; 1973, p. 100).

div.head: Apocalypse
div.p: Holloway (1961, pp. 75–80): The king’s end is like the end of the world: not the Day of Judgement, but the universal cataclysm which was to precede it. Twice…the idea is mentioned explicitly [2577–8, 3224].…For the Elizabethans, the End of the World was a living conviction and even something of a current fear, quoting Hooker, Donne, Burton, and others. Mack (1965, pp. 85–6): In the scenes on the heath, the elements are at war as if it were indeed Armageddon. When Lear awakes with Cordelia at his side, he imagines that already apocalypse is past, she is a soul in bliss, he bound upon a wheel of fire. Appearing in the last act with Cordelia dead in his arms, he wonders that those around him do not crack [86] heaven’s vault with their grief, and they wonder in turn if the pietà they behold is the promis’d end or image of that horror. These are but some of the overt allusions. Under them everywhere run tides of doomsday passion that seem to use up and wear away people, codes, expectations, all stable points of reference, till only a profound sense remains that an epoch, in fact a whole dispensation, has forever closed. Lascelles (1973, pp. 73 ff.): The passion of fear evoked throughout the play is partly owing to a visual allusion: the Doomsday paintings, especially those over the chancel arch in so many English churches,…established in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. In these, (p. 75) Christ sits in judgment at the apex; at the bottom, the blessed are led to a heavenly gate and the lost towards a hell mouth, marshalled by fiends, and then tormented, while other souls emerge from their graves. The souls are almost always naked. The paintings represent the Athanasian Creed and Matt. 24 and 25. Allusions to Doomsday recur through Lr.: e.g., 1706, 2794–7, 3224–5. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974) downplays Job and emphasizes Revelation, with its ideas of apocalypse. Wittreich’s (1984) study of apocalyptic and other prophetic strands in Lr. emphasizes particularly the influence of the Book of Revelation. For the influence of descriptions of the apocalypse in Matt. 24, Mark 13, Luke 21, and Rev. 16, see nn. 433–44, 440–1, 441–2, 1584, 2133, 3224–5.

div.head: Biblical Influence Generally
div.p: Milward (1973, passim) finds numerous parallels in Elizabethan homilies and sermons, generally Christian commonplaces of Biblical origin. Colie (1974, p. 122): In the play, biblical echoes recur, largely to Old Testament and apocryphal moral books: to the patience of Job, the endurance enjoined in Ecclesiastes and Psalter, to the experienced consideration of Ecclesiasticus and the Book of Wisdom, as well as to such New Testament themes as the charity of the Gospels and of Paul.…Upon the political parts of King Lear, Proverbs offers an almost constant gloss; similarly, many verses from Job, Ecclesiastes, and Wisdom speak to the private moral and psychological problems of Lear and his friends, deepened now and then by echoes from Mark and the Epistles. Coursen (1976, p. 285): Lear’s struggle back to Cordelia…is a journey to a truth that has its analogue, among others (Job, Jonah, the Prodigal Son, the Wandering Jew) in the journey of the Magi. (P. 290): Lear’s reawakening in 4.7 is like the raising of Lazarus, and his kneeling to Cordelia is like the kneeling of the Magi. Such analogues lend deeper emotional impact. Guilfoyle (1989; 1990, pp. 111–127) finds Christian analogy and imagery throughout Lr. (P. 112): In the opening scene and at intervals up to the middle of Act III there are Old Testament analogies with the Creation disaster and the Creator’s wrath and disillusion with his Creation.…From [2042] to [2526], Lear is absent from the stage while Gloucester is the central figure in two powerful New Testament evocations, with scenic forms from the blindfolding and buffeting of Christ as well as the temptation by Satan.…At the end of the play the images of the Grail story and of the cycle plays come together in an icon of the Deposition from the Cross. Guilfoyle adduces many analogies from the Bible and the cycle plays, recognizing medieval scenic form and Christian typology in Lr.

Countless allusions to particular biblical passages, detected by Carter (1905), Noble (1935), Colie (1974), Milward (1987), Shaheen (1987), and many others, are recorded in the commentary notes. They are listed in the index.

div.head: Medieval and Renaissance Writers
div.p: The most important medieval influence on Lr. is of course Geoffrey of Monmouth; see .

Siegel (1955, pp. 325–36): Boethius’s (5th c.) De Consolatione Philosophiae taught the value of adversity, which was directed by divine providence (a stoic idea). The idea was repeated by fathers of the church, Christian humanist followers, and circulated in Sh.’s time in such writers as Thomas Elyot, Thomas More, Pierre de la Primaudaye, Coverdale, Bacon, and others. Presson (1965, pp. 423–4): The ethical and metaphysical foundations of [Boethius’s] De Consolatione and [424] King Lear are remarkably similar, but many of the answers that satisfied Boethius no longer satisfy Shakespeare.…Pessimism…takes the place of optimism; wonderment replaces certainty; questions are substituted for affirmation.

Guilfoyle (1987; 1990, pp. 97–109) suspects that references to Dover, Salisbury, possibly Lipsbury, Merlin, Camelot, the Dragon, etc. are all intentional, intended (p. 109) to color the Lear story with reminiscences of Christ’s supreme sacrifice and of the legendary figure [Joseph of Arimathea] who brought the blood of that sacrifice to Britain in the Holy Grail and thus provided the basis for the Arthurian legends. She notes that in FQ 2.10, the canto in which the Lear story appears, there is reference (st. 53) to Joseph and the Grail, and that 10 stanzas later is a reference to Uther Pendragon, father of the prince Arthur who is Spenser’s hero. In a similar vein (1987, pp. 215 ff.) she finds analogies with Malory: Arthur leads an army from France and lands at Dover to confront a would-be usurper of his throne, Mordred; (p. 216) both Arthur and Cordelia appear at times as Christ-figures; Mordred, like Edmund, is a bastard and the King’s son. (P. 218): Igraine is a near anagram of Regan. In Malory, characters in the wilderness run mad, but like Lear may emerge as changed men. Dover takes on a mystic dimension with Christian overtones. Lear carrying Cordelia prefigures the Arthurian legends of finding the Holy Grail.
Thompson (1978, pp. 71–2, 81–2) finds only two certain links to Chaucer, in the Monk’s Tale’s description of Nero as a fisherman, and in the apocryphal Merlin’s Prophecy; see nn. 2004–5, 1735.

Goldsmith (1955) traces many popular and literary sources of the tradition of the wise fool, Erasmus’s Praise of Folly (1509) being one. Like most critics who describe Lear’s Fool and Sh.’s outlook as Erasmian, he stops short of claiming that Sh. had read Erasmus or was directly influenced by him. Indeed, (p. 98) It is not even certain that [the Fool] is the focal center of one of the play’s important ideas—the wisdom of seeming folly. Edgar, though he wears no motley, probably comes as close as the Fool does to Erasmus’ conception of the wise fool—one of those simple souls with whom God peoples the Kingdom of Heaven. Kaiser (1963, p. 99): Erasmus’s Folly prefigures Shakespeare’s greatest fool in her humanity, her optimistic faith in human nature and her realistic acceptance of the vicissitudes of mankind.…[Sh.’s] debt to Erasmus may well have been enormous, a statement given no further support. Reibetanz (1977, pp. 94 ff.), similarly: Sh. was familiar with the tradition, on stage and off, of moriae encomium, of which Erasmus’s The Praise of Folly (1509) was the best-known example. Cordelia imprudently speaks the truth and comes close to being the archetypal Christian fool described by St. Paul and Erasmus. So do Kent and Edgar. (P. 100): Most of the Fool’s traditional topoi and witticisms come in I.iv, and in fact that scene gives rise to a sustained moriae encomium. The play as a whole presents a great stage of fools. Edmund, Goneril, Regan, and Oswald are fools whose worldly villainy undoes them. Lear and Gloucester exhibit and come to recognize enormous folly; Albany is a virtuous fool. But Sh. (p. 106) breaks out of the controlling vision of the moriae encomium, for Erasmus’ and similar satires are based on the premise that diying to this worlde is the beginnyng of a better life.…Shakespeare leaves us with no such comforting assurance, and so he checks Folly’s ultimately unperturbed laughter. Evans’s (1990) study in Humanist Intertextuality asserts Erasmus’s influence on the play but shows none in particular. Sh. in Lr. used both the secular and the Christian folly themes: the former more obvious in the beginning of the play—the destructive folly of self-love, pride, and anger—and the latter at the end, after Lear has traversed the dark kingdom of madness and found new life in the redemptive folly of Cordelia, a Christ-figure. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 105–6): The Pauline paradoxes about wisdom appearing to be folly and vice versa animate Erasmus’s Praise of Folly, which Shakespeare may have known either in the Latin or in Sir Thomas Chaloner’s translation (1549, reissued in 1577).…[106] The play’s ironic reversals and paradoxes seem to recuperate something of the spirit of Erasmus and Montaigne. Bate (2000, pp. 29, 31): True wisdom comes not in Gloucester’s and Edgar’s words of Stoic comfort or Albany’s hapless faith in divine providence, but in moments of folly and love…[31] those essentials of the Erasmian and Montaignian—that is to say the counter-Renaissance—Christian vision.…The Shakespeare who wrote King Lear…was not a historian. He was not a philosopher. He was a foolosopher. Butler (1986, pp. 511 ff.) shows the applicability of some of Erasmus’s Apophthegms, all too commonplace to show direct influence on Sh.

A few Italian sources have been proposed. Cairncross (1976) detects echoes of Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso in the trial by combat in Act 5, as does Mueller (1994); see n. 3037–42. Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 182–7): Sh. had used Cinthio Giraldi’s Hecatommithi (1565) for MM and Oth. The ten stories in the eighth decade, from which Sh. derived MM, explore the theme of ingratitude. The third exemplifies female ingratitude; Don Aulo’s story is of a ruler almost 80 years old, Apesio, King of Scythia, who marries two daughters to the sons of the previous king (he himself being a low-born general elected to kingship upon his predecessor’s death). The resentful son Anemero cannot persuade the mild daughter Agatia to murder her father, nor can the wild daughter Omosia persuade her mild husband Eumonio; so Anemero and Omosia agree to murder their spouses, marry, and take over the kingdom. Anemero kills the old king by hurling him down some stairs. Later Omosia dies in childbirth, Anemero’s sons are killed before him, he is sent into exile and dies of a long and painful illness. (P. 184): This story gives the very atmosphere of aggressive evil that is so marked a feature in King Lear, the theme of filial ingratitude is specifically and powerfully associated with women, one husband is an essentially kindly man, one woman transfers from a good to bad husband, and its protagonist (p. 185) has the regality that distinguished Lear from the private catastrophe of Timon and that (p. 186) transforms stories of foolish weakness [Timon, old Leir] into a drama of classical proportions, in which Lear represents James’s ideas of kingly greatness. (P. 202): The father-daughter confrontation was perhaps suggested originally by Giraldi. Furness (ed. 1880, p. 407) translates the query of Klein (1866, 1:891) whether the hint of presenting assumed and real madness and professional folly in the same play and scenes may not have derived from Cristoforo Castelletti’s Le Stravaganze d’Amore (Rome, 1585), since as far as we know, no drama exists before Lear and Hamlet wherein feigned insanity is depicted at all except for this play. Colie (1966, pp. 461–81): Lear illustrates a number of Renaissance paradoxes, as enumerated in Ortensio Lando’s Paradossi (1543).

Contemporary prose romances (other than Sidney’s Arcadia discussed above; see ) seem often to provide rather broad generic similarities than close likeness suggesting particular influence. Smith (1946, pp. 153 ff.): Richard Johnson’s Arthurian prose romance Tom a Lincolne, whose second part was entered in the Stationers’ Register 20 Oct. 1607 [well after Lr. was written], has parallels with Lr.; its Wild Man of the Woods theme may be reflected in speeches of mad Lear and Poor Tom. Nonetheless (p. 161) the similarities are mainly generic, and similar parallels could also be traced with other romances, such as Valentine and Orson, the Latin Vita Merlini, and the Irish Buile Suibhne. Such generic parallels are the hero-king, madness and old age, strife in the kingdom, nakedness during madness, lamentation, beast-like suffering during a storm, then shelter, concerned servants who entertain and annoy the king, complaints about the cold, and a non-fatal leap from a cliff. Hamilton (1974, p. 191): Thomas Lodge’s prose romance Robert Second Duke of Normandy (1591) is certainly a direct source for King Lear; Robert progresses from wickedness through suffering to repentance, takes shelter with a hermit in a wood, does penance by taking on the role of a Fool, and fights incognito to save Christendom. (P. 191): Besides the central theme of the humbling of a proud man, there are suggestions here for ways to develop the Fool, the philosopher Edgar at the hovel, the incidents between Oswald and Kent, the trial by combat, and the use of Cordelia. See also Reibetanz (1977, pp. 116–17) and .

Jorgensen (1967, pp. 39–40) shows the multiple editions (hence popularity) of Sir John Davies, Pierre Boaistuau, Thomas Wright, Pierre de La Primaudaye, and (later) Pierre Charron, suggesting that Sh. might have looked at treatises on self-knowledge. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 109): If Shakespeare knew the translation by George Pettie of [Stefano] Guazzo’s Civil Conversation he would have found support in it for Montaigne’s attitude to senile parents, and a strong recommendation that old fathers ought to acknowledge their insufficiency and want of judgment, and to referre the ordering of their house and liuing to their children, who are of discretion to deale in such waighty matters; see n. 382. Kinney (1980) finds parallels with the political thought of the neo-Stoic Lipsius in his Sixe Bookes of Politickes or Civil Doctrine, tr. William Jones (1594), admitting that (p. 14) the political thought in Lear…is so commonplace that Shakespeare needed no source at all. Taylor (1982, p. 397 n.) and Salingar (1983, p. 163) agree that the parallels are too general to show influence. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 109 n): The general bent of Justus Lipsius seems to me to anticipate the authoritarian writings of James I rather than King Lear. Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 186 ff.): In Basilikon Doron (Political Works of James I, ed. C. H. McIlwain, 1918, p. 36) James explicitly warns his son against adultery, using the example of the king his grandfather, whose begetting a rebellious bastard bred the wracke of his lawfull daughter and heire. (P. 188): In both Basilikon Doron and The Trew Law of Free Monarchies (1598) he [ed. McIlwain, p. 54] spells out the obligations and sacred bonds of parents to children and children to parents. He links this, especially in the latter tract, to the obligations of subjects to kings.…[194] This absolute authority he…applies…(in True Law of Free Monarchies) [to] chastisement and correction of children who offend, [196] so long as (he says in Basilikon Doron) he first digests his passion before his royal anger breaks out. (P. 205): The play uses James’s view on kingship and kingliness to explore the nature of authority in a fallen world, here divorced from divine sanction, and so doomed…to failure. Without claiming direct influence, Nicholl (1980, pp. 152 ff.) argues for a correspondence with alchemical ideas, a series of parallels between the plot and imagery of the play and the patterns and symbols of alchemy. Brownlow (1987, p. 27) detects the influence of the recusant Robert Southwell’s Epistle of Comfort (1604); see nn. 2949, 2956. For similarities with Thomas Harman’s Caveat (1567) see n. 1265, and with George Puttenham’s Arte (1589), n. 1735.

div.head: Annesley, Allen, Hansby, Dudley, Lambert, Shakespeare
div.p:
Hales (1876, p. 306; see DP n. 17) notices in an epitaph in the wall of the church tower at Lee, Kent, a daughter named Cordell Lady Hervey, who erected a monument to her father Bryan Anslie (d. 10 July 1604) out of dutifull loue vnto her father and mother. We may fondly trust that Grace and Christian, the elder sisters, by no means corresponded to Goneril and Regan. The epitaph is also noticed independently by M. A. S. M. (1884, p. 29), who specifies that Cordelia Anslye married William Harvey. S. H. A. H. (1884, p. 77) and Hall (1885, p. 35) note that William Harvey’s first wife was Lady Southampton, mother of Sh.’s patron, to whom he dedicated Ven. and Luc. The text of the epitaph, transcribed by S. J. Low of Pembroke College, Oxford, is given below as it first appears in Hales (1876); in its reprints in Hales (1884, pp. 271–2) and Bullough (1973, pp. 310–11), some spellings and pointings are changed:
Here lyeth buried the bodyes of Bryan Anslye, Esquier, late of Lee in the county of Kent, and Avdry his wife, the only davghter of Robert Turell, of Bvrbrooke in ye county of Essex, Esquier. He had issue by her one sonne and three davghters, Bryan, who died wthout issve; Grace, married to Sr John Wilgoose, Knight; Christian, married to the Lord Sands; and Cordell, married to Sir William Hervey, Knight. Ye said Bryan the father died on the xth day of Ivly, 1604; he served Qveene Elizabeth as one of ye band of Gentlemen Pencioners to her matie the space of xxxtye yeares. The said Awdry died on the xxvth of Novebeber (sic), 1591. Cordell, the youngest davghter, at her owne proper cost and chardges, in further testimonie of her dvtifull love vnto her father and mother cavsed this monvment to be erected for the p’petvall memorie of their names against the ingratefvll natvre of oblivious time.
‘Nec primus, nec ultimus; multi ante
Cesserunt, et omnes sequetitur.’ (sic).

And thereby hangs a tale. Stopes (1922, p. 274) notices in the Cecil papers at Hatfield (CI.163) a letter from John Wildegoose and Samuel Lennard [dated 18 Oct. 1603] asking Robert Cecil to have Sir Brian Annesley of Lee, Lewisham, Kent declared unfit to manage his affairs. In response, his daughter Cordell wrote to Cecil on 23 Oct. asking, if Brian must be declared lunatic, that he be put in charge of Sir James Croft. Stopes makes no connection with Lr. Merrifield (1936, p. 204) gives a detailed account of these affairs from records in Somerset House and in the Cecil papers, and from Stopes, adding that in 1604 Wildgoose contested (unsuccessfully) the will of Brian (dated 1600) on grounds that he was not of sound mind when he made it. Young (1948, p. 300–1), seeming to have discovered the Annesley story independently, claims that the widow Wildgoose (not her husband John) tried to get her father certified incompetent and later, as wicked sister, contested the will. [Merrifield, however: It does not appear that Grace and Christian <the other two daughters> played the parts of Goneril and Regan. It was John (Wildegos), mentioned in Cordell’s letter, who was the agent.] Isham (1954, pp. 150–1): Cordell Annesley’s name was given as Cordelia when she was married and when she was buried. [E. G. Withycombe, Oxford Dictionary of English Christian Names, 3rd ed., 1977, however: Cordell or Cordelia Harvey was buried at St. Martin-in-the-Fields in 1636.]

Mack (1965, p. 46 n.): The incident is not easy to reconstruct. The sisters’ married names were Lady Grace Wildgoose and Lady Christian Sandys, but there is no mention of the latter’s participating in the proceedings against Annesley. Lady Wildgoose, the elder, and her husband seem to have initiated the case, Wildgoose, Timothy Law, and Samuel Lennard representing to Cecil on Oct. 18, 1603, that they had visited Annesley as Cecil (apparently in response to their overtures) had authorized them to do, and that they had found him altogether unfit to govern himself or his estate. On Oct. 23, Thomas Walsingham, James Crofts, and Lennard, instructed by Cecil to take inventory, reported to him that they had done so, and had sealed up Annesley’s chests and other things of value, but that in view of the present emulation between the two gentlewomen (Lady Wildgoose and Cordell) for the government of his person, a determination of guardianship would have to be made by Cecil. It was at this point that Cordell intervened, asking that custody of her father be bestowed on Sir James Crofts, who out of the love he bare unto him in his more happier days, and for the good he wisheth unto us his children, is contented upon entreaty to undergo the burden and care of him and his estate without intendment to make any one penny benefit to himself…as also to prevent any record of Lunacy that may be procured hereafter.

Bullough (1969, pp. 43–9) gives a more detailed account of the Wilgosse [sic] family, their relations, holdings, overseers of the will, and the whole contention. (P. 47): She [Cordell] did not deny that her father was out of his mind, but she was rightly afraid of what might happen to him if he were taken away from her.…To be recorded a lunatic meant the loss of all civil and human rights, to be entirely at the mercy of one’s guardian, who might take one into his household, make use of one’s property, and ill-treat the patient without redress. Cordell feared such a fate for her father in addition to the disgrace it would bring on his name and family. Apparently Grace was willing to connive at such treatment, if she did not instigate it.…[48] Of the three Annesley sisters only one is known to have taken part against her father.…Unlike Cordelia, Cordell was not rejected by him; on the contrary she was his favourite during his last years, as his Will and Testament proves.…She certainly tended him with love.

Idem (1973, p. 270): Cordell protested to Robert Cecil that her father’s long service deserved a better agnomination, than at his last gasp to be recorded and registered a Lunatic. She refused to let Sir John Wildgose make an inventory of her father’s domestic property and seems to have succeeded in keeping him and his wife at bay. When Annesley died in July 1604, they disputed his will, which left them little and most of his property to Cordell. The Prerogative Court upheld the will on 3 December. One of the execu-[271]tors was Sir William Harvey, third husband of the Dowager Countess of Southampton, mother of Shakespeare’s early patron. And after that lady’s death in 1607, he married Cordell Annesley.

Two documents from the Cecil papers (A and B) are here reproduced from the Royal Commission on Historical Manuscripts, Calendar of the Manuscripts of the Most Hon. the Marquess of Salisbury, vol. 15 (ed. M. S. Giuseppi, 1930), pp. 262, 265–6; a third (C), abridged in that source, is here reproduced in full from Stopes (1922, p. 274).

item.p: A. Sir John Wildegos and others to Lord Cecil (p. 262).

1603, Oct. 18.—According to your letter of the 12th of this present, we repaired unto the house of Bryan Annesley, of Lee, in the county of Kent, and finding him fallen into such imperfection and distemperature of mind and memory, as we thought him thereby become altogether unfit to govern himself or his estate, we endeavoured to take a perfect inventory of such goods and chattels as he possessed in and about his house. But Mrs. Cordall, his daughter, who during the time of all his infirmity hath taken upon her the government of him and his affairs, refuseth to suffer any inventory to be taken, until such time as she hath had conference with her friends, by reason whereof we could proceed no farther in the execution of your letter.— From Lee, 18 Oct, 1603.
Signed: John Wildegos, Tymothe Lawe, Samuel Lennard.
B. Sir Thomas Walsingham and others to the Same (pp. 265–6).

1603, Oct. 23.—According to the authority given us by your letters, we repaired to the house of Mr. Bryan Annesley, and there in the presence of his two daughters, Lady Wildgosse and Mrs. Cordell Annesley, have sealed up all such chests and trunks of evidence, and other things of value, as they showed us to be his. We were informed that he holdeth divers things by lease, which for not payment of the rent might be in danger to be forfeited. We have therefore requested Sir James Croftes, whom your lordship hath associated to us in this business, to take care of the payment of such rents as are reserved upon any lease made to the said Mr. Annesley and also for the receipts of rents due to him. As touching the government of his person and family, though by nature his two daughters may seem fittest to perform this duty, yet respecting the absence of Sir John [266] Wildgosse at this time, and the present emulation between the two gentlewomen, we have referred the determination thereof to your lordship.—From Scadbury, 23 Oct., 1603.
Signed: Tho. Walsingham: James Croftes: Samuel Lennard.
C. Cordell Annesley to Lord Cecil (p. 274).
