Matthews (1913, p. 287): The poet ousts the playwright, and the dramatic poem planned as a play to please the public in the playhouse becomes an epic poem of a world-wide universality for which the theater is altogether too small.…The drama is not only unfitted for performance on our modern picture-frame stage, with its realistic scenery; it is almost equally unfitted for performance on the medieval platform-stage.

In contrast, C. F. T. Brooke (1913, pp. 88–91): The cause of King Lear’s relative failure to appeal on our stage is that Shakespeare stands here at odds…with the conventional tragic standards and with the general public’s estimate of life. The play suffers, not from excessive grandeur, but, on the contrary, because its most significant situations manifest to us, visually presented, something less than tragic proportions.…Not only has [Sh.] chosen to present under the tattered veil of mythical royalty a bourgeois family group; he has even dethroned all the conventional tragic passions and elevated to the highest place in the whole hierarchy of sin his detested petty vice of selfishness.…[91] To give the semblance of tragedy to such a theme, the poet has been driven to an artificial heightening of his effects.…The result is both a triumph and a failure. Alden (1922, p. 270): Modern actors wisely hesitate to put it on.

Granville-Barker argues that the play’s dramatic vitality emerges when theaters abandon the conventions of realism (1927; 1946, 2:5–10): All of these things of which Bradley complains, the confusion of pathos, humor and sublime imagination, the vastness of the convulsion, the vagueness of the scene and the movements of the characters, the strange atmosphere and the half-realized suggestions—all this [Sh.] needs for Lear’s experience and ours. Personally, I do not find quite so much vagueness and confusion. To whatever metaphysical heights Lear himself may rise, some character (Kent and Gloucester through the storm and in the hovel, Edgar for the meeting with the blinded Gloucester), some circumstance, or a few salient and explicit phrases will always be found pointing the action on its way. And if we become so one with Lear in his agony that for the time its full significance escapes us, may not memory still make this clear? For that is very often true of our own emotional experiences. We are in confusion of suffering or joy at the time; only later do we realize, as we say, what it all meant to us. It is, I suggest, this natural [6] bent which Shakespeare turns to his account in these larger passages of King Lear. In the acting they move us profoundly. The impression they make remains. And when the play is over they, with the rest of it, should cohere in the memory and clarify; and…the meaning of the whole should be plain. Shakespeare, I protest, has not failed; he has—to the degree of his endeavor—triumphantly succeeded. But to appreciate the success and give effect to it in the play’s performance we must master and conform to the stagecraft on which it depends.…[9] Upon a realistic stage the thing cannot well be done. With Shakespeare made to delegate half his privileges to scene-painter and property-man a like dissociation will be forced upon the actor. And it is not only that the apparently real heath and hovel and the all but real thunder and lightning will reduce the characters which move among them to mere matter of fact also, but that by the dissociation itself, the appeal to our imagination—upon which all depends—is compromised. For the strength of this lies in its unity and concentration. It is the unity of the appeal that allows Shakespeare to bring so much within its scope. And, with time, place and circumstance, night, storm and desolation, and man’s capacity to match them in despair all caught into a few lines of poetry, it should not be so hard to absorb besides—he willing—the ego of the actor who speaks them. [10] Then he will stand before us not physically ridiculous by comparison with them, but invested with their dynamic quality.

Yet some critics demur. For Jacox (1875), Wilson (1898), Courthope (1903, 4:167), and Luce (1907) Lr. is better read than acted. Drew (1937) sides with Lamb against Granville-Barker. Ridley (1940, p. 202): Lr.’s universality is not…representable by any actor, or in any theater but that of the mind. Webster (1955, p. 220): I cannot believe that King Lear ever was or will be a good play. Harbage (ed. 1969, p. 1061): More often than not our experiences in the theatre confirm [Lamb’s] view [that Lr. cannot be acted]. There have been fine productions, but not very many: one touch of insincerity can rot everything away. Kennedy (1976, p. 43): There are too many themes, it is too consciously multifarious, for the stage to contain it all. Bloom (1998, p. 476): Our directors and actors are defeated by this play, and I begin sadly to agree with Charles Lamb that we ought to keep reading King Lear and avoid its staged travesties. Orwell (1947; 1950, p. 39) charts a middle course: Tolstoy is right in saying that Lear is not a very good play, as a play. It is too drawn-out and has too many characters and sub-plots. One wicked daughter would have been quite enough, and Edgar is a superfluous character: indeed it would probably be a better play if Gloucester and both his sons were eliminated. Nevertheless, something, a kind of pattern, or perhaps only an atmosphere, survives the complications and the longeurs. Lear can be imagined as a puppet show, a mime, a ballet, a series of pictures. Part of its poetry, perhaps the most essential part, is inherent in the story and is dependent neither on any particular set of words, nor on flesh-and-blood presentation.
In contrast, Leggatt (1988, p. 9), speaks for many late-20th-c. critics in emphasising how fundamentally theatrical it is, how much of its essential thinking is done by means peculiar to the theatre.

Other critics express unease about the play’s onstage horrors, in particular the blinding of Gloucester, which for Warton (1754, p. 312) ought not to be exhibited on the stage. Likewise Gentleman (1770, 362): We heartily wish that the insignificant, cruel, offensive scene, where Gloster’s eyes are put out, had been left to narration; the subject of it, while in action, is shocking, and Cornwall’s scuffle with his domestic, ludicrous. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159): I am not able to apologise…for the extrusion of Gloucester’s eyes, which seems an act too horrid to be endured in dramatick exhibition, and such as must always compel the mind to relieve its distress by incredulity. Yet let it be remembered that our authour well knew what would please the audience for which he wrote. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:59) also disapproves, but Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 614 ff.) defends the scene in literary though not in theatrical contexts: If he had in any wise derogated from the dignity of his art, then certainly he would have deserved the reproach of having unjustly pandered to the rude taste of the masses. But…may not our poet just as well have sought for a means of using the horrors of the coarse tragedy in Marlowe’s style for a higher moral and artistic aim, making the wildness and atrocity of passion, carried to the utmost bounds, serve as the true aim and object of a work of art? Must not a mind of this magnitude have felt that the strongest poetic genius finds alone the scope necessary for it in the representation of the strongest passions? Must he not have felt that there was good reason why the ancients took their subjects from the old primitive heroic ages, where they could venture to invest the more grandly-formed natures with mightier powers? And is it not an acknowledged fact that Shakespeare attained the highest excellency of his art in the delineation of this unrestrained humanity, in Macbeth, in Hamlet, and especially in Lear? How often has Lear been called the grandest and noblest of all his dramas!…[633] We cannot justify the putting out of Gloster’s eyes upon the stage; although Shakespeare, by the singular circumstance of making a nameless and unknown servant take instant vengeance on the perpetrator of the deed, has given prompt satisfaction to the natural indignation consequent upon such an atrocity. The blinding indeed was Shakespeare’s express intention, but this could certainly have been attained as well if the action had been placed behind the scenes. Similarly Bradley (1904, p. 251): The blinding of Gloster on the stage has been condemned almost universally; and surely with justice, because the mere physical horror of such a spectacle would in the theatre be a sensation so violent as to overpower the purely tragic emotions, and therefore the spectacle would seem revolting or shocking. But it is otherwise in reading. For mere imagination the physical horror, though not lost, is so far deadened that it can do its duty as a stimulus to pity, and to that appalled dismay at the extremity of human cruelty which it is of the essence of the tragedy to excite. Thus the blinding of Gloster belongs rightly to King Lear in its proper world of imagination; it is a blot upon King Lear as a stage-play.

Other critics who condemn the staging of Gloucester’s blinding include Wilkes (1877); Dawson (1888); Boas (1896, p. 450): a barbarous outrage, that violates our emotions instead of purging them through pity and terror; and Matthews (1913, p. 283), who blames the baser likings of the Elizabethan rabble.…Simply hideous,…it is dramatically useless. It is introduced because of its brutality, for the sheer effect of theatrical shock, since there is really no motive for it, as Regan would naturally order Gloster to be killed at once, which is what she later regrets not having done. Bridges (1925, p. 181) likewise explains it as a concession to the taste of the groundlings. In contrast, Clarke (1863, p. 189): I have no more wholesome defence to set up for the poet, than to refer to the period of civilisation in which all the events of the story were transacted;— a period when mutilation, and even homicide produced not more excitement, than in our day would ensue upon seeing one man knock another down in the street.

Spens (1922, p. 21) defends the episode in theatrical terms: It was essential to give Lear’s feelings of the hard selfishness of his daughters an objective expression, to save his passion from degenerating into sordid domestic squabble. Traversi justifies it in terms of literary symbolism (1952, pp. 140–1): The preoccupation with sight, with eyes and their loss, which can be detected running through the earlier part of the play like a hidden thread, here [in 3.7] comes to the surface in concrete dramatic form. As it does so, we realize more clearly than heretofore that this blinding incident has more than a factual meaning in the structure of the play. The physical suffering inflicted upon Gloucester, indeed, is almost intolerable, and only in relation to the vast conception of the tragedy, in which it forms a turning-point, can [141] its inclusion be justified in artistic terms. For it is no accident that the moment in which Gloucester loses his sight, the victim of what seems to be, and is, a gratuitous act of evil, is also that in which the birth of his spiritual understanding is confirmed. Likewise Charney (1969, p. 63): By showing us directly this scene of almost unbearable cruelty, Shakespeare is insisting that the evil at the heart of the play is real and unmetaphoric. Pechter (1978, pp. 182–4) defends the episode in relation to the extraordinary power of King Lear to make us suffer.…The play’s violence pervades generally and inheres deeply in the way it presents its characters and involves its audience.…[183] No other play of Shakespeare’s involves an audience so directly and so deeply with its characters.…[184] We are made to pay for our mistakes in King Lear, and it hurts, over and over again, to have to beat at this gate that let our folly in.
See n. 2140 for further critical opinions and for the customary stage treatments.

Another source of unease for critics has been the ending of the play, especially the death of Cordelia. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159): Shakespeare has suffered the virtue of Cordelia to perish in a just cause, contrary to the natural ideas of justice, to the hope of the reader, and, what is even more strange, to the faith of the chronicles.…A play in which the wicked prosper, and the virtuous miscarry, may doubtless be good, because it is a just representation of the common events of human life: but since all reasonable beings naturally love justice, I cannot easily be persuaded, that the observation of justice makes a play worse; or, that if other excellencies are equal, the audience will not always rise better pleased from the final triumph of persecuted virtue. In the present case the publick has decided. Cordelia, from the time of Tate, has always retired with victory and felicity. And, if my sensations could add anything to the general suffrage, I might relate, that I was many years ago so shocked by Cordelia’s death, that I know not whether I ever endured to read again the last scenes of the play till I undertook to revise them as an editor. Other critics who disapprove of the deaths of Lear and Cordelia include Theobald (1715), Cooke (1731), A. B. (1752), Lennox (1754), Taylor (1774), Davies (1784), Duport (1828). Wilkes (1877, pp. 379–80) condemns as heartless…the abhorrent hanging of the sweet and low-voiced Cordelia, that filial saint.…There [380] was no need, in order to reach the susceptibilities of his audience, to hang that angel of gratitude and goodness, Cordelia. Frye (1922, p. 297): The last act is obviously a blunder. I can imagine nature in her stubborn courses stumbling into some such blind and bloody shambles; that is not the difficulty—the untowardness of insentiency. But I can not recognize in Lear the logic or raison d’être of the genre, the bare technical congruity of the literary form which is evident in the most brutal Zolaesque impressionism.…The deaths of Cordelia and her father are impertinent not merely morally but theatrically; they are extrinsic and superfluous. Weisinger (1957, p. 160): Shakespeare forces the action on to the shambles of the Grand Guignol of Act V, completely cancelling the calming and cleansing effect of the tragic vision already attained with Lear’s self-awareness [at 2814–7].

The Romantics, characteristically, defend Sh.’s ending. Hunt (1808; 1949, pp. 16–17): Shakespeare made his play end unhappily, because he knew that real nature required such a catastrophe.…As to the Doctor’s [Johnson’s] old argument that poetic justice did not allow the innocent to suffer with the guilty, I think it is completely refuted, not so much by the common ill fortune of virtue, which he seems to consider as the only argument against him, but by the evident maxim that error is never so exemplary in its effects as when they involve the innocent with the guilty; nay, the very death of a virtuous person seems to be a sort of triumph over persecution; the calm repose which [17] we see in the dead body, and the lively enjoyment which we fancy the soul has just fled to partake, form a strong contrast with the anticipated end of the guilty, and with their turbulent pleasures on earth. It appears to me also that the old age of Lear has been too much shattered by his repeated madness to survive a second change of fortune, and that the exhaustion of which he dies in Shakespeare is in every respect natural and unavoidable. Schlegel (1808; tr. 1815, 2:208): [Cordelia’s] death has been thought too cruel; and in England the piece is so far altered in acting that she remains victorious and happy. I must own, I cannot conceive what ideas of art and dramatic connexion those persons have who suppose that we can at pleasure tack a double conclusion to a tragedy; a melancholy one for hard-hearted spectators, and a merry one for souls of a softer mould. After surviving so many sufferings, Lear can only die in a tragical manner from his grief for the death of Cordelia; and if he is also to be saved and to pass the remainder of his days in happiness, the whole loses its signification. According to Shakespeare’s plan the guilty, it is true, are all punished, for wickedness destroys itself; but the auxiliatory virtues are every where too late, or overmatched by the cunning activity of malice. The persons of this drama have only such a faint belief in Providence as heathens may be supposed to have; and the poet here wishes to show us that this belief requires a wider range than the dark pilgrimage on earth to be established in its utmost extent. Hazlitt (1817; 1930, pp. 269–72): The concluding events are sad, painfully sad; but their pathos is extreme. The oppression of the feelings is relieved by the very interest we take in the misfortunes of others, and by the reflections to which they give birth.…[272] Our natural sympathy with actual suffering is lost in the strong impulse given to our natural affections, and carried away with the swelling tide of passion, that gushes from and relieves the heart.

A number of early critics express indignation at Tate’s altering Sh.’s intentions. Lamb (1811, p. 138) calls Tate’s ending sickening.…The paltry consideration of poetical justice, which is established on grounds very unphilosophical, ought not to be brought in competition with the tenderness, the sublimity, and the various beauties of the original tragedy of King Lear. Hudson (1848, 2:278): Why, the catastrophe, as it stands, is the sublimest one in the whole Shakespeareian drama.…It is the crowning glory of the whole play, which sets the seal to all the glories that have gone before, and without which they are aimless and meaningless. Clarke (1863, pp. 184) decries the presumption of that man, Tate, whose unhallowed ignorance converted this sublime effort of passion, endurance, and poetical justice consummated, into the vulgar finale of a holiday tale:—And so, they were all married, and lived very happy afterwards.…Theatrical enormities enough have, indeed, been perpetrated, but no one sacrilege has ever yet equalled Tate’s mutilation of the tragedy of King Lear. See also Farren (1824); Anon. (1831); Jameson (1833); Knight (1849, pp. 344–52) for detailed criticism of Tate’s inferiority; Gervinus (1849–50); Reed (1855, pp. 373–4); Hugo (1864); Mézières (1865); Moore (1895); Brandes (1895–6); Dawson (1888); Woodbridge (1898); Raleigh (1907); Creizenach (1909); Alden (1922); Stuart (1928). For further analysis of Tate’s motives and occasional defenses of his results, see , .

Nineteenth-century critics often justify Sh.’s ending on moral or ethical grounds. Horn (1823, 1:196; tr. in Furness ed. 1880, p. 452): It is in accordance neither with history nor ethics always to give to virtue the victory.…Was he [Sh.] to allow England to be conquered by France, so that the Prince of France should ascend the British throne with his wife Cordelia? Or was he bound to give us the pleasure of seeing the aged Lear restored to health, and again wielding the sceptre?…Whoever has undergone what [Lear] underwent cannot suffer death; he welcomes it. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, pp. 197 ff.): Cordelia pays the penalty of the fault she committed, when, instead of affectionately humouring the weakness of her aged father, she met him with unfilial frowardness, and answered his, no doubt, foolish questions with unbecoming harsh-[198]ness and asperity; a father’s curse lights upon her head, and its direful consequences cannot afterwards be avoided. The slighter her failing may appear, the deeper is the tragic effect of its heavy penalty. For the true force of the tragic lies exactly in this, that the trivial faults of the good are overwhelmed in the same ruin as the most revolting offenses of the bad; with this difference, however, that whereas to the former purification and atonement (and consequently true life also) is conveyed in its annihilation, to the latter temporary destruction and punishment bring likewise eternal death.…[204] The tragic impression [of Lear’s death] loses its crushing and oppressive horror, and is transmuted into the calm consolatory feeling of a gentle death and a blissful peace. Snider (1887, pp. 199–202): The death of Cordelia is often felt to be unjustifiable, and the play was once altered to suit this feeling. But a true comprehension of the nature of Dramatic Art will vindicate the poet. The end of Tragedy is not that somebody get killed, or even that a villain be brought to justice; it must show the collision of two ethical principles, both of which have validity in the reason of man.…[200] Cordelia’s profoundest impulse is devotion to Family—a very lofty principle of action; but she is led by it into a collision with the State—a still higher principle.…[201] On what ground [does Sh. alter the received ending of the story of Cordelia]? Assuredly not to show the good woman overwhelmed in her goodness; that is not Shakespeare’s view of the moral order of things. An innocent person may perish in the world of accident, but not in the ethical world of which Shakespeare gives the picture. Like his [202] characters in general, she is caught in the antithesis of opposing principles. Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 227 ff.): Dr Johnson, with his sturdy British morality, could not endure to read the last scenes of King Lear, and declared in favour of Nahum Tate’s improvement on Shakspere’s play, according to which Edgar makes love to Cordelia, and she retires in the end with victory and felicity. To die is so exceedingly uncomfortable; to live, and be a happy wife is so eminently satisfactory. Shakspere’s morality is somewhat more stern than that of the great moralist. Shakspere introduces into the world no little ethical code. Such a little ethical code would flutter away in tatters across the tempest and night of Lear’s agony. But Shakspere discovers the supreme fact,—that the moral world stands in sovereign independence of the world of the senses.…[228] That which satisfies our heart, that which brings us strength and consolation, is not that by happy concurrence of circumstances Cordelia should succeed in her enterprize, but merely that Cordelia existed. Lesser happiness can be dispensed with if we are granted the presence of beautiful, heroic souls. Cordelia has strengthened the bonds of humanity; she has enriched the tradition of human goodness.…[268] Shakspere opposes the presence and the influence of evil not by any transcendental denial of evil, but by the presence of human virtue, fidelity, and self-sacrificial love.…We feel throughout the play that evil is abnormal; a curse which brings down destruction upon itself; that it [269] is without any long career; that evil-doer is at variance with evil-doer. But good is normal.

Bradley (1904, pp. 251–3) is ambivalent: Doubtless we are right when we turn away with disgust from Tate’s sentimental alterations, from his marriage of Edgar and Cordelia, and from that cheap moral which [252] every one of Shakespeare’s tragedies contradicts, that Truth and Virtue shall at last succeed. But are we so sure that we are right when we unreservedly condemn the feeling which beyond question comes to many readers of King Lear who would like Tate as little as we? What they wish, though they have not the courage to confess it even to themselves, is that the deaths of Edmund, Goneril, Regan and Gloster should be followed by the escape of Lear and Cordelia from death, and that we should be allowed to imagine the poor old king passing quietly in the home of his beloved child to the end which cannot be far off. Now, I do not dream of saying that we ought to wish this, so long as we regard King Lear simply as a work of poetic imagination. But if King Lear is to be considered strictly as a drama, or simply as we consider Othello, it is not so clear that the wish is unjustified. In fact I will take my courage in both hands and say boldly that I share it, and also that I believe that Shakespeare would have ended the play thus had he taken the subject in hand a few years later, in the days of Cymbeline and the Winter’s Tale. If I read King Lear simply as a drama, I find that my feelings call for this happy ending. I do not mean the human, the philanthropic, feelings, but the dramatic sense. The former wish Hamlet and Othello to escape their doom; the latter does not; but it does wish Lear and Cordelia to be saved. Surely, it says, the tragic emotions have been sufficiently stirred already. Surely the tragic outcome of Lear’s error and his daughters’ ingratitude has been made clear enough and moving enough. And, still more surely, such a tragic catastrophe as this should seem inevitable. But this catastrophe, unlike those of all the other mature tragedies, does not seem at all inevitable. [253] It is not even satisfactorily motivated. In fact it seems expressly designed to fall suddenly like a bolt from a sky cleared by the vanished storm. And although from a wider point of view one may fully recognise the value of this effect, and may even reject with horror the wish for a happy ending, this wider point of view, I must maintain, is not strictly dramatic or tragic. For other comments on the ending see n. 3216.

Twentieth-century critics sometimes praise the play as prophetic of modern attitudes. Mack (1965, pp. 25 ff.): In a number of ways, our own century seems better qualified to communicate and respond to the full range of experience in King Lear than any previous time, save possibly Shakespeare’s own. We are familiar with the virtues of the bare, unlocalized Elizabethan platform stage, and can recover them at will, with the immense added resource of modern lighting. After two world wars and Auschwitz, our sensibility is significantly more in touch than our grandparents’ was with the play’s jagged violence, its sadism, madness, and processional of deaths, its wild blends of levity and horror, selfishness and selflessness, and the anguish of its closing scene. We have not the Victorians’ difficulty, today, in discerning behind its foreground story of a family quarrel inti-[26]mations of mortality on a far grander scale: we know that we go to see in Lear one who is as much a portent as a man…and that the play as a whole, with its kings, beggars, fools, blindness, madness, and storm, casts shadows of unearthly grandeur on any twentieth-century imagination that will submit itself to it.…[97] The bent of the play is mythic: it abandons verisimilitude to find out truth, like the story of Oedipus; or like the Rime of the Ancient Mariner, with which, in fact, it has interesting affinities. Foakes (1993, pp. 181–2): One might say that King Lear is released from history, and can always therefore be seen as essentially a contemporary play.…[182] The play is at once ancient and modern, and because it is not located in a specific place…or specific time, we are not troubled by a sense of contradictions or anachronisms.…The vague suggestions of antiquity in the play, and its mythic resonances, work to enrich and deepen a design that throughout emphasizes the present moment and looks to the future that depends upon each act. Thus the play is political in the largest sense, and its possible local reference to the age of James I is of less importance than its pervasive concern with wider issues that bear powerfully on the political consciousness of the present time, ours and everyone’s. Hunt (1995, p. 128) sees affinities with postmodernism: Extreme anti-formalism in [Lr.] amounts to evidence of the perceived intensification of the shattering and degeneration of social and natural worlds.…Lear’s profound reason-in-madness resembles the postmodern trait of contradictory reasoning designed to transform the structure of reason itself.…Postmodern imploded binarism, in which the Other becomes the Same and the Same the Other, clarifies the collapse of sexuality on both large and small scales in King Lear.

Lr. has been compared with various other Shn. works: with Ham. by Jones (1995, pp. 186–208); with Oth. by Muir (1958, pp. 145–62); with Mac. by Held (1995, pp. 39–47); with AYL by Kernodle (1945, p. 187), Mack (1965, p. 64), Jones (1971, pp. 171–3) and McCombie (1980, pp. 67–80); with 1–3H6, Jn., Tit., AWW, TN, and Cym. by Jones (1971, pp. 163–94); with Shr. by Wells (1980, pp. 55–66); with LLL by Booth (1983, pp. 61–78), who finds both plays permeated with demonstrations of indefiniteness (p. 62); with MND by Black (1982, pp. 52–68), who interprets both plays as teratologies (i.e., stories about monsters); and with Tmp. by Hamlin (1995, pp. 125–30) and Setti (1988, pp. 71–80), who also compares it to Karen Blixen’s Peter and Rosa. It has also been compared with Sophocles’s Oedipus plays by Lamb (1811, p. 299), Shelley (1821), Jameson (1833, pp. 241–5), Girardin (1849, pp. 125–45), Seeley (1851, pp. 1–51), Blaze de Bury (1868, pp. 234–5), Watt (1908, pp. 274–85), Chiesa (1925, pp. 123–52), Bodkin (1934, pp. 280–4), Pratt (1965, pp. 49–57), LaBelle (1969, pp. 343–7), and Lupton & Reinhard (1993, pp. 189–229), who employ a Lacanian interpretive framework; with Aeschylus’s plays by Shelley (1821), Swinburne (1880), Elton (1966, pp. 212–19); with the tragedies of Seneca by Pratt (1965, pp. 49–57) and Lerner (1962, pp. 353–69); with Seneca’s Oedipus specifically by Pratt (1983, pp. 6–9); with Euripides’s Herakles and Seneca’s Hercules Furens by Braden (1993); with Euripides’s Bacchae by Gray (1985); with Sophocles’s Oedipus at Colonus and Euripides’s Bacchae by Poole (1987, pp. 209 ff.), focusing on their concern with death and justice; with Corneille’s Clitandre by Montagu (1769, pp. 74–9); with Racine’s Phédre by Lerner (1962, p. 362); with Webster’s Duchess of Malfi by Heilman (1960, pp. 18–19) and Hunt (1993, pp. 21–42); with Marston’s Malcontent by Cohen (1985, pp. 338–43); with Everyman by Salter (1954, pp. 47–50); with Rastell’s The Four Elements by Mikalachki (1998, pp. 86–90); with the Book of Job by Nevo (1972, pp. 260 ff.), Holloway (1961, pp. 85–8), Ornstein (1960, pp. 272–3), Pack (1991, pp. 251–76), and Muir (ed. 1952, p. lv); see also , ; with Boethius’s De Consolatione by Presson (1965, pp. 406–24); with Giraudoux’s La Folle de Chaillot by Hugo (1952, pp. 3–11); with Jonson’s Volpone by Musgrove (1957, pp. 21–39) and Norton-Smith (1983, pp. 203–14); with The Brothers Karamazov by Rosen (1960); with Père Goriot by Girardin (1849, pp. 140–5); with Turgenev’s A King Lear of the Steppes by Knights (1963, pp. 27–8);with Conrad’s The End of the Tether by Gillon (1968, pp. 15–22); to Hooker’s Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity by Young (1986, pp. 98–104); with Wole Soyinka’s The Strong Breed by Brockbank (1983, pp. 11–19). Iwasaki (1999), compares Lr. to Noh plays. Conrad (1995, pp. 95–132) discusses, as continuations of Lr., Schiller, Die Räuber; Balzac, Le Père Goriot; Turgenev, Fathers and Sons; Williams, Cat on a Hot Tin Roof; Broken Lance, dir. Edward Dmytryk; Smiley, A Thousand Acres; Blixen, Out of Africa; Stow, To the Islands; Ran, dir. Kurosawa. For Lr.’s influence on other works, see .

div.head: Genre
div.p: Although, in F1, Sh.’s fellow actors identified Lr. as a Tragedy, the earlier Q1 named it a History. On the likelihood that the Q1 title page was an unauthorized invention of the publisher, modeled on that of the earlier source-play Leir, see n. 0.3. Most commentators discuss the play as a tragedy, though often disagreeing about what kind of tragedy it is.

Saintsbury (1897, p. 396) is representative of critics who interpret Lr. as a tragedy of character in which the tragic catastrophe results from the protagonist’s own faults of character and the mistaken actions resulting from them: The tragedy of Lear…is in the retribution of Lear’s petulant and self-centered impulsiveness, in the retribution which must have followed in some other way even if the king had never made his rash disposition of the kingdom, which could only be avoided by his correcting his whole nature, as he does not, in fact, correct it, till the final moment. Heilman (1948, pp. 31–7): That disaster follows from the hero’s tragic flaw implies that the world is a moral organism in which events are morally meaningful.…[32] Most of the action is organized with Lear and Gloucester as centers, and what happens in the play is to be seen as proceeding from them and as having a certain impact upon them.…We see good and evil in conflict in the world, but by the structure we are reminded that the conflict is an emanation of that in the individual soul.…[37] Thus we move from melodrama, which represents the externalized conflict as reality, to tragedy, in which the externalized conflict corresponds to the war within the soul and is indeed begotten by the war within the soul. See also Campbell (1930, pp. 185 ff.). Tamblyn (1922, pp. 72–73) objects: Lr. is (p. 73) not a tragedy of character, in the ordinary sense.…[72] To some extent, certainly, Lear’s own troubles come from his disposition and the act of folly, but Shakespeare no more asks us to consider Lear primarily responsible for his tragedy in and through his octogenarian whim or even perhaps his imperious temper than he would attempt any single explanation of that imperious temper itself. Character is mystery made by fate, rather than the reverse. Chambers (ed. 1906; 1926, pp. 241–2): King Lear belongs to the later manner of Shakespearean tragedy…[which] seems to shift from the nature of man to the nature of what is around and above man, and to seek the primary causes of tragic [242] disaster, less in the imperfect mettle of a hero…than in external forces which are conceived of…as unmoral and blind in their working.

Some critics employ Aristotelian categories, focusing less on the cause of the tragic action than its cathartic effects (variously understood) on the reader or the protagonist. Chambers (ed. 1906; 1926, p. 240): Among the tragedies of Shakespeare, King Lear stands out as, in the Aristotelian sense of the word, the most tragic. It is the most tremendous in design, brings into play the most elemental forces, makes the most irresistible demand upon those emotions of pity and awe, the purification of which is the function and deliberate end of tragedy. I say purification, not purgation, since…the actual effect of tragedy is not to purge away or eliminate pity and awe from the soul of the spectator, and is to purify and ennoble those emotions, by calling them from the personal to the universal and fixing them upon just those elements in the totality of things which, essentially and in themselves, are the most pitiful and the most awful. This ideal of tragedy is realized in King Lear, as it has only been realized some dozen times in the history of literature, largely by virtue of the cosmic scope of the play. Maclean (1951; 1952, pp. 600–2): Shakespeare uses actions, which are more discernible than emotions, to mark [Lear’s] descent into the pit. Sh. also added thought to action and emotion, and thought in many ways is more precise than either of the other two.…[602] Our pity and fear for Lear are both magnified and mitigated.…In addition, the action is arranged from beginning to end…in such a way that fear does not become horror, or pity some kind of excruciating anguish. For Purdom (1963, p. 166), the purification is specifically in the crisis of the dramatic action, when Lear himself is purified. In that crisis, not in anything concerning the other characters, is contained the equilibrium…which follows from the evil being accepted. Archer (1982, p. 122): Shakespeare’s crafty employment of incomplete catharsis is what marks this play as a tragedy; one made all the more tragic by the reader’s seeing what it is Lear fails to see: the character and endurance of love. Rosen (1995, p. 27) relates the notion of catastrophe in Renaissance tragic theory to the characters’ inability to find causal connections between events.…It is…the nature of catastrophe to come from outside the plot.…The catastrophe stands for the unmotivated, and thus the arbitrary, the contingent, the unexpected.

With Snider (1887, pp. 132–3), we shift focus entirely from the protagonist’s inner nature to the surrounding world and interpret the tragedy in Hegelian terms as a dialectical conflict of values: We shall find the entire drama [133] separating into two parts or movements, the first of which embraces three Acts and shows the breaking up of the Institutional World by an inner disease, which has been introduced by Lear and Gloster. The very persons who have violated institutions have obtained control of them and are administering them, in order to banish and destroy those who have shown most truly the institutional spirit. It is the mighty collapse of society, in which the individual and the social order around him fall into complete discord. This is the Perverted World, in which the wrong ones have the right, and the right ones have the wrong. But with the Fourth Act, the return out of disorder begins; the shattered Institutional World purifies itself in the fire of war; the faithful ones assert their right of control, and the faithless ones become faithless to one another, while their power disintegrates of itself. Such is the second Movement, showing the restoration, and the whole drama is a grand social cycle, including the essential process of history, giving a picture of a world destroyed and then restored, the tragedy not merely of individuals, but of institutions, yet with the recovery of the latter from their malady.

In contrast, it has also been seen as a domestic tragedy. Rapp (1843; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 457): Divested of the historical costume, the features of Lear look out upon us with the naturalness of ordinary life, so that we seem to see an unhappy citizen of the year 1600 wrestling with madness rather than an old English king, much as Lear insists upon his regal dignity. Here is the charm which the poem has for the great public: Lear suffers from the domestic cross which is never wholly absent in any single family. Ruskin (1870; 1905, 20:31): Lr. is essentially domestic in [its] strongest motives of interest. Bayne (1881; 1880–6, p. 223): The drama of Lear, whatever else it may be, is first and supremely a domestic and personal tragedy. Brooke (1913, p. 89): Lear is one of the boldest examples of the bürgerliches Trauerspiel, a type always ungrateful to the snobbery of audiences and the conservatism of tragic tradition. Idem (1911, pp. 398–9): In Shakespeare’s treatment, King Lear and his daughters lose the vague royal dignity which the earlier anonymous play on the same subject allows them, and become practically bourgeois types; while the kingdom of Britain could [399] be replaced without dramatic loss by a farm. Poel (1929, p. 48): Lr. is domestic tragedy, that is to say it should not be regarded as an historical tragedy, or as grand tragedy in the sense of the word associated with grand opera. McFarland (1981, p. 95): The play itself might be seen as an exalted version of the domestic tragedy of the period—as an elevated form of such structures as A Woman Killed with Kindness or even Arden of Faversham.

Others see similarities with classical Greek and Roman tragedy. Fansler (1914, pp. 184 ff.): Lear is a combination of Senecan and Elizabethan [tragic] structures.…[192] The Lear-Cordelia tragedy as Shakespeare presents it is a Greek-Senecan action with a continued downward fall from the beginning.…[194] The Goneril-Regan-Edmund love story and the Gloucester-Edgar-Edmund struggle have together a progress independent of the overtragedy. Their course exemplifies what is sometimes called typical Elizabethan structure; that is, the actors rise from the contemplation of wicked deeds to the execution of them and undergo the reaction that brings death. Miola (1992, pp. 143–74) characterizes Lr. as a tragedy of furor…in [144] which Hercules Furens serves as a model.…Lear’s furor…is both error and heroic response to evil.…Seneca and Senecan traditions clearly contribute to the complex polyphonies of King Lear.…Rhetorical devices and motifs [e.g. stichomythia] as [145] well as dramatic conventions [e.g. the nuntius and chorus] constitute Senecan presence in the play.…[173] In King Lear Shakespeare confronts and solves the dramatic problem of creating a sympathetic Senecan protagonist…[174] by creating the wrath of Lear, a wrath which…is ultimately unique: his is not a passion that leads to scelus but one that transforms character, brings insight in madness, thirsts for justice as well as revenge, and finally modulates into a pained and human protest against the cruel fates.…The inscribed Senecan models prove to be as inadequate to Lear’s rending experience as do those of the morality play, likewise evoked and, finally, repudiated. Bowers (1980, pp. 13–14) views Lr. as a modified classical tragedy, i.e., (p. 14) a fifth-act tragedy [in which] we cannot expect…the formal climax that takes place in the third act of a five-act Renaissance drama. For the possible influence of classical tragedy as a source for Lr., see .

Critics who interpret Lr. as a Christian tragedy include Sewall (1959, pp. 68 ff.), who finds in Lr. Christian tragedy in its full development…the meeting in a single action of the non-Christian (Greek, pagan, or humanist) with the Christian to produce a world…in which the certainties of revealed Christianity lose the substance of faith and become only tantalizing possibilities hovering about but not defining the action.…[73] But whatever redemption the hero wins is not through Divine Grace but, like the Greek hero, through his own unaided efforts. He has no comforter on the dark voyage, no Heavenly City as his destination, where his bundle of sins drops miraculously from his back. What is Christian about Christian tragedy is not eschatological but psychological and ethical. For other interpretations of the play as Christian tragedy, see below, , and for biblical influences, see above, .

Various critics find other ways of classifying Lr. as a tragedy. For Frye (1967, pp. 99 ff.) Lr. is a tragedy of isolation, in which (p.118) the hero becomes a scapegoat, a person excluded from his society and thereby left to face the full weight of absurdity and anguish that isolated man feels in nature. Gellért (1988, p. 347) finds in Lr. the recipe of the original Dionysian ritual plays. Other critics who relate Lr. as a tragedy to ritual sacrifice include Bodkin (1934, p. 281) and Holloway (1961, p. 97).

McAlindon (1992, pp. 85–8) calls the play the supreme exemplar of Sidney’s claim that tragedy serves a political function, that is, works against tyranny, by virtue of its capacity to excite admiration and commiseration, to draw…an abundance of tears, and to move and mollify the hardened heart.…[87] King Lear is, in a special sense, a [88] tragedy of the heart.

In contrast, Vivas (1971, pp. 846–65), focusing on the relation of tragedy, as poetry, to the tragic vision that the reader or spectator discovers to be the informed substance of a tragic poem, describes Lr. as (p. 847) an unmitigated tragedy.…It presents an action that, to our sense of equity reaches the extreme limit of gratuitous or arbitrarily ordained catastrophe.…The rationale of the unmitigated tragedy is more difficult to grasp than that of the moralistic or psychological tragedy and remains dubious throughout the whole play.…It directs the mind to a transcendent source of the disasters it presents.…[848] An unmitigated tragedy cannot have for its stage an exclusively human world. To be totally unmitigated it must somehow involve the universe.…[862] What King Lear does is to reveal, which is to say to tear the veil of, moral aporiai at the heart of its cosmos.…[865] No one can live sanely from day to day while facing the dread portent of unmitigated tragedy. But without its help we are not likely to see, unless we are endowed with the poetic powers of a Shakespeare, into the depths of the abyss.

Faas (1984, p. 109) goes further, calling the play a post-tragic anti-tragedy: King Lear…inverts the mainly classical paradigms of tragedy.…Suffering…is shown in Lear to be neither purposeful nor ennobling. Although the king temporarily achieves pathei mathos, or learning through suffering, he dies in sheer misery and madness, mouthing curses against his best friends. Nor are we purged of fear and pity in watching his slowly drawn-out agonies.…Although the expectation of tragic effects has been aroused in us, we find ourselves experiencing their opposites. Salgādo (1984, p. 39) likewise: King Lear includes and transcends, and by transcending raises doubts about, the claims of tragedy to be a true and ennobling report on human life. Similarly Holbrook (1994, p. 134): A critical light is…thrown upon tragic assumptions in King Lear, where the suffering of the king and other elite characters…is understood in the context of the daily, anonymous, untragic suffering of the mass of society.…A measure of Lear’s ethical rehabilitation is a newfound concern for this mass—and implicit within this is the recognition, remarkable indeed for a tragedy, that the misery of poor people weighs as much as a king’s. This recognition amounts…almost to an ethical dismantling of the social basis of tragedy. Goldman (2005, p. 214): The questioning of tragic value itself is a crucial part of the experience of King Lear—of the ambivalent responses that the play seems deliberately to arouse toward its painful itinerary.

Such views of Lr. as a comfortless anti-tragedy have clear affinities with characterizations of the play as absurdist drama, an idea anticipated by Knight (1930, pp. 184 ff.): The core of the play is an absurdity, an indignity, an incongruity. In no tragedy of Shakespeare does incident and dialogue so recklessly and miraculously [185] walk the tight-rope of our pity over the depths of bathos and absurdity.…The whole tragedy of Lear witnesses a sense of humour in the gods which is in…bad taste.…The gouging out of Gloucester’s eyes is a thing unnecessary, crude, disgusting; it is meant to be. It helps to provide an accompanying exaggeration of one element—that of cruelty—in the horror that makes Lear’s madness. And not only horror: there is even again something satanically comic embedded deep in it. The sight of physical torment, to the uneducated, brings laughter. Shakespeare’s England delighted in watching both physical torment and the [186] comic ravings of actual lunacy. The dance of madmen in Webster’s Duchess of Malfi is of the same ghoulish humour as Regan’s plucking Gloucester by the beard: the groundlings will laugh at both. Moreover, the sacrilege of the human body in torture must be, to a human mind, incongruous, absurd. This hideous mockery is consummated in Regan’s final witticism after Gloucester’s eyes are out: [quotes 2170–1]. The macabre humoresque of this is nauseating: but it is there, and integral to the play. These ghoulish horrors, so popular in Elizabethan drama, and the very stuff of the Lear of Shakespeare’s youth, Titus Andronicus, find an exquisitely appropriate place in the tragedy of Shakespeare’s maturity which takes as its special province this territory of the grotesque and fantastic which is Lear’s madness. We are, indeed, pointed to this grim fun, this hideous sense of humour, at the back of the tragedy.…[189] But indeed this recurrent stress on the incongruous and the fantastic is not an element in Lear: it is the very heart of the play. We watch humanity grotesquely tormented, cruelly and with mockery impaled: nearly all the persons suffer some form of crude indignity in the course of the play.…[191] The tragedy of Lear is most poignant in that it is purposeless, unreasonable. It is the most fearless artistic facing of the ultimate cruelty of things in our literature.…[192] Nor does the use of the words comic and humour here imply disrespect to the poet’s purpose: rather I have used these words, crudely no doubt, to cut out for analysis the very heart of the play—the thing that man dares scarcely face: the demonic grin of the incongruous and absurd in the most pitiful of human struggles with an iron fate. It is this that wrenches, splits, gashes the mind till it utters the whirling vapourings of lunacy. And, though love and music—twin sisters of salvation—temporarily may heal the racked consciousness of Lear, yet, so deeply planted in the facts of our life is this unknowing ridicule of destiny, that the uttermost tragedy of the incongruous ensues, and there is no hope save in the broken heart and limp body of death. Lear is of all the most agonizing of tragedies to endure: and if we are to feel more than a fraction of this agony, we must have sense of this quality of grimmest humour. We must beware of sentimentalizing the cosmic mockery of the play. Similarly, for Fluchère (1953, pp. 241 ff.), Lr. is the Tragedy of Disorder in its unbounded confusion. The characters, the action, the poetry—all are stamped by a tremendous effort to reach out beyond the facts of the real world to the vague regions of the Absolute, and to bring there the shock of destruction.… in Lear there are no longer any frontiers between the sublime and the ridiculous, between the sane and the insane, between man and beast, perhaps even between man and God. Rossiter (1961, pp. 270 ff.) likewise discusses the comic-ironic-grotesque in Lear. Utterly unlaughable, it has all the wit of a malevolent commentator as pitiless and well-informed as the records of the Day of Judgement. Ultimately it suggests (p. 290) a universe with a malevolent grin on its face: or, worse, one from which the grin has faded away, like the Cheshire Cat’s. King Lear is informed throughout with that drastic and terrifying suspicion…that man’s whole endurance may be utterly meaningless. Esslin (1961, p. 234) explicitly places Lr. within a theatrical tradition of the absurd because of its strong sense of the futility and absurdity of the human condition (quotes 2221–2). Kott (1964, pp. 99 ff.) famously compares Lr. to the new theatre of the absurd: Grotesque takes over the themes of tragedy and poses the same fundamental questions. Only its answers are different.…Tragedy is the theatre of priests, grotesque is the theatre of clowns.…[100] When established values have been overthrown, and there is no appeal, to God, Nature, or History, from the tortures inflicted by the cruel world, the clown becomes the central figure in the theatre. He accompanies the exiled trio—the king, the nobleman and his son—on their cruel wanderings through the cold endless night which has fallen on the world; through the cold night which in Shakespeare’s King Lear will turn us all to fools and madmen.…[104] In King Lear, Shakespeare shows the paradox of pure theatre.…The stage is empty throughout: there is nothing, except the cruel earth, where man goes on his journey from the cradle to the grave.…[105] On this earth, through which the tempest has passed leaving only stones, the King, the Fool, the Blind Man and the Madman carry on their distracted dialogue.…[121] Buffoonery is not only a philosophy, it is also a kind of theatre. To us it is the most contemporary aspect of King Lear. Only it has to be seen and interpreted properly. For this reason one must reject all the romantic and naturalistic accessories; the opera and melodrama about the old man who, driven out by his daughters, wanders about bareheaded in a storm and goes mad as a result of his misfortunes. But as in the case of Hamlet, there is a method in this madness. Madness in King Lear is a philosophy, a conscious cross-over to the position of the Clown. Cohn (1972–3, p. 223): The plot [of Lr.] is as Beckettian as anything out of Molloy or Malone Dies; the scene, a metaphysical farce which ridicules life death, sanity and illusion. Zak (1984, p. 38) likewise sees a poetic universe repeatedly leveled by nearly farcical irony. Other critics who see the play as absurdist include Holland (1978, pp. 18–44). Kolve (1966, pp. 181 ff.) objects: The middle of the play is a superlative example—progenitor, if you like—of the theater of the absurd. However, (p. 182) the text exists and is larger than that reading.…Its catharsis, its reassurances, are in fact so careful, so precisely delimited, that they possess possibly a greater validity than does the look into the void alone.…[184] The play goes a long and beautifully managed journey through chaos, but it is a journey through that condition. It begins and ends elsewhere. Fricker (1966) and Graczyk (1993) likewise argue, contra Kott, that the world of Lr. is neither absurd nor grotesque.

Other critics discuss Lr. as a history play. Wendell (1894, p. 293): King Lear was evidently set forth as a chronicle-history; and indeed it differs from what we recognize as chronicle-history more in substance than in manner. Ribner (1957, pp. 249–52): As a play about kingship which deals with basic ethical questions…inseparable from political questions,…[252] King Lear fulfills many of the functions of the history play. Flahiff (1974, p. 232): In a literal sense King Lear stands as the earliest of Shakespeare’s British histories (in its subject matter, not the order of its composition). Shanker (1975) finds elements of history-play structure (see below, ). Wittreich (1984, pp. 76 ff.): The title page, linking tragedy and comedy and subordinating both to history, indicates that the concerns of the play are political as well as personal, social as well as individual. Tragedy and comedy do not cancel one another out in history but, rather, are absorbed by it, giving history its different contours.…[82] The effect of Shakespeare’s generic mixture here is to stretch the boundaries of tragedy and comedy and to create for them a containing form of history—of history conceived prophetically and climaxed apocalyptically. In contrast, Curran (1999, p. 2) finds Lr.unique among the extant Galfridian chronicle plays treating the pre-Roman era of British history in its escape from history.

The play has also been characterized as epic. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 642): The poet in this work, in this creation of his own, approaches the most comprehensive works of epic national poetry, the growth, as it were, of centuries; and Aristotle, could he have seen this, would now more than ever have awarded his praise to tragedy: that with smaller means it attained to the great object of the epos. Miller (1900, p. 15): Both [Lr. and Cym.] have a strong infusion of the Epic.…In epic poetry…the Power above the world is placed openly in the foreground. Men are the recipients of the influence, they are almost the tools of the supreme Controller, rather than centres of influence themselves.

Lr. is sometimes described as a morality drama. Thus Campbell (1948, p. 94): Lr. is a sublime morality play, the action of which is set against a backdrop of eternity. Lear’s problem and his career resemble those of the central figure in the typical morality play, who is variously called Genus Humanum, Mankind or Everyman. And the action of Shakespeare’s play is his greatly modified version of man’s endless search for true and everlasting spiritual values, rewarded, in this case, by the final discovery of them just before he must answer Death’s awful summons. Danby (1949, pp. 40–1): The characters…call for the same kind of treatment as the characters of Morality.…[41] The play presents the fate of man, the situation of man, in general. For Heilman (1948, p. 32), The children [of Lear and Gloucester], like the Good and Evil Angels in Marlowe’s Faustus, represent the different elements that are in conflict in the fathers. Similarly Traversi (1952, p. 43): There is a very real sense in which the whole action of [Lr.] might be described as a projection of the conflicting issues supremely present in the mind of the central protagonist. As father, Lear produces in his daughters contrasted reactions which reflect different and contradictory facets of his own mind. Rosier (1954, pp. 576–7): Lear represents Everyman in the Morality Play, insofar as he has arrived at a point in life where his unreasonableness and lack of self-[577]knowledge catch up with him in the form of negative consequences, imposed upon him by the law of nature. Whitaker (Mirror, 1965, pp. 216–36): Edgar is analogous to Knowledge in Everyman, Cordelia is [217] Love. Even the sisters approximate Lust, and Edmund is still Ambition; Lr. is thus (p. 236) an exemplum of the evil effects of wrath and lust. Ribner (1960, p. 117): [Sh.] availed himself of the morality play formula which was so much a part of the dramatic tradition of his age. The didactic and homiletic tradition of medieval drama afforded tools by which Shakespeare might shape a complex action to reflect the universal role of man in conflict with evil. Jones (1971, pp. 157–8) finds that the motif of the coming of death not only links King Lear with [158] these earlier native plays but may have been the reason why Shakespeare originally chose to treat his new tragic subject in what must have seemed a pointedly archaic style.…The downward curve of the typical morality play plot, which brings the hero to his knees and finally prostrates him in death, possibly accounts for a similar movement clearly discernible at the centre of the tragedy despite its great profusion of character and episode. Kronenfeld (1998, pp. 205–8) also sees affinities with morality plays: The corrupted mock trial in Lear…shares the general Christian theme of the imperfection of earthly justice with dream visions and morality plays not all that far removed from it in time.…[207] The trials of Lady Meed or Cloth Breeches versus Velvet Breeches are part of a widely available and long-standing Christian [208] understanding of the limits of earthly justice and the role that Avarice plays in society. See also Spivack (1958, pp. 413–14), Creeth (1960, pp. 390–1), Rose (1972, passim), Erzgräber (1981, pp. 83–110), and Martin (1987, pp. 33–45). Schell (1983, pp. 194–5) sees the play as both the culmination and undoing of morality form: King Lear may, indeed, be Shakespeare’s most Shavian play in the way that it turns a familiar dramatic form against itself and the assumptions it embodies. Just as Shaw appropriates the narrative conventions of nineteenth-century melodrama in order to bring melodramatizing thought to the surface and set its romantic fictions against reality, so Shakespeare reworks the Lear story along the lines of dramatic moral allegory and draws out the forms of thought associated with it, only to confront allegory with tragic reality. The result is that what we once thought of as a moral allegory we must now think of as moral romance.…[195] King Lear is not a moral tragedy but a tragedy of a moral system. Lear’s entrance with Cordelia’s body virtually marks the end of a long-lived way of understanding experience and of the dramatic form created to express it. For morality-play influences, see above, .

The tension in Lr. between symbolic or emblematic modes of characterization akin to morality drama and dramatic realism is a recurrent critical issue. While Brooke (1911, p. 398) calls it his greatest realistic play, Stoll (1927, p. 112) argues that Shakespeare often sacrifices psychological consistency to dramatic situations as in the behavior of Cordelia, Kent, and Lear in 1.1; Putney (1944, p. 312) objects: The tragedy of Lear is profoundly moving because its characters are actuated by common emotions and its situations are essentially human. For Brooke (1963, p. 10) the play seems, at almost any given moment, to possess just that immediate sense of naturalism which, regarded overall, one might expect it to lack. In this respect, Lear resembles Shakespeare’s last plays, whose plots if merely read, or reflected on outside the theatre, seem merely absurd; but which in actual performance often seem utterly convincing, in the naturalness with which speech corresponds to situation. Departures from realism are defended by Clarke (1863, p. 170): The main incident, the characters of the principal agents, and their course of action being all strained to the utmost tension of probability, [Sh.’s] naturally fine instinct at once prompted him, that to preserve a harmonious proportion throughout, it was necessary that he should aggrandise the moral qualities of the inferiour persons in the dramatis personæ. We therefore notice that all the contrasted passions are thrown into high lights. The virtuous characters become glowingly conspicuous by their juxtaposition with the vicious ones; and not merely so, for by themselves, and uncontrasted, they are perfect specimens of truth, honour, disinterested love, and self-devotion. For Dow (1885, pp. 231–2), this is a flaw in Lear. In this tragedy, as in no other of Shakespeare, have we characters tending to lose the vivid and individual emphasis of their personality in characteristics. The twist of nature in the two daughters and in Edmund is so abnormal, and their ingratitude strikes us with such a dead chill, that their persons half melt from their individual limning.…[232] We seem at times to be moving in a world where evil influences have assumed a human form.

Bradley (1904, p. 263–5): Considered simply as psychological studies few of [the characters], surely, are of the highest interest.…[264] We seem to trace the tendency which, a few years later, produced Ariel and Caliban, the tendency of imagination to analyse and abstract, to decompose human nature into its constituent factors, and then to construct beings in whom one or more of these factors is absent or atrophied. This, of course, is a tendency which produces symbols, allegories, personifications of qualities and abstract ideas…and, while [265] it would be going too far to suggest that he was employing conscious symbolism or allegory in King Lear, it does appear to disclose a mode of imagination not so very far removed from the mode with which, we must remember, Shakespeare was perfectly familiar in Morality plays and in the Fairy Queen. For Fraser (ed. 1963, p. xxxi), The appeal to realism…is at all costs to be avoided.

Mack (1965, pp. 56 ff.): The distinctive feature of King Lear [is] its combination of parable and parable situations with acute realism.…[67] The complication in Shakespeare’s management of character…is simply that at any given instant characters may shift along a spectrum between compelling realism and an almost pure representativeness that resembles (and evidently derives from) [the] esse of the Morality play, though it is not necessarily allegorical.…[69] Finally we meet in King Lear, to a degree nowhere else paralleled in Shakespeare’s tragedies, a form of organization that is as much homiletic as it is dramatic, and sometimes more the former than the latter. We may see one aspect of the play’s homiletic bias in…the characters who are pure states of being, unmixedly good and bad; or the scenes and episodes that have the quality of visual exempla, essentialized moments in a human history we all share, like Kent sitting in the stocks, Lear raving in the storm, Gloucester taking his desperate leap, a madman [71] preaching to a blind man, etc. We may see another aspect of this bias in the fact that the play reverberates with preaching. The Fool preaches, Kent preaches, Albany preaches, Edgar preaches, and the two elder daughters preach to their father, so that when Lear says to Gloucester in Dover fields: I will preach to thee: mark [2622], it not only comes as a poignant climax, but makes us wonder whether the incoherence of his immediately succeeding utterances is not a reflection and summing up of the previous babble of creeds.…[77] In conclusion, the play calls for a performing style that has [78] absorbed both epic disengagement and psychic intimacy, renders the implausible event plausible, moves easily from personification to personality, effectively marries the tragic to the absurd, and, above all, represses the urge to regularize and unify by twentieth-century psychological principles a play whose actual mode of unity is partly medieval and homiletic.…[83] More of the play becomes intelligible and significant if a view of it is taken that relates its conventions to literary modes to which it is genuinely akin, such as Romance, Morality play, and Vision, rather than to psychological or realistic drama, with which it has very little in common.

Other critics who see Sh. employing a symbolic mode in Lr. include Watkins (1942, p. 9): Most conspicuously of all the plays King Lear shows Shakespeare’s mixed technique…a combination of psychological realism and symbolical stylization, the latter tending towards allegory. Lothian (1949, p. 12): Part of the greatness of this play is that so many of the characters, without becoming abstractions, are charged with symbolic significance, and their interaction takes on a spire of meaning, a kind of allegory, a pattern or diagram of the forces operative in human life, at all times and all places. Wilson (1957, pp. 182–7): As Shakespeare tells it, the story of King Lear is a folktale, not merely in the opening scene, but throughout; and the dramatist has not wished to alter the folktale arbitrariness and simplicity of its archetypal form.…[187] The method of King Lear eschews psychological realism, the nice analysis of motive, or any standard of historicity; it seems to cultivate deliberately a certain arbitrariness and illogicality in the contriving of the plot, the behaviour and interrelations of the characters; it invokes the simplicity of the folktale and draws constantly upon its resources—and it does all this to provide the proper vehicle for a poetic drama in which the impression of large, sometimes vague, but always imposing symbols and values symbolically projected, emerging from and dominating a radiant poetic vision, is the ultimate effect. Yet the play is intensely dramatic. Dauphiné & Richer (1979, p. 108) call Lr. an allegorical piece in the best sense of the word. Anderson (1987, pp. 4–16): King Lear…[is] vitally allegorical at its core.…[9] from realistic improbability and disjunction, to conspicuous mythic characterization, sustained structural significance, radical puns and thematic words, insistent reiteration of meaning, allegorical projection, interiorized landscapes, persistent allusiveness [10] to the forms, images, and words of earlier literary texts, and in short, to a concern with meaning as meaning that is not naively abstracted from earth but is radically discontinuous with it.…[16] The initial conflict in King Lear resonates with ideas like those in Book II [of The Faerie Queene] and dramatizes a similar impasse. Zimbardo (1990, pp. 3–4): because Shakespeare’s unconscious consciousness was shaped by medieval conceptions of perception and artistic representation, King Lear is not…a [novelistic] story, but rather, it is a complex, emblematic pattern.…[4] There are in King Lear neither characters, in our modern, novel-conditioned sense of the term (i.e., fictional simulations of persons like ourselves having interiority and psychology) nor dialogue (i.e. fictional simulation of conversation or discursive exchange). Rather there are emblematic figures and iconic rhetorical set-pieces set in various juxtaposition which together comprise a medieval/Renaissance discourse of patterning, a calligraphic system of signs.

Garber (2004, p. 677): Nowhere in literature is allegory more effectively naturalized. It is for those moments in King Lear that open up toward the sublime, as the speakers’ generalizations on human nature begin to approach the condition of aphorism.…and not for its commentary on seventeenth-century monarchy or the plight of early modern mendicants, that the play is regarded as one of Shakespeare’s most magnificent achievements. Hawkes (1995, p. 26) also sees Lr. as emblematic rather than naturalistic, evincing the sort of non-naturalistic art, put on in the afternoon in daylight and in the public gaze, with little attempt at make-up, costume, or realistic sets, and with all its female parts played by male actors, which aimed to engage with real life, not at the private, personal, psychological level, but at the level of the broad, general issues of the common weal and in the mode of public debate.

Other critics object to symbolic or emblematic interpretation as reductive. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 9 ff.): The characters inhabiting this dialectical world are…never fixed entities, but dynamics, sustained by the tension among their conflicting values and impulses.…[327] As long as the characters are not diminished…into symbols or stereotypes of good and bad, of dimensionless saints and devils, if their full polyphonies of mixed qualities are realized, they clamor for us to perceive with some awe, and [328] sharply experience, their complex, unruly, terrible, recognizable passions.…The dark, deadly, grimly comic world of Lear evokes so wide and intense a range of responses on so many levels of consciousness because it reflects so many varieties of human possibility, from the transcendent to the animal—so many that it must defeat any attempt to enclose its meaning in limited formulae such as redemption, retribution, endgame, morality, etc. We may find some rest in the assurance that Shakespeare shares our preference for love over hate, honesty over falsehood, loyalty over disloyalty, order over disorder, but we cannot go on to extract morals from his play: that order will triumph, love conquers all, suffering redeems, recompense waits in the next world—unless we invent them. Lesser (1970, p. 158) emphasizes psychological verisimilitude: An understanding of the first scene in general and the interplay between Lear and his daughters in particular rests upon the kind of elemental knowledge of the heart which we begin to acquire as infants and share with all human beings by the time we are grown-up.

Kettle (1988, pp. 74–5) denies that Lr. is an allegory or that we should use a word like symbolic to describe it. For Shakespeare does not work in abstractions. He is a supremely realistic writer who presents us all the time with actual situations, actual relationships, and what general observations he offers are always based on particular observations and insights. He is not, of course, a naturalistic dramatist, attempting a slice of life kind of realism, and he uses every resource of his teeming imagination to create means of penetrating, through words and fantasy, to the inner processes of the situations and people he presents.…[75] But every device of art is used to produce, not some effect above or beyond reality, but the deepest, most complex exploration of the actual nature of reality, its texture and its implications, its movement and its interconnectedness. The tension between parable and realism is also discussed by Bevington (ed. 1997, pp. 1168–9). For Paris (1991, p. 107), Lr. is a highly realistic drama; for Carruth (1992, p. 519), it is Shakespeare’s most realistic play. Linville (1990, pp. 310–11) observes that In practice, treating Lear’s emblematic dimensions as dominant has often meant offering an enlarged sense of Lear’s own place in the play, whether the interpretive coordinates employed are derived from traditions of medieval allegory or, as in Freud’s reading of the work, from the symbology of pagan myth.…[311] Conversely, foregrounding the psychological realism in King Lear, whether in the play as a whole or in key scenes and segments, has often meant denying Lear’s character quite such emphatic dominance and deference. The critic’s capacity to see feelingly makes even Goneril, Regan, and Edmund important candidates for empathetic understanding.

Perhaps surprisingly, critics often find affinities with comedy in Lr., particularly in Sh.’s characteristic mingling of tones. Shelley (1821; 1968, p. 114): The modern practice of blending comedy with tragedy, though liable to great abuse in point of practice, is undoubtedly an extension of the dramatic circle; but the comedy should be as it is in King Lear, universal, ideal, and sublime. It is, perhaps, the intervention of this principle which determines the balance in favour of King Lear against the Œdipus Tyrannus, or the Agamemnon, or, if you will, the trilogies with which they are connected; unless the intense power of the choral poetry, especially that of the latter, should be considered as restoring the equilibrium. Ruskin (1838; 1903, 1:173–4): Again, Shakspeare has been blamed by some few critical asses for…the fool in Lear [and other comic elements in the tragedies] because, it is said, these bits interrupt the tragic feeling. No such thing; they enhance it to an incalculable extent; they deepen its degree, though they diminish its duration. [174] And what is the result? that the impression of the agony of the individuals brought before us is far stronger than it could otherwise have been, and our sympathies are more forcibly awakened. Wendell (1894, p. 295): Only when we understand that King Lear, for all his marvelous pathos, was meant, in scene after scene, to impress an audience as comic, can we begin to understand the theatrical intention of Shakspere’s tragedy.…At once ranting and grotesque, the madness of Lear, to-day so supremely and solely tragic, was probably the trait which chiefly made the Elizabethan public relish the play. Brooke (1911, p. 399): In Shakespeare’s treatment, King Lear and his daughters lose the vague royal dignity [with] which the earlier anonymous play [Leir] had invested them; Lear, Goneril, Regan, and Cordelia are all fundamentally creatures of the hard actual world; and their egotisms and bickerings belong to the same type and have obviously the same source in contemporary observation as dozens of the cynical or satirical scenes in the city comedies of Jonson and Chapman. Knight (1930, p. 176): in Lear there is a dualism continually crying in vain to be resolved either by tragedy or comedy. Thence arises its peculiar tension of pain: and the course of the action often comes as near to the resolution of comedy as to that of tragedy. Leech (1950, pp. 76–7): There seems to run parallel to the tragic pattern an undercurrent of fierce [77] comedy. Marks (1957–8, p. 106) praises Sh.’s reconciliation of humor and pathos and the artistry by which the threatened dissolution of the pathos by the mockery, and the threatened discrediting (as in bad taste) of mockery by suffering, are kept from happening. Gardner (1967, pp. 8–10): The comic element is ubiquitous and cannot be located in certain scenes, which can be labelled as comic relief, or lodged in certain characters.…[9] The peculiarity of King Lear is that this comic undercurrent, this sense of absurdity, does not touch the wicked characters or play over the lower-[10]class characters, who usually provide what is called comic relief.…It is in the very heart of the play, in the scenes of the passion of Lear and Gloucester.…No other tragedy gives us this sense of the world as a great stage of fools. But no tragedy also so turns upside down and confuses our notions of what is wisdom and what is folly. Edwards (1968, p. 129): For the plan of the play, Shakespeare returned to the three-part movement of the festive comedy which he had not touched for five years or more. Long (1976, p. 218): Lr. is a tragic play with a festive-comic structure and the metaphysical summary of a whole tragic vision whose roots are in festive comedy, a vision which recognizes the savageness of nature’s destructiveness as well as the sense of indestructible joyfulness which is so convincingly realized first in the fertility of Lear’s imagination and then in the spring or release for the creation of which that fertility is the only guarantee. Hyland (1985–6, p. 170): With its dominating images of a topsy-turvy world, King Lear is oddly like comedy…and this is reflected by the successful use of the comic device of disguise in the play. See also Woodbridge (1898, p. 173); Creizenach (1909; tr. 1916, p. 243); Alden (1916, p. 99, and 1922, pp. 271–2); Traschen (1976).

Besides elements of comic tone, formal conventions of comedy have been seen in Lr. For Stockholder (1968, p. 44), the play’s ambiguous vibration between [the] two poles [of Christian orthodoxy and grotesque absurdism] results from Shakespeare’s deliberate intermingling of the devices of and the vision inherent in comedy, fairy tale, and farce on the one hand and tragedy on the other.…The continuously shifting balance of emotional response evoked by these genres contains the play’s meaning. Miller (1975, p. 3): King Lear…is from a formal standpoint a comedy, deriving much of its incomparable power from a radical tension between the emotional texture of the events and the generic form into which the events have been cast. The fairy-tale beginning, the double plot, the humor of the Fool, the lack of proper motivation, the parody of the Green world, the gratuitous death of Cordelia—anomalies noted by countless critics—are…outward signs of Shakespeare’s overall strategy of using the comic form to delineate a terrible vision. Coursen (1976, p. 237) describes Lr. as a comedy swallowed up in tragedy.

Snyder (1979, pp. 140 ff.): King Lear is full of the structures, motifs, and devices of comedy. It has a double plot and a developed Fool; it is concerned, like many comedies, with the passing of power from old to young; two of its characters are disguised throughout most of the play, one of them in a series of personae that allow him to manipulate other characters; the protagonists are forced out from society into educative confrontations in a natural setting and then return to society again; and this process is completed by the traditional disorder of comedy—social hierarchies turned upside down, logic and even sanity violated. The plot disregards probability as flagrantly as any romantic comedy, from the love test that sets it in motion to the conclusion of the Gloucester action in chivalric challenge, triumph of disguised hero over villain, deathbed repentance of villain. [141] These constant appeals to the world of romantic comedy function in a complex way. They are often twisted to serve, and intensify, the immediate tragic effect. Yet they simultaneously allow for a long-range hope, based on the well-established assumptions of comedy, that all the confusion and pain is leading to a positive conclusion though this hope is deliberately shattered. (P. 179): Shakespeare in King Lear is not rewriting the Purgatorio or anticipating Endgame; he is setting one vision against the other, and in their uneasy coexistence lies the play’s peculiar tragic force.

In contrast, Partee (1971, pp. 60–1) sees a divine comedy in the play’s fundamentally comic movement.…[61] Lear by the end has finally conferred his state on younger strengths [specifically, Edgar], but rather than crawling unburdened to death as he had planned, he is spared, by the clearest gods, the indignity of ending his days as a trivial old man. Bryant (1977, p. 27) likewise discusses comic themes and strategies in Acts 1–4.
