Thompson (1988, p. 19) summarizes recent criticism: The play contains a large number of comic elements, including the double-plot itself (unusual in tragedy of this period but very common in comedy), the presence of the professional Fool with his witty comments on the action, the central concern with the handing over of power from the older to the younger generation, the love affairs of the latter, the use of a natural setting (the heath) for educative purposes, the use of disguise, the flouting of probability in some aspects of the plotting. The play’s principal sources, King Leir and the Arcadia, are themselves a comedy and a pastoral romance respectively. Miola (1994, p. 330) discusses complex adaptations of New Comedy in particular: Deploying familiar characters and configurations, Lear subverts comedic design, i.e., the inner dynamic and its agencies—be they natural or supernatural—by which comedy comes to happy conclusions. The comedies and this tragedy variously use the same agencies—human effort, Providence, sheer luck—but to precisely opposite ends. Greenblatt (1985, p. 180) compares Lr. to Renaissance Italian tragedia di fin lieto, i.e., tragicomedy.

The play has also been discussed in terms of the pastoral mode. Mack (1965, pp. 63–5): In Lr. a scheme of things long associated with [pastoral] romance…is turned topsy-turvy and charged with unprecedented power.…The protagonist [of most Renaissance pastoral romances] moves out in a sweeping arc from the world of everyday, where he has confronted problems or experiences that threatened to disintegrate him, to some sort of Arcadian countryside or forest, which is more fully in sympathy with human feelings and states. There he undergoes a learning process that consists in considerable part of discovering his own problem reflected in those he meets. Having viewed his prob-[64]lem in another, having sometimes undergone in the process something like a ritual death and rebirth, he is able to return to the everyday world, restored to serenity and often to temporal felicity.…[65] King Lear alludes to such patterns…but turns them upside down. It moves from extrusion not to pastoral but to what I take to be the greatest anti-pastoral ever penned. Young (1972, pp. 76 ff.): It follows in its outlines the pattern of the pastoral romance as developed in Spain and Italy and elaborated by English romance writers and dramatists. That is, it deals with characters who are forced to leave society and undergo a period of sojourn in a natural setting, and with their eventual return. As in the more serious pastoral novels, the period of sojourn is one of psychological adjustment, with the natural setting acting as a mirror to the mind. Again typically, the emphasis on the workings of Fortune creates a curious compound of philosophical speculation and spectacular turn of event. Moreover many of the features of the stories—disguises, unaccountable and uncontrollable emotions, errors of identity and allegiance which disrupt the natural social bonds, extensive use of opposites—are readily apparent in Lear.…[93] King Lear employs the pastoral pattern in order to negate it.…It denies its characters and audience the consolations supposed to accompany poverty, isolation, and humiliation.…It suggests that renunciation is no insurance against suffering. Lindheim (1974, p. 181): The play uses pastoral structure to get at pastoral ideas—to arrive at basic man and a purified order of human values that encompasses public justice and private compassion—but once having arrived at the theme of human feeling, Shakespeare goes on to treat his material according to the tragic mode. Zak (1984, pp. 58 ff): Imagery and conventions peculiar to the pastoral mode extensively cluster around Cordelia, the Fool, and, at times at least, Kent. Together the three of them form an ideal community, a contentedly peaceful and gracious social order whose simple existence confirms the play’s version of pastoral, a better way than the brazen and [59] contentious sophistications of the others at Lear’s court. On Lr.’s recessive pastoral pattern see also Colie (1974, pp. 302–16), Jones (1971, pp. 171–3), and McCombie (1980, pp. 67–80). Hamlin (1995, pp. 125–6) argues that pastoral in Lear is inseparable from political critique.…[126] Lear, like The Tempest,…is obsessively concerned with human unaccommodation and with the category of the monstrous. For discussions of pastoral in Lr.’s sources, see above, .

Reibetanz (1977, pp. 116–17) sees affinities with romance rather than pastoral: Lr. (p. 117) takes hold of the romance tradition only to overturn it.…[116] The Lear world’s…extreme characters, illogical actions, spatial and temporal discontinuities—not to mention wicked sisters, a fairy prince, and ubiquitous castles: these find their home in romance. Like Pericles, The Tempest, or numerous narrative romances, King Lear takes us to a remote setting and invites us into a world where mundane logic is frequently left behind, a world that makes us accept its own logic. The places we visit are highly expressive of themes and of the characters and actions depicted in them, and the weather and topography act on the characters anthropomorphically. What goes on in the Lear world is also redolent of romance: spiritual wandering, the testing of patience, the opposition of court and country, brothers waging mortal combat against each other, and the separation and reunion of loved ones. By the time we reach Act V, this romance atmosphere has prepared us to accept the exciting denouement of turn and counterturn which also belongs to romance. For Salingar (1978, p. 8) likewise, King Lear can be described as very largely a romance inverted. Uphaus (1978, pp. 307–8): By the end of Act III …the main characters themselves begin to feel the exhaustion of tragedy and intimate a realm beyond tragedy.…[308] Edgar and Cordelia, in particular, attempt to reverse tragic time.…They define their romance actions against tragedy. Turner (1988, pp. 96–7): Our response to the central focus of the Lear-Cordelia relationship is shaped precisely by two complementary traditions of romance:…the romance of the ruler whose education is completed by exposure to feel as his subjects feel and the complementary romance of the subject, in which a dependant’s patience is rewarded after long abuse; however, (p. 97) the reconciliatory rituals of romance are here seen to be ineffective when faced with the powerful social contradictions which it is commonly their business to reconcile. According to Parker (1995, pp. 112 ff.), Lr. both invites us to participate in romance and holds us back from doing so. It represents (p. 114) the passage into the madness of romance as both desirable and dangerous, thereby anticipating the late plays. Jones (1995, p. 213): From the tragic standpoint the Quarto text of King Lear is riddled with romance as with a mortal cancer; F, however, turns romance into tragedy.

Welsford (1927, p. 297) sees the influence of masque form: In King Lear there are no intrusive lyrical interludes, no momentary changes from the tragic to the romantic or symbolical key, but the central scene of the play [3.4] is lyrical.…Shakespeare could hardly have produced it had he been catering for an audience less accustomed to hybrid forms, and to the frequent insertion of masques.

Some critics associate Lr. with popular antiauthoritarian dramatic modes derived from or akin to folk drama. Thus Bristol (1985, pp. 209–12): In King Lear, the Battle of Carnival and Lent is acted out in an [210] extremely painful variant. The central scenes showing the liminary outcasts on the heath are a procession of defeated and expelled Carnival, pursued by the temporarily victorious energies of Lenten civil policy.…[212] The multiple deaths at the end of the play do not create a reconciliatory image of saturnalian clarification.…Secular authority, in both its majestic, charismatic and its practical, administrative manifestations, has been changed into a festive effigy and symbolically destroyed. Weimann (1978, pp. 40–1): In King Lear, where the nonsensical heritage of ritual action [i.e., the topsy-turvydom of the Mummers’ Play] is replaced by a new convention of reason in madness,…the inverted vision of the world has become a means of criticizing society and of expressing the profound realism of a thoroughly dramatic apprehension and understanding of the world. In King Lear, the visionary quality of speech is linked with the conventional notion that madness is a dramatic form of social license. At the same time, the representation of Lear’s madness involves new mimetic [41] standards of psychological realism which supplement more traditional forms of popular inversion and invective. At this level the topsy-turvying vision again raises questions with some utopian significance, but it does so with a different kind of consistency: we no longer have a trivial dream of the Land of Plenty, but rather a dramatic interpretation of the connection between true need…and a just distribution of goods.

Other critics employ various generic categories. For Hudson (1872, 2:353), Lr. is the highest specimen we have of what is aptly called the Gothic Drama; for Moulton (1903, p. 141–3), it is a problem drama; for Danby (1949, p. 15), a drama of ideas—such a drama of ideas not as the Morality play had been, a drama of abstractions; nor such a drama of amusing talk about theses as Bernard Shaw’s is; a drama of ideas, however, none the less, and Shakespeare’s own creation: the real Novum Organum of Elizabethan thought. Honigmann (1984, p. 47) identifies a subgenre…the Oedipus-Everyman play, in which the hero is, characteristically, a sinner who becomes a thinker; in the course of the play he suffers rather than initiates action. Martin (1987, pp. 7–16) classifies Lr. as ironic drama: The confusion of generic elements alien to conventional tragedy means that (p. 15) King Lear is not a tragedy, if judged by Aristotelian standards. (P. 16): Sh. has not merely reconciled tragedy and comedy, but he has amalgamated all the notable genres familiar to Elizabethan playwrights.…Shakespeare, perhaps disenchanted by…the limited views of life presented by each of the conventional dramatic types, has indissolubly knit all these traditions and formed a composite drama which deals with the manifold complexities of life. This ironic drama is characterized by therapeusis rather than catharsis, stasis rather than catharsis. Cohen (1985, p. 344) finds a split within [the] tragedy between satire and tragicomedy. The generic tension corresponds to the contradiction in the play between demystification and retotalization. Hodges (1985, pp. 70–87) relates Lr. to anatomy as a literary mode or genre: In a broad sense, Lear is about the paradoxes of [the] dismembering mode of representation [proper to anatomy]: it demonstrates how a process of ordering can obliterate unity and a process of decomposition can compose a world.…[87] [Sh.’s] anatomizing mode of drama, which opens up the depths to our eyes and brings us close to the animal passions and the ideals of love and bond that exist beyond form, also requires the brutal disintegration of the bodies of man, the state, and his own media, language and drama. Smidt (1990, p. 130) describes a compound of fairy-tale plot, Job-like lament, metaphysical debate, moral satire and great poetry.

div.head: Moral, Religious, Philosophical
div.p: Lr. is a play whose main characters, forced to endure terrible agony, memorably try to make sense of their experience, pointedly asking far-reaching questions about the nature of humanity and the nature of whatever metaphysical system—if any—may lie behind their world, questions which seem to implicate and challenge the beliefs of audiences and readers of the play. Consequently interpretive criticism of the play frequently confronts issues of moral, religious, and philosophical significance. The extreme examples of good and evil in the characters’ behavior likewise encourages these emphases in criticism of Lr.

Many of the earliest critics are preoccupied with the play’s putative moral lessons. Thus Gentleman (1770, 1:364) excuses the Dover cliff episode, despite its improbability, because it gives so fine a warning against the worst of crimes, suicide, and inculcates so useful, so moral a lesson of bearing up under temporal affliction. Griffith (1775), relentlessly moral, systematically isolates passages for approval and disapproval; Lear’s curse (789–802) and Gloucester’s expression of despair (2521–2) are both condemned on moral grounds.

Later critics too find moral lessons in Lr. For Carstairs (1918, p. 169) the lesson is that goodness, nobleness of character is the one priceless, imperishable thing. James (1951, pp. 77 ff.) argues that Lr. should be understood as making a genuine contribution to human knowledge: King Lear explores life itself.…[78] It represents a great labour of knowledge: not indeed of understanding but of perception; it therefore constitutes (p. 79) a contribution to human knowledge…in spite of the fact that it is not an expression of faith, nor a work of metaphysic, nor a piece of natural philosophy. Besides, it does not set out to please our desires or seek to submit the shows of things to them; it has nothing to do with what we want; it is a genuine exploration of experience.…[116] In this play Shakespeare is,…above all, concerned to exhibit certain moral ideas or states, imaginatively apprehended indeed, yet still ideas of good and evil. His imagination sifts out these essences.…[117] It is suffering love…that we contemplate.…[121] [Lr.] confronts us with mystery in the face of which there is nothing to be said. It exhibits the limits merely of our human experience as they are reached by souls of surpassing excellence and beauty. These are also the limits of secular art.…[125] King Lear is, so far, if you will, didactic. Hyman (1984, pp. 150–5) argues that the literary power of this play depends on the fact that neither our aesthetic nor our ethical feelings are subordinated to the other. Sh.’s (p. 155) power to take and to give delight in what shocks the virtuous philosopher requires the presence, and not the suspension, of our moral attitudes. We need the conflict between our ethical and our aesthetic feelings to create the poetry. Palmer (1992, p. 215) discusses characters in Lr. to demonstrate the morally educative power of literature.

Since Lr. is a play about fathers who wrong their children and children who either betray their fathers or sacrifice themselves on their behalf, it is not surprising that early critics discuss the play’s concern with the mutual duties appropriate to parents and children. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, pp. 192–4): In King Lear, parental affection and filial reverence are contemplated as the focus towards which all the ties of life converge, and the family—in its largest and historical import—is the particular grade of life in which the poet has here taken up his position within the domain of poetry.…[193] In order to show that a moral corruption is never solitary, but is in its seed and principle universal, and ultimately resting on the sinfulness of the whole human race, he has taken the noblest families as representative of the great family of man, and made them the victims of the moral pestilence.…[194] While in the one case the open folly of the parent is answered by the open and shameless crimes of the children, in the other secret sins are met by hidden and sanctified enormity. In the former case the family tie is broken, together with the false and rickety foundation on which it rested; in the latter it is annihilated by the retributive poison of a single sin, which from the first had eaten away the only stay of domestic happiness—true purity of heart. Young (1851, p. 66), perhaps influenced by Ulrici, also praises the morality of the play, especially in displaying and inculcating parental and filial affection. See also Hudson (1872, 2:380). Schwartzkopff (1868, pp. 109 ff.) finds in Lr. an affirmation of the Fourth Commandment. In contrast Berger (1997, p. 233): The fathers tilt the so-called bias of nature in their direction to protect their interests against their children, to preserve their power against indirect and legitimate no less than direct and illegitimate filial exchanges, and—above all—to maintain self-esteem, especially when doing things that jeopardize it. I gave you all is thus the founding gesture of a discourse by which the fathers reify a moral system favorable to them, and use it to monopolize the resources of self-justification in their strategic warfare with the next generation.…The initial premises are gradually subverted to expose the deep fears and contradictions that give rise to them.

Other early critics as well as some moderns find the play especially concerned with the evils of ingratitude. Hall (1879, p. 37): The chief cause which leads up to and produces the tragic result is the vile ingratitude of Goneril and Regan. Brandes (1895–6, tr. 1898, 2:130): In what frame of mind did Shakespeare set himself to this work?…The drama tells us plainly enough. Of all the different forms of cruelty, coarseness, and baseness with which life had brought him into contact, of all the vices and infamies that embitter the existence of the nobler sort of men, one vice now seemed to him the worst—stood out before him as the most abominable and revolting of all—one of which he himself, no doubt, had again and again been the victim—to wit, ingratitude. See also Hewitt (1917). However, T. G. D. (1754, p. 99) objects: The Moral of this Play, is not to expose the Ingratitude of Children, more than the Folly of Parents. Similarly Ridley (1937, p. 170): I doubt whether [the main theme] is, for all Lear’s harping on the topic, what is ordinarily called ingratitude; I think that it is rather impiety in the Roman sense, and particularly that cruelty which is the worst offence against pietas. See also McCullen (1952, p. 339).

Other moral vices discussed by critics of Lr. include flattery and hypocrisy. Draper (1938, p. 245): Flattery is the symbol of villainy in King Lear; and it is the characteristic weapon, not only of Goneril and Regan, but also of the treacherous Edmund. Vickers (1979, p. 82): The devastation at the end of King Lear is sufficient proof of the destructiveness of hypocrisy, once it is believed. Davidson (1984, pp. 190 ff.): Hypocrisy in the pursuit of a private and sinister kind of self-defined wisdom—a wisdom that must be hidden so as to seem to be something other than actual foolishness—provides…the paradox around which the visual tableaux and iconography of King Lear are organized.…[196] The iconography of the world-upside-down topos becomes a major factor in King Lear and illustrates emblematically what the ascendancy of Goneril, Regan, and Edmund means in the political sphere.…[199] [Cordelia] must be seen as an emblem of the highest wisdom which paradoxically is also the greatest foolishness.

Other moralizing critics emphasize self-will and pride. Clarke (1863, p. 167): The play of King Lear…is a practical example of the calamities resulting from unbridled, unguided self-will. Will, independent of, and irresponsible to, justice and rationality, is the pivot upon which turn all the disasters that befall its leading characters. Courthope (1903, 4:161): The play comprehensively illustrates Marlowe’s tragic principle of Will resolved in the pursuit of its own ends, and the Greek tragic principle of divine Nemesis following the commission of sin from one generation to another. The medieval doctrine of the vanity of the world…is made to modify the doctrine of Machiavelli, that all things are permissible to absolute Power. Haller (1952, p. 14): Lear and his daughters have fallen into the first of all sins, namely pride, the love and worship of self, the beginning of all deceit, hatred, hardness, enslavement to evil and disruption.

That Lr. illustrates the danger of passion is asserted by others. Thus Masefield (1911, pp. 188–9): One of the chief lessons of the play is that man is only safe when his mind is perfectly just and calm. Any in-[189]justice, trouble or hunger in the mind delivers man to powers who restore calmness and justice by means violent or gentle according to the strength of the obsession. The play begins at the moment when an established blindness in two men is about to become an instrument for the violent opening of their eyes. Likewise Goddard (1951, p. 525): The predestined end of unmastered human passion is the suicide of the species. That is the gospel according to King Lear. Campbell (1930, p. 207), drawing on Renaissance psychological treatises to argue that Shakespeare’s tragic heroes are slaves to passion, interprets Lr. as a tragedy of wrath: King Lear as the tragedy of wrath…was planned as a tragedy of old age. In Lear and Gloucester Shakespeare represented old men bestowing benefits unjustly, led by flattery to give unwisely, led by anger to withhold unjustly and to seek revenge for imagined slights. Both the evil and the folly of their anger are brought out. The evil lay in their inflicting evil on others. The folly lay in the evil they brought upon themselves. Even Kent, the friend and loyal follower, is led in anger to go beyond the command of reason in his treatment of Oswald and hence to bring further misfortune on the King. Cornwall is killed in an angry fight with his servant, but the servant is also killed for his righteous anger. The whole is a welter of passion. But the picture is relieved by Cordelia, who cannot be moved by passion; by Edgar, who acts as reason dictates even in the guise of a madman; and by Albany, who at the last is the calm arbiter of the gor’d state. Brooke (1963, pp. 27 ff.) objects: It was of course an Elizabethan commonplace that reason should control affection, and that is [in 2.1] both demonstrated and abused. For Edmund the superiority of reason is a matter of power; but what unsettles Gloucester is rational proof. Reason thus becomes doubly questionable, both as capable of stimulating affection, and as incapable of judging it. Similarly (p. 28) Lear opposes Regan’s reasonable condemnation [of his followers in 2.4] not with evidence to the contrary, but simply with an oscillation between passionate anger and appeals to affection.…[29] The oscillations are only dubiously reasonable; but the will to sustain affection, and the violence provoked by its violation, are manifest. With every evidence of the unreliability of feelings, it is on them that we base our judgment. Lr. represents a disturbance of orthodox attitudes to reason and affection.…[30] The distinction between reason and affection becomes one of the distinctions between sub- and main-plot.

Some critics see Lr. preoccupied with the evils of unmastered sexual passion in particular. Thus Wilson (1929, p. 37) asserts that Gloucester’s punishment was in part deserved, and that the person chiefly responsible for it, his bastard son Edmund, had suffered a more grievous wrong at his father’s hands than even the loss of his eyes. Heilman (1948, pp. 90–1) finds a theme of lawless sexual passion figured in a pattern of images associated with the storm in Act 3: The storm and madness are tremendously real, but we are never allowed to forget the moral disorder of which they are both symbols.…[91] In the storm…we see human nature torn loose from all law and order, and, in its orgiastic quality, the moral derangement of the human agents.…Yet the tragedy as a whole affirms the pre-eminence of order; the paradox of tragedy is that order comes out of a world wracked by disorder, that chaos proves order. There cannot be a breach in nature unless there is a nature. Klevar (1972, p. 119) also comments that the breach of nuptial vows has contributed to the disorder of the social world.

Other critics find in Lr. a more pervasive disgust with sex and procreation. Danby (1945, p. 23): King Lear is not only anti-authoritarian and anti-social, but also anti-sexual. Love is stripped of its Spenserian glamour, and the revulsion expressed crudely. Sitwell (1948, p. 55): This play would seem to be largely a diatribe against procreation. Empson (1951, p. 150) refers to the sex-resenting Shakespeare. West (1960, pp. 55–8): One of the major contributions to the impression of pessimism that the play may leave comes from a suspicion of Lear’s which is parallel to the suspicion of Gloucester’s that the gods are like wanton boys. Lear’s is a suspicion not about killing as a joke of the gods, but about procreation as one of the devil’s.…[56] Lear seems in his madness to imply that sex is an insult to mankind and mercilessly alien—or that man is a beast.…[57] The dramatic clarity of madness connects directly with sex: the hatefulness of the children belongs to the carnality that made them.…[58] The rationale of the pessimistic suspicion that tears Lear and through him affects the audience is logically naive, but resistless to the mad king and, in the sight of his suffering, impressive to us. Everett (1989, p. 67) finds the play pervaded by a grittily commonplace sexuality, a remorseless sexual pain.

Other critics discuss as central to the play a contrast between selfishness, cupidity, and covetousness on the one hand, and generosity and charity on the other. Thus Snider (1887, pp. 138–40): Charity in its universal sense…[140] is the test by which the leading characters of the play are gauged. Jayne (1964, p. 277) also sees as central to Lr.’s concerns the theme of charity in human relations: the desperate need which human beings have for each other, and their paradoxical inability to satisfy that need. Stauffer (1949, p. 193) sees Lr. affirming the spiritual realities of good and evil, and defining the latter in terms of the hard cold workings of calculated selfishness. Traversi (1952, pp. 209 f.): The excesses of the acquisitive passion have their roots ultimately in personal cravings and thus can be ascribed in the last analysis to a lack of natural feeling similar to the passion-driven egoism which prompts unnatural children to expose their parents to indigence and torture. The social situation, in short, is…intimately related…to a moral flaw, to the [210] inversion of natural order in the personal sphere. Battenhouse (1969, p. 278): From covetousness…springs the irresponsibility and self-undoing of Gloucester and Lear. This is the root cause of tragedy. Koch (1990, pp. 86–98) displaces charity from a moral to an anthropological interpretive framework: Charity is considered as part of a larger structure of exchange, and the play’s dramatic action is seen as a conflict between two opposed systems of exchange and valuation, i.e. between a kind of gift exchange in which the very act of reciprocity is more important than the precise value of the gifts and a system of exchange which derives value from material equivalence.…[87] These two systems of exchange…also represent the real social conflicts evident in England in 1605 involving the opposition of feudal charitable exchange and modern monetary exchange.…[98] Throughout King Lear, Shakespeare dramatizes the dangerous effect that a new system of values—a system with property at its base and money as its medium—could have on the more ambivalent, more God-instilled feudal values of charity and hospitality.

Sharp (1902, p. 56) discusses love and pity as sources of morality, arguing contra Kreyssig that Lr. is not a drama of Kant’s categorical imperative: The attitude of the nobler combatants toward crime and moral heroism alike is not determined in its essentials by the relation in which they suppose themselves to stand to any supersensible power. Aggeler (1993, p. 329) discusses the play’s affirmation of the redemptive power of good pity. See also Coursen (1976, passim) on kindness. Smidt (1990, p. 146) finds that a large number of expressions of pity which we find in the Quarto are absent from the Folio, as if there were an attempt to make the world an even harsher place for man than in the original conception. Wolf (1998, p. 263) argues that both the language and imagery of King Lear attack Harsnett’s lack of good pity.

Orwell (1947; 1950, p. 46) focuses on renunciation: What exactly is the moral of Lear? Evidently there are two morals, one explicit, the other implied in the story. Shakespeare starts by assuming that to make yourself powerless is to invite an attack.…First of all, therefore, there is the vulgar, common-sense moral drawn by the Fool: Don’t relinquish power, don’t give away your lands. But there is also another moral. Shakespeare never utters it in so many words, and it does not very much matter whether he was fully aware of it. It is contained in the story, which, after all, he made up, or altered to suit his purposes. It is: Give away your lands if you want to, but don’t expect to gain happiness by doing so. Probably you won’t gain happiness. If you live for others, you must live for others, and not as a roundabout way of getting an advantage for yourself.

Figurative blindness and moral impercipience are frequent themes in criticism of this play in which the fathers’ tragic errors are based on failures to recognize the truth about their children and in which one father is literally blinded at the moment he learns the truth about his sons. Many critics find suggestions of a growth in moral awareness in the tragic protagonists. Ruskin (1852; 1909, 36:129): It was not without a meaning that in Lr. the catastrophe is brought on by an old man’s weakness and hastiness. I see that Shakespeare knew long ago…that the sorrow of the whole world is all the consequence of Mistake; and its chief miseries are brought about by small errors and misconceptions, trifles apparently, which our own evil passions leave us to be prey of. Wilson (1949, p. 46): The world closed in upon Lear because he did not maintain eternal vigilance against the active principle of evil. Egri (1946, p. 3): Blind trust leads to destruction is the premise of the play. Heilman (1948, pp. 28 ff.) sees a more far-reaching pattern of contrasts between shallow shrewdness and true wisdom: In Lr. we see, ultimately, the shrewd, sharp-thinking worldly people (Goneril, Regan, Edmund) balanced against a set of apparently helpless incompetents (Edgar, the Fool, Lear). Yet the former stop at a superficial understanding of things, and the latter come to profound insights.…[30] That [man] can ultimately learn, through representative suffering, is one of the fundamental intimations of the pattern of Lear. Sh. presents (p. 289) not only characters who retain their insight when the world argues compellingly for blindness, but also those who, partially stricken with blindness, can regain their lost intuition of truth. Lear and [290] Gloucester do not persist in error, as a cynic might make them do; rather they come to distinguish, one from another, their two kinds of children, and thus, at last, to distinguish, and make a right choice between, the kinds of moral capacity in themselves which are externalized in their children.…That the saving perspective, which brings evil into focus, is possible to man after he has made serious mistakes, is the play’s ultimate assertion. See also Idem (1964, ’Twere Best, pp. 89–98). Similarly Goddard (1951, p. 556): Lr. shows that there is a mode of seeing as much higher than physical eyesight as physical eyesight is to touch, an insight that bestows power to see things invisible to mortal sight as certainly as Lear saw that Cordelia lives after her death [sic]. Dye (1964, pp. 514–17): Lr.’s blurring of locale suggests an immense world (ultimate reality) necessarily dim and gloomy because of man’s inability to clearly comprehend reality.…[516] In this handy-dandy world, where trusted, indulged children turn on their parents like pelicans, and where evil forces prevail by deception…even the forces of good must work in disguise.…The Fool, whose common sense is so intricately played against Lear’s confusion and madness, represents yet another sort of misapprehension of the nature of man.…Through the illusion of death Gloucester is led to an acceptance of the afflictions of life—a form, however shadowy, of an acceptance of reality.…[517] Lear’s anxiety when faced with reality (both anxiety and reality symbolized in the storm) is excruciatingly intense. Blissett (1974, pp. 114 f.) similarly identifies recognition as a central theme: In Lr. recognition begins almost at once and is spread over the widest possible dramatic field; so perfect is it at the end that it is not the protagonist but the spectators, in so far as they continue to cling to the life of the self, who are in ignorance of their true condition.…[115] Lear comes to see what we see, and we come to see as he sees; at the end he dies healed and contrite, and we experience what a good death might be, though without any of its imaginable consolations. Brooke (1963, pp. 14–15) discusses the idea of seeing, well or ill…in both the relating and the distinguishing of the two plots [Lear’s and Gloucester’s]. Other critics who discuss the contrast between appearance and reality and the difficulty of attaining true insight include Fraser (1962), Clemen (1972, pp. 177–83), Rosenberg (1972, pp. 336–45), and Albrecht (1978, pp. 620–1). Jorgensen (1967, pp. 39 ff.): The prosaic theme of nosce teipsum run[s] beneath the spectacle of Lear’s suffering; the play is (p. 103) a typically Renaissance study of nosce teipsum. Nagata (1990, pp. 171 ff.) interprets Lr. as a tragedy of the exterior and the interior…a theme common to both Renaissance audiences and to contemporary readers. The tragedy (p. 170) is a result of the vision-oriented mentality which does not see the invisible interior. Gibbons (1993, p. 85) similarly finds that the contrast and conflict between outer and inner ways of seeing, between outer and inner imperatives, is fundamental to the play; it is a concern which is apparent also in The Taming of the Shrew and Titus Andronicus, two plays which are illuminated when compared to the later King Lear. Dundas (1985–6, pp. 48–56) sees a concern with sight and hearing as opposed alternative means of understanding: To set Lear…in the context of the paragone of the senses [of sight and hearing] is to grasp the step-by-step rejection of these senses, in order to affirm one thing: the heart and its affections as the seat of moral life.…[56] Shakespeare is at pains to undermine our faith in both speech and spectacle.

Not everyone accepts the idea that Lr. is fundamentally concerned with a theme of blindness and insight. Alpers (1962, pp. 133–4) criticizes Heilman’s interpretive schema: The data of the sight pattern simply are not there: in the numerous references to the eyes there is no dominating pattern of sight for insight.…[134] If we treat events and feelings in Lear as paths to or equivalents of insight, we necessarily dilute the intensity and human reality of all the suffering, malice, and love that we find in the play. And if we assume that moral truths are as clear as day, we find ourselves in the insufferable position of patronizing Lear for his moral confusions. Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 274–8) likewise denies that references to sight and blindness reveal the characters’ growth in moral insight; more significant is the act or failure of recognition: Lear does not attain his insight until the end of the fourth Act, and when he does it is climactic. This suggests that Lear’s dominating motivation to this point, from the time things go wrong in the opening scene, is to avoid being recognized. The isolation and avoidance of eyes is what the obsessive sight imagery of the play underlines. The blinding of Gloucester (p. 275) symbolizes (it instances) the psychic cruelty which pervades the play; but what this particular act of cruelty means is that cruelty cannot bear to be seen. It literalizes evil’s ancient love of darkness. This relates the blinding to Cornwall’s needs; but it is also related to necessities of Gloucester’s character.…[277] For if the failure to recognize others is a fail-[278]ure to let others recognize you, a fear of what is revealed to them, an avoidance of their eyes, then it is exactly shame which is the cause of his withholding of recognition.…For shame is the specific discomfort produced by the sense of being looked at, the avoidance of the sight of others is the reflex it produces. Carpenter (1991, pp. 204–5), considering memory and forgetting in the play, finds the treatment of awareness and recognition more paradoxical: King Lear is a play in which there seems at least the possibility that memory might lead to salvation, but (p. 205) forgetting becomes the prerequisite of forgiveness, and forgetfulness…a dominant characteristic.

Several critics, have seen significant implications in the characters’ putting on and taking off clothing and in references to clothing and nakedness in the dialogue of the play, beginning with Heilman (1948, pp. 69 f.), who perceives a systematic commentary upon appearances that are misread, upon the difficulties of perceiving the world truly, upon the failure—which may itself be a spiritual affirmation—to put up a good appearance, upon, that is, naïveté, defenselessness, innocence. This commentary appears in the clothes pattern, as components of which we find, on the one hand, larger dramatic elements such as the clothing and nakedness of characters, and, on the other, the recurrent imagery of clothes.…[70] [Edgar’s] nakedness becomes a symbol of that defenselessness in the world which Edgar has already shown and indeed of innocent people generally, unprotected by worldliness or pretense in a world swept by the storms of ambition and other uncontrolled emotions. But Edgar’s nakedness is also a defense, and in terms of the play the innocent have always a defense, if not against immediate enemies, at least against ultimate corruption. The naked wretches may ultimately have a better protection than those who are proudly arrayed in what the world values. To strip oneself may be folly; but nakedness may be an aid to understanding. The clothes pattern, like the sight pattern, contains its paradoxes, and thus is woven into the main fabric of meaning. Greenfield (1954, pp. 281–4): In contrasting gorgeousness and nakedness, Shakespeare used a motif of [282] ancient and highly respectable lineage.…[284] [The clothing motif] is wholly fused with the structure, the poetic language, and the physical representation of the play.…Morally, the motif is used…to contrast inferior and superior values. Rosen (1960, p. 43): In stripping off his clothes, Lear divests himself of the husks of appearance, the accidents of power and rank. Charney (1974, pp. 81–7): The nakedness-clothes theme is a moral polarity, in which the truth of nakedness is contrasted with the false appearances created by clothes.…[87] Clothes represent the values of society, of the status quo, of an externally, socially conceived morality, whereas nakedness is the traditional image of unadorned truth; of innocent and vulnerable babes, fools, and madmen; and also of a wild and bestial nature, untempered by law, kindness, or justice. See also Clay (1956), Waith (1975). Frye (1965, pp. 18–28) is skeptical that nakedness is ever a positive value in the play: In King Lear, the villains force disguises upon characters of whom we approve, and these disguises are symptomatic of the disorder that has been let loose upon the world.…[25] When Lear divests himself of power, and then is divested of the additions of a king, he is left without protection and, rather than finding himself, he discovers the extent to which his identity has depended upon things which he [26] bore but which were not himself.…Poor Tom, not the shepherd [of Golden Age pastoral], is the symbol of natural man, without clothes, without position or protection, outside the law.…[28] Lear’s nadir occurs when he accepts Edmund’s [naturalistic] view [of man’s animality]—which is a semi-philosophical equivalent for the attitudes of all the villainous characters—though his acceptance is a self-destructive gesture of despair, not a principle on which to act. Accordingly when Lear recovers sanity, he is dressed in fresh garments. Goldberg (1974, p. 129) sees clothing as only a metaphor for the mask by which [Lear] conceals and protects himself from any deeper self-awareness.…All his talk about it is an example of the very thing it represents to us: a guise to conceal and flatter reality. Rackin (1978, p. 94) finds the play’s treatment of clothing and nakedness to be radically ambivalent.

Kronenfeld (1998, pp. 74 ff.) criticizes many previous critics’ thematic interpretations of clothing and nakedness: Most of the critical discussions that focus on clothing in King Lear…attempt to locate the values of the play in nakedness and its apparent or presumed textual analogues—silence, the heart, what we feel, plainness—and do tend to seek a univalent meaning for nakedness. The authors of these discussions—like most critics—hear the text speak in terms of values that are still recognizable as values that overlap with their own, and at the same time, are values that may be [75] ascribed to the playwright’s culture.…Both these formal and these political readings tap into only a small part of the rich meaningfulness of concepts of clothing and nakedness; they would benefit from a more complete and more precise account of the relations of contiguity or contrast in which various types of clothing—decent, ragged, whorish, and so forth—appear, as well as of the referents to which such terms point in actual Renaissance use.…[90] Whether nakedness is seen positively, or negatively (as appears to be more often the case, on balance), an awareness of the paradoxical malleability of such categories as naked and clothed, plain and elaborate, was built into the culture.…

p.quote: Most of the critics of King Lear…read that text’s dichotomies largely in accordance with what appears to be our own cultural dichotomy between the falsely artful and the nakedly true (and the reasons why that dichotomy is salient for us may have something to do with the historical ascendancy of Protestantism in part, as well as with our living in a post-Romantic age). As such, these critics may downplay Lear’s serious concern with affronts to the deference and dignity marked by such symbols as retinues and gorgeous apparel [1569], his need for ceremonious affection [588], his need to reason not the need for the superfluous too strictly [1564–5]. They may fail to notice that Edgar who goes naked as Poor Tom, or speaks like [91] a peasant, can also appear fair and warlike [3098] in full military regalia, to defend his right and contest his brother Edmund’s in the eloquent language of formal challenge [3080–96]. They may also fail to notice that the plain-spoken Cordelia is described by the Gentleman who attends on her in the most courtly and elegant language.…The culture values both nakedness and proper clothing. Attempts to identify religious and political positions exclusively with one or the other may well be ill advised.…[234] The political affiliation of particular characters in the play and the political values of the play itself cannot be derived from its metaphors of nakedness and clothing.

div.p: The play’s representations of madness have also been related by critics to various moral, political, and philosophical ideas. Heilman (1948, pp. 180–1) discusses madness as a theme or motif recurrent in the language and action of the play: The madness pattern…is concerned with the ways in which men interpret phenomena, the meanings which they find in experience, the general truths which they consciously formulate or in terms of which they characteristically act, the kind of wisdom, or sophistication, which they achieve. What men see and what men believe, of course, are intimately related; yet it is possible to focus attention on what goes on in the foreground or on what lies behind. The latter is the special area of the madness pattern. Its materials are men’s philosophic attitudes to the world of which they are a part, their grasp, more specifically, of the problem of evil. Lear’s madness is, in one respect, a result of his inability to bring an obdurate universe under intellectual control: the difficulty is too great, and his mind fails. Gloucester, the typical man of despair, formulates a pessimistic position which makes [181] only suicide meaningful. The implied metaphysics of Lear’s elder daughters is…something quite different. Other minds mould the materials of life in still other ways. The play indeed puts together an almost schematic pattern of the relationships of minds to experience. In this structure, the madness of Lear is focal; hence the term madness pattern.

Other critics too find suggestions of a higher reason in madness. McFarland (1966, p. 160) sees Lear’s madness as an integral symbol of the humiliation of reason which constitutes the play’s paradoxical educative process. Kettle (1988, p. 76): The very word madness needs our thought. It can no more be taken for granted in Lear than in Hamlet. The more one examines the play the more one comes to feel that Lear’s madness is not so much a breakdown as a breakthrough. It is necessary. Similarly Erlebach (1995) argues that Lr. progresses from irrationality to suprarationality.

In contrast, Felperin (1977, pp. 101–5) finds in Lear’s madness the utter negation of meaning and morality: It is only Shakespeare’s protagonists—Hamlet, Othello, Lear, and Lady Macbeth—as characters whose role-playing is precarious and whose naked humanity is therefore most vulnerable, who are capable of true madness. Their foils are immune to madness, precisely because they are too thoroughly engrossed in their protective roles for an underlying self ever to be exposed in its naked frailty. Lear in his madness thus stands in contrast to Gloucester, who naïvely wishes he could go mad like Lear, mistaking madness for a protection against pain when it is in fact an exposure to it: [quotes 2732–9]. Like his nakedness—to which it is the psychological correlative —Lear’s madness also stands in contrast to Edgar’s stagy and conventional madtalk of sin and foul fiends. Edgar’s madness…is actually the antithesis of the true madness of Lear, since the latter arises from the breakdown of roles whereas the former is itself a role and therefore a protection against a maddening overperception.…It [102] has the status of a sign emptied of its significance and divorced from the realities of nakedness and madness to which it refers, the absent referent in both cases being supplied by Lear. Within the universe of Shakespearean tragedy, madness is thus the opposite pole of morality, a vision of undifferentiated anarchy as opposed to one of a wholly mapped-out order. Sh. (p. 105) leaves us in the end with not a choice of either morality and meaning or madness and absurdity, but more like an ultimatum of neither morality and meaning nor madness and absurdity, an ultimatum that becomes inescapable as a result of Lear’s own strenuous and futile effort to remain within the realm of choice.…The aporia toward which not only Lear, but Shakespeare’s other great tragedies, move represents the very negation of the possibility of unity, coherence, and resolution, of the accommodation that all our systems of explanation provide, be they pious or modernist, consoling or painful, older or newer.

Leed (1978, pp. 60–2) discusses madness as the liberation of passion.…[62] The tragedy is that it is only in madness that [Lear] can experience his full emotional life.…In Lear we have a figure through whom we see the richness that we must forgo in order to lead possible lives. For Salkeld (1993, pp. 100–11), Lear’s confusion [i.e., his madness] is as much political as cerebral, provoked by discontent with the old, absolutist system and a lack of any cogent, practical idea of how to produce anything new.…Absolutism is demonstrated as a sterile political doctrine having no conceptual progeny or institutional evolution. It marks a limit in the play, as it did in English politics at the outset of the seventeenth century, beyond which madness lies—the unthinkable—later to be realised in a revolution. At the close of the play this sterility is figured in the bodies of Lear and his dead daughters.…[101] Madness in the play is the effect of ideological failure. It (p. 103) occurs not within the minds of Lear and [104] Edgar but in their discourse and on their bodies.…[111] Lear’s stately dreams of paternalism, sketched in bare outline on the great map, are broken by a femininity represented in Goneril and Regan which has learned to use the political strategies of patriarchy for its own ends. Dumoulié (1994) compares Lr. to Seneca’s Hercules Furens and Strindberg’s The Father, focusing on the conjunction of madness with monarchical and patriarchal power; madness is merely the exacerbation of the discourse of power. (Fr.)

Critics also frequently discuss the theme of folly, most prominently represented by Lear’s fool, in moral terms. Welsford (1935, p. 269): Lear’s tragedy is the investing of the King with motley; it is also the crowning and apotheosis of the Fool. Heilman (1948, pp. 185–6): We have…two implied definitions of folly. As the word is used by Kent, it implies that the wise man will protect himself at least negatively, so to speak, by the mere avoidance of such needless actions as putting one’s enemies into power. As Goneril applies the word folly to Albany’s arguments, she implies that the wise man’s duty to himself is taking affirmative, self-aggrandizing action, regardless of who gets hurt in the process. Yet these definitions have one sense in common: folly is not looking out for oneself in the world. Looking out for oneself in a worldly sense is at best a slippery business, in which one may slide almost impercep-[186]tibly from thoughtless mistakes to an overlooking of injury to others. Thus in his folly, as in his introduction of a wrong scheme of values, we see the relationship between Lear and his daughters. At the same time we are fully aware of the ultimate moral distance between them. French (1959, p. 424) reads Lr. as a play about Christian folly, which is paradoxically to be interpreted as a kind of wisdom according to Paul and Erasmus. In contrast, Elton (1966, pp. 303–4) relates Lr.’s treatment of the theme to the Renaissance secularization of folly found in (p. 304) Erasmus, Rabelais, Franck, [and] Bruegel. Reibetanz (1977, p. 95) likewise refers to Erasmus: Shakespeare uses the tradition [of moriae encomium] to support a process of characterization involving intense moral oppositions; he creates a pattern of references to fools and folly that reinforces these oppositions. Involved in our experience of King Lear is an Erasmian anatomy of humanity, a distillation of mankind into those who are wise fools and those who are vicious fools. In contrast, Colie (1974, Energies, pp. 139 ff.) focuses on biblical contexts: Though the play condemns the folly proscribed in Proverbs, it praises the folly prescribed by Paul (1 Cor. 1). Folly does not bring rewards on earth, but it can, somehow, bring spiritual comfort.…[140] The deep undercurrent of spiritual language running through the play, its reference largely to the stoical books of the Old Testament, provides some holdfast upon the idea, at least, of moral order, to remind us, through all the shifting of fortune and point of view, that moral order is an ideal that society cannot afford to let go. The play does not refer to a transcendent morality at all—rather, it produces a rockbed morality, fundamental if comfortless and unyielding, a minimum prescription for social survival.…[141] The morality is simple not because life is uncomplicated, but because it is not; because only a morality forged to maximum economy upon the anvil of cruel experience—the experience of Job, of captive Israel, of the Preacher, of Lear—is appropriate to the incalculable hazards between birth and death.…From the language of paradox, beloved of the rigorous stoics, fused with that resonant language celebrating human endurance, the proud magnificence of oppressed Israel, Lear draws much of its strength. Evans (1990, p. 4) discusses the theme of Erasmian folly in a Christian reading of the play: Shakespeare used both the secular and the Christian folly themes: the former more obvious in the beginning of the play—the destructive folly of self-love, pride, and anger—and the latter at the end, after Lear has traversed the dark kingdom of madness and found new life in the redemptive folly of Cordelia. Lukes (1980, pp. 40–1) relates folly to the political limits of liberating laughter: In the case of Lear’s fool, and that of Lear as fool, the lack of serious preoccupation with convention that distinguishes them as fools entails an inability or [41] unwillingness to function effectively in the physical world. For other discussions of folly in Lr., see , , .

Coleridge (1930, 1:62) observed that Old age…is itself a character in Lr., and some critics have discussed moral themes related to old age in the play. Heilman (1948, pp. 135–6): In King Lear we find…a twofold view of age. On the one hand age is allied with Nature: it has a certain position to which a certain response is obligatory. If man adheres to the order of the whole, he cannot withhold from age what is its due from an ordered humanity—respect and loving kindness. On the other hand, age becomes an isolated fact whose significance lies only in its relevance to the situations of those who must deal with it, and they are under no obligation to apply to it any other standard than that of interest. Their view is pragmatic; the pragmatists are Goneril, Regan, and Edmund. Nearly all the other characters in the play regard [136] age as having established rights within the realm of humanity. These characters are those who understand Nature as nomos, and in whom…there is a strong religious sense. Elton (1966, pp. 241, 243): in Lear old age stands for a code of values.…[243] Old, with its connotations of primogeniture, legitimacy, and hierarchy, has in Lear, as in Macbeth, a eulogistic sense. Spens (1916, p. 100), in contrast, sees Lr. concerned with the pathos of the passing of virile manhood.

Critics have also found in the language of the play a particular concern with evaluation and quantification, which they also relate to the moral vision of the play. Heilman (1948, p. 158) identifies a motif he calls the values pattern, which involves the existence throughout the play of an evaluative attitude to life. Experiences, kinds of possession, qualities, physical properties, and so on, are not merely named, or dealt with passively as they occur in the plot; but often, by a rather unobtrusive use of language, their value to man is suggested. We are reminded, repeatedly, of the preciousness of parental and filial affection, of judgment, of sight and insight, of compassion; of the world’s attitude to poverty; of misfortune as a producer of insight. By these means the play always maintains our consciousness of its concern with the problem of values. Elton (1966, pp. 123–4) relates the moral theme to the history of ideas: In the seventeenth century’s new atomistic and fragmented universe, all in pieces, all coherence gone, the hard clarities of number began to be shored up against the frustrating mysteries of providence: if humankind could not know, it could at least reckon.…[124] in Lear those characters who are busily quantifying mystery finally divide up nothing and at the end become, like the hero of the first act, an O without a figure. For it is an irony of calculation that precision is ultimately meaningless under the ambiguous pudder of the thunder and within a shifting world without a frame. Both the villains’ ethic of calculation and the hero’s hubristic quid pro quo are ironically thrown up against the screen of cosmic ambiguity. In Shakespeare, as in Sophocles, the self-confident pursuer and measurer becomes the thing enigmatically pursued and measured, but by mysterious divinities themselves beyond rational reckoning.

Hawkes (1995, pp. 32 ff.) relates the concern with evaluation and quantification to the themes of reason in madness and wise folly: Lear certainly reaches and goes beyond the limit of his rational faculty. However, the effect of that is to reveal how limited a notion of that faculty has hitherto engaged him whereas (p. 33) the concept of a superior form of reasoning is firmly rooted in the character of Cordelia from the beginning.…Lear’s response to Cordelia’s non-rational rejection of an assessing process that would have made her rich is to brand his daughter foolish in the extreme. Of course, by that token, he also links her with the official representative of foolishness in the play.…[35] The Fool will speak of values which exist above the rational level on which they can be known or shown, and which outstrip the computation of Lear’s Nothing will come of nothing precisely because of that: [quotes 647–9, 656–7]. In fact, the Fool’s mockery of Lear’s arrogant mathematics is virtually overt, pointing directly to the crime that Lear has committed in equating the value of land with that of love.

Jones (1995, pp. 171–80) also finds that Sh. was sensitive to quantity in King Lear,…[176] a mental itch which is also a symptom of something else.…[180] The very marked tendency of [F/Q] variants to cluster round quantity is the statistical alter ego of the author’s breath on the page.…[The] significance [of these variants] is at once affirmed and unexpounded because unexpoundable. Hopkins (1994, p. 37) sees a conflict between the play’s moral treatment of the theme of quantification and the practice of academic literary criticism: Our very skills as readers…serve to militate against the degree to which we can intelligently read King Lear, since in order to align ourselves with the pro-qualitative, anti-quantitative stance which Cordelia appears to be taking we will be forced to work against our own preconceived beliefs about duplication and multiplication; as decoders trained specifically in the detection of themes, we too keep score, at exactly the same time as we are disapproving of Lear for doing so. For other discussions of evaluation and quantification, see Fowler (1988), Freeman (1993), Marienstras (1993).

Many critics of Lr. have found in the play not only a concern with a growth in moral awareness on the part of the protagonists but a positive affirmation of the idea that suffering leads to such moral growth or, further, that suffering leads to spiritual purification, an idea they see demonstrated in the experiences of both Lear and Gloucester. Reed (1855, pp. 359 ff.): The tragedy teaches the restoration of Lear’s moral nature.…[374] Surely we are taught that—There is in mournful thoughts a power to virtue friendly [qtd. from Wordsworth, The Excursion]. Especially influential is the assertion of Bradley (1904, p. 285), that Lear is redeemed by suffering: Should we not be…near the truth if we called this poem The Redemption of King Lear, and declared that the business of the gods with him was neither to torment him, nor to teach him a noble anger, but to lead him to attain through apparently hopeless failure the very end and aim of life? C. F. T. Brooke (1913, pp. 96–7): Viewed in its widest significance, the drama is a record of the schooling of Lear’s self-love.…The chaos of meanness gives place to a universe whose good is ordered from above, where selfishness and malice become the agents of chastisement and regeneracy. It is (p. 97) the story of [Lear’s] redemption.

Knight (1930, pp. 214–16): It is a play of creative suffering. Mankind are working out a sort of purgatory. The good ones know it; the bad seem not to.…[215] Mankind in Lear are continually being ennobled by suffering. They bear it with an ever deeper insight into their own nature and the hidden purposes of existence.…In some strange way the suffering they endure enriches them, brings them peace.…[216] We watch humanity, pained and relieving pain, and finding peace. Gloucester’s purgatory was contingent on his first lending aid to Lear and raising the hate of the adverse party: thus an act of goodness buys the inestimable gift of purgatorial agony. Chambers (1940, p. 48): Lear and Gloucester, led by Kent and Cordelia and Edgar, climb the mountain of Purgatory. And like the souls in the Purgatorio (xi, 31–3), in the midst of their own crushing sorrows, Lear and Gloucester, Kent and Edgar and Cordelia are praying and thinking for others—[quotes 1809]. We begin to see the world as Keats saw it—not so much a Vale of Tears as a Vale of Soul Making, till Lear, consoled, ends by teaching patience to Gloucester and to Cordelia. Likewise Fraser (ed. 1963, p. xxii): Lr.’s primary story is…the ascent of the King as he climbs the Mountain of Purgatory and is fulfilled. Idem (1962), pp. 131–4: The play is a kind of Commedia.…[133] Lear puts on the new man.…[134] And grace is bestowed on him. Lothian (1949, pp. 27 ff.): Reduced to its simplest analysis…the spire of meaning in this play is the spiritual history or regeneration of King Lear and the tremendous wrench with which it is effected.…[79] It is in Lear’s mind that the tragedy is perceived, in his soul that it is experienced; his words provide the light by which we read the events. Siegel (1955, p. 326): The suffering of Gloucester and Lear is…more than punishment; it is a purgatory which burns away their previous selfishness. Adversity brings for the good the miracle of love, a heightening of their humanity. Kernan (1966, p. 64): The fall from the cliff stage-managed by Edgar in 4.6 dramatizes the truly miraculous salvation found by the wanderers and outcasts on the heath. All their lives are miracles in the sense that, just as they thought their humanity was about to disappear into bestiality and nothingness, they discovered their human reality in a way they had never expected. Birenbaum (1983; 1989, p. 256) discusses that ultimate ripeness towards which the play evolves, a ripeness that grows in agony, old age and death, for such knowledge is the source of love. Rice (1984, pp. 50–60) also finds the play to be redemptive though not doctrinally Christian. Kettle (1988, pp. 74–8) describes a regeneration consistent with Marxist materialism: [Lear’s] story, put in its simplest terms, is the story of his progress from being a king to being a man, neither more nor less. It is a story so fearful and yet so wonderful that all human society is shaken by the terrible beauty of it and at its supreme moments man and the universe are seen in relationships which it is scarcely possible for words other than Shakespeare’s own to describe.…[78] The new humanity which Lear achieves is not simply a self-knowledge acquired by introspection or any kind of mystical or religious experience; it is an outlook gained through experience and action.…The experience results in a turning upside-down, handy-dandy, of accepted social assumptions. Hawkins (1991, pp. 181–5): King Lear is a tragedy of regeneration, of rebirth.…[183] The disintegration of [Lear’s] old self releases new and tremendous energies; each step down into madness marks an access of awareness and spiritual power; death and regeneration go on simultaneously.…[185] Lear is driven to the very limits of suffering—and then beyond—that he may see and know the meaning of the love he claimed as his right at the beginning of the play. Other critics who discuss purgative suffering and spiritual regeneration include Snider (1887, p. 174); Laffan (1904); Taylor (1907, pp. 221–4); Balmforth (1925, pp. 70–81); Tomlison (1925, p. 452); Ashwell (1926, pp. 145–64); Wilson (1929, pp. 40–2); Bethell (1944, pp. 52–61); Harbage (1947, p. 176); Traversi (1952, pp. 221–6); Muir (ed. 1952; 1972, pp. xlix ff.); Spalding (1953, pp. 148–57); Danby (1961, pp. 69–72), Holloway (Correspondence, 1961, pp. 168–9), Muir (Correspondence, 1962, pp. 68–9); Srinivasa Iyengar (1964, pp. 470–92); Schumann (1965, pp. 200–1); Harrison (1967, pp. 662–71); Kampmann (1972, pp. 53–75); Sharma (1975); Hills (1976, passim); Grimes (1983, p. 88); Jorgensen (1985, passim); Beyer (1991, pp. 225–41); Fabiny (1994, pp. 461–78).

Many of the critics who find purgative suffering in Lr. also find in the play an assertion not only of the value of Love but of its triumph. Beale (1881, p. 59): The subject of the play then is not personal affection, but that loyal love or piety which draws us first to those who are nearest, as members of one family, or state, or church, but afterwards binds us to all whose needs we can fill, unites us to all humanity. Its bonds are not broken by sin, it is a Christlike redeeming love, which must mingle with sorrow, ere suffering can purify. Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, pp. 45–6): That Lear’s triumph is short-lived, makes it no less a triumph.…[46] It is blessing, forgiving, sacred love, that behind all encircles the rolling world. Walters (1889, p. 74): The play…ends in the redemption of man through the supreme triumph of woman’s love. Luce (1907, pp. 308, 426): Briefly, I take this…to be the lesson of King Lear—There’s nothing we can call our own but love.…[426] Love, far from being destroyed by the tragedy, is more than triumphant; it is actually created.…There is no poem more sublime in its ethical purpose than King Lear. Knight (1930, p. 225): Human life is shown as a painful, slow struggle, in which man travails to be born from animal-nature into his destined inheritance of human nature and supreme love.…The primary persons in Lear, good and bad, die into love. Clarke (1934, p. 380): The chief justification for Cordelia’s death—both dramatically and poetically—is to be found…in the quality of the father’s and daughter’s love for each other, a quality which constitutes not Lear alone, and not Cordelia alone, the true hero of the tragedy, but Lear-and-Cordelia as a third entity, greater than either. Chambers (1940, pp. 49–52): King Lear is, like the Paradiso, a vast poem on the victory of true love.…[52] As the world vanishes from Gloucester and Lear and Kent, their strings of life begin to crack in a passion of love which, after all they have suffered, they cannot sustain. This world passes away, and the fashion of it, and we are left, as at the end of the Divine Comedy, with The love that moves the sun and all the stars. Spencer (1943, p. 150) cites Lear’s recovery into love. Sisson (1962, pp. 96–8): The end of the play is surely the triumph of love, of positive goodness.…[98] It seems to be the true conclusion of King Lear that power and justice, human or divine, are none of them ultimately important after all. Lyons (1968, p. 117): The recognition of the value of the love shared by Lear and Cordelia, her forgiveness and their mutual compassion, transcends the image of the dying Lear who imagines that Cordelia lives. Cox (1969, p. 10): Lr. celebrates love in all human relationships. Hiramatsu (1973–4, pp. 33–4): Lr. (p. 34) is a tragedy of love produced from the Renaissance contradictions between (p. 33) self-devotional [i.e. self-sacrificing] love,…a product of the psychological stability of the people who were satisfied with their sense of belonging to the medieval systematic order, and egotistic self-love, a product of a sense of free competition of the people who were exerting themselves to escape from the medieval constraints to acquire personal freedom. Everett (1989, pp. 72–3): The heart of the tragedy is that passion which moves bad and good alike [i.e., love].…The characters’ continually calling on gods tells us less about what Lear calls divinity than of what these human beings themselves make of their love.…[73] Shakespeare’s tragic centre…lies in the suffering of the good [characters] who are caught at the crossing of love with power. See also Knights (1955), Champion (1976).

That religious concerns are central to this play is clearly indicated by the number of times the characters raise questions about the gods or appeal to them. Unsurprisingly, then, specifically religious language is used by a number of critics who find in the action of the play a redemptive pattern like that suggested by Bradley—not a specifically Christian redemption of the immortal soul but a vaguer kind of moral or spiritual regeneration. Turnbull (1892, p. 59): Like the great Greek tragedian with Œdipus, our poet has recourse here to a religious procedure, of which there are three distinctly defined stages of development to be noticed. There is first the process of purification, effected by the awful ordeal of pain and passion through which he is compelled to pass. Then there is the deliverance and restoration of the care-clouded brain and child-wounded soul, through the sacred balm of a daughter’s love. And, finally, there is the consecration of the aged and weary hearted Lear in death. It might almost be said that the apotheosis and martyrdom of the eponymous hero of the poem are one. To use his own words when speaking of the captive Queen Cordelia, it is upon such sacrifices alone that the gods themselves throw incense. This is the spiritual motive that controls the tragedy. This is the supreme fact in the field of vision on which Shakespeare’s curiosity fastens; the chief centre of interest for his imagination and ours. Sheldon (1897, p. 215): In the last two acts of the play Shakespeare gives us the story of a redemption and a picture of a Paradise Restored.

Other critics discuss the significance of the religious experience of the characters of the play, who frequently importune the pagan gods of the play world or at other times affirm or question the benevolence of these gods. Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 269–71): Each of the principal personages of the play is brought into presence of those mysterious powers which dominate life, and preside over human destiny; and each according to his character is made to offer an interpretation of the great riddle. Of these interpretations, none is adequate to account for all the facts. Shakspere (differing in this from the old play) placed the story in heathen times, partly, we may surmise, that he might be able to put the question boldly, What are the gods? Edmund…discovers no power or authority higher than the will of the individual, and a hard trenchant intellect.…[270] His self-indulgent father is, after the manner of the self-indulgent, prone to superstition; and Gloucester’s superstition affords some countenance to Edmund’s scepticism.…Edgar, on the contrary…discovers that the gods are upon the side of right, are unceasingly at work in the vindication of truth, and the execution of justice.…And as Edgar, the justiciary, finds in the gods his fellow-workers in the execution of justice, so Cordelia, in whose heart love is a clear and perpetual illumination, can turn for assistance and co-operancy in her deeds of love to the strong and gentle rulers of the world: [quotes 2763–4]. Brink (1895, pp. 243–4) sees Sh. affirming the ultimate goodness of the world order in the play’s references to the gods: In the fate of its inhabitants is seen clearly the hand of Nemesis: the wicked fall victims to their own crimes; but is there not also revealed the ruling of a benign Providence in the fortunes of Lear, and, above all, in the lot of Cordelia?…The poet does not deny a Providence,—he believes in a divine government of the world,—but he is content to worship in humility the mystery in which it enshrouds itself. He paints the world as he sees it, and it appears dark to him; but it is at night that the stars become visible.…The optimism which the poet does not renounce even in Lear is of a [244] purely ethical nature; he appeals to our conscience. In loud tones he preaches the duty of resigned endurance, of manly steadfastness, of strenuous moral conduct; he makes us feel how the Good, totally regardless of any outward success, is in itself a thing most real, to be striven for above all other things. He strengthens our faith in virtue and incites us to it in figures like that of Kent, and, above all, in the gracious and lofty figure of Cordelia; he animates us with hope in the eventual triumph of the good in this world in the fortunes of Edgar. Bradley (1904, pp. 271–3) sees Lr.’s concern with the gods as a source of the play’s sublimity and profundity: As we contemplate this world, the question presses on us What can be the ultimate power that moves it, that excites this gigantic war and waste, or, perhaps, that suffers them and overrules them? And in King Lear this question is not left to us to ask, it is raised by the characters themselves. References to religious or irreligious beliefs and feelings are more frequent than is usual in Shakespeare’s tragedies, as frequent perhaps as in his final plays. He introduces characteristic differences in the language of the different persons about fortune or the stars or the gods, and shows how the question What rules the world? is forced upon their minds.…[273] Almost throughout the latter half of the drama we note in most of the better characters a pre-occupation with the question of the ultimate power, and a passionate need to explain by reference to it what otherwise would drive them to despair. And the influence of this pre-occupation and need joins with other influences in affecting the imagination, and in causing it to receive from King Lear an impression which is at least as near akin to the Divine Comedy as to Othello.

Knight (1930, pp. 204 ff.) sees a subtle and gradual progression towards spiritual significance in the play’s references to the gods: The gods so often apostrophized are…slightly vitalized: one feels them to be figments of the human mind rather than omnipotent ruling powers—they are presented with no poetic conviction. And exactly this doubt, this questioning, as to the reality and nature of the directing powers, so evident in the god-references, is one [205] of the primary motives throughout the play. The gods here are more natural than supernatural; the good and bad elements in nature are, too, natural, not, as in Macbeth, supernatural. Lear is throughout naturalistic. The gods are mentioned in various contexts where humanity voices, under stress of circumstance, its fears or hopes concerning divinity: they are no more than this. However, (p. 208): The return to nature which [Lear] endures in the play’s progress paradoxically builds in him a less naturalistic theology.…Slowly, painfully, emergent from the Lear naturalism we see a religion born of disillusionment, suffering, and sympathy: a purely spontaneous, natural growth of the human spirit, developing from nature magic to God. On the gods as merely embodiments of natural forces, see also Bacon (1857, p. 243) and McAlindon (1991, p. 193).

Other critics also find in Lr.’s references to the gods an affirmation of belief in a transcendent supernatural order. Grace (1942, pp. 434, 442): Shakespeare’s understanding of tragedy is directly related to his cosmic sense—a sense that enables him to see the relations of the particular to the universal, of the microcosm to the macrocosm, not only in a contemporary but also in a highly personal, vivid way.…[442] King Lear shows the pitiless insignificance of a man cut off from an organic supernaturalism and left at the mercy of a nature of which he is not undisputed master. Fairchild (1944, p. 45): By wiping out social institutions in King Lear, Shakespeare cleared his way to bring natural man into direct relation with the ultimate powers of the universe. Heilman (1948, pp. 271–8): Passages which indicate religious attitudes…are sufficiently numerous to evidence a pervading consciousness of deity, not a self-conscious adoption of suitable modes of religious expression, but a largely unconscious, habitual reliance upon divine forces whose primacy is unquestioned; the passages occur most frequently in the lines of the chief tragic characters, who must be chiefly concerned with the fundamentals of human experience; and enough of them are spoken by other characters (Kent, Albany, Edgar) to make clear the religious climate of the action.…[277] The religious pattern, through which we see not only an age that is technically pagan but also a play that is pervaded by Christian influences, exhibits the kind of belief which makes [278] it possible to assert the lesser importance of the world. That is, there is a realm of eternal law and justice, of enduring reality which demands the loyalty of mortals, and through that loyalty they achieve their humanity. This achievement is the ultimate one, no matter what man’s fate in the world. Hole (1968, p. 233) likewise finds in Lr. the abiding presence of [a religious] world order, manifested in the characters’ constant awareness of the gods and their influence on human life. Goddard (1951, pp. 527 ff.) also describes the play as religious: King Lear is a story of how a king in the worldly sense became a king in the fairy-tale sense, of how a bad king became a beautiful man.…[529] Its innermost secret is religious.…[533] There is a spiritual lightning that illuminates the lost soul.…[534] Angels…come to the aid of this stricken monarch.…[556] King Lear and his child were lifted up into the realm of the gods. Stauffer (1949, pp. 190–1, 209) sees the affirmation of a supernatural order which is inscrutable but ultimately benevolent: What power or powers rule this world? Shakespeare has been accused of mocking ambiguity. Are they the conventional Roman gods, Apollo, Jupiter, Juno, that are called on in oaths? Or is [191] it Nature, whom Edmund in his crude materialism takes as his goddess? Or is it a fatalistic world ruled by fear and superstition as Gloucester sometimes believes, a world in which omens are potent and planetary influence has cracked nature into ruinous disorders?…Or is the governor that hate which Gloucester, his eyes torn out, sees so clearly: human beings are flies mutilated and destroyed for the amusement of the callow gods. Or is Fortune tiptoe on a tickle globe, blindfolded, her wheel crazily spinning? All these conceptions, in the larger framework, are symbols of carelessness, ignorance, unrest, disease, or pain. Shakespeare deliberately mutes the Christian references or overtones and pluralizes and depersonalizes the heavens and the gods. Fortune with her wheel may be the intermediary between divinity and man, as she had been in the millenium since Boethius; but above Fortune are inscrutable powers. As all the references to the gods build up, they appear clearly as implacable instruments of justice and age-old order. But also they are allied with patience and mercy.…[209] The tragedy generates miracles through misery. But the miracles are no less true than the misery; and the gods, kind and avenging, seek to give losses their remedies. See also Charlton (1948) and Ginger (1964). Whereas Elton (1966, pp. 329–34) finds the gods of the play world to be either deaf to human prayers or else indifferent or malicious, Williams (1986, p. 361), examining the responses that the gods make to specific petitions addressed to them, finds a pattern in those responses that sustains a positive view of this pagan world, even an optimistic one.
