Similarly Grene (1992, pp. 191–2): What we experience at the end of a performance of King Lear is not an assured conviction of the empty absurdity of the world, but a deeply troubled awareness of its inscrutability.…[192] King Lear drives its audience…towards the essential emotions that animate belief itself.

A number of 20th-c. critics discuss Lr. as a specifically Christian drama in which, despite the pagan setting, Sh. presupposed his audience’s shared assumptions of a universe governed by divine law, of love as sacramental and redemptive, of suffering as purgative and leading to faith and hope as well as charity, and of a system of providential guidance including apocalypse and grace. Bethell (1944, p. 59): May we not at least suspect Shakespeare of deliberately intending to present a world without revelation, in order to determine how far human nature could penetrate its mysteries and achieve religious and moral order apart from the gift of supernatural grace?…It is unlikely that Shakespeare went momentarily pagan for the writing of King Lear…but more than likely that he should clinically isolate the pagan mind in order to work out a particular problem. Danby (1949, pp. 204–5): Lr. is not only our profoundest tragedy; it is also our profoundest expression of an essentially Christian comment on man’s world and his society, [205] using the terms and benefitting by the formulations of the Christian tradition. King Lear, I feel, is at least as Christian as the Divine Comedy. Maxwell (1950, pp. 142, 147): King Lear is a Christian play about a pagan world.…Each character creates—or, if that is too strong a word, attaches himself to—a religion which reflects his nature.…[147] A Christian outlook is both presupposed and expressed. Rosier (1954, p. 574): To call Lear a pagan drama, a non-Christian tragedy…[is] nothing less than wrong-headedness.…Underlying the basic theme and structure of the play…there is an implicit context of the Christian universe in Elizabethan terms.…The universe as a whole and in its component parts, figured in the metaphor of the great chain of being, is governed by law: the lex aeterna. Speaight (1955, pp. 91 ff.): There is, of course, a profound teaching in Lear,…the teaching of the Cross.…[93] Lear’s divesting himself of kingship…like all sin…was an offense against unity.…[94] [In 1.1] Cordelia’s love is expressed in sacramental and not in sentimental terms. To apply to her profession the canons of romantic emotionalism is disastrously to misconceive the nature of Shakespearian agape.…[100] In Goneril, as in Iago, we meet the mystery of evil.…[121] In a metaphysical sense…Edgar and Cordelia are one. They are the male and female, the active and passive counterparts of a single redemptive process. They answer, for those who have ears, the tragic agnosticism of the play. Turner (1959, p. 27) calls Lr. a study in the redemption of man…strikingly comparable to the Divine Comedy of Dante. Hathorn (1960) interprets the play as an antinaturalist affirmation of Christian faith. Whitaker (Mirror, 1965, pp. 210–28) argues that Lr. expresses the Christian concept that God permits suffering to try and to refine the natures of men.…[213] Through the purgatorial experience of suffering and of having brought home to them their error, both Lear and Gloucester find redemption, not in the order of nature…but in the order of grace.…[228] This play is pre-Christian in time, and the word salvation is never uttered; but it is…profoundly Christian in thought. Stein (1969, pp. 106–52): In the mystery of the play’s catharsis…[107] Shakespeare reveals the rebirth of hope within a truly absolute despair.…[125] Shakespeare takes us to the extreme verge, as Pascal does, and ruthlessly insists that we distinguish and choose between forced hope and the force of hope.…[128] The deaths that conclude the play are empowered to evoke (though not to presume or assert) an incipient eschatological perspective.…[131] Lear is, indeed, like the Pensées, an exposure in depth of radical antinomies—pointing to faith.…[145] Cordelia’s life and death fall within a significatory pattern—incomplete at the point where the play ends (the point where common sense ends)—defined by the Gospels—and whose completion lies beyond common sense.…[152] Such a catharsis can only be religious. Battenhouse (1969, pp. 272 ff.): The total story…has a kind of echoing parallel to biblical history.…[273] The developing drama is thus thoroughly realistic in its accounting for evil, while at the same time not pessimistic as regards man’s potentialities for regaining moral health.…[275] The ultimate outcome of a quest for infinite love can hardly be dramatized except as in a glass darkly; hence the final events in Lear have the quality of apocalyptic signs.…With due proportion they figure the possibilities the poet posits for man’s development under divine providence.…Moreover, the coast of Dover seems to have significance as moral geography.…Once the play’s action has revealed at England’s geographical center of wild midlands an apocalypse of tyranny in the blinding of Gloucester in his own castle, all the characters in the play find themselves moving eastward, as if toward a place and moment of more final judgment and accounting.…[293] Probably no Shakespearean play illustrates so well as King Lear the thesis of St. Augustine in the City of God, Book I, that calamities are profitable, both for refining away the selfishness in good men and exterminating the corruption of wicked men.…[302] Shakespeare, by placing his story in primeval times, perhaps wished to suggest to his Elizabethan audience the pit from which they were digged. That is, they could here review the agonizing quest that would be necessary to make progress again toward Christian mystery, should England ever be deprived of its Christian heritage.

Fortin (1974, pp. 316–21): Sh.’s object seems to be to explore…whether it is pos-[317]sible to discover supernatural dimensions in human experience.…[319] A central intuition of the play [is] that rational and natural explanations of evil are inadequate. Likewise the good characters’ (p. 320) unpublished virtues, rising beyond self-interest and even reaching at times the splendid absurdity of sacrifice, point to a dimension of grace in human behavior, to some kind of discontinuity between man and nature—a motiveless benignity as incomprehensible as the motiveless malignity of the villains.…[Although] King Lear cannot be said to affirm unequivocally the traditional Christian world view,…[321] the play [suggests] that the religious hypothesis is at least as convincing as the natural hypothesis, which seems incapable of accounting for the mystery of human vice and virtue. Idem (1979, pp. 114–18): To consider the secular reading as exclusively valid is as much an act of dogmatic assertion as is the comforting vision offered by the Christian interpreters, since the assertion in either case [115] is based upon a selection of evidence as well as a selective interpretation of that evidence.…[118] For the Christian critic the opaqueness of the Lear world is no insurmountable obstacle, for the very structural ironies which purportedly impeach the Christian worldview provide, when seen from a different perspective, a strong support for a Christian reading.…The ending of King Lear…presents a demythologized Christianity that offers mystery rather than justice and that is founded upon hope rather than fulfillment.

Davis (1974, p. 134): Lr. offers an insight into the very heart of [Christian sacrifice]. Reibetanz (1977, p. 120): Lr. directs us to a realm of meaning that exists outside the Lear world…primarily from the association of Cordelia with Christ. Milward (1975, pp. 7 ff.): If ever [8] work of human literature breathed an intense faith in God, it is surely King Lear,…[38] the tragedy in which [the] theme of innocent suffering and sacrifice [pervasive in Sh.’s comedies and tragedies] is brought to its climax of pity and indignation.…[73] [Various] threads of thematic meaning from the Parable of the Prodigal are…drawn together by [Sh.] in [Lr.]. Here he almost seems to stand the Parable upside down, as in both the main plot and the secondary plot it is the fathers—Lear and Gloucester—who prove to be the Prodigals, and their respective children—Cordelia and Edgar—replace the father in the Parable by welcoming their own fathers back after a period of wandering and destitution.…[89] Amid his sufferings in the storm [Lear] is not only a patient Job, but also a suffering Servant, despised and rejected of men, and (as he proclaims to the elements) more sinn’d against than sinning. Even at the height of his madness there remains in him the authority and royal nature of the Messiah.…[90] [In the] sacred tableau [of Lear holding dead Cordelia]…we may recognize in Lear, not only a child-changed father in a rever-[91]sal of roles from the Parable of the Prodigal Son, but also a woman-changed man, as the mother in him wells up towards his heart and he comes to represent Mary mourning over the body of her Son on Calvary in a stage image that recalls nothing so vividly as the Pietà of Michelangelo. Lynch (1986, p. 161): In some ways Shakespeare’s play may be even more Christian than its predecessor [Leir]. Whereas both dramas follow the morality pattern of sin, suffering, and redemption, Shakespeare’s tragedy depicts a process of spiritual growth that is more prolonged and profound. Cotterill (1995, p. 169) likewise notes its compatibility with Christian truth. Edwards (2000, pp. 18–29) sees the play’s vision as true to the Christian idea of a fallen world: Lr. is a play that pushes to a limit the moral discomposure of a world where good and evil are inextricable and conveys the desire to overcome an immense loss and a present lack, and the recognition of an as yet unobtainable transcendence.…[29] King Lear is surely an eminently Christian work, whose faith and hope are not in a future world but in this world where, if God seems absent, grace is present.

That Lr. affirms a specifically Christian providential order is maintained by several critics. Bickersteth (1946, pp. 156–70): However ugly, irrational, wicked, and therefore painful [the world of the play] may seem in itself…it does, in fact, when spiritually lived [157] with, compel us to accept without question its beauty, its reasonableness, and its moral worth. Sh. (p. 170) was unconsciously inspired by…some such myth as the Harrowing of Hell.…Divine love, symbolized by Cordelia, enters a kingdom already divided against itself, which is the Christian definition of hell.…It enters there as a disorganizing force, which must needs make the confusion yet more confounded before it can restore all things to order, as in the end it certainly will. Ribner (1958, pp. 34 ff.): King Lear is an affirmation of justice in the world, of a harmonious system ruled by a God who in his ultimate purpose is benevolent.…[35] All the elements of King Lear are shaped by the theme of regeneration which dominates the whole.…[53] In King Lear character and action are shaped by a controlling design, which is in itself an intellectual statement. In its totality King Lear asserts the perfection of God’s harmonious order and the inevitable triumph of justice, with the forces of evil preying upon and destroying themselves.…[54] Shakespeare affirms the possibility of human salvation, and he does this by placing in an imaginative setting the regeneration from evil of two aged men. Dunlop (1920, pp. 275–83): A tragedy of love in martyrdom,…[283] the drama as a whole amply justifies the providential order of the world. Merchant (1964, pp. 75–8) Lr. depicts a self-consistent universe within which it is possible to make judgements of value.…[78] The tragic end of Lear is given its final import by its setting within a traditional eschatology. Myrick (1964, pp. 62–70) sees a grimmer form of providentialism, which he calls Christian pessimism: The fact…that in King Lear Shakespeare raises the problem of evil with unexampled force does not distinguish his outlook from that of the most pious man in England.…[67] One by one, the five villainous characters in Lear are destroyed in the exact circumstances in which the Elizabethans had been trained to see and dread the judgment of an angry God.…[68] What to so many moderns suggests a merely irrational world would suggest to the Elizabethans the power of a superintending wisdom and justice.…[70] The dark view of man which we find in King Lear is normal in Elizabethan Christianity. Cheetham (1988, p. 63): Shakespeare plots a development from a pagan to a Christian theology, which…presents us with a divine power whose ways may be mysterious and inscrutable, which may not intervene to save the innocent or punish the wicked, as we might wish, but which is essentially caring and compassionate rather than vengeful and punitive, and without which life would be meaningless and chaotic. Kernodle (1989, p. 375): Not only the love and religious concern of the main characters but the very structure of the play is a magnificent assertion of order and meaning in the universe.

Others who interpret Lr. as both Christian and redemptive go even further, finding intimations of immortality for Lear and other characters. Thus Bridges (1925, p. 60) sees a suggestion of immortality at play’s end. The greater Lear does not die. Campbell (1948, p. 107): The old man’s heart breaks in a spasm of ecstasy. For only to earthbound intelligence is Lear pathetically deceived in thinking poor Cordelia alive. Those familiar with the pattern of the morality play realize that Lear has discovered in her unselfish God-like love the one companion who is willing to go with him through Death up to the Everlasting Judge. This knowledge enables Lear to meet Death in a state of rapture.…[108] Like Lear, Gloucester dies at peace and in hope. Like Lear, too, he is saved by contrition from eternal darkness. Weilgart (1952, p. 56): What characterizes this drama of decay more than any other tragedy of Shakespeare, is its pointing toward the world beyond. Lear has to be reformed before he is worthy to die. Siegel (1955, pp. 332–6): In Cordelia’s love, which finds no cause for ceasing in the injury he has done her, Lear has found the perfect pattern of love, which he is now able to see and follow. His education and redemption are now complete. But it is for heaven that Lear has been redeemed, not for earth.…Lear’s final conviction that Cordelia is alive might be regarded as the mysterious insight believed to be granted to a man on the point of death, the last blessing conferred upon him as he is kneeling by the corpse of his daughter.…[335] There is…hinted to the poetic imagination a miracle,…the redemption of Lear for heaven, a redemption analogous to the redemption of mankind, for which the Son of God had come down to earth.…[336] King Lear ends with a poetic suggestion of what was flatly presented in the morality plays. Ribner (1960, pp. 130 ff.): Death [promises] a reunion in heaven for Lear with the Cordelia who has preceded him there. If Lear’s final belief, as his heart breaks, that Cordelia lives is contrary to fact, this is of small significance, for Shakespeare’s audience could not doubt that she dwelt, in fact, where her father soon would join her. Kirby (1989, pp. 149–57): Shakespeare…[implies] that the crimes [the wicked characters] have committed…carry an eternal as well as temporal punishment—they are, indeed, cut off amid the blossom of their sins.…[153] [Gloucester, Kent, and Cordelia die] in a state of grace.…[156] It is unthinkable and illogical that [Lear] dies in despair.…[157] Lear dies of joy, not because he believes Cordelia to be alive, but because he knows that their last parting has come and has gone, and that he will never need to say goodbye to his beloved daughter again.

In contrast, other critics sees the play as Christian but not redemptive. Coursen (1976, pp. 237 ff.): The play is a history of the world…[238] from its pagan beginnings…to a Christian moment of repentance and forgiveness, and on into a world where invocations of deity reverberate against an emphatically dead sky…and where the Last Judgment delivers only a negative sentence.…[239] King Lear is a cosmic tragedy…because the earth is denied Lear’s insight into what he has learned.…[295] Lear has achieved a specifically Christian revelation. However, (p. 298): the final scene explicitly denies the providence Edgar arranges for Gloucester and cancels forever Lear’s awakening to a new dispensation.…[302] Cordelia’s death is not to be construed in any context of redemption or of hope. Guilfoyle (1990, p. 127): The symbolism reflects not the redemption of Lear but rather some aspects of the pattern of Christian salvation as it had been shown in the pantomime of the cycle plays. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 197): The play is not about the redemption of King Lear, but about his damnation; damned not on account of any sin he has committed, but, like the good pagans of Dante’s Inferno, condemned because he lives before Merlin (and Christ).…There is no pattern of spiritual development in the play. Basney (1994, p. 32): King Lear contains many actions clearly taken over from Christian experience without offering a cultural or historical redemption as its final vision.…[34] Shakespeare’s art is religiously anti-religious.…[35] The ending…seems to imply a Christian scepticism about the realization of ideals in cultural institutions like the state or the theater.

Some critics focus on particular Christian virtues. Danby (1952, pp. 119–26) discusses Christian patience: Of the four people in King Lear who exhibit reactions to adversity within the traditional scheme [of Christian patience] two show patience and two defective patience. The group is meticulously balanced. Cordelia is the perfection of Christian patience that suffreth long and is kind. Her father is an instance of extreme falling-off—first into rage and then into madness. Gloucester and Edgar occupy a middle range between these two limits. The son is steadily patient. The father wavers on the edge of grace and despair and is only saved in the end by the ministrations of his son. Adumbrated in the Shakespearian pattern are Coverdale’s two spheres of nature and spirit.…[126] The Nature which ripens man through adversity is, by implication, the Christian rather than the heathen thing. Yellen (1984, pp. 457–64): Through suffering Lear learns the two great lessons of charity and humility, which have long been preached, if not always practiced, by Christianity.…[464] [A] sense of healing and goodness, of benediction and grace…pervades the closing scenes of the play.

Other critics relate the play to particular Christian sacraments or devotional practices. Cunningham (1984, pp. 9–16): Sh. draws upon the ancient rite of baptism…in [10] describing the renewal of the old king.…[16] In the darkness of the storm, Lear…puts off his clothes and figuratively goes into the waters, asking judgment of sin and calling down destruction upon it. Doebler (1994, pp. 161–8) refers to the traditional practices concerned with dying a holy death: In characterization, plot, and imagery, the play balances the old assumptions of the ars moriendi: sin and forgiveness, suffering and release, damnation and redemption. The very depth of despair an audience must feel when confronted with what the false children…can be, stripped of loyalty and true reason, undeserving of mercy, is designed to offer the opposing necessary glimpse of the manna of grace. The false children are on one level displacements of demons tempting to despair, while the true children are displacements of the guardian angels.…[168] The end of the play, however heartbreaking, would have illuminated for Shakespeare’s audience the life that transcends the material.

Others refer to particular theological doctrines. Levin (1959; 1976, p. 181): Perhaps the ultimate meaning of Gloucester’s fall [onto the stage in 4.6] is its symbolic gesture of expiation, reenacting his own original sin, as well as the fall of man and his consequent progression toward self-knowledge. Gaull (1967, pp. 334–9): Placing King Lear in the intellectual climate in which the play was conceived, one finds a conflict on the thematic level between two kinds of love: divine love, expressed in an ordered cosmic, social, and spiritual hierarchy, and erotic love, a kind of subterranean energy which is the source of chaos, disorder, and destruction.…[338] Edmund, the child of eros, serves not only as the voice of the anarchical group but also as the source of its daemonic energy.…[339] Lear’s insanity involves his recognition of the emotional basis of his relationship with Goneril and Regan, a love professedly filial but essentially corrupt, profane, erotic.…It is divine love, the love which created and maintained the cosmic order, embodied in Cordelia, which restores Lear to his rationality and to his royal position. Harris (1976, pp. 255 ff.), focusing on four different sorts of resolutions…in the final act of the play, finds that Lr. (p. 263) manifests the Christian conception of time which will make all things plain. According to Bryant (1977, p. 29), The pride, fall, and exile [of Nebuchadnezzar] provide the pattern for the first four acts of King Lear. Keefer (1988, pp. 147–8): Calvin’s God—who was for most purposes also the God of the Elizabethan Anglican Church, and [who is similar] to Blake’s tyrannical Urizen,…[148] is a pervasive presence in the play.…By a species of synecdoche it is Lear himself who makes us aware of this presence, and…the play incorporates a sustained dramatic meditation upon what Calvin called accommodation, the process by which a wholly unintelligible and incomprehensible deity represents himself, in human terms, to mankind.

For other Christian interpretations, see Gill (1937); Rogers (1953); Howse (1955, pp. 61–72); Oppel (1957, 1968, 1979); Rosati (1958, pp. 21 ff.); Dunkel (1958–9, pp. 359–65); Fraser (1962, passim); Hawkins (1963–4, pp. 3–9); Peck (1967); Schuster (1967); Rosinger (1968, pp. 491 ff.); England (1982); Butler (1992); Andic (1996); and (most baldly) Lloyd (1947, p. 530): At his bedside in Lent the Christian should have two books. If one of them is the Bible, the other is undoubtedly King Lear.

A Buddhist interpretation is offered by Howe (1994, pp. 182–7): King Lear has an astonishing moment in [4.6] when his orientation toward himself and the world seems very like a Buddhist’s.…[183] As his madness has passed its climax of rage and [184] reached catharsis, it has swept his self-belief away. He is no longer in anguish, therefore; his mood has quieted, even sweetened. He accepts the grotesque situation of the play and dissolves it into unimportance.…[185] He converts samsara to nirvana.…[187] He carries this wisdom back into his world of sanity in [4.7]. However, he cannot maintain this renunciation. Having found that Cordelia forgives and loves him, he falls into dependence on that love.

Some critics express skepticism about Christian readings of Lr. Orwell (1947; 1950, p. 47): The morality of Shakespeare’s later tragedies is not religious in the ordinary sense, and certainly is not Christian.…All of these tragedies start out with the humanist assumption that life, although full of sorrow, is worth living, and that Man is a noble animal—a belief that Tolstoy in his old age did not share. Everett (New, 1960, pp. 326–32): Those critics who find in the play either a partial, or a total Christian allegory, are alike in one thing, however different their respective approaches may be: this is an interest in such parts of the play as seem to make a statement that is differentiated from the plot (that is, the story as it would stand in a prose tale). They are interested in the kind of poetic statements which the play seems to make, in contradistinction from what actually happens.…It is obviously impossible to decide, simply, whether or not King Lear is a Christian play. She objects to Muir’s Arden introduction and studies by Knights, Chambers, and Danby as (p. 332) doctrinal and didactic. West (1960, pp. 58–9): The given morality of King Lear suits Christianity, certainly, and no doubt it suits many other creeds, but to feel its force in the play does not require a Christian account of it nor any account that [59] fits into a system.…Lear and Gloucester and Kent genuinely yearn toward universal order. But at their best by neither word nor deed can they do more than assert the given morality.

Other critics go further, arguing that the play’s tragic vision is too dark and pessimistic to accommodate a Christian world-view. Chambers (1926, pp. 245–8): It is worth observing with what care Shakespeare has arranged every detail of the play so as to give edge to his indictment of the forces that make sport of man’s nothingness. The plot, which deliberately rejects the Christian interpretation of the universe, is set in a pagan environment. The [246] heavens are invoked in a pagan terminology, as Nature, or under the names of the classic deities. Pains are taken, contrary to the usual disregard of anachronism in the plays, to avoid the introduction of Christian language or Christian sentiments. The source-play’s happy ending would not have suited Shakespeare’s design, because it would not have borne the burden of the final victory of evil. Raphael (1954, p. 361): Contra Danby, though the play may fit Christian ethics, it cannot fit Christian theology. Knoll (1957, p. 376): On a Christian basis, Shakespeare has erected a play not essentially Christian. Looking into the heart of darkness, Shakespeare finds human conceptions of right and wrong insufficient to explain the glory and the terror of human life.…Here the Elizabethan drama of choice is deserted in favor of the Greek drama of fulfillment. Stampfer (1960, pp. 1–10): Part of the poignance of King Lear lies in the fact that its issues, and the varieties of evil that it faces, are so central to Christianity, while it is denied any of the mitigation offered by a well-defined heaven and hell, and a formal doctrine of supernatural salvation.…[10] with Lear’s death, each audience, by the ritual of drama, shares and releases the most private fear to which mankind is subject, the fear that penance is impossible, that the covenant, once broken, can never be reestablished, because its partner has no charity, resilience, or harmony—the fear, in other words, that we inhabit an imbecile universe. Savvas (1966, p. 560–2): By the end of the play, we have realized that there are no longer any frontiers between the wise and the ridiculous, between the sane and the insane, between man and beast, or even between man and the gods.…There is no justice among men and there is no justice in the Universe. Men do not forgive and neither do the gods—this is a world without forgiveness.…[561] If Lear, or Gloucester, must suffer and endure in order to achieve wisdom, then wisdom or self-knowledge appear undesirable since they run parallel with madness, [562] torment, and death. Good and bad, under this light, are not only inseparable but indistinguishable. Frye (1967, p. 115): All we see is an old man dying of an unbearable pain. The hideous wrench of agony which the death of Cordelia gives to the play is too much a part of the play even to be explained as inexplicable. And whatever else may be true, the vision of absurd anguish in which the play ends is certainly true. Sewall (1967, p. 215): I see no resolution in this play; Edmund and the evil sisters are destroyed, to be sure; but so are Lear and Cordelia, and if their reward is heaven, Shakespeare says nothing whatsoever about it.…I see no Christian piety or transcending Christian spirit attending Lear on his quest any more than Starbuck’s piety influenced Ahab.…[Lear’s] daughters become the center of his monomaniac vision—his own peculiar white whale.…Cordelia with her holy water is a late arrival, and the metaphoric implications of her death are a bitterly ironic comment on her redemptive effect on her father. Coursen (1968, p. 438): Edgar’s efforts to translate the universe into a pattern of providence are denied. Kernan (1987, pp. 225–32): King Lear is the greatest literary theodicy written in English. However, (p. 232) theodicy fails in the end, for the play is unable to comprehend suffering and loss in some scheme of things.

Various critics challenge Christian interpretations of Lr. on the basis of viewing Christianity itself, with its promise of ultimate justice, as incompatible with the tragic vision of utter loss. Thus Barnet (1955, pp. 85–92) criticizes advocates of Christian tragedy (if there is such a genre) for asserting that Shakespeare’s dramas, too, have their note of regeneration. However, (p. 92) although Lear learns humility through suffering, at the conclusion he is still capable of the misconceptions and unstoical emotion which are the stuff of tragedy. An audience feels not merely relief for his death but also horror for his ultimate false perception that Cordelia lives.

Rosenberg (1966, pp. 135–46): Christian allegorical interpretations convert horror into purgation, agony into ecstasy, mutilation and murder into salvation.…[136] Although there are no dogmas in Lear—only the pitiless denial of all certainties—and although we live in an age hostile to faith, the anti-dogmatic King Lear has become a refuge for misplaced piety.…[137] King Lear asserts nothing, though it questions everything. It poses for our staggered imaginations the possibility that the cosmos is amoral, perhaps malevolent, more likely a vast nothing—a word which in its several variations echoes like a diabolical chorus throughout the play, provides the Fool with his bitterest jests, and culminates in Lear’s fivefold repeated never.…[144] In its convulsive travail the cosmos of King Lear destroys all that is most noble along with all that is most base. Radical evil consumes itself, like the monsters of the deep; only mediocrity survives its destruction.…[146] King Lear is a play which is neither a sublime affirmation nor [pace Kott] a grotesque denial but a savage and beautiful confrontation of the ambiguity of human experience. Waller (1972, p. 62): The play’s total effect is to call in question any sense of universal providential judgement.

Nevo (1972, pp. 259–72): It is the inadequacy, if anything, of love to redeem that is the burden of the play.…What is enacted is a [260] titanic agon rather than a purgatorial progress.…[261] The play is a Shakespearean version of the Book of Job, raising the problem of undeserved suffering with a similar insistence, power, and intensity.…What is dramatized in the action of Lear is the opposite of resignation. It is the way in which an erring man’s passionate protest against injustice and humiliation affirms human dignity despite the most relentless cruelty, cynicism, and degradation that can be brought to bear on it.…[272] In nearly all moralistic and redemptive readings of Lear…it is a prime element in the case that Lear’s sufferings are justified by the repentance they finally produce. The fact of the matter is that Lear has needed no more than two days to know the woe that too late repents. Similarly Snyder (1979, p. 177): Religion in King Lear does not contradict heroic self-assertion but reinforces it. Roche (1981, pp. 140 ff.) too is skeptical that a tragic hero attains a kind of knowledge that redeems him, his suffering, and reconciles his claims to the world he leaves impoverished for his loss, an idea he ascribes to (p. 146) an attempt to divorce common morality from literary perception, an attempt to establish literature as a secular replacement for religion.…[148] I see no way in which the suffering of Lear can be related to Christian redemption except in the way that Yeats transforms tragedy into gaiety, that is, by poetic fiat and not by examination of the text as delivered to us by Shakespeare in the early seventeenth century.…[149] King Lear, based as it is on historical sources, is meant to depict the plight of man before the Christian era, that is, before the salvation of man by Christ’s sacrifice was available.…[156] The ending of Lear is as bleak and unrewarding as man can reach outside the gates of hell. There is no transcendence that we ourselves do not impose on the play. Every gesture of Lear’s love is countered by an equal and opposite gesture of hatred.…Every optimistic surmise by any character who calls upon the gods is denied.…[160] For Shakespeare the story of Lear was part of history, and all of history was part of that providential plan that would eventually bring good out of evil. But Shakespeare changes Lear’s success in history to defeat in fiction.…We lament the impossibility of tragedy in the modern world because we have romanticized [161] our own heroic inadequacies, understanding neither heroism nor inadequacy. What Shakespeare saw as all too human failure we have converted into triumph, unjustified and undefined.

Barber (1980, pp. 196–9): [Rather than] intimations of a Christian resolution in Shakespeare’s tragedy…he presents versions of the Oedipus complex tragically unresolved. His tragedies present the post-Christian situation where, with some of the expectations and values of Christianity, we do not have God and the Holy Family, only the human [197] family. In this situation he makes us feel that human life is supremely valuable as well as terrible.…Shakespeare presents social arrangements in the Christian terms of his society, and with a critical perspective that implies part of the Christian norm. But only a part. The full Christian norm would deal with the need for a complete union in love, the need Lear looked for from Cordelia…by redirecting it to divine objects.…[198] So a Christian Lear might be provided with the Presence whose lack drives him to madness; his daughters might be spared the demand that they be that presence, that all their tenderness be arrogated to a father who asks them to make him, in effect, their god.…As regularly happens in Shakespeare’s mature work, religious language comes into play to express investment in the family bond.…What the play presents, however, is not a Christian resolution, but the tragic consequences of this investment.…Shakespeare understood the destructive side of human bonds, the value of which he so movingly expresses. He presents (p. 199) the modern situation where religious need, or need cognate to what had been dealt with by worship of the Holy Family, has no resource except the human family, and its extensions in society, including the problematic idea of kingship.

Wymer (1986, pp. 71–2): The Christian answer, exemplified by Edgar and Cordelia, that despair is succeeded by comfort has its place in the play, but it is not the final place. The Cliffs of Dover episode…tells us that comfort is always at hand, but the play in its entirety tells us that comfort is not always enough. In the end we are reduced to the bedrock of [72] tragedy—that the price of wisdom is suffering, and such a price may not be worth paying. Kirsch (1988, pp. 166–9): At the center of most of the play’s…paradoxes is the phenomenon of the denial of death.…[169] In the pagan world of King Lear the New Testament’s conception of death, and life, is the denial; the reality is that of Ecclesiastes, the pilgrimage of the heart in the Old Testament that insists above all else that death cannot be denied. Whitehead (1992, p. 29) finds an appalled acceptance that there are no superhuman presences which either control the universe or purposefully guide human destinies.

Other critics go further and see Sh. deliberately challenging Christian premises. Elton (1966, p. 338): Although its realistic depiction of heathen religious attitudes, far from simple camouflage, is not intended to provide allegorical one-to-one correspondences with the world of Jacobean Christianity—and could not, without serious consequences to its author—its contemporary analogical significance would not have been lost on some members of a sympathetic audience, circa 1605, undergoing in related terms its own theological crisis. By depicting a superstitious pagan progressing towards doubt of his gods, [Sh.] secured for the play the approbation of the less devout, who saw in its direction the victory of the True Faith.…Moreover, he obtained for it the interest of those more troubled and sophisticated auditors who were not to be stilled by pious assurances in the unsteady new world of the later Renaissance. For the latter, [Lr.] carried its own tua res agitatur significance: it made more vivid the image of that horror, the all-dissolving chaos, for those who could not turn aside and stop their beating minds. Sinfield (1983, p. 128): From the security of its pagan setting King Lear focusses upon Reformation thought a three-pronged critique. It requires us to consider the implications of a god of systematic retribution, rejects this for the idea that the world may be governed by blind fortune, and poses against these two versions of the divinity a subversive ethic of generosity. Wittreich (1984, pp. 122–5): There is no escaping the conclusion that King Lear is a play of carefully orchestrated ironies that, one after another, impeach the promises of Christianity as they are found in the Gospels and Epistles.…The Christian analogy provided by the Apocalypse, while a clue to interpretation, does not proclaim the play to be Christian.…[124] For Shakespeare, the essential problem is to rescue the Apocalypse and read it back into the human world; and his way of dealing with that pro-[125]blem is to demystify the Apocalypse and thereby humanize it—is to turn over responsibility for the shaping of history to man and thereby secularize the Christian prophecy. Strier (2000, pp. 181 ff.): Unlike Hamlet, which seems committed to leaving its questions open, Lear might be said to participate less in Pyrrhonian than in Academic skepticism—instead of leaving everything open, neither asserted nor denied, it might be said to move all the way to negative dogmatism.Lear seems to present a world that is truly and utterly disenchanted.…[187] [Lr.] truly reject[s] the dream of magical or even providential exorcism of evil.…For Shakespeare, the truth might be that the redemptive as well as the demonic are purely human affairs.

Arguments that the play is anti-Christian often rely on pointing to or asserting bitter ironies that emphasize the hollowness of Christian comfort. What follows is a list of critics who interpret Lr. thus, as fundamentally pessimistic. Melville (1850, p. 126) relates Lr. to the power of blackness he perceived in Hawthorne’s fiction: Through the mouths of the dark characters of Hamlet, Timon, Lear, and Iago, [Sh.] craftily says, or sometimes insinuates the things which we feel to be so terrifically true, that it were all but madness for any good man, in his own proper character, to utter, or even hint of them. Tormented into desperation, Lear, the frantic king, tears off the mask, and speaks the sane madness of vital truth. Swinburne (1880, pp. 171–2): Lr.’s fatalism is of a darker and harder nature than that of Æschylus. (P. 172): Requital, redemption, amends, equity, explanation, pity and mercy, are words without a meaning here. [quotes 2221–2] Here is no need of the Eumenides, children of Night everlasting; for here is very Night herself.…For in this most terrible work of human genius it is with the very springs and sources of nature that her student has set himself to deal. The veil of the temple of our humanity is rent in twain. Nature herself, we might say, is revealed—and revealed as unnatural. In face of such a world as this a man might be forgiven who should pray that chaos might come again. S. A. Brooke (1913, pp. 198–9) finds Lr. more savage than either Aeschylus or Sophocles. Fagus (1923, p. 169): It is Lear who strangles Cordelia. We should add that it is Gloucester who, by his son, strangles Lear’s daughter; it is Lear who, by his daughter, tears out Gloucester’s eyes.…With the best intentions in the world, the fool who torments Lear with his ill-timed wit and Edgar, the sham madman who finishes him off with his maddening talk, have no small share of responsibility for his madness. And later, Edgar, through an excess of zeal causes his father to die of shock.…Cordelia herself and her inflexible truthfulness, almost aggressive for a moment and ill-timed, abandons her father, whom she knows well, to her sisters, who also know him too well. She cannot lie any more than Edgar and the fool can hold their tongues. Well then, there is nothing more terrible. (Fr.) Lewis (1927, p. 180): The punctual arrival of [the dead] Cordelia, brought in like a Christmas present, so narquois and so pat, cannot be anything but what it forces us at once to see it as: an expression of the poet’s mockery at the vanity of human supplications, and notions of benevolent powers, of whom we are the cherished children. Bailey (1929, p. 172): The dominant impression left by King Lear is that of the weakness of men, their helplessness in the hands of powers outside them, their insignificance in the universe which contains and overwhelms them. Empson (1949, p. 204): The play shows a malcontent view of Nature as the supreme clown. Idem (1951, pp. 150–6): The gods of the play are criminal lunatics. The play’s verbal patterns suggest (p. 156) a fundamental horror, an idea that the gods are such silly and malicious jesters that they will soon destroy the world. Harrison (1951, p. 159): The lesson, motive, and motto of Lear is contained in Gloucester’s words: [quotes 2221–2]. Brooke (1963, pp. 57 ff.): The process of the play seems…calculated to repudiate every source of consolation with which we might greet the final disaster.…[58] The last two Acts of the play…are constructed of a series of advances and repudiations of visions of hope,…a dialectical pattern, of exchange between theory and experience, which is continually repeated.…[59] The final sense is that all moral structures, whether of natural order [60] or Christian redemption, are invalidated by the naked fact of experience.…When Lear dies, the moral voices are silenced. We are left with unaccommodated man indeed: naked, unsheltered by any consolation whatsoever.…We are left to Lear’s deluded death without even the aesthetic consolation of formal patterning. We are, in short, forced by the remorseless process of King Lear to face the fact of its ending without any support from systems of moral or artistic belief at all. Idem (1964, pp. 85–7): The process of [the] last two Acts…has not only made it impossible to retain any concept of an ordered universe, but has also promoted the reflection that any system of order results in strange notions of justice. And in the end the subtlest and most tempting order of all is undone—the order of repentance, forgiveness, redemption and regeneration is reversed in unregenerate Lear’s tottering [86] broken-hearted into madness and death.…[87] The greatness of King Lear is in the perfect completeness of its negation, and in the superb energy with which it is enforced. Elton (1966, p. 334): A pattern of gratuitousness…appears to pervade not only the beginning and end but also two of the play’s crucial events, Gloucester’s blinding and Cordelia’s hanging. Accompanied by the irrational menacings of the thunder, the willful operations of an upside-down providence in an apparently deranged universe would suggest an implicit metaphysical absurdity.…What is expressed in the relation of the lines and in the sequence of dialogue and event [confirms] an implicit direction of the tragedy: annihilation of faith in poetic justice and, within the confines of a grim, pagan universe, annihilation of faith in divine justice. In this dark world, the last choruses tell us, we find the promised end, or the image of that horror, in which man’s chief joy is to be removed from the rack of this tough world and in which man’s pathetic solace is—ultimate irony!—the illusion that that which he has loved most still breathes.…No redemption stirs at this world’s end; only suffering, tears, pity, and loss—and illusion. Stuart (1967, p. 179): King Lear does not end with an affirmation. It rather looks backward to the waste and shame and corruption that has taken place. Nothing to come will excel what has gone before, either in a good or bad sense. One learns the truth too late, and he who knows the truth must die. Marks (1967–8, p. 169): King Lear does not offer the comfort we demand from great tragic literature; it does not give a final shape to suffering, a meaning to death and so to life. It ends instead with a sad statement of the intensity of Lear’s suffering, unmitigated by any attribution of meaning. Jayne (1964, p. 285) denies significant moral regeneration; no one really achieves anything very significant in the play. Every single character fails in his effort to re-establish a bond with society. See also Vivas (1971).

Other critics counterargue that the play is optimistic or affirmative rather than merely pessimistic—that its evidence for goodness, order, love, forgiveness, kindness, justice, charity, and individual heroism outweighs its terror and gloom. Bradley (1904, pp. 279 ff.): Man is not represented in [Sh.’s] tragedies as the mere plaything of a blind or capricious power, suffering woes which have no relation to character and actions; nor is the world represented as given over to darkness. The keynote of Lr. is surely to be heard neither in the words wrung from Gloster in his anguish, nor in Edgar’s words the gods are just. Its final and total result is one in which pity and terror, carried perhaps to the extreme limits of art, are so blended with a sense of law and beauty that we feel at last, not depression and much less despair, but a consciousness of greatness in pain, and of solemnity in the mystery we cannot fathom.…[303] On the one hand we see a world which generates terrible evil in profusion. Further, the beings in whom this evil appears at its strongest are able, to a certain extent, to thrive. They are not unhappy, and they have power to spread misery and destruction around them.…[304] On the other hand this evil is merely destructive: it founds nothing, and seems capable of existing only on foundations laid by its opposite. It is also self-destructive.…Thus the world in which evil appears seems to be at heart unfriendly to it. And this impression is confirmed by the fact that the convulsion of this world is due to evil, mainly in the worst forms here considered, partly in the milder forms which we call the errors or defects of the better characters. Good, in the widest sense, seems thus to be the principle of life and health in the world; evil, at least in these worst forms, to be a poison. The world reacts to it violently, and, in the struggle to expel it is driven to devastate itself.…There is in the world of King Lear the same abundance of extreme good as of extreme evil. It generates [305] in profusion self-less devotion and unconquerable love. And the strange thing is that neither Shakespeare nor we are surprised. We approve these characters, admire them, love them; but we feel no mystery. We do not ask in bewilderment, Is there any cause in nature that makes these kind hearts? Such hardened optimists are we, and Shakespeare,—and those who find the darkness of revelation in a tragedy which reveals Cordelia.

Others who argue against the idea that Lr. projects a pessimistic view of the human condition include C. F. T. Brooke (1913, p. 97): King Lear is a play of good cheer, a powerful witness to the presence and potency in this world of faith, hope, and charity…pervaded by the kind of optimism which is most truly characteristic of [Sh.]. Mais (1923, p. 45): That love should be capable of such grief is in itself a triumph. We leave the theatre after seeing King Lear as we leave it after seeing Hamlet, in a state of spiritual exultation at the victory once more of good over the powers of evil. Stevenson (1914, p. 26): It is not pessimism to prefer death with the good to life with the bad. See also Knight (1928, pp. 411–14). Perkinson (1939, p. 211) ascribes the apparently gratuitous pessimism and the more than tragic intensity of King Lear to the result of his technical solution of an immediate problem…when [Sh.] telescoped the Cordelia story [including her death] into the chronicle history of King Lear. Ellis-Fermor (1945, p. 75): The conversions that flow in rising and cumulative waves through the last two acts of the play all set towards a positive, though undefined, interpretation.…The tragic balance is readjusted. The perception of evil is as full as in the Oedipus or the Oresteia, but there is an undefined, but no less positive, perception of order emerging again from casualty. Harbage (1947, p. 146): Phrases about the play’s tearing the universe from its hinges and hurling charges against destiny itself must be viewed as rhetorical flourishes. The enemy in King Lear is not God but human unkindness. Knights (1959, pp. 99–119): Shakespeare’s total view of human life in this play has a toughness and actuality that make most pessimism look like sentimentality.…In the successive stripping away of [100] the layers of appearance, what remains to discover is the most fundamental reality of all. In the play it takes the form of the love and forgiveness of Cordelia. But that love has to be earned in the way in which all things most worth having are earned—by the full admission of a need, the achievement of honesty and humility, the painful shedding of all that is recognized as incompatible with the highest good, by, in short, making oneself able to receive whatever it may be.…[118] At the end…[119] the mind, the imagination…is directed towards affirmation in spite of everything. Stein (1959, pp. 375–7): Shakespeare reveals the rebirth of hope within a truly absolute despair.…[376] If affliction must be borne—and the play makes us see that it must—the world ceases to be bottomlessly absurd. The mere fact of moral exposure—exposure to [377] that ultimate imperative that denies a man the choice of death—even as it seems to seal his cosmic entrapment, indicates a measure of shelter: shelter from the maddening image of Tom, the thing, shelter from manhood stripped of humankindness: shelter from ultimate exposure to Nothing. To this extent, Tchehov also…transcends desperation…Lear descends more deeply into the heart’s mind—and it is the depth of its penetration of patience that releases the play’s tragic joy. Skulsky (1966, p. 19): What we have been allowed to take part in is a victory, not of good over evil, but of the tragic vision over the absurd; a tribute not to the power of goodness, but to its reality. Idem (1976, pp. 124–65) discusses Lr. as a poetic laboratory testing whether the supposedly intrinsic values of justice and charity persist…[125] with the vanishing of order.…[132] There is…no sign of optimism in King Lear, least of all about men’s capacity for moral perception and decency. The assumed ground of the human claim to respect and care seems, instead, to be quite simply the human capacity for [133] joy and suffering. Yet (p. 165) The end of the play is mysteriously affirmative…. The scheme of things may…tolerate pointless calamity and malignity, in an alternation with their opposites as arbitrary as Edmund’s cult of the amoral. But the arbitrariness does not extend to the moral alternatives themselves. Chaudhuri (1981, p. 166): In King Lear, the accidents of individual character and situation are unusually overwhelmed by the sense of collective experience. The capacities of the individual are heroically enlarged.…In this all-inclusive humanity, the entire range of man’s experience serves to aggrandize him; sin, pain and loss are seen to stimulate and expand the faculties. Standard moral concepts grow meaningless here. Ogden (1983, p. 184): The impression that the universe may be cheerless, dark and deadly is balanced by the feeling of pride due to the impression that we have seen men like ourselves facing this terror with full awareness and heroic endurance. Summers (1984, pp. 110–13): At the end we respond to Lear’s death as heroic rather than merely pathetic.…[113] Lear’s final convictions that Cordelia is alive and that her lips move are overwhelming recognition of the reality that he has come to know: that the things he has learned from Cordelia about the nature of love…are more truly alive than anything else in the world. Mehl, 1986, p. 103): There is a general idea of humane behavior implied in the tragedy as a whole and insisted on with unconventional intensity, and this is by no means despairing or indifferent. Bonnefoy (1985–6, pp. 490–1) finds Lr. more optimistic than Ham.: We meet in an arena of error, of crime, of dreadfully unjust death, in which even the very idea of Heaven seems missing; and yet, the center holds, meaning manages to survive and even to take on new depth.…[491] In spite of the crisis of modern times, [poetry is able] to make manifest what is hidden beneath the impoverished forms of everyday thinking, beneath the dissociations and alienations imposed by science and culture—and thus it will be an intervention, the assumption of a neglected responsibility. Other critics who see Lr. as affirmative rather than pessimistic include Boas (1896), Balmforth (1926), Knight (1928, pp. 411–14), Wilson (1932, pp. 124–7), Jones (1964), Knights (1967), Collins (1989), and Ishikawa (1989).

Some critics argue that the play builds into itself a dialectic of opposites that makes a choice between redemptivist and absurdist interpretations impossible. Thus Mack (1965, pp. 114–17): We are offered two ways of being sentimental about Lear’s final vision, both of which we must make an effort to eschew. One is to follow those critics who argue that, because [his] last lines probably mean that Lear dies in the joy of thinking that Cordelia lives, some sort of mitigation or transfiguration has been reached which turns defeat into total victory.…[115] The other sentimentality leads us to indulge the currently fashionable existentialist nausée.…[116] We face the ending of this play, as we face our world, with whatever support we customarily derive from systems of belief or unbelief.…[117] Tragedy never tells us what to think; it shows us what we are and may be. And what we are and may be was never… more memorably fixed upon a stage than in this kneeling old man whose heartbreak is precisely the measure of what, in our world of relatedness, it is possible to lose and possible to win. The victory and defeat are simultaneous and inseparable. Rabkin (1967, pp. 10–11): In King Lear as in Hamlet Shakespeare creates a universe susceptible of contradictory interpretations which are voiced by the characters in it and, more importantly, made equally plausible by the action. In order simply to interpret the plot, we find ourselves constantly driven to make up our minds about what kind of universe the characters live in. We want to know why Lear and Cordelia and Edgar—and we ourselves—are being made to suffer. But as the intensity of our experience with the play, especially in the theater, makes us long for a sense of closure in the perplexing world in which Shakespeare involves us, we find ourselves able at almost any point in the play to read its world as godless or divine; these are the terms implicit in the action of King Lear and explicit in its language. If we choose the atheistic or naturalistic interpretation, we must still interpret the nature which we see constantly operant, and we find ourselves unable to determine whether it is mechanistic or ravening or somehow ordered consistently with what we consider humane in the play’s best characters and in ourselves. If we entertain the possibility that there are gods who rule the world of the play, we are given adequate evidence to support both the thesis that they are indifferent to human concerns and its antithesis, that they care about us. If we allow the play to persuade us that the gods are concerned about us, we cannot determine the nature of their concern: We find ourselves tempted at any point to agree with formulations by characters who assert that the gods are malicious or pedagogical or benevolent or retributive, that they are interested in destroying us or redeeming us. One can easily think of fictions in which the action suggests many interpretations as straw men to be disposed of by a satisfying final resolution; but in King Lear the ending achieves much of its power precisely because it can equally sustain any one of these readings at the expense of all the others. The tragedy is thus a profoundly skeptical exploration, even though skepticism is too univocal an attitude, too much a single kind of faith, to seem anything like an equivalent to the vision King Lear leads us to. McElroy (1973, pp. 161–2) argues for the complementarity of redemptivist and absurdist interpretations: Views or attitudes which are diametrically opposed in such a way that each must logically exclude the other…exist together, side by side, in perfect artistic unity and [162] harmony in the play.…Ethics and experience are the two principal poles of the Lear dialectic, and that dialectic is complementary in that both elements have inexorable demands to make and there is no resolution or meeting ground between them.…The Lear dialectic forces us at once to assent to both the necessity and intrinsic worth of ethical values, the basis of redemptive readings, but at the same time to contemplate the utter inability of such values to cope with experience, the basis of absurdist readings. In contrast Saunders (1988, p. 127) sees opposed tendencies toward pessimism and optimism located in textual variants: The Quarto version [of Lear’s dying speech], with no glimmer of transcendence or illusion, is tailor-made for the pessimistic school of interpretation.…The Folio version—especially if we see Lear’s last two lines [3282–3] as an addition made by Shakespeare at the time he was writing his late plays when he was much preoccupied with the theme of redemption—lends some support to those who have found in the ending of the play some flickerings of hope or mystic vision. Czubak (1989, pp. 164–71) discusses the opposition between life and sterility, a theme which is firmly set in [a] system of negation and affirmation characteristic of (p. 171) the bi-polar universe of the play.

The same characteristics and qualities of Lr. that provoke critics to raise moral and religious questions also stimulate thinking about a range of philosophical issues both broadly and narrowly defined. Critics who find the play concerned in various ways with finding meaning in human experience include Bush (1956, pp. 88–96): Lr. is a play about believing.…[96] The question is whether natural causes are enough to explain and save ourselves—whether, more simply, it is enough to be a man. Michel (1961, p. 647): The plot may be said to criticize the pretensions of humanism. Johansen (1972, pp. 110–27): The drama develops from the viewpoint that the world HAS a given meaning to the problem of ASCRIBING to it a given meaning. The ending of the drama enacts a (p. 126) transition from the cosmos possessing divinely recognized legality to something inscrutable.…[127] [Lr.] is the tragedy of Unredeemable Time. Elton (1975, p. 48) sees Lr. as preoccupied with the problem of certainty, correlated to crises of belief and knowledge in European theological and philosophical thought. Anderson (1971–2; 1986, p. 185): The fragile world of Lear shares many concerns with [Montaigne’s] Essaies; it is a critique of justice, reason, nature, social structure—perhaps Shakespeare’s deepest glance into the abyss. Each theme is a compound of disproportion. Joughin (2002, p. 72): Lr. constitutes a type of exemplary text precisely because it continues to remind us of the limits of our attempts to engage in meaningful interpretation.…The paradox is that Lear can still remain valuable for us only in its wider perception that modern culture is increasingly found to be lacking in value; and thus, in the same process, Lear’s value is somehow to survive the experience of outliving its own utility.

A number of critics see philosophical Stoicism as relevant to interpretation of Lr. Dowden (1875; 1879, p. 259): To Stoicism the mere phenomenon of human existence is a vast piece of unreason and grotesqueness, and from this unreason and grotesqueness Stoicism makes its escape by becoming indifferent to the phenomenon, and by devotion to the moral idea, the law of the soul, which is forever one with itself and with the highest reason. The ethics of the play of King Lear are Stoical ethics. Campbell (1948, p. 94): Lear is not so much an erring Christian as a completely unstoical man and he is converted to a state of mind which is a mixture of Stoic insight and Christian humility. Haydn (1950, pp. 638–51): The whole play is unmistakably concerned with a dying order, in which the protagonists of Nature and Stoicism fight for supremacy.…[641] [Edmund, Goneril, and Regan are Machiavellian] naturalists [who] substitute virtù for virtue in the traditional sense whereas Stoicism is demonstrated (p. 642) in the characters of Cordelia and Edgar and the juxtaposition of Kent and the Fool, as well as in the points of view of many other characters toward the nature of nature and the moral order of the universe, and in the hard primitivism advocated by many characters in the best Stoic-Cynic manner.…[651] In the end…it is a true Stoic world, in which retributive justice is enacted. But it is not a world in which love and mercy play a positive and effective part. Gloucester and Lear are allowed to undergo purgation by fire and to reach the promised land of Stoic patience, but not to enjoy it. The almost gratuitous deaths of the Fool and Cordelia establish only the grim unpredictability of fatum, and the fact that man’s only refuge is the acquisition of his unconquerable soul. Chang (1966, pp. 50–2) also sees a conflict between Stoicism and Machiavellianism in Lr. Rinehart (1953, p. 228) likewise finds a world of stoic philosophy in Lr., as does Kolve (1966, p. 186): The two protagonists both learn patience, but it is a lesson closer to the resignation taught by the Stoics—the absence of desire, the freedom from hope—than it is to the patience exampled by Christ in his sufferings—stillness and humility designed to earn (or make manifest) a heavenly crown. An explicitly Christian ending is deliberately avoided. Miola (1992, p. 155–6): Clearly inscribed in King Lear, the Senecan opposition between wrath and patience is, as in Hamlet, profoundly ambivalent and subject to searching inquiry. Schneider (1995, par. 12): When we look at King Lear through a Stoic lens, many shadowy places become distinct. See also Shanker (1975, pp. 174–6).

Other critics deny the relevance of Stoicism to Lr. Danby (1948, p. 305): What has often been taken for Stoicism [in Lr.] is no Stoicism at all but rather the orthodox teaching on Christian Patience. Monsarrat (1984, p. 146): To speak of Stoics and Stoicism in King Lear seems to be a misconception of that philosophy or a misreading of the play. Jones-Davies (1989) finds the play criticizing both Stoic and Machiavellian notions of reason as perverse and inhuman. Bate (2000, pp. 25–9) places Lr. in an historically identifiable philosophical, or rather anti-philosophical [i.e., anti-Stoical], tradition seen in Montaigne and Erasmus. (P. 26): King Lear comes to a similar conclusion [concerning the inadequacy of Stoic virtue], but it does so not though thinking, in the manner of Montaigne, but through enactment—through performance.…[29] True wisdom comes not in Gloucester’s and Edgar’s words of Stoic comfort or Albany’s hapless faith in divine providence, but in moments of folly and love. Elton (1966, pp. 97–9) also discusses the inadequacy of stoicism in Lr.

Some modern critics relate the play to existentialism. For instance, Baker (1962, pp. 546 ff.) applies five existential categories to show how Lr. (p. 550) deals profoundly with the existentials of the human condition. (P. 546): The basic existential categories are as follows: First, being born into this world and finding ourselves here. Secondly, being towards others and finding ourselves existing among other people who are similarly bounded as ourselves.…Third, experiencing certain elementary emotions, especially anguish, (p. 547) defined as one’s feeling in the face of existence as a whole.…Fourth, the human experience of time and of being headed towards death. And, finally, the possibility of transcendence of these space-time limitations. McFarland (1966, pp. 130–4): The action of King Lear has no favored perspective for judgment. And this fact points towards one of its deepest motive truths: King Lear presents no protagonist because it presents no achieved identity; the movement of the play, precisely, is the quest for identity. If the action of King Lear can thus be described, in its largest terms, as a simultaneous search, on the part [131] of all its major characters, for a meaningful self, the search is ironically laid out by the tragedy’s time, its place, and its religious reference. From none of these boundary dimensions does there issue help for struggling man, and, joined in their bleakness, they provide mockingly ironic assurance of equal conditions and fair play for all.…[134] The moral concern of Lear…receives its configurations in situations beyond good and evil.…Just as there is no protagonist to command our easy approbation, so likewise does no character fit into a traditional framework of blame and the ascription of evil. Weitz (1971, p. 32): Philosophically central in King Lear—an important if not central strand of the whole drama—is man’s worth in a morally indifferent universe. Shakespeare’s answer, I propose, is that man’s worth resides in his commitment to his humanity: a commitment without any metaphysical justification. Chakravorty (1990, pp. 1 ff.) reads Lr. as an excellent illustration of the Existentialist ethos of Freedom and Choice,…[122] an Existential Drama on the universal situation of man. Willams (1985, p. 2) relates Lr.’s patterns of deliberate reduction and reorientation to the concept of reduction in existential phenomenology. See also Blau (1964).

Besides discussing particular schools of philosophy, critics also discuss Lr.’s treatment of such perennial philosophical topics as nature, justice, and love. The concept of nature in Lr. is discussed by a number of critics, who are often concerned with contrasts between traditional concepts of natural law and the more modern ideas about naturalism. Hales (1875; 1884, pp. 252–3): King Lear deals especially with the natural man as opposed to the artificial man.…[253] So that in this play we have presented to us humanity in its purest and simplest elements—humanity unsophisticated, denuded of all its lendings, with its natural impulses all unchecked and potent. Knight (1930, pp. 197 ff.): The thought of nature is as ubiquitous here as that of death in Hamlet, fear in Macbeth, or time in Troilus and Cressida. The phraseology is pregnant of natural reference and natural suggestion; and where the human element merges into the natural, the suggestion is often one of village life. The world of Lear is townless. It is a world of flowers, rough country, tempestuous wind, and wild, or farmyard, beasts; and, as a background, there is continual mention of homely, countrified customs, legends, rhymes. This world is rooted in nature, firmly as a Hardy novel.…Now there are two main directions for this animal and natural suggestion running though the play. First, two of the persons undergo a direct return to nature in their purgatorial progress; second, the actions of humanity tend to assume contrast with the natural world in point of ethics.…[201] Lear revolts from man, tries to become a thing of elemental, instinctive life: since rational consciousness has proved unbearable. Hence the relevance of animals, and animal symbolism to madness. For madness is the breaking of that which differentiates man from beast. So Lear tries to become naked, bestial, unsophisticated; and later garlands himself with flowers.…[202] Thoughts of nature are also related to human vice. The evil of mankind is often here regarded as essentially a defacing of nature, since this is now human nature, and human nature is moral. Milne (1947, p. 247) sees the play as antinaturalistic: Cordelia’s death [is] the culminating point of attack upon nature which is the moving force and final message of the play. In contrast, Heilman (1948, p. 115) sees an affirmation of natural law: All of the characters who think about nature at all claim the aegis of nature; some ignore the subject entirely, but no one is willing to be an enemy of nature. So nature has different meanings in the usage of different moral agents. To most of the characters in the play, nature is a fundamental principle of order; it is the lex naturalis, the divinely ordained cosmic scheme; it implies a distinction between good and evil, and the operation of an eternal justice. On the other hand, nature is understood simply as vital force, the physical drive and the impulses of the individual, the totality of unfettered and uncriticized urgencies. The two senses compete with each other; thus they set up a special tension; and this tension qualifies the total dramatic statement.

Danby (1949, pp. 15 ff.): King Lear can be regarded as a play dramatizing the meanings of the single word Nature.…[19] Two main meanings, strongly contrasted and mutually exclusive, run through the play. On one side is [20] the view consciously adopted by Edmund, and tacitly assumed by Goneril and Regan. On the other is the view largely held by the Lear party. This latter is the traditional and orthodox view. Its limiting expression is Cordelia.…The view of the Lear party is the same as that found in Bacon and Hooker. Edmund’s philosopher (just old enough in 1606 to have seen Edmund on the stage) is Hobbes.…[21] The idea of Nature…in orthodox Elizabethan thought, is always something normative for human beings. It is impossible to talk about Nature without talking also about pattern and ideal form; about Reason as displayed in Nature; about Law as the innermost expression of Nature; about Custom which is the basis of Law and equally with Law an expression of Nature’s pattern; about Restraint as the observance of Law, and the way to discover our richest self-fulfillment.…[38] Edmund, on the other hand, admits of no connections in Nature save connections of material cause and effect. And Nature is a closed system. For him, as for us, it is a structure laid down, devoid of intelligence, impervious to Reason.…As Nature goes dead, community becomes competition, and man a nexus of appetites. Reason is no longer a normative drive but a calculator of the means to satisfy the appetites with which we were born.

Similarly Traversi (1952, pp. 135, 49): King Lear is a great tragedy precisely because it is a play about human nature before being a play about the abuses of government or social inequality.…[49] The relation of Gloucester to his two sons…constitute [sic] a study…of the complexity implied in the term nature. Edmund’s natural bastardizing destroys the still more natural relationship between the father and his true-born son; in the same way passion, though natural to the full development of man, may yet wreck the harmony of his experience and destroy his peace. Ribner (1958, p. 39): There are two concepts of nature at war within the play. One is the orthodox nature of Hooker’s Humanism, of Cordelia, Kent, and Edgar; the other is the nature of Renaissance skepticism, of Edmund, Goneril, and Regan. Likewise Whitaker (Mirror, 1965, p. 211): The plot of King Lear, insofar as it operates in the order of nature, is a thorough working out of the concept that nature is order until man’s folly destroys the equilibrium. Elton (1966, pp. 76, 296 f.): Cordelia’s bond, ultimately merciful as it relates to an affirmation of divine justice, is one expression of natural law. However, (p. 296) Committed to the pleasure of destruction, the villains identify cruelty and murder with natural law. Such inferences follow inevitably from the dissolution of traditional natural law’s restraints.…[297] Since vicious cruelty conforms to the law of nature, and God tortures and repudiates mankind, there is nothing to stop one from torturing and repudiating one’s fellow men. Such ultimate nihilism is, in practice, deduced by the sadistic villains. Yet it is also sensed by the protagonists themselves amidst the seeming cosmic sadism which kills men, like flies, for sport and which later gratuitously slaughters the innocent. Bauer (1968, p. 360) also perceives a conflict between competing ideas about nature, between nomos—nature as law—and physis—nature as vital force.

Other critics object to this binary opposition between a moral natural law and an amoral naturalism. Rosenberg (1972, p. 76): In Lr. the views of Nature…are many more than two.…Lear is not a debate: the views of nature are functions of individual characterizations, and not vice versa.…The word’s meaning changes as the personae change. McAlindon (1991, pp. 173–4): Shakespeare, in responding to the old play’s uncomplicated endorsement of the benignant nature championed by theologians, was not simply intent on testing it by reference to the malignant nature of the new philosophers; rather, he was appealing to, and endorsing, a unitary theory of nature which [174] embraces both perceptions. In that theory…all nature is animated by sympathies and antipathies, love and strife.

For other discussions of nature in Lr., see Masefield (1911, pp. 189–90), Craig (1925, pp. 101 ff.), Knights (1959, pp. 117 ff.), Lökse (1960, pp. 158 ff.), Fraser (1962), Mason (1975), Erlebach (1981, pp. 105–17), Freed (1987), Orgel (2002, pp. 1482–3).

Many critics have discussed the idea of justice in Lr., a play whose suffering characters memorably question whether justice can be found either in human institutions or in nature or in the heavens. Critics divide especially over whether justice is affirmed or denied by the ending of the play. Preston (1869, pp. 53, 58): Sh. shows us the vengeance of Heaven lighting upon the unjust father, as heavily as upon the undutiful daughters.…[58] The persecutions which Cordelia suffered from her father reconcile me, in a measure, to that father’s subsequent sufferings. He deserved them. Doyle (1877, p. 166): We feel when the tragedy ends that God is just, crushing in his anger those who have broken through the holiest ties of nature, when prompted to do so by avarice and ambition; and with his utmost gentleness dismissing Lear, in spite of his weakness every inch a king, to the gracious and healing rest of death. Lounsbury (1901, p. 414) praises the catastrophe as true to the moral laws which control the results of human action. So does Watt (1908, p. 285): But, finally, the truth stands clear, and it emerges that the ills and sorrows are but heaven’s judgment’s on the deeds of men. Siegel (1957, pp. 169–70) goes further: The suffering that Gloucester and Lear undergo has in it elements of poetic justice of the kind which the evil characters meet. Gloucester, blindly credulous…is punished by being made actually blind.…His blindness, an impairment of one of his senses, is also a form of retribution for his sensual indulgence.…[170] Lear acted with insane anger in disinheriting Cordelia and dividing the kingdom.…He becomes indeed mad. To this Rosenberg (1966, p. 139) objects: Like Job’s pharisaical comforters, those critics who find poetic justice in King Lear are guilty of a morally shocking reading of the play. Empson (1949, p. 207): Shakespeare cannot have believed all through the play that Gloucester deserved to have his eyes put out; the sort of justice imputed to the gods is what is called poetic, happening through agencies which have obviously no real sense of justice.

Critics who find in the play a challenge to conventional notions of justice include Goldberg (1974, pp. 14 ff.): It may perhaps be that the last scene is so unbearable not because it denies us the justice we want, but because it gives it to us; and also perhaps that some of the mystery of which Bradley spoke, is to fathom in ourselves how much, as human beings, we can love justice if we are able to love at all.…[101] The action of the play has irresistibly involved us…unwittingly in complicity with the logic by which [Cordelia] is killed.…[110] We do not need the mad Lear to suggest the kinship between the love of justice and the love of cruelty.…[131] The element in man that (most clearly in Lear) needs an answering moral order, justice, seems to become most intensely real and active just when the will, pressed by its own helplessness, drives itself against the world in a blaze of mad disorder.…[182] King Lear…is not the expression or the affirmation of some moral or metaphysical or epistemological truth or of the ultimate supremacy of some particular value. Felperin (1977, p. 99): [Lear’s] mad enactments of the forms of justice on the heath work to undermine the morality vision they represent. In that older drama, the satiric castigation of judicial corruption deals in such negative exempla as Lear offers, but only on the way to establishing a true vision of justice. Lear’s recourse in his madness to this strain of morality rhetoric and imagery, however, works to strip away these social and religious legitimations to the emptiness and arbitrariness of the idea of justice itself, its fundamental disjuncture from a human nature that exists beneath or beyond moral and legal categories.

Critics concerned with juridical forms of justice and their significance include Moseley (1988, p. 66), who identifies five trial scenes: 1.1 (p. 69: a trial of love), 2.2 (the stocking of Kent), 3.6 (Lear’s imagined trial of Regan and Goneril), 3.7 (Gloucester’s interrogation and blinding) and 5.3 (Edgar and Edmund’s trial by combat). Szabó (1988, p. 346), drawing on Paul Ricoeur’s discussion of the hermeneutics of testimony, finds that quasi-legal procedures…are embedded in the emplotment of the tragedy; the mock-trial of 3.6 anticipates the crucial moment when Lear will not be a mere victim but a martyr for truth and true love. Honigmann (1989, pp. 288–90) observes that Lr. is more explicitly concerned with crime and punishment, and justice, than any of the other tragedies.…[290] A clear connection is made between human judgement generally and legal judgements and the implied judgements of the play.…The dramatis personae and we, the spectators, are often trapped in judgements that are only locally true, if that. Shakespeare challenges us to think for ourselves by presenting poetic justice side by side with punishments that appear to be no less valid but perhaps are not meant to be. Green (1995, p. 63): Repeated references to the law and to judgment, both secular and divine,…rather than offering hope of a fair judicial decision or a merciful reprieve, intensify and mirror the characters’ experiences of heavenly wrath, human cruelty, and hopeless pain. Scott (2002) discusses Lear’s abdication and division of the kingdom in the context of contemporary legal contracts.

The relation between justice and love concerns other critics.
