Lowenthal (1994, p. 415): This play about justice tries in fact to demonstrate that it has a natural base in our social nature, and that, even when we perceive the delicate ways in which self-interest tends to intermingle with our love of others, this attachment is still real. It is a concern for others that lies at the bottom of justice—a wish to see them properly treated, and an abhorrence at their being mistreated.…It can therefore be said that Shakespeare emphatically disagrees with Lear’s conclusions—and Kent’s—at the end of the play. The examples of love he sets before us are far more impressive than the examples of wickedness. In contrast, Kahn (2000, pp. xi ff.): The destruction of love by law and of law by love is a central theme of King Lear.…The primary concern of the play…is…political psychology.…[xviii] The play begins with the problem of orderly governmental succession, takes up the problem of leadership and loyalty, and then deals with issues of treason and invasion. The play also deals with a number of symbolic representations of love: that of father for daughter, subject for ruler, and of lovers or would-be lovers. Most importantly, it gives us a representation of the universal love for all mankind…which is at the heart of the Christian tradition. King Lear offers a rich set of representations against which the reader is invited to meditate on the relationships among these forms of love, and their relation to law.…[xix] Whatever the virtues of a love beyond law that Lear reaches on the heath, that love cannot be brought back into the political order. From the perspective of law, it looks more like madness than an ultimate transcendence of finitude. Where love dreams of the equality of judge and defendant, law insists on the distinction. Where love would overcome the distinction of citizen and enemy, seeing only the bare, forked animal that is man, the thing itself, law insists on the distinction between those who aid and those who injure the state.…This is not just Lear’s tragedy but ours as well.

Several modern critics discuss the significance of a perceived motif of destruction and rebuilding, or reduction and renewal, or creation and destruction. McFarland (1966, pp. 137–64) emphasizes reduction and renewal: A reductio toward nothingness characterizes the movement of King Lear. All determinations of its cosmos are reduced to the brink of nothingness in the search for that which is essential for human life. Those characters (p. 151) who suffer the reduction of their identities and their world are rewarded, not necessarily by happiness, but by intensified experience.…[164] A renewal of spirit, emerging from madness and nothing, lay[s] the basis for a recreation of the cosmos of King Lear and a new reality in the relationships of its inhabitants. Hargrove (1980, pp. 42–51) finds in the theme of destruction and rebuilding a brilliant unifying device and a powerful comment on human experience.…From the ruins of his former self, Lear changes to some extent into a new person.…[51] The play is both optimistic and pessimistic, for destruction and rebuilding are mixed throughout and especially in the ending. Storozynsky (1991, pp. 163–9): Lr. is a story of creation and destruction, and especially of separation and division.…[169] The pattern was readily at hand in the mythological and biblical accounts of creation in which the world, born of Chaos, is readily turned upside-down, destroyed, and reduced once more to nothing. Magister (1992) and Demastes (1998) relate Lr. to modern chaos theory.

Various particular philosophical concepts are the concern of other critics. Pogson (1950, pp. 23 ff.) sees the play concerned with mystical wisdom: the subplot constitutes a clear allegory concerned with the tragedy of the inability of unawakened Man to distinguish between Truth and Falsity.…[43] The closing scenes of the play represent a kind of mystical death and re-birth for Lear [a tragic figure who is ourselves]. Nigro (1984) compares Lr.’s variations of the movement away from a calculation of things to a confrontation with nothingness to the mystical via negativa’s symbolic progression toward truth and authenticity by way of negation. Presson (1965, p. 421) comments on the problem of free will or determinism. Needless to say, though both attitudes are represented, no simple conclusion emerges. For Burke (1969, p. 12), Lr. is concerned with the paradox of substance:…Insofar as a man’s person gains substance from social powers which are not intrinsic to him yet with which, by reason of his role in life, he becomes associated, what can he essentially be, once these extrinsic underpinnings are removed? Cavell (1969; 2002, p. 324) sees Lr. representing a loss of presentness concomitant with the rise of skepticism: [Lr.’s] characters, having for whatever reason to forego presentness to their worlds, extend that disruption in their knowing of it (Lear and Gloucester knowing they cannot be loved, Regan knowing the destination of Gloucester, Edgar knowing he is contemned and has to win acceptance). But…how do we learn that what we need is not more knowledge but the willingness to forego knowing? Willig (1979) sees Sh. aligned with Franciscan nominalism. Lear’s perception of Gloucester as androgynous in 4.6 demonstrates the madness of a totalitarian hunger for power that strives to encompass all qualities: age, youth, masculinity, femininity, strength, and weakness. (Ger.) Wells (1980, pp. 59 f.) identifies as a central theme the dualism of mind and body.…[60] The contrast between [Gloucester’s physical and Lear’s mental suffering] is merely the most obvious aspect of an exploration of the relationship between mind and body which may be held to underpin the structures of the entire play. Danson (1981, pp. 133–5): Lr. shows man, despite all our Edgar-like graspings toward infinity or our Gloucester-like descents toward nothing, still (while we are in this life) suspended, incapable of reaching either secure extreme.…[135] [Lr.] has shown us man in the form given him by nature, suspended between the two abysses of infinity and nothingness. Homan (1986, p. 194) characterizes Lr. as a play that in its catholicity, in its exhilarating yet potentially stern challenge to the playwright’s artifice, celebrates at once the gamut of life and the physical basis on which the idiosyncrasies of metaphysics so depend. Wawrytko (1986, p. 393) asserts that Lr. reflect[s] the essential need for [the Confucian virtue] hsiao in society, as the sine qua non of civilized coexistence both within the family and within the state. Yang (1987) discusses Chinese translators’ use of the word hsiao in rendering Lr.’s bond. According to Scott (1990, pp. 73–82), The liar paradox [a self-undoing paradox] has some affinities with scepticism in philosophy, which is also relevant to Shakespeare’s play.…[82] A frank avowal of fiction or artifice, in the manner of the liar paradox,…carries Lear to the far side of authority of any kind…and past any experience that the saddened bystanders…can formulate. The play, in driving itself paradoxically beyond itself, is sceptically humble before paradox. Salkeld (1993, p. 105): King Lear reads as an exact corollary to Descartes. Whereas for the latter, the body is finite, mutable and an unreliable source of knowledge, in the former, the body solidifies into the only sure ground for all knowledge, meaning and subjectivity. Cantor (1996, p. 231): Shakespeare shows his awareness in King Lear of the dark truths about human nature taught by modern thinkers like Machiavelli [and Hobbes].…But ultimately Shakespeare’s affinities seem to lie more deeply with ancients like Plato and Aristotle, especially in his vision of the philosophic potentiality of humanity embodied in Lear’s learned Theban.

Several 20th-c. critics find mythic and archetypal patterns central to the meaning of the play. Heilman (1949, p. 45) sees Lr. as concerned with the apparent decay of myth and the mythic habit of mind.…In this view, the complex and elusive King Lear becomes a myth about myth: its theme is the myth in crisis. Specific myths are the concern of Sitwell (1948, pp. 51–2): In this play we see…the reversal of all [mythic] histories. In the beginning of the legend, Cronos devoured his own offspring. In King Lear, the brood devours the parent, in whom Age had become Time, and Time a fifth element. In the myth of Œdipus, son of Laius, King of Thebes, the Theban King, having learned from the oracle that he was doomed to die by the hand of his own son, exposed that son upon Mount Cithaeron immediately after his birth, with his hands and feet tied together. Here it is Lear, the father, who having first cast from his bosom his child Cordelia, is then shut from the gates to wander under the extemitie of the skies as an outcast. The eyes, not the feet, of Gloucester, the father of Edmund, are pierced, and he is thrust outside the gates, to wander in blindness. In the Fourth Scene of the Third Act…[52] [Lear] is no longer Œdipus, but is the Sphinx, who must ask the great question.…And it is the naked man exposed upon the mountains—one more naked even than the questioner—one who has nothing but his bare humanity, who is now Œdipus the Theban, who can give an answer to the Riddle. No longer does the Sphinx, as in the ancient legend, put an oblique question to which the answer is: This is Man. Instead, bare and terrible, the question is put. Lear, the Sphinx, asks: Is Man no more than this? But in this work of Night, no answer comes from the Naked Man,—no direct answer, only a few meaningless words, like dust from the ruins. But behind that huddle of meaningless words lies the true answer: Man is nothing. Likewise Hardison (1975, p. 228): The Ixion myth had a general influence on the play, extending from the first scene to the last.…The myth…supplied Shakespeare with the philosophical issues in terms of which the action of the play developed. Hughes (1992, pp. 257–62) finds in Lr. as in all Sh.’s works a complex refiguration of the myth of Venus, Adonis, and the boar.

Other critics find more general archetypal patterns. Henn (1956, p. 155): Between the poles of the heroic and the homely, king and beast, the play oscillates on its violent sea. At its centre the Fool and the Blinded Man stand beside the King: one in danger of whipping for speaking his wisdom, the other blinded for a night’s pleasure, both now wiser than the King. Over all is the sense of power that has been borrowed, and which has released evil, and must work itself out in convulsion. Driscoll (1977, pp. 159–60): Archetypal stages and patterns structure [Lr.’s] vision.…[160] The early Lear…[embodies] the wrathful, unconscious, and contradictory animal nature Yahweh exhibits.…The sea monster emblematizes Yahweh’s terrible anima—Goneril.…At the next stage stands Job, the man who must suffer Yahweh’s injustices. Lear’s mortification, torment, madness, and the journey to the unconscious it represents, together with his temporary realization of expanded consciousness in humility and patience when he reunites with Cordelia, dramatizes this stage.…With Cordelia’s violent death, Lear enters the third stage, where he fully grasps the reality of evil and suffering by becoming a defiant Promethean figure.…The highest or goal stage is that of fulfillment, wholeness, or enlightenment and…is identified with Christ as an alchemical symbol. Cordelia stands at this stage.

Long (1976, p. 218) sees a seasonal mythic pattern: Shakespeare realizes the tragic paradox in all its intensity by working with a model for understanding human life which has its basis in a metaphysic of the seasons, built in its turn on the popular dialectics of seasonal folk-lore, superstition, and magic. Liebler (1995, pp. 197–8) emphasizes the social function of myth, interpreting Lr. as festive tragedy: Lr. represents the subjectivity, the subjection, and through it, the precariousness of political/cultural identity.…[198] In King Lear, when the fundamental inscription of known national identity is altered, the definitions of all relations are destabilized, including…the definition of human. At the spatial center of the play is the question of what that word means, and with it the definition and possibility of civilization.…Lear’s cartographic gerrymandering…creates the statusless limbo of liminality which dissolves the security of familiar social structures.

Ritual action is the concern of other critics, such as Coursen (1976, pp. 259–93): The first scene has been an anti-ritual, not a ceremony celebrating contact with deeper mysteries, but a set piece dictated by the needs of Lear the man for further furbishing his self-esteem.…[277] The trial scene [3.6] is…a parody of the initial love test, the justice of the second reflecting the justice of the first in an ironic mirror.…[288] The reconciliation scene [4.7] is sacramental; it (p. 292) resonates with overtones of the Sacrament of Baptism. Pilikian (1977–8, pp. 26–30): There are numerous indications that Lear’s love-game of the first scene [27] is actually a seasonal celebration of national fertility.…Cordelia, by refusing to respect the ritual rules of the fertility-game, is committing an offense of such socio-political seriousness, that it can only be qualified as the ultimate State-Treason, deserving capital punishment because by her behavior she is inviting the evil of infertility, hence, DEATH upon Lear’s kingdom.…[30] Lear [had intended an incestuous Sacred Marriage with Cordelia [in 1.1]. [He] identifies himself with Dionysius, the ritual bridegroom of ancient Athenian ritual.…Lear allows himself such a blatant act of incest because Cordelia is a bastard-daughter [p. 28: the offspring of an adulterous female (the Queen)]. Boose (1982, p. 332): The tragic action derives from colliding, incompatible ritual structures: the attempt of the man who is both king and father to substitute the illegitimate transfer of his kingdom for the legitimate one of his daughter.

A few critics specifically identify ritual sacrifice as the archetypal pattern underlying the action of Lr. Bodkin (1934, pp. 85–6): In the reader’s or spectator’s experience of tragic catharsis, something is present corresponding to the emotional meaning that belonged to ancient rituals undertaken for the renewal of the life of the tribe.…[86] Lear dies, but those who have shared with awe and pity the anguish of his last convulsion gather themselves together to sustain the gored state. See also below, . Holloway (1961, p. 98): Running through the work, besides its other interests is something which might be called the vertebrate structure of its intrinsic design; the developing line, unabridged, of a human sacrifice. Brockbank (1976, pp. 129–32): In Lr., Sh. internalize[s] the tragic-sacrificial experience, to realize it in the hidden structures of language and consciousness.…[132] The playwright is presiding over a sacrifice; and the playwright, in the span of the theatre’s few hours, is himself the clearest god who makes honours of men’s impossibilities [cf. 2518–19]. Smith (1991, pp. 79–80) likewise finds the play enacting ritual parricide…the [80] scapegoating of the patriarch, thereby invok[ing] a sense of declining monarchy itself. However, the ending reemphasizes the patriarchal system that had been disrupted in the play. See also Davidson (1931), Stéphane (1964).

Other critics find in this fictional drama a self-conscious concern with issues of fiction-making or with the nature of drama itself. MacIntyre (1982, pp. 34–5) discusses paradoxical relations between truth, lies, and fiction: Long before their deaths, [Lear and Gloucester] learn the folly of their trust in falsehoods. Yet, strangely, much of the good that befalls them itself is built upon falsehoods by characters who intend to benefit them [i.e., Kent and Edgar]. The relationship between telling the truth, telling lies, and inventing fictions—the posy of Kent and Edgar—shapes the play’s most important actions. This relationship parallels the 16th century’s awareness of the need to tell the truth, an aware-[35]ness most important in the justification of poesy (the creation of fictions) against charges that to make them is to lie. Righter (1962, p. 185) discusses Lr. as metadrama: For the most part…the play metaphor appears in connection with Lear and his followers, and always as an expression of futility and despair.…The necessity for the adoption of disguise, of false identity, in order to remain oneself is one of the most painful paradoxes in King Lear. Van Laan (1974, pp. 63 ff.) likewise finds Lr. to be concerned with play-acting: By establishing play-acting as a viable mode of action [in 1.1], Lear has created the great stage of fools he will eventually refer to explicitly [2625]. The central importance of this theatrical metaphor is demonstrated by the thoroughness with which it applies to the [66] action. Almost every character engages in play-acting of one kind or another, and his skill or lack of skill in play-acting is a crucial factor in determining the nature of his experience. Similarly Egan (1975, p. 20): Shakespeare’s artistic purpose is reflected within the play itself through attempts by its characters to deal with, influence, or alter the circumstances of their world directly through exercises of dramatic art. Hubert (1983, p. 86) discusses the verbal overdetermination [in Lr.] not only of such active elements of dramaturgy as writing, staging, directing, improvising, prompting, but also of its most static aspect, the role of the audience. Melchiori (1988, p. 78): The metaphor of the theater as world and of the world as theater…is indeed the synthesis of the whole play of Lear in its outer and inner structure. Lear is Shakespeare’s supreme tribute to the power of metaphor. Desmet (1992, pp. 114–20): The play explicitly addresses the relationship between voice and vision in dramatic illusion.…[120] Rhetoric’s limited ability to shape both self and world is figured thematically in the play by a contrast between the antique, largely oral culture that Lear has lost and a hostile, literate world where information is processed dispassionately through the eye rather than the ear. See also McIver (1978) and Berger (1985; 1997, p. 67).

Other modern critics either find Lr. to be concerned with the proper function of language, or they find in the play support for various ideas about language. Burckhardt (Quality, 1961, pp. 33–45): Lear tragically treats [words] as substances, as entities, which carry their own truth within them: they create for him his daughters’ loves, as they are to create…their realms.…[45] The knowledge that is his madness…is the harvest of Lear’s proud faith in the substantiality of his words; Nothing now has come of nothing, the word as entity has created its meaning and drawn the universe into the chaos of universal negation. The name has become absolute: Lear, utterly divested of all that gives meaning to the name of king, is now king in name only and so, paradoxically, king absolute and essential. German (1964, p. 10) sees a central concern with the breakdown of communication between human beings. Danson (1974, pp. 165–78): Lear’s ritual for declaring love…shows that language must somehow be redeemed from the fate inherent in its public nature.…The play…may be, in effect, an effort to create some more capable language.…[178] The language of the play imitates one of the play’s dominant actions, the breaking down and stripping away of old social forms until they are as naked as the thing itself and ready (possibly) for a rebirth in a new dispensation. Zitner (1974, pp. 3 ff.): Its language is not only the vehicle for King Lear’s questions, but one of them…The uses of language are as intended and systematic a motif as the uses of love.…[4] Shakespeare’s prohibition of nice pieties at the end of the play…suggests that the demands of form and decorum in language may lead to untruths.…Language as literature, therefore language at the top of its bent, declares itself inadequate for the task it has just performed.…[14] In a play so paradoxical, so problematic, such truths as can be hazarded must be enveloped in ironic verbal textures: snatches of song, riddle, burlesque prophecy, and quip. Having little application, conventional wisdom is relegated to the merely rhetorical artifice in which sentence began. Valesio (1980, p. 43), similarly, finds in 1.1 one of the most striking illustrations of the rhetoric of antirhetoric. Hawkes (1977, p. 29): Cordelia’s silence is Shakespeare’s own addition to the story. Its purpose is to demonstrate the limitations Lear imposes on language by his insistence on words alone as the carriers of meaning.

De Grazia (1978, pp. 379–83) in contrast sees Lr. more concerned with ethical failings than linguistic theory: In [Sh.’s] period, linguistic deterioration was seen as a sign of moral corruption, not of inherent inadequacies in language itself.…[383] In King Lear, language in the storm scenes deteriorates to the only partially coherent and familiar sounds of mad Lear, crazed Fool, and possessed Tom.…In each case, the breakdown, the babbling is the fault of the speaker rather than of the linguistic medium available to him. In each case the problem might have been avoided or resolved with the traditional antidote of charity.

Aers, Hodge & Kress (1981, pp. 77–98), employing a theory of language as ideology, find that Sh. exemplifies the social construction of individuals.…[78] A speaker’s choice of a given linguistic form always arises out of the ideological system which is relevant and operative for him at that point. It is thus possible to infer a speaker’s values from the linguistic forms he uses.…Within the society of King Lear, individuality may be defined and expressed in one of two distinct modes. Either an individual [e.g. Albany] realises himself through socially given characteristics, apprehended by him as what is conventionally acceptable, hence accepted and internalised as natural without any examination; or else the individual [e.g. Kent] takes a critical stance towards the categories of the social world and attempts to express his individuality in a way which, while inevitably social, [79] is not passively dependent on external and imposed definitions of socially appropriate identity and values.…[84] However, King Lear is not about a simple dichotomy between the two modes of perceiving self.…A character may assume either position at different times.…[85] Conditions of stress…cause the characters to move unwittingly and unwillingly out of their habitual forms of perception. Ultimately (p. 98) the play…disclose[s] the old [social] order as generating its own supersessions.

Whittier (1989, pp. 367–77), for whom Lear is at once Shakespeare’s most misogynist and rhetorically selfconscious tragedy, attempts to regenitalize the play’s poetic body, to uncover the tissue of its sexual and linguistic pessimism, and to articulate the dynamics of its genders under the aspects of idea, imagery, diction, and those rhemes [i.e., blocks of rhetorical structure] which…Valesio [p. 44] calls the biology of the text.…[377] In this tragedy as in no other, words are made to take on the displaced burden of maternity in a motherless world, and to redeem both the potential sterility of what is solely male and the potential disorder of what is solely female.

Grundy (1990, pp. 181–8): The central tragic source in King Lear is that the action is made to imitate the poetic rather than the natural model of language; this involves (p. 182) the denial of the referential function of language and causes (p. 182) a lack of coherence between language and experience.…The incoherence of the Lear-world is regularly suggested in a way that [184] prepares us for a potentially unifying New Speak resolution. Lear sees (p. 188) the poetic code as Orwellian Newspeak. Goneril et al. attempt to make poetic language (p. 187) a true New Speak,…an original code not interpretable, by trying to discount its rhetorical status and enforce a referential function on it.

Graham (1994, pp. 192 ff.): In King Lear…Shakespeare subjects [rhetorical] plainness to the full force of a skeptical challenge, yet shows it withstanding that challenge in a somewhat altered form.…Shakespeare shows how conviction that seems abso-[193]utely true and powerful when silent can be diminished when compelled to speak and act. Yet he also shows that the necessity of performance can make conviction most real if the plainspeaker [sic] acknowledges that knowledge and actions are rhetorically mediated.…[205] For characters such as Cordelia, Kent, Edgar, and the Fool, plainness to a considerable degree comprises the conviction and performance of [206] love, and their plain love enables them to escape from the self-justifying prison of a purely antirhetorical plainness to the contingent relations of a rhetorical engagement with the world.

Magnusson (1999, pp. 150–3) focuses on social dialogue in the play: Lr. insists on the extraordinary power that the banalities of conversation exert in constructing and holding in place the structures of reality that the characters in Lear inhabit.…[153] It makes visible the normal conversational mechanisms of acknowledgment, or reciprocal self-maintenance—mechanisms which usually function apart from the awareness or conscious intention of the participants. That making visible does not, however, enable characters like Cordelia or Kent to change their practices of acknowledgment or to alter their needs for acknowledgment, because these forms of acknowledgment are what make and sustain their own quotidian selves.

Poststructuralist theories of language and discourse provide an interpretive framework for others. Schehr (1982, p. 62): Lear’s madness…is a reflection of the violence of language and of the limits of culture. And all the monsters of the play, most notably Lear himself, are the products of the incongruity of the nature/culture opposition, revolving around the nothing, yet perpetually covering, discovering and re(dis)covering it. Humphries (1983, pp. 31–5): Lr. expresses the failure of epistemology. It partakes of dualism, of fear, of repression, of relativity, differentiation and fragmentation, and of epistemological failure, all of which exceed the palpably real and can be expressed only through exploitation of the inductive properties of language. This would mean that Saussurean linguistics, differential philosophy, and Freudian psychology—being as compellingly and disturbingly excessive as Lear itself—offer models and terminologies which may be equal to the perilous and slippery exigency [Danson, 1981, p. 119] which Shakespeare’s play dramatizes.…[35] Shakespeare seems to understand, or be groping toward an understanding, that language must be understood within a metaphysic of absence. Reiss (1980, pp. 183–5): in Lear we are shown a confusion and an inversion that are not simply those of an order [of discourse] that has lost ground, but that proceed from a direct clash of different classes of discourse, of different ways of thinking and acting, of different conceptions of power, of the place of the self and the role of the other. Unlike other Renaissance tragedies Lr. (p. 185) does not aim to constitute the subject (or to show, perform, its impossibility) but rather to set in motion the operation and confrontation of power.…In the play of conflicting powers no conclusion will be reached: save perhaps the indication that confrontation is utterly inadequate to produce anything new that may be socially or politically useful. For, in the end, Lear may be showing us that a new class of discourse cannot spring simply from confrontation—that it can only arise with a quite different, within an other (logical or discursive) space, that it can only arise on the basis of a prior—and essential—displacement.

Eagleton (1986, pp. 81–3), in a self-described exercise in political semiotics, focuses on the theme of language and value: The paradox which King Lear explores is that it is natural for the human animal to transcend its own limits, yet this creative tendency to exceed oneself is also the source of destructiveness. Being untrue to their own nature is natural to human beings: what we call culture or history is an open-ended transformation of fixed boundaries, a transcendence of mere appetite or rich surplus over precise measure. But when this process transgresses the body’s confines too far, it violates the bonds of sensuous compassion and begins to prey on physical life itself.…[82] What is superfluous or excessive about human beings, King Lear suggests, is nothing less than language itself, which constantly outruns the confines of the body. The worst is not, declares Edgar, So long as we can say This is the worst ([2210–11]). By naming an ultimate limit, speech transcends it in that very act, undoing its own pronouncement by its own performance. Language is the edge we have over biology, but it is a mixed blessing.…[83] Language, like much else in the play, has a problem in pitching itself at the elusive point between too much and too little—except, perhaps, in the formally precise yet generously affectionate discourse of Cordelia. Cordelia blends largesse and limitation on her first appearance in the play, when she reminds Lear that her love, though freely given, must be properly divided between himself and her future husband; and the same balance is present in her combination of physical rootedness and freedom of spirit. In this sense, she symbolically resolves many of the play’s formal antinomies. The only problem, however, is that she dies. Edgar’s closing injunction—Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say—is no trite tag, denoting as it does that organic unity of body and language, that shaping of signs by the senses, of which Cordelia is representative; but the play has also demonstrated that to speak what one feels is no easy business. For if it is structural to human nature to surpass itself, and if language is the very index and medium of this, then there would seem to be a contradiction at the very core of the linguistic animal which makes it natural for signs to come adrift from things, consciousness to overstep physical bonds, values to get out of hand and norms to be destructively overridden.…King Lear is a tragedy because it stares this contradiction full in the face, aware that no poetic symbolism is adequate to resolve it.

Evans (1986, pp. 224–31) discusses Lr.’s discourse on representation: In King Lear the abyss of subjects and signs, complete with its ideological disclosures and abnegations, appears as an almost physical presence, conjured up near the cliffs of Dover during [4.6].…[225] Madness is produced in the play’s language as a signifier cut free of its signified and as voices that disperse the unified subject.…The heath and the cliff are…places of transformation that reverse the supplementary mark of the linguistic and theatrical signifier.…[226] The view from the cliff-edge, inscribed in the theatrical trope of the supplement, is the absent centre of the play, a regress into the nothing spoken by the Fool revealing the text’s discourse on the linguistic and theatrical signifier, produced as the nothing or the excess that precedes the essences engaged in the discursive closures of conflicting ideologies.…[228] Madness, the theatre and traditional forms of festive upheaval are brought into a particularly sharp conjunction, through which the locus conflict between a feudal nature reformulated by the ideologues of the absolutist Tudor state, and the discourses of competitive individualism is played out behind allusions to the festive ideal of equality and plenty.…[231] The discourse on representation in King Lear, which incorporates timeless prophecy, the imaginary abyss of language, and actors acting (actors acting) madness that contains reason, is a particularly convoluted production of the aesthetic ideology of nothing.…While the internal distances and inversions of the text it proposes may disclose the contrivance of ideological discourses that present themselves as natural, the textuality that gets in the way of the conflicting doctrines in King Lear also traps in its regresses the egalitarian festive ideal.…The historical transformations of festive inversion and abuse evident in the play are powerless in the face of the sort of essentialist discourse they debunk.

Goldberg (1988, pp. 245–56) identifies a compensatory pattern…focused on the word Dover.…[246] The word names a site of desire, the hope for recovery, or, at least, repose, restoratives to answer eyeless rage, or the final closing of the eyes in a sleep without end.…[247] [However,] after Gloucester’s reiterated questions to Edgar [at 2245, 2256] the word Dover never appears in King Lear. Instead of the place, we arrive at Dover Cliff only in the lines that Edgar speaks to his father in IV.vi.…It suffices to say that Dover Cliff exists only in Edgar’s lines and nowhere else in the play. The refusal to allow the word Dover to arrive at the place it (apparently) names, the failure, in other words, for signifier to reach signified—the failure of the sign—establishes the place that Dover occupies in the text. It is the place of illusion—the illusion of the desire voiced by Kent or Gloucester, the illusion of recovery and the illusion of respite and end.…The limits that Dover represents in the text are the limits of representation themselves.…[256] Edgar’s imagined Dover is a working out of illusion that rests on nothing: silence, invisibility, blindness.

Cavanagh (1991, pp. 158–61): King Lear dramatises the need to define, i.e., the need to disentangle sense from the pressing confusion of circumstances. Lr. (p. 159) exposes definition to an often terrifying light that reveals the wilfully closed authoritarian cruelty that can inhere within the formulation of sense.…[160] Characters, good and evil alike, become victims of the way they have made sense of the world.…[161] This continual rupturing of the parameters of sense and definition is one source of King Lear’s power and, like its characters, readers of the play have preferred a censored version of its reality.…By restoring a final sense to the play—by discovering, or even replacing, its essence—its remorseless challenges to the ability to define can be erased.

Other critics employing poststructuralist concepts of language include Cope (1988, p. 275), who suggests a certain timid rapprochement between the metaphoric language about language of Derrida and the more furious poetry and radical claims against the paradox of language in Lear. Downes (1988, pp. 225 ff.): The play seems to be preoccupied [226] with linguistic issues. This is perhaps less the result of the author’s interest in language as such, but rather the product of language itself being constitutive of social norms and conventions.…[245] But there is no easy equation of rhetorical styles and falsehood, or plainness and truth.…[254] What is foregrounded [in 53–9]…is the problem of institutional love in a context where social identity is constituted in hierarchies of authority, and the reliability of language in this context. Harrison (1991, pp. 56–7): What [1.1] forces upon our attention is not reality…[57] but the nature, and the limitations, of our own representations of reality. Armstrong (1994, pp. 415 ff.) focuses on uncanny duplicity: In King Lear [sic], the division of the kingdom(s) in the first scene of the play stages a duplication which sends disseminatory repercussions both forward and backward.…This dissemination haunts the action of the play throughout, not only in the multiplicity of conflicting messages (mis)directed [416] across the stage, but also in the doubling and division of plot, action and character. Finally, certain effects of division can be shown to exceed the play and structure the reactions of audiences, readers, critics and editors.…[431] The most uncanny element of all, the gaze,…becomes apparent at several moments in the play: Lear’s mirror image of folly, Gloucester’s blind gaze, the aftermath of the fall from Dover cliff. At these points the audience finds itself transfixed in the gaze of the Other, where the play both looks back at the audience and shows itself showing itself.…A reading of the uncanny moment suggests how an illusory relationship between representation and reality can only be maintained through certain repressions and the institution and naturalization of specific perceptual rubrics which become liable to disintegration, duplication or reversal. Davis (1999, pp. 121–37) examines aspects of King Lear which fall under the [Lacanian theory of the] sway of the signifier in two readily specifiable forms: letters and numbers. (P. 124): Awareness of the early modern era’s emotionally charged debate over mathematical approaches to the practical reckoning of worth can be a valuable part of the interpretive equipment that one brings to the play.…[137] Early modern cultural anxieties about algoristic practices and the new zero…have a very pervasive bearing on the play’s conceptual design.…This helps to account for a particular shaping given to the conflict set up by the action between letters placed as external to authentic processes of communication, and numbering treated as a projection of the intrinsic.

div.head: Psychological
div.p: Lr., with its harrowing representations of cruelty within families and moving depictions of love between fathers and their children, is sometimes interpreted as a myth or fantasy satisfying readers’ or audiences’ primal psychic needs. Goddard (1951, pp. 522–5): The theme of King Lear is the same one that dominates Greek drama, the relation of the generations,…the authority of the past over the present as symbolized by the father.…[524] What we see…is the conversion of the father into the likeness of the child.…Lear ends with authority and force put off, with love and tenderness put on.…[Cordelia’s] conduct involved the paradox of both discontinuity and continuity with the older generation. The present [525] must break with the past, her story seems to say, in order to become conscious of itself and of its freedom; whereupon it must mend the breach it has made lest it cut itself off from the only energy whereby it can live. We must repudiate the past, for it has sinned against us; we must forgive and love it, for it has given us life. This is irrational, but it is true.

Rosenberg (1972, pp. 329 ff.) describes The Lear Myth thus: At the heart of King Lear lies a fantasy deeply embedded in human consciousness. It is a fantasy that a child readily recognizes, but that grown men generally learn to disguise in the dress of art.…[330] The child, insatiable for love and self-esteem, insistent on the role of the sole favorite, inevitably makes demands upon a parent that are rejected, because nobody can have—be—everything. The rejection often seems to be accompanied by a favoring of the child’s rivals—brothers, sisters, the other parent. The child compensates in fantasy.…The Lear fantasy is more cunning [than the Oedipus fantasy]: the parent suffers—dies—because he wrongs the dreamer, who himself may die, or at least endure noble martyrdom: for the suffering and death of the child dreamer is in this context the worst possible punishment for the father.…The theme sounds in some religious mythology, and reverberates in fairy tales and folklore.…[331] This generic fantasy seems most satisfying when it is complete with its second part: when, as in Lear, the parent who rejects the innocent child not only is made to realize, often through much suffering, how wrong he was, and is very, very, sorry, but is also rescued by the child, and begs the child’s forgiveness.…[332] As made by Shakespeare, Lear seems motivated by a fate of his own choosing, but he is also in the grip of a psychic destiny: the guilty father, and the guilty, offending siblings must be punished, while the true child is vindicated in terrible suffering.…[335] Every important character in the play is designed to release for the audience passions normally repressed in life.

Similarly Stockholder (1976, pp. 24–6): King Lear…activates the family structure in which our primal phantasy life originates. At the same time the extension by analogy of that structure to nation and cosmos satisfyingly confirms the tremendous importance of that primal time without making us feel in danger of regressing to a childlike level of involvement.…The aggressive destructive com-[25]ponents of the play satisfy…infantile, aggressive feelings in a more directly infantile way than either popular or folk literature, for not only is the action directly brutal and horrendous; it is also action taken directly by children against parents, with hands rather than weapons, and it does, in the end, destroy those parents. The action is accompanied by constant verbal reinforcing in the persistent imagery of beasts, bestiality, monsters of the deep, so that part of the defence level arises from the judgement of that infantile aggression as less than human, at the same time that the satisfaction in part derives from unleashing those less than human elements from the stultifying false ceremony presented to us in the play’s opening. On the phantasy level, Lear’s three daughters work as two aspects of the self as child. The tendency of evil aspects to split into several figures while the good remains single…may relate to the single figure of the good parent of pre-individualized infancy in contrast to the many figures the growing child and adult meets who later function in parent roles.…The sub-plot repeats this pattern, but on a more mature emotional level.…The satisfying complexity of the play as the two plots intertwine, and figures from one start acting on those from the other, seems to reproduce the complexity that results when the phantasy demands of individuals start interacting on each other in the actual world.…[26] The play associates the rage of Goneril and Regan with the fury of the storm on the heath to which Lear is subjected, though that depersonalized, somewhat oceanic rage seems a relief, in so far as we identify with Lear, from civilized Oedipally-torn domesticities.…At whatever level one wishes to state the meaning of [Lr.], whether on a political level having to do with a concept of the state, or on a metaphysical level having to do with the nature of reality, or in terms of Elizabethan cosmology, all of these meanings are about ways in which deep phantasy levels find fulfillment in the external world, and about the consequences for that world of the different ways of fulfilling different phantasies.

Adelman (1978, pp. 1–7): King Lear is an unusually harrowing experience for its audience…because of its insistence on our sympathetic participation in [the experiences that it portrays].…[6] However foreign the setting, however motiveless the actions, these characters seem familiar to us: familiar from our childhood, when we knew all about the three daughters, and knew that the scorned youngest was the best.…We have all faced, in one way or another, the dilemma that faces Lear’s daughters. We have had to choose, with Cordelia, between a dutiful display of love made meaningless because it is not freely given, and a withholding of the display, a refusal to demean our love by producing it on demand, as if for a reward.…[7] As we have faced the dilemma of the daughters, so have we faced the anxieties that prompt Lear’s question: the desire to control exactly that which loses its value once it is not given freely is partly an attempt to repair the damage of our first fall, the first recognition of the separation of self and other that makes us so frighteningly aware of our dependence on everything that is outside ourselves, everything we find that we cannot control.…We understand these characters at the start partly insofar as we allow their dilemmas to find echoes within us; and we are encouraged to participate in their psychic lives by those very elements that make King Lear seem remote to us, and removed from our ordinary ways of understanding.

Others who discuss the psychology of family relations include McFarland (1981, pp. 105 ff.): The family image in Lear is what in Christopher Lasch’s rubric is termed haven in a heartless world.…[113] The sexual disgust of King Lear …should be seen …as a deliberate eviction from the play of the only force that in both common experience and psychological observation challenges the satisfactions and securities of the family.…[116] The truth, both of the play and of human life, is that human inattention destroys the family as haven. But the family as haven, though it undergoes vicissitudes that reveal it to be largely illusion…complements the idea of a heartless world. Asp (1986, pp. 192–203): With a ruthless, almost anti-humanist clarity, the play depicts the implacable conflicts that exist between the generations: the narcissistic, infantile, and latently incestuous demands made by the aging father on the daughters and the aggressive rejection of these demands by the offspring. The play (p. 197) is structured…around the dynamics of repression and negation.…[203] The lack, or loss of a nurturing maternal principle within the world of the play is the terrifying absence at its heart. Cole (1985, p. 138) finds even in the good children ambivalence toward the father: Cordelia’s smiles and tears; the presence of the French army attempting to protect a British king; the exhausting pursuit of Lear (a benign version of her sisters’ attempted pursuit to the death); Edgar’s conscious trickery of his father, trifling with his despair; and the deathblow given Gloucester by the son’s revelation of himself as son do not in the least undermine the genuinely benevolent designs of Cordelia and Edgar as mourners-caretakers, yet they are clearly expressions of the ambivalence which characterizes ritual mourning for the lost father. Bloom (1998, pp. 484–91): What the drama of King Lear truly outrages is our universal idealization of the value of familial love—that is to say, both love’s personal and love’s social value. The play manifests an intense anguish in regard to human sexuality, and a compassionate despair as to the mutually destructive nature of both paternal and filial love. Maternal love is kept out of the tragedy, as if natural love in its strongest form would be too much to bear, even for this negative sublimity.…[491] The Freudian, witty oxymoron of family romance loses its wit in the context of King Lear, where familial love offers you only a choice between destructions.

Some critics find Lr. specifically concerned with the threat of incest in father-daughter relations. Thus Lucas (1951, pp. 65–6) following Pauncz: The first fatal scene between Lear and Cordelia becomes more [66] intelligible, and more pathetic, when we see in it a lovers’ quarrel, though neither of them knows it. Melchiori (1960, p. 73): In Lear, the bawdiest of Shakespeare’s plays [?], the problem [of father-daughter incest] which was to be set out and even solved more coolly and calmly later [i.e. in the romances], was seething underneath. Cavell (1969; 2002, p. 300): It is part of the miracle of the vision in King Lear …that we do not care whether the kind of love between [Lear and Cordelia] is forbidden according to man’s lights. We care whether love is or is not altogether forbidden to man, whether we may not altogether be incapable of it, of admitting it into our world. We wonder whether we may always go mad between the equal efforts and terrors at once of rejecting and of accepting love. McCabe (1993, p. 179), responding to Hugo’s reflections (see ), argues that Under such extreme circumstances traditional distinctions between the sacred and the profane tend to collapse.…During the course of the play Shakespeare conducts an anatomy of parental and filial emotions almost as brutal as that to which Lear would submit Regan. See also below.

Adelman (1992, p. 104) finds maternal deprivation to be a central concern: This text about fathers insistently returns to mothers: discovering what he is father to, confronting the implications of his own paternity, Lear is brought to acknowledge their absent presence; and even Gloucester, unproblematically father to his sons, is made the victim of their awesome power.…Much of the play’s power comes…from its confrontation with the language of maternal deprivation or worse, from the vulnerability and rage that is the consequence of this confrontation and the intensity and fragility of the hope for a saving maternal presence that can undo pain. In the characteristic way of the return of the repressed, that is, the excision of the mother that seems initially to allow for a fantasy of male parthenogenesis ends by releasing fantasies far more frightening than any merely literal mothers could be, fantasies that give emotional coloration to the entire play in part because they are not localized in (and hence limited to) any single character.

Danson (1998, p. 245) emphasizes the misrecognition of fathers: The evidence throughout Shakespeare’s career suggests that the complement of the playwright’s strong urge to father-daughter reunion is his equally strong avoidance of the father-son reunion—a reunion he is nonetheless drawn repeatedly to attempting. Edgar’s ostensible reason for his delay in revealing himself to Gloucester has the feel of a rationalisation…and possibly it feels like a rationalisation because what Shakespeare really delays or defers could be the intolerable recognition that Edmund’s wish, the bad son’s wish to supplant the father, is also always the good son Edgar’s unavoidable destiny.

Other critics focus on the psychology of the characters rather than that of readers or audiences. Berger (1979; 1997, p. 27): The [characters’] language reveals the complementary pressures of a self-justifying function and a scapegoating function. It shows us that characters tend to avoid recognizing their own contributions to the difficulties they face, while magnifying the complicity of others. Their scenarios are frequently cast in the simplistic mode of folklore, fairytale, or parable.…These parabolic conceptions often reinforce the character’s sense of the inevitability of his or her plight, and they seem to have the effect that Freud ascribed to dreams in that their displacements and condensations enable the dreamer character to go on sleeping, to delay reentry into a world or knowledge or self whose reality is feared. Idem (1997, pp. 300–23): In the perspective of redistributed complicities, the good characters are those who try to hide their darker purposes primarily from themselves, and the wicked are those who try, or pretend to try, to hide them from others.…[301] At the core of the network of ethical discourses is a small knot of volatile interactions among the discourses of the victim, the revenger, the sinner, the villain, the donor, the hero, and the saint or savior.…[323] Edgar, Lear, Cordelia, Gloucester, and Kent all try to ensconce themselves in the victim’s discourse, and most of them at one point or another enact its passive-aggressive potentialities. Zak (1984, pp. 12 ff.): Shakespeare sees the essence of the tragedy in King [13] Lear as a flight from shame that keeps man from a redeeming participation in human community.…Shakespeare presents all the principal characters in King Lear as self-cover’d thing[s], for shame. But the shame that drives Cordelia, Kent, and the Fool into love’s disguises is primarily a matter of discretion, not disgrace.…In Lear, Edmund, Edgar, and Gloucester, however, the matter is reversed. Banishing discretion, they…hide, even from themselves, in a desperate and isolating flight from the sense of their own disgrace.…[20] The play is tragic not because its characters inhabit an imbecile universe but because well-intentioned men, with opportunities to do so, do not act to make the play the romance it could and should have been.

Critics indebted to Freudian psychoanalytic theory draw various conclusions about the meaning of Lr. Kanzer (1965, p. 11): The dominant fantasy that we feel justified in reconstructing from King Lear is one of childbirth which, on a deeper layer, encloses a sadistic primal scene. Chaplin (1969, pp. 34–45): To say that King Lear’s form is dream-like is another way of saying that Shakespeare has found the appropriately dramatic way of representing the ideational content of Lear’s repressed infantile desires, his primitive animistic mode of expressing them, and the neurotic symptoms they betray.…[45] Through a dream-like penetration to the primitive and archetypal sources of both imagination and desire, Shakespeare has brought us to confront the essentially human paradox: the incompatible needs of a child changed father, their representation through wrong imaginations and through Reason in madness, and the image of their origin and their end—unaccommodated man. See also Kanzer (1951), Pauncz (1951), Idem (1954), and Barron and Rosenberg (1970).

A variety of psychological theories besides Freudian psychoanalytic theory are adduced by critics discussing Lr. Thus Sinfield (1976, pp. 2–15): The relations between the main characters in King Lear can be made more comprehensible by using [R. D.] Laing’s concepts and approach.…[15] Indeed, King Lear may be regarded as a vast image for the suffering of the inadequate self. McLaughlin (1978, p. 37) employs the ideas of Alfred Adler: Not only Lear, but also his three daughters and Edmund are driven by the need to achieve social, personal, and sexual power. Snyder (1982, p. 451): Lear’s career from [his] reluctant abdication through struggle and pain to his reconciliation with Cordelia parallels the course of many dying patients observed by Elizabeth Kübler-Ross and other students of death and dying, from initial denial to acceptance. Indeed the stages of response Kübler-Ross outlines in her study [i.e. denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance] all have their correspondences, naturalistic and symbolic, in the action of the play. Bevington (1989, passim) also discusses the psychology of dying in Lr. Pandit (1990, pp. 248–53) uses the ideas of Jacques Lacan, focus[ing] on the theme of authorial subjectivity in the context of intersubjective mirroring in the Shakespearean text, and arguing that aesthetic pleasure results from the emotional identification of the reader with the author, and of both with the character(s). At 898 and 2794, (p. 253) The emotional synchronicity of: <I did her wrong> <you do me wrong> <they did me wrong> [sic], before the onset and after the quieting of the great rage inscribes in the discourse of the play the mark of Lear’s subjectivity. The ear and gaze of the Other are for Lear those of the author. Richards (1991, p. 166) also employs Lacanian concepts: Light is shed on Lear’s internal development and the structure of the drama in its received, traditional form, by viewing it as the dramatization of a primal crisis at the Mirror stage, resolved through the shifting play of the scopic drive. Herold (1991, pp. 174–8), focusing on Shakespeare’s treatment of madness, argues that Sh. anticipates (p. 178) what therapists call object relations. S. Wilson (1995, pp. 154–68), reading as a cultural materialist, identifies a peculiar psychological theme, the hystericity of history, whereby Lr. thematizes the trauma of the origin as a repetition. King Lear presents itself as a representation of the origin of Great Britain and the origin of history itself by historicizing these origins as traumatic repetitions.…[168] The space or context of this trauma…is fantasized or thematized as female jouissance.

Blending psychology and anthropology, Hogan (1995, pp. 184–93) finds that In King Lear, the most baffling section concerns a suicidal mortal jump that never should have occurred—and didn’t.…The related oddity…is a blinding. As in King John, the blinding precedes and in some sense precipitates the jump. Moreover, in each case, what is baffling is the sudden introduction of blinding when execution had previously been ordained. These inconsistencies, viewed in light of classical and biblical myth, reveal (p. 193) the epitedic structure of King John and King Lear [i.e., their associative rather than causal structure]. Specifically, blinding and exile appear as individual punishments for violation of the marriage laws by which society is in part organized. Moreover, they are punishments visited upon the culpable individuals themselves. The mortal fall, in contrast, is part of a social rectification or social disruption deriving from a violation of the laws governing authority.

Several modern critics find in the play’s characters or its internal logic signs of male anxiety about femininity. Erickson (1985, pp. 104–13): For various male characters, the comfort of male bonding is a defense against female contamination. Yet, (p. 113) However poignant the relations among Lear’s company of supportive men, this male bonding is finally a minor resource compared with the unequivocal centrality of Cordelia for Lear.…In contrast to Othello, King Lear places greater structural emphasis on the final phase in which the male protagonist regains his perception of the woman’s innocence. Kahn (1986, p. 47) regards the embarrassed shrinking from recognition [which Cavell (1976) identifies at the heart of the play] as part of a masculine identity crisis in a culture that dichotomized power as masculine and feeling as feminine. Simpson (1986, pp. 22–7) identifies a destructive Lear-syndrome: Lear does not mean to exterminate all the women in the play, but it is true to the terms of the Lear-syndrome that he do so.…It is sexuality, of the male variety, that is at the heart of the Lear syndrome,…fear of the female, and of the sexual urge that puts men into relation with women.…[25] Shakespeare means to criticize Lear on the issue of his irascibility and immaturity, but at the same time there is evidence of a covert approval of the events he brings about.…[27] The great energy of the play comes from the unrestrained exercise of male sexuality and fantasy, and its appearance as a strictly negative function. Bono (1992, pp. 105–23) finds a masculinist anxiety about the rival reproductive power of women, inextricable from the social, political, and metaphysical uncertainties of the time.…[107] The presence of just such a maternal subtext in Sidney’s Arcadia [is] that text’s major influence on King Lear.…[122] In compensation for what it shows and what we cannot speak about, [Lr.] makes a naked appeal to maternal feeling that can support a nascent Christian theology.…[123] Lear is a play that finally rests on our kind nursery, in the pre-Oedipal realm of the maternal gesture.

Lupton & Reinhard (1993, pp. 5 ff.): King Lear holds the position of…the text at the limit of Oedipal interpretation, the play that casts and casts out femininity as the cause…of radical loss, foreclosure, and psychosis.…[147] In the Shakespearean textuality of psychoanalysis, Freud’s three caskets pass into and are retrospectively allegorized as Lacan’s three orders [the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the Real].…The language of thing, object, and nothing marks the intersection of King Lear and psychoanalysis insofar as each discourse describes and is marred by a textual (and sexual) hole at the core of representation and exchange.…Lear functions as both the hidden thing inhabiting the discourses nestled around it, and the outer limit that conditions and situates their modes of disclosure.…[229] The itinerary of Lear enacts a psychotic parody already situated within the family complexes dramatized in the Oedipus trilogy. In so doing, Lear’s hallucinatory traversal isolates the mortifying moment of the real, hung—like Jocasta and Antigone—within the Oedipal scene of symbolization.

Rudnytsky (1998–9, pp. 292–8), viewing King Lear through a feminist psychoanalytic lens, interprets Gloucester’s blinding as (p. 293) a symbolic castration, which leaves him with a bleeding vagina.…[295] Lear, a male hysteric, fears that he harbors within himself the internal organs of the despised female body.…[296] The play’s relentless dichotomizing of good and evil characters is based on a gendered polarity.…[298] The incest theme that subtends the Lear plot inevitably finds its double in the Gloucester subplot.

Of course not all critics approve of psychologistic criticism. Campbell (1953, p. 468) may speak for many who object to psychoanalytic criticism in particular: If King Lear is in essence the story of an old man’s morbid attachment to his daughter, it loses all its tragic splendor and all its exalted religious meaning.…The zealous application of psychoanalytic knowledge to the characters in Shakespeare’s plays reduces the most comprehensive imaginative vision of human experience in all literature to a mere collection of case histories of neurotics and psychotics.

Critics have often focused on the representation of women in Lr., which seems to them to include both hostility and idealization. Discussions of this subject tend to blur the boundaries between psychological and social or political interpretation.

Among early critics, Warton (1754, p. 308) observes that Lear in 4.6 makes some very severe reflections on the hypocrisy of lewd and abandon’d women. Ruskin (1865; 1905, 18:13) focuses on idealization of woman: The catastrophe of every [Shn.] play is caused always by the folly or fault of a man; the redemption, if there be any, by the wisdom and virtue of a woman, and, failing that, there is none. The catastrophe of King Lear is owing to his own want of judgment, his impatient vanity, his misunderstanding of his children; the virtue of his one true daughter would have saved him from all the injuries of the others, unless he had cast her away from him; as it is, she all but saves him. Snider (1887, p. 135) observes, It is a curious fact that the wife of neither [Lear nor Gloster] appears; long since she dropped out of this world of domestic discord, possibly was its first victim. Strindberg (1908; 1966, pp. 97–8) imagines that Lear’s misogynist railing in 4.6 is occasioned by an unhappy marriage: There’s his wife, I thought, because he has no reason for concerning himself with his daughters’ erotic life.…There can be no doubt that an unhappy memory has come into the old man’s brain and that in his daughters’ cynical attacks on Edmund he has recognized their mother, whom they probably take after. However, (p. 98) Shakespeare’s supposed hatred of women is beautifully disproved in Act V when Cordelia has come back to him: [quotes 2950–3]. In good and evil, with her roots in the dirt and her flower in the light, the most beautiful grafted to the most ugly, the masterpiece of creation but utterly spoiled, hating when she loves, and loving when she hates, that is how Shakespeare depicts woman, the sphinx, whose riddle cannot be solved, because it is unsolvable, or does not exist!

A number of modern critics insist that Sh. projects a disturbingly misogynistic and repressively patriarchal imaginative vision in Lr. Oates (1974/5, p. 25): The promised end is…in another [sense], the inevitable horror that follows when nature (or woman) is given the freedom to act spontaneously, to upset ritual, rising in rebellion against masculine authority. All the goddesses…must die, the kingdom must be totally purged of the female, not in order that mere evil be eradicated, but that the life-force itself be denied. McLuskie (1985, pp. 98, 106): In King Lear…the narrative and its dramatisation present a connection between sexual insubordination and anarchy, and the connection is given an explicitly misogynist emphasis. The action of the play, the organisation of its points of view and the theatrical dynamic of its central scenes all depend upon an audience accepting an equation between human nature and male power.…[106] The misogyny of King Lear, both the play and its hero, is constructed out of an ascetic tradition which presents women as the source of the primal sin of lust, combining with concerns about the threat to the family posed by female insubordination. However the text also dramatises the material conditions which lie behind assertions of power within the family, even as it expresses deep anxieties about the chaos which can ensue when the balance of power is altered. Callaghan (1989, pp. 172, 59 ff.) discusses the discourses which circumscribe masculinity [in Lr.] by constructing a category of woman that is always placed just outside it, at the point of tragic transgression. Thus Cordelia’s (p. 59) female transgression…is constructed as rebellion against patriarchal authority while Lear’s masculine transgression is (p. 62) constructed in a way that…displace[s] the blame and guilt onto representations of women.…When Lear banishes Cordelia, Kent and the audience may think he is being foolish but they do not think he has consciously violated some immutable moral law or longstanding social code. He has not acted unnaturally. The unnatural behaviour is that of Goneril and Regan—not even that of Edmund since he is exhibiting the behaviour commonly expected of an illegitimate son.…[91] The female corpse [is] central to tragic denouement even though that centrality is constructed via the male gaze. In Lr. a sense of lost masculinity…needs to be regained and reasserted through symbolic union with the dead female figure.…Phallic power in the form of sovereignty has, during the course of the [92] play, been unmasked as both vulnerable and impotent, and as a final movement Lear is rendered subject to Cordelia’s castrating gaze. Adelman (1992, p. 116): If the play relentlessly returns Lear to the dark and vicious place initially occluded, forcing him to acknowledge his complicity in the stench of female corruption, it is nonetheless the women who pay the full cost of his return. And if the cost is high for Goneril and Regan, it is even higher for Cordelia. For the monstrous mother/daughters Lear finds in them are in part Cordelia’s psychic progeny, generated out of his terrible need for her; and as a consequence, she must become the sacrificial antidote to maternal malevolence in them. Acting out Lear’s fantasied relation to the occluded mother through all three of the daughters who are her projections, the play divides and conquers her, recontaining her in the daughters who are her derivatives, all three of whom die in an instant. The wheel indeed comes full circle and the play ends where it had begun, with the eradication of the problematic female body.

Women’s speech and women’s silence are particular concerns of some critics who find elements of misogyny in Lr. Luckyj (1993, p. 37): The culture that produced and watched King Lear may have experienced Cordelia’s silence as both reassuringly submissive and dangerously subversive—a complex nexus for competing views of women’s silence. Rutter (1994–6; 1997, pp. 174 ff.): Lear makes the metaphors of this play; Goneril and Regan literalize them.…In [Sh.’s] theater (where language is not just iterative but creative, where words work like God’s, to realize, to materialize) the metaphors men speak women embody, women play out. Lr. enacts (p. 175) the clear patriarchal need to shift onto women what begins…as male transgression.…It is men who let loose the demons of this play; it is women who are demonized.…[184] In the theater, and in the text, Cordelia speaks out [in 1.1]. The lines make her disruptive. She doesn’t say nothing. The Nothing she eventually does say is mediated by the somethings she says first. Paradoxically the asides contrive both to make and to unmake her the virtuous silent woman of the stereotype.…[185] Lear’s opening scene plays ambiguously upon the issue of women’s speech; and…women’s speech is [186] both the matter of the scene and likewise the matter with the scene, for speech is what the King requires, and speech withheld provokes the crisis, yet the act of speaking makes women deviant.…[209] [In 5.3] Shakespeare…requires his audience to look at a stage full of female death where the Lear family is together again and we are re-membering the opening scene, defamiliar/refamiliar.…And so Cordelia and her sisters, dead silent, re-play the problematics of female speech that once again matter to the scene. The monsters Lear made, they have become; the spectacle of their dead bodies is the play’s Medusa. Callaghan (1989, pp. 178–80) also discusses the discursive logic of female silence and utterance.

Others seek to defend the play from charges of misogyny and patriarchy. Taylor (1907, p. 209): Without the underplot we might have been tempted to suspect in the play some traces of the tedious old masculine satire on the opposite sex.…It is the episode of Gloucester, with its pair of contrasted sons, which…makes it clear that the passions exhibited for our edification are neither those of woman nor those of male humanity, but belong to human nature universal. It is the undutiful child, not the undutiful and untender daughter, to whom our attention is directed. Jorgensen (1967, p. 126): The anatomy of the female was not introduced [in Lear’s mad speeches in 4.6] because Shakespeare was sick—possibly not because Lear was sick—but in part because Lear was in his self-discovery investigating man’s condition, and only woman’s body could suffice to illustrate the full depravity of man. Holbrook (1989, pp. 150–1): Shakespeare, through Lear’s mad outburst [in 4.6], is exploring at the unconscious level the universal dread of woman’s mysterious power of parturition and the terrible mystery of birth out of her bowels—out of her menstruation. This is the connection between woman and death—between copulation and mortality.…[151] But though she is feared, and is shown in this play to be capable of being hateful, she is not hated. Woman is redeemed by the devotion and love of Cordelia.

Several critics go further, arguing that Lr. implicitly criticizes or undermines misogyny and patriarchy. Goddard (1951, pp. 523): It is intimated that the redemption of man from violence must come from woman—not from women alone, but from the generic woman who, whether expressed or hidden, is an integral part of both the sexes. Gardner (1967, p. 13): Throughout the play there are suggestions that a narrowly-conceived manhood becomes associated with evil, is evil. Novy (1979, pp. 281–8): Lr. includes implicit criticism of the prerogatives of the father and an exploration of some behavior that patriarchy fosters in men and women.…Although Lear is more concerned with the mutuality between father and daughter [than Sh.’s comedies are], it deals with aspects of that mutuality which are also experienced by husband and wife in a patriarchal society, where the authority of fathers over their families, husbands over wives, and men in general over women are all related and analogous. Too great an imbalance in this power makes it likely that [282] attempts at mutuality will be flawed by male coercion and female deception.…[288] In [Lear’s] final vision of what [his and Cordelia’s] relationship would be, alone and happy in prison…parent kneels to child. The need for forgiveness reverses hierarchies of both age and sex, and suggests their limitations.…Shakespeare suggests that in a patriarchal society mutuality between man and woman must include the mutuality of forgiveness and repentance, because the powerful are so likely to abuse their power.…[290] Much of Lear and Cordelia’s sufferings are related to the particular vulnerabilities of men and women in a patriarchal society. Hoover (1985, p. 87) also sees the play repudiating misogyny: The king’s movement from…egocentric love…through anti-eroticism and anti-feminism, to disinterested love…involves rejecting both his early idealization and his later condemnation of women.…The various sex dramas and fantasies of other male characters…not only foreshadow [Lear’s] transformation but are contained and to some extent resolved in the king himself.…Edmund stands out as a notable and menacing exception. McEachern (1988, pp. 281–90) finds Sh. exposing the consuming nature of patriarchy as revealed in Lear’s attempts [in 1.1] to engineer a version of exogamy that will disguise—if only rhetorically—the loss that marriage entails.…Lear tries impossibly to fuse familial and political authorities, to combine the impulse to conserve the integrity of the family with the social demands of exogamy. He defames Cordelia in the hope that Dower’d with [his] curse [224], others will refuse her. Contra McLuskie, Sh. (p. 290) does not become another patriarchal bard.…He does not replicate ideology; rather, he exposes its assumptions.

Other critics emphasize the power of the feminine characters. Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 202–3): Male phallic rigidity in conflict with the fluidity and resilience of the feminine is the powerful psychological and mythic pattern underpinning the play. In Lear the long dialectical debate on the male/female dichotomy, which Shakespeare had conducted from Hamlet onwards, reaches its negative climax.…Ostensibly Shakespeare leaves no doubt in the play about which side of the deconstruction debate he is on. The evil individualism of Goneril, Regan and Edmund and the benign individualism of Cordelia lead to the [203] same sterile isolation, a world where dialogue is no longer possible, where men are islands. Of necessity this world collapses through its own incoherence.…Yet the power with which he endows the feminine and, even more, the brief glimpse we get of a world of love unstructured by authority in the scenes between Lear and Cordelia at the end, suggest an imaginative grasp of a different kind of order: what Holinshed describes (with different intention) as the gunarchie of Queen Cordeilla. Foakes (1993, p. 215), contra Mcluskie: Even if in general, Shakespeare, like others of his age, assumed as natural a patriarchal order,…King Lear is dominated by its women. When Goneril and Regan have power, indeed, they are as strong and ruthless as Lear himself had been, and show they have the courage and toughness to hold sway in a masculine world.…The controlling image at the end of the play is that of the three dead daughters, destroyed, it might be said, by their intervention in a man’s world, but at the same time having shown they could compete in it, and change the course of future events. Hawkes (1995, pp. 37 ff.): What the play chronicles…is a fundamental challenge to…male reason, a condemnation of its parameters as narrow and constricted, and of its processes as divisive and reductive. It is significant that such a challenge comes from the female Cordelia, or from her surrogate voice, that of the Fool. It is significant that it comes in the form of the super-rational, whose mode can be termed intuitive.…There are powerful moments in the play when the text yields itself quite readily to a specific notion of the female, which Lear longs to embrace.…It is as if his abandonment of reason genuinely involves the abandonment of a tough and heartless maleness.…[40] Perhaps this makes possible a reconciliation with a feminine dimension that has hitherto been fiercely excluded.…To the extent that that the play is critical of an instrumental reason, it can be said to be critical of the sort of maleness whose instrument that reason is.
Thompson (1991, p. 119) discusses the quarrel between feminist readings and materialist readings of this family-centered tragedy.

div.head: Historical, Cultural, Political
div.p: Many critics searching for the thematic import of Lr. have focussed not on those parts of the play which are foregrounded in a theatrical performance—the actions, passions, and speech of its main characters—but rather on their historical, cultural, and especially political backgrounds, insofar as these may be glimpsed or inferred from the play’s three hours’ traffic. Early historical criticisms often devoted attention to Sh.’s portrayal of the legendary, pre-Christian, seemingly prehistoric Britain found in sources of the Lear story from Geoffrey onwards. Later critics, especially those throughout most of the 20th c., concentrated on ways in which, they believed, the play reflected and implicitly commented upon contemporary Elizabethan and Jacobean events and concerns. Especially in the last third of the 20th c., when it became the fashion for scholarly criticism to focus on discussions of Theory—much of it historiographical or sociological—rather than on practical criticism, much critical discussion treated the play as ostensibly exemplifying and supporting general theories about history, human society, or culture. At the same time, critics often found the world view of Lr. applicable to events of modern life.

Early critics found it significant that the early Britain of Sh.’s play was an age remote and barbarous…dark and ferocious (Drake, 1838, p. 559). Schlegel (1809–11; tr. 1815, 2:207): To save in some degree the honour of human nature, Shakespeare never wishes that his spectators should forget that the story takes place in a dreary and barbarous age: he lays particular stress on the circumstance that the Britons of that day were still heathens, although he has not made all the remaining circumstances to coincide learnedly with the time which he has chosen. From this point of view we must judge of many coarsenesses in expression and manners; for instance, the immodest manner in which Gloster acknowledges his bastard, Kent’s quarrel with the Steward, and more especially the cruelty personally exercised on Gloster by the Duke of Cornwall. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, pp. 201–2) praises the consummate skill with which Sh. has…contrived in this drama to…blend the private and domestic fortunes of his dramatic personages with a general historical interest.…The tragedy sets before us the public fortunes of a great nation in the first instance, and ultimately the history of the whole world, as affected by the morality or immorality of private life, and it becomes consequently, not merely in its ideal subject-matter, but also by the course taken by the represented fable, a matter of history in general. At the same time, the poet’s reasons for placing this one alone of his five great tragedies upon the soil of heathenism, and for exhibiting it under a heathenish view of things, becomes apparent. Such a wide-spread corruption of morals…could never occur, except in a state of human nature still exposed to the old sin in all its power; among Christians it could only be possible as an exception—as an isolated [202] case.

Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 617–20) argues for the significance of the play’s being set in the heroic and mythic period of the Gallic and Teutonic nations.…In like manner the ancients sought their tragic fables beyond the civilised ages, in stories of pre-Trojan date, and the fearful history of the houses of Laius and Tantalus was the source from which ancient tragedy drew its richest nourishment. Transported into such times, we delight in the historical record of these heroic forms, of this haughty colossal manhood, of these striving natures, of these demi-gods and titans; we find the wanton growth of impulse and passion natural to these races; we are less shocked at the abundance of cruelty, because we feel ourselves involuntarily attracted by the greater strength which was able in those days to endure heavier burdens and sufferings.
