Nor are we even repelled and misled by the idea that this species of manhood was in itself a myth and a fable, too far from the human nature familiar to us ever to have had reality; we know from the well-authenticated history of the Burgundian and Merovingian houses, that such times and men did exist, that family horrors, as we read them in Lear, have abounded for centuries even among Christian races, and that the crimes of Tantalus in the old tragedy are not necessarily, and from their very nature, myths and fables. Into such times as these Shakespeare has [618] transported us in the most tragic of his tragedies.…In Lear the poet places us in the very centre of such an age, and brings actively before us a whole race endowed with that barbaric strength of passion in which, almost without exception, the resistance of reason and conscience over the emotions of passion is powerless or dead.…[619] Special weight is laid upon the fact that it is a heathenish time; nature is the goddess of Lear as well as Edmund; chance reigns above, power and force below. The best of this race know of no inner strength, of no noble will, of no calmness and self-command, and of no moral principle, whereby the power of the blood can be broken, the impulse of passion controlled, and immoderate desires bridled.…[620] All human nature, in such a generation, goes blindly to extremes. Even goodness, where it does appear, fidelity, uprightness, modesty, and self-rule, are all in the extreme. It is a humanity as yet uncultivated, knowing no religious ordinances, no moral laws, no ripeness of experience; a generation near akin to the bare, forked animal of Edgar, cast rough out of nature’s hand. In this state of nature it is relationship that first imposes a law and sets a limit. The tie of blood everywhere first quenches the thirst for ruling and possessing, and destroys the selfishness of the individual. But here self-love rends even these ties of nature. Likewise Hudson (1848, 2:221–2): The tragedy of Lear seems written on purpose to exemplify the virtues and vices of a barbarous age.…[222] The play exhibits throughout an extreme diversity of character, a violent antipathy and antithesis of moral complexion, and especially a boldness, a gratuitousness, a lustihood in crime, which the order of civilization would as little produce as tolerate. Reed (1855, pp. 73, 74–5): The wondrous sagacity of the poet sought for a remote period of history, where royalty still wore something of its patriarchal state, so that filial ingratitude should, at the same time, be treason, and filial piety be identified with all that is noble and beautiful in loyalty and truth.…[74] The scene of such a drama is well laid, too, in a pagan age and country.…The wild spirit of the heathen father’s revenge is in harmony with his times; and appropriate to a mysterious and barbarous age is the sublime threatening [75] of his vengeance.…Placed as the drama is, in the darkness of paganism, the fury of the elements, when Lear is driven forth into the storm, acquires a wild significance, as if the lightning and the thunder were conscious powers of evil in mysterious alliance with the wicked hearts of his daughters…and we see no power in a pagan creed to interpose against them. Mézières (1865, p. 285) ascribes the play’s horrors to its setting, in which ferocity is a an element of local color. So does Hall (1879). Bransom (1934, p. 183): There is no play of Shakespeare which reads so much like authentic history as King Lear. It has…a most remarkable verisimilitude.

Some modern critics also emphasize the play’s primitive setting. Charlton (1948, pp. 190 ff.): Shakespeare’s heavy stressing of the primitive both in the people and in the world of King Lear.…[207] a dramatic cosmos which is little more than stark nature’s universe…a circumambient atmosphere from and within which an elemental human world may have its being, a rude and simple universe wherein life and man are both at their beginnings, [208] fresh from nature’s moulds, a universe of nature whose turbulent winds and flashing lightnings are macrocosmic passions resurgent in the anger and the lust of its aboriginal human denizens.…[227] Behind the darkness of the foreground, human kindliness is strengthening itself into habit; and habit is stoutly corroborating itself as custom. A spiritual civilisation is dimly emerging and man is making or discovering a morality. But the price of it is heavy in blood and tears. Hoeniger (1974, pp. 98 ff.): The story which reached Shakespeare was not only primitive in its setting but also primitive in its origin…In transforming the simple story into a complex and powerful drama, he explored the primitive in all its depth and terror. He refers to the work of folklorist Giuseppe Cocchiara, concluding that the data point to some amazing correspondence between Shakespeare’s play and folktales and the [initiation rites of primitive tribes] from which they come. Mikalachki (1998, pp. 16, 70) reads Lr. as a tragedy of native origins, relentless in its terrible revelation of ancient British isolation and barbarity.…[70] Shakespeare exploded the elements of topographical and historically based nationalism in his tragedy of British prehistory.

Some critics find Sh. particularly interested in Celtic social customs or racial characteristics. Hales (1875; 1884, pp. 245 ff.): Not only has Sh. purposely and deliberately conducted us into heathen times, and by this heathenizing acknowledged the chronology of the old traditions, but he has also provided (p. 249) a strikingly faithful picture of the Celtic race,…[250] a race highly inflammable, headstrong, flushed with sudden angers, and breaking out into wild violences, but also, in its better children at least, of a deep tenderness and sincerity; in short, a highly emotional race, quickly stirred to good and to evil. Likewise Boas (1896, p. 441): In Macbeth he had dealt with the imaginative and mystical elements in the Celtic nature.…But in King Lear he singled out a different characteristic of the race—its uncontrollable and wayward passion, which links it not with the spirit-world, but with the untamed, ravening forces of purely animal or natural life. Thompson (1883–4, pp. 8–9): The clue to the matter [of Lear’s divestiture of power] is that the French and English versions of the story misrepresented what Lear did at the start, because they did not understand the old Celtic usage upon which his act rested itself.…Lear’s procedure was to accept his sons-in-law as chief tenants under his authority, with reserve of his rights of maintenance [9] as the English called it when they came into Ireland. He did not divest himself of his royalty, although his sons-in-law may have borne, in the oldest versions of the story, a title as dignified as his own.

In contrast, Belloc (1911, pp. 267–70) describes the play as a reflection of the English national soul: First it is not designed to its end [i.e., it is unactable].…This quality which makes so many English things growths rather than instruments is most evident in the great play. Again, it has…a sort of formlessness [which], if it mars the framework of the thing and spoils it, yet also permits the exercise of an immeasurable vitality.…[268] The play is national, again, in that permanent curiosity upon knowable things—nay, that mysterious half-knowledge of unknowable things—which, in its last forms, produced the mystic, and which is throughout history so plainly characteristic of these Northern Atlantic islands.

Other critics deny authorial concern with historicity in the play’s setting. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:158): Shakespear, indeed, by the mention of his Earls and Dukes, has given us the idea of times more civilised, and of life regulated by softer manners; and the truth is, that though he so nicely discriminates, and so minutely describes the characters of men, he commonly neglects and confounds the characters of ages, by mingling customs ancient and modern, English and foreign. Prat (1855) denies any intention to represent an actual historical setting. Likewise Snider (1887, p. 129): There can be no greater mistake than to explain King Lear by referring it to a barbarous period. It is Elizabethan, even in its most revolting incident, the putting out the eyes of Gloster. Its manifold anachronisms we never think of, except by an effort of erudition; then the entire play becomes one monster of anachronism, which swallows all the rest. The poet himself, in a passage suspected by some editors, laughs at his violations of chronology: [quotes 1749]. Still, the setting is mythical and not historical; the poet takes his mythus from a time before history, and pours into it the thoughts and feelings of his own age. Clutton-Brock (1916, p. 126) finds a peculiar quality of unworldliness.…We [seem to] see souls independent of time and place. For Campbell (1948, p. 109), the setting is wholly imaginary and symbolic, and the issue of foreign invasion irrelevant. Stauffer (1949, p. 186): Here is an image of the state of man, not of an island garrison. Though Shakespeare shows more than his casual awareness of the historical sense, Lear is not a picture of primitive Britain, and one must think twice to remember that the play is full of wars between nations and rumors of civil wars. For the tragedy is timeless, and man’s fate is involved no less surely than in the Garden of Eden. Gardner (1967, pp. 6 ff.): Lr. is unhistoric in the sense that we ask no questions about the past and care nothing about the future, it is unhistoric also in the conduct of the action.…Both time and place are handled with extreme casualness.…Even more striking…is Shakespeare’s entirely deliberate refusal to localize King Lear in history.…I do not think it is true to say that he sets it far back in a remote past.…[7] But Shakespeare…makes it quite clear that whatever the time of the play the world he presents is not a Christian world. In contrast to the Roman plays, nobody feels that, in removing King Lear from the Christian context in which the other tragedies are so firmly set, Shakespeare was concerned to present a world that was in some ways different from the world he knew, governed by different moral [8] imperatives, with different concepts of man’s relation to powers other than human. Rosenberg (1972, p. 18): The play disclaims primitivism, except, in an ironical dialectic, the savage primitivism of sophisticated man—an irony Shakespeare seems constantly to have intended. The Lear world suffers the pains of civilization, with robed and furred gowns of wool and silk, women gorgeously dressed and perfumed, a court fool, an elegant nobility at home visited by princely courtiers from abroad, with justice advanced enough to be perverted, and a lavish monarchical economy so sophisticated it casually spawns the bedlam beggars and poor naked wretches of the audience’s experience. Wells (ed. 2000, pp. 33–4): Shakespeare opens up the play’s action, replacing specificity by multiplicity of suggestiveness, by a technique of delocalization. In contrast to Leir, it is often impossible to assign the action to any specific location.…[34] Equally, Shakespeare withdraws, or muddies, the sense of period. See also Guizot (1852, pp. 220–1) on the indeterminacy of the play’s setting.

Much of the political and cultural criticism of Lr. draws analogies between the world presented in the play and the contemporary Renaissance world, and much of this commentary is based on the premise that, like the Lr. world, in which an old order is disintegrating, the Elizabethan-Jacobean world was a transitional period in which many medieval institutions were giving way to modern or early-modern ones. Hawkes (1992, pp. 124–9): Lear’s division of the kingdom…offers to tease out for its audience the ramifications of a political and social disaster whose proportions [125] foreshadow and comment on contemporary events, or pseudo-events, such as the Gunpowder Plot. As a result it takes its place as part of a symbolic field extending beyond the theatre to the culture at large. He calls for a (p. 129) historicist criticism capable of recognizing the complexities of this kind of permanent contestation of meaning both on the past and in the present. In much of such criticism the events and personages of the play are read as kinds of allegories or parables pointing to Sh.’s contemporary world.

The most general kind of comparison finds in both worlds a breakdown of an old stable system of hierarchy, of a harmonious arrangement of the world into a great chain (or stair, or ladder) within which each thing has its own place and correspondences exist between one degree and the next, and the microcosm of man mirrors the order in the macrocosm. Thus Spencer (1943, pp. 135–42): Shakespeare uses the three inter-related hierarchies given him by the assumptions of his age to make King Lear the largest and most profound of all his plays. Nowhere else does he so completely fuse the contemporary concepts of the world, the individual and the state into a single unity; correspondences and parallels between them, amalgamations of one concept with another, are everywhere; they embody the vision of life and [136] they form the texture of the style.…[Yet][141] in King Lear: everything is turned loose. Lear’s own passions, the fury of the elements, the lustful desires of Goneril and Regan, all are horribly released from order.…[142] Natural law, justice and religion are concepts which permeate the play, the validity of which the action seems to violate. Voss (1995, pp. 11–12) describes the play in terms of the influences changing contemporary England: Thus the textual map which is King Lear is localised by the intersection of a number of pairs of co-ordinates: Lear’s life and death, primogeniture and partible inheritance, Old Testament and New, oral and visual culture, roles and jobs, land-capital and money-capital, pre- and post-enclosure, king and thing, feudalism and capitalism. On the one hand these are [12] sequential in time, but they can also be seen as dynamic complementarities, defining human interaction in society more generally. Not all critics agree that the world presented in Lr. is so fluid. de Grazia (1996, pp. 21–31): King Lear blocks the mobility identified since the nineteenth century with the Modern—through its locking of persons into things, proper selves into property, subjectivity effects into personal effects—in an attempt to withstand flux or fluidity, superflux or superfluity.…[31] There is nothing handy-dandy or pellmell about the shaking of superflux, the undoing of excess: it follows the precise course of primogeniture and succession. Burnett (1997, p. 86): In its representation of master-servant relations and hierarchical structures, King Lear reveals a profoundly paradoxical stance. Spotswood (1998, p. 265): Lr. did not deconsecrate privilege, status, or hierarchy. Distinctions within the aristocracy and, more importantly, between aristocrats and commoners are enforced, both on stage and in public, through performance. Differences in clothing, language, and manners maintain hierarchy.

Several critics observe in the play adumbrations of the decline of the traditional medieval, feudal social system and the concomitant rise of a new and ruthless political individualism. Their emphasis is on a changing ethos, from a comity of mutual allegiance and dependence to a struggle for power and riches. The spokesmen for and practicers of the new ethos are variously identified as Machiavels, (greedy) individualists, New Men, materialists, the bourgeoisie, and capitalists. E. Muir (1947, pp. 7 ff.): In Lr. two ideas of society are directly confronted, [8] and the old generation and the new are set face to face, each assured of its own right to power.…[9] It is [their attitude to power], more than their ingratitude, that estranges Lear from Goneril and Regan. (P. 14): The members of the new generation [Goneril, Regan, Edmund and Cornwall] are bound together by common interest…but their most immediate bond is a common way of thinking, a spontaneous intellectual affinity resembling that of a chosen group to whom a new vision of the world has been vouchsafed, a vision resembling (p. 16) the theory and practice by which [Fascism] was upheld in modern Italy and Germany. (P. 18): Their shallowness is ultimately that of the Machiavellian view of life as it was understood in [Sh.’s] age, of policy, or Realpolitik, whichever we may choose to call it.…If we read Burckhardt, if we reflect that Machiavellianism was a current preoccupation in Shakespeare’s time, and consider further that the Renaissance gave to the individual a prominence he had not possessed since classical times, and that personal power, especially in princes, appeared sometimes to be boundless, we need not shrink from regarding Edmund and his confederates as political types.…To understand [Sh.’s] attitude to the new generation we must finally consider his identification of them with nature.…[19] In almost everything [Lear] says, whether in anger or kindness…he sets against the idea of natural freedom the sacred tradition of human society,…[23] a society bound together not by force and appetite, but by a sort of piety and human fitness, a natural piety.…The communal tradition, filled with memory, has been smashed by an [24] individualism that exists in its perpetual shallow present. Danby (1949, pp. 52 ff.): Because the play is an allegory of ethical systems and people, it must also be an allegory of community [involving two opposed social systems]. For according to one of the systems at least we are all members one of another. This society is that of the medieval vision. Its representative is an old King.…It is doting and it falls into error. The other society is that of nascent capitalism. Its representative in chief [Edmund] is the New Man—and a political machiavel. I have no doubt that if Shakespeare were forced to take sides, he would prefer Lear to Goneril and Regan, Gloster to Edmund. Shakespeare, however, has an alternative to the simple either-or.…[53] By a profound instinct for the Utopian root of art, Shakespeare saw in the medieval dream and the Anabaptist equalitarianism an alternative to Edmund and a fulfilment of the old King’s real Nature. The vision of the new order is given in Lear’s prayer and embodied in the King’s rejected daughter. The prayer (p. 186) shows that Shakespeare is following the traditional schema of spiritual regeneration laid down in the devotionalists. [It expresses] the sentiment of Christian communism which…itself forms a part of a long tradition still active in the sixteenth century, and ready to emerge into the world of seventeenth-century politics whenever the opportunity offers.…[187] It is a Christian levelling of society—the logical and full expression of charity—which is pointed to. Likewise El-Gabalawy (1978, pp. 228–34): Lr. expresses a vision of Christian communism [which] regards the levelling of society as the logical and full expression of charity.…[234] Lear’s new awareness of social evils…implies rejection of [a belief that] the social order, given its inequalities of possession and opportunity, has been divinely ordained.…In his pilgrimage from paganism towards religion Lear gradually transcends the old proud self until he ultimately assimilates the Christian virtues of love and humility. Colie (1974, Reason, pp. 189 ff.): Lr. is a play deeply rooted in its own period, a play which draws some of its power from the playwright’s insight into the peculiar aristocratic situation of the time in which it was written, the situation Lawrence Stone has been at such pains to delineate.…[196] In different ways, Lear, Gloucester, and Kent are old-fashioned aristocrats, theirs the noble ethos in the process of erosion during the Renaissance; equally, Albany, Cornwall, Goneril, Regan, and Edmund are domesticated in a new world of power and might, which they intend to keep well within their control.…Neither way of life is sanctified, neither is regarded as an unqualified success. Cohen (1980, pp. 113 ff.): Lr. is Sh.’s fullest treatment of the conflicts that…divided the English people in the early seventeenth century.…[114] Goneril, Regan, and Edmund, the leading amoral individualists of the play, destroy traditional feudal relationships in the family and the state by their singleminded pursuit of political, economic, and social power. Nowhere else is Shakespeare’s attack on capitalism so devastating. At the same time, however, King Lear is also Shakespeare’s most powerful critique of feudal values, and particularly of royal absolutism.…Although capitalism is irretrievably evil, feudalism may perhaps be redeemed if it can combine its traditional human bonds with serious moral content. Thus, the poor and the dispossessed play a crucial, if often passive, role in Shakespeare’s attempt to create a new synthesis capable of breaking the historic impasse between the rival sectors of the ruling class and of justifying the exercise of power. Kavanagh (1985, p. 156–8) views Lear’s related tyranny and incestuousness [sic],…Gloucester’s weakness and adultery, and both fathers’ misrecognition of real loyalty as symptoms of an individualist ideology that lives the world as a field of calculation, self-gratification and perverse desire.…[157] Counterpoised to this is the hierarchical ideology of fealty, faith, and restraint, which lives the world as a field of reciprocal obligation.…King Lear effectively hurls these two ideologies against each other, in what is here certainly no clash of mere opinions but of whole modes of living—what the play constantly defines as opposed Natures. However, the play’s (p. 158) egalitarianism is finally more at home within bourgeois republican than within aristocratic Christian humanism, and King Lear appropriates egalitarianism for the latter only in order to occupy and control—in a conjuncture that still allows such a manoeuvre—a strategically important ideological terrain. The play attempts to incorporate the strongest element of bourgeois ideology in its language and images as an unequal, dominated element of a transformed aristocratic ideology—one that is now stronger for its unprecedented unitary cast and universalized appeal, but one also now attached to a discourse which can only undermine that discourse’s own legitimacy.

Most often the rising individualism is associated with bourgeois acquisitive greed. Sen (1964, pp. 80–5): The central polarity of the play is the opposition between feudal authority and bourgeois appetite.…[85] In the face of [the] unanswerable and inevitable grief [of the ending] it is absurd to be offered [spiritual or moral] consolation.…There is no penance in Lear but a knowledge of what his world was, the horror it contained and the appetite it had inevitably to let loose. The vision is the transformation of opposites, absolutism giving birth to unbridled license, feudal sanctities to bourgeois individualism. And this was progress, without irony but pregnant with tragedy. Delaney (1977, pp. 430–37): In King Lear Shakespeare displays [an] attachment to traditional and aristocratic values, combined with a distaste and fear of the acquisitive, unscrupulous bourgeois values (as they appear to him) that are taking their place. Edmund anticipates the Hobbesian view of primitive culture as a war of all against all and denies the medieval standards of Elizabethan society. Lear and Gloucester (p. 435) view social inequality from the traditional perspective of Christian charity, with its ideal of an organic, hierarchical state in which all are linked together in brotherly love. The remedy for the sufferings of the poor is that the rich should treat them better, not that they should demand redress of their own initiative.…[437] Edmund embodies no hope for the future, but only the most destructive aspects of the new era of bourgeois transformation.…The struggle between the old order and the new is therefore bound to be a tragic one, whose outcome is too dark and bloody to be redeemed by the vapidly moralistic Edgar. Markels (1991, King Lear, Revolution, p. 11): King Lear dramatizes a revolution in which the cosmology, politics, and ethics of feudalism, which the play nostalgically idealizes, are supplanted by the bourgeois politics and ethics which the play abhorrently idealizes and which continue to define our culture. Idem (1991, Shakespeare’s Materialism, p. 101): A connection between King Lear’s ideological deliberateness and its emotional power…can be traced to a latent historical materialism.…[103] Edgar’s climactic emergence as Edmund’s conqueror…may look at first like traditional providence but…[Edgar] has had to secede ideologically from the old world of Cordelia and enter the new world of Edmund, thereby acquiring (p. 104) a shape-shifting mobility that incorporates the entrepreneurial power of improvisation which also animates Edmund. Lear recognizes (p. 107) that it was he himself who authorized the cancellation of justice and the unleashing of violence that opened his community to the bourgeois revolution in social relations. That this is accomplished only through…a personal collapse of reason inseparable from the public collapse of justice as defined by the old social relations, is another sign of Shakespeare’s materialism.

Other critics see the bourgeoisie’s acquisition and exploitation of land—real (royal) estate—as a lethal blow to feudalism that is deplored in the play. Kozintsev (1966, pp. 224–9): The system of images of this tragedy…echoes the processes of the epoch of primary accumulation.…The [225] land became something to be traded for money; those who used to work it were expropriated and turned into beggars.… Not one uniting factor remains between man and man: nothing, not one single form of social existence. However, contra Danby, (p. 249) it is difficult to label Goneril, Edmund or Regan as either feudal or capitalist. They display characteristics of the new era, but the purposes which these people pursue are, for the most part, of the traditional kind. Kernan (1981, pp. 8 ff.), viewing Sh. as a profoundly conservative writer, sees in the division of the kingdom (p. 11) a reflection of the central social issue of the time: the transfer of land from the old aristocracy to new entrepreneurs, and from one type of management stressing a natural relationship between estate, lord, and tenant to a new type of exploitation of the land for profit. Selden (1987, pp. 151–66) also sees the play responding to the crisis of feudalism in Sh.’s time, reflected in discontent over enclosure and statutes to address the decay of tillage and the increased vagrancy which threatened social order.…[155] The tragedies of both Lear and Gloucester are connected with the ownership of land.…[156] It seems reasonable to link Edmund with those rising classes who acquired land and wealth by ingenuity and not by birth. Kettle (1988, p. 77): Lear’s incapacity to deal with the inhumanity of the new people is what drives him into a solidarity, and, later, an identification, with the poor.…His direct personal contact with ruling-class inhumanity leads him to question the validity of property itself and the authority and exemption from elementary human moral values it confers. In this, Lear’s development is not at all unlike that of later seventeenth-century radicals like Winstanley.

The acquisitive attitude is as often as not identified with capitalism, but since there are no proper capitalists in the play, the terms used are usually proto- or nascent or rising capitalism. Smirnov (1936, pp. 68–71): The king is absorbed in the illusion of kingship…divorce[d] from its material attributes.…The two elder daughters embody the same feudal ideals with the addition of traits…typical of primary accumulation [i.e., proto-capitalism]—perfidy, cruelty, greed, ruthlessness. In the storm Lear (p. 69) begins to sense the monstrous injustice of the feudal-aristocratic system.…[70] Shakespeare depicts Edmund as the plundering aristocrat, who follows the worst practices of primary accumulation.…[71] Cordelia and Edgar…are profoundly humanist in the Shakespearean meaning of the word [i.e., (p. 26): emancipated from feudal bondage]. Šimko (1967, p. 209): The struggle of the bourgeoisie to break up the feudal bonds of birth privileges was progressive in its time since it helped society to forge ahead in its development, but…[Sh.] detected the shortcomings inherent in the rising capitalist society and organization. Shanker (1975, pp. 155–61): Lr. is a work in which authority as ideology is radically examined.…[158] Edmund and his associates…signify the rising forces of capitalism, the enemies of James and the court faction.…Lear…symbolizes the form rather than the content of feudal society.…[160] Shakespeare is calling for a new order of compassion based upon a new vision of reality, of man, and society.…[161] Out of the turmoil, anguish, and suffering depicted in the universe of Lear comes a new, a transcendent, faith in man’s potential for altering society. Wallis (1991, p. 231): The structure of feeling embodied by the text of Lear, especially the tension between emblematic and psychological elements in the characters, is a result of the slow but inexorable, enthralling but also terrifying process of change from a basically feudal order to a basically capitalist one.

Other commentators focus on the corrupting rationale for acquisition. Rotman (1987, pp. 78–81): The play engages the disruption and moral disintegration inherent in capitalism’s threat to commoditise social reality.…[80] Lear’s transaction, by arithmetising [love], by forcefully inserting it into a system of mercantile exchange and making it an object of deals, replaces [Cordelia’s] produced love, the continuous result of a lived [81] practice, by love neutralised into a commodity, an item within a system of measurable values. And in doing so rapes it. Margolies (1992, pp. 20 ff.): The actions of the play are a dramatic testing of real social attitudes.…Tradition-directed and inner-directed [social] types are brought into dramatic, formal opposition.…[37] Goneril and Regan…are offering a new system, a rationality of atomistic humanity against which [Lear’s] unexamined geniality of traditional relationships cannot stand. Hawkes (1995, pp. 7, 30): Lear’s insistence on putting a price on love has a potential which, once activated, lifts it well clear of the merely personal and pathetic.…It also…helps us to identify in Lear’s acts a recurring and finally characteristic pattern. A dividing, measuring, weighing, and assessing mode is its central feature. The tearing apart of his country’s unity, and the calculation of his daughters’ love, both confirm his involvement in and commitment to a huge process of diminution which proceeds by division and quantification. The play exposes (p. 30) the withering, reductive nature of instrumental, weighing, measuring, assessing reason that Lear has unleashed upon the world.

Not everyone is convinced that the play manifests a feudal vs. bourgeois (or capitalist) dichotomy. Liebler (1995, pp. 199–201): The battle between old and new (or old and young) is real enough in this play; but however repulsive and dangerous Edmund, Goneril, and Regan appear to be, Shakespeare makes it clear that the fathers broke the rules first by violating the same traditional bonds whose loss they come to regret.…[200] The play not only interrogates a moribund feudal-aristocratic system; it also exposes the structures of civilization per se as system, articulated in relationships that require careful, consistent protection by some structure of hierarchy and communitas. The feudal structures of King Lear are the particular instantiations of system in general.…[203] Simplistically read, Lear’s revelation [1807–17] might result in a radical re-ordering of the play’s social structures. But when we see what in fact happens, we see too that such a re-ordering does not occur, and indeed may not be possible. Wherever they go people carry with them the positions they have occupied in the social structure.…[208] Family relations, domestic relations, the relations of comitatus, appear to be the focus in these scenes.…If Shakespeare addressed contemporary developments in economic practices, as Selden and others suggest, he did so in the context of the breakdown in family relations and codes of loyalty and reciprocal responsibility. Levin (1997, p. 154): Marxist interpretations confuse a necessary condition with a sufficient cause. The society of the play, where kings and fathers have absolute power, property is inherited, and so on, makes the tragic actions possible, since they could not occur (at least in the same way) in another kind of world, but it does not cause these actions, since other people living in this society do not act in this manner; indeed all the witnesses to Lear’s rejection of Cordelia view it as a shocking departure from the norms of their society. Kronenfeld (1998, pp. 100 ff.): The division between feudal and bourgeois bonds—whether seen as a division between the old-fashioned authoritarian and the new individualist, or as a division between the charitable and the calculating—does not necessarily map onto late Renaissance uses of the term.…[109] Thus a contract between a parent and his child providing raiment, bed, and food in exchange for an endowment or inheritance—if not a dominant pattern in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—hardly entailed Puritanism or capitalism.…[113] Such legalistic attitudes…are not necessarily new in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, nor, certainly, the result of a change from feudal bonds to contractual bonds.

A few critics argue that feudalism is shown in the play to contain the seeds of its own destruction. Halpern (1991, pp. 220 ff.): King Lear is largely about the divorce between the signs and the material realities of royal power.…[242] One of the weaknesses of many historical readings of Lear is that they equate the collapse of the play’s social order with the collapse of feudalism, whereas in fact the play collapses back into feudalism.…[255] King Lear employs the parceling of landed property as its founding emblem for the zero-sum economy [of feudalism].…It portrays all other human or spiritual realms as similarly bounded.…[256] The materialist and antitranscendental strain in Lear prevents the access of any divine or genuinely supernatural supplement to the play’s original portion; and the nature of domestic relations, quite brutally implicated with and modeled on property relations, forecloses the possibility of an emotional or affective supplement as well.…[269] The play does not passively watch the collapse of a social order which it portrays. It throws this order—or its declining values—over the edge, consumes it in a massive act of dépense [destructive expenditure]. Turner (1988, pp. 100–11): Lear’s irresponsible vanity [in 1.1]…strikes at the heart of the relationship between love and property which is, ideally, the cornerstone of the feudal system and which all its ceremonies of allegiance are designed to reinforce—and in doing so it draws out that system’s latent contradictions into open conflict.…[101] The true subject of King Lear [contra Danby et al.] is not an old [feudal] order succumbing to a new [bourgeois capitalist] but an old order succumbing to its own internal contradictions.…[111] Simply, Shakespeare has turned his historical and romance materials upside-down: the heroic past out of which Tudor and Stuart moralists drew their mythical charter yields in King Lear an understanding of the present as a time and place of abiding injustice, where morality remains problematical and reciprocity incomplete. Moretti (1982, pp. 7–17): The historical task effectively accomplished by [Shn. tragic] form was precisely the destruction of the fundamental paradigm of the dominant culture.…[16] As Lear heightens the absolutist claims made in Gorboduc, it simultaneously diminishes the counterclaims of the aristocracy, who are no longer allowed…to inscribe events within an organic and rational framework of meaning.…[17] The close of King Lear makes clear that no one is any longer capable of giving meaning to the tragic process; no speech is equal to it, and therein lies the tragedy. Likewise Strauss (1999–2000, pp. 33–4): The play functions brilliantly as a device for probing the nature of feudal society (and doing so in a very radical way).…The querying of feudal forms in the play takes the form of an eruption—an eruption born out of feudalism’s own internal tensions.…[34] There are times when the disintegration seems to herald a new beginning. But despite repeated hints of a return, a renewal, there is actually no cure. The play ends with exhaustion, with emptiedness.

One critic seems to find the cause of feudalism’s demise in the modern dynamism of the Renaissance. McLuhan (1962, pp. 12–17): In King Lear …Shakespeare shows an utter clairvoyance concerning the social and personal consequences of denudation and stripping of attributes and functions for the sake of speed, precision, and increased power.…[14] King Lear is a kind of elaborate case history of people translating themselves out of a world of roles into the new world of jobs. It offers a complete demonstration of how it felt to live through the change from medieval to Renaissance time and space, from an inclusive to an exclusive sense of the world.…[17] King Lear is a kind of medieval sermon-exemplum or inductive reasoning to display the madness and misery of the new Renaissance life of action. Shakespeare explains minutely that the very principle of action is the splitting up of social operations and of the private sense life into specialized segments.
For other interpretations of Lr. in relation to the decline of feudalism, see Rosati (1958); Klotz (1976); Margolies (1985).

A few critics suggest that the play reflects and anticipates egalitarian attitudes and even encourages later radicalisms. Swinburne (1880, pp. 174–5) finds in Lr. evidence…of a sympathy with the mass of social misery more wide and deep and [175] direct and bitter and tender than Shakespeare has shown elsewhere.…Surely has the author of King Lear avowed himself in the only good and rational sense of the words a spiritual if not a political democrat and socialist. See also Idem (1902, pp. 6, 8). Blaze de Bury (1885, p. 207) sees Shakespeare preoccupied by the question of the proletariat. Hobday (1979, p. 63) relates the Fool’s prophecy and some of Lear’s mad speeches to a tradition of popular radicalism, egalitarian and sometimes communist, which was rarely put into literary form by its English supporters before the 1640s. Likewise Cohen (1984, p. 51): Various echoes of the radicals may perhaps be heard in King Lear with its subversive egalitarianism, rejection of authority, and possible advocacy of utopian communism.…Insofar as the play locates its ideological norm in the lower class, it anticipates the Puritan political appeal to those groups. Even the metaphysical questioning of King Lear looks back to Anabaptism and forward to the Familists, the Grindletonians, the Muggletonians, and especially the Diggers. Idem (1985, pp. 345–56): Edgar’s accession to the throne violates the logic of [the play’s] experience, in its impossible effort to integrate a properly communist vision into a monarchical order. King Lear points to the future, only to show that the way there is barred.…[356] King Lear takes its place in a tradition of popular radicalism…that may extend without a break from the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 to the present. Jordan (1990, p. 88) argues that Shakespeare’s representation of the conflict in King Lear adopts a Machiavellian perspective on political power by divorcing the authority of office—in this case of the king—from the actual power required to force obedience to his dictates. He depicts as a fiction the so-called mystery of kingship and its supposed attributes. Heinemann (1992, pp. 76–82): The drama empowers ordinary people in the audience to think and judge for themselves of matters usually considered mysteries of state in which no one but the natural rulers—the nobility and gentry and professional élites—should be allowed to meddle.…[78] The central focus is on the horror of a society divided between extremes of rich and poor, greed and starvation, the powerful and the powerless, robes and rags, and the impossibility of real justice and security in such a world.…[79] There may also be an echo [in 2608–12] of antinomian discourse, implying that our categories of right and wrong, sin and righteousness, are meaningless and evil.…The mock-trial vividly makes the case…against the whole intrinsically ridiculous pretence of justice in an unjust society. [80] The resistance to evil too has an upside-down dimension, coming first from the weak, the oppressed lower orders, the peasants and servants.…[82] The upside-down discourse…echoes Utopian ideas which survived in a serious and organized form, more or less underground, in late-Elizabethan and Jacobean times, among radical religious sects such as the Family of Love, and were to surface again forty to fifty years later in the revolutionary years, first with the Levellers, and after their defeat with the Ranters and Seekers. Strier (1995, pp. 176–99): In both versions of King Lear Shakespeare dramatized and espoused the most radical…ideas about obedience. (P. 189): The ethic of Lear is deeply anticourtly. In the actions of Cornwall’s servant, Sh. (p. 193) is presenting the most radical possible sociopolitical act in a way that can only be interpreted as calling for his audience’s approval. In so treating (p. 194) the paradox of service through resistance, Sh. (p. 199) clearly espoused active resistance in Lr. Kiernan (1996, p. 106): It is Shakespeare’s most Gothic tragedy, because the closest in feeling to the masses, the experiences of the poor, and some of their modes of thought and speech. They are not—not yet—in revolt; what is breaking in on the minds of at least a few among their masters is the fundamental wrongness of the social fabric, whose axioms or truisms are turning out to be lies. We may be closer in touch here with Shakespeare’s own deepest feelings than anywhere else.

Not everyone is persuaded that the play is subversive or endorses a radical distribution of property. Levin (1997, p. 151): All the tragic actions involve relations between members of the ruling class, so it is hard to see how they can be caused by class divisions. Kronenfeld (1998, p. 126, 172 ff.): A strong belief in spiritual equality or Christian egalitarianism clearly coexisted with a recognition of…the social hierarchy and paternalism felt to be utterly necessary to the stable functioning of society.…[172] In fact, distribution, excess, enough, superflux—the terms of Lear’s and Gloucester’s speeches, which [some] critics view as radical or subversive—are all terms that belong to the traditional and authoritative, not to say authoritarian, discourse of charity, a charity used by Elizabethan and Jacobean legislators and administrators—city and town aldermen, justices of the peace, churchwardens, and overseers of the poor—and by Anglican and Puritan ministers. The sentiments these words express are not radically egalitarian, but entirely compatible with homiletic exhortations to private [173] and public charity, with the poor laws and other governmental mechanisms of charity, and with Protestant social thought as a whole. All of these were perfectly accordant with—indeed, dependent on—the existence of a hierarchical social order, and plausibly had at least the partial motive of reinforcing it.

Much political criticism is concerned not with such large-scale topics as feudalism, capitalism, and egalitarianism, but with more limited topics of immediate interest to a Jacobean audience. Inevitably a play about a king, written by one of the King’s Men, and presented before the king in 1606 would invite comment on its possible relevance to King James himself and to his interests. Since one of his chief interests when this play was being written was his plan to bring Scotland and all of Britain into a Union, and since a play about a king bringing disunion to his kingdom would be potentially very pertinent to that plan, many scholars and critics since Malone (ed. 1790) and Chalmers (1799) have discussed Lr.’s possible relation to the issue (see nn. 7 and 43–6, and , ). Draper (1937, pp. 179 ff.): Shakespeare wrote [Lr.] between 1604 and 1607, during the years when King James was trying to get Parliament and its commissioners to pass favorably on the Union, and when…he was citing the misfortunes that division brought to early Britain.…[180] The entire plot depends on this division of the kingdom…and the distraction of the whole commonwealth that cannot but ensue.…[181] In the final division, the two realms of Goneril and Regan must roughly have corresponded to England and to Scotland. The titles of the respective husbands bear this out.…[182] Neither Holinshed nor Leir, nor Shakespeare’s other possible sources…portray the misery of the nobles and the people that results from this division. See also Draper (1936, pp. 85 ff.). Jones (1961, p. 74): If James seemed to unite Britain…Lear sought to divide it. In this important respect, Lear is James’s anti-type, his figural antithesis. It is Lear’s act of dividing the kingdom which makes possible all the happenings and developments of the tragedy, not least of which is the break-down of law and order. Wickham (1973, pp. 35–9): The Lear story itself [cannot] be isolated from its wider context of legendary history that stretches back to Trojan Brutus and his division of the British Isles between his three sons and forward to Gorboduc who repeated this folly with equally disastrous results. All three stories came thus to be linked with Merlin’s prophecy of a second Brutus, desired in the fullness of time to return to New Troy and reunite the Kingdom. This figure had already been recognised in the person of James I by Samuel Daniel, Thomas Dekker, and Anthony Munday in poems and pageants before Shakespeare turned his attention to the Lear story.…[39] The legend of British descent from Trojan Brutus, his founding of New Troy, or Troynovant, on the banks of the Thames, his disastrous division of the kingdom between his three sons and Merlin’s later prophecy of the coming of a second Brutus who would restore what was lost, all of which had appealed so strongly to the early Tudor chroniclers, could not be bettered as a vehicle for the projection of James’s message of Peace through union and prosperity through Peace. Dubu (1983, p. 46): Sh. emphasizes unequivocably but with great tact the political wisdom of James I’s great design of the union of Great Britain. Dutton (1986, p. 149): This optimistic dimension of the play must, in fact, have been far more apparent than it is today; and it is far from incidental to the tragedy.…Like Antony and Cleopatra, King Lear is a play in which harrowing personal tragedy paves the way for re-born peace and stability, enriching the society which emerges from it.…arguments against modern sentimental pessimism. Wortham (1996, p. 111): The play warns that not to recognize Britain as a de facto union may be as dangerous as to take a hatchet to a united kingdom.

A few find the play’s message about Union somewhat more ambiguous. Again Wickham (1973, p. 43): Shakespeare prudently chose to…[balance] the happy reunion of father and daughter presented in the old play against Monmouth’s tragic conclusion, thus combining his own artistic purposes with deliberate ambiguity in the political treatment of the story: rather than burn his boats with a public declaration that the second Brutus had finally arrived in the form of James I, he reserved judgment. The possibility is admitted through making Albany the agent of Lear’s reunion with Cordelia, but Shakespeare refrains from joining Daniel, Dekker, and Munday in projections which time and events could easily prove premature. Patterson (1984, pp. 60–71): Lr. is a play that was indeed designed to be ambiguous…intended to be experienced differently by different audiences, or even to mediate between them, by showing that the questions under dispute were not capable of easy resolution. Something is present in the text of what both James and his opponents wanted to hear; but beyond such slight gratifications is a larger analysis,…finely reticulated, of the conflict between the loyalty due to the sovereign and the perception that a particular sovereign’s inadequacies are dangerous to the nation.…[71] A play so deeply ambiguated, so clearly referential in some way to the Union debate, but so utterly resistant to assimilation by either side in the controversy,…could safely take its place in a theater usually vulnerable at that moment to state interference,…could even, with impunity, be presented before the king. By grotesque somatic metaphor and puns Berry (1999, p. 136) relates Lr. to anxiety over James’s project of a unified Britain, finding a strikingly scatological refiguration of James’s new British kingdom.…A morally compromised kingship is implied to have an unsettling association with a suggestively feminized anality: a breach or fissure in the body politic that marks the site of the uncanny.…The political heart of Lear’s tragedy is the king’s sacrifice of the centre or seat of his breached kingdom or sovereignty.…Cordelia’s jointure is figuratively digested and, it is implied, excreted by her brothers-in-law. What it becomes is the discarded waste/waist land, whose spectral uncanniness signals the concealment of the animating spirit or soul of royal power within the centre of the land.

Another interest of King James, his conception of kingship as requiring near absolute authority, appears to several critics to be implicated in the play. One of them sees authority as Lear’s dominant concern; Seehase (1979) declares that the relationship between authority and individuality is at the heart of Lear’s anger towards Cordelia. Several commentators see Lear’s abdication as (to a Jacobean audience) a frightening dereliction of a necessary strong authority, no less reprehensible than sin or blasphemy (Miller, 1993, p. 22). Craig (1948, pp. 207–8): When Lear gives over his kingdom, he commits a sin against nature and the law of God.…throughout the play appear the consequences of the violation of fundamental laws of nature.…[208] The underlying concept of King Lear…is not ingratitude.…It is authority.…The basis of King Lear is belief in authority, in a strong single rule. Ribner (1960, pp. 118–19): Lear’s resignation of his throne and division of his kingdom would have been regarded by a Jacobean audience with a horror difficult for a modern audience to appreciate, for these acts were a violation of the king’s responsibility to God, and they could [119] result only in the chaos on every level of creation which is the subject of the play. Fraser (1962, p. 63): No other play mirrors with such clarity or terror the horror attaching to anarchy, to the abdication of order and degree.…Shakespeare, exalting order, appeals to sanctions almost mystical on their face but, in essence, prosaic, entirely practical. Axton (1977, pp. 136–9, 143) describes the legal theory of the king’s two bodies as (p. 143) a political tradition [Sh.] both needed and transcended in Lr. The play is a deeply speculative tragedy,…[137] a sensitive study of the disintegration of an inhuman political ideal, and (p. 138) a tragedy of kingship.…For forty years opponents of the Stuart claim had insisted that there was no difference in law between a king and a subject. Clearly Shakespeare’s tragedy rests on a legal structure which suggests a terrible difference.…[139] Politically, Lear commits the original sin. Shakespeare, writing of it, holds out no hope of forgiveness and no palliative for the inexorable punishment. Lear’s political error is more heinous than any committed by a comparable Elizabethan player king.…Lear makes an utter travesty of kingship by not only dividing the realm, giving away the power of his office and sundering the crown, but by retaining the name of king and thus the responsibility for all the ensuing disasters. Barker (1993, p. 90): Lr. presents a dramatic argument for the inescapability of domination, or sovereignty in the extended sense. If it gives some ground to the demystification of sacred monarchy, it is in order to secure the widest purchase of its deepest commitment to fixed order at the level of the political. Kernan (1995, pp. 96–102): Shakespeare’s paradigmatic political play and his most magisterial image of the true king, King Lear…stages James’s conception of the absolute king.…[102] Lear fleshes out [James’s] theoretical version of kingship, putting onstage a titanic divine-right king who stands astride his kingdom and his people, a king who speaks to the gods. The kingdom disintegrates when the true king no longer rules, but it is as perdurably lasting as its king, and though rocked to its foundations, it is still shakily in place, as is the institution of kingship, at the end of the play.…In this play Shakespeare was not simply extending the legitimation of his patron’s theories…, he was improving upon them. Whereas James took the king and his order as the prior reality, Shakespeare portrayed the moral emptiness of the heath as the primary fact of existence. For the playwright the established order with which his play begins is a social defense against an always threatening anomie.

Other commentators see Lr. as referring to James’s more benign conception of his kingly concerns. Elton (1966, pp. 92–3) thinks that the play’s treatment of miracles appeals to James’s attitudes toward pretended possession, fraudulent miracles, and superstitious astrological prognostication, and that (pp. 243, 245) its favorable treatment of old age may have been related to the expedient affirmation of the antiquity and right of the foreign intruder who in 1603 had intruded hard upon the nearly half-century reign of the beloved English queen.…[245] Gratifying his patron’s genealogical concerns, [Lr. and Mac.]…also vividly reminded the Stuart king’s new English court and public of the venerable seniority of his line. Perry (1997, pp. 121–37) discusses Lr. and Mac. in relation to James I’s self-representation as a nourish-father,…part of an ideological construct which includes gift-giving but also resonates with a larger, resolutely patriarchal conception of nature as both cornucopian and safely masculine.…[123] Lear and Duncan are both introduced as bountiful, as representatives of a principle of cornucopian plenty, and as self-replicating fathers.…[125] Generally speaking, the relevance of King Lear to the Jacobean state is both underscored within the play and given as an interpretive problem.…[136] King Lear is primarily interested in exploring the governmental failure of royal benignity.

Some find the play critical of royal absolutism. Crawford (1916, pp. 254–5): In King Lear the dramatist undertakes to portray the blighting effects of absolutism on the spirit of the monarch.…It is not the subjects of despots who suffer most, but the despots themselves. R. S. Sharma (1982, pp. 12 ff.): Shakespeare’s treatment of the king and kingship in this play was in essence influenced by the contemporary anti-authoritarian, antiabsolutist, monarchomachic [13] thought.…[25] The play dramatizes, in a tragic form, some aspects of the issue of obedience to secular authority as it impinged on the European Consciousness in an area of sectarian controversy and emerging authoritarian, absolute, dynastic monarchical rule. Lr. shows a strong familiarity with contemporary ideas of society, power, authority, the nature of relationship between the secular ruler and the subject and issues of obedience and resistance as reflected in the Renaissance and Reformation thought in general and in the writings of thinkers like Erasmus, More, Bodin, and Buchanan in particular. The order-disorder dialectic of the tragedy communicates in a most effective dramatic manner the social dialectic between the forces of just rule (Rex Justus) and the forces of tyranny (Tyrannos). The dialectical conflict between the King and the Tyrant is organized dramatically at various levels of feeling and emotion and of personal and social relationships so that the play acquires multiplicity of patterns, each autonomous, yet contributing to the intensity and totality of the others. Baldo (1996, p. 174): In Lr., eye and ear are regularly pitted against one another and used as a way of designating, by a kind of shorthand, political alternatives.…Perhaps more critical of Renaissance sovereignty than any other [play] Shakespeare wrote, King Lear tells the story of the dethronement of what Phineas Fletcher…calls the noblest sense [i.e., eyesight].…King Lear is equally a story that instructs the eye to take on a new function, the conveyance of recognition and sympathy rather than authority and control. See Siemon, , on iconoclasm. Kronenfeld (1998, pp. 118 ff.), on the other hand, questions the play’s concern with absolutism: For all the ease with which the father-king analogy lends itself to absolutist political thought, it was not the unique property of absolutists.…[121] Thus, if [1.1] of Lear levies a critique, that critique may have been read by a contemporary audience, and especially by the king in power, as a critique of failures of fatherly, kindly, and temperate kingship, rather than as a critique of those aspects of the father-king analogy that lend themselves to the defense of patriarchal absolutism.

A few recent commentators detect criticisms of the conduct of James’s court. Boehrer (1990, p. 245): Lear in effect…plans to go on progress forever. Although never specifically mentioned in Lear, the idea of the royal progress thus permeates the structure of the play, which develops as a tragedy when its hero elects to separate the progress as social practice from the material circumstances that permit it to exist.…King Lear functions…as a play about problematical changes in current social practice, and especially in the display of royal power. Archer (1992, pp. 187 ff.): Lr. is an example of how sovereign power was represented following the death of Queen Elizabeth. The rule of King Lear and the order he represents is seemingly constituted by the sort [188] of visual court ritual that we see in the first scene.…Yet it is also underlain by…courtly observation, the tissue of glances among servants of the prince.…some elements of surveillant power developed within a sovereignty of display, which concealed the practices of courtly observation just as the idea of the state was later to conceal surveillance itself. Furthermore, the emergence of surveillance from observation and display [in the Renaissance court] caused the crisis in the representation of sovereign power [found] in Lear.…[189] [In 1.1] the King’s darker purpose is to displace the Dukes’ competition into the rhetorical contest among his daughters.…[190] Lear precipitates a political crisis by doing what Foucault claimed all properly sovereign rulers did—rule principally through ceremony and display. He drives a wedge between power and the display of power.…[192] Cordelia and Kent are driven to espionage when the older forms of power through display, and displayed punishment, are taken away from the king. Heinemann (1990, p. 193): Centrally the play deals with a decaying social order…breaking down in conflict between the arbitrary old king and the predatory royalty and ambitious upstarts who surround him—all at the expense of the helpless suffering poor, who are ever-present in the poetic imagery though not in the cast list.…The flattering, cadging courtiers and upstarts were seen at the time as flattering, cadging courtiers and upstarts, like James’s expensive and much resented Scottish favorites (or, prophetically, like the Duke of Buckingham…). Butler (Topicality, 1992, pp. 2–3): The word knight carried equivocal connotations in the early years of James I’s reign.…[3] Criticisms of armed retainers who had no function but to inflate status had found their way onto the stage before Regan and Goneril uttered them.

A few comment on the play’s portrait of the king himself and find it to be ambiguous, balancing faults and virtues, indictments and defenses. Smith (1988, pp. 34 ff.): Opinions which were similar to those of James’s critics were put into the mouths of Lear’s oppressors. Thus, although the pomposity of James might have been reflected in Lear’s speeches [in 1.1] (and the language of the play is full of echoes of speeches, especially from James’s famous oration at the opening of Parliament in March, 1604), possible references to James’s liberal creation of noble titles, the expense of his household and his frequent lack of interest in affairs of state in favour of hunting are contained within Goneril and Regan’s complaints to Lear about his excessive burdening of the state in maintaining large numbers of knights and hunting. It may be that…parts of the play were considered too close to the royal bone. Yet the play remains ambivalent in its presentation of any line of criticism. King James is ultimately praised while seeing an image of kingship not uncritical of his own person.…[35] Cordelia’s invasion may be seen as a form of resistance which would have been consistent with King James’s viewpoint. In this sense King Lear finds in the recently developed resistance theory new matter for tragic drama.…[40] Is there [in Lr.] some distanced portrait of the ill-tempered, pompous Scottish king, whose own sexuality is transposed in Lear’s hatred of his daughters, and brought to tragic violence in the gouging out of eyes (eyes being shaped like eggs or wombs, and suggesting the sexual order of nature)? Marcus (1988, pp. 149 ff.) considers what effect any criticisms of the king would have had on its audience (including the king) in the court performance on St. Stephen’s Night of 1606: If the 1608 quarto version is richer [than F] in topical details evoking the royal Project for Union, it is also richer in particularized materials which can easily be interpreted as criticism of King James I.…In the quarto King Lear the fool brings up the monopoly system, taunting his royal master for giving away his land and rents to his daughters.…[150] In the quarto King Lear, the wronged king attempts to create a commission of judges very like a Chancery commission to pronounce on the justice of his daughters’ behaviour.…The royal commission of the hovel Lear appoints to arraign and try those daughters who [151] have stripped him of his authority and exacerbated the diuision of the Kingdomes is a madman’s eerie echo of James I’s actual tactics—in the matter of Great Britain and on numerous other occasions—for attempting to work his will upon recalcitrant subjects.…[153] In King Lear, James I’s notions about the organicism of Britain under the king as head are themselves placed on trial…. [But] [155] It is easy to see how [the] liturgical context [of the Feast of St. Stephen]—inescapable for anyone who went to church on the holiday as English subjects were required to—would frame the play itself, solve and disentangle some of its interpretive cruxes.…[156] It is also easy to see how the play’s lesson about succour for the needy and downtrodden could be given moral application, according to the Jacobean line, as reproof against those in the English Parliament and elsewhere who, like Goneril and Regan in the play, were hard-heartedly denying the nation’s obligatory responsibility to the needy Scots.…What are we to make of the elements of the quarto King Lear that appear to criticize King James I and his notions of prerogative—the very notions which stood behind such arbitrary gestures as his attempt to enforce holiday hospitality by royal decree? To a degree, these elements take on a degree of ritual humiliation on the part of one of the powerful in connection with the holiday’s strong message of Deposuit potentes.…[157] Through his presence at the performance of King Lear, James I provided a perspective on the play from which it could be read as both a royal acknowledgment of the king’s sins of state and a dispersal of just the type of legal authority which sought to undercut his absolutism. In keeping with the example of St. Stephen, James I could be interpreted, through his very tolerance of the play’s critique, as forgiving his enemies—at least to the extent that public acknowledgment of hostile criticism can be taken as a kind of forgiveness. Hofele (1997, p. 95): Lr.’s images of authority… desubstantialize kingship by presenting it as a play between the two contrary forces of elevatio and reductio.

Among more general areas of contemporary concern, not focused on the king, to which commentators have found allusions in the play are religion, property law, dispossession and social unrest, medicine and madness, and new intellectual developments. A play that borrows from Harsnett’s satiric anti-Catholic Declaration but uses its language to express human suffering sympathetically has been read as both anti- and pro-Catholic. Thus Whalley (1748) finds elements of anti-Jesuit topical satire in the Fool’s prophecy as well as in Edgar’s echoes of Harsnet, while Wilkes (1877, p. 383) finds evidence of sympathy for Catholicism in Lr.’s mockery of the whole of Harsnet’s statements…in Edgar’s…Bedlamite ravings. Murphy (1984, pp. 12 ff.) sees Lr. concerned with religio-political polemics, specifically the battle between the miraculous faith and the justifying faith with special attention to their implications for politics in England and Scotland and justifications for treason and murder.…[13] The text of King Lear does not endorse the miraculous faith of the exorcists [exposed by Harsnett]. Rather King Lear closes with the miraculous doctrine of the King’s Two Bodies.…[14] In King Lear, as elsewhere, Shakespeare is an impassioned Royalist and the most profound apologist for hierarchy and degree as answering to the deepest needs of humanity that one can find in English literature.…[200] Since…one clear meaning of this world of darkness, devils, imprecations, revenge, and murder is that it is a world of some English Roman Catholics, the task of Edgar is to [201] restore balance and peace to this world.…The dramatic action is concerned with leading this British king [Lear] and this British noble [Edgar] out of the blasted heath, even though an invasion on their behalf fails, the British princess who is queen of France is killed, and both men die. Greenblatt (1985, pp. 104–22): The institutional strategies in which both King Lear and Harsnett’s Declaration are embedded…are part of an intense and sustained struggle [for cultural authority] in late sixteenth- and early seventeenth-century England.… In early modern England…rivalry among elites competing for the major share of authority is expressed in struggles over religious doctrine and practice. Harsnett’s Declaration is a weapon in one such struggle, the attempt by the established and state-supported Church of England to eliminate competing religious authorities by wiping out pockets of rivalrous charisma.…[105] Harsnett wishes, in effect, to cap permanently the great rushing geysers of charisma released in rituals of exorcism.…[116] King Lear’s relation to Harsnett’s book then is essentially one of reiteration, a reiteration that signals a deeper and unexpressed institutional exchange. The official church dismantles and cedes to the players the powerful mechanisms of an unwanted and dangerous charisma; in return the players confirm the charge that those mechanisms are theatrical and hence illusory. However, (p. 118) in Shakespeare the realization that demonic possession is a theatrical illusion leads not to a clarification—the clear-eyed satisfaction of the man who refuses to be gulled—but to a deeper uncertainty, a loss of moorings, in the face of evil.…[121] Lear’s sorrows are not redeemed; nothing can turn them to joy, but the forlorn hope of an impossible redemption persists, drained of its institutional and doctrinal significance, empty and vain, cut off even from a theatrical realization, but like the dream of exorcism, ineradicable. In contrast, Brownlow (1993, pp. 126–8): The effect [of Edgar’s performance as Poor Tom] is surely…an initiation of the audience into some realities that the signs of possession might portend. Similarly, when Edgar takes his father through the strange ritual of the false suicide, the effect should not be to turn the audience against miracles but to make them wonder what the definition of a miracle might be.…[128] King Lear is…an immense prophetic miracle play on religious and political subject matter, composed as a romantic tragedy of outrageous indecorum, appropriating or engulfing Harsnett’s own book, and situating its contents in a landscape of violence and alienation that, whether we read it as pre- or post-Christian, offers a devastating commentary on the spiritual condition of contemporary England. Taylor (Forms of Opposition, 1994, pp. 294–5): There can be no denying that King Lear draws [295] upon a series of incidents in recent recusant history—or that it was read by some of its first readers as a pro-Catholic play.

The conflict over inheritance that begins the play has also seemed related to contemporary property law. Greenblatt (1990, pp. 195–7): Lr. is powerfully situated in the midst of precisely the concerns of the makers of [Elizabethan and Jacobean] maintenance agreements, i.e. legal contracts by which, in return for the transfer of family property, children undertook to provide food, clothing and shelter. These concerns include the terror of being turned out of doors or of becoming a stranger even in one’s own house; the fear of losing the food, clothing, and shelter necessary for survival, let alone dignity; the humiliating loss of parental authority; the dread, particularly powerful in a society that adhered to the principle of gerontological hierarchy, of being supplanted by the young. Lear’s royal status does not cancel but rather intensifies these concerns.…[97] What enables [Lear] to lay aside his claim to rule, the [opening] scene suggests, is the transformation of power into a demand for unbounded love, a love that then takes the place of the older contractual bond between parents and children.…Against paternal and monarchical absolutism, Cordelia opposes in effect the ethos of the maintenance agreement, and this opposition has for Lear the quality of treason. R. Wilson (1993, pp. 230, 220–4): The tragic cultural implications of testamentary power were unfolded in King Lear.…[220] The legend of local [Kentish] exceptionalism that made gavelkind [as in Kent, equal division of a deceased man’s property among his sons] such a precious relic for codifiers of England’s ancient constitution…haunts Shakespeare’s ancient British tragedy.…[222] With [his] inducements to his co-heiresses to deny equalities ([9]), and tender for a third more opulent than your sisters ([92]), Lear jolts the ancient rite of succession abruptly into the capitalist land market, with its unfettered testation.…[223] He behaves, that is to say, not as a feudal monarch, but as a modern landowner.…[224] In the tragedy the legal ground is shifting beneath the characters, as it was in England, as their culture slides from partibility to testation. Voss (1995, pp. 4 ff.): At a historical moment which seems to us, in retrospect, to have been heading towards absolutism in both monarchy and property, and hence to primogeniture, Lear insists on partible inheritance.…At a time when authority and precedent are lodging ever more firmly in the written document, Lear insists on an oral process. But Lear’s love-contest generates an (p. 6) impetus towards a moral cash economy,…entering the world of jobs and leaving the world of roles. Spinosa (1995, pp. 149 ff.) sees King Lear as the English myth of the first use in the word’s legal sense (land-holding for profit). Lr. attempt[s] to develop a sharp understanding of the nature of the problems in personal identity, property, and law associated with the proliferation of the use. It shows what would become of property, identity, and law by employing a prototypical use to organize an entire political society.…Two structurally different forms of the early modern identity [150] (self-constituting supervisorial identity revealed in Lear, on the one hand, and deep psychological identity hearkened to by Kent and Cordelia, on the other) organize themselves around the use, each in conflict with the other. In contrast to these early modern selves, Goneril and Regan stand out as representatives of a feudal, calculative organization of identity, and consequently they…fail fully to grasp the point of the proto-use Lear establishes in granting his land to his daughters. (P. 173): For Shakespeare, then, the practices of the use that come to dominate landholding include not only the production of the self-constituting self trying to organize a public space but also the response to this of certain selves as vexed inward selves.

Since two main characters of the play are a Bedlam beggar and a king-as-outcast, commentators have found echoes of a contemporary problem, dispossession. Voss (1995, pp. 7 ff.): The enclosure movement subtends aspects of both the structure and the texture of King Lear.…[8] Together Lear, Poor Tom and the Fool generate a convincing image, of which enclosure and its related social practices are important elements, of the vagrant, landless life of the masterless poor on and off the roads of England [ca. 1605].…[11] Lear’s experience as a common vagrant turns him away from his own kingdom to seek a private life outside history. Barker (1993, pp. 16–17): The play calls up, and is haunted by, the imagined voices of the figures of the masterless, the displaced, the dangerously unfixed populace, which troublingly populated the anxious imagination of early modern power. However, as in the wider structure of the tragic formation,…this dialectic of dispos-[17]session from identity, and identity discovered in reduction to unaccommodation, is not even-handed. The association of the reduction to a core of humanity on the heath with the ordinary dispossessed and with these thematics of injustice, corruption of power and oppression, is in fact an essentialisation of oppression. Carroll (1996, pp. 184–5): Shakespeare’s powerful encounter between monarchical power [Lear] and social marginality [Poor Tom] physically enacts more than a century’s worth of symbolic confrontations, but this representation comes with a major difference: the humbling of Lear, the king’s descent to the level of the beggar, is not only a critical moment in the play but a skeptical one—part of an important Shakespearean interrogation of the dis-[185]courses of poverty and power. Lear’s remarkable prayer is part of a powerful dramatic process that will expose the arbitrariness of class, power, wealth, and so identity. The beggar and the king’s confrontation, facing one another in similar positions of deprivation, deconstructs the traditional binaries of authority and subjection, wealth and poverty, identity and nothingness. Dubrow (1999, pp. 104–15) finds a housing crisis at the heart of the play: Not the least of the many connections among the ethical characters in the play is that virtually all of them lose their homes.…Throughout the play the loss of that material version of protection the abode creates represents the denial of the ability to [105] protect and be protected in other respects, though at the same time the loss…may engender new forms of guardianship. Hence…literal shelters trope broader questions of safety, responsibility, and subjectivity.…In representing imperilled dwellings…King Lear repeatedly engages with seventeenth-century cultural and social pressures, notably the danger of trespass and other threats to housing and to property ownership.…[108] Male subjectivity…is in no small measure formed by the ability to shelter and deformed by its absence.…[109] King Lear connects housing and its absence with the loss and restoration of Lear’s mind, his dignity, and his power. Cornwall and Regan’s commandeering of Gloucester’s house (p. 111) would also have signalled the insecurity of dwelling places in their own historical moment. Mehl (1975, p. 156), however: A historically-minded reading will lead to the conclusion that the plight of the poor is not a major concern of the play. Elton (1966, pp. 287–8) finds topical relevance to a breakdown of Renaissance hospitality.

A play including three different kinds of madmen has invited discussion of contemporary theories of madness and its treatment. Feder (1980, p. 119): In dramatizing the very structure of Lear’s emotions and thoughts, Shakespeare incorporates medieval assumptions about human nature and institutions as well as the current scientific skepticism which had begun to challenge them. His portrayal of Lear’s mind functioning on levels of consciousness and awareness previously unexplored in literature elucidates the process of discovery characteristic of the Renaissance and is one of its profoundest manifestations. Williams (1984, pp. 188–99), noting it is remarkable how regularly Shakespeare throughout his career links proper diet, proper rest, and suitable and recreative occupation or activity, finds (p. 199) the fullest exposition of the three medicatives in action…in the sickness and cure of Lear. Hoeniger (1984), discussing the function of music in 4.7, surveys classical, medieval, and early modern theories of music as therapeutic. Mazzaro (1985–6, p. 98): the play’s depiction of real and feigned madness reveal[s] not only how much a Simonidean memory system based on correspondences between a microcosm and a macrocosm has taken root [in Renaissance culture] but also how, by positing an intermediate ordering reference point in a demicosm (much like the interior ordering vanishing points in a Renaissance painting), a basis for worldly or human understanding is created. Leggatt (1996, pp. 128–37): Shakespeare is much closer.…[to the] social realities [reflected in contemporary documents].…[137] Other plays of the period cope with the horror of madness by stylizing and distancing it; King Lear confronts it directly. Thiher (1999, p. 85): Shakespeare’s pivotal example demonstrates that at the beginning of the seventeenth century, in spite of the sclerosis of medicine, it became possible to view madness as something other than an accident produced by humors, or diabolical possession, or animal lust, or the position of the stars—to evoke the principal fantasies that had allayed our fear of madness. Madness in Hamlet and King Lear is a position in a context, a relation that must be interpretively explored, and one that can be positively evaluated. In fine Shakespeare offers an understanding of madness unsurpassed since the Greeks. Milne (2002, p. 55): The play’s dramatization of tragical death reveals how an Elizabethan or Jacobean audience might associate tragic poetics with medical diagnosis in ways that create difficulties for modern performers and audiences.
