The older, frequently disputed view that the turn of the century marked a crisis or revolution in intellectual attitudes may be seen in Greenlaw (1931, pp. 150–1): Lr expresses the intellectual disillusionment that marked the closing of the great queen’s reign and the dawn of a new century. Sh.’s (p. 151) pessimism is national and can be traced in other writers of the time. It reappears in Canzano (1993, passim): Lr.’s depiction of a world gone mad reflects the crisis in Renaissance intellectual culture described by Danby. Somewhat similarly, Peterson (1995, pp. 97, 104): Lr. shows a deep…concern over an emerging crisis of epistemology, evident in Sh.’s (p. 104) continuing interest in dramaturgical modes of mimesis and their limitations and in whether human events are random or teleological. Philosophical debates about belief and skepticism, astrology, and the like are referred to throughout the notes of this edition and are named in the index. A scientific revolution is cited by Crane (2004, pp. 3 ff.): Early modern debates about the nature of matter: whether it is infinitely divisible or not; whether substance itself depends on divisibility; whether a void or a vacuum exists, or not; whether nature was created ex nihilo, or not; whether or not a materialist atomism is necessary to explain phenomena like evaporation, condensation and weight—all of these…are echoed in the language and imagery of the play, and significantly structure its treatment of epistemological and ethical questions. [He suggests] a contemporary English locus for such debates, in the circle of Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and followers like Thomas Harriot and William Warner, whose speculations about atomism were widely known.…[5] In King Lear, Shakespeare responds to a growing realization that the structures developed by existing systems of thought to explain the invisible and counter-intuitive workings of matter no longer worked.…And because Shakespeare was a poet, his complex engagement with images of the physical world also structures his understanding of social and ethical problems.…[12] Although Marxist criticism has tended to argue that Goneril and Regan join Edgar [sic] as proponents of a new materialism, while Lear and Cordelia hold to older, spiritually informed values, their attitudes toward divisibility seem roughly opposite this received interpretation.

The many letters in the play have occasioned recent discussions of Renaissance literacy. Erwin (1990, p. 85): By foregrounding the alienations of living speech inherent in his own text [through exchanges of letters and the parody of Scripture]…Shakespeare could make audiences see his letters as suns bright enough to challenge King James’ eclipse of Hecate-blessed Elizabethan mythopoiea. Schwarz (1991, pp. 63–74): The many letters…transmitted and exchanged in King Lear…are sites in which the text’s relationship to its historical moment is played out, signifiers of an increasingly troublesome intellectual and physical relationship of both the art object and the perceiving subject to a rapidly changing social space.…[70] It is in the subplot…that the issues of technology and its structural redefinition of the subject are played out. Postal carriers signify (p. 73) the newly acquired symbolic authority of the technocrats, as represented by its mobilization and authorization of signifiers.…[74] The play’s obsession with written signifiers…[calls] attention to vast transformations in the social fabric of early English capitalism. Jardine (1996, p. 79) finds Lr. concerned with the controlled production of feeling as discussed in Erasmian handbooks on letter-writing.…King Lear elicits our revulsion towards such efficiency by presenting us with the prospect of a world in which real affection is deprived of instrumentality…precisely to the extent that a cynically operated technology of affect—of warmth and intimacy generated by letters—debases the heart’s expressive resources, leaving nothing to be said.

In recent decades, much critical discussion has treated Lr. as ostensibly exemplifying and supporting general theories not only about Elizabethan-Jacobean times but also about history, human society, or culture in general. Some center on the importance of individual moral choices in shaping history; others emphasize the influence of historical and cultural forces and of social or political systems; and one treats of a particular divine purpose beyond general providence.

Older theorizing emphasizes that the basis of a working society is fellow-feeling between citizens, and conversely that lack of such feeling leads to disintegration. Natural affection between members of a family is often seen as the basis for the larger community, hence Lear’s destruction of his family leads to chaos in the kingdom. Stauffer (1949, pp. 191–6): Shakespeare’s dual themes of personal love and the stable social order here blend into a single embracing conception, whose symbol is the family.…[196] The imaginative identification between the father-child symbol and the conception of universal harmony or universal discord is a bold one, but it is made so easily and confidently that when a father misjudges his daughters, machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders follow us disquietly to our graves.…This wider conception of love as a social obligation is seen also in terms of the state, though it is framed in the symbols of the larger cosmos as well as the smaller unit of the family and its dependents. In this sense, the theme of the play is authority and allegiance.…[204] The drift of the play has been from the selfish court to the broad commonalty of the poor. Some of its great speeches are Edgar’s pictures of base beggars and the forsaken castaways of society, [205] and from these pictures rise naturally the other great speeches of Lear and Gloucester on just distribution and sympathy.…Lear and Gloucester, each himself a poor banished man, are initiated into the wide fellowship of the poor; and from the inhabitants of hovels and heaths and prisons, from low farms, poor pelting villages, sheepcotes and mills, from drinking the green mantle of the standing pool and being drenched by the rain and persecuted by the thunder, swell the great prayers of sympathy with human misery. Compassion builds a classless society, for in suffering all men are equal. Barish & Waingrow (1958, pp. 348–50) discuss Lr.’s depiction of social relations in terms of true and false service: As servants of God we discover the true and whole meaning of service: that by promoting concord between individuals of different rank, it ends by minimizing distinctions of rank. In contrast, instead of progressing towards a uniquely human kind of solidarity, above the prevailing relationships of rank, false service plunges society downwards into a bestial chaos.…[349] The quintessence of the good servant and the touchstone for service throughout the play is Kent.…[350] Oswald is Kent turned inside out, the bad servant anatomized, and their altercation in the courtyard of Gloucester’s castle presents in almost schematic form the confrontation of true service with false.

Sewell (1951, pp. 108 ff.) discusses social relatedness as a pervasive and significant concern of the play: King Lear is the play in which Shakespeare returns once again to see man as a human soul, not in opposition to society, not rejecting society, but finding in society the sphere of fulfillment.…Social order is the condition, as it is the resultant, of sweet and affirmative being, without which man relapses into a beastly and self-destructive individualism.…[110] There is nothing in the play to cast suspicion on the rightness of external order—there is much in the play to make us feel that without it we are lost, to affirm that not discipline but indiscipline destroys. But there is also much to support the view that even discipline will destroy where it is not involved in self-discipline and love. King Lear …is the only one of Shakespeare’s plays in which personal relationship is treated as an end and not as a means; the only [111] play in which personal relationships seem to determine character rather than to have an effect upon character.…All the characters are conceived…in their relationships with other people, in their relationships with each other, and society is a vital complex of such relationships. In King Lear, then, not only is individual character differently conceived, but also living society itself.…In King Lear personal relationships are the field of character-fulfillment.…[113] Personal relationships, however, are conceived in two different ways—in loyalty and consideration which are owed according merely to the bond, and in that going out of [114] oneself which makes of love and loyalty something more than is demanded by the bond.…[116] The movement of the play seems to be from conduct (and character) in which reason is governed by self-regard, to conduct (and character) in which reason is transformed by compassion. In an image, this compassion becomes a healing and medicinal balm [quotes 2176+8–9 and 2776–9].…[117] But it is not a merely secular society in which these characters are conceived to have their being. Nor, on [118] the other hand, do I think it can be said (even through allegory) to be a society understood in terms of Christian theology. Nevertheless…we certainly get the impression in the play that the characters are imagined not only as members of each other but also as members of a Nature which is active both within themselves and throughout the circumambient universe. Man is nowhere so certainly exhibited as a member of all organic creation and of the elemental powers. Man’s membership of society is more than legal, is more than political, because it is subtended in a wider membership, in which plants and animals, the wind and the thunder are also included. And is it too extravagant to suggest that this natural universe is, in the earlier part of the play, peopled not only by men but also by beings of a primitive pagan belief…and that the dominion of these beings is, in the action of the play, superseded? Is it, indeed, too extravagant to suggest that in the play we have a veritable change in dispensation? What the final dispensation is, however, is difficult to determine, for Shakespeare seems not to specify it. The most we can say is that…there are moments and images towards the end of King Lear which give promise of grace and benediction. Similarly Mack (1965, pp. 100–13): There can be no question that the most powerful single dimension of the play’s world for its spectators is its continual reference to and evocation, through ear and eye alike, of the nature and significance of human society.…The circumstantial sociality of the Lear world…defines and gives body to this closing vision of human achievement and its cost. In writing King Lear, Shakespeare’s imagination appears to have been so fully oriented toward presenting human reality as a web of ties commutual that not only characterization and action, but language, theme, and even the very mise en scène are influenced.…[102] Shakespeare’s concern with relation as the ultimate reality for human beings also expresses itself strongly in the plot of King Lear and in the [103] language of social use and habit to which the plot gives rise and which it repeatedly examines. To an extent unparalleled in the other tragedies, the plot of the play depends on and manipulates relations of service and of family.…[110] Existence is tragic in King Lear because existence is inseparable from relation; we are born from and to it; it envelops us in our loves and lives as parents, children, sisters, brothers, husbands, wives, servants, masters, rulers, subjects—the web is seamless and unending.…[111] Man’s tragic fate, as King Lear presents it, comes into being with his entry into relatedness, which is his entry into humanity.…[113] So far as human wisdom goes, the choice of relatedness must be recognized as its own reward, leading sometimes to alleviation of suffering, as in the case of Gloucester’s joy in Edgar, but equally often to more suffering, as in the case of Lear. Knights (1957, p. 120): King Lear establishes the grounds of any politics that claims to be more than a grammar of power. Behind hierarchy and authority, behind formal justice and public order, is a community of persons bound by holy cords…Which are too intrinse t’unloose. The basic political facts of this play are that men can feel for each other, and that this directness of relationship—expressing itself in the humblest of ways as well as in the most exalted forms of loyalty and sacrifice—is the only alternative to a predatory power-seeking whose necessary end is anarchy. Ignatieff (1985, pp. 30–6) reads Lr. as a reflection on the claim of need, on the role of the natural and the social in the grounding of the claim.…It is a play that sets out to show us why we must take the needs of others on trust, by showing how murderous and pitiless a place the world can become without such trust. The claim of need makes the relation between the powerful and the powerless human, but the nightmare of the powerless is that one day they will make their claim and the powerful will demand a reason, one day the look of entreaty will be met with the unknowing stare of force.…[36] Lear defends a world in which each person would have enough, but he also defends a proposition much less familiar to modern ears: that dignity reposes in difference, not equality. Wharton (1988, pp. 117, 113) interprets Lr. as a deliberate counter-statement against the scepticism and destructiveness of [moral] experiments in Jacobean drama, (p. 113) promoting and reinforcing the very doctrine of human ties and bonds that the experimental heroes of Jacobean drama deliberately set out to violate.

To the contrary view that material conditions rather than a feeling such as pity are paramount in shaping a society, others object. Dollimore (1984; 2004, pp. 191–7): In Lr., far from endorsing the idea that man can redeem himself in and through an access of pity [(p. 190): a humanist view which mystifies suffering and invests man with a quasi-transcendent identity], we might be moved to recognise that, on the contrary, in a world where pity is the prerequisite for compassionate action, where a king has to share the suffering of his subjects in order to care, the majority will remain poor, naked and wretched. The point of course is that princes only see the hovels of wretches during progresses (walkabouts?), in flight or in fairy tale.…[192] So, far from transcending in the name of an essential humanity the gulf which separates the privileged from the deprived, the play insists on it.…[197] King Lear is, above all, a play about power, property and inheritance.…Human values are not antecedent to these material realities but are, on the contrary, in-formed [sic] by them. Levin (1997, p. 153) objects: This reading…makes the play virtually unrecognizable by reversing our moral judgments, since the apparently good characters are wrong and the apparently evil ones are right, and by negating our emotional engagement, since we cannot sympathize with those reactionary essentialist humanists. McAlindon (1992, p. 88), contra Dollimore: Pity is shown to be the first prerequisite for socio-political understanding. Idem (1995, pp. 838–43): It is demonstrably wrong to claim that pity here is ineffectual, produces no significant alteration, is not redemptive.…[839] In fact a central idea of the play is that people commit and tolerate injustice precisely because…they will not feel.…[841] Fortitude is nowhere devalued [in Lr.]. What it signifies is not political quietism but rather the capacity to endure what cannot be changed or avoided for the time being.…[843] The categorical denial that suffering is redeemed in Lear by the sufferers’ growth in knowledge and understanding…is extraordinarily unconvincing and offhand. Davidson (1996, pp. 292–5), also contra Dollimore: Shakespeare in fact was not affirming the value of subversion, of skepticism linked to self-interest, of materialist analysis of forces whether cosmic or national or personal.…[295] By placing the contemporary problem of belief in dramatic form Shakespeare has provided reference points by which human beings may come to terms with their own anxiety concerning earthly imperfection—the reality of evil in this world—and the possibility of transcendence and the redemptive power of grace.

Others emphasize individual action rather than feeling. Hays (1979, pp. 98–114): King Lear is not the great metaphysical opus that critics from Bradley on have claimed it is. Rather, (p. 99) the primary antithesis Shakespeare established in the play is between (pro)creative human activity based on an order of law and egocentric activity which has no rational, that is, social, justification.…[100] These contrasts between private irrationality and a rationally ordered social system, between meaning found in the community and rampant egocentrism, are the building blocks of the play as a whole.…[111] As the play proceeds it exposes the reality behind the mystified structures of feudal-aristocratic society at the same time that it exposes the distance between rhetoric and experienced reality.…[114] The final struggle in the play is between Edmund and Edgar—between rational egocentrism and social rationalism. Somewhat similarly, Ryan (1989, pp. 46–72) denies the notion that Shakespeare’s tragedies depict as fixed and inexorable the destructive forces to which individuals find themselves subject, and that the wisdom they preach is submission to conditions human beings cannot change. Rather Lr. specifically affirms (p. 67) that everything which occurs, however horrific, follows all too clearly from the fact that men / Are as the time is [2973–4] rather than as nature or the gods direct, whatever the [68] characters themselves may blindly assert to the contrary. Lr. (p. 72) leaves us no choice but to identify the problem as the indefensible subjection of men and women to the injustices of a stratified society, and to seek the implied solution in the egalitarian standpoint created and vindicated by the play as a whole. See also Idem (1995, pp. 38–9).

For some, the play’s lessons of political morality are not unequivocally clear. Leggatt (1992, pp. 181–200): Its value system is to a great extent familiar: loyalty, kindness and charity all play on the audience’s sympathies.…[199] But through the last moments of the play the commentary becomes increasingly inarticulate.…[200] so that with the excitement goes a certain frustration and discomfort. Gellrich (1988, pp. 218–25): The whole tragedy mobilizes conflicts that disrupt moral categories and ethical identities, thus rendering evaluative interpretations of character and action a hazardous business.…[223] while seeming to elicit expectations of morality drama in the first act of King Lear, Shakespeare destabilizes differences between good and bad, justice and injustice on which the instructive potential of such drama rests.…[225] There is [also] an excess of pathos in King Lear that eludes the rationalization of disaster in the doctrine of moral instruction.…King Lear does not settle our souls in the way Renaissance and neoclassical critics argue it should, through structural properties and clarity of moral vision. White (1988, p. 182–96) finds in Lr. an unresolved though integrated dialectic, about political attitudes and social actions.…[195] The underlying logic of King Lear is subversive of all forms of authority.…[196] It is the play in which the concepts of authority and social justice are most starkly opposed and yet most intimately linked in an evolving vision that demonstrates both the rigorous logic and the intimations of utopian hope and despairing realism of philosophical anarchism.

In recent years much theorizing about Lr. has centered on the nature of power—its sources, systems, and effects. Some of it is affected by feminist criticism, dwelling on the influence of a social and cultural system, patriarchy, upon the exercise of political power. Hodge (1990, p. 63): Lr.’s ending is a repudiation of history and myth, morality and political ideology…a savage and pessimistic social critique, directed at the contradictions of patriarchy and its lethal consequences for the sexual life of men and women, a mimetic construct which has as its semiosic effect the projection of Shakespeare as a social critic challenging the consensus truth of his day. So also Cohen (1993, pp. 94 ff.), emphasizing the political dimension that contextualizes the killing of Cordelia in terms of sex and gender distortions which the play produces.…[108] The reason she dies is forcibly and definitively to validate a structure of nature and kinship that patriarchy has consoloidated as its own.

Tennenhouse (1986, pp. 132–42) considers a more specific system for holding and transferring power: Lr. displays the political consequences which unfold when the monarch divests himself of the patriarchal prerogatives traditionally inhering in his body.…[134] Shakespeare’s Jacobean version of the story interrogates the very notion of the Crown as a corporate essence in perpetuity. His Lear thus poses a threat to legitimate authority that had never been at issue before. Out of this historically later contest between the king’s two bodies, a Jacobean thematics can be said to emerge. The metaphysics of the Crown itself is called into question so that it may be displaced onto the state as a ubiquitous presence which exists prior to and ontologically different from any of its natural embodiments.…[135] When [Lear] determines the rules of inheritance according to his will and not according to the principle of primogeniture, he appears to deny the metaphysics of the body politic and the special status of the king’s blood. By dismantling his iconic body, Lear…initiates a series of conflicts which threaten the stability of the state as well as the coherence of its signs and symbols. Sh. (p. 139) seems [especially] interested in depicting the consequences of severing the iconic bond between the powers inhering in the blood and the blood itself.…[141] Shakespeare assures us that only those survive at the end of the play who have maintained belief in the primacy of blood over all other signs, instruments, or manifestations of power.…[142] It is more than coincidental, then—or rather it is coincidental in precisely the way that ideology arranges the coincidence of such events—that no direct heir to the throne of Britain remains alive at the end of King Lear. Under such conditions,…power reverts back to its metaphysical source—the patriarchal principle itself. What matters most in maintaining the order of the state is loyalty to the principle of blood—the metaphysical body of power—and not the individual who wields it. For this is the form of power that Shakespeare displays by his revision of Elizabethan materials.

Matz (1994, pp. 223–4): Literally and metaphorically, torture provides a response to King Lear’s potentially subversive questioning of monarchic authority.…[224] The king’s authority is finally substantiated on the tortured body.

Grady (1996, pp. 160, 138–42) considers the will to power itself in relation to the postmodernist theme of reification. Concerned with the general possibilities of meaning under conditions of emerging reified modernity, he finds that Lr. (p. 138) enacts a logic of resistance to power…consistent with Habermas’s treatment of problems of legitimation.…[140] King Lear takes place in a space in which…[an] understanding of the legitimating, ideological functions of formerly unquestioned theology and cosmology has begun to rise to consciousness.…As the major cultural signifying systems begin to be seen as essentially ideological…the play focuses on the workings of a reified power system that had, outside the repressed text of Machiavelli’s The Prince—and the privileged, equivocal space of the theatre,…largely escaped conceptualization.…[142] In King Lear sex and power are linked through the depiction of sadism and sexual domination at work in the otherwise impersonal subjectivities of the three principal rulers [Cornwall, Regan, and Goneril]. This theme is part of a larger probing of the possibilities of an innate human will to power—evil, a kind of pessimistic essentialism. And yet the play follows this logic of essentialist pessimism to its darkest moments, only to project an alternative notion of human possibilities in the figures of Edgar and Cordelia. The ending leaves us…poised between a utopian vision of human possibilities and a devastating reality principle that will allow no easy affirmations of any positivity. Neither, however, will Lear’s logic allow any essentialist conclusions about a human nature shown capable of the widest possible range of motivations and actions.

It remains to mention a theological view of historical change whose presence several critics have sensed lying behind the events of Lr. A number of earlier critics have remarked on the number of references in the play to the coming of Doomsday. Lascelles (1973, p. 73) finds that scenes in Lr. create a visual allusion [to] the Doomsday paintings, especially those over the chancel arch in so many English churches. Oppel (Phenomenon, 1978, pp. 215 ff.) finds intimations of apocalypse in the breathtaking course of events.…[216] The phenomenon of acceleration is familiar to us through the Christian doctrine which views the course of history as the history of salvation.…[217] Christian belief is based upon the conviction that world history is being rapidly propelled toward its end and its fulfillment…at the irrevocable Last Judgment.…[219] The disquieting aspect about [Lr.] is the way this play takes up this theme of acceleration and thereby touches upon concepts within the realm of Protestant theological history, but at the same time radically reverses all Christian concepts related to the promised end with trust in a blissful Second Coming. Davidson (1992, pp. 80–4): The theatrical spectacle throughout most of the play is illustrative…of a topsy-turvy world—indeed, of a world turned upside down, a topos medieval in origin.…[81] Shakespeare has turned the traditional topos of the world upside down to a use not foreseen by the medieval and ancient writers.…[84] The play shows violations of all the seven Corporal Acts of Mercy.…These reversals of merciful deeds are omens of Doomsday, when Christ as Judge will return as in the final pageants in the Middle English cycle plays to regard those who have done or failed to do the Corporal Acts of Mercy. And the conclusion of Shakespeare’s drama…will also be a judgment scene. See also Holloway (1961, pp. 75–9), Morris (1985, pp. 127 ff.).

The idea that Lr. depicts apocalypse is treated at book length by Wittreich (1984, pp. 12 ff.): In accordance with the historical chronicles, Shakespeare makes the terrifying vision of a Last Judgment the locus of his play, yet, more troublesomely, appears to deny that event its Christian significance, either beyond time or within it. There is no transcendence here.…Here there is death without deliverance, an end without a new beginning, no heaven apparently and no new earth—just the tears of things.…Or so it seems.…[16] Not only must James’s pet concerns and political attitudes come into play in interpretation, but such contextualization presses James’s own conception of history, of apocalyptic history, upon a play-world that seemingly defies it.…[19] In the case of the Lear story the [typological] message was political, as well as ethical; the very history in which it was embedded, in conjunction with typology, became a political weapon used to advance James to the throne and to sustain his court.…[20] Shakespeare means to acknowledge James’s efforts to unite England and Scotland.…The troubled and divided court, the afflicted kingdom, the disjointed and destabilized world [of Lr.], Shakespeare implies, will become healthy and whole again under the aegis of James.…[31] Yet Shakespeare also withholds from the king the sort of idolatrous flattery that was currently enveloping him in the apocalyptic myth.…This is a play, after all, in which a king becomes truly a king only after he has become first, and daringly, a man. Shakespeare seems, furthermore, to cast a dubious eye on apocalyptics.…Indeed, if apocalypse is viewed as a declaration of hope in man’s darkest hour, as a proclamation that God rules history and will bring out of it, independent of human participation, a glorious future, then Shakespeare may be seen resisting apocalypse by withdrawing such promises.…[36] King Lear …presents history within a new literary structure, Shakespeare implying that elements in the play not found in tradition, or in the chronicles, may nevertheless belong to history.…[39] The triumph of Britain in the war with France, whatever its historical veracity, makes an important symbolic point and, further, reinforces the typological play between two kings, two separate moments of history, while reminding us that typology itself was a popular way of writing history in the Renaissance—a way of abolishing past history except as a type-source for a new history.…[44] Shakespeare introduces prophetic and apocalyptic elements into his play and allows them to authorize his astonishing revision of a received tradition whose view of history is grimly pessimistic—indeed to legitimate the claim that King Lear is a presentation of True Chronicle History.…[90] The apocalyptic element in King Lear is thus ambiguous, so much so that it may be construed as lending all degrees of darkness to the play or, conversely, as shattering that darkness by letting in the light, however scattered, of Revelation itself.…[95] If the whole center of the play creates the ambience of apocalypse and the exchange between Kent and Edgar [3224–5] brings us to its verge, that center finds its circumference in the apocalyptic trumpets that terminate the play’s action.…Besides the blaring trumpets, the play contains numerous other signatures of Apocalypse.…[98] Characters in Shakespeare’s play also exhibit an archetypal connec-[99]tion with figures in the Apocalypse.…[101] Through such apocalyptic images, themes, and ideas, Shakespeare implies a flickering analogy between secular and sacred history.…[103] Apocalyptic reference…lodges King Lear within…an historical phase, the first woe, that antedates the Incarnation and that for all its adumbrations of last things is but an image of that horror.…Apocalyptic reference, besides imparting mythic dimensions to this play, also turns the apocalyptic myth against itself in such a way as to challenge received interpretations of it. Like the Lear legend, the myth of apocalypse is first ravaged, then created anew, in a play whose chief aesthetic features…derive from a poetics that King Lear shares with the last book of the Bible.…[105] Through an elaborate system of allusion involving the Book of Revelation, Shakespeare edges history, tragedy, and comedy toward, and then into, a prophetic mode. The play, repeatedly referring to prophecy, itself becomes a prophecy that would warn the present and wrest from it a new future; and in its last act, the play veers toward, seems to stand at the very verge of apocalypse. Lear is a prophecy not in the vulgar sense of predicting the future, but in the Renaissance sense of interpreting existing prophecy in order to bring mankind to a new stage of consciousness and increase the distance the eyes may pierce [869].

Often politically minded critics have applied the play’s lessons to political issues in their own times. Thus Anon. (1792, pp. 107–111), alarmed by revolutionary France, finds support for political conservatism, and cites the opening lines in support of primogeniture. Likewise Chalmers (1799, p. 416), decrying Jacobinism: The moral of Lear…is the most important, which can be exhibited by scenic action, to a people; in order to inculcate, by examples, the dangers of division, and the benefits of union. Miller (1900, pp. 23 ff.) applies the lesson of King Lear to the situation of the India of our own day, to argue (p. 109) that the transition from the first stage of civilized society to that which ought to develop out of it, can be safely made only when that public spirit, that postponement of self to the common good, that devotion to the great ends that society subserves which Shakespeare sets forth as love has place and power in the everyday machinery of the community.

Since World War II, however, readers and audiences have felt a different kind of affinity with Lr. Hamlet, a play about an idealistic young man in constant doubt where the truth lay, spoke especially to the Victorian age, dealing with the upsetting ideas of Lyell, Darwin, Marx, and ultimately Freud. Lr., a play about the possibility of infinite loss, has been especially meaningful to the twentieth century of two world wars, mechanized warfare, genocide, and the possibility of atomic annihilation. Wilson (1929, p. 45): I do not think that a generation that has survived the Great War is likely to shirk the ending of the play. Rowe (1943, pp. 207–13): The sense of a world in moral chaos which may lead to disillusion and despair is not unique to our generation; Shakespeare confronted it in King Lear and transcended it.…[213] In the years before naziism was unleashed upon Europe, King Lear, in my experience, was a play of Shakespeare’s to which students were least readily responsive. They were left cold by it as unreal, or were left rebellious, without finding the catharsis of tragedy. In the last two years it has seemed to become of immediate meaningfulness and satisfaction. They find that they are not the first to know chaos, and they gain equanimity for their own world… Spencer (1944, pp. 302–3): Lear embodies much of the nobility and many of the weaknesses peculiarly inherent in our post-medieval Western civilization.…[It] is the tragedy not so much [303] of an individual as of a civilization. Knight (1944, pp. 52–3): Lear gives up his sovereignty in all but name, sentimentally wishing for ease…just as Great Britain, in our time…has tried to relinquish that power which is yet her pressing destiny, thinking to preserve her royalty on easy terms.…[53] The play is written, broadly, from a sense of oncoming disaster in Renaissance civilisation related to lack of family piety.…Like Timon, though less obviously, the play is a warning. Heilman (1948, pp. 287–8): To us, in our world, Lear should not be too difficult or seem too bitter. We are familiar enough with the revolt against sanctions, with the cult of success, and, above all, with the rejection of all the claims that are not consistent with the belief that our sole destiny is mastery of the immediate, tangible world. We can see a world in solution, an exacerbated sense of circumstance, a preoccupation with the here and now, a mastery of practical psychology and of the manipulation of the human mind, an unprecedentedly skillful awareness of things and objects—and a despair of the longer vision. We should have no trouble in seeing that Shakespeare has caught a world in extremis, when the quality [288] of man’s reasoning about reality is the main problem; in seeing that he has caught metaphysical evil in a particular historical formulation. We should easily understand the rightness of his picture. When the old order changeth, it is far less likely that wild bells ring in the new than that utter human anguish precedes and accompanies the enlargement, if so it be, of the old insight, or the recovery of an old insight which in the context seems new. All that anguish Shakespeare has infused into the play. Mack (1965, pp. 85–6) suggests that fear of nuclear annihilation brings King Lear close to our business and bosoms today.…Intimations of World’s End run through it like a yeast. In the scenes on the heath, the elements are at war as if it were indeed Armageddon. When Lear awakes with Cordelia at his side, he imagines that already apocalypse is past, she is a soul in bliss, he bound upon a wheel of fire. Appearing in the last act with Cordelia dead in his arms, he wonders that those around him do not crack [86] heaven’s vault with their grief, and they wonder in turn if the pietà they behold is the promis’d end or image of that horror. These are but some of the overt allusions. Under them everywhere run tides of doomsday passion that seem to use up and wear away people, codes, expectations, all stable points of reference, till only a profound sense remains that an epoch, in fact a whole dispensation has forever closed. Davis (1974, pp. 153–60) associates Edmund’s nihilism with modern politics of emancipation. Orkin (1987, pp. 156–7) relates Lear’s relinquishing of his power and the problem of Regan’s and Goneril’s takeover directly to the South African Land Act of 1913, and further relates the play’s depiction of an apparently legitimate but actually ruthless and cruel ruling class to (p. 157) the present state of emergency in South Africa, criticizing the depoliticized use made of the text in the country’s educational system. Likewise Visser (1998, p. 215): Today, in South Africa, the great number of people left landless and homeless through what are at bottom the same social and economic forces glimpsed in King Lear…await the more equitable distribution of the social product recognized as essential by both Lear and Gloucester. See also Basu Roy (2001). Cameron (1992) reads Lr. as a parable of global capitalism. Foakes (1993, pp. 213–14) seeks a political explanation for the play’s paramount status among Sh.’s works in the 20th century: King Lear exposes the contradictions between, on the one hand, the importance our society places upon individual expression and fulfillment, upon the freedom and autonomy of each person, and on the other, the diminution of the individual to a nobody, another entry in the computer lists of the government, banks, police and advertisers, marking the social, economic and political insignificance of each person in a mass society. In this sense King Lear remains to the end a powerfully political play, and the pathos of the final image of Lear is largely generated by our awareness of this contradiction, as it is embodied in what happened to him. Perhaps there is yet another political dimension to the play, reflected in its resurgence as Shakespeare’s greatest play since the Second World War and especially since 1960 or so, at least as it relates to Britain, where it has been staged more often in recent years than ever before.…Perhaps it is not altogether fanciful to associate Lear, clinging to the power he has given away and losing everything, [214] with Britain, clinging to an imperial role it no longer has any claim to, having given its empire away, while declining all too rapidly into one of the poorest countries of Europe.

Readings of the play as drame à clef are chiefly a product of the late-19th, early-20th century heyday of bardolatry and its obverse, anti-Stratfordianism. However, such readings occasionally appear in recent decades as well.

A number of critics have found in Lr. a reflection of Sh.’s bitter personal experience or profound disillusion. Thus Duvall (1900, p. 232) supposes that in the love of Lear for Cordelia was some of the remorse which Shakespeare felt at having abandoned Susanna and Judith for so long. (Fr.) Strindberg (1908; tr. 1966, pp. 210–12) sees an expression of Sh.’s personal despair: Cordelia’s death is perfectly natural for Shakespeare, who in [211] this period of his life seems to have seen through the whole mess, and to have lain on the rack of torture.…What bitter experiences Shakespeare had lived through one does not know, but he had daughters and was not happily married. Most likely his competitors, too, made his life bitter.…His own life was stormy and irregular, and various admissions in the sonnets imply that he had early in life learned the secrets of life and its joys.…[212] When a human being despairs, he first of all doubts God’s goodness, and that is close to blasphemy. Shakespeare blasphemes (the gods) in King Lear. Watt (1908, p. 275) also supposes a basis in Sh.’s biography. Harris (1909, pp. 328–30): Lear is a page of Shakespeare’s autobiography, and the faults of it are the stains of his blistering tears.…[330] The note of this tragedy is Shakespeare’s understanding of his insane blind trust in men; but the passion of it springs from erotic mania and from the consciousness that he is too old for love’s lists. Idem (1912, pp. 185 ff.): It is his faithless mistress [Mary Fitton] who has infected the poet’s imagination.…[197] Jealousy has bred despair, and the despair shrills to madness and the more awful dread of madness. Chambers (1930), too, speculates that while writing the tragedies Sh. underwent mental strain, exhaustion, possibly even a breakdown (1:86): Shakespeare’s spirit must have been very nearly submerged in Lear. However, he later concedes (1:274) this may all be fanciful, very likely only…a whimsy of my own. Murry (1936, pp. 337 ff.) judges that Lr. reflects a period in which Sh.’s imaginative mastery was inhibited by his obsession with a negative vision. In Lr. Shakespeare [seems] out of his depth.…[338] One is conscious of the strange sexual undercurrent which disturbs the depths of his uncontrolled dramas—a terrible primitive revulsion against sex.…The theme of venery is intertwined with the theme of filial ingratitude [viz. Goneril and Regan].…It is some vast upsurge of the animal, destroying humanity, of which Shakespeare is apprehensive.…[341] A man possessed, as Shakespeare may have been possessed, during the writing of King Lear, by the vision that is continually breaking forth in it, cannot imagine with his whole being.…Many of the scenes are evidently the work not so much of a tired, as of a divided man…intermittently possessed by a vision that is inimical to the spontaneity of Imagination. Muir & O’Loughlin (1937, pp. 179 ff.) likewise claim that Lr. reflects Sh.’s pained emotional life. Southhampton’s unspecified betrayal and break with Sh. ca. 1598 led Sh. to be obsessed with betrayal and ingratitude, making him bitter and pessimistic, probably attempting to bury his memories in sexual indulgence. Sh., by the time of Lr. and Tim., (p. 195) was disgusted with sex. He is a man tortured by his own thoughts, disgusted by his own feelings, hating his fellow men…a man bound on a wheel of fire, a man to whom life was a nightmare, a man who…was on the last verge of sanity, a man who was saved only by his sense of humor, and by the detachment which that implies. Fripp (1938, pp. 665–7) also finds that in Lr. Shakespeare is oppressed with the sense of human corruption. He was, as all thinking men then were, Calvinistic. He believed in the Fall, and in man’s inability to rise without divine Grace.…[667] We are left…feeling with Shakespeare the moral insufficiency and insipience of life, and its injustice and meaninglessness without life to come, convinced that goodness reveals not only human nature but the Divine. Brown (1949, pp. 140–1): For ten years Sh. lived a phase of Dark Vision. When writing Lr. and Tim. he (p. 141) was living in a world of darkness unqualified and experienced (p. 179) constant surrender to disgust with the physical side of love. Similarly Rowse (1963, p. 376): The obsessive disgust with sex that is so characteristic of Shakespeare at this period…must indicate something in his state of mind, if not of body. Likewise Holbrook (1964, pp. 142–3): Having found the frail and mortal nature of man, and perhaps the whole of worldly reality…almost unacceptable…too dreadful and treacherous ever to bring to hopeful order, Sh. found his disgust too strong to control.…Lear would seem to have been the crucial turning point, towards acceptance, peace, [143] inward order, and a belief in love and continuity. Brewer (1966, p. 98): Could it be…a possibility that Shakespeare did contract a [venereal] disease which increased the vehemence with which he denounced women and railed against sex at this time? De Moor (1960, pp. 56 ff.) finds Sh., in whom the unity of woman and poet is evident, embodying in Lear’s daughters aspects of his self. (P. 58): We do not consider Lear in any way a tragedy of filial ingratitude, but the same tragedy as Hamlet and Othello, in different circumstances, with images of women the focus of both idealization and disgust with the world. Teplitz (1970, pp. 205–9) imagines a psycho-biographical basis for Shakespeare’s hostility to female progeny for inheritance in Lr., deriving from (p. 209) the frustration of single, legitimate male inheritance in Sh.’s own family due to the death of young Hamnet.

Psychoanalytic concepts provide an interpretive master-key for Sharpe (1950, pp. 218 ff.): Shakespeare dramatized an old conflict, a conflict not of age but of childhood and infancy re-activated in the poet’s maturity.…[219] The poet in maturity re-experienced with all their original massive power the genuine emotions of childhood. Psychically he regressed to the loves and hates of early childhood.…[226] In this play there are evidences of Lear’s mother’s two pregnancies (i.e., the poet’s mother). One occurred when his sphincter control was not stabilized, and he became incontinent, this being dramatized in the Goneril-Lear quarrel concerning his knights. The second pregnancy occurred when the child was accustomed to walk about independently. He ran away from where he was staying for a day, a night, or even longer.…He was found exhausted, dirty, and decked with the flowers of late summer.…[227] The decision to stay with each daughter a month in turn is the outcome of the complexity of emotional reactions concerning phantasies arising in childhood from the observations of signs of the mother’s menstruation.…[231] The frustrations of which Lear complains include in their range at different ages, loss of the breast, less and less attention to His Majesty the Baby so long accustomed to occupy the attention of everyone, and the anal deprivations.…These grievances are at the same time a subtle defence used unconsciously to fool his father and to hide from him and himself his knowledge of the father’s sexual love for the mother.…[233] [The] dramatizations in King Lear of removal from place to place are a symptom of obsessional doubt. Cordelia dies because (p. 235) she is the symbol of Lear’s hysterical identification. For Mirsky (1994, pp. 15 ff.), too, Lr. enacts Shakespeare’s dream life, his obsessions.…[19] King Lear is a story of a dying man’s desire for his daughters. Sh. (p. 20) foresaw his own old age, a man overwhelmed by desire for his daughters. In addition, (p. 41) Shakespeare increases sexual tension in his Folio changes.

Hughes (1992, pp. 257–62) provides a more mystical psycho-spiritual allegory based on Sh.’s lifelong obsession with the myth of Venus and Adonis: Lear…confronts (rather like Shakespeare drafting his own will in 1606) three women, i.e. the Goddess who incorporates in some form still hidden from him, the Queen of Hell, but who mainly embodies the love on which his sanity depends.…[261] The Boar, which is in some ways his birth labour, and which is also the Storm of the disintegration of the old ego, is also, as always, the Queen of Hell. In his battling crawl towards his rebirth, Lear seems to be fighting his way into the teeth of the hurricane [262] of her diabolical terrors—as if in some hope of reaching the very source of the Great Witch: the source of the Goddess! (See also Freud on Cordelia as the goddess of death, below, .)

A few critics find Sh. settling personal scores. A satire on Sh.’s fellow dramatists is suggested by Cartwright (1864, pp. 32 ff.): Jonson is marked out most clearly and unmistakably as Edmund; Cornwall is Marston, Albany = Dekker, Kent = Chapman, Gloucester = Lyly, Burgundy = Fletcher, and France = Beaumont. Goneril and Regan are (p. 66) the muses of Decker [sic] and Marston, and Cordelia is the romantic muse. Knight (1973, p. 55): Edmund immortalizes Edmund Lambert as one who illegitimately stole the paternity [i.e. patrimony] of a brother [in-law, Sh.’s father].

Other critics have read the play as a historical allegory commenting on the sixteenth-century Reformation and wars of religion. Bowden (1899, pp. 324 ff.) finds evidence for Shakespeare’s Roman Catholicism in Lr.’s drame à clef: Lear is the development of the doctrine which was involved in Henry VIII.’s theory of Empire.…The monarch has the monopoly of loyalty and obedience, and whoever gives only a divided allegiance is a traitor. Goneril acts as an English Protestant, Cordelia as a French Catholic; Lear’s alienation from Cordelia is (p. 326) much the same as the English government’s inability to reconcile itself with the English Catholics. His (p. 327) sacrificial reunion and death leads to a conversion of Albany. Creighton (1913, pp. 19 ff.) reads the play as a religious allegory of the [Henrician] Reformation in England.…[79] The Lear of the opening scene must be understood as Henry himself, whereas the tragic Lear of all the great scenes is changed to a…[82] symbol of the national conscience and its superstitions. Gloucester is (p. 101) the monastic system. His blinding symbolizes the dissolution of the monasteries. Edmund stands for (p. 103) Thomas Cromwell, the Machiavelli of the English Reformation. Goneril symbolizes the papacy, Regan (p. 55) the protestantism of the Protectorate, and Cordelia (p. 47) the truth and plainness of humanism. Burgundy = Erasmian humanism, France = Montaigne, Oswald = Wolsey, Kent = Skelton and Sir Thomas More, Albany = the old Catholic baronage, Curan = the Duke of Somerset, and Edgar-as-Tom = Kyd, Nashe, Lodge, and Dekker. Winstanley (1922, pp. 145, 211): King Lear is really a political play, in which the nations themselves are protagonists and in which the ungrateful children mean the factions of a civil war, tearing their fatherland to pieces. Lear’s suffering and death at the hands of his daughters represents the murder of Darnley by his wife, Mary, Queen of Scots, as well as the murder of Coligny in the St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre; in paralleling the latter he comes to stand for France itself, (p. 211) while the whole idea of France slipping and falling to destruction suggests a possible meaning for Gloucester and the precipice scene. Allen (1930, pp. 344–68) follows Winstanley (apparently) in both her Scottish and French allegorizations, especially the latter. In the Scottish allegory, Lear = Darnley, Goneril = Mary, Oswald = Rizzio (Mary’s low-born Italian servant), Edmund = Bothwell, Regan = Lady Bothwell, and Kent = Murray. In the French allegory, Lear (p. 347) is Coligny, Admiral of France, a proposition which…leads to a…powerfully convincing piece of evidence in support of our case for [Edward DeVere, Earl of] Oxford as Shakespeare. Coligny (p. 349) was born not far from waterish Burgundy, and was the subject of a biography by Oxford’s uncle Arthur Golding; he was powerful (p. 350) in and around the region of the Loire (Lear). (P. 354): Golding wrote how Coligny was in a storm that blew his hat off and left him bareheaded, like Lear. (P. 355): Lear’s storm is symbolical of the tempest that had burst over France. Lear (p. 361) is also in part Oxford, as well; Kent also (p. 345) stands for Oxford. (P. 351): Guise [is] the Edmund of the play. (P. 352): Catherine de Medicis [is] the prototype of Goneril. (P. 359): Jeanne de Navarre, protestant mother of Henry IV, was the historic original of Cordelia in Lear. (P. 361): Edgar is Henry of Navarre, Albany is Charles IX, and Cornwall is Henry III. E. Clark (1931, p. 601), also approaching Lr. as an Oxfordian, finds a less religious basis for historical allegory: The three daughters of King Lear are…intended to personify the three lines of descent from Henry VII. Goneril represents the line of Margaret Tudor, who married James IV of Scotland; her descendant, James VI, Duke of Albany, became King of Britain, as did the Duke of Albany in Sh.’s play. Henry VIII, who inherited the title of Duke of Cornwall, is represented…by Regan…wife of the Duke of Cornwall. Cordelia represents Mary Tudor, Henry VII’s youngest daughter and favorite sister of Henry VIII. She was affianced to Charles, Duke of Burgundy, before marrying the decrepit French king Louis XII. Moreover, into the character of King Lear, Lord Oxford wrote some of the bitterness of soul he was experiencing in 1589 and 1590, stemming from the Marprelate controversy (which caused the dissolving of his dramatic company, Paul’s Boys, in 1590) and Elizabeth’s failure to back his patriotic endeavor to support the throne; when she failed him, he wrote down in King Lear of the blackness of ingratitude. Kent represents Drake, and Edmund is Lord Henry Howard, whose lies caused Oxford, like Edgar, to be banished from Court and (p. 609) become a vagabond (i.e. an actor), etc. Milward (1975, pp. 105–9) is a Stratfordian who sees in the play an allegory expressing Sh.’s crypto-Catholicism: The great breach in the abused nature of his time and his country over which [Sh.] grieves with no less bitterness than Cordelia over her sleeping father, or Lear himself over his dead daughter…is nothing but the breach with Rome, effected by Henry VIII.…[108] Edgar, who is content to suffer in patience and to recommend a like patience to his fellows in service and suffering, represents one alternative for persecuted English Catholics. The other is chosen by Kent, who maintains a secret contact with the continent while moving about in Britain, and encourages Cordelia to use her influence in France to give losses their remedies. He is therefore surrounded by an atmosphere of conspiracy which also infects the whole of Gloucester’s castle.…[109] The planned invasion of Britain by the French forces [is an] evident parallel with the Spanish Armada.

Other critics read the play as a philosophical allegory. Thus Bacon (1857, pp. 204 ff.), reading Sh.’s plays in general as shadowed parables of Baconian philosophy and rational progressivism: It was the experiment of the unarmed prerogative, that the old popular tale of the ancient king of Britain offered to the poet’s hands, and that was an experiment which he was willing to see traced to its natural conclusion on paper at least.…In the poet’s hands, the debased and outcast king, becomes the impersonation of a debased and violated state.…[205] For this is the grand social tragedy.…[215] It was necessary to the purpose of the play to exhibit man’s dependence on art, by means of his senses and his sensibilities, and his intellectual conditions, and all his frailties and liabilities,—his dependence on art, based on the knowledge of natural laws, universal laws,—constitutions which include the human. It was necessary to exhibit the whole misery, the last extreme of that social evil, to which a creature so naturally frail and ignorant is liable, under those coarse, fortuitous, inartistic, unscientific social conglomerations, which ignorant and barbarous ages build, and under the tyranny of those wild, barbaric social evils, which our fine institutions, notwithstanding the universality of their terms, and the transcendent nature of the forces which they are understood to have at their disposal, for some fatal reason or other, do not yet succeed in removing. Ruggles (1895, pp. 162 ff.) likewise reads Lr. as a fable or apologue in dramatic form illustrating Baconian philosophy. (P. 211): It is almost one continuous inquiry into causes.…The whole dialogue of [212] the play is a tissue wrought out of inquiries into causes, and the assignment of them and of their effects, expressed in an endless variety of forms, and typifying the mind’s desire for knowledge and the use of experience in the intercourse of life.…[239] The play, taken as a whole, is an image of the moral world…furnishing a dramatic illustration or analogon to that model of the world which Bacon says it is the aim of his philosophy to build in the understanding.

Swinburne (1880, p. 175) finds evidence of Sh.’s progressive political ideas: The author of King Lear [has] avowed himself in the only good and rational sense of the words a spiritual if not a political democrat and socialist.

Dauphiné & Richer (1979, passim) read the play as an allegory symbolizing human spiritual development through the emblems of Fortune’s wheel, the twelve zodiacal signs (associated with Lr.’s pervasive animal imagery), and Tarot. Sh.’s metaphysical doctrine is assimilable to a sort of esoteric Christianity, permeated by Neo-Pythagorism and the Kabbala. In Lr. Sh. wished to describe various types of destiny and several modes of retribution. The piece is constructed upon the association of four wheels, each corresponding to a group of three zodiacal signs. Fire and water, factors simultaneously interior and exterior to man, are conceived of as agents of destruction, and thus the characters of water and the characters of fire perish, including Cordelia. Cordelia corresponds to the sign of Leo, associated with the human heart, and to the Tarot emblem of the lion, a symbol of strength. She plays the role of psychopomp to Lear. Lear himself, a choleric king, represents the first sign of the zodiac, Aries, associated with fire and with royalty. As Aries, he is a sacrificial ram. He also represents the Tarot figure of the emperor. Lear is also Saturnian, a figure of Cronos, devourer of his children. Edmund corresponds to Virgo in his cold calculating ruthlessness, Goneril to Scorpio (a diabolic sign), Regan to Cancer, Gloucester to Capricorn, the Fool to Sagittarius, Kent to Aquarius, Albany to Libra, etc. According to Nicholl (1980, pp. 144 ff.), The whole story, the whole unfolding process, of King Lear is deeply and intentionally alchemical.…[152] What Lear undergoes is something very like an alchemical transmutation; he can be emblematically read (p. 158) as Raw Stuff, matter that must undergo the pains of transformation, the hero of the [160] redemptive drama of the magnum opus.…[168] The alchemical playgoer of c. 1605…saw the sick King as an emblem of corrupt matter, and heard the Dragon as a signal for that matter to embark on its purgatorial journey. He would also discern, in the images describing Cordelia and Goneril, certain echoes from alchemical literature which suggest to him that Lear’s daughter is that twofold transforming principle the alchemists call Our Mercury.…[216] King Lear is, among many other things, the most extraordinary alchemical myth ever written. Cordelia is (pp. 207–9) recognizable as the anima mercurii, i.e., Mercury as quintessence (p. 209). The Fool is Mercury (p. 179). Goneril (p. 175) is the wolf antimony, devouring the King; the serpent Mercury, who causes the nature wherewith she is united to vanish.

Finally, Martin (1987, pp. 34–45) suggests a morality-play allegorical pattern in which the vicious characters exemplify the seven deadly sins: Burgundy (p. 34) represents the sin of Pride, Cornwall is (p. 35) the representative of Wrath, Edmund is (p. 37) the representative of Avarice, Goneril (p. 38) of Lust, (p. 39) Regan represents the sin of Envy, Oswald (pp. 42–3) represents Gluttony, and Curan (p. 44) the sin of Sloth.

div.head: Structure
div.p: Critics have focused on two different though related structural questions: the advantages and disadvantages of the double-plot structure, and the large structural patterns found in one or both plots.

From the beginning, critics have differed over whether the double plot, in combining the story of Lear and his daughters with that of Gloucester and his sons, produced mainly excessive complications or enriched the experience of the play. Warton (1754, p. 312), objects to it: The plot of Edmund against his brother…distracts the attention and destroys the unity of the fable. In contrast, Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159) finds that The injury done by Edmund to the simplicity of the action is abundantly recompensed by the addition of variety, by the art with which he is made to cooperate with the chief design, and the opportunity which he gives the poet of combining perfidy with perfidy, and connecting the wicked son with the wicked daughters, to impress this important moral, that villany is never at a stop, that crimes lead to crimes, and at last terminate in ruin.

The Romantics and their successors characteristically admire the double plot. Schlegel (1815, 2:206–7) praises the ingenuity and skill with which the two main parts of the composition are dovetailed into one another!… It is the very combination which constitutes the sublime unity of the work. The two cases resemble each other in the main; an infatuated father is blind towards his well disposed child, and the unnatural offspring, to whom he gives the preference, requite him by the destruction of his entire happiness. But all the circumstances are so different that these stories, while they make an equal [207] impression on the heart, form a complete contrast for the imagination. Were Lear alone to suffer from his daughters, the impression would be limited to the powerful compassion felt by us for his private misfortune. But two such unheard of examples taking place at the same time have the appearance of a great commotion in the moral world: the picture becomes gigantic, and fills us with such alarm as we should entertain at the idea that the heavenly bodies might one day fall out of their regular orbits. Similarly, Hazlitt (1817; 1930, p. 268): Indeed, the manner in which the threads of the story are woven together is almost as wonderful in the way of art as the carrying on the tide of passion, still varying and unimpaired, is on the score of nature. Likewise Drake (1817, 2:459–60): The two portions [460] of which the fable consists…influence each other in so many points, and are blended with such consummate skill, that whilst the imagination is delighted by diversity of circumstances, the judgment is equally gratified in viewing their mutual co-operation towards the final result; the coalescence being so intimate, as not only to preserve the necessary unity of action, but to constitute one of the greatest beauties of the piece. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 616) also admires the coordinated plenitude of the play’s double plot: We are not here confined especially to individual characters.…Twofold or still more manifold actions are united; characters equally important and fascinating move in greater number, in mutual relation; the actual matter gains greatly thereby in richness, extent and compressed fulness; and we have only to select the enterprises of a Kent or an Oswald, to find what a mass of facts in well-connected order lies almost concealed even in subordinate parts, though at first glance it may be easily overlooked in the abundance of matter. Other 19th-c. admirers of Sh.’s plot construction include Guizot (1852, pp. 218–19), Mézières (1865, pp. 286 ff.), and Hallam (1873, 3:84). Yeats (1903, pp. 339–40) follows the Romantics in emphasizing the rich plenitude of the double plot: Poetry and imagination [are] always the children of far-off multitudinous things.…[340] The Shakespearean Drama gets the emotion of multitude out of the sub-plot which copies the main plot, much as a shadow upon the wall copies one’s body in the firelight. We think of King Lear less as the history of one man and his sorrows than as the history of a whole evil time. Lear’s shadow is Gloster, who also has ungrateful children, and the mind goes on imagining other shadows, shadow beyond shadow till it has pictured the world.

For Bradley (1904, pp. 262, 254–5), the chief value of the double action lies in the fact—in Shakespeare without a parallel—that the sub-plot simply repeats the theme of the main story.…This repetition does not simply double the pain with which the tragedy is witnessed: it startles and terrifies by suggesting that the folly of Lear and the ingratitude of his daughters are no accidents or merely individual aberrations, but that in that dark cold world some fateful malignant influence is abroad.…Hence too, as well as from other sources, comes that feeling which haunts us in King Lear, as though we were witnessing something universal. However, he finds that a (p. 254) principal structural weakness of King Lear …is felt…in the Fourth and the first part of the Fifth [acts]. And it arises chiefly from the double action.…[255] The number of essential characters is so large, their events and movements are so complicated, and events towards the close crowd in upon one another so thickly, that the reader’s attention, rapidly transferred from one centre of interest to another, is overstrained. He becomes, if not intellectually confused, at least emotionally fatigued. The battle, on which everything turns, scarcely affects him. The deaths of Edmund, Goneril, Regan and Gloster seem but trifles here; and anything short of the incomparable pathos of the close would leave him cold. There is something almost ludicrous in the insignificance of this battle, when it is compared with the corresponding battles in Julius Caesar and Macbeth; and even though there may have been further reasons for its insignificance, the main one is simply that there was no room to give it its due effect among such a host of competing interests.

Other critics also criticize the structure as overfull, too crowded or complex to maintain a satisfying effect of unity. Woodbridge (1898, pp. 14–15): The structure of Lear is marred by the too frequent changes of scene, not because these destroy the illusion, but because every such change demands [15] a fresh adjustment of the reader’s mind to the new conditions, and such use of his energies is waste of his energies unless there is some compensating gain. Matthews (1913, p. 281): So far as its earlier acts are concerned, King Lear is one of the most skilfully constructed of all his dramas. But in the fourth act…we observe the slacking of interest and the confusion of aim which so often characterize this portion of an Elizabethan play.…Even in the final act, when we are eager to follow the fate of Lear himself, our attention is distracted by the prolonged episode of the challenge and duel of Edgar and Edmund. To Croce (1920, p. 295), the adventures of Gloucester and his son are not completely satisfactory, grafted as they are upon those of the king and his daughters, either because they introduce too realistic an element into a play with an imaginary theme, or because they create a heavy parallelism.…The origin for this parallelism may perhaps really be due to the need for theatrical variety, complication, and suspense, rather than to any moral purpose of emphasising horror at ingratitude. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:10) also finds that Lr. suffers somewhat under the burden of its double plot. See also Wilson (1898) and Baker (1907, pp. 267–8, 274). James (1951, pp. 112–13): After the third Act…the soul of the play and the body of the plot have fallen apart; they have indeed to be made to look as if they have not; but they have, all the same.…[113] Edgar has to be made into a fighting man, Cordelia into the leader of an army; and it simply will not do. Shakespeare could not take it; we cannot take it. The Cordelia and the Edgar whom we know are one thing; the Cordelia and the Edgar who fight battles and engage in combats are another; and they cannot be reconciled. The souls of Cordelia and Edgar are not in the stage figures who in battle and combat thus serve the purposes of a plot which a dramatist has to get on with and bring to a conclusion. In Cordelia and Edgar Shakespeare is contemplating figures of spiritual perfection who cannot move, with [114] any substance of reality, at this level of the plot’s working. Evans (1979, p. 149), examining the practices, i.e., deceptive actions that generate dramatic irony, finds that their abundance exhibited in King Lear surpasses that found in any other plays, whether comedies or tragedies.…But in fact, if we take the core of the tragedy to be the suffering and redemption of Lear, this vast and complex machinery contributes only negligibly. Smidt (1990, pp. 136–49) finds various unconformities in the structure: Structural and other anomalies…indicate that Shakespeare worked in a state of excitement and perhaps under pressure of time during the composition of Lear. He had urgent ideas but no design preconceived in detail to guide the development from scene to scene. Consequently he abandoned or changed early conceptions en route and left major as well as minor loose ends and inconsistencies.…[149] Though King Lear is one of the great tragedies of all time it is not without faults of construction.

Fly (1976, p. 90) counters objections that Sh. lacks control, finding an unusual form of coherence in the formative action (or praxis) that unifies and reveals the full imaginative design of the play.…Shakespeare’s experimentation with his medium has taken him to the point where he can create the effect of going beyond extremity in regard to theme and structure.…Appearing to violate dramatic propriety, while actually endowing his art with new force and magnitude, he can exploit his medium to create a desired illusion of immediacy. Likewise Orange (1984–5, pp. 3–16): The abundance of potential meanings on offer, the number of possible interpretations which the play puts forward about itself…leads at times to a sense of incoherence. However, (p. 16) The play’s own coherence masters the varieties of incoherence it makes use of.

Others critics differ over whether the main- and sub-plots are complementary or competing, or they discuss various dramatic effects resulting from the imperfect parallelism of the two plots. Price (1894, pp. 177 ff.): The story of Lear’s character and the picture of his mental decay…form the pathos and vital charm of the poem; but…the passion and the action of Edmund, the rise and downfall of his fortunes…supply the form of the drama and its dramatic movement.…[179] The climax scene…[180] stands almost at the beginning.…All the remainder of the tragedy…is thrown together in one huge catabasis.…[181] But, in order to sustain the movement of this otherwise unwieldy and drooping catabasis, [Sh.] has blended the emotion of the Lear tragedy with the regular and stirring action of the story of Edmund. Perkinson (1943, pp. 324–7): When Shakespeare swiftly projects his hero into a period of physical ignominy and, by contrast, of increasing spiritual nobility, both beyond anything in the sources, then Lear (p. 326) becomes an actionless hero.…Shakespeare then faced a double task of filling out his five acts and of emphasizing further his tragic conclusion.…The Gloucester subplot…reinforces his thinned-[327]out plot, and for unusual intervals carries the play itself.…[There are] two particular results of Shakespeare’s procedure…the chronicle structure and the specious and probably intentional complexity. The former is justified by the quasi-historical nature of the material.…The latter…was perhaps designed to cover up the thinness of the material as well as the type of actionless hero in this chronicle structure. Unfortunately, today the episodic structure…suggests to some a worn-out and careless genius. Similarly Mincoff (1950, p. 64): The Gloucester plot leads to a fairly regular alternation of abruptly contrasting scenes and an even greater complexity of network than in other plays, but also to a kind of double climax in two succeeding scenes [3.6–7].…One may note how the farmhouse-scene with its imaginary trial of Lear’s daughters leads back to the opening scene…[and] how the climax is in fact inverted, a climax of despair with a subsequent turn towards a renewed hope; and how Lear, remaining a technically passive figure after as before the climax, is eliminated for most of the fourth act, while the rather disappointing intrigues of Edmund and the sisters are used to fill out the waning interest of the descent. Levin (1967, pp. 432–44): In King Lear …the plots seem to be unrelated at first and then gradually coalesce through a series of reciprocal interactions…until at the end they are inextricably entangled.…[437] Having set up [a] basic parallel between his plots, [Sh.] has then very carefully and consistently differentiated them so that the subplot is in all respects less internalized and less serious than the main one.…[444] The tragedy of Lear seems even more extraordinarily moving because our response to it is continually readjusted, and thereby heightened, in relation to the emotions evoked by Gloucester’s fate, which is poignant enough in itself for any ordinary tragic effect, and yet is seen to be so much less serious and internalized than Lear’s. Rabkin (1967, p. 33): The parallelism of the double plot serves…to provoke an experience in which understanding plays as large a part as emotional response.…The double plot tends to complicate the issues while making them clearer: we learn something about Lear’s inadequacies as father as we see Gloucester implicitly parodying them, but what we learn tends to make us both more sympathetic with the king’s suffering and more annoyed with him. Rees (1971, pp. 34–5): The last acts of King Lear constitute a working of…reconciliation and retribution plots, the two being conducted simultaneously.…The retribution material lends itself more readily to varied dramatic treatment than the reconciliation material does.…[35] The expected reconciliation between Gloucester and Edgar is achieved offstage and reported.…What is there for Lear and Cordelia to do? A coup de théâtre is needed at the end to pull attention sharply to where it should rightly be, on Lear and his enormous sufferings. The coup de théâtre is a shocking death [Cordelia’s].…Shakespeare [may have written] this most discussed of scenes because of a limitation in the plot material he was working with. Evans (1979, p. 148) emphasizes the opportunities for dramatic irony provided by the Gloucester subplot: Sh. chose to surround the story of Lear’s travail with an elaborate added structure that offered abundant opportunity to develop exploitable secondary gaps [in awareness] to compensate for the absence of a central one. Thompson (1984, pp. 58–68) finds in the play Shakespeare’s most ambitious use of the mirror structure to relate parallel plots. (P. 62): It is remarkable in this play how Shakespeare constantly disrupts the apparent simplicity of the parallel plots by having his characters ignore the similarities the audience can see and suggest others which we know to be false.…[64] Thus misunderstanding, deception, disguise and madness all contribute to a manipulation of the characters’ awareness of the situation which complicates and unsettles our own view as well.…[65] But it is a major difference between the two plots in Lear that, while the subplot comes to a relatively conventional conclusion in which all three members of the Gloucester family arrive at a state of awareness concerning events which is virtually identical with that of the audience, the main plot eschews these satisfactions.…[66] It is quite striking how little Lear himself understands about the plot by the end of the play.…[68] Thus by the end these two apparently similar plots have reached conclusions which feel very different indeed. In a way the Gloucester plot has been a tragedy of intrigue from the beginning.…The Lear plot on the other hand has never been a plot at all in this sense. Pavel (1985, p. 99): In their narrative appearance…the two plots are largely different. Dramatic-effect [sic] derives, among other things, from the common problems of the two plots unfolding as dissimilar structures.…Lear’s plot…is a highly compact development.…In contrast, Gloucester’s plot…precisely because of its diversity…lacks the dynamism and momentum of the main plot. Hattaway (1992, p. 217): The story of Gloucester is a play within the play, and…an example of how not to write a play.…The Gloucester story…is essentially formulaic and consequently…on its own unmoving. House (1992, pp. 99 ff.): Rather than merely simplifying, the Gloucester plot makes the Lear plot look both odder and more normal, makes it more appalling and more affecting.…[111] The subplot’s comic, domestic, bizarre and didactic transformations of the main plot throw that into relief, show us more clearly what it is, but they also indicate the absurdity latent in the extremism of tragedy.

Many critics discuss the two plot strands as thematically parallel or complementary. Snider (1887, p. 131): An outer link connects the two stories, the relation of parents and children, but also an inner link connects them in a common idea, in a common charity and uncharity. Spencer (1943, p. 136): The sub-plot re-inforces the main plot; it is not, as in all the other plays where a sub-plot occurs, a contrast to it. Heilman (1948, pp. 32–3): Lear and Gloucester evince certain faults of understanding, and the justification for having them both in the play is that these flaws complement each other, and thus, because presented jointly, become a movingly inclusive dramatization of man’s liability to error. Lear imposes certain mistakes upon the world; the world—most conspicuously as it acts through Edmund—imposes certain mistakes upon Gloucester. The men are the active and passive forms of that moral frailty by which man may fall into very serious [33] trouble. Stauffer (1949, pp. 196–7) sees the Gloucester subplot providing choric com-[197]ment on the total action.…Since the governing ideas are made verbally clear in this less important part of the piece, the main action can present them in terms of pure character, emotion, and story. For Ribner (1960, p. 117), The double action affords us another hero who is Lear on a slightly lower social plane, and his career by paralleling closely that of Lear reinforces the universal validity of the play’s theme [regeneration]. Alpers (1962, p. 145): The subplot’s relation to the main plot can best be understood by considering how differently Lear and Gloucester stand for Everyman. Gloucester is Everyman in the sense that he is ordinary—indistinguishable from other men in temperament and intelligence.…Lear is Everyman because he is the individual human being who most eloquently stands for all men. Bennett (1962, p. 149): The events in the Gloucester plot regularly precede and serve as interpretive preparation for parallel events in the Lear plot in a way which is a refinement of the old dumb-show technique, as exemplified in the preliminary dumb-show in Hamlet’s Murder of Gonzago. Mack (1965, p. 71): Though the subplot’s line of action sometimes crosses and even merges with that of the main plot in an external way, the relation of the two plots remains homiletic rather than dramatic: Gloucester’s story is never permitted to discharge its full energies into the consciousness of Lear. The experiences of Gloucester and his sons are all events of tragic import as we see them in the theatre, which come to Lear’s attention only dimly (when they come at all) and make no part of his tragic experience. Their presence in the play is entirely dictated by their meaning for us. Likewise Schanzer (1969, p. 109): The long chain of echoes consists chiefly of correspondences between the spiritual journey of the two fathers [rather than the misdeeds of the villains].
