By mirroring in the person of Gloucester Lear’s tragic suffering, the process of ennoblement and of learning to see which grows out of this suffering, the paradox of gain in and through loss, Shakespeare has made it impossible for us to overlook the importance of these themes. Champion (1976, p. 157): The parallel experiences of Lear and Gloucester…[force] each of them to gaze directly at the emotional void that results from egomania and to reaffirm the supreme value of selfless love.…[160] Lear and Gloucester for the spectators are separate-but-related reflections of the same tragic dilemma. Stein (1969, pp. 141–3): The Gloucester plot is thoroughly at home within the tragedy’s total idiom and poetic logic.…[143] To see the final facts as rivalling and disowning—rather than as fulfilling—the structuring significances of the advancing drama is to dismember the entire defining structure. For Cavell (1969; 2002, p. 280), Gloucester [becomes] not just a figure parallel to Lear, but Lear’s double; he does not merely represent Lear, but is psychically identical with him. So that what comes to the surface in [their] meeting [in 4.6] is not a related story but Lear’s submerged mind.…In this fusion of plots and identities, we have the great image, the double or mirror image, of everyman who has gone to great length to avoid himself, caught at the moment of coming upon himself face to face. Hunter (ed. 1972, pp. 23–43): The addition of the Gloucester story to the Lear story produces precisely the same kind of synchronous dimension as Lévi-Strauss discovers in the repetitions and parallelisms of the Oedipus story…tak[ing] the emphases of the play away from the linear processes of motive and sequence.…[34] A world of competing values is established, and the values are, on the whole, larger, more complex, and more interesting than the people who profess them.…[42] The role of plot in relation to character is to flatten self-assertion.…[43] The gigantic quality of King Lear might seem to be tied in with its lack of interest in the details of character which separate one person from another. Olsson (1985–6, pp. 251–3) suggests a shift of emphasis from [a parallel between] Lear and Gloucester to [a parallel between] Lear and Edmund.…Each of them triggers off a far-reaching chain reaction. Like Edmund, Lear commits an (p. 252) assault on the established order which threatens the maintenance of feudal loyalties, and he (p. 253) simply follows his own nature. Both characters show what Love can achieve in those who receive Love.

Elton (1966, pp. 267 ff.) sees both parallels and antitheses in the double plot: Among other explanations for the double plot is that which identifies in Lear and Gloucester traditional aspects of the sensitive soul: the irascible and the concupiscible matching the protagonists’ anger and lechery.…[278] While the superstitious-concupiscible character might be seen as passively accepting, the skeptical-irascible might be regarded [279] as a dynamically rejecting type. Contemporary ideas of belief and unbelief, of the passive and the active, could also in this manner be assimilated to antithetical structural elements.…Indeed it may be possible to regard the double plot as a developing metaphor, opening up the principal action into two parts that mirror each other. Such a device would be appropriate to a play in which the protagonist expresses a dissociation between his name and his identity…so that his person dissolves into a double personage, a character in search of himself.…[283] Ultimately, then, the double plot is an instrument of complexity, the assurance of a multifaceted ambivalence which, contrary to the salvation hypothesis, probes and tests, without finally resolving, its argument of mysterious human suffering.

A number of modern critics emphasize thematic differences between the two plots, including Brooke (1963, pp. 16 ff.): The juxtaposition of the two plots…challenges our belief in ultimate justice; and…it is the moral story of Gloucester and his sons which [is] the more superficial of the two.…[39] [It seems] harsh and false.…[53] Edgar’s play…is allegorical in character.…By contrast with it Lear’s play seems more natural, and therefore more profound. Frye (1967, pp. 113–18) similarly views the Gloucester plot as a straight tragedy of order…a morally intelligible tragedy, in contrast to Lear’s (p. 118) tragedy of isolation, (p. 115) a vision of absurd anguish. Likewise Lyons (1974, p. 25): The subplot simplifies the central action, translating its concerns into familiar (and therefore easily apprehensible) verbal and visual patterns. The subplot is easier to grasp because its characters tend to account for their sufferings in traditional moral language; it also pictorializes the main action, supplying interpreted visual emblems for some of the play’s important themes. The clarity of the subplot and its didacticism are related, furthermore, to the old-fashioned literary forms, like the morality play and the chivalric romance, through which it represents experience. These give expression to the idea of convention, and therefore to a world of recognizably structured perceptions and values—the very opposite of dislocation and madness. But the verbal and visual simplifications of the subplot do not merely provide a contrast with what goes on elsewhere in the play; they help to reveal the nature of Lear’s experience by being so obviously inadequate to it. Lear’s sufferings are heroic because they cannot be accommodated by traditional formulas, moral or literary, and the subplot exists partly to establish that fact. Goldberg (1974, p. 79): The similarities between the two sets of figures ought not to distract attention from the differences between them, which are probably more important in the end. Axton (1977, pp. 138–40) also emphasizes differences rather than similarity. Felperin (1977, pp. 91–3): It is precisely the pervasive Christianizing of the sub-[92]plot that puts into question its supposed parallelism with the main plot. It is almost as if the older Christian structure deliberately dismantled in the story of Lear is just as deliberately reconstructed in the story of Gloucester, which had been only implicitly Christian in Sidney. With its black-and-white contrasts of good and bad, lawful and illegitimate, natural and unnatural sons, its clear symmetries of cause and effect, sin and retribution, moral blindness and physical blinding, the Gloucester action is basically as simple and homiletic in structure as any of the neat little tragedies of A Mirror for Magistrates and the long medieval tradition of the falls of illustrious men that lies behind it. The Gloucester action, like the medieval and morality-derived models of the Lear action, is not tragic at all.…The Gloucester subplot turns out to be a simple dramatic exemplum illustrating the educative abasement of the complacent sinner.…The action, that is, illustrates a fortunate fall and issues in redemptive suffering, a sadder but wiser man, and a happy death.…[93] The Gloucester action at no point puts into question its initial assumptions concerning the origin of evil or the meaning of suffering, for in its fulfillment of a conventional Christian design those questions are answered in advance and those answers only confirmed by its outcome. Something always comes of something, evil of illegitimacy and good of legitimacy. The universe of the Gloucester action operates by strict and transparent laws of cause and effect, which are at no point challenged, though of course they can be disobeyed: I stumbled when I saw. The assumption here is that he now sees feelingly and truly. Just as his pilgrimage to Dover has an attainable goal, though it is not the one he intended, so experience has an ascertainable meaning, though it may not be ascertained until the end. Halter (1990, p. 96): Sh., by breaking some of the major conventions of the dénouement, pushes to the limits a basic antithesis…between the world of the subplot, whose characters keep up a belief in a divine order, and the world of the main plot, in which the characters either move toward despair and madness or are relentlessly crushed at the end of the play. Alulis (1994, pp. 374–6): As the main plot becomes increasingly private, the subplot highlights political affairs.…[376] The subplot concludes with Edgar’s ascension to the throne. (But see n. 3295.)

Finally, Zimbardo (1990, p. 25) argues that there is no plot in King Lear—no less a plot and an ancillary subplot. An emblematic scene may point backward as well as forward.…None is more important than another. They are emblems whose pattern of relationship is to cross, slide, interpenetrate or challenge one another.
In addition to the double plot, critics also discuss other structural features of the play.

The treatment of time and place in the construction of the plots has been discussed by several critics. Daniel (1879, pp. 215–23) identifies ten days’ duration for the action of plot. However, apparent inconsistencies in the play’s time scheme are discussed by Brink (1895, p. 221): If we follow the scenes in which the king appears, from the point where Goneril first shows her disregard toward him to the night when he wanders shelterless upon the heath, and calculate the time that has elapsed between these two time periods, we shall find that it comprises but a limited number of hours—at most a few days. During this same time, however, Cordelia in France has received information of the base treatment her father has experienced, has found opportunity to communicate with Kent by letter, nay, more, French troops have already landed on the British coast. But what does it matter? Similarly Greg (1940, pp. 438–9): The closely-knit time scheme up to [4.3]…is intentional, and [shows] that Shakespeare [439] deliberately hurries his audience along at whatever cost to probability. This cost, however, was undoubtedly a heavy one, for the schedule I have extracted from the time-indications that link the several scenes proves…manifestly impossible, and is indeed flatly contradicted by several definite statements in the text. In contrast, Raysor (1938, pp. 22–37): All problems of time are solved in Lear by the sub-plot.…[35] [4.3 and 4.4] may probably be regarded as dramatic padding [to allow time for Edmund’s and Oswald’s travels].…Everyone notices in reading Lear the way in which the play seems to come approximately to an end with the third act, only with difficulty getting under way again for the true conclusion.…[36] Time is needed while the two British armies gather and combine to face the invader, while all the chief characters are brought to confront each other for the last crisis at Dover. And the sub-plot must give this time.…[37] The sub-plot accordingly begins a fresh exposition for the falling out of the sisters over Edmund’s love…a filler action. Sen Gupta (1961, p. 161) argues that the time scheme is purposely confused: There is progress from the beginning to the middle and from the middle to the end but these stages are not separated from each other by intervals of time or points of rest; this process of interpenetration, which is both progressive and regressive, demands new technical devices which are indifferent to temporal sequence. Knowles (1999, pp. 42–8) similarly describes the treatment of time involving Cordelia’s return from France as a departure from [Sh.’s] usual practice.…[46] No explanation exists for Cordelia’s return because Shakespeare deliberately refrained from providing one.…[47] That is, he may deliberately have sacrificed clarity about the invasion in order to gain other dramatic advantages,…allowing the play to move towards its crisis and resolution without any pause in momentum or emotional intensity and (p. 48) protecting the pathos of the king’s madness by keeping it brief as well as avoiding the suggestion that the early French invasion must have sprung from entirely selfish motives on the part of Cordelia and her husband. (P. 49): Shakespeare is practicing some very clever sleight of hand. See also Muir (ed. 1952; 1972, p. xlvi) and nn. 811, 926, and 1242.

Other critics are concerned with acts and scenes as structural units. Thus Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2: 11): F’s act-division has…much dramatic validity, and a producer may legitimately choose to abide by it. Jones (1971, pp. 160–3): King Lear makes use of the two basic principles of dramatic organization which Shakespeare seems to have inherited: the division into five acts and into two parts. The act-division is quite clear, and the Folio numbering can be accepted.…The first three acts are planned as a continuous action.…[161] What Lear undergoes in these three acts…is a progress in weakness.…[163] The second part…may be said to be far closer to romance or tragicomedy than the first.…What we have in the first half is the mingling of comic with tragic forms; in the last two acts we have the mingling of tragicomic with tragic forms. In contrast, Seltzer (1981, pp. 174 ff.): Lear…consists of three large movements (and not five acts). Bowers (1980, pp. 14–20): Although [the division of the kingdom and rejection of Cordelia] is the turning-point of the full Lear story, it is not the turning-point of the play in terms of its five-act structure. What Shakespeare has done is to move up into the first scene of his play what is the turning-point of the total story—instead of leaving it undramatized in the classical manner as a past event that must be narrated.…[17] The moral change that [Lear] underwent in the storm…marks the turning-point of the play, taken as a dramatic unit.…What we have in the storm scene… is Shakespeare’s use of the device of anticlimax as a means for effecting in the tragic close a reconciliation of protagonist and audience.…[20] For the climax that governs the action [of a five-act Renaissance drama], King Lear substitutes the anticlimax, or ethical reversal, that governs the interpretation and reception by the audience of the action that follows on the tragic decision dramatized in the first scene of the play. Rose (1972, pp. 28 ff.) discusses scenes as structural units, focusing on 1.1, 2.2–4, and 3.1–6: Shakespeare’s scene divisions generally define units of meaning as well as units of narrative; they are based on (p. 30) the principle of thematic, or conceptual, integrity. Scenic design is characterized by (p. 39) shapeliness…symmetry and careful proportioning…the mark of a master craftsman.…[Sh.] must have planned scenes very thoroughly in advance. In contrast, Stuart (1928, p. 236) criticizes the arrangement of scenes: in Act 3, Sh. breaks into the representation of Lear’s madness and the storm by inserting two scenes which foreshadow the coming of the French King. This procedure diminishes the cumulative effect of the scene on the heath.…[Also] scenes are often sketchy. In King Lear the intrigue of Edmund with Regan and Goneril is so briefly presented that it scarcely makes a dramatic impression, and it keeps Lear and Cordelia off the stage.

Various other ways of describing the structure include Dow (1885, p. 231), who describes Lr. as a fugual play involving complex counterpointing of various motifs. Larner (1991, pp. 31–2): Lr.’s abrupt rhythms, repetitions and parallelisms unite when viewed as something like musical phrases, shaped into overarching structures and vertical harmonies. Its lines weave together into patterns of dissonance and harmony, of ironic counterpoint.…[32] The tragic action of the play resembles what was later to become known in the classical period as a sonata allegro, with three subjects developed in an arc of irony. Moulton (1893, pp. 205 ff.): The…structure of the plot corresponds with the simple structure of a scientific proposition. The latter consists of two unequal parts: a few lines are sufficient to enunciate the problem, while a whole treatise may be required for its solution. So in King Lear a single scene brings about the unnatural state of affairs, the consequences of which it takes the rest of the play to trace. The catastrophe, or turning point of the play…appears…close to the commencement: at the end of the opening scene Lear’s act of folly has in reality determined the issue of the whole action; the scenes which follow are only working out a determined issue to its full realisation.…The consequences flowing from what Lear has done make up three distinct tragedies, which go on working side by side, and all of which are central to the full solution of the problem. First there is the nemesis [206] upon Lear himself and then a second tragedy in the sufferings of the faithful Kent and the loving Cordelia, and finally that which is concerned with the mutual intrigues of Goneril and Regan, intrigues ending in their common ruin.…To this main plot is added an underplot equally elaborate.…[207] Thus as the main and underplot go on working side by side, they are at every turn by their antithesis throwing up one another’s effect; the contrast is like the reversing of the original subject in a musical fugue.…The three tragedies which make up the consequences of Lear’s error have their analogies in the three tragedies which flow from the intrigue of Edmund. First we have the nemesis on Gloucester.…Next…the suffering of the innocent Edgar. Then, as before we saw a third tragedy in the way in which the power conferred upon Goneril and Regan is used to work out their destruction, so in the underplot we find that the position which Edmund has gained involves him in intrigues, which by the development of the play are made to result in a nemesis upon his original intrigue.…[223] The intricate drama of King Lear has a general movement which centres the passion of the play in a single Climax [3.6]. Thus intricacy of plot has been found not inconsistent with simplicity of movement, and from the various parts of the drama the complex trains of passion have been brought to a focus in the centre. Kernodle (1945, pp. 186–8) sees a two-fold structure marked partly by the key position of Cornwall in the first part [I–III] and of Albany in the second part [IV–V]. Wentersdorf (1965, p. 648): In King Lear there are two contrasted lines of action: the external fortunes of the protagonist, which decline—with minor, suspense-raising advances—from beginning to end, and the old king’s spiritual fortunes, which slowly but surely progress until at last he emerges from the struggle, cleansed of his weaknesses by the purgatorial fire of earthly suffering.…King Lear therefore has the structure not of a pyramid but of a diagonal cross. Had Shakespeare followed the normal pyramidal pattern, the process of regeneration would have been restricted to the latter half of the play. By starting with the turning point in Lear’s worldly affairs, the dramatist is able to devote almost five acts to the falling action.

Jones (1971, pp. 153 ff.) praises the high degree of artistry in the play’s design.…[154] What we are given is a sense of widening circles, ramifying side-lines of interest, even as late in the action as [155] Edmund’s soliloquy in v.i a promise of yet further intrigues—all merging with the spectacle of things simply running down, a progressive randomness.…We seem to move from episode to episode without much sense of what the final destination is to be.…[156] This uncertainty about the final destination of the action, about where we are going, is accompanied by another characteristic feature of King Lear. This is the recurrence of scenes of a curiously static nature, scenes of brooding, reflection, or, in a more impassioned style, of declamation.…If these features of the play are taken together, they amount to so many reasons why King Lear should be comparatively unpopular as a stage play.…King Lear is more exacting, more painful and exhausting to experience; it gives less immediate pleasure. And this can in part be explained in terms of structure: for despite its scenes of episodic heightening, the over-all action lacks, or appears to lack, a clear terminus ad quem—we are given nothing specific to wait for. Nothing, that is, except perhaps something which can not be brought about by any foreseeable move in the plot: the death of the old man who is the hero.…[159] The personal theme of the coming of death is set within another larger theme of the ending of the world: both are epitomized in Albany’s phrase this great decay [3269]. The impression we have in the later scenes of King Lear of increasing randomness and inertia—The centre cannot hold—is part of Shakespeare’s governing artistic idea; unless we recognize this we shall merely find the play structurally defective.

Other modern critics who discuss the play’s overall structure include McElroy (1973, p. 150), who describes the structure as unstintingly linear, proceeding without digression or abatement.…Time and space are drastically compressed.…So economical is the dramaturgy of Lear that many of its most memorable points are made not through spoken words but through a series of intense visual images. Barroll (1974, pp. 368–9) identifies a Coriolanus structure: multiple provocations of the protagonist by variously motivated agents.…[369] Lear’s madness is itself almost a complete negation of the importance of demonstrated decision making to this kind of structure.…He requires no more plausible motivation than the random directions that madness might take from casual encounters with any stimuli. We err if we simply assume that the old king’s mad speeches are necessarily ethical pronouncements by which we are to understand the values implicit in the drama.…The dilemma of whether Lear’s mad speeches indeed are characterization or ethical statement raises a further observation about the kind of tragic structure with which we deal here.…If the provoking of the protagonist is not to be the concentrated result of one character, but the function of many figures, then the multiplicity of the provoking agents has its own effect. Agents provoke in terms of viewpoints, and thus a complex of purely ethical commentary and counter-commentary comes into being. We are thus led to debate values. Shanker (1975, pp. 135–73): At least three major structures exist in King Lear—the conventionally historic, the dramatic, and the symbolic.…[168] As a history play, King Lear has the conventional Shakespearean structure of his rise and fall of rebellion.…As a logical structure, the play is grounded upon a thesis-antithesis [i.e. the masterful use of contrast for purposes of mordant irony (p. 151)] resolved by a vision of synthesis.…But King Lear also contains a symbolic structure.…[173] In King Lear the act structure is historical in pattern, while individual scenes are constructed on the thematic principle of contrast or are based upon…the dramatization of symbolic events. Reibetanz (1977, pp. 34–5): Sh. employs an anti-narrative structure characteristic of Jacobean drama; rather than cumulative progression we find momentary effects and poses, dramatic emblems, and suppression of story elements.…[35] The incidents, characters, and settings of King Lear form a vast hall of mirrors reflecting Lear. Taylor (To Analyze, 1985, pp. 188–235) examines in detail Shakespeare’s disposition and arrangement of his material in Act 1 to show how (p. 235) the sheer bulk or mass of impressions we receive…in Act I of King Lear predisposes us to see the eventual face-to-face confrontation between Lear and Goneril from the perspective of Lear’s party. Young (1990, pp. 78–86) finds in the play a tension between expansiveness and intimacy.…Lear has a public structure and a private style.…[86] The structural expansiveness…not only opens to a new generic inclusiveness…but also drives toward an emblematic or symbolic representation of human experience that has led commentators to allegorize and directors to existentialize. Tayler (1990, p. 30) identifies proleptic form as an organizing device in Lr.: As spectators, we travel, so to speak, through the play on two tracks—one of plot, where we may find ourselves more or less surprised by the turn of events or even by the possibility of a happy ending, and the other of proleptic form, where through repetition [of the words no, nothing, etc.] we gather and retain a number of expectations about the promis’d end. Foakes (1993, passim) identifies a four-part movement, comprising division, expulsion, confusion, and war.

Other critics are concerned with the sense of closure or its absence at play’s end. Kermode (1967, p. 82): In King Lear everything tends toward a conclusion that does not occur; even personal death, for Lear, is terribly delayed. Beyond the apparent worst there is a worse suffering, and when the end comes it is not only more appalling than anybody expected, but a mere image of that horror, not the thing itself. The end is now a matter of immanence; tragedy assumes the figurations of apocalypse, of death and judgment, heaven and hell; but the world goes forward in the hands of exhausted survivors. Edgar haplessly assumes the dignity; only the king’s body is at rest. This is the tragedy of sempiternity; apocalypse is translated out of time into the aevum. The world may, as Gloucester supposes, exhibit all the symptoms of decay and change, all the terrors of an approaching end, but when the end comes it is not an end, and both suffering and the need for patience are perpetual. We discover a new aspect of our quasi-immortality. Booth (1983, pp. 11–21): When Lear enters howling in the last moments of the play, Shakespeare has already presented an action that is serious, of undoubted magnitude, and complete; he thereupon continues that action beyond the limits of the one category that no audience can expect to see challenged: Shakespeare presents the culminating events of his story after his play is over.…The fact that King Lear ends but does not stop is only the biggest of a succession of similar facts about the play.…[21] Repeated evocation of a sense of indefiniteness generates a sense of pattern and thus of the wholeness, the identity of the play. Similarly Halio (ed. 1992, p. 31): The play indeed seems to end several times before it is over. In contrast, Leggatt (1988, p. 8): In King Lear the last scene completes, with terrible exactness, the action begun in the first.…The play’s end is latent in its beginning, and the main clues to this are theatrical: the arrangement of characters on the stage, the voice of Lear breaking against the silence of Cordelia. Spinrad (1991, pp. 231–9): In Lear’s death, Shakespeare has denied us our expected forms of closure so that we may reach a kind of catharsis not covered by our standard dramatic theories.…[239] Perhaps we need to be shaken out of our dramatic expectations at the end in order to learn the heroism of compassion.

Finally, other critics find in the logic of the play’s structure a denial of hope in a beneficent world order. For Elton (1966, pp. 329–34), structural irony is a principle of action which, with the safety of indirection, probes the ways of the gods to man.…[330] Sequential ironies…are exposed like a series of trapdoors in Lear.…[334] In the relation of the lines and in the sequence of dialogue and event is expressed annihilation of faith in poetic justice and, within the confines of a grim, pagan universe, annihilation of faith in divine justice. Adelman (1973, pp. 8–10) likewise finds implicit in the structure a denial of a coherent, providential universe. In King Lear…the assertion that ripeness is all is at least as significant as in Hamlet. Most of Edgar’s speeches are devoted to the explication of this coherence. But the sense of providential order is, despite the assertions, almost entirely absent: the dramatic structure itself [9] does not permit us this luxury.…Lear begins with a dramatic logic so taut that the end in illogic is almost intolerably disturbing. Old men who do not have faith in their children and who trust instead to the aural and ocular evidence of their evil children will cast out the good children and be badly mistreated by the evil ones. The plot is shocking but inexorable: there is nothing accidental or gratuitous here. But suddenly this logical rigor of plot collapses. When Albany’s forces triumph and Edmund repents, the providential order seems to assert itself; and there is now no reason why the play should not end happily.…But instead…Lear enters with the dead body of Cordelia in his arms; and our sense of order is forever shattered. There is neither narrative nor moral necessity for her death.…There is not even a historical necessity.…We have been caught up in the working out of a providential scheme when a perfectly gratuitous act destroys this scheme.…[10] There are no answers—only relentless questions, asked by the dramatic structure, by the unfolding events of the play itself.

div.head: Stagecraft and Dramaturgy
div.p: Rosenberg (1972, p. 9) speaks for many critics in arguing that Lr.’s world is made of sight, sound, and word, and it cannot be comprehended unless the three components are perceived in a single gestalt. Jackson (1966, pp. 27–8) finds Sh. employing a kind of iconographical system borrowed in part from Renaissance painting, sculpture, literature, liturgy, and music.…The result of its particular use in King Lear is that many situations are not given rational explanations of the kind established in Greek tragedy; on the contrary, Shakespeare, like Wagner and the Contemporary writers, used the method of music and the plastic arts in giving major realities figuration.…The dramatic structure of King [28] Lear…was articulated in a plastic grammar: in a richly textured and highly figured theatrical language, through which the playwright’s own symbols found a greater reality and a heightened brilliance.

Visual effects, particularly the arrangement of characters in theatrical tableaux or speaking pictures, are frequently the focus of criticism. Fraser (1962, passim) finds traditional moral emblems represented in the actions as well as the words of the characters (see above, , ). Rosenberg (1972, pp. 337–9) emphasizes complexity and ambiguity: Lear’s language of gesture has a cumulative symbolic content and texture that command the eye and mind to a special poetic experience as subtle and deeply stirring in its way as the ear-mind’s experience of the words.…[338] Words [often] fail in Lear; and sight-sound imagery must complete the communication, especially when latent, subconscious impulses must be conveyed.…Shakespeare created a string of speaking pictures, every line and shape of which say something to the mind.…Some attempts have been made to reduce Shakespeare’s speaking pictures to the terms of contemporary emblems; but as an artist he was always breaking and restructuring the familiar.…[345] These images…and their associated sounds, support an organic structure of symbols rich in denotative detail and connotative reverberation and ambiguity.…They can only be known in performance. Reibetanz (1974, pp. 39–52): With notable frequency, the play’s characters arrange themselves into fleeting but memorable tableaux, pictorial realizations of abstract themes, a technique (p. 43) characteristic of private-theatre drama.…[52] What Shakespeare has done…is to employ elements of the disjunctive private-theatre structure to reinforce the emphatic effect of a conventional structure associated with public-theatre drama. The structure is therefore a perfect vehicle for both the dramatic and the emblematic aspects of Shakespeare’s art; since it is both tumultuous and recurrently fixed, it satisfies both needs at once. Brown (1975, pp. 375–83) discusses the antithesis of king and beggar which is so repetitive a motif in the vocabulary of [Sh.’s] imagination but which [in Lr.] is…actualized in visual and dramatic terms…deeply embedded in the imaginative texture of the play: the dramatic and psychic experience both of the hero and of other characters leads to and away from it in ways which, though intricate, do not obscure its archetypal significance.…[378] The experience of the hero is only the central focus of a drama which in astonishing imaginative coherence repeats the main action in a variety of secondary modes.…[383] In his growing sense of impotence Lear’s mind, mirrored by the play as a whole, reaches out to gestures and images derived from a range of experience—of poverty, of wretchedness, of alienation—to which the mythical omnipotent king of the opening scene was blind, but which is now becoming a reflection of his own condition. Hargreave (1970, p. 491) emphasizes the visual contradiction of word by stage image. Siemon (1985, pp. 281 ff.) goes further, arguing that the visual tableaux are iconoclastic, i.e. anti-emblematic: in a violent way, Lr. employs word and action to turn the probings of our meaning-hungry vision back on themselves.…[282] The iconoclasm in Lear most typically takes the form of giving one too much of the sensory particular in proportion to the general meaning it should serve. Thus at 3277–83, rather than composing a secular pietà (cf. n. 3216), Lear’s (p. 249) attention to the broken particulars of physical existence subverts the decorous generalizations of emblematic vision, which would seek to enwrap the scene in meaning and so solidify living flux into significance.…[251] The insistent refusal of this final scene to halt its action around a significant figure or a metaphorical summing up is the last struggle of a conflict between action and emblem apparent throughout the play.…[272] The Dover Cliff incident [is also] profoundly iconoclastic while (p. 273) Gloucester’s blinding and the duel of the brothers—both highly emblematic moments and neither the product of a character’s rhetorical strategies—implicate the audience for its own idolatrous eagerness to accept the visual schemata for the all of the action. Rosen (1988, pp. 188–93), who likewise finds Sh. visual[ly] comment[ing] on the spoken word by means of (p. 190) the actualization of images in the rhetoric of a scene, argues that The villains [are able] to wrest the Shakespearean rhetoric to their own purposes. In contrast, Edgar (p. 193) keeps trying to recuperate the images of a providential world; yet he ends the play with a naked antirhetoric beyond any other in its despair. Leggatt (1992, pp. 181–5), considering Lr. as a play for the Globe audience, concludes that (p. 182) some of the play’s theatrical power comes from its use, and abuse, of the gestures that define personal and family relations.…[185] The visual language of social relations is also crucial. Likewise King (1984, p. 83), discussing the parting of the coronet in 1.1 as an emblem of the realm about to be torn in two, argues that Shakespeare has used an emblematic stage picture to undercut and deny Lear’s spoken words. Davidson (1984, pp. 190 ff.) also discusses the visual tableaux and iconography of King Lear as does Sillars (1997, pp. 278–96). Womack (2002, p. 104) sees in the play’s stage pictures a straining for religious effects: In Lr. it is as if Shakespeare were reinventing the religious drama which the English Reformation had just brought to an end. What needs to be added to that context, though, is that if this is sacred theatre, it is also a particularly theatrical kind of sacredness which moves the dramaturgy still further away from the level rendition of life. The theatrical images are unnatural not only in the sense that they are sacred, but also in the sense that they are fakes. The expansive view of general human nature is obscured by a murky mixture of theophany and showmanship, the generic Protestant term for which is superstition.

Nonverbal aural effects, including silence, are the focus of other critics. Howard (1984, pp. 42 ff.) discusses as instances of Shakespeare’s aural dramaturgy both 4.3, which provides an aural bridge that…demonstrates the close link between the aural orchestration of the play and the needs of the listening audience, and dramatically powerful moments of silence in 1.1 and 5.3. She discusses visual spectacle as well as aural design in 1.1, 2.4, and 5.3 (p. 120): These scenes are orchestrated, both visually and aurally, to make palpable and immediate the grinding force of men’s will to power and the cruel dialectic between weakness and strength, pain and aggression, that it is this play’s special achievement to enact. The (p. 127) aural, visual, and kinetic elements of 3.6 are (p. 126) orchestrated to suggest how close the king, his world, and the play’s scenic structures are verging on incoherence and fragmentation. (P. 156): Crescendo effects are produced in 2.2–4 and 3.1–7. McGuire (1985, pp. 97–121) discusses the presence and the ramifications of open silences during the final moments of King Lear.…[120] By virtue of its final silences, King Lear gives us a variety of possible endings, each with its own coherence, each with its own validity. He criticizes (p. 121) stage traditions, editorial practices, and habits of interpretation that minimize the impact of the open silences that mark the final moments of King Lear. Berge (1994, p. 212): When Shakespeare imposes a silence on Cordelia and the Fool, effectively halting their fulfillment, he denies Lear the chance to gain the dramatic completion which Regan, Goneril, and Edmund enjoy.

The function of physical gestures and stage properties concerns other critics. Rosenberg (1972, p. 337): What Shakespeare says with faces and bodies—and things—involves a special kind of poetry.…Lear’s language of gesture has a cumulative symbolic content and texture that command the eye and mind to a special poetic experience as subtle and deeply stirring in its way as the ear-mind’s experience of the words. Goldman (1981, pp. 25–44) discusses the histrionic imagery of King Lear, i.e., various motifs…of enactment: mental, physical, and emotional movements the actor is called upon to make that are particularly related to his basic work of sustaining the part in performance.…[39] [These] various motifs of performance…require that the actor keep renewing his sensations, opening himself to a particularity of suffering.…[44] And it is against the same background that we see one of the play’s familiar sights—people supporting each other, one leading another by a hand or arm, two supporting one, one touching another. Edgar, Lear, and Gloucester seem to spend much of the play reeducating themselves in feeling through the exercise of touch, and this, too, adds to the impression of a fragile thread of feeling poised against the storm. Leggatt (1988, p. 13) comments on Lr.’s staged violence: We seem to be watching the playground violence of children: striking, tripping, kicking. Instead of the epic clash of armies, which Shakespeare’s theatre could suggest by exciting hand-to-hand combat, we are watching the low, undignified essence of violence, the hard, angry striking of body against body. Tetzeli von Rosader (1991, p. 35): The near-nakedness of the body…becomes visible as a dramatic sign of great potency. Brown (1995, pp. 109–18): The reliance on physical action [rather than rhetorical language to render Lear’s and Gloucester’s suffering] was extraordinary and risky.…[110] Shakespeare has presented the consequence of violence so that the audience has to shoulder responsibility for its own reactions.…[118] To understand how Shakespeare held the mirror up to the violence of his times, and so to the violence of ours, it is necessary to pay attention to what is done as well as what is spoken.

Critical discussions of stage properties in Lr. include that of Lusardi (1991), who discusses (pp. 31–41) the theatrical possibilities of the map and coronet in 1.1; (pp. 99 ff.) the joint-stool in 3.6; (pp. 126–8) the note of 2970; (pp. 146 ff.) and the looking-glass, (supposed) feather, and button in 5.3. The button is also discussed by McGuire (1985, pp. 98–103). Gurr (2002, p. 46) sees in the royal crowns and ducal coronets one of the strongest visual marks of the play’s progress and its point as royal propaganda. Avery (1998, pp. 51–3): The map itself…because of its ability to display possession (and therefore generosity) and represent power (and therefore Lear’s self-image), becomes as important as the territory that forms the actual possession.…[53] King Lear, finally, shows the map to be just another form of rhetoric. The play displays a failed attempt at coercive cartography. Leggatt (1992, pp. 182–4) also discusses props and costumes. Bergeron (1993, pp. 159–74): Shakespeare has placed an extraordinary reliance on letters in the Gloucester story in order to open up another level of discourse, one in contrast to Lear’s.…[162] For [Lear], saying things makes them true—a flaw in his royal character that the play will tragically exploit.…[164] Gloucester in Lear’s position in scene one would have had little difficulty in dealing with Cordelia’s nothing [93]; he would have seen it as a possible indirection. Similarly, Lear in Gloucester’s position would have accepted Edmund’s nothing [366] and moved on.…[174] Shakespeare holds in solution the opposing discourse of Lear and Gloucester. By the end, Gloucester has been…delivered over entirely to report as he becomes wholly dependent on the disguised Edgar as his means of knowing what is happening. Lear has come to recognize that where the possibility of a lie does not exist, truth cannot exist either; he discovers the gap between his sentence and his power. Holmes (1960, pp. 186–7) also comments on letters in the play: There must have been many original spectators of King Lear who had stood in the crowd a few months earlier to see Fawkes hanged, and to them, at any rate, Edmund’s assortment [187] of compromising correspondence would be no playwright’s extravagance but a natural feature to be expected in such cases, as experience had lately shown. Teague (1992, p. 100) argues that the stage-motif of a forged letter used to seduce Gloucester to evil action is derived from JC; which suggests that both plays are concerned with how an individual reads—sources, letters, characters, portents. See also Farcy (1990, pp. 260–3) and Jardine (1996).

The dramatic use of disguise is discussed by Maclean (1960, p. 50–2), who contrasts Edgar’s judicious use of disguise with Kent’s: Once disguised, the individual must guard against three temptations. He must not leave anything to time, but must actively intervene at the proper moment; he must not allow himself to be led astray by his emotions and throw off his disguise too soon; and he must not become so fascinated by the game of disguising that, missing the moment for action, he will retain the disguise beyond the point at which it ceases to be necessary. Kent illustrates all these mistakes. Righter (1962, p. 176): The tendency to regard disguise as a state of negation and symbolic death, an image of nothingness, recurs strongly in King Lear. Holly (1973, p. 172): Shakespeare’s tragic vision in Lear is integrally related to deception and self-deception which in turn is inseparable from his use of the device of disguise.…There is an inverse proportion between masks and self-deception in the plays; i.e., characters who don masks most frequently [i.e., Kent and Edgar] practice the least amount of self-deception and in general are characters who see themselves most honestly and clearly. Sharpe (1959, pp. 19–26) identifies a technique of impersonative irony which is characteristic of Edgar’s disguises. Hyland (1985–6, p. 169): Shakespeare wants Kent and Edgar in disguise so that he can use them as emblems of disorder and as victims of the upside-down world.
For discussions of theatrical doubling, see above, .

Motion through time and space is a focus for other critics. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:17): In working out a theme so full of incident and of contending characters Shakespeare allows for no distraction of attention at all, certainly not for the breaking of continuity which the constant shifting of realistically localized scenery must involve. The action, moreover, of [the] later scenes is exceptionally dependent upon to-ings and fro-ings. Given continuity of performance and no more insistence upon whereabouts than the action itself will indicate, the impression produced by the constant busy movement into our sight and out again of purposeful, passionate or distracted figures, is in itself of great dramatic value, and most congruous to the plot and counterplot of the play’s ending. Levin (1959; 1976, pp. 176–9) discusses Sh.’s exploitation of the unlocalized stage in the Dover Cliff episode: Remember that we are just as blind as Gloucester. Theatrical convention prescribes that we accept whatever is said on the subject of immediate place as the setting.…[178] On a proscenium stage, the whole situation would be impossible. Thus the episode is a (p. 179) trick that Shakespeare has played upon ourselves, his audience. Hills (1976, p. 4): Aided by his stage geography, Sh. presents a one-way procession from the Court to the plain near Dover, creating dramatic motion as opposed to stillness.…Lear’s unplanned movement through time and space [dramatizes] the emotional rigidity out of which he is jarred and the stillness to which he finally comes. Seltzer (1981, pp. 183–4): Lear takes place primarily in space itself—not space as a cosmos, but space as a stage. If we envisage the reality of this play as creating itself, moment by moment, beat by beat, phrase by phrase, in an absolutely open acting space, the reality of tempo, of image, and of idea will be heightened inevitably.…[Lr. and Tmp.] demand an acknowledgment of the stage as a magic and wild place which can be anywhere and everywhere, and which is contemporary and real precisely [184] because the feelings projected from that place are specific and real. Turner (1997, p. 165) discusses the relationships between the categories of place and space.…No play more than King Lear so self-consciously engages the power of the early modern open stage to take up and transform, in the process of its fiction and for the duration of that fiction only, the spatial medium in which a dramatic action took place.…Indeed, one of the central questions the play forces us to confront is finally this: how might the open stage allow the exploration of a series of spatial concepts in a way that is beyond print or words, even beyond the language of poetry?

Another dramaturgical technique in criticism of Lr. is the use of ceremonial or ritualistic action. Hockey (1959, pp. 389 ff.) sees Sh. presenting several kinds of trial in order to comment dramatically on two major themes—love and justice.…Acting as judge [in 1.1], Lear purports to weigh the evidence presented by his three daughters. Like any judge, though, Lear himself is judged—by the audience—and convicted of poor judgment.…[390] The trial motif [in 1.1] is emphasized by the puzzled questions France puts to Lear about Cordelia’s offense and by Cordelia’s plea to be acquitted.…[392] By using the trial pattern of action [in 3.6] and…combining it with madness Shakespeare dramatizes the supremacy of love over justice, for justice can neither force love nor punish its shortcomings.…[393] Just as Lear’s suffering in the storm took the form of trials, so does Gloucester’s blinding come in a trial scene.…Another kind of trial is employed to conclude the play—trial by combat.…[395] The movement of the plot, the character of Lear’s mind, and, above all, the larger meaning of the play have been dramatized with incredible aptness as trials. Stroup (1977, pp. 143–6) discusses Lear’s division of the kingdom and the removal of his clothes in Act 4 as ceremonial actions heightening the sense of significance. Kendall (1992, pp. 241–2): In the trial by combat we witness precisely what the rest of the play negates: a vision of deep order, a working out of natural and, of course, poetic justice.…It is an enterlude that, in calling attention to itself as artifact, reveals the fragility of all scripts, all [242] artifacts of order, even the script of King Lear itself. Palmer (1995, p. 33) sees Sh. using ceremonial pageantry ironically: Pageantic pomp and honor…is turned to bitter reversals of expectation.

Hardy (1987, 1997, pp. 190–200) examines the function of narration in King Lear, which is always concerned to explore and appraise mind, feeling, speech, ordering, and social interaction.…[200] The narrations in King Lear, like the whole play, tell the audience tragic truths.

Other unique dramaturgical techniques are identified by critics. Knight (1930, p. 195): The technique here—the vagueness of locality, and of time, the inconsistencies and improbabilities—all lend the persons and their acts some element of mystery and some suggestion of infinite purposes working themselves out before us.…Nor, till we have clear sight of this peculiar Lear-atmosphere, shall we appreciate the fecundity of human creation moving within it. Krutch (1930, p. 498) finds expressionist techniques: Lr. not only anticipates the completest nihilism ever achieved by a Strindberg or an Andreyev, but anticipates also even their method of expression. Walker (1938, pp. 45 ff.) sees Sh. drawing from a common stock of knowledge derived from medieval and Tudor dramatic conventions for describing emotion rather than from technical treatises on psychology. (P. 57): The description of emotion in King Lear …is based on extremely simple and common ideas. The mere embellishments which current psychology or physiology could have supplied are conspicuously absent. In describing the development of Lear’s madness Shakespeare relies almost entirely upon repeated dramatization of an effort of control, the voice of control passing back and forth between Lear himself and other characters. Spencer (1943, p. 142): Re-inforcement through expansion, expansion through re-inforcement, in the worlds of nature, of the individual and of the state, each inseparably linked to the others so that when one falls, they all fall—such is Shakespeare’s technique in King Lear. Isenberg (1951, p. 185) identifies another technique: Cordelia is continuously present both to Lear’s mind and our own; and the silence, the absence are not only compatible with [her] visionary presence, they are the positive pledge and proof of its reality. Block (1959, p. 512) finds balanced and shifting sympathies: Thanks to the artistry and skill with which Shakespeare deviated from his sources, balancing and shifting the audience’s sympathies toward the characters, King Lear is throughout permeated with a continuous suspense that would otherwise be lacking. Rackin (1970, pp. 30–4) discusses delusion as resolution: The complex and paradoxical universe of the play admits of no easy answers—often, it seems of no answers at all.…Any attempt at resolution runs a tremendous danger of seeming false. Shakespeare avoids this danger…by presenting his resolutions as false, at least from certain angles of vision. The results look wonderfully true. Through Edgar, Shakespeare perpetrates delusions—plays practical jokes on other characters, and these jokes have the effect of resolving the major issues of the play, even though they never lose their delusory quality.…[34] [Likewise] Lear’s death is triumphant…because his final assertion of faith…is a completely creative act. To use the language of the play, it has no reason and no cause: it is something that has come of nothing. Clemen (1972, pp. 87–9) discusses Sh.’s technique of preparation, i.e., of preparing the audience for action to follow. Colie (1974, pp. 354–5) discusses Sh.’s analytical decomposition of literary forms and literary decorum: Like Troilus and Cressida, King Lear works in travesty: characters are again and again en travesti: dressed up as something else either literally or spiritually.…[355] Characters take on, try out, experiment in various roles, voluntarily and involuntarily. They act beyond received and assigned decorums to be other than themselves, or other than what others take them to be. Jacobs (1977, pp. 133–4): The entire interaction between Edgar and Gloucester after the beginning of Act IV is a rather grotesque example of a tragic device that occurs with some frequency in Renaissance drama [i.e., aural theater].…[134] First, a character is deprived of sight. Then a second character or group of characters contrives an aural presentation designed to delude the blinded character and create an illusory situation in the latter’s mind.…[The device has] a didactic function. Matchett (1979, pp. 185 ff.): Lr. is unrivalled in the way it gains major effects through…direct manipulation…of [the] audience’s responses.…[188] Shakespeare misleads an innocent audience…through keeping before it the assumption—not merely the hope, but the expectation—that Lear and Cordelia will eventually win through to reconciliation and a happy ending.…[189] Even with Gloucester, we are constantly trapped into hope.…[190] Every time Shakespeare raises our hopes, he pulls the rug out from under us. This is the rhythm of King Lear, and it remains consistently so to the end of the play.…[201] The effect is surely to force us to concentrate upon the [tragic] event itself, abandoning such contingencies as might be used to protect ourselves from experiencing it. Black (1980, p. 35): In King Lear Shakespeare is deliberately breaking forms, purposefully overturning conventions and received techniques and in many ways turning his own dramatic art upside-down. Similarly Bilton (1985, p. 105): Asking what King Lear does to us, we find that Shakespeare designed it to build up and build on many different kinds of expectation in us, only to frustrate them all, a pattern which culminates in the premised or promised end. Peat (1980, pp. 43–51) discusses the tension of uncertainty: It is in the nature of King Lear to stimulate contrary responses.…King Lear forces every spectator to choose between the contrary possibilities that it holds in unresolved opposition.…[45] The play provides evidence to support conflicting interpretations of Lear’s last lines and…the decision we make about those lines finally determines the direction of the whole movement [Walton (1960, p. 14)] of the play.…[49] The scene [of Dover Cliff likewise] precludes…certainty.…[51] Throughout [much of 5.3] the possibility that Cordelia lives remains open and the audience continue to alternate between hope and despair. In this world of uncertainty, this is the greatest uncertainty of all. Honigmann (1984, p. 50): Another highly original technique in the play [is] the way human beings talk past one another, as if insulated from one another—as if they cannot hear properly. Calderwood (1986, pp. 5–18) discusses creative uncreation: Shakespeare uncreates King Lear…[7] strip[ping] his own theatrical art to a kind of nothingness. Lr. (p. 18) begins with art—with the ordered, ritually stylized, word-dominated world of its opening scene and, before that, with the created forms of King Leir and the Arcadia—and subtracts from it toward nature as the chaotic immediate, the nothing to which the verbal artist reduces all prior forms and meanings in order to begin again. Brittin (1989, p. 90) discusses dramaturgical foresight, whereby later actions are anticipated in earlier ones: Shakespeare’s dramaturgy in Lr. shows his foresight in controlling his characterizations as well as in complicating his plot. Cartwright (1991, pp. 182–226) discusses response-guiders: Response-guiding characters, standing between the audience and the action, affect spectatorial distance.…[183] But King Lear makes the mediation of such characters both fundamental and problematic: Characters who set the play’s moral coordinates (for better or worse) [particularly Kent and Edgar] sometimes proceed to fall away from or contradict the very qualities they seemed to represent.…[184] The play’s ensemble acting urges as a theatrical experience…a certain detachment from the Lear-group (figured by Kent) yielding to an engagement with the play’s heroes (prompted by Edgar).…[226] Lear’s secondary characters… invite early spectatorial interpretations and then undermine those interpretations, keeping the audience always at risk.

Finally various critics have discussed Sh.’s dramaturgical techniques in representing madness. Warton (1754, p. 274): The assumed madness of Edgar and the real distraction of Lear, form a judicious contrast. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:58) Edgar’s false madness tak[es] off part of the shock from the true, as well as displaying the profound difference.…In Edgar’s ravings, Shakspeare all the while lets you see a fixed purpose, a practical end in view;—in Lear’s, there is only the brooding of the one anguish, an eddy without progression. Hunter (ed. 1972, pp. 10–16): It is not that madness augments the pathos that the King’s position already presents. Indeed the effect is opposite. [11] The pathos of the old King Leir play is almost wholly swallowed up in the terrifying maelstrom of words and images that express man’s need to see himself as meaningful. And this is a depersonalizing process.…[15] Lear’s madness is a means of diverting our attention out [16] of the natural world of effects (where the other versions of the story have their being) and into the metaphorical world of causes. In the mad scenes nothing happens, in the ordinary meaning of the word. But these scenes convey that sense of an irreversible change of state which an earlier dramaturgy…derived from Ovid’s horrific stories of metamorphosis—the sense of a world now frozen in the grotesque forms of despair, and using the grotesque actions that derive from this. In King Lear this world is focused not (as in the earlier plays) on public revenge, but on spiritual change, and the actions reflect this. Wenzel (1994, p. 65) employs typologies drawn from…text linguistics and theatrical semiotics to describe briefly the verbal and non-verbal devices which mark the state of madness in Lr.

div.head: Language and Style
div.p: The first critic to comment on the style of Lr. is Warton (1754, 2:273), who praises as judicious and affecting Lr.’s use of broken utterance to communicate passion.

General assessments of the style of the play include Gentleman (1770, 1:377): The language of King Lear is of mixed nature, verse and prose; where the former occurs, we find it bold, nervous, figurative, and, with some few exceptions, flowing; the latter is compact, pregnant and spirited. Masefield (1911, p. 192): The verse is as great as the invention. It rises and falls with the passion like music with singing. All the scale of Shakespeare’s art is used; the terrible spiritual manner of [quotes 1658–9] as well as the instinctive manner of a prose coloured to the height with all the traditions of country life. Arnold (1911, pp. 44, 152) finds the language of soliloquies in Lr characterized by introspection and conscience and (p. 152) a change from the epigrammatic to the analytical. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:18–23) praises the dialogue’s combination of freedom and power and the molding of verse and prose into such a variety of expressive form that it is a wonder any unity of effect is kept at all—yet it is.…[23] The whole scheme and method of its writing is a contrivance for its effective acting. Williams (1951, p. 57) notes that combination of dramatic and poetic genius which one expects to find in Shakespeare in critical passages…writing of the highest intensity. Gardner (1967, pp. 3 ff.): The language…of King Lear is dramatic through and through, in that the poetry is hardly detachable from its contexts and derives part of its power from continual striking juxtapositions of rhythms and styles.…[8] At its peaks of poetry it is the language of common life, raised to its highest peak of expressiveness, that moves us so profoundly. Young (1990, pp. 87–93): The counterpoint to Lear’s expansive and capacious structural features is a curious inwardness and intimacy in its language.…[93] The stylistic complement to the play’s tendency to pose large questions about human fate and metaphysical order seems…to be its extraordinary capacity to produce expressive force from simple details…embedded in the play’s language.

A number of critics describe the style as pushing at the limits of verbal expression and signification. Hunt (1808; 1949, pp. 17–18): He who can read the shuddering conceits of Edgar…without peopling the atmosphere about him with visions; or can listen [18] to the artless reasoning of the abused old father without reproaching every little grief he may have occasioned a fond parent, has neither a head to fancy nor a heart to feel.…I can easily conceive that a poet arises from fancies like these…with a pulse disordered by inspiration. The imagination looks out into other worlds with an eagerness stretched beyond its natural tension, and it returns back in languor and irritability. Luce (1907, p. 437): Passion sometimes threatens if it does not destroy form, and the torrent of verse outstrips drama. Belloc (1911, p. 269): It is written as though the pen breeds thoughts. It is possible to conjecture as one reads, and especially in the diatribes, that the pen itself was rapid and the brain too rapid for the pen. Matthews (1913, pp. 292–3): His thoughts tumble out so many and so fast that they seem to trip each other up; and sometimes it is only with difficulty that we can follow them as they fall from the lips of the actors.…In the full plenitude of his power as a poet and profoundly inspired by the epic appeal of the awful story he was telling, he neglects the noble harmony of thought and expression, as he dis-[293]regards also the exigencies of the stage. He writes as one carried up into the night by the strong wing of his own soaring imagination and pouring forth his soul not so much for the delight of others, or even for the relief of self-expression, but simply because he must. Mack (1965, pp. 99 f.): As it uses for the most part the barest bones of language…to point at experiences that lie beyond the scope of language, so it uses stripped-down constituents of personality… to point to complexities of being [100] and of human reality that lie beyond the scope of the ordinary conventions of dramatic character. Rosenberg (1972, p. 7): The play reaches toward extremes, beyond extremes, where words ultimately fail, where language abdicates before the unspeakable, and only gesture or silence function. The love Cordelia cannot bear to say comes to nothing; the pain that Lear will feel cannot be said, only howled. Roles reverse sharply: men move from base to top, from throne to mire; values zigzag: all offend, none offend. Men should not treat animals as they treat each other in this play; but men are animals, too, and make animal sounds. The words and sounds reflect the nervous equilibrium of the whole system: the conditional mood permeates it, unsettles it, infects it with the whipsaw of choice. There is, accordingly, much interrogation, a wondering of which? who? why?—a multitude of question marks, asking, asking, from Fool’s insistent riddling to Lear’s cosmic puzzlement. McElroy (1973, p. 150): All elements in the world of the play seem to be pushed almost from the outset to violently conflicting extremes. The middle ground, which forms so much of life in even turbulent or disruptive times, is eliminated entirely. Fly (1974, p. 63): Characterization in Lear—like plot, scenario, and language—may be understood as a dependent part of a larger design…approximated most succinctly in the phrase to top extremity—a phrase that encompasses the play’s insistent urge to press beyond the extreme limits of dramatic presentation. Weiss (1981, p. 68): Language in this play, more than that of other words, consists of haunting verbal relics from a world largely vanished: words, once possibly effective and satisfying, accepted as identical with reality and the gods, now dilapidated, having little to do with the actual lives of the characters. Booth (1983, p. 35–7): Verbal instabilities subvert our comforting belief in irrelevancy by arousing our sense of the irrelevant—by making us aware of open avenues for thought which the play does not pause to acknowledge and which thus feel to us like momentary vagaries of our own minds. The attractive nuisance of ideational static tempts an audience’s mind within inches of the extravagance which, for differing reasons and with differing effects, is a common denominator of Lear’s thinking, the Fool’s and Edgar’s as they leap from one frame of reference to another…[extending] poetic patterning beyond the boundaries of system. The speeches are pulled together by nonsignifying alliteration…and by a phonetic equation…that impinges on our consciousness as a mad substitute for a logical one. Likewise for Leggatt (1988, pp. 67–8): The characters’ words are an unreliable key to their natures; nor can they always manage the easier feat of analysing other characters.…[68] The realities about which the play is most articulate are the brute physical realities in the face of which all individuals are alike; Tom is cold; Gloucester is in pain; Cordelia is dead. In the torture chambers in which Shakespeare would find one of the more recognisable links between his time and ours, it is the body that is used to break the mind, to turn the inarticulate individual into someone who no longer knows what he thought he knew, believes what he thought he believed, or is what he thought he was. The world of the play is, as Kent calls it, a rack, and the lines of continuity we try to follow through the personalities of the central figures are like sinews that twist and break. McAlindon (1991, p. 170): Debasing what is noble and ennobling what is base, the contrary language of King Lear is a kind of continuous paradox. Rutter (1994–6; 1997, pp. 172–3) notes the bizarre, radically unstable poetry of King Lear; a poetry that breaks nature apart as it inverts human experience: the king is made a subject, the nobleman, bedlam beggar; the bastard is legitimized, the dearest child stranger’d, then new adopted to our hate, made a foster-child of alienation; women change arms at home to put the distaff in their husbands’ hands while they take up the sword; men turn to women and weep.…[173] Both grotesquely alien and insanely familiar, Lear becomes a female domestic, a mad pastry chef.…Catechresis of this order asserts itself as the standard poetic trope of King Lear.

Wells (ed. 2000, pp. 53–4): To its early audiences, the language of King Lear must have seemed very strange, as original in its day as that of James Joyce or Dylan Thomas in theirs.…Over a hundred words or compounds…either represent or predate OED’s first recorded use (absolutely or in this sense), and though this is not entirely reliable, it gives some idea of the innovativeness of the play’s vocabulary. There are also many rare words and expressions, some literary, others deriving from specialist vocabularies that defeat scholarly investigation. The language constantly strains meaning beyond its normal limits. Margreta de Grazia notes its inclination to superfluity, its use of superlatives and super-superlatives and pejor-pejoratives, and links this with the way the play itself goes to extremes [1998, p. 282].…Frequently, too, syntax is strained to the point of contortion, and (even allowing for textual problems) characters express themselves so cryptically that they risk becoming incomprehensible. [54] To say all this, however, is not to deny that the language of the play can rise to incomparable heights of calculated eloquence in both verse and prose, or indeed that it may at times speak with a sublime simplicity that seems all the more powerful for the knotted tortuosities that have gone before. Honigmann (1980, p. 160): The fact that Lear’s high language requires so little apology, in the scenes in which he is enraged but not yet mad, proves…that Shakespeare felt confident that verbal extravagance would not be misunderstood.

Negative assessments of the style include Wendell (1894, pp. 288 ff.): murky, passionate, despairing confusion.…[289] The style of the play is overpacked with meaning.…[291] Philosophizing with no dramatic purpose often deepens the obscurity.…[292] On the stage such a style could never have been effective. Norwood (1925, p. 594) deplores the play’s rankness or morbid artificiality of style.

In contrast, Bradley (1904, pp. 292–3) notes the simplicity of [Lear’s] language in the mad scenes. The language is more than simple, it is familiar. And this familiarity is characteristic of Lear…from the time of his madness onwards, and is the source of the peculiarly poignant effect of some of his sentences.

Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:19–22): For more reasons and in more directions than one, Shakespeare seeks strength in simplicity in King Lear. The noble conventional speech of its beginning will not serve him long, for this is the language of such an authority as Lear discards. There is needed an expression of those fiercer, cruder strengths which come into play when a reign of order ends and a moral code is broken.…[21] [Sh. also uses] an even more simple device, recurrent throughout the play…with varying purpose and effect…[the] device of iteration [e.g. Nothing, base, howl].…[22] It is a simple device indeed, but all mature artists tend to seek strength in simplicity of expression. It is, at its simplest, a very old device, and older than drama. Iteration casts, of itself, a spell upon the listener, and the very sound of that echoing Never can make us sharers in Lear’s helplessness and despair. Blunden (1929; 1934, pp. 198 ff.) likewise comments on the iteration of Nothing and of swearing by gods, and Summers (1984, pp. 105 ff.) also discusses Lear’s incredulous, exclamatory, and mad repetitions. Charlton (1948, pp. 207 ff.) finds in Lr.’s formal simplicity a poetic primitivism suggesting the universality of its themes: Shakespeare the dramatist chooses the arena in which Shakespeare the poet can be dramatically himself in the fullness of his poetic power. The dramatist calls up his human characters, strips them of all perquisites but the primitive strands of human life, and releases them to live in a dramatic cosmos which is little more than stark nature’s universe…a rude and simple universe wherein life and man are both at their beginnings.…[218] As is the metaphysical world of King Lear, so perforce are its earthly institutions, its material furnishings, and so perforce are its people in their nature and their habits.…[221] They are, indeed, creatures of passion and of instinct.…The men and women of King Lear are and feel themselves to be near companions of the beasts.…[226] As the heavens and the earth of it, as its men and its women, so is the theme of King Lear.…resolved into elemental simplicity.…Its plot is a simple domestic circumstance…within the imaginative capacity of all mankind.…So by its very simplification, King Lear universalises the tragedy which it represents. Leider (1970, pp. 52–3) also finds plainness rather than complexity: King Lear is a tragedy of reduction. It moves away from superfluities, toward necessity, simplicity and truth.…[53] For Lear…plainness is [the] language of truth. According to Draper (1937, p. 36), the plainer style of Sh.’s Jacobean plays arose from the royal taste. Weis (1986, pp. 198 ff.): In King Lear Shakespeare engages in an intensely dramatic exploration of the language and the limits of a radically uprooted moral vision born from, and only answerable to, experience.…[207] Rhetoric and suffering are more emphatically irreconcilable in King Lear than anywhere else in Shakespeare’s work. The play’s action (p. 209) creates as the standard of civilized being a moral primitivism. The unfailing insistence in the play of a credible answerability of language to experience, on the interdependence of expression and perception, is rooted in the same symbolic and physical nakedness.…[214] In the play’s style [we see] a use of language which, while remaining expressive, is perceived manifestly to be striving to be different in order to be true. Toliver (1989, pp. 141–52) also finds an opposition between rhetoric and poetry in the language of the play: Whereas rhetoric offers a language to champion a given order and sometimes a language of reason to link orders, poetry becomes finally a matter of suffered consequences.…[144] In the wake of Lear’s tragedy, the rhetoric of command and the language of felt connections…look very far apart.…The best relations, the ones that make the tragedy tragic, will have to be lyricized apart from, rather than in the midst of, society.…[151] Shakespeare…undoes all…versions of mastery and power and their public idiom, so calculated to spoil the expression of sentiment and heartfelt worth. Although the poetry of confessed filial devotion [152] has authenticity, it has no authority.…It merely guarantees the closure of an affective form with a definitive ironic loss. Kallendorf (1992, pp. 11–13) rejects the dichotomy of plain truth vs. elaborate falsehood: Eloquence…functions as a guide to character in King Lear. Those whose use of [rhetorical] figures calls attention to itself—Cordelia, France, Lear, Gloucester, Edgar, and Kent—are the ones who struggle to attain the selfless love of the angels. Those whose usual pattern of speech is unfigured—Goneril, Regan, and Edmund—are the ones in [12] whom self-interested appetite predominates, as with a beast of prey.…[13] Over the course of the play, the good characters draw much more heavily on the ordered patterns of the figures than the evil ones.

Some critics find grandeur rather than plainness the hallmark of the verse. Saintsbury (1908, 2:44–5): The decasyllables of Lear’s ill-judged and ill-fated bid for his daughters’ hypocrisy are of the very finest type.…This luxuriance…recurs in him and in others, though not in all, and not always in those who use it. It is the properest of all media for the splendid central scenes, and especially that more than Æschylean opening [1656–64].…[45] There is no spirit from the infinite deep of prosodic possibility that the poet cannot call, and none that dare disobey the calling. Swinburne (1909, p. 64): All the magnetism of tempest is in the very words and cadences of the verse.

Maeterlinck (1905, pp. 193–4) emphasizes lyricism: The youngest, the most unchangeable of tragedies is also the most organically lyrical dramatic poem that was ever realised, the only one in the world in which the magnificence of the language does not once injure the probability, the naturalness of the dialogue.…[194] As it seems to be accepted that a hero who expresses his inner life in all its magnificence cannot remain probable and human on the stage except under the condition that he be represented as mad in real life (for it is understood that here fools alone express that hidden life), Shakespeare systematically unsettles the reason of his protagonists and thus opens the dyke that held captive the swollen lyrical flood. Thenceforward, he speaks freely by their mouths; and beauty invades the stage without fearing lest it be told that it is out of place. Thenceforward, also, the lyricism of his great works is more or less high, more or less wide, in proportion to the madness of his hero.…No otherwhere does it overflow as in King Lear, torrential, uninterrupted and irresistible, hurling together, in immense and miraculous images, the oceans, the forests, the tempests and the stars, because the magnificent insanity of the dispossessed and desperate old king extends from the first scene to the last.

In contrast, Nowottny (1960, pp. 49 ff.): Perhaps one reason why King Lear has been mistaken for an unactable play is that it is so nearly an unreadable play: taken passage by passage, it is so flat and grey. She notes the absence from Lear of resplendent imagery, idiosyncrasy of mind expressed in mannered style, indeed of poetry that survives quotation out of context.…What is really peculiar about the language is the freedom and unexpectedness of its melodic line; Lear himself is unfailingly astonishing, and this property of his words is resistant to explanation in terms of the recurrence of [thematic] patterns.…[50] Lear’s language…[51] is resistant to familiar critical tools.…Its impact is due not to displayed deviations from the language of common life but to its exploitation of the common responses we cannot avoid making when confronted by expressively ordered language.…What is effective in Lear’s language is its free line, the apparent absence of contrivance in the sudden blazes that illuminate the prosy syntax and commonplace vocabulary of Lear’s utterances.…Lear’s domination of the play is a linguistic domination; his is the most powerful of the voices that speak out of sufferings. Shakespeare concentrates upon Lear the style that gives a felt experience of the incommensurateness of human nature to what it must endure.…[52] The play is deeply concerned with the inadequacy of language to do justice to feeling or to afford any handhold against abysses of iniquity and suffering.…One of the things this play has to say about feeling and suffering is that they are beyond words. This poses the basic problem of the play’s dramatic language.… [53] The minor characters are used to support the language of its hero, who must use language not as the adequate register of his experience, but as evidence that his experience is beyond language’s scope.

Barton (1971, pp. 25–7): Over and over again, in the vital moments of the play, it is stated explicitly that language has failed.…[26] Not…by accident are repeated words so characteristic of this tragedy. The last two acts are filled with frenzied repetitions.…One comes to feel that these words are being broken on the anvil in an effort to determine whether or not there is anything inside.…[27] Truth and love in this world are tongue-tied and silent. The glib and the verbally adroit, the Edmunds, Oswalds and Regans, are deeply suspect. Only madness and folly are truly articulate, and their speech hovers continually on the edge of the meaningless, the place where words dissolve into pure noise or inarticulate cries.

Many critics have commented on Lr.’s poetic imagery. Farren (1824, pp. 83–4) finds flowers to be emblematic…of the state of Lear’s mind…[84] emblematic of the sources and variety of the disease under which he labours. Blunden (1929; 1934, p. 213) argues that the nature imagery in speeches in act 4 and in 5.1 serves to lighten the movement of the passions and allure the audience along, yet so, that the ultimate darkness must be deepened. Others focus specifically on animal imagery. Kirkman (1879, pp. 386 ff.): We find…in King Lear, an extraordinary frequence in the mention of the lower animals, a constant allusion to animal nature and its destructive or deceitful instincts, and in a vast majority of the instances with one special reference, the reference of comparison with the ways of men, according to the resemblance between the two…[387] for the most part in a morally unsavoury relation.…[389] Mr. Darwin…would state on biological grounds precisely the same fact in nature as Shakspere has worked out on moral or psychological principles. Bradley (1904, pp. 266–7) notes as a very striking characteristic of King Lear—one in which it has no parallel except Timon—the incessant references to the lower animals and man’s likeness to them.
