These references are scattered throughout the whole play as though Shakespeare’s mind were so busy with the subject that he could hardly write a page without some allusion to it. The dog, the horse, the cow, the sheep, the hog, the lion, the bear, the wolf, the fox, the monkey, the pole-cat, the civet-cat, the pelican, the owl, the crow, the chough, the wren, the fly, the butterfly, the rat, the mouse, the frog, the tadpole, the wall-newt, the water-newt, the worm—I am sure I cannot have completed the list, and some of them are mentioned again and again. Often, of course, and especially in the talk of Edgar as the Bedlam, they have no symbolical meaning; but not seldom, even in his talk, they are expressly referred to for their typical qualities.…[267] As we read, the souls of all the beasts in turn seem to have entered the bodies of these mortals; horrible in their venom, savagery, lust, deceitfulness, sloth, cruelty, filthiness; miserable in their feebleness, nakedness, defencelessness, blindness; and man, consider him well, is even what they are. Knight (1930, p. 198) finds that the animals are often homely, sometimes wild, but neither terrifying nor beautiful. They merge into the bleak atmosphere, they have nothing of the bizarre picturesqueness of those in Julius Caesar, and do not in their totality suggest the hideous and grim portent of those in Macbeth. Heilman (1948, pp. 92 ff.) links the animal images with sex imagery: The (p. 104) accumulation of sexual terms used pejoratively and of sardonic comments upon sexuality…suggests a corruption of creative energies.…Under certain circumstances human beings undergo a kind of liberation that enables them to plunge vigorously and masterfully into the world and apparently to gain possession of all things valued in the world—yet their unchecked energizing has in it the seeds of their destruction. Likewise sex is used consistently to support the impact of the animal imagery: the whole mass of sex and animal references functions as part of an effort to define, to find a rationale for, human conduct which falls below the norms of everyday experience. What we have is a powerful statement of the animal in man, not a reminder that the animal always triumphs, but an insistent reminder that the animal is always there to be dealt with. McCloskey (1962, pp. 321 ff.): The tragic disaster toward which [Lear] proceeds…is expressed to a remarkable degree by images from the padding, stalking, creeping, crawling, slithering world of animals, insects, and the more repulsive denizens of the waters, and the images are evoked to express or to intensify [Lear’s] anger, rejection, indignation, wrath, and vengeance. The imagery of the lower animals…suggests the moral derangement of the world in which Lear has hitherto thought himself secure.… [323] While anger is often imaged forth in feral terms, blindness, stupidity, weakness, and helplessness are presented in images from the still lower stratum of animate things, that of the snail, the oyster, and the eel.…[325] The climax of descent in terms of animal imagery…coincides with the climax of the play…[in] Lear’s reaction to the injustice of Cordelia’s death. Micheli (1981, p. 341) finds in the play’s references to animals shifts from literal to figurative language which articulate the structure and enhance the power of this tragedy, particularly in the speeches of Lear and Edgar. Thompson & Thompson (1987, p. 83) analyze Lr.’s animal metaphors in terms of linguistic semantic-field theory and find the difficulty of the metaphors residing in the familiar-heightened-to-the-point-of paradox rather than…the strange or eccentric. This grounding of metaphors in the commonplace, even the cliché, has obvious advantages for an audience which needs to grasp the basic meaning at once in a single hearing. Such conventional or familiar content allows for an unusually complex interchange between vehicle and tenor.

According to Spurgeon (1935, pp. 338–42), The atmosphere of buffeting, strain and strife…[339] is [greatly] increased by the general floating image, kept constantly before us, chiefly by means of the verbs used, but also in metaphor, of a human body in anguished movement, tugged, wrenched, beaten, pierced, stung, scourged, dislocated, flayed, gashed, scalded, tortured and finally broken on the rack.…[341] The idea of unnatural horrors, of human beings preying on themselves like monsters of the deep, or like wolves and tigers tearing one another’s flesh, is also constantly before us.…[342] The large number of animal images…also…very distinctly augment the sensation of horror and physical pain.…To this is added…the fury of the elements, described…wholly in terms of the human body.

Some mid-20th-c. critics approach the play as a poetic statement to be interpreted in terms of thematic or symbolic patterns of imagery. Clemen (1936; 1977, pp. 133–7) argues that In King Lear, action and imagery appear to be particularly closely dependent upon each other and are reciprocally illuminating; the imagery, in fact, seems to have taken over some functions which so far—in Shakespeare’s earlier plays—belonged to other mediums of artistic expression.…[137] The imagery…transforms human matters into mighty universal events.…The words atmosphere, background, no longer suffice to designate how nature, landscape and the animal world are evoked by the imagery. This atmosphere here becomes a world in itself; we almost forget that it is only through the words of certain characters that life is given to this world of nature. Heilman (1948, pp. 24–5), examines recurrent imagery and recurrent statements on certain themes.…[25] The nakedness, the storm, the blindness, and the madness…become symbols.…The dramatic and poetic elements are reciprocally illuminating and animating; they are interdependent in the manner of the parts of an organism; together they form rich and stimulating patterns of meaning. Keast (1949; 1952, pp. 127–36) objects that the meaning of King Lear becomes, on Heilman’s reading, a commonplace repetition of Christian parables.…[136] Nothing in the text of the play, nothing in Shakespeare’s habits as a dramatist, nothing in the circumstances of its composition and production, nothing in Elizabethan dramatic practice in general, nothing in the dramatic criticism of Shakespeare’s day—nothing, in short, internal or external, suggests or has been thought until recent years to suggest, that a literal reading of King Lear will fail to account for essential features of the play and that the tragedy must be interpreted, therefore, as an organized body of symbols.

For Traversi (1952, p. 43), too, Lr. exemplifies Sh’s development of dramatic symbolism…which derives originally from an extension of the scope and purpose of the poetic image in the dramatic scheme.…The poetic image, expanding by a continually growing number of contacts with the surrounding verse, becomes more intimately and more variously related to the exigencies of story and character, until the very possibility of a sharp distinction between the action and the poetry through which its meaning in emotional and spiritual terms is conveyed, becomes inconceivable. The plot, thus conceived less in terms of common realism than as an extension of the poetry, becomes in itself an expanded image, the symbolic reflection of an experience which the poet, following the promptings of his creative impulse, is concerned to mould into a finished artistic form. Likewise Echeruo (1963, p. 46): It is the imagery…that makes sense of the play, that saves it from being the unresolved picture of chaos many have unfortunately called it. Knights (1963, pp. 37–8) describes Lr. as a highly complex metaphor,…[38] a moving image of life…that sets in motion those powers of apprehension through which we simultaneously become aware of and make our world. Other discussions of Lr.’s iterative imagery include Kernodle (1945), Prior (1947, pp. 84–92), Stauffer (1949, pp. 188–9), and Gurr (1988, pp. 37–46).

A number of critics focus on the play’s images of sight and blindness. Kreider (1933, pp. 121 ff.): Persistently recurrent words directly or indirectly naming eyes and sight show Lr. to be a tale of physical and spiritual blindness. Such repetition is (p. 132) one of the artistic devices for securing remarkable unity in the play. Heilman (1948, pp. 51–62): The sight pattern prepares us for the study of evil that finds its main treatment in the madness pattern.…[61] Shakespeare has found in sight a flexibly responding symbol for the problems which arise in connection with the point of view from which man judges the meaning of experience.…[62] By a full and varied use of all the functions of men’s eyes [including tears] Shakespeare has achieved a rich, multivalued expression of man’s moral make-up. Thompson (1965) discusses references to smell in relation ideas of blindness: The sight pattern in King Lear has been the object of exhaustive study, but this motif, in its relation to the sense of smell, forms an important and neglected aspect of the play’s structure.

Fraser (1962, p. 15) finds in the poetic imagery traditional moral emblems derived from the analogies of proverb lore, the continued and fixed representation of themes and allegorical conventions like the Dance of Death or the Seven Deadly Sins, the illustrations in catechisms, in tapestries, in the Biblia Pauperum, in emblem books and bestiaries, and on Elizabethan title pages, [and] the traditional arrangement of the figures in street pageants.…The iconology of King Lear…[displays] the following central motifs: the idea of Providence; of Kind; of Fortune; of Anarchy and Order; and Reason and Will; and Show against Substance; and Redemption. Other critics who focus on emblematic iconographic imagery include Soellner (1984, pp. 274–89), who emphasizes the figures of circle and wheel as significant in a tragedy whose wheel turns mercilessly downward as the characters experience human and cosmic upheavals. King Lear testifies to Shakespeare’s masterful use of iconographic, philosophic and dramatic means to develop a seminal situation to its starkly tragic conclusion. Iwasaki (1966–7) sees the emblem Veritas filia temporis as central, and Idem (1992, 13 ff.) discusses Lr. in terms of the emblem of the world upside down.

Other discussions of imagery include Ellis-Fermor (1945, p. 90): In the speech of Regan there is a slight preponderance of images drawn from calculation, wealth contrasted with poverty; in that of Goneril a similar preponderance of images drawn from passion and the uncurbed experience of the senses. In the speech of Edmund, images from disease and maiming conflict (especially at the beginning of the play) and alternate with those drawn from the elemental energies of nature, and both are crossed again by others, from the exercise of skill, of adroit and successful manipulation. Heilman (1948, pp. 69 f.) also discusses at length the recurrent imagery of clothes as thematically significant; see . For Morse (1983, p. 125), images of unnatural food and objectionable ingestion are intimate[ly] relat[ed] to the themes of witchcraft, madness, and treason. Fisher (1990, pp. 84–8) discusses the controlled counterpoint of energetic word and rational number in 2.4: The dramatist is using number, the prime instrument of Reason, to circumscribe and contain a dangerous explosion of Energy.…[88] The letter O becomes as complex a semiotic device as can be construed in a single symbol. Contra Rotman on the semiotics of zero (see below ), the meaning is not merely negative.

The play’s syntax interests other critics. Berkelman (1938, p. 359) finds that Lear’s speeches are characterized by exclamations, compound words, and his habit of apostrophe. To Nowottny (1957, pp. 90–7), Lear’s habit of asking questions [is] of fundamental importance in the play.…[97] The whole play is a dramatic answer to the one question in which all Lear’s questions are subsumed: What is Man? Doran (1976, pp. 97 ff.) finds Lear’s speeches to be characterized by commands, hortatory prayers, emphatic assertions of intent, astonished questions, and sententious declarations.…[98] The fact that these types of sentences are repeated to some degree in the speech of other characters than Lear indicates that they are not limited in function to the distinguishing of character.…[99] The reason is that the syntax is so intimately appropriate to the fable, as Shakespeare conceived it.…[100] The generally not very complicated syntax of the play—with its plain and emphatic declaratives, its commanding or hortatory imperatives—fits the fairy-tale world of absolutes: good and evil, truth and falsehood, love and hate. According to Moss (1987, p. 16): In King Lear a technique that may be labeled addition or cumulation controls the development of tension, fact, and idea; in no other work does Shakespeare employ this device with nearly the same frequency, variety, and versatility.…The dramatist heaps up words to emphasize and clarify his points, unifying (p. 17) words or word groups…by semantic correspondence, by grammatical coordination, and by conjunctive linkage.

Prosody is a concern of others. Brooke (1963, p. 11–13): The rhythms in Lear are varied through as great a range as the experience, and in this sense the use of verse becomes an essential economy; it establishes both more fully, and more immediately, the quality of each experience.…[13] Lear …stands with Antony and Cleopatra as the supreme achievement in [creating a musical coherence]. Sedlak (1969) focuses on the expressive variety of blank-verse forms in Lear’s speeches. See also Clemen (1969, pp. 10–23). Wood (1961, pp. 465–6): The spondaic character [and] pounding effect [of Lear’s speeches] proves on closer inspection to be concentrated in a habit of speech that is peculiar to Lear before his regeneration, a [466] group of four syllables, usually monosyllables, often standing at the beginning of a line or speech, the four syllables calling for almost equal emphasis [see 165, 1297, 1783]. A caesura follows, often a significant pause.…After the great rage…is killed in him this mannerism is succeeded by a habit of…repetition of monosyllables [see 2629, 2948, 3217]. Tarlinskaja (1987, p. 170) finds unusual patterns of stress in Lear’s short utterances and monologue.…A mad verse rhythm…emphasizes King Lear’s eccentric character and final madness. See also Walker (1854), Bathurst (1857), Abbott (1870, §§516–29), Bayfield (1920), Halliday (1954, pp. 155–8), and David (1935).

Other critics discuss the style and function of Lr.’s prose. Crane (1952, pp. 160–7): The prose of King Lear performs many and varied functions: it establishes a tone of cynical realism in the dialogue of Goneril and Regan; a tone of bluff frankness in the prose disguise of Kent; the Machiavellianism of Edmund; the madness of Lear and the pretended madness of Edgar; and it ultimately combines with verse to produce, [161] in the extraordinary harmonies of the trial scene, a blending of forms that is unique in Shakespeare.…[167] The apparent breakdown of the distinction between prose and verse, as in the scene of the mock trial, actually points not to a violation, but to a transcendence of the prose convention. Prose and verse are normally contrasted in Shakespeare’s plays. But King Lear, while keeping the element of contrast (the Edmund-scenes against the Lear-scenes), introduces a new synthesis of forms, such as would have been impossible in the earlier plays, in which the distinction between forms is strongly marked. Vickers (1968, pp. 351–2): The prose of King Lear is not…closely related to one character or situation.…Indeed it is…widely distributed.…The dramatic applications of the medium are equally varied…[352] conditioned by the complex demands of character or situation. Riemer (1993–4, p. 24): By means of the jagged rhythms of prose, Lear’s mad speeches convey a linguistic image or picture of his wandering mind…a mimesis of insanity. Hart (1954, p. 8): In Lear’s mad speeches, the effect of incoherence is produced in part by the use of both verse and prose, rather than by prose alone, as Bradley would lead us to believe [1904 pp. 288–9].

Other general linguistic categories discussed by critics include bawdry, discussed by Partridge (1947, passim), Colman (1974, pp. 126–31), Williams (1994), and Idem (1997); and figures of speech, discussed by Joseph (1947, passim). Freeman (1993, p. 1) analyzes 1.1 according to the emerging theory of cognitive metaphor, showing that metaphorical structures arise from a competition between the framing bodily experiences of balance [figured in terms of financial accounting] and linking [Cordelia’s bond] that define ways of understanding crucial to the larger patterns of the play. Jacobson (1980, p. 599) is concerned with the technique of naming: in Lear not merely the language and characterization but even the development of the action is informed by the significant names of the three sisters.

Certain key words are the focus of other critics, notably the word nothing. Mahood (1957, p. 183) finds in the wordplay upon nothing an expression of different attitudes to the problem of language. Rosenberg (1972, p. 69): Nothing has multiple valences independent of theology; it is another small word symptomatic of the verbal substructure of the play. Nothing comes of nothing but so does everything, spiritual wholeness seems possible from material nothing, man is all and nothing, nothing is nothing. What needs further to be noticed, in the critical attention to the word, is that, while it evoke continuous tension, it is itself part of a larger, pervasive pattern of denial in the Lear tapestry. Linked negative words spread through the language like a dark shadow: besides the thirty-odd nothings, no sounds one hundred fifty times, not almost three hundred times, neither, nor, none, ne’er, and never another hundred. Against this the rare affirmatives—yes less than ten times, yea and aye some twenty-five times—cast only a faint light and some of these are functionally negations. Miller (1993, pp. 18, 33–4): The word nothing is the most central word, from which everything in the play develops.…[33] What we see in the play…is an elaborate symphonic development upon the notion of nothingness and stripping, of reduction to some sort of hypothetical zero which in [34] fact is never reachable because there is always the possibility that the world will do something worse to you than what you have already anticipated. Willbern (1980, pp. 244 ff.), reading psychoanalytically, argues that Sh’s Nothing encompasses positive and negative senses, reciprocal yet equal.…The notion of absence or lack…[245] includes bawdy meanings…a specific, though latent, bodily sense of Cordelia’s nothing—as no thing.…[246] Not having, or having nothing, is Cordelia’s loss, and ultimately Lear’s. Through its language of licentiousness denied and organs deprived, the language of Cordelia’s defense alludes to the hidden genital significance of her Nothing.…[247] Yet this design of denial and negation traces only half of our original circle. Its reciprocal, the positive half, represents fullness rather than emptiness, presence rather than absence, whole rather than hole. It rests on or borders its negative twin in a relationship of primary creativity. Nothing, in other words, is the very ground of being, just as silence is the very ground of speech. We come to recognize the potential positive generativity of Shakespeare’s Nothing—although what is generated is not always benign. Considers (p. 252) several senses of O as sign and sound and symbol—various significations that circumscribe and circulate through Shakespeare’s Nothing…in King Lear. Shengold (1991, pp. 23–4) also interprets the word in terms of psychoanalytical symbolism: The confrontation scene between Lear and Cordelia with its repeated nothings can be seen as a portrayal of a child who wants milk and sexual gratification from the mother and instead feels presented with nothing—the rejecting breast and the female genital, which he takes to be castrated. Lr. also (p. 24) contains a post-oral, anal development of nothing and of everything. Rotman (1987, p. 80): The play shows the destruction of a world and a self by a force derived from nothing; a force wearing the mask…of zero.…[86] The play is Shakespeare’s encounter with the empty doubleness of nothing, with the spectre that he saw in those transactions…not in terms of abstract meta-signs or some grand metaphysical void but as zero, painfully concretised in the buying and selling of knighthood, self and love through numbers. Tayler (1990, pp. 17–21): Shakespeare repeats the word nothing, along with other words signifying negation,…in an artistic pattern, almost geometric in its exactitude, to guide our responses to what we see and hear…[especially] at the end of the play.…[18] In the art of Shakespeare’s theater, negation leads to anagnorisis.…[21] No has some connection with Know… Hawkes (1995, p. 54): The crucial word nothing has a capacity for serious punning which the play exploits. Its homonym is the word noting. Since noting refers (via the sense of intense observation, or even that of musical sound) precisely to a range and mode of perception to which the non-verbal, non-discursive sign—beyond the reach or words—appeals, these homonyms seem almost to enact, even to affirm, the committed pre-literate orality on which they depend, and to which they are addressed. In King Lear’s case, what is clearly at stake in the nothing/noting nexus is the range of meanings that lies beyond the reach of explicit, rational words, including the body’s kinesic contribution as an adjunct to and a moderation of whatever words say. Grady (1996, p. 145): Most of the time nothing turns out to have a rather precise meaning: it is that fearful condition when one’s name has been lost, when one has been severed from the feudal signifying systems, with their property and inheritance laws and customs. The repetition of nothing is also discussed by Blau (1963, pp. 122–32) and Cederstrom (1993, pp. 40–49).

The word nature is discussed at length as centrally significant by Danby (1949, passim); see above, . Other discussions of the word’s significance include Bald (1948, p. 339): In King Lear the key word to denote the regulating principle not merely in human relationships but within the cosmos as well is not order or degree but nature. Nature and its derivatives…occur more frequently in this than in any other play of Shakespeare, and most often with reference to the relation of parent and child. Gomme (1967, p. 113): If King Lear is the comedy of the grotesque, a vital part of the comedy comes from an exploration of the grotesque pun on nature, which is hinted at in the opening conversation and is thereafter never far from the centre of the action. See also Cederstrom (1993, pp. 33–40). Danby (1949, pp. 129–30) also discusses the key word bond: For both the sixteenth century and the romantics…a bond is a potentially frigid thing. For the Middle Ages and for Cordelia, on the other hand, the word means…[130] the inclusive scheme of natural law which Kings as well as ploughboys can violate. Hawkes (1959, pp. 178 ff.) focuses on love: O.E.D. gives as a developed meaning of Love, v.2 (OE lofian praise) to appraise, estimate or state the price or value of.…[180] Shakespeare’s grasping of the pun upon Love…can be detected without doubt in King Lear. Not surprisingly, Goneril’s Love presents a fairly precise, tabulated catalogue in the manner of an estimate.…[181] Cordelia’s remark at a very early stage in the proceedings has indicated her direct rejection of the whole immoral nature of Love as an expressible value. She seizes on the fact that the true sense of Love implies something which it is impossible to conceive of and estimate or state the value of in any terms. Empson (1951, pp. 125–35) discusses the various meanings of fool: All through the play…the idea of renunciation [cf. Orwell, above] is examined in the light of the complex idea of folly; and this would imply that you are losing a great deal if you do not give its full weight to fool, a key term which is used (by the way) forty-eight times. Possible meanings alone or in combination include simpleton, clown, knave, and lunatic. The half-mad clown is the typical or central meaning of the word in Lr. (p. 135). See also Righter (1993, pp. 243 ff.). Mack (1965, pp. 104–5): The term service, with its cognates and synonyms, tolls in the language of King Lear like that bell which reminded John Donne we are all parts of a single continent, but it is only one of a host of socially orientated terms to do so. Almost as prominent, and equally pertinent to the playwright’s concern with human relatedness, are the generic terms of social responsibility: meet, fit, proper, due, duty, bond, and the generic appellations of social status and social approbation and disapprobation: knave, fool, villain, rogue, rascal, slave, and many more.…[105] Two other titles that the play first manipulates and then explores in visually expressive episodes are gentleman and fellow. See also discussions of service in Barish & Waingrow (1958, pp. 347–55); Shanker (1975, pp. 150–4); Mahood (1992, pp. 159 ff.).

Among other critical discussions of key words, Nowottny (1957, pp. 92–3) focuses on the word flesh: Through the impact of the storm Shakespeare has…brought home to us Lear’s belief that all a man can know is what he knows through the flesh. Further, in Lear’s defiance of the storm, his involvement with the problem of guilt has been brought to the fore. By a master-stroke, Shakespeare now establishes an intimate relation between Lear’s several preoccupations, by using for them all the one symbol of the flesh: the flesh that suffers, knows, begets, is punished for its guilt.…[93] It is the discovery of the metonymy, the flesh, wherewith to advert to all the problems vital to the play which gives the language of the latter part of the tragedy its characteristic mark of simplicity charged with power.…Much of the sombre power of the most memorable utterances of the mad scenes is due to the subtle interplay between the flesh as mere flesh and the qualities the flesh embodies, and to the interplay between the different members of that whole complex of ideas of which the flesh has been made a symbol. Knights (1963, pp. 32–7) discusses the word justice. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 6–7) sees as key the sequence if-but-yet: Well over a hundred times the word [if] sounds, more than twice as often as the substantive words.…The word is symptomatic. The Lear world is full of uncertainties. Even the eternal basic values Shakespeare affirms—love, kindness, loyalty—have corrupting shadow sides.…[7] In this if world where fulfillment of expectations is tenuous, but occurs even more often (122 times), yet about half as much…casting doubt on what has gone before, complicating expectation, equivocating. Also (p. 7): Aptly, in [Lr.’s] impossible search for understanding, the word know in various forms, and in various degrees of certainty, occurs over a hundred times. Colie (1974, pp. 302–16) discusses breeding and kindness. Humphries (1983, p. 32): Woven throughout is an elaborately plaited chain of symbols which play on the several meanings of [the word] orb: circle, cyclical period, astral orbit, the earth, the globe of the eye, the [globe] surmounted by a cross forming part of the regalia, a certain rank or station, and also, beginning in the thirteenth century, childless, bereaved (OED). This three-letter word contains the entire play. Occhiogrosso (1984, p. 16): Lr. is filled with references to the hands…as a means of making connection, union, a bond, and that is why the single most frequently recurrent line of the play, in one variant form or another, is Give me thy hand. Astington (1985, pp. 330–4): Bawdy punning on the word fault is important to the structure of the play as a whole. (P. 334): in 1.1, it shows the sexual pathology of Lear’s realm in action. McAlindon (1991, pp. 175–9): Referred to about sixty times in the play, the heart is arguably its major image.…[182] The heart is the central microcosm in the correspondent and contrarious universe of King Lear.

Other critics who discuss aspects of the play’s style at the level of the single word include Rubinstein (1986, p. 348), who finds sexual puns in Lear’s speeches quite similar in function to dream material in psychoanalysis and suggests that Shakespeare may have at times intended that his wit be fully understood only by an inner circle. Thomson (1993, p. 82): The un- prefix occurs sixty-three times in the Folio version of King Lear, and sixty-two times in the Quarto.…Certainly the negating construction is in keeping with the overall impression of a chaotic world; indeed, the language, or the perceptions it signifies, is as much a cause as it is a result of the inversions of proper order in both the main and subplots. Hodge and Kress (1982, p. 144), analyze shifts between thou and you in terms of the semiotics of power and solidarity, finding the ultimately unresolved tension between ideological account and material reality, as the main content of the play.

Other aspects of language and style discussed by critics include the use of sententiae. Andresen (1974, pp. 152 ff.): Shakespeare freely exploits sententiae for revelation of character. In King Lear, indeed, the sentence is a touchstone for the quality of a character’s understanding of the profound truths of life. In Lr., nearly everyone speaks aphoristically at one time or another, and many characters work variations upon the same commonplaces [such as puer senex, Veritas Filia Temporis, and senectus mundi]. Precisely in these variations lie important clues to the psychological and moral states of each character. Reibetanz (1977, p. 118): Even though Shakespeare gives an extraordinary number of sententiae to the characters of King Lear—more than he gave to even the prodigiously sententious figure of Polonius—none of them can deal satisfactorily with the events of Act V.…So many speeches in King Lear invite us to view them as distillations of the whole, the Lear world in a grain of sand, but in fact none is. Shakespeare throws out a large collection of sententiae, both optimistic and gloomy, which—depending on our predilictions—we can choose among for epigraphs; but the play itself resists such summary treatment. Hammond (1991, pp. 80 ff.) discusses quotation and commonplace: King Lear is particularly concerned with the major commonplaces of the age.…But the play has always seemed not an anthology of clichés but a work which thrusts upon us questions which are so profoundly painful that they interrogate us below the level at which we can muster replies: they disturb the very structures of thought. One of the ways in which King Lear damages us is that it holds before us the commonplaces of life which we thought were stable, and frames them in such a way that they fade into clichés. And this process of framing, of exhibiting our truths as fragile constructions, calls into question the procedures of rational thought, and, like the Moriae Encomium, leaves our authorities without power.…[93] One of this play’s characteristic dramatic methods…is that of quotation.…[128] By its various techniques of verbal and theatrical quotation, it holds up the mirror not to nature but to the web of rhetorical devices through which we represent self-interest and expediency as the common laws of the natural order.

Various unique descriptions of the play’s style include the identification by Nowottny (1960, pp. 53–5) of a technique of montage in the language of the play: Shakespeare mounts (and of course places) a passage in such a way that its depth of meaningfulness is inferred from something not strictly contained within the passage itself. This technique is sustained variously: by contrasts, by preparatory passages…and by surprise.…[Thus] the Fool fills in the pauses in which Lear casts about for suitable reaction to what confronts him.…The bluntness of Kent, if it had no other function in the play, would have been worth inventing for the sake of Lear’s reaction to it in the scene of the stocks.…[55] This mounting of great passages in verbal encounters that prepare for them (and even, ultimately, on characterization and plot) is a continuous technique, and to bear it in mind may make some apparent miracles of style less impregnable to commentary. Colie (1966, pp. 466–70) notes in the language and plot of Lr. a number of stock paradoxes in Renaissance literature, submerged beneath the moving surface of the play, worked into one another in a substructure that itself keeps the surface moving in its irregular but recurrent patterns. To change the metaphor, the paradoxes in this play are wound into a strong twist spiraling in to converge upon one essential consideration. Whichever paradox one begins by examining…or at whatever point in the play one begins the examination, one is soon drawn into all the other paradoxes, narrowing together upon the central theme of the play, the discovery that individual self-discovery is also the revelation of the human predicament.…[470] Between the worlds upside down of most paradoxical literature…and the world upside down in King Lear there is a great difference, the difference between detachment and involvement, between satiric and tragic irony.…The paradoxist’s inversion in tragedy is not so much an intellectual as a factual inversion: the paradox is itself contradicted, the metaphor un-metaphored, as irony turns into truth. Hoy (1973, pp. 53–5) sees Lr. sharing with mannerist painting the representation of different levels of reality by way of different levels of style.…[55] The most sublime and the most loathsome imaginings inhere in the language of the play, from one scene to the next. Atwood (1976, pp. 42–54) discusses style in 1.1 in relation to Renaissance rhetorical ideas of decorum. Leith & Myerson (1989, pp. 71–7) analyze the rhetorical relation of speakers to their utterances in 1.1. Kermode (2000, pp. 195–7) finds in the play’s verbal irony a sort of authorial savagery; irony is too civilised a word for it.…[197] There is a cruelty in the writing that echoes the cruelty of the story, a terrible calculatedness that puts one in mind of Cornwall’s and Regan’s.

div.head: Albany
div.p: Critics frequently find Albany lacking as a man, either weak, confused, or incompetent. Hall (1879, pp. 26–7) calls him a weak and indecisive man…totally unfitted for troublous times.…[27] There is a want of manliness and courage in Albany. Elton (1966, pp. 300–2): Although Albany, like the protagonists and Edgar, is deceived by a close relative, he is slowest to be undeceived.…Albany’s is primarily a timed explosion, a retarded awakening to human evil.…After Lear’s madness and Gloucester’s blinding…he is never man so chang’d [2270]; yet, perceiving the moral reversal in his world [quotes 2275–6], he smiles bitterly and does nothing. His last stage emphasizes Albany’s almost invariable lateness.…He is too late to prevent the French invaders’ landing [2271]. When, at long last, he is stirred to action, he discovers himself, too late, in the ironical position of one who is wedded to a loathed enemy with whom he must patriotically ally to combat a desired friend. When he gradually resigns the kingdom to Lear…it is again too late, for some ten lines later Lear is dead. And, most notably, as he exclaims [quotes 3192, 3205], his absolute power [3272] is too late to prevent the murder of Cordelia.…[301] In the marriage of Albany and Goneril, hierarchical justice and degree are wedded to unfathomable evil and chaos, their conjunction suggesting the Hobbesian beast coupled with civilized order. Standing for human decency, against the blood-dimmed tide, Albany for a time seems to lack conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity. Firm in the last act, however, the duke demands distributive justice, even on the battlefield…and later promises their due to Kent and Edgar.…It is the judgment of the heavens, moreover, which Albany repeatedly invokes.…In contrast to the [302] pitiful Edgar,…Albany’s discovery involves only justice. Inclining here to the terror, rather than the pity, of the Aristotelian tragic effect, the duke exclaims at the death of his wife and his sister-in-law: [quotes 3185–6]. Yet, while occupying antithetical moral positions, Albany with his poetic justice…and the villains with their lex talionis seem analogous.…At the end he appears to transcend a private confusion perhaps only to achieve a cosmic one.…It is, appropriately, this personage whom Shakespeare chooses to uphold distributive and cosmic justice at the end [3274–6]—in effect to explicate, like Job’s comforter, the mystery of suffering…—and to be undercut by Lear’s unsatisfied outcry [3277–80]. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 253–4): Against Goneril’s fire and strength, he has seemed, indeed, a usurper of her bed, her body. Before 4.2, he has been without force or even forthrightness: Lear’s knight had felt [in 1.4] the coolness in the Duke as well as Goneril. Lear acknowledged this, and the memory of it urges him, in [4.6], to dream of stealing upon his sons-in-law to kill, kill, kill. Albany clearly does not satisfy Goneril maritally. Until 4.2, only a misleading outline of Albany’s milder side [had] appeared; only then are the dialectic of the design, the polyphony, the moulding and shading…foreshadowed.…[254] Albany’s own position is, of course, ambiguous. Neutral to Lear or worse in [1.4], he allowed the Good old man to go angrily out into the night—the act for which [in 4.2] he…flay[ed] Goneril. Albany believes Lear wronged—yet he will fight against him. So the design, as with the other characters, has its built-in restlessness, unresolved inner conflict. Friedenreich (1979, pp. 295 ff.): Albany functions…as the major instrument by which Shakespeare makes us imagine that we do indeed see some glimmer of light on the horizon, false light though it may be.…[305] Albany is a decent man in a situation calling for more than decency; he is a man whose valor is tied as it should be to his honor, but who finds himself outmaneuvered by those less honorable than himself; he has great faith in the power of time to assuage civil wounds…but time betrays him. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 127–8): Readers of King Lear believe that Albany is simple and honest and good because he proclaims his own innocence on several occasions, because he is outraged by Gloucester’s blinding, because he defends Britain against foreign invasion, and because he presides over the trial that brings Edmund to justice. But not one of these virtuous acts is presented unequivocally by Shakespeare. Each is the locus of significant variants. Despite his virtue, Albany is censured as Cornwall’s partner first by Kent and then by Lear. Despite his outrage, Albany does nothing to relieve either Gloucester, Lear, or Cordelia. Despite his conquest of the enemy, his defense of Britain is shown in its consequences to be a tragic blunder. [128] And finally, Albany’s needless urgency to try Edmund leads him to ignore the danger to Lear and Cordelia, a negligence that contributes directly to their deaths. Albany is indeed a good man, just as Brutus is a good man; but like Brutus, Albany makes choices leading to tragedy. Gurr (2002, p. 51) describes him as fumbling and uncomprehending.

However, some critics find him wholly admirable. Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, p. 20): He is a gentle and dignified spirit…a calm, rich being, swayed and illumined by the light of reason alone. Mackail (1930, pp. 78–81): He is generally thought of as only on the second plane of the drama, and as of little importance. Really, he is the pivot on which it all turns. He is central, inasmuch as he is the one character in the play who is from first to last completely sane, balanced, and normal. Sparing of words, unhurried and even slow in action, he is never either confused or hustled; and he can strike, when the time comes, with unhesitating certainty.…[81] Edmund thought that Albany was a stupid man; he left him out of account. On that one mistake, on that single defect of human insight, [his] adroit and complicated and successful schemes of villainy crashed like an egg-shell. Lökse (1960, p. 123): Albany is throughout the last scene the master of the ceremonies, and he is ceremonious to such an extent that only the peculiar nature of the play allows it to bear the burden of the ceremoniousness. It is in the light of his task in this last scene of the play that we must see his well balanced words earlier in the play, his quiet statements and his sense of proportion. Great damage will be done if the representation of him at any stage is given a touch of the ridiculous. Stevenson (1965, p. 262): Albany emerges as an archetypal figure, like the Albion of Blake’s prophetic books, pointing to the spiritual reintegration not merely of the British people, but of mankind. Brower (1971, p. 390): Albany attains to something like heroic stature.

Various critics emphasize his growth in moral stature over the course of the play. Bradley (1904, p. 297): Albany is merely sketched, and he is so generally neglected that a few words about him may be in place. He too ends the play a better and wiser man than he began. When the play opens he is, of course, only just married to Goneril; and the idea is, I think, that he has been bewitched by her fiery beauty not less than by her dowry. He is an inoffensive, peace-loving man, and is overborne at first by his great love for his wife and by her imperious will. He is not free from responsibility for the treatment which the King receives in his house; the Knight says to Lear, [quotes 589–91]. But he takes no part in the quarrel, and doubtless speaks truly when he protests that he is as guiltless as ignorant of the cause of Lear’s violent passion. When the King departs, he begins to remonstrate with Goneril, but shrinks in a cowardly manner, which is a trifle comical, from contest with her. She leaves him behind when she goes to join Regan, and he is not further responsible for what follows. When he hears of it, the scales drop from his eyes, Goneril becomes hateful to him, he determines to revenge Gloster’s eyes. His position is however very difficult, as he is willing to fight against Cordelia in so far as her army is French, and unwilling in so far as she represents her father. This difficulty, and his natural inferiority to Edmund in force and ability, pushes him into the background; the battle is not won by him but by Edmund; and but for Edgar he would certainly have fallen a victim to the murderous plot against him. When it is discovered, however, he is fearless and resolute enough, besides being full of kind feeling towards Kent and Edgar, and of sympathetic distress at Gloster’s death. And one would be sure that he meant to retain this strength till the end but for his last words [3294–5]. See also S. A. Brooke (1913, p. 205). Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:62–4): Albany is at the opposite pole [from Cornwall]. He prefers a quiet life with Goneril while he can contrive it, even at the loss of some self-respect.…His milky gentleness, his harmful mildness ring true enough as accusations: does he think to tame a tigress with a platitude? His wife, quite naturally, departs to seek Regan’s help without him. Much has happened, though, by the time we see him again, when Goneril is on the full tide of reckless triumphant wickedness.…[63] That Albany had loved his wife is plain. We hear him speak of the great love he bore her. He has been slow to think ill of her. But he is of those who let their wrath gather beneath a placid surface till, on a sudden, it boils over, and if the cause of it lies deep they are never the same again.…The first stern clash with Goneril wins Albany the authoritative standing that he now needs in the play.…Albany, once in action, is as distinguished a figure as any in the play. Shakespeare endows him with a fine sense of irony. The slight sting in the tail of his compliment to Edmund after the battle…[64] the cutting courtesy…his cool preparation of his stroke; the stroke itself…are not bad for a moral fool. Nor does he trust to the appearance of the unknown champion for Edmund’s undoing. He throws his own gauntlet down. A touch of gallantry, though Shakespeare does not—does not need to—compromise his dignity by setting him to fight. And he is left from now to the play’s end in command of its action. Kirschbaum (1960, pp. 20–8): Albany’s growth from nonentity to greatness qualifies the bleakness of the play’s ending. (P. 21): He is a prominent but not immediately perceivable part of the play’s architecture, because Shakespeare at first purposefully makes him two-dimensional.…The [opening] scene [suggests] that Albany and Cornwall must have or should have moral or psychological problems arising from the nature of the strong, forceful, bad women to whom each is married. In 1.3 he is (p. 22) negative, uninformed, inconsiderable.…[23] This man, we are ready to affirm, may be good, but he appears a weakling; there is no strength in him, no impulse to lead or control. He is dominated by his wife.…When we are allowed to observe him once more [in 4.2], he will be very different. He will be shown as one whom the fact of evil is changing from a negative personality into a positive one, who is now the psychological and moral equal of his wife. Albany’s transformation suggests that (p. 24) within the King Lear tragic world there has occurred a melioristic phenomenon of the utmost spiritual importance. That which was weak and ineffective has been changed through the very fact of evil itself into something ethically aware and strong.…[25] Now, how much the play requires us to pay attention to Albany’s queer moral dilemma—loving Lear but yet fighting Cordelia and her army who are there for Lear’s rescue—I do not know. Perhaps, Shakespeare’s shortness with the problem is evidence that the exigencies of the plot are paramount.…[27] The Albany who enters in [5.3] has a markedly increased spiritual stature. He is now, and feels he is, the dominant figure on the stage…able to speak scornfully to this woman who has spoken so scornfully to him.…It is as though he were taking over a power which the evil group have hitherto arrogated to themselves.…[29] Strength, charity, justice, lack of sentimentality are all illustrated in his final speeches as well as a corresponding humility.…And this great man, great in psychological strength, great in physical power, great in piety and morality, was the nonentity with which the play began! And King Lear is often described as totally dark! Mortenson (1965, pp. 217–25): A fully developed guardian of order and natural law who emerges at the end as its solid exponent,…Albany reiterates, on an independent level, the spiritual and moral growth of Lear and Gloucester, and consequently expands the total statement, i.e., the reassertion of order. (P. 219): Albany comes to stand for…that state of government which adheres to proper form and justice and creates a climate which will nurture the forces of good.…[221] In his meticulous correctness, Albany reflects the hierarchy at its most conservative.…His conservativism or reticence in this respect may be almost exasperating, but it is not dramatically fortuitous. His manner of statement never rises above the most traditional rhetoric; his vocabulary patterns recall copybook maxims.…[223] Insofar as…Albany is…an organic part of [the play’s general] pattern,…his decision [to oppose Cordelia’s army] is simply and instinctively right, not wrong.…[224] Albany is the only major character in King Lear who loses neither moral rectitude nor high temporal position. Since he alone is never displaced, he is not a tragic figure and thus cannot have the dramatic appeal of those who are. But this is not to say he is a weakly drawn or arbitrary figure. Albany represents the basic and enduring principle of order in his growth.…In Albany’s development may be found a further delineation of the self-knowledge theme and regeneration theme to be found in the Lear and Gloucester plots; as a champion of the reassertion of goodness and order he achieves full [225] integration. We may feel a sense of dissatisfaction with Albany’s conservative diction and his failure to achieve the higher vision of Lear, but this does not invalidate his enduring rightness. Harris (1976, p. 261): Deep in his wife’s shadow during most of the play, in 5.3 Albany at last shines with the strength and knowledge that the tragedy has allowed him to acquire. He finally proves to be his wife’s master and master of the realm. When order returns, he strengthens it by becoming what he never was. See also Leggatt (1988, pp. 52–5). Smidt (1990, pp. 140–2) defends Albany while doubting the idea of his moral growth: There is no reason to think that Albany has not all along had a complete moral system opposed to that which Goneril comes to demonstrate.…We do not have to believe the aspersions cast on Albany by those who are biased against him.…[142] In the end he loses his central standing to Edgar. He does not change dramatically, but has more questionable qualities of leadership and is no longer, in the Folio, the most natural successor to Lear.

Psychologizing critics include Bransom (1934, p. 151): Goneril’s power, beauty, and extraordinary sex-attraction had bewitched her husband. With the aid of this attraction and her natural force of character she easily imposed her will upon him, too easily for him to retain her respect. Hence her contemptuous estimate of his character. But the cause of his submission lay not so much in any weakness of his own will as in something closely akin to sexual pleasure which he found in submitting to hers. Reaction followed, almost revolt. There was disgust at himself, shame and humiliation. He was conscious of disgust, but not conscious that it was disgust at himself. The true cause of his disgust was repressed, and it found expression only as disgust at his wife; that is to say it was an indirect expression and was transferred from himself to his wife. Zak (1984, pp. 39–41): We watch with an understanding of inevitable human weakness as the well-intentioned Albany inconspicuously slides into allowing the fatal delay in the return of the captives whom he, as commander-in-chief, had demanded of Edmund as the first priority. In the process he surrenders his generous power to rescue the king and Cordelia to his personal hurt and subconscious rage to settle his marital scores against Goneril and Edmund.…Our sympathy for him does not shield him later as he suddenly blurts out his lapse of memory—[quotes 3192].…[40] Nor does he cut much of a figure as he lamely tries to establish an official tone and juridical atmosphere in the midst of the unspeakable waste of life all about him and the deflating interruptions of Lear’s nearly mad raving.…He acts the fool, absurdly declaiming.…Albany’s manner of expressing his intent [3268] to abdicate because others, he blindly presumes, would better sustain the weight of state clearly invites us to recall the darker purpose…[41] of Lear’s fast intent [43] at the outset.…Both kings are, in fact, pretenders, even perhaps to themselves, each in the indulgence of his self-conceived helplessness feeding the illusion that this self-protective reservation for himself is instead a generous act or at least a disinterested token of respect.

Some recent critics emphasize differences between the Quarto and Folio versions of the role. Warren (1978, p. 99): The part of Albany is more developed in Q than in F, and in Q he closes the play as a mature and victorious duke assuming responsibility for the kingdom; in F he is a weaker character, avoiding responsibility. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 125–6): The variants in the Folio shape Albany’s character in a number of complex ways. Clearly his instincts are [126] to act sympathetically toward Lear, but the Folio text amplifies the conflict in Albany between his humane instincts on the one hand and on the other his rigid principles of justice and his flaccid ethical practices.…Variants in the Folio text of [5.3] amplify Albany’s performance as a vigorous prosecutor of treason committed against himself. Further variants create for him in the Folio a series of disjointed actions that give credence to his remarks about his own inner turmoil. The display of emotional tension in the Folio makes Albany’s second abdication [if it is one; see n. 3295] at the end of the scene justifiable, because Albany’s need to withdraw from active life has been shown so convincingly. In contrast, Albany’s statements about his inner crises are not very compelling in the Quarto, since they have no consequence or observable counterpart in his actions. Therefore his second abdication may be interpreted as inconclusive, especially considering the Quarto’s ascription of the final speech. In both texts Albany is a complex and ambiguous figure. His intentions are not commensurate with his actions and their consequences. Gurr (1988, pp. 115–18): The Folio’s changes consistently make Albany clearly a figure of authority but also a ditherer, hesitant, unsure, upset and easily distracted.…In both versions of the play…Albany is not in any way at the end his country’s saviour, but (p. 116) in the revised Folio text he is never in control, either of his own mind or of the events in the kingdom over which he comes to be the sole ruler. At play’s end (p. 118) he has learned nothing. Albion, under Albany, is not restored to real health. Weis (ed. 1993, pp. 11–12): There is no question that F’s Albany is a greatly impoverished character.…F’s text begs questions of psychological credibility.…[12] It is Albany’s innocence or folly which leads him to think that Goneril is no longer the woman he once loved, but a monster. In fact, his life with her was all along built on false assumptions. Albany’s failure even [in 4.2] to see this…shows that his pain and predicament in the Q text of the play are partly those of a betrayed husband. F, on the other hand, turns him into a two-dimensional figurehead whose sole identity seems to be that of a dispassionate and upright soldier-leader. Knowles (1997, p. 71) is skeptical: The reduction [of Albany’s role] is more quantitative than qualitative.

Other views include Snider (1887, p. 201), who interprets Albany as an instructive contrast to Cordelia: He takes the State as his ethical principle, though he has to act with those whom he hates and against those whom he loves.…The consequences of their actions are seen in the catastrophe; Cordelia perishes, while Albany survives as the ruler of his country. Draper (1945, p. 44) describes him as sanguine. Pogson (1950, p. 40): The Duke of Albany represents the spirit of Britain, the national character, justice.

div.head: Cordelia
div.p: Critics have often idealized Cordelia. Bottoms (2002, p. 112) discusses the process by which 19th-century commentators turned Cordelia into a heroine well suited to the psychological fantasy needs of dutiful Victorian daughters. Thus Jameson (1833, p. 228): If Lear be the grandest of Shakspeare’s tragedies, Cordelia in herself, as a human being governed by the purest and holiest impulses and motives, the most refined from all dross of selfishness and passion, approaches near to perfection; and, in her adaptation as a dramatic personage to a determinate plan of action, may be pronounced altogether perfect.…The whole character rests upon the two sublimest principles of human action—the love of truth and the sense of duty; but these, when they stand alone (as in the Antigone), are apt to strike us as severe and cold. Shakspeare has, therefore, wreathed them round with the dearest attributes of our feminine nature, the power of feeling and inspiring affection. The first part of the play shows us how Cordelia is loved, the second part how she can love.…What… lends to Cordelia that peculiar and individual truth of character which distinguishes her from every other human being…is a natural reserve, a tardiness of disposition,…a subdued quietness of deportment and expression, a veiled shyness thrown over all her emotions, her language and her manner, making the outward demonstration invariably fall short of what we know to be the feeling within.…This deliberate coolness…is beautifully represented as a certain modification of character, the necessary result of feelings habitually, if not naturally, repressed. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 637–8): She is one of the tenderest of Shakespeare’s creations, hard to be understood, yet simple and clear to those who feel rightly.…Richer in love than in tongue, she possessed not the glib and oily art to speak and purpose not.… The ready speech and flattery of her sisters would have been despised by her…most of all because she had none of that craving and self-seeking which makes them so eloquent. Feminine simplicity and modesty, a want or tardiness in nature, as her future husband calls it, helps to chain her tongue in the opening scene, and makes her utter the fatal word which decides her fate.…Above all she is actuated in her decision by a sickening contempt and scorn of her sisters, which she cannot longer suppress.…[638] She is a being such as Shakespeare in his Pericles has depicted in the holy, pious Marina and dies a martyr to her filial love as before to her love of truth. In this unsuspiciousness, in this involuntary obedience to the promptings of sacred feelings, she resembles Desdemona. Reed (1855, p. 51): She is a personification of all that is graceful and dutiful in womanly nature—a being, the very embodiment of filial piety, whom every parent, the wide world over, may bless, and every daughter reverence. Clarke (1863, p. 172): Cordelia is so forcibly drawn,—though with so few brief touches,—that we marvel at the masterly hand that could delineate a female figure known to us as perfectly as our sister’s, by means so succinct. There is a certain conciseness in all that is said of Cordelia, as well as all that she herself says, which consists singularly with her own character,—this being the extreme of reticence.…There is a curious combination of loftiest dignity with lowliest humility in her nature, which combine to form the beautiful piece of womanhood known to us as Shakespeare’s Cordelia. Hugo (1864; tr. 1886, pp. 246–7): The father is the pretext for the daughter. [247] That admirable human creature, Lear, serves as a support to this ineffable divine creation, Cordelia. All that chaos of crimes, vices, manias, and miseries finds its justification in this shining vision of virtue. Shakespeare, bearing Cordelia in his brain, in creating this tragedy was like a god who, having an Aurora to establish, should make a world to put her in. Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, p. 42): She displays a filial perfection that might be the fountain head of daughterly love to feed forever the hungry father heart of the world. Elliott (1885, p. 232): She is the casket of gems engulphed in the remorseless deep. Price (1894, p. 172) sees in her the highest type of complete womanhood. Goddard (1951, pp. 523–4): Cordelia, with her abruptness and bluntness, her strain of disdain, is closer to most of us than the innocent and angelic Desdemona. If to err is human, to forgive divine, they are both divine, but Cordelia is more human. It is a triumphant mark of Shakespeare’s art that the two supreme heroines of his tragic period should be so similar yet so antipodal.…[524] Cordelia loves her father deeply and sincerely, but underplays her confession of affection—partly from a congenital truthfulness and hatred of display that bends backward at the hypocrisy of her sisters, but even more, perhaps, through a well-grounded fear, possibly unconscious, that if her father’s plan goes through she will be given to the worldly Burgundy whom she could only have despised rather than to the unworldly France whom she loves.…[542] Cordelia, we know, is a spirit [cf. 2799].…[552] Shakespeare confers upon her existence in the Imagination itself, which, as William Blake saw, is our only [553] word for Eternity. Other idealizing critics include Drake (1817; 1838, p. 560); Lewes (1894, pp. 289–97); Taine (1864; 1871, 2:100); Hall (1871, pp. 246–8); Hales (1875; 1884, pp. 264–70); Walters (1889, p. 61); Turnbull (1892, pp. 45–9); Stone (1925, p. 166); Reibetanz (1977, p. 120). Schlegel (1809–11; tr. 1815, 2:208) compares the heavenly beauty of soul of Cordelia to that of Antigone, a comparison often repeated in the 19th century and afterward; for instance Heine (1838; tr. 1891, 1:366): She is the modern Antigone, who in depth of soul and feeling far surpasses her antique sister; likewise Girardin (1845; 1849, pp. 125 ff.), who describes her as surpassing Antigone in tender pity if not in virtue. Analogously, for Mézières (1860; 1865, p. 300) she is the Iphigenia of British legend, the sacrificial victim of a barbarous age. (In Fr.).

She has frequently been described in sacral terms. Hudson (1848, 2:259 ff.) sees a peculiar fitness between Cordelia and the part she was designed more particularly to act; which was, to exemplify the workings of filial piety, as Lear exemplifies the workings of paternal love. To embody and illustrate this sentiment, [260] the whole character, in all its movements and aspects, must needs be essentially religious.…[262] Thus she imparts and infuses the sweet, divine grace of her nature so cunningly, and silently, and sacramentally, that the recipients thereof feel not their obligations to her, or rather to heaven for her, while she is with them, and know not what her presence is doing for them until she is gone, and it may be truly said, her absence alone can reveal her to them. See also Idem (1872, 2:374–80). Meany (1859, p. 18) speaks of her gift…of real without visible presence.…She comes to us by inspiration rather than by vision. Ruggles (1895, p. 193):Cordelia may be regarded as a household divinity,—not so much one who is worshiped, as one who blesses others, one who hourly puts good thoughts into good works and thus becomes an earthly type of divine love, and adumbration of that Truth, whose Word is his Deed. Knight (1930, p. 220): Cordelia, in that she represents the Principle of Love, is idealized: Edmund is of the past, Lear of the present, Cordelia of the future dispensation. She is like a soul in bliss. Her tears are holy water and her eyes heavenly [2347+31]: she alone here has both goodness and fascination. Fabiny (1994, p. 465): She desperately fight[s] to deliver Lear from the invisible process of the internalization of evil.…[466] For…Cordelia the blind, sinful state of mind of [Lear] is like a sickness that must be cured by a kind of Christian psychoanalysis.…[470] She appears as a saint, a redemptive agent whose voice is not from this world. See also Womack (2002, pp. 103–4).

Various critics compare her to Christ. Heine (1838; tr. 1891, 1:366): The sad bitterness with which Cordelia plays upon the hypocrisy of her sisters…has all the character of that irony which the Master of all Love, the hero of the gospel, sometimes employed. Bethell (1944, pp. 66–8): From first to last [she] is associated with theological terminology and Christian symbol.…[68] It seems more than likely that Shakespeare wished to suggest the foreshadowing of Christ in pure natures before His coming. Bickersteth (1947, p. 170) calls her a Christ figure, a symbol of divine love within a pagan setting. Campbell (1948, p. 107): It is not what the earthly creature Cordelia is, but what she represents that is important for the meaning of the play. It is her spirit not her bodily presence that redeems her father. And…she is hanged, as Christ was crucified, so that mankind might be saved. Siegel (1955, p. 335): The Elizabethans…would have more readily apprehended than we do that Cordelia’s ignominious death completes the analogy between her and Christ. Gomme (1967, p. 114): She suffers, like Christ, for the salvation of others—not for Lear, but for us, the audience, who take part in the action of the play as its symbolic heirs, as we are the spiritual heirs of Christ. Milward (1975, pp. 39 ff.): In her, as also in Edgar, the ideal of a sacrificial victim for the expiation of sins and the salvation of sinners is seen in its purest form; and of all Shakespeare’s characters she comes closest to the figure of Christ, the suffering Saviour of the world. Additionally, like the heroines of the romances, she also functions as a figure for (p. 152) Mary as Second Eve, who was conceived without stain of original sin and cooperated with Christ in his work of redemption. England (1982, p. 70): She has a redemptive and Christlike role. Guilfoyle (1989; 1990, p. 117) also calls her a Christ-figure; Morris (1985, p. 155): Cordelia serves as restorer-redeemer-savior to a Lear reborn. Evans (1990, p. 15): She is an image of Christ; Langford (1991, p. 24) calls her a redemptive Christ-figure: Cordelia’s death stands as a reenactment of the climax of the Christian story. In contrast, Cavell (1969; 2002, p. 302): If Cordelia resembles Christ, it is by having become fully human, by knowing her separateness, by knowing the deafness of miracles, by accepting the unacceptability of her love, and by nevertheless maintaining her love and the whole knowledge it brings. One can say she redeems nature ([2648]), but this means nothing miraculous, only that she shows nature not to be the cause of evil—there is no cause in nature which makes these hard hearts, and no cause outside either. The cause is the heart itself, the having of a heart, in a world made heartless. Coursen (1976, pp. 278–99): In the first scene she represents that part of the outer mystery which expresses truth but which, like Christ, must be recognized, must resonate against the inner mystery of man. Her muteness before Lear is similar to Christ’s before Pilate.…[283] France discerns in her…a sacramental depth of which her substance is but the outward manifestation.…Cordelia’s love emerges from the deep premises of a world order that must be felt inwardly to be understood.…[284] Cordelia’s ethic is that of the New Testament, based on spiritual value, on the inner meaning of the law, on the fulfillment of the law that Christ states is his mission (Matthew 5:17).…[287] Cordelia [is linked] to the agape most completely embodied in Christ. However, (p. 299) to make Cordelia a Christ-figure would be to suggest that Shakespeare is oriented toward truth, as Auerbach suggests the Bible is. Since Shakespeare is oriented toward response, he creates a character representing truth—not a figure in an allegory. Driscoll (1977, p. 160) identifies her with Christ as an alchemical symbol.

Elton (1966, pp. 76 ff.) views her as a virtuous pagan, a believer in providence and divine justice, whose words and deeds form a meaningful pattern of pious and reverent belief.…Cordelia demonstrates her consistency with order, the principle of the bond, when she prays [2763–5], where breach and discord are to be replaced by a cured wholeness and harmony, analogous to a restored cosmic harmony, related to the Platonic conception.…Like Shakespeare’s royal patron, who had recently united Scotland and England, Cordelia is devoted to curing division. Strife between north and south, between such aptly named figures as Albany and Cornwall…has its antithesis in Cordelia’s healing and restoring forgiveness. She prays for a cure in this great breach, in Lear’s abused nature, and her love would repair those…harms [2764, 2778]. Recalling the highest virtue as the highest love (the Augustinian summum amor), she summons up also its Boethian and Chaucerian bond of love. For it is love and its correlative, pity, which in Lear are the binding forces and which Cordelia preeminently reflects.…[79] Cordelia unites in herself the Renaissance-sundered pietas and sapientia.…Unlike Lear, Cordelia, anticipating the higher virtues of faith, hope, and charity, seems to approach the contemplative virtues of wisdom (sapientia), knowledge (scientia), and understanding (intellectus). In sum, she embodies Albany’s association between Wisdom and goodness [2303+7].…[82] As a pagan antedating Christ, existing under a natural rather than a revealed theology and under a dispensation of nature without grace, Cordelia appears limited to works…without hope of heaven but rather out of good conscience and mere recognition.…[83] It may be concluded that…Cordelia could in all probability have been identified as approximating the pagan prisca theologia, like Sidney’s Pamela. Contrary to Dante, who placed virtuous heathens in the First Circle or limbo of his Inferno, in Shakespeare’s day the controversy over the salut des infidèles might, according to the indications in King Lear, have been decided in her favor. Brower (1971, p. 411): Cordelia is Shakespeare’s purest symbol of another way than the heroic of meeting the worst, the way of submission and suffering, of selflessness and compassion. If these virtues and the language through which they are expressed are in part pagan, they belong to a pagan tradition that like Virgilian humanitas was easily absorbed into Christianity.

Critics have frequently turned her into a secular symbol as well. Hugo (1864; tr. 1886, p. 244): Maternity of the daughter toward the father. Profound subject! A maternity venerable among all other maternities, so admirably translated by the legend of that Roman girl who in the depth of a prison nurses her old father. The young breast near the white beard: there is no holier sight! Such a filial breast is Cordelia. Freud (1913; tr. 1950, 4:255): Cordelia is death.…It is in vain that an old man yearns for the love of woman as he once had it from his mother; the third of the Fates alone, the silent Goddess of Death, will take him into her arms. Mitchell (1992, p. 100): As Freud’s goddess of Death, Cordelia speaks with the inexorable voice of the law, of Antropos, the third of the Muses, the ineluctable one who keeps the register of truth and reality. See also Ramnoux (1968, p. 19). Danby (1949, pp. 124–6): Cordelia is the other Nature Edmund, Goneril, and Regan [125] ignore.…She is a figure comparable with that of Griselde or Beatrice: literally a woman; allegorically the root of individual and social sanity; tropologically Charity that suffereth long and is kind; anagogically the redemptive principle itself.…[The] normative humanity embodied in Cordelia incorporates the traditional ideals of natural theology and…this ideal requires not only perfection in the individual, but perfection in the community also.…Cordelia cannot stand for individual sanity without at the same time standing for rightness in the relation of man to man—social sanity.…[126] Cordelia expresses the utopian intention of Shakespeare’s art. Idem (1952, p. 120): The habitual terms applied to her in the play would be extravagant in respect of a mere woman. They are quite natural when applied to a woman who is conceived as a Griselda or Beatrice. Wilson (1930, p. 201): She represents the redemptive power of love. Traversi (1952, pp. 44 f., 212 ff.): Cordelia is a norm of harmonious completeness.…[44] Only in Cordelia are…objective [45] nature and subjective impulse, truly united.… [212] The queenliness of Cordelia [in Act 4]…stands out in contrast to her father’s passion-torn regality, as a complete, harmonious unity to its broken and disrupted parts. As such, it gives fulfillment in dramatic terms to the royal side of Lear’s divided nature, just as Goneril brings consistency to its passionate, wilful aspect. The harmony of her being [is] due to her conformity to nature itself. Speaight (1955, p. 121): She is Nature redeemed and remade…the bias from which her world had fallen; and…the symbol and clue of its recovery. Fraser (ed. 1963, p. xxxi): Less real than symbolic, her affinity is more to a creature of fairy tale like Cinderella than to a heroine of the realistic drama like Blanche DuBois. Gaull (1967, p. 340) calls her an embodiment of divine love. Iwasaki (1966–7, p. 3): Cordelia is truth…conform[ing] with the traditional idea of Veritas filia temporis. Reibetanz (1974, p. 54): Cordelia…exists as a dramatized emblem. There is never any question of this Cordelia’s being romantically repelled (as in King Leir) or attracted (as in Tate’s play) to anybody. Unlike Desdemona or even Ophelia, Cordelia has none of the dimensions of the romantic heroine. Hays (1979, p. 113): Cordelia embodies the just, maternal, protective ideal which the declining feudal-aristocratic society created as an image of itself. Erlebach (1981, p. 115) calls her a personification of divine reason. Perry (1980, pp. 101–15): Seen from the vantage point of the [integrative] tradition of erotic spirituality, she is the Cor or heart, viewed by Leone Ebreo as the mediator between man’s mind and body, and Delia the moon, the sign of reconciliation between heaven and nature, spirit and matter. Moreover…the Delian person, whose center is the human heart, is expert both at binding that subtle knot that makes us man and, when need be, in unbinding man from all nonhuman attachments.…[115] It is for [her] withdrawn and contemplative father that Cordelia is the death-wish [cf. Freud], but for the inhabitants of the kingdom she is very much the opposite.…Her emblematic essence [is] as an ideal link between heaven and earth and as humanity’s bond with nature and with one another. Zak (1984, pp. 27–71): She is the symbolic discretion that could and should lead,…a reading that is [28] reinforced by the fact that in the Renaissance the word discretion referred both to the freedom to act according to one’s own judgment and with circumspection and to the ability to hold one’s counsel, to be silent when speech would be inconvenient or…inappropriate.…[71] Though Cordelia remains one of our literature’s most successfully realized ideal heroines…she simultaneously comes to stand as a richly stylized symbol of pastoral grace. Kettle (1988, p. 80): Towards the end of the play Cordelia…is seen explicitly as the alternative to the old [political] order (which by her honesty she has exposed) and to the new people who hate and fear her.…Sunshine and rain at once, the image of the rainbow, the pledge of future harmony arising out of contradiction, is associated with Cordelia. She seems to express in her very person the better way to which Lear has come through… a kind of utopian promise. Sandona (1990, pp. 109–10): She is not a personification; nor does she reflect a complete person to be judged for ulterior motives.…Like Solveig in Ibsen’s Peer Gynt, she exists at the beginning and at the end of the play as if representing a truth which exists behind the scenes, behind the screens of this world. She is (p. 110) the paradoxical voice of silence, the paradoxical act of patience. Holahan (1997, p. 417): The play sets the construction of value in the lady, dramatizing a worth to her objective presence in stages of absence, reported return, and actual appearance. It then reveals the force of her value and presence in the repair of Lear, which will survive further losses, including that of the lady herself.…Her character is at once value and value’s instrument. Berry (1999, p. 154): She is a subtle refiguration of sovereignty as the bond or knot of Union. In contrast, Boling (1995, p. 19): By choosing to empty herself and be nothing in death, Cordelia eludes the various representations of her death that others would impose upon her and gains the representational triumph of the thing itself, helping Lear see better and choose transcendence.

Perhaps in reaction to such idealization, other critics have emphasized normal human qualities. Ruskin (1879; 1906, 25:417): Shakespeare clearly does not mean her to have been supremely beautiful in person.…Had she been entirely beautiful, [France] would have honoured her as a lover should, even before he saw her despised; nor would she ever have been so despised—or by her father, misunderstood. Swinburne (1880, pp. 173–4): Cordelia, the brotherless Antigone of our stage, has one passing touch of intolerance for what her sister was afterwards to brand as indiscretion and dotage in their father, which redeems her from the charge of perfection. Like Imogen, she is not too inhumanly divine for [174] the sense of divine irritation. Godlike though they be, their very godhead is human and feminine; and only therefore credible, and only therefore adorable. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:45): The simple secret of Cordelia’s nature is that she does not see things from the standpoint of her own gain or loss. She did not beg, she does not bargain. She can give as she could lose, keeping a quiet mind. It is no effort to her to love her father better than herself.…Neither good fortune nor ill can touch Cordelia herself; this is her strength and her weakness. Norwood (1925, pp. 597): She is a woman perfectly ordinary in nature and conduct.…She acts precisely as nine women out of ten would have acted. Ridley (1937, p. 169): She is not a great, and hardly an attractive figure.…She is utterly honest, and she is also somewhat inarticulate. Kellogg (1866, p. 114) and Preston (1869, p. 55) praise her good sense.

Others are more critical of her behavior. For instance, various critics scold her for not speaking more lovingly to her father in 1.1. Thus Gentleman (1770, 1:353) criticizes that unjustifiable, cynical roughness, which Shakespeare has stamped upon Cordelia, in the barren, churlish answer she gives her father. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:54) too finds some little admixture of pride and sullenness in Cordelia’s Nothing. Oechelhäuser (1871; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, pp. 464–5): Cordelia should have yielded to Lear’s bizarre, yet harmless idea of pleasing himself with his children’s protestations of love, and should, as she knew her father, have foreseen the consequences of her refusal to contribute to this pleasure. Following that first, one-sided impulse, she does not do so, and indirectly all the after misery springs from her refusal.…Thus is Cordelia’s death justified. Doyle (1877, pp. 161–2): There is a certain dryness and stoniness of fibre in Cordelia herself, coupled, moreover, with that specially unfeminine quality or non-quality, want of tact. These are deficiencies which hinder us from believing that Shakspere intended Cordelia as a representative of the very highest class of women. She is…[162] a spoilt child. Stockton (1887, p. 495): Cordelia was a virago…almost vulgar. Snider (1877; 1887, p. 162): She becomes uncharitable. She disregards the age, weakness, and temper of her father, and hands him over wholly to the two sisters, whose character she well understands.…As her conduct is undaughterly, so it is unsisterly, when she sarcastically bids farewell to her sister.…Cordelia’s act is thus the source of the terrible calamities which befall Lear and the State; with all her virtues she has not reached the highest, which is charity. But she will reach it, and this is the interest and beauty of her character; she develops. Crawford (1916, pp. 262–83): Sweet and beautiful she is, but obstinate and perverse as well.…[283] She is…manifestly a victim of her own obstinacy.
