Mackenzie (1924, p. 291): She is so wholly engrossed by her own judgment of the situation, her proud refusal to do the smallest thing to put herself on her sisters’ level, that she utterly fails to see it from any other point of view.…She does not pity, because it has never occurred to her to perceive, the horrible sense of being no longer effectual that is one of the tragedies of old age.…A weaker, less fiercely upright woman might have seen it.…But Cordelia…is very much her father’s daughter. Bailey (1929, pp. 174–5): She shows obstinate disagreeableness in 1.1. (P. 175): When led in as a prisoner [in 5.3] she is brief, proud, and bitter. Gerwig (1929, p. 12): However much we may admire her innate and absolute honesty she certainly lacks one of the qualities which constitute woman’s charm—tact. Menon (1938, p. 114) views her as excessively proud in 1.1, more anxious to taunt her sisters and to please the husband she has not yet secured than to answer her father’s question. Haller (1952, p. 16) too sees an initial sin of pride: Cordelia loved her father but loved him less than she loved her own way and hated her sisters. Sewell (1951, pp. 61–2): Is not Cordelia’s conduct—even though, morally, she could do no other—the kind of conduct for which she must go down on her knees and ask forgiveness?…[62] She must ask forgiveness, surely, for taking out on an old man, however silly his game might have been, her disgust with her sisters. Lesser (1970, p. 165) blames her behaving like a spoiled child, and blames her sulkiness and recalcitrance on her unconscious awareness of the excessive, incestuous element in her father’s love.…Had she been more comfortable about her own feelings for her father, which however strong were under firm control, and had she been able to face his love for her consciously and calmly, she would have realized that it would never lead to demands she could not readily and guiltlessly satisfy. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 58 ff.): The critics who found Christ in Cordelia pass over her first mute response, and her next two answers [in 1.1], and explain her concession that she loves according to her bond as a noble transaction.…But the first answers are insistently there; the searcher out of religious parallels should perhaps observe that they are outright denials; and that altogether she denies Lear thrice. No amount of explanation can make anything kind, charitable, or loving of an answer, to the offer of love, of Nothing. Various constructive impulses have been seen in Cordelia [in 1.1]…but if they exist, they are not realized in her own explication of her one-word text. It is cold-blooded.…The quantifier [of love] is Cordelia; she is the one who measures out, so much here, so much there. And as she does, she regresses to self-pity.…[61] In the complex of emotional material in the Cordelia design, then, the feelings of love, kindness, sympathy, all the virtues that later will seem her special property, [initially] hide in her shell of self-involvement.…[81] [Her parting words to her sisters contain] impulses of hostility that only harm [Lear].…A daughter concerned for this father could hardly manage a less effective way of appealing to her sisters to care for him. Berry (1984, p. 427): Cordelia committed the grossest of solecisms in 1.1; she flouts all of the decencies which in aggregate conduce to the decorum of existence. Wawrytko (1986, p. 399): Had Cordelia been aware of the dual demands of love (ai) and respect (ching) comprised by hsiao, a more appropriate, and productive response would have ensued [in 1.1]. Foakes (1993, p. 185): In 1.1, As he is a tyrannical old despot making a nonsense of the idea of love, he deserves her effective rebuke; as he is a pathetic old man and her father, he needs her kindness and love. She claims to speak truth, but ceremonial occasions have little to do with truth; in fact she speaks less than truth in saying she loves her father according to her bond, no[r Q] more, nor less.…She is right and wrong, both true and false at the same time, and more than a little like her father in their clash over the word nothing. Ghose (1993, p. 109): Cordelia’s behaviour in 1.1 shows that she has been waiting for an opportunity to alienate her father, that she has done so in order that she may be disinherited by her father.…She has fallen in love with…the King of France, and is consequently desperate to prevent the perilous event, which could easily transpire, of some chance determining her father to give her away in marriage to…the Duke of Burgundy. Ryan (in Hunter, ed. 1996, 2005, p. xlvi): Her blank refusal to indulge her father’s ploy to bestow on her A third more opulent [92] than her sisters’…evinces an inflexible obstinacy and a presumption of moral superiority.…There is a steely glint of spite in [her] clinical words [at 108–110+1] whose truthfulness cannot disguise their barbed intent to wound.

In contrast, Cavell (1969; 2002, p. 293) defends her behavior in 1.1: The truth is, she could not flatter; not because she was too proud or too principled, though these might have been the reasons, for a different character; but because nothing she could have done would have been flattery—at best it would have been dissembled flattery. There is no convention for doing what Cordelia was being asked to do. It is not that Goneril and Regan have taken the words out of her mouth, but that she cannot say them, because for her they are true (Dearer than eyesight, space and liberty…). She is not disgusted by her sister’s flattery (it’s nothing new); but broken-hearted at hearing the words she wishes she were in a position to say. So she is sent, and taken, away. Or half of her leaves; the other half remains, in Lear’s mind, in Kent’s service, and in the Fool’s love. Likewise Zak (1984, pp. 77 ff.): Playful parody, consummate tact, and secret generosity are…the hallmarks of Cordelia’s controversial behavior in the first scene.…[88] Rather than risk humiliating Lear with the naked truth, she would cloak herself, risk being mistaken for an ungrateful and dishonorable daughter and, thus, raze her likeness but also lovingly refuse to insult Lear’s dignity in his shame.…[89] What Cordelia would have Lear learn through the example of her speech is that while we are powerless to demand or insure love, we can accept this weakness with dignity—without self-contempt—because it always remains in our grand human power to give love. Chakravorty (1990, p. 35) describes her as an existentialist: In 1.1 she is creating her own morality or moral value by her own free choice. She is refusing to allow Essence precedence over Experience.

A number of critics ascribe traits of her character to heredity. Heine (1838; tr. 1891, 1:366): I believe that she is a little self-willed, and this small spot is a birth-mark from the father. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 637): In the milky gentleness of her disposition there is mingled a drop of gall from her father’s obstinacy; by this delicate stroke Shakespeare has linked her to the age and to the family character. Clarke (1863, p. 168): She inherits, in a degree and kind, the self-will and obstinacy of her father. Taylor (1907, p. 218): Her cussedness is explained by heredity. Fijn van Draat (1936, p. 357) also sees the paternal strain in her character as a tragic flaw. Stauffer (1949, p. 195): Cordelia shows…a touch of that pride which makes her her father’s child. Blok (1966, p. 18): She has inherited her father’s stubbornness, his limitless pride, his terrible inability to compromise. See also Idem (1966; 1967, p. 371); and Figgis (1912, p. 273), Hammond (1913, p. 112), Anon. (1944, p. 43). Traversi (1952, pp. 44–6) cites heredity as a virtue rather than a fault: Her insistence upon the bond is affirmed with an unyielding decision that is itself part of the family character (for Shakespeare, although not here primarily concerned with personal motive, is careful to relate the family behaviour to an appropriate psychological explanation).…Cordelia’s behaviour during [1.1], far from reflecting the stubbornness of which she has so often been accused, represents a norm, a plenitude, in relation to which the imperfect or distorted motives of the other members of the family are seen in their evident partiality.…[46] The firmness with which Cordelia clings with unadorned simplicity to the position which she rightly regards as sanctioned by nature is…clearly hereditary. In contrast, Strindberg (1908; 1966, p. 98) emphasizes maternal inheritance, imagining that Cordelia is her mother’s beautiful image which survived her, a palette of pure gold on the black slate, and which the eighty-year-old had seen in his youth with the sharp eyes of love, ripped out, framed, and hidden in his heart!

Some have condemned her for lack of charity. Morris (1957, pp. 142 ff.): In apparently trying to weigh and [143] juggle with imponderables, Cordelia reproduc[es] Lear’s error [of quantifying love]—and…she is doing this deliberately.…[151] The wrath that Cordelia brings down upon herself comes as much from her affront to the dignity of Lear’s soul as from her defiance of his power.…[154] By appearing to set up the value of truth as of more weight than the claims of authority, Cordelia not only implies the slightness of her love for her father, but also asserts that the formality and power in which he takes pride is shallow, if not ridiculous. Roy (1965, pp. 68–9) also sees her as measuring and quantifying love.

She has also been criticized for leading a French army into Britain. Thus Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 637–41) defends the justice of Cordelia’s death by the fact that she attacks England with a French force in order to restore her father. The whole responsibility of this step falls upon her. Snider (1887, p. 198): She brings a French army into England.…She thus assails the highest ethical institution of man—the State; in defending a right, she unwittingly herself commits the greatest wrong. Watt (1908, p. 284): The sacrifice of Cordelia in Shakespeare’s play was demanded by an instinct of patriotism. The soldiers of a foreign kingdom must never tread to victory on our shores. Moulton (1903, pp. 46–7) objects: Cordelia is an innocent victim, not (as commentators have asserted) punished for sin against patriotism.

Critics sometimes find a tragic flaw in her psychology. Bradley (1904, pp. 315–22): An expressiveness almost inexhaustible gained through paucity of expression; the suggestion of infinite wealth and beauty conveyed by the very refusal to reveal this beauty in expansive speech—this is at once the nature of Cordelia herself and the chief characteristic of Shakespeare’s art in representing it.…The devotion she inspires almost inevitably obscures her part in the tragedy. This devotion is composed, so to speak, of two elements, reverence and pity.…The memory of Cordelia thus becomes detached in a manner from the action of the drama. The reader refuses to admit into it any idea of imperfection, and is outraged when any share in her father’s [318] sufferings is attributed to the part she plays in the opening scene.…But Shakespeare’s was the tragic point of view. He exhibits in the opening scene a tragic situation for Cordelia as well as for Lear. At a moment where terrible issues join, Fate makes on her the one demand which she is unable to meet.…In this failure a large part is played by her inability to speak. Tender emotion, and especially a tender love for the person to whom she has to speak, makes her dumb.…But…[320] this dumbness of love was not the sole source of misunderstanding.…[321] Cordelia’s hatred of hypocrisy and of the faintest appearance of mercenary professions…is mingled with…a touch of personal antagonism and pride.…This side of her character is emphatically shown in her language to her sisters in the first scene…and again in the very last words we hear her speak [2947].…[322] Strange last words for us to hear from a being so worshipped and beloved; but how characteristic! (But see Everett (1989, pp. 77–8): Bradley’s distinguished essays on the play have taught generations of readers to believe in a wonderfully wordless Cordelia. But the fact is [78] that the Princess is by nature eloquent; it is Lear who reduces the royally poised woman of [4.3 and 4.4] to something nearer the difficult, though principled and sympathetic, girl of the first Act.) Fleissner (1962, p. 126): Her inability to communicate successfully with Lear at the outset…is a sufficient tragic flaw to motivate her death. Byles (1989, pp. 54–5): While Cordelia unconsciously rejects the incestuous components of Lear’s demands in 1.1, she later, in 4.7 and 5.3, accepts [a] limited psychic space, submitting herself to her old father’s needs.…[Her] inability to maintain a separate, objective identity, one not based on masculine perception and need, leads to her death. Paris (1991, pp. 113–16) calls her a distinct psychological type whose behavior is intelligible in the light of her defense system…a person who cares above all about rectitude and self-respect.…[114] Her fear of incurring self-hate…prevents Cordelia from reassuring her father after he has been hurt and from attempting to assuage his anger.…[116] Her desire for revenge on her father is far more deeply repressed than is Edgar’s. It does not show up in her behavior, except in a few very oblique ways; but it seems to be enacted by the plot, in which Lear is severely punished for what he does to her. Crick (1997, p. 74) sees her as incestuous: Her being is so utterly rooted in and derived from the bond with her father that she cannot acknowledge France or his love.

Other critics reject attempts to find in Cordelia’s character or psychology the cause of her failure to indulge Lear in 1.1. Raleigh (1907, p. 135): It is a character invented for the situation, so that to argue from the character to the plot is to invert the true order of things in the artist’s method. Perkinson (1943, p. 320) too rejects attempts to discover a fault in Cordelia. Likewise Ribner (1960, p. 135): Cordelia cannot be judged by any standards of psychological verisimilitude. The tendency to censure her for her conduct in the opening scene comes from a failure to perceive that she is not a real person, that her function here is a thematic one, to emphasize the nature of the bond which Lear rejects, and not to humour a foolish father as a real daughter might have done. She serves…as a symbol of love and self-sacrifice, a reflection of the love of God.

In contrast to the tendency to idealize Cordelia which dominated earlier criticism of her character, a number of critics in recent decades are quite harsh in their judgment of her. Riemer (1966, p. 36) finds her unimaginative and ineffective…little more than a shadow. Goldberg (1974, pp. 20 ff.): In 1.1, in refusing to have any truck with fiction or a social role based upon it, and acting partly out of an unacknowledged weakness in herself—that is, out of a need to feel and to appear more righteous than her sisters—she succeeds in turning her truth into falsehood…[23] ignoring altogether the unutterable plea for reassurance that prompts such questions as [Lear’s].…There is something wrong with a heart that answers only to the demand rather than to the need (or the love) behind it.…[101] And yet [in Act 4] what she represents is precisely the kind of inner justice, a justice of the heart, that answers to the balance that men are impelled to find, or to make, in acting upon the outward world of nature itself.…[141] She represents a possibility of reconcilement so beautiful, so moving, and so desirable that it is easy to let it swamp our whole consciousness. Real though that possibility is, it is after all only a model, and a miniature one at that, of a fullness of being which eludes everyone else in the play, and which…eludes her as well.…[142] It is so precious for being so rare and fragile, but…it is so fragile because it has to leave so much out.…[143] The art Cordelia represents is one that enables life only by diminishing certain of its possibilities. Habicht (1978, p. 109) describes her as politically counterrevolutionary, a source of suffering to the state. Hays (1979, pp. 100–1): Her love is as petulant and self-centered as Lear’s. There is (p. 101) a certain arbitrariness and a lack of imagination on Cordelia’s part; both of which help to explain…why Cordelia, like Lear, is unfit for the role of reestablishing a legally constituted social order. Berger (1979; 1997, pp. 44 ff.): Cordelia, for reasons of her own—not all of them available to her—accepted Lear’s challenge [in 1.1], asserted her merit over and against his nature-in-her, and by her stonewalling helped him bring on her plight. At the same time she helped Lear commit himself to her sisters’ professed bosoms, after which Lear (with Kent’s aid) worked with Regan and Goneril to bring out the worst in them. Yet nowhere in the play does Cordelia—or do her words—show the slightest recognition of her complicity in the skewing of relationships. Rather, she has a persistent habit of publishing her unpublished virtues.…I find it disarmingly ingenuous that she has to protest she was not blown across from France by political ambition. But I also find a touch of smugness in her echoing the words of Christ (my father’s business), and this is of a piece with other indications in her Dover scenes that she is here as a merciful redeemer, one who was more sinned against than sinning but has forgiven her tormentors and now returns to restore them from their crimes and woes. She joins others in viewing herself this way.…[300] Cordelia…ensconces herself first in a Cinderellan version of the victim’s discourse and later in the discourse of the saintly redeemer; she disowns knowledge of her complicity with great success, and apparently minimal effort. Valesio (1980, p. 45–6) sees her exemplifying the rhetoric of antirhetoric: Cordelia, (p. 46) the good sister, is insincere (if we look at the real politics of the discourse over and against its ideology). For she embodies…a rhetorical strategy…that implies a violation of the framework established by the king.…Thus Cordelia exploits the nostalgia of all of us, the hypocritical readers, for a utopic world of complete sincerity. Halpern (1991, pp. 248–51): Cordelia has more than a little in common with the play’s villainous characters, including her sisters.…[249] Her wounding economy of words foreshadows Goneril’s and Regan’s cruelly rational system of household management; she poses a fundamental challenge to [Lear’s] authority and, moreover, means to do so.…[250] She redoubles [Lear’s grandiose] gesture by depriving herself of a kingdom.… It is…the powerfully aggressive nobility of her gesture that takes the King of France with an unanticipated desire.…What Cordelia does in [1.1] is break the monopoly of the absolutist word-order and thereby release an aristocratic game of challenge and counterchallenge, expense and counterexpense.…Cordelia’s motives, or apparent motives, should not be allowed to conceal the actual result of her actions: she wins a total victory over her father, who by the end of the play is reduced to groveling and self-abasement.…[251] Cordelia…begins more and more to resemble Edmund: like him, she challenges paternal and political authority, and like him she ultimately becomes a military commander. Her role too is to reintroduce the feudal war machine, to break the monopoly of the absolutist word-order, to unleash an atavistic movement in which the values of a militarized aristocracy are revived, even if in tragic form. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, pp. 86–91): Cordelia also shows herself to be jealous.…Indeed, the jealousy she feels toward her sisters has…become nothing less than an idée fixe.…Throughout the tragedy Cordelia appears to show implacable rancor towards [her sisters], and fear, feelings that seem to have their origins in the distant past.…[88] Cordelia’s attention is centered on her sisters and only secondarily on her father, both in the opening scene and in many of her subsequent appearances.…When her sisters show that they are able to satisfy their father’s primitive need for praise and Lear publicly announces that his kingdom is to be divided among his three daughters, Cordelia does something to maintain her privileged place in her father’s heart: she transforms her favored status into negative supremacy. If she cannot have all of her father’s love, she must have all of his hatred.…[90] Essentially, Cordelia appears to have feelings only for her family and regards everybody else with indifference.…[91] [Lines 2379–80] are in fact the crucial key to a full understanding of this character. Her statement is a Verneinung, a negation that reveals the very desire that it seeks to conceal and disown.…Without realizing it, Cordelia admits that blown ambition has led her to take up arms. Kiernan (1996, pp. 112–13): She did not fully capture Shakespeare’s imagination; and the cause of this may be that she is a well meaning woman caught between two eras, belonging in part to them both, and suffering from this, dramatically, more than her sisters do. We first see her as partaking, with the problem play heroines, of a certain angularity, a virtuousness which can only preserve its purity, in a tainted soil, at the expense of some more ingratiating qualities.…We next see Cordelia, now queen of France, leading a French army of invasion into her native land (her royal consort tactfully absenting himself). She is enmeshed now in an older code, on a par with that of the fighting dynasts in the Wars of the Roses.…[113] Cordelia is careful to disclaim any motive of ambition; but she has found her father mad as the vexed sea [2352]: if he is put on the throne she and her husband will be the real power.…It can be no more than a charitable guess if we suppose her conscience to be pricking her for her obduracy in the first scene, and what it has led to; but what she is doing now is worse. For Cordelia as self-serving see also Levin (1994, pp. 208–9). Held (1995, pp. 47–84) defends the excellence of her character from the prejudices of modern critics.

Various critics have described her as a dynamic character, one who develops and changes over the course of the play. See Snider above, . C. F. T. Brooke (1913, p. 96): The Cordelia of the last two acts is a much wiser and nobler character than the self-righteous girl who is so forward at the beginning to defy parental authority and convict parental unwisdom. Bransom (1934, pp. 27–9): At first she is motivated by a strong moral reaction from the life around her, from its flattery, its sordidness, its unchastity, its constant cringing to authority.…[28] This reaction to the things around her had caused her to make a moral code rather harsh and joyless for herself, and rather intolerant and contemptuous of the persons and things from which she was reacting.…[29] When she reappears Shakespeare makes it plain that experience has been at work within the deep places of her heart and has revealed a great love and almost infinite tenderness. Whitaker (Mirror, 1965, p. 238–9): Hard and unyielding in Act 1, by Act 4 she has grown…in the theological virtue of charity or love. Battenhouse (1969, pp. 282 ff.): Cordelia…does not initially understand love as forgiveness. Her behavior in the opening scene’s crisis, while less gravely faulty than Lear’s, is nevertheless allied to his and helps precipitate his hideous rashness. For she too seeks self-justification and acts from a sense of rightness tinged with self-regard.…[296] Cordelia’s subsequent fate in the play is to become (as in Greek legend) a discarded child who is then (figuratively) adopted and raised by a king of another country, after which she becomes (as in Christian legend) an atoning child who goes about her father’s business. Sharma (1975, p. 6): [In 1.1] Cordelia is resentful—a condition which does not admit of the flexibility of mind and ease of manners demanded by social intercourse.…She needs to be schooled by experience both of love and suffering, to win the necessary freedom and poise which alone constitute true sovereignty. Coursen (1976, p. 278): Cordelia…undergoes a change during the play—from truth to love. Garber (1981, p. 24): She is not static; her action in speaking and her willingness to speak [in 4.7] mark a change, if not in her moral rectitude and purity of love, then in her capacity to translate that love into a social act of reintegration.…This ability to come to terms with the world around her, its social necessities as well as its moral issues, demonstrates maturity. Leggatt (1988, pp. 63–6): She too is a developing character. As there are unexpected affinities between Edgar and Edmond [sic], so Cordelia’s development follows a line parallel to that of Goneril and Regan. Her nothing in response to Lear’s demand for a statement of love is in its own way as extravagant, as detached from reality, as her sisters’ elaborate protestations. She too is exaggerating to [64] meet the demands of the occasion. In 4.7 her reply [2833: No cause, no cause.] is in its own way, as absurd and irrational as the cruelty into which Goneril and Regan have fallen.…But this is a saving absurdity. It breaks [66] out of the closed circle of service and reward, crime and punishment.…Though her language is still simple, the Cordelia of Act 4 seems a richer, more extraordinary character than the plain-spoken but cold and prickly girl of the first scene. Linville (1990, pp. 314–15): Cordelia…has an identity throughout the play that is not confined to an allegorical or emblematic one, or to disengaged modes of response appropriate to them.…[315] In part [this] is because what she might become—wife, mother, queen, autonomous voice—is at issue from the play’s outset.…Although many critics have seriously entertained the notion that she exhibits… psychological complexity of character only in the context of her resistance to authority at the play’s beginning, her much reduced opposition to paternal pressure can be seen as what makes her more of a character in Act 5. In contrast, Adelman (1992, p. 125): Insofar as the Cordelia of 1.1 is silenced, insofar as we feel the Cordelia who returns more as an iconic presence answering Lear’s terrible need than as a separate character with her own needs, Shakespeare is complicit in Lear’s fantasy, rewarding him for his suffering by making for him the Cordelia he had wanted all along. Berge (1994, pp. 219 f.) sees a different kind of development, leading in acts 4 and 5 to a striking manifestation of despair. Her last speech (p. 220) reveals a changed Cordelia. The devaluation of divine justice may be a sign that Cordelia is bitter.…It is perhaps feelings of distressing isolation which prompt her to call for the sight of her tormentors. Kahn (2000, pp. 140–1) describes the change in her character as a loss of innocence: She infuses the conventional life within which she finds herself with the erotic passion of her soul. Her love for all is deeply in tension with political obligation, which she seems not to understand at all.…Yet, we are attracted to her love because it combines a kind of childlike innocence with an intimation of universal acceptance. There is, nevertheless, something unstable about this love, located just in its childlike quality. As [141] Cordelia matures into political responsibility, we see this innocent love disappear. To Cordelia’s love of her father at the end of the play, we have to add a new hatred of her enemies.…[151] As she enters politics, her love is no longer innocent.…she wants revenge. Pugliatti (2000, pp. 149 ff.): If we forget that her will has prevailed unhesitatingly in the first scene of the play, we thin out the density of her character, we simplify and soften it: if we forget that Cordelia is, at the beginning, complicit in the situation, we disperse her mystery.…[153] Cordelia’s torment in the first scene of the play originates in the mystery of fatherhood itself, in the enigmatic, ambiguous bond which links fathers and children, in the equivocal alternative between nature and duty which she seems to be unable to either solve or altogether reject.…Her tenderness to Lear [in Act 4], which is usually considered a natural fact, is the outcome of a painful, silent struggle with feelings and language, with emotions and the ability to express them; a struggle which, till the last, she is unable to successfully resolve. Lökse (1960, pp. 134–5) denies that she changes: she is not proud and obstinate in 1.1; (p. 135) Sh. makes her consistent all through the play.

Some proponents of the idea that the Folio text presents Sh.’s revision of the Quarto perceive significant changes in her role. Taylor (1980, p. 31): The Folio…systematically remov[es] verbal and visual reminders of the French presence, so that Cordelia seems to lead not an invasion but a rebellion, like Bolingbroke’s or Richmond’s. Foakes (1993, pp. 110 ff.): The Cordelia of the Folio is a less prominent figure than in the Quarto, but also stronger and tougher, and not likely simply to be thought of as an emblem of holiness and pity. In Act 4, she seems to be (p. 201) in Q an almost holy figure, no longer measuring love according to her bond, but the very emblem of caring pity. F omits the elaborate establishment of a quasi-religious aura about this new Cordelia.…Her presence leading an army [relates] to her boldness in the opening scene, as now Cordelia has made it her business, she says, to restore our aged father’s right [rite F]. Her use of the royal plural is notable.…It would seem that there is after all, and in spite of her denial, some blown ambition [2379] in what she is doing; she is not merely rescuing Lear, but aiming to give him back the power he so abused. It would seem that she is caught up in the confusions caused by her father’s initial act, for here she defends herself as acting out of pity and love, which merge with and at the same time are paradoxically alien to the [202] image of the war she is seeking.…[204] There is an element, unintended on Cordelia’s part, of cruelty about [her reunion with Lear].…[205] [She] is determined not only to restore her father to a life he would be glad to relinquish, but also to restore him to the power and majesty he can no longer command, and has given up.…In seeking to restore him to his right, his rule, by heading an army in battle against the British forces led by Albany and Edmund, she ends by inflicting on him yet more suffering.…[206] Why does Cordelia not simply take him back with her to France? The play does not raise this question, but it does show her determination to seek conflict, to restore Lear to power, and, apparently, to revenge herself on her sisters. See also Idem (ed. 1997, pp. 139 f). Knowles (1999, p. 46) objects: There is simply no evidence that Cordelia is ever a general leading invading troops, or that this soft-spoken girl is more active and warlike in either text.…No explanation exists for Cordelia’s return because Shakespeare intentionally refrained from providing one. See n. 2347+2–+7, 2919.

Other critics discuss Cordelia in relation to feminist issues, including gender and patriarchy. Millard (1989, pp. 144–51): She not only suggests the doomed Virago of Renaissance legends but also assumes the role of the tragic hero.…Cordelia presents a tragic paradigm as a woman who first rejects the self-obliterating role of daughter/mother demanded by her father, only to be defeated later by her attempt of the heroic militant role reserved for the son/father.…[150] Since there is no patriarchal order after Lear’s abdication and subsequent madness, all his daughters’ actions, however motivated, can only [151] contribute to the chaos. Whittier (1989, p. 391–3) describes her as an androgynous figure: In dramatizing Cordelia’s androgynous poise, Shakespeare distances Cordelia the speaker from Cordelia the physical stage presence, presenting her vocally in what is primarily a male mode, but visibly in the female.…In a playworld where being demands speech and speech is masculine, Cordelia’s silence of death is a silence of gender as well: there is no female Redeemer. Rudnytsky (1998–9, p. 302) As the distillation of the patriarchal ideal of femininity, Cordelia is the logical culmination of the misogyny that characterizes all the virtuous male characters in the play. Cox (1998–9, pp. 143–57) discusses Cordelia’s embodiment of virgo and virago topoi derived from both Christian and secular intellectual traditions.…[146] Most significant in relation to the virgo/virago paradigms is Cordelia’s silence.…[149] In refusing to speak as expected she places herself in a twofold position of gendered otherness that reifies the virgo/virago paradigms.…[153] Though curiously asexual in effect and behavior, Cordelia is nonetheless gendered—bigendered, we might say, since she embodies the characteristics of both masculine and feminine.…[155] But, as befits the virgo/virago conventions, Cordelia’s polysemous gender identity is regarded with an uncomfortable ambivalence in the play.…[156] Thus, while Cordelia’s character exhibits a dimension of moral goodness, she nonetheless displays unnatural gender which poses a threat to natural order; her [157] idealized virgo status is reified only in absence of any further speech.…Cordelia is killed off owing to both her womanly and unwomanly goodness.

Others emphasize the political significance of her role. W. Cohen (1985, p. 337): She is figuratively connected to the lower classes.…Through Cordelia’s covert linkages with the lower classes, King Lear also acknowledges the mediating role between elite and popular culture often played by such women.…In Cordelia’s murder sexual and class oppression coalesce. D. Cohen (1993, p. 107) describes her as the leader of an armed revolution against patriarchy. Grady (1996, p. 175): She concentrates and expresses the utopian element of the play’s subaltern resistance but generalizes it, perhaps allegorizes it, putting under erasure, as it were, its specific social markings with her dreamlike reappearance in the play as an empowered queen at the head of a justice-bringing army, a folk-tale-like transformation from her previous departure in disgrace from her father’s Symbolic order.

She has been connected to literary archetypes. Johansen (1972, pp. 120–2), employing a structuralist analysis, finds that the Cor.-figure [sic] unites…three traditions—those of the innocent victim, the magical heroine, and the heroine’s defilement and pseudo-death. Cor.’s death must…be seen as the destruction of one element from one structure in and by its entering into another.…The [121] French camp at Dover… is a crossing point from one universe to another for Cor.; it is precisely in this place she is left by France as the figurative expression of her entrance into the corrupt cosmos. Stated in another way, one can say that she from her static position in the hierarchy goes over to the chaotic universe’s dynamism.…[122] Cor.’s defeat and death mark the dissolution of transcendence through a collision with historicism. Novy (1980, pp. 260–2) discusses her in terms of the problematic image of the woman as actor in Sh.’s tragedies: At first, she exemplifies what Jonas Barish calls the nontheatrical protagonist, characterized by rectitude rather than plenitude.…Cordelia refuses not only to pretend, but also to say anything that might be interpreted as pretense. The kind of acting that she refuses in the first scene is the emotional expression, on cue, of feelings that are really hers. She loves Lear, but she does not want him to control her expression of that love. Later, in 4.3 and 4.4, she also play[s] the role of audience…providing a voice, [262] a mediation for the sympathy of the offstage audience.…In [the] reunion scene [4.7], [Lear and Cordelia] each can be moved by the other, like an audience, and can express feelings, like an actor, in a kind of mutual dependence. But Cordelia reaches Lear here partly because she has proved herself by her earlier refusal to say anything that could be construed as pretense. Mueller (1994, p. 310) calls her a Sleeping Beauty whose death is surrounded by surprise and uncertainty. Miola (1994, p. 339): She is a tragic version of the Italianate woman as wonder common in New Comedic romance. Throughout King Lear Cordelia exhibits the luminous spirituality of those comedic and redemptive figures.

She has also been connected to psychological archetypes. Stockholder (1976, p. 25): On the phantasy level…Cordelia confirms our inarticulate inner goodness and intuitive rightness, the childhood integrity unseen by and unrecognized by parents and the rest of the external world. She suggests pure being, stripped bare (as Lear later attempts to strip himself) of the accumulation of individual traits, all coloured and perhaps produced by the conflicting experience of early childhood. She is totally at one with herself, totally sure of her stance. She also, in the shifting relations of the play, takes on the aura of the good mother, nurturing, open, non-manipulative, as Goneril and Regan take on the overtones of the bad mother, ravenous, manipulative, devouring. Coursen (1984, p. 80): Cordelia would seem to be one of Jung’s introverted irrational types. Irrational here does not connote a value judgment; nonrational or arational might be more precise. Irrational in Cordelia’s case corresponds to intuitive. Adelman (1992, pp. 119–22): As Cordelia is the original site of [Lear’s] vulnerability, only she can serve as reassurance against the dark mother Lear’s rage releases into the play. Physically separated from the place of this mother—the place of the storm—through her long absence, she comes to epitomize the antidote against it; on her return, she is identified as the one daughter, / Who redeems nature from the general curse / Which twain have brought her to [2647–9].…Cordelia can return—can redeem the nature that they [Goneril and Regan as much as Adam and Eve] have cursed—only insofar as she is exempt from the maternal inheritance, in essence remade as the second Eve, the Virgin Mother who can undo harm.…[120] Only thus redefined as the holy mother can Cordelia safely return to love her father all.…[121] But the cost for Cordelia is too high: she can occupy this space, repairing the breach that twain have made, only by sacrificing her own [122] separateness, her own individuality; and Shakespeare makes it plain that this sacrifice is no accident, that it is just what Lear requires. If Cordelia’s insistence on her separateness initially defines Lear’s fall into mortality, his fantasy of recovery requires that she give up her separateness, along with the sexuality that is its sign.

div.head: Cornwall
div.p: Critics generally find Cornwall repellent. Bradley (1904, pp. 298–9): Cornwall seems to have been a fit mate for [299] Regan; and what worse can be said of him? It is a great satisfaction to think that he endured what to him must have seemed the dreadful disgrace of being killed by a servant. He shows, I believe, no redeeming trait, and he is a coward, as may be seen from the sudden rise in his courage when Goneril arrives at the castle and supports him and Regan against Lear [1491–2]. But as his cruelties are not aimed at a blood relation, he is not, in this sense, a monster, like [Edmund, Goneril and Regan]. See also Blaze de Bury (1885, pp. 187–8). Leggatt (1988, p. 47): The evil of Cornwall…is not so much negative as simply weak. His achievements are to put one old man in the stocks, and blind another once he is safely tied up and held down by the servants. Despite Lear’s persistent questions he confesses to having put Kent in the stocks only when Goneril has entered and all his allies are on stage. He needs support.…The more Cornwall parades his strength the more we sense his underlying weakness. Heinemann (1992, p. 80): He is merely the Nazi-type brute.

However, Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:61–2) defends the dramaturgical effectiveness of the role: Cornwall has character in abundance.…He justifies in action and speech Gloucester’s description: [quotes 1367–9]. [62] He is a man, we may suppose, in the prime of life; old enough, at least, to say to Edmund [quotes 1994–5]. He is by no means a stupid man: the cynical humor with which he appraises Kent shows that. He asserts himself against his wife as Albany does not. He can speak up to Lear when need be, but he is not too swift to do it. In his vindictiveness he still keeps his head.…But this hardly makes him the more likable. And though we might allow him some credit for doing his own dirty work, it is evident that he enjoys Gloucester’s blinding, for he sets about it with a savage jest. The taste of blood seems to loose all the wild beast in him; and, like a wild beast, Shakespeare has him dispatched. Yet Cornwall is a forceful character; and there are those who—having no more concern with them than to profit by their forcefulness—can find, strangely enough, something to admire in such men. So he may be allowed a certain dog-toothed attractiveness in performance.

Moseley (1988, p. 75) finds him a tragic figure: In [2.2], we first see Cornwall as a person, green as yet in power. In [3.7]…Cornwall is not only a tyrant but an appalling sadist. And here he ends, killed by his own servant. The two [scenes] together are a play in little—the tragedy of Cornwall, a man released into action by Lear’s repudiation of his obligations, who causes havoc in the name of power, and turns himself from (one presumes) a perfectly acceptable nobleman into a monster.

Bransom (1934, pp. 57 ff.) finds a degree of psychological complexity: Cornwall is interested [in Edgar’s supposed conduct in 2.1] because he is aware that Edgar may have political motives…connected with the dispute between the dukes.…He is something of a bully, and like most bullies a coward.…[58] Loud when there is nothing to be afraid of; cowed in the presence of the king, who was a man of strong nature; grossly cruel to Gloster, [he is] a man of weak nature. The blinding of Gloucester (p. 84) was the result not of his intention but of his own hot and fiery character reacting to circumstances. That reaction was determined probably in the grim recesses of his unconscious mind.…[85] He intended to put Gloster to death.…The blinding was not premeditated. So does Heilman (1948, pp. 250–2), who also relates him to moral themes: In Cornwall we find…the man of reason whose emotions are fatally close to the surface. Spurned emotions ultimately betray all the plotters; but Cornwall has so little control that in a scheming world his survival value is small. Compared with Oswald, of course, he is a man of intellectual stature. In analyzing the type to which he thinks Kent belongs, he shows the same kind of brilliance that characterizes Edmund’s debunking of astrology: [quotes 1170–9]. That Shakespeare gives to characters such as Cornwall speeches which are keenly penetrating rather than shocking or absurd has been noted by various critics. But…such sharp, independent minds, although they are often masterly in the analysis of a situation or of the minds of others or of human types, are incapable of transcending this partial profundity to arrive at an understanding of themselves or at tenable standards of conduct.…[251] His own tendency is to fall in with the casuistry of the usurping sisters; on Regan’s obvious rationalization of letting Lear go out into the stormy night and of barring the castle against him, Cornwall comments My Regan counsels well [1613]. But if Goneril, Regan, and Edmund are ultimately betrayed by lapses from rationalistic standards, they are, compared with Cornwall, models of self-discipline. When any kind of pressure is applied, Cornwall becomes wholly a creature of emotion.…Here is a man of sharp mind appar-[252]ently coming into control of a kingdom: but his own kind of madness betrays him. If Cornwall’s evil is to be defined, like that of Goneril and Regan, as a combination of reason and nature, perhaps we may say that his nature, his impulse, is definable by the modern term sadism. He has a passion for the infliction of physical suffering: thus he symbolizes the appetite for evil generally. In fact, in terms of the play, appetite—man-as-nature, man-as-animal—is appetite for evil; man achieves human goodness when the self is mastered by loyalties and by transcendent insights.

In contast, Mortenson (1965, p. 219) describes him in wholly symbolic terms: Cornwall stands for that state of government in which evil forces find official sanction for their operations, for individual Machiavellian autonomy.

Elton (1966, pp. 293–4): Where Albany is inaction, Cornwall is the fury of the deed itself, a rough beast whose unswerving cruelty, too destructive to survive, comes to deadly use.…[294] Self-consumingly, the fiery Duke [1380] is without issue. Yet for a time he finds a son in Edmund, as Edmund plots against his own father.…That filial relationship is shortly to be dissolved, when, in the exchange of the blinding scene [3.7], Edmund loses his father substitute near the instant that his own father is deprived of his eyes.…Complementary to each other, Cornwall in his outward villainy contrasts with Edmund in his inward Machiavellian guile, as, in effect, the lion with the fox. Indeed, in contrast at least to the initial behavior of the other villains, Cornwall is relatively uncourtier-like and bluntly to the point. Although in this he parallels Kent, Cornwall ironically indicts him as hypocritical.

Kahn (2000, pp. 101–4) focuses on his greatest outrage, the blinding of Gloucester: In 3.7, the issue for Cornwall is France and the coming war.…[104] Cornwall’s error is not in the punishment of Gloucester, but in the conduct of the trial.…Cornwall dies for failing to follow the legal forms of justice, not for doing evil.

div.head: Edgar
div.p: Most early commentators focus on Edgar’s impersonation of Poor Tom, often praising Sh. for distinguishing between Edgar’s feigned and Lear’s true madness. For instance, Warton (1754, p. 274) notes that Tom’s supposed sufferings are enumerated with an inimitable wildness of fancy.…The assumed madness of Edgar and the real distraction of Lear, form a judicious contrast. Likewise Gentleman (1770, 1:361): In all Edgar’s flights, we may most plainly perceive a laboured diffusion of ideas, a methodical strain of images, and a studied wildness, adverting to no particular leading subject; in the execution of this, our author has been amazingly successful, beyond imagination luxuriant. Farren (1833) also discusses Edgar’s role of Poor Tom as a contrast to Lear’s madness. Ray (1847, p. 305): Had it been Shakespeare’s design to represent a case of real demonomania, or of chronic mania [rather than feigned madness], we should unquestionably have had something very different from the part of Edgar. Ross (1867, pp. 37–8): In creating Edgar’s role as Mad Tom, Shakspere has…very happily distinguished the true from the false character.…Edgar’s insanity is…sudden and complete. His feelings do not appear to be touched at all; he is not monomaniacal, and [38] the delirium he affects does not issue from his mind, as in genuine lunacy.…He is, in fact…an imposter, nothing more. See n. 1265 for the suggestion of a historical basis for Poor Tom as recognizable type of character.

When they comment on Edgar’s role in propria persona, early commentators almost invariably find him praiseworthy and admirable, though Tate (1681, p. A2v) expresses unease that Edgar’s Disguise was a poor Shift to save his Life. Hudson (1848, 2:268): Edgar, controlling himself even because of his generosity, is always calm, collected and deliberate.…disguising himself for his own safety, and then turning his disguise into an opportunity of service. See also Idem (1872, 2:383–5). Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 634–6): We see Edgar, Lear’s godson (the poet forgot, in this designation, that these were heathen times), the innocent and pure soul, so far from evil that he suspects none, stirred by no passionate blood, driven by no wild desire like all the rest; he has inherited his father’s mildness, with a nature more calm and a mind far more versatile. Suddenly surprised by ill-fortune…he rapidly resolves with foresight, adroitness, and a skillful compliance with circumstances, to play the part of one of those Bedlam beggars, who in wild attire and with a madness half feigned were accustomed to wander over England. When he first makes his appearance in this condition…he hints that he has been tempted to suicide as his father was afterwards. This trait, as well as his feigned madness, might [635] induce us to believe that we have another Hamlet before us, a good soul who would rather endure wrong than avenge it. But this he is not. There is nothing in the healthy youth of this sickly sentimental nature. As soon as he has seen Lear’s greater misfortune he manfully collects himself, showing himself in this the son of a new and better age, and he is ready as the stronger man to bear his smaller sorrow patiently. He warns himself to be ever circumspect, and to watch the storm of time like a wise pilot. A greater blow awaits him; he meets his blinded father, and becomes convinced of Edmund’s treachery. Even this, instead of overwhelming him, rouses him in contrast to his easily depressed father, to fresh self-command and mastery over his grief and misery.…He is to his father, in himself alone, all that Kent, the fool, and Cordelia are to Lear. All that Kent is, for he is also a disguised and faithful though disgraced attendant; all that the fool is, for he carries on his vocation, playing the fool to sorrow, although, more discerning than the fool, he knows it to be a bad trade, angering itself and others; all that Cordelia is, for he heals the inward despair of his father, like a spiritual comforter. He is, in this age of obstinate and rude characters, the versatile, Odyssean spirit which is never lacking in such heroic times, at once a sufferer and a hero, brave and prudent in the midst of the dangers surrounding him; he grows greater at every step. To play this character a man must be every inch an actor. He changes his part at least six times. At first he is Edgar; then poor Tom; then, forgetting himself while his mind is occupied about his father, he falls somewhat out of his assumed part; after this he describes the immeasurable cliff, as if he stood shuddering on the edge of it; then he is the dweller on the seashore, where Gloster imagines himself to have fallen; then, after the meeting of his father with Lear, he is again another beggar, and before the steward he becomes changed into a peasant; in the lists with Edmund he is an unknown champion; and finally he is himself again. In these various [636] characters he is cunningly circumspect to the extreme; his father, on first meeting with poor Tom, is faintly reminded of his Edgar; then, and whenever the fear of recognition appears greater, his dissembling becomes stronger. But this dissembling is not, therefore, induced by a fear and excitability like Hamlet’s; Edgar goes from his father’s corpse, from Kent’s death-struggle, from emotions the most violent, to do battle with Edmund, and comes off victorious. Endowed with such self-command under sorrow, we feel that Edgar is able to perform the most important services for his father in disguise; he sustains him physically and saves him mentally.…We also, readers and spectators, go away from this accumulation of woe with emotions softened and satisfied. See also Guizot (1852, pp. 219–20); Mézières (1860; 1865, pp. 296–7); and Snider (1887, pp. 186–95), who emphasizes Edgar’s moral development.

Sympathetic accounts of Edgar continue in the 20th century. Many critics emphasize Edgar’s praiseworthy qualities including his mildness, goodness, courage, versatility, piety, intelligence, wisdom, fortitude, and ability to learn and grow. Armstrong (1913, pp. 103–4) is wholly admiring: Edgar is one of those splendid secondary characters in which Shakespeare abounds.…[104] He is not revealed in any one particular scene, nor by his own or anyone else’s actual word of mouth. His actions alone are given to us to judge him by. He is certainly prompt to take action, and discreet with the discretion that is genuinely the better part of valour. The nature of the methods proves his valour. Poor Tom is a-cold. Though pretending to be mad he is not by any means pretending to be cold or to suffer. He shows wonderful wisdom, tenderness, and strength of character. He lies very low, but it is not for the sake of his own skin. He never falters. And his reward is that he is eventually able to close his poor old father’s eyelids in death, to save the remnants of the situation and do some good in this maelstrom of terror and wickedness. Is there not something akin to Hamlet in his pretended madness? But Edgar is more independent. The tragedy does not strike so near home. He can put his antic disposition on or off at will. There is no fear of its becoming a Nessus-shirt. Edgar is the antidote to Lear, the direct opposite. Stone (1925, p. 163) praises his keen insight into the evolution of natural laws. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:58–61): Edgar is a slow starter.…[59] Edmund flashes upon us in pinchbeck brilliance; the worth of Edgar waits discovery, and trial and misfortune must help discover it—to himself above all.…His very reserve at the beginning can give him a stamp of distinction, and should be made to do so. And the notion of that strange disguise would not come, we may say, to a commonplace man. Through the ravings of Poor Tom we can detect something of the mind of Edgar with its misprision of the sensual life—of his father’s life is it? We can certainly see his pitiful heart; this Shakespeare stresses. But only in the soliloquies that end [3.6] and begin Act [4] do we discover the full mind of the man.…[60] We seem to have found the play’s philosopher.…Edgar’s philosophy of indifference to fortune, of patience with life itself, of the good comfort of fellowship, is now, certainly, to dominate the play.…[61] Edgar, in fact, has become a man of character indeed, modest, of a discerning mind, and, in this pagan play, a very Christian gentleman.

Elton (1966, pp. 84–5), likewise finding Edgar to be sympathetic, emphasizes the centrality of the role: If Cordelia is silent and absent, Edgar seems loquacious and ubiquitous, a Proteus with more lines than anyone but the protagonist himself. The most enigmatic character in the play, perhaps, he occupies a role which is far out of proportion to his secondary-plot origin. Last to be introduced, excepting the Fool and Oswald, he is billed on the Quarto’s title-page with the titular hero.…[He] [85] is, for much of the drama, a series of personae. Indeed Poor Tom speaks of having been made to course his own shadow for a traitor [1838]. By the second act, as Mann ohne Schatten and hombre sin nombre, Edgar is involved in a quest for his own identity and, under the newly recognized cosmic dispensation, for that of man himself.

A number of critics emphasize his growth and development. Bradley (1904, pp. 305–7): Of [the] four [extremely virtuous] characters Edgar excites the least enthusiasm, but he is the one whose development is the most marked. His behaviour in the early part of the play, granted that it is not too improbable, is so foolish as to provoke one. But he learns by experience, and becomes the most capable person in the story, without losing any of his purity and nobility of mind.…[306] He is the man on whom we are to rely at the end for the recovery and welfare of the state: and we do rely on him.…There is in Edgar, with much else that is fine, something of that buoyancy of spirit which charms us in Imogen. Nothing can subdue in him the feeling that life is sweet and must be cherished. At his worst, misconstrued, contemned, exiled, under sentence of death, the lowest and most dejected thing of fortune, he keeps his head erect. The inextinguishable spirit of youth and delight is in him; he embraces the unsubstantial air which has blown him to the worst; for him the worst returns to laughter. Bear free and patient thoughts, he says to his father. His own thoughts are more than patient, they are free, even joyous, in spite of the tender sympathies which strive in vain to overwhelm him. This ability to feel and offer great sympathy with distress, without losing through the sympathy any elasticity or strength, is a noble quality, sometimes found in [307] souls like Edgar’s, naturally buoyant and also religious. It may even be characteristic of him that, when Lear is sinking down in death, he tries to rouse him and bring him back to life. Look up, my lord! he cries. See also Watt (1908, pp. 280–1). Heilman (1948, p. 80) too emphasizes his intellectual and spiritual growth: The end of Edgar’s nakedness coincides exactly with his dual change of status with regard to his father: he is now Gloucester’s guardian, and Gloucester knows the truth about him. Both as a man upon whom are thrust the responsibilities of protector and as a son who has regained his father’s love, he gains strength and defenses; he is no longer the unprotected wanderer, so to speak, the Theban, the Athenian, the Persian that Lear had taken him for; spiritually he is again at home in his native country, in his own home. Likewise Gardner (1967, pp. 12, 15): Edgar…gives an immediate impression of weakness and pliability. He allows himself to be bustled off the stage, instead of waiting to confront his father. Against the image of Cordelia refusing Lear what she believes he has no right to ask, and bearing the consequences without flinching, we have the image of an amiable young man, confused by his clever brother’s patter, ignominiously hiding away from the supposed anger of his father.…[15] The transformation of Edgar is striking.…Outcast, he accepts the outcast’s role, and presents to Lear’s eyes the very essence of unaccommodated man, who being stripped of all, knows the secrets of things, Lear’s philosopher. As such he is fit to be a learned justicer and sit with the King, the Fool and the honest man, Caius, on the bench at the trial of Goneril and Regan. He emerges from this a philosopher indeed, the moralist of the play. In contrast, Evans (1979, p. 166): Edgar assumes his lunatic’s role ignorant of the truth, and ignorant he remains during the long period in which he deceives, with his disguise, all those he meets. As proprietor of the play’s most exploitable and most exploited secret, he yet occupies the lowest rung on the ladder of awarenesses.

Other sympathetic critics include Siegel (1955, p. 328): Edgar has learned to understand the meaning of life as a result of the adversity he has faced. Skulsky (1966; 1976, p. 139): In the Dover cliff scene, It is clear that Edgar has delicately honored the sensibility of the man he is trying to teach. Jorgensen (1967, p. 88): Edgar adopts the role of Poor Tom because he apparently…wants to find out what humanity means in a tough world. Stuart (1967, p. 177) emphasizes compassion: However Christian Edgar’s words may sound, he has learned resignation not from any institutional creed, but by looking around him. His moment of truth comes when he sees a fellow human being suffering. Only then does the world come into perspective for him. Dillon (1989, pp. 82 ff.) finds Edgar to be a believable person who grows from fear and shame to chastened power and who also (p. 91) becomes a final fruition of the play’s main theme: that the problem of justice is ultimately a problem of love. Partee (1991, p. 177): We see in detail Edgar’s steady progression towards insight and strength. Aggeler (1993, p. 323): He feels the sufferings of others, and it is this very capacity to feel and pity that accelerates his moral development and makes him capable of exercising what Montaigne would call virtue.

Bradley (1904, p. 306) describes him as religious: He interprets everything religiously, and is speaking [at 3133–4] from an intense conviction which overrides personal feelings. With this religiousness, on the other side, is connected his cheerful and confident endurance, and his practical helpfulness and resource. He never thinks of despairing; in the worst circumstances he is sure there is something to be done to make things better. And he is sure of this, not only from temperament, but from faith in the clearest gods. Similarly Hole (1968, p. 222): Edgar is directly aware of divine intervention in human affairs, carried out by gods, who are not harsh or incomprehensible, but impartially just. In contrast, Elton (1966, pp. 113–14): In Cordelia’s kind gods, Edgar voices no unequivocal confidence, his piety seeming largely filial. Although as Mad Tom he refers to the sweet face of Heaven [1869], echoing Lear’s desperate prayer to the heavens’ sweet sway [1480], the ejaculation is in keeping with the confessional tone of his lunatic speech and his mingled chime of catechism, homilies, and commandments.…Lacking legitimate miracles, [114] Edgar through his sympathy brings the comfort of illusion to the despairing and the suffering. For in the ironic universe of the tragedy life seems made bearable by illusion, as, ultimately, Lear’s death appears attended by illusion. Bevington (1994, pp. 12–14): Edgar shares much of Edmund’s existential view of [13] humanity’s endless capacity for self-deception. Both sons find their father’s superstition hopelessly outdated, even though Edgar remains tolerant of his father’s need for a faith in the gods. We perhaps catch a glimpse of what Edgar thinks of providentialism himself when he arranges a mock suicide for his despairing father.…The phrasing [of 2517–19] does not suggest Edgar’s own belief in divine providence. Religion is instead, for Edgar, something that his father needs, and so the dutiful son creates for him a fiction.…Edgar is like his villainous brother in discounting superstition and in dispelling (for himself, though not for his father) the comfortable illusions with which human beings delude themselves.…[14] His is a Stoic view that refuses to depend on foolish hopes of the gods’ intervention on behalf of the virtuous, though he need not be regarded as a skeptic in the full sense of that term; he acknowledges the gods as a meaningful ideal even while denying any easy notions of providentialism and allowing that what most people mean by the gods is hopelessly superstitious. Edgar is accordingly a useful counterpart not only to Edmund but to Albany and his need to believe in providential vindication.

A number of modern critics find off-putting qualities in the role, finding Edgar to be gullible, self-righteous, moralistic, ineffectual, arrogant, evasive of the truth, manipulative, or power-seeking. Bradley (1904, pp. 305–6) notes in Edgar touches which a little chill one’s feeling for him. [quotes 3131–4] —one wishes he had not said to his dying brother those words about their dead father.…It may be [306] suggested that Shakespeare merely wished to introduce this moral somehow, and did not mean the speech to be characteristic of the speaker. But I doubt this: he might well have delivered it through Albany, if he was determined to deliver it. This trait in Edgar is characteristic. It seems to be connected with his pronounced and conscious religiousness. Haydn (1950, p. 645): One can make an excellent case for his development from a largely good but as yet untried young man to a conscious Stoic philosopher, but Edgar at his best is still a little prissy and self-righteous. Blok (1966, p. 19): See how many arid masks Edgar must change, how much he has to dissemble, how laboriously and…how prosaically he makes his way forward. At the last victory is his, he appears as the avenger of ill deeds; but even here he is not bright and there is no radiance about him; he is just the unknown black knight. Mason (1967, p. 230) objects to his cheap moralizing. Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 282–4): Why does Edgar wait, on seeing his father blind, and hearing that his father knows his mistake, before revealing himself to him?…[283] What Edgar does is most directly described as avoiding recognition.…This links him…to Cornwall and the sphere of open evil. The scene at Dover cliff (p. 284) is not…a picture of mankind making its way up Purgatory [pace Chambers 1940]; for Gloucester’s character is not purified by it but extirpated.…To fill this scene with nourishing, profound meaning is to see it from Edgar’s point of view; that is, avoid what is there. Edgar is Ahab, trying to harpoon the meaning of his life into something external to it; and we believe him, and serve him. He is Hedda Gabler, with her ugly demand for beauty. In the fanciful, childish deceit of his plan, he is Tom Sawyer in the last chapters of Huckleberry Finn, enveloping Jim’s prison with symbols of escape instead of opening the door. To this Foakes (1993, p. 199) objects: In maintaining his disguise he always remains in control of himself, aloof from, and when necessary able to manipulate, the feelings of Lear and Gloucester, and so is able to become an agent of their recovery. Only by avoiding emotional commitment does Edgar remain clear-sighted and become a force for renewal and restitution; this is the main reason why Shakespeare does not permit him to reveal himself to his father until the very end.

Other negative judgments of Edgar include that of Goldberg (1974, pp. 115–21): He is a true member of the Gloucester family, all of whom in one way or another seem insecure and anxious about themselves, and whose characteristic psychic style is defensive beside the bolder, more [116] challenging, self-consciously active style of the Lear family.…[121] Some of the sharpest ironies of the play are reserved for Edgar, almost as if Shakespeare felt slightly irritated by such adept, talkative, but fundamentally self-protective moralism.…Edgar…can see a moral principle in the world all right but no positive principle of human energy.…He is not so much unable to find anything to say, as unable to restrain the impulse to act.…Edgar is the most lethal character in the play. Edwards (1978, p. 122): He too has this tinge of arrogance in assuming the role of providence, he too seems to delight too much in acting, he too seems to believe that men are persuaded more by fiction than by the truth; and the successes which he achieves are ironic and questionable. Kettle (1988, p. 73): The relation between Tom and Edgar remains ill-defined or, rather, too well-defined. Edgar simply pretends to be Tom and then becomes Edgar again. Tom is a richer character than Edgar because he includes Edgar, whereas Edgar doesn’t include Tom. Edgar is not really changed by being Tom, though the play is, through the experiences of Lear and Gloucester. But the Edgar of the last act is essentially St. George, the feudal hero, and he has to be, for he will become king [but see n. 3295]. Only in the last four lines of the play does a doubt creep in and we are allowed to wonder whether Edgar perhaps remembers Tom. Zak (1984, pp. 41 ff.): Edgar’s actions are characterized by avoidance and delay.…[42] If we…compare his burden to Kent and the Fool’s burden of active love, Edgar’s philosophical consolation shades into mere rhetoric.…He does not really know the meaning of the satisfactions of the companionate suffering he speaks of. For Edgar, bearing’s fellowship [cf. 2056+5–10] implies no genuinely communal fellowship but only the self-centered satisfaction of knowing someone is under burdens heavier than one’s own. Though his words speak of it, he does not know the miraculous birth of muted but mutual joy from the ashes of suffering love.…[43] Edgar, though earnestly seeking to do good, merely usurps himself as he persists in playing out a series of needlessly artificial roles rather than simply presenting himself to his father.…[44] [In Act 5] he is apparently so distracted with imagining the orchestration of his own heroic virtue that he has no time for the trifling checks of common sense.…[51] Edgar offers hopelessly simplistic solutions to questions the complexity of which he does not even understand; he is unconsciously intent on himself primarily.…[53] In [Edgar’s last words] he reveals himself as another pretender to kingship.…He ought to remember that words, the tools of creative self-discovery, always prove ineffective shields when used as defense against vulnerability.…[61] In his absorption in his own miseries [in the role of Poor Tom] Edgar is, of course, always unaware that his behavior is but a self-involved parody of those in greater need than he. But that fact should not completely exonerate him from moral culpability in the matter. Though Edgar always acts with conscious generosity, he does so unwittingly in contempt for the man in himself and in others he meets, because, rather than fully participating in their plights, he subtly imposes upon, trifles with, and needlessly bullies those even weaker than himself.…[62] What makes Edgar’s pattern of behavior more exasperating and pathetic than heinous and brings to his wantonness a degree of exculpation is the implicit contempt in which he seems to hold himself.…His central crime, like Lear’s, is a sin against himself. Hattaway (1992, 2:222) condemns the unattractive self-righteousness of Edgar, a man who seems to enjoy mortifying his father. Euridge (1994, p. 65): His attempt to explain the suffering in the play is a means through which he can appropriate power and bolster authority—his trivialization of the suffering in the play is a necessary adjunct to his social and political function.

Some disapproving or ambivalent critics seek deep, often unconscious (and usually unsavory) psychological motives for his actions. Empson (1951, p. 141): I think we are really meant to doubt his sanity.…Perhaps he may have felt that to go on pretending madness was a sort of penance to bring good luck, but one may suspect darker feelings to be at work. After all, his function towards Gloucester is a direct parallel to that of the Fool towards Lear, and the Fool does not neglect his trade of mocking. After Edgar has imposed a false death on the father who has wronged him he describes himself as a sort of grotesque devil. Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 284–5): If one wishes a psychological explanation for Edgar’s behavior, the question to be answered is: Why does Edgar avoid his father’s recognition? Two answers suggest themselves. (1) He is himself ashamed and guilty. He was as gullible as his father was to Edmund’s invention. He failed to confront his father, to trust his love, exactly as his father had failed him. He is as responsible for his father’s blindness as his father is. He wants to make it up to his father before asking for his recognition—to make it up instead of repenting, acknowledging; he wants to do something instead of stopping and seeing. So he goes on doing the very thing which needs making up for. (2) He cannot bear the fact that his father is incapable, impotent, maimed. [285] He wants his father still to be a father, powerful, so that he can remain a child. For otherwise they are simply two human beings in need of one another, and it is not usual for parents and children to manage that transformation, becoming for one another nothing more, but nothing less, than unaccommodated man. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 152–3): Edgar’s madness is not only pretence to foreshadow the reality in Lear; it has its touches of brilliant lunacy, madness in reason, as Lear’s will have its reason in madness. Edgar is like Hamlet in that his ecstasy will sometimes carry him momentarily beyond pretence into the reality of the unreality he pretends.…[153] There is, in the design of Edgar’s restless action, which grows frenetic in Act III, a movement between decisiveness and the irrational. His acts will often be convulsive, while his imagery will be in the direction of repression, punishment, pain, for himself and others. Even his greatest kindliness will be edged with a curious opposite, that, as he will say near the end, he recognizes as a fault. So the design requires him to act under compulsions he does not understand; and their force may be made visual [in 2.3] with a brutal physicality that in the theatre sometimes has been manifested with a painful, masochistic attack on his vanishing self.…[214] His design suggests the undertaking—or enduring—of a process that he will see as a purification, but that must appear ambiguous to an audience.…[246] Those who see Edgar as simply a noble and good son may miss the evident cruelty of his behavior in Act 4 as well as his resistance to insight.…[248] Why does Edgar withhold love, deny his identity, play fool, deprive Gloster of his dream of seeing Edgar in his touch? Blaming himself later—he is a steadfast blamer—Edgar will call it what it obviously is and much more: a fault.…Edgar’s fooling is masochistic as well as sadistic—ang’ring itself and others. Something of the design of Edgar’s complex ambivalence, that will lead him while nursing his father to torture him—and himself.…[266] Certainly impulses to love and support move him; but they seem clouded by motives of revenge and punishment.…Edgar, the actor, indulges the bad trade of playing fool to sorrow. Stockholder (1976, p. 26): Edgar, in adopting the persona of Poor Tom, portrays himself as victim of niggling and humiliating harassments.…The Poor Tom side of himself expresses [the] outrage…of the unswervingly dutiful, but wronged son. He expresses his rage through his role as Tom O’Bedlam, while as Edgar he continues to function as the dutiful son and rational guide to spiritual ends. One might say, however, that he, like Edmond [sic], uses calculating intelligence to express his Oedipal hatred for the father, disguised under the appearance of moral didacticism. In action, his playing with his father’s despair, even though he says that tis done to cure it, takes on the same qualities as Edmond’s manipulation of Gloucester.…[We] are left with a figure who, having split himself in this way, becomes the adult, successor to power. At the play’s end we see him re-introducing the ritual elements that opened the play. This doesn’t bode well for an end of the cycle, for that split in Edgar promises another though lesser Lear to tear the world apart again. Adelman (1978, pp. 3–20): Edgar gains his title as the play’s philosopher not through his immersion in experience but through his attempts to escape from it. He tries more insistently than any other character to gain some distance on suffering, and hence relief from it, by making it conform to a comprehensible pattern. His disquisition on the tendency of things to get better ([2179–92]), interrupted only by the appearance of his newly blinded father, is the extreme example of this attempt and amply illustrates its dangers.…[8] The absolute goodness and nobility of Edgar…has been assumed in much criticism of the twentieth century, perhaps partly because in a play in which the wicked are so palpably and purely wicked, we long to find the good as palpably and purely good.…But Edgar’s absolute goodness can be assumed only at the price of overlooking certain questions raised by his behavior: and our best warrant for overlooking them is a concept [9] of character that allows us to declare that, at certain moments, Edgar takes on an emblematic quality that absolves him from the ordinary responsibilities of human beings.…[11] [However,] Edgar’s status as moral emblem need in no way impair our acknowledgment of his psychological state.…[14] As we watch Edgar becoming Poor Tom, as we watch the enthusiasm with which he embraces the vulnerability and even the self-inflicted pain of Poor Tom, we must feel that Poor Tom serves the needs of Edgar as well as those of the play.…[15] Despite Edgar’s attempt to keep himself separate from poor Tom, the likeness between Edgar and Poor Tom is finally as striking as the difference. For characteristic of both is a passivity, a willingness to see oneself as victim (and indeed to be victim), which borders on the masochistic.…[19] The role of Poor Tom continues to serve Edgar’s needs as long as the knowledge of his father’s anger, and hence his own desire for revenge, continue to make action impossible.…Edgar’s disguises throughout are emblematic partly of Edgar’s own distance from what he can recognize as himself. As he moves from mad beggar to poor man and peasant, then to armed and nameless noble, and finally to the resumption of his own identity, the progression reflects his increasing integration with his own experience and, at the same time, his increasing integration back into [20] the human community. And as he is able to reclaim more of himself, he is able to reclaim more of his father. Berger (1985; 1997, pp. 62–3): To assume the Christlike posture may—since Edgar is not quite Christ—act back on the darker purpose [i.e., unconscious aggression] and intensify it: In view of what I am doing for him, what he has done to me seems worse than ever. Hence the impulse to forgiveness and atonement may converge with a renewed impulse to administer justice. From the cliff scene to his account of Gloucester’s death, Edgar will show that he fully merits the titles bestowed on him by Lear: most learned justicer, robed man of justice.…Edgar had entertained the idea that blindness would be a just symbol, if not a just [63] punishment, for Gloucester’s inability truly to see him. Presumably what he cannot bear about his father’s maimed appearance is his having entertained this idea.…It is the shock of complicity that must have scared Poor Tom out of his good wits and into a bad…trade that may not earn him the release he desires. Hall (1991, pp. 58–60): There is no decisive split…but a recognisable Edgar character, or underlying self, which his various roles subserve.…The divergent roles attest to and serve to develop the Edgar character so that he emerges as a stronger individual, though recognisably the same one, by the end of the play.…[59] Edgar’s role above all suggests the impossibility of knowing and therefore the folly of trying to second guess the divine scheme.…[60] He adopts the manipulative role of providence shaper, a role both coercive and constricting, yet his metamorphosis into the mad and marginal beggar is a creative one.…These two roles [can be seen as] parallel impulses within the Edgar psychology. In this reading the Poor Tom persona springs from Edgar’s almost masochistic sense of being victimised by forces beyond his control…while the providence shaping derives from a contrary impulse: Edgar’s more aggressive need to establish control by demonstrating the operation of a benevolent deity, even if he has to concoct the evidence for it himself. Mirsky (1994, p. 26): The bland, gullible Edgar becomes in his metamorphosis a lewd sexual buffoon, motivated by anger and possible fascination with the sexual indiscretion of his father.

Bloom (1998, pp. 480–4) is unusual in being both psychologistic and sympathetic: Why does Edgar assume the lowest possible disguise? Is he punishing himself for his own credulity, for sharing his father’s inability to see through Edmund’s brilliant deceptions? There is something so profoundly disproportionate in Edgar’s self abnegation throughout the play that we have to presume in him a recalcitrance akin to Cordelia’s, but far in excess of hers.
