Whether as bedlamite or as poor peasant, Edgar refuses his own identity for more than practical purposes. The most extraordinary manifestation of this refusal is his consistent unwillingness to reveal himself to Gloucester, his father.…[482] The play’s central consciousness perforce is Edgar’s, who actually speaks more lines than anyone except Lear.…Edgar, whose pilgrimage of abnegation culminates in vengeance, ends overwhelmed by the helplessness of his love, a love progressively growing [483] in range and intensity, with the pragmatic effect of yielding him, as the new king, only greater suffering.…His final wisdom is to submit to the weight of this sad time [3298], a submission that involves his reluctant assumption of the crown, with the ghastly historical mission of clearing a Britain overrun by wolves [according to legends concerning the historical King Edgar].…Edgar is the center at play’s end, and we [484] can wonder why we are so slow to see that it is, except for Lear, Edgar’s play after all.…[491] Edgar nevertheless emerges impaired from his long ordeal of abnegation. Not least of these impairments is his horror of female sexuality, the dark and vicious place [3133]. A high price has been exacted for the long descent into the sullen and assumed humor of Tom O’Bedlam. The cost of confirmation for Edgar is a savage wound in his psyche.

Critics often find it difficult to see Edgar as an integrated character because he plays so many roles. Some critics see his character developing and growing in understanding through playing these various roles. Peck (1967, pp. 220–36): Edgar’s actions in the play are part of an effort to approach the humanistic questions of man’s identity and meaning in the universe. As such they serve as a foil to Lear’s self-searching.…[222] Unlike Edmund, Edgar learns to use disguises without doing damage to his soul. He is one of few people in the play who learns to see appearances for what they are, and then use them to discover not only his individual identity but also a social identity which is consistent with his individual identity.…[234] In Edgar’s efforts to outface adversity, discover his personal identity, and re-establish his public identity, we see in small part the struggle which Lear himself goes through.…[235] Edgar’s comic pilgrimage…explores and affirms the need for human companionship and mutuality.…Through Christian analogues Shakespeare makes Edgar’s achievement more universal.…Edgar’s comic pilgrimage has a choric function at the end of the play.…[236] Edgar’s comic pilgrimage emphasizes the tragic hero’s greatness, which surpasses the moral categories of good and bad from which men normally evaluate human actions.

Other critics argue that his roles express hidden sides of Edgar’s real personality which are not immediately obvious. S. A. Brooke (1913, p. 203): Edgar is at first the pink of propriety—as admirable in morals as in manners. He would not be out of place in a London drawing-room.…Yet what in him lay unexpressed? All that we listen to from the lips of Poor Tom! In his disguise he lets loose the original thoughts, the unconventional things which his soul had mused on and concealed. Similarly Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:59): Through the ravings of Poor Tom we can detect something of the mind of Edgar with its misprision of the sensual life. Bransom (1934, pp. 102 ff.): Edgar acts the madman badly. He seems, however, to have thought out some method with considerable care. He might almost have read a modern medical treatise on the neuroses.…[104] [The] rake’s progress [described in 1865–79]…has its origins in [Edgar’s] experience.…[209] Shakespeare conceived of him as a man who had at one period of his life indulged in sexual sin, and had turned from it, turned consciously and with effort, setting before himself as the outcome of a bitter experience a new standard of conduct. Mercy and forbearance had a large part in his new code. Feder (1980, p. 133): Edgar’s choice of servingman…as the former occupation of poor Tom and his bitter description of his lust, greed, and deceitfulness, suggest that…he has associated his own plight with episodes of betrayal that he has witnessed in the past.…His own assumed role has made him conscious of the deceits that had been an accepted part of his life at court. Leggatt (1988, pp. 61–3): In his insight that Tom is punishing his own flesh, Lear may have hit on a truth about Edgar. It is not that Edgar has any particular sin to punish himself for; for a chaste and moralising young man the natural feelings of the body are sin enough. And so he creates—and…moralises—the image of a naked madman pursued by demons. Edgar’s concern that the world is just, may have, then, a dark side.…[62] Edgar shows no sign of hating his father; on the contrary. But there is unexpected, self-satisfied cruelty in his reference to the way the gods have punished Gloucester.…[63] We catch glimpses of a dark side to [Edgar’s] virtues: the sense of justice has an edge of cruelty, perhaps even of self-contempt; and the kindness is a way of prolonging suffering. Even the complexity and elusiveness of Edgar make their own point: it is hard to get a fix on the character, hard to be sure of our judgement of him. The sheer variety of his roles…makes him as much a chameleon as Richard III or Iago, and this is odd company to find him in. But Shakespeare may be suggesting that in the treacherous world of this play—which includes the instability of human nature itself—virtue can only survive by constant adaptation. And we may wonder how far it can adapt without betraying its own integrity. Everett (1989, pp. 71–2): At no point does gentle philosophical Edgar wholly lose an effect of impotence, yet Edgar is himself a child of the Court who lives always in Gloucester’s shadow and according to his pattern. Thus throughout the play, and especially in the storm scenes, there glint…fascinating glimpses of some high world that Edgar has left, or Tom dreamed about.…[72] As a result, Edgar’s devil-haunted disguise of Poor Tom in all his nakedness has a curious ersatz quality, sharply contrasted with the pain of Lear’s madness and the grinding truths of the Fool. Like the false disguise of Tom, all these spectres of power—Dauphin, Caesar, the Giant Child Roland—hint perhaps that the ruined worldling cannot become innocent simply by taking off his clothes. Paris (1991, p. 129): The role of Poor Tom allows Edgar to express not only his self-pity and his sense of victimization, but also his feeling of rage. Alulis (1994, p. 378): As Poor Tom, Edgar conveys his ideas of the good and the just by indicting Edmund’s understanding as madness or folly. Parker (1995, p. 114) notes his obstinate-helpless adherence to consciousness, which inhibits the amnesia necessary to the working of romance. Carroll (1996, p. 203): As Poor Tom, Edgar performed the role of suffering and marginalization, but also profoundly experienced it, just as the counterfeit madmen of the period may have feigned self-mutilations that were essentially indistinguishable from the real thing. This disguise is an escape for Edgar, because it saves his life; it is a release for him, because it allows his own bitter fury to be anonymously released through the madman’s voice; it is a deep necessity, because through it he can beg for the love that has been denied him; and finally it is a torment to him, as much the cause as the relief of his suffering. To be dispossessed, to be stripped of all social bonds, to be reduced to the basest and most poorest shape, to surrender one’s body to the winds and persecutions of the sky—this experience of alienation forces Edgar to feel what it must, in part, be like to be his brother Edmund. These half-brothers exchange the voice of dispossession in the course of the play: as Edgar disappears into Tom when Edmund becomes Earl of Gloucester, so Edmund disappears altogether when Edgar becomes Earl of Gloucester. See also Idem (1992, pp. 21–2). Leggatt (1996, pp. 132–3): Though Edgar’s asides keep reminding us of his presence behind Tom, Tom seems to a surprising degree to be a character in his own right.…[133] Edgar creates his role not by going into conventional stage madness but by imitating the real thing.
Other critics argue that his role-playing often serves to serve the needs of the plot rather than revealing Edgar as an autonomous agent acting in character.

For some he serves as teacher or healer to Gloucester, Lear, and the audience. Frye (1967, p. 106): Poor Tom is the providence or guardian spirit that shows Lear the end of his journey to find his own nature. McCullen (1969, pp. 43–9): Edgar is a paradox…an optimist who disguises himself as the most pessimistic figure.…[47] His wisdom is a point of view promulgated by consolation books of the Renaissance: that good and evil are indeed relative and that ultimate evil comes only through despair.…[49] Though [Lear’s] opinion of Edgar seems erroneous, it is correct: the Bedlam emerges as the soundest philosopher in the kingdom. Milward (1977–8, pp. 25–6): As the mad beggar at the heart of the play, Tom…has a triple function, which he largely fulfills by means of soliloquies and asides. The first is…where [26] he welcomes the mad king into his fellowship…and undertakes to initiate him into his Theban or Athenian philosophy. The second is where he performs the same office for his blinded father.…Edgar’s third function as the mad beggar [is] to witness the meeting mad king and the blind father—and the encounter of the two plots of the play. Battenhouse (1979, p. 5): He is Lear’s philosopher…bringing Lear to self-knowledge, by deflating his self-righteous reason and substituting a down-to-earth recognition of human folly, or of the foul fiend that blights human judgment. Idem (1969, p. 297): On Tom there…devolves an opportunity to serve obscurely as his King’s tutor. Coates (1986–7, p. 9): It is not his poverty and physical distress which are the most significant things about Poor Tom, but his spiritual fear and his spiritual need; those assaults by the devil which are evidence to a contemporary of the existence of an absolute evil and its inevitable corollary, an absolute good.…[11] Shakespeare intended Edgar [as Poor Tom] to be seen as a spiritual guide to Lear [as well as to] Gloucester. Schleiner (1985, p. 340–3) relates Edgar’s cure of Gloucester in 4.6 to Renaissance theories of treating the imagination by the imagination and praises (p. 341) Edgar’s ingenuity as a therapist. Butler (1988, pp. 24–5) cites contemporary medical and theological arguments to defend Edgar’s behavior in act 4: contra Rosenberg, We are spectators…of a successful psychodrama, staged by a son for [a] therapeutic purpose…[25] Playing fool to sorrow, and trifling with despair are healing stratagems. He doubts if he can by reason persuade his father to abandon his suicidal despair: so he politickely confirms him in his fantasy the better to fasten his cure upon him. That cure is, of course, theological. Fabiny (1994, p. 469): He is both wise teacher and the devoted doctor of his father.

He is also seen as a chorus, guiding the audience (in its response) as well as his father. Knight (1930, pp. 199 ff.): In the role of poor Tom Edgar enacts the Lear philosophy, expresses its peculiar animal symbolism, and raises the pitch of the madness-extravaganza of the central scenes. Here he acts the appropriate forms which the Lear vision as a whole expresses. His words and actions are therefore most important. So, later, he becomes the high priest of the Lear religion: a voice, a choric moralizer. He has little personality: his function is almost purely symbolical. [200] Thus his slaying of the prim courtier Oswald in his guise of a country yokel with broad dialect (IV.vi) suggests the antithesis between the false civilization and the rough naturalism which are the poles of the Lear-universe. So, also, his challenge of Edmund at the end, suggesting a universal judgement.…[216] Edgar, so often the voice of the Lear philosophy,…in leading his father to suicide, in saving him, and in pointing the moral—in limning his picture of the fiend on the cliff edge, in urging that the gods have preserved him, in all this he is, as it were, the high-priest of this play’s stoicism, of endurance which forbids a facile exit in self-murder. He thus understands his father’s purgatorial destiny, and thus helps to direct it. Elton (1966, pp. 95–8): While the king conducts the protagonist’s business, Edgar is left to voice its developing rationale, feeling. Ironically, only the mad beggar can give adequate expression to the disorder Lear experiences: I will keep still, the king cries, clinging to Edgar, with my philosopher [1959]. [96] Like the Fool, simultaneously involved and disengaged, Edgar humanizes and translates for both characters and audience the almost unbearable suffering. As the Fool strives grotesquely toward the release of laughter, Edgar interposes the solace of tears.…To the spectators the innovation of Edgar’s quick changes, like that of the Fool’s jesting, could have made him more theatrically acceptable. In addition, while the Fool’s quasi-comic viewpoint permits a distancing on pain, Edgar’s sympathetic perspective facilitates the pathos which, according to Walpole, makes a tragic view possible.…[98] In Edgar, the genealogy of the man of feeling recalls Renaissance countercurrents against Stoic rationalism and suppression of emotion. Reibetanz (1977, pp. 110–18): Edgar claims our attention by taking over both the Fool’s role as sympathetic choral interpreter and Edmund’s as chief stage-manager, and as the play progresses we see more and more of its events through his eyes. He witnesses and approximates Lear’s madness on the heath, and deals with Gloucester’s blind despair on Dover Cliffs. Edgar is the only one of the three noble sufferers who establishes a direct relationship with the audience through soliloquies and asides, and he faithfully tries to reckon with the play’s actions and help us to comprehend the Lear world.…[118] [He] does not embody the ultimate vision of King Lear, but he provides us with a perspective on it.…Edgar is our Virgil, the well meaning guide who can take us only to the threshold of the highest truth. Mooney (1985, p. 164): It is Edgar…who…establishes much of the play’s tone, Edgar who serves as the play’s choric voice, Edgar whose experience we emulate in viewing the play. We are, in fact, even closer to Edgar than to Lear. Cartwright (1991, p. 184): Edgar unexpectedly invites [spectatorial engagement]. Edgar’s shallowness, even his own detachment, provide [sic] surprising ground for our engagement with those heroic qualities that he does possess, although heroism in Lear tends to express collective rather than individual attributes. Likewise his penchant for disguise actually confirms the play’s rising action. Seehase (1973) argues that Edgar’s choric speeches express the experience and wisdom of the masses.

Critics also describe him as an actor, a dramatist, or a creative artist. Hunter (1954, pp. 219 f.): Shakspere seems to have conceived for Edgar, as for Hamlet, a sort of self-realization through his skill as an impersonator though Edgar, the great impersonator…[220] is himself, an enigma. Elton (1966, p. 87): Concomitant with his other roles, Edgar, like Hamlet, assumes the role of actor. His entrance is theatrically announced by the malevolently histrionic and truly hypocritical Edmund [quotes 463]. Like Hamlet, too, he assumes an antic disposition and prepares in public to don his Bedlam make-up [1260–3]. On this great stage of fools, Edgar’s play-within-a-play employs theatrical asides, actors’ terms, and quick changes of symbolic garb. His trade plays fool to sorrow [2224]; his tears mar his counterfeiting [2020], and he cannot daub it further [2241]. Moreover, Edgar intensifies the emotional impact by showing it almost break through the limits of his actor’s role as actor. If we consider that actors might be statutory vagabonds and rogues, often shelterless, Edgar’s assumed outcast role and roguish madness [2176+6] foreshadow both Cordelia’s coupling of Lear with rogues forlorn [2787] and the king’s reference to poor rogues [2953].…While he partakes of the chameleon’s dish as actor, he also stage-manages Gloucester’s suicide [4.6] and remains to the end the régisseur of human compassion. For Sahel (1975, pp. 339–44) he is a would-be dramatist attempting to impose artistic order on his world. Bryant (1977, pp. 33–4): There is…an undeniable sense of the role-playing asserting itself through [the] very caricature of madness and through the role-player’s superiority to the situation which is expressed as sheer performance.…The role-playing of Edgar demands to be viewed as a histrionic end in itself.…[34] The mode is the mode of pantomime. Felperin (1977, p. 93): In Edgar’s appearance as Poor Tom and later as unnamed challenger, there is nothing of the groping toward self-definition we associate with Shakespearean tragic role-playing. His roles are as easily and completely put on and off as the costume or visor they depend on: Edgar I nothing am [1272]. They are mere expedients contrived for the temporary purpose of preserving himself, bringing Gloucester through despair to repentance, and recovering his own legitimate rights, and once they have successfully achieved those purposes they are shed as the mere disguises they are. Greenblatt (1985, pp. 175–8), discussing Edgar’s role as Tom in relation to Harsnett’s attack on spurious exorcism, also emphasizes theatricality: Not only is Edgar’s desperation as Poor Tom bound up with the stress of counterfeiting, but (p. 176) in much the same manner as the exorcists’ theatrical suggestion, Edgar tries to create in Gloucester an experience of awe and wonder.…For Shakespeare as for Harsnett this miracle minting is the product of specifically histrionic manipulations; the scene at Dover is a disenchanted analysis of both religious and theatrical illusions. Walking about on a perfectly flat stage, Edgar does to his father what the theater usually does to the audience: he persuades his father to discount the evidence of his senses. In addition, since (p. 178) the fraudulent possession and exorcism are given to the legitimate Edgar, who is forced to such shifts by the nightmarish persecution directed against him, Edgar’s situation has an odd and unsettling resemblance to the situation of the Jesuits if viewed from an unofficial perspective. See also Idem (1986, pp. 340–6) and . Young (1990, pp. 97–8): Edgar is an artist of a kind, making local habitations and names out of airy nothing and warming himself with the energies and inventions of the mind cast into a wilderness of exposure and near-despair.…[98] In a play in which most of the characters are wildly and helplessly expressive with language, showing us their pain, humiliation, malice, and bewilderment, Edgar has more than a modicum of control and purpose. He has what Keats, trying to define Shakespeare’s genius, called negative capability, the capacity for entering into a reality beyond one’s own consciousness. McAlindon (1991, pp. 185–6): Edgar’s art…extends well beyond the care and cure of his father to effect both his own survival and a complete change in the unfolding plot [2725] of the nation’s history. It is associated more with drama than with medicine, its constituent elements being disguise, role play, plotting, and [186]—in the cliff scene—a stunning eloquence. Like drama itself (as understood by most Renaissance playwrights), it is an art whose feigning is ultimately instrumental in disclosing truth.…It should be compared with the art of Camillo and Paulina in The Winter’s Tale and, especially, with that of Prospero in The Tempest. Kahn (2000, pp. 110–11): We can also read the drama Edgar scripts at Dover not as a psychological cure, but as a commentary on political order. Edgar remains disguised because he is creating a political space for Gloucester. All political order…is a matter of roles taken on and played out.…[111] Edgar’s disguise…symbolizes his latent power to reorder the state.…[112] Edgar recreates for Gloucester the divine, mythical foundation of [the political] order.

Other critics, rejecting the idea that Edgar is a consistent character (in contrast to psychologizing critics), ascribe his behavior to his dramaturgical function in providing generic elements of comedy, intrigue, horror, or moral or ironic comment. Thus Wendell (1894, p. 294): Startling as the obvious conclusion may seem, it is unavoidable: the character of Edgar, at least so far as his feigned madness went, was intended to be broadly comic. In this respect, too, it was conventional. Bradbrook (1935, p. 67) discusses Edgar’s impersonation of Poor Tom as an example of a disguised character depersonalized for the sake of the intrigue…to add to the complexity of the emotional structure of the play.…There is no reason for his elaborate practising of his disguise when he is alone with the mad Lear or his blind father. But a madman is needed in the storm scenes, and though the audience’s knowledge that Edgar is not really mad adds to the horror, that is, as it were, one of the calculations in the margin. Lothian (1949, p. 72): The part of Edgar is a great opportunity for a versatile actor, but it is doubtful that Shakespeare conceived the character all of a piece. Kirschbaum (1957, pp. 9 ff.): Edgar is not a mimetic unity; he is a dramatic device. Each of his roles contributes not to a rich psychological unity but to Shakespeare’s poetic purpose.…[10] The role of Poor Tom has four major functions—which are, of course, not mutually exclusive: to provide spectacle, to be a component of Lear’s re-education, to enforce the religious querying running throughout the play, and to contrast with Oswald.…[16] In the Dover Cliff scene, Edgar is not so much Edgar as, literally, a deus ex machina. His rapid assumption of roles in this [17] part of the play tends to obliterate his personal identity. Mack (1965, pp. 61–2): In…Edgar we see a character whose possible Morality backgrounds are…various. His unblinking attitude towards his father’s transgressions and his strict code of retribution, both expressed as his wicked brother lies dying under his judicial hand—[quotes 3131–4]—are less (one must think) characteristics of the solicitous and patient guide of Gloucester and the pitying observer of Lear than necessities of his role as presenter of legitimacy and polar opposite to his brother’s Appetite. On the other hand, in his scenes on the heath as Mad Tom, many of his words and actions relate him to the hero figure of the Moralities after this figure has fallen on evil days and ways. Perhaps this is designed to keep before us the inner metaphysical and moral cost of Appetite while the intervening scenes are exhibiting its gross outer efficiencies in the successful plot of Edmund against his father. At any rate, Edgar is attended by fiends, who have misled him through a partly moralized landscape of fire and famine, bog and quagmire [1833–5], and has been tempted to suicide with knife and [62] halter, as happens often to the Morality hero. Recollections of the Seven Deadly Sins, which he has practiced…and of the Ten Commandments, which he now bids his hearers keep…run through his wild chatter, in which we recognize at some moments the Morality theme of Pride and Corrupt Sensuality turned out of doors to grovel amongst the lowest living things for food…and at other moments the outcast naked wretch who by virtue of total alienation has indeed become the thing itself—the fork’d animal [1888–9], the worm [2217]. Edgar’s career in the play as a whole, especially after he has laid aside his madness, gives him a further kinship to one type of Morality hero—the naïf and dupe who out of deception and harsh experience gains wisdom. Toward the play’s close this pattern becomes insistent. Frye (1953, p. 274) also sees affinities with character types in morality drama: Edgar, with his bewildering variety of disguises, his appearance to blind or mad people in different roles, and his tendency to appear on the third sound of the trumpet and to come pat like the catastrophe in the old comedy, seems to be an experiment in a new type, a kind of tragic virtue, in contrast to Edmund as tragic vice. In contrast to Elton’s emphasis on compassion (above), Stockholder (1968, pp. 58–9) discusses Edgar’s dual role as comic eiron: On one level Edgar replaces Goneril and Regan as eiron. This is hopeful, for as the play’s philosopher he makes explicit one aspect inherent in the eiron’s role—causing his victim first to enact and then to know his own folly so that he may make himself and his world better.…However, this is only half the picture, for Edgar’s disguise…dramatically creates another reality that takes on a force of its own.…[59] As Poor Tom and grotesque fiend he becomes an abstracted and extended version of the heartless comedians Goneril and Regan, and makes explicit another, opposed element inherent in the role of comic eiron as he manipulates Gloucester to expose in action his spiritual error, seemingly for the malicious delight in degrading and ridiculing him. The two elements of the eiron become so polarized that they rack out the play between them rather than merge or cancel each other out. McElroy (1973, p. 158): Edgar can best be regarded as multiple personae rather than a single characterization. Champion (1976, pp. 166–7): The function of Edgar as a stylized character through whom Gloucester is made to articulate his spiritual struggle is in large part similar to that of the Fool.…When he assumes the role of Tom o’ Bedlam, he is—like the [167] Fool—essentially a dramatic device without individual personality. Snyder (1979, pp. 150–2): His disguise as Poor Tom…is… in the comic tradition,…a role assumed for self-protection but functioning as a positive source of new insight. The Bedlam disguise does more than cover Edgar: it possesses him in some way.…[151] There is…a certain wild exuberance in Edgar’s bizarre world-making. It releases something in him even while it expands Lear’s vision and that of the audience.…Edgar gives the impression of reveling in his talents for adaptation and in his growing ability to control situations. Quick changes are an important feature of the manipulator’s stock-in-trade, and this last switch into dialect feels like a direct importation from comedy.…It is easy to recognize in Edgar the virtuosity of the accomplished disguiser and the unrestrained word-spinning of the clown.…[152] He changes from gullible alazon to powerful eiron, and this transformation helps to raise comic expectations about the whole course of the action. Evans (1979, p. 180): At play’s end, we know Edgar not at all; Edgar is a non-entity, whose original dim image has been obliterated by his successive roles. Styan (1979, pp. 130–40): Edgar’s character as the chameleon agent in King Lear is naturally inscrutable; the Edgar who remains when Poor Tom and his successors have been put aside is all but nonexistent.…[140] He has the weakest character and the strongest role in the play. Booth (1983, p. 46): Edgar’s disguises make us uneasy about an identity of which we are certain.…Poor Tom…seems more Edgar’s fellow character than his persona. White (1984, pp. 307–20) Edgar’s role as Poor Tom constitutes almost the major problem of the play. He challenges (p. 309) our notion of character as something already constituted…an anti-tragic belief.…[314] Poor Tom’s significance to the play is far more than that of a disguise figure, because in dramatic terms he has an identity of his own, very differently constituted than Edgar’s.…[318] While remaining only a stage phenomenon—not even a person in the fuller sense that Edgar himself is—he yet makes us feel that we are in contact with a real social victim; a product of particular circumstances.…[320] There is no absolute core of being either to Poor Tom or to Edgar; during the storm this very concept of individual identity has proved subject to violent imaginative metamorphoses, to the extent that the play has seemed to be pointing towards a disturbing (and incipiently modern) notion of subjects being constituted in terms of tragically limited contingencies of the present moment. Murphy (1984, pp. 197–9): The language in single speeches of Edgar need not be taken back to some postulated unity of a coherent psychological self which in turn confers a unity of character upon the speaker and which character in turn must be plausibly motivated by the actions and reactions of the persons of the scene and of the play.…Individual speeches synthesize…a dramatic play of voices, unified by a situation.…The technique governing Edgar’s speeches may be modelled on devices in Harsnett’s Declaration since (p. 198) Edgar is disguised both as a bedlam beggar and as an energumen, one possessed by devils and demons. These two dimensions are essential for the dramatic functions Edgar exercises in these parts of the play. Harsnett’s Declaration, the contemporary literature, and an immense body of careful descriptions of possessed persons emphasize again and again the startling contrast in the voices that characterize these matters. It is this contrast…that is exactly counterfeited by Edgar. His usual expected natural voice is that of Poor Tom, the bedlam beggar’s whine.…[199] Harsnett has delineated the dramatic persona of Edgar/Poor Tom in his account of [the Jesuit Father] Edmunds, who played three parts in one.…Edgar’s passages should establish clearly these three modes of speaking and vocalizing as three distinguishable manners. Mooney (1985, pp. 153–5): Readers who share Professor Cavell’s perspective overlook the functions Edgar performs as a choric character and as the symbolic figure of Poor Tom, preferring to limit their focus to psychological examinations of his realistic persona.…The recognition that Edgar serves multiple functions also implies that he performs his roles from different figural positions in respect to the play’s illusionistic frame. Each of Edgar’s personae, that is, requires a different kind of audience awareness about the relationship among a character and his role(s), his stage position and the play’s modes of presentation.…[154] The three dimensions to Edgar’s role correspond to different figural positions within the play’s illusionistic frame and to different realistic, representative, and choric personae.…[155] The contradictory feelings about Edgar that Stanley Cavell has engendered derive from the failure to distinguish his role as an active participant in the illusionistic action from his function as the symbolic figure of Poor Tom or as a commentator who stands, as it were, outside the play. Smidt (1990, p. 142): Edgar is a nonentity until Act IV and even after that not very credible as a person.…Edgar’s main usefulness is in the scenes with Lear in the storm, where he joins the Fool in a duo of fool and madman, embodying, even allegorising a central theme of confusion and reflecting the mind and behaviour of the King. Then, as he abandons his assumed madness to conduct his father, he turns philosopher and speaks some of the most balanced wisdom of the play. Still there is little preparation for Albany’s praise of his royal nobleness ([3138]): we can only assume that he is being belatedly groomed for the role of ruler which he enters upon at the end of the Folio version. Leggatt (1992, pp. 196–7): There may have been in Edgar’s impersonation [of Poor Tom] an element of play that we miss now.…It is out of Tom that Edgar emerges. That may seem to be putting it backwards, but in theatrical terms we know so little of Edgar before he becomes Tom that Tom is our first and most powerful impression of him; the character we know as Edgar develops later. This means that Edgar, as shape-shifter, is not just an aristocrat driven into poverty but—more powerfully—a figure who rises from humble origins to heroic action.…[197] Like an apprentice hero, he emerges from oblivion to chivalric achievement, acting out the audience’s own romantic fantasies. Miola (1994, pp. 334–5) sees affinities with intriguers of New Comedy. Keyishian (1995, p. 76): Edgar functions as the overall avenger and redeemer in the play.…The nature of his achievement may be illuminated by noting the several qualities and strategies he shares with Hamlet. Both adopt madness as a self-protective disguise; both are forced to work in isolation for long stretches of time; both are driven to severe and illuminating introspection before coming to positions of metaphysical security…from which they may acknowledge and submit themselves to a providence that delivers their enemies intro their hands.

For several critics Edgar and the various roles he plays function as one or more thematic symbols of moral, religious, political, or philosophical ideas. Draper (1945, p. 44) claims that Edgar exemplifies the sanguine humoral temperament. Danby (1949, pp. 189–91): Poor Tom is a highly appropriate congeries of meanings. He is a human bankrupt, haunted by the fiends of past and now [190] meaningless lusts, cast out from society, shut out from the spirit, incapable of regeneration. He is the Courtier-Beggarman who of his corn cries woe: [quotes 1865–78]. As in the Fool’s verse, the imagery of the corrupt affections intertwines with the imagery of corrupt society. Poor Tom is a scarlet sinner, and also a landed gentleman who ran into debt.—All the same, of course, Poor Tom is Edgar in the first of his disguises: a simular of virtue.…For Edgar is the machiavel of patience, of ripeness, of God’s ultimate revenges.…[He] slips from role to role. Poor Tom is followed by the peasant, the peasant by the gentleman, the gentleman by the shining champion, until Edgar is himself again, and, with Kent, is made King of England. The roles in their sequence suggest two things: the singleness of the essential nature of man at every level and in every social function; second, the ability of the seed of natural honesty to quicken in [191] the Beggarman and transform the beggarman into a King. Edgar at the end of the play is the national champion of the Faulconbridge tradition; the kingly nature considered as inherent in the stuff of valiant humanity rather than in any dynastic title to a throne. Ribner (1958, pp. 45, 52): Edgar’s function as Poor Tom is to serve as a visible symbol of man as Lear in his delusion sees him, reduced to the level of a beast.…[52] In his combat with Edmund, Edgar becomes a symbol of divine justice which will triumph over evil and re-assert the harmony of God’s natural order. Idem (1960, pp. 134–5): Edgar is adapted to various purposes in different parts of the play. As Poor Tom he serves as a symbol of man reduced to the level of beast; that he is in disguise symbolically underlines that in reality man is not so. There is no need to search for other reasons for his adoption of this particular disguise. Shakespeare wishes merely to provide a visual symbol of man as Lear in his [135] delusion conceives him to be. As he leads his blind father, Edgar takes on a different role. Here he becomes a symbol of the very opposite of Poor Tom—of human devotion, of those qualities which raise man above the level of the beast and link him to God. As such he is able to teach his father the lessons necessary for his redemption. Finally, in his combat with Edmund, Edgar becomes a symbol of divine justice triumphing over evil to reassert the harmony of God’s natural order.…There is little logic in Edgar’s behaviour from first to last, and that there is but slight psychological consistency in his character is an irrelevant consideration in the total design of Shakespeare’s play. Elton (1966, p. 87): As the protagonists suggest the Renaissance idea of decay, Edgar, alluding to the world’s strange mutations [2191], appears to act out the Renaissance notion of mutability. Kolve (1966, p. 187): Tom is…the central philosophical image of the play, the source of the strongest and deepest affirmations. That is, pity, compassion, duty can grow out of—should grow out from—this recognition of one’s vulnerability within the suffering and the vulnerability of others. In contrast, Hole (1968, p. 223): Poor Tom is a gentleman servant, an upstart, aping the affected manners of a fashionable master, to the Elizabethans a conventional object of ridicule and satire. Blok (1966; 1967, p. 372): Edgar is sacrifice and retribution; by his strength he atones for his father’s weakness. Cohen (1980, p. 115) sees his significance in the play’s representation of the treatment of the poor: Edgar functions primarily to…[connect] Lear’s personal development…to the future of the kingdom. At the beginning of the play, he is a naively ineffectual, though well-intentioned aristocrat. Social conflict within the ruling class drives him to adopt the disguise of a mad beggar, and in the subsequent acts he personally endures the misery of the poor and vicariously observes both the sufferings and the insights of his father and his king. His new understanding enables him to serve…as the worthiest successor to the crown [if he is; see n. 3295]. Edgar’s triumph suggests that at least some small portion of what Lear has come to represent will survive the final catastrophe. Without this limited victory, the ending of the play, with the indiscriminate destruction of good and bad alike, could easily border on absurdity. Chaplin (1969, p. 42): Edgar is another dream-like persona of Lear, overtly disguised, like a dream figure, to represent displaced identity. Flahiff (1974, p. 227) compares him to Hal in 1 & 2 H4 in that he comes to act with cunning and deliberateness reminiscent of Hal’s cunning and deliberateness; and to the historical Saxon king Edgar: Edgar’s succession [promises] precisely those prospects of renewal and consolidation that Sir Thomas Elyot saw realized in the reign of King Edgar, who provides Sh. a literal, factual, historical prototype and source for him. In contrast, Pinciss (1982, p. 88): Edgar is perhaps the most powerful, poignant and comprehensive presentation of the savage man in literature. Adams (1988, pp. 78–86) sees his significance in the role’s suggestions of hope for the future: Edgar’s progress from anonymity to sovereignty suggests that (p. 86) there is a chance that the sick, divided kingdom may be restored to wholeness and the damage wrought by Lear’s initial folly undone. Chakravorty (1990, p. 101): Poor Tom’s most vital part in the play is…[to] establish the [existentialist] philosophy of Lear by externalising it on the stage…that man is…no more than his bare, unadorned self, which means that philosophically and essentially, man is no more and no less than his freedom. Cantwell (1993, p. 31): Edgar’s performance of Poor Tom represents the relation between folklore and official culture. Hawkes (1995, p. 45): Poor Tom would surely have been recognized by the audience as a representation of a well-known bugbear from real life, and at the time the source of periodic bouts of moral panic; one of that band of half-starved, half-crazed figures who were beginning in increasing numbers to gather on the periphery of communities in the early modern period…masterless men. Grady (1996, p. 167–79): Edgar’s (multidimensional, [168] overdetermined) theatricality can be interpreted as an affirmation of the possibility of human change; he is (p. 179) the figure most evocative of human non-essentiality and open-endedness in the play. Berry (1999, p. 161): Edgar’s disguise is additionally intended to evoke a still more archaic or barbarous state of man, before the existence of private property, in which the bareness of ancient British life is combined with images of a British otherworld inhabited by spirits. Burnett (2005, pp. 76–8): Edgar as Poor Tom is enlisted in order to point up how derelictions of duty are revealed in multiple ways and through several identifications and impersonations. Edgar’s rehearsal of his fictive history—[quotes 1865–72]—[77] at once aligns him with a number of errant servant types elaborated in contemporary Protestant polemic.…By implication, social descent and immoral aspiration are clearly tied together, and a basis for vagabondage is furnished in the failing individual rather than the flawed social fabric.…Poor Tom features as a further variation on the likes of Edmund and Oswald, both of whom dishonour service via an unholy dedication to a mistress.…[78] More generally, as befits his function as a servant that concatenates other servants, Poor Tom is tied through excremental imagery to a further tier of monstrosity.

Battenhouse (1969, pp. 294–7) finds a narrative of Christian redemption in Edgar’s career: The naive Edgar…has a touch of his father’s pleasant vices. Though to a lesser degree than his father, Edgar loves too much this present life, is too curious of its secrets, and too eager for the seductive kind of friendship offered by a bastard. Specifically, Edgar unstates himself by listening to Edmund’s astrological lore, and then to Edmund’s proposal that Edgar protect himself against danger, not by seeking reconciliation with the father, but by seeking safety in evasion and masquerade. Such a course of action soon leads to antics very much like those of black magic. However, [296] Edgar decides to put off his old Edgarhood…and to accept instead the lot of a Tom of Bedlam.…[297] His own commitment to humiliation implies on his part a pilgrimage in search of charity. And in this quest his taking on of a disguise role enables him, in actual fact, to work out a kind of penance.…Under [the role’s] surface wildness, Edgar can rehearse (albeit in a heightened and surrealist form) the causes and consequences of his personal folly. Confession in this mode provides medicine for himself and also aids a fellow sufferer, Lear. Furthermore, (p. 276): Shakespeare [may] have patterned his pre-Christian Edgar in the light of…a paradigm [of divine Kingship]. Morris (1985, pp. 147–8) interprets him as a Christ figure: Edgar is Christ champion and ultimately Christ victor. Early in the play he undergoes the mortal ministry such as outlawry…, temptation by the devil…, and passion (at least the scourging and crowning with thorns…). Thereafter, in a way…possibly representative of the Comforter, he works for the salvation of a father [148] deep in despair, and, that completed successfully, he puts on the armor of the church militant to combat the dragon error,…restoring the kingdom to goodness as the last of its forces of darkness expire. Likewise Rice (1984, p. 50): Redemption…is incarnated in Edgar.…[51] In the role of Poor Tom, Edgar is transformed into a man of intuitive faith, living in accord with Christ’s irrationalist counsels. Cheetham (1988, p. 58) also finds him a Christlike figure.…By his self-inflicted and undeserved suffering he atones, at least in part, for the vices of others; he inspires virtuous behaviour in Lear and Gloucester, both of whom take pity on him and are moved to show him particular acts of kindness…; he exemplifies and preaches a philosophy of endurance and trust in God; and finally he leads others to emulate his example. Miller (1993, pp. 27–31): The way in which Edgar humiliates himself, becoming a Bedlam beggar, a wanderer in anonymity on the heath, and undergoes mockery, disdain and humiliation, only to return as this great soldier of Christ at the end, is…unintelligible outside the mesh of Christian iconography.…[31] Not only should we have in mind a Christian image, but also some sort of vision of figures similar to the holy fools in Dostoevsky. Edgar should present a Prince Mishkin-like figure who almost seeks the role which is forced upon him by misfortune.

Some modern critics see significant differences between the Quarto and Folio texts’ versions of the role. Warren (1978, pp. 99 ff.): The part of Edgar is shorter in F than in Q; however, whereas in Q he ends the play a young man overwhelmed by his experience, in F he is a young man who has learned a great deal, and who is emerging as the new leader of the ravaged society.…[105] In Q Edgar remains an immature young man and ends the play devastated by his experience.…In F Edgar grows into a potential ruler, a well-intentioned, resolute man in a harsh world. However, Hamilton (1983, pp. 37 ff.) argues that the capacity of the name Edgar to evoke kingly associations from English and Scottish history means that [35] there is little change in the meanings of the ending in Q and F, both of which promise renewal. Taylor (King Lear: The Date, 1983, pp. 425 ff.), focusing on the Folio’s reassignment of the last speech, argues that Edgar fills the role of chief moral survivor much more comfortably than either Albany or Kent and that (p. 427) in strengthening Edgar the Folio therefore strengthens the promise of moral continuity after the tragedy. In contrast, Weis (ed. 1993, p. 26): Q’s Edgar is a consistently more important part than F’s, particularly in the crucial third act where Edgar appears as Poor Tom. For further discussion of changes in Edgar’s part, see , , , , , , , , , , , , , .

div.head: Edmund
div.p: Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:50–1) influences later critics both in identifying him as the main agent and prime mover of the plot and in proposing psychological motives for his villainy: From the first drawing up of the curtain he has stood before us in the united strength and beauty of earliest manhood. Gifted thus with high advantages of person, and further endowed by nature with a powerful intellect and a strong energetic will, even without any concurrences of circumstances and accident, pride will be the sin that most easily besets him. But he is the known and acknowledged son of the princely Gloster. Edmund, therefore, has both the germ of pride and the conditions best fitted to evolve and ripen it into a predominant feeling. Yet hitherto no reason appears why it [51] should be other than the not unusual pride of person, talent, and birth, a pride auxiliary if not akin to many virtues, and the natural ally of honorable impulses. But alas! in his own presence his own father takes shame to himself for the frank avowal that he is his father—has blushed so often to acknowledge him that he is now braz’d to it. He hears his mother and the circumstances of his birth spoken of with a most degrading and licentious levity—described as a wanton by her own paramour, and the remembrance of the animal sting, the low criminal gratification connected with her wantonness and prostituted beauty assigned as the reason why the whoreson must be acknowledged. This, and the consciousness of its notoriety—the gnawing conviction that every shew of respect is an effort of courtesy which recalls while it represses a contrary feeling—this is the ever-trickling flow of wormwood and gall into the wound of pride, the corrosive virus which inoculates pride with a venom not its own, with envy, hatred, a lust of that power which in its blaze of radiance would hide the dark spots on his disk, [with] pangs of shame personally undeserved and therefore felt as wrongs, and a blind ferment of vindictive workings towards the occasions and causes, especially towards a brother whose stainless birth and lawful honors were the constant remembrancers of his debasement, and were ever in the way to prevent all chance of its being unknown or overlooked or forgotten. Hudson (1848, 2:233–4) follows Coleridge in emphasizing motives of pride and suspicion of contempt (unlike Goneril and Regan, he is not gratuitously wicked): Whatever predisposition he may have towards filial piety is discouraged by his father’s open impiety towards his mother; nay, even his duty to her seems to absolve him from all obligation of gratitude to him: the religious awe with which we naturally contemplate the mystery of our coming hither, and the mysterious union of those who brought us hither, is killed or kept out of his mind by his father’s looseness and levity respecting his birth and her who bore him. Thus the very beginnings of religion are stifled in him by the impossibility of revering his parents. See also Idem (1872, 2:359–63).

Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 632–3): In Edmund, Shakespeare has repeated the main features of Richard III. and Iago.…He invests him with the premeditated wickedness and bitterness of Richard, a bitterness awakened in Richard by disgust at his natural deformity, and in Edmund by annoyance at the defect of his birth and family prejudices. Like Richard, Edmund aspires (and indeed without declaring it) after the prospect which offers itself with regard to the kingdom.…With this far-reaching ambition, Edmund unites Iago’s cold reason and selfish calculation, his realistic free-thinking, his indifference to any means that suit him, his hypocrisy which considers lack of dissimulation as mental weakness, and his perseverance and skill in changing the modes by which he pursues his ends as opportunity serves.…He strides forward throughout with the security [633] of a master-spirit, careless in his open knavery, nay, even straightforward in his artful intrigues.…Success in arms, however, over-elevates him; forgetting his prudence, he ventures to challenge truth and justice in a battle by ordeal, and falls under the avenging sword of his brother. In the dying man one spark of satisfaction is still kindled in the feeling that he was yet beloved; and some pity for Lear and Cordelia is at last kindled within him, though this only in consequence of a casual mention of their names, and, as it were, in spite of his nature; he dies, like Lear’s daughters, obdurate and unrepenting.

Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 265–6) also explain[s] the evil in Edmund’s heart by his resentment of his bastardy: He has been thrown abroad in the world, and is constrained by none of the bonds of nature, or memory, of habit or association. A hard, sceptical intellect, uninspired and unfed by the instincts of the heart, can easily enough reason away the consciousness of obligations the most sacred.…His mind is destitute of dread of the Divine Nemesis. Like Iago, Like Richard III., he finds the regulating force of the universe in the ego—in the individual will.…We can, therefore, in some degree account for Edmund’s bold egoism and inhumanity. What obligation should a child feel to the man who, for a moment’s selfish pleasure, had degraded and stained his entire life? Likewise Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, p. 14): No thinking being, taking Edmund just where he is found, can forget that before one step has been taken a softening veil of charity and tenderest pity is spread before the villany [sic] to be, and we are made to feel compassion before we are allowed to condemn, or to see the wreck of a noble creation warped, tortured by that for which he is not wholly accountable. Snider (1887, p. 141–2): His course and character are simply the logical result of his situation.…All the safeguards which have been [142] built up to protect the individual, as Family, State, Law, are turned to his degradation and destruction. The illegitimate child, therefore, is the natural villain—hostile to the Family, to Society, to Law, to Morality; in him institutions become contradictory to their purpose, and he must bear the sting of their wrong. Littleton (1897, p. 178): Here is the key to his character. He never forgave his father for his birth. Cruelly branded, his high-strung nature felt keenly the injustice of his lot; for he was innocent. The sense of an irremediable wrong embittered him against his race, and, like Ishmael, he felt that every man’s hand was against him and his hand was against every man. The case of Sisyphus was no sadder.

In contrast, White (1877, p. 75) downplays the significance of Edmund’s bastardy: It suited Shakespeare’s plot that the villain should be the bastard; that is all; and Lear’s legitimate daughters Goneril and Regan are as base, as bad, and as cruelly ungrateful as Gloucester’s illegitimate son. Shakespeare knew human nature too well, and handled it with too just and impartial a hand, to let the question of legitimacy influence him one way or another. Stoll (1940, p. 278): He is not ill-treated or impoverished…and his illegitimacy, like that of Don John and others in Elizabethan drama, like Richard’s physical monstrosity and Shylock’s racial one, is meant to be taken as an indication of villainy rather than an extenuation of it. Embittered by the baseness of his birth, he is eloquent in his resentment; but he is cynical and skeptical, vindictive, and cruel, and shows no sign of affection thwarted or blighted. Lökse (1960, p. 110): The notion of any desire on the part of Edmund for revenge for unjust treatment must be dropped.…The driving force in Edmund is cold greed and cold cruelty, not passion.

Some critics express a degree of sympathy for him. Thus Hazlitt (1817; 1930, 4:258–9): The absence of [hypocrisy]…at times reconciles us to him [though see 3.5]. We are not tempted to exaggerate the [259] guilt of his conduct, when he himself gives it up as a bad business, and writes himself down plain villain. (For a contrasting view of Edmund as hypocrite, see Elton [1966, pp. 133–4]: Like a Vice Dissimulation or Faux Semblant, the Machiavellian [134] Edmund panders to Gloucester’s fixed credulity; he is hypocritical, too, in the face of his ally Cornwall [quotes 1979–83].) Mézières (1860; 1865, pp. 299 f.) sees Edmund as less wholly evil than Iago, his crimes motivated always by his ambition. Courthope (1903, 4:162): His nature is not without an element of nobility, which appears in his dying moments. Mackenzie (1924, p. 293): As with Richard, there is something in him almost likeable. One feels that they deserve to die, but is glad that it should be decently, in fight. And one pities them for their courage and for the gaiety with which they defy the isolation of deformity or the bend sinister. Wilson (1929, p. 43) too finds him an engaging character. Lothian (1949, p. 15): He has some right on his side. He is a figure of tremendous force and significance, a type of the rebellious intellect and ruthless will…a prototype of the great figure of Milton’s Satan. See also Swinburne (1902, p. 4).

Bradley (1904, pp. 245 ff.): Edmund, though of course essentially distinguished from Iago, often reminds us of him. However, (p. 300) Edmund is apparently a good deal younger than Iago. He has a lighter and more superficial nature, and there is a certain genuine gaiety in him which makes one smile not unsympathetically as one listens to his first soliloquy, with its cheery conclusion, so unlike Iago’s references to the powers of darkness, [quotes 356]. Even after we have witnessed his dreadful deeds, a touch of this sympathy is felt again when we hear his nonchalant reflections before the battle.…[301] Edmund is an adventurer pure and simple. He acts in pursuance of a purpose, and, if he has any affections or dislikes, ignores them. He is determined to make his way, first to his brother’s lands, then—as the prospect widens—to the crown; and he regards men and women, with their virtues and vices, together with the bonds of kinship, friendship, or allegiance, merely as hindrances or helps to his end. They are for him divested of all quality except their relation to this end; as indifferent as mathematical quantities or mere physical agents.…He preserves this attitude with perfect consistency until the possibility of attaining his end is snatched from him by death.

p.quote: Like the deformity of Richard, Edmund’s illegitimacy furnishes, of course, no excuse for his villainy, but it somewhat influences our feelings. It is no fault of his, and yet it separates him from other men. He is the product of Nature—of a natural appetite asserting itself against the social order; and he has no recognised place within this order. So he devotes himself to Nature, whose law is that of the stronger, and who does not recognise those moral obligations which [302] exist only by convention,—by custom or the curiosity of nations. Practically, his attitude is that of a professional criminal. You tell me I do not belong to you, he seems to say to society: very well: I will make my way into your treasure-house if I can. And if I have to take your life in doing so, that is your affair. How far he is serious in this attitude, and really indignant at the brand of bastardy, how far his indignation is a half-conscious self-excuse for his meditated villainy, it is hard to say; but the end shows that he is not entirely in earnest.

As he is an adventurer, with no more ill-will to anyone than good-will, it is natural that, when he lost the game, he should accept his failure without showing personal animosity. But he does more. He admits the truth of Edgar’s words about the justice of the gods, and applies them to his own case (though the fact that he himself refers to fortune’s wheel rather than to the gods may be significant). He shows too that he is not destitute of feeling; for he is touched by the story of his father’s death, and at last pants for life in the effort to do some good by saving Lear and Cordelia. There is something pathetic here which tempts me to dream that, if Edmund had been home during those nine years when he was out, he might have been a very different man.…[303] Stranger than this emergence of better feelings, and curiously pathetic, is the pleasure of the dying man in the thought that he was loved by both the women whose corpses are almost the last sight he is to see. Perhaps, as we conjectured, the cause of his delay in saving Lear and Cordelia even after he hears of the deaths of the sisters is that he is sunk in dreamy reflections on his past. When he murmurs, Yet Edmund was beloved, one is almost in danger of forgetting that he had done much more than reject the love of his father and half-brother.

div.p: Knight (1930, p. 219): Edmund is a throw-back in the evolutionary process. He is a natural son…a son of nature. He is uncivilized—he rejects civilization because civilization has rejected him. He is unprincipled, cruel, selfish—but he has fascination. He has a kind of sex-appeal about him. Goneril and Regan fall readily before his charm. He is beautiful as an animal, physically a paragon of animals, with an animal’s lithe grace, a cat’s heartless skill in tormenting the weak. Edmund is not cruel: he, catlike, lacks the gift of sympathy. He is playing a game. And he has an impudent charm of conscious superiority and sex-attraction. We cannot resist his appeal—we are glad that so rich a personality meets his end with some dramatic colour. His life he has regulated with a fine theatrical sense, and he closes it with a touch of fine tragedy.…This is a fitting conclusion to the schemes of Edmund; he is, as it were, always trying to stage a combination of events in which he shall figure prominently. He has a sense of his own romantic self-adventure. Witness his exquisite remark to Goneril before the battle [quotes 2293].

Gardner (1967, pp. 12–19): Though a master of duplicity, he must be open and frank with us; and we instinctively respond to any character who takes us into his confidence.…In this play such frankness is almost a passport to the affections; it is a relief as a contrast to [Goneril and Regan].…[13] He has two gifts that charm: gaiety of spirit and humour.…[14] Edmund has the gambler’s temperament; he is fundamentally an adventurer though (p. 15) the gaiety and nonchalance, the wit and gusto, of his first two appearances drop away [in act 3]. When he betrays his father into the hands of Cornwall and Regan he is appalling.…There is no comedy in Edgar’s grim decision [16] to acquaint the Duke instantly of Gloucester’s courtesy to Lear and none in his horrid cant of loyalty when he speaks with Cornwall. He is sickening here as Goneril and Regan are. But at the close distinctions appear again.…Edmund changes sides. He is given a long death scene, in front of the audience, and at the last moment of his life he suddenly does good. He dies with the commandment to save Lear and Cordelia on his lips.…It is a good act, done for no reason; and, like many good acts in this play, it does no good. It is beautiful in itself. Contra Granville-Barker, (p. 17) It is not true that Shakespeare does not prepare us for this moment. Edmund is the one character in the play who is given a long death scene. All the other deaths in the play are sudden deaths and most of them take place off-stage. Edmund’s forgiveness of Edgar is human, generous, and in character.…[19] Shakespeare has throughout softened the character of the bastard son of Sidney’s Arcadia. Edmund’s crimes are at second-hand; he is not shown as cruel and ferocious. We may make excuses for him. He has a motive in his bastardy. He has been abroad nine years when the play opens and he is to be sent abroad again to carve out a career. He is not Edgar’s boyhood companion and Gloucester has been no true father to him. The monstrous passion of Goneril and Regan for him is the first love he has known.

Dean (1977, p. 30) sees a transition from object of a joke to tragic hero. Leggatt (1988, pp. 48–51): His recognition of an opposed scheme of values, and his willingness to pay it the backhanded compliment of irony, show in him a moral awareness that Goneril and Regan lack. Though he has the dangerous attraction of a jungle cat, his appeal is not simply at an animal level. The surprise he holds for us at the end of the play, when he attempts to reprieve Lear and Cordelia, is complementary to the surprise we get from Goneril and Regan. As their self-protective common sense turns to astonishing cruelty, so his predatory selfishness turns in the end to magnanimity. A more conventional playwright would have shown Edmond as a repentant convert. Shakespeare is subtler than that: Edmond’s virtue is of a piece with his evil. The position he aspires to involves not just property but style, and it is one of the play’s more acute social observations that the parvenu takes greater care to behave like a gentleman than do the [49] established aristocrats, who never think twice about such matters. We see this most of all in the last scene, in Edmond’s response to Edgar’s challenge.…[and] in the sporting flourish with which he takes his death.…[51] Through the figure of Edmond we are warned not to be too confident about dividing the characters into good and bad. There may even be a closer relationship between the two brothers than we might at first think.…Each brother is a resourceful improviser, a shape-shifter, a deceiver. Opposed though they are, there is a mysterious rapport between them that works against the division of the cast into black and white teams, and that makes each character more open and dynamic than such a division would allow. Bloom (1989, pp. 77–8): Edmund’s mysterious and belated metamorphosis as the play nears its end [is] a movement from playing oneself to being oneself.…Shakespeare seems to have wished to give us a virtuoso display of his original art in changing character through the representation of a growing inwardness. Outrageously refreshing at his most evil (Edgar is a virtuous bore in contrast to him), Edmund is the most attractive of Jacobean hero-villains, and inevitably captures both Goneril and Regan, evidently with singularly little effort. His dangerous attractiveness is one of the principal unexplored clues to the enigmas of Shakespeare’s most sublime achievement.…[78] The Faustian Edmund is not only overtly Marlovian, but indeed may be Shakespeare’s charmed but wary portrait of elements in Christopher Marlowe himself. Idem (1992, pp. 4–7): Edmund astonishingly combines aspects of the personalities of Faulconbridge and of Don John, though he is even more attractive than Faulconbridge, and far more vicious than Don John of Aragon.…[6] The negation named Edmund is something very enigmatic. Iago’s negative theology is predicated upon an initial worship of Othello, but Edmund is amazingly free of all connection, all affect.…Edmund has no passions whatsoever; he has never loved anyone, and he never will. In that respect he is Shakespeare’s most original character.…He is convinced of his natural superiority, which extends to his command of manipulative language, and yet he is not a Marlovian rhetorician, like Tamburlaine, nor is he intoxicated with his own villainy, like Richard II [sic] and Barabas.…[7] Edmund’s driving force is Marlovian nihilism, revolt against authority and tradition for revolt’s sake, since revolt and nature are thus made one. Revolt is heroic for Edmund.…It is an irony of Shakespearean representation that we like Edmund least when he turns so belatedly towards the good. The change is persuasive, but by it Edmund ceases to be Edmund. Hamlet dies into apotheosis; Iago will die stubbornly Iago, in silence. We do not know who Edmund is, as he dies, and he does not know either. Miller (1993, p. 27): He is in some respects…a Miltonic Lucifer. Hawkes (1995, pp. 21–2) admires his attractive, convention-shattering energy…offer[ing the] audience…a kind of anarchic fellowship.…[22] The story’s clear injunction to us to disapprove of illegitimacy turns out to be drastically at odds with the rhythm, the tone, the gestures, the alliterative and bodily momentum which builds up its overwhelming energy in Edmund’s lines [in 1.2].…Edmund…here speaks powerfully, and literally from the centre of the stage, on behalf of those whom his society wishes to silence, and then marginalize. McFarland (1981, pp. 113–15): He is a figure invested with deep pathos.…[114] It is intriguing that Shakespeare had a brother named Edmund, who also became an actor, and who fathered a bastard son named Edward.…The presence of Edmund and Edward, brother and bastard, in Shakespeare’s familial awareness somehow per-[115]tains to his creation of Edmund and Edgar.

The degree of sympathy critics find for Edmund sometimes depends on their interpretation of his dying speeches, in particular whether or not he repents. McNeir (1968, pp. 188 ff.): The best explanation of Edmund’s delay in attempting to save Lear and Cordelia is in terms of Elizabethan doctrine on the subject of repentance.…[206] When he falls, fatally wounded.…Edmund’s physical crisis rattles his belief in his unholy gods just as suddenly as Gloucester’s blinding destroys his faith in divine providence.…The process of his repentance is clearly marked.…[207] as he gropes his way toward membership in the human community.…[208] [However,] the movement of his mind outward and beyond the self to an expanded sympathy for others halts and turns inward with his vision of a dreadful conjunction, expressed by the archetypal motif of the death wedding, which in this context becomes a mockery of holy matrimony.…[210] Edmund’s homage to [the lust of Goneril and Regan] and his mistaking it for love…transforms his repentance into a travesty of itself.…Edmund fails to save his victims [Lear and Cordelia] because of his stubbornness of heart in yielding to the stirrings of conscience; his incomplete repentance likewise fails to save him because it is unacceptable in the orthodox Elizabethan view. In contrast Matthews (1975, p. 29) describes Edmund as converted and redeemed by love: Edmund’s experience is Lear’s writ small—a movement from pride and stupidity and arrogance and ignorance through personal suffering and awareness of mortality…through compassion and an exploration of the ironies of strict justice, finally into love and an act of repentance. Turner (1988, p. 110): We should perhaps best understand Edmund’s ideology, opposing nature to society and thereby turning Cordelia’s vision upside-down, as a perverse parody of the pastoral fantasy that shapes our romance expectations of the play—the fantasy that the injustices of civilization may be repaired by invoking the ideal equity of nature.…Nothing could be further from the easy certitudes and naive moral reparations of romance than what Shakespeare has made of the traditional romantic pattern of the rise, fall, and death-bed conversion of the villain—for Edmund…is not converted, and he does not repent.…It seems that his one good act will be done to spite himself and the world he has built in the image of his own conception. Waith (1993, p. 158) discusses the sympathy invited for Edmund at his death: The revelation of his vulnerability is potentially moving, not because it offers a psychological explanation, much less a justification, of his villainy, but because it removes him from the stereotype of Vice-figure, diabolically committed to evil. It gives him an individual self which must be acknowledged in its complexity. Kahn (2000, pp. 158–9): Edmund’s recognition that he was beloved…[159] is…a glimmer of the transcendent love experienced by Lear [in Act 4]. In contrast, Boling (1995, p. 9): His dying repentance is a patent fraud.

Some critics emphasize realistic verisimilitude in his psychology. Price (1894, pp. 173–4): Over against this manifold force of intellect, there was, however, one intellectual fault in Edmund, the fault that for the safety of human society is almost always found in men so clever and wicked. He was himself so devoid of real feeling, so incapable of real affection, as to be unable to make the right estimate for their existence and power in others.…[174] And thus, in sheer abuse and disdain of love, he brought upon himself, through the love of these women for him, the turn of fortune that crushed him. Masefield (1911, pp. 192–4): One of the most wonderful and least praised of the inventions in the last scene is that of the dying Edmund.…[193] He can hardly hope to live for more than a few minutes. The death of his last two victims cannot benefit him. A word from him would save them.…Yet at the last minute, his one little glimmer of faithfulness keeps the word unspoken. He is silent for Goneril’s sake. If he ever cared for any one in the world, except himself, he may have cared a little for Goneril. He thinks of her now.…The death of Lear will benefit her. It will be to her something saved from the general wreck, something to the good, in the losing bout. An impulse stirs him to speak, but he puts it by. He keeps silent about Lear, till one comes saying that Goneril [194] has killed herself. Still he does not speak. The news pricks the vanity in him. He strokes his plumes with a tender thought for the brightness of the life that made two princesses die for love of him. When he speaks of Lear it is too late.

Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:56–8): Edmund is, in wickedness, half-brother to Iago. Having no such great nature as Othello’s to work on, Shakespeare has no need of such transcendent villainy; and he lessens and vulgarizes his man by giving him one of those excuses for foul play against the world which a knave likes to find as a point of departure. His first soliloquy is a complete enough disclosure…finer by its surprise for us in the mouth of the modest young man of the earlier scene.…There is a sporting and imaginative touch, perhaps, in the trick that finally gets rid of Edgar.…But for the rest, a strict attention to business, and a quick eye to one main chance after the other, suffice him. And this, really, is almost the loathliest thing about the man. He is (p. 57) snivelingly hypocritical with Cornwall…but once he is in the saddle, and when not one royal lady, but two, have lost their heads over him, what a change!…[58] Ironically patronizing [Albany], he los[es] his head…in the flush of his fire-new fortune. Bransom (1934, p. 205): It is a great mistake to group him with the great schemers like Richard III and Iago. He had just as little nerve to strike Albany as he had to strike his father or his brother. Then two royal ladies fell in love with him, and one [Goneril], whose ambition aimed at the crown of Britain, invited him to share it with her. He again fell to the temptation but had not the force of character to grasp the prize. He doubted, vacillated, hesitated, and was lost. It was the disturbed politics of the time that threw these temptations in his way, but he had not the strength or the ability to avail himself of them. Here, then, is a very commonplace character, very skillfully delineated. Fijn van Draat (1937, p. 183): It is safe to assume that Edmond, who in hardly any respect features his father, reproduces his mother’s character. She must have been a fair, voluptuous, wily, unprincipled, treacherous, ambitious woman, endowed with a powerful intellect and energetic will, but only, as a woman of her class would be, intent on her own advantage; greedy and covetous, not content with her place in society.

Heilman (1948, pp. 236–47, 126–7) describes Edmund as both a libertine skeptic and a reasoner, the possessor of a detached mind, whose thinking demonstrates (p. 237) the coalescence of the two meanings of rationalize. For, whereas Edmund appears, on the one hand, to be disinterestedly seeking a ratio, an intellectually tenable position, with regard to certain facts of experience, it is clear that what he is actually doing, on the other hand, is seeking justification for an emotionally determined course of action: he has already decided to top th’ legitimate [355], and he is seeking a quasi-logical formulation of an emotive commitment. As with the sisters, his mind is reduced to instrument.…[239] Except for the rigor of calculation which excludes every iota of moral concern…Edmund’s deceptive process is not intrinsically brilliant, depending chiefly upon a sure knowledge of the relatively unperceptive individual to be seduced.…[240] The finesse which Edmund exhibits in [his] dealings [with Gloucester and Edgar] is that of what we have come to know as the propagandist—the agent who uses his mind as machinery but is indifferent to the moral quality of his end, who gains technical understanding of how men’s nervous systems function and without scruple manipulates them for pleasure or profit.…[241] With Edmund as with the sisters, the rational prosecution of advantage ironically falls down when the complexity of experience becomes too much for it.…Except for his step against Lear and Cordelia, Edmund the hard schemer has become very ineffectual by Act V.…[244] There are two forces that may be supposed to be influencing Edmund and causing him to lose his original aggressive firmness.…One of these forces is a kind of sentimental vanity or egoism; the other is some latent capacity to respond to traditional appeals—to what Edmund himself calls the plague of custom. Perhaps the latter has also a sentimental cast with him, and what we see in all his final actions is merely the kind of softness that the hard rationalist frequently falls into—and that is quite likely to be mistaken for moral quality. Edmund’s sentimental vanity is suggested by his inability to do anything decisive about the triangle: he cannot give up the role of heartbreaker, one very flattering to an ego which has suffered as much damage as Edmund’s.…[245] Perhaps we should take him at the psychological level and say that his whole trouble is that he has never received love. Under any circumstance, however, we see Edmund overtaken by a force which his view of life could hardly accommodate. One can imagine what the contemptuous iconoclast, who wanted land and power, ought to be saying about the value of the passion of two dead women. The sentimental side of Edmund appears also…in his acceptance of Edgar’s challenge.…[246] In Edmund there is some residuum of traditional responsiveness [to an old code of personal honor].…The unreconstructed remnant of the old order in Edmund comes closest to authentic expression, to winning a pure assent from him, in his agreement with Edgar’s moralizing comment on Gloucester’s adultery…and his further reply [quotes 3135–6], which…is virtually a recantation of his nature credo.…But the sentimental element in Edmund’s bowing the knee to the moral tradition is clear.…[247] He is savoring a feeling, perhaps also enjoying his own death scene.…[126] What is more, there is some evidence that Edmund recants [quotes 3136].…[127] By implication he refutes his own theory—the theory of the man begotten by stealth of nature and therefore naturally licensed to take what custom does not allow him.…He revolts against the implied inevitability of character [of 459–61] and acts in a way contrary to the that I am in which he has believed.

Others who discuss him in terms of plausible psychological motives include Kirsch (1966, p. 205): The fact of his illegitimacy has created a complex in him; and Blok (1966, p. 19): The time and the way he has been brought up…have made of Edmund a cynical free-thinker. Goldberg (1974, p. 74): Even at first glance we surely recognize him as one of that familiar type, the consciously brilliant young man on the make, and the cheap naturalistic commonplaces he flashes about are obviously self-fortifying rationalizations rather than a deeply pondered philosophy that requires all the resources of scholarly criticism (aided, of course, by Shakespeare’s dramatic skill) to expose. What is interesting about them is not their validity or invalidity as beliefs, but the kind of inner weakness that needs them.…[75] As the action unfolds, it becomes clear that, however much Edmund drives his will towards socially acknowledged position and power, it always drives him to self-concealment. He cannot say anything to another person that is not false; more to the point, he is driven to be just as false to himself.…[78] As an element in the over-all design, he is as close to Lear and Cordelia as to Goneril and Regan. Berger (1985; 1997, pp. 58 ff.): As the darkest purpose [i.e., aggression against the self] is displaced from father to son it changes into the melodramatic caricature that confirms Edmund in his fantasy of virile and autonomous villainy. But since he represents so many of his father’s features, we can respond with an oddly pungent mixture of amusement, pity, and apprehension to the profound dependency the caricature betrays. We see that he needs and relies on Gloucester as much as Gloucester needs and relies on him. Edmund’s role as Vice and bravo sits uneasily atop other feelings that derive from his dependence on the father he contemns.…[314] From the beginning Edmund seems bothered primarily by the low social standing, the baseness, of bastards. Parading as nature’s nobleman, he clearly respects the values of the society whose rules he intends to flout.…Far from wanting [315] to tear down the patriarchal order, he would like it to remain alive and well so that, by short-circuiting its legal impediments, he can enjoy its rewards.…[316] The soliloquy that begins with a counter-patriarchal appeal to Goddess Nature ultimately reveals itself as an act of reauthorizing the father. Carroll (1996, pp. 186–97): What Edmund wants to do is become someone else, almost anyone else, because he cannot stand himself. His goal is to become Edgar, and he does, and then he becomes his father as well, dispossessing him as he himself was dispossessed. Edmund therefore does not really want to overthrow the social order.…Instead, he wishes to render the social order arbitrary, dissociated from the order of nature, and to stand where the order of law has instead placed his brother.
