Throughout the play he will speak and write in the stolen or forged voices of his brother and father, endeavoring to replace them by becoming them.…[197] Poor Tom’s sufferings…are Edmund’s as well. Displacement links them together, as does their fate to be nothing more than natural bodies, forbidden by law or culture from any place in the social hierarchy; Edmund’s bastardy and Edgar’s vagrancy are mirrored forms of arbitrary social exclusion. The link between Edmund and Poor Tom is both implicit…and explicit.

Others argue against interpreting him realistically. Wilkes (1877, p. 380): He is made too wicked to be human. Stoll (1940, p. 278): The means whereby he is made acceptable or endurable…are not psychological or sociological; they lie mainly…in the management of the story on the stage and in his eloquence and poetry, his sarcasm and wit. He is not justified or explained, but made interesting, and kept from being repellent. Barnet (1956, p. 16): Strength of intellect is not given to Edmund to make him psychologically consistent, but to lend force and immediacy to the power of evil. Felperin (1977, pp. 93–4): Edmund’s role-playing is…superficial. There is none of that mystery behind his Vice-like plot of ambition and intrigue that there is in the case of Iago, with whom he is often misleadingly equated. Edmund’s motivation is only too clear from the patronizing treatment we see him receive at Gloucester’s hands and from his own soliloquy on his status as bastard. [94] To be a bastard is, as Edmund makes clear, to be superfluous, to have no rightful or legal place within the social structure. He therefore attempts to legitimate himself in the name of an amoral nature that exists prior to social forms, to create a rival structure proceeding from and centered on the self. All this is perfectly logical, as Richard III’s And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover…/ I am determined to prove a villain [R3 1.1.28–30 (30–2)] is logical. But in neither case is it psychological; it points to no hidden depths. Edmund has in fact more in common with such early and morality-derived Shakespearean villains as Aaron the Moor, Don John, and Richard III, who carry around with them an external sign or stigma that serves as badge and pretext of their villainy, than he does with Iago, whose alienation goes deeper and carries no badge, who is at some level a mystery to himself, and whose cultivation of a Vice-like evil can be neither fully explained nor fully demystified. For unlike that of Iago, Edmund’s role can be put off as easily as it was put on: [quotes 3196, 3200–1]. See also . Evans (1979, p. 179): Edmund begins splendidly, but we see the best of him in his first two soliloquies, after which he is a shadowy figure whom we glimpse only occasionally and of whom we hear from time to time as being concerned with neither the mischief that he initiated nor with Lear; and by the time his final purpose is unexpectedly announced at the tag-end of his soliloquy in [5.1], we have to greet him almost as a stranger and a newcomer.

Various critics emphasize his function in the plot rather than his psychology. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 14 ff.): The chief role Edmund will play is the playing of roles.…[87] In the theatre he has been shrunk to a cheerful rascal, carrying the audience lightly with him over even the darker moments. At the other extreme he has been saturnine, scowling, fierce, weighting the play down rather than lifting it along. He has also seemed to be only a put-upon young man, motivated only by the wrongs and deprivations done him; conversely as if acting only out of his own panache, or with a paranoid compulsion. The role demands a very strong, very supple dramatic identity, as supple as Edgar’s. Somewhere in the Bastard’s flamboyance lurks the generosity to make him, dying, do some good; and also the vision that he will realize of absolute power.…He moves with purpose, as the play does, between light and shadow. Barroll (1974, p. 368): If Edmund plays Iago to Gloucester’s Othello, it is interesting to note that, in the tragedy as a whole, Edmund’s structural function is, curiously, to precipitate symbol. He makes possible not a Brutus-like soul-searching, but a poor Tom, as he drives Edgar into exile; he precipitates a blind Cupid as he tricks and betrays his father into mutilating punishment as well as attempted suicide. It is interesting to note this change in structural function for such a tempter-figure. Not stimulating Lear’s character-reactions, he populates the pageantry of the drama, manufacturing material, not for the primary characters, but for those figures whose function may be ethical commentary. Milward (1977–8, pp. 21 ff.): Too much attention has been paid to Edmund’s…emphasis on his bastardy and his peculiar…concept of Nature.…But from the viewpoint of the audience it is more important that…he presents himself as not merely one of the characters in [the secondary] plot, but rather as its stage-manager.…[22] He believes not so much in an abstract Nature as in his concrete self. Smidt (1990, pp. 135–6): Although Edmund comes alive much more vividly than his brother Edgar,…[136] there is really not much use for him between III.v, when he betrays his father to Cornwall, and V.iii, when he dies, and it may be for this reason that he is made to play a part in a subplot involving the rivalry of the two sisters for his love.

Others interpret him thematically, symbolically, or allegorically. Ruggles (1895, p. 197): Edmund, by his dark treachery and great personal beauty is a fitting symbol of the speciousness and villainy of the world. Traversi (1952, pp. 48–9): Edmund’s own declaration of belief in his first speech…shows him to be the enemy, not only of custom, of accepted usage, but—in his own despite—of reason itself.…The connection of rationalism with a disruptive force founded ultimately upon the blood is as clear in Edmund as it was formerly in Iago.…[49] The contrast in terms of linguistic vitality and poetic organization, between the surface energy of Edmund’s utterances and the emotional completeness associated with Cordelia and gradually built up in her by exposure to experience, is essential to the whole play.…Behind Edmund’s apparent self-sufficiency there lies, indeed, a remarkable contradiction. Like Iago, his use of reason, which bears fruit in the seeming rationality of his claim to an unprejudiced reading of experience, is itself a product of the passion which inspires him to revolt against sanctions which have, for him, no relationship to the forces of instinctive life.…Edmund’s philosophy, with its appearance of objectivity covering uncontrolled impulse, is itself a product of the breaking of the bond which led originally to his begetting. A child of Gloucester’s own disordered passion, traces of which survive to undo him in his senility, his destruction of the filial bonds imposed by nature is a consequence of the natural manner of his conception.

Spivack (1958, pp. 413–14) associates him with figures in morality drama: His gay alacrity in deception and dissimulation, the breach his stratagem achieves between father and son, and, beyond anything else, his absolute awareness of the moral [414] position…[are] the evolved product of the Christian homiletic drama. Likewise Mack (1965, pp. 60–1): His name could be Appetite— sprung from his father’s appetite and seeking to devour all that lies in his way: brother, father, mistress, the kingdom itself.…The solid shape under the idiosyncratic accent remains that of the Vice figure of the Morality plays, who confides his scorn to the spectators in a similarly insinuating tone and always [61] identifies himself for them by attacking the moral bases of the life they lead. Seiden (1979, pp. 205–6): Edmund is one kind of Natural; Nature working in its regular fashion has produced the sort of person we might call a superb specimen; he incarnates the amorality of sheer process; his bastardy, symbolic morally of who he is, is biologically symbolic of what he is: elemental vitalism, life staining to create and destroy life.…[206] If for no other reason, Edmund and the Fool are kin in that they exemplify in a pure, unalloyed state the moral natures with which they are endowed. Dachslager (1986, pp. 8 ff.): Shakespeare’s major villains are villains not only or even mainly because of the villainous deeds they commit (the deeds being symptomatic) but rather because of their heretical religious beliefs, more especially their image as infidels.… Edmund is essentially a pagan, a worshipper of false gods.…[9] Edmund is a misbeliever and Goneril and Regan, disbelievers.…[18] He falls in the line [of villainous infidels] established by [Marlowe’s] Barabas and ending with Caliban. Miola (1994, p. 332) discusses Edmund in relation to the conventional characters of New Comedy: see .

A number of critics see him as a representative of modernity, often relating his words and deeds to religious and philosophical heterodoxy. S. A. Brooke (1913, pp. 201–2): Edmund belongs to [the play’s savage] world…but his vices are rather the vices of a civilised society.…Then his repentance is modern. His speeches then seem out of harmony with the general note of the play.…They breathe of the reckless life of that Italy which Shakespeare knew from the stories of the novellisti. Draper (1938, p. 133): Edmund is the personified antithesis of all that was regarded as good in the state, in society and in religion. He is a younger son, and yet in his brother’s life-time usurps his place, and rises almost to the very throne, the seat of God’s Anointed. Yet worse, he is base born. Being a natural son, he takes Nature for his goddess, and so renounces both religion and the laws of human society. With unspeakable impudence, he even calls on the gods to stand up for bastards. He uses witchcraft and astrology and so allies himself with the devil and all his works. James I was especially horrified at witchcraft; and it was generally considered one of the worst of crimes. Bald (1948, p. 347): He is in Renaissance terms a libertine free-thinker, an extreme and dangerous individualist who scorns the conventional restraints and for whom the ordinary bonds of society and morality have no meaning. Ribner (1960, pp. 123–4): The chief symbol of Renaissance scepticism,…Edmund denies the system of correspondences between the mind of man and the phenomena of nature which was so integral a part of the Elizabethan doctrine of order and degree.…[124] It is fitting that Edmund should be a bastard, for, conceived outside of God’s harmonious order with its moral standards, he can deny all benevolent human feelings which are a part of it, proceeding directly from the love of God. Merchant (Sh.’s Theology, 1964, p. 76): Within the larger Lear universe, set within the relative antiquity of early British history, Edmund’s milieu is deliberately contemporary, a conscious anachronism.…Edmund’s beliefs have their source in the political commonplaces of Machiavellian amoralism and in the Pyrrhonism which, rightly or wrongly, the Elizabethans derived from Montaigne. See also Bauer (1968). Danby (1949, pp. 46–50): Edmund belongs to the new age of scientific inquiry and industrial development, of bureaucratic organization and social regimentation, the age of mining and merchant-venturing, of monopoly and Empire-making, the age of the sixteenth century and after: an age of competition, suspicion, glory.…[48] Edmund is the New Man. Shakespeare’s understanding of the type is so extensive as to amount to real sympathy. The insight comes, I think, from Shakespeare’s being in part a New Man himself. This would account for the colour and charm with which he always invests the figure.…[50] Edmund is the last great expression in Shakespeare of that side of Renaissance individualism which has made a positive addition to the history of the West.…But in spite of the attractiveness of the portrait, Edmund still…is a Shakespearean villain. And condemned with him in the apocalyptical judgment of the play is the corrupt society he represents. Elton (1966, pp. 125–36): The raisonneur of rationalism.…[126] Edmund witnesses the Jacobean disintegration of natural law and ethical absolutes.…[127] To this change Edmund, as a confessed naturalist, gives voice; and as a libertine naturalist, despite his pagan devotions to the fertility goddess Natura, he would tend to be considered an atheist.…[128] Edmund is like the Arcadia’s Cecropia, a defender of relative morals and man-made gods.…Furthermore, Edmund’s rebellion is not only against the stigma of bastardy but also, implicitly at least, against the very basis of nobility and monarchy, right by birth and inheritance.…He also impugns the law of primogeniture.…In denying these principles of order, and in stressing conception, rather than birth, Edmund helps demolish the bond, which Lear, in actions as well as words, had already demolished.…[134] Finally…[135] [Edmund’s] concern with honor and chivalry at the combat scene…points to his craving for respectability. His ironically self-preoccupied outcry, at sight of the sisters’ bodies, [quotes 3196], significantly passive, indicates the similar basis of his needs. At the end his single virtue [3052], which he has trusted, fails him; he had staked all against fortune on his solitary and self-sustaining virtù.…[136] Although he musters all his virtù against the misfortune of his coming into the world,…he is conscious of his social exclusion [336–44] and lovelessness [3196]. Sharing the deterministic overtones of the Bastard in [Ado], Edmund might, in one sense, concur with Don John: I cannot hide what I am.…The Bastard, in effect, reveals the paradoxical determinism of the emancipated will. Kozintsev (1966, p. 254) calls him a poet glorying in the might of brigandry. In this, he is a hero of the Renaissance.…He is one of the destroyers of feudal and patriarchal relationships. Vivas (1971, p. 853): Edmund is a thorough Machiavellian, as the term was understood in the seventeenth century—or, rather, popularly misunderstood—as indeed it is still misunderstood among us today. But Edmund’s ruthless immorality did not stem from his belief in a nature that is opposed to the curiosity of nations and the plague of custom.…The heart of Edmund’s view of nature is better described as Hobbesian than as Machiavellian, in spite of the anachronism. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 20): Edmund stands for a whole class of anti-Establishment individualists, who, in every age, are thought to be finding it too easy to pull down the decencies of society. Davis (1974, pp. 47–8): Edmund is indeed in advance of his time, not in the sense that he anticipates some later phase of human progress, but that his type does not usually appear until a more advanced stage of decay has set in. The negative [48] analysis whereby he justifies his schemes is the kind of thinking that is usually caused by widespread corruption. This lends an appearance of righteousness to the apostate’s ideas, which often deceives him as well as those around him. No such corruption exists in the play. Edmund’s negativism is devoid of any pretense that he is turning his back upon a sinful world and seeking blessed freedom from the rules and prohibitions to which men pay lip service only. Dollimore (1984; 2004, pp. 197–201): Like Montaigne, he insists that universal law is merely municipal law. He repudiates the ideological process whereby the latter is misrecognised as the former; he rejects, that is, a way of thinking which represents the contingent [198] as the necessary and thereby further represents human identity and the social world as metaphysically determined (and therefore unalterable).…Yet this revolutionary scepticism is discredited by the purpose to which it is put.…Edmund’s scepticism is made to serve an existing system of values; although he falls prey to, he does not introduce his society to its obsession with power, property and inheritance; it is already the material and ideological basis of that society. Edmund embodies the process whereby, because of the contradictory conditions of its inception, a revolutionary (emergent) insight is folded back into a dominant ideology. Cohen (1985, pp. 331–2): The principal theorist and practitioner in the play of the instrumental reason diagnosed and deplored by the Frankfurt school,…[332] Edmund also derives from the Vice figure of popular dramaturgy and is therefore potentially compatible with a critique of capitalism that sees in bourgeois ideology the enemy of all that makes life worth living.…In this role, then, he performs the traditional task of subverting the serious aristocratic concerns of the play from a popular perspective. Halpern (1991, p. 242): This supposedly proto-capitalist character drives the society of the play not forward into some postfeudal condition but backward into a fully feudalized mode.…Edmund’s dominant role in the play…is not to be midwife to capitalism; rather, it is to reintroduce the feudal war machine and thus fully reconstitute a baronial culture that had degenerated into ceremony and property rights. Euridge (1994, p. 61): It is a mistake to attribute Edmund’s actions to…a psychological preoccupation with his own legitimacy.…Edmund’s bastardy is, both to him and to us, a matter incidental; Edmund does not covet Edgar’s legitimacy but his land, and not land as feudal blazon but as real-estate to be developed—with all the equanimity of a corporate raider. Kahn (2000, pp. 52 ff.): Edmund is a revolutionary.…[53] Recognizing no limits from outside of himself, he would remake the entire world.…Even had he been born with his brother’s birthright, he would still be reaching out for more power. Yet (p. 156) the solitary character of his experience is too insubstantial a thing to rely on in the end [and he sees his fall as divine punishment].…Edmund, stripped of the conventional appearance of success with which he had clothed himself, nevertheless continues to measure himself against that conventional order. He remains deeply of the House of Gloucester. No less than Edgar, he is his father’s son.

Taylor (1980, pp. 33–4) claims there are significant differences between the character in Q and F: In the Quarto Edmund is to a large extent the victim of his own hubris.…In the Folio, Edmund, who dismisses his army so that he can plot with the Captain the murder of Lear and Cordelia, as a result finds himself tactically outmanoeuvred by Albany; he thus has no real choice but to fight. But because he is not self-deluded, the Folio Edmund becomes more [34] dangerous.…Equally important, by making Edmund the victim of a trick, a (theatrical as well as political) coup, the Folio makes him more sympathetic. He is, again, the underdog. Knowles (Merging, 1999, p. 275) answers these claims in detail.

Finally, there are various other interpretations. Draper (1945, pp. 62, 97): Edmund is innately melancholy though he counterfeits a sanguine disposition. (P. 97): This travelled youth should be played as a past master in exotic elegance so combined with an affected modesty as to charm the rough nobility of a barbarous age. Parr (1953, p. 83): Edmund’s career shows him to be in large measure the living embodiment of astral influences exerted by the malignant constellation of Ursa Major. Elton (1966, p. 138) discusses certain affinities between [Sh’s] Edmund and some elements of the seventeenth-century Don Juan tradition. Dumoulié (1994, p. 121): He is Lear’s monstrous double. Both display erotic fury linked to the will to power. (In Fr.) See also Armstrong (1913, 105–6); Matthews (1913, p. 284) for Edmund as a lesser Iago; Anderson (1927, p. 169); Brock (1937, pp. 45–8); Harbage (1947, p. 66); Block (1959, pp. 509–10).

div.head: Fool
div.p: Early commentators betray a sense of unease concerning the role’s challenge to conventional notions of dramatic decorum. Thus Griffith (1775, p. 357) insists on the good sense of Sh.’s fools in contrast to those of modern times. Hunt (1808; 1949, p. 15) approved of Tate’s omitting from the stage the Fool, which is now out of date, though he appreciated the Fool in Lr. as a text for reading (1846, p. 9): The jests of the Fool in Lear are the sighs of knowledge.

Romantic critics generally praise the role for contributing to the pathos of the play rather than merely providing comic relief (though the value of comic relief is defended by Granville-Barker [1927; 1946, 2:50]). Müller (1808, p. 80): The Fool’s role is essential—not to counteract the woe and pain and thus neutralize it, but, rather, to invest the action with tragic dignity. (In Ger.) Coleridge (1811; 1856, pp. 26–7): The contrast of the Fool wonderfully heightens the colouring of some of the most painful situations.…[27] In no instance can it be justly alleged of [Sh.], as it may be of some of the ablest of his contemporaries, that he introduced his fool, or his clown merely for the sake of exciting the laughter of his audiences. Idem (1813; 1960, 1: 56): The Fool [is] no comic buffoon to make the groundlings laugh, no forced condescension of Shakespeare’s genius to the taste of his audiences. Accordingly he is prepared for—brought into living connection with the pathos of the play, with the sufferings. [Quotes 602–3.] The Fool [is] as wonderful a creation as the Caliban—an inspired idiot. Schlegel (1809–11; tr. 1815, 2:145 ff.) defends the Fool in Lr. etc. as providing bold irony and describes him as (p. 205) Lear’s wisest counsellor, as well as a good-hearted fool. Hazlitt (1817; 1930, 4:260) finds a mixture of comic relief and pathos in the Fool, whose well-timed levity comes in to break the continuity of feeling when it can no longer be borne, and to bring into play again the fibres of the heart just as they are growing rigid from overstrained excitement. The imagination is glad to take refuge in the half-comic, half-serious comments of the Fool, just as the mind under the extreme anguish of a surgical operation vents itself in sallies of wit.…In another point of view it is indispensable, inasmuch as while it is a diversion to the too great intensity of our disgust, it carries the pathos to the highest pitch of which it is capable, by shewing the pitiable weakness of the old king’s conduct and its irretrievable consequences in the most familiar point of view. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, p. 198) finds the role profound and sublime: All the profound thoughtfulness of view on which the tragic view of the world ultimately rests, lies hidden in the deep meditative humour of the Fool, against which the tragic form of art is, as it were, broken, in order to display more clearly its inmost core. This genuine humour of the Fool plays, as it were, with the tragical; to it pain or pleasure, happiness or misery, are all the same; it makes a sport of the most heart-rending sufferings and misfortunes of earthly existence; even from death and destruction it can derive amusement. By these qualities he is raised high above this earthly existence; and he has already attained to that elevation of the human mind above all the pursuits or sorrows of this earthly life, which it is the end of this tragic art to set forth, and which is, as it were, personified in him. The humour itself is, in its very essence, the sublime of Comic.

Emphasizing his faithful devotion to Lear, a number of early critics suggest a sentimental view of the role. Thus Horn (1823; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 452): In Shakspeare’s rich gallery of fools, the Fool in Lear is the grandest and most tragic. He has more sense than all the rest of the men in the play put together. His disposition is truly noble and loveable. No one can see more clearly the great weakness of the old king, fast growing childish, than he, but no one can cherish towards him a more faithful love. Wonder not at the many cutting and bitter speeches that he makes; he must say them, for it is his office. We may be sure that he, the wise fool, knows that, in such terrible sufferings as those of the old king, a momentary annoyance is a sort of relief; at all events, far more easily borne than a state of constant depression. Schick (1833; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 453): It is not only his wit, never running dry, although indeed alloyed by many a platitude, nor his invariable good humor and his clear understanding, by which the Fool commands our sympathy, but, in an almost still higher degree, it is the loveableness of his character that interests us. He has pined away—as we learn before he appears—after the youngest of the princesses has gone to France, and has sorrowed the more for what the knight who relates his condition cannot mention to the king, namely, the unhappy circumstances under which the departure of Cordelia has taken place. And how faithfully does he cling to the king in that fearful night, and, by forcing himself to appear merrier than he possibly could be in that condition, try in every way to calm the wild excitement of his master, and lure him from his heartrending, maddening pain at the shameful ingratitude of his degenerate daughters. But the more the Fool is saddened at the sight of Lear’s failing mind, the fewer are his words, until at last the Poet, and with perfect truth, lets him disappear from the scene.…It is highly probably that the Fool’s heart was broken by trouble and grief at Lear’s cruel fate. Hudson (1848, 2:273): He is the soul of pathos in a sort of comic masquerade; one in whom fun and frolic are sublimed and idealized into tragic beauty; with the garments of mourning showing through and softened by the lawn of playfulness.…There is all along a shrinking, velvet-footed delicacy of step in the Fool’s antics, as if awed by the holiness of the ground; and he seems bringing diversion to the thoughts, that he may the better steal a sense of woe into the heart. See also Idem (1872, 2:380–3). Dowden (1875; 1879 pp. 273–4) quotes Hudson approvingly. Hense (1856; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 460): Genuine humour breaks forth only out of a loving heart.…Only in slight allusions does he touch the fault of the king, for roughly to waken up the injury done were the office not of love but of scorn.…As…the old king draws ever nearer to the brink of the abyss, the arrows of the Fool, aimed at the folly of the king, grow fewer, he catches oftener at some harmless, jesting remark, to cheer the suffering of his master, and to lighten the burthen of his own grief. Clarke (1863, pp. 176–9): He is that gracious emanation of all that is gentle, and constant, and cheerful, and true.…In the character of this most illustrious creation we recognise a tender, fondling nature.…[178] The constancy of attachment between the two opposite natures of Lear and his Fool is one of the most masterly, as well as beautiful creations that ever entered the mind of any poet.…The Fool’s own struggles be-[179]tween his heart’s sadness and his duty’s jesting, form one powerful self-contrast; and the way in which Shakespeare has used this humour of the Fool, as a forcible heightening of the mournful and the tragic in the play, forms another. There is an admirable poetic harmony in the jarring of the Fool’s words against the old king’s words, with the tumult of the elements, and the fearful moral discord that reigns through all. No one but so great a genius as Shakespeare would have dared to place the grotesque levity of the Fool’s expressions against the sublime of Lear’s passion. He knew that they only served to render more terrible that storm of grief in appeal, with their affecting attempts at pleasantry in the midst of distress. Their very license makes them only the more startling in their effect of forced mirth, as the poor Fool labours to out-jest his master’s heart-struck injuries. Idem (1873, pp. 398–400): Fidelity of attachment is at the root of the fool’s philosophy.…[399] It is the spirit of affectionate attachment which causes him to try and divert Lear’s thoughts when he perceives them to be dwelling with too-late remorse and awakened truth of perception.…[quotes 898–916] [400] This principle of fidelity in attachment is finely sustained throughout the tragedy, as compensating counterpart to the cruelty and self-will which form its mainspring of passion and character. Hetherington (1879, p. 732): He is a half-mad, half-inspired child of Nature, giving up his heart, nay, his life itself, in a love that was very precious. The infinite tenderness of the Fool is perhaps his most marked characteristic. Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, p. 18) calls him a marvelous example of this highly wrought being, who with a heart of richest capacity, struggles to hide it in a flood of wit that is the thinnest sort of mask, only serving to call attention to its utter uselessness as a screen, and making more obvious his shrinking soul. Littleton (1897, p. 180): Lear’s Fool is simply sublime. Self was swallowed up in Life’s mission. Poel (1929, p. 52): He is a foil to the king, physically as well as mentally; very young and frail, he might even be lame or a dwarf, but the face should be beautiful and infinitely sad to look upon.…He is never in manner bitter or sardonic.

This sweet fool is countered by the bitter fool proffered by other critics, who view his bitter words as painful—even harmful—to Lear. Drake (1817; 1838, p. 285): The horrors of the scene are…heightened by [his] seeming thoughtless levity. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 631): The fool’s strokes at Lear’s follies are from the first beyond a joke; instead of distracting his thoughts they drive him to dwell upon those which torture him; even when driven out in the night of the storm the fool carries on the biting satire; and however well his jests may serve the aesthetic purpose of not allowing the spectator to dwell too painfully and continually upon the violent outbursts of Lear’s madness, they are, on the other hand, psychologically considered, inappropriate and injudicious as a remedy against this very malady. Bridges (1925, p. 183): He is introduced not to give comic relief, but rather to heighten, by his bitter commentaries, the terror and pity of situations already tragic.…His barbed words bring no comfort either to Lear or to the onlooker. They intensify his master’s pain. Ridley (1937, p. 171): He can hardly (like Desdemona) open his mouth without saying the wrong thing; he sees the situation with perfectly clear appraisement…but he does not see that Lear is far past the point at which any comment on the situation, however just, can help. As a result his comments are equally sensible and disastrous. Empson (1951, pp. 132–3) suggests an element of malice: I do not deny that the Fool is affectionate towards Lear and Cordelia, his only protectors…only that he is [133] supposed to be a high-minded and self-sacrificing character; also I think that the malice which is part of his role comes out plainly enough in his jokes to Lear.…the Fool understands about madness because he is mad himself. Ellis (1968, p. 265): It is not clear that the fool ever hopes for Lear’s redemption.…Joined together in negation, the fool would reduce Lear to the same awareness of desolation that he has; but not, it seems, in order that he might lead him through it to an acceptance of his situation. Consequently, he cannot, any more than his master, be redeemed, for he rejects the openness that would exchange loss with loss and so build community. Rosenberg (1972, p. 107): His role—his costume—gives him a power over the king, and he uses it. In language he never gives comfort to Lear, at best only advice to come in out of the rain; he never verbally commiserates with Lear for his suffering. Fool mainly recalls the king’s folly, and recalls it, and recalls it. Yet subtextually, in visual imagery, in his own mock kingship, sceptre and all, he is a mirrored shadow of his master.…He is Lear’s looking-glass. Bloom (1992, pp. 2–4): The Fool’s love for Lear is accompanied by a capacity for terror, on Lear’s behalf as on his own.…The Fool drives us a little mad, even as perversely he punishes Lear by helping Lear along to madness. To instruct in Folly, even in the Erasmian sense, is to practice a dark profession, since one is teaching unreason as the pragmatic alternative to knavery. Folly is a kind of Renaissance version of Freud’s Death Drive, beyond the pleasure principle. Blake’s Proverb of Hell that if the Fool would persist in his folly, he would become wise, is perfectly exemplified by Lear’s Fool, except that this Fool is uncannier even than that. Lear lovingly regards him as a child, and he is or seems to be a preternaturally wise child, but a child who cannot grow up, almost as though he were more sprite than human.…[3] Perhaps Lear’s Fool, even more than Shakespeare’s other displaced spirits, incarnates what Nietzsche thought was the [4] motive for all metaphor, and so for all literature: the desire to be elsewhere, the desire to be different. See also Speziale-Bagliacca below.

Some critics have argued over the Fool’s age: is he a boy or a man? Clarke (1873, pp. 397–8): He is a youth, not a grown man.…[398] His delicacy of frame…is indicated by some slight but significant side touches. Concerning his disappearance after 3.6, Shakespeare evidently meant to infer [sic] that the fragile lad—weakly in frame, susceptible in temperament, and rendered doubly so by the delicacy of his nurture in the court-household as the petted boy-jester of his royal employer—never recovered from the rigours and terrors of that tempestuous night. See n. 626. Bradley (1904, p. 313): He is if not a boy then boyish: a timid, delicate, frail being; Brown (1963, pp. 166–7): The fluency of the Fool’s rimes [and] his sudden shifts in subject…imply an accompaniment of restless bodily antics that spell the charms of a child’s gay and tireless energy and love of life.…[167] I see no reason why Shakespeare should prefer the more or less ganglionic atavism of an adult to the charm of a boy’s natural spontaneity. Elton (1966, p. 320): The Fool may be partly related to the [convention of the] puer senex or wise youth. McEwan (1976, pp. 215): recognizing the fool as a boy rather than a grown man clarifies relationships among the terms child, knave, and fool. Others who see him as a boy include Lloyd (1875; 1894, p. 450); Moulton (1893, p. 223): He is a tender and delicate youth; Bransom (1934, pp. 78–9); Draper (1945, p. 99).

Nineteenth-century critics concerned to argue that the Fool was a man were hardly less sentimental than those emphasizing his boyishness. Oechelhäuser (1871; qtd. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 464): I would have the Fool represented as an elderly man, as a sort of family piece in the house of the eighty-year-old king.…His speeches bear the stamp of the biting irony which is not an acquired thing, but which usually comes with age in one whose humble station does not correspond with his intellectual abilities. However this may be, the effect of this rôle would be greatly increased if, in the stormy night, the mask of the Fool is allowed ever more and more to fall off, and the sad, faithful servant becomes more and more prominent. Holland (1885; 1894, pp. 71–84): His keen insight into character, his commonsense view of looking at things, his distrust of mere words—and, indeed, the coarseness of some of his allusions to [72] women, all militate against the boy theory.…[84] His was a duty for duty’s sake, which is higher than any instinct ruled by fear or greed—that sense of duty which fixes the soldier to his post, the captain to his ship, in the face of imminent death—that duty which was Nelson’s most stirring watchword, and has been the conspicuous characteristic, as well as the pride, of the Englishman, century after century, making him fittest of all to rule as well as to obey. Never was there a truer, more thorough-going Englishman than Shakespeare, and he nobly dared to place this highest perfection of duty for duty’s sake in a poor Fool. Others who argue that the Fool is a man of middle age include White (1877, p. 73) and Slicer (1895, p. 380). Miller (1993, p. 35): The boy fool is simply someone who is politically junior to Lear, or socially junior, and nothing more than that.…If the fool is presented as an old man who is exactly the same age as Lear, who has grown up with him, every single one of his otherwise gnomic, runic formulae becomes understandable.

Critics have also debated whether or not the Fool should be considered a half-wit or natural fool. To Douce (1807; 1839, p. 419), he is a mere natural with a considerable share of cunning. Hardinge (1818, 3:4): Contra Douce, he is not silly by nature.…He is a Counterfeit, who, under the license and shelter of the Fool’s apparel, implement, and manners, talks not only wit, but shrewd sense; to which I add, and lay stress upon it, moralizing Satire—a distinction between him and all the other Fools of art, either in History, or in Shakespeare himself. Bradley (1904, pp. 311–14): To suppose that the Fool is, like many a domestic fool at that time, a perfectly sane man pretending to be half-witted, is surely a most prosaic blunder.…Being slightly touched in the brain, and holding the office of a fool, he performs the duties of his office intentionally as well as involuntarily.…Unless we suppose [312] that he is touched in the brain we lose half the effect of his appearance in the Storm-scenes.…His heroism consists largely in this, that his efforts to outjest his master’s injuries are the efforts of a being to whom a responsible and consistent course of action, nay even a responsible use of language, is at the best of times difficult, and from whom it is never at the best of times expected. It is a heroism something like that of Lear himself in his endeavour to learn patience at the age of eighty. But arguments against the idea that the Fool is wholly sane are either needless or futile; for in the end they are appeals to the perception that this idea almost destroys the poetry of the character. Harrison (1927, p. 74) calls him a natural, a half-wit, with the divine simplicity of the half sane. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:51): He is not a half-wit, but—the old word fits—a natural; he does not, that is to say, draw all our practical distinctions between sense and nonsense, the wise thing to do, and the unwise. But he lives in a logical world of his own. Lear has petted him as one pets a dog; he shows a dog’s fidelity. It is foolish of him, no doubt, to follow his master into such a storm—but, then, he is a fool. Shakespeare, having had his dramatic use of him, drops him incontinently; this alone should label the part of merely incidental importance to the scheme of the play. But even this he makes a part of the human pathos of the creature. Coghill (1959, p. 14): He is a half-wit…in the tradition of the natural…an idiot of genius. Bennett (1962, pp. 144–5): The Fool’s remarks are not inspired idiocy, but rather the indiscretions of [145] a boy (as Lear calls him) whose mind is sane but has failed to develop into maturity.…He is child-like, unsophisticated, and uninhibited, rather than insane. Frye (1967, p. 105): The Fool is a natural in the sense of representing something still unspoiled and innocent in the middle of a fallen nature.

Various critics argue that he should not be viewed as a plausibly motivated psychological character. Watkins (1942, pp. 20–1): That astonishing re-creation of the Fool so dear to Romantic critics…is based on the assumption that Shakespeare’s characterization of the Fool is [21] by the same method of psychological realism which he employs in Hamlet and to some extent in Lear. This lovable Fool, heroically outjesting his master’s calamities, cannot survive one glance at the text. If we insist on psychological realism here, the Fool becomes a monster of sadism, taunting Lear with his follies, diabolically fingering the raw nerve at every conceivable opportunity.…Perhaps it is going to the other extreme to say that the Fool has no character at all; but he is personalized only enough to get by in a cast of characters. He is more a dramatic and poetic device than a characterization, and is presented almost entirely by the stylized symbolical method.…The Fool is virtually a personification of the bitter truth tormenting Lear to madness.…He is, in a sense, a psychological device, but stylized and un-realistic; he is a dramatization of what is really going on in Lear’s mind, which otherwise we learn only from a few of his remarks. Danby (1945, p. 21): The idea that the Fool is a character may be allowed to lapse. He is best regarded not as a self-contained monad but as part of Shakespeare. Nosworthy (1939, pp. 265–6): Intellectually eccentric but emotionally normal, he is hard to classify morally as he lacks any marked moral consciousness. Thus, his amorality transcends or evades most of the situations and he is able, for a time, to solve his problems intellectually as no other character can. As the situations grow more intense this ability decreases, for intellect and emotion are not enough, and in his professional [266] capacity as court-jester (i.e. intellectual commentator) he is a hindrance and has to go. Riemer (1966, p. 37): so passive, and perhaps even indifferent, that he seems sub-human, a dry rattle of protest without any commitment to the play’s problems. Styan (1975, p. 195): Always more role-player and commentator than character, his license [is] more that of the eternal clown than that of the court fool. Champion (1976, p. 161): A character totally without individual personality and totally without narrative purpose, he in effect is a stage device for Lear’s articulation of his emotional condition. Bryant (1977, p. 35): He plays no roles because he is a role…the comic and theatrical dimension is paramount. Seiden (1979, pp. 197–211): Of course the Fool has a personality; yet he cannot be perceived as being a person. He expresses but does not genuinely experience feeling. He is engaged in the action; yet he is not changed by his engagement in ways that can be understood by any psychology or logic of human behavior.…[199] It seems correct, therefore, to describe the ontological status of the Fool as one of pure character—all the accidents of birth, family, education, and social, economic, and political relationship having been expunged from the record, if ever such human data can have existed. In another sense, however, the Fool is precisely characterless.…[211] [The Fool] is the nothingness of Death, if not the death to which all life returns, then pre-death, so to speak, that chaos out of the darkness of which emerged light, form, and life.

Others, however, insist on interpreting him in terms of realistic psychology. Thus Bransom (1934, p. 100): The fool soon suspects that Tom is only feigning madness, and feigning it badly, and at last recognizes him. Goldberg (1974, p. 90): He is limited by what he cannot understand about Lear—how hard a man who is able to expect justice can stick by his right to get it.…The Fool cannot expect justice; instead, he is clear-eyed about so much of life just because he cannot afford the luxury of demanding more. Zak (1984, pp. 113 ff.) deplores the misguided nature of readings of his character that would reduce his role in the play into purely functional terms of embittered choral commentary.…Ridicule is the only language he can use to get through to Lear.…[114] The Fool derides Lear because it is the only instrument he can use to drive Lear’s shame out into the open and free him from its stranglehold.…He may sound cynically delighted when he ridicules Lear, but actually he regrets the need to do so.…[138] The Fool lovingly confronts Lear with a sweet and bitter image of himself. Gaiser (1986, pp. 117, 116) speaks of his absolute detachment from a reality which leaves no hope for the future. (P. 116): He has retreated into a counterworld devoid of all existential necessities: to him, life is but a game. Bloom (1998, pp. 495–7): His acute ambivalence toward Lear, founded upon an outrage at Cordelia’s exile and Lear’s self-destructiveness, is one of Shakespeare’s crucial inventions of human affect.…[497] From the Fool’s perspective, Lear indeed is culpable, but only because he was not patriarchal enough to accept Cordelia’s recalcitrance in expressing her love. On that view, Lear is condemned for having forsaken his own fatherhood.…The Fool’s visionary terror is…curiously Nietzschean in that it, too, insists upon the image of fatherhood as being the necessary middle ground that alone can keep origins and ends from turning into each other. And the Fool is accurate…precisely apocalyptic in his forebodings.…Yet what drives the Fool? Once Lear has divided Cordelia’s portion between Goneril and Regan, it is simply too late for warnings and admonishments to make any difference, and the Fool knows this. Ambivalence runs wild in the Fool: yet punishing Lear by increasing his madness can do no good, except to drama itself: [quotes 913–19]. The Fool and Lear sing trios with the undertaker, in this great spiritual chorus of things falling apart.

The Fool’s relation to dramatic and literary traditions of clowning and foolery is the concern of other critics. Welsford (1935, pp. 253–4): Sufficiently life-like to be tragically convincing,…he is also the fool of the sottie, and, although evidently half-witted, is endowed with a penetration deeper and more far-reaching than that superficial sharp-wittedness and gift for smart repartee which went to the making of a successful court-jester. He is in fact the sage-fool who sees the truth, and his rôle has even more intellectual than emotional significance. For King Lear is…[254] true to a definitely intellectual tradition and makes use of the conventions of fool-literature which were…clerical rather than popular in origin, and were used as the vehicle of a reasoned criticism of life. The Fool, therefore…is here used both as a commentator whose words furnish important clues to the interpretation of a difficult play; and also as a prominent figure caught up into the drama, whose rôle and nature form a vital part of the central tragic theme.…His business, however, is not to deal out satirical commonplaces, but to emphasize one peculiarly useful instance of the reversal of position between the wise man and the fool; indeed he labours this point with a maddening reiteration which is only excusable because his tactless jokes and snatches of song spring so evidently from natural grief. Wenzel (1982, p. 226) sees his roots in homiletic literature: he is descended from the domestic or court fool who teaches his master a moral lesson and thereby effects his conversion, a change of his ways to the better. This figure made his appearance in handbooks for preachers and in sermons from at least the beginning of the fourteenth century onward and continued in vogue well into Shakespeare’s time. McCombie (1980, pp. 69–71) compares him to Touchstone in AYL. Weimann (1978, pp. 41–2), discusses him in relation to conventions of the Mummers’ Play. Shickman (1991, p. 76) asserts that Shakespeare’s Fool, in all probability, actually is meant to carry a mirror on the stage.…In so doing, he presents emblems of folly, prudence, and self-knowledge, consonant with the tragic polarities of the play. See nn. 744, 1686–7. Leggatt (1992, p. 193): The Fool is the obvious part for the company clown. The way his entrance is built up by Lear’s repeated requests for him shows a conscious playing on the audience’s desire to see the clown. For his dramatic predecessors see Busby (1923).

He has also been discussed in terms of his role as professional entertainer. Mason (1967, pp. 45–6): We shall not see him properly if we cannot see him literally. First and foremost he is a royal privilege.…Lear’s maintaining him when he is no longer king is a further mark of his unwillingness to learn the new duties imposed by abdication.…Secondly…his behaviour is as much of a disguise as Kent’s and later, Edgar’s. He is a professional fool. We don’t find him very funny and we are embarrassed by the thought that Shakespeare may have found him a satisfactory clown.…I think we should be doing wrong…if we were induced to attribute to the Fool, as some have done, a passionate love of and devotion to his master, equal to Kent’s. By and large it is better to consider his function rather than his motive. His job is to minister medicine to Lear, the kind that produces madness but prepares the way for the superior brand Cordelia [46] has to offer. Hotson (1952, p. 100): For Shakespeare’s audience it is plain that Lear’s Fool, in his unobtrusive and humble robe of motley,…belonged to the contemporary scene, and his introduction by Shakespeare into tragedy was therefore a step toward realism. Black (1984, pp. 83–97), attempting a sort of job description for Shakespeare’s fools in their working-day world, finds that (p. 94) Lear’s Fool has a strong sense of his vocation…and recognizes that it is difficult to keep the profession free of interlopers, including kings.

He has also been discussed as a dramaturgical device in the service of the play. Bennett (1962, p. 144): It is the solution of [the technical] problem of how to keep before the audience Lear’s guilt and folly that produced the Fool, perhaps Shakespeare’s boldest stroke of genius.…He has been described as a kind of external conscience, but it is not Lear’s injustice but his folly that the Fool harps on. He does, however, in some respects, act not only as a reminder, but as a representative of Cordelia, appealing to Lear’s affections by his doglike devotion, depending on him for protection, and so keeping Lear human in that part of the play where Cordelia cannot appear, keeping the audience reminded of her and of Lear’s capacity for love. Wood (1972, p. 222): The Fool creates a pervasive ironic tone and a basic tragi-comic structure, dominant in the tragedy until the putting out of Gloucester’s eyes. Bloom (1992, p. 2): The Fool’s dramatic function, like Horatio’s, is to be a surrogate for the audience, mediating Lear’s sublimity for us even as Horatio mediates the sublime aspects of Hamlet. The Fool and Horatio are floating presences, rather than proper characters in themselves.

Various critics comment on his connection with Cordelia. Thom (1885, pp, 171–2): He supplies the place of the loving child-element in Cordelia’s absence, and is, so to speak, her complement by contrariety. This explains the Fool’s early disappearance from the play: (p. 172) The poet does not allow Cordelia to speak of the Fool even once. She was the thing suggested by him; she the substance of which he was the lengthened shadow. Hence we are to look forward past him to her. Having attained her, it would be anticlimax to revert to him, and we are not allowed to look back. Elton (1966, pp. 324–6): Both Fool and Cordelia…are, at the start, childlike dependents upon Lear, and both follow and are devoted to him unto death. Yet both share an unyielding devotion to truth, Cordelia’s initial refusal to temporize suggesting the truth-telling function of the Fool. Moreover, there appears a connection in Lear’s mind between him and the daughters.…Shakespeare also [325] appears, in the Fool’s irrelevant jests, to plant ironical foreshadowing of Cordelia’s end.…[326] From the above may be deduced an evident intention to infuse part of the Fool’s symbolism into the pathos of Cordelia’s death and of Lear’s ultimate anagnorisis. Anshutz (1964, p. 245) absurdly supposes that he is (literally) Cordelia in disguise. Berge (1994, pp. 220–1): The Fool, in his privileged role as Lear’s verbal antagonist, is very like Cordelia in regard to the unspoken truth.…The Fool completes his action and speech in the play much like Cordelia.…The Fool despairs of common sense while Cordelia surrenders to feelings of bitterness. See also the critics who argue that the role was doubled with the part of Cordelia, .

The Fool is sometimes said to perform a choric function, speaking with authority as a moral teacher or psychoanalyst. Ey (1880): He functions as chorus and becomes superfluous when Lear becomes insane. (In Ger.) Knight (1930, p. 178): From the first signs of Goneril’s cruelty, the Fool is used as a chorus, pointing us to the absurdity of the situation. He is indeed an admirable chorus, increasing our pain by his emphasis on a humour which yet will not serve to merge the incompatible in a unity of laughter. He is not all wrong when he treats the situation as a matter for a joke. Much here that is always regarded as essentially pathetic is not far from comedy. Goldsmith (1955, pp. 66 ff.): He is a wise fool in the Erasmian or Pauline sense…[74] who expresses in his heartfelt devotion to Cordelia and to his king the Christian virtues of patience, humility, and love. Ribner (1958, p. 53): He serves as a reminder to both Lear and the audience of the folly of Lear’s initial behavior. Bryant (1977, p. 36): Moral horror is patent in his speeches, which constitute a searing commentary on the deforming power of sin. Rose (1969, p. 938) speaks of the Fool as Lear’s psychoanalyst; Battenhouse (1979, p. 5) as Lear’s schoolmaster. See also Orwell (1947; 1950, pp. 40–1). However, Davis (1974, pp. 79 ff.), citing (p. 81) the unbelievable strangeness of the demented fool, argues that (p. 79) we can never so simplify our view as to make the fool a chorus for the play.…[84] Were simplicity all, we would be almost correct in dismissing the decorum of royalty as nonsense and in seeing elemental wisdom as the truth that really matters behind facades of punctiliousness. But the fool…is a defender of the very thing we would be thereby dismissing. He is a violation of the new order, which in turn is a violation of the old.

Wittreich (1984, pp. 49 ff.) sees the Fool invested with the authority of a prophet: Through this fool [Sh.] reminds us that the gift of prophecy is inextricably linked with foolishness, that fools themselves strike a subversive relationship with the society they summon to judgment.…Neither spurious nor irrelevant, the Fool’s prophecy is essential to King Lear—a quintessential manifestation of its cosmos.…[50] The vatic role assigned to the fool in Renaissance culture, and also in Shakespeare’s play, has powerful religious sanction as well…[51] for the system of references in Shakespeare’s play has some astonishing moments of correlation with a similar system of references involving fools and folly in the Old and New Testaments.…[53] And there is progression in [the Fool’s] speeches as well—a movement from legendary Britain to James’s [54] England, from oracular irony to full-blown prophecy, from shadowy types to truth, with the Fool in this progression exploding not just Lear’s illusions, but James’s and the world’s as well.…[57] Merlin, according to the fiction of Shakespeare’s play, find[s] his prototype in Shakespeare’s Fool, who, like Merlin, is a kindly helper, a faithful advisor to his king, especially in times of trial and struggle and who, again like Merlin, delivers an artfully artless prophecy of an ardently political nature.

Other critics argue that he functions as Lear’s conscience or as various other aspects of his consciousness. Moulton (1893, pp. 220–3): The function of the Fool in King Lear is to keep vividly before the audience (as well as of his master) the idea at the root of the main plot [Lear’s moral error].…[223] The Fool becomes an outward conscience to his master: he keeps before Lear the unnatural act from which the whole tragedy springs, but he converts the thought of it into the emotion of self-reproach. Boas (1896, p. 444): But the Fool in this play has a curiously specialized function. The one theme upon which he harps without rest is the egregious folly of Lear.…Hence it is that, unlike his fellows in other plays, he is nameless, with no more distinguishing badge of individuality than plain Fool. For he is scarcely a person, a unit to be counted in a census of population. He is a wandering voice—the voice of Lear’s conscience taking outward form in this grotesque, yet wistful figure, the soul of pathos in a comic masquerade. Empson (1930; 1956, p. 46): The Fool acts a sort of divided personality externalised from the King. Heilman (1948, p. 186): At one level he may be understood as the conscience of Lear, the inner voice—externalized. Traversi (1952, p. 52): His comments…represent…submerged aspects of Lear’s own thought, truths present in his mind but discarded as contrary to his desires, and only here emerging in clipped and enigmatic forms. Auden (1954, pp. 44–5): The fool…seems to stand for Lear’s sense of reality which he rejects. Not for his conscience. The fool never speaks to him, as Kent does, in the name of morality.…[45] [The fool’s appearance is] the dramatic manifestation of [Lear’s] shift [toward madness].…As long as passion has not totally engulfed him the fool can appear at his side.…There is still a chance, however faint, that he may realise the facts of his situation and be restored to sanity.…But when this chance has passed and Lear has descended into madness past recall, there is nothing for the fool to represent and he must disappear. Kirsch (1966, p. 218) employs Jungian terms: The Fool acts as a typical spiritus familiaris, the object spokesman for Lear’s unconscious. Chakravorty (1990, pp. 82–3): Fool acts out Lear’s Bad Faith, somewhat like a Bad Angel or Temp-[83]ter in a Morality, taunting him for his misery and goading him constantly to revoke his abdication or renunciation, in short, to give up his Freedom. Fool, like the Storm, resides within Lear. Both are the externalized appearance of the reality within him, and have no meaning, value or essence outside of Lear himself. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, pp. 95–9): He is emblematic of a well-defined psychic presence.…[97] Lear’s Fool acts at the prompting of the old king’s projective identifications.…[98] [Love] is what Lear is trying to achieve and the Fool is trying to prevent by all possible means.…By using the technique of speaking nonsense, the Fool strikes at the king’s heart and paralyzes him. All of his sayings and jokes revolve around one single piece of advice: Why do you need your daughters’ love, Lear? You ought to worry about your own crown! The proverbial language used by the Fool is concerned with self-protection and property rights.…The Fool represents the sadistic and perverse voice of Lear, a voice that attacks all bonds in order to avoid being abandoned. [99] Having been betrayed in his earliest infancy, Lear does not want to repeat the experience. Thus, subtly, often seductively…he castrates every impulse, every manifestation of disinterested affection.…The Fool mocks and subdues the king, makes him feel foolish and inadequate. Lear does not want to be derided or taunted, and yet he helps the Fool to deride and taunt him.

In contrast to the view of the Fool as an aspect of Lear’s consciousness, McLuskie (1985, p. 105) argues that the Fool comically undermin[es] the focus on Lear…subverting if not denying the emotional impact of the scenes in which he appears. In an important sense the Fool is less an alter ego for Lear than for his daughters: like them he reminds Lear and the audience of the material basis for the change in the balance of power. However, where they exploit Lear’s powerlessness with cruelty and oppression he denies that necessity by his continued allegiance. In modern productions this important channel for an alternative view of events is closed off by holding the Fool within the narrative, using him as a means to heighten the emotional appeal of Lear’s decline.

Modern critics have associated the Fool with a wide range of thematic or symbolic ideas. Some critics find in his words a terrifying grotesquerie suggesting an absurdist vision. Danby (1945, pp. 18–21): The Fool’s trick is to keep a see-saw of ambivalences constantly in motion.…There is no fixed centre, only a to-and-fro between extremes. More still, the extremes act together, one up the other down, but both in partnership.…[19] There is neither sanction nor unction for his loyalty. While it is a fact, it is a fact brutish, irrational, and indefensible. The alternative to Knavishness is part, for him, of a cosmic handy-dandy, nor can he say who is really the Knave and who the Fool. Wiseman, Knave, and Fool—all three engage in a giddy pas de trois. The Fool has a foot in every camp. He strives for an original Marriage of Heaven and Hell.…The Fool’s model of cautionary excellence is the canny capitalist and self-denying puritan combined.…The ideal is…mean and contemptible.…[21] He expresses and fixes what might be called a pre-tragic phase of existence—a potentiality in the mind at once terrified, bewildered, mean and pathetic: something Shakespeare felt inside himself as hard, localised, fatal, and yet as extraneous as cancer. Idem (1949, p. 113): The Fool can be regarded as the consciousness of a split society. Like man, its creator, the society is a twin-headed monster at strife with itself. The Fool constantly uses the imagery of disease and perversity. Complementary ill-healths counterbalance in perpetual handy-dandy. He sees rich man and poor man, head and heart, sympathizes with neither, yet cannot dissociate himself from the conditions of the strife. Harsh as the handy-dandy world of corrupt society is, there is no escape from it.…The Fool…stands for the unillumined head—the intellect— as Lear is the soul, and Cordelia the spirit. He can discern in his cold light the alternatives between which he cannot choose. Brooke (1963, pp. 23–4): The Fool is fundamentally an anti-body, a complete contrast to everybody, as one feels in his bare prose, and in his verse, which is more unlike other poetries even than prose. In one sense, this is a form of parody, the serious themes seen as a joke; the Fool does make us laugh. But in another sense it represents a kind of clarity; the Fool sees the issue in its bare essentials.…[24] Strip the play of poetic visions, and you arrive at this: salutary common sense, which is also the negation of any real sense of value.…It is not surprising, then, that the Fool is melancholic.…The simplicity of the Fool’s verse can be seen as the simplicity of nature thought of as without any grand order, and without the least vestige of human pride; he does not question whether the pride is true or false, he simply omits it. Hence his speech is always melancholy, and fragmentary. Kott (1964, pp. 123–4): He is looking from the outside and does not follow any ideology. He rejects all appearances, of law, justice, moral order. He sees brute force, cruelty and lust. He has no illusions and does not seek consolation in the existence of natural or supernatural order, which provides for the punishment of evil and reward of good. Lear, insisting on his fictitious majesty, seems ridiculous to him. All the more ridiculous because he does not see how ridiculous he is. But the Fool does not desert his ridiculous, degraded king, and accompanies him on his way to madness. The Fool knows that the only true madness is to regard this world as rational.…His language is that of our modern grotesque. The same grotesque [124] that exposes the absurdity of apparent reality and of the absolute by means of a great and universal reductio ad absurdum. Elton (1966, pp. 311–21): As raisonneur of chaos, the Fool is the incessant chorus of value inversion. In this he is reminiscent of…[312] the world-upside-down topos.…Structurally, as well as conceptually, the world-upside-down motif, which embraces the play, manifests also the Fool’s principles.…[314] Since the world upside down is thus not only a physical but also a moral revolution, subversion becomes inversion, and all values change places [2597].… in Lear, further, the cosmos seems enlisted in that reversal, against order and on the side of anarchy.…[319] The Fool, Lear’s partner in irrationality, functions analogously to Lear’s other Doppelgänger, his partner in suffering, the double plot’s Gloucester.…The eventual identity of king and jester lies in the recognition that under the omnipotently sportive deities all men, whether solemn or foolish, are ludicrous.…[321] If eventually in the physical sense superfluous, the contradictory clown seems eclipsed only in propria persona by the higher irrationalities. In contrast, Orwell (1947; 1950, pp. 40–1): His jokes, riddles and scraps of rhyme, and his endless digs at Lear’s high-minded folly, ranging from mere derision to a sort of melancholy poetry…are like a trickle of sanity running through the play, a reminder that somewhere or other in spite of the injustices, [41] cruelties, intrigues, deceptions and misunderstandings that are being enacted here, life is going on much as usual.

Other critics focus on whether the role is politically subversive. Seehase (1973, pp. 88–100) sees the Fool as the choric voice of the plebeian masses as does Mohamad (1990, p. 11): He represents the long history of the plebs, particularly the peasants, in their version of class struggle. Kettle (1988, p. 79): His comments—the shrewd and cynical paradoxes, the irreverent thrusts at Lear’s dignity—form a kind of choric counterpoint of the main themes of the play which not only adds a depth and complexity but helps define the essential popular element within this play of kings and nobles. It is not easy to get a consistent pattern from the Fool’s remarks. His Blakean prophecy (at the end of Act III, Sc. ii) is puzzling and apparently inconsistent, yet it expresses with an exciting vividness the historical tensions and contradictions which lie behind the whole play. Perhaps it is the cynical realism of his comments which is most striking. He has been ground down too long to have much hope of salvation, so that his resilience is spasmodic, his pessimism deep-rooted. He reminds one a little of the old soldier whose hatred and contempt of the army has been fed on a lifetime of chastening experience and who cannot—for all his irreverence—shake off the habits of servitude he despises. One might think of him as the opposite of the eternal butler, an eternal batman, a sort of Elizabethan Schweik. Heinemann (1992, p. 81): The Fool stands in a direct theatrical tradition of the clown as prophet…iconoclastic, egalitarian, anti-Popish…and a champion of the poor. Rutter (1994–6; 1997, p. 194): The Fool teach[es] Lear a new language, catechizing him in a political grammar whose morphology grotesquely anatomizes the king’s body (eyes, nose, crown, buttocks) and whose syntax, the riddle, skews meaning to put it straight.

Leinwand (1987, pp. 229–32) denies the role’s subversiveness: The fool identifies himself not merely with the court, but with an absolutist’s conception of the court.…The Fool harps on topsyturvydom, even though he can do little to set things right, because he wants so badly for Lear to regain his equilibrium.…[231] The Fool seems to have a contradictory but nonetheless understandable vision of a suitable sovereign. One and the same man is to be father-businessman and absolute monarch, an amalgam that accounts for both capitalism and absolutism.…[232] Surely Shakespeare’s hopes for Lear (and James?) are not the Fool’s. Leggatt (1992, p. 193–4): Though it is part of his job to bring the King down to earth,…his jokes about a world turned upside down embody a wish to see proper order restored.

A few critics have discussed the fool as embodying the sympathetic or creative imagination in conflict with rational calculation. Heilman (1948, pp. 186–7): In his love for Lear and his devotion to Lear when there was every practical reason for his getting aboard the political band wagon,…the Fool is a man of imagination who by imagination grasps a value that cannot be demon-[187]strated rationally and whose deed is the dramatic opposite of the conduct of the rationalists in the play. His speech is always the imaginative speech of poetry: he is always ironic, he depends on symbols (the coxcomb, the crowns of the egg, the hedge-sparrow fed the cuckoo so long), on riddles and analogies, on similes (like the breath of an unfee’d lawyer), metaphors (truth’s a dog), and paradoxes (thou mad’st thy daughter thy mother). The Fool’s education of Lear is in part a re-education of his imagination, an implied attack upon the calculating rationalism by which Lear had inaugurated all his troubles. Traversi (1952, pp. 52–60): The Fool’s comments…reduce the whole action to a contrast between gratuitous folly, on the one head, and the cold-blooded following of self-interest on the other.…[59] This application to Lear’s fortunes of a pessimistic reading of human motives clashes, however, in the Fool’s own words, with a contrary sentiment, indefinable in terms of common-sense but capable of affecting, almost in spite of himself, the speaker’s choice of his own course of action.…[60] There exists, in fact, a distinction between head and heart, between rational common-sense and moral feeling, which corresponds to the two readings of nature as order, harmony, and as the unchecked following of self-interest, with which Lear’s own tragedy is mainly concerned. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 11) calls him a living manifestation of that world of irony and metaphor in which every experience can throw light on every other one. Similarly Alter (1989, p. 229): The particular kind of wild and scathing wit [Sh.] unleashes through the Fool in King Lear is also a realization of the peculiar logic of multifariousness that generally characterizes the liberal imagination.

Various other moral and thematic meanings are identified with the Fool’s role. Thus Calkins (1888, p. 58): The Fool was created to illustrate the moral that the noblest virtues flourish best and bear their choicest fruit in the soil of poverty. Ruggles (1895, pp. 202–3) calls him an embodied fable,…[203] a good dramatic representative of that doctrine termed by Bacon Serious Satire, or the Insides of Things, which treats of the impostures and hypocrisies which are opposed to the virtues and duties proper to the different relations of life. Everett (1989, p. 67): The Fool brings with him from the Shakespearian comic world that bred him an incurable ache in the sweet tooth of love—a grim wisdom as of the detached mind in the sensual body. His natural element is the submerged life of feeling in the play, the whole current of the romantic erotic glimpsed through the political stuff of the story.…[He] embodies that powre to hurt which in Shakespeare’s Sonnets attends love. Zimbardo (1990, pp. 5–8): The emblematic configuration The King and The Fool…points toward the ineffable nothing that underlies all human existence.…[8] What the Fool stands for is necessary to what the King stands for as zero is necessary to the name of one. The medieval/Renaissance emblem The King and The Fool, then, is the emblem of our condition and our consciousness, the whole of our disparity.

Some recent critics have argued for significant differences between the role in the Quarto and Folio texts. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 219, 230): In F, the Fool is consistently a wise and worldly jester, more urbane and oblique than his predecessor.…[230] In the Historie, where the Fool is less a court jester than a sage natural, covetous of his Nuncle’s attention, the commonsensical kind of folly is sparsely represented.…The changes in the Fool’s part are Shakespearian. Foakes (1985; 1993, pp. 103–5) is more cautious: The changes in F are generally consistent in reinforcing the general sardonic commentary of the Fool, but they do not…transform a blathering natural in Q into a canny rationalist in F. It would seem rather that from the beginning Shakespeare has a many-sided conception of the Fool, and that there is a complexity in both texts allowing a range of perspectives on him.…[104] The text of Q…shows that the Fool was conceived from the start as a professional court fool, a clear-sighted analyst of Lear’s condition, not simply a sort of village idiot.…On the one hand he can be seen as a devoted, humble attendant on Lear, perhaps a youth…who might be thought of as frail, easily cowed, perhaps a little feminine…and hence a reflection of Lear’s conscience.…On the other hand the Fool can be seen as a sharp, rational, mature professional, turning [105] Lear’s language back on him…a figure who establishes through his generalizing comments a note of social protest in the play. The Fool’s early scenes (1.4, 1.5) tend to emphasize the first set of images, while the later scenes (II.4, III.2, III.4, III.6) bring out the other range of possibilities; but Shakespeare took pains by small additions in F to keep alive the King’s tenderness for his knave even as the Fool is displaced by Edgar to become a more marginal figure. Idem (ed. 1997, p. 116): There seems little doubt that [the differences in the Fool’s part between Quarto and Folio] were made as conscious revision and that Shakespeare was responsible for most if not all of them. Whether they form a coherent pattern, making the Folio Fool superior dramatically to the Quarto Fool, is less clear.…It would seem rather that from the beginning Shakespeare had a kind of double vision of the Fool, and that there is a radical indeterminacy in his conception of the role. For doubts that the few changes to the Fool’s part represent authorial revision, see , , .

div.head: France
div.p: For such a small role, France has attracted a surprising amount of comment. Some critics comment on his personal attractiveness. Thus Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:61): The spirit and quality of France’s speeches should keep him a pleasant memory to the play’s end. Blok (1966, p. 19): Compared to Cordelia and Edgar, we cannot but be struck by the youthful fire, the naïve spontaneity and light-heartedness of the King of France. He seems to be an apparition from some other world, and so, in fact, he is; in that world, everything is somehow simpler and easier, people are more trustful, turning to their fellow without ulterior motive, not expecting to find in him a secret enemy. Mahood (1992, p. 159): Small as the role is, it has subtleties which call for skilled acting.

Some critics see him as a national type. Mackenzie (1924, pp. 289–90): There is something that is genuinely French about the precise tone of his [290] ironically courteous contempt of Lear and Burgundy and the beau geste towards Cordelia herself. He brings into the tangled emotions a Latin clear-headedness, a sense of the shape as well as the colour of things, that serves as an artistic point of rest, and his speeches sum the situation just before its crisis. Akhmanova et. al. (1989, pp. 79 ff.): His speech portrayal was meant to represent the French way of saying things…[81] the rhetoric of French feelings and French pathos, which are, of course, quite different from the English ones.…[80] The [unusually high] frequency of [Romance] words, their Frenchness, their mere length completely change the prosody of the French king’s speech.…[81] There are also specific points of grammar which could be used as further evidence.…[82] The solecisms were intentional…Shakespeare’s way of portraying the French character, thus adding to the cumulative effect of strangeness and foreignness created by the whole manner of the king’s speech.

Others see him as a representative of ethical ideas endorsed by the play. Snider (1887, pp. 162–3) sees France’s true love for Cordelia as the cause of her growth in love to her father. Battenhouse (1969, p. 285): He [France] has taken to himself a bride that he might perfect her—a concept that is basic to the New Testament idea of marriage. In this sense his act is figurally Christian, although he lives in pre-Christian times. Idem (1979, pp. 6–7) describes him as a better counselor to Lear than Kent. Champion (1976, p. 174): France voices the major theme of the play—the lesson that both Lear and Gloucester are to painfully learn—in his assertion that true love is not measured by material concern. Willson (1983, pp. 147–8): France’s role can readily be described as precursing the climactic transformation of Lear’s character. His presence lends to the opening scene the mood of experiencing the future in an instant.…[148] France’s role can in fact be described as choric.

Others view him with suspicion. Bransom (1934, pp. 193–9) imagines his invasion to be motivated by self-interest: The French king was by no means reconciled to the permanent loss of the richest province of Britain, which he still regarded as his by right of his wife’s dower, and had his secret service men everywhere. These kept him informed of political movements in Britain, and he bided his time. His abandonment of Cordelia is (p. 199) both ignominious and unchivalrous. Similarly Greg (1940, pp. 441–5) raises the question of the French king’s motive. If, taking advantage of the antagonism between Albany and Cornwall, he planned [442] invasion as soon as he returned to his own kingdom, it was not planned to avenge the treatment Lear had received at the hands of his elder daughters, as we are later led to believe, and as is essential for any sympathetic feeling towards the invaders.…[444] I…feel bound to assume that [after] further leave-taking…[327] France—the hot-blooded France of [1505]—incensed at some fresh insult to Cordelia, departed in a rage, determined to wrest by force her portion from the favoured son-in-laws, Albany and Cornwall. Such is the situation when France and Cordelia land at Dover. But…[445] Cordelia succeeded in persuading her husband to abandon his purpose of wresting a portion of the kingdom for himself and retire to his own land, thus leaving her free to use his army in defence of her father, should the need arise. Kahn (2000, pp. 123–4): France presumably came [to England] because his political ambitions were set on England, particularly an England in which there were already rumors of strife between Cornwall and Albany.…Cordelia’s use of the army for the sake of love violates the political order, of which the king is the embodiment.…[124] France is an image of the dangers of allowing love to rule a state. Though less suspicious, Bevington (ed. 1992, p. 1168) finds the character ambivalent: The King of France is in part a hero out of romance, who makes selfless choices and rescues the heroine Cordelia from her distress; yet his motive must also be appraised in the context of a bitter struggle for power. Why does he leave court in choler, and why does he return to England with an army? Is it only to aid his wife and her beleaguered father, or is he negotiating for military advantage?…The dual focus of the play [its opposition of parable and realism] invites conflicting interpretation.

Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 141) supposes that Q retains traces of a version of King Lear in which the King of France played an active role, as he does in other versions of the story known to Shakespeare. Knowles (Cordelia’s, 1999, pp. 46–9) demurs: There is simply no evidence that France was ever intended to lead the army into the final battle in Q (or in an imagined earlier version) but not in F.…[49] Why Cordelia and France have invaded [remains] intentionally vague, incomplete, and enigmatic, and of a piece with rumors of an impending civil war that never materializes and with puzzling, apparently untrue references to the mistreatment of Lear by both dukes.

div.head: Gloster
div.p: Many critics compare Gloucester to Lear, generally to Gloucester’s disadvantage.
