Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 632–4): A good, mild, unexcitable man, of easy mind and manners, lax and superstitious, Gloster has created his own trouble, just as Lear has drawn down his misery upon himself. He has a natural son, through whom his breach of the marriage-vow is to be avenged; he has indeed in addition done everything in education and treatment that could provoke the bastard against him.…[633] Like Lear, he bethinks himself upon poverty for the first time in his own need, and preaches that community of goods which he had never thought of when he possessed them.…[644] Like Lear, also, he despairs of the world and records the triumph of the wicked, expressing it in that fearful sentence—[quotes 2220–1]. Even before his eyes were put out, when oppressed only by his own and Lear’s family troubles, Gloster called himself almost mad; subsequently, at the sight of Lear he wishes for himself the same fate, that his thoughts might be severed from his griefs. But his softer and more elastic nature prevents this; despair drives the less obdurate but equally abandoned one to contemplate suicide, which never entered the thoughts of the revengeful Lear. Bradley (1904, pp. 293–5): The parallel between Lear and Gloster…is, up to a certain point, so marked that it cannot be accidental. Both are old white-haired men…; both, it would seem, widowers, with children comparatively young. Like Lear, Gloster is tormented, and his life is sought, by the child whom he favours; he is tended and healed by the child whom he has wronged. His sufferings, like Lear’s, are partly traceable to his own extreme folly and injustice, [294] and, it may be added, to a selfish pursuit of his own pleasure. His sufferings, again, like Lear’s, purify and enlighten him: he dies a better and wiser man than he showed himself at first. They even learn the same lesson, and Gloster’s repetition (noticed and blamed by Johnson) of the thought in a famous speech of Lear’s is surely intentional. And, finally, Gloster dies almost as Lear dies. Edgar reveals himself to him and asks his blessing (as Cordelia asks Lear’s): [quotes 3159–61].…And in character too Gloster is, like his master, affectionate, credulous [295] and hasty. But otherwise he is sharply contrasted with the tragic Lear, who is a towering figure, every inch a king, while Gloster is built on a much smaller scale, and has infinitely less force and fire. He is, indeed, a decidedly weak though good-hearted man; and, failing wholly to support Kent in resisting Lear’s original folly and injustice, he only gradually takes the better part. Nor is his character either very interesting or very distinct. He often gives one the impression of being wanted mainly to fill a place in the scheme of the play; and, though it would be easy to give a long list of his characteristics, they scarcely…compose an individual, a person whom we are sure we should recognise at once. See also Taylor (1907, pp. 210–11). Harbage (ed. 1969, p. 1063): Gloucester also represents Man, but his distinction from Lear suggests the distinction between ordinary and extraordinary men. Gloucester is amiably confused about his past…and sentimentally fumbling in the present. What appears in Lear as heroic error appears in him as gullibility. Burckhardt (King’s, 1961, p. 382): There is something ludicrous about Gloster’s fall; Lear, even at his maddest, is never ludicrous. London (1965, p. 181): A crushed worm beneath a great wheel, Gloucester is immensely pathetic but not tragic. Kozintsev (1966, p. 257): Hot-tempered and despotic in his own home, he is quiet enough at court. He is a vassal. All his views are based on this concept. Nevo (1972, p. 295): Gloucester has from the beginning believed in the great opposeless wills, which he is content to think tyrannical, determining men’s fortunes in arbitrary mystery. He has never felt Lear’s need nor made Lear’s imperious demand for an absolute justice made manifest and intelligible. He has never required Lear’s God. Therefore he is not compelled to Lear’s promethean agon, and his salvation is irremediably undignified. His renunciation of the world is a submission of the will, an escape from that before which his intellect stands defeated. Ellis (1972, p. 275): Gloucester’s fumbling and confused response to the deception contrasts with Lear’s tragic strength and will in the face of the machinations against him by his own children. However, Perret (1985, p. 89) interprets the contrast to Gloucester’s advantage: Unlike Lear, who expresses his concern for others primarily though words, Gloucester expresses his through words backed by deeds. As a parallel character, the earl helps us to see the king better, which is not necessarily to think better of the king. Gloucester grows in moral stature as the king does not. Others who compare the roles include Leggatt (1988, pp. 70–2), who emphasizes contrast rather than parallel to Lear; and Cunningham (1988, p. 26): Readily receptive to the notion that his child, like Cordelia, does not love him, Gloucester, too, feels the need for love and the anxiety to assert his authority as still effective.

A number of critics judge him morally responsible for his suffering. Clarke (1863, p. 170) emphasizes selfishness, judging him another of the victims to the effects of an irresponsible self-will, and of the selfishness inherent with it. His self-indulgence in early life, and scanty dispensation of justice to his natural son, Edmund,—one part of a vicious system in morals, and which proves to himself so bitter a scourge in the sequel,—and his blind rage against the legitimate son, both emanate from his ruling passion, and both concur in effecting his downfall. Siegel (1955, p. 327): Gloucester has been a man who, although having good intentions, has been yielding before power wrongly used, heeding his ease rather than his duty and loving himself more than humanity; however, his selfishness is purged by suffering. Others emphasize sensuality rather than selfishness. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:52–6): Gloucester himself is the [53] play’s nearest approach to the average sensual man. The civilized world is full of Gloucesters. In half a dozen short speeches Shakespeare sets him fully before us: turning elderly but probably still handsome; nice of speech if a little pompous; the accomplished courtier (he seems to be Lear’s master of ceremonies); vain, as his mock modesty shows, but the joking shamelessness that succeeds it is mainly swagger; an egotist, and blind, knowing least of what he should know most, of his two sons.…Gloucester, like so many sensual men, is good nature itself, as long as things go their easy, natural way; but when they fail to he is upset, rattled.…We must not, however, appraise either his simplicity or Edgar’s [regarding Edmund’s deceit] with detachment—for by that light, no human being, it would seem, between infancy and dotage, could be so gullible. Shakespeare asks us to allow him the fact of the deception, even as we have allowed the partition of the kingdom. It is his starting point, the dramatist’s let’s pretend, which is as essential to the beginning of the play as a let it be granted to a proposition of Euclid. And, within bounds, the degree of pretense makes surprisingly little difference.…Thus Shakespeare makes Gloucester, with his pother about these late eclipses of the sun and moon, the sort of man who might at any moment be taken in by any sort of tale; the more improbable, indeed, the better. He makes Edmund plausible even if the [54] incriminating letter is not.…The sensual man does not stand up very resolutely against blows dealt to his complacent affections. Disillusion leaves Gloucester not only wax in Edmund’s hands but more helpless than it belongs to him to be…in the alien troubles that now center around him. Shakespeare’s maneuvering of him…from the welcome to the noble arch and patron to the moment when his guest’s honored fingers are plucking at his eyes—is a good example of the fruitful economy with which, once a character has come alive, its simplest gesture, its very muteness is made significant.…Fate’s worst revenge on him is that, blinded, he comes to see himself so clearly as he is, and to find the world, which once went so comfortably with him, a moral chaos. We might wonder at the amount of agonized reflection in this kind allotted to him. But mark its culmination: [55] [quotes 2733–9]. The one thing, it seems, that the average sensual man cannot endure is knowledge of the truth. Better death or madness than that! Yet which of us must not feelingly protest that the Gloucester, who threads and fumbles his way so well-meaningly about the family battlefield his house is turned into (much against his will) is very harshly used.…[56] Is this poetic justice upon a gentleman, whose worst fault has been to play for safety, his worst blunder to think ill of a man without question and to believe a liar? Wilson (1957, p. 199): He is presented as the easy-going man of the world, comfortably licentious, slyly priding himself on his spirit in having produced a presentable bastard in Edmund, and yet innocently gullible and superstitious, an ineffectual but well intentioned libertine.…As Gloucester’s fibre is coarser and weaker than Lear’s, as his mode of life is simpler, less imaginative, and more earth-bound, so his suffering, appropriately, is physically brutal, while Lear’s is mainly of the spirit. Likewise Pechter (1978, p. 195): Gloucester is not a hero. Gloucester is l’homme moyen sensuel.

Others criticize him as morally imperceptive. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, p. 194): His light, superficial estimate of marriage, and the other relations of life, which leads him superstitiously to look upon the moral liberty of man as dependent upon a physical necessity, and the actions of man on the phenomena of nature, and the latter itself as a ball in the hands of the gods, has completely blinded him, and for this darkness of the moral vision he is visited with blindness of the physical organ; he is deprived of the sight of his eyes because he was without a pure light of the mind. Heilman (1948, pp. 41–265): Gloucester’s tragic flaw is a special kind of lack of insight. Gloucester is not a stupid man, but he is a man who does not ask enough questions, who takes evidence at its face value, who confounds appearance and substance. He is the man of the world, the sophisticate, as we might say, who has the naïveté ironically inseparable from the type. His whole history is consistent. Long before the time of the play he enjoyed an adulterous liaison…which indicated that he viewed sex morality entirely as a man of the world. His unperceptive worldliness [42] is the opening note of the play.…The light in which he sees things lights up only the surface of the world. It is quite consistent that he is inclined to get on with the new political regime: he plainly has his doubts about the way things are going, but that a principle is involved, a principle on which he should take a stand, simply does not occur to him.…[43] The de facto, the immediate, the circumscribing world hypnotize him: he cannot question. Yet Gloucester is not unalterably a bandwagon man; he can rise to become a tragic figure, and finally, shocked into a new alertness, he undertakes the commitment to Lear which is his ruin in the practical world whose creature he has been, but at the same time the salvation of his soul. But his spiritual awakening is very subtly managed; there is a fine stroke in the ambiguity of the terms in which Gloucester tells Edmund that he intends to aid Lear (III.iii). There is no doubt whatever that he pities Lear and realizes—note his phrase this unnatural dealing [1753–4]—at last that more is involved than political bad taste. But it is also true that he has been abused and mistreated by the usurpers, and that he says, [quotes 1761–4]. He is waking up to the moral state of affairs, but in his consciousness there is also some hint that to be pro-Lear may be a good thing; and he is at least in part maneuvering toward the comfortable stream of history. Gloucester does not consciously seek evil, or deliberately hunt for feather beds; it is simply that he is tragically slow in seeing what is implied in the situations in which he finds himself.

p.quote: His being blinded, then is an ironic completion of his career.…[44] Thus all the evidence of drama and language points to the conclusion that Gloucester’s hamartia is…failure to see essential things. Furthermore, it seems clear, this failure is meant to be evidenced in the original adultery which Coleridge regards as Gloucester’s originating moral misdeed. Near the end the philosophical Edgar, speaking of Gloucester, says to Edmund, [quotes 3132–4].…The [45] place was dark because years before, Gloucester was exhibiting a characteristic failure to see what his deed involved.…[48] He is deprived of the organs which he once used so superficially. Yet this happens just as he is coming to real insight.…[50] Perhaps the final guarantee of his insight is his loss of outward sight. The vile jelly, the material seeing, had but caught reflections from the outward surfaces of life; as long as these were available to him, the seeing Gloucester was spiritually blind. The sisters and Cornwall cut him off from this outer world, which…circumscribed his vision; hence their fury is self-defeating, for they give him what their general conduct has already prepared him for—inward vision. His physical and material loss is spiritual gain: he who would find his life must lose it.…[265] In Gloucester [we see] a gradual transformation from the man in whom a jaunty worldliness is dominant to the man who finds it essential to be in harmony with the gods; and, as we would expect of a character in whom such opposites come into play, there is, even after the transition, a discernible wavering. It is his old dubiety and skepticism, the reactivation of his old susceptibility to despair, once in a secular, now in a religious context. Between the early and the late Gloucester we can see also an intermediate position which logically bridges the extremes: as the old courtier begins to realize that he and the court are in a serious situation, his first effort to come to grips with it is, in terms of understanding, his eclipse theory, and, in terms of action, the tendency to ride along with the dominant forces as an unpleasant necessity. He is a what-will-be-will-be, spirit-of-the-times man—until he is shaken and forced into the deeper channels of understanding of which he is capable. For the will of history he substitutes the will of god; his sense of authority moves from a temporal orientation to an eternal, from a naturalistic to a divine.

div.p: Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 276–8) likewise emphasizes impercipience: I cannot understand [Gloucester’s] immediate and complete acquiescence in the fate which has befallen him (his acknowledgment of his folly, his acceptance of Edgar’s innocence, and his wish for forgiveness all take just twenty syllables) without supposing that it strikes him as a retribution, forcing him to an insight about his life as a whole. Not, however, a necessarily true insight. He has revealed his fault in the opening speeches of the play, in which he tells Kent of his shame. (That shame is the subject of those speeches is emphasized by Coleridge; but he concentrates, appropriately enough, on Edmund’s shame.)…He recognizes the moral claim upon himself, as he says twice, to acknowledge his bastard; but all this means to him is that he has a bastard for a son. He does not acknowledge him, as a son or a person, with his feelings of illegitimacy and being cast out. That is something Gloucester ought to be ashamed of; his shame is itself more shameful than his one piece of licentiousness.…[278] Gloucester suffers the same punishment he inflicts: in his respectability he avoided eyes; when respectability falls away and the disreputable come into power, his eyes are avoided. In the fear of Gloucester’s poor eyes there is the promise that cruelty can be overcome, and instruction about how it can be overcome. That is the content which justifies the scene of his blinding, aesthetically, psychologically, morally.

Goldberg (1974, pp. 79–88) judges him psychologically insecure: Gloucester is wavering, uncertain, fearful, and confused. At bottom he is a much more various personality than Edmund or Kent, because far more open to experience. But he is obviously so afraid of what might happen to him, so little confident of his own vitality, so unable, for all his air of jocular complacency…to rest secure in his ego, that he would indeed unstate [himself] to be in a due resolution [429–30].…[80] The contradiction of Gloucester’s tender and entire love for Edgar being so ready to believe the worst of him is very obvious.…As with Lear, his desire for justice on Edgar is so savage and extreme that it clearly betrays the open wound underneath it.…The point is not so much Gloucester’s confusion or weakness of mind as his helplessness every time in the face of his deepest feelings.…[88] Gloucester’s very mistrust, the very recessiveness of his will, makes the lurking savagery he both exhibits and meets in the world seem not only more vividly, more objectively real to us, but also…utterly inescapable. Similarly Zak (1984, pp. 140 ff.), who describes him as the king’s foil, playing a suicidal Jocasta to Lear’s Oedipus.…Based on the things Gloucester says and does after his mutilation by Cornwall, it would certainly be difficult to defend a claim for any significant growth in his understanding of himself and his condition.…[141] Even blind, he is so ashamed of his shameful acts that he flees from an acknowledgment of their shamefulness.…To shield himself from his own misery, he holds to a fanciful and delusive hope (as against true and generous hope), speciously imagining he can triumph over the vulnerability he suffers and the catastrophic mistake he has so clearly made.…[142] Gloucester persists in trying to enforce [the] charity of oblivion for himself rather than accepting charity for himself and giving it to others.…Gloucester…stubbornly sins against generous love for the king in his own self-regarding grief. Berger (1985; 1997, pp. 55–8): Edmund’s plot enables him to confirm apprehensions about his legitimate heir which he seems…almost too eager to entertain.…If a father loves his children for what he feels they owe him, his anxiety is aroused by what he feels he owes them. From Gloucester’s point of view the whoreson is owed nothing, the legitimate son everything. His distrust of Edgar may be something he desires no less than something he fears. And to have found such suspicions groundless might well have exposed him to the inner retribution of the darkest purpose [i.e., aggression against the self].…[56] Luckily he finds in Edmund a willing instrument to help…make his suspicion come true. That is, he fends off the darkest purpose by relying on the bastard who embraces its distorted mirror image, the villain’s formula [more sinning than sinned against].…[58] Gloucester fends off the guilt associated with family betrayal by redistributing complicities in such a way as to present it to himself and others in the form of manly shame and victimage. Taylor (1990, pp. 39–40): Gloucester accepts [Edmund’s forged] letter as Edgar’s…because within Gloucester there is already predilection to find the favored son inadequate or treacherous.…[40] In accepting all the horrific implications of the letter Gloucester is in effect willing the world to be worse than it is.

Other negative judgments include that of Battenhouse (1969, p. 438 n.): A slothful man…superstitiously honoring demonic gods, Gloucester is also characterized by (p. 278) lack of faith and covetousness. According to de Grazia (1996, p. 28), From the first to the last, the play stigmatizes him as the indiscriminate dispenser of both economic and sexual purses, coin and seed. Most strikingly, Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, p. 127): Gloucester betrays [Regan’s] respect and trust, and at the same time betrays his country. Nor does he do this with noble intent but, rather, (the context suggests) out of pure opportunism: [quotes 1761–4].

A number of critics characterize him as superstitious. Snider (1887, pp. 143, 149–50): Gloster is superstitious fundamentally; he sees in Nature, in the eclipses of the sun and moon, the collisions of the moral world; he is always ready to assign to blind physical causes the obliquities of man’s action. By thus ignoring human freedom, he would seem to try to get rid of his own guilt.…[149] We see that this habit has grown into the very fibre of his character, and is that through which he is moved. That little talk of his at the beginning of the play, gives the germ: he has been guilty of a wrong, and has tried to shuffle off the responsibility for his act from himself by making guilty the sun, the moon, the stars. The result is, he becomes superstitious, a believer in the doctrine that man is governed by external [150] agencies, is not a free being, and hence not accountable. It is the attempt to smother conscience by self-excuse, till he succeeds; it is the lie which he tells to his own soul so often and so long, that at last he comes to believe it—the source of all his calamities.…Another result we must notice: Gloster, in releasing himself from moral responsibility, releases himself from inner control, and gives himself over to passion, as he gave himself over to the external powers of the planets. Thus he shows no patience, no charity, and herein he is again like Lear. Bradley (1904, pp. 295–6): Gloster is the superstitious character of the drama,—the only one. He thinks much of these late eclipses of the sun and moon. His two sons, from opposite points of view, make nothing of them. His easy acceptance of the calumny against Edgar is partly due to this weakness, and Edmund builds upon it, for an evil purpose, when he describes Edgar thus: [quotes 972–4]. [296] Edgar in turn builds upon it, for a good purpose, when he persuades his blind father that he was led to jump down Dover cliff by the temptation of a fiend in the form of a beggar, and was saved by a miracle: [quotes 2514–19]. Elton (1966, pp. 153–4): He is an identifiable superstitious type.…In his weak vacillation between terror and appeasement the earl is the antitype to his king’s continuing defiance. Projecting his personal insecurities onto the screen of the cosmos—his fear, as Greville would say, fashioning gods unto man—he seems to create the gods in the counterpart of his own image. In contrast to Cordelia’s steadfast faith and devotion, Gloucester’s perfect fear casteth out love. His attitude to the governing powers is expressed symbolically in his passion, at the hands of Cornwall and Regan: [quotes 2125–6]. The implication of man as a baited bear torn, pour le sport, by human curs is present in the image, but the microcosmic image corresponds also to Gloucester’s macrocosmic theology of pointlessly hostile divinities. Moreover, a summary of Gloucester’s expressions regarding himself and regarding the cosmos would show a certain congruence: in the first act he reveals himself to be credulous, rash, and vengeful, while he appeals blindly for harsh personal retribution to the heavens; he vacillates between sensual boasting regarding his adultery…and a misplaced sense of shame…; he is melancholy, [154] gloomy, and pessimistic, being struck by portents in eclipses, the ensuing decay of the world, the significance of predictions and almanacs, and the conviction that necessity rules via nativity and that the heavens, governing all, produce men’s vices and virtues; in the third act he exhibits fear, suspicion, and desire for vengeance, while on a cosmic level he falls into a kind of Stoic resignation and an acceptance of endurance and appeals to the presently kind gods for mercy; in the fourth act he shows humility and repentance, seeing man as the lowest animal, while ruling all are cruel gods, killing men for their sport; he expresses sympathy for the poor and views suicide as a release, while the gods are seen as punishing powers, alternately as possibly good, then as cruel and invincible, and as tyrants making men’s lives unbearable; later Gloucester is to repeat his conviction of the decay of the world, along with his acceptance of the truth, too, that ripeness is all, while ironically the gods in his cruelly blinded eyes become gentle.

Other critics are more indulgent. Bräker (1780; tr. 1979, p. 96): Gloster, noble Gloster, your fate moves me most deeply of all! See Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877) above, . Richmond-Green (1882, pt. 2, pp. 34, 40): Gloucester treads a Via Dolorosa.…His patience and fortitude, his forbearance and resolution, his love for the wronged Edgar welling above his own flood of woe, give us a nature rare and sweet, strong and charitable, and he lifts himself above the errors of his life, and shows us the clear ways of God.…[40] Gloster’s sufferings form the climax of the tragedy. Watt (1908, p. 279) calls him a beautiful figure, of humble fidelity and noble troth while for Armstrong (1913, p. 106) he is a gentleman and a sportsman, who does not seek to excuse himself, and bears manfully his awful punishment. Stone (1925, pp. 162–3): He is [163] fundamentally good and true…a simple man in a particularly dark hour. Lökse (1960, pp. 125–6) argues that he is neither sensual nor superstitious. Likewise Skulsky (1966; 1976, p. 139): There is no reason to suppose, with some critics, that Gloucester is, by the presumed standard, superstitious. See n. 433–44. Gardner (1967, pp. 14–15): Gloucester, the dupe of his clever son, is lifted beyond our patronage by the horror of the fate that falls upon him, the direct result of his first act of moral worth in the play. Gloucester is a follower of Cornwall, my worthy arch and patron. He has made his choice as to which rising power he will attach himself to. He has taken the Fool’s advice: [quotes 1334–5]. But there is a core of decency in him.…His conscience revolts. In the brief scene with Edmund the politic Gloucester, wanting to keep in with all sides, in the end comes down on the side of loyalty. His pride is injured by Cornwall taking command in his own house, he has heard rumours of the French invasion, the King’s injuries will be revenged—all these things sway him; but in the end he speaks simply in terms of moral obligation: [quotes 1768–9]. [15] The Gloucester who goes out into the tempest with his torch and meets the mad Lear, the Fool and the Bedlamite speaks a new language [quotes 1923–4]. And for the first time he speaks with the accents of wounded love: [quotes 1945–50]. When, at the end of the scene of his agony, he is thrust out to smell his way to Dover, he has ceased to be Edmund’s dupe and become Lear’s fellow-wanderer. Paris (1991, p. 139): He is a pious man who is trying to live by religious ideas, but he is unable to do so with any consistency.

Various critics emphasize moral or spiritual growth. Knight (1930, p. 215): Gloucester moves beyond self-interest, through suffering, to the nobility and grandeur of his prayer: [quotes 2473–9]. Knights (1959, pp. 107–8): The progress of Gloucester is something like a simplified projection of the Lear experience on to a morality plane.…[108] The Gloucester who listens to Lear’s tirades [in 4.6] is someone quite other than his earlier self, someone incredibly—miraculously, the play suggests—better. And the change in him, defined and emphasized by the touching simplicity of the verse he speaks, is something that our imagination completely endorses. Ribner (1960, pp. 130–1): He is, like Lear, a redeemed sinner: We are not to suppose that the fate which overtakes Gloucester is mere retribution for lechery, for his sin goes deeper than that. Gloucester violates the laws of primogeniture, as surely as Lear violates the duties of kingship. Gloucester’s sin is thus a denial of God’s law and of the harmonious order of the universe.…[131] Gloucester must suffer for his violation of order, just as Lear suffers for his, and through suffering he must undergo a like purgation, come to a state of Christian stoicism, and die joyfully. See also Idem (1958, p. 49). Long (1976, p. 164): The citizen Gloucester [is] at first entailed by a crudified version of Law as brute power and then repelled by it as more flexible and humane conceptions of the civilized stir within him. Rosinger (1968, pp. 493 ff.) sees Gloucester’s moral development displayed in his change from act[ing] and speak[ing] as if he were a god—an irresponsible god who creates in order to satisfy his lust, to accepting guilt. (P. 504): Gloucester’s charge against the gods is not offered by Shakespeare as a weighty judgment on life, but rather as an obstacle to be swept aside before moral regeneration can take place. Womack (2002, p. 104) relates him to figures in medieval saints’ drama: He can be seen to withdraw not only from the plot but from the world: luridly maimed and wandering in the wilderness, accompanied by a mysterious beggar who is part demon and part friendly animal, he is both a kind of martyr and a kind of ascetic, moving via a spectacular miracle and an obscurely purgative process to a death which is also a blissful reunion. His trajectory too is a kind of displaced sanctification; a whole area of the play is being made out of hagiographical material. See also Heilman (1948, pp. 41–265), cited above, as well as the various redemptivist critics cited above on .

Some critics find that psychological consistency in the role is sometimes sacrificed to dramatic situation. Stoll (1933, pp. 442–5): As he busies himself to save the King, he steadily comes nearer to being an heroic and tragic figure.…So far, however, does this tragic change and transfiguration proceed within him that I confess to some difficulty in recognizing the homely old fellow we knew, particularly after the blinding.…[443] The maundering greybeard, with his rambling prose, has vanished.…[444] Gloster…keeps all his good points, but almost none of his weak ones, a few external manner-[445]isms, but not the deeper-seated ones; in his suffering and his human relations he fairly seems himself, but in his utterances concerning life and fate he seems to pass a little beyond his range. Mason (1967, pp. 214) cites Gloucester as an instance of Lr.’s radical incoherence: In Act 4 Gloucester…rises in stature to a major figure and is conscious to the finger-tips of having squared his accounts with life. Like a hero in a Greek play he knows he has reached a limit. He thinks the wrong he has done his son is irreparable. In the world of a Greek play his attempted suicide would be noble. What are we to make of it here? Is it a case of diabolic possession, and are we therefore glad to see him abused once again and once again the victim of a baby trick? Or if we take his resolution to be noble, is it not a pitiful come-down to find him so easily converted by Edgar? Can we see unambiguously what Shakespeare, what the play wants with Gloucester? In contrast, he is for Smidt (1990, p. 130) the limit of realistic portraiture in this play (i.e., the most realistically plausible).

Various other views of the role include Kahn (2000, pp. 52 ff.): Gloucester is a classic conservative…not well adapted to changing political circumstances.…[109] He believes what he is shown, even when it clashes with what would otherwise seem obvious.…His blindness is an exact metaphor for this latent incapacity.…[110] Gloucester is…the paradigmatic political subject. He pulls together in his own person theater and politics.

div.head: Gonerill
div.p: Most critics discuss Goneril and Regan together, and thus most of the following comments include Regan as well as Goneril.

Contrasts between Goneril and Regan begin with Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 624–6): At the first…the two sisters display no characteristic difference; as like as a crab is to a crab, says the fool: on a closer inspection it is surprising what a wide and clearly defined contrast there is between the two. The elder, Goneril, with the wolfish visage and the dark frontlet of ill-humour, is a masculine woman, full of independent purposes and projects, whilst Regan appears more feminine, rather instigated by Goneril, more passive, and more dependent. Goneril’s boundless, unbordered nature, which renders her a true child of that fearful age, shows itself in bloody undertakings, originating in her own brain; whilst Regan’s evil nature appears rather in her urging on the atrocity of others, as when Kent is set in the stocks and Gloster’s eyes are torn out.…Goneril at first appears to govern her husband, who recognises her depth of foresight, and…she pursues her aims independently, scarcely listening to him, and scarcely deigning to answer him.…Regan, on the contrary, is obsequious and dependent toward the gloomy, laconic, and powerful Cornwall.…Regan cannot hurl forth vehement and hasty words like Goneril; she has not the same fierce eyes, her glance (though Lear in his madness indeed calls it a squint) is more full of comfort, her nature is softer and more cordial, and Lear, it seems, hardly trusts himself to penetrate her character closely; when, in his delusion, he sits in judgment upon her, he desires to have her heart anatomised. She utters inoffensively harsher things to her father than Goneril does, and yet her father hesitates to pronounce his curse upon her as upon her sister; a curse even twice repeated against [626] Goneril. The latter receives it with marble coldness, but Regan shudders, and fears to draw upon herself the like malediction. It is not until Goneril in her presence has entirely laid open her own cruel and unblushing barbarity towards their old father, that Regan grows bolder also, and drives away the king’s train of knights.…After the brood of serpents have got rid of the old father, there begins a domestic feud between the two families.…Here, again, Regan appears less blameable and vile; she makes no engagement with Edmund till after Cornwall’s death; she unsuspectingly confides letters for Edmund to Goneril’s treacherous servant; she falls a victim to her sister’s poison, being herself clear from all attempts of the kind; in every respect she is more contracted in her nature than her sister, whose woman’s will is of undistinguish’d space. This emphasis on Goneril as the more formidable sister is repeated by many subsequent critics. Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 263–4): Goneril is the calm wielder of a pitiless force, the resolute initiator of cruelty. Regan is a smaller, shriller, fiercer, more eager piece of malice. [264] The tyranny of the elder sister is a cool, persistent pressure, as little affected by tenderness or scruple as the action of some crushing hammer; Regan’s ferocity is more unmeasured, and less abnormal or monstrous. Regan would avoid her father, and while she confronts him alone, quails a little as she hears the old man’s curse pronounced against her sister: [quotes 1452–3]. But Goneril knows that a helpless old man is only a helpless old man, that words are merely words. When, after Lear’s terrible malediction, he rides away with his train, Goneril, who would bring things to an issue, pursues her father, determined to see matters out to the end.

Waller (1882, p. 78) accepts this pattern of contrasts but finds Regan less repulsive than her sister: Of the two, Goneril is the vilest, for she is the initiator of all the cruelty and crime.…Regan is a much more feminine character; she is less fierce, and in her wickedness greatly dependent upon Goneril.(p. 82) It is through the influence of Goneril that Edmund has ordered the death of Cordelia.

Critics often seem to try to outdo each other in expressing loathing for the sisters. For instance, A. B. (1752, p. 254): The daughters are intended as examples of divine vengeance, and as objects of detestation. Hazlitt (1817; 1930, p. 258): They are so thoroughly hateful that we do not even like to repeat their names. Horn (1823, 1:193; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, pp. 451–2): It would be an interesting subject for a prize essay which of the two is the worse, Regan or Goneril. I must confess, I am not able to answer the question satisfactorily. I believe Shakspeare meant to leave it a question. It may be said that Goneril, as she was the first to ill-treat her father, was the worse; but it may be justly replied, that Regan was still worse, inasmuch as the sight of the tortured old man, so far from moving her, only causes her to torture him anew, so that nothing is left but madness, which, as we have already intimated, can be regarded as only a relief. On the whole, the Fool was in the right when he said that both [452] were of a height, and that one tasted as much like the other as a crab does to a crab. Boas (1896, p. 443): These two terrible figures are by far the most revolting creations of the dramatist. They are not simply unsexed women, they are Gorgons, monsters in female shape, whose looks turn us to stone. With all the motiveless malignity of Iago, they are wanting in his genius, his humour, his magnificent audacity.

In fact Goneril and Regan are frequently regarded as inhuman monsters or types of wickedness rather than fully human characters. Hudson (1848, 2:227–31): There is no accounting for the conduct of Goneril and Regan but by supposing a thorough fiendishness of nature, a very instinct and impulse of malignity. With but little of soul, and that little concentrated in the head, they have no heart to guide and inspire their understanding, and but just enough understanding to seize occasions and frame excuses for their heartlessness.…[228] It is difficult to think of them otherwise than merely as instruments of [229] the plot; not so much ungrateful persons as personifications of ingratitude.…[231] Thus we are let to see, that whether they are drawn together or drawn asunder, still it is from an appetite for sin; that if they unite, it is to do evil, and if they divide, it is to do the same. It is a significant fact, that their passion for Edmund grows out of his treachery to his father; as though they saw in his proceedings an apology for their own.…It is worthy of remark, also, that they are both of the self-same mind and metal; indeed they are so much alike in character, that we can scarcely distinguish them as individuals; seem almost too much like repetitions of each other to be realities. See also Idem, 1872, 2:356–9. Reed (1855, p. 362): They are incarnations of guilty passions and self-tormenting cares. Hugo (1864; tr. 1886, p. 246): Sh. takes Ingratitude, which begins with a caress, and he gives to this monster two heads. Doyle (1877, p. 161): Regan and Goneril, are not pourtrayed by Shakspere in his happiest manner. They serve their purpose, and that is all. As important elements in an important play, they are perhaps nearer lay figures, and conventional impersonations of stage wickedness, than any other characters in the whole of Shakspere’s works. Everything spoken by Regan might belong to Goneril. Everything belonging to Goneril might come from Regan. There is no difference between them, unless we say that Goneril…is the more enterprising and unscrupulous she-devil of the two. Norwood (1925, p. 596): These women are mere simulacra dressed out in exaggerated vices and blazing with theatrical devilry. Even as fiends they are wooden and unreal; when the comparatively normal plane is left behind, they never move like animate beings, but jerk convulsively into incredible depravities. A play which depends for its action so considerably on two such glaringly-daubed puppets cannot be accounted, whatever its other merits, as taking high dramatic rank. Watkins (1942, p. 23): Goneril, who is the most astonishing characterization in the play, represents this fusion [of psychological realism with symbolism] perfectly.…Her subtlety is poetic, not psychological, though psychology is present.…She is a magnificent embodiment of evil, and no less one of Shakespeare’s greatest character creations because, unlike Lady Macbeth, she is superhuman, an allegorical figure. Novy (1979, pp. 282–3): The contrast between Goneril and Regan, on the one hand, and Cordelia, on the other, owes something to the traditional tendency in Western literature to split the image of woman into devil and angel, Eve and Mary.…[283] Goneril and Regan are much less psychologically complex than most Shakespearean characters of comparable importance. Few of their lines carry hints of other motivations than cruelty, lust, or ambition, characteristics of the archetypal fantasy image of the woman as enemy. Shakespeare gives them no humanizing scruples.

Other critics insist they are plausibly human. Gentleman (1770, 1:375): Goneril and Regan are characters infamously black, but not as Dr. Warton [1754, 2:312] seems to doubt impossible or even improbable; for we have too many originals of filial ingratitude in real life, to verify such mimic representations of it. Clarke (1863, pp. 175–6): History presents no parallel in criminality to the two elder daughters of Lear; and the poet, with unerring instinct in ethics, has extended their hard and cruel undutifulness towards their husbands, as well as their parent.…Throughout their career of wickedness, we cannot fail to be struck with the tact and feeling of the poet, in toning down the externals of their natures upon those occasions when they are brought into communion and contact with their father. Then we find that their speeches are subdued, and delivered with a certain air of deference, as though the paternal authority were not wholly extinct in their minds. The unfilial deportment bursts forth, and is displayed when he has quitted the scene.…[176] There is also another point in which the two characters attract attention, and that is in their individuality. It has frequently been observed that there is no distinction or predominance in the cruelty of the two daughters of Lear. They are twins in wickedness, and yet there is a characteristic difference in the mind-manner of the two women. Gonneril [sic] is more towering and haughty in her deportment. She never, for a moment, loses sight of her descent—she never forgets the aristocrat. Her conduct toward her husband is uniformly that of one who has descended from a higher sphere to ally herself with, and to tolerate a husband; and whom (when she encounters a person more agreeable to her fancy) she plots to assassinate. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:41–3): With regard to Goneril and Regan [Sh.] is quite content to assume—we shrink from the assumption nowadays—that there are really wicked people in the world. That admitted, these two exemplars of the fact are lifelike enough.…They are both realists. Their father wants smooth speech of them and they give it, echoing his very phrases and tones.…Left alone together…they are under no illusions at all, we find, about their own good fortune.…They are as wide-awake to the chances of trouble ahead; but while Regan would wait and see, Goneril means to go to meet it.…What a good case Goneril makes for herself.…And Regan, though she needs Goneril’s prompting, makes an even better case of it; the weaker nature is the more plausible.…[42] How then can we call Regan and Goneril double-dyed fiends? They played the hypocrite for a kingdom; but which of us might not? Having got what they wanted and more than they expected they found good excuse for not paying the price for it. Like failings have been known in the most reputable people. Their conduct so far, it could be argued, has been eminently respectable, level-headed and worldly-wise. They do seem somewhat hard-hearted, but that is all.…But from now on the truth about them grows patent. Does prosperity turn their heads? It releases hidden devils.…And the weaker Regan grows the more violent of the two; she turns crueler even than that bloody wolf, Cornwall, her husband. For amid the scuffling a little later she can even think to tell Gloucester that his own son has betrayed him; and even as he faces her, blinded and bleeding, she can jeer at him. The devil of lust comes now to match with the devil of cruelty.…In their plot upon their father they were clever enough, self-controlled, subtle. But, the beast let loose in them, they turn reckless, shameless, foolish. Regan, with a little law on her side, presumes on it; so Goneril poisons her as she might a rat. And the last note of Goneril is devilish pride.…[43] We may see, then, in Goneril and Regan, evil triumphant, self-degrading and self-destructive. It may also be that, from beginning to end, Shakespeare, for his part, sees little to choose between hot lust and murdering hand and the hard heart, in which all is rooted. Sharma (1965, p. 83): Women like Goneril and Regan are barbarous; their conduct is unnatural but not improbable. History—both British and Indian—has many parallel examples.

Various critics seek psychological explanations for their actions. Doyle (1877, p. 162) suggests that Lear’s preferential treatment of Cordelia may have embittered them. Somerville (1929, pp. 161 ff.) describes Goneril as a mental monstrosity,…[162] a type of mind in which emotion, tender or otherwise, is but feebly represented—or possibly lacking altogether. Love, gratitude, hate, pity, remorse and purposive cruelty apparently find no place in her. It is even doubtful if she has any feelings of fear or natural desire. She is neither moral nor immoral. She is simply non-moral.…[164] If there is such a thing as moral insanity—a debatable question—then she was morally insane.…[167] Goneril poisons her sister not out of jealousy, as Edmund thinks, but because Regan was an impediment in her path to the throne…and her reasoning for committing suicide was, probably, because she saw no other course open for her. Abenheimer (1945, p. 329) describes the sisters as narcissists, adding that Blinding is symbolical of castration.…Women who narcissistically crave omnipotence always include this destruction in their fantastic destructive aims. Faber (1967, pp. 314 ff.): Goneril’s desire for Edmund as well as her profound marital discontent may have been fostered to some extent by Lear himself, who…lavished the better part of his fatherly affection on Cordelia.…Goneril’s longing for Edmund [can be understood] by remembering that he represents to her the possible satisfaction of frustrated dependency needs which cannot reach their ultimate fulfillment in the marital relationship because for Goneril the marital relationship is too reminiscent of an unrewarding or nongratifying parent-child relationship. In a word, Goneril’s lusting after Edmund is a psychopathological lusting, rooted primarily in the frustrations and dependencies of childhood and only secondarily in the matured physical emer-[315]gencies of the adult. Davis (1974, pp. 59–71): Goneril has that all-engulfing selfishness which interprets the world about her according to her moods.…[61] She is a tempestuous beauty, magisterial, disdainful of the opposition she can ignore, furious at the annoyances she cannot.…[70] Goneril is quite expansive in her enumeration of the king’s faults, as expansive as she was when professing her great love for him, and is false on each occasion.…[71] She has an eye for the faults of those nearest her, we might almost say a psychological need to condemn in order to explain away her perpetual dissatisfaction with life. Boredom is a chronic affliction with her, to a degree that makes a well-balanced life virtually impossible. Goldberg (1974, pp. 104–5): Goneril is more than a hypocritical ingrate.…[105] She does know Lear’s heart—in the only terms in which he has given it to her, but more importantly in the only terms she can know anything: that is, of threats from, and aggression towards, the external world.…[106] The rampant ego can see personal relationships only as power-relationships.…The power of her verse lies in the security and freedom achieved by keeping the facts wholly outside herself, and the strict command she can thereby exercise over them within. Leggatt (1988, p. 42–7): In Act 1 and 2.1, they appear to be not attacking Lear but simply protecting themselves: their tactics are to withdraw and deny. So far we seem to be dealing with petty meanness, an evil—if it is evil—that has no scale, no spiritual dimension, nothing like Iago’s divinity of hell. But as Lear puts pressure on them, a moral abyss begins to open.…[43] Muir’s insight [1949, p. 41] that there is something missing is acute; but I wonder if it is memory.…I think what is missing might better be called censorship. Most people have cruel or violent impulses but are able to suppress them; we know there are certain things we are not supposed to do. Goneril and Regan do not appear to know this.…[44] What begins as common sense opens out into a terrifying blankness, a moral idiocy. In Goneril and Regan we confront…the banality of evil.…[45] They may think of their later rivalry for Edmond as love, but the passion that drives them is not love for Edmond but jealousy of each other.…They are incapable of natural sexual [46] enjoyment.…[47] Shakespeare’s Goneril and Regan are not created out of such normal feelings [as Gonorill and Ragan display in Leir] but out of absence and withdrawal. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, pp. 127–36): Rather than being monsters of ingratitude,…they have been contaminated by Lear’s own cruelty.…[128] Giving away his kingdom conceals Lear’s wish to tighten the hold on his daughters so that he will have them constantly at his disposal.…[129] They refuse to accept the blackmail implicit in Lear’s pelican-mother devotion, which is a healthy sign. They must defend their own integrity.…It can reasonably be assumed that [Lear’s] daughters have been raised in a despotic yet probably seductive atmosphere; they have grown up with the conviction that they must be submissive at all times or else be repudiated.…However…on a level that is in a sense magical and ephemeral, their grandiloquent words of praise fulfill Lear’s real, primitive needs.…[130] The two horrible ingrates realize that their father’s violence is an authentic danger, but they do not turn him into a dragon (or only to a limited extent). On the contrary, they (particularly Goneril) continually try to make him reason on the basis of an inadequate but firm and realistic logic.…[132] Goneril’s error, if it can be called that, is to alternate between a parental attitude comprising a mixture of perverse blandishments and severity and an adult attitude that requires mutual respect. This she does while failing to understand that before her stands a man who is on the verge of madness. At another level, the two sisters feel so harassed by their father that they react with extreme ferocity—the very ferocity of Lear himself.…[135] Are the daughters afraid of freedom? Regan’s hesitations and Goneril’s hesitations are signs of their insecurity. They still harbor a strong desire to revive, at the social level, a flesh-and-blood father able to protect them from the same primitive terror evoked by the dragon, as well as another Saint George father figure able to [136] alleviate their feelings of guilt toward a parent who has been attacked and is furious. Does their sudden, theatrically abrupt and almost gratuitous love for Edmond express this compelling need?…This coup de foudre allows Goneril and Regan to continue their attempt to keep love separate from rage. While Lear continues to be the object of their hatred for a tyrannical father, the primal love for a father who (Lear gives us to understand) had once known how to be warm and passionate is transferred to Edmond.

Some critics excuse their behavior to varying degrees, often ascribing their behavior to traits inherited from Lear. Thus Johnston (1884, p. 97): Shakespeare provides some excuse for their behavior, foundation, insufficient as it might be, for conduct not only wholly inexcusable in its inception.…The monarch had not considered that these daughters must have inherited some of the spirit that had made their father a ruler. Wendell (1894, pp. 296–9) comments on the excellent reasons which Goneril and Regan have to justify what is commonly held to be their gross ingratitude. In the first place, these women have inherited from their father an impetuous, overbearing temper, of the kind which is especially sensitive to the exhibition of its weakness by other people. Constitutionally, then, they would be specially liable to provocation by a man so like them as their father. In the second place, their professions of filial devotion are [297] not essentially insincere; they are simply elaborate manifestations of such formal etiquette as still appears in the formulæ of correspondence. Cordelia’s sincerity is an excess of too mannerly virtue; Goneril’s and Regan’s protestations of love are only what court manners conventionally require. Lear, quartered with Goneril, behaves outrageously, and she is justifiably angry; her anger manifests itself, characteristically, not by a direct outburst, but by orders, quite in accordance with court etiquette, that Lear and his rowdies be treated with abruptness.…[298] Lear’s behavior is in no way conciliatory. Finally, before he plunges off into the storm, both of his daughters have been worked up into such a rage that if they had acted as modern moralists command they would have been too good for human nature. Given their temperaments, the conduct of Lear, and the misunderstanding involved in the clash between the character and the disguise of Kent, and [sic] nothing could be more humanly justifiable than their behavior. Yet so carefully is the intention of the plot preserved that to this day these passionate, human women are considered to be what Lear and the audience were expected to find them,—monsters of ingratitude. S. A. Brooke (1913, p. 207): Sh. provides some reason for their cruelty: They had inherited their father’s temperament, but had been forced to keep it down for all these years and to suffer in the repression. In contrast, Armstrong (1913, 106–7) suggests heredity from their mother: One trembles to think where they got [107] their villainy from. Lear is evidently a widower. Madam is never mentioned—a fact for which there is probably good reason. Cordelia probably takes after her father. Hammond (1913, p. 112): We have in the main plot of King Lear a study in heredity.…In the older daughters we see but Lear’s worse passions turned back and visited upon him even as Gloster’s sin finds him out at Edmund’s hand. Taylor (1907, pp. 219–21) also notes hereditary traits and reasonable objections. C. F. T. Brooke (1913, pp. 91–2): Goneril and Regan are always thought monsters of evil, and [92] so they indubitably appeared to Shakespeare. Yet the spectator who watches them through the first two acts and a half may find it difficult to justify his detestation. Till the beginning of the storm scenes in Act III, worldly reason would even pronounce in favor of the two daughters as opposed to their domineering and vindictive father. The dramatist’s purpose, indeed, is to dethrone just this cold reason of the law-court, which freezes the sympathies and apotheosizes self-interest. Ashwell (1926, p. 157) says of Gonerill: Every housekeeper will agree with me that her position was most difficult, the whole situation become intolerable. It is exactly that rightness, that persistent, nagging, peevish, wailing rightness, which makes the shrew. Block (1959, p. 506): What Shakespeare has attempted to do in Act 1 is to balance the audience’s sympathies between Lear and Goneril, first by presenting Lear in as unfavorable a light as possible and, then, by emphasizing what Goneril has had to put up with not only from Lear’s knights but from Lear himself. See also Harbage (1947, p. 66). Alfar (1996, p. 375): Their evil is defined by acts of will, power, desire, sexuality—acts which disrupt both conventional morality and the patrilineal order’s definition of appropriate femininity and consequently must be met with punitive consequences. However, the presumption that Goneril and Regan are evil reifies female subjectivity as stable and whole, rather than multiple and complex.…[Their] actions are not evidence of their innate evil but are symptomatic of the patrilineal structure of power relations in which they live and to which they must accommodate themselves. Kahn (2000, p. 64): The conflict between love and law is the source of Goneril’s evil. In Acts 1 and 2 there is no dramatic evidence that [Lear’s] daughters are acting out of malice or even mistreating him. They have the familial obligation to support him in his old age. They accept this burden. They seek to perform it, however, in a way that does not endanger the public order.…Goneril and Regan are, at this point, the voice of reason in the state.…[118] The development of Goneril’s character is… a consequence of, her exercise of political responsibility, which has led her away from the roles of [119] daughter and wife. Each compromise with the traditional values of the House has made her more open to the next step, until there is nothing left but the defense of power itself. Furthermore, (p. 137) we are in no position to condemn Goneril’s love for Edmund, in place of a husband whom she seems never to have loved.

Mack (1965, pp. 31–2) objects to those who make excuses for Goneril: Lear is not an easy domestic guest.…But to justify Goneril is to obscure from the audience the relentless movement by which the man who is cynically humored so long as (in the Fool’s phrase) he bears bags is maneuvered into surrender by two daughters whom Kent calls dog-hearted [2347+46], Albany calls Tigers, not daughters [2303+9], and the gentlest voice in the play calls Shame of ladies! [2347+28].…[32] In the play’s terms, Lear being her father, nothing can possibly justify Goneril.…On the one hand, she is like the flood which cannot be border’d certain in itself [2303+2], and will, given the opportunity, as Ulysses says in Troilus and Cressida, make a sop of all this solid globe; on the other hand, she is like the branch that tears itself from the fostering tree. Throughout the play Shakespeare brilliantly humanizes both Regan and Goneril by the shifting passions and appetites he traces in their speech, but this is a different matter from motivation. The motivation of the sisters lies not in what Lear has done to them, but in what they are. The fact that they are paradigms of evil rather than (or as well as) exasperated spoilt children whose patience has been exhausted gives them their stature and force. Likewise Taylor (To Analyze, 1985, pp. 192–3): Modern criticism derides as sentimental or melodramatic any [193] interpretation which too thoroughly blackens Lear’s daughters, and yet the sentimental melodramatic Tate has done his best to find excuses for them, often the very excuses paraded by their latter-day apologists. Sentimentality is the refusal to believe…in irredeemable evil. Evans (1990, p. 12) calls Goneril irredeemably evil, forever cut off from grace

Other critics even find suggestions of tragic grandeur in Goneril and sometimes Regan as well. Mézières (1865, p. 299) compares them to the heroines of Racine and Corneille. Ruskin (1865; 1905, 18:114) describes the sisters as frightful exceptions to the ordinary laws of life; fatal in their influence also, in proportion to the power for good which they have abandoned. Thom (1885, p. 167): Goneril is a character but little inferior to Lady Macbeth in the strength of will to execute what her strong mind conceives though she fills us with more of disgust than the terrible Scotch Queen, because her powers are exerted in pursuit of the lusts of the flesh rather than of the lust of the intellect. Swinburne (1902, p. 4): A champion who wished to enter the lists on behalf of Goneril might plead that Regan was so much more of a Gadarean sow than her elder sister as to be, for all we know, incapable of such passion as flames out in Goneril at the thought of foreign banners spread in a noiseless land. Beast and she-devil as she is, she rises in that instant to the level of an unclean and a criminal Joan of Arc. Her advocate might also invoke as an extenuating circumstance the fact that she poisoned Regan. Bradley (1904, pp. 299–300): The differences between the sisters, which are distinctly marked…are all in favour of the elder and more terrible.…Edmund judged right when, caring for neither sister but aiming at the crown, he preferred Goneril, for he could trust her to remove the remaining impediments to her desires. The scornful and fearless exclamation, An interlude! with which she greets the exposure of her design, was quite beyond Regan. Her unhesitating suicide was perhaps less so. She would not have condescended to the lie which Regan so needlessly tells to Oswald: [quotes 2394–8]. [300] Her father’s curse is nothing to her. She scorns even to mention the gods. In this she stands alone among the more notable characters of the play.…Touches of Goneril reappear in the heroine of the next tragedy, Macbeth; and…we are sometimes reminded of her again by the character of the Queen in Cymbeline.…Horrible as she is she is almost awful. Bransom (1934, pp. 17 ff.) admires Goneril extravagantly: Shakespeare meant to endow her with personal beauty of face and form, perhaps too with a certain voluptuousness.…[18] Goneril is as clearly differentiated from Regan as she is from Cordelia. Indeed the eldest and youngest were in some respects more alike; and they certainly bore a stronger resemblance to their father than Regan did.…[51] The tragedy of Cordelia and the tragedy of Goneril are both compressed and included in the tragedy of King Lear. In fact, (p. 165) The tragedy of Goneril is more bitter than the tragedy of Lear, and, like Lear’s, it is a tragedy of character.…[197] The mainspring of Goneril’s conduct was a vast ambition [to rule Britain without corrival] dating from the opening of the play, or, in embryo, even before. In Act 1, (p. 41) Goneril suspected the existence of [a] conspiracy to restore the king, and she felt in consequence how great was the danger latent in the king’s retinue. She therefore determined to get rid of it. This led to a quarrel with her father, as a result of which he abjured her roof and in a mighty rage sought shelter with Regan. But Goneril was aware of disputes between her husband and brother-in-law which might lead to war. She knew that in such an event an alliance between her sister and father might be decisive against her victory. So she determined to be present at their interview to prevent it. In Acts 1 and 2 Goneril displays (p. 53) admirable resolution and resource; and when we consider that she acted with the fear inspired by the curse still in her heart, I think we may accord her our admiration. That Goneril was incapable of saying anything in a conciliatory way…should…[54] be regarded as constitutional and compared with the difficulty Cordelia found in speaking at all.…[62] She has affinities with what we may describe as [Lear’s] tragic type, and one cannot help indulging the useless regret that she has not been more elaborated. Also, supposedly (p. 49) Goneril was a girl about to become a mother. But Rosenberg (1972, pp. 47 ff.) dismisses this as unlikely: There is no direct hint…of pregnancy; and…if it existed, the Bastard, who so shrewdly casts his balances in soliloquy, might be expected to weigh this item. Goneril and Regan (p. 49) are passionate women, with some humor, social grace, and the physical strength to ride long hours through the night and preside at battles.…[50] It has been said that Goneril’s first speech shows her to be a quantifier, [51] a measurer, answering with calculation her father’s request for love [cf. Hawkes (1959)].…But the invitation to quantify is initiated by Lear himself; and if Goneril weighs carefully later, moving between calculation and passion, she certainly does not do so [in 1.1].…[52] Goneril’s own tragic history, as well as Lear’s, must not be diminished by visualizing her only as a witch. Reducing her—and Regan—at once to wicked stereotypes destroys both the dialectic and the suspense of character and action.…[251] To see her as simply lascivious or serpentine is another way of reducing the whole Lear equation to a morality. Goneril’s passion [for Edmund], like her ambition, is oversize, Lear-size; she would be a queen with a king of her choice. She has some of the stature of Lady Macbeth—whose love was not necessarily lust because she was an accomplice to murder.…Powerful and passionate, she yet has touches of grace and humor. Long (1976, p. 182) finds a perversely passionate and hotly energetic and explosive quality to the evil displayed by Goneril and Regan. Driscoll (1977, p. 160) sees in her an emblem of Yahweh’s terrible anima.

For others, however, she and her sister are merely repellent in a commonplace way. Beale (1881, p. 62): Goneril’s violence is not strength, but weakness, the result of fear. Mackenzie (1924, pp. 295–6) describes her as a person absolutely sure both of her rightness and her power, and [296] quite stupid. Muir (1949, p. 41): Having no memory, they have no responsibility, and no need, therefore, to treat their father differently from any other troublesome old man.…They seem to have come from nowhere and to be on the way to nowhere; they have words and acts only to meet the momentary emergency, the momentary appetite; their speech is therefore strikingly deficient in imagery, and consists of a series of pitiless truisms. Gardner (1967, pp. 12–14) deplores the awful self-righteousness, the monstrous [13] acceptance of themselves as being right and justified, the cold priggishness of Goneril and Regan.…They sound like the unsympathetic matrons of an old people’s home.…Goneril and Regan are both plainly beautiful women, but charm, a quality not inconsistent with depravity, they do not possess, for they have no capacity for enjoyment.…[14] They never laugh any more than they weep and are forever on guard to keep what they have and get more. Barnet (1956, p. 15): Each is, in the view of the audience, a she-fox whose baseness is not mitigated either by the evil of the other, or the faults in Lear himself. Blok (1966, p. 20): Both are thoroughly commonplace, vulgar pieces; in both, the human being has died, leaving them with nothing but immutable instinctual urges. In any other epoch they would have been spiteful gossips; in that age they became black-hearted criminals. Kozintsev (1977, p. 69): Beauty, even with fateful undertones and a taste of the infernal, is death to such characters as Goneril and Regan. Regan tells her father that she has not enough food to keep him and his train; Goneril storms at her husband, using coarse words of abuse like a fish-wife. One must see the horrifying commonplaceness of these obscene heartless old women. Basney (1994, p. 31): The evil in Goneril and Regan is not, most of the time, Dionysiac and volcanic. It is quiet, polite, fitting; it is a parody of obligation.

Goneril and her sister sister have been interpreted as representing various political positions. Ingram (1984, p. 254): She is partly made to resemble a puritan parvenue—rational, hypocritical, and lustful.…Thus she threatens three hierarchies: monarchical, familial, and class. Weimann (1967; tr. 1978, p. 237): Turned in on themselves and imprisoned by their own egotism…Goneril and Regan represent a new individualism. They are so far removed, not only in moral outlook but also in physical space, from the plebeian audience and its collective understanding of the world and of art, that they occupy a Figurenposition that permits knavish speech and self-revealing aside but not that type of proverb and wordplay that is rooted in the common experience and inherited traditions of the people. In fact they are not given any forms of speech that recall the festive element and ritual origins of audience contact.…Their outlook, regardless of how brilliantly it is presented, does not permit any sustained downstage position. That is one reason why they do not conclude the play. Cohen (1988, p. 124): Like most of Shakespeare’s villains, the sisters demonstrate only a fragmented connection with history. Their mode, typically, is the present and future, their vision is clearly focussed on gaining control of their world by looking at what is, rather than what was, in order to determine what shall be. Märtin (1992, pp. 140 ff.): Goneril and Regan compose a realistic image of cruelty and destructiveness in societies focused on power and property. (In Ger.) Euridge (1994, pp. 57–9), rejecting the rigid critical Trinitarianism which binds Goneril, Regan, and Edmund indivisibly, argues that (p. 59) Goneril and Regan destroy each other not because of any inherent weakness in their new order…but because they remain fully integrated with the old order and its many weaknesses, because they remain entrapped by the nexus of gender and social constructions that inform the play.

Several modern critics discuss the sisters in relation to ideas of women’s gender roles and representations of women. Harding (1969, p. 250): Gonerill is a less interesting conception than Lady Macbeth precisely because she makes a success of the male role; she is a convincing imitation of an unscrupulous man, eventually overthrown, it is true, as many villains are, but not divided and defeated by her femininity. Adelman (1992, p. 115): In the portrayal of Goneril and Regan, the play’s dramaturgy is entirely complicit with the fantasy of the dark and vicious place (i.e., Lear’s subconscious fear and loathing of the feminine). For the play simultaneously illuminates their genesis in Lear’s need [to scapegoat women] and embraces Lear’s vision of them, making them monstrous as he himself could have wished: as it progresses, they are increasingly identified as the source of evil; finally removed wholly from the realm of human sympathy—as Edmund never is—they die as monsters, consumed by their own excess.

Goneril and Regan’s language has been discussed by other critics. Guyol (1966, p. 319): Goneril’s controlled language reflects her controlled and limited universe. Valesio (1980, pp. 45–6): The bad sisters embody…a frank and straightforward rhetorical approach. They are…sincere…in the only serious sense that this word can have applied to any discourse—namely, their rhetorical performance conforms to the explicitly established pattern. Rutter (1994–6; 1997, p. 198): Goneril’s role collects up and literalizes the metaphors of speech and silence that monster Lear’s daughters.

They are often discussed as symbols or embodiments of themes. Snider (1887, pp. 205–6): Their very faithlessness becomes universal. Having been faithless to their father, they naturally become faithless to the Family in all its relations; [206] they are now portrayed as violating the great fundamental virtue of the Family—chastity. Heilman (1948, p. 228): They are rationalists whose considerable shrewdness is used entirely for the gratification of their desires.…The animal and the practical intelligence are joined in a calculating mechanism which, within certain limits, is terrifyingly efficacious. Thus they can be seen as aspects of Lear: We may recall that the spirit of calculation was first set free, so to speak, by Lear, and that the kinship between him and his daughters symbolizes his responsibility for them, and his momentary, but inaugural, participation in the fallacious method of judging values.…If they are considered as a kind of extrusion from him, a developing into life-size of a part of his personality, freed from the counterbalance of the rest of the personality, we can see how tight the unity of the play is.…[234] The paradox is that these free minds, unburdened by any conventional or traditional allegiance, become slaves to the uncontrolled animal desire, mechanisms for the attainment of irrational objectives.…[235] Hence the portrayal of the sisters in the triangular passion is a dramatic elaboration of Lear’s metaphor for them—Centaurs: we see rational mind unmistakably in conjunction with, and what is more, in the service of, the animal body.…[236] They are defeated by their nature despite their sharp minds because they have lacked the power of imagination by which they might get hold of disciplinary, saving values. That they are morally lost was clear from the start; the final little joke upon them is that they are also practically lost. In their reason is a double madness. Similarly, Traversi (1952, pp. 46–7): In Goneril and Regan the passions which lurk in the darker recesses of [Lear’s] undifferentiated humanity are given independent life and logical consistency.…Events will show that…in spite of their impressive appearance of control, of dominating the event, [they] share their father’s incapacity to control the promptings of passion. For it is a fundamental part of the play’s conception that father and [47] daughters are to be regarded as complementary aspects of a single development within the unity of the family. Empson (1949, pp. 197–8): The internecine lust of the two sisters…illustrate[s] the [198] themes of sex-horror and the self-destructiveness of evil. Elton (1966, pp. 117–21) places Goneril in the Renaissance literary tradition of the Machiavellian atheist: Despite her paganism, the striking thing about Goneril is that she never mentions the gods at all, an indication that her Renaissance garb has completely covered her natural condition; totally self-occupied with her lusts and the expansion of her will, she is deaf to such counsels as Edgar’s to Gloucester, do but look up [2501].…[119] As a heathen villainess, sprung fully grown from the head of the Renaissance Machiavel, Goneril exhibits few differences from her sixteenth-century Italian model; the implication is that, sharing the common ground of atheism, the pagan and the Machiavellian are expected to behave in a similar manner against God and their fellow men.…Further, in contrast to Cordelia’s governance and knowledge, Goneril’s ideals are practical judgment and action; remarking Lear’s poor judgment [316] in worldly self-regard, she is quick to act in what she conceives as her own self-interest.…Indeed, for her, mind [522] is almost the same as will…, a far leap from the Aquinian or Hookerian nous, or reason; her world is a visible one, without cosmic hierarchy and principle, and must be constructed through frenzied acquisition, status claims, climbing, and opportunism; lacking Cordelia’s bond, Goneril ironically creates disorder and is, in-[120]deed, in herself an aspect of disorder—chaos and evil being twins in the Elizabethan view.…[121] Goneril and Regan move within a universe of confused proportions in which the only unit of measurement is quantitative, and the main value word, more. Their motive is not service but the new [122] appetitus divitiarum infinitus. For them love means both physical and material gratification. Dachslager (1986, p. 17), in contrast, finds Goneril and Regan theologically neutral, neither faithful nor unfaithful, orthodox nor unorthodox. Stockholder (1976, p. 25) discusses the sisters as projections of psychological fantasy: Goneril and Regan express the rage, hatred, fury, unrelenting desire for revenge on those who do not recognize Cordelia, i.e. the phantasy figure of the self as good and beautiful. Goneril and Regan vengefully deny and humiliate the actual parent, until with them we experience the satisfaction of having the father at the feet of the child, and finally closing the door against him. Booth (1983, p. 45) describes them as exemplifying the principle of simultaneous likeness and difference which constitutes the primary quality of Lr. Shakespeare goes to some trouble to establish Goneril and Regan as a single evil force… but we come to recognize Goneril’s superior intelligence and managerial skill and to see that Regan trails behind her, compensating for dullness with exaggerated brutality. By Act V, when their mutual antagonism has become the most virulent in the play, Goneril and Regan are surely no longer a single unit; but in their squabble over Edmund they again seem interchangeable to us (one has to think a moment to remember which sister is murdered and which is the suicide).…Goneril and Regan are a unit and are also detached elements free to relate with or oppose any others. Turner (1988, pp. 111 ff.): The sisters…emblematize all the envious malice still at the heart of family life.…[107] Despite the rationalizations of self-interest which they offer, they are in fact seduced by the perverse pleasures that lie on the other side of prohibition.…The secret heart of these pleasures is envy. Spinosa (1995, p. 173) characterizes the sisters as feudal rather than (pace Danby et al.) modern, and argues that Goneril and Regan are…both innocent of having any abiding relation to their country’s style, which Lear seeks to embody, and any single passionately felt sentiment that organizes all their excessive desires, such as Cordelia’s love for Lear. They are, in the terms of this play, characters innocent of character. Grady (1996, pp. 149–50) relates them to the theme of reified power. They become merely subject-positions for the carrying out of the dictates of power, with…[150] an added dimension of sexuality. They become virtually allegorical.

McLeod (1983, pp. 175–85) argues for significant differences between the Quarto and Folio versions of Goneril: As soon as we contrast the texts,…we see that [Goneril’s] plan [in 1.3] to slack service in F is relatively cool; it reads like the reasoned tit for tat of a woman who is conscious of propriety and principle, and who responds to provocation slowly and in proportion. The Q Duchess by contrast seems to have lost her grip on herself, and her Q-only vituperations seem to offer an inner glimpse of a woman so insecure about the authorities that hee hath giuen away that she is impelled to force his hand by breed[ing] from hence occasions. When we contrast Q and F it seems that Gonerill the Bitch has yet to appear in The Tragedie; in The Historie, however, Gonorill is now taking on monstrous dimensions. In 1.4 also (p. 179) Gonerill’s self-control and the specificity of her grievance with her father in The Tragedie [contrast] with Gonorill’s general wildness in The Historie.…[185] From [4.2] to the end of the play one’s impression of Gonerill is that she is ever more self-possessed than her Quarto counterpart, but that her comparable perversity is paradoxically both more chilling and theatrically attractive—as was Edmund’s—by virtue of wit. Foakes (1993, p. 106) likewise finds that F variants provide a softening of [Goneril’s] personal hostility to Lear and more reasonable cause for [Goneril and Regan’s] attitude toward their father. Knowles (1997, p. 68) objects: How can such minutiae really alter our judgment of Goneril when weighed against her whole career of heartless ingratitude, greed, lust, connivance, attempted murder of her father and husband, and actual murder of her sister, and against the repeated judgments of Cordelia, Kent, Lear, the Fool, Gloucester, Edgar, and Albany that she like Regan is unnatural, bestial, monstrous, even demonic?

div.head: Kent
div.p: Early critics unfailingly admire Kent.
