Davies (1784, 2:187): The generosity of Kent is not to be matched in any other drama, antient or modern.…None but a Shakspeare ever conceived so noble an example of persisting goodness and generous fidelity. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:54): Kent [is] the nearest to perfect goodness of all Shakespeare’s characters, and yet the most individualized. Lamb (1811; 1935, p. 310): He is the noblest pattern of virtue which even Shakespeare has conceived. Horn (1823, 1:199; tr. Furness, ed. 1880, p. 452): Even the poorest and humblest servant still has a respectable name, but Kent takes no such title; he calls himself Caius. Of all names, this is the meanest; it is hardly a name, as in all schools, in Manuals of Logic, Grammars, &c. it stands as a makeshift for all names. Just on this account, it is here excellently chosen, for Kent who, as a count and knight, is banished, will be nothing now, and believes there is no need that he should be anything else than a mere helper of the king, and, by this pure self-abnegation, he becomes the most faithful friend of the miserable king. Clarke (1863, p. 181): Kent is the personification of a brave, uncompromising, all-enduring friendship. What in almost any other writer would appear like a crude melo-drame friendship, by the force of genius, assumes the air of a perfectly natural course of action. We are surprised at no sacrifice on the part of Kent in behalf of his master: we feel that he would have gone to his death to have rescued him from his miseries; and this, not from a blind, serf-like obedience; for Kent is a reasoning man, and in the day of Lear’s power is the only one who stands between him and his perversity, and endeavours to protect him against himself. The blunt, rough-speaking of many honest friends is not altogether free from an impertinent conceit of superiority that we reluctantly resent: in Kent it is the manifestation of disinterested love and fidelity; with a sense to foresee the consequences of the king’s headlong career, and the power to rescue him from its consequences: and this he would have done with as little ceremony of speech as he would in act, had his master been about to cast himself into a torrent. Boas (1896, p. 443): In Kent we have Shakspere’s most elaborate picture of the ideal liegeman, who holds his life but as a pawn to wage against his king’s enemies, yet who is not afraid to protest when he sees him rushing blindly to his own destruction. Strier (1995, pp. 182–3), however, sees Kent as a Renaissance courtier rather than a feudal retainer.…Shakespeare does not present Kent as naturally or habitually boorish or even plain-spoken.…[183] Kent’s rudeness is chosen, under pressure, as a moral stance. Bridges (1916; 1925, pp. 60 ff.) extravagantly sentimentalizes Kent as a model to emulate.…[204] Through his fidelity we are enabled to retain our faith in the worth of life.

Bradley (1904, pp. 307–10) also finds the role attractive but is not wholly uncritical: Kent is one of the best-loved characters in Shakespeare. He is beloved for his own sake, and also for the sake of Cordelia and of Lear. We are grateful to him because he stands up for Cordelia, and because, when she is out of sight, he constantly keeps her in our minds. And how well these two love each other we see when they meet. Yet it is not Cordelia who is dearest to Kent. His love for Lear is the passion of his life: it is his life. At the beginning he braves Lear’s wrath even more for Lear’s sake than Cordelia’s. At the end he seems to realise Cordelia’s death only as it is reflected in Lear’s agony. Nor does he merely love his master passionately, as Cordelia loves her father. That word master, and Kent’s appeal to the authority he saw in the old King’s face, are significant. He belongs to Lear, body and soul, as a dog does to his master and god. The King is not to him old, wayward, unreasonable, piteous: he is still terrible, grand, the king of men. Through his eyes we see the Lear of Lear’s prime, whom Cordelia never saw. Kent never forgets this Lear. In the Storm-scenes, even after the King becomes insane, Kent never addresses him without [308] the old terms of respect.…In acting the part of a blunt and eccentric serving-man Kent retains much of his natural character. The eccentricity seems to be put on, but the plainness which gets him put in the stocks is but an exaggeration of his plainness in the opening scene, and Shakespeare certainly meant him for one of those characters whom we love none the less for their defects. He is hot and rash; noble but far from skilful in resistance to the King; he might well have chosen wiser words to gain his point. But, as he himself says, he has more man than wit about him.…One has not the heart to wish him different, but he illustrates the truth that to run one’s head unselfishly against a wall is not the best way to help one’s friends.

p.quote: One fact about Kent is often overlooked. He is an old man. He tells Lear that he is eight and forty, but it is clear that he is much older; not so old as his master…but, one may suppose, three-score and upward.…If his age is not remembered, we fail to realise the full beauty of his thoughtlessness of himself, his inces-[309]sant care for the King, his light-hearted indifference to fortune or fate. We lose also some of the naturalness and pathos of his feeling that his task is nearly done.…Kent in his devotion, his self-effacement, his cheerful stoicism, his desire to follow his dead lord, [310] has been well likened to Horatio. But Horatio is not old; nor is he hot-headed; and though he is stoical he is also religious. Kent, as compared with him and with Edgar is not so. He has not Edgar’s faith in the clearest gods. He refers to them, in fact, less often than to fortune or the stars. He lives mainly by the love in his own heart.

div.p: Likewise Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:46–8): His dominant quality is his unquestioning courage; akin to this the selflessness which makes it as easy for him to be silent as to speak.…Through the first three acts there is never a stroke in the drawing of Kent which is merely conventional, nor yet an uncertain one.…And for a small sign of Shakespeare’s confidence in the sufficiency of his creature, see the shrewd critical thrust which he lets Cornwall have at him: [quotes 1170–2]. Even though it be a Cornwall disparaging a Kent, the thrust is shrewd enough for Shakespeare not to risk it unless he is confident that Kent’s credit with the audience is firm. This variety and apparent inconsistency give great vitality.…[47] But it is of a piece with the character that when misfortune overwhelms Lear, Kent should sink himself in it, that his colorfulness should fade, his humor wane, and the rest of the play find him tuned to this one key of vigilant unquestioning service; till he comes to the final simplicity of [quotes 3296–7]. Nevertheless Shakespeare does seem in Act IV to lose interest in him.…[48] What his purpose may be in sustaining his disguise…is never very clear. But Shakespeare’s own purpose here is clear enough; not to spoil Lear’s reconciliation with Cordelia, by adding to it a reconciliation with Kent.

Other modern critics sympathetic to Kent include Traversi (1952, p. 51): The attitude of Kent [stresses] the reasonable, the truly natural attitude of the subject to his King.…Kent’s attitude corresponds, in the public sphere, to that of Cordelia in her interpretation of the duties of a daughter. Both are plain-speaking where matters of principle or judgment are concerned. Cordelia’s lack of the glib and oily art of flattering speech is fairly balanced by Kent’s pride in his ability to deliver a plain passage bluntly. His confession of principles [544–7] is indeed a summary of the virtues which find their highest expression in true loyalty; the determination to be consistent with his own nature…to show and expect fair-dealing…to reflect more than to speak…above all, to cling to traditional sanctions of moral behaviour…are all qualities which the world around him, encouraged by the example set by its lawful ruler, is busily engaged in inverting. Kent’s plainness is founded in the first place on a maturity of judgment which reveals itself most typically in a domination of sensual impulse—at forty-eight, he affirms that he is [quotes 568–9]—but at the back of it lies a clear conception of natural order, a belief that true authority needs to be exercised (and accepted) if chaos and tragedy are to be avoided. See also Brown (1953, pp. 292–3), for whom he is the voice [293] of Lear’s own better self. Goldsmith (1958, Kent, pp. 94–8) characterizes him as a conventional stage type: the plain, blunt Englishman. The role is a countertype to the fawning courtier and the flattering counselor. (P. 98): The truly cathartic aspect of his role lies [99] in that Kent gives voice to our own thoughts and pent emotions, providing (p. 98) emotional relief and moral justification in scenes of otherwise unbearable tension. Champion (1976, p. 172): He exemplifies the selfless devotion that enables Lear and Cordelia (as well as Gloucester) to rise above the world even at the moment it destroys them. Egan (1981, pp. 146–54): Kent’s responses to the central action of King Lear, being repeatedly those of an interested and empathetic spectator, significantly shape and modulate the audience’s experience of the play.…[154] We suffer with and through Kent, and that suffering…grounds our aesthetic comprehension in the truth of a concrete, directly-felt experience. Everett (1989, pp. 73–5): Somewhere inside the life of heroic service and high principle, as Kent’s face looks out from the hood of Caius, there is a romantic who, like all [74] romantics, lives in the thought of the promis’d end, the unimaginably good tomorrow when love is mutual and happiness begins.…Kent’s promis’d end is to be still Kent: a man incapable of not loving. Kent’s existence is precluded from mere pathos by its disguises, its silences, which at once double the sense of his pain and close it from our view. Reticence is his armour. Moreover, his life has its own dark logic. Heroically good and sympathetic as he is, Kent is as much as Gloucester and Edgar a man of the Court.…Kent’s romantic idealism springs from that feeling for Authority which, as he says himself, holds him to the King; and it brings with it a high pride and sense of honour which include minor details like a preference to stay clear of mad beggars.…Hence the complex tacit bitterness of Edgar’s account of the grieving Kent, which closes on that aspect of Edgar’s and Kent’s service most agonizing to their shared courtly sense of honour: [quotes 3168+16–18].…This is conceivably a motive for Kent’s enigmatically violent rage at Oswald.…[75] All in all, Kent’s silence or reticence throughout the play…create[s] a deep image of human love in its shame or inhibition, its self-defeating self-sacrifices, its life improper for a slave. Rozett (1987, p. 238) describes him as a tragic figure: Caught up in a sequence of events that alters the lives of everyone around him, Kent shares certain of the Elizabethan tragic protagonist’s characteristics: noble, uncompromising, and well-intentioned, he makes a series of choices from which his isolation and tragic loss eventually result. Rather than a tragedy of error and recognition, Kent’s is a tragedy of betrayed expectations—a tragedy the audience shares, because our expectations [that Kent will be acknowledged by Lear by the play’s end] have also been overturned. Kahn (2000, pp. 12–13): Since Kent is the only person in the play who is wholly and completely a public person, one who has no competing private domain of family,…[13] Kent’s presence and the parallel between him and Cordelia make an important point: Love is possible within the public domain. See also Bloom (1960, p. 472); Burckhardt (1960, p. 468).

Elton (1966, pp. 285 ff.) is also sympathetic: Kent is the disinterested feudal liegeman in a self-seeking Jacobean world.…[289] His loyal strength matches the virtù of the treacherous Edmund. He is the truly noble Earl of Kent, in contrast to the falsely ennobled Edmund, Earl of Gloucester; and his Cynic forthrightness is, like Timon’s, the obverse to libertine hypocrisy. As his diction indicates, Kent is the plain, blunt man of the country, complementing, in truth-speaking, the relatively oblique and court-bred Fool. His encounter with the symbol of false service, Oswald [2.2], is consummated by the rustic-guised Edgar’s dispatch of the villain [2683–2714]. Anticipating Gloucester’s proxy role…for the king’s hardships, Kent, claiming to carry years on my back [569–70], is sturdier than his master, who, at the start, [290] would Unburthen’d crawl toward death [46]. Yet Kent’s initial inability to vanquish Oswald foreshadows Lear’s frustration against his adversaries, as Edgar’s slaying of Oswald later prefigures their downfall.…Kent…mirrors the virility of [Lear’s] manhood.…Hence, Kent is neither so young as to defeat the comparison nor so old as to destroy its effectiveness; he is…at the final verge of, or past, virilitas but not yet within the protagonists’ senium.…But…Kent…is too old to learn the new ways of disservice. Further…he is also Lear’s symbolic evidence of strength.…Yet he is unlike the old lecher Gloucester.…For, in contrast to Lear, who has just submitted his all to his evil daughters, Kent identifies himself as above womanly weakness. Kent also evinces Stoicism: While Kent’s [quotes 2347+34–6] seems, like the Servants’ and Albany’s exclamations, choral hyperbole shaken loose by the cumulative horrors, it also reflects a Stoic [291] fatalism. Kent also shows Stoic fortitude in the stocks…and alludes, like Cordelia, to fortune.…Further, Kent, like the stoical Brutus and Macbeth, fatalistically stakes his destiny on th’event. Finally, Kent’s [quotes 3224] may carry overtones not only of the Last Judgment but perhaps also of the well-known Stoic notion concerning the antici-[292]pated periodical consumption (ecpyrosis) of the entire world. Haydn (1950, p. 642) likewise describes him as an almost perfectly doctrinal Stoic.

Perhaps consistent with this view of Kent as stoical is an emphasis on his lacking a belief in divine providence. Thus Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 271–2): Kent possesses no vision, like that which gladdens Edgar, of a divine providence. His loyalty to right has something in it of a desperate instinct, which persists in spite of the appearances presented by the world. Shakspere would have us know that there is not any devotion to truth, to justice, to charity more intense and real than that of the man who is faithful to them, out of the sheer spirit of loyalty, unstimulated and unsupported by any faith which can be called theological. Kent, who has seen the vicissitude of things, knows of no higher power than fortune. Therefore, all the more, Kent clings to the passionate instinct of right-doing, and to the hardy temper, the fortitude which makes evil, when it happens to come, [272] endurable.…Accordingly there is at once an exquisite tenderness in Kent’s nature, and also a certain roughness and hardness, needful to protect, from the shocks of life, the tenderness of one who finds no refuge in communion with the higher powers, or in a creed of religious optimism. Likewise Sharp (1902, pp. 216–18): Those about Kent profess at one time or another their faith in an all-just Providence; Kent is silent.…[217] Kent was not always an unbeliever. At the beginning of the play, when he is still one that fortune loves, he addresses his master: [quotes 148–51]. This is no mere conventional mode of speech.…[218] Then comes overwhelming misfortune to one he loves, coupled with the revelation of malignant wickedness in those whom he has personally known. As a result, God is gone from his world. The sufferings and the heartlessness in his master’s family cost him not only his life but his religious faith. In contrast, Battenhouse (1969, pp. 286–8) sees spiritual growth in implicitly Christian terms: As with other characters in this play, a combination of suffering and strange new discoveries gradually enlarges Kent’s understanding.…[287] His stoic virtue has, as its ultimate potential, a sense of call to a new kind of service—spoken of as a journey.…[288] Insight rather than accolade is Kent’s true reward.

Some critics condemn his impulsiveness. Hudson (1848, 2:269–70): Kent is continually getting himself into trouble in trying to get others out. Blunt, downright, impassioned alike in his sympathies and antipathies, he pushes right on as regardless of times and occasions as of himself; is as intemperate and reckless in virtue as others are in crime: indefatigable in loyalty and affection, he is present whenever there is suffering to be relieved, or treachery to be defeated; and, while rivalling the worst in endowments of mind, he at the same time rivals the best in a noble use of them.…In his impulsiveness, however, Kent can hardly help doing too much: rash, reckless, I might almost say, fanatical in honesty, he often mars what he would mend, hinders where he would help, injures whom [270] he would serve: his noble but indiscreet and ill-timed endeavours to arrest, only go to aggravate Lear’s judgment on Cordelia, while at the same time they provoke a similar judgment on himself; and, afterwards, his generous rashness and saucy roughness in behalf of the king, while it draws on himself the malice of the sister fiends, only quickens and sharpens their persecution of Lear. Such is Kent’s virtue; beautiful indeed, but unavailing. See also Idem (1872, 2:383–6). Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 631): His just anger against Lear in the opening scene shows him to be a truly faithful servant, but it only still more aggravates the contradictory spirit and the obstinacy of the passionate king.…He has more man than wit in him; he appears in his genuine and just wrath as unrestrained as Lear in his ungrounded fury, and he helps by his vehemence to increase the bitter discord between the latter and his daughters. With restless activity he aids the king in his abandoned condition; he sacrifices himself, and dies at last worn out with excess of true devotion; but all this, merely on account of his disguise, is entirely unavailing for the comfort and support of his aging sovereign. Boas (1896, p. 443): He is not without his share of Celtic impetuosity.

Others criticize him for being imperceptive, ineffective, or brutal. Schlegel (1809; tr. 1815, 2:207): Even the virtue of the honest Kent bears the stamp of an iron age. Blok (1966, p. 20): His kindly heart is calloused; he is a watch-dog with inflamed red eyes, guarding his master even in sleep, ready to sink his teeth into any passer-by and to tear him to pieces, who will not let himself be either stroked or patted. Jayne (1964, p. 280): Kent fails to solve the problem of relating himself to the rest of humanity because of a tactless lack of charity. Rosenberg (1972, p. 13): Kent swing[s] erratically along the man-beast axis. His goodness, his frankness, even his loyalty, are crossed with a dark savagery. Goldberg (1974, pp. 69–73): The condition of Kent’s virtue is one (pretty limited) kind of self-abnegation—an abnegation of the merely selfish or self-seeking—and its product one (pretty limited) kind of patience.…[70] He is not the kind of man who could really know Lear, of course: how to feel, how to think, how to act, never become problems for him.…He is not much more than he claims to be: his nature—his very capacity to feel and act—seems constrained by his very virtues, his ethical character.…[71] The tone and accent of Kent’s speech all through the play are obviously stoic—plain, rather terse, unambiguous, without much metaphoric complexity. It is a language not much open to experience; indeed, it is usually tightened around its virtue like a fist to oppose the world.…[72] Thus the kind of justice Kent looks for is apparently quite simple and straightforward.…The only trouble is that we can also recognize it as too simple—or rather, as simple in the wrong way. It is too external, too abstract, and yet too much directed to confirming the self-directed ego.…[73] For Kent the sight of the dead Cordelia in Lear’s arms causes the whole structure of his world to break apart.…Endurance now seems to him to have been pointless all along, since the only point it had lay in some expected future vindication, in a morally intelligible Final Judgment. Evans (1979, pp. 154–66): Kent’s practice [i.e., his disguise and secret attendance upon Lear] proves only marginally effective and his identity gradually becomes irrelevant.…[157] No explanation except deliberate intent can account for his behaviour [in 2.2] when he (p. 161) bring[s] things to an abrupt head; rather than let the agony of slow recognition gnaw at the old king, he kindle[s] the fires of rage in Lear. Yet (p. 166) Kent’s practice…yields only insignificant dramatic effect during the action and proves superfluous at the end; certainly Shakespeare never brought a major practice to a lamer conclusion. Leggatt (1988, pp. 52–3): Kent’s savage description of men of Oswald’s type [1151–3]…could be a hostile description of himself. His salient quality is loyalty; so is Oswald’s.…Kent’s hostility to Oswald is the most naked and simple hostility in the play; on their second meeting he beats him not so much for what he has done as for what he is. Is this because Kent recognises in him the dark side of his own virtue?…[53] Increasingly, an air of futility hangs over him. Shakespeare’s arbitrary plotting is to some degree responsible for this: in the later scenes Kent keeps losing track of his master. Though he is a strong presence in the first half of the play, his impact fades considerably towards the end.…In Kent we see one of the most popular types of the Elizabethan stage: the honest counsellor. Shakespeare saves him from the woodenness that often afflicts such figures by giving him a brusque, excitable manner that makes him distinctive. But he also hedges his virtue about with reservations, and cuts short his expected dramatic career. Paris (1991, pp. 116–17): Kent is a perfectionist, who speaks not so much out of a concern for Lear, which would have been better served by a greater degree of tact, as out of a need to obey his own inner dictates.…[117] If Kent had not had to prove that he is not one of those smiling rogues he so despises, he would have been able to give Lear his good advice in a less offensive manner. Cartwright (1991, p. 184): Kent demonstrates the spectator’s oscillating distance from Lear, for Kent frequently intervenes as an audience-surrogate and moral counselor, only to become tarnished by his actions. Foakes (1993, p. 186): Kent’s loyalty may be admirable in itself, and [his] violence to Oswald may draw a warm gut response, but [he] is at the same time sycophantically pandering to Lear’s obstinacy.…Kent’s behaviour works to prevent Lear from understanding his situation, rather than enabling him, as Kent desired in the opening scene, to see better. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, pp. 114–22) is extravagantly suspicious: As Caius, Kent acts like an overprotective mother who caters to her child’s every whim so as to keep him perennially dependent, even at the risk of his becoming dull and conceited.…[117] Kent is a mixture of ingenuousness and Machiavellianism—what might be called a split Machiavellianism (that is, totally remote from his consciousness).…Clinically speaking…he probably belongs to the category of perverse individuals with a dual personality.…Kent’s secret design—secret for him, too, being perhaps an unconscious design—is most probably to replace the three daughters in the king’s affections, with the whole plan culminating in a great scene of reconciliation. In order to do this he must separate the daughters from their father. Kent’s hatred for Oswald is excessive—a paranoid hatred—while the steward himself is totally loyal to Goneril. Presumably Kent is so hostile toward him because he has projected onto him the part of himself that wants to sever the ties between father and daughters.…[122] It could further be suggested that Kent employs the masochistic technique of letting himself be put in the stocks in order to arouse anguish and indignation in Lear and thus strengthen the bond between them.

Some critics find a lack of psychological consistency. Stoll (1933, pp. 431–6): At the beginning of the play, for the situation, Kent is…more tactless and uncompliant than Cordelia; and later, as, to accompany his master, he puts on disguise, he must needs cloak his character too. For a while, he must, like Hamlet, play a part, and in a measure be a different man. The account of his reaction to Gloster’s death is unconvincing: (p. 436) Certainly Kent did not bellow. Lökse (1960, pp. 140–1): It is a strange task for the polite and ceremonious Earl to perform the task of instigating quarrels and getting into the stocks, and it is made possible only by the fact that Kent is in disguise.…The Kent-Oswald period is necessary for dramatic purposes but must be disregarded as far as judgment on Kent’s character is concerned.…[141] Kent is essentially the Perillus of Leir. Holmes (1960, p. 187) also emphasizes Kent’s theatricality: he takes service in his malcontent disguise (probably, in those days, a black cloak like Hamlet and a black hat like Guy Fawkes). Mason (1967, pp. 44, 150–1): Apart from some poor jokes, Kent in 1.4 is very much a function and very little a character. As such he serves as a foil to the Bad Servant.…[150] The Kent who rails at Oswald [in 2.2] is a new character. He has a flow and a vivacity quite out of keeping with the rest of his part in the play. This is more than plainness, it is the abundance of riot. If we had not thought it at the time, we now look back on Kent’s previous treatment of Oswald and begin to [suppose] that if Kent stood for the Good Servant he might also have stood for the Bad.…[151] Once Kent is clapped in [the stocks] and we begin by watching the balance swing to the side of guilt we may well congratulate Shakespeare on doing with Kent what in the name of character consistency I have deplored. For it may then cross our minds that Kent’s uncharacteristic unmannerliness was as it were by replacing that of his knights an extension of Lear. He for the moment is Lear’s guilt, his unnatural folly. Snyder (1979, pp. 149–50) relates Kent’s disguise as Caius to comic conventions: Shakespeare apparently invented Kent’s disguise, borrowing from comedy the notion of serving the loved one incognito.…Kent has affinities as well with another conventional comic type, the father in disguise protecting his child. He thus joins Cordelia and the others as a parent figure for the child-Lear and reinforces the sense of hierarchies overturned, both as earl turned servant and as servant protecting master. Interestingly, Kent as Caius shows traces of the traditional comic freedom granted by disguise, mainly in his scenes with Oswald.…Kent appears to take pleasure in shedding the dignity of an earl, pleasure the audience delightedly shares, though (p. 150) his servant role represents no radical change of outlook, and its freeing powers are correspondingly limited. As he watches and weeps for Lear, we easily forget the fact of his disguise. Certainly it permits no sustained escape or detached overview. Smidt (1990, pp. 131–3) finds various unconformities or inconsistencies in Kent: His age and weakness seem to be invented as excuses for his inaction, and he is ready to die by the end of the play. But though he gives his age as 48 when he seeks service with the King…and Cornwall calls him ancient knave and reverend braggart,…48 after all was no hoary age [132] even in the Elizabethan era, and Kent in the first half of the play certainly gives the impression of having the vitality of youth.…[133] Kent was apparently the victim of authorial second thoughts. M. Warren (1983, pp. 60–7) sees significant differences in the role in Q and F: Whether as a central aim of the [putative] revision or as an incidental consequence of revisions with other major objectives, the part of Kent undergoes such substantial change between Quarto and Folio in the last two and a half acts that in the Folio he becomes a marginal figure until his entrance just prior to Lear’s final scene,…[67] reduced in the fourth act from a residual figure of honesty and loyalty to almost a cipher. See , , .

Other, unusual interpretations include Snider (1887, p. 207–8): Some critics have imagined that his death is given in the play, but this is certainly a mistake of a fact, and also a misunderstanding of a principle. The truth is, the poet wishes to preserve all the faithful; but, to do so consistently, he must keep them out of the collision with the State. Seehase (1973) claims that Kent’s judgments on Lear express the wisdom of the common people. (In Ger.) Burelbach (1987, p. 132) claims that he was perhaps named in reference to the custom, unique to Kent, of Gavelkind since both Lear and Gloucester…moved toward a greater awareness of the need to treat progeny equally, or at least equitably.

div.head: Lear
div.p: While many share the judgment of Coleridge (1823; 1990, 1:27) that Lear is the most tremendous effort of Shakspeare, as a Poet, radically opposite views of the role appear even in the earliest comments on the character. According to an anonymous Jacobean elegist, c. 1619, quoted in Chambers (1923, 2:309), he was played by Burbage as Kind. See . However, to Hill (1735), King Lear’s most distinguishing Mark is the violent Impatience of his Temper. As we will see, the capacity of the role to provoke both pity and terror has been interpreted in widely various ways.

Many critics respond sympathetically and sometimes indulgently to Lear. Griffith (1775, p. 359) regards him as a real object both of commiseration and esteem, notwithstanding the weakness, passion, and injustice he has so fully exposed in the beginning of the Play, and she praises Sh. for rendering his mixed character, as true to nature. Similarly Davies (1784, 2:205): He is a character, amiable in many respects, brave, generous, frank, and benevolent though at the same time, wilful, rash, violent, and headstrong. Schlegel (1809–11; tr. 1815, 2:204): The threefold dignity of a king, an old man, and a father, is dishonoured by the cruel ingratitude of his unnatural daughters; the old Lear, who out of a foolish tenderness has given away every thing, is driven out to the world a wandering beggar; the childish imbecility to which he was fast advancing changes into the wild-[205]est insanity, and when he is saved from the disgraceful destitution to which he was abandoned it is too late: the kind consolations of filial care and attention and true friendship are now lost on him; his bodily and mental powers are destroyed beyond all hope of recovery, and all that now remains to him of life is the capability of loving and suffering beyond measure.…[207] Great qualities have not been superfluously assigned to the King; the poet could command our sympathy for his situation without concealing what he had done to bring himself into it. Lear is choleric, overbearing, and almost childish from age, when he drives out his youngest [208] daughter because she will not join in the hypocritical exaggerations of her sisters. But he has a warm and affectionate heart, which is susceptible of the most fervent gratitude; and even rays of a high and kingly disposition burst forth from the eclipse of his understanding. Hudson (1848, 2:240–53): His mind is sliding into…second childhood…; and while appearing as weak as a child he at the same time appears as loving and unsuspecting.…[242] Nothing can be more touchingly beautiful, than the spectacle of the aged king…doing away the constraints of authority to admit more unequivocal demonstrations of love, and resigning his power over his children to rest on his power with them.…[249] But the great thing in the delineation of Lear, is the progress and effect of his passion in re-developing his [250] faculties. For the character seems designed in part to illustrate the power of passion to reawaken and raise the faculties from the tomb wherein age hath quietly inurned them.…Lear’s very infirmities of body serve but to unfold, enlarge, and impress his splendours and energies of mind; his resurgent powers coming forth with a strength, a vigour, and intensity unknown, perhaps impossible before, like the resurrection to a higher, a larger, a more glorious life. [253] All things considered, the difficulties of the subject as well as the grandeur of the results, it can hardly be questioned, that Lear is Shakespeare’s masterpiece of individual characterization. See also Idem (1872, 2:363–70). Salvini (1884, p. 563): The division of the kingdom is the outgrowth of a generous heart and a natural trust in filial love. Bradley (1904, pp. 280–1) assumes that readers’ sympathy for Lear is so strong that it is necessary to remind them of Lear’s responsibility for his tragic fate: The position of the hero in this tragedy is in one important respect peculiar. The reader of Hamlet, Othello, or Macbeth, is in no danger of forgetting, when the catastrophe is reached, the part played by the hero in bringing it on.…It is otherwise in King Lear. When the conclusion arrives, the old King has for a long while been passive. We have long regarded him not only as a man more sinned against than sinning, but almost wholly as a sufferer, hardly at all as an agent. His sufferings have been so cruel, and our indignation against those who inflicted them has been so intense, that recollection of the wrong he did to Cordelia, to Kent, and to his realm, has been well-nigh effaced.…[281] Yet it is essential that Lear’s contribution to the drama should be remembered…because otherwise his fate would appear to us at best pathetic, at worst shocking, but certainly not tragic.…[282] Lear, we see, is generous and unsuspicious, of an open and free nature, like Hamlet and Othello and indeed most of Shakespeare’s heroes, who in this, according to Ben Jonson, resemble the poet who made them. Lear, we see, is also choleric by temperament—the first of Shakespeare’s heroes who is so. And a long life of absolute power, in which he has been flattered to the top of his bent, has produced in him that blindness to human limitations, and that presumptuous self-will, which in Greek tragedy we have so often seen stumbling against the altar of Nemesis. Our consciousness that the decay of old age contributes to this condition deepens our pity and our sense of human infirmity, but certainly does not lead us to regard the old King as irresponsible, and so to sever the tragic nexus which binds together his errors and calamities.

Other predominantly sympathetic interpretations of the role include Hofmannsthal (1905; 1952, pp. 264–5): I know nothing that so grips the heart as the tone of Lear’s voice when he speaks with Edgar. To his daughters he talks like a furious prophet or a patriarch drunk with pain. To his Fool he speaks harshly. But to Edgar, that naked madman whom he has found in a cave, he speaks in a tone (wherein, to be sure, there is something of madness) whose keynote is an extraordinary politeness of the heart, an indescribable courtesy, which [265] makes us realize how this king could sometimes make his people happy when in a gracious mood. Blaze de Bury (1868, p. 229) sees Lear as good humored, a bon vivant. Bridges (1916; 1925, p. 57) finds in Lear a heart naturally fashioned to be blessed in itself and blessing in its influence. Likewise Stone (1925, p. 167): Lear is one of the noblemen of the earth, too far removed from pettiness and morbidity to conceive of misery and ingratitude at the hands of his loved ones, his generosity prompts him to give away his hearth and realm. His casting off of Cordelia is a grave mistake in an otherwise admirable character. Blunden (1929; 1934, pp. 211–13): He is a curious student,…a lover [212] of the English scene,…a reader of the classics, and a sportsman. (P. 213): In short, Lear is…as gifted and as generous a sovereign as ever could have the title of the King of Britain. Sitwell (1948, p. 66): How shall it be explained by what sublime genius this old King, so wilful, so terrible in his passions, is yet so near to our hearts that we would cradle him in our arms like a child? James (1951, pp. 94–5): It is easy enough, and no doubt natural enough to call Lear selfish, impulsive, and crass; but this is not the whole [95] truth about him.…He is patient, or at least tries to be patient, when he is disposed to acknowledge that his daughters’ evil is also his own.…[96] The changed man that Lear became was only the victory of something in him which had always been there.…It is no miracle which is wrought in Lear; he has genuinely grown to what he has become at the end of the play. The issue has been between anger and judgement on one side, and patience and forgiveness on the other. Bush (1956, p. 91): His belief in nature…commands our pity and respect.…He is like a child, as Goneril and Regan remind him; he asks for things from this world. Yet for this reason he becomes a figure of great and tragic presence. Stauffer (1949, pp. 194 ff.): Lear begins as the picture of a spoiled child, but (p. 205) every inch a king, his most truly regal qualities are a sensitive heart and a magnanimous mind. The generosity of his nature dwarfs even his deep faults. Harbage (ed. 1969, p. 1062): He is proud and peremptory, and it is better to be humble and temporizing, but there are occupational hazards in being a king, perhaps even in being a father. Is his charge not true that the world has lied to him, telling him he was wise before he was bearded, returning yea and nay to everything he said? His guilt is widely shared, and his flaw like that of Oedipus seems mysteriously hereditary. And it is linked inextricably with his virtues. We applaud the resurgence of youthful might that cuts down Cordelia’s assassin. We admire the valor of his attempts (and they come quite early) to be patient, to compromise, to hold back womanish tears, to cling to his reason. Nothing is more moving than his bewildered attempts to meet social obligations as he kneels by Cordelia’s body. We love his manliness. Pride has its value too. Schoff (1962, pp. 163–8): If we follow the guidance of Shakespeare in the lines of the play, we find no evidence that Lear is meant to be considered a horrible example of stupidity, senility, or wrathfulness, nor yet a man who sins against his responsibilities as king.…[167] Lear…is shown to us through action and reliable report as a man of intelligence, integrity, and at least a degree of magnanimity, capable of seeing [168] himself as he is and learning of the world’s agony through his own; as a man who inspires great love; and as a man with a sense of humor. Gardner (1967, pp. 20–2): Much has been said of Lear’s impatience of temperament; but along with it there goes from the beginning a generous unwillingness to see offence before he must.…Along with [his] impatience over trifles, there is a touching striving after fairness.…He is terribly slow to understand the negative cruelty of Regan. When he cries outside Goneril’s castle [quotes 918–19] and again in Gloucester’s courtyard, as he looks on Kent: [quotes 1328–30]; or when, as he prepares to leave Regan, he prays [quote 1571]; or when, as he goes out into the storm, he cries O fool, I shall go mad! he shows he understands the dangers of a passionate temper that he has attempted and does attempt to master. It is not wholly true that he hath ever but slenderly known himself. It might more truly be said that what he has to learn is less his own nature than the nature of the world.…And if his impatience at the beginning has been exaggerated and his efforts at self-control passed over, by those critics who would make the theme of the play Lear’s moral redemption, the rage and cries for vengeance that alternate with his moments of gentleness and pity and self-reproach have been perhaps rather overlooked too. From Gloucester we can learn a moral lesson, of patience and resignation and endurance.…But with Lear we explore passionate experience: his discovery of what the world offers to a heart that loves and asks for love in return.…[22] What we honour and what moves us in Lear is his vulnerability. He cannot steel his heart against pain or joy.…Hope never dies within him. Jorgensen (1967, pp. 44 ff.): Lear, rather than Brutus or Hamlet, is [Sh.’s] most impressive depiction of a hero thinking his way toward self-discovery.…[67] Lear is not so contemptible in intellect as Knight and others have felt [see below, ].…[116] As an unwilling student of himself, he is impelled by his own considerable intelligence, and by the precepts of the age in which he was created, to go well beyond himself in his quest for self-knowledge.…Lear’s ultimate self-discovery is…what it means to be a man. Napieralski (1973, p. 444): His doom issues in the main from only noble impulses to enjoy the freedom and security of his daughter’s love and to guarantee the order and peace for his kingdom. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 186): Perhaps it is not so surprising in an age when kings have been either outlawed or emasculated and the authority of fathers questioned, that Shakespeare’s presentation of his great King has been so misunderstood. His very act of wisdom and generosity in giving up power while he is still able to manage an orderly succession has been described (by those duly taking their pensions at 65) as political irresponsibility. His failure to detect flattery in the voice of decorum and love in the voice of rudeness has been condemned by an age as suspicious of politeness as it is approving of the kind of personal integrity that discounts the feelings of others. Lear’s imperiousness, his aggressive authority, today associated with tyranny and selfishness, would to his early audiences appear as certain signs of greatness in a king. We can be sure of this because we have James I’s opinion on the matter and Lear is every inch a Jamesean king. Cantor (1996, pp. 218–19): Shakespeare depicts Lear’s confusion of nature and convention more as a kind of occupational hazard of kingship than as the peculiar failing of a particular man.…[219] Lear is undeniably a great king.

Numerous critics find heroic grandeur in Lear. Hugo (1864; tr. 1886, p. 247): And what a figure is that father! What a caryatid! It is man stooping. He does nothing but shift burdens for others that are heavier. The more the old man becomes enfeebled, the more his load augments. He lives under an over-burden. He bears at first power, then ingratitude, then isolation, then despair, then hunger and thirst, then madness, then all Nature. Masefield (1911, p. 191): King Lear is a grander, ironic invention, who hurts far more than any of [Sh.’s other tragic heroes] because he is a horribly strong man who is powerless. He is so strong that he cannot die. He is so strong that he nearly breaks the net, before the folds kill him. Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:25–40): He is old and uncertain; but a mighty man, never a mere tyrant divested of power. He has genius, warped and random genius though it may be, and to madness, as it will appear, very nearly allied. And Shakespeare’s art lies in showing us this in nothing he does—for what he does now is foolish—but in every trivial thing that he is. After 1.5, Lear passes (p. 28) from personal grievance to the taking upon him, as great natures may, the imagined burden of the whole world’s sorrow—and if his nature breaks under it, what wonder! And Shakespeare brings about this transition from malediction to martyrdom with great art, by contrivance direct and indirect, by broad strokes and subtle; nor ever—his art at this is at its greatest—does he turn his Lear from a man into an ethical proposition. The thing is achieved—as the whole play is achieved—in terms of humanity, and according to the rubric of the drama.…[37] Shakespeare has led Lear to compassion for sin as well as suffering, has led him mad to where he could not hope to lead him sane—to where sound common sense will hardly let us follow him…to a deep compassion for mankind itself.…[39] Lear’s last scene…[40] is human tragedy brought to its simplest terms, fit ending to a tragic play that has seemed to outleap human experience. From power of intellect and will, from the imaginative sweep of madness, Shakespeare brings Lear to this; to no moralizing nor high thoughts, but just to [quotes 3219–23]. Wilson (1957, pp. 191 ff.): Lear is a commanding figure, an imposing presence in his folly.…We are horrified by his rashness, but our horror is mingled not with pity but with awe.…[193] Lear is the grandest of all Shakespeare’s tragic heroes, and his faults are on the scale of his grandeur.…The ultimate effect of his fault is to enlarge the tragedy beyond the measure of justice, of hybris and nemesis, with the emergence of Lear’s purified love.…[205] Lear has all the virtues of Coriolanus and Timon—the frank, unqualified generosity, the heroic nobility, a grandeur that includes all their [206] greatness and far surpasses it.…In his final suffering, Lear inspires us with reverence, with awe; in his tragic figure, the value of human life is vindicated, triumphantly and secure. Everett (1960, New, p. 335): The one gift that he possesses is a colossal power of life itself. Burckhardt (1961, King’s, p. 382): His fall…derives its terrifying grandeur from being not passive but willed. Kozintsev (1966, p. 263) sees a white-haired rebel, denouncing injustice, demanding that things should change or cease. Brower (1971, pp. 383 ff.) characterizes Lear as a blend of pagan hero and Christian saint: Lear begins as a [son] of Achilles blinded by honey-sweet anger, but (p. 393) in the storm he swing[s] from commanding to suffering acceptance.…[398] The hero gives up commanding the universe, choosing rather to command himself, that is, to lose himself. In the mad speeches of 4.6, (p. 405) The higher controlled reason of the hero gives way to Reason in madness. But to see how the world goes, as Lear does, is to regain some control, some power over self, and to attain to a degree of moral heroism, however precarious.…It takes greatness to look into darkness with Lear’s gentleness and clarity. Although (p. 406) the play is not an illustration of Christian doctrine, and Lear is not redeemed or saved, nonetheless (p. 415) in the presence of the truth that Job faces—that evil can not be explained—Lear…finds a resource…in Christian selflessness.…To love and hope with full tragic knowledge of the injustice, cruelty, and confusion of life is to pass beyond god-like hero to something god-like indeed. Hunter (ed. 1972, pp. 7 ff.) emphasizes Lear’s giant features,…the scope and sweep of the conception,…the demonic energy he manifests—those who think of him as an enfeebled [8] old man should read again.…[29] Lear represents both the terrifying [30] and mana-laden god-king, whose verse has the sweep and majesty of one whose thoughts are laws.…[34] Any temptation to think Lear’s character responsible for what happens is in fact much limited by the absence of any dimension of self-doubt or self-scrutiny in his nature; it would be like assuming an interest in God’s character. Davis (1974, pp. 4–31): Lear himself is the authority that commands respect. After his downfall all those who condemn the action are inspired by a devotion to the man himself.…[11] When he first steps before us, there is nothing of the senile or foolish old man that so many commentators have inferred from the folly of which he will shortly be guilty.…[31] Lear symbolizes authority: authority fully recognized and rightly venerated.

In contrast, Kozintsev (1977, pp. 62–3): The greatness of his personality lies…in his boldness, of thought, his power of spiritual response.…He is heroic…in that having once been the overlord, he recognizes and lays completely bare the absurdity of power, the worthlessness of its actions and the falsehood of words.…He becomes great only when he understands that he is like any other man. Have there ever been despots who were capable of recognizing this at the end of their lives? At the beginning of the action one cannot yet recognize Lear: one can see a mask of power in an abstract and illusory form.…His extreme cruelty, his condemnations without trial and without investigation, all these banishments [quotes 223], promises of death for attempting to behave as befits a man—what is elevated or great about this? However, Lear tears off the mask of power, and throws it away. Only then does his face become visible: suffering has made him beautiful and human.

Other heroic interpretations include Feder (1980, pp. 134–5): Lear in his madness is an explorer of consciousness.…[135] His obsessions and hallucinations reveal that, in his very retreat from the anguish of his present despair, he unconsciously strives toward a restitution of his own ego—a construction of a continuous, integrated sense of his real existence in relation to time, nature and society, cause and effect.…In recreating his own character on stage—an act unique in drama—Lear is a heroic figure. Summers (1980, pp. 80–9), observing that Lear’s most terrible and poignant moments are marked by sudden reversals of beliefs and emotions and determinations, a pattern which is continually repeated, finds that (p. 89) at the end we respond to Lear’s death as heroic rather than pathetic…because his final powerful fluctuating responses cast doubt on the realities which we often assume as objective and self-evident. Danson (1981, pp. 121 ff.): Lear is a giant form who dwarfs even the other Shakespearean heroes. Hamlet and Macbeth are more fully articulated; Hamlet, at least, is psychologically more various. But no one, not even Othello or Coriolanus, has Lear’s massive musculature. In him duration becomes magnitude; he is so hugely active for so long that finally the most remarkable thing to be said is that he has borne most: [quotes 3300–1]. Lear endures his tough world until he seems less a victim than another aspect of the wind and rain and thunder and spouting hurricanoes in which he hugely exists. And all this bigness in the play’s central character demands from us an equally sympathetic response. It takes all our energy just to keep up with that awful old man whose demands—on his children, his subjects, nature itself, and on us as audience—are so monstrous and inspiring. Hawkins (1991, p. 183): Lear’s noble anger transfigures him. In his madness, he takes on numinous power, the mysterium tremendum of thunder and lightning. Bloom (1992, p. 9): His rashness is matched by his furious sincerity, and overmatched only by his mysterious authority, an eminence that survives madness and petulance, and every error of his palpably bad judgments.…Lear is gigantically wrong, but never less than titanic, at least a daemon and sometimes a hint of something larger, a man who is a god.…Except for the Yahweh of the original portions of what are now called Genesis, Exodus, and Numbers, Lear remains the largest Western instance of a literary character raised to the heights, to the Sublime. Idem (1998, pp. 493 ff.): Lear is Shakespeare’s most sublime and most demanding character.…Outrageously hyperbolical, insanely eloquent, Lear nevertheless always demands more love than can be given (within the limitations of the human), [494] and so he scarcely can speak without crossing into the realms of the unsayable. He is thus Hamlet’s contrary: we feel that Hamlet says everything that can be said, much more than we can say, whoever we are. Lear overwhelms us, by Shakespearean design, because he somehow succeeds in saying what no one else…could ever say.…[506] Lear, surging on through fury, madness, and clarifying though momentary epiphanies, is the largest figure of love desperately sought and blindly denied ever placed upon a stage or in print. He is the universal image of the unwisdom and destructiveness of paternal [507] love at its most ineffectual, implacably persuaded of its own benignity, totally devoid of self-knowledge, and careening onward until it brings down the person it loves best, and its world as well.…King Lear is also the ultimate image of royal, legitimate authority, and more mysteriously the image of the wayward, frightening Yahweh of the J writer, earliest of Hebrew authors. The death of Lear is the end of the father, of the king, and of that part of the godhead that is father-king.…After Lear something vanishes from the Western literary representations of the father-king-God.

Other critics emphasizing the grandeur of the role also compare Lear to figures from the Bible and classical mythology. Sitwell (1948, pp. 51–2) compares him to both Oedipus and the Sphinx. Sewall (1959, pp. 72 ff.): Caught up in the action which he had unwittingly precipitated, he refuses to default or compromise…and presses on in heroic pride to justify himself.…[74] Like Job and Oedipus, Lear shows himself more than sinner, more than sinned against. He does evil, and evil is done to him; but in the course of his ordeal, which in part he brought upon himself, he transcends both these categories. Like the other heroes, he ends victor as well as victim. Nevo (1972, pp. 261–3): Like Job, Lear takes his initial prosperity as a sign of heavenly favor; like Job in affliction, he calls the heavens themselves to heavenly account. Like Job, though he die for it, yet he will affirm his own conviction of what injustice is. Like Job, his natural egotism reaches beyond itself to embrace a universe of suffering creatures and returns to the bedrock reality of the suffering creature. Like Job he refuses to compromise with pain and with evil; refuses to surrender to the plot of optimistic quietism whereby pain and evil are denied, are made into goods, disciplinary or deserved or redemptive; are made nonexistent. Lear, raging in the storm, is no hero of renunciation but of an enormous expostulation. (P. 263): Interpretations which make of Lear at the very beginning of the play a senile, obtuse, or crass materialist, who must be chastened into learning what every Sunday-school child knows by heart are vulgarizations of the tragic predicament. Milward (1975, p. 51): Lear himself, as he runs unbonneted in the tempest and faces the fury of the fretful elements, is Shakespeare’s dramatization of the Biblical Job in the context no less of Elizabeth’s England than of Holinshed’s Britain. In him he gathers together all the sufferings of his innocent contemporaries and presents them in an archetypal form that not merely emulates, but also surpasses the sufferings of Job—viewing them as he does, not merely in the light of Job, but also in that of the suffering servant of the Old Testament, and of Christ himself in his Passion. Driscoll (1977, pp. 159–60) compares him to the wrathful Yahweh and to Prometheus. Bloom (1989, p. 72): Shakespeare invoked the Book of Job in order to emphasize the absolute negativity of Lear’s tragedy.…Shakespeare allows him a diction more preternaturally eloquent than is spoken by anyone else in this or any other drama, and that evidently never will be matched again. Lear matters because his language is uniquely strong, and because we are persuaded that this splendor is wholly appropriate to him. Others who compare him to Job include Gardner (1948, 1:175) and Muir (ed. 1952; 1972, p. lv).

Bloom (1998, pp. 477–9) reconsiders the idea of Job as paradigm for Lear and suggests Solomon instead: Since he wrote King Lear as a servant of King James I, who had the reputation of being the wisest fool in Christendom, perhaps Shakespeare’s conception of Lear was influenced by James’s particular admiration for Solomon, wisest of kings.…[478] Shakespeare sought what we tend now not to emphasize in our accounts of Lear: a paradigm for greatness.…Lear is at once father, king, and a kind of mortal god: he is the image of male authority, perhaps the ultimate representation of the Dead White European Male. Solomon reigned for fifty years, and was James I’s wished-for archetype: glorious, wise, wealthy, even if Solomon’s passion for women was not exactly shared by the sexually ambiguous James. Lear is in no way a portrait of James…but Lear’s greatness would have mattered to James: he too considered himself every inch a king. I think he [479] would have recognized in the aged Lear the aged Solomon, each in their eighties, each needing and wanting love, and each worthy of love.…The crucial foregrounding of the play, if we are to understand it at all, is that Lear is lovable, loving, and greatly loved by anyone at all worthy of our own affection and approbation.

London (1965, p. 174): also sees Lear as Promethean, apocalyptic and Titanic. Elton (1966, p. 239) calls Lear a defiant Prometheus…Lear-Agonistes. Wittreich (1984, p. 97): Lear’s heroic stature is…measured, and in part defined, by his association with the fifth angel of the Apocalypse. Flahiff (1986, p. 26) calls him an unlikely Noah: An old man, the last of his kind and the first Monarch of the world—three children—the Deluge—his own nakedness observed—his curse upon the observer—the division of his kingdom as well as a would-be Jehovah…calling up—and down—that deluge of which he is a victim, and whose embodiment he becomes. For other similarities with classical and biblical heroes, see .

In contrast, some critics find weakness rather than grandeur or sublimity. Armstrong (1913, pp. 104–5): Lear is just what he describes himself to be, a fond, foolish old man. Almost entirely devoid of any wisdom, foresight or insight, he is fond of his daughters, but apparently still more fond of their affection. He is like a lovesick, importunate girl, to whom words mean more than acts.…[105] He is a kind, good, not particularly bright old man. He is painfully and bitterly surprised and deceived, where, had he been a little more intelligent, perhaps a little less vain, he might not have been either. Shore (1920, p. 155) complains of the silliness of Lear. It is difficult to feel sorry for him. Ridley (1937, p. 168) calls him an egotistical, petulant, and stupid old man. Fijn van Draat (1937, pp. 178–9): I take Lear to be a man well on in his fifties and no older. But he is old in the pregnant sense of the word long before his time. Always highly strung his quick, irascible temper, his fits of passion bordering on insanity, the hysterica passio that enfeebles his mind; drink and debauch with the inevitable sleeplessness in their train, all these have frayed his nerves that could not stand the racket.…[179] Until his tragic end Lear is devoid of all dignity, majesty, nobility of soul. Mason (1967, p. 34): The principal fact established [in 1.1] is that Lear is an impotent old fool. Some actors have wished us to see him as a terrible awesome Dragon, but he rather resembles the King in Alice in Wonderland. Miola (1994, pp. 336–8): Withholding Cordelia’s dowry in [1.1], Lear plays in a…specific New Comedy configuration—the familiar senex iratus blocking a marriage.…[338] Angry withdrawal and fulminating misanthropy characterize the comedic idiotes—self-important, isolated, inflexible, anti-festive, and ridiculous.…Lear’s angry withdrawal to the heath and his declamatory rage against the world thus describe a progress archetypally comic as well as tragic. Combe & Schmader (1996, p. 34) see merely an example of unsuccessful aging. Weiss (1977) notes that Lear is inarticulate in moments of the greatest excitement in accordance with his choleric old age. His typical form of speech is the question, which distinguishes him in particular from the other characters. (In Ger.)

Other critics emphasize a mixture of strength and weakness. Gildon (1710, p. 406): He is a truly Tragic Character not supremely Virtuous or Scandalously vicious; he is made up of Choler, and Obstinacy, Frailties pardonable enough in an old Man, and yet what drew on him all the Misfortunes of his Life. Dowden (1875; 1879, p. 272): Lear is grandly passive—played upon by all the manifold forces of nature and society. Brink (1895, p. 238): He is a strange mixture of strength and weakness, of heroism and childlike helplessness, of manly passion and childish wilfulness. Knight (1930, pp. 177–220): The images he creates of his three daughters’ love are quite false, sentimentalized: he understands the nature of none of his children, and, demanding an unreal and impossible love from all three, is disillusioned by each in turn. But, though sentimental, this love is not weak. It is powerful and firm-planted in his mind as a mountain rock embedded in earth. The tearing out of it is hideous, cataclysmic. A tremendous soul is, as it were, incongruously geared to a puerile intellect. Lear’s senses prove his idealized love-figments false, his intellect snaps, and, as the loosened drive flings limp, the disconnected engine of madness spins free, and the ungeared revolutions of it are terrible, fantastic. This, then, is the basis of the play: greatness linked to puerility. Lear’s instincts are themselves grand, heroic—noble even. His judgment is nothing. Stockholder (1968, p. 46) finds that he is in part a fool, a comic alazon as well as the mythic origin of the polarized forces of good and evil embodied in his three daughters. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 20 ff.): The character is a dynamic equation, the terms of which are constantly changing, new terms drawn in, vanished ones reengaged.…He is the primary if-but-yet character of his if-but-yet world.…[21] Strength and weakness will pair in Lear: physical strength and psychic fatigue; spiritual force and bodily exhaustion. Similarly wisdom and folly will coexist, alternate, reciprocate; as will madness and sanity, age and vigor, love and hate, anger and kindness, authority and submission, conditioning and impulse. Lear will need to be absolute, alone; and dependent, nourished.…On subtler levels, the Lear design suggests masked motives to which the names narcissism, regression, repression, incest wish, or death wish may apply.…There are various familiar archetypal gestalts assembled and opposed in [the Lear design]: king, father, man (old, wise, foolish, childish), child, lover, fool, madman.…Shakespeare restructured and distorted the familiar gestalts, sometimes blurred the boundaries among them. Never a king with so absolute—and apparently earned—authority so undermined by qualities and experiences deadly to his role. The image of kingly power leans on the archetype of wise old age, then collapses in a whirlpool of counter-images of decay, folly, and madness. King-father, man-father, mad-father, mad-man, man-child, man-animal, man-fool—they all clinch and coalesce.…[68] The story of this king figure brought low is a reprise of the archetypal fantasy of assault on the most high. Lear’s invocations are, dramatically, not a test of the gods, but of Lear the invoker. His assumption of semidivinity, of a comradeship with deity, is undercut by his humanity, and his animal heritage.…[198] Lear has been likened to Prometheus; he is different, more complex,…less Prometheus than a failed Zeus: he would take vengeance on all who oppose him, especially the young. He will not recognize in himself the secret faults for which the others must be made to pay, his obsession with trial and punishment is [throughout Act 3] nearly absolute.

Various critics have interpreted Lear in symbolic terms, an approach which generally reinforces a view of the grandeur of the role. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, pp. 199–201) anticipates Bradley (see above, ) in emphasizing the symbolic and cosmic repercussions of Lear’s fall into madness: The madness of the King cannot be justified on mere psychological grounds; it would be highly censurable if it had not a poetic justification, in the organic structure of the entire work.…As the family tie—the first and absolutely indispensable foundation of all moral and intellectual development has been irremediably broken, and thereby the whole of human existence unsettled, being let loose from its primary source and reality in God; [200] this convulsion and the extreme enormity of sin must be exhibited both internally and externally.…[201] It was only by such an affliction that a character like his could be brought to repentance; and by such means alone could the propitiatory element of tragedy be manifested in his case. It was not until his kingly spirit, his haughty virtue, his energy and sovereignty of will, had been utterly overthrown, that he could be brought to the humility which is the parent of true love, and that love in him could be purified. Bodkin (1934, pp. 17 ff.) describes Lear as an archetype of tragic sacrifice: his status as king is loaded with significance for the sources of which we must go far back in the story of the race and of the individual.…The figures of both father and king tend to retain within those deeper levels of the mind to which poetry may penetrate…something of the mana that invested the first representative of a power akin to, but vastly beyond, that of the individual emerging into self-consciousness.…[281] It is the same magic of poetic speech that transforms the raving Lear into a majestic figure who seems to bear the imagined burden of the whole world’s sorrow [Granville-Barker, 1927; 1946, 2:28]. The glory that the poet’s art reveals, within the old man broken to madness upon the desolate heath, may in part be traced…to the collective emotional energies vested, through personal and racial history…within the person and function of a king. The power, daemonic or divine, glorifying the contemplated figure, which is also seen with perfect distinctness in its human limitation, weakness, and misery—such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art, I am a very foolish, fond old man—moves the spectator with the authentic tragic feeling that has, among its mingled aspects, the character of a purgation, and hence an atonement. Kingly greatness, beheld in a form so broken and pitiful, is no longer a possible object of the personal self-seeking and power-craving that isolates the individual from his kind. (P. 284): As a ritualized sacrificial figure, Lear is related to Christ. Holloway (1961, p. 97) also identifies Lear as a ritual scapegoat: He is a Jack-a-Green, at once hero and victim of a popular ceremony.…He is the man who begins as centre of his whole world, but who is progressively set, both by the other characters and himself, apart from it and against it. Similarly, Bristol (1985, p. 210–11): It is easy to recognize Lear as a figure of Carnival misrule whose withdrawal from the arduous political efforts of kingship into the celebration of festive hospitality leads to his transformation into a mock-king, and who is (p. 211) driven away by Lenten severity. Pilikian (1977–8, p. 26): Lear is…a fertility symbol, the source of all blessing for the beneficent fertility of his kingdom.

Some critics discuss Lear as a symbol of universal mankind. Watkins (1942, pp. 24–5): Lear is only partially a psychological creation since the play is (p. 25) simultaneously a psychologically realistic individual tragedy of ingratitude, and a symbolical tragedy of man’s inhumanity to man.…Lear is not only Lear but Everyman. Traversi (1952, p. 126): In Act 3 Lear assumes a stature that is more than merely personal, becomes man, the microcosm of the universe, exposed to a suffering to which the frame of things itself contributes, but which finds its acutest symbol in the intimate disunion which the earlier action of the play has introduced into the family bond. Rosen (1960, pp. 17 ff.): Sympathizing with Lear’s values and his precarious position, through his speech we move into his consciousness; we see the world with his eyes, we are committed to his point of view.…[27] Not character, but values become most important; not personality, but a situation typical of tragic human destiny.…[29] We move from the plight of individual man to the terrors of everyman.…[40] In searching for his own identity in the midst of chaos, he does so for all mankind.…[42] This stress on the responsibility of one man for all makes Lear one with all humanity and binds all humanity into oneness.…[47] Lear, like many of Dostoevski’s characters, loses himself to find himself part of all humanity.…[51] His vision of truth and his complete change of character give us a sense of the nobility of spirit which can transcend the confinements of man’s condition. In contrast, London (1965, p. 183): Lear is an epitome (not a symbol) of man. Milward (1975, p. 8): In a sense Lear is Adam; and his original sin consists, not in the laying aside of his kingship, but in his rejection of grace in Cordelia, or rather in his antecedent pride and inclination to flattery and falsehood. Even as king he is already the old Adam, but in a manner disguised from himself and others. Only when he lays aside his kingly power does the old Adam in him come into the open.…[18] In…his knowledge of himself as Man, apart from the pomp and commodities of human life, he comes to know the common human condition he shares with other men.…This is for him the beginning of salvation. Long (1976, p. 161): The figure of the King is an archetypal imagining of everything that it is to be a social man.

Other symbolical interpretations of the role include that of Wilson (1929, p. 46): He is a symbol of man’s unconquerable soul, of the triumph of spirit over the worst that material forces can do against it. It is impossible to contemplate the death of Lear without thinking of Calvary. Danby (1949, pp. 174–5): Lear himself is the Soul, in a middle place between Edmund [the Flesh] and Cordelia [the Spirit]. As such he is capable of rejecting the Spirit. As such, too, of course, he is capable of being recalled and of turning again.…[175] All depends on the transactions that take place between the King and Nature. For the King should be representative man, the expression of every man’s natural honesty, and as such the embodiment of the health of the state. Righter (1962, p. 133) discusses Lear as Player King, a symbol of flawed rule: He has rashly placed himself in the paradoxical position of the man who plays the king’s part on the stage. Everett (1989, p. 64): He is Eros Tyrannos, Tyrannicke love in person. As such he becomes extraordinarily elusive in moral terms, not simply because he learns and changes in the course of the play…but because from the opening scene he releases into the tragedy all the moral anarchy of love.…[79] His love for his daughters is both creative and destructive, a heroic search for meaning that both makes and breaks. Chakravorty (1990, pp. 4–8) interprets him as a type of existentialist hero: King Lear, so long immersed in Bad Faith, suddenly awakes to the consciousness of freedom and decides to assert it.…[5] Lear’s choice to abdicate is his exercise of freedom.…[7] Lear’s madness in this drama is also the objective correlative of man’s Existentialist consciousness which is essentially irrational. In the storm Lear (p. 8) invokes his own creative power to blow and strike in order to change and create the order of things anew and thereby create his own freedom. Linville (1990, p. 316): An aged figure who…repudiates filiation and devours his children, be becomes a type of Chronos or Father Time. Perry (1997, p. 123) sees an image of a nourish father as formulated by James I, a fantasy of patriarchal kingship as quasi-maternal. Spinosa (1995, pp. 163–5) argues that in 1.1, Lear attempts to make himself into the primary figure of English authority that, as such figures do, has the job of gathering together the excessive sentiments and feelings of the kingdom and showing the appropriateness and worthiness of such feelings.
The many psychological interpretations of the role, including discussions of the madness of Lear, tend to emphasize flawed humanity rather than grandeur, and particularity rather than universality.

A minor quarrel in the 18th century concerned whether Lear was driven mad by the loss of royalty or his daughters’ ingratitude. Warton (1754, p. 307): Madness being occasioned by a close and continued attention of the mind to a single object, Shakespeare judiciously represents the loss of royalty as the particular idea which has brought on the distraction of Lear, and which perpetually recurs to his imagination and mixes itself with all his ramblings. Murphy (1754, pp. 91–2): I am really surprized that the Critic in the Adventurer should impute the Madness of Lear to [92] the Loss of Royalty. The Behaviour of his Children is always uppermost in his Thoughts, and we perceive it working upon his Passions, till at Length his Mind settles into a fixt Attention to that single Object. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159–60): Lear would move our compassion but little, did we not [160] rather consider the injured father than the degraded king. T. G. D. (1754, p. 97) says that loss of royalty and ingratitude of children are both important, and closely linked. Hunt (1808; 1949, p. 17): There has been question whether his misery proceeds so much from his disappointed tenderness as from his loss of royalty; but if the latter appeared to be the first cause, it would certainly lessen the natural pathos of the story, and I think the question might have been settled by simple reference to his first interview with Cordelia, when he returns to reason and becomes calm and penitent at the sight of his injured daughter without once adverting impatiently to his lost sovereignty: if they tell him that he is in his own kingdom, he merely begs them not to abuse him: he has no pride, no impatience, no revenge, before his forgiving angel. The very first reason he gives for Edgar’s apparent misery, when he meets him as a wandering maniac, is filial ingratitude; he insists that nothing could have made a human being so wretched but his ungrateful children; and it is wonderful to see the consummate art with which Shakespeare has preserved in these two pictures of madness that single occupation of thought which at once fixes and distracts the mind.

Early critics (and some moderns as well) have also argued about whether Lear should be considered mad at the outset of the play. See nn. 1, 3–10, 115–27. Lennox (1754, 3:287): Lear does not run mad till the third Act; yet his Behaviour towards Cordelia in [the] first Scene has all the Appearance of a Judgment totally depraved.…What less than Phrenzy can inspire a Rage so groundless, and a Conduct so absurd! Lear, while in his Senses, acts like a mad Man, and from his first Appearance to his last seems to be wholly deprived of his Reason. Heine (1838; tr. 1891, 1:365): In the first scene There is a little cloud already in the intellect of Lear, which will thicken anon to the blackest mental night. He who in such fashion gives all away, must be already mad. Anon. (1844, pp. 32–3): He was insane…[33] from the beginning of the play, when he gave his kingdom away, and banished as it were Cordelia and Kent, and abused his servants. The ill-usage of his daughters only aggravated the disease and drove him to raving madness. Kreyssig (1862; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 461) likewise sees the behavior of a man already unsettled in his understanding, and emphasizes Lear’s terrible wrath rather than any sympathetic qualities. With differing emphases, Leed (1978, p. 62) likewise asserts that Lear is mad from the beginning of the play, arguing as well that his reconciliation with Cordelia does not reverse his madness but extends it.…[67] He is a character of such awesomeness to us because he goes into the forbidden psychic realm where there is no constraint upon the expression of passion.

In contrast, various critics argue that Lear is sane and wise rather than mad or foolish at the beginning of the play. Bransom (1934, p. 213) calls him a man of great intellectual power and imagination…of a very high order. Elliott (1959, pp. 261–2): Lear’s folly is not due to senile dementia. Lear’s mind, throughout the first scene, is remarkably creative and powerful.…[262] Shakespeare in the outset of this drama tries to make Lear, like his other main tragic heroes, as humanly representative as possible. Nevo (1972, pp. 263–8): Rather than [exhibiting] Coleridge’s signs of senility,…Lear is impressively in command of the court and his faculties. It is (p. 268) not the original proposed division of the kingdom, nor even the love-test as such, that constitutes Lear’s fatal error, but, specifically and precisely, the redistribution which actually takes place, the disinheritance of Cordelia and the giving of entire power into the hands of the wicked sisters. For the wisdom of Lear’s plan for the division of the kingdom, see nn. 7, 43–6, 53–8. Birenbaum (1983; 1989, pp. 235–8) also defends Lear’s scheme: Lear is in fact a kind of visionary idealist. He is being magnanimous in relinquishing his throne, and he is showing a care for all his daughters in granting them all kingdoms. He is even being realistic in acknowledging the fatigues of old age. We should respect (p. 238) the decency of his dream. Likewise Berry (1984, pp. 428 ff.): Lear commits an irreparable folly in banishing Cordelia, but his appraisal of forces, up to that point, is highly defensible.…[422] The dispositions which Lear makes for the security of his realm are an intelligent attempt (p. 426) to set up a system which will survive [him], while permitting him a guiding hand in late old age. Partee (1992, p. 36): Lear is not senile or foolish; the planned division was brilliantly conceived but carelessly executed in that the king has wildly over-estimated the political sophistication of his youngest daughter. Held (1995, pp. 63–4): He understands well enough Cordelia’s reasons for not wanting to participate in the love test.…He has foreseen her reaction, and creates the love test precisely in order to elicit this reaction from her.…[64] as a pretext for denying her a dowry.

As Muir (1960, p. 38), observes, It has often been observed by doctors of widely differing views that Shakespeare is clinically accurate in his presentation of the symptoms of madness; accordingly, it is not surprising that various medical diagnoses have been suggested for Lear. Willis (1823, p. 69) discusses Lear to illustrate the idea that bodily disease takes place prior to any mental derangement. Ray (1847, p. 292): Assuming Lear to be an historical portrait instead of a poetical creation, we should say there existed in his case a strong predisposition to insanity, and that if it had not been developed by the approach of old age, or the conduct of his daughters, it would have been by something else. Bucknill (1867, pp. 177–96) argues that Lear is mad from the start of the play, though not incoherent until his exposure to the storm brings his mental disease to a point of crisis. His behavior in the first scene illustrates exaggerated passion, perverted affection, weakened judgment; all the elements, in fact, of madness, except incoherence and delusion. Sh.’s (p. 196) profound knowledge of mental disease is shown by his understanding of insanity as a disturbance of the emotions rather than of the intellect. Ross (1867, p. 31) also praises Sh.’s intimate knowledge of the phenomena of insanity.
