Flint (1904, p. 269) sees in Lear a study of the form of insanity known as senile dementia, as does Taylor (1907, p. 214): Lear is himself already over the verge of senile imbecility. Edgar (1934, p. 161) and Cunningham (1988, p. 25) both call him a case of…senile dementia. Somerville (1929, pp. 121–32) likewise emphasizes psychological realism in the depiction of Lear’s madness: Rightly judged, his attacks of mania are to be regarded as unconscious attempts to escape from an enemy world into himself.…[132] It is best that Lear should die, not only to end his troubles, but also because if he had lived he would almost certainly have been a hopeless dement—a living being without a mind. Andreason (1976, p. 1868): Lear has a mild organic brain syndrome that develops under stress into a reactive psychosis. Barnes (1986, p. 216): The stages and development of Lear’s derangement are, in two important and basic respects, wholly compatible with the view of psychosis held by existential psychologists.…The madness is to some degree chosen, and it is purposeful. Draper (1940, p. 537) cites humoral theory: Some have thought his madness a perfect case of senile dementia as understood by modern alienists; and so it well may be: in its development and symptoms, it is also a perfect case of melancholy dotage as the Elizabethans conceived of it. See also Idem (1945, p. 76): Lear’s choleric humor dries to melancholy with old age and mental shock. Rosenberg (1972, p. 216) objects: To give Lear’s madness a scientific classification is meaningless. Hoeniger (1992, p. 317), however: Shakespeare’s conception of Lear was influenced by Stoic and later views of anger as brevis furor (and habitual anger as furor or madness), as well as by stories of kings who are punished for their repeated tyrannical rages with madness, though in Shakespeare’s play there is no hint of divine punishment. Both traditions suggest that Shakespeare and his Jacobean audience thought of Lear as mentally unstable (and thus ill) from the start but not therefore as less responsible for his conduct. See also n. 53–8. Thiher (1999, p. 84) sees his madness manifested in that Lear cannot judge how language functions.…Like many medieval minds, he confuses the literal with the rhetorical, the existential with the semantic.

A number of psychoanalytically-minded critics explain Lear’s behavior as motivated by incestuous passion for one of his daughters. Bransom (1934, pp. 221–5): The evidence of [2567–72 shows] that in Lear’s life there had been some unusually disturbing sexual experience.…It is possible that it was an old, repressed, incestuous passion for one of his daughters [probably Goneril].…[224] When Lear mounted his throne, divided his kingdom, proposed his love-test, and came into conflict with his daughters, a group of emotions, separated from consciousness, was to a large extent in control of his conduct.…[225] Lear’s insanity, therefore, must be regarded as originating, in the main, in this group of emotions. That is to say, long before Lear actually became insane his conduct was affected by factors which were eventually responsible for his insanity. See Freud (1934) for his approving response. Pauncz (1952, pp. 58, 74) identifies a Lear Complex, seen in his attachment to his daughters, especially [Cordelia]. Not fatherly affection, in the everyday sense of the word, is meant here, but rather a specifically erotic affection, which may readily be compared to the child fixation in the Oedipus Complex as described by Freud, except that it is reversed.…[74] Is it too daring and far-fetched to look at Lear’s kaleidoscopic transformation in terms of a meaningful unity, to try to understand all Lear’s fantastic ideas and imaginings, his actions and conduct, his guilt and shame as the manifestations of his most basic longing: To be united as the bridegroom, with Cordelia the bride? Donnelly (1955, p. 153): It is total, and therefore incestuous, love that [Lear] wants from [Cordelia] though he does not realize the incestuousness of his attachment.…Evidence of the extent of Lear’s sexual phantasies is readily found in the scenes in which he is insane. Stetner & Goodman (1968, p. 89): Lear’s darker purpose in 1.1 is incestuous desire: We do not pretend that the incest motif is any more than one of the elements in the most complex of Shakespeare’s designs, but we do contend that it is a major element, and that it is indeed designed. Chaplin (1969, pp. 31–2): The insistence that Lear’s desires are free of sexual content, and that latent incest would objectify itself as an accept-[32]tance of sexual overtures, inadequately gauges both Lear’s behavior and the nature of latent incest itself. Dove & Gamble (1969, pp. 313–14): The possessive Lear had no intention at all of allowing his favourite daughter to leave Britain, perhaps for good, in the arms of either France or Burgundy. On the contrary, he wants her to stay in Britain with him as the prop of his old age, and with this in mind he offers her the glittering and totally unexpected bait of the opulent third of the kingdom, which he never for a moment doubts that she will accept with adoring gratitude.…[314] In a certain sense, we may say that Lear is the third suitor, and the great rivals are not only rivals with each other but with him. Lesser (1970, pp. 161–2): There is a not wholly desexualized—a repressed incestuous—element in Lear’s feeling for Cordelia.…[162] Cordelia’s unanticipated behavior [in 1.1] thwarts a whole cluster of unconscious, or at any rate unacknowledged, desires. Wheeler (1980, p. 163): In his longing, Lear destroys Cordelia by creating her presence in the image of his own need and imprisoning her in that image. But the consequences of Lear’s actions extend throughout the world of the play. He has tragically altered the conditions of an actual world in which Cordelia must be destroyed, cannot be retrieved, cannot be used. In the play’s symbolic action, the malevolence of that outer world mirrors the inner destructiveness of Lear. Blechner (1988, p. 319): We can see in King Lear a love-tragedy between father and daughter. In the first scene the father banishes the loved daughter after having attempted in vain to prevent her from marrying. In the final scene, he achieves his wish, the taboo is broken, the love is expressed, and…the transgressing characters die. Parker (1991, p. 140): Lear is the third suitor for Cordelia in 1.1; his true motivation—his darker purpose—shows him to be a far more intelligent and scheming man than many have given him credit for. See n. 41. Dudley (1993, p. 74): Lear’s incestuous longing is…emotional rather than physical—yet still unwitting. Crick (1997, p. 76): Lear’s obsessive screams of sexual revulsion in 4.6 express his own pathological recoil from the hideous prospect of imagining the detested bride-groom, the hot-blooded France [1505], enjoying his beloved daughter. Such unendurable thoughts may also carry him to the brink of becoming conscious of the forbidden sexuality of his own need to possess Cordelia’s person. See also Wile (1935, pp. 325–6), Ravich (1964, pp. 28–35), Grinstein (1965, pp. 121–41), Rose (1969, pp. 938–40), Stockholder (1985), Whittier (1989, pp. 388 ff.), and Ford (1998, pp. 41–2). For the evidence supposed to imply incestuous inclinations in Lear, see nn. 105, 109, 238, 1644, 1708, 2567–71, 2640–1, 2949, and , , , , , , .

Other modern critics employ a range of psychological concepts when interpreting Lear. Abenheimer (1945, p. 328) labels Lear a narcissist: His exaggerated sovereignty, and his attempt to be even above common reason, parental love and obligations, and loyalty towards devoted friends express the narcissistic intolerance for any limitation of the ego. At the same time he craves liberation from the burden of being an ego. Therefore he throws away all his power and makes himself weak like a little child who has to be cared for and looked after.…Blindly he chases after the impossible aim to shelter in the love of a perfect mother. Likewise Simon (1988, p. 105): Lear’s narcissistic character structure entails defects in empathy, rage at his inability to control natural and familial processes, and delusional attempts to reconstruct and control his shattered world. The themes of uncreation and destruction of meaning and meaningful connection typical of the play King Lear emanate from and are entwined with the traits of the character Lear. Riemer (1966, pp. 33–9) characterizes Lear as solipsistic: Lear sees himself inhabiting an egocentric universe—a universe where concepts and other people have significance and existence only in so far as they fall into a meaningful relationship with himself. Tragically, (p. 39) in the process of attaining…wisdom and…harmony, Lear becomes (p. 42) dull and lacking in imaginative vigour and vitality. Kirsch (1966, p. 220): He had projected his anima image onto Cordelia.…It was [the] sudden loss of the anima projection which…unleashed Lear’s affectivity. Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 286–99): Lear’s behavior in [the first] scene is explained by…the attempt to avoid recognition, the shame of exposure, the threat of self-revelation.…[288] There is reason to assume that the open possibility—or the open fact—that [his two older daughters] are not offering true love is exactly what he wants. Trouble breaks out only with Cordelia’s Nothing, and her broken resolution to be silent.…[289] Lear knows it is a bribe he offers, and—part of him any-[290]way—wants exactly what a bribe can buy: (1) false love; and (2) a public expression of love. That is: he wants something he does not have to return in kind, something which a division of his property fully pays for.…Cordelia is alarming precisely because he knows she is offering the real thing.…She threatens to expose…his terror of being loved, of needing love. Similarly, in 5.3, Lear (p. 297)does not renounce the world in going to prison, but flees from it.…[298] The ideas of love and death are interlocked in his mind—and in particular of death as a payment or placation for the granting of love. His own death, because acknowledging love still presents itself to him as an annihilation of himself. And [Cordelia’s] death, because now that he admits her love, he must admit, what he knew from the beginning, that he is impotent to sustain it. [299] It can be said that what Lear is ashamed of is not his need for love and his ability to return it, but of the nature of his love for Cordelia. It is too far from plain love of father for daughter. Even if we resist seeing in it the love of lovers, it is at least incompatible with the idea of her having any (other) lover. Goldberg (1974, pp. 26 ff.): Whatever is said by critics seeking profound moral faults in his behaviour to explain why his later suffering is so providentially just, his division of the kingdom had not been attempting to calculate the worth of his daughters’ love against material possessions or vice versa. The division being already settled, he was surreptitiously asking them, and especially Cordelia, rather to measure his love by the generosity of his gift,…but it is precisely because he was giving Cordelia love with his gift that her response has hurt so badly. She has seemed to deny not so much the gift as the love…in a way moreover that denies him by denying his ability to respect himself as a man of careful justice, noble generosity, and love for (especially one of) his children.…[27] The kind of love he wants would at once acknowledge the only image of himself he can respect and therefore acknowledge, remain silent about the need, and thereby enable him not to be conscious of the terrifying vulnerability from which it springs.…[109] The violent effort of Lear’s will to hold together a consciousness of his manhood, fatherhood, and power—a familiar shape or identity, whose authority lies in the abstract roles it assumes, is so badly shaken not because it is denied, but because its hidden premiss [is] helpless emotional need.…[113] He needs others’ respect in order to respect himself. Yet…the very urgency of this need betrays the fear behind it—which is a form not of self-ignorance, but rather of self-mistrust, as if he cannot believe…in his mere self as worth the love and respect it needs.…[129] Lear is largely moved by self-pity and self-will. Berger (1979; 1997, pp. 31–47): In Act 1, his darker purpose [cf. 41] seems to be to play on everyone’s curiosity and to stir up as much envy and contention as he can among the younger strengths with the aim of dominating and dividing them, humbling and punishing them.…[32] He can hardly be unaware that his giving was a form of taking; his paternal kindness a form of hostility; his renunciation an effort to retain power; his retention of power a response to the terror of the impotency of old age.…The source of his fear must lie in patterns of feeling, behavior, and relationship that predate the opening scene of the play.…[33] Even the weakest twinge of recognition, the dimmest sense of his complicity, could have brought home to him the reason for, the justness of, his suspicion that he was unloved—the sense that is, that he had never truly loved his children, that he had always used his paternal authority to command, demand, tease, and humiliate.…In hurting and punishing Cordelia he is trying to hurt and punish himself.…[34] We can, then, distinguish in [Lear’s] speech and behavior the working out of two purposes additional to his own consciously proclaimed darker purpose—by which he means dark to the others but not to him. The two I have in mind are initially both dark to him, and I shall speak of them as darker and darkest: the darker purpose moves him to aggression against others; the darkest purpose moves him to aggression against himself. The darker purpose justifies itself accord-[35]ing to the logic of the victim’s formula, more sinned against than sinning; the darkest purpose justifies itself according to the logic of more sinning than sinned against. Lear quickly discovers the presence within him of the darker purpose, and its usefulness, and he puts it to work. Among its uses are its effectiveness against the efforts of the darkest purpose to make itself known. It is the darker purpose, of course, that counsels madness. At the same time, to the degree that the darker purpose is effective in this policing function, it exacerbates the darkest purpose. Aggression against others, the projective distortion of guilt feelings, is the bad faith that creates, intensifies, and festers the darkest purpose.…We should note…the extent to which Lear provokes Goneril and Regan into their aggressive and mean behavior.…He shares in their complicity more than he seem willing to admit.…[47] When Lear comes onstage with Cordelia’s body [in 5.3],…what he does is make sure she is dead before bringing her back to life; he controls her return, and he sends her back again to death. Pirie (1980, p. 6): Lear matures belatedly into an awareness of the adult world’s complexity. But he does so only to panic back into a regressively simple-minded horror of the post-pubertal body [cf. 2568–71]. Schwartz (1980, p. 27): The center of the play is Lear’s refusal to mourn the loss of maternal provision, a refusal that leads him into a persecutory universe within which the breakdown of psychic and social boundaries reaches its most devastatingly powerful Shakespearean form.…The play comes full circle in Lear’s desire to find, and his failure to find, symbolic nurturance from Cordelia’s mouth. Schuman (1983, pp. 88–90): Lear’s madness is restitutive rather than retributive. Beginning with a need to regress to the preoedipal level of development, Lear (p. 90) had to become mad in order to expose his self-deceptions and to gain control over the feelings of rage which otherwise would have continued their destructive course. Coursen (1984: pp. 76–84): Lear’s problem is exacerbated by his being what Jung calls the extroverted thinking type. This personality-type tends to discern his reality in the external world and tends to employ thinking as his means of ordering that received reality.…[83] Lear, as characterized, clings to his rationality, rejects his intuitions, is victimized by his feelings—as thinking types are.…[84] Lear must undergo self-destruction—the eradication of the ego, or all that conscious orientation thought it knew—in order to experience regeneration, the establishment of what Jung calls the Self, a consciousness that incorporates the deeper, previously ignored, energies of the psyche. Zak (1984, pp. 27 ff.): Some blockage in Lear’s consciousness always prevents him from seeing his own situation and action clearly enough for him to become his own best counselor.…[29] An unacknowledged but no less burning shame, as Kent specifically remarked of Lear’s final refusal to face her, repeatedly and persistently detains him from Cordelia [2347+43–7].…[33] His tragic nobility emerges out of his agonized and unspeakable suspicion that he is neither rightful king nor deserving of love.…In Lear vulnerability remains simply a horror to be fled.…[173] All the miseries he endures are subtly self-glorifying, an indulgence in pain to help him avoid the acknowledgment of his own evil. Stockholder (1987, pp. 118–19) imagines Lear as the dreamer of the play world: King Lear defines himself as both legitimate king and father, and generates a world in which familial and social authority function as strong analogues for each other.…In this structural configuration, by casting himself as father to all women figures he renders all sexuality incestuous.…In relinquishing his crown while keeping the privilege of kingship he unknowingly empowers the feared desires that his role as king had been designed to restrain.…[119] To preserve an image of female purity he…casts himself as a son and victim to images of evil mothers, while permitting himself to regress to more childlike stages of sexuality that he associates first with boyish boisterousness, then with humiliation and deprivation, and finally with disgust. His object in passing through these stages is to know himself as a man rather than as king and father, and to reclaim Cordelia. For a moment he subtly recasts her as an appropriate object of his desire. But as the horrific images he has momentarily dispelled rush back upon him he…seeks the consummation of love in the grave. Leggatt (1988, pp. 73–8): From the beginning there is a tension in Lear between the desire to surrender…and the desire to cling to power, authority and love. Yet in clinging to these things Lear violates them.…[74] Beneath the titanic arrogance Lear is vulnerable, anxious, needing to be assured of his future, with the contradictory wants of a child: ease and power, love that is given and love that is secured by being bought. Behind his arrogance lies the simple human fear, Old Adam’s fear in As You Like It of unregarded age in corners thrown (II.ii.43). And behind that in turn lies the fear of loneliness and neglect, a fear that can be felt at any age.…[78] Part of King Lear’s overall tension is that while the play as a whole is constantly moving towards new insights, new discoveries, the central character is fighting a tremendous battle against knowledge, a battle in which, paradoxically, every loss is an advance. A related tension is that between Lear’s awareness of the world around him and his preoccupation with himself. Stern (1990, pp. 306–8): Lear’s transference of the kingdom…seems engendered by and surely to engender in him…a transference in the psychoanalytic sense: that is, an awakening in the present of powerful infantile feelings and attitudes.…[308] The story…that frames the story of Lear’s traumatic loss of Cordelia in the play is thus a barely spoken story of the loss of her mother, and the trace, perhaps, of an unspoken story of lost maternal responsiveness in his own childhood. Paris (1991, pp. 109–19): Lear is a predominantly narcissistic person who (p. 110) has been treated like a spoiled child all his life, and, as a result…has become permanently infantile.…[119] Given the intensity of his reactions to the relatively minor frustrations of the opening scene, it is not surprising that he is driven mad by the total rejection of his claims that he encounters later. Mitchell (1992, pp. 100–1): In retreat from Cordelia’s truth, i.e., the necessity of death, Lear revert[s] to a regressive infancy.…Fighting to deny his impotence…, he becomes a mother in labor through a process of identality. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, pp. 85–104): The king feels a desperate need for gratitude and love on the part of his daughters but…he cannot acknowledge this need.…He gives the impression of being a person who has probably never experienced the delicacy of genuine feelings of true love. And even if he has, he was unable to recognize it for what it was.…The type of insensitivity Lear displays is symptomatic of a lack of affection during his childhood.…He is infantile.…[93] With her unexpected refusal to enter the competition, Cordelia turns into a wicked mother in Lear’s eyes. A terrible, primitive mother who denies him her understanding.…[104] Unable to keep the wretched parts of himself internalized, Lear is forced to project them. That is his real tragedy.

Several psychologistic critics find Lear struggling with gender. Sharpe (1946, p. 24): Lear is psychically driven into an hysterical pretence of being his mother, the corrupt thing inside her is him, they are of one flesh, one body.…[Quotes 1328, 1515–19.] This method of psychical retreat from reality is a way of controlling aggression against the real mother external to himself. More important still is the fact that we see here a retreat from the reality of his masculinity. Novy (1979, p. 285): Lear’s attack on women in 4.6 is a form of scapegoating [related] to patriarchal society’s split of human qualities into masculine and feminine. Patriarchal society exerts social and psychological pressure on men to deny qualities in themselves that would be seen as feminine and instead to project them on to women.…Lear’s disgust with women’s lust is especially strong because it is really disgust with himself; at the same time, his initial expectations of Cordelia’s kind nursery are especially high because he identifies her with nurturing qualities and vulnerabilities not easily admitted by a king whose royal symbol is the dragon. Gohlke (1980, pp. 156–8) detects deep fantasies of maternal betrayal.…[157] It is birth itself, the condition of owing one’s life to a woman and the ambivalence attending an awareness of dependence on women in general, which structures much of Lear’s re-[158]lations to his daughters. Coursen (1984: pp. 83–4): He resists feminization, stiffens into a kind of god-figure who threatens in relation to his loss of power, externalizes the revenges that his own psyche is committing upon him, and becomes more and more childish as his compulsive male persona perpetuates itself. Feminization involves the male’s contact with his anima, the feminine soul of his androgynous nature. As insisting on absoluteness drives Lear towards ludicrous immaturity, so insisting on total maleness drives him towards stereotypical femininity—[84] stereotypical because, without contact with his androgyny, the externally derived stereotype is all that is available to him. Kahn (1986, pp. 41–5): Lear’s madness is essentially his rage at being deprived of the maternal presence. It is tantalizing, though I can imagine no way of proving it, to view this rage as part of the social pathology of wet-nursing in the ruling classes.…[45] Regan and Goneril betray and disappoint Lear by not being mothers to him, but in a deeper, broader sense, they shame him by bringing out the woman in him. Adelman (1992, p. 104): Lear’s confrontation with his daughters…repeatedly leads him back to the mother ostensibly occluded by the play: in recognizing his daughters as part of himself he will be led to recognize not only his terrifying dependence on female forces outside himself but also an equally terrifying femaleness within himself—a femaleness that he will come to call mother [1328]. Rutter (1994–6; 1997, p. 175): Does the progressive feminization of Lear evoke terror and grief, the deterioration of the masculine being the tragic issue? Or should we see Lear’s appropriation of the feminine as an appalling act of cultural aggression that—even as he makes his daughters male monsters, Centaurs, and himself the mother—perverts the feminine and occupies the feminine space to wreck it? At the end might we feel not pity but rage? In contrast, Deats (1996; 1999, pp. 28–9): Lear discovers the long-sought-for mother in the storm before his reunion with Cordelia.…He ultimately finds this nurturing parent not in Cordelia but in himself.…[29] Lear learns to integrate his feminine and masculine qualities, seeking both relatedness and autonomy, balancing empathy with strength.

Leggatt (1996, pp. 134–7) argues for the verisimilitude of Lear’s madness: Lear’s wilderness journey could…be straight reporting.…[137] Other stage madmen are performances; Lear is the thing itself. He thereby agrees with earlier critics, such as Walpole (1768, p. 89): The finest picture ever drawn of a head distempered by misfortune is that of king Lear. His thoughts dwell on the ingratitude of his daughters, and every sentence that falls from his wildness excites reflection and pity. Likewise W. N. (1818, p. 293): I know no narrative, either historical or dramatic, conducted with more good sense and deep reflection than the account of Lear’s madness from its commencement to its consummation.…infinite art and sagacity.…[Shakespeare] has…provided the world with a complete historical representation of this mental disease, with philosophical acuteness, tracing it from its remote causes, and marking its progress in all its various stages. See also Staël-Holstein (1828, p. 127), Farren (1833), Ray (1847, p. 291), Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 629–30), Clarke (1863, pp. 185–6), Kellogg (1866, p. 17), Hudson (1872, 2:370–4), Moulton (1893, pp. 214–5). Bradley (1904, pp. 288–9): The most obvious symptom of Lear’s insanity, especially in its first stages, is of course the domination of a fixed idea. Whatever presents itself to his senses is seized on by this idea and compelled to express it; as for example in those words…which first show that his mind has actually given way: [quotes 1830–1]. But it is remarkable that what we have here is only, in an exaggerated and perverted form, the very same action of imagination that before produced those sublime appeals: [quotes 1479–82] and [quotes 1669–79]. Shakespeare, long before this, in the Midsummer Night’s Dream, had noticed that the resemblance between [289] the lunatic, the lover, and the poet; and the partial truth that genius is allied to insanity was quite familiar to him. But he presents here the supplementary half-truth that insanity is allied to genius. He does not, however, put into the mouth of the insane Lear any such sublime passages as those just quoted. Lear’s insanity, which destroys the coherence, also reduces the poetry of his imagination. What it stimulates is that power of moral perception and reflection which had already been quickened by his sufferings.…It is this same strain of thought which…issues in those famous Timon-like speeches which make us realise the original strength of the old King’s mind. And when this strain, on his recovery, unites with the streams of repentance and love, it produces that serene renunciation of the world, with its power and glory and resentments and revenges, which is expressed in the speech: [quotes 2948–59].

In contrast, other critics, besides those inclined to symbolism discussed above, reject the idea of realistic verisimilitude on which psychological interpretations generally depend, viewing Shn. character as merely a a function of plot or dramatic convention. Stoll (1944, p. 280) argues that Lear’s behavior is stylized, not realistic: it is the securing of an emotional effect at the cost of realism. He also claims that Lear dies sane, not mad. Olson (1961, pp. 197 ff.), approaching Sh.’s treatment of the story from the point of view of the working dramatist, emphasizes the priority of plot to character: (p. 206) Lear must endure degradation from kingship, and to suffer from this on principle, i.e., as an affront to his honor, he must be proud; he must suffer ingratitude and betrayal, and to suffer from these on principle, he must be just; he must suffer from the privation of affection, and to suffer from this as deeply as possible he must be the kind of man to whom affection is most necessary, and to whom affection may well outweigh all other things.

Many critics have attempted to identify a tragic flaw in Lear’s character or an error of his judgment which precipitates his tragedy. Thus he has been seen as behaving like a barbarian despot. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:158) refers the seeming improbability of Lear’s conduct in 1.1 to the histories at that time vulgarly received as true. And perhaps if we turn our thoughts upon the barbarity and ignorance of the age to which this story is referred, it will appear not so unlikely as while we estimate Lear’s manners by our own. Such preference of one daughter to another, or resignation of dominion on such conditions, would be yet credible, if told of a petty prince of Guinea or Madagascar. Reed (1855, pp. 355–8): Lear is a barbaric chieftain—a heathen monarch;…[356] the very personification of unlimited despotism, lawless and selfish.…[358] And yet, beneath all this, there is something which shows that these are the ruins of a noble nature, overgrown, indeed, with all the weeds that rankly luxuriate in the habit of tyranny. Other critics who blame his despotic tendencies include Turnbull (1892, p. 157): He is simply the impersonation of a fatuous absolutism; and Crawford (1916, p. 257): In acquiring unlimited sovereignty over his dominion and over his family, he had completely lost sovereignty over himself. Similarly, Spencer (1943, p. 140): The division of the kingdom and the testing of his daughters are only the climax of a life composed of hasty imperious decisions, based on an unthinking acceptance of his own importance and what was due to him as king and father.

Several Romantic critics were influenced by the description of Lear as the man of mere sensibility (i.e., emotional susceptibility, in contradistinction to rational self-control) proffered by Richardson (1784, pp. 77 ff.): Shakespeare has exhibited the madness of Lear, as the natural effect of such suffering on such a [78] character.…[80] He becomes more interesting towards the close of the drama; not merely because he is more and more unhappy, but because he becomes really more deserving of our esteem. His misfortunes correct his misconduct; they rouse reflection, and lead him to that reformation which we approve. Hunt (1808; 1949, p. 17): The character of Lear has been well defined by Professor Richardson to consist of mere sensibility, he is fond, capricious, and revengeful, and it may be observed that, during his first ill-treatment, we are not so much moved with pity for himself as with horror at his daughters. It is when misfortune has begun to humble him that we pity, because we esteem him more, and our sympathy regularly increases with his humility. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:49–56): The strange, yet by no means unnatural, mixture of selfishness, sensibility, and habit of feeling derived from and fostered by the particular rank and usages of the individual; the intense desire to be intensely beloved—selfish, and yet characteristic of the selfishness of a loving and kindly nature—a feeble selfishness, self-supportless and leaning for all pleasure on another’s breast; the selfish craving after a sympathy with a prodigal disinterestedness, [50] contradicted by its own ostentation and the mode and nature of its claims; the anxiety, the distrust, the jealousy, which more or less accompany all selfish affections, and are among the surest contradistinctions of mere fondness from true love, and which originate Lear’s eager wish to enjoy his daughter’s violent professions, while the inveterate habits of sovereignty convert the wish into claim and positive right, and an incompliance with it into crime and treason;—these facts, these passions, these moral verities, on which the whole tragedy is founded, are all prepared for, and will to the retrospect be found implied, in the first four or five lines of the play.…[56] Old age, like infancy, is itself a character. In Lear the natural imperfections [are] increased by life-long habits of being promptly obeyed. Any addition of individuality [would be] unnecessary and painful. The relations of others to him, of wondrous fidelity and frightful ingratitude, sufficiently distinguish him. Thus he is the open and ample play-room of nature’s passions. Hazlitt (1817; 1930, 4:258): It is his rash haste, his violent impetuosity, his blindness to every thing but the dictates of his passions or affections, that produces all his misfortunes, that aggravates his impatience of them, that enforces our pity for him. Drake (1817; 1838, p. 560), following Richardson in ascribing Lear’s behavior to the impulses of sensibility, praises Sh.’s psychological acumen. Lear’s madness was, in fact, the necessary consequence of the reciprocal action of complicated distress and morbid sensibility; and, in describing the approach of this dreadful infliction, in tracing its progress, its height and subsidence, our poet has displayed such an intimate knowledge of the workings of the human intellect, under all its aberrations, as would afford an admirable study for the enquirer into mental physiology. Staël-Holstein (1828, p. 115) groups Lear with Henry VI and Richard II as men of weak minds,…doomed to an inglorious destiny. Girardin (1849, p. 131): We are not surprised that, with this violence of the passions which Shakspeare has given him, Lear should lose his reason as soon as the ingratitude of his children enabled him to see his folly. Passionate and weak natures who do not wish to anticipate evil, although warned of it beforehand, cannot support it when it comes. Such is King Lear. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, pp. 622–40): He had never learned to control himself; the best and soundest of his time had been but rash or passionate. This was his nature; it had become his habit through power and greatness, through the prosperity which had never left him, and had never permitted a thought of misfortune and misery. Such a father fosters hypocrisy and flattery in his children only too commonly for his own punishment; this flattery, again, in its turn, only increases still more his violence and irritability.…If [623] this haughtiness of the ruler both at home and abroad, a haughtiness which had never learned to bear the truth nor to suffer contradiction, except from the mouth of the fool whom the whip could keep within bounds, if this haughtiness were a natural imperfection, nourished by the habits of a long life, we can imagine that these faults would be increased still more by the unruly waywardness, the weakness, and sensitiveness of his infirm years. If we picture such a man still endowed with that strength of passion which makes him not only the child but the very king of that heroic age, we shall require nothing further for the full understanding of his conduct in the opening scene, which has so often been censured.…The whole ungovernable nature of a man who had never learned to master the ebullitions of his passion bursts violently forth.…[640] Had he lived and triumphed with Cordelia, revenge might have governed him again; it might have robbed him of our sympathy, and might not have permitted him to attain that peace to which the poet intends to lead him. The death of his child forcibly retains him in that peace and gentleness in which he is to depart to a better life. See also Mézières (1860; 1865, pp. 289–93) and Blaze de Bury (1885, p. 173). Price (1894, p. 179) describes him as a sentimentalist…in whom the passion for love is strong and the sense of duty feeble.

Other criticisms of his moral flaws or his errors in judgment include that of Horn (1823, 1:185; tr. in Furness, ed. 1880, p. 451): His resignation from rule is his greatest error, and hence a great sin; for, except in rare cases, when a higher will makes itself manifest, man is bound never to desert his post in the State—it is not accident that has placed him there. Also to blame is the fantastic character of Lear, that he should resolve to divide his kingdom according to the measure of love which he receives; and, as he would settle the matter at once, [that] the measure must be determined by words. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1846, pp. 192–3): Like the love of Romeo, and Othello, that of Lear is far from being pure from dross and earthly alloy; in him, too, it possesses a character of passionateness, as is shewn in his hasty and unjust banishment of Kent and Cordelia.…[193] Accordingly, we must look upon Lear himself as the author of his own fate, no less than the crimes and sufferings of his daughters. He falls the victim of the errors and weakness of his own affectionate heart. Thus invariably does the lovely and noble of this earth hasten to perdition whenever unpurified and earthly: it neglects to look back to its divine origin for its true strength and support. Snider (1887, pp. 154–7): He has used arbitrary power till his individuality is inflated to the size of the universe; he regards himself as greater than institutions.…[157] There is the same contradiction in his love that we see in his surrender of power; he deems himself greater than love, as he deems himself greater than authority, yet both are what he most needs. Tomlison (1925, pp. 451–3): His offenses were faults of temperament and evidences of incomplete development.…That Lear had fallen short of greatness was largely due to his unwillingness to endure discipline.…chiefly because of wilfulness.…[453] We must also hold Lear somewhat responsible for the character and behavior of those viciously inclined and lustful daughters, who display the effects of a bad environment. If Cordelia escaped deterioration, it was because she was of more delicate fibre. Chambers (1926, pp. 242–5) discusses Lear as a sentimental egotist. Campbell (1930, p. 189) draws on Renaissance psychological treatises to argue that we have in Lear the habitually wrathful man, advanced by years to that age when his self-esteem takes offence suddenly, easily, without reason and without regard to justice. He is indeed the slave to habitual wrath. Ashton (1932, pp. 532–6) also sees Sh. shaping into drama the development of the choleric temperament of Lear into madness.…[536] By the skilful handling of that material he builds up…an effective and affecting picture of the tragic fault which is Lear’s weakness. See also Schücking (1938, p. 24). Likewise Rosier (1954, p. 578): The conflict arises because of the king’s wrath, which causes in turn self-love, vain coveting of his daughter’s affection, and excessive curiosity. His basic flaw or frailty of character is irascibility. (In contrast, Keyishian [1995, p. 71]: Lear is not merely a choleric man, the slave of his humors, but a conscious individual reasonably capable of free choice whose mistaken decisions are fully tragic because they are fully considered.) Philip (1931) sees inordinate desire of power as Lear’s great flaw. Heilman (1948, pp. 164–71): Lear invites tragedy by three errors: he mistakes the nature of kingship; he establishes a wrong method for evaluating love; and he misinterprets the value of certain statements about love. In each case he is calculating an advantage; his imagination is not working.…[171] Lear wanted to measure love, which is a state of the soul, in material terms (property).…There are various ingredients in Lear’s tragic flaw, but the most important is his failure to recognize what areas of value are most capable of rational formulation. That error becomes the whole being of Goneril and Regan. Fluchère (1948; tr. 1953, p. 244): The part played by error in the tragic hero’s career is so important that it is surprising to find it has not been methodically investigated. Lear is doubly mistaken: he takes for love the simulation of it, and he takes for indifference the true love whose expression cannot compete with that of dissimulation. The reversal of values that takes place in proportion as he is led to attribute truth to each appearance—this is his tragic purgation, and it is the subject of the play. Traversi (1952, pp. 46–51): Lear’s insistence, as father, upon the respect due to his paternity leads, through the imperfect self-knowledge which vitiates it, to the division of his family into parties, both of which reflect contrasted elements of the family nature simultaneously present in himself.…[51] Lear’s abdication logically releases a corresponding egoism in those whom an ordered conception of social relationships regards as freely subdued to authority. Ribner (1958, pp. 36 ff.): Lear himself has unleashed the forces of evil which cause his suffering.…Lear’s division of his kingdom and resignation of his throne would have been regarded by a Jacobean audience with a horror which it is difficult for a modern audience to understand. In Act 3, (p. 43) Lear glories in the savagery of nature, not realizing that the storm is merely the reflection in nature of his own sin in the sphere of man.…[46] In denying authority [in 4.6], Lear is again denying his own position as a king appointed by and responsible to God, just as he had denied it in his resignation of his throne. Dye (1964, p. 515): Lear’s tragic flaw [is] his inability to recognize the inner truth unless it is clothed with outer show.…Goneril and Regan, in their selfishness, their misconception of the nature of love, their quick use of flattery, their misuse of authority, exhibit many of Lear’s traits which he attempts to rationalize under the guise of king and father. Taylor (1964, pp. 509–10): The play is…primarily about Lear himself and his tragically limited self-knowledge. (P. 510): Shakespeare opens an unbridgeable chasm between Lear’s presumptions about himself and the surrounding actualities which those very presumptions have always kept him from understanding. Willson (1972, p. 167) condemns Lear for being materialistic and describes 1.1 as an auction…based on the perception of human beings and the kingdom as material, saleable, and therefore debased commodities. McElroy (1973, pp. 168–87): His tragic errors all stem from two false assumptions: first, that identity is inherent in an individual, is stable and immutable, and is defined largely by one’s place in a fixed hierarchy; second, that the forces of nature and his own indomitable will are in such close harmony as [169] to be practically synonymous. (P. 186): When his private universe…crashes…[187] he embraces the inverted madman’s vision with the savage energy typical of the character and the play. Boose (1982, p. 332): In substituting his public paternity for his private one, the inherently indivisible entity for the one that biologically must divide and recombine, Lear violates both his kingly role in the hierarchical universe and his domestic one in the family. Liebler (1995, p. 9): Lear’s tragedy springs in part from his belief not only that he can reify and redistribute the meaning of abstractions such as kingdom, love, and loyalty, but that he knows what they are in the first place, and that he can legislate their operations. What he is to learn through the tragedy (among other things) is that these abstractions are labels for certain kinds of human relations that are negotiable and fragile, and that these relational bonds are protected and insured by ritual action that wards off both spiritual harm and physical disease, prevents the fiend and kills vermin. Kahn (2000, pp. 63–5): Lear tries and fails to remake the state on the basis of familial love. He (p. 65) suffers from the political delusion that love can be managed and measured by reason.

Many critics argue that Lear grows in wisdom or moral awareness or that he is spiritually purified or regenerated as a result of his terrible suffering. Those who find him attaining wisdom through madness include Bransom (1934, pp. 220 ff.): In madness thoughts deep-buried come to the surface: though at first he acts his futile desire for revenge in his mock trial, later a finer lunatic apprehension glimpses profound human truths. His thoughts fix on the sex-inhibitions of civilized man, delving into the truth of man’s civilized ascent. He finds sex to be a pivot-force in human affairs, sugared though it be by convention. All human civilization and justice are a mockery. He is all the time working deep into that which is real, in him or others, facing truth, though it be hideous. He has been forced from a deceiving consciousness of self-deception, sentiment, the tinsel of kingship and authority, to the knowledge of his own and others’ nature.…He wins his purgatorial reward in finding that which is most real to him, his love for Cordelia. For the first time he compasses his own reality, and its signs are humility and love. He falls back on the simplicity of love: next of death. His purgatory then closes. This is the movement from civilization, through a return to nature and a revulsion from civilized man to death, which is later massively reconstructed in Timon. Sitwell (1948, p. 65): In King Lear, we have one to whom the darkness of the mind brought a wisdom greater than Socrates (one who, like Socrates, is soon to cast off the chains of the body). Heilman (1948, pp. 83 ff.): If we see the movement of Lear from well-accoutered king to half-clad fugitive, we also observe his progress from eyeless rage to seeing beneath the surfaces that deceived him. Once a victim of angry pride,…[128] Lear…has had to emend and rephrase his initial theories of life. But he is so beaten about by the tumultuous world that, although he has come…to some remarkable insights, he cannot finally resolve his sense of life’s meaning into aphoristic finalities.…[129] Lear is an imaginative man rather than an intellectual, and he cannot forge orderly paradigms of wisdom. At death he is…what might be called orthodox. In the latter part of the play he appears, however, not as a master of the rules but as an inquirer and learner.…For Lear, as well as for seekers of pat formulae, many questions remain unanswered: only the ancient metaphors for experience remain. And the ability to use those metaphors is evidence of how far Lear has gone toward salvation.…[195] Madness is the expression of a certain conflict in Lear between his heresy of material equivalents, i.e., (p. 196) his philosophy of calculation or (p. 218) his quid-pro-quo rationalismon the one hand, and a true understanding of spiritual values on the other. (P. 219): But Lear’s un-reason accommodates a kind of reasoning; we see, in place of his earlier calculative spirit, a restored imagination which, even though at his death he is still battling fundamental enigmas, is capable of effecting austere syntheses out of the materials of the new disorderly world. [220] In place of his old myopia there is a new uncompromisingness of insight. In the experiences before his madness, in the storm scenes in which he goes mad, but most of all in [4.6], Lear has developed an imaginative awareness of evil which he did not have when he was making the trial of his daughters; he has come to a compassion for humanity—a compassion which, as Cordelia’s tears indicate symbolically, is a kind of insight; and, as both his direct statements and his figures show, he has come to some knowledge of himself and his liability to error. He is a very different man from the Lear of Act I.…But his imagination is restored. If such a process were not going on, the madness scenes would have been merely pathetic or grotesque or sardonic. Yet they are no such thing. Not that the madness is not real; but it is ambivalent, and the meaningfulness is as authentic as the clinical detail. Shakespeare takes pains to point out literally that Lear is as much a man of understanding as he is a raving lunatic, or rather that lunacy of demeanor can co-exist with a most penetrating insight. See also Idem (1964, ’Twere Best, pp. 93 ff.).

Muir (1960, p. 38): Precisely because he is mad, Lear is freed from the conventional attitudes of society. He is able, at moments, to see more clearly and piercingly than the sane, because the sane buy their peace of mind by adjusting themselves to the received ideas of society. Lear recognizes the way he has been shielded from reality by flattery. He also sees the hypocritical pretensions of society with regard to its treatment of criminals. And, finally, he sees that human life is inescapably tragic. Weidhorn (1962, pp. 310–11): The developments [of Lear] may be segregated into the discoveries about: the family, by Lear the father; the other self, by Lear the flattered, self-centered man; the polity, by Lear the king; the human race, by Lear the judge; Lear’s own self, by Lear the proud man.…[311] The insights into the family situation and into the plight of the other, that is, into the people immediately about him, occur in the earlier stages of Lear’s education. The subsequent findings involve matters that are at a greater remove—his past years of rule, the human race as a whole—and are therefore arrived at more gradually, in the later acts of the play.…Perhaps the most important development in Lear is his growth to the stage where he can say I am old and foolish, where he attains self-knowledge. Egan (1975, p. 34) sees Lear growing as a dramatic artist: As he grows in moral vision the aesthetic terms in which he couches [his] vision…increase in sophistication,…culminating in an exercise of overtly dramatic art (i.e. the mock-trial in 3.6). Doss (1978, p. 65) similarly compares him to Prospero, as an old man who comes to open his eyes to the ways of mankind. But unlike Prospero, Lear does not like what he sees. Siemon (1985, pp. 261–7): Madness releases Lear from his idolatrous relationship to his representations.…[267] One who accepts the significance of emblem undergoes a dramatic experience negating the assumptions that had grounded his notions of correspondence. Not that this process is simple or easily brought to completion. Lear’s emblematic vision is still functioning after the storm; it leads him, for example, to find an embodiment of the human condition in Edgar/Tom, and he believes strongly enough in schematization to attempt the arraignment of Regan in the person of a joint-stool. But utterly mad Lear is incapable of keeping his emblems within the boundaries of decorous generality: they tap a reservoir of disgust and violence that makes full acceptance of any one of them impossible.…Only the wrenching power of dissimilitude can free one who has been so dominated by the emblematic. Also emphasizing a growth in understanding is Keyishian (1995, p. 68), for whom Lear’s offstage killing of the jailor in 5.3 is a heroic feat which shows he has learned from his mistakes. When he had power, he abused it by punishing good and rewarding evil.…Now…he is angry at last…at the right person, at the right time, for the right reason; and he takes the right revenge.

Those who emphasize a regeneration and purification of Lear’s moral nature include Reed (1855, pp. 370–2): But most impressive is it to trace the effect of the severe chastening upon the king’s moral nature. His closest sympathy [in Act 3] is with the lowly fool, and this sympathy expands with a more comprehensive one for all suffering humanity.… [372] Lear [does] not pass away from life in the darkness of insanity. His recovery in Act 4 shows him purified of selfishness. Dowden (1875; 1879, pp. 272–3): Though he is in part delivered from his imperious self-will, and learns at last what true love is, and that it exists in the world—Lear passes away from our sight, not in any mood of resigna-[273]tion, or faith, or illuminated peace, but in a piteous agony of yearning for that love which he had found only to lose forever. Does Shakspere mean to contrast the pleasure in a demonstration of spurious affection in the first scene, with the agonised cry for real love in the last scene, and does he wish us to understand that the true gain from the bitter discipline of Lear’s old age, was precisely this—his acquiring a supreme need of what is best, though a need which finds, as far as we can learn, no satisfaction? Snider (1887, p. 203): The revengeful Lear pleads for charity, the unlimited monarch recognizes his limits in full. He is indeed redeemed with a marvelous baptism; having been immersed in the dark river of madness, he comes out a new sane man. Not only reason he has, but love now in its true sense. However, Lear did not attain a perfect restoration, he was not absolutely self-centered, the last trial was too hard for him. Yet the complete man must meet such a trial.

Bradley (1904, pp. 284–5): There is nothing more noble and beautiful in literature than Shakespeare’s exposition of the effect of suffering in reviving the greatness and eliciting the sweetness of Lear’s nature. The occasional recurrence, during his madness, of autocratic impatience or of desire for revenge serves only to heighten this effect, and the moments when his insanity becomes merely infinitely piteous do not weaken it. The old King who in pleading with his daughters feels so intensely his own humiliation and their horrible ingratitude, and who yet, at fourscore and upward, constrains himself to practise a self-control and patience so many years disused; who out of old affection for his Fool, and in repentance for his injustice to the Fool’s beloved mistress, tolerates incessant and cutting reminders of his own folly and wrong, in whom the rage of the storm awakes a [285] power and a poetic grandeur surpassing even that of Othello’s anguish; who comes in his affliction to think of others first, and to seek, in tender solicitude for his poor boy, the shelter he scorns for his own bare head; who learns to feel and to pray for the miserable and houseless poor, to discern the falseness of flattery and the brutality of rank and raiment to the common humanity beneath; whose sight is so purged by scalding tears that it sees at last how power and place and all things in the world are vanity except love; who tastes in his last hours the extremes both of love’s rapture and of its agony, but could never, if he lived on or lived again, care a jot for aught beside—there is no figure, surely, in the world of poetry at once so grand, so pathetic, and so beautiful as his. C. F. T. Brooke (1913, p. 96) writes of his cleansing from the mire of egotism in which he, as well as his two daughters, has been steeped. Danby (1949, pp. 185–91): Under Thunder, the miracle of Lear’s rehabilitation is achieved.…[186] Charity, repentance, a renewed will to amendment, an awareness of his neighbours accompanying the new awareness of himself, the falling away of original egocentricity, of anger, revenge, impatience with the Heavens—the prayer shows Lear’s mind settling into its proper frame. However, when he goes mad, (p. 191) he is spared the real suffering of remorse or the real agony of compassion. Maclean (1951; 1952, p. 601): In contrast to Hamlet and Othello, King Lear is a tragedy in the course of which the protagonist becomes worthy of being a tragic hero. Wilson (1957, p. 204): In his latest moments, Lear is freed of every motive but the love of his child. He has forgotten his wrongs, or any thought of retribution; and, as he joins Cordelia in death, his love has been made perfect by suffering. Adams (1960, p. 226): Lear achieves insight through his active, creative acceptance of suffering. Provost (1961, p. 71) contrasts Lear to Richard II: Lear’s self-pity and evasion of guilt, unlike Richard’s, are finally brought under control.…He becomes humble in the face of truth as Richard could never have done. Whitaker (Mirror, 1965, p. 228): He has been stretched so long upon the rack of this tough world, not so much because he can endure no more as because he has become patient and resigned, perfected in the ripeness that is all. He is a higher kind of man for the stretching! Kirsch (1966, pp. 202 ff.) views Lear’s redemption in Jungian terms: King Lear [is] a process of individuation.…[212] Lear, in finding himself, experiences God, though not in a form that is concordant with the conventions of his time.…[314] At the moment of death, the coniunctio occurs and in this vision Lear perceives ultimate truth, achieves full consciousness, and thus experiences [315] redemption. Rosinger (1968, pp. 494 ff.) describes a process of moral development in which Lear goes from acting like a god to accepting guilt.

Ribner (1960, p. 130) considers Lear a sinner redeemed by suffering: in Act 5, He has attained an ideal of Christian stoicism through an acceptance of human love, which is a reflection of the love of God and of the perfection and harmony of the universe—all of which in his madness he had denied. See also Siegel (1955, pp. 328–32) for another view of Lear as redeemed sinner. Rosen (1960, pp. 41–9): Lear’s whole personality undergoes a complete transformation. From a desire for personal vindication and personal recognition, his thoughts turn to sympathy for each individual being.…[49] Lear reaches the very lowest state of existence, unaccommodated man, he loses that which distinguishes man from animal, his reason, but from nothingness he progresses to Truth.…a secular vision of love and the community of mankind. Battenhouse (1969, pp. 272 ff.) describes an implicitly Christian pattern of redemption: Lear is…tortured by a hard-heartedness, not solely in his daughters but principally in himself. [273] And its cause, basically, arises not from nature but from a fiendishness of spirit, which Lear’s will has permitted to enslave his nature and abuse it.…[277] When Lear prefers the flattering words of fair-faced Goneril and Regan to Cordelia’s plain honesty, is he not committing, unwittingly, a kind of spiritual adultery?.…[278] We may say further…that what [Lear and Gloucester] have in common is covetousness—the characteristic vice of old age.…We can discern in Lear, although he cannot, a coveting of honor and glory.…[280] This subconscious and ignorant motive precipitates Lear’s tragedy. At play’s end, however, he shows (p. 289) a faith beyond reason. A dream of new life is summoning him—as, indeed, had been his experience…when he awoke to an imagination of Cordelia as a soul in bliss.… Lear’s bewilderment in both episodes suggests a mind groping toward supernatural fact.…[290] Those critics who see Lear as dying deluded and insane are arbitrarily truncating the logic of moral discovery which has characterized the play’s whole structure.…[291] The total story of Lear’s purgation, if we study its windings for the essential pattern, can be seen as his gradual learning to put off, not so much his lendings as his initial self-centeredness.…[292] Once Lear knows himself utterly humiliated, he can call out for a surgeon, and can half-conjecture some kind of rescue. He is thus being made apt for a new stage in another world. Chaudhuri (1981, pp. 169–70): Essentially his experience is constructive, purgatorial.…Lear changes and grows, gradually evolves his moral conceptions, admitting the full reality of human experience and even enlarging its boundaries.…[170] Lear…deliberately draws upon himself an increasingly intense weight of suffering.…He appears to call upon his own head the suffering due for all man’s evil.…We have here an obvious approximation to the suffering of Christ himself. In fact, Lear seems to unite the characters of the first and second Adam, and draw upon himself the suffering of both.…This combination of two opposed but complementary roles brings out the paradoxical compound of Lear’s heroism, the spiritual strength that transforms the nature of vice and frailty by an indomitably suffering acceptance. Morris (1985, p. 162): He is the main evil at the outset of his drama insofar as he has made the great refusal both in state and family [i.e., by (p. 115): breaking the sacred bond between parent and child as well as committing (p. 116) the greater sin of repudiation of God by his (p. 117) removal of himself as top link in the chain of being]; but he has been redeemed by play’s end through recognition of his sins, through contrition for them, through confession that he has severed himself unacceptably from rule and from daughter, through satisfaction paid by his suffering and death, and chiefly through the absolution given by Christ himself in the symbolic figure of his daughter with whom he is totally and lovingly reconciled.

Empson (1949, pp. 208–14), who describes Lear as a holy fool, sees a more paradoxical sanctification: There is a sort of terror about the pathos of Lear, and it arises chiefly because he is always on the edge of absurdity.…[214] Lear has made a fool of himself on the most cosmic and appalling scale possible; he has got on the wrong side of the next world as well as the wrong side of this one.…By being such a complete fool Lear may become in some mystical way superlatively wise and holy. Idem (1951, pp. 145 ff.): His impatience and his clowning are what have taught him to understand the nature of the world. He appears in 4.7 and 5.1 as a mysteriously wise imbecile.…We are to think of him as sane and yet leave him all the halo that he acquired in his madness and all the inconsequence that he learned from the clowns.…[157] The scapegoat who has collected all this wisdom for us is viewed at the end with a sort of hushed envy, not…really because he has become wise but because the general human desire for experience has been so glutted in him; he has been through everything. He also remarks (p. 138) that it is ridiculous and rather sordid of Lear to find the horror of sex an exciting topic.

Other critics emphasizing inner growth include Hoover (1989, p. 350): Lear relinquish[es] misogyny as a necessary prelude to [his] reunion with Cordelia. Nagata (1990, p. 170) discusses the inner change of Lear—from a man of seeing to a man of listening. Exposure to the storm…helps him to realize the interiority of human beings in contrast to the exterior impersonal world. Yoshioka (1991–2, p. 224) argues for Lear’s spiritual growth.…His identity [eventually encompasses] a wider spectrum of humanity,…integrating masculinity and femininity, fatherhood and motherhood. Butler (1992, Erasmus, p. 21): Lear undergoes a terrifying vivification, is driven across a series of apocalyptic frontiers into a new awareness of himself, of life, and of love. Lowenthal (1994, p. 416): Lear begins by being a very good but hardly a perfect king.…Under the impact of his daughters’ ingratitude and the storm, he becomes juster and wiser still.…In the final scene he seems to join together the perfections of king, father and man all at once: then he is King Lear in the fullest sense. Holahan (1997, pp. 407–8): Lear changes by looking for and imitating Cordelia’s soft voice. For other discussions of Lear as morally or spiritually purified and regenerated see .

Other critics deny that Lear becomes significantly wiser or purer. Thus Schücking (1922, pp. 185–9): It is true that a number of expositors…see in Lear’s tragedy a great process of purification, by means of which he is freed from the dross of vanity and selfishness and is led out of his blindness to a proper recognition of the true values of life.…[186] But the question is whether it is really consistent with Shakespeare’s philosophy to see in this sequence of events an ascent of the character to a higher plane, a process of purification and perfection.…[187] That Lear in the further course of his madness comes to reject all that is unnatural and all claims that are morally unjustified, though sanctioned by tradition and authority, cannot be disputed. But it must be noticed that in this he does little more than follow the beaten track of the melancholy type, whose humour especially delights in unmasking all kinds of shams.…Lear’s criticism…is but an aspect of a mood and dependent on a state of mental derangement.…It would have to be confirmed by him in some form or other after his reason had been restored to sanity in order to make us see in it a real revolution of his philosophic outlook and a stage of his development.…[189] The whole course of the drama [is] the story of a breakdown, of a decay accompanied by the most wonderful and fascinating phenomena comparable to the autumn decline of the year when the dying leaves appear in their most beautiful colours. It is not a development, but a decadence manifesting itself in a variety of forms, among others in that feeling of weakness which creates in the masterful old man, who so far has been centred entirely in himself, a sympathetic interest in the distress of others which he has never known before.…It is therefore a complete misunderstanding of the true state of affairs to regard Lear as greater at the close than the beginning. Barnet (1955, p. 92): Although Lear learns humility through suffering, at the conclusion he is still capable of the misconceptions and unstoical emotion which are the stuff of tragedy. Birrell (1958, p. 106): The storm does not really change Lear essentially.…Lear’s self-deception remains with him to the very end. Alpers (1962, p. 152) deplores the primary mistake of equating Lear’s being humbled with the virtue of humility. Bennett (1962, pp. 148–50) especially questions the idea that a higher reason appears in Lear’s madness: The significance of [4.6]…lies not in the truth of Lear’s biting satire, his Reason in madness, but in his state of mind—his generalization of the injustice he has suffered (of his daughters’ cruelty) to include all humanity, at the same time that he is exhibiting his own injustice and cruelty to the blind Gloucester.…Lear’s madness is a more penetrating analysis of the overthrow of reason by forces within—and they are evil forces, reflecting the ancient notion of possession by evil spirits, supported by Biblical authority.… Lear’s bitter speeches are a part of the expression of his madness, they are not sane comments, Lear’s or Shakespeare’s.

Taylor (1964, pp. 511–12): Shakespeare never permits a full sense of his failures in both his family and his kingdom to cross Lear’s consciousness. Shakespeare has him state his regret for his stupid misjudgment of Cordelia, and the consequent injustice to her. After Lear recovers from his madness, however, Shakespeare does not grant him any awareness of the condition of his kingdom following the division of it.…[512] The flashes of insight which illuminate Lear’s flow of words in madness are shadowy conceptualizations which Shakespeare has all along let stand in direct contrast to the sharp actualities which have gored the state. Gaull (1967, pp. 339 ff.) argues that his instincts remain escapist and regressive. Arnold (1972, p. 207): Lear’s spiritual renewal depends upon his learning to see himself as more than simply a victim of a loveless universe. Not one of [his] comforters ever expresses the conviction that Lear achieves such saving insight. Their sense of frustration seems justified by what happens in the play and particularly by the carefully developed contrasts between the resolutions of the Lear and Gloucester plots. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 208–9): It is doubtful that Shakespeare meant Lear’s madness to carry a positive value, to be instructive, regenerative, as is sometimes argued. Levin Schücking, opposing, went too far in insisting Lear is no better after madness; for the design will show Lear able to love Cordelia, to recover briefly that giving impulse of kneeling and praying in the storm. But the madness is a painful interruption; his mind’s furious hyperactivity will leave Lear drained, as it would in life; he will have regressed to the helpless innocence of the dependent child when, with Cordelia, in [4.7] and the beginning of [5.3], he briefly resumes the learning begun in [3.4]. Nor did Shakespeare use the madness for a moral lesson; nor—as Orwell would have it—as a mask to express safely dangerous socialist opinions about society.…Shakespeare created this madness…to fit the multiple dialectic that is Lear.…[209] In the full dialectic, returning lucidity would energize the face, reason and unreason would struggle, alternating rage, cupidity, craftiness, with sudden, open-hearted tenderness—the voice of love, never entirely stilled, sometimes heard crying under the howls of hate. Long (1976, pp. 193–5): Elemental vitality and…inalienable life com[e] to their fierce climax in his madness.…It is always a sense of this gamesome quality of Lear that seems…to be absent from most accounts of his trauma—a sense of his recklessness, his merriment, the devouring hilarity of his madness.…[195] We would go grotesquely wrong if we thought of the essence of [his trauma] as residing in his learning—humility, or what not. Roche (1981, p. 156): Lear dies a failure, poignant but a failure, certainly no hero, or Shakespeare need not have rewritten history.…[161] What has Lear learned? Nothing. Not even suffering has taught him anything. Archer (1982, p. 122): Lear learns little since he fails to acknowledge…his misconception of love. Dollimore (1984; 2004, pp. 195–6): Lear’s madness is less divine furor than a process of collapse which reminds us just how precarious is the psychological equilibrium which we call unity, and just how dependent upon an identity which is social rather than essential. What makes Lear the person he is—or rather was—is not kingly essence (divine right), but, among other things, his authority and his family. On the heath he represents the process whereby man has been stripped of his stoic and (Christian) humanist conceptions of self.…[196] For Lear dispossession and displacement entail not redemptive suffering but a kind of suffering recognition—implicated perhaps with confession, depending on how culpable we take this king to have been with regard to the great image of authority which he now briefly demystifies. Cf. Cohen (1988, p. 125–6), who focuses on Lear’s attempts to connect the pre-play past…with the situations he faces in the play, necessitating (p. 126) a radical reconsideration of the formerly stable self. Holbrook (1994, p. 137): His tremendous noble egoism…never really dissipates or changes into something new. Erickson (1985, p. 114): His momentary openness to human contact in 4.7 is superseded by a withdrawal into the hollow posture of omnipotent fantasy in 5.3. Cordelia is subsumed into the escapist vision Lear constructs for both of them; she is not consulted.…This appropriation of Cordelia is not an act of love but a violation of it that echoes and repeats Lear’s ritual of possessiveness in the opening scene. Simon (1988, p. 108): He remains narcissistic. Lear, when all is said and done in the play, has achieved only a limited awareness of the need for differentiation and relinquishing control over one’s children. Miller (1993, p. 34): You do not get in Lear a recovery, a reconciliation, or a discovery.…He has learned nothing; he has picked up fragments of wisdom but has not achieved a comprehensive moral vision in the way that Gloucester has, and certainly in the way that Edgar has. Dudley (1993, p. 74): By the fifth act it is apparent that Lear has learned very little: he is the same man who needed public professions of love from his daughters; the same man who throughout the play looked from one daughter to the next to serve as his other—his echo. Liebler (1995, p. 204): Lear cannot jettison the hierarchic structures of his former life. In contrast, Danson (1974, p. 197): Lear’s unregeneracy, his obstinate refusal to learn the lessons we think appropriate for him, is more exactly right than any of those hopeful lessons learned could be. And Leggatt (1988, pp. 94–5): Lear is not so much a character who has been saved or educated as a character who has been through an intense experience, one that has presented him—and us—with basic images of the human condition, hurled at us with brutal speed and impact: the naked madman, the crying baby, the soul in bliss, the dead child. His death is the completion of a life lived at the extreme.…[95] Asserting his power over his own life, Lear began the play by asking his daughters to say how much they loved him. He ends by demonstrating his own love, and our mortal helplessness, in a manner beyond words.

Elton (1966, passim) argues that Lear’s suffering causes him to lose his faith in his gods. At the close of the play, Lear is (p. 54) recognizable in Renaissance terms, if not in our own, as an outward skeptic. Sh. (p. 178) strongly established Lear’s pagan piety at the start in order to have a norm against which to work and against which to measure Lear’s departures at the end.…For if anything is clear in this tragedy, it is that the protagonist’s faith in the gods whom he adores is severely shaken by the events of the tragedy.…[200] Lear gives voice to a…series of notions which the Renaissance spectator would have associated with questioning rather than acceptance, especially (p. 212) in his attitudes to thunder. In Act 4 (p. 229) his denunciation of human justice becomes…more savage. And as it does, it implies a more-than-secular attack on authority, on the powers that be, which he has so long worshipped and represented.…Lear, the guardian of justice himself and the vicar of the gods on earth, turns against law and piety in an implicit self-enunciation that at once transforms his earth and his cosmos.…The gods are viewed as dubiously unattainable.…[238] After the death of an illusion, Lear is taken back to life by Cordelia’s forgiving grace. To say, with some commentators, that Lear repents and attains humility and patience, thus becoming fit for heaven, in a kind of revivified morality pattern, is to underestimate the complexity both of the play and of Lear’s character.…Lear…returns purged, but with a difference.…The living martyrdom has been intellectual as well as physical, religious as well as secular, and has gone too far.…[239] The defiant Prometheus and Lear-Agonistes of the previous passages comes back to us in the final scene.…[258] Lear’s end involves more than an in-consolatio. For as in life he has transgressed against the ars vivendi, so at his death he violates the ars moriendi.…The ars moriendi included the method of handling the five [259] temptations: unbelief, despair, impatience, vainglory, and worldly attachment, as to relatives. Yet in his concluding scene, the old king, long past the usual age of reconciliation, seems prey to all of these, including defiance of the heavens, commission of a confirmed murder [3239], and a final heroic vaunt [3240–2].…[263] The obstacles to an orthodox theological reading of King Lear, in which the protagonist moves from sin and suffering to redemption, are more formidable than has generally been realized. The so-called stumbling block, to the Shakespearean neo-Christianizers, of Lear’s last appearance is…scarcely a hapax legomenon but a carefully anticipated culmination of Lear’s previously expressed tendencies. In contrast, Hole (1968, p. 229): Lear’s awareness of [the power of the gods] is shown in the religious terminology with which he comes increasingly to express his thought. Skulsky (1966; 1976, pp. 152 ff.) also counters Elton’s view that Lear is a skeptic who repudiates Providence.

Clayton (1983, p. 122) argues that alterations in Lear’s role from the Quarto to the Folio are part of an evident, emphatic, and functional pattern that combines the progressive peeling away of layers of attire, appearance, affectation, and at last anatomy itself with an ultimate regression (or progression) to a state of second childhood. See .

Finally Honigmann (1976, pp. 107 ff.) argues that Lear’s mind…makes special demands upon the audience. It is elusive as all buried treasure. Lear exists in a twilight world of acute perception and withdrawal, of poetry and gabble; whereas Hamlet’s mind works as a wonderfully efficient instrument, a surgeon’s knife probing the imposthumes of society, Lear wields an axe, he hacks at man’s false pretensions, denouncing or cursing, then retreats one knows not whither, and mutters to himself in the soul’s recesses. He is (p. 108) the most inaccessible and unknowable hero of all the central tragedies.…[109] The many occasions when, instead of conversing with others, he talks to himself…[are] often indistinguishable from true soliloquy or aside in that we believe him to be thinking aloud and cannot always tell whether or not other stage-characters are supposed to hear him.…[114] Lear’s mind works…in ever-changing thought patterns and, blurring the seen and unseen, becomes the play’s central thoroughfare, where past, present and future meet, wishful thinking and random recollection, odds and ends of experience that could not otherwise be mixed—so that an exceptional range of words and images passes through this, the most inclusive of all Shakespeare’s plays.

For other discussions of Lear, see Knight (1849, pp. 347–8); Hales (1875; 1884, pp. 256–64); Doyle (1877, pp. 159–61); Blaze de Bury (1885, pp. 211–5); Brandes (1895–6; tr. 1898, 2:136); S. A. Brooke (1913, pp. 205–24); Croce (1920, p. 231); Anderson (1927, p. 169); Miles (1940, pp. 295–6); Spencer (1944, pp. 324–5); Egri (1942; 1946, p. 74); Ribner (1947); Draper (1946, pp. 123–4); Campbell (1947, p. 181); Brown (1953, pp. 292–3); Siegel (1956, pp. 342–3); Morris (1957); Ribner (1958, pp. 39–40); Block (1962); Brittin (1962); McCloskey (1962); Chang (1966, pp. 50–2); Blok (1966, pp. 21–4); Partee (1971, pp. 60–1); Barroll (1974, pp. 368–9); Bache (1975); Novy (1979, p. 285).

div.head: Regan
div.p: Most critics discuss Regan together with Goneril, and discussions of the two sisters together are surveyed above, . For comparisons with Goneril, generally finding Regan weaker and crueler than her sister, see the comments on Goneril above by Gervinus, Clarke, Dowden, Swinburne, Bradley, Granville-Barker, and Booth. This section is limited to discussions of Regan apart from her sister.
Coleridge (1813; 1836, 2:199): Regan is not, in fact, a greater monster than Goneril, but she has the power of casting more venom.

Clarke (1863, p. 176): Regan is only equal to her sister in undutifulness. Her mind is of a coarser grain. There is a ribald ferocity in her nature which one would suppose it impossible to transcend. When she and Cornwall, her husband, her really other self, act the frightful scene of tearing out Gloster’s eyes, Regan’s behaviour and language bear the character of a butcher in a slaughter-house, jesting at the resistance and contortions of his tethered victim. Beale (1881, p. 61): Regan is a parasite by nature, she clings to others, but to destroy them. She does not originate schemes, as do Goneril and Edmund, but she makes each of them more wicked.
