Bradley (1904, pp. 299–300): That Regan did not commit adultery, did not murder her sister or plot to murder her husband, did not join her name with Edmund’s on the order for the deaths of Cordelia and Lear, and in other respects failed to take quite so active a part as Goneril in atrocious wickedness, is quite true but not in the least to her credit. It only means that she had much less force, courage and initiative than her sister, and for that reason is less formidable and more loathsome.…But, to set against Regan’s inferiority in power, there is nothing: she is superior only in a venomous meanness which is almost as hateful as her cruelty. She is the most hideous human being (if she is one) that Shakespeare ever drew. Mackenzie (1924, p. 314): Regan is smaller than either [of her sisters]. She has her father’s vehemence and the family lack of comprehension and certainty that their own point of view is the only one there can be: but she is shrill and shallow beside Goneril’s solid driving power or the steadfast spirit of Cordelia.…Leaving out Pandarus and Thersites, she is probably the most horrible figure Shakespeare ever created—certainly one of the very few for whom one feels a quite unmitigated loathing. Bransom (1934, pp. 62 ff.): Regan inspires detestation to about the same extent as Cordelia inspires affection.…Regan had no pride and a much more voluble manner than either of [her sisters]. She was far inferior to Goneril in intellect, and, in a less degree, to Cordelia.…[63] Goneril’s cruelty always had motive behind it, for the most part weighty motive.…Regan’s seems to have none.…[64] The new psychology would describe Regan as sadistic. Elton (1966, pp. 118–19): As Edgar complements Cordelia in goodness,…Regan complements her sister in evil. Like Goneril, she reduces divine reason to practical consideration [quotes 331] and action [quotes 1070–1]; and, like her, she measures value by material gain. Déracinée, like Goneril, Regan also spares mentioning the gods, except once, hypocritically, before Lear [quotes 1452]—a [119] silence which may be eloquent regarding her beliefs. She thus represents an antithesis to Gloucester’s concern regarding the heavenly forces. Her ethics are pat. They involve vengeance of inordinate kind [quotes 1027]; a devilish parody of poetic justice [1606–8]; an ironic perversion of the relation between goodness and pity [quotes 2165–7]; and the proper place of weakness vis-à-vis power [quotes 1494]. Cavell (1969; 2002, pp. 281–91): In 3.7, Regan assumes that [Gloucester] is going to Dover because in her mind, the man she is sending on his way to Dover is the man she knows is sent on his way to Dover: in her paroxysms of cruelty, she imagines that she has just participated in blinding her father.…[291] She has no ideas of her own, her special vileness is always to increase the measure of pain others are prepared to inflict; her mind is itself a lynch mob. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 162–3): Her evil is not obvious [in Acts 1 and 2]. Suspense is…part of the design.…Again and again she will pray her father to change, even entreat him.…In the theatre she has been most effective—[163] partly because it contrasts her with Goneril—when she has seemed sweet; in fact bittersweet, emasculating Lear with an insistent, tender concern. Ingram (1984, p. 255): Regan is more…an Ugly Sister than…a politically threatening tragedy Queen. Lusardi (1991, pp. 73–5) finds her individualized by the pattern [74] of Regan’s need to outdo the doings of others; she (p. 75) seems driven by an insistent psychological need. She is…the richer character in her malignity, though probably the more difficult sister to play.

div.head: Steward
div.p: Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:121 n.) briefly observed, I know not well why Shakespeare gives the Steward, who is a mere factor of wickedness, so much fidelity. Generally, however, critics have been wholly unsympathetic. Coleridge (1813; 1960, 1:55–6): The Steward (as a contrast to Kent) [is] the only character of unredeemable baseness in Shakespeare. [Observe] even in this the judgement and invention. What could the [56] willing tool of a Goneril be? Not a vice but this of baseness was left open for him. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875; 1877, p. 631) censures that time-serving soul of baseness…whom no insolence and mistreatment can excite into bitterness and passion. Clarke (1863, pp. 186–7): He is the reverse of Kent. He, from the mere servility of slavish obedience, would perpetrate any enormity of vice or of good service with the implicit punctuality and passiveness of a machine.…Among the mistakes that Dr Johnson has made in commenting upon Shakespeare, may, I conceive, be included his [187] summary of the character of the steward. He deems it inconsistent in the poet to give to this man, whom he styles a mere factor of wickedness, so much fidelity. As if fidelity were the accident of his character, and wickedness the basis; whereas, it is his serf-like fidelity to his mistress which is his leading characteristic, and which, in fact, is the cause of, and produces his evil deeds; they being merely her promptings or commands carried into action. The poor wretch is base enough in all conscience, but it is the baseness of servility and dogged servitude. Hudson (1872, 2:385–6): To call the Steward wicked were a waste of language: he is absolutely beneath the sense of that term; one of those convenient pack-horses whereon guilt often rides to its ends. Except the task of smoothing the way for the passions of a wicked mistress, no employment were base enough for him. None but a reptile like him could ever have [386] got hatched into notice in such an atmosphere as Goneril’s society: were he anything else, there could not be sympathy enough between them to admit the relation of superior and subaltern.

Bradley (1904, p. 298) calls him the most contemptible of the characters. Yet twice we are able to feel sympathy with him. Regan cannot tempt him to let her open Goneril’s letter to Edmund; and his last thought as he dies is given to the fulfilment of his trust. It is to a monster that he is faithful, and he is faithful to her in a monstrous design. Still, faithfulness is faithfulness, and he is not wholly worthless.

Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:64–5) emphasizes historical specificity: A modern audience must lose almost as much of the flavor of Oswald as of the Fool; and more still must be lost if he is stripped of his doublet and hose, forbidden his swagger and his curtseys and thrust back into the dark ages. We cannot be expected to cheer—as I doubt not Shakespeare’s audience did—when Kent breaks out with [quotes 1145–6] nor to take the precise point of Lear’s [quotes 579] that newfangled fellow, neither gentleman nor plain servant, mimicking the manners of the one, doing dirtier work than the other.…[65] Oswalds have existed in every age and been good game for abuse, but the London of Shakespeare’s day had evidently produced an unusually fine crop of them. It follows then that his Ay, madams and No, madams, his I’ll not be strucken, my lord, his Prithee, if thou lovest me, tell me, and his Out, dunghill,…must answer exactly in accent and attitude, as he himself in look and manner, to the very sort of being Shakespeare had in mind. Kirschbaum (1957, p. 14) likewise sees him as representative of Sh.’s age: Oswald belongs body and soul to the new world of opportunity, selfishness, immorality and cruelty. Halpern (1991, pp. 243–5): He rather than Edmund is the Renaissance new man.…[244] Lacking a distinguished lineage, landed wealth, or military prowess, Oswald can only adopt the manners, gestures, bearing, and clothing of a gentleman: in short the consumption-signs of aristocracy.…He thus represents the end term of the transformation of the old baronial class to a new courtly one.…As a class and sexual hybrid …[245] Oswald…concentrates…the collapse of sexual and class boundaries. Kozintsev (1966, p. 252) sees the type as universal rather than narrowly historical: A little cell of flattery, boot-licking and impertinence. He bobs up wherever there is injustice, wherever someone is preparing to finish off a man already down, wherever there is a demand for those who can find greatness in vileness.

Critics who express some limited measure of sympathy for him include Heilman (1948, pp. 249–50): Kent shows up Oswald as not the brightest of faithful camp followers; Oswald gets his principles of rational worldliness at second hand, and he attempts to move in company which is too fast for him. When Albany calls Oswald sot after Oswald has reported to him Gloucester’s treachery and Edmund’s loyal service [2273–4], Albany’s word nicely exhibits the moral and intellectual obtuseness of Oswald. On the one occasion when his wits impel him to take the initiative to advance his fortune (by killing Gloucester), he is quickly killed [2675 ff.]. His moral madness is penetrated by [250] an ironic ray of selflessness as he is dying: he wants Goneril’s note taken on to Edmund [2701–2]. Smith (1952, p. 64): Oswald becomes human even in his villainy. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 93–4): Inevitably he is a loser, and there is comedy in his discomfiture; but unless he has dignity to go with his loyalty, he diminishes the two with whom he has the strongest relationships: Kent and Goneril. Oswald is subtly involved in the male-female and master-follower dialectics. He generally appears as one of the young enemies of the aged.…[94] Before [Goneril’s] strength, he is supple and compliant, as he also retreats before Kent’s masculinity; but he has learned to look down on Albany’s submissiveness—hence will be surprised by the Duke’s strength in IV. His loyalty is a curious mirroring of that of Kent, his first antagonist, and that of Edgar, his last.…The mixture in his role of his relative masculinity and his serving role take [sic] shape in the loyalty of his relationship, erotic or otherwise, with Goneril.…[282] Oswald’s dignity survives [in 4.6].…His last act, after asking to be buried, is loyalty to Goneril.…As he dies, the repetition in his last words is curiously touching, individualizing. Speziale-Bagliacca (1998, p. 119) defends his behavior in 2.2: Not only is Oswald polite to Kent but he clearly does not recognize him and even seems to take him for a member of Cornwall’s court.

Others who discuss him include Strier (1995, p. 186), who argues that as a steward in a major household he was not at all poor, but actually quite grand. de Grazia (1996, p. 28): He stands for the possibility the play abhors (despite its own generic hybridity)—of hybridization, mongrelization, heterogeneity teeming its way into the hierarchy. Kahn (2000, pp. 54–5): Oswald represents the appetitive aspect of desire [within the public order].…[55] Such [sycophantic] subjects will push a paranoid style of political power. They corrupt power without even thinking about it. Burnett (2005, pp. 72–3): Oswald is associated with mixture and shape-shifting…Oswald is figured in terms of plurality and impurity, with the latter idea reaching its extension in Kent’s equation of the steward with waste and promise to daub the walls of a jakes with him.…Oswald’s imaginative possibility can be traced both to contemporary anxieties about the unstable composition of servants and to a mindset that saw as synonymous a neglect of proper duty and shit.…[73] Yet…in the case of Oswald, the movement toward an interpretive resolution does not run smooth: the steward’s later pledge to honour his mistress’s command—[quotes 2404]…recalls an observance rather than an avoidance of Protestant service ideals.

div.head: Others
div.p: Burgundy, according to Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:61), gains enough character from his laconic indifference. Rosenberg (1972, p. 74): He is something more than a stalking horse, he cares enough for Cordelia to try to make a deal, when it seems none is possible. Mahood (1992, p. 159) dismisses him as a despicable and near-comic contrast to the serviteur of courtly love. Kullmann (1987) interprets him as a figure representing the Netherlands; as a negative foil to France, he suggests Sh.’s contrasting attitudes toward the two countries. (In Ger.)
Curan may be the Messenger (Gentleman) in 4.2, according to Mahood (1992, p. 169). See n. 2312.

The First Servant in 3.7 is often praised. Craig (1949, p. 255): The nameless first Servant in King Lear is as great a hero as can be found in the plays of Shakespeare. See also Wilkes (1877, p. 392), Traversi (1952, pp. 141–2), Kirschbaum (1957, pp. 14 ff.), Elton (1966, p. 295), and Wertheimer (1990). Pechter (1978, pp. 197) sees a mixture of the compassionate and vindictive instincts.…The episode is typically sentimentalized and moralized.…[198] His compassion for Gloucester expresses itself in the offering of at least part of the winged vengeance the Earl had sought. Mahood (1992, p. 168): The important, the revolutionary fact about the First Servant is that he is not…a shocked bystander; a performance reveals him to be one of the group of servants who have dragged in and bound Gloucester on Cornwall’s orders.…[His] possession of a weapon exposes [Cornwall’s] contempt for civilised custom. Burnett (2005, pp. 78–9): The servant steps beyond prescribed norms in claiming for himself interpretive superiority: he grants himself the right to define good service and thereby accedes to a prohibited autonomy.…[However,] from the position of the values of the dominant order…the servant constitutes an extreme version of the riotous knight [cf. 750–2].…[79] Yet Cornwall’s and Regan’s…aristocratic principles are thrown into parodic relief by their dependant’s own defence of the values of courtesy.…In brief, the actions of the servant work to open out social complexity, to heighten difference and to reinforce the difficulties of the sources of stable authority. The Second and Third Servants, according to Mahood (1992, pp. 170–1), are Gloucester’s servants, not Cornwall’s. Their (p. 171) failure…to come to [Gloucester’s] defence…weakens the effect of their comments and actions once the atrocity has been committed. Thus they are cut from F.

Critical comment on the Gentleman of 3.1 and 4.3 largely focuses on the style of his speeches. Clarke (1863, p. 188): What little we have of this character is developed with exquisite taste and gentleness. His general bearing and fulfillment of his mission, perfectly harmonise with the nature of his calling, and the sphere in which he moves. The rich eloquence put into his mouth is at once consistent with his station, and it also displays the prodigality of the poet in investing so unimportant a character with such language. Bransom (1934, pp. 82, 153) finds him a very life-like person; loquacious and with a good opinion of his own powers of description. Sh. (p. 153) has invested the gentleman with a touch of comedy. He is really very commonplace, but affects a poetic diction of which he is absurdly incapable. Rosenberg (1972, p. 257): The sweetness of his tone is so cloying.…But consider the Gentleman’s verse as characterization, especially in its contrast with Kent’s crisper verse.…The description of Cordelia has some of the delicacy of that perfumed lord who so infuriated Hotspur. There is a touch of Osric in this Gentleman, a touch of the court poet with his artificial antinomies, that are pretty echoes of the deeper oppositions of the play. Howard (1991, p. 203) focuses on cuts to the role in F: The Quarto Gentleman is a character who, though minor, participates fully in the play, both poetically and theatrically, and dignifies the character, and the player, on the periphery of the action; in comparison, the trimmed-down Folio Gentleman is a cypher, testifying to his own insignificance. Interestingly enough, the necessity of the sacrifice of an important minor part to the modern theatrical values of concision, contrast, and surprise seem to go totally unquestioned by both Stone [1980] and Urkowitz [1980].

Of the Knight or seruant in 1.4, Mahood (1992, p. 162) observes: The suggestions of a closely knit family in the Knight’s use of the possessive [my at 602], and his concern for a retainer whom Goneril’s servants merely chide [507], round out the portrait of a man of choice, and rarest parts such as Lear at line [776] asserts each of his followers to be. In short, the Knight’s function is to give the lie to Goneril’s account of him and his companions as riotous, insolent and deboshed. Of the Gentleman (seruant) of 2.4, (p. 164): For Shakespeare to have replaced the Knight [in 1.4] by the Gentleman in 2.4 makes good sense…in terms of the play’s development.…The Gentleman represents a different type of service from that rendered by the Knight and his companions…[suggestive] of the kind nursery which Lear looked to receive from Cordelia.…Then, at the beginning of the third act, the Gentleman suddenly becomes voluble.…Discreet and self-effacing in his attendance on the King, the Gentleman talks freely with the disguised Kent.…His eloquence calls for a good voice, and it is tempting to speculate that the original actor of France took on this further role. The reassignment of the Doctor’s lines to him in F is (p. 166) deliberate and dramatic, rather than enforced and [167] theatrical. The Doctor is called by Egan (1975, p. 48) a kind of dramatic artificer. Kellogg (1866, p. 110) sees him as an authoritative practitioner.
On the number of servants in the play and their various names—Servant, Knight, Gentleman, Doctor—see nn. 580, 874, and 1615.

The Captain is said by Blau (1964, p. 100) to possess a wealth of personal distinction…rugged, prideful, competitive—a man of destiny in small. He serves himself as much as the plot. Mahood (1992, pp. 175–6): calls him one of the richest small parts in Shakespearean tragedy,…the very extreme of depravity. See also Howard (1991).

The Old Man of 4.1 is said by Clarke (1863, p. 188) to be a first-class yeoman and by Rosenberg (1972, p. 248) a foil for Gloster’s anguished, erratic mood. The role is also discussed by Granville-Barker (1927; 1946, 2:65) and Mahood (1992, pp. 171–5). See n. 2193.

div.head: Stage History
div.p: This section of the appendix has four parts. The first presents chronologically the fragmentary knowledge we have of 17th-c. performances of Sh.’s original play. The modern stage history begins with Nahum Tate’s The History of King Lear (1681), a radical revision of Sh.’s play that, with various alterations made over time, replaced it on the stage for a hundred and fifty years and continued to influence acting editions and productions for another fifty. Since the influence of Tate’s version is so important to an understanding of the stage history of Lr., the second part of this section is a description of the text on the modern stage, beginning with Tate’s changes and recording the gradual return to Sh.’s original. The third part is a survey of significant modern productions and notable performers. A full stage history of performances from 1681 to the present, even a survey limited to revivals on the London and New York professional stages and in the major Sh. festivals, is quite beyond the scope of this edition. Finally, a few film versions, adaptations, and offshoots are mentioned in the fourth part. Much of the information about actual performances may be found in standard stage histories, especially those of Genest (1832), Brown (1903), Winter (1915), Odell (1920 and 1927–49), Hogan (1952–7), Kemp & Trewin (1953), The London Stage 1660–1800 (1960–8), Trewin (1964), Speaight (1973), Wearing (1976–93), Shattuck (1976–87), Mullin (1980, 1994), Beauman (1982), Leiter (1986), and Williams (1990); from studies of Lr. in particular, esp. Derrick (1940), Harris (1966), Rosenberg (1972), Bratton (ed. 1987), and Leggatt (1991); and from reviews in the London Times, The New York Times Theater Reviews, 1870–1970 (1971–), and a variety of Sh. and theater journals. Other particular sources are cited locally. For the 20th century, the notable performances that were filmed or sound-recorded are now increasingly available.

div.head: Seventeenth-Century Performances
div.p: 1605, spring?Many since Malone (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 1:322; ed. 1790, 1:352–3) have argued that the old play Leir (Stationers’ Register 8 May 1605) was published in order to cash in on the current stage popularity of Sh.’s play, which must therefore have been in performance by early in 1605. There is no factual evidence for performances at that time, and many reasons exist to think that a date of composition in or before 1605 may be too early; see .

1606, summer?As Barroll (1991, pp. 154–5, 176–7) points out, although the public theaters were closed for plague during the late spring, early summer, and autumn of 1606, the King’s Men performed before James at Greenwich and Hampton Court to honor the visit of the queen’s brother Christian of Denmark in August, and Lr. could have been performed then. Both Ham. and Mac. have also been proposed; see Paul (1950, pp. 317–31). There is no record of which (if any) of Sh.’s plays were performed for that occasion, and the sportive nature of the celebrations may not have invited the presentation of any tragedies at all; see .

1606, 26 Dec., court.Nathaniel Butter’s and John Busby’s Stationers’ Register entry on 26 Nov. 1607 for the manuscript that would become Q1 Lr. reads in part (as transcribed in Greg, BEPD 1:24): Mr Willm Shakespeare his historye of Kynge Lear as yt was played before the kinges maiestie at Whitehall vppon St Stephans [deleted k]night at x&ptilde;ist&mtilde;s Last by his maites servantes playinge vsually at the globe on the Banksyde. The title page of Q1 also advertises a royal performance at Whitehall on St. Stephen’s Day (26 Dec.). As Price (1894, p. 165) asserts, this first known performance of Lr. may conceivably have been its first anywhere, although an opening performance at court would have been extraordinary. Barroll (1991, p. 155) argues that the play would not have been performed at that time if it had already been acted before the court only four months earlier for the visit of Christian of Denmark, or at the previous (1605–6) Christmas festivities. Since Sh.’s company did not play at court on Shrove Monday or Shrove Tuesday 1606, nor during Lent (which ended at Easter, 20 April), and because plague prevented any company from playing in public or at court before 26 Dec., Barroll concludes that King Lear had its debut either at court on Christmas 1606 or in public [at the Globe] between April and June 1606 before plague returned to London. The play might have been ready for acting by spring 1606: see . Greg (1940, p. 303): In a private letter [Sir Edmund Chambers] writes: The court was at Whitehall by 1 November 1606, and does not seem to have moved again until the following spring. There was not yet a permanent theatre at court, and I think we may take it that Lear was given in the Great Hall. Here the Offices of Revels and Works could certainly fit up some temporary erection corresponding to the threefold public theatre stage [i.e., presumably, platform, alcove, and balcony].…I should suppose that anything put up for 26 December would stand throughout the winter’s performances, although the mask on 6 January, 1607, might entail some rearrangement. Derrick (1940, p. 14), assuming that the Great Hall was being made ready for Campion’s masque of 6 Jan., believes that Lr. was performed in the adjoining Great Chamber. Wells (ed. 2000, p. 5) notes in support that The Great Chamber was made ready for the plaies in December 1606 (Malone Society, Collections, vol. 6, Oxford, 1961 [1962], p. 101). Considering the simplicity of stage resources required for Lr., Greg entertains but ultimately rejects the possibility that it was written specifically for this court performance rather than for the public stage. Teague (1991, pp. 185–6) lists the properties called for in Q and F. Except for Lear’s chair in F 2771, none implies a significantly different staging; even the colors in 4.4, 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 could have been used in Q even though not explicitly called for. Several critics—Battenhouse (1969, p. 144), Hassel (1979, pp. 22 ff.), Wittreich (1984, pp. 114–15), Marcus (1988, pp. 154–9)—finding correlations between themes in Lr. (persecution, equity, patience, hospitality, charity, forgiveness, earned wisdom) and the story of St. Stephen, speculate that the play was chosen for performance on that saint’s feast day to suggest particular moral lessons to James and his court. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 91): Both the idea that the play had a special relevance to St Stephen’s Day (Marcus, 155–6) and the suggestion that it came perilously close to presenting a fictional portrait of the king himself (Patterson, [1989], 106) seem implausible to me. In dividing the kingdom and bringing about his own downfall, Lear behaves in a way directly contrary to the advice James gave to his son in Basilikon Doron.

Doubling of roles by Sh.’s actors is generally assumed. Bentley (1981, p. 54): In addition to…thirteen sharers and boy apprentices, the playwright had probably in 1604 about a dozen hired men…for minor roles, such as Curan, or the Doctor, or the Herald, or the messengers. In Lr. he counts twelve major roles: Lear (765 lines), Edgar (397), Kent (379), Gloucester (344), Edmund (323), the Fool (253), Goneril (196), Regan (187), Albany (156), Cordelia (117), Cornwall (110), Oswald (80). In addition there are about 25 smaller parts; each hired man could handle two or three of these. Ringler’s (1981, pp. 193–4 nn.) assessment differs slightly: For the performance of King Lear in 1606 the twelve adult actors available were the seven shareholders, Robert Armin, Richard Burbage, Henry Condell, Richard Cowley, John Heminges, William Shakespeare, and William Sly; and the hirelings Alexander Cooke, Samuel Gilburne, John Lowin, Nicholas Tooley, and probably Samuel Crosse.…[194] King Lear has only eleven speaking parts of any consequence…; but a number of mute attendants are needed, especially in the first and last scenes. If one of the (two) attendants at I, i, 33 bears the coronet, the entire Act I can be produced with fifteen players without doubling Edgar or Oswald.…The finale can be performed with fifteen players.…Extant records indicate that probably only three boy actors were with the company in 1606: Robert Goughe, the only one of the three whose name later appeared in the Folio Principall Actors, who presumably played the parts of Cordelia and the Fool; John Edmans (mentioned in Pope’s will in 1603); and James Sands (mentioned in Phillips’ will in 1605). In addition to a few hirelings for attendants and soldiers Engelen (1927, pp. 121–3) would need only twelve players (nine men and three boys) for the major roles: Lear, Gloucester, Edmund, Edgar, Goneril, and Regan would be undoubled, and the other roles would be doubled as follows: Cordelia=Fool (third boy), Cornwall=Doctor=Knight, Albany=Curan, Kent=Old Man, Burgundy=Oswald=Captain, and France=Gentleman=Herald. Darton (ed. 1928, pp. xlix ff.), casting a modern production, would not allow doubling of Cornwall, Cordelia, the Fool, Edgar, and Oswald, and so counts twelve major (undoubled) roles, five actors for more minor (and doubled) speaking roles, and several supers. Howard (1991) proposes the doubling of Cordelia=Fool, France=Edgar, Burgundy=Oswald, Kent=Old Man, Gloucester=Herald. King (1992, p. 91 and tables 69–70) believes that the principal roles of Lear, Kent, Gloucester, Edgar, Edmund, Fool, Regan, Goneril, and Cordelia were not doubled, but he conjectures the possible doubling of France=Oswald and Cornwall=Gentleman. By his computations, both Q and F would have required nine actors playing eleven principal male roles, and three boys playing three principal female roles; Q would require an additional six men playing fifteen small speaking parts and seventeen mutes, and F would require ten men playing sixteen small speaking parts and twenty-two mutes. Bradley (1992, p. 232), assuming less doubling, estimates casts for both Q and F Lr. of sixteen men and three to five boys. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 148): It is possible that the King’s Men staged their plays as lavishly as their resources allowed, and if they had a hectic daily repertory like that at the Rose and Fortune (as listed in Henslowe) actors may have welcomed an alternation between large and small roles, and there may have been less doubling than is often suggested. Baldwin (1927, pp. 228–9, table III), assigning named roles to members of Sh.’s company according to their supposed lines (characteristic skills), casts the play as follows: Lear = Richard Burbage, Gloucester = John Lowin, Edgar = Henry Cundall, Kent = John Heminges, Edmund = William Sly, the Fool = Robert Armin, Oswald = Richard Cowley, Cornwall = Alexander Cooke, Albany = Robert Goffe, King of France = Samuel Gilburne, Goneril = Jack Wilson, Regan = John Edmans, Cordelia = James Sands. These speculations are widely questioned because of doubts that the actors were so closely identified with particular acting specialties as Baldwin believes.

That the great actor Richard Burbage (1568–1619) acted Lear is attested by an anonymous elegy ca. 1620, On ye. death of ye. famous Actor R. Burbage, attributed in one MS to Jo ffletcher. Halliwell-Phillipps (1889, 2:88) identifies five MS versions of it. It was first published in Gentleman’s Magazine 95 (June 1825), 498–9, by Eu. H[ood] (pseud. for. Joseph Haslewood), who dated it 1620. Munro (1909, 2:273) dates it about 1618–19. Haslewood printed it from a MS accidentally lacking the following three (of four) lines found in other doubtlessly authentic MSS:
No more young Hamlett, ould Heironymoe.
Kind Leer, the greued Moore, and more beside,
That liued in him, haue now for ever dy’de.

On the controversy over John Payne Collier’s deletion of these and other lines and substitution of forged lines of his own in several variant longer versions of this elegy, see Chambers (1923, 2:309) and Ingleby (1881, 2:169–82). The phrase Kind Leer might seem more easily to suggest the mild protagonist of the old Leir play than Sh.’s wrathful king, but Lear is called kind at 906, 1637 (F), and 1800, and there is no reason to think that Burbage ever acted in Leir, a Queen’s Men play, or would have been remembered for playing its passive hero rather than Sh.’s titan. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 148): If Richard Burbage, the leading actor in the King’s Men, played Lear, he would have been about forty-two years old when King Lear was staged before James I in 1606, and…is likely to have presented a powerful figure.

Like others before him, Baldwin (1927) assigns the Fool to Robert Armin, the actor who ca. 1600 (see Knowles, ed. AYL, 1977, pp. 374–7) replaced William Kempe as the principal clown of Sh.’s company and is thought to have played Touchstone, Feste, and Lavache. The assignment is accepted by Hotson (1952, pp. 100–1), Felver (1961, p. 58), Bradbrook (1969, p. 50), Lippincott (1975), and most recent commentators. Parrott (1934, p. 70): Perhaps the most striking instance of Shakespeare’s consideration of an actor occurs in King Lear.…We may well imagine Armin objecting to so poor a rôle [as the Clown in Oth.]. As if to recompense him Shakespeare introduced into his next play King Lear, the part of the Fool—for which there is no corresponding part in the old source—a rôle which would at once tax and exhibit all of Armin’s quality as an actor. Sprague (1966, p. 34): The Fool in King Lear, as we recognize at once in the theatre, is a broadly comic part, though one which at moments transcends comedy. To the gifted and mature Robert Armin, with his particular interest in the subject of court and domestic fools, the role must have seemed his by right, and only his. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 50–1): In his own play The Two Maids of More-clack (1608) he doubled in the parts of an idiot clown and a witty steward, and showed off his skill in both. In creating the role of the Fool in King Lear, Shakespeare may have had in mind the spectrum of Armin’s skills. These skills would have included singing. The casting has not gone unchallenged, however. Brown (1963, p. 166) and Ringler (1981, pp. 188–9), taking literally Lear’s epithets pretty knave and boy, think that the middle-aged Armin was too old for the role, which would have been taken by one of the company’s boy actors. Much critical opinion favors an older character, however; see n. 626 and . Foakes estimates Armin’s age in 1606 as almost forty. Nungezer (1929) gives no birth date; Felver (1961, p. 10), on the authority of Hotson (1952, p. 107), estimates 1568, making Armin about thirty-eight. Holmes (1978, pp. 183–5), arguing that Armin, pupil of Richard Tarlton, probably played a bluff, critical, argumentative,…robust and sometimes knockabout comedy, thinks he would have played Kent.

The assumption that Cordelia’s role would naturally be played by one of the three boy actors in the company has been challenged and extensively debated in the past century. In 1894 Brandl (pp. 31–2, 179), finding parallels between the roles of Cordelia and the Fool and no overlap of the characters on stage, proposed that the same actor doubled in both of these roles. Those who have supported the idea include Tolman (1925, pp. 93–4), Engelen (1927, p. 121), Quiller-Couch (1932, p. 108), Stroup (1961), Adler (1977, p. 30), Booth (1979, pp. 126–7), Ringler (1981, pp. 188–9), Meagher (1984, p. 18), and Abrams (1985). Halio (ed. 1992, p. 35) sums up the usual reasons: Doubling would be feasible, since Cordelia leaves the action [in 1.1] before the Fool enters in 1.4 and returns [in 4.4] only after the Fool’s final exit in 3.6. The lines introducing the Fool ([600–3]) and the ambiguous reference in my poor fool is hanged ([3277]) provide thematic or conceptual linking of the two roles. Like several others, Ringler believes that a boy actor played both roles: The doubled role of Cordelia (117 lines) and the Fool (253 lines) would be the fourth most important in the play—after Lear, Edgar, and Kent—and so would be played by the most accomplished boy actor. Others think a more mature actor is required, indeed Robert Armin. Although casting a thirty-eight year old man to play Lear’s youngest daughter is on the face of it improbable, Adler, for instance, argues that Armin had the versatility to have played women, he had a singing voice that could have imitated a woman’s, and perhaps a diminutive stature (to judge by his diminutive nicknames Snuff, Pink, and Robin, and the fact he left his cloak to his sister).

Both hypothetical castings (boy, Armin) have been vigorously attacked. Lawrence (1927, pp. 72–3): Proof that leading female characters [73] were ever doubled is wholly lacking; and to me the postulate is incredible. It involves a very troublesome case of [back and forth] character alternation. Beyond doubt, minor female characters were—in fact (from the scarcity of boys) had to be—doubled, a boy playing a female attendant at one juncture playing another at another; but the doubling of a male and female character was an irksome task, viewing the difference in attire and the difficulties of female make-up—all the more so if alternation were demanded. The evidence for mixed doubling of this order is very slight and admits only of the deduction that none but adult players ever resorted to it, and that the female characters so doubled were of an elderly type, citing the casts for Duchess of Malfi, Shoemaker’s Holiday, and (as sole exception) The Wild Goose Chase. Thaler (1930, p. 122; cf. 1929, pp. 38, 257 ff.): The difficulties…—the changes in make-up, dress, bearing, and voice, required to metamorphose the tempest-tost Fool into the Queen seem insuperable.…The Fool is…always nervous and sharp-tongued.…He is…usually strained to an almost hysterical pitch…whereas Cordelia’s voice—!…Shakespeare purposely made it ever soft, gentle, and low. Sprague (1966, pp. 33–4): The notion is very implausible. With two boy actors already required for major [34] parts, as Goneril and Regan, it seems most unlikely that Shakespeare would make such extraordinary demands on a third. Nor could the supposed casting have found favour with that important member of the company the first comedian. Berry (1993, p. 17): The supposed doubling is an academic fancy: both Fool and Cordelia are major parts, and therefore Robert Armin, the company’s fool, would not have yielded to a boy actor playing Cordelia or have been allowed to play another key part in the same play. It seems inherently probable that Armin exercised territorial rights over the role. Would the allowed fool of the company yield his part to a boy, in a tragic masterpiece? Foakes (loc. cit.): Armin, who seems to have been small in stature, ugly, and at the same time highly intelligent, combined the physique of a natural fool or clown with the mental agility of a professional. Fleissner (1991, p. 176), fantastically: More probably Archee [sic] Armstrong happened to take both roles. But the coarse and impudent style of James’s Scots fool is beyond imagining in, e.g., the reunion of Lear and Cordelia in 4.7.

Depriving Armin of the Fool’s role, Ringler (op. cit., pp. 190–1) assigns him Edgar’s: In the play that Armin wrote for himself [Two Maids of More-Clack] and in which he played the principal part disguised in four different roles, he was only partly a fool and clown, much more a scheming servant, but most of all a quick-change artist, an actor of multiple impersonations. The one character who indulges in multiple impersonations in King Lear is Edgar; so,…Armin could have been the actor who was assigned Edgar’s part.…Mention [on Q1 title page] of his assumed humor of Tom of Bedlam stresses his [Edgar’s] multiple role-playing. In the course of Shakespeare’s play Edgar assumes six different characters, legitimate son, Poor Tom, peasant, man at bottom of cliff, Zomerzet rustic, and armored champion, while often (p. 191) before the audience he maintains himself by means of…asides. Halio (ed. 1992, pp. 35–6) On the other hand, would Armin’s small size suit Edgar, especially as the champion against Edmond in 5.3? He adds, Note that Edgar’s absence in 1.1 may be explained by the need for the actor to play the King of France.

1606–1642.There is no record of any performance in the public theaters before their closing. Halliwell-Phillipps (2nd ed., 1882, pp. 144–5; 1889, 1:219): No record of the character of its reception by the Court has been preserved, but it must have been successful at the theatre, for the booksellers, late in November of the following year, made an arrangement…for the publication of the tragedy. The alterations made in the F text, some of which seem non-Shn. in vocabulary and versification (see ), may indicate revision for one or more revivals before 1623; but the evidence is slight. Thomas Pavier was familiar enough with the play to reprint it as Q2 (1619), but his acquaintance may have derived only from the printed book Q1, not from the theater. Brown (ed. 1976): The play’s early success is attested to chiefly by its publication in 1608.… But King Lear can never have been a runaway popular success. It is a long and complex work, and no recorded production has ever played the complete text.…Its hero wins no battle, revenges no father, and neither seeks nor defends bride, mistress, or country. Lear is more than eighty years of age…, and for more than half the play, he is on the verge of madness. A ballad of King Leare and his three Daughters (see ) was printed in its third edition in 1620. Wells (ed. 2000, p. 57): Its existence tells us that the play was popular enough to generate a song likely to have been sung in the streets of London.…In its descriptions of Lear in his madness and his death over Cordelia’s body it gives us what may well be unique eyewitness impressions of moments from the play as performed by Shakespeare’s company. The evidence of theatrical cuts and additions in the Folio text (see ) may suggest revision for one or more revivals before 1623, but such changes cannot be dated with any certainty.

A few echoes in contemporary plays and other works, a few of them pre-dating the publication of Q1, may suggest a number of performances at the Globe. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 46): There is no evidence to suggest that King Lear made much impact during the seventeenth century. In the list of allusions to Shakespeare from 1591 to 1700 collected in The Shakspere Allusion Book, King Lear occupies a very lowly position, less mentioned than even Pericles or The Merry Wives of Windsor, and far outshone by Julius Caesar, Hamlet, and Othello. Hardin (1995, pp. 274–5) offers no compelling evidence that Lr. influenced John Ross’s Latin account of Cordelia and Leir in his Britannica (Frankfurt, 1607). Schücking (1916–17) demonstrates verbal and thematic echoes of Lr. in both The Revenger’s Tragedy (1606–7) and The Atheist’s Tragedy (1607–11); those in the latter play are discussed by Ornstein (1960, pp. 80–103) and Frost (1968, pp. 197–8). Apparent echoes in Dekker’s The Bel-man of London (1608; see n. 1265) of Poor Tom’s outcries in 1839–42 simply repeat well-known Bedlamite language (see n. 1839) and do not show Dekker’s familiarity with Lr., contrary to Black & Smith (1931, p. 5) and Parrott (1949, p. 299). Proudfoot (1992, p. xxviii) detects a half-dozen echoes of Lr. (and several other Shn. plays; see nn. 1673–5, 2056+12, 2352, 2353–5, 3217) in the anonymous MS play Tom a Lincolne (ca. 1611), possibly by Heywood. Some have thought that Lear’s use of mirror and feather to show breath stirring in 5.3 may be consciously imitated in Webster’s White Devil 5.2.38–9 (1612), though such usages appear in earlier and later plays and may be simply well-known tests; see nn. 3222, 3227. Bosola’s Breake heart in Duchess of Malfi (ca. 1614) may echo Lear’s (or Kent’s) final line or similar lines from other Shn. plays: see n. 3285. Munro (1909, 1:200) thinks that Fletcher’s The Woman’s Prize 2.4.92 (1611?; 1604–ca. 1617), Petruchio: Come: something I’ll do; but what it is, I know not echoes Lr. 1580–1, but that line itself has many precedents: see n. 1580–2. Maxwell (1939, pp. 141–3), detecting similarities of theme and one simile between Lr. and Middleton, Rowley, and Massinger’s The Old Law (ca. 1618), suspects a recent revival of Lr.; the evidence is slight. To buttress it Maxwell further argues that the King’s Men objected to Pavier’s printing of Lr. in 1619 because the play was still part of the company’s repertory: Of the plays fraudulently dated…Lear is the only one written after 1600, and if the King’s Men objected to the republication because they were still acting some of the plays, then certainly Lear was the one most likely to have been recently or still upon the stage. The King’s Men, however, apparently objected to Pavier’s independently publishing any of their plays, not just Lr. A line in Massinger’s A New Way to Pay Old Debts (1625), I will…tread you into mortar, like its counterpart in Lr., is probably proverbial; see n. 1138–9. The use of music to treat Meleander in Ford’s Lover’s Melancholy (1628) may echo Lr. 4.7, though the treatment was traditional; see n. 2775+2. John Suckling’s The Goblins (1638) has The Prince of darkenesse…Mahu, Mohu; see n. 1921–2. For further, generally doubtful echoes in other works, see .

Collier (ed. 1858, 5:615): The earliest notice we recollect of King Lear (probably the older play from the spelling of the name) is in a book, printed by Boscard at St. Omer’s in 1614, called The Life and Death of Edmund Gerringes. [sic] where the writer is speaking of those who admire affected words.…In the margin opposite the name are inserted the words A booke so called; and no doubt a play-book was intended. This allusion, brought to Collier’s attention by Thomas Rodd the bookseller, is pointed out in a note pasted into Collier’s copy of ed. 1844, BL C.134.f.1, vol. 7, between pp. 150 and 151. The work erroneously referred to is John Geninges’s memorial to a relative martyred in 1591, The Life and Death of Mr. Edmund Geninges priest (STC 11728). On p. 4 is a poem The Avthor to his Booke, whose stanzas 4 and 5 read,
Affected wordes, or Courtly complement,
Do not expect, who euer reades this story;
Vertu’s my ground, it needs no ornament,
And to deceyue you so, I should be sory.
If any such there be, post to Kinga Book
so called Liere,
He hath applause, seeke not contentment heere.
Poets may paynt, and diuersely adorne
Theyr feygned passions, and Chymera’s strange;
Teaching theyr pennes to weepe as one forlorne,
And vp and downe in barren deserts range.
But if true griefe do once possesse theyr mind,
They feele theyr combats in another kind.
My authour’s playne,…

A printed book rather than a manuscript playbook is surely referred to, either Leir (1605) or Lr. (1608). Although Halliwell-Phillipps (2nd ed., 1882, p. 285; 1889, 2:339) and Chambers (1930, 2:339) agree with Collier that the old Leir play is meant, Sh.’s play was more likely to be familiar enough to be subject to an allusion in 1614. Leir had not been performed in London since 1594, and the company that had owned it, the Queen’s Men, had disbanded by early 1603. Moreover, criticisms of affected wordes and ornament more easily apply to the verbal fireworks of Lr. than to the determinedly plain style of the older play.

1609–42? Blackfriars?The division of Lr. into numbered acts and scenes in F, uncharacteristic of plays performed in the public amphitheaters, may reflect the playbook’s adaptation in or after 1609, when the King’s Men began to use their indoor theater in Blackfriars, where act intervals seem to have been regularly observed, perhaps to allow for trimming or replacing candles used for stage lighting; cf. n. 2743. It is entirely possible that some of the cuts, additions, and other changes from Q that are evident in the F text resulted from one or more revivals in the Blackfriars, though it is impossible to date these alterations with any certainty. There is one indication of a Blackfriars revival before the closing of the theaters. Nicoll (1923, pp. 314–15) reprints from papers in the Lord Chamberlain’s department of the Public Record Office (L.C. 5/137, p. 343) a list of Plays allotted to D’Avenant (Dec. 12, 1660): Whereas Sr William Davenant, Knight hath humbly prsented to us a proposition of reformeinge some of the most ancient Playes that were playd at Blackfriers and of makeinge them, fitt, for the Company of Actors appointed vnder his direction and Command.… The list of eleven plays includes nine by Shakespeare, one of them Kinge Lear. The warrant proceeds to forbid any but D’Avenant’s actors to present these plays. It does not clearly require that the plays be reformed before presentation after 1660, nor apparently was Lr.: see below s.v. 1664.

1610, Candlemas (2 or 3 Feb.), Gowthwaite Hall, Nidderdale, West Riding, Yorkshire.Sisson (1942, pp. 134 ff.) discovered from Star Chamber documents (St. Ch. 8. 19/10) a performance of king Lere by a provincial company of actors performing at the house of Sir John Yorke and Lady Julyan Yorke. Almost everyone assumes with Sisson that the play was Sh.’s newly published Lr. rather than the older Leir play, though Wells (ed. 2000, p. 56) reserves judgment. Murphy (1984, pp. 93–118; cf. 1987, pp. 57–63) details government suspicions of the Yorkes for possible involvement in the hiding of priests and the Gunpowder Plot. For their entertainments in the Christmas season of 1609–10 both the Yorks and the company of players, whom Chambers (1923, 1:304, 328; 2:339) calls the Simpsons’ Company, but whom Sisson prefers to call Sir Richard Cholmeley’s Players, were tried for sedition, the players for having acted a seditious play, of Catholic purport, at York’s house, Gowthwaite Hall, at Christmas. The players were Catholic recusants who for several years had played for mostly Catholic audiences throughout Yorkshire. The seditious play was an unknown Saint Christopher in which, according to the Star Chamber records, a Popish priest, armed with a cross, won a disputation with an English minister, armed with a Bible. The remaining repertory of the Simpsons in that season consisted of three new and newly published plays from the London stage, The Travailes of the Three English Brothers (Q 1607), Pericles (Q 1609), and (if the play was indeed Sh.’s) Lr. (Q 1608). At Candlemas Per. and the Lear play were performed, probably on successive nights. The assumed choice of Lr. has been variously explained. Hassel (1979, pp. 100 ff.) suggests that Lr., like the feast of Candlemas, celebrates purification into good will and selfless love. Murphy (pp. 114–16) suspects that Lr., because of its ambivalent use of Harsnett, was of interest to Yorkshire Catholics who knew of Harsnett’s attacks on the sign of the cross, the subject of the St. Christopher play. Sisson (p. 139): The Simpsons not only wanted the latest plays available but also the best.…All the evidence goes to show that both Pericles and Lear were very popular plays, and likely to make the Cholmeley’s Players’ repertory exceedingly attractive. Mowat (1997, pp. 213–17): The players may have believed that a play authorized for printing and reading was ipso facto allowed for playing. Sh.’s Lr., likely starring Burbage and advertised for both its court performance and its virtuoso role of Tom o’ Bedlam, was in all probability better known in 1610 than the old Leir, which seems to have been acted only by the traveling Queen’s Men in the years before 1603. Elsewhere Sisson (1961, p. 80) points out personal parallels between Lady Julian York and Cordelia (see ) but does not offer them to explain the choice of this play.

1626, Dresden?Fleay (1886, p. 311): The play Lear, King of England, performed in Dresden in 1626–7 by a company of Englishmen (Cohn, 1865, pp. cxv f.) was From the old Queen’s play [i.e., Leir].…Yet is it strange that it should be called a tragedy. It would hardly be Shakespeare’s play, as no other of so late date occurs in the list. Chambers (1923, 2:286) is noncommittal about the authorship of the Dresden play, though it is listed in the index (4:417) under Lear, King, among other references to Sh.’s play. Idem (1930, 1:470): A Tragoedia von Lear König von Engelandt in John Green’s Dresden repertory of 1626 may have been derived either from Lear or Leir. Both the term tragedy and the spelling Lear may more readily suggest Sh.’s play; both works had been available in quarto for some two decades. Whichever it was, it would have been acted in translation; the English companies had been performing in German for many years (see Limon, 1985, pp. 21–2).

1642–81.Furnivall (1886, pp. 111, 154) notes that lines 1921–2 of Lr. are quoted in Suckling’s The Goblins (ca. 1638; 1646, p. 25), and that lines 726–8 may be echoed in John Cleveland’s Character of a Country-Committee-Man (ca. 1644; Poems &c., 1677, p. 100). Heinemann (1980, pp. 253–4) finds two allusions in John Harris’s Leveller newspaper Mercurius Militaris (24–31 Oct. 1648, p. 17); Harris had once been an actor. Bentley (1945, p. 3) notes a quotation in John Cotgrave’s Wits Interpreter (1655). Munro (1909, 2:76, 115, 126) finds a few more allusions: W. London’s A Catalogue of the Most Vendible Books in England (1658, sig. F4) lists King Leare, and his three Daughters, with the unfortunate life of Edgar, doubtless Jane Bell’s quarto of 1655. The play is also listed in Francis Kirkman’s 1671 Catalogue, spelt Leir but attributed to Sh. Some anonymous commendatory verses in Gratiæ Theatrales (1662, sig. *4v) predicts of one of the plays in this collection, This I’le dare to foretell, although no Seer, | That Thorny-Abbey will out-date King LEAR. Thorn-Drury (1920, pp. 22–3) finds three allusive quotations from Lr. in William Winstanley’s almanac Poor Robin of October and November of 1678.

1655.Jane Bell inherited from Richard Oulton the right to publish Leir, but since the Stationers’ Register entry misspelled the title as Lear, she mistakenly assumed the right to reprint Lr. from Q2 (see ). The fact that she did so, when texts of Lr. were available in Q1 (1608), Q2 (1619), F1 (1623), and F2 (1632), may suggest continuing interest in the play, which of course was not being acted in the public theaters at the time.
1660, 12 Dec. Salisbury Court.Sir William Davenant, leading the New Duke’s company, was granted a warrant to act nine Sh. plays including Lr. See above s.v. 1609–42, and Van Lennep (1965, 1:22).

1664, Jan. Lincoln’s Inn Fields.Near the end of the period between Michaelmas (29 Sept.) 1663 and Lady Day (25 Mar.) William Hamon (or Hammond) entered in his journal (Folger MS v.a.422) that he took his wife and sister to see Lr. (Van Lennep, 1965, 1:75, assigning the date of Jan.). Malone (ed. 1790, 2:268): Sir William D’Avenant’s Company, after having played for some time at the Cockpit in Drury Lane, and at Salisbury Court, removed in March or April 1662, to a new theatre in Portugal Row near Lincoln’s Inn Fields.…They represented the following plays of Shakspeare…King Lear. The theater opened in June 1661 and remained the company’s home until they moved to their new theater in Dorset Garden in 1671. Munro (1909, 2:438–9, 442) quotes John Downes, Roscius Anglicanus (1708, p. 26; cf. p. 33): There were several other Plays Acted, from 1662, to 1665, both Old and Modern: As…The Tragedy of King Lear, as Mr. Shakespear Wrote it; before it was alter’d by Mr. Tate. On p. 52 Downes identifies Lear as a role acted by Thomas Betterton (1635–1710) but does not specify a time before Tate’s adaptation of 1681, when Betterton did play Lear. (Downes was in Davenant’s theater in Lincolns-Inn Fields from its opening in 1662, and was book-keeper and prompter for the Duke’s, the United, and the Betterton’s companies until Oct. 1706.) Though Betterton would have been only twenty-nine in 1664, Malone (ed. 1790, 2:268), Spencer (1927, p. 75) and Derrick (1940, p. 40) think he probably played Lear at that time; Derrick further speculates that Henry Harris = Edgar, James Noakes = Fool, Thomas Lovell = Gloucester, [John] Richards = Kent, and Mrs. Saunderson (m. Betterton Dec. 1662) = Cordelia. Nicoll (1923, pp. 82–3): When the theatres opened in 1660, they were naturally supplied by plays taken from the repertoire of the pre-commonwealth playhouses. By the King’s company from the commencement of their acting at the Red Bull to May 1663, the date of their removal to the Theatre Royal in Bridges Street, we find revived three tragedies of Shakespeare [Oth., JC, Tit.].…By the Duke’s actors before the opening of the Lincoln’s [83] Inn Field playhouse in June 1661 were revived…Shakespeare’s Pericles. Later, from June 1661 to May 1665 [when plague closed the theaters], the same company produced Hamlet, Romeo, Henry VIII, King Lear, Macbeth,… Wells (ed. 2000, p. 62), on the 1663–4 performance(s): The fact that they were succeeded by a heavily adapted version suggests that they had no great success. An unaltered Lr. was performed again in 1675, however.

1666–71, Lincoln’s Inn Fields?Because Downes (1708, p. 33) in a later paragraph than that in which he lists plays of 1662–5 (see prev. entry) associates Lr. with performances, specifically at Lincoln’s Inn Fields, of Davenant’s alteration of Mac. ([1663; seen by Pepys in 1664, 1666, and 1667] and the Davenant-Dryden Tmp. (1667), Derrick (1940, pp. 37–9) surmises that Lr. was performed there again after 1665, before the company moved to its new theater in Dorset Garden. No performance of Lr. in these years is recorded.

1675, 29 June. Dorset Garden.Van Lennep (1965, 1:234): Nell Gwynne attended the Duke’s Company performance on 29 June. Malone (ed. 1790, 2:277–80): Between the year 1671 and 1682, when the King’s and the Duke of York’s servants united, (about which time [278] Charles Hart, the principal support of the former company, died,) King Lear, Timon of Athens, Macbeth, and [279] The Tempest, were the only plays of our author that were exhibited at the theatre in Dorset Gardens; and the [280] three latter were not represented in their original state, but as altered by D’Avenant and Shadwell. The statement is mainly true, but H8 and Ham. were also occasionally performed during that period. The theater opened Nov. 1671. The United Company, which dissolved in 1695, used the Drury Lane Theatre for plays, Dorset Garden for opera and spectacle.

1680–1, October to March.Nahum Tate’s adaptation, The History of King Lear (date of first performance unknown; see Van Lennep, 1965, 1:294; Black, ed. 1975, p. xxxiv; Maguire, 1991, p. 41, n. 13). The 1681 edition gives the cast, including Lear = Betterton, Cordelia = Mrs. Barry. In his Dedication Tate credits his Esteemed Friend Thomas Boteler, Esq. for suggesting that he alter Lr. Summers (1922, p. 280) conjectures that Boteler was a nobleman of the family of the Duke of Ormond, but Spencer (1965, p. 413) objects: The Duke’s eldest son, Thomas Butler, Earl of Ossory, died in 1680 and in any case would not have been Thomas Boteler, Esq. Ayres (1964, p. 28) declares that he was a son of Robert Butler of London, b. 1652 and mentioned in two of Ormond’s letters of Nov. 1680, seeming to be a confidant to matters of political importance, and Scouten (1942, p. cxii): Among the contributors to Dryden’s edition of Ovid’s Epistles, Translated by Several Hands (1680), to which Tate contributed three pieces, is a Mr. Butler; so possibly the Boteler of this dedication was a member of a circle of minor poets and translators. Black (p. xvii) surmises that Boteler’s awareness of similarities between Lear and Tate’s earlier The Loyal General (1679)—an irascible king tired of ruling, plots against him, civil strife, wandering on a moor during a storm, the death of a loyal daughter—prompted him to suggest that the adaptation of Sh.’s play would be an easy task; Tate did in fact repeat from his earlier play the love interest and the virtuous heroine saved from rape.

The mixture in Tate’s play of readings from both Q and F Lr. invites explanation. Since there is no evident reason why Tate needed to collate minutely two versions of a play he intended radically to revise, possibly his text merely reflects theatrical practice as embodied in the company’s promptbook. Though Black (p. 99) thinks that it is highly unlikely that a free-lance worker such as Tate could have had access to the Duke’s Theater scripts or promptbooks, possibly a family connection would have gained him access. It may be merely coincidence that Charlotte Boteler, whom Colley Cibber (Apology, ed. Lowe, 1889, 1:163) calls the daughter of a decay’d Knight), was an actress in the Duke’s Company, and might have provided access to a playbook. Massai (1995, p. 186) is open to this suggestion: By the 1680s, Tate was an established playwright and his previous dramatic works, Brutus of Alba (1678) and The Loyal General (1679), had both been performed at Dorset Garden by the Duke’s company. There seems therefore to be no reason why Tate should not have had access to the company’s library.…The fact that [Charlotte Boteler] was the daughter of a decayed knight…would account for the honorific Esq. in Tate’s dedication. If such a connection could be proved, Charlotte would represent a direct link between Tate and the company. All that is known of Charlotte Butler is summarized by Judith Milhous and Robert D. Hume (HLQ, 1980, pp. 316–19), who doubt that she was with the company until the season of 1679–80. Because two of Tate’s plays had been mounted by the Duke’s Company in 1678 and 1679, Langhans, Milhous, and Hume (all privately, 1998) believe that Tate should have had no real trouble (pace Black) in acquiring from John Downes or Thomas Betterton access to the Duke’s Company’s promptbook of Lr., which would have been in the Dorset Garden library after Sh.’s Lr. had been performed there on 29 June 1675.

Tate’s alteration has been discussed in detail by Erzgraeber (1897, 1899), Summers (1922), Spencer (1927), Derrick (1940, pp. 46–59), Spencer (1963, 1965), Merchant (1965), Nameri (1976), Hammond (1991, pp. 121–8), Marsden (1995), Massai (2000), and others. In his dedication to Boteler Tate indicates that his aim in revising was to make a better play. To remedy the Disorder of Sh.’s Jewels, unstrung and improve the Regularity and Probability of the Tale, he added the continuous thread of the Love betwixt Edgar and Cordelia; Cordelia’s love, unknown to Lear, explains more probably her rejection of Burgundy and her Father’s Passion, and gives a more heroic-romantic Countenance to Edgar’s Disguise, adopted secretly to protect Cordelia. Tate also capitalized on changed theatrical conditions (women on stage), adding the amorous tryst of Edmund and Regan in a grotto, and a part for a fourth actress, Cordelia’s confidant and chaperone Arante. He also adapted the play to the taste of the age, eliminating the Fool as a comic part indecorous in a serious play (as well as an impudent critic of royalty); providing a happy ending that both gave Success to the innocent distrest Persons and avoided laughably incumbr[ing] the Stage with dead Bodies; adding further disguises, mistaken identity, and the openly sexual actions of an attempted rape and an adulterous assignation; sentimentally heightening the Distress of the Story, as by an added scene of a tearful encounter of the virtuous outcasts and by prolonging scenes of pathos; and flattening much of the language, complementing Sh.’s images and language…so odd and surprising less by added Quaintness of Expression than with moral abstraction, literalness, correct grammar, modernization, and simple elegance. Potter (privately): The Fool appears to have been associated in critics’ minds with the unsophisticated pre-war drama that the Restoration theatre was trying to reform, citing Davenant’s Playhouse to be Let (1663; Works, 1673, 2:73): till the nation be more civiliz’d, | Your Fool and Devil may be entertain’d; | They’l get money; none now but very choice | Spectators will vouchsafe to see a Play | Without’m.

As several commentators have pointed out—see esp. Wikander (1986), Bate (1989, pp. 59–60), Maguire (1991; 1992, pp. 41–2), Dobson (1992, pp. 80–5), Clark (ed. 1997, pp. lxv-lxx), and Hardman (2002)—in changing tragedy to tragicomedy Tate, who alludes in the last line of his Prologue to the Popish Plot, was also clearly playing to the royalist preferences of his Restoration audience: avoiding regicide, eliminating a foreign invasion so as to emphasize the horrors of civil war, and, in Edmund’s drive for power, underlining topical parallels with the current Exclusion Crisis, the Whigs’ attempt to substitute Charles’s ambitious illegitimate son the Duke of Monmouth for James Duke of York. See also . Strier (1995, p. 211) argues that the play’s political stance is more Whig than Tory. The success of Tate’s adaptation is alluded to in Robert Gould’s Poems (1689, p. 177), quoted by Munro (1909, 2:296). Among modern critical editions are those of Spencer (1965) and Clark (1997); a facsimile of the 1681 edition was published by Cornmarket Press (1969).

1681?–1700? Dublin, Smock Alley Theatre.Evans (1996, pp. 1–4), on the Smock Alley promptbook (Folger Library) and its three hands: Probably the production for which it was prepared, though almost certainly before 1700, was after 1681.…Since only two London performances of Shakespeare’s Lear…are recorded (1664/65 and 1675) before Tate’s 1681 adaptation and since Smock Alley tended to take its cue from London successes, it is probably unlikely that Lear would have been seriously considered for production before 1681.…[2] The Smock Alley prompt-book shows no evidence, structural or verbal, of influence from Tate’s version until the final scene (V.iii). At this point all advance character calls suddenly cease, the last such call being for Edgar and Gloucester (at V.i.54) in preparation for their entry at the beginning of V.ii. The cessation of advance calls at this particular point suggests, strongly, I think, despite a few cuts by Hand II in V.iii, that Hand I…intended to conclude the play with a somewhat adapted version of Tate’s happy ending. Bizarre, even unlikely, as this may sound, it is, in fact, exactly what George Colman concocted…in his alteration of Lear first performed in 1768. (Not exactly: Colman made other changes.) Hand III, which disappears after 2.4, is a late 18th-c. hand, since it inserts readings drawn from 18th-c. eds. from Rowe (1709) through Jennens (1770), perhaps drawing the earlier ones from Jennens’s record of editorial emendations from Rowe through Johnson. The absence of actors’ names, of advance warnings for sound effects, and of secondary cutting suggest that the play never reached actual production.

1687–8, court.Van Lennep (1965, 1:358, 362) records performances at court by the United (Duke’s-King’s) Company on 9 May 1687 and 20 Feb. 1688. Hardman (2002, p. 923): Presumably, since he saw it twice, the king found the treatment of the subject congenial. By then the promised future of 1681 had become reality, though James did not enjoy it for long. Exclusionism had failed, James had succeeded his brother, Monmouth’s rebellion had been put down, the Duke executed and his supporters systematically destroyed.

1688–9?Van Lennep (1965, 1:368): A reprint of Tate dated 1689 advertises the play as Acted at the Queen’s Theatre, possibly indicating a revival. Van Lennep does not identify the Queen’s Theatre, perhaps a hall at court. Potter (privately) suggests a topical interest: Lear’s abdication in favor of his daughter and son-in-law is precisely equivalent to James’s.

1689?–1702?Munro (1909, 2:364, 426): In a MS note in a copy of Langbaine’s An Account of the English Dramatick Poets (1691, p. 458) William Oldys writes, The Play of Lear is said to have been prohibited acting by Lord Dorset in King Williams Reign (1689–1702). J. Drake, in The Antient and Modern Stages Survey’d (1699, p. 206) includes Sh.’s Lr. among Plays…generally known and approved. Van Lennep (1965, 1:508) records only one performance, by Rich’s company at Drury Lane on 3 Feb. 1699, and Avery (1960, 2:28) lists another at Drury Lane on 30 Oct. 1702, a half-year after William’s death, and above a dozen more performances in the remainder of the decade. Hardman (2002, p. 923): Perhaps the gap after 1688 is explained partly by the association of the play with the ousted régime.

div.head: The Text on the Stage, 1681–2000
div.p: This section of the appendix is a survey of the text of King Lear as it appeared in the important published acting editions and some recent promptbooks. Most of the texts are associated with major theatrical productions in London or New York. A few are included as evidence, sometimes from decades after the original performance, of the longevity of popular stage versions. Both types of printed acting editions contribute to the complex history of the performance text of Lr. Nahum Tate’s radical revision of the play in 1681 was not unusual for the period; but unlike most other Restoration alterations—only Colley Cibber’s Richard III lasted longer—Tate’s version overwhelmed the original onstage for a hundred and fifty years and influenced acting editions and productions for another fifty.

Tate’s play, The History of King Lear, was printed five times between 1681 and 1712, and several additional 18th-c. acting editions are virtually complete versions of Tate’s play. But before the last of these appeared in 1775, George Colman and David Garrick made the first restorations from the original text, using much of Shakespeare’s first four acts, in conjunction with Tate’s happy ending. Fifty years later, in 1824, R. W. Elliston and Edmund Kean reversed the Colman-Garrick equation, restoring Shakespeare’s tragic ending to the first four acts of Tate’s play. In between was the influential version of J. P. Kemble, based on The History and more notable for omissions of Tate’s original material than for its minor restorations of Shakespearean language. In any event, like most of the versions before the advent of William Charles Macready—and several American ones thereafter—these are all hybrids of Shakespeare’s Lr. and Tate’s.

Macready’s 1838 achievement was a production based almost entirely on Shakespeare’s text. Yet Tate’s stagecraft lived on in his influential omissions and transpositions. Macready’s seminal version, which restored not only the tragic ending but also the Fool, still retained many of Tate’s structural changes, which persisted through the 19th c. Macready, however, also eliminated Shakespearean material that Tate had retained—such as the blinding of Gloucester—and thus inspired a long line of actor-managers, including Charles Kean and Henry Irving in England, and Edwin Booth in America, who pared the play down to focus on the pathos of Lear. Meanwhile, the Elliston-Kean Lr. endured, thanks in part to the American actor Edwin Forrest. The textual dichotomy is reflected in the fact that the theatrical bookseller Samuel French was publishing Macready’s Shakespeare-based version in London during the 1870s, at the same time that the company was publishing Elliston-Kean’s modified History in New York.

At the turn of the 20th c. there is a gap, as the play lay dormant for theatrical and scholarly reevaluation—much as had happened in the 1810s, when George III’s insanity kept the mad King Lear off the stage and romantic critics considered Shakespeare’s great poem unfit for performance. After World War I, and through the mid-century, producers gradually reinstated the text. Scholarly directors restored Shakespeare’s fluid structure, and audiences sobered by the catastrophic world events of the 1930s and 1940s were receptive to the existential tragedy of the play. Productions such as the Granville-Barker/Gielgud Lr. in 1940 were the most faithful to Shakespeare’s play since the mid-17th c., and Donald Wolfit took his Lear to the provinces. By the early 1980s, two versions were made especially for television audiences, one with a published script with minimal cuts, and both were widely available on videotape.

div.head: The Versions
div.p: Following is a list of the major available acting texts in chronological order. For the 18th and 19th centuries, these are published performance editions. For the 20th c., when published acting editions became less common, the entries are mainly for promptbooks. The first version, by compulsion, is a 17th-c. adaptation.
1. Nahum Tate, 1681: The History of King Lear. Acted at the Duke’s Theatre. Reviv’d with Alterations. By N. Tate. London…1681. (Cornmarket Press Facsimile, 1969.)
Dramatis Personae: Betterton (Lear), Barry (Cordelia)
Line numbers refer to The History of King Lear, ed. James Black, Lincoln, Nebr.: 1975.

Any discussion of the performance text of Lr. must begin with a description of Tate’s alterations. First, Tate’s changes must be understood in order to follow the discussion of subsequent stage versions, which incorporated elements of The History for more than 150 years. Moreover, Tate’s dramatic restructuring of Shakespeare’s material lasted even longer than his creative additions to the story. Long after the restoration of Shakespeare’s original language onstage, many of Tate’s basic omissions and transpositions endured. So while Tate’s accretions and his rewording have been rejected, it is important to see that his dramaturgy was stageworthy to the extent that later producers of Lr., sometimes working independently, often came to similar conclusions.

The History is an extensive Restoration adaptation of the Folio text, with numerous omissions, several transpositions and the addition of considerable original material. Approximately one third of The History is original, with a third of those lines comprising the happy ending.

The play opens with the Bastard’s melodramatic Thou Nature soliloquy from 1.2 (335–56), a transposition that readily identifies most later texts based on Tate’s. Edmund’s plot against Edgar is already afoot, allowing Tate to telescope the Gloucester subplot. In his Epistle Dedicatory to Thomas Boteler, Tate says that to add Probability of motive—and the popular element of heroic romance—he created A Love betwixt Edgar and Cordelia, eliminating the King of France. In Tate’s play, the love story becomes the subplot. The first of six major interpolations is a 47-line dialogue between the lovers after the first court scene (1.1.188–234). Otherwise, Tate generally followed the first half of Shakespeare’s play.

In Tate’s Act 3, however, Lear’s storm scenes alternate with original material. In 3.2 (124 lines) and 3.4 (115 lines), Cordelia, disguised and abroad in order to search for Lear, is seized by Ruffians. She is accompanied by her maid, Arante, whose appearance is another Tate giveaway. (In some later versions of The History, as in the original, Arante, or Aranthe, is in the play, but not listed in the DP.) Edgar saves Cordelia from Edmund’s intended rape, and she declares her love. The History again follows the Folio from the blinding of Gloucester in 3.7 to the duel in 5.3. The major original scene here is Tate’s Act 4 opener, A Grotto. Edmund and Regan amorously Seated, Listning to Musick, 49 lines of bombast that never reappeared in any of the subsequent adaptations of Tate’s History. The Grotto is preceded by a 27-line soliloquy by the blinded Gloster, All Dark and Comfortless! (3.5.67–93). The fifth addition is the end of 4.2 (65–110), Tate’s expansion of Cordelia’s reappearance in Shakespeare’s 4.4.

In Tate’s dedicatory letter, he also claims that the love story led to making the Tale conclude in a Success to the innocent distrest Persons. The last 260 lines of his play are almost completely original. Tate replaced the tragic ending that would so dismay Dr. Johnson with a happy one, in which Lear and Cordelia, saved by Edgar from being hanged in prison, live to reign in triumph. Gloster also survives. The three villains do die—though not onstage, avoiding what Tate described as the encumbrance of dead Bodies that makes many Tragedies conclude with unseasonable Jests. In addition, by proving, as Edgar says in the curtain line, That Truth and Vertue shall at last succeed, the new ending also satisfied the critical doctrine deplored by Addison (1711) as the chymerical Notion of poetical Justice. Another 100 lines original to Tate are found in scattered minor passages.

The substantive change that endured longest onstage was Tate’s excision of the Fool—a comic and low-born character that breached royal as well as literary decorum, even if the play was no longer a tragedy. Unlike later producers, however, Tate did retain three controversial elements: the blinding of Gloucester, Gloucester’s suicide attempt, and the evil and sexuality of Goneril and Regan. In fact, with the advent of actresses on the Restoration stage, Tate enhanced all the women’s roles. The older sisters’ wickedness and lust are exaggerated: They usurp their husbands’ roles, woo the villain boldly, and melodramatically poison each other. But the character who undergoes the greatest transformation is Cordelia, whose virginity and goodness take center stage, as she bears the burden of many of Tate’s most un-Shakespearean lines: What have not Women dar’d for vicious Love, | And we’ll be shining Proofs that they can dare | For Piety as much (3.2.106–8).

Tate also restructured Shakespeare’s sprawling play, tightening and combining scenes. In his dedication, Tate described Lr. as a Heap of Jewels, unstrung and unpolisht; yet so dazling in their Disorder. To make the material more manageable for the stage, Tate omitted numerous small scenes or discrete parts of scenes. Typically, these are the quiet transitions, often brief dialogues, that Shakespeare used before or after more dramatic passages. In addition to shortening the play overall, these omissions allow a scene, or an act, to begin or end more dramatically.
The following list of scenes or discrete parts of scenes that Tate omitted from the Folio will be useful throughout this discussion.

list.item: end of 1.1 (310–32): Goneril and Regan, Sister…it’h heate
1.3 (506–28): Goneril and Steward, Did my Father…dinner
end of 1.4 (830–72): Goneril, Albany, Steward, Doe you marke that…euent—omitted when Lear’s great curse (789–803; see Text on Stage, , ) is transposed to end Act 1
1.5 (874–925): Lear, Kent, Fool, Goe you before…shorter—likewise omitted when the great curse is transposed
beginning of 2.1 (928–42): Bastard and Curan, Saue thee Curan…sir
end of 2.4 (1587–1613): Cornwall and Regan, Let vs withdraw…storme—to end Act 2 on Lear’s I shall goe mad (1586)
3.1 (1615–53): Kent and Gentleman, Whats here beside foule weather?…other—to open Act 3 on Lear’s Blow wind (1656)
4.2, part (2287–2311+8): Goneril with Bastard, then Albany, ere long you are like to heare…What newes
4.5 (2383–428): Regan and Steward, But are my brothers…well
4.6, part (2650–62): Edgar and Gentleman, Haile gentle sir…sir
beginning of 4.7 (2745–61): Cordelia and Kent, O thou good Kent…king
beginning of 5.1 (2847–901): Bastard, etc., Know of the Duke…time

div.p: Tate’s minor omissions are legion. He pruned speeches throughout, reducing his play to three quarters of the length of the Folio. Despite The History’s many additions, it has 2450 lines (counting stage directions, as in through-line numbering), to the Folio’s 3303. For example, Lear’s first long speech, 19 lines in F (41–59), is only 10 lines in Tate (1.1.67–76); Lear’s 13 lines at 115–27 become 5 lines. Even with the addition of Tate’s original material, his version of Lear’s first scene is 146 lines (1.1.56–187), compared with Folio’s 254 (37–291). Similarly, Tate’s first storm scene (3.1) is about half the length (47 lines) of Folio’s 3.2 (94 lines). As Tate cut, he clarified the language and regularized the prosody, so that many of The History’s Shakespearean lines are recast in Tate’s image. In Regan’s first speech (74–81), Sir I am made of the selfe same mettal… becomes My Sister, Sir, in part exprest my Love… (1.1.86). Regan’s Which the most precious square of sence possesses (79) becomes Sense has no other Joy that I can relish (1.1.88). Lear’s powerful and complex Blow wind [F: windes]…man (1656–64), cut to five lines, tamely concludes: Spout Cataracts, and Hurricanos fall | Till you have drown’d the Towns and Palaces | Of proud ingratefull Man (3.1.3–5).

On the other hand, Tate’s original material borrows generously from Shakespeare. Edgar’s first avowal of love (O heav’nly Maid that art thy self thy Dow’r, 1.1.205) uses language from the absent France (264). Before Lear enters, Gloster tells Kent: Alas! ’tis the Infirmity of his Age, | Yet has his Temper ever been unfixt, | Chol’rick and suddain… (1.1.53–5). The lines are from the Goneril-Regan dialogue at the end of Shakespeare’s first scene, which Tate omitted. The first line is Regan’s 318, the second is a version of 319, and the third uses cholericke from 324 and the idea of vnconstant starts from 325. Some of Tate’s appropriations of Shakespeare’s language are more far-fetched. In 3.2, Arante says, In such a Night as This? Consider, Madam, | For many Miles about there’s scarce a Bush | To shelter in (102–4). The first phrase is Shakespeare’s (1799), which Tate uses in place at 3.3.16. The second line is Gloucester’s at the end of Shakespeare’s Act 2 (1604–5), a line that Tate omitted. The last three words are Tate’s clarification.
