Tate’s major transpositions usually combine similar scenes, in contrast to Shakespeare’s alternation of dissimilar scenes. Tate’s consolidation is often achieved with the help of omissions. He also transposed material in order to begin or end a scene or act more dramatically.
The Bastard’s Thou Nature soliloquy (335–56) opens Tate’s History.

Lear’s great curse is transposed to the end of Act 1: harke [F: Heare] Nature…child (789–803) is moved forward, to follow the subsequent father’s curse (life and death! I am asham’d…for euer, 814–29). The remainder of the act is omitted.

The Kent-Steward altercation from the beginning of 2.2 (1075–116), Good deuen [F: dawning] to thee friend…helpe, is transposed back into 2.1, following 1023, in order to combine the two Cornwall-Regan scenes (1024–73 with Gloucester, and 1117–1227 with Kent).

The end of Act 3 is consolidated: A pastiche of selected lines from 3.6 are transposed back into 3.4. Thus Shakespeare’s two scenes with Lear and friends are combined into Tate’s 3.3, while Shakespeare’s scenes 5 and 7, Cornwall in Gloucester’s house, become Tate’s 3.5. Tate’s two scenes are separated by the attempted rape of Cordelia and her reunion with Edgar (3.4).

There are three minor transpositions in Act 4:
4.4: Cordelia’s Alack tis he…corne (2351–6) is transposed back to Tate’s 4.2.65.
4.5: Regan’s It was great ignorance…life (2394–7) and If you doe chance…off (2424–5) are transposed back to 4.2 (Tate’s 4.3), where the lines are given to Goneril.
4.6: Lear’s It were a delicate…kill (2626–9) is transposed forward, to follow 2643 and end the long scene.
Tate’s History was reprinted: Q2, 1689; Q3, 1699; Q4, 1702?; Q5, 1712.

Between 1717 and 1775, there were some 25 additional editions, which differ only in accidentals. A few have cast lists. The frontispiece of a 1735 edition depicts five players, including the Fool, who is not in the printed play.
2. George Colman, 1768: The History of King Lear. As it is performed at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. London…MDCCLXVIII. (Cornmarket Press Facsimile, 1969.)
DP: Powell, Yates

This is the first acting edition after Tate’s to restore Shakespearean text. Yet it is possible that some of Tate’s excesses were omitted in performance during the century between the two versions. Indeed, given the critical interest in the subject of Shakespeare’s Lr. versus Tate’s, and the widespread omission of some of Tate’s original material such as the Grotto scene (4.1), it seems unlikely that The History survived completely intact on the stage in the decades before Colman’s radical restoration of Shakespeare’s lines. Black (1967, p. 43) notes that playbills for three performances of Lr. at Lincoln’s Inn Fields in January 1743 advertise a production With Restorations from Shakespeare, as does a Covent Garden bill for 13 Dec. 1744.

George Colman, dramatist and manager of Covent Garden, based his first four acts almost entirely on Shakespeare’s play, even including some lines that are unique to the Quarto (most notably in 4.3, but also in 3.6 and 4.2). Nevertheless, he used Tate’s ending. In Colman’s thoughtful Advertisement to the printed edition, he attacks Tate for the insipidity of the love story, but quotes Dr. Johnson on the success of the happy ending. Thus Colman’s first grand object was to reconcile the catastrophe of Tate to the story of Shakespeare. His version is unique in omitting the romance (and Arante) and retaining the King of France. Colman also says that he jettisoned his thought of retaining the Fool, lest the drama sink into burlesque. He did retain the blinding scene, though he was the first to move the unpleasing act offstage. Finally, he was the first to omit the utter improbability of Gloucester’s suicide attempt and the following dialogue (2481–524), forestalling the leap with Lear’s entrance.

Colman omitted most of the small scenes omitted by Tate (see ), though he retained the end of 1.1, all of 1.3, and all of 4.4. He also used most of Tate’s transpositions: the great curse to the end of Act 1, Kent’s part of 2.2 into 2.1, and lines from 3.6 into 3.4, where he followed Tate’s selection and arrangement of lines. Colman’s History reverts to Tate’s after the reconciliation scene, which begins Act 5. However, Colman’s last act omits much of Tate’s enhancement of the Goneril-Regan rivalry: Tate’s 5.1 (Goneril’s plot to poison Regan), 5.2 (the Bastard’s soliloquy on the sisters), and 5.5.58–114 (the exit of the three dying villains).

The productions of Colman’s version of Lr. overlapped with Garrick’s. The two men had worked together at Drury Lane, and may have been inspired by the recent editions of Shakespeare by Johnson and Capell. But Colman’s version—which was to be the most thorough adoption of Shakespearean language until the 1830s—was published before Garrick’s.

3. Bell’s, 1773: King Lear, A Tragedy, by Shakespeare, As Performed at the Theatre-Royal, Drury-Lane. Regulated from the Prompt-book, With Permission of the Managers, By Mr. Hopkins, Prompter. An Introduction, and Notes Critical and Illustrative, Are Added by the Authors of the Dramatic Censor. London: Printed for John Bell…MDCCLXXIII. (Bell’s Edition of Shakespeares [sic] Plays, vol. 2, 1774.)
DP: Garrick, Barry (Drury Lane); Ross (Covent Garden)

Bell’s was the first series of acting editions that claimed to publish a play as it is now performed at the Theatres Royal. Though the text was long thought to be Garrick’s October 1756 version with restorations, Harris (1971) has shown that Garrick only gradually restored Shakespeare’s original language, and that Bell’s edition actually reflects his 1770 revival (see ). One argument is in the brief introduction by Francis Gentleman, which praises this hybrid as more nervous than Tate’s and much more agreeable than Mr. Colman’s late alteration. Garrick’s version had a longer publishing history than Colman’s: Bell’s text was reissued by Whitworth (1775) and Barker (1794), in slightly altered form by Bathurst, and, into the 19th c., in Roach’s series.

Bell’s edition, like Colman’s, shows substantial restorations of Shakespearean text from the first four acts, and concludes with a truncated version of Tate’s happy ending. Garrick, however, relied more heavily on Tate’s text. Bell’s omits all of the passages omitted by Tate, except for the beginning of 2.1, and makes almost all of Tate’s transpositions (although the play begins with Kent and Gloucester, not the Bastard). As in Tate’s History (and Colman’s), the Fool is omitted. The major difference from Colman’s version is that Garrick retained most of Tate’s Cordelia-Edgar love story, including Edmund’s attempted rape (though not the Grotto scene, 4.1). The blinding follows Tate’s text, though Garrick, like Colman, moved the deed offstage. Garrick was unusual in retaining Shakespeare’s dialogue after Gloucester’s suicide attempt.

4. Harrison, 1779: King Lear. A Tragedy. As it is Acted at the Theatres-Royal in Drury-Lane and Covent-Garden. Written by Shakespeare. London: Printed for Harrison and Co.…MDCCLXXIX. (No. 18 of The Theatrical Magazine, vol. 3.)

This acting edition is a virtually complete History, with a few minor restorations. Published between two editions of Garrick’s more Shakespearean version, Harrison reflects the continued popularity of Tate’s adaptation.

5. Bathurst, 1786: King Lear, A Tragedy: Altered from Shakspeare by David Garrick, Esq. Marked with the Variations in the Manager’s Book at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane. London. Printed for C. Bathurst…M.DCC.LXXXVI.
DP: Garrick, Younge (DL); Henderson, Mrs. Kemble (CG)
The text is similar to Bell’s, but restores several additional lines in the first half of the play, including some lines unique to the Quarto.

6. Lowndes, c. 1795–1800: Shakspeare’s King Lear: As Altered by N. Tate, Newly Revised by J. P. Kemble, and Acted by Their Majesties Servants, at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. Printed by C. Lowndes, No. 66, Drury-Lane, Next the Stage-door, and Sold in the Theatre. [N.d.; c. 1795–1800.]
DP: Kemble, Siddons

This is the first published version of John Philip Kemble’s influential version of Tate’s alteration, first produced at Drury Lane in 1792. Instead of building on Colman’s and Garrick’s restorations, Kemble reverted to Tate’s text, making only minor restorations of original Shakespearean language. These are mainly in the first three acts, notably Kemble’s use of Shakespeare’s text instead of Tate’s for Lear’s great curse (789–803). More substantial are Kemble’s omissions, mainly in the second half of the play. Of Tate’s original material, Kemble omitted Gloucester’s lament after the blinding (an expanded All dark and comfortless!, 3.5.67–93) and the next scene, Edmund and Regan in the Grotto (4.1). Kemble followed Colman in omitting Gloucester’s suicide leap and the following dialogue. Like Colman and Garrick, Kemble began Act 5 with the reconciliation scene (4.7) and shortened Tate’s ending by significantly reducing the rivalry of Goneril and Regan over the Bastard. But Kemble also omitted Lear and Cordelia’s We Two…Incense (5.4.70–9). Kemble transposed Tate’s last speeches, to end the play with Lear instead of Edgar.

7. Roach, 1801: King Lear, A Tragedy, By William Shakspere. Adapted for Theatrical Representation, As Performed at the Theatres-Royal, Drury-Lane and Covent-Garden. Regulated from the Prompt-books, By Permission of the Managers…London: Printed by and for J. Roach…MDCCCI.

Although the DP lists Kemble, this small theater edition is essentially Garrick’s more Shakespearean version, though it does have a few of Kemble’s minor restorations. Despite the popularity of Kemble’s own Tate-based version, Roach’s was reprinted in 1809.

8. J. P. Kemble, 1808: Shakspeare’s King Lear, (with Nahum Tate’s Alterations, [sic]). A Tragedy, revised by J. P. Kemble; and now first published as it is acted at The Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. London: Printed for the Theatre. 1808.
DP: Kemble, C. Kemble (Edgar)

Kemble, says Shattuck (1974, 5:xiv), was the first actor-manager in the English-speaking theater who systematically published his own acting versions. This Lr., a lightly revised version of the text in Lowndes, reflects Kemble’s 1808 Covent Garden production. In 1815, Kemble’s promptbook was reissued in a series for John Miller’s Select British Drama.

9. Inchbald, 1808: King Lear; A Tragedy, In Five Acts; By William Shakspeare. As Performed at the Theatres Royal, Drury Lane and Covent Garden. Printed Under the Authority of the Managers from the Prompt Book. With Remarks by Mrs. Inchbald. London…1808. (The British Theatre; or, A Collection of Plays. Vol. IV.)
DP: Kemble, Siddons (DL); Cooke (CG)

For her widely published acting series, Elizabeth Inchbald, an actress, playwright, and novelist, adopted Kemble’s alteration, though she followed Tate’s text over Kemble’s in a dozen minor instances. In her twenties (during the 1770s), Inchbald had played Cordelia to the Lear of her husband, Joseph, in the provinces.

10. Elliston, 1820: Shakspeare’s Tragedy of King Lear. Printed chiefly from Nahum Tate’s edition, with some restorations from the original text, By R. W. Elliston. London…Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. 1820. (Cornmarket Press Facsimile, 1970.)
DP: Kean, W. [Sarah Cooke] West

This is the first version by actor-manager Elliston, probably representing Edmund Kean’s 24 April 1820 Drury Lane performance, only months after the January 29 death of the troubled King George III and the lifting of the eleven-year ban on the play. It is basically Kemble’s alteration of Tate’s History, complete with the happy ending, with a few independent restorations of Shakespeare’s language, including Blow wind (1656–64) and Rumble thy belly full (1669–79). Elliston also restored some of Cordelia’s lines, and used All blest secrets (4.4, 2366–69) to open Act 5, along with lines from Shakespeare’s reconciliation scene (2763–6 and 2774–9). Elliston’s introduction inaugurates the 19th-c. interest in historical accuracy by including a long excerpt from Holinshed.

11. Oxberry, 1820: Oxberry’s Edition. King Lear, A tragedy; Altered from Shakspeare, by Nahum Tate.…The only edition existing which is faithfully marked with the stage business, and stage directions, as it is performed at the Theatres Royal. By W. Oxberry, Comedian. London.…
(The New English Drama, vol. 10.)
DP: Kean (DL); J. Booth (CG)
Engraving: West as Cordelia

William Oxberry’s edition is essentially Kemble’s version of Tate’s, plus Elliston’s limited restorations. While very similar to the editions of Kemble, Inchbald, and Elliston, Oxberry’s is not exactly the same as any of them. For example, it omits Tate’s 2.5.161–8, Hold now…Love, which is retained by the others. The preface, however, regrets that an acting edition has to use a Tate-based text. Oxberry, an actor, criticizes the happy ending and mentions the satire of the fool, a character absent from this version. He ridicules Dr. Johnson and asks: Is not the restoration of Lear to felicity, after so much suffering, an anti-climax? (p. iv).

12. Dolby, 1824: Dolby’s British Theatre. King Lear, A Tragedy, In Five Acts. By William Shakspeare. Printed from the Original Edition, with Remarks. To Which Are Added, A Description of the Costume, Cast of the Characters, Sides of Entrance and Exit, Relative Positions of the Performers on the Stage, and the Whole of the Stage Business, As Now Performed at the Theatres Royal, London. (Dolby’s British Theatre, vol. 6, London, 1824.)
DP: Kean, West (DL, 1824)
Engraving: I. R. Cruikshank/White: Edgar strikes with his staff

Dolby’s is the first publication of a hybrid version that was apparently more popular in print than onstage. The text contains the first major restoration of the 19th c., Elliston’s Drury Lane revival of the tragic ending for Edmund Kean in 1823. The ending is grafted onto the first four acts of Elliston’s 1820 version of Tate’s History, though here Elliston followed some of Oxberry’s minor omissions. There are also independent omissions of material original to Tate: Gloucester’s remarks on the state (3.2.34–44) and Regan’s invitation of the Bastard to the Grotto (3.5.24–9), since the Grotto scene itself had been eliminated by Kemble. Dolby’s Act 5 opens with minor restorations of Cordelia from Shakespeare’s 4.4 and 4.7, followed by Tate’s reconciliation scene. The remainder is a 350-line version of Shakespeare’s Act 5—though some of Tate’s is used to flesh out the short 5.2 with Gloucester’s soliloquy (5.3.6 ff.). Omitted are the confrontation of Albany and Goneril (3107–19), Edgar on meeting Kent (3168+1–+18), the sisters’ deaths and Kent’s return (3169–99), Edmund’s death and Albany’s resignation offer (3264–76), and the 18 lines after Lear’s last words, F’s Do…there (3282–3).

The irony is that while Dolby’s emphasized stage authenticity, introducing an edition of King Lear as now acted, Elliston’s experiment with restoring the tragic ending was apparently short-lived onstage. Still, this particular hybrid had a long publishing life in the major acting editions—from Cumberland’s to Modern Standard Drama to French’s Standard Drama, as each publisher was taken over by the succeeding one. The introductory Remarks are largely a quotation from Hollingshead.

13. Cumberland, c. 1828: King Lear. A Tragedy, In five Acts, by William Shakspeare. Printed from the Acting Copy, with Remarks, Biographical and Critical, by D.—G. [George Daniel]. To which are added, A Description of the Costume,—Cast of the Characters,—Entrances and Exits,—Relative Positions of the Performers on the Stage, and the Whole of the Stage Business, As performed at the Theatres Royal, London.…London [n.d.]. (Cumberland’s British Theatre, vol. 2; Cornmarket Press Facsimile, 1970.)

The series of acting editions originally called Dolby’s British Theatre became Cumberland’s British Theatre. The text is almost the same, while the Dolby stage directions are condensed. A cast list for Covent Garden, dated 1828 and headed by Kean, is added alongside that of 1824. What is new is the introduction by George Daniel, a piece of serious criticism with quotations and stage history, and contemporary comment on J. P. Kemble and Edmund Kean. D. G.’s Remarks first appeared in some 1826 editions of Dolby’s, where they are paginated for the later edition.

14. Pattie, 1839: The Dramatic Works of Shakspere; After the Most Correct Stage Copies, and Approved Readings; with Notes, Glossary, and A Life of the Author.…Part V. King Lear. London: J. Pattie…Covent Garden. 1839 [pp. 295–374]. (The Popular Standard Library Edition of Shakspere. Dedicated, with Permission, to W. C. Macready, Esq.)
DP: Macready, Faucit, Horton (Fool)

Pattie seems to be the first acting edition based almost entirely on Shakespeare’s play rather than on Tate’s. (Fourteen lines of Tate’s Gloster, The Fight grows hot…, 5.3.6–12, 17–23, are added to 5.2.) Pattie is unique. With a DP for Covent Garden, 1839, the edition clearly owes its existence to Macready’s groundbreaking production of the previous year, including his restoration of the part of the Fool. But in many respects Pattie harks back to the promptbook for Macready’s 1834 production, which was based on Shakespeare’s text, but still minus the Fool. Most important, Pattie contains a shortened version of 3.7, the blinding scene, albeit with the SD Gloucester is taken out by the Servants inserted in the middle of 2142, between Giue me some helpe and O cruell, O ye Gods! It was not until 1838 that Macready inaugurated the 19th-c. omission of the blinding. Thus Pattie is the only 19th-c. acting edition that includes both the Fool and the blinding scene (with the exception of Flower’s later Memorial Theatre Edition, which prints the blinding dialogue in small type, indicating that it was omitted onstage). Typically, Pattie’s 3.7 retains more lines than Macready’s 1834 promptbook. Pattie is also the first acting edition since Garrick (and the only one in the 19th c. other than Flower’s) to print Rowe’s SD for Gloucester at 2480, He leaps, and falls along, even though it is not in Macready’s promptbooks. Like Macready, Pattie omits the ensuing dialogue on suicide.

While many individual lines are omitted, Pattie is structurally more complete than the much more widely printed Lacy’s (see No. 16), retaining the end of 3.6 from Q (2056+1–2056+18), about 75 lines of 3.7, most of 4.3 (from Q), all of 4.5, and Edgar and Gentleman in 4.6 (2650–62). Many of Pattie’s omissions, though not all, are the same as Tate’s. Pattie omits the end of 1.1, the end of 1.4, Kent’s That such a slaue as this… (1145–61 from 2.2), the end of 2.4 (1588–613), the Fool’s song at the end of 3.2 (1734–49), the end of 3.7 in Q, the post-suicide dialogue (2481–524), the beginning of 4.7, the end of 4.7 in Q, Edgar on meeting Kent (3168+), and the deaths of Goneril and Regan (3169–80). Lear’s curse is transposed (786–803 follows 830), in conjunction with the omission of Lear’s first exit (809–11) and most of 1.5, except for 899–906, which is transposed ahead to 2.4. Pattie does not have Macready’s condensation of Act 3, but prints 3.4 to 3.7 as four separate scenes, with only a few lines of 3.4 inserted into 3.6. It is possible, however, that the editor chose not to print these complex transpositions—like Flower, who printed 3.4 to 3.7 sequentially, while noting that Macready’s condensed version was still current onstage. The familiar costume list in Pattie is from Dolby/Cumberland.

15. Modern Standard Drama, 1848: King Lear. A Tragedy in Five Acts. By William Shakspeare. With the Stage Business, Casts of Characters, Costumes, Relative Positions, etc. New York: John Douglas…1848. (Modern Standard Drama, Edited by John W. S. Hows, No. LXXI. Reprinted by Wm. Taylor & Co., N.Y. and Baltimore, n.d.)
DP: Kean, West (DL, 1824); Forrest, Wallack (Broadway, 1848); Booth, Burke (Arch St., Phila.)

This widely published American acting edition is the direct heir of Dolby/Cumberland—i.e., Elliston’s hybrid of Tate’s first four acts and Shakespeare’s tragic ending. In a new introduction, John W. S. Hows praises the restorations of the great Macready but concludes: The Modern Standard Drama, being a faithful transcript of plays as they are acted, we have necessarily taken Tate’s alteration as our text book.
16. Lacy’s, 1857?: King Lear. A Tragedy, In Five Acts, by William Shakespeare. Thomas Hailes Lacy…London [n.d.]. (Lacy’s Acting Edition of Plays, vol. 31.)
DP: Macready, Faucit
Engraving: R. Smirke/R. Sherratt: Lear and Cordelia [4.7]

The major acting edition in England at the mid-century, Lacy’s probably reflects Macready’s mature stage version, even though the DP still lists the historic Covent Garden production of 25 Jan. 1838, with Miss P. Horton as the Fool. This is the first acting edition based completely on Shakespeare’s text, albeit with many of the by now familiar omissions and transpositions. Lacy’s makes many more small restorations than Pattie (No. 14), but Lacy’s sizable omissions make it the same overall length. (Halstead (1983, 13:467) notes that Lacy’s acting editions generally included more text than was performed onstage, and that Lacy’s Lr. retains more text than Macready’s promptbooks. But only 26 lines are marked with asterisks, indicating that they are usually omitted.) The most significant new omission is the majority of 3.7, the blinding scene, from Gloucester’s entrance at 2088 to the end. Lacy’s also introduced Macready’s consolidation of Act 3: various lines from 3.6 are transposed back into 3.4, and 3.5 is combined with the beginning of 3.7. In these Act 3 alterations, Macready not only followed Tate’s outline, but even used some of his text. The dialogue after Gloucester’s suicide attempt (2481–525) is omitted in Lacy’s, as in Pattie’s; but Lacy’s also omits the leap, reverting to Colman’s (and Kemble’s) use of Lear’s entrance as an interruption. To lengthen 5.2, instead of using Tate’s language, Lacy’s borrows from Shakespeare’s 4.6, how stiffe is my vild sence (2733–9).

Lacy’s, like Pattie, omits the end of 1.1, the end of 1.4, the end of 2.4, the end of 3.2, the end of 3.6 (from Q), the end of 4.7, and Edgar on meeting Kent in 5.3. Unlike Pattie, Lacy’s also omits all of 4.3 (from Q), 2650–62 from 4.6, and most of 4.5, except for several lines of Regan’s, which, in the manner of Tate, are transposed back to 4.2 and given to Goneril. Lacy’s restores a few passages omitted by Pattie: most of 1.5 (transposing 882–919 ahead to 2.4, following 1278), the beginning of 4.7, and the Gentleman with a bloody knife and news of the deaths of Goneril and Regan (3169–80). The other transpositions are similar to those in Pattie (and Tate’s History): Lear’s curse is moved to the end of Act 1, and his It were a delicate…kill (2626–9) to the end of 4.6.

17. Charles Kean, 1858: Shakespeare’s Tragedy of King Lear, Arranged for Representation at The Princess’s Theatre, with Historical and Explanatory Notes, by Charles Kean, F.S.A., As First Performed on Saturday, April 17, 1858…London [n.d.]. (Cornmarket Press Facsimile, 1970.)
DP: Charles Kean, Kate Terry

While this version is similar to Lacy’s, Kean made even more omissions of Shakespearean text, many in small increments, perhaps to leave time onstage for his elaborate scenic effects. He omitted all of 3.5 (Cornwall and Bastard) and the blinding in 3.7 (except for Steward’s lines on Dover, 2074–9, transposed ahead into 4.2), 4.5 (Regan and Steward), and the short 5.2 (Edgar and Gloucester). Like Macready, he omitted the end of 1.1, the end of 1.4, the end of 2.4, all of 4.3 and 4.5, the post-suicide dialogue in 4.6, and the beginning of 4.7. In addition to the basic Tate-Macready transpositions, after the omission of the blinding, Kean transposed the first two scenes of Act 4, in order to announce Gloucester’s blinding before Edgar meets him. Like Elliston, Kean opened Act 5 with the reconciliation scene. Each of the five acts is followed by Historical Notes, in an effort to place and date the action.

18. Edwin Forrest Edition, 1860: King Lear. No. 1 of the Edwin Forrest Edition of Shakspearian Plays, correctly marked, with the kind permission of The Eminent Tragedian, from his own prompt book, and as performed by him at Niblo’s Garden, New York, under the management of James M. Nixon, Esq. W. A. Moore & C. S. Bernard, Niblo’s Garden, and the American Dramatic Institute…N.Y. (1860)

This version, though broadly similar to the Modern Standard Drama (i.e., Dolby/ Cumberland), departs from it significantly enough to make it unique. In this Forrest edition, the publishers thank him not only for the use of his promptbooks but for his personal revision in proof, before going to press. However, despite the innovations of his rival Macready, Forrest’s version is an old-fashioned hybrid of Tate’s play and the tragic ending. The SDs are the same as in Dolby/Cumberland (and MSD), and the text is similar—though not the same—for the first three acts. Like Pattie, Forrest restored Edgar’s Q-only soliloquy at the end of 3.6 (2056+5–+18), but he transposed it back to follow Lear’s Act 3 exit in Tate (3.3.170), noting: When Lear is carried off Edgar enters, and speaks this speech from the original text. Forrest omitted the blinding, but used some Shakespearean text at the end of Act 3—three lines of 3.5 (1979, 1982–3), yoked to the beginning of 3.7. He used a version of Kean’s transposition of 4.1 and 4.2, conflating Tate’s text with Shakespeare’s language after the Messenger enters (2313). He omitted the end of Tate’s 4.2 (65–110), as well as Gloucester’s leap and the following dialogue. He finally switched to Shakespeare’s text in Act 5, which he cut heavily, omitting the long beginning of 5.1 (2847–78), the Bastard’s soliloquy, and, in 5.3, dialogues of Cordelia and Lear, and the Bastard and the Captain (2938–2981+2); most of the speeches of Goneril and Regan, and their deaths; and Edgar on meeting Kent. Forrest ended with Lear (3283), plus one line, Breake hart… (3285), which he gave to Edgar.

19. French’s Standard Drama, before 1878: King Lear. A Tragedy In Five Acts. By William Shakespeare. With the Stage Business, Casts of Characters, Costumes, Relative Positions, etc. New York: Samuel French Publisher [n.d.]. (French’s Standard Drama, No. LXXI.)

This is French’s repackaging of the Modern Standard Drama (and the early French’s American Drama), complete with the Hows introduction and three cast lists. From French’s name and address on the title page of later editions, it is evident that most extant editions date later than 1878 and are later than this one. Thus the standard American acting edition well into the second half of the 19th c. was the old Elliston/Kean 1824 hybrid of Tate’s first four acts and Shakespeare’s tragic ending.
20. French’s Acting Edition, 1872–78?: King Lear. A Tragedy, In Five Acts, By William Shakespeare. London: Samuel French…[n.d]. (French’s Acting Edition (Late Lacy’s).)

This is French’s English edition—literally, Late Lacy’s on the new cover, the American publisher French having bought the London company Lacy’s in 1872. Thus French’s Acting Edition contains Macready’s version of Shakespeare’s Lr. and is therefore very different from the Tate-Shakespeare hybrid that was being published at the same time in New York as French’s Standard Drama. (After 1872, both FSD and FAE give NY and London addresses.) The DP still cites Macready and Horton at Covent Garden, 1838.
21. Edwin Booth’s Prompt-Book, 1878: The Prompt-Book. Edited by William Winter. Shakespeare’s Tragedy of King Lear, As presented by Edwin Booth. New York…1878.

This is Booth’s late Lr., subsequent to several hand-marked promptbooks. Winter’s introduction notes the gradual movement away from Tate’s play. The text of this version is entirely Shakespeare, but the demands of the current stage make it a faithful condensation. A unique version, with heavy omissions and transpositions, Booth’s is closest to Charles Kean’s. The text omits 3.1, 3.7, the beginning of 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, the post-suicide dialogue, and the beginning of 4.7. It also omits so many passages at the end of the play that Booth’s is the shortest version of Shakespeare’s Act 5: the beginning of 5.1, 5.2, the beginning of 5.3, all the Goneril-Regan-Albany dialogue, Edgar on Gloucester as well as on Kent, the sisters’ deaths, and the last 12 lines. In the first four acts, however, Booth omitted fewer lines than Kean. Booth used the standard transpositions, but was the only one to follow Tate’s transposition of 2.1 and 2.2, combining the two Cornwall scenes. Winter (1915, pp. 448–9) later wrote, although I edited Booth’s Prompt Books,…I did not always approve the cuts and transpositions of the text that he elected to make.…In preparing King Lear for the stage I should make considerable restorations. Still, Winter defended his use of cuts, transpositions, and the omission of horrible business or vulgar words, saying, Some modification of the language and the business of even Shakespeare’s stupendous tragedy of King Lear is essential in the present day (p. 367).
22. Flower, 1883: King Lear: A Tragedy, by William Shakespeare. Edited by C. E. Flower. London: Samuel French…[n.d.]. (The Memorial Theatre Edition. Printed in Stratford-upon-Avon.)

This is one of a series edited by the founder of the Stratford Festival, Charles Edward Flower, which presented Shakespeare’s plays as performed in the Memorial Theatre toward the end of the 19th c. Lr. was first performed there in 1883, starring William Creswick; but while Flower at one point transcribed a Creswick promptbook, Flower’s edition differs from it. His brief but sophisticated introduction discusses omissions and transpositions onstage, including not only Tate’s, but the Folio’s alteration and abridgement of the Quarto. In the second edition (n.d.), Flower says that the goal of the series is to present the original text in its entirety, using the device of printing the material usually omitted onstage in smaller type: This [edition] may, indeed, serve as a substitute for the traditional acting editions, which were often most carelessly cut, and which have been entirely discarded in the admirable revivals of late years. The stage omissions in this Lr., however, are indicated on an already bowdlerized text, Flower explaining that offensive language has been omitted or softened. More important, Flower notes that even at this late date, Macready’s version…is the one usually acted, and the Stratford text is clearly based on it. Still, this is an independent version, with some minor omissions and even more restorations that differ from those in both Pattie and Lacy’s. Flower echoes Pattie more closely in the first half of the play, Lacy’s in the second half. In the introduction, he approves of the yoking of 3.4 and 3.6 printed in Lacy’s, but objects to the multiple minor transpositions in these scenes. Flower printed 3.4 to 3.7 sequentially, but set 3.5 and 3.7 (the blinding) in small type (usually omitted), with a note that sometimes fragments of these scenes are transposed forward (as in Lacy’s). Noting that the Folio itself made omissions, Flower followed Lacy’s in omitting Q-only passages that Pattie retained, such as the end of 3.6 and all of 4.3. Flower’s edition also differs from Pattie in omitting 4.5 and part of 4.6 (2647–62), so that his structure is more like Lacy’s.

23. Henry Irving’s Lyceum, 1892: King Lear, A Tragedy in Five Acts, by William Shakespeare, As Arranged for the Stage by Henry Irving, and Presented at The Lyceum Theatre, on November 10th, 1892. London: Nassau Steam Press, Ltd. 1892.
DP: Irving, Ellen Terry

Having published a complete works, The Henry Irving Shakespeare, in 1889, Irving here explains: This version…has been made for practical use on the stage, the play being necessarily reduced to reasonable length to suit the exigencies of the present time. In the curtailment, all superfluous horrors have been omitted. Irving thus omitted all of 3.7 (the blinding) and the suicide leap. But while his substantially cut version is closest to Charles Kean’s, the Lyceum Lr. is unique. It omits 3.5, but retains 3.4 and 3.6 as separate scenes, unlike Tate and Macready, who inserted parts of 3.6 into 3.4. Irving’s unique revision of Act 4 starts with Kean’s transposition of 4.2 and 4.1, then moves to 4.6, then to 4.3, omitting 4.4 and 4.5, and ends with 4.7. Though Irving made numerous minor omissions, especially in 5.3, several of his restorations are unusual in this era. The Lyceum is the only 19th-c. edition other than Pattie to restore most of 4.3. Irving also retained lines at the end of 1.1, in the mock trial, in the post-suicide dialogue (2489–93), and some of the sisters’ deaths. Cutting even more than Kean, Irving also omitted parts of 1.4 (660–98) and 3.2 (1694–1713), all of 3.3 (Gloucester and Edmund), and all of 4.4 (Cordelia’s return).
Irving’s was the last of these published acting editions for 75 years.

24. Stratford, 1932 (W. Bridges-Adams directs Randle Ayrton): King Lear, 3 May 1932. Shakespeare and the Stage. Series 4. Prompt Books from the Shakespeare Centre Library, Stratford-upon-Avon. (Harvester Microform. Part 2, reel 35.)

Bridges-Adams’s 1931–2 production was the first important Lr. of the 20th c. In the promptbook, the great curse is not transposed, the blinding scene is intact, and Gloucester’s suicidal fall is followed by Shakespeare’s dialogue. But the director had used the same promptbook in 1924, and there are multiple markings on the printed Temple edition—e.g., 3.1 and 4.3 marked one way as completely omitted, the other way as partially omitted. In fact, while the artistic director at Stratford from 1919 to 1934 was nicknamed Unabridges-Adams for his newly inclusive texts, the more extensive omissions seem to belong to the later production. Still, there were no transpositions. Bridges-Adams even retained the dialogue after the curse, ending the long tradition of a curtain after the crescendo. He also broke ground by generally maintaining Shakespeare’s alternation of large scenes and small ones, notably the indoor-outdoor sequence in Act 3. Omitted in one or both versions are: Lear’s reentry after the curse (809–29); various of the Fool’s rhymes (e.g., 678–91, 1322–7, 1680–7, 1734–49); Edgar’s soliloquy from Q at the end of 3.6 (2056+5–+18); all of 4.5; Gentleman and Edgar in 4.6 (2646–59); the end of 4.7 (2843+1–+11); the beginning of 5.1 (2847–63); the short 5.2 (2920–37); and Edgar’s 5.3 accounts of Gloucester and Kent (3137–3168+18). Hundreds of other lines are omitted throughout, mostly in cuts of one to ten lines. Five acts with curtain drops are marked. The interval is after 3.7, the blinding, with the Quarto ending (2176+1–+9) omitted.
25. John Houseman directs Louis Calhern, National Theatre, N.Y., 25 Dec. 1950 (Shattuck promptbook No. 110)

Houseman’s promptbook, a typescript, omits only one complete scene, the short 5.2 (2920–37), but there are several long omissions and numerous small ones, more in the first half of the play than in the second. Houseman also made several transpositions, a few of them unique. He omitted speeches by the Bastard (1001–16) and Kent (1146–62, 1303–27, 1627–1638+4), by the Fool at the end of 3.2 (1734–49), the end of 4.7 (2843+1–+11), and Edgar on Kent (3163–3168+14). Cordelia’s 4.4 reappearance is omitted, except for ô deere father… (2373–81), which is transposed ahead to the end of the reconciliation scene (4.7), following 2843. Lear’s two curses are transposed, along with additional minor transpositions: 785 is followed by 812–30, 786–808, 834–6, 831–2, and 856–72. Lear does not reenter at 809, and the line …fiftie of my followers… (810) is transposed back, before the great curse, to follow 758. Lines 837–55 are also omitted. Another complex set of transpositions and omissions reorders the deaths of Goneril and Reagan (3168–99), whose bodies are not brought onstage.

26. Stratford, 1962 (Peter Brook directs Paul Scofield): King Lear, 6 November 1962. Shakespeare and the Stage. Series 4. Prompt Books from the Shakespeare Centre Library, Stratford-upon-Avon. (Harvester Microform. Part 2, reel 36.)

The promptbook for Brook’s existential Lr. omits only 355 lines, most of them unique to the Quarto. Only six lines are omitted in Act 1, and the only complete scene omitted is Q’s 4.3. Again the interval is after the blinding, with the good servants at the end of 3.7 (2176+1–+9) pointedly omitted. Brook’s other sizable omissions are most of the Bastard’s speech at 996–1015; the Fool’s song at the end of 3.2 (1734–49); Edgar’s When we our betters see at the end of 3.6 (2056+5–+18); Gentleman and Edgar in 4.6 (2646–62); and, in 5.3, 29 lines including Edgar’s account of Kent (3163–74), and the 23 lines of confusion that precede Lear’s final entrance (3192–215).
27. French’s Acting Edition, 1967: King Lear, By William Shakespeare, London, Samuel French Limited, 1967. The play produced, edited and illustrated by George Skillan.

After the mid-20th-c. revival of Lr., French published this heavily annotated acting edition on a complete, conflated text. The extensive commentary, which is critical as well as directorial, leaves little to the imagination.
28. BBC TV, 1982 (Jonathan Miller, director): King Lear. The BBC TV Shakespeare. London, 1983.
DP: Michael Hordern, Brenda Blethyn

The published acting version of this television production is marked with the limited omissions and transpositions that Miller made on the Peter Alexander edition (1951). Only about 250 lines are omitted, including all of 4.3, the only complete scene. Other sizable omissions are lines of Edmund and Gloucester in 2.1 (980–1014), almost half of 3.1, Edgar on Kent (3163–3168+18), and other lines in Act 5. There are only minor transpositions of a few lines.
29. New York Shakespeare Festival, 1996.

This unpublished script for the 25 Jan. 1996 production directed by Adrian Hall and starring F. Murray Abraham has omissions marked on a xeroxed text of Harbage’s Penguin edition. The only transposition divides the short 5.2, moving the first half of the scene (2920–25) back before 5.1, to give Edgar time to go to battle and return. More than 600 lines are omitted. The only full scene omitted is 4.3, but other passages unique to Q are also omitted: Edgar at the end of 3.6 (2056+5–+18), the end of 3.7 (2176+1–+9), Edgar on Kent in 5.3 (3163–3168+15). The numerous smaller omissions are mostly of difficult lines, though Kent and Fool lose 25 lines in 2.4 (1303–27). There are many small cuts in 5.3. Only 30 lines altogether are cut from Goneril and Regan. Hall, who had directed Lr. twice, invited the cast to work on the omissions. John Dias, longtime dramaturge at the NYSF, said that every promptbook depended on the actors on hand—an intriguing note on which to end this survey.

div.head: Transpositions and Omissions
div.p: This section describes the transpositions and omissions used in stage versions over the centuries, as well as their likely motives. (Many of the lines at issue are discussed in greater detail in the Commentary Notes.) While transpositions became less common in the 20th c., as directors accepted Shakespeare’s fluid alternation of scenes, Lr., like most of the plays in the canon, has always been cut for the stage. From at least the time of the Folio version, there was an effort to reduce the number of scenes, or dialogues within scenes—either by simply omitting a passage, or by transposing a passage to connect with a similar one, thereby merging two scenes into one. Frequently, an omission was made in conjunction with a transposition. A reduced number of locations became even more important with the advent of changing scenery and closing curtains. At the end of the 19th c., Flower (ed. 1883, 2nd ed., n.p.) wrote: Shakespeare’s plays, which in his days were, probably, simply declaimed without much stage action, or with no waits for change of scenery, are too long for the patience of modern audiences. The heavily cut Memorial Theatre version still ran four hours. In America, Winter (1915, p. 412) thought Shakespeare’s plays should be reduced to three hours’ traffic: There are, indeed, many changes of scene, and for the modern stage cuts and a few transpositions are essential.

Many of the enduring omissions and transpositions originated with Tate’s radical alteration. Others began with Colman and Garrick, though their partial restorations of Shakespeare’s language had no direct heirs, but were followed onstage by Kemble’s reversion to Tate’s History. The pre-modern text of Lr. was Macready’s, a version of which was published by J. Pattie in 1839, the first edition since the Folio to be almost wholly based on Shakespeare’s language, albeit with omissions and transpositions. A somewhat different version of Macready’s Lr. was more widely published by Lacy’s, and as late as 1883, Flower said that Macready’s version still prevailed onstage (see No. 22). Yet much of the structure of Macready’s Lr. had its inspiration in Tate’s History.

div.head: Transpositions
div.p: Gentleman (ed. 1773), defending Garrick’s version in Bell’s edition, described Shakespeare’s tragedy as in many places, too diffuse, and in others obscure. To tighten and clarify the structure, Tate transposed dialogue (see ). His transpositions endured, even after his language was abandoned. A hundred and fifty years later, Macready’s Shakespearean text still incorporated most of Tate’s major transpositions. The exception is the transposition of the Bastard’s soliloquy to open the play, which was used only by the Tate-based versions of Kemble, Inchbald, Elliston, Oxberry, Dolby/Cumberland, and Forrest. As Flower (ed. 1883, 2nd ed., n.p.) explained a half century after Macready’s time, The exigencies of modern scenic representation require the occasional transposition of scenes.

Tate’s most enduring transposition moved Lear’s great curse forward, to the end of Act 1—a tradition that died so hard that in the mid-20th c. it was still being defended by Donald Wolfit (ed. 1956, pp. 7–8) as the correction of a textual error. George Daniel (ed. 1826, p. 8), describing Kemble’s performance, wrote: But the climax of all acting was the curse upon Goneril. Regardless of who played Lear, this transposition, usually made in conjunction with the omission of a hundred less dramatic lines, ends the act with the emotional power of Lear’s most famous speech—allowing for applause or a curtain, and sometimes both. While there are many variations, the basic transposition moves the great curse, harke [F: Heare] Nature…child (789–803), forward, to follow Lear’s fathers cursse (814–29); the remainder of Act 1 is omitted (the end of 1.4, 830–72, between Goneril and Albany, and all of 1.5, 874–925, mostly Lear and the Fool). The transposition also usually eliminates Lear’s awkward (and anticlimactic) exit (803) and reentry (809). In The History, Lear starts to exit at 1.2.71 (785), but meets Albany entering.

Colman, Garrick, and Kemble all followed Tate in transposing the great curse to follow the father’s curse and omitting the rest of the act; Lear does not exit between the curses. There are minor differences between Colman’s and Garrick’s selection of Shakespearean lines in this passage, while the great curse is one of Kemble’s few major restorations of Shakespearean language. Only Tate used a few lines of the Goneril-Albany dialogue (based on 848–9) after Lear’s exit at the end of the great curse. In the 19th c., Macready, Charles Kean, Booth, and Irving all still transposed the great curse and omitted the end of 1.4 and Lear’s mid-scene exit. But with the inclusion of the Fool, Macready retained some of 1.5 (899–906 in Pattie; 882–919 in Lacy’s), which he transposed ahead to 2.4 (following 1278), a similar scene; Act 1 still ended on the great curse. Kean, Booth, and Irving followed suit, though there are again variations in line selections. Bridges-Adams’s novel solution to the problem of the curses was to omit Lear’s exit and the entire father’s curse (809–29), though he omitted only five lines from 1.5, ending on Lear’s Come boy (922). As late as 1950, Houseman still transposed the curse.

The transpositions at the end of Act 3 are more complex. Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.) observed that Macready’s version takes great liberty with the third act. To reduce changes of scenery, Macready made two scenes out of four. First he yoked two scenes with Lear in the storm, 3.4 and 3.6. This outdoor scene was followed by an indoor scene that yoked 3.5 and a shortened 3.7, both with Cornwall. The consolidation, of course, was very much like Tate’s, whose basic structural change here was to insert two sections of 3.6 back into 3.4. In Tate’s 3.3 (Storm still), first the Lear-Edgar dialogue from Shakespeare’s 3.6 (2007–38) is transposed back to yoke with the Lear-Edgar dialogue in Shakespeare’s 3.4 (inserted after 1919). The scene continues with the end of Shakespeare’s 3.4 (1895–1968), then ends with eight reordered lines from the end of Shakespeare’s 3.6 (2033–42), concluding with Lear’s exit, Weele…morning. In The History, this storm scene is followed by Edmund’s attempted rape of Cordelia (3.4), which is in turn followed by Tate’s 3.5, a combination of Shakespeare’s 3.5 (Cornwall and Edmund) and 3.7 (the blinding).

Colman, Garrick, and Macready (and of course all the editions based on their versions) used a similar combination of Shakespeare’s 3.4 and 3.6, followed by some combination of Shakespeare’s 3.5 and 3.7. (Only Garrick separated the two scenes with Tate’s 3.4 rape scene.) As for Colman, who generally restored more Shakespearean language than Garrick did, this Act 3 consolidation is one of the sections where he hewed closer to Tate’s text. Macready’s version (in Lacy’s) still closely parallels Tate’s, especially in the outdoor scene; at the end of the scene—which is the end of Macready’s Act 3—almost the same lines are used, in slightly different order (Tate: 2047, 2050–1, 2033–4, 2041–2; Macready: 2033–5, 2047–51, 2041–2). Lacy’s, in fact, follows the History so closely here that it is one of the rare passages that makes use of some of Tate’s transitional lines (3.3.89–90, 102–3, and, separately, 104). Booth used his own radical reordering of selected lines—after 1951: 2014+16, 2014+6, 2014+21–2, 2027–32, 2035–7, 2004–6, 1954–5, 1966–8, 2037–5. Irving did not transpose these scenes. Instead, he ran Lear’s storm scenes in sequence: 3.1; 3.2 and 3.4 as one scene, followed by 3.6; he simply omitted the three Cornwall scenes—3.3, 3.5, and 3.7.

Macready used a few lines of Shakespeare’s 3.5 as the opening of Act 4, yoked directly to the beginning of 3.7 (2060–87). Flower marked 3.5 as usually omitted, as it was by Kean and Irving. Booth, like Macready, used a few lines from each scene, though not the same ones. Kean virtually eliminated 3.7, loosely borrowing a few lines of the Steward (2074–9) and transposing them forward to 4.2. For all of them, the great departure from Tate was the elimination of most of 3.7, the blinding of Gloucester (see ). Toward the end of the 19th c., Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.) wrote that he saw no occasion for the six or eight transpositions of the dialogue in these scenes. He printed 3.4, 3.5, and a truncated 3.6 as discrete scenes. (He also printed 3.5 and 3.7 in small type, indicating that they were usually omitted onstage.) The big Act 3 transpositions eventually ceased. Houseman ended Act 3 on Gloucester’s Come, come away (2056), transposing ten lines of Edgar’s When we our betters see (2056+5–+18) back a few lines, to follow the Fool’s And Ile go to bed at noone (2043). Occasionally, other scenes in Act 3 have been moved: Houseman transposed Kent’s description of the storm in 3.2 (Things…force [F: feare], 1694–1701) to the very beginning of Act 3, and Booth, who omitted 3.1, transposed 3.2 and 3.3.

Tate’s Act 4 transpositions were more modest, as were those of later versions, with the exception of Irving’s. Tate’s transposition of a few lines each from 4.4 and 4.5 resulted from his omission of those small scenes (). In 4.6, at Lear’s exit, Tate transposed It were a delicate stratagem…kill, kill, kill (2626–9) forward a few lines, to follow 2643, omitting Then theres life int…Sa, sa, sa, sa (2644–5), allowing the king a more dramatic—and dignified—exit. Colman and Garrick, restoring Shakespeare’s language, used Tate’s transposition. In Lacy’s, Macready made the same basic transposition, which was followed by Kean and Booth. In fact, the only popular transposition that does not echo Tate is Charles Kean’s transposition of 4.1 and 4.2. In versions that omit the blinding, this change allows the Gentleman (2312–47) to tell Albany—and the audience—about Gloucester’s eyes (and Cornwall’s death) before Edgar meets his father poorlie,leed (2189). Booth and Irving followed Kean. But Irving’s rearrangement of Act 4 was unique. He transposed the long 4.6 back, to follow 4.2 and 4.1. Kent and Gentleman in 4.3 came next, announcing Cordelia’s return, which followed immediately in the reconciliation scene (4.7).

Transpositions have also been used to deal with the impossibly short 5.2, in which Edgar runs to the battle and back, leaving his father in the shaddow of this bush (F: Tree, 2921). In Lacy’s, Macready transposed Gloucester’s how stiffe is my vild sence… (2733–9) from the end of 4.6 to 5.2, to follow his Grace goe with you sir (2925), to give Edgar time offstage. Again the concept was Tate’s, who wrote his own 19-line addition (5.3.5–23; see ). The scene still provokes alterations: The only transposition in the 1996 New York Shakespeare Festival version moved the first five lines of the scene back before 5.1, giving Edgar real time to leave and return.

div.head: Omissions
div.p: The textual omissions fall into five categories: material that is exclusive to the Quarto and omitted from F; the small scenes first omitted by Tate; controversial matter in the blinding of Gloucester and his suicide attempt, as well as in scenes dramatizing the wickedness of Goneril and Regan; the multiple omissions in Act 5; and minor omissions for a variety of substantive and stylistic reasons.

div.head: Quarto Lines
div.p: One obvious category of omissions is material that is unique to the poorly printed 1608 Quarto. Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.) began his introduction by deploring stage adaptations: Probably in Shakespeare’s own days the play was altered and considerably abridged, for we find that in the first folio, while some lines are inserted, many passages (including one whole scene) which appear in the earlier quartos are cut out. Whatever the origin of the Folio version of Lr., the 1623 text lacks about 300 lines that are in Q, two thirds of them grouped in discrete segments. The Folio Lr., whose differences from the Quarto probably reflect the company’s stage version, is, in a way, the first acting edition—though like many later acting editions, it probably contains more lines than were acted onstage.

Tate based his History on the Folio version, except for a few emendations from the Quarto in Act 1, such as the addition of to loue my father all (110+1). Thus modern readers used to a conflated Lr. should keep in mind that Tate’s highly influential play, like F, had no 4.3 (Kent and Gentleman), no mock trial in 3.6, no good servants at the end of 3.7. Tate also omitted two small scenes containing only a few lines unique to Q: 1.3 (Goneril and Steward) and 3.1 (Kent and Gentleman). Colman and Garrick, who had access to the 18th-c. editions of Theobald, Johnson, and Capell, used a bit more of the Quarto. By the 19th c., when all nontheatrical texts were full conflations of Q and F, producers did not necessarily know the provenance of specific passages. Yet in the introduction to Lr. in the Complete Works edited by actor-manager Samuel Phelps (1851–4, 2:339), he says of the differences between Q and F: The variation…may be reasonably accounted for by presuming that as usual the folio was reprinted from the prompter’s acting copy of the play, and that a certain judicious condensation had been adopted to render the delivery of the speeches less fatiguing to the performers. The traditional omission of Quarto material onstage endured well into the 20th c., with the gradual exception of the mock trial. By 1935, with the publication of editions like the New Temple, which identified Q-only and F-only passages, and with the revision of Granville-Barker’s Preface, in which he discussed the relative merits of the Q-F discrepancies, no self-respecting director could claim ignorance of the major differences.

Scene 4.3 (2347+1–+56), in which Kent and a Gentleman discuss Cordelia’s return, is the only complete scene unique to Q, and that has given producers an excuse to cut it, even in comparatively complete modern productions like Miller’s. The scene is also one of those quiet dialogues of exposition rather than action that were omitted from the time of Tate. There are also narrative problems: Kent repeating an explanation of his disguise, as well as several loose ends—the movements of the King of France, the single mention of M. la Far, and the placement of Lear ith towne. Dramatically, the rhetorical description of Cordelia’s emotions can seem unnecessary compared with her own smiles and teares in subsequent scenes. Among the early acting versions, only Colman’s included 4.3, using half its lines and omitting France and la Far (2347+2–+9) and much of Cordelia (2347+20–+38). In the 19th c., Pattie printed most of 4.3 while Lacy’s omitted it completely, reflecting either Macready’s variations or an editor’s reluctance to cut a complete scene. All later 19th-c. editions omitted 4.3, except Irving’s. Using all but 11 lines of it, he moved the scene ahead, between 4.6 and 4.7, as a reintroduction to Cordelia, having omitted 4.4. Bridges-Adams tried 4.3 both ways, fully and partially omitted. Houseman omitted most of the scene, while Brook omitted it completely. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 228), calling it a carpentered scene, spoke for the many who do without it: I could better believe that Shakespeare cut it than wrote it. At the New York Shakespeare Festival, where Adrian Hall made all other omissions with input from the cast, 4.3 was his only mandatory cut.

Three of Shakespeare’s quiet scene codas are unique to the Quarto, and all are frequently omitted: the endings of 3.6, 3.7, and 4.7. The end of 3.6 (2056+1–+18) comprises Kent’s Oppressed nature sleepes and Edgar’s When we our betters see.… As Granville-Barker (1927, p. 227) noted, Edgar’s speech is dramatically redundant with a speech in 4.1, which is more appropriate as he is about to confront his blind father. Here it takes the spotlight off Lear’s exit from the storm. The end of 3.6 has been omitted in all versions except the following: in the 19th c., Pattie, which omits Kent (2056+1–+4), and Forrest, who omitted Kent and attached Edgar’s speech to the end of Tate’s 3.3; and in the 20th c., Houseman, who used half and transposed it back a few lines to follow 2043, and Miller, the only one to use all of it in place.

A more loaded passage is the end of 3.7 (2176+1–+9), Cornwall’s good servants after the blinding. In the post-Shakespearean theater, these moral beings potentially have the last words before the act-interval. They were of course omitted throughout the 19th c., along with the rest of the blinding scene (see ). Bridges-Adams, who in 1931–2 reinstated the blinding, omitted them before his interval. Brook did the same, in order to emphasize the horror of the blinding. Miller cut only 2176+5–+8. The end of 4.7 (2843+1–+11), Kent and Gentleman exchanging news, including the awkward rumor that Edgar had joined Kent in Germany, was widely omitted to allow Act 4 to end on the high point of the reconciliation scene. The passage was omitted in all versions through the 19th c., as well as by Bridges-Adams and Houseman.

In fact, the one substantial Quarto-only passage that directors have widely retained, at least in the 20th c., is the mock trial in 3.6 (2014+1–+30), Lear’s imagined arraignment of his eldest daughters. The passage is not in Tate’s History, probably because it is not in the Folio. It was not restored by Colman or Garrick, or by any of the Kemble line of adapters of Tate. At last Macready restored a third of the lines—but not the same ones in Pattie (mostly from the first half, 2014+1, +4–+5, +11–+16) and Lacy’s (all of the lines are Lear’s—2014+4, +6, +16–+18, +22, +26–9—and they are part of the transposition of 3.6 back into 3.4). But Kean used only three lines; Booth, nine. Flower used half of the passage, including lines not used in either Macready text (2014+23–5). By the end of the 19th c., Irving used most of the passage, omitting 2014+2–+3, +9–+13, +18–+20. It was not until the 20th c. that the complete mock trial was restored onstage. Bridges-Adams was the first to do so in 1931–2. Houseman omitted only Fool’s 2014+2–+3, Brook only 2014+14, and Miller 2014+19–+21. Occasionally, the mock trial is still omitted, as it was in the 1959 production at Stratford, for which director Glen Byam Shaw used the Folio text. The most obvious reason for the omission is time, the mock trial being part of a very long scene that was often combined with another long scene, 3.4. Also, as we shall see, early versions tended to reduce the roles of the wicked daughters. Finally, as suggested by the varied staging of this passage (Adrian Hall had the actors playing Goneril and Regan enter, briefly, as gauzily-covered nude apparitions), it is difficult to project the visions of a madman onstage, and it is conceivable that the mock trial, compelling as the text is, was omitted from the Folio because it was not immediately accessible to the audience.
Finally, as detailed below, Edgar’s Q-only description of the dying Kent (3168+1–+18) is among the many excisions in Act 5.

div.head: Small Scenes
div.p: The dozen small scenes or parts of scenes omitted from F by Tate were widely omitted in later versions, not only by his followers, but also by the restorers of Shakespeare’s text. These are Shakespeare’s quiet dialogues, transitions between scenes that are bigger in length, action, and dramatic intensity. Many small scenes are conversations between secondary characters who comment informally on the action, before or after major events or speeches. These passages are seen as dispensable because they are not necessary to the plot, and they are sacrificed because they are relatively undramatic. A minor example is the Edgar-Gentleman dialogue in 4.6 (2650–62, Do you heare ought of a battell toward…), Shakespeare’s transition between Lear’s exit and the killing of Oswald. The lines were omitted from every version through the 19th c., as well as by Bridges-Adams and Brook.

Some of these passages are codas to big scenes, and omitting them allows the scene to end on a more dramatic moment: the end of 1.1; the end of 1.4, in conjunction with 1.5; and the end of 2.4. The precedent, of course, is in the Folio’s omission of the scene codas unique to the Quarto. The end of 1.1 (310–32) is the Goneril-Regan dialogue after the opening court scene, in which they agree only to further thinke and doe something (331–2). Tate replaced it with the first dialogue between his lovers. Colman, so often the exception, restored it, but most later editors omitted it, possibly as anticlimactic to Cordelia’s farewell (With washt eyes, 293). After Tate, the scene was also cut in the general diminution of the roles of Goneril and Regan. A universal omission from Garrick through Flower, the end of 1.1 was restored only partially by Irving, Bridges-Adams (who omitted 318–30) and Houseman (omitted 327–30).

The next two common omissions are the end of 1.4 and 1.5, both eliminated from the time of Tate, in order to end the first act on the dramatic high point of Lear’s great curse. The end of 1.4 (831–72) is considered dispensable for several reasons: first, little is said that is not acted out later; second, 14 lines are only in the Folio; and third, the main character is Goneril, the target of many omissions. In its vulnerable position following Lear’s two curses, the passage was universally omitted through the 19th c. scene 1.5, a quiet dialogue between Lear and Fool, was likewise omitted by Tate’s followers. It was first restored, in part, by Macready (only 8 lines in Pattie, all but 12 in Lacy’s); but he transposed it ahead into 2.4 (following 1278), linking it with a similar Lear-Fool exchange. Booth’s 1.5 followed Lacy’s, Irving omitted a few more lines, Kean omitted even more, and Flower marked the whole scene as usually omitted. By the 20th c., Bridges-Adams omitted only three lines of 1.4 and four of 1.5, while Houseman cut eight lines from 1.5.

Similarly, the omission of the end of 2.4 (1587–1613), in which Cornwall tells the sisters twill be a storme, allows the act to end on a major speech of Lear’s, O reason not the deed [F: need] (1564), concluding on the crescendo of O foole I shall goe mad (1586). Tate used one line of decompression, ’Tis a wild Night, come out o’th’ Storm (2.5.188, based on 1612–13), but every one of his followers omitted it. The whole passage was universally omitted through the 19th c. Again, the substance of the dialogue (The King is in high rage, 1598) will be acted out, and the wicked sisters were often muted. The end of 2.4 was mostly restored by Bridges-Adams, who omitted 1588–97 (This house…return’d).

Four other dialogues are Shakespeare’s low-key preludes to major scenes, and omitting them allows the action to open more dramatically: the beginnings of 2.1, 4.7, and 5.1, and the whole of 3.1. Tate, typically, omitted the minor dialogue between Bastard and Curan at the beginning of 2.1 (928–42). The History has no Curan, and his news, at any rate, is dispensable: Cornwall’s approach is announced (twice) in the subsequent passage, and the rumors of likely warres…twixt the two Dukes are not only eare-bussing arguments, but are never realized. Colman, Forrest, and Booth omitted the whole passage. It was restored by Macready, and he, Kean, Irving, and Houseman cut only a few (different) lines in the middle.

Tate’s omission of 3.1, Kent and Gentleman in the storm, allowed the act to open more dramatically. Instead of the Gentleman’s description of the king Contending with the fretfull element (1619), the storm is introduced directly by Lear’s Blow wind (1656), bellowed against the accompanying sound and light show. Tate also eliminated further talk of the diuision…twixt Albany and Cornwall (1628–30), for which he later substituted a peasants’ rebellion. Garrick and Colman, and all of Tate’s followers, omitted the whole of 3.1.

Macready was the first to restore 3.1. But the scene still has so many problems that it is never restored altogether. First there is the textual complication of 20 lines unique to Q (1622+1–+8 and 1638+1–+12) and eight lines, possibly overlapping, unique to F (1631–8). Kent’s from France there comes a power | Into this scattered kingdome (1638+1–+2) may have been omitted from F for political reasons (see nn. 1631–1638+12, 1631–8, and 1638+1–+12). But Macready (and Flower) omitted the stylistically difficult F-only lines—Seruants…Which are to France the Spies and Speculations | Intelligent of our State and snuffes, and packings of the Dukes— and 1638+10–1643 (I am a…containes). Kean omitted a few more lines from each Q speech, and Irving omitted a few lines more than Kean. Even so, the conflated 3.1 is a conundrum, and it was completely eliminated by Forrest, who generally followed Tate’s text, as well as by Booth, who followed Shakespeare’s. Understandably, 3.1 is one of the scenes that Bridges-Adams tried both ways: either omitting it entirely, or only partially (cutting 20 lines, among them 1622+1–+8 and 1631–1638+1). The advice of Granville-Barker (1927, p. 226), to shorten this prelude to Lear’s great entrance, was followed by Houseman (who omitted 1629–1638+5), Brook (omitted 11 lines of Kent, among them 1634–1638+1), and even Miller (omitted 1618, 1622+1–+8, 1623–5, 1631–8, and 1648–53).

Tate also omitted the beginning of 4.7 (2745–60), Cordelia and Kent’s quiet prelude to the reconciliation scene. This omission became even more important when Colman and Garrick began the tradition of starting Act 5 with the reconciliation—Garrick using Tate’s text, Colman a combination of Tate’s and Shakespeare’s, beginning with O you kind Gods…father (2763–6). The reconciliation opens Act 5 in the versions of Kemble, Elliston, Dolby/Cumberland, Pattie, Kean, and Forrest, all of which omit the passage. Houseman omitted 2752–9.

Elliston, however, while mostly following Tate’s version of 4.7, used four Shakespearean lines from 4.4, All blest secrets…distresse (2366–9), which he transposed forward to open Act 5, as a lead-in to the reconciliation, while omitting the rest of 4.4. Even this combination may have been inspired by Tate. Tate omitted 4.4, the reappearance of Cordelia, since his Cordelia never disappears; but he transposed the first six lines (2351–6) back to his 4.2.65. Garrick and Kemble omitted the whole scene. While it was printed in both Pattie and Lacy’s, it was excised in Macready’s 1838 promptbook. Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.) notes with regret that 4.4 was sometimes still omitted in performance, as it was by Irving. Houseman used only the end (Cordelia and the messenger, 2372–81), but he transposed it far ahead, to follow the reconciliation at 2843.

div.head: Controversial Material
div.p: As extensive as Tate’s revisions were, in some substantive ways he was truer to Shakespeare than most other producers in retaining the play’s most controversial elements: the horror of Gloucester’s blinding, the improbability of his suicide attempt, and the viciousness and lechery of Goneril and Regan. Until well into the 20th c., this material was either toned down or omitted altogether.

div.head: The Blinding of Gloucester
div.p: Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159) thought the extrusion of Gloucester’s eyes…an act too horrid to be endured in dramatick exhibition; Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 97) considered it beyond the outermost mark and ne plus ultra of the dramatic. The blinding has been diminished more often than not, and as late as 1940 it was played after the interval at the Old Vic, to allow audience members to avoid it by returning late to their seats. Tate retained the incident, though he had Cornwall order his servants to do it. The stage direction reads: They put out his Eyes (3.5.46). Tate’s blinding scene was a short version of Shakespeare’s, but The History was to be the only published theatrical version of Lr. in which Gloucester was blinded onstage until the 20th c.

Colman and Garrick both followed Tate’s dialogue here, using Cornwall’s Slaves perform your Work (3.5.42). But their stage directions vastly altered the action, sending Gloucester offstage for the violence. In Colman’s edition, 43 is followed by Ex. Glo. and servants; when Glocester (sic) cries out at 45, he does so [without]. In Bell’s, at the Duke’s speech, They force Gloster off. They put out his eyes. Kemble, who moved the blinding scene to open Act 4, retained most of Tate’s dialogue and likewise did the deed offstage: The Servants take Gloster away. With Gloucester offstage, Kemble omitted his closing soliloquy, Tate’s 27-line version of 2160, All darke and comfortles, which Colman had also omitted; Garrick, who only shortened it, had to bring Gloucester back onstage. Kemble’s heirs—Inchbald, Elliston, Oxberry, Dolby/Cumberland, and Modern Standard Drama—followed him in retaining most of Tate’s blinding scene (minus the closing soliloquy) but moving the blinding itself offstage.

The horror of the blinding, of course, is not confined to the stage direction but permeates Shakespeare’s dramatic poetry: the scene is painful even if we do not see the gruesome act. Nineteenth-century producers experimented with the challenging material. Macready, in an 1834 promptbook, retained 34 of the 90 lines after Gloucester’s entrance, as well as most of the beginning of 3.7. Cornwall orders the servants to perform your work, and Gloster is dragged out. Pattie, the first published version of Macready’s restored Lr., retains an additional 20 lines. More significantly, Pattie is the only acting edition between the Folios and the 20th c. to include any of Shakespeare’s text of the blinding. (Pattie omits 2098, 2100–1, 2103–19, 2130–6, 2139–40.) Nevertheless, Pattie echoes Colman, Garrick, and Kemble in sending Gloucester offstage after 2142: Gloster is taken out by the Servants. Cornwall’s out vild Ielly lines (2158–9) are omitted, and Gloucester’s last four lines (2160–1, 2168–9) are said without. Phelps, too, struggled with the blinding. While he did not publish an acting edition, there is evidence in his mid-century promptbooks that he retained some of the dialogue and experimented with keeping the act onstage; in his 1845 promptbook (Folger), the servants bind Gloucester in a chair, his back being to the audience, and behind [center] pillar. In his Works (1851–4, 2:380), Phelps notes that the blinding took place on the secondary stage made use of in theatres at that time—that is, not in full view of the audience, but still onstage.

The radical change came with Macready’s mature version, which omitted the blinding dialogue completely—excising almost a hundred lines starting with Gloucester’s entrance (2088–2176+9), the single longest omission in Lacy’s. For the next hundred years, the entire episode was banished from published acting editions—except by Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.), who printed it in small type (meaning that it was usually omitted) and took for granted the impossibility of representing the terrible details of the blinding of Gloucester. Even when Macready omitted the blinding dialogue, he restored the beginning of 3.7 (2058–87), which opened his fourth act (Pattie and Lacy’s both omit only 2070 and 2075–7). Forrest used a version of Macready’s beginning of 3.7, but Kean and Booth used only a few lines, and Irving completely omitted 3.7.

Without the cruel and repulsive scene, the play produced by the Victorians was more sentimental. The omission also reduced the subplot, focusing the drama more directly on Lear. A secondary effect of omitting the blinding was the partial softening of Regan, who appears at her most vicious in 3.7. Tate had cut only some of her cruelty when he tightened the scene: both eyes are gouged at once (losing One side will mocke another, tother to, 2143), and Cornwall, instead of Regan, kills the rebellious servant. Tate retained a version of Regan breaking the news of Edmund’s treachery (thou calst on him that hates thee, 2165); but all of Tate’s followers omitted his If thy Eyes fail thee call for Spectacles (3.5.60). Colman’s limited restorations included the Cornwall-Regan exchange Wherefore to Douer? (2120–7) and her brutal Goe thrust him out at gates, and let him smell | his way to Douer (2170–1), which Tate had assigned to the Duke. But the major distinction is that Tate, Colman, and Garrick, as well as Kemble and his followers, all retained the blinding scene, while the 19th-c. restorers omitted it.

The blinding was not rehabilitated until the 20th c. The earliest Stratford promptbook with the scene is that of Bridges-Adams (1924, 1931/2). However, we know from reviews that some version of the scene, including fearful shrieks, was in Benson’s 1902 production, though it is possible that the actual blinding may have been obscured, or even done offstage. In any event, in 1931, presenting this by now unfamiliar play, Bridges-Adams thought it only fair to warn the squeamish that we are retaining the scene in which Gloucester’s eyes are put out (SCL scrapbook 24:70). He omitted only Gloucester’s rhetorical flourishes in 2131–7 (the steeled [F: Stelled] fires, etc.)—the same lines omitted by Tate in 1681, and by Miller in 1982—concluding with All cruels else subscrib’d, considered by Furness (ed. 1880, p. 223) the most puzzling phrase in this play. By the time of Granville-Barker’s 1940 production at the Old Vic, the evil and the violence were again front and center. Production notes by Hallam Fordham (1942, n.p.) read: Gloucester is brought in by servants. He is bound, and made to sit on a low stool in the front, centre, with his back to the audience.…Cornwall advances towards him and gouges out one of his eyes with his thumb.…This scene is played with vivid realism—so much so that some audience members were seen to grope towards the exits with unbecoming haste. Peter Brook, who omitted the good servants at the end of 3.7 (see ), also omitted Gloucester’s appeal to a higher justice, O cruell, O ye Gods! (2142).

Phelps (1851–4, 2:380) deplored graphic versions of the blinding: Painfully horrible as this scene is…, it was rendered more unnecessarily repulsive by the introduction in modern editions of stage directions, which led to the impression that Gloster’s eyes were plucked out in sight of the audience. A century later, French’s Acting Edition places Cornwall behind the chair, Regan in front, masking the application of bloody grease-paint. When Cornwall gouges out Gloucester’s other eye, Skillan (ed. 1967, p. 148) notes: He throws the eye up stage behind the chair.

div.head: Gloucester’s Suicide Leap
div.p: Q has stage directions: He kneeles (2473) and He fals (2480); F has none. Although there is no stage direction in The History, Tate clearly retained Gloucester’s suicide attempt and most of the subsequent dialogue, following Shakespeare’s text from the beginning of 4.6, When shall we come toth’ top of that same hill? (2431) to Edgar’s Bare [F: Beare] free & patient thoughts (2525). Garrick also used the entire passage, following Shakespeare’s text and adding Rowe’s SD, He leaps, and falls along, although Bell’s edition notes: Tho’ this incident has been objected to, we think as imagination works with peculiar strength, on a despairing mind, it is very defensible (p. 60). But Garrick was the last to include the leap and the dialogue until the 20th c. Colman (ed. 1768, p. iv) quoted Thomas Warton on The utter improbability of Glocester’s imagining, though blind, that he had leaped down Dover Cliff (Adventurer, No. 122), adding that in the representation it is still more liable to objection than in print. So Colman retained the beginning of the scene—to preserve Edgar’s celebrated description of the Cliff—but omitted, without scruple, the fall and the following dialogue, from Now fellow fare thee well (2480) to patient thoughts (2525). Colman thus made Lear’s entrance and Edgar’s but who comes here (2526–7) the standard interruption to Gloucester’s suicide, which by and large disappeared from the stage for more than a century.

Kemble, while generally following Tate’s text, made virtually the same omission as Colman, eliminating the leap and the following dialogue (4.4.38–69), skipping from Gloucester’s farewell to Lear’s fantastic appearance. All of Kemble’s followers did likewise, and the suicide and attendant dialogue were eliminated by Inchbald, Elliston, Oxberry, Dolby, Cumberland, MSD, and Forrest. Oxberry’s SD—Prepares to fall, when Edgar advances and catches him—was followed by Dolby, Cumberland, MSD, and Forrest. Macready, at least in Lacy’s, despite a Shakespearean text, excised the same material as Colman and Kemble (2481–525); the SD is Edgar stays him, as he is about to leap. Charles Kean and Booth made the same 45-line omission, as did Flower. Once again, Irving’s solution was unique. The SD Gloster is about to leap, when Edgar catches him is transformed by Irving’s restoration of six of Shakespeare’s subsequent lines: Gloucester’s Away and let me die (2489) and part of Edgar’s response, Hadst thou beene…thou dost breath…Thy lifes a miracle (2490–3; 2497). Without actually leaping, this Gloucester imagines that he has done so; Irving still cut the other 39 lines.

There are reasons beyond improbablility for excluding this episode, such as the religious proscription against suicide. There is also the fact that in a production with distinct scenes, 4.6 is disproportionately long, and the subplot was often vulnerable. Finally, the comic elements in this passage, such as Edgar’s fantastic description of the thing on the cliff, threaten to undercut the pathos—though as Gentleman (1770, 1:364) objected, why the mere matter of falling on the stage should be laughable we know not.

When Bridges-Adams restored the suicide attempt and most of the dialogue in the early 1930s, he had Gloucester fall from a kneeling position. Fordham (1942, n.p.) described Granville-Barker’s Gloucester as, apparently from a kneeling postion, he rises quickly and, throwing his cloak up over his face, falls to the ground, where he lies stunned. G. Wilson Knight (1930, p. 187) called Gloucester’s suicide attempt the play’s ultimate expression of the grotesque merged into the ridiculous. A generation later, Brook put that perspective onstage. Marowitz (1963, p. 21) says that for Brook, the metaphysical farce of the suicide was the germinal scene; he was the first to retain it all.

div.head: The Wicked Sisters
div.p: The fortunes of Goneril and Regan have ebbed and flowed onstage. Tate exaggerated their evil; during the next two centuries, their roles were reduced, literally and figuratively; by the mid-20th c., their roles were largely restored. Today, like many compelling villains, Goneril and Regan threaten to overwhelm their opposite—the silent and largely absent Cordelia. This discrepancy between the sisters was not a problem in The History, where Cordelia’s role was expanded to heroic—and romantic—proportions, at least in part because it was to be played by a woman. In Tate’s black-and-white moral universe, Gonerill and Regan are cruelty and lust incarnate, wielding power to further their ends. Regan invites Edmund to the Grotto even before her husband, Cornwall, is wounded (3.5.24); in Tate’s version of 4.2, the indecisive Albany is absent, and the messenger announces Cornwall’s death to Gonerill alone; in 5.4, Gonerill, not the Bastard, bribes the Captain to kill Lear and Cordelia (5–9).

The adapters of Tate omitted many of his excesses, but in doing so, they also weakened the characters. Colman (ed. 1768) called Edmund’s criminal commerce with Gonerill and Regan…the most disgusting part of the original, and deplored Tate’s amplifications. Both Colman and Garrick omitted Tate’s wholly original Grotto scene (4.1), in which he made Regan, as well as Gonerill, an adulteress, telling Edmund that her husband’s wound grows Dangerous—I hope Mortal (20). The scene never appeared again, except in texts based entirely on The History (as late as Harrison in 1779). Kemble and his followers likewise omitted the Grotto. Colman and Garrick, and later Kemble, also omitted Gonerill’s plan to poison her sister at a banquet (5.1), another passage found only in complete reprints of The History. Finally, all three omitted 5.5.58–114, Tate’s melodramatic expansion of 3107–19, the sisters’ squabbling over the wounded Edmund and their announcements of mutual poisoning. Tate had given his female villains a grandiose exit; in later adaptations, they leave the stage unceremoniously at the end of 5.4, 173 lines earlier.

While Tate expanded the roles of the wicked sisters with his own material, the list of Shakespearean scenes he omitted includes seven in which they appear—every single one of their scenes, in fact, except for the ensemble scenes.
