Most of these scenes are discussed elsewhere. Three are the small coda scenes discussed above: the ends of 1.1, 1.4, and 2.4. The others are 1.3, 4.2, 4.5, and 5.1. When the 19th-c. restorers of Shakespeare’s text omitted these same scenes, they sacrificed fully half the lines of the wicked sisters, and when they also omitted the blinding, they lost Regan at her worst. In an era when Shakespeare’s heroines were prized as models of female behavior, and even Lady Macbeth was recuperated as a loving but ambitious wife, the Victorian Lrs. mitigated much of the sisters’ evil, their sexuality, and their power, as well as their dramatic potential for upstaging their idealized little sister.

Despite Macready’s pioneering reliance on the original text, his substantive treatment of Goneril and Regan in the first three acts was not very different from that of his predecessors. He reduced the sisters’ roles by omitting the ends of 1.1, 1.4, and 2.4, as did every other 19th-c. version (except for Irving’s restoration of 10 lines of the end of 1.1). And in all 19th-c. versions except Pattie, Regan is lost with the blinding scene. The only exception was Macready’s restoration of most of 1.3 (Goneril and Steward), a scene that only Colman had previously restored (though both omitted Q, 522+1–+4; Macready also omitted 525–7). In the 19th c., only Forrest omitted 1.3 completely. The common partial omissions were the exaggerated Euery houre | he flashes into one grosse crime or other (510–11), omitted by all except Booth; most of Q at 522+1–+4; and Goneril’s last speech, And let his Knights haue colder looks among you (525–7), which she has already said in substance (all except Booth). Kean and Irving also omitted If you come slacke… (516–17). In the 20th c., Bridges-Adams omitted 520–3, Houseman 522–522+4 and 525–6.

Except for the blinding (3.7), Goneril and Regan disappear in Shakespeare’s Act 3. Goneril reappears in 4.2, with Steward, then Edmund, and, finally, in a confrontation with Albany, before a messenger enters to tell Albany about the blinding of Gloucester. Tate used only some of this scene, focusing on Goneril by omitting both Edmund and Albany. While Garrick, and later Kemble, followed Tate, Colman restored most of the scene, omitting about 35 lines, most of them only in Q, and most of them Albany’s (2303+1–+7, +11, +14–+17; 2307+1–+2, +4; 2311+1–+8), as well as Goneril’s single speech at the end of the scene (One way…answer, 2330–4). With minor variations, the versions of 4.2 by Macready, Kean, and Flower were similar to that of Colman. Irving cut about twice as much, and Forrest and Booth omitted everything before the entrance of the messenger (2267–2311+8). In the 20th c., Bridges-Adams still omitted about 35 lines of 4.2, beginning with Oswald (2273–83); but he also diminished Albany, omitting not only his Q lines (2303+1–+8) but also you are not worth the dust which the rude wind | Blowes in your face (2302–3), which only Colman had previously omitted. Finally, Bridges-Adams also omitted most of the messenger. Houseman omitted only the two usual Albany passages, Q’s 2303+1–+5 and 2311+1–+8, and 2306–7.

The other common omissions in 4.2 are Goneril’s sexually assertive lines to Edmund. Tate had eliminated Edmund from the scene. Through the 19th c., all later versions except Colman’s and Flower’s omitted …ere long you are like to heare…A mistresses coward [F: command] (2287–9); this kisse if it durst speake | Would stretch thy spirits vp into the ayre (2290–1) was not printed until the Flower and Irving editions. Goneril’s boldest speech here is Oh, the difference of man, and man | to thee womans seruices are dew | My foote [F: Foole] vsurpes my body (2295–7). Tate had cut the lines here but borrowed them for Regan in the Grotto (4.1.23–4). When his adapters omitted the Grotto scene, they lost the lines altogether. Colman restored the lines but changed body to duty. Macready changed body to Tate’s bed in his 1834 promptbook (as in Pattie) and to hand in later promptbooks, as Kean did; Lacy’s has body. Irving omitted the three lines, which were also eliminated by Forrest’s and Booth’s excision of the entire passage.

Scene 4.5, between Regan and the Steward, is the kind of minor scene that Tate eliminated without softening the sisters. In fact, he borrowed Regan’s strongest lines here and gave them to Goneril in his version of 4.2 (The History’s 4.3)—the viciously shrewd observations, It was great ignorance, Glosters eyes being out | To let him liue (2394–5) and If you doe chance to heare of that blind traytor, | Preferment fals on him that cuts him off (2424–5). Again, when the 19th-c. restorers omitted 4.5, they lost not only the Steward’s motivation but Regan’s sexual politics (My Lord is dead, Edmund…more conuenient is he for my hand | Then for your Ladies, 2417–19). The scene was completely omitted by Kean, Booth, Flower, and Irving. It is included in only one 19th-c. acting edition, Pattie. It is gone from Lacy’s, though Macready followed Tate in salvaging Goneril’s lines about Gloucester and transposing them back to the end of 4.2.
As detailed below, the traditional omissions in Act 5 are considerable, and Goneril and Regan continued to be primary targets.

div.head: Act 5
div.p: Act 5 is cut, heavily or lightly, in every one of the acting editions surveyed here. Even the modestly pruned BBC version (No. 28) notes: Apart from the omission of [4.3], any serious editing…has been limited to the closing scenes of the play (p. 37). The multiple components, some of them seemingly repetitious or digressive, were pared down or omitted entirely. The first restoration of Shakespeare’s tragic ending was in the Elliston-Kean version published in the 1824 Dolby and reprinted in Cumberland (c. 1828). However, this was attached to the first four acts of Kemble’s version, which was, of course, largely Tate’s. Dolby’s Act 5 begins with Elliston’s restoration of four lines from 4.4 (All blest secrets, 2366–9), but most of the reconciliation scene was still Tate’s, including Cordelia’s Act 4 curtain soliloquy (The Gods restore you…King, 4.5.59–72). Dolby continues with Shakespeare’s 5.1, much of which had been omitted by Tate and his followers. The History is used again to flesh out the short 5.2 with Gloster’s soliloquy The Fight grows hot… (5.3.6 ff.).

Other than this cobbled beginning, the Elliston-Kean restoration of Shakespeare’s Act 5 set the pattern for the 19th c.: The original scene order is followed, but omissions increase as the act proceeds, simplifying Shakespeare’s complex denouement in order to focus on the main character. Dolby/Cumberland omits about 120 of the 460 lines in Folio’s Act 5. Lacy’s (which keeps the reconciliation scene at the end of Act 4), prints more Act 5 lines than any other contemporary edition—omitting only 75 F lines—though not every line was necessarily delivered onstage. Charles Kean’s last act started with 75 lines of the reconciliation; his ending omitted about 145 F lines. Forrest’s entire last act, a version of Dolby’s combined 4.7 and Act 5, is only half as long as Dolby’s. Booth’s version of F’s Act 5, the shortest, was under 200 lines, while Irving used about 320 lines. Flower’s fuller text was similar to Lacy’s.

Dolby/Cumberland describes five distinct scenes in Act 5. The last, in a nod to Tate, is set in A Prison; but for the first time in over a century, the play includes the stage direction Enter Lear…with Cordelia, dead, in his arms. Lacy’s text (and Flower’s) used the Folio’s three scenes. Later editors simplified. Charles Kean had only two scenes, the first being the reconciliation. Booth played his truncated last act in a single scene; Irving’s had two scenes with the same setting.

As late as the Modern Standard Drama (1848), while most of Folio’s 5.1 (2845–916) was printed, the scene was marked as usually omitted in the Representation. There are many reasons for this popular omission: the complicated scene has four separate parts, lines unique to the Quarto, and explicit sexual rivalry between Goneril and Regan. Forrest’s 1860 text omitted all of 5.1 except Edgar’s petition to Albany (2880–901), but noted: This scene is usually omitted in the Representation. Tate and all his followers, including Colman and Garrick, omitted the beginning of 5.1 (2845–78), an unsavory dialogue between the Bastard and Regan, followed by problematic lines between Albany and Goneril, eight of them from Q. Booth made the same omission.

The Bastard-Regan dialogue was generally restored by Dolby/Cumberland and Macready. Still, every 19th-c. edition omitted the Q-only lines (2859+1–+3) and a sexual allusion of Regan’s that even Edmund finds crude: But haue you neuer found my brothers way, | To the forfended place? (2858–9). Flower forbore to print this line, even in small type, while Pattie, apparently working from a full text, retained a footnote to forfended, even though the lines were excised. Dolby/Cumberland and Kean also omitted Regan’s I neuer shall indure hir, deere my Lord | bee not familiar with her (2861–2). Irving, as usual, made his own selection, omitting the same lines as Lacy’s, as well as 2847–9 and 2851–2. Bridges-Adams reverted to omitting all of the Edmund-Regan dialogue (2847–63); Houseman omitted only Q’s lines; and Miller omitted the first six lines of 5.1 (2847–52), Edmund’s discussion of the Duke’s last purpose, which requires the presence of an officer. After Albany and Goneril enter (2864), the usual omissions were Q’s for this busines…nobly (2868+1–+5), omitted not only through the 19th c. but also by Houseman and Miller in the 20th. Flower marked Goneril’s next speech, Combine…here (2870–2), as also usually omitted. Charles Kean dispensed with Goneril altogether.

Scene 5.1 concludes with the Bastard’s soliloquy on the romantic rivalry between Goneril and Regan, To both these sister [F: Sisters] haue I sworne my loue (2902–16). Tate’s version intensifies the sexuality when the Bastard says of Regan, already | I have enjoy’d her (5.2.6–7). While Colman and Garrick followed Tate, Kemble and his followers deleted the soliloquy by omitting all of Tate’s 5.2. When Dolby/Cumberland restored the tragic ending, Shakespeare’s comparatively modest soliloquy was restored. The only line omitted was the blunt neither can bee inioy’d | If both remaine aliue (2905–6), which was omitted in every 19th-c. edition.

The short 5.2, in which Gloucester is left under a tree while Edgar exits to check on the battle and then reenters almost immediately, is awkwardly brief unless the battle itself fills the stage. To expand it, Tate gave Gloster a despairing 18-line soliloquy: The Fight grows hot (5.3.6–23). Colman used 9 lines of it, Kemble 13. The early restorers also tried to fix 5.2. Elliston, having used original language from the end of Act 4, reverted to Kemble’s version of Tate here. These lines from Tate’s text were used as late as Pattie, though they are not in Macready’s promptbooks. Lacy’s suggests that Macready filled the gap by transposing six lines from 4.6 (2733–8), Gloucester’s how stiffe is my vild sence.… Kean, Booth, Irving, and Houseman simply omitted the entire scene. Flower (ed. 1883, n.p.) notes Spedding’s ingenious suggestion to make the division between Acts 4 and 5 at Edgar’s exit, though Flower says that it has not generally been adopted. The scene was still omitted by Bridges-Adams and later by Houseman. Even Miller omitted Edgar’s first lines (Here father…comfort, 2921–4), thereby eliminating his mid-scene exit.

The long 5.3 begins with Lear escorting Cordelia to prison (2938–68), a poetic interlude completely omitted by Forrest and Booth. Tate had used Lear’s No, no, no, no: come lets away to prison… (2948–57) and given his Vpon such sacrifices…The Gods thēselues throw incense (2961–2) to Cordelia. Colman and Garrick followed Tate, but Kemble and his followers omitted all but the first three lines of Lear’s speech, possibly because of religious scruples (see ). Dolby/Cumberland began the restoration of this section. In Shakespeare’s next passage, the Bastard bribes the Captain to murder the prisoners (2969–2981+2); Tate made Goneril bribe the Captain. Colman and Garrick, as well as Kemble and followers, omitted the passage, along with their general diminution of the wicked sisters. Dolby/Cumberland again instituted the restoration, but this passage, too, was later omitted by Forrest and Booth.

Shakespeare’s last 321 lines are one continuous movement. First the disposition of prisoners of war degenerates into a family feud (2982–3035). Tate shortened the bickering in 3001–35, probably because of the informal style of repartee, and transposed it back to precede the section with Lear and Cordelia. Dolby/Cumberland restored the passage, with several small omissions, as did most later 19th-c. editions. Only Forrest and Booth omitted 3001–35 (except for Albany’s arrest of Edmund, 3027–8). All except Macready and Flower omitted the low comedy of Gon. That were the most, if hee should husband you. | Reg. Iesters doe oft proue Prophets (3012–13). Similarly, all except Macready and Flower omitted the sarcasm of Albany’s If you will mary, make your loue to me, | My Lady is bespoke and Goneril’s An enterlude (3033–5). Every 19th-c. text except Pattie bowdlerized the sexual bluntness of Goneril’s Meane you to inioy him then? (3022). It was omitted by Dolby/Cumberland, Forrest, and Booth. When the line was restored, Lacy’s and Flower changed inioy to marry, Kean used wed, and Irving possess. Kean also omitted Regan’s unladylike power play, That’s as we list to grace him (3001–6), and her married sister’s inappropriate retort, Not so hot…, while Irving omitted the beginning (3001–19) and the end (3029–35) of the passage. In addition, all 19th-c. versions except Pattie omitted Goneril’s Hola…squint and Regan’s first sign of sickness, Lady I am not well… (3014–17), in preparation for minimizing the sisters’ deaths. It is Flower’s only omission here. Some of these Goneril-Regan omissions lasted through Bridges-Adams, who omitted their first exchange (3001–9) and Albany’s sarcasm (3029–34).

Tate also eliminated some of Goneril and Regan’s minor lines before and after the duel; instead, he inserted a grandiose 42-line quarrel over the wounded Edmund (5.5.73–114), which concludes with the sisters’ announcements that they have poisoned each other. In both Shakespeare’s play and Tate’s, these are Goneril’s and Regan’s final lines. Because of the florid melodrama of Tate’s passage (Die, Circe, for thy Charms are at an End…, 96), this addition was eliminated by every single adapter of The History. Thus when Tate’s followers used his outline here but omitted his original material, they lost Goneril and Regan’s exit lines in both versions of the play—and the wicked sisters left the stage many lines earlier and much less dramatically. Some of the restorers also omitted Shakespearean lines. Before the duel, Forrest and Booth omitted both of Regan’s last lines—Sicke, ô sicke (along with Goneril’s If not, ile ne’re trust poyson, 3043–4) and This sicknes growes vpon me (3055). Kean omitted only the latter. The nasty Albany-Goneril dialogue after the duel (3107–20) was completely omitted by Dolby/Cumberland, Forrest, and Booth. These versions thus deprived Goneril, too, of her exit lines (Say if I do…for’t, 3116–17). Irving omitted all of Goneril’s lines, except 3116. Goneril’s rationalization (This is meere practise Gloster…, 3108–11) was omitted by Kean, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman.

As for the duel between the brothers, Tate may have found the challenger’s incognito unconvincing, because Albany identifies Lord Edgar to Edmund (5.5.15). Colman and Garrick halved the long and rewritten speeches that follow in The History. Of the restorers, only Irving reduced the brothers’ speeches (3080–106) in the 19th c. and Bridges-Adams and Houseman in the 20th.

Edgar’s long account of Gloucester’s death, List a briefe tale…Burst smillingly (3144–62), was shortened slightly by Dolby, Macready, and Forrest. As a mournful story that competes with Lear’s imminent death, it was completely omitted by Kean, Booth, Flower, and Irving. Bridges-Adams again tried it both ways, omitting it completely and partially. His partial version, like Houseman’s and Brook’s, cut the speech in half by omitting scattered lines. Editors also pared lines before and after this speech. Booth and Irving began the omission with Albany at 3137, Kean at 3138, Macready and Flower at 3142. The lines between Edgar’s account of Gloucester and his account of Kent (3163–8) were omitted by all 19th-c. texts, as well as by Houseman and Miller. Flower indicated that both speeches and the link (3142–3168+18) were usually omitted. In the case of Booth, who also omitted the subsequent material (the deaths of the sisters), the excision ran from 3137 to 3199 (also excluding the 18 lines of Q). Irving began the omission earlier, at 3124, skipping most of Edgar’s speeches and his dialogue with Albany.

The single most popular omission in all of 5.3 is Edgar’s account of Kent, This would haue seemd a periode… (3168+1–+18)—universally omitted in the 19th c., but also widely omitted in the 20th—by Houseman, Brook, and Miller; Brooks-Adams tried it both omitted and partially cut. The reasons are many: It is all unique to the Quarto; it is filled with linguistic difficulties; and directly following Edgar’s poignant account of his father’s death, the speech is anticlimactic, if not repetitious. With Gloucester dead and Lear about to die, most producers are willing to sacrifice Kent as the strings of life, | Began to cracke. Moreover, he is about to reappear.

The wicked sisters were often deprived of their brief but spectacular demise—a servant’s entrance with Goneril’s bloody knife and her confession of poisoning Regan (3169–80). The passage was not used by Tate, who left their deaths to Edgar’s announcement in the last scene: …your imperious Daughters | Gonerill and haughty Regan, both are Dead, | Each by the other poison’d at a Banquet (5.6.128–30). Everyone who used Tate’s ending followed suit. The restorers, however, were slow to include Shakespeare’s graphic and purposefully disjointed passage, and by the end of the 19th c., only Flower had printed all eleven lines. Dolby/Cumberland, the first text with the tragic ending, omitted the entire passage of the deaths and their aftermath (3169–99), leaving the news to Kent’s quiet lines at 3259–60, Your eldest daughters haue foredoome [F: fore-done] themselues. Macready’s promptbooks show several versions. Lacy’s printed a fuller version, including the bloody knife stage direction and Gentleman’s Its hot it smokes, it came euen from the heart of— (omitting only What kind of helpe, | Speake man, 3171–2). Pattie, which omitted both of Edgar’s long speeches, also omitted the sisters’ deaths, jumping from Edgar’s Worthy Prince I know’t (3141) to Kent’s entrance (3181). Booth omitted even more, from 3137 to 3199. Charles Kean omitted the smoking knife, and used his own brief announcement of the deaths. Irving, who also cut much of the preceding material, used a condensed three-line announcement after Goneril’s desperate exit at 3120. Bridges-Adams followed Macready, omitting only 3171–2, but Brook eliminated the melodrama of the first five lines (Its hot it smokes…), lessening the sense of desperate confusion in this scene.

Using various small omissions and even transpositions, every editor who retained at least part of the sisters’ deaths struggled with this passage, trying to make sense of the multiple plot twists of the bloody knife, Kent’s entrance, the sisters’ bodies, Kent’s speech, Albany’s forgetfulness and the undoing of Edmund’s plan—all in less than fifty lines. At one extreme, Houseman made several transpositions within 3170–99; omitted 10 lines (cutting Albany’s lines at Kent’s entrance and the bringing of the bodies, 3181–8); and inserted four lines from Edgar’s earlier account of Kent (3168+15–+18), the rest of which he omitted.

Stage directions in both Q and F clearly call for the bodies of Goneril and Regan to be brought onstage. It is a cumbersome stage direction, literally and figuratively, and probably the one most often ignored in this play. Indeed, Albany’s Produce their bodies, be they aliue or dead (3183) was omitted by every version listed until Miller’s in 1982. Depending on the means of conveyance, the bodies might also detract from the impact of Lear’s entrance with Cordelia in his arms. Lacy’s omitted the first eight lines of Kent’s entrance (3181–8), as did Flower and Irving, while Pattie omitted only Albany’s 3183–5. The character of Albany is thereby subtly diminished. Every single 19th-c. version further omitted his return to the subject of Goneril and Regan (3194–9), depriving him of his reaction to his wife’s death, the Websterean Euen so, couer their faces (3199). The Euen so refers to the Bastard’s self-serving description of the sexual triangle, Yet Edmund was beloued (3196–8), which was also omitted. More important, the absence of the bodies eliminates the source of Albany’s distraction from the urgent problem of Lear. Phelps’s Works, which generally followed F’s stage directions, used Q here—Kent’s slightly later entrance, just before Albany’s O tis he (3186), and the bodies not brought in until 3194, at Albany’s Seest thou this obiect Kent? In Q’s dramatic sequence, the gruesome sight distracts Albany just as he starts to respond to Kent’s jarring query about Lear. All 19th-c. versions except Pattie also omitted the Bastard’s Nay send in time and Albany’s Runne, runne, O runne (3204–5). For Forrest and Booth, these lines were part of still larger omissions (see , ); Irving also omitted the entire passage with Kent (3181–200).

The foreshortening of Act 5 continued into the 20th c. Bridges-Adams omitted Albany’s 3186–8 and his distraction (3194–9). Although Granville-Barker (1927, p. 155) argued that the sisters’ bodies were necessary to reunite the cast of characters in the play’s opening scene, the 1940 Gielgud production eliminated them after the audience laughed. Brook continued his heavy Act 5 omissions, cutting 3181, 3186–8, and the whole rescue attempt, from Great thing of vs forgot to Edmund’s exit (3192–215); thus Kent’s entrance to bid my King and maister ay good night (3190) is immediately followed by Lear’s entrance (3216). Even Miller, who may have been the first to bring in the bodies since the 17th c., perhaps because of the technical possibilities of television, omitted Albany’s distraction (3194–5) and his mourning (3199).

There are numerous small omissions even after Lear’s final entrance. Albany’s cryptic Fall and cease (3226) was omitted by Lacy’s and by Bridges-Adams, who also omitted Edgar’s Or image of that horror (3225). Brook omitted the obvious Tis noble Kent your friend (3232). Some editors even cut Lear’s lines. Irving omitted Prethe away…for euer (3231–4). Kean omitted most of the exchange between Lear and Kent/Caius, If Fortune bragd…steps (3245–55), Irving omitted all except the recognition (3247–8), and Bridges-Adams omitted 3248–53.

There has long been dissatisfaction with the trifle of Edmund’s death (3266–7), coming as it does after Cordelia’s death. Tate had Albany say, I left ev’n now the Traytor wounded Mortally (5.6.75). Dolby/Cumberland omitted the announcement of Edmund’s death, as did every other 19th-c. edition—though some, like Lacy’s, show Edmund expiring earlier, after his last speech (3214), with an added Oh! (dies in the arms of the Knights). All except Macready continued this excision by omitting Albany’s problematic abdication speech, you Lords…deseruings (3268–76). In the 20th c., Bridges-Adams retained Edmund’s death but omitted Albany’s speech; Houseman omitted Edmund’s death and the last half of Albany’s speech.

The final major omission is the very end of the play. In the 19th c., directors did not care whether Albany (Q) or Edgar (F) delivered Shakespeare’s last speech because they did not use it—or any of the last 11 lines of the play (3291–301). Dolby/Cumberland, making the first reinstatement of Lear’s death, ends the play on his final lines in F, Do you see this?…looke there (3282–3), eliminating the last 18 lines of the play. Dolby/Cumberland includes a unique stage direction: after Lear’s Looke her lips (3282), he Kisses her. Though the punctuation varies, from that time on, every Lear delivered the more complex lines of the Folio. Pattie used one line after Lear’s death, Edgar’s He faints my Lord… (3284), while Forrest added only Breake hart… (3285), assigned to Edgar. Lacy’s, Kean, and Irving omitted that problematic line, but used 3284 and ended the play with Kent’s three-line speech Vex not his ghost…longer (3287–9). Booth used one additional line, ending on Edgar’s O he is gone indeed (3290). Flower reverted to ending with Lear. Bridges-Adams restored Shakespeare’s ending, omitting only Kent’s The wonder is… and Albany’s Beare them from hence… (3291–4), a weighty command that is sometimes ignored; he gave the last speech to Albany.

div.head: Minor Omissions
div.p: In addition to the many scenes and parts of scenes that have been omitted, there are numerous smaller omissions, sometimes a few lines, often part of a long speech. The reasons are many. The Fool’s part, for example, was cautiously kept small, even after the character was restored. Moreover, sometimes his lines were cut because they are obscure or indecent. Throughout the play passages were omitted because they are difficult, or sexual, or irreverent. A smaller category consists of lines that call for awkward stage business. Finally, there is material that seems repetitious or simply unnecessary.

Many omissions, of course, suggest complex causes. For example, Lacy’s and Flower note that the dialogue among the three sisters toward the end of 1.1, Prescribe not vs our duties… (301–9), is usually omitted onstage. One reason is that these lines introduce the Goneril-Regan dialogue at the end of 1.1, which was often omitted. Cordelia’s farewell at 300 makes a more poignant scene ending. In addition, Goneril’s You haue obedience scanted, | And well are worth the worth that you haue wanted (304–5) is also difficult (it was omitted by Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams), and Cordelia’s Time shal vnfould…derides (306–7) is both epigrammatic and a rhymed couplet. The neatly rhymed couplets of Shakespeare’s early plays, which diminished over the course of his career, were completely out of fashion by the time of the Romantic poets at the turn of the 19th c. Epigrammatic speech was probably rejected as singsong in style, moralistic and generalized rather than dramatic in content, and often obscure in its allusions. Finally, there are omissions whose motives are unclear, such as Lear’s an excellent thing in women (3237), which was omitted by Dolby/Cumberland, Modern Standard Drama, Kean, and Forrest. Altogether, an impressive number of these minor omissions were first made by Tate.

The part of the Fool was restored only gradually. Tate had completely omitted the impolite and impolitic jester from his heroic play. When Macready and his successors reintroduced the character, they included the pathos but not the Fool’s full range of sarcastic, indecent, and allusive speech. We have already noted the loss of the Fool’s lines as parts of larger omissions—his song at the end of 1.4 (835–41), his lines in 1.5, and the mock trial in 3.6. But the character was reduced throughout, a few lines at a time—some of them nonsense, some obscure, some vulgar, most of them indecorously comic. In addition, the Fool’s speech is mostly commentary on the plot, rather than part of the action, and he is given to sententious versifying, all of which enhances his expendability.

The omissions from 1.4, the Fool’s first scene, are typical. For many editors, there was simply too much jesting for such a long, important scene, the prelude to Lear’s great curse. The first popular omission comes only ten lines after the Fool’s entrance at 624: Flower indicated (with small type) the usual omission of how now nuncle…then two tens to a score (634–57), though only Kean omitted all of it; Macready omitted the first ten lines. Flower did not even print the rude couplet about thy drinke and thy whore (654–5), a line that was also omitted by Macready and Irving. Booth, who omitted only Lear’s A pestilent gull [F: gall]… (644), softened stincke (643) to weep. Bridges-Adams omitted 634–9 (from would), 642–4 (from when), and 653. Irving was the only one who excised 50 lines of the Fool’s catechism, from can you make no vse of nothing vncle to I had rather be any kind of thing then a foole, | and yet (660–98), a passage that includes 11 lines unique to Q, That Lord that counsail’d… (669+1–+11). Houseman omitted seven lines of Q. The first of many of the Fool’s proverbial jests to be omitted is when thou clouest thy crowne…thou borest thy asse… (674–6), cut by Macready, Kean, Flower, and Irving. The naughtily undignified for when thou gauest them the rod, and put’st downe thine own breeches (686–7), another passage Flower considered literally unprintable, was omitted by Macready, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. Kean continued cutting heavily and even transposed a few lines, omitting 670–7 (to durt), 678–83 (from if I speake, also omitted by Booth and Bridges-Adams), and 692–9 (to Nuncle). After Goneril enters, Booth and Irving omitted the Fool’s seven lines on nothing at 705–11. Also omitted were his cryptic asides so out went the candle, and we were left darkling (728–9), omitted by Pattie, Kean, Booth, and Bridges-Adams (who omitted from 726); May not an Asse know…whoop Iug I loue thee (735–7), omitted by Macready, Kean, and Booth; and Lears shadow (744), omitted by Macready and Kean.

When the end of 1.4 and all of 1.5 are omitted in connection with the transposition of Lear’s great curse (see ), the Fool does not reappear until 2.4. The Fool’s quip on when a mans ouer lusty at legs (1282–5), possibly perceived as sexual, was omitted by Kean; Booth and Irving omitted from Horses, and Bridges-Adams omitted 1284–5 (from when). The sententious F-only Winters not gon yet…in a yeare (1322–7) was omitted all or in part by Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. The motives are mixed: the speech is sententious, and some of the proverbial allusions obscure; it is rhythmic doggerel and partly rhymed; Dolors is a pun, and arrant whore impolite; it does not further the plot. Every 19th-c. edition except Lacy’s omitted the Fool’s next sententious list, Weele set thee to schoole to an Ant… (1340–9); Bridges-Adams omitted the first four lines, Houseman 1341–4 (all…stincking) and 1347–9. The Fool’s singsong but cryptic words at 1350–7 (That Sir…perdy) was completely omitted by Miller, while Pattie, Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams omitted from 1354. Every 19th-c. edition omitted the Fool’s comic examples of the Cockney and the eels and her brother who buttered his horse’s hay (1398–1402); Bridges-Adams omitted only the latter.

In 3.2, all 19th-c. texts except Booth’s and Flower’s omitted the Fool’s irreverent and obscure Court holly water in a drie house… (1665–6). All 19th-c. texts, plus Houseman and Miller, omitted his licentious and sententious rhymes on the codpiece (1682–7); Bridges-Adams omitted 1680–90. The crude heers Grace, & a codpis (1692) was omitted by all 19th-c. texts. The Fool’s anticlimactic Prophesie (1734–49) was omitted not only during the 19th c., but by Bridges-Adams, Houseman, and Brook, reflecting the widespread belief that it is spurious. Miller transposed 1746 to follow 1739. In 3.4, the Fool’s immodest jest Nay he reseru’d a blanket, else we had beene all sham’d (1846–7) was omitted by Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Macready omitted the sexual now a little fire…were like an old leachers heart…all the rest in bodie cold (1892–4), as did Kean, Booth, Flower (who also omitted this is a naughty night to swim in, 1891–2), and Irving. In an already truncated 3.6, Lacy’s omitted the yeoman riddle (2007–12), one answer to which is only in F, as did Kean and Booth. The Fool’s And Ile go to bed at noone (2043), his exit from the play in the Folio, was omitted by Macready and Kean, in order to end the scene on Lear’s exit lines (2041–2) instead of on the jest.

Most of the other characters whose parts are reduced have already been discussed in relation to various major omissions. The extensive omissions of material unique to the Quarto reduced the key characters of Edgar, Albany, and Kent, as well as unnamed characters like Cornwall’s servants at the end of 3.7 and the Gentleman with Kent in 3.1 and 4.3. Only rarely does a minor omission remove a character entirely from a scene, as was the case with the Gentleman at the beginning of 2.4 (1276–8), who was omitted by every version from Tate through Dolby/Cumberland, reinstated by Macready, and omitted again by Booth and Irving. The only remaining characters to discuss are Burgundy and France. Shakespeare’s unlikable Burgundy, who appears only in 1.1 and must have been played by an actor with more than one part, has only twelve lines. Tate condensed the part to six lines (1.1.180–7), and Kemble and his followers used only three of Tate’s. Colman and Garrick used only two of Shakespeare’s lines: Pardon me…conditions (225–6). The 19th-c. restorers continued to omit most of the Burgundy dialogue, including Lear’s lines to him, possibly finding the bargaining over Cordelia’s dowry ungentlemanly, as well as saving time in a long scene. Macready, Kean, and Flower used only the same two lines as Colman and Garrick, omitting 207–15 and 220–23. Booth and Irving omitted 215–23, beginning at Lear’s Sir there she stands.… The King of France, who was excised from Tate’s History, was a stranger to the stage before Macready’s version, having appeared only in Colman’s short-lived Lr. Colman and Bridges-Adams omitted France’s first speech, This is most strange… (234–44), Irving omitted all but the first line, and Macready, Kean, Flower, and Houseman omitted the last six difficult lines. At the end of this passage, all 19th-c. versions and Houseman omitted France’s chiding challenge to Burgundy, …what say you to the Lady?… (260–74), with Burgundy’s churlish response and what might have been perceived as Cordelia’s unladylike retort, Peace be with Burgundie.…

Difficult lines were readily omitted, whether the difficulty originated from textual problems, outdated or obscure references, or Shakespeare’s unique use of language. For example, seven lines into the play, Gloucester’s for equalities are so weighed, that curiositie in neither, can make choise of eithers moytie (9–10) is omitted by Colman, Macready, Kean, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. Following is a compilation of many similar cruxes that have been omitted, not including those problem passages embedded in the more substantial omissions described above.

Regan’s protestation of filial devotion (77–81), which includes the difficult Which the most precious square of sence possesses (79), was omitted by Colman, Pattie, Kean, and Flower. Kent’s and let me still remaine, | The true blanke of thine eye (170–1) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Macready, and Kean. Gloucester’s subscribd his power, | confined to exhibition (359–60) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Kent’s If but as well I other accents borrow…likenes (531–4) was omitted by Macready, Kean, Flower, and Irving. The last six lines of Goneril’s all-licenc’d foole speech, which ends with that then necessitie | must call discreet proceedings (720–5), was omitted by Pattie, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, Houseman, and Brook. Even Lear’s lines are cut when he is opaque, as in his discernings | are lethergie (741–2), omitted by Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, and Bridges-Adams, though 742 may also be omitted because of the king’s unpoetic ha!

In 2.2, Kent’s cryptic humor is cut. His debatable reference to Ajax, None of these roges & cowards… (1201–2) was omitted by all 19th-c. editions, as well as by Bridges-Adams, Houseman, and Brook. A good mans fortune may grow out at heeles (1233–4) was omitted by Macready, Kean, and Irving. The crux nothing almost sees my rackles [F: miracles] | But miserie (1242–3) was omitted by Colman, Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman; and shall find time…seeking to giue | Losses and [F: their] remedies (1245–7) was omitted by Colman, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman; Brook omitted 1244–7. It is surprising that only Booth omitted the entire speech (1237–50), given that it is a compendium of causes of omissions—difficult lines, aphorisms, the plot questions raised by the letter, and the staging challenge of leaving Kent asleep in the stocks.

In 2.4, the difficult locution of Lear’s exaggerated tis worse then murder, | To doe vpon respect… (1298–9) was omitted by Garrick in Bell’s and by Kean; And am fallen out with my more hedier will…for the sound man (1386–8) was omitted by Garrick (Bell’s), Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. The grammatical challenges of Regan’s Nature on you…better thē you your selfe (1426–32) were variously doctored by Colman, Garrick, Kean, and Houseman. Her Giue eare sir to my sister… (1528–31) was omitted by Colman and Garrick and every 19th-c. edition; Houseman omitted 1529–30. And in Lear’s O reason not the deed [F: need] monologue, the confusing double use of gorgeous in If onely to goe warme were gorgeous…warme (1568–70) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Macready, Kean, Flower, and Bridges-Adams. In Act 4, Gloucester’s obscure and paradoxical full oft tis seene…Proue our comodities (2200–2), omitted by Tate in a speech otherwise untouched, was likewise omitted by Colman, Macready, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. So much of the remainder of the play is cut for other reasons that there is only one more example of a line omitted primarily for its difficulty, Goneril’s our wishes on the way | May proue effects (2282–3), cut by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams.

The omission of sexual language in Lr. skewed the play toward the sentimental. While such deletions were legion during the Victorian era, they were made as early as Colman and as late as Bridges-Adams. Many sexual allusions were lost along with the major omissions of the Fool’s lines and the Goneril-Regan material. Smaller omissions began at once with Gloucester’s references to the Bastard’s mother: wherupon shee grew round wombed (17) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Macready, Kean (17–18, …bed), Flower, and Bridges-Adams. Some or all of yet was his mother faire, there was good sport at his makeing, & the whoreson must be acknowledged (25–7) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Macready, Kean, and Flower. Booth and Irving omitted most of this dialogue on the Bastard’s conception (15–27). Flower’s double standard for omissions is obvious here: whereas a crux like equalities…moytie (9–10) is printed in small type, indicating that it is usually omitted onstage, the sexual lines just cited are not even printed. In short order, Gloucester loses some of his complexity, as well as his relationship to other characters.

Tate began his play with the Bastard’s Thou Nature… soliloquy (335–56). Colman omitted the graphic who in the lusty stealth of nature…got tweene a sleepe and wake (345–49), and was followed by Kean, Booth, Flower, and Irving; Pattie omitted only the phrases doth within a stale dull lyed [F: tyred] bed (347) and got tweene a sleepe and wake (349), while Lacy’s omitted only 349. In the Bastard’s foppery of the world soliloquy (447–61), my Father compounded with my Mother…rough and lecherous (457–9) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, all 19th-c. editions, and Bridges-Adams. (Flower did not print my Father…vnder the Dragons taile, 457–8.) Kean and Flower continued the cut through 466, omitting had the maidenlest starre…twinckled on my bastardy (460–61), while Booth changed bastardy to birth. In 1.4, Goneril’s epicurisme, and lust…brothell (753–4) was variously omitted by Colman, Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, and Bridges-Adams.

Kent’s earthy speech as Caius in 2.2 was a target: Kean omitted many scattered phrases from A knaue, a rascall…addition (1087–97). Booth changed whorson (1091) to knave and omitted 1092–7 (from one truncke). Booth and Kean also omitted the obscure draw you rogue…draw? (1103–6), which contains another whorson (1105), while Flower simply did not print the two whorsons and changed bitch (1095) to cur. Irving excised Thou whorson Zedd (1137); daube the walles of a iaques with him (1139–40) was omitted in full or part by Pattie, Kean, Booth, Flower (who did not print whorson and of a iaques), and Irving. The fact that such material was kept intact by Colman and Garrick suggests that their audiences were closer to this sort of humor. Edgar’s bawdry as Poor Tom was another target. In his resume as A Seruingman in 3.4 (1865–80), serued the lust…and did the act of darkenes with her (1866–8) was omitted by Macready, Kean, Booth, and Flower (who did not print it); one that slept in the contriuing of lust, and wakt to doe it (1869–70) was omitted by Colman, Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, and Flower. Irving omitted Edgar’s entire speech, as well as the preceding lines (from Lear’s flesh Begot | those Pelicane daughters, 1855), also losing Edgar’s commit not with mans sworne spouse (1861–2); Kean omitted 1858–63. Kean also omitted keepe thy foote out of brothell, thy hand out of placket (1876–7), while Flower changed Brothels [F] to taverns. In the 20th c., directors still omitted these lines; Bridges-Adams cut the end of the speech (1874–80), and Houseman cut 1868–72 (swore…Turke) and 1874–78 (let…fiend).

Once again, Lear’s lines are not immune. In his 4.6 catalogue of adultery (2557–73), the wren goes toot, and the smal guilded flie | doe letcher in my sight, let copulation thriue (2558–9) was omitted by Colman, Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower (not printed), and Irving. Colman and Booth also omitted for Glosters bastard son…daughters got tweene the lawfull sheets (2560–1). Pattie changed got tweene the lawfull sheets to sprung from the lawful sheets, Kean to Got in the lawful bed, and Flower to Born in a lawful bed. The remainder of the speech, a repugnant description of female lust (behold yon simpring dame, 2563–73) was omitted by Pattie and Kean; Booth and Irving omitted through consumation (2571). From this section, Lacy’s omitted only whose face between her | forkes presageth snow (2563–4), and Flower did not print fichew nor the soyled horse goes toot with a more riotous appetite (2565–7). Lear’s address to the rascall beadle who hotly lusts to vse a whore (2603–6), which also glances at the church, was omitted not only by Kean, Booth, Flower, and Irving, but also by Bridges-Adams and Houseman. Lacy’s changed whore to wench.

Finally, Edgar’s the darke and vitious Place where thee he gotte, | cost him his eies (3133–4) was omitted by all 19th-c. versions except Macready’s. Two related passages were undoubtedly deleted because they are repulsive. One is Lear’s somewhat difficult The barbarous Scythyan…to gorge his appetite (123–7), omitted by Tate, Colman, Garrick, Kemble, Macready, Kean, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. The other is Edgar’s eats | cow-dung for sallets (1910–11), omitted by Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, Flower, and Bridges-Adams.

Irreverent passages, at least in a Christian sense, are limited in Lr. because of the pagan setting. The only major omission on possibly religious grounds is Gloucester’s suicide attempt and the ensuing discussion (see ). Elsewhere, Lear’s by Iupiter (192) was omitted only by Tate and his followers; Lear and Kent swearing by Jupiter and Juno (1295–6) was omitted only by Kemble and his followers. Both exclamations may also have been rejected as unpoetic speech. The natural astrology of Lear’s By all the operation of the orbs, | From whome we doe exsist and cease to be (118–9) was omitted by Macready, Kean, Flower, and Irving. France’s Gods, Gods! tis strãge… (279–80) was omitted by Colman, Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman; it is also a rhymed couplet. In 2.1, in a passage largely restored by Kemble, he and his followers, as well as Kean and Booth, omitted the Bastard’s coniuring the Moone | to stand’s auspicious Mistris (973–4); Bridges-Adams omitted 972–5. In the same scene, only Kean and Irving omitted …the reuengiue [F: reuenging] Gods, | gainst Paracides… (981–2), as part of a five-line omission (980–4).

The one apparent reference to a supreme deity, Lear’s And take vpon’s the mistery of things | As if we were Gods spies (2956–7), may seem presumptuous, if not blasphemous. Tate retained most of the lets away to prison passage (Sh. 2948–68; Tate 5.4.67–82), though he did change Gods to Heav’ns and gave Lear’s Vpon such sacrifices…The Gods thēselues throw incense (2961–2) to Cordelia. But Kemble and his followers omitted most of Tate’s version, as Forrest and Booth later omitted Shakespeare’s (in the latter cases, as part of a longer deletion from 5.3; see , ). When Dolby/Cumberland first restored this passage, only And take vpon’s…Gods spies (2956–7) was omitted. Pattie and Kean omitted from 2953, and heare poore rogues, to 2957. The most un-Christian lines of the play may be Gloucester’s As flies are toth’ wanton boyes, are we toth’ Gods, | They bitt [F: kill] vs for their sport (2221–2). This nihilistic observation was omitted by Tate, but restored by Colman and Garrick. It was omitted again, not only by Kemble et al., but also by Macready, Kean, and Irving. It was still omitted by Bridges-Adams, along with other lines. But only a few years later, in what seems to be the first mass market paperback edition, G. B. Harrison (ed. 1937, p. 144 n.) noted simply, This is the motto for the play.

Gloucester’s flies simile is also the kind of sententious speech that Lr. directors of all eras have found expendable. In addition to the many previous examples, Edgar’s the worst is not, | As long as we can say, this is the worst (2210–11) was omitted by Tate, Colman, Bell’s, Pattie, Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams (with other lines); his bad is the trade…maister (2224–5) was omitted by Colman, Pattie’s, Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Lear’s thoud’st shun a Beare…meet the beare it’h mouth (1789–91), omitted by Tate, was also cut by Colman, Bell’s, Macready, Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams.

Finally, Lear’s bear example is also expendable because it slows the flow of his long dramatic speech. Directors have often excised such parenthetical remarks. Kent’s more hard then is the stone…denide me to come in (1718–20), which the Folio actually set in parentheses, was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Brook. The disguised Edgar’s asides to the Jacobean audience apparently became less fashionable on the stage. I would not take this from report…my heart breakes at it (2585–6) was omitted by Bell’s, Macready, Kean, Irving, Bridges-Adams, Brook, and Houseman, who cut the whole passage (2581–93). Lear himself is given to self-interruption. His yea are you free? | Some other time for that (1410–11) was omitted by Tate, Colman, Garrick, Kean, and Irving. His return to the subject in 1490–3 (how came my man it’h stockes?), which seems to distract from the main business of Goneril’s arrival, was omitted by Tate, Bell’s, Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, Flower, and Irving (partially). Sometimes, as in 1493 (Lear’s You, did you?), the targets are short, choppy lines, often questions, the kind of prosaic dialogue that Tate omitted.

A few lines are omitted because they call for awkward stage business. Edgar’s intention to bury the dead Oswald, heere in the sands, | Thee ile rake vp…leachers (2726–8) was omitted by Pattie, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, and Miller. A few lines earlier is an example of stage business that is not only awkward to do but too obvious to articulate; Edgar’s lets see his pockets…Hee’s dead…Their papers is more lawfull (2709–14) was omitted all or in part by Colman, Kean, Irving, Bridges-Adams, Houseman, Brook, and Miller. A different kind of challenge—for actor and audience—is Edgar’s assumed accent in this scene (2687–98); a rustic dialect that may have been conventional on Shakespeare’s stage (and Tate’s) was partly omitted by Colman, Kean, Irving, Bridges-Adams, Houseman, and Miller.

In the reconciliation scene, Lear’s lets see, | I feele this pin pricke (2807–8) raises the question of why he has a pin on his freshly arrayed body, and the words were omitted by Tate, Colman, Garrick, Kean, and Booth. In 2.1, Gloucester’s impractical suggestion to distribute Edgar’s picture…farre and neere (1019–20) was omitted by Tate, Colman, Garrick, Lacy’s, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, Houseman, Brook, and Miller. A more complex awkwardness has led most editors (except Colman, partially) to omit the Bastard’s preceding speech, When I disswaded him…seeke it (1001–14). Edmund’s indirect quotation of Edgar, which is of course fabricated, goes on for so long that an audience may misunderstand it as exposition. The Gloucester-Bastard dialogue in 2.1 also seems repetitious after the long 1.2. Both reasons contribute to one of the few long omissions by Miller, 981–1014. Oddly, 980–92 was one of Kemble’s major restorations.

Yet another kind of awkwardness is linguistic. In 4.2, the Messenger’s shorthand report on the blinding, going to put out | the other eye of Gloster (2314–15), raises questions: Who was going, and why begin with the other eye? We know from Act 5 that Shakespeare sometimes mined the drama of a stressed messenger, but in this case, most editors and directors rejected it. Tate, whose Gloster loses both eyes at once, avoided the problem of reporting one blinded eye at a time, and his text was followed by Garrick, Kemble, and even Dolby/Cumberland. Lacy’s, in a rare rewrite, substituted who interposed his arm to save | The eyes of Gloucester. Pattie restored these lines, but omitted Albany’s lost he his other eye (2326), as did Colman, Pattie, Kean, Booth, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. Many editions also shortened the Messenger’s description of the righteous servant and Albany’s moral response, especially when the blinding itself had been omitted. Pattie omitted A seruant…other eye (2317–26). Kean omitted Albany’s lines and inserted lines on Gloucester’s culpability, loosely based on 2074–9. Forrest rewrote 2314–15 and omitted 2325–34 (from But). Booth omitted 2317–22 and 2327–34, and changed 2326 to Lost he his eyes? Irving omitted 2321–27 and 2330–4 (to tart). In the 19th c., only Flower retained the entire passage. Bridges-Adams omitted 2317–22 and 2325–7 (from But). Houseman omitted only lost he his other eye…both my Lord (2326–7). A few lines later, Goneril says, One way I like this well, | But… (2330–1). Her cryptic another way | the newes is not so tooke [F: tart] (2333–4) was omitted by Colman, Macready, Kean, Booth, Irving, and Houseman.

In the reconciliation scene, Lear’s nonsensical (and possibly spurious) Not an houre more, nor lesse (2816), which appeared in F, was omitted by Tate, Colman, Macready, Kean, and Flower. The Q-only louder the musicke there (2775+2) may sometimes be omitted in order to avoid playing music; but the lines were omitted in Lacy’s and Booth, even though music is indicated in stage directions. Kean, using a transposition in Phelps’s Works, moved those four words to follow a short version of Cordelia’s 2781–90. The words were also omitted by Miller. If musicians are onstage, the command may be superfluous, or even awkward. The later theater, of course, did not need a realistic source for music.

Finally, numerous lines are omitted because they seem unnecessary or repetitious. Whether Tate used a Folio or a Duke’s promptbook, many such lines are absent from his Lr. and have a long history of being dropped onstage. The first group of cuts, however, consists of most of the remaining lines unique to the Quarto (after the major omissions of Q material; see ), which were apparently considered expendable at least from the time of the First Folio, so that lines such as Goneril’s I would breed from hence occasions, and I shall, that I may speake (527+1–+2) were omitted by Colman, as well as Macready, Kean, Flower, and Irving, who omitted 525–8. Of the two overlapping lists of astrological predictions in 1.2, Gloucester’s These late eclipses…Graues (433–44) and the Bastard’s as of vnnaturalnesse…I know not what from Q (473+1–+5), the latter was omitted by Colman, Garrick (Bell’s), Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. However, the part of Gloucester’s list that is unique to the Folio, This villaine…Graues (439–44), was also widely omitted—by Tate, Colman (most of it), Garrick, Macready (partially), Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. The Lear-Fool dialogue I should bee false perswaded I had daughters (744+1–+4) was omitted by Pattie, Kean, Booth, Flower, and Bridges-Adams; Lacy’s and Irving omitted only the Fool’s Which they, will make an obedient father. In 2.2, Gloucester’s His fault is much… (1220+1–+4) was omitted by Kean, Houseman, and Brook, and partially by Macready, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Edgar’s list of Fiue fiends… (2248+1–+5) was omitted by every text except Miller’s.

Lines unique to the Folio were cut less frequently. Only Tate, with his rigid prosody, omitted Lear. Nothing? | Cor. Nothing (94–5). Also in 1.1, Lear’s Our son of Cornwal…preuented now (46–50) was omitted only by Tate and Garrick; Pattie omitted 48–50 (We…now). Lear’s parenthesis at 54–5 was omitted by Tate, Garrick (Bell’s), Kean, and Houseman. Lear’s and with Champains rich’d…Riuers (69–70) was omitted by Tate, Kean, and Houseman. The Vines of France…interest (90–1) was omitted by Tate and Garrick. The Bastard’s goe arm’d speech in 1.2 (487–91) suffered various small omissions by Tate, Kean, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Part of Regan’s I cannot thinke… speech in 2.4 (1420–4) was omitted by Irving. And F’s addition to Edgar’s first speech in 4.1 (2184–7) was omitted by Colman, Kean, and Houseman.

Of the remaining minor omissions, many again began with Tate. In Shakespeare’s 1.2, the Bastard’s deception of Gloucester by means of a purported letter from Edgar is about 90 lines. Tate’s condensed version is only a third as long; after all, his play opens with the Bastard’s plans. While later adapters, too, may have judged the pace slow, they also might have questioned Gloucester’s utter gullibility here. Lines 363–4 were omitted by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Booth, and Irving; 376–9 by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Irving, and Houseman (partially); 397–401 by Kean, Booth, and Irving; 404–8 by Pattie, Kean, Booth, and Flower; and the Bastard’s ten lines and Gloucester’s response at 413–22 by Macready, Kean, Booth, Flower, Irving, Bridges-Adams, and Houseman. Gloucester’s sententious quip on nothing, the qualitie of nothing…spectacles (368–70) was omitted by Colman; Macready, Kean, Booth, and Irving retained only lets see. Bridges-Adams and Houseman omitted only the first line, Flower omitted only the second, if it bee nothing I shall not neede spectacles (369–70), an unseemly joke, in hindsight. None of these lines are in Tate’s History.

Omissions in the long 2.4 also originated with Tate. Gloucester’s repetitious how vnremoueable and fixt he is | in his owne Course (1368–9) was omitted by Colman, Garrick (Bell’s), Pattie, Kean, Booth, and Irving. Lear’s anticlimactic curse, You nimble lightnings… (1448–51), was omitted by Colman and Garrick (from Strike, 1445), Kean, Irving (1445–49, to eyes), and Houseman (1445–6). Lear’s extended comparison of Regan to her sister, her eies are fierce… (1456–61), was omitted by Kean and Booth, and variously cut by Colman, Garrick (Bell’s), Macready, Irving, and Bridges-Adams, all of whom omitted Tis not in thee…coming in, except Pattie, which retained Tis not…words; Houseman omitted 1461–3 (thou…gratitude). Lear’s But yet thou art my flesh…bloud (1515–19) was omitted by Colman, Garrick, and Kean; his graphic metaphor, thou art a bile, | A plague sore, an imbossed carbuncle | in my Corrupted bloud (1517–19) was omitted by Macready, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Regan’s sith that both charge and danger.…impossible (1535–8) was omitted by all 19th-c. editors, as well as by Bridges-Adams and Houseman.

The remaining omissions have multiple causes. From the time of Tate, the last ten lines of Kent’s first long speech, from What wilt thou doe ould man (155–64), were considered expendable. An unnecessary development of his theme, and a somewhat cryptic one, the passage was omitted by Colman, Garrick, Kean, Booth (to 159), and Irving; Bridges-Adams omitted only 158–9, the sententious To plainnes honours bound | when Maiestie stoops to folly. The voluble and jocular Kent is even more heavily cut as Caius in 2.2. His long and highly rhetorical description of the Steward, such smiling roges as these…Camulet (1146–57), and the lines following, were completely omitted by Houseman (through 1162); Pattie, Kean, and Irving (through 1161), and Booth (through 1159). Bridges-Adams and Brook omitted through 1153, Macready and Miller through 1150. Most of the 20-line Cornwall-Kent dialogue on Caius’s blunt speech, And constraines the garb…too’t (1172–89), was marked by Flower as usually omitted, as it was by Pattie, Kean, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Lacy’s omitted only the last ten lines, including Kent’s parodic flitkering Phoebus front (1183), but marked the previous lines as usually omitted. Lines 1180–9 were likewise omitted by Booth, Houseman, and Brook. Only Irving omitted all of Lear’s third big speech in the storm, Let the great Gods…sinning (1702–13); Kean and Brook each omitted a few lines. But Irving was not alone in shortening Kent’s anticlimactic description of the storm, Alas sir…force [F: feare] (1694–1701), which became even less necessary as stage thunder and lightning improved. Bridges-Adams omitted from the difficult The wrathfull Skies… (1695), Booth from Since I was man… (1697), while Brook omitted only The wrathfull Skies…caues (1695–7). Houseman transposed Kent’s entire speech to open 3.1.

The Gloucester subplot is targeted again at the end of 3.4, when his Canst thou blame him…Grace (1942–51), in which he compares his filial loss with Lear’s, slows Lear’s progess. But there are almost as many variations as there are editions. Houseman omitted all but the last line; Bridges-Adams all but the first and last lines. Flower indicated that the usual omission was from I had a sonne… (1946); but Pattie omitted only O that good Kent…banisht man (1943–4), while Lacy’s and Kean omitted 1943–4 and 1946–50. Irving omitted only I lou’d him friend | No father his sonne deerer (1948–9), while Booth and Brook omitted only 1943–4. In 4.1, Gloucester’s lines on the superfluous and lust-dieted man (2251–6), an awkward version of something that Lear says better—and more than once—was omitted by Kean, Booth, Irving, and Bridges-Adams. Lacy’s omitted only the difficult That stands [F: slaues] your ordinance (2253). Finally, the Steward’s report to Goneril in 4.2 on Albany’s changed attitude (2270–8), which was omitted by Tate and Garrick, was also omitted or shortened by the restorers. Again, there are many variations. Macready omitted from of Glosters treacherie (2273)—Pattie to the end of the speech, Lacy’s to 2276. Bridges-Adams followed Pattie. Booth and Irving omitted it completely, Booth as part of a much larger omission, Irving from the beginning of the scene. Kean omitted only 2278–9, Brook only 2277–8. But this speech is a good example to end on, because the reasons for cutting it are many, reminding us that we do not always know why a particular omission was made. In this case, the possible motivations are the absence of the blinding scene in some versions, the undignified description of Albany, which borders on the comic, and the fact that the Steward, having already made his point, is simply, but unnecessarily, elaborating.

div.head: King Lear in Performance 1681–2000

epigraph.quote: Even when you’re producing King Lear…, plumbing the most abysmal of abysms, you’re puttin’ on a show.

div.p: It has often been said that King Lear was to the 20th c. what Hamlet was to the 19th. Onstage, however, Lr. did not become the touchstone Shakespearean play until World War II, when Lear became the signature role of both the classical Shakespearean actor John Gielgud and the populist one, Donald Wolfit. Peter Brook’s 1962 Lr. was arguably the most influential Shakespearean production of the mid-century. There followed several films, and by the 1990s, there were numerous productions in London. At the turn of the millennium, for the mature male actor, the role of Lear was the height to scale.

Of course, this was not always the case. Like many other Shakespearean plays, Lr. was drastically revised during the Restoration. In The History of King Lear (1681), Nahum Tate tightened the action by omitting and transposing scenes, refined the language, and gave the play a love story and a happy ending. (The major acting editions referred to in this essay, beginning with Tate’s adaptation, are described in The Text on the Stage, ). As we know from Samuel Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159), the alteration was an enduring success: The publick has decided. Cordelia, from the time of Tate, has always retired with victory and felicity. However, even as Johnson wrote, tragedians were slowly restoring the original, and for much of the next century, most stage versions and acting editions of Lr. were hybrids of Tate’s play and Shakespeare’s. As late as 1815, Richard Wroughton (who played Kemble’s Edgar) could with impunity crib Lear’s lines over the dead Cordelia for his adaptation of Richard II because they were not used in contemporary productions of Lr. The widowed queen borrows lines from 3217–83: O, you are men of stone…O, he [sic] is gone for ever…Look there, look there! (Shakspeare’s King Richard the Second, 1815, pp. 70–1).

The textual complications must have made a challenging role even more difficult. David Garrick played a gradually more Shakespearean text over several decades. Edmund Kean—who once told John W. Francis (Old New York, 1858, p. 227) that none but a young man could perform old Lear—began in Elliston’s hybrid with Tate’s ending (1820), then tried the tragic ending briefly (1823), but soon reverted to Tate’s. William Charles Macready only gradually reinstated Shakespeare’s play, performing his first Lear with no Fool at his side (1834). A young Edwin Booth acted with his father in an old hybrid, then dropped the part for a while, until he revived the original in 1870. Indeed, Tate’s History was not completely banished from the English stage until the mid-19th c., and even later in America.

The difficulty of the leading role was described succinctly by a 20th-c. German Lear, Werner Krauss (quoted by Rosenberg, 1972, p. 23 n.): When you have the strength to play it, you lack the wisdom; when you have the wisdom, you no longer have the strength. Some actors attacked the role with the reckless energy of youth—Garrick at age 25, Gielgud at 26—and then developed it over a lifetime. Others, like Macready and Henry Irving, postponed it until they felt ready, and then prepared it carefully. A few, like the American Edwin Forrest, owned the part. But it always presented a challenge. Marowitz (1963, p. 22) wrote: [Peter] Brook spoke of the play as a mountain whose summit had never been reached. On the way up one found the shattered bodies of other climbers strewn on every side. Olivier here, Laughton there; it’s frightening. Brook made another observation to keep in mind during this survey, which focuses on the central role: he said that Lr. is so difficult to stage because it is Shakespeare’s greatest play and needs not only a capital performance in the part of Lear but equally illuminating acting all the way through (Roberts, 1962, pp. 20–1).

John Downes (1708, p. 26), the prompter of the Duke’s Company, tells us that Lr. had been presented between 1662 and 1665 as Mr. Shakespear Wrote it; before it was alter’d by Mr. Tate. It is tempting to imagine that the original was performed by a young Thomas Betterton, who went on to become the leading Restoration actor; but there is no evidence. What we do know is that at the age of 46, Betterton was the first actor to play Tate’s altered Lear, at the ten-year-old Dorset Garden Theatre, in 1681; he also heads the dramatis personae list in the first quarto of The History of King Lear (1681). William Smith, the Duke’s second lead (who had played the title role in Aphra Behn’s The Rover in 1677), was Edgar, Tate’s romantic hero. Cordelia, a role greatly enhanced for one of the new English actresses, was introduced by the first among them, Elizabeth Barry, then 23, who also spoke the Epilogue. (Later, Cordelia was played by the third in the Betterton-Barry acting-managing triumvirate, Anne Bracegirdle.) Regan, for whom Tate wrote a love scene with Edmund, was played by Lady Slingsby, described by John H. Wilson (All the King’s Ladies, 1958, p. 104) as the leading tragedienne and villainess of the Duke’s Company. Gonerill was one of the last roles of Mrs. Shadwell, who, as Anne Gibbs, had been one of the six original actresses hired by Davenant.

Although Betterton seems to have played the part of Lear over three decades—the last time only two months before his death in 1710—we know virtually nothing about his portrayal. Downes (1708, p. 52) lists it as one of his major roles. Charles Gildon (The Life of Mr. Thomas Betterton, 1710, pp. 115–16) is the first critic to single out the great curse on Goneril (789–803) as the touchstone speech of the actor playing Lear, maintaining that Betterton thought it should be delivered with an elevated Tone and enraged Voice…in a Fury next to Madness. Thomas Davies (1783, 2:274–5), after doing some homework, concluded that it is in vain…to talk of Betterton’s Lear, for we know nothing of it. Davies surmised that the lack of evidence meant that this tragedy…was not in an such equal degree of favour, with the public, as Hamlet, Othello, and many other of our poet’s dramas. Colley Cibber, who had played both Edmund and Gloster, did not discuss Betterton’s Lear in his Apology (1740). Neither did Anthony Aston in his Brief Supplement to Colley Cibber (ed. R. W. Lowe, 1889), though when he praises John Verbruggen’s Edgar, he has in mind Tate’s romantic hero (2:311): In Edgar, in King Lear, Jack shew’d his Judgment most; for his Madness was unlimited: Whereas he sensibly felt a Tenderness for Cordelia, in these Words, (speaking to her)—As you did once know Edgar!

In the quarto of Tate’s History there are three brief stage directions for the storm, as well as for Lightning and Thunder, all common stage effects of the day, especially at the well-equipped Dorset Garden. Given the popularity of stage machines for creating such special effects as flyings of persons and objects (Avery, 1960, 1:xxvi), Cordelia’s lines me thought I heard | The charming Voice of a descending God (5.6.87–8; citations to Black’s edition of Tate, 1975) might suggest a special effect. But there is no stage direction for a deus ex machina, and her comment is probably a rhetorical flourish similar to that in Tate’s The Ingratitude of a Commonwealth (1682, p. 61), where Coriolanus asks that some kind God descend t’inform me. In his generally nasty satire on The Play-House (1685), Robert Gould praises Shakespeare and says of Timon, Lear, and The Tempest: These have been alter’d by our Poets now, | And with Success, too, that we must allow (in Montague Summers, The Playhouse of Pepys, NY, 1934, p. 308). The records available to The London Stage for this period show that Tate’s King Lear was performed At Court (Whitehall) on 9 May 1687 and 20 Feb. 1688, and at Drury Lane on 3 Feb. 1699, all with casts unknown. The play was reprinted in 1689, when it was Acted at the Queen’s Theatre, as advertised.

Black (1975, p. 35) says that Tate’s version flourished after 1700, with at least one performance a year every year between 1702 and 1715, except 1707. But in a letter of 1723, actor-manager Barton Booth mentioned the play, along with other adaptations that were box office disappointments (in Judith Milhous and Robert Hume, A Register of English Theatrical Documents, 1660–1737, 1991, 2:678). Theophilus Cibber says that Booth’s own Lear (between 1714 and 1727, at Drury Lane) was godlike, even in the mad scenes, his Sceptre of Straw like the Thunder-bolt of a Jupiter Tonans (The Lives and Characters of the Most Eminent Actors and Actresses, 1753, 1:81). Garrick’s other predecessors as Lear included George Powell, Robert Wilks, Anthony Boheme, John Mills, Dennis Delane, and James Quin. Quin, the leading man at Covent Garden when Garrick debuted, was his chief rival through the 1740s, though Lear was not one of his best roles.

King Lear became the signature role of the great David Garrick. Harris (1966, pp. 440–2) lists 87 performances, all but 10 between 1742 and 1763. Garrick’s Lear evolved over his long career. He began with Tate’s version, on 11 Mar. 1742 at Goodman’s Fields, at age 25. He then played Lear at Drury Lane 18 times through 1745. At Covent Garden in 1746, Susannah Maria Cibber, who was to become Garrick’s leading lady, first joined him as Cordelia. In 1747, he returned to Drury Lane, for an eventual total of 55 performances. On 28 Oct. 1756, Garrick produced and played King Lear with restorations, in what was long thought to be his final version but has been shown by Harris (1971) not to be (see ).

Garrick is often credited with (and blamed for) popularizing the sentimental Lear. Garrick was small (five feet five), and his Lear was a weak and pathetic old man and father. An early biographer (and sometime actor), Arthur Murphy (The Life of David Garrick, Esq., 1801, 1:19), wrote: He had no sudden starts, no violent gesticulation; his movements were slow and feeble.…During the whole time he presented a sight of woe and misery. Davies (1783, 2:280), who had played Edgar in 1752 and Gloster to Garrick’s Lear in 1759, described him throwing away his crutch, kneeling on one knee, clasping his hands together, and lifting his eyes towards heaven in preparation for the curse, which he rendered so terribly affecting to the audience, that…they seemed to shrink from it as from a blast of lightning. After the curse, he burst into tears—copious enough, in earlier performances, to warrant a handkerchief. Audiences wept. At his last performance of Lr., in 1776, even his Goneril and Regan cried (London Chronicle, in Stone, 1948, p. 103). Yet Garrick’s sentimental interpretation had darker shadows. In a 1773 letter, he wrote, Lear is certainly a Weak man, it is part of his Character—violent, old & weakly fond of his Daughters (Letters, ed. D. M. Little and G. M. Kahrl, 1963, 2:682–3).

Garrick’s Cordelias, being Tate’s, had major roles. The first was Peg Woffington. Davies (1783, 2:320) thought that Mrs. Cibber, the most pathetic of all actresses, was the only Cordelia of excellence and described The discovery of Lear, in prison, sleeping with his head on her lap, his hand closed in her’s. In the engravings based on Benjamin Wilson’s lost 1761 painting of Lear in the storm, a small, frail Garrick wears a royal version of contemporary Georgian dress: knee breeches and ermine-trimmed surcoat. He is hatless and clean-shaven. Lightning crackles in the background; in the foreground is a fallen tree. The actresses, too, wore current styles, as shown in Pieter van Bleeck’s 1755 portrait of Susannah Cibber and her Aranthe: elaborate gowns of velvet and satin, cloth headdresses, and delicate shoes with pointed toes and curved heels.

Francis Gentleman (1770, 1:370, 368)—playwright, critic, and occasional actor, who played Gloucester at the Haymarket the same year The Dramatic Censor was published—praises Garrick’s Lear, though he gives no specifics other than the feebleness of Mr. Garrick’s deportments. Gentleman’s subject matter is a detailed comparison between Colman’s 1768 adaptation and Tate’s. The fact that Gentleman discusses Garrick only as an actor, not an adapter, argues that he had not yet presented his major restoration. In fact, Gentleman concludes with the hope that Garrick will undertake a compromise version somewhere between the latitude of tate, and the circumscription of colman. It is not until the introduction to Bell’s edition in 1773 that Gentleman says he prefers Garrick’s version to Colman’s.

Since at least the time of Addison (1711), various critics had decried Tate’s alteration, so it is not surprising that a number of contemporaries appealed directly to the preeminent actor-manager to restore the original version of his best role. The anonymous A Word of Advice to Mr. G--rr—ck, appended to An Examen of the New Comedy, Call’d The Suspicious Husband (1747), admonishes the actor (and co-manager of Drury Lane): Why will you do so great an Injury to Shakespeare, as to perform Tate’s execrable Alteration of him? (p. 35). The author urges Garrick to present Lear in the Original, Fool and all, concluding, How can you keep your Countenance when you come to the Spheres stopping their Course, the Sun making halt, and the Winds bearing on their rosy Wings, that Cordelia is a Queen! (p. 39). Genest (1832, 4:475), quoting liberally, attributes this pamphlet to Samuel Foote, actor, playwright, and manager, who discussed Garrick’s Lear in his Treatise on the Passions (1747).

Indeed, it was George Colman the Elder, actor, dramatist, and rival manager at Covent Garden, who first produced and published a largely restored version of Lr. Colman had assisted Garrick at Drury Lane until 1767, and there is evidence that they worked together on this play; Davies (1783, 2:266) says that they considered restoring the Fool. But Colman decamped to Covent Garden, apparently bringing his version with him. He aired his grievances in A True State of the Differences Subsisting Between the Proprietors of Covent-Garden Theatre (1768); the payment of £70 he received for altering Lr. and another play was only one bone of contention. Colman refers to Garrick with respect, but argues: If the celebrated manager of Drury Lane had ever attempted to execute my projected plan of altering King Lear, my labours on this occasion would undoubtedly have been superseded (pp. 40–1).

Colman’s version is much more Shakespearean than Garrick’s. There is even a tantalizing contemporary reference to Colman’s having restored the original distressed Catastrophe, an undertaking John Potter, author of The Theatrical Review or, New Companion to the Play-house (1772), deplored as a circumstance not greatly in favour of humanity or delicacy of feeling, since it is now, rather too shocking to be borne (p. 334). But there is no other evidence that Colman experimented with the tragic ending, and his published version has Tate’s happy one.

Colman’s Lr. opened at Covent Garden on 20 Feb. 1768, with William Powell as Lear. Powell had first played Lear at Drury Lane in 1765, in Garrick’s slightly modified version of Tate’s History; he thus became the first in a long line of actors to undergo the transformation from Tate’s abused good old king to Shakespeare’s more complex monarch. Colman’s alteration had a limited run. Powell played Lear nine times in the next fifteen months, until his sudden death in 1769. David Ross took over the lead, and by 6 Oct. 1777, he was playing a Lr. that once again included Tate’s Arante, a character eliminated by Colman.

Harris (1971) has shown that Garrick’s mature restoration dates from 1770. Based on the character name Curan, which first appeared in the Drury Lane cast list for 31 Oct. 1770 (and was first printed in Bell’s), Harris suggests that Garrick’s revised Lr. was introduced by none other than Spranger Barry, the dashing Irish actor who had been Garrick’s rival back in 1756. Barry began his long career of interpreting Lear at Covent Garden on 26 Feb. 1756, weeks after Garrick’s 12 Feb. Lear at Drury Lane. He even, like Garrick, played opposite Susannah Cibber. The rivalry with Garrick was captured in several popular verses, including: To Barry, they give loud Huzza’s, | To Garrick only Tears (quoted in Theophilus Cibber, to David Garrick, Esq.; with Dissertations on Theatrical Subjects, Second Dissertation, 1759, p. 43). Barry began doing Lear at Drury Lane on 21 Oct. 1767. As for Garrick, it may have been the new version that prompted him to play Lear again, substituting for Barry seven times during the early 1770s. Stone (1948, p. 101) says that because of Garrick, there were twice as many performances of Lr. in the period 1741–1776 as there were in 1702–1740.

William Winter (1915, p. 434) remarks that Lr. was never popular in America. Shattuck (1976, 1:9) says it was probably first presented soon after the 1752 Shakespearean debut of Lewis Hallam’s company in Williamsburg, Virginia; this undoubtedly would have been some version of Tate’s play. This troupe gave the first recorded performance of Lr. in New York on 14 Jan. 1754, at the Theatre in Nassau Street, with Patrick Malone as Lear, Hallam as Kent, and Mrs. Hallam as Cordelia; Mrs. Rigby was Aranthe. By 1768, Lewis Hallam, Jr., played Lear. As in London, the tragedy was usually followed by an afterpiece. A 1786 bill for King Lear advertises not acted these thirteen years (Odell, 1927, 1:245). At the end of the 18th c., when theater was attacked by Puritanical critics, the American Company billed Shakespeare’s plays as Moral Lectures. In Philadelphia in 1788, Lr. was advertised as The Crime of Filial Ingratitude (Shattuck, 1976, 1:16).

In Europe, Jean-François Ducis made the first French version of Lr., his third Shakespearean adaptation. His neoclassic Le Roi Lear, in rhyming alexandrines, loosely follows Tate’s History. It was presented before the court of Louis XVI at Versailles on 16 Jan. 1783, with Jean-Baptiste Brizard as Lear and a teenage Mme. Vestris as Cordelia; Marie-Antoinette wept. On 20 Jan. the production moved to the Comédie-Française. Friedrich Ludwig Schröder presented his own version of Lr. in Hamburg in 1778, and went on to become the first important German Lear, legendary for the power of his anger (Williams, 1990, p. 115). Williams also says that Schröder’s version, which retained the Fool and saved Cordelia at the end (but not Lear), was the standard German stage version well into the 19th c. (pp. 82–4). It was the version produced in 1796 when Johann von Goethe was director of the Weimar court theater.

John Philip Kemble was the only major player whose later portrayals incorporated more, rather than less, of Tate’s text. Kemble first played Lear on 21 Jan. 1788 at a Drury Lane benefit for Sarah (Kemble) Siddons, his Cordelia (and his older sister), sometimes called the greatest tragic actress of the English stage. This was Garrick’s mature version, and the play was advertised as not acted these 9 years (Van Lennep, 5.2:1036). Kemble was not a success as Lear, and there were only five more performances. Kemble’s own adaptation, which used more of Tate’s text than Garrick’s, did not open until 6 Mar. 1792, at Drury Lane. He gave only intermittent performances over the next decade.
