Kemble revived Lr. at Covent Garden in 1808, the year he published his influential promptbook.

Kemble’s classical style—statuesque poses, grand gestures, and a slow, stately delivery—was unsuitable for the passionate, mad Lear. James Boaden said, He was too elaborately aged, and quenched with infirmity the insane fire of the injured father (Memoirs of the Life of John Philip Kemble, Esq., 1825, p. 213). Yet George Daniel (ed. 1826, p. 8) preferred Kemble to the young Edmund Kean: Kemble’s Lear was a study for Michael Angelo.…But the climax of all acting was the curse upon Goneril. On his knees, bare-headed, his white locks streaming…with heaven-ward eye, quivering lip, and hands clasped together in convulsive agony. Just think, muses Daniel, what Kemble might have done with the tragic ending! The only other actor Daniel singles out is Charles Kemble (J. P.’s brother) as the disguised Edgar, this singularly wild and romantic creature of poetic fancy. Perhaps closer in sensibility to the audience for the Quarto of Lr., which bills Edgar along with Lear, Daniel adds, Mr. Charles Kemble’s appearance was highly picturesque.

In stage design, J. P. Kemble was an early proponent of historical accuracy and romantic antiquarianism. With the enlarged theaters and the new fly galleries, there was a greater interest in scenery, in contrast to the stock sets of Garrick’s era. Tate’s consolidation of scenes allowed for Kemble’s dozen-plus Saxon scenes. Kemble, in white wig and mustache, wore a lace collar and white stockings, though he also introduced Saxon costumes. Kemble’s Lear was unfortunately immortalized by Lamb (1811, 2:308–9; 1903, 1:107) as an old man tottering about the stage with a walking-stick, a portrayal that helped convince Lamb—who probably never saw Shakespeare’s version—that Lear is essentially impossible to be represented on a stage. Like critics before and after him, Lamb also deplored the contemptible machinery by which they mimic the storm.

In America, Winter cites the Lears of William Warren the elder (c. 1805), Thomas Abthorpe Cooper (1809), and James Fennell (1810). They were soon joined by the English émigré George Frederick Cooke. But in England in 1811, Lr. was banished from the boards because of the madness of King George III—who, we are told in a modern biography, insightfully compared himself to King Lear, comforting himself with the thought of his three Cordelias (Christopher Hibbert, George III, 1998, p. 287).

The romantic actor Edmund Kean played Lear the same number of times Garrick did—about 90; but Kean did so in the comparatively short span of 13 years. Fully half of those Lears were presented outside London, including two tours in the United States. Although Kean first acted at Drury Lane in 1814, he did not essay Lear until 24 Apr. 1820, three months after the death of the king. The text was Kemble’s, with minor restorations by manager R. W. Elliston. Critics like Hazlitt (1820, p. 686) were disappointed by the happy ending, because Kean had boasted about the anticipated response of the London audiences…when they came to see him over the dead body of Cordelia. The Times of London reported that the repeated applause came not only at points of climax, but also in less obvious moments, such as the dialogue about the fierie Duke in 2.4, which elicited many peals of prolonged applause (Harris, 1966, p. 146).

Kean seems to have played a more vigorous Lear than Garrick did. Harris (1966, p. 404) notes that the promptbooks show that while Garrick fell into Kent’s arms after the curse, Kean strode offstage. Hazlitt (1820, pp. 687–8) described Kean delivering the curse: He threw himself on his knees; lifted up his arms like withered stumps; threw his head quite back, and in that position, as if severed from all that held him to society, breathed a heart-struck prayer, like the figure of a man obtruncated. Yet Hazlitt complained that Kean’s delivery of the curse was mostly rant and rage: he tore it to tatters, to very rags. The Times critic (25 April) singled out the reconciliation scene (4.7, played as the beginning of the 5th act): There was scarcely a dry eye in the theatre. While it lasted, the silence would have rendered the fall of a pin audible; and it was followed by a burst of applause, unanimous, long, and enthusiastic. Hazlitt wrote that at To be my child Cordelia, Mr. Kean staggered faintly into Cordelia’s arms with sobs of tenderness (p. 690).

Elliston advertised the costumes and the elaborate scenery, giving credit to the multiple designers. The highlight was in Act 3: A Land Storm. After the manner of Loutherbourg’s Eidophusicon, a miniature scenic exhibition that used, among other vivid effects, lights and moving colored filters (Odell, 1920, 2:163–65). Drury Lane offered not only rain (created by a magic lantern with changing colored transparencies), but animated trees (branches moving noisily in the wind), accompanied by flashes of lightning, waterfalls, and a fiery red glare (Harris, 1966, p. 149). The Times reviewer (25 April) wrote, The scene of the storm was less effective than many others, because the manager, by a strange error, had caused the tempest to be exhibited with so much accuracy that the performer could scarcely be heard amidst the confusion. Macready (1875, p. 149) recalled the flashy storm: as a scenic effect it was a noisy failure, and as an illustration of Shakespeare’s text, which tells us, for many miles about there’s scarce a bush, a ludicrous blunder. Though generally not well reviewed, the production ran for more than two dozen performances.

In 1823, Elliston and Kean finally restored the tragic ending. The Drury Lane playbill for 10 Feb. announced: In obedience to the suggestions of Men of literary eminence, from the time of Addison, that the original fifth act of the Tragedy of King Lear should be restored, the Proprietor deems it his duty to pay deference to such opinion; and, this Evening, Mr. Kean will conclude the character of Lear, as originally written by Shakspeare. The production was a failure. Critics such as John Bull (16 Feb.) were disappointed that Elliston and Kean had merely attached a shortened Act 5 to the first four acts of the Kemble-Elliston version of Tate’s play. As for the ending, Genest (1832, 9:186) says that the diminutive Kean staggered under the weight of his dead Cordelia (Mrs. W. West); this is said to have set the audience into a laugh, which continued till the curtain dropt, especially when he repeated Never five times. Others found Lear’s death slow—or as the critic for the New Times (11 Feb.) called it, unnaturally tardy, which again prompted laughter. Daniel (ed. 1826, p. 8), comparing Kean unfavorably to Kemble, said: Kean is, in truth— A very foolish fond old man; But he is not— Ev’ry inch a king. Given Kean’s limited success with the tragic ending, it is noteworthy that Daniel concludes, Mr. Kean’s dying scene (for, to his credit be it spoken, he plays the character nearly as Shakspeare wrote it), though somewhat deficient in power, is deeply affecting.

Unfortunately, there is no evidence that Kean played the tragic ending beyond four documented performances at Drury Lane. (Tradition says three, but Harris, 1966, p. 163, cites a review of a fourth, in 1824.) There may have been a few others on tour. But in America, in 1826, James Henry Hackett (1863, p. 227 n.) saw Kean play Tate’s ending, for which Kean apologized, telling Hackett that in my soul I was ashamed of the prevailing taste. A more enduring legacy of this production is the often-reprinted costume list that first appears in Dolby’s (1824): King Lear.—First dress.—Richly embroidered Saxon tunic of rich crimson velvet, ditto cap; flesh-coloured arms, legs, and sandals.—Second dress.—Black.

The first British actor to play Lear after the royal ban was lifted was actually Junius Brutus Booth, on 13 Apr. 1820. After Elliston announced Kean as Lear for Drury Lane, Henry Harris, Covent Garden manager, asked the young Macready to do a rival Lear. When Macready agreed only to play Edmund, Harris plucked the 24-year-old Booth from the Coburg, a non-patent theater, where, Winter (1915, p. 393) says, he was in William Moncrieff’s The Lear of Private Life, a domestic melodrama (see ). Booth’s Lear played only three times. Later that year, Booth played Edgar to Kean’s Lear. The following year, Booth moved to America, where he performed, largely on tour, for another quarter-century. Booth’s style was passionate like Kean’s, and he once told an impatient audience: Shut up! Keep still, and in ten minutes I’ll give you the goddamnedest Lear you ever saw in your lives (Shattuck, 1976, 1:46, quoting Richard Lockridge, Darling of Misfortune: Edwin Booth, 1932, p. 24).

In Germany, even before the Schlegel-Tieck translation of Lr. in 1832, Williams (1990, p. 116) documents a performance tradition of a fairly full text. But 19th-c. German Lears retreated from Schröder’s powerful monarch. Actor-manager August Wilhelm Iffland was a noble but ultimately pathetic Lear in a lavish production at the Berlin Royal Theater in 1808. The most renowned German Lear of the period was Ludwig Devrient, at the Nationaltheater in Berlin (1815); Rosenberg (1972, p. 25) says that under the influence of Schlegel’s criticism, Devrient began the play old and with a touch of the madness to come. The two long-playing Lears of the Vienna Burgtheater were more sentimental. Heinrich Anschutz reigned from 1806. In 1822, Josef Schreyvogel directed Anschutz as a pitiable king; Schreyvogel’s text was almost complete, except for the Viennese ending, in which Cordelia and Lear survive after Looke there. In the second half of the century, Adolf von Sonnenthal was even more pathetic and senile, though eventually the death of Cordelia was allowed on stage (Williams, 1990, p. 126).

In the performance history of King Lear, the single most important figure after Nahum Tate is William Charles Macready, the eminent tragedian who finally restored Shakespeare’s text, albeit with many of Tate’s omissions and transpositions. Macready’s slow but steady path to the role is well documented, in voluminous diaries and in three distinctive promptbooks for his productions of 1834, 1838, and 1844.

Lear was ultimately among Macready’s great roles, second only to his Macbeth. Between 1833 and his retirement in 1851, he played Lear a total of 80 times—at all the major theaters in London, as well as on tour, in the British Isles and during two trips to the U.S. A cautious player, Macready (1875, p. 306) first played the king—the last of the great characters of Shakspeare that I have left unattempted—in August 1833 at Swansea, still in an old version. The following May, Macready wrote in his diary, The truth is I can give my mind to nothing until the fate of this Lear, which indeed is my fate, be decided (1912, 1:139). Finally, on 23 May 1834, Macready presented the first Lr. since the 17th c. from the text of Shakespeare. The production was a milestone, even though the Fool was still absent. To temper our awe at the occasion, there is the typically crowded Covent Garden playbill for Monday, June 2, 1834: a somewhat reduced Lr. followed by two afterpieces, the Last Act of The Revolt of the Harem! with the Evolutions of the Female Army and Milton’s Masque of Comus! Over the next eight months, there were only six more performances.

Almost four years later, on 25 Jan. 1838, Macready re-mounted Lr. at Covent Garden, at last reinstating the Fool. John Bull correctly predicted that the date will be marked in the annals of the stage (28 Jan., in Odell, 1920, 2:194). Macready’s diary (1912, 1:438) explains that the actor he had cast in the challenging role, Drinkwater Meadows, was inadequate in rehearsals. Confiding his dismay to colleagues, wrote Macready, I described the sort of fragile, hectic, beautiful-faced, half-idiot-looking boy that he should be, and stated my belief that it never could be acted. George Bartley (who played Kent) suggested a woman, and Macready exclaimed, Miss P[riscilla]. Horton is the very person. In the promptbook (at the Victoria and Albert Museum), the name of Meadows is crossed out and changed to Miss P. Horton, who later that year played Ariel in Macready’s Tempest. Bound in the promptbook is the music for five songs for the Fool (including a verse from the Twelfth Night version of the rain it raineth). The restored Fool was eagerly awaited, and Horton’s entrance was greeted with applause (Harris, 1966, p. 230). Though her reviews were mixed, the 19-year-old began a tradition of women playing the Fool that survives today, while the immediate influence was a series of sweet and sentimental Fools, their cynicism softened and their indecencies omitted.

In a critique of the reinstated role in the Examiner (4 Feb. 1838; formerly attributed to Charles Dickens), John Forster wrote: Mr. Macready’s Lear, remarkable before for a masterly completeness of conception, is heightened by this introduction of the Fool to a surprising degree. Forster saw the Fool as a necessary contrast to the tragic passion of Lear, especially during the storm. He notes that the Fool sings even here—though the line he cites, And Ile go to bed at noone (2043), is not in the promptbook. Forster also describes the curse on Goneril, which Macready delivered on his knees, with arms upraised and head thrown back. Macready was often applauded after the curse, and even called before the curtain, though sometimes he was praised for staying in character even when applauded. At ile not weepe (1583), Macready wept on the Fool’s shoulder—and a new point for applause was born.

Possibly inspired by the complexity of the restored text, Macready’s characterization of Lear was newly powerful, aided by the actor’s strong voice and substantial physique. Macready (1875, p. 149) wrote that Garrick, Kemble, and Kean had all based the character on the infirmity and the feebleness instead of the vigor of old age. But Lear’s was in truth a lusty winter: his language never betrays imbecility of mind or body. Macready noted that Lear was still strong enough to ride, to hunt, to run wildly through the fury of the storm, to slay the ruffian who murdered his Cordelia, and to bear about her dead body in his arms.

This production played fifteen times in 1838–9. As in 1834, Lr. was only the first offering on the program. That first season, with young Queen Victoria in the audience, Macready (1967, p. 132) claimed that he boldly addressed Poore naked wretches (1809) to her. Helen Faucit, only 21 but already principal tragic actress at Covent Garden, reluctantly agreed to play Macready’s Cordelia, though she did not like the part. Faucit’s husband, Sir Theodore Martin, later reported on their visit to the dying tragedian, whom Faucit hadn’t seen in years: When we entered the room Mr Macready…was asleep on a couch. My wife stole gently to a chair at the foot of the couch, and sat watching him intently. After a little time his eyes opened, and he gazed at her with a look of pleased surprise, which, she told me afterwards, reminded her of the beautiful expression which, when playing Cordelia, she used to see come over his face when Lear wakes and finds Cordelia by his side (Helena Faucit, 1900, pp. 316–17). The engraving of Macready and Faucit in Act 5 is the first of an actor with a dead Cordelia (in Winter, 1915, facing p. 398). Macready may have created a trend for long white hair; he also wore a short beard, which Winter cites as a first. Fanny Kemble, Macready’s Cordelia in 1848, said that she disliked being dragged and pulled about in the last scene, and that Macready, who carried her in, acknowledged that necessarily the scene was a disagreeable one for the poor corpse (Records of Later Life, 1884, p. 639).

Macready’s adoption of Tate’s consolidation of scenes allowed for enhanced production values such as stage pictures—scenic groupings of main characters and numerous extras, ranged against important scenery. John Bull (28 Jan., in Odell, 1920, 2:210–11) praised the Saxon costumes, the Stonehenge settings, the various Processions, marches, groups, and the verisimilitude of the storm, which included sheets of rain, howling wind, and Forked lightnings. As usual, other critics found the sound effects excessive. George Scharf included three drawings of this production in his published portfolio Recollections of the Scenic Effects of Covent Garden Theatre during the season 1838–9, dedicated by permission to W. C. Macready Esq.

Macready introduced his original Lr. to American audiences at New York’s Park Theatre on 27 Sept. 1844, a significant departure from that of his American rival Edwin Forrest, who throughout his career presented the old hybrid play. Macready continued to perform Lear at least half a dozen times a year, including his penultimate farewell performance in 1851.

Samuel Phelps, who produced 31 of Shakespeare’s plays at Sadler’s Wells between 1843 and 1862, first played Lear in 1837, outside of London. That same year, Macready hired Phelps at Covent Garden, though legend has it that Macready jealously held him back, saying, Are you aware of the struggle I had to hold my own against Young, Charles Kemble, and Kean? Of the degradation of playing second fiddle as Edmund to the Lear of that amateur boy Booth? (in Trewin, 1955, p. 102).

Although Phelps played Lear many times in his long career, he was not known for his interpretation, which was in the sentimental tradition, with the feeble old man losing his mind early on. His own first production was on 5 Nov. 1845. He was nonetheless compared favorably to Macready, who was playing Lear at the Princess’s. Phelps was the first major producer since the 17th c. to use a male Fool (Henry Scharf), described as an acerbic moral satirist, probably in contrast to Macready’s sweet Fool. Even at the end of Phelps’s career, the critic for the Examiner (1 June 1861) said that after the storm, everything is exquisitely done…with regard to its pathos, not to its terror. The king is utterly lost in the father. Phelps is generally credited with restoring Shakespearean text; the pleasantly surprised Athenaeum reviewer (8 Nov. 1845) said he follows the text and order of Shakespeare’s scenes, with some few inevitable omissions, but with no alterations. There are three promptbooks of Phelps’s productions—1845, 1855, 1865—and each is multiply marked, a reminder that an actor’s interpretation, like his text, can change over time.

Charles Kean’s 1858 production at the Princess’s Theatre ran for only eight weeks. In the Preface to the published version, Kean (ed. 1858; see No. 17, ) describes the play as a harrowing picture of filial ingratitude and paternal despair aggravated into madness. But he spends the rest of his preface on the historical accuracy of the production. Kean set the play in the Anglo-Saxon era of the eighth century, as a time sufficiently remote but still recognizably British. Each act is followed by pages of Historical Notes, which include excerpts from sources such as Holinshed and Dekker’s Belman of London, notes from various editors (Malone, Steevens, etc.), explanations from works such as Joseph Strutt’s antiquarian studies, and even a commentary on the sweet and sour role of the Fool, based on an account of William I’s fool.

Kean’s Lear was kindly, genial, even humorous. Kate Terry, a seasoned player at fourteen, was Cordelia. The real star was the scenery, created by multiple designers; several sets of lavish illustrations survive. In the Magazine of Art (1892), Edward Strange wrote that the best scenes were the Room of State in Lear’s palace (Lloyds), with its adornments of hunting trophies and weapons, Cuthbert’s Exterior of the Duke of Gloster’s Castle, and Gordon and Grieve’s two views near Dover, in which a strong suggestion from Turner was marked (in Odell, 1920, 2:352). The storm featured moving clouds, howling wind, flashes of lightning and moonlight, and finally rain and thunder. A review in the Illustrated London News (24 Apr. 1858) speaks of clouds and electric fluid travelling rapidly across the sky. G. K. Hunter, in his introduction to the Cornmarket Press facsimile (1970), says that Kean lost £4,000 on the production, even though the royal family attended four times.

When Winter (1915, p. 427) saw Kean in New York in 1865, he delivered the curse beginning solemnly and speaking in a fervid whisper, which gradually changed into a gasping, choking outcry. His business was the simultaneous action of throwing away the spear and falling upon his knees. Winter added: The part of the Fool was made specially pictorial and pathetic by Miss Poole…who sang some of the bits of verse allotted to that character (p. 425). A photograph of Poole shows a middle-aged woman with knee-length dress, fool’s cap and stick, women’s shoes, and cross-gartered (Parsons and Mason, 1995, p. 112).

The two most prominent American Lears in the 19th c. were Edwin Forrest and Edwin Booth, though there were others. Winter (1915, p. 444) lists nineteen actors between 1837 and 1884, some of them Englishmen on tour. Among the most interesting were those who experimented with a restored text, including James W. Wallack, Jr., and James Stark, both ca. 1850. Stark’s 1852 Astor Place promptbook boasts that it is from the Original Text of William Shakespeare without any interpolations whatever. Carlisle (1969, p. 273 n.) notes that although James Hackett announced Lr. at New York’s Park Theatre in 1840 as terminating according to the great dramatist’s text and original catastrophe, his version included Tate’s Aranthe. Hackett—whose memoir treats the text and Tate’s revisions in some detail—restored Lear’s hot tears in order to soften the curse (1863, pp. 98–9). While Hackett found Macready’s 1847 Lear too vigorous, he had a copy made of Macready’s promptbook, as did several other Americans.

Edwin Forrest, who had played Iago to Edmund Kean’s Othello during Kean’s 1826 visit to America, debuted in New York as Othello the same year. He also played Lear that first season (27 Dec., Bowery Theatre), a bold choice for the 19-year-old. Othello and Lear remained his best Shakespearean roles. Though contemporary with Macready, Forrest played an old-fashioned version of the Edmund Kean hybrid, with even more of Tate’s text, but also with the tragic ending. Forrest thought it his best role. Complimented on playing Lear, he said: Play Lear! What do you mean, sir? I don’t play Lear! I play Hamlet, Richard, Shylock, Virginius, but by God, sir, I am Lear! (Arthur Hornblow, A History of the Theatre in America, 1919, 2:36).

With a resonant voice and commanding figure, Forrest specialized in what George William Curtis called the muscular school of acting. In 1836, between Macready’s first two restorations, Forrest, the first important American Lear to perform in England, played at Drury Lane. His biographer William Alger (1877, 1:395) described Forrest’s curse, which often brought down burst after burst of applause. Describing Forrest’s later Lear, He beat his breast as if not knowing what he did. His hands clutched wildly at the air as though struggling with something invisible. Then, sinking on his knees, with upturned look and hands straight outstretched towards his unnatural daughter, he poured out, in frenzied tones of mingled shriek and sob, his withering curse, half adjuration, half malediction (2:786). The tragic ending was still something of a novelty on the American stage. Alger said: He stood erect and still, gazing into vacancy. Not a rustle, not a breath, could be heard in the house. Slowly the head nodded, the muscles of the face relaxed, the hands opened, the eyes closed…and his form sank upon the stage, while the parting salvos of the storm rolled afar (2:790–1).

The Examiner critic John Forster (a friend of Macready’s) wrote: Mr. Forrest played Lear as a foolish fond old man. He expressed weakness tolerably well; he shed an abundance of tears;…and he walked as a very old person might be supposed to walk. But this is not Lear (in Shattuck, 1976, 1:74). Hackett (1863, p. 97), on the other hand, who was known for his Falstaff, found Forrest too stern and proud to be sympathetic, and recoiled from his startling paroxysms of rage. Forster, among others, criticized Forrest for his extreme transitions—e.g., the leap to the fury of the curse from the calm preceding it, and the quiet entrance to the storm scene. The criticism was seconded by Macready, who saw Forrest in New York in 1843, playing what Macready (1912, 2:229) called the disgusting trash of Tate! In an often engraved photograph of Forrest in Act 4 (in Shattuck, 1:76), he has full white hair and beard, wields a scepter of straw, and wears a long royal gown and an elaborate crown of wildflowers. Charlotte Cushman was Forrest’s Goneril at the Park in 1837.

In a late letter Forrest wrote: For forty years I have studied and acted Lear. I have studied the part in the closet, in the street, on the stage, in lunatic asylums all over the world, and I hold that next to God, Shakspeare comprehended the mind of man (Alger, 1877, 2:797). Winter (1915, pp. 439–41), who considered Forrest’s early portrayal too powerful,—the animal element predominating over the mental and spiritual, missed the pathos. But he felt that Forrest grew into the part and finally gained the involuntary tribute of tears. Still, Winter deplored Forrest’s realism—including pigeon toes and drool upon his beard. The New York Times reviewed one of Forrest’s last Lears, at the age of 65, after a three-year absence from the stage. Forrest was not only greeted with applause upon entering, but was repeatedly summoned before the curtain (7 Feb. 1871). The reviewer agreed with Winter that Forrest had finally added pathos to poor old Lear, though there were still some blemishes of mannerism…of exaggerated transition. The critic noted that of all Shakespeare’s plays, Lear is that with which the greatest liberties are taken in the acting, the example of Tate being followed very freely by performers and managers, adding that Forrest had considered reinstating the Fool but did not want to be accused of copying his rival Macready.

Ira Aldridge, a black American billed in London as the African Roscius, went abroad for better acting opportunities. He first played Lear in 1858 in St. Petersburg, at about age fifty, and scored a big success, even though the rest of the cast was speaking German.

Edwin Booth—small, sensitive, intellectual—excelled as Hamlet rather than Lear. But he finally overturned Tate’s version in America, and even revived the original in England. Like many other actors, Booth transformed his portrayal of Lear during his long career. William Winter, Booth’s biographer (and the editor of his promptbooks), wrote: At first he acted Lear,—as his father and as Forrest had done,— in the old Tate version, modified by Kemble (Life and Art of Edwin Booth, NY, 1893, p. 182). Later, Winter (1915, p. 446) wrote: About 1860 Booth discarded the part from his repertory, in order to forget it…and thus to facilitate for himself a careful and thorough study of the original. Booth finally played his own restored—and heavily cut—version in 1870 in Chicago (McVicker’s Theatre), and on 16 Nov. 1875 (at Daly’s Fifth Avenue) in New York. The New York Times reviewer (17 Nov.) felt that Booth lacked the pathos as well as the power for Lear. Nevertheless, he was called before the curtain again and again.

A decade later, a New York Times review (9 Feb. 1886) compared Booth’s performance unfavorably to Forrest’s force and grandeur: The pathos of Mr. Booth’s Lear is affecting in a larger degree than its fury is awe inspiring. He does not try to rouse the groundlings with Every inch a king, but the tenderness of the performance is irresistible. Tears flowed freely in the auditorium during the later scenes of the play. This review also looked back on Booth’s impact in England, where he had played Lear at the Princess’s in 1881. Ignoring Charles Kean and Phelps, the critic says that although London preferred Irving’s Hamlet to Booth’s, no prominent English actor, since the retirement of Macready, has attempted successfully to portray [Lear]. The symmetry, eloquence and pathos of Booth’s Lear moved London playgoers to tears and the critics to adulation. They had no performance in their memory to compare it with. Booth played Lear in London again in 1891, a year before Irving did.

Winter (1915, p. 449) wrote: Booth was tender and affectionate, but he was highly intellectual and still more highly spiritual. Like many of his contemporaries, Booth was praised for the reconciliation scene; Winter thought it the best he ever saw: I remember him,—indeed, who that saw him could ever forget?—sitting on a stool; his attenuated figure, his haggard face, his beseechful eyes, his bewildered glance at his clothing, his timid, hesitant, forlorn manner as he gazed on Cordelia, the doubting, questioning look which bespoke the slow recurrence of memory, the piteous, feeble movement of the hands, one upon the other, and the pathos of the heart-breaking voice (p. 447). This is the very scene painted by Jarvis McEntee, showing Booth seated, with a long white beard and a haunted look (engraving in Winter, 1915, facing p. 448). In the last scene, Booth played with the rope that was still around his Cordelia’s neck.

Two of Booth’s contemporaries also played Shakespeare’s Lear. One was Lawrence Barrett, whose first New York Lear was in 1876 at Booth’s Theatre. Using his own version, Barrett played the kind old father. The production was grand, with sets of Stonehenge and Dover Cliff, a hundred extras, and Cordelia entering the battle on a real horse. As in the best London productions, lightning toppled a large tree. In the late 1880s, Barrett managed tours for Booth, then acted with him (playing Edgar to Booth’s Lear).

Winter’s favorite Lear was the Irish-born John Edward McCullough, in some respects, the best I have ever seen (1915, p. 453). McCullough was Forrest’s heir, literally (he worked with Forrest in the 1860s and was his Edgar) and stylistically. Winter says that when Lear rushes out into the storm, Forrest’s impression was one of strength, Booth’s lurid, electrical, meteoric celerity…thrilling, and McCullough’s human, even temperate (p. 456). McCullough’s first Lear was in 1873 in San Francisco, his first in New York in 1877. Winter says that he first played the old hybrid Lr., then switched to Shakespeare’s. Winter especially praised McCullough for developing the madness gradually, calling him the first actor to distinguish between the agony of the awareness of going mad, and the jolly babbling of a man already mad (as played by J. B. Booth, E. Kean, and Forrest). Despite Winter’s penchant for a sympathetic, even sentimental Lear, he was impressed by the strength of McCullough’s Lear and praised his power and authority. The New York Times review, from London, of Henry Irving’s 1892 Lr. (13 Nov.) attributes the greater popularity of this play in America to the prevailing style of acting there: The fact that the methods of the old robust school of tragedians have survived so much longer on the other side of the Atlantic than here has kept this fierce test of dramatic strength well alive on the American stage. In France, a young Sarah Bernhardt played Cordelia at the Odéon in Paris in 1868 in Jules Lacroix’s translation.

William Creswick, who had played the role for years, was the first Lear at the four-year-old Shakespeare Memorial Theatre in Stratford, in 1883. The version was still basically Macready’s, which was likewise the basis for C. E. Flower’s Memorial Theatre Edition [1883]. In the introduction, Flower says that this version, cuts and all, lasted four hours. The Fool was played by Miss A. Chippendale. Creswick was called before the curtain at the end of each act. A review in the Stratford-upon-Avon Herald (23 Apr.) says that the scene where the curse is pronounced upon Cordelia…raised the enthusiasm of the audience to such a pitch that Mr. Creswick had to appear before the curtain. The surprising notice of the curse on Cordelia might seem to be an error about an unfamiliar play; but it also appears in later reviews. Presumably, the reference is to Well let it be so…for euer (115–23); but since the barbarous Scythyan (123–7) was omitted, leaving only seven lines, maybe the following six lines, come not between…Her father’s heart from her (130–4) were considered part of the speech. Lr. was done again at Stratford in 1890, by Osmond Tearle.

More exciting were two Italian actors. Ernesto Rossi played Lear in London in 1876 and 1882, and during an American tour in 1881–2. He used an Italian translation, supported by an English-speaking cast. The English actor and producer William Poel (1913, p. 177), declaring, We have no tragic actors, thought that Rossi was the only great Lear. Rossi played the king very old and weak, as well as mad from the beginning. He compensated for the language barrier with actions such as taking a full minute to awaken in the reconciliation scene. Tommaso Salvini, called by Odell (1920, 2:262) perhaps the greatest actor of modern times, did Lear in the U.S. and England in the mid-1880s, at first in an Italian translation, and later with the rest of the cast speaking English. A large man, Salvini created a sensation playing a powerful Lear, physically and mentally; Rosenberg (1972, p. 22) described him as the archetype of the archetypal titan. Although a New York Times reviewer called him a hot-blooded, agile, gesticulating southron (9 Feb. 1886), Salvini began the curse in unusual quiet; afterward he strode out. His Lear was still strong in the storm, and not fully mad until 3.6. At the end, an exhausted Lear dragged Cordelia’s body onstage. Henry James, while acknowledging that Salvini’s Lear is, like everything he does, magnificent, still felt compelled to write: Lear is a great and terrible poem,—the most sublime, possibly, of all dramatic poems; but it is not, to my conception, a play (The Scenic Art, 1948, p. 178).

Like Macready, Henry Irving put off Lr. for decades. He, too, had played Edmund in his youth. Irving typically planned a production over a long period, even researching past performances. (The Old Man was played by Henry Howe, an octogenarian, who had worked with Macready, and whose entrance was greeted with applause.) Still, Lr. was by many years the last of the great Shakespearean tragedies Irving undertook, having done Hamlet, Macbeth, and Othello in the mid-1870s.

Irving finally presented Lr. at the Lyceum on 10 Nov. 1892. The correspondent for the New York Times (13 Nov.) said that the production was anticipated as the most important step in his long and active managerial career. The critic explained that while the play was more popular in America, the London audience watched it as an almost complete novelty. In fact, he said, There is an entire generation of English playgoers who have never seen King Lear at all. Irving had broken away from the old repertory system of rotating several different plays, and introduced the extended run of a single production. In three months, he played Lear a record 76 times. In an article called Four Favorite Parts (English Illustrated Magazine 10, 1893, p. 929), Irving observed: It broke down my physical strength after sixty consecutive nights, and when I resumed it after a brief rest I was forced reluctantly to the conclusion that there is one character in Shakespeare which cannot be played six times a week with impunity.

Despite its run, Irving’s Lr. was not considered a success, and he never revived it. Still, he told Winter (1915, p. 429): The best thing I ever did…was my performance of King Lear. They would not have it…but it was my greatest work.…My performance was psychological, and I know it was right. I wish you had seen it. Irving’s was the only London production between 1890 and 1899. King Lear would once again be considered unplayable.

Everything the 20th c. disdained about 19th-c. productions culminated with Irving—a sentimental old madman in a truncated text, surrounded by scores of extras choreographed against stupendous scenery in elaborate stage pictures. The sets included three different palaces of late Roman Britain, and the souvenir program illustrates armies massed at Dover Cliff. Lear’s knights were accompanied by live dogs. The storm was very dark and very loud, with twenty minutes of thunder, lightning, wind, rain, and fog. G. B. Shaw repeatedly cited Irving’s Lr. as the nadir of Shakespearean production: When Sir Henry Irving tried to interpolate a most singular and fantastic notion of an old man between the lines of a fearfully mutilated acting version of King Lear, he was smashed (Bernard Shaw: Collected Letters, ed. Dan H. Laurence, 1965, 1:661).

There are different descriptions of Irving’s Lear; apparently he played the role sometimes very old, sometimes more powerful. The tinge of insanity appeared as early as the first scene. But he was always sympathetic, especially as the wronged father. The New York Times (13 Nov.) described Irving as subtler than not only Forrest, but Booth and McCullough as well. Irving’s rejection of footlight declamation meant that it was sometimes hard to hear his weak voice, a problem compounded in reviews by his famous first-night nerves. As James Agate (1943, pp. 190–1) observed, The part is largely a solo for the voice. Unfortunately, said Agate, Irving’s Lear had pathos, but only a clever simulation of power; it was useless for him to spout cataracts and hurricanoes in a voice which broke to a piping treble. A photogravure (after a painting by J. Bernard Partridge, in Winter, 1915, facing p. 428) used for the souvenir program shows Irving in long hair and beard, wearing a voluminous oriental robe and wielding a large sword.

The New York Times (11 Nov.) reported that the fall of the curtain after each act was the signal for an outburst of enthusiastic applause. Irving delivered the curse on one knee, with arms up, then across his chest, building from quiet to rage; at the end, there was a shriek from Goneril. The applause after this scene was so loud and prolonged that Mr. Irving had again and again to appear upon the stage (The Daily Chronicle, 11 Nov., in Harris, 1966, p. 272). Two lines addressed to the Fool—Let me not be mad (918) and the Act 2 curtain line, I shall goe mad (1586)—were similarly points, as was the business of Lear’s escape at the end of 4.6.

The sentimental favorite, again followed by multiple curtain calls, was the reconciliation scene (4.7) with Ellen Terry, Irving’s longtime costar (who was then 44). At Be your teares wet (2827), Irving put his finger on her cheek and tasted her tears. Yet her interpretation was new, with a hint of Cordelia’s rigidity. In Four Lectures on Shakespeare (1932, p. 156), Terry said: Cordelia is a most difficult part. So little to say, so much to feel! Rarely does an actress fathom the depths of those still waters. At the end, after carrying Terry onstage, Irving toyed with the rope around her neck and kissed her, as if to bring her back to life. A man, William Haviland, played an old Fool, and a young Gordon Craig modeled his Oswald on Irving’s Malvolio.

Irving notwithstanding, change was in the air. William Poel’s Elizabethan Stage Society apparently never did Lr.; but in 1889, Jocza Savits played an Elizabethan-style version on the new Shakespeare stage at the Munich court theater.

In America, the English émigré Frederick Warde, who had played Edgar to Edwin Booth’s Lear, and Edmund to Lawrence Barrett’s, began his own touring company in the 1880s but did not play Lear until 1896, when he was 45. In his autobiography, Warde (1920, p. 254) wrote that he had previously not felt ready for the role: Certain personal experiences, however, had made me realize the relations between a parent and his adult children: the period when the judgment of the parent and the child may differ, and in spite of paternal and filial affection must be considered, and then I felt that I could better comprehend the conditions that existed between King Lear and his daughters. His son, Ernest, had played the Fool, a character Frederick discussed in The Fools of Shakespeare (1913).

During the 20th c., Lr. was transformed from a play that was considered unactable to the central Shakespearean drama of our times. A mid-century production turned the traditional interpretation upside down, and the stage richness of the final decade began with three London productions in 1990. In addition, Rothwell and Melzer (1990) list 40 filmed versions, performances, or adaptations (see ).

At the turn of the 20th c., there were few productions of Lr. Herbert Beerbohm Tree, the dominant Shakespearean producer, at least in full dress mode, never presented it. In America, Winter (1915, p. 434) said, revivals of it have been effected only at long intervals. Bradley (1904, p. 243) famously concurred, observing that while Lr. may be Shakespeare’s greatest work, it also is certainly the least popular of the major tragedies, the least often presented on the stage, and the least successful there. He argued that Lr. was great poetry, not a great play—such poetry as cannot be transferred to the space behind the foot-lights, but has its being only in imagination (p. 270). Bradley even confessed to wishing for a happy ending onstage (p. 252). As G. K. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 52) later observed, Bradley, like Lamb, had probably never seen the real thing.

However, there were scattered attempts at a new interpretation. Frank Benson, who undertook to do the entire canon at Stratford from 1886, finally presented the unfamiliar Lr. in 1902. Benson played Lear beardless, with a male Fool and Constance Benson, his wife, as Cordelia. As with the 1883 Stratford production, a reviewer praised the scene in which Lear pronounces the curse on Cordelia and banishes Kent (Birmingham Gazette, 21 April). Benson boldly included the blinding, prompting another reviewer to protest that the added horror of gouging out the old man’s eyes, accompanied by fearful shrieks, might, we think, have been spared the audience (Birmingham Post, 21 April). Benson remounted Lr. in 1904 and 1906. But Stratford was not yet considered a major venue, and the play was not done there again for another two decades.

On the continent, André Antoine, also undertaking the entire canon, in French, in 1904 starred in an Elizabethan-style production of continuous action, which ran for 100 performances at Théâtre Antoine in Paris. The translation by Pierre Loti introduced the unadapted text to the French stage. In 1908, Max Reinhardt directed Albert Basserman in an elaborate production at the Deutsches Theater in Berlin.

When Norman McKinnel played Lear at the Haymarket in 1909, it was the first important London production since Irving’s in 1892. Directed by Herbert Trench, it ran for 35 performances. The design by Charles Ricketts was comparatively bare, with a big Dover Cliff. Poel (1913, p. 183) wrote of the sensationalism of the blinding in this production. Lr. was not among the Elizabethan-style productions of Harley Granville-Barker at the Savoy (1912–14). The only other London production of note was Ben Greet’s at the young Old Vic in 1918, starring Russell Thorndike and his sister, Sybil Thorndike, as the Fool. Gordon Crosse (1953, p. 51) said: Miss Thorndike’s halting gait, hanging lip, and nervous demeanour suggested the half-witted youth perfectly. Legend has it that during an air raid, Lear cried, Crack nature’s mould, all Germans spill at once (Trewin, 1964, p. 73).

In America, the only significant Lear was Robert Bruce Mantell, whose manager first talked him into playing the role as a novelty in 1905. Lr. had not been done by a major actor in New York since Salvini (1885) and Booth (1886). The six-week run was extended to eight. Rejecting the new naturalistic delivery in favor of old-fashioned declamation, Mantell argued that at least you could understand what he was saying. Eventually, on tour from 1906, Mantell did more Lr. than was done in all of London during the same period. Mantell’s third wife, Marie Booth Russell, played Cordelia at first; but being a big woman and a limited actress, she switched to Goneril, becoming the subject of the first known photograph of an actress playing one of the wicked sisters (in Shattuck, 1987, 2:234). Mantell’s planned world tour of Lr. for the tercentenary in 1916 was cancelled because of the war.

The 1920s saw a few short runs. In 1920, Russell Thorndike played Lear again at the Old Vic. Henry Baynton, who had worked with Granville-Barker, played Lear at the Savoy in 1922. In 1924, the Phoenix Society, a Sunday-night drama society specializing in rare plays, gave an Elizabethan staging at Regent Theatre. Also in 1924, 25-year-old William Bridges-Adams—once Poel’s assistant and now the first director of the New Shakespeare Company at Stratford—directed his first Lr. there, with Arthur Phillips as Lear and Dorothy Green as a fierce Goneril. And Nugent Monck, another disciple of Poel, presented Lr. at the imitation Elizabethan Maddermarket Theatre in Norwich in 1926. That same year the Memorial Theatre in Stratford burned down, and Allardyce Nicoll, who wrote that Lr. possesses epic characteristics ill adapted for stage representation (British Drama, NY, 1925, p. 174), founded the Shakespeare Institute.

Trewin (1964, p. 115) describes the 1928 production at the Old Vic—Andrew Leigh directing Ernest Milton—as the first of a new sequence of Lears, a part overlong neglected. In Europe, Lr. was done in Moscow in 1920 (Frand Dramatic Theatre), in Florence in 1923 (Polizana Nationale), and in Germany in 1925, where Eugen Klopfer collapsed sobbing after rejecting Cordelia.

Finally, in April of 1931, English theatergoers were once again offered rival performances of Lr. At the Old Vic, young John Gielgud did the first of his many Lears (discussed below), while in Stratford, Bridges-Adams directed Randle Ayrton in a converted cinema. Writing in the Spectator (25 Apr.), Peter Fleming noted the phenomenon in an era when A single important production of King Lear is rarer than a two-headed calf (p. 658). The newly inclusive Bridges-Adams promptbook, a reworking of his 1924 script, can be considered the first modern performance text. The world had been through a great war, and the time was ripe for a new kind of Lr. Bridges-Adams staged the blinding so realistically that he saw fit to warn the audience (see ). Unfortunately, because of limited rehearsal time, it was obvious that some actors did not know their parts in this unfamiliar play. Still, there was enough interest for a tour; afterward, the production came home: Shakespeare’s heretofore unactable tragedy was among the plays chosen to inaugurate the new Memorial Theatre in the spring of 1932. The 20th-c. rehabilitation of Lr. had begun.

In 1927, Granville-Barker published his first Prefaces to Shakespeare, which included his essay on the dramatic poetry of Lr., and the radical notion that the play was meant to be acted. An advertisement in the Third Series (1937) quotes J. Dover Wilson’s Inaugural Lecture as Regius Professor at Edinburgh, in which he praised Granville-Barker for challenging Lamb’s preference for private reading over public performance. It is one of the most important literary discoveries of our age that Shakespeare wrote, not to be read, but to be acted; that his plays are not books, but, as it were, libretti for stage performance. It is amazing that so obvious a fact should so late have come to recognition. Believing that this change of attitude was prompted, in part, by the scholarly rediscovery of the Elizabethan stage, Dover Wilson said that Granville-Barker has shown us that no school of dramatic criticism is…safe, which is divorced from theatrical experience.

This revolutionary theatrical awareness was a far cry from W. J. Craig’s 1901 Arden edition, which did not even mention performance. For the stage, a more significant edition was M. R. Ridley’s New Temple in 1935, inexpensive and widely reprinted, whose small, square, open-faced format was used for several promptbooks. Although lightly annotated, Ridley’s edition marked material unique to Q and F. During the 1930s, the mass market paperbacks of Shakespeare’s plays, such as G. B. Harrison’s 1937 Penguin edition of Lr., meant that each actor could now mark his own promptbook.

In 1934, Hugh Hunt directed 22-year-old William Devlin at London’s Westminster Theatre; Dorothy Green was again Goneril. Agate (1943, pp. 200–1) preferred Devlin’s powerful and earthy Lear to that of Gielgud and his annoying intellectuality. Though Hunt omitted the meeting with Gloucester (4.6), Agate praised him for the extraordinary notion of presenting the play as a whole, or very nearly…through the use of curtains and a simple, stylized setting. Devlin continued to play Lear for twenty-five years, and struck a modern note with hints of incestuous feelings toward Cordelia.

Ayrton returned to Stratford in 1936 and 1937, this time directed by the renowned Russian Theodore Komisarjevsky. In the cast were Donald Wolfit (as Kent) and Rosalind Iden, Wolfit’s future costar and wife, as Cordelia. Komisarjevsky, making his own omissions and transpositions, emphasized what T. C. Kemp (in Trewin, 1964, p. 169) called the cosmic quality of Lear’s desolation. He also created a stir with his single minimalist set of steep staircases set at angles, and dramatic colored lights against a cyclorama. Kemp’s review described the finale: The lights dimmed slowly, and darkness descended step by step down-stage. Line by line the motionless soldiers and courtiers faded from view: the light lingered for a moment on the dead Lear and Cordelia before they too dissolved in the dark.

In Russia, Salomon Mikhoels played a weak and foolish Lear in a Yiddish translation at the Jewish State Theater in Moscow in 1935. In 1941, Grigori Kozintsev directed at Leningrad’s Bolshoi Dramatic Theatre, with a bare stage and music by Dmitry Shostakovich, in a production emphasizing social injustice.

By mid-century, however, M. St. Clare Byrne (1960, p. 205) observed: When Granville-Barker so triumphantly vindicated the play’s acting quality he fixed our acting style. The note was grandeur. Grandeur and the tremendous solo performance have brought the play back into the theatre as the diploma piece for the mature actor. The most renowned Lear of the century was John Gielgud. Like many of his predecessors, he played the part often over a long career, with differing interpretations. He had a walk-on part in Lr. at the Old Vic in 1922, later claiming that he wasn’t good enough to be entrusted with a line. The first of his four stage portrayals of Lear was in 1931 at the Old Vic, directed by Harcourt Williams. Gielgud was 26. After four exhausting hours, the audience applauded for ten minutes. Agate (1943, p. 196), never a Gielgud fan, thought him too young, too weak in physique and voice, and hardly perceptible madness. Agate liked only Ralph Richardson’s extremely moving Kent. Dorothy Green reprised Goneril.

Gielgud’s second Lear, on 21 Apr. 1940, also at the Old Vic, is now considered one of the two most important productions of the 20th c., alongside Peter Brook’s in 1962. It was also Gielgud’s favorite. The official director was Lewis Casson (who played Kent); but the genius of 1940 was Granville-Barker himself. In his Prefaces, he had described Lear as powerful and arrogant; he now warned Gielgud: Lear is an oak; you are an ash (in Gielgud, 1963, pp. 51–2). Gielgud recalled: He had only ten days to work with us on King Lear, but they were the fullest in experience that I have ever had in all my years upon the stage.

Gielgud said further that Granville-Barker’s first concern was certainly for the speaking of the verse and the balance of the voices, but that he also encouraged grand entrances and exits centre-stage, a declamatory style, imposing gestures (pp. 53–4). There were two letters from Granville-Barker after he returned to Paris: first, My dear Gielgud. Did we ever agree as to the precise moment at which Lear goes off his head? I believe that Poor Tom’s appearance from the hovel marks it. The next day, a postscript: Translate the Hamlet-Ghost business into terms of Lear and it will about give you the effect (pp. 132–3). Gielgud’s Stage Directions includes his own notes on Granville-Barker’s directorial hints—e.g., at Nothing, I haue sworne. I am firme (269): Real, sulky. Big Ben striking. Pass by exit, cut her dead (pp. 122–3). For the curse on Goneril, Gielgud was relatively quiet, arms raised, palms out: The curse sudden, surprise the audience. Speak nicely to Albany, going, then down to her. Strange, not loud. Deadly. Ride it. In Prefaces, Granville-Barker (1927, p. 142) had said to locate the storm in Lear’s voice, to make Lear and the storm as one. (The 1927 version is livelier than the revision, 1946, 1:265–6.) Gielgud’s notes for 3.2: Tune in. Pitch voice. Low key. Oratorio (p. 125). This production also broke with the tradition of saintly Cordelias: Jessica Tandy was a strong chip off the old block, as Granville-Barker advised. At the end, Gielgud said Looke on her (3282) with joy.

Gielgud’s third Lear was at Stratford in 1950, a production he codirected with Anthony Quayle. The program noted, with acknowledgments to the late Granville-Barker, and in Gielgud’s opening night curtain speech, he thanked the spirit of Harley Granville-Barker who taught me all I know about this play (Trewin, 1964, p. 216). While Gielgud still played a strong Lear, he was criticized as both too reserved in the first half and too sympathetic at the end. The Renaissance costumes were more opulent than Granville-Barker had advised, and the setting included a large symbolic riven oak center-stage. The production was divided into three acts, the second being Folio’s Act 3; Granville-Barker had used a single interval after Act 3. Peggy Ashcroft was a complex Cordelia: she started sweet, but wore a breastplate and carried a sword in 4.4.

Gielgud’s fourth Lear was in the infamous Stratford touring production that played at the Palace Theatre in London in 1955. The director was George Devine (who also played Gloucester), but the distractingly futuristic sets and costumes were designed by Isamu Noguchi (who, the program stated, aimed to find a setting and costumes which would be free of historical or decorative associations). Underneath the bizarre costumes lurked a modern Lear. Less noble and sympathetic than in the past, Gielgud’s king was a stubborn old man who was responsible for his problems and a bit mad from the beginning. Gielgud’s signature voice and melodic versification were compromised by his realistic depiction of aging, while the emotional center of the production was Claire Bloom’s Cordelia.

Unfortunately, Gielgud was never fully captured on film as Lear, though in 1994, he recorded the play for radio with Kenneth Branagh’s Renaissance Theatre Company. Branagh, who plays Edmund, used the Folio text, though scenes were recorded out of sequence. Emma Thompson is Cordelia; Judi Dench, Goneril. In an interview for his 90th birthday, Gielgud said he agreed to do it because Lear’s a part I love. I knew it (New York Times, 28 Oct. 1993).

In the middle of Laurence Olivier’s debut season at the Old Vic in 1938, he played The King of Nowhere, in which, as a half-mad actor, he recited Blow wind [F: windes] (1656). In 1946, he played his only stage Lear, with the Old Vic company at the New Theatre; he also directed. As usual, Olivier elicited mixed reviews: he accentuated the humor of the role, playing it madcap in the opening, e.g., whispering to Cordelia. The Times critic, noting It is a period extraordinarily rich in notable Lears (25 Sept.), appreciated Olivier’s unexpected humour, a judicious comic light which exposes what is vain and tyrannical. But the reviewer for Theatre Arts (Dec.) considered Olivier too tame, a good-natured but fussy old gentleman (p. 702). However, they agreed that he was superb when crowned with wildflowers (in 4.6).

Agate, Tynan, and Ivor Brown all compared Olivier’s Lear with his more successful Shallow in 2H4 (1945). Agate (Go, Dec. 1946, pp. 35–6) declared Olivier’s Lear the event of the season. He praised just the right amount of testiness in the opening and the quiet at the end so that death took place without one’s knowing the exact moment of passing, but he felt that Olivier’s performance was calculated rather than genuinely moving. Tynan (1975, pp. 39–40), who compared Olivier unfavorably to Wolfit, felt that Olivier lacked Lear’s deluded grandeur and relied on tricks like the stabbing finger and nodding head. Alec Guinness was generally more successful as the Fool, one of the first of several clowns in whiteface—quiet, frightened, and pained—though Tynan observed that he could also be vindictive. And while Agate thought that Guinness was born to play the part, he disliked the constricting makeup. Brown (1946) noted that the production was unusual for fully incorporating Goneril and Regan. This was the first post-WWII version of Lr., and even though Brown complained that the storm was over-noisy and that there were too many small changes of scene (p. 15), he could assert: Lear is no longer dismissed as unactable or treated as endurable only in a completely garbled text. We live…amid more horrifying circumstances than our fore-fathers…. Let the hurricane whistle and roar, let Gloucester’s eyes be gouged out like jellies, let mortals die like flies beneath the thumbs of wanton boys; Britain can take it (p. 3). In France, Charles Dullin directed and starred in an absurdist, existentialist version in 1945 at Théâtre Sarah-Bernhardt.

The other great Lear at mid-century was Donald Wolfit, the last of the actor-managers. His biographer, Ronald Harwood (1971, p. 95), summarized: Wolfit embodied the heroic, earthy force; Gielgud the lyrical and aesthetic. Wolfit’s Lear was also recorded, though in a heavily cut version (Living Shakespeare, 1962).

At Stratford, Wolfit had played Hamlet in 1935; in 1936 and 1937, he had played Kent to the great Lear of Randle Ayrton (Wolfit 1954, p. 212). Shortly thereafter, he founded his own company. In 1942, Wolfit felt ready to undertake the greatest task of all in a production of Lr. that opened in Cardiff, coproduced by Nugent Monck. The time seemed opportune. If ever the sorrows of Lear, the cruelty and the blinding, staggering sickness of this great tragedy could be understood by the mind and heart of the people, surely the time must be now. Half our cities lay in partial ruins and there was worse to come.…We were indeed on the open heath as a nation, defying the elements (p. 211).

Wolfit told the designer Ernest Stern that he wanted to do Lr.:
Quite right, he said, I did it with Reinhardt; he had a hundred knights. Magnificent!
Yes, said I, but I shall have to do it with six.
Very good, replied the indomitable Stern, I did it first of all with Reinhardt with six knights and it was much much better. You do it with six.

Wolfit’s first West End Lear was in 1943, at St. James’s, and he played the role in London on and off through 1953. In the early years, his Advance Players’ Association had a rivalry with the Old Vic, and Wolfit did Lear in 1946, the same year as Olivier. The challenges facing Wolfit’s touring company are captured in Harwood’s play The Dresser (1980; 1983 film by Peter Yates); there is also an account of a typical performance in Harwood’s biography (1971, pp. 159–65). In one three-month period in 1944, Wolfit played not only Lear, but also Richard III, Othello, Touchstone, Hamlet, and Malvolio—though he eventually had to drop Othello and Richard III while doing Lear. Wolfit (1954, p. 213) also needed only one attempt to realize that he could not play Lear twice in one day. Instead, I arranged to open the week with King Lear and play one other performance towards the end, preferably on the Saturday so that there would be the Sunday to rest my voice and recover my strength. He was astonished at how rarely even Shakespeare’s major plays were presented outside of London. In Glasgow, Lr. had not been done for fifteen years, but in many of the large cities I played it had not been presented professionally for more than thirty years.

Wolfit was the last of the titanic Lears—powerful, emotional, and ultimately sympathetic. In 1946, Agate (1961, pp. 247–8) called Wolfit’s Michelangelesque Lear the greatest piece of Shakespearean acting I have seen since I have been privileged to write for the Sunday Times. Speaight (1962, p. 51), who had played Edmund in Gielgud’s 1931 Lr., said, Wolfit has, in a greater degree than any other actor who has essayed the part, the sheer physical bulk and bigness, the incontestable presence—though Speaight had never seen him in the role, and Wolfit’s Lear had a wagging head and shaking hands. Tynan (1975, pp. 23–4), who saw all of Wolfit’s Shakespearean roles in 1944, wrote: There has never been an actor of greater gusto than Wolfit: he has dynamism, energy, bulk and stature, and he joins these together with a sheer relish for resonant words which splits small theatres as Caruso shattered wine glasses. Among his greatest roles was, of course, his Lear, majestic and devastated. Harwood noted that the storm was never loud enough to drown out Wolfit’s voice. Richard Goolden played what Tynan (1975, p. 125) described as a macabre Fool with a senile stoop and a child’s skipping legs, and Rosalind Iden (Mrs. Wolfit) played what Agate (1961, p. 248) called the gormless Cordelia.

If Wolfit’s acting was old-fashioned, his dramaturgy was not. In his Autobiography (1954, p. 212), he recalls Stern’s simple setting and the opportunity for speed. He adds, We had one interval only, as Granville Barker suggested, after the blinding of Gloucester. Music and costume were likewise simple, solemn, barbaric (Granville-Barker’s word). In 1956, Wolfit (ed., pp. 3–4) wrote an insightful introduction to the Folio Society edition of Lr. (illustrated with Noguchi’s modernist costumes). He noted the revival of the Elizabethan form of inclusive texts and scenic fluidity: Never since the Puritan closure of the theatres in the middle of the seventeenth century has the full text, with a minimum of cutting, been so consistently played before audiences as during this last quarter of a century. Finally, Wolfit grasped the new stature of King Lear: It seems probable that there have been more performances of this, the greatest of Shakespeare’s tragedies, in England in the last twenty-five years than at any previous time since the play was written. It has appeared with great regularity in the repertoire of both the Memorial Theatre, Stratford upon Avon, and the Old Vic. My own company of players have given more than two hundred performances.

The unprecedented popularity of Lr. made possible a 1949 revival of Tate’s History by the Oxford University Players, directed by Nevill Coghill, at London’s Fortune Theatre. The Times (9 July) said the text was based on an early Garrick version (1742), with the undergraduate Peter Parker playing Garrick playing Lear. (The following year, Parker and his Oxford colleagues played Shakespeare’s Lr.)

In the 1950s, Shakespearean production in England migrated increasingly from the West End to Stratford. There had been only one Lr. at Stratford since Komisarjevsky’s: in 1943, Peter Creswell directed Abraham Sofaer. But Stratford became a major player only around 1950, in part because of the respected Gielgud-Quayle production of Lr. that year. In London, the Old Vic presented Stephen Murray as Lear in 1952, in a production by Hugh Hunt; and Paul Rogers in 1958, in a production by Douglas Seale. At Stratford, in 1953, George Devine directed Michael Redgrave. The tall Redgrave was old but grand; Marius Goring was an acrobatic Fool. More than forty years later, Judi Dench (in Bate and Jackson, 1996, pp. 197–8) recalled the excitement of the performances and the spare, abstract, revolving sets by Robert Colqhoun. In 1955, Gielgud’s Noguchi version (a Stratford production) played at the Palace, but this was the only West End Lr. in the 1950s besides Wolfit’s.

For Stratford’s 100th season, in 1959, Glen Byam Shaw directed Charles Laughton, who played Lear as everyman. Grandeur was out, and Laughton’s all-too-human Lear—a kind of throwback to the kind old father—was controversial. Laughton, who was heavy, played Lear as old, genial, and hearty. The curse was relatively low-key, almost conversational; the storm, too, focused on his voice, rather than noises off. Shaw used the Folio text, and the production was rare in omitting even the mock trial. The notable cast included Ian Holm as the Fool (who explicitly died at the end of 3.6), Albert Finney as Edgar, and Zoe Caldwell as a stubborn Cordelia.

In the U.S., in 1950, John Houseman directed Louis Calhern at the National Theatre, N.Y. Orson Welles, who had played Lear on television in 1953 (see ), played it onstage in 1956 in a seat-of-the-pants production at New York’s City Center. Having injured both ankles, Welles, a roaring boy of a Lear, was pushed around in a wheelchair by his acerbic Fool, Alvin Epstein.

Arguably the most important production of Lr. in the second half of the 20th c. was Peter Brook’s, which opened in Stratford on 6 Nov. 1962, only two years after the founding of the Royal Shakespeare Company; the production moved to the Aldwych in London and toured in Europe and the U.S. Brook’s view was an existentialist version of the comedy of grotesque that G. Wilson Knight had seen in the play back in 1930. The current inspiration was Jan Kott’s interpretation of Lr. through the lens of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame, in which, Kott (1964, p. 90) said, Grotesque is more cruel than tragedy. Brook himself described Lr. as Shakespeare’s greatest play, the arch example of the theatre of the absurd, from which everything in good modern drama has been drawn (Roberts, 1962, p. 22). Tynan (1975, p. 343) began his rave review: Lay him to rest, the royal Lear with whom generations of star actors have made us reverently familiar; the majestic ancient, wronged and maddened by his vicious daughters.…A great director…has dared to direct King Lear from a standpoint of moral neutrality. Others found Paul Scofield’s Lear too unsympathetic—a powerful but difficult man, with a flat voice, lumbering gait, and untraditionally short hair and beard. Lear’s knights were really riotous in 1.4, and the daughters’ treatment of Lear seemed largely justified. Some observers found the production bleak and even amoral. Mack (1965, p. 41) deplored it as rationalizing the irrational, regularizing the irregular, and compared Brook’s efforts to those of Tate and Garrick, going so far as to use Lamb’s metaphor of a hook in the nostrils of Leviathan (). Brook later conceded that his production was more relevant to Eastern Europe, and less successful in America.

The subplot gained in importance, if not sympathy. Cornwall gouged out Gloucester’s eyes with golden spurs. Charles Marowitz (1963, p. 28), assistant director, said that Brook cut the words of the good servants after the blinding to remove the tint of sympathy. The houselights came up for the single interval as Gloucester groped his way offstage—with servants, in fact, pushing him. Central to the production because of its grotesque aspect was Gloucester’s attempted suicide, a scene often deleted in the past for this very reason. Brook also emphasized the Fool, played by Alec McCowen. At the end, the body of Edmund (whose repentance was omitted) was left onstage, for Edgar to drag off. Irene Worth’s Goneril was complex, and even sympathetic, with tears in response to the curse. Diana Rigg’s Cordelia was spirited, her father’s daughter.

Brook, like Komisarjevsky, was his own designer. He used a timeless minimalism also drawn from Beckett: a bare stage; a few props of wood and metal; two large off-white screens; for the storm, lowered sheets of rusted metal that shook like thunder; nonspecific leather costumes; and harsh, bright lighting. Kozintsev (1977, pp. 22–3), who saw the production in Russia, said the design enclosed the action of the tragedy in a cold and timeless emptiness. It was as if all the clocks in the world had stopped.

In the U.S., in 1961, Herbert Blau directed a proto-Brook production at the Actor’s Workshop in San Francisco, absurdist yet apocalyptic, with Michael O’Sullivan as an unsympathetic Lear. The major American Lear was Morris Carnovsky, who played the role in two 1963 productions at Stratford, Conn., directed by Alan Fletcher—first as a tired old man, then with more power. Speaight (1973, p. 241) said that the Lear of Carnovsky, with his deep and resonant voice…was probably the finest Shakespearian performance in post-WWII America. Again, there was some sympathy for Goneril and Regan. Carnovsky’s Lear is one of the first to be preserved on video, though only in selected scenes. In 1968, Lee J. Cobb played an everyday Lear at New York’s Lincoln Center, directed by Gerald Freedman, with Stacy Keach as Edmund.

In England, Jonathan Miller directed a Lr. set during the Thirty Years War (Nottingham, 1967), and Trevor Nunn directed Eric Porter at Stratford (1968). Porter was a Scofield Lear, stern and unsentimental, though he was close to his Fool (Michael Williams), and carried him in in 3.4. Ben Kingsley was Oswald, Patrick Stewart Cornwall. In 1966, the Stewart Headlam Players performed Tate’s History in Richmond and London.

The 1970s opened with two important feature films (see ), directed by Peter Brook and Grigori Kozintsev, both of whom had directed Lr. onstage. The two had corresponded, and after Kozintsev’s death, his thoughts on Korol Lir were published in King Lear: The Space of Tragedy: The Diary of a Film Director (1977). In Italy in 1972, Giorgio Strehler directed Tino Carraro at Piccolo Teatro in Milan. Kott described this production as To my mind the most faithful to my book, extremely cruel (in Kennedy, 1993, p. 219). Successful and influential, Strehler’s circus version, with Lear as Ringmaster, played in repertory for five years, and toured Europe. One actor (Ottavia Piccolo) doubled as Cordelia and the Fool (a clown in top hat).

In 1973, Edwin Sherin directed James Earl Jones as a sympathetic Lear at the New York Shakespeare Festival, with Raul Julia as Edmund. A film of this production, televised in 1977, offers proof that the tradition of applause after the curse lasted well into the 20th c. In Stratford, Buzz Goodbody directed a popular abridged version at The Other Place in 1974. Tony Church was Lear, in a domestic drama with strong women. Among the excised characters were all three sons-in-law. Then came three modern-dress productions. Trevor Nunn directed Donald Sinden as a powerful, cigar-chomping military figure in a WWI setting (Stratford, 1976). In 1979, Peter Ustinov’s bumbling (though also cigar-chomping) Victorian king was directed by Robin Phillips in Stratford, Ontario (see Maurice Good’s rehearsal journal, Every Inch a Lear, 1982). In 1982, Adrian Noble directed a strong Michael Gambon in an eclectic Stratford production that was part fin-de-siècle. Antony Sher’s memorable Fool was a music hall clown in whiteface and red nose. The storm found Lear and his Fool up a ten-foot pole, and parts of 3.6 were played in a drum, echoing Beckett’s Endgame; on let them anotomize Regan (2033), Lear stabbed at her, a pillow held by the Fool, and mortally wounded him.

This was also the time for two Lrs. made for television, both available on video and therefore widely discussed (see ). Jonathan Miller, who had directed Michael Hordern onstage at Nottingham in 1969, and for British TV in 1975, did so for The Complete BBC Shakespeare in 1982. In 1983, Michael Elliott directed Laurence Olivier for Granada TV. These small-screen versions are mentioned here because they neatly illustrate the opposite sides of the design debate: The BBC cast wears ornate Renaissance dress, while the Granada actors, in simple robes of ancient Britain, wander among Stonehenge pillars.

In 1984, John Neville-Andrews directed John Wylie at the Folger Theatre in Washington, D.C. They tried to use only the Folio text, but partly abandoned that goal in rehearsal. The same year, Ingmar Bergman directed the play in Stockholm, with seventy cast members always onstage, a line of naked wretches on the heath.

In 1985, the Riverside Shakespeare Company in New York offered Tate’s History of King Lear, directed by W. Stuart McDowell. In an original prologue set in 1756 (the presumed date of Garrick’s partial restoration), the actor (played by Eric Hoffmann) wants to restore Shakespeare’s original, while his friend Dr. Johnson says he will play Kent only if Garrick uses Tate’s version; they compromise. Onstage, Tate’s version worked surprisingly well, even with the musical interludes used in Garrick’s time.

Deborah Warner’s first Lr. was for her own Kick Theatre Company at London’s Almeida Theatre in 1985. Her signature spare design featured three stepladders and simple modern dress. Hilary Townley doubled as Cordelia and the Fool. In 1986, Anthony Hopkins, directed by dramatist David Hare at London’s National Theatre, played a tough-guy Lear. Hopkins spoke in a dark throaty growl and sported a close-shaven head (Nightingale, 1997, pp. 237, 232). Clare (1995, p. 55 n.) tells the backstage tale of the advice Horden gave to Hopkins: Don’t let Tony Sher play the Fool.

The 20th c. ended rich with Lears, with three productions in England in 1990. All were modern-dress; all tried to spell out the Fool’s end, instead of letting him simply disappear; all suggested the contemporary taint of incest. At the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Stratford, Nicholas Hytner directed John Wood as a pathetic old man whose daughters suffered from lack of love. The text was basically the Folio, though the mock trial was added. The Fool was Linda Kerr Scott—fragile, twitchy, and loyal; Ralph Fiennes was Edmund. At the National Theatre, in a full, conflated text, Deborah Warner directed Brian Cox in another domestic drama; Lear’s throne was a wheelchair, which he used at the end to cart in the dead Cordelia. The Fool (David Bradley) was left onstage alone, as if dead, at the end of 3.6, followed by the intermission. Ian McKellen was Kent. Finally, Kenneth Branagh, actor-manager of the Renaissance Theatre Company, directed Richard Briers as Lear (at the Dominion and on tour in the U.S.), with Branagh as Edgar, and Emma Thompson as a tough Fool in whiteface. In New York, however, the only Lr. in 1990 was Lee Breuer’s reversed-gender version (see ); in a New York Times review (26 Jan.), Frank Rich noted that Lr. has not received a major New York revival in years.

In 1991, Fritz Weaver was directed by Michael Kahn at the Shakespeare Theatre in Washington, D.C. Again the emphasis was on family dysfunction, with the wicked sisters justified at first. Ted van Griethuysen was Gloucester. In 1993, at Stratford, Adrian Noble directed Robert Stephens as a dying old man. The blinding motif was expanded: Edgar (Simon Russell Beale) blinded Oswald as he killed him, and tried to do the same to Edmund in the duel. The Fool (Ian Hughes) made his last exit (3.6) with a knife in hand. Also in 1993, Max Stafford-Clark directed Tom Wilkinson at London’s Royal Court in a harsh political interpretation set during WWI. In 1996, Adrian Hall directed F. Murray Abraham at the New York Shakespeare Festival. Jeffrey Wright, the Fool, used a raw egg at 673–4. The wicked sisters were distinct: a serious Goneril (Margaret Gibson) and a sensuous Regan (Elizabeth Marvel).

In 1997, Martin Esslin began a review with: Once generally regarded as unactable, King Lear has now become almost ubiquitous (Plays International, Nov., www.alanhoward.org.uk/learplaysint.htm). The most acclaimed Lear of the decade was Ian Holm, directed by Richard Eyre at the National Theatre’s intimate Cottesloe in 1997. Benedict Nightingale (New York Times, 4 May 1997) called it an emotionally wrenching major Shakespearean performance: If Scofield emphasized the…harsh tyrant at the expense of the loving father, Mr. Holm is both. Holm’s performance was also physically memorable: short and squat, he disrobed completely at off off you leadings (F: Lendings, 1888), and began the reconciliation scene on all fours. Michael Bryant played a Fool as old as Lear. The simple, spare, timeless production was filmed for TV (see ). In the same year, a woman, Kathryn Hunter, played Lear at the Haymarket Theatre in Leicester, directed by Helena Kaut Howson. Lr. was also the last production of Peter Hall’s repertory run at the Old Vic in 1997, with Alan Howard as a heroic Lear in a traditional production of an uncut Folio text. In 1999, Nigel Hawthorne played Lear at the Barbican; and Michael Kahn directed Ted van Griethuysen at Washington’s Shakespeare Theatre. Kahn emphasized Cordelia’s silence by making her literally mute, the Fool translating for her.

A producer as well as a critic, Esslin attributed the renewed popularity of Lr. to the increased ability of directors to use a fast-moving, truly epic style that relies on the verse and the strong story-line rather than scenery and spectacular effects. The 21st c. began auspiciously for the play by coming full circle: King Lear was performed at London’s new Globe theater in 2001, with Barry Kyle directing Julian Glover.

div.head: Films, Adaptations, and Offshoots
div.p: Accounts of film and television versions of Lr. may be found in Ball (1968), Manvell (1971), Jorgens (1977), Coursen & Bulman (1988), Rothwell & Melzer (1990), Lusardi & Schlueter (1991), Coursen (1992), Rothwell (1999), and Brode (2000). Many of these once rare films—from Frederick Warde to Orson Welles and Peter Brook—are now widely available.

Silent versions begin with a lost Italian or German film (1905, 100 m.) which may have starred the Italian tragic actor Ermete Novelli. Vitagraph’s 1909 (960 ft.) Lr., directed by and starring William V. Ranous, attempted to include too much action for its 10-minute running time. Milano Film’s Lr. (1910, 565 ft., dir. Giuseppe De Liguoro) omitted the Gloucester subplot, as did a version by Film d’Arte Italiana (1910, 1072 ft., dir. Gerolamo Lo Savio), in which Ermete Novelli played a doddering, self-pitying Lear. In the American Shakespeare version (Thanhouser Film Corp; 1916, 5 reels, 43 min.), which also omitted the Gloucester story and kept the Fool alive, Frederick Warde was an impressive Lear, and the battle scenes were spectacular; Warde’s son Ernest directed and played the Fool. The only filmed version of the 1930s was the so-called Yiddish King Lear (Lear Pictures, 1935), based by Harry Thomashevsky on a play by Jacob Gordin (see below).

A BBC production (1948, 200 min.) featured a majestic William Devlin, who had played Lear in London the year before. A 73-minute version, shown in the U.S. on Omnibus in 1953, was directed by Andrew McCullough and Peter Brook; it included music by Virgil Thomson and paired Orson Welles with an acrobatic Fool played by Alan Badel. Peter Brook’s influential 1962 stage production became a radically cut (137-minute) version filmed in Jutland and released in 1971 by Filmways (London) and Athena/Laterna Films (Copenhagen).
