Set in a bleak, wintry countryside where the characters were housed in caves and dressed in furs and leather, and featuring an especially violent storm and the burning of Cordelia’s ships, Brook’s grim film purportedly reflected his outrage at the recent war in Vietnam. Paul Scofield played a cold, dehumanized Lear who learned nothing, opposite Jack MacGowran’s sensitive Fool; Annelise Gabold played a sullen and bitter Cordelia, and Irene Worth and Susan Engel played Goneril and Regan as glamorously heartless. Some found the liberal use of such devices as jump cuts, surprising camera angles, zoom lenses, and underexposure to be intrusive. Grigori Kozintsev’s more traditional Lenfilm version (140 min.), filmed in black and white in Estonia and released in the Soviet Union in 1970 and in America in 1972, presented the story of Lear more simply, as a folk tale with political overtones. Adapted from a translation by Boris Pasternak and including a musical score by Dmitri Shostakovich, the film showed the journey of a slight but still-vigorous old king (Yuri Yarvet) through humiliation and bitterness to forgiveness and newfound wisdom, as he comes to identify with the proletariat and turns his and Cordelia’s downfall to a joyous assertion of moral victory.

Some television versions were based on previous stage productions: examples are those of Triple Action Theatre/British Film Institute (1976, 45 min.), of Radiotelevisione Italiana (1979, 195 min.), and of PBS’s film (1975, 120 min.) of a live performance of Joseph Papp’s production (1973) in New York’s Central Park, notable mainly for the Lear of James Earl Jones. Other versions were filmed originally for television. For the BBC series The Shakespeare Plays, Jonathan Miller directed (1982, 120 min.) Michael Hordern as an unmajestic, overwhelmed father. In 1983, for Granada TV, Michael Elliott directed an aging and physically weakened Laurence Olivier, whose despotic patriarch was by turns whimsical and deeply pathetic. The cast included John Hurt (a loving Fool), Dorothy Tutin (Goneril), and Diana Rigg (Regan). The 1998 PBS version was based on Richard Eyre’s National Theatre (Cottesloe) stage production of 1997, like it featuring bare scenery, simple lighting and costume, and Ian Holm’s nudity in the storm scenes. Michael Bryant’s Fool was as old as Lear. In accordance with some modern interpretative trends, Lear’s knights were shown as unruly and the elder daughters as aggressively adulterous.

Tate’s History (1681) anticipated several later stage adaptations, some of them even more remote from the original. William Moncrieff’s The Lear of Private Life (London, Coburg Theatre, 1820) is based on Amelia Opie’s Father and Daughter (1806), a novel about a woman who returns home from seduction and elopement to nurse her mad father. Jacob Gordin based two Yiddish plays on the Lear story. The first, Der Yidisher Kenig Lir (The Jewish King Lear, 1892), showed the disintegration of Russian-Jewish family life; starring Jacob Adler, it enjoyed hundreds of performances at New York’s Windsor Theater and became the source of a film in 1935. Mirele Efros (The Jewish Queen Lear, 1898), depicting a strong matriarch, continued on the stage for much of the 20th c. Ossip Dymow rewrote the play for a film version (Credo Pictures, 1939) made by Joseph Berne and Roman Rebush. Gordon Bottomley’s proto-feminist verse play King Lear’s Wife (1915; His Majesty’s Theatre, 1916) depicts Lear’s mistreatment (adultery, mental cruelty leading to death) of his wife Hygd because she had produced a third daughter instead of a son; in revenge, Goneril, a virgin huntress, kills Lear’s mistress. Edward Bond’s Lear (1971, Royal Court Theatre) shows the effects of state-sponsored violence—rape, butchery, oppression—on modern society. Though a Cordelia-like character defeats Lear’s two elder daughters in a revolution, she herself initiates a reign of terror. The elder daughters are executed (Goneril is literally anatomized), Cordelia is raped, and Lear is himself blinded and dies ingloriously. In Elaine Feinstein’s Lear’s Daughters (Women’s Theatre Group, 1987), the father, who wanted sons, denies love to his artistic daughters, and his Queen dies. In Howard Barker’s Seven Lears (1990), Lear and his daughters conspire to kill his virtuous queen (their mother) Clarissa and hate his mistress (their grandmother) Prudentia. In Melvin Bragg’s King Lear in New York (1992) an aging film actor returns to play Lr. on the stage.

Nicoll (1955, 4:88–91; 1959, 5:358, 703–4, 785) names several travesties: Anon., King Lear and his Three Daughters, burletta (Royalty Theatre, 1812); J. R. O’Neill (Hugo Vamp), King Lear and his Daughters Queer, pub. 1830; John Chalmers, King Leer and his Three Darters (Bower Saloon, 1848); Joseph Halford and Charles James Collins, King Queer and his Daughters Three: An Extravaganza Burlesque (Strand Theatre, 1855); Anon., Kynge Lear and Hys Faythefull Foole, burlesque (Britannia, 1860); E. Elton, King Lear and his Daughters Queer, burlesque (Britannia, 1871).

Several films borrow situations, characters, and themes from Lr. without closely imitating the play. The silent film Le roi Lear au village (1911, 1177 ft., dir. Louis Feuillade) is an adaptation to ordinary modern life. In Joseph Mankiewicz’s House of Strangers a banker (Edward G. Robinson) divides the family business among two sons after the favorite third son is sentenced for his father’s crimes. In the western Broken Lance (Edward Dmytryk, 1954) the favorite half-breed son of a domineering cattle baron (Spencer Tracy) is mistreated by his two half-brothers. In The Big Show (1961), after a circus owner (Nehemiah Persoff) loses the love of a young son, his other two sons wrest control of the circus from him; a circus dwarf is the counterpart of Lear’s Fool. Paul Mazursky’s Harry and Tonto (Twentieth-Century Fox, 1974) depicts abuse of the elderly. An aging English teacher (Art Carney), who quotes from Lr., is evicted from his apartment and then shunted from one child to another, accompanied by his cat Tonto (his Fool). Peter Yates’s The Dresser (1983), based on Ronald Harwood’s play (1980), depicts a character resembling the great actor-manager Donald Wolfit (with his dresser as Fool) in his last wartime performance of Lr. Akira Kurosawa’s Ran (Chaos; 1985) converts Lr. to a samurai epic in 16th-c. Japan, in which the sons of a domineering warlord (who has a loyal and loving Fool) fight for succession in violent, billiantly colorful battle scenes, and revenge is taken by the women the Lear-figure has wronged. The chaotic Golan-Globus Lr. (1987), directed by Jean-Luc Godard, is a film about making a film about a Mafia godfather, Don Learo. The fluid cast included Norman Mailer, Burgess Meredith, Woody Allen, Molly Ringwald, and Peter Sellars. In the Danish The King Is Alive (2000, dir. Kristian Levring), stranded tourists facing apparent death in the Namibian desert rehearse for a performance of Lr. to keep up morale, and come to resemble the play’s characters.

Finally, the story of Lr. has inspired a number of novels. In Balzac’s Pere Goriot (1834) the daughters of a miller take and waste the wealth he spent a lifetime acquiring. In Ivan Turgenev’s novella A King Lear of the Steppes (1870) a father, having given his property to his daughters, is denied an allowance and dies tearing down the house. In Emile Zola’s La Terre (1888) a peasant, having divided his land between a daughter and two sons, is stripped of everything by his children and is murdered by one of his sons. In Jane Smiley’s A Thousand Acres (1991) a tyrannical midwestern farmer sinks into alcoholism and madness, and his land is divided among his three daughters. The youngest loves him most, while the older ones recover memories of paternal incest. Jason Robards played the father in the film (1997).

div.head: Music
div.p: Discussions of musical cues within the text, of the meaning of musical terms used in the play, of the textual and interpretive problems concerning the use of music, of the likelihood that some lines of the text were sung, and of the dramatic functions of such musical moments, are all to be found in the line-by-line commentary notes. The following is a brief discussion of the play’s use of vocal and instrumental music in general, of possible contemporary musical settings for some of its lines, and of later music inspired by the play.

div.head: The Use of Music in General
div.p: In Lr. there are virtually no lyrical moments, no opportunities for extraneous song or instrumental playing to entertain or delight. The play supports Moore’s (1916, p. 82) generalization that in the large, there are in Shakespeare no songs devoid of dramatic function. Armin’s pathetic song in 3.2 mainly serves to widen Lear’s perceptions, and the one moment of soft instrumental music in 4.7 serves wholly to effect the restoration of his wits.

Stevens (1964, p. 39): King Lear, so rich and complex in every other respect, does not speak with particular emphasis to the musician. There is, to be brief, a pattern of noise in the play, filling out its dramatic shape; the trumpet signals of Lear are gradually silenced by those of Goneril and Regan; his horns are heard only once (I.4); after this we hear Storme and Tempest, Storme stille, until they are replaced by the drums, alarums and retreats of Act V and the formal combat of Edgar and Edmund, with its three [sic] trumpet calls. At the end, exeunt with a dead March. There is one respite (not in all the texts): healing music for Lear’s condition in the scene where he and Cordelia are reunited (IV.7). The Fool’s and Edgar’s snatches of song are dramatic master-strokes, but they have no truly musical significance. Their elliptical, enigmatic wisdom is all in the words.…But it could be said that, character-wise, their music signifies the privileged, impersonal detachment of fools and madmen.

Long (1971, 3:162 ff.): Shakespeare associated music in performance only with Lear or the main plot; and for the most part, music sounds only in the presence of the old king.…[163] The royal court with Lear as king has its music, the music of ceremony and ritual, music in its public function, which in this case is to elevate human actions and to mark the orderly processes of state.…In contrast…the song scraps which are scattered throughout the unredeemed Nature that is the second locale reflect the anguished mind of Lear. The songs of the Fool, Edgar as Tom o’ Bedlam, and (by report) the king himself…provide one means by which we are made to hear as well as see, and therefore to feel more intensely, the nightmare and her ninefold. As in Hamlet, the vocal music aids us in probing the depths of a distracted mind. But it is to the therapeutic music of an instrumental consort that Lear escapes from his untuned mind to the harmony of Cordelia’s love which redeems Nature itself.…[164] The consort music which aurally presents the king’s return to sanity, and the trumpet fanfares announcing the trial by combat in act 5, are…balanced like opposite spokes of a great wheel against the sennet and flourishes heard in act 1.…The Fool expresses himself using bits of ancient folklore—wise saws, riddles, and fragments of ballads and old songs.…The song scraps he offers are part of his general gnomic-choric function. They suggest a moral or comment on an action by reminding Lear and the audience of analogous situations in the folk-histories—the ballads. It is difficult to determine which of the Fool’s jingles and rhymes are sung and which are spoken. There is no stage direction in either the Q or F texts to indicate that the Fool sings at all.

div.head: Vocal Music
div.p: Sternfeld (SQ, 1963, p. 487): The Fool, who so accurately assesses the positions of Lear, Goneril, and Regan, articulates his perceptions in a surprisingly large number of songs. The interfusion of these lyrics into the tragicomic canvas is one of the marvels of Shakespeare’s poetry. Ingram (1964, p. 171): Music itself which symbolises…stability seems almost stripped of its power. The Fool’s words are wise but they are more and more coloured by terror. The more unnatural and horrifying aspects of such [fragmentary] singing are exploited in Poor Tom’s wailing and maundering, a wild conglomeration that is half speech and half song, half sense and half nonsense. The weak and pitiful singing of this pair mark the highest triumph of unreason over the powers of music. In the opinion of most commentators, Edgar does not sing at all, and the Fool sings the lines here marked with an asterisk. The fragments of verse that might suggest singing are at 1.4: 648–57, 669+1–+4 (Q only), *680–3, *687–91, 710–11, 726–8, 837–41, all Fool; 2.4 1323–5, 1350–7, Fool; 3.2 1682–5, *1729–32, 1736–48, all Fool; 3.4 1900–3, 1916–18, 1966–8, all Edgar; 3.6 2014+8–+10 (Edgar the first line, the Fool possibly singing the latter two), 2014+19–+21, 2023–30. Other lines for which Gooch & Thatcher (1991, pp. 634–50, passim) list musical settings for non-dramatic vocal performance include 42–134, 669+1–+4, 1571–86, 1656–79, 1809–17, 2014+9–+21, 2234–5, and 2943–59. The following passages are those for which contemporary music has been found. Lear’s Fool may have sung some of his lines to these tunes.

div.head: Fooles had nere lesse wit in a yeare (680–3)
div.p: Seng (1967, pp. 200–1): The original music for the Fool’s song—if it is a song—is not known. [John] Caulfield ([Vocal Music in Shakespeare’s Plays,] n.d., II, 93) gives an anonymous tune, but there is no reason to suppose it is either [201] early or authentic. Sternfeld (1963, p. 160) thinks that the lines are sung, and (1964, p. 20) he sets the words to the contemporary tune called Robin in the Ballet Lute Book (Dublin, Trinity College, MS. D.1.21); his score is reproduced below. Long (1971, 3:167–8), without explanation, conjectures that the verses could also be set to the ballad tune Rogero, along with 687–91; see item 3 in the next section, below. Duffin (2004, p. 148) suggests the ballad tune Jog On (or Hanskin), appearing in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book (ca. 1619), the MS Het Luitboek van Thysius (ca. 1620), and John Playford’s English Dancing Master (1651).

figure.figDesc: Score: Fooles had nere lesse wit in a yeare

div.head: Then they for sudden ioy did weep (687–91)
div.p: For versions of the extant ballad, sometimes called John Careless, dated as early as 1564, and for later quotations from it found in Nashe, Heywood, Henry Lok, and Lr., see the commentary note. Its tune was apparently well known in Sh.’s time. Rollins (1920, p. 47): As early as October 8, 1583, a ballad called A Declaration of the death of John Lewes…was written To the tune of John Carelesse, and Some men for suddaine joyes doe weepe is the tune of The Confession of a Penitent Sinner (The confession of a Pænitent Sinner, [ed. J. W. Ebsworth, 1883–97,] III., 168) [STC 5627, ca. 1635]. A ballad of John Careles, &c., was licensed for publication on August 1, 1586, John Carelesse on December 14, 1624, and Sir John Careles on February 9, 1635,—all undoubtedly broadside versions of the ballad. What the original ballad tune was is not clear, and three possibilities have been proposed, none conclusively.

1. Seng (1958, pp. 583–5) reprints the only near-contemporary melody discovered so far for either the Fool’s song, or for the Ballad of John Careless, in two staves of manuscript music in the BL copy (K.1.e.9) of Thomas Ravenscroft’s Pammelia, Musicks Miscellanie (1609; STC 20759), sigs. A1v-A2, datable confidently before the middle of the 17th c. Sternfeld (1963, p. 176), without affirming the identification, prints the music in modern notation, putting a repeat sign at the end but not after bar 7, and matching the tune to the words of both the original ballad and the Fool’s adaptation of it. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 344) prints this tune without indicating any repeat. Simpson (1966, p. 534 n.) is dubious: Seng’s stave may be a harmonizing part and not the melodic line itself. Sternfeld (1964, pp. 20 f.) sets Sh.’s words and Seng’s music as a round for three voices, interpreting the repeat sign after bar 7 as the signal for the next voice to enter, and completely writing out the overlapping lines and phrases. Duffin (2004, p. 376) sets Seng’s words as a round to a different tune, If Care Do Cause Men Cry. The following is Sternfeld’s original notation for Seng’s tune alone:
Score: Late as I waked

2. Since Heywood’s quotation from the ballad of John Careless is prefaced, in his same stanza, by two lines quoted from another ballad, Sternfeld (1963, p. 177) deduces that both ballads were set to the same tune: The first two lines of Heywood’s lyric are obviously a variant of the well-known ballad (Wooldridge [1893] I. 92): When Arthur first in Court began,… Falstaff quotes [the ballad] in 2 Henry IV, II.iv.33 [1062]. The ballad of King Arthur was sung to the tune Flying Fame (Wooldridge [1893] I. 91). This tune proved to be one of the most popular melodies of the time accommodating, among others, Chevy Chase and the Lamentable Song of the Death of King Lear [see ]. It seems reasonable therefore, to fit both Heywood’s and Shakespeare’s quatrains to this tune, Flying Fame. Seng (1967, p. 203) rejects this conclusion: But nearly all ballad-lyrics and ballad-tunes are interchangeable because they share a common form; moreover, the song in Heywood’s play may be an ad hoc medley. It was probably sung on the stage to the tune of its opening lines, viz., Flying Fame, but this fact indicates nothing about the tune of the Fool’s song in Lear. The score below is reprinted from Sternfeld (1964, p. 22); two different but related tunes to Chevy Chase are printed by Simpson (1966, p. 97), who does not associate them with Lr.

figure.figDesc: Score: Then they for sudden joy did weep

div.p: 3. Long (1971, 3:166 ff.) finds that a ballad, The confession of a Pænitent Sinner (STC 5627; S.R. 8 Apr. 1635) is directed to be sung To the tune of, O man in desperation: or, Some men for suddaine joyes doe weepe. Assuming that these two titles refer to the same tune rather than to two different ones, he extrapolates further from Rollins’s (1920, p. 164) identification of the tune of Diana [and her darlings dear] as evidently equivalent to O man in desperation, though neither tune is known, and Rollins’s further conclusion (1921, p. 860) that it is unquestionably true that the tune of Diana [registered 1565–6], The Quarter Braules, Rogero, and O man in desperation were interchangeable. Possibly they were identical. Long therefore (pp. 166–8) prefers Rogero as the Fool’s tune: If Rogero is also the tune to which Some men for suddaine joyes doe wepe was sung, we have found in Rogero a possible setting for the ballad of John Careles &c and also, possibly, for the two stanzas [i.e., 680–3, 687–91; see above] sung by Lear’s Fool.…[168] It is the oldest of the three tunes and therefore probably the most familiar to Shakespeare and his audience when the play was first produced. The Italian Ruggiero came to England from Italy in the first quarter of the sixteenth century, and by 1585 Rogero was the tune both for popular songs and for lute variations or divisions. Harmonizing the ground in Thomas Dallis’s lute book in Trinity (Dublin) Library, MS 410 (D.3.30), p. 20, Long gives a score in modern notation, reproduced here despite its doubtfulness. Chappell (1859, 1:94) and Wooldridge (1893, 1:231) each give a quite different tune for Rogero, and Simpson (1966, pp. 533–6, 612–14) yet different tunes for both Rogero and O Man in Desperation.

figure.figDesc: Score: Fools had ne’re less grace

div.head: Hee that has a little tine witte (1729–32)
div.p: Sternfeld (1963, pp. 188–92): No source earlier that the eighteenth century is known for this lyric. In 1772 there appeared in London a volume of songs from the repertory of the famous Vauxhall Gardens, entitled The New Songs in the Pantomime of the Witches; the Celebrated Epilogue in the Comedy of Twelfth Night…composed by J. Vernon.…[192] Whether Joseph Vernon (1738–82) composed a new tune for Shakespeare’s comedy or whether he arranged a traditional melody, is difficult to determine now.…[Sternfeld gives (pp. 189–91) a transcription from the 1772 volume.] In 1859 William Chappell published a variation of Vernon’s melody (Chappell [1859] I.225), though curiously he does not mention his source. His version is in G major [rather, E minor], while Vernon’s composition is in G minor, and there are several melodic variants.…Chappell said of his illustration that it was still sung on the stage to this tune. It has no other authority than theatrical tradition.…The lack of antiquity in the tradition of the tune induced Wooldridge, when he revised Chappell’s standard work in 1893, to omit the song altogether. Chappell’s tune has however, been reproduced with words from TN by Elson (1900, pp. 321–2), John Long (Shakespeare’s Use of Music, 1955, 1:182), and others. Duffin (2004, p. 449) suggests a contemporary tune Tom Tinker because, in Cyril Tourneur’s (?) Laugh and Lie Down (1605, sigs. B4v-C1), after a reference in one paragraph to singing Oh the winde, the weather, and the raine, that tune is cited for a ballad beginning Whilom I was. Sternfeld’s score (p. 191) of Chappell’s version, set to words of both TN and Lr., is given here because of the tune’s long traditional use.

div.head: Blesse thy fiue wits, Toms a cold (1839)
div.p: The phrase Poor Tom’s a cold and the Bedlamite’s requests for bacon and his blessings on the donor’s five senses were formulaic street cries echoed in contemporary songs and poems (see n. 1839). The astonishing number and variety of Mad Tom songs, which remained popular throughout the 18th c., is evident from lists and collections of them in Chappell (1859, 1:328–36), Wooldridge (1893, 1:175–82), Simpson (1966, pp. 263–6, 710–13), and Loving Mad Tom: Bedlamite Verses of the XVI and XVII Centuries, ed. Jack Lindsay, 1927. Carroll (1996, p. 194, n. 8): All of these songs are later than 1605; even Edgar/Poor Tom’s cries of pain were sentimentalized, showing up in comedies and entertainments in the later seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Isaac D’Israeli noted that Poems composed in the character of Tom-o’-Bedlam appear to have formed a fashionable class of poetry among the wits; they seem to have held their poetical contests, and some of these writers became celebrated for their successful efforts. In The Compleat Angler, he notes, Izaak Walton refers to Mr William Basse as one who has made the songs of the Hunter in his Career and of Tom-o’-Bedlam, and many others of note. Idem (2002, pp. 85–6) attributes the fashion for these songs to the appearance of Sh.’s Bedlam in 1606, who Carroll believes may have sung at eight different moments in the play: After King Lear, Poor Tom’s singing becomes conventional, and other singing beggars proliferate. Duffin (2004, pp. 402–5), sets one song, From the hag and hungry goblin, to a tune from a lute manuscript (BL 38539, ca. 1620), and another, Forth from my sad and darksome cell, to a tune called Gray’s Inn attributed to John Coprario, from a masque manuscript (BL 10444, after 1623).

It seems possible, therefore, that some in Sh.’s audience might have associated Edgar’s phrases with current tunes. Sternfeld (1963, pp. 177–80) provides music (below) from one setting of the street cries: We have no certain knowledge whether Mad Tom sings or speaks the lines derived from the traditional Bedlam call. A musical source for what must have been a well-known London cry is a composition by Orlando Gibbons (1583–1625) for voices and viols. It is entitled The London Cry and survives in three different sets of part-books preserved in manuscript in the British Museum: Add. 17792–96, [179] 29372–76, 37402–06. He discusses the musical form—an In nomine, in which the chant melody (Gloria tibi trinitas) is a cantus firmus below the treble; only a fragment of the melody is set to the words, and the rest is played by viols. There is no way of knowing how closely a piece by a professional composer, based on a liturgical chant, resembles the street cries of a Bedlam, and the words are provided by Gibbons, not Sh.

div.head: Thorough the sharpe hathorne blowes the cold wind (1827–8; cf. 1878–9)
div.p: Long (1971, 3:170) conjectures: The line can easily be set to a strain of the ballad tune Drive the Cold Winter Away. He gives the music (below), taken from Chappell (1859, 1:193–4), who found it in Playford’s The English Dancing Master (1651). Chappell and Simpson (1966, pp. 197–9) think that the tune may be from the 16th c.

figure.figDesc: Score: Through the sharp hawthorne blow the winds

div.head: Swithald footed…arint thee (1900–3)
div.p: Though most editors do not mark these lines as sung, Long (1971, p. 171) proposes the first eight measures of a lute piece in BM Add. MS 38,539, fol. 14r, whose tune also appears in John Playford’s Musick’s Delight on the Cithren (1666, no. 33) with the title Tom a Bedlam, and which was probably the setting for several ballads.

figure.figDesc: Score: St. Withold footed thrice the old

div.head: Child Rowland, to the darke towne come (1966–8)
div.p: Long (1971, pp. 172–3) offers his wild surmise that Edgar could have sung his [first] line to Loth to Depart, a tune associated with the Shirburn ballad Rowland’s god-sonne. It is given by Chappell (1859, 1:173), Wooldridge (1893, 1:102), and Simpson (1966, p. 456); Long adds Sh.’s words.

figure.figDesc: Score: Child Rowland to the dark tower came

div.head: Come ore the broome Bessy to mee (2014+8)
div.p: For the appearance of this (or a similar) phrase in a variety of ballads amatory, political, and religious, see the commentary note. Stevens (1961, p. 348) lists most of the known versions. Of extant music, some settings seems more susceptible than others to quotation by Lear’s Fool. The Ritson manuscript in the British Library (BM Add. MS 5665), first reproduced in facsimile in Halliwell (ed. 1865, 14:466), is a three-part setting from the early 16th c., titled (after its opening words) Come O’er the Burn Bessy. Its leading tune is quite different from later settings more contemporary with Lr., and its elaborate counterpoint seems unlikely to have sprung to the mind of a clown in the public theater. Sternfeld (1963, pp. 181–3; 1964, pp. 26–7) provides a transcription in modern notation, with the ballad’s original words. A later MS of a lute solo in a Cambridge University MS, titled Over the Broom Bessy, has been transcribed in whole or part by Wooldridge (1893, 1:121), Naylor (1913, p. 52), Sternfeld (1963, pp. 185–6, 187; 1964, p. 28), and Long (1971, 3:175). Though the transcriptions differ slightly, and there may be some confusion about the identifying numbers of the MS, the tune in all of them is essentially the same. Long dates this lute MS 1595?–1605?, and says that the composition, titled Toy—Francis Cuttings and bearing a subscription —ouer the broome Bessy, is a series of divisions or variations by the lutenist Francis Cuttings on an older tune. Sternfeld’s transcription (essentially) is reprinted by Hunter (ed. 1972) and in the score below. Another lute solo appears in Dorothy Weld(e)’s Lute Book, fol. 6r, named Browne Bessé, sweet Bessé, come over to me. Sternfeld (1963, p. 187; 1964, p. 28) extracts from its elaborations a melody very similar to that in the Cambridge University MS.

figure.figDesc: Score: Come o’er the bourn, Bessy

div.head: Sleepest or wakest…take no harme (2014+19–+21)
div.p: Long (1971, 3:176–7), though conceding that almost any text written in the common tumbling meter could be fitted with any one of many ballad tunes, thinks that Flying Fame, also proposed for 687–91, then…among (see above), is the most likely, if indeed he sang the lines. For other possibilities see the commentary note.

div.head: Instrumental Music
div.p: The play’s instrumental music is on the whole associated with royal entrances, processions, or ceremonies or with military combat. There are directions for Sennet (37), Flourish (202, 291, 1073, 2982), Hornes within (538; perhaps implied at 518), and Tucket within (1014, 1466). Trumpet calls for battle or duel are indicated in SDs or dialogue at 2926 (retreat), 3058, 3063, 3064, 3065, 3066 (= Q 3067?), and 3106. A drum is called for explicitly at 2349, 2737 (Q 2739), 2845, 2864, 2918, 2938; it may be played in the Alarums at 2918, 2926, and 3107, and probably plays for the dead March (3302). Quiet music, probably by a consort of recorders or viols, is implied (in Q only) at 2775+2. Except at 37, 2739, 2775+2, 2918, 2926, 3058, and 3106, the musical cues have been added in F, the more theatrical text; F’s omission of Q’s soft music at 2775+2 presumably reflects a change in staging (see n. 2775+2). Though none of the original music is known, contemporary examples suitable for use have been suggested. Scores for various trumpet calls and fanfares and for drum tattoos and marches are provided by Naylor (1896, pp. 208–11) and Long (1971, 3:269–72). For soft offstage music in 4.7 (2775+2) Long (p. 179) provides from Antony Holborne’s Pavans, Galliards, Almains, and Other Short Aeirs (1599, no. 17) a consort piece called Paradizo, scored for two voices; with added inner voices, Holborne’s score may be arranged for three recorders—alto, tenor, and bass—with a sackbut or trombone to sound the lower bass notes. Manifold (1956, p. 149) suggests The Earl of Salisbury’s Pavan.

The lists in Gooch & Thatcher (1991, pp. 592–630, 638–46, 650–1) of instrumental music inspired by Lr.—overtures, incidental music, film scores, ballets, tone poems, symphonies, etc.—supplant earlier listings such as those by Greenhill, Harrison, & Furnivall (1884, pp. 18–19), Dean, Moore, & Hartnoll (1964, pp. 256–7), and Boustead (1964, p. 10). These compositions range from solos, duets, and pieces for small ensembles to works for full concert bands and symphony orchestras, and in style from classical to very modern, including jazz and electronic music. Among well-known composers who have produced musical impressions of Lr. are Milli Balakirev, Granville Bantock, Hector Berlioz (most famously), Henry Bishop, Marc Blitzstein, Henry Cowell, Peter Maxwell Davies, Claude Debussy, Paul Dukas, Marcel Dupré, Niels Gade, (possibly) Josef Haydn, Aram Khachaturian, Franz Liszt, Otto Luening, Charles Mackerras, Modest Mussorgsky, Ivor Novello, Vincent Persichetti, George Rochberg, Ned Rorem, Dmitrii Shostakovich, Vilhelm Stenhammer, Morton Subotnik, Virgil Thomson, and Felix Weingartner. Appreciations of some of these pieces may be found in Wilson (1922, pp. 50–3) and Fiske (1964, pp. 177–241, passim).

div.head: Operatic Versions
div.p: Among those who have considered and then abandoned the idea of basing an opera on this play are Ernest Bloch, Benjamin Britten, Claude Debussy, Henri DuParc, Edward Elgar, Pietro Mascagni, (possibly) Giacomo Puccini, and most notably and regrettably Giuseppe Verdi, who prepared a complete libretto before abandoning the project (see Schmidgall, 1985). Dean (1965, p. 82): Lr. has defeated every composer who has attempted it. Among Lr.’s other challenges, its great length and complex double plot make it an uncongenial subject for opera, allowing little latitude for extended arias and ensembles. An exceptional modern example, Aribert Reimann’s Lear (1978), has its musical admirers (see Schultz, 1984; Littlejohn, 1992, pp. 256, 261–3), but its demanding, dissonant, often cacophonous score seems not to have won it popularity. Dean (1964, p. 168; 1965, p. 89) and Dean, Moore, & Hartnoll (1964, pp. 256–7) list only seven other operatic settings, none by well-known composers; Hotaling (1990) lists some dozen known operas and another dozen reported ones of unknown status. Gooch & Thatcher (1991, pp. 630–4, 646), by including adaptations, works assimilating only parts of Lr., and rock, country-rock, burlesque, musical-comedy, and ballet versions, extend their list to some three dozen works, many unpublished, as well as (pp. 647–9) a half dozen cantatas. A few titles listed by Clarke (1888, pp. 460–1) and Squire (1916, p. 78) are obscure, doubtful, or erroneous, including Cordelia (1823) by Conradin Kreutzer, apparently unrelated to Sh.’s play.
